Catalase sits in nearly every air-breathing organism, concentrated in liver, kidney and red blood cells, where it destroys the peroxide those cells make as a by-product of their own chemistry. TRY IT: add dish soap to strong peroxide and the same reaction gives the classroom 'elephant's toothpaste' column -- which comes out hot, around 75 C, because the peroxide's breakdown releases heat all by itself. Either a mineral salt (potassium iodide) or a spoonful of living baker's yeast will start it, and neither is used up. Sources: Scientific American, 'The Liver: Helping Enzymes Help You!'; Wikipedia, "Elephant's toothpaste".

question: A boy boils a piece of liver, cools it and drops it into drugstore hydrogen peroxide. A raw piece made the beaker erupt, the work of an enzyme in the meat called catalase. This piece barely stirs it, and nothing was rinsed away. What did the boiling do?
answer: It warped the catalase out of its working shape
choices: It warped the catalase out of its working shape
It drove the iron out of the catalase's core
It boiled off the water the catalase needs to work
It sealed the meat against the peroxide
context: Boiling denatures catalase. Heat unravels the enzyme's folded three-dimensional structure, and the active site -- a narrow channel about 3 nm deep leading down to an iron-bearing heme -- is deformed, so hydrogen peroxide can no longer dock. Every atom is still present; only the shape is gone. Enzymes are catalysts, and for a catalyst built of protein, shape IS function. Scientific American's version of this test just microwaves the liver for 20 seconds and the bubbling largely stops. That same physics is why a very high fever is dangerous: between roughly 40 and 44 C human enzyme systems begin to malfunction as proteins unfold and clump, with heatstroke core temperature around 41-42 C. Sources: Scientific American, 'The Liver: Helping Enzymes Help You!'; Grokipedia, 'Catalase'; Hashim, 'Clinical biochemistry of hyperthermia', Annals of Clinical Biochemistry 2010.

question: A cube of raw liver turns a beaker of peroxide into foam in seconds. Each catalase molecule in it has four working spots, and each spot grabs one peroxide molecule, splits it and lets go, with no partner and no stored energy. How many peroxide molecules does one catalase get through in a second?
answer: About 40 million
choices: About 4,000
About 400,000
About 40 million
About 4 billion
context: Catalase (EC 1.11.1.6) decomposes up to about 40 million molecules of hydrogen peroxide per second per enzyme molecule (~4 x 10^7 s^-1) -- one of the highest turnover rates known for any enzyme. It is a tetramer: four identical subunits of roughly 60 kDa, each carrying one iron-bearing heme, and each active site sits at the bottom of a narrow hydrophobic channel about 3 nm deep that lets H2O2 in and shuts larger molecules out. It is found in nearly all aerobic organisms and lives inside cell compartments called peroxisomes. Source: Grokipedia, 'Catalase'.

question: Johann Wolfgang Doebereiner aimed a fine jet of hydrogen gas at a lump of spongy platinum at the University of Jena in 1823. No candle or spark was near, yet the platinum glowed red-hot and the hydrogen caught fire on its own. He saw he could sell the trick. What did he turn it into?
answer: A pocket lighter for making flame on demand
choices: A pocket lighter for making flame on demand
A safety lamp for the tunnels of coal mines
A furnace for smelting platinum from its ore
A burner for filling army hydrogen balloons
context: Doebereiner's lamp: zinc granules in roughly 25% sulfuric acid generate hydrogen (Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2); opening a stopcock sends a jet onto a platinum sponge at the nozzle, which glows red-hot and lights the gas. Close the stopcock, pressure builds, the acid falls away from the zinc, and the flame dies. Doebereiner -- a coachman's son and self-taught apothecary's apprentice -- owed his Jena professorship to the backing of the poet Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who bought one of the first lamps, funded the platinum research and wrote a poem in its honour. Doebereiner filed no patent on it. Grokipedia records roughly 20,000 units in use in Germany and Britain by 1828; the largest maker, Heinrich Gottfried Piegler of Schleiz, kept building them until about 1880. John Walker's first friction matches went on sale only in 1827 -- the lighter beat the match to market. Doebereiner also proposed the element 'triads' around 1829, foreshadowing the periodic law. Source: Grokipedia, "Doebereiner's lamp".

question: A garage mechanic pulled a dead catalyst pack from an American car soon after the 1975 model year, and no cleaning would bring it back. Its tiny beads, coated with platinum and palladium, were meant to turn carbon monoxide and unburned fuel into carbon dioxide and water. What had killed it?
answer: One tank of leaded petrol
choices: One tank of leaded petrol
One tank of petrol cut with kerosene
One tank run down to fumes
One tank of the new unleaded petrol
context: Burning leaded petrol produces elemental lead plus lead oxide, chloride and bromide. The lead alloys with the platinum-group metals while its compounds coat the catalyst surface. The UN Environment Programme states flatly that a converter 'can be destroyed by a single tankful of leaded fuel'; a Ford patent puts it bluntly: lead 'will deactivate catalysts formed from materials such as platinum, palladium, ruthenium, rhodium, iridium'. Poisoned metal cannot be regenerated in a garage -- the part is replaced. Other real catalyst poisons: sulfur, phosphorus and zinc from burnt engine oil, silicon from coolant leaks. The 1975 units were two-way oxidation converters (about 74% CO and 68% hydrocarbon reduction) that did almost nothing about nitrogen oxides; the three-way design, which adds rhodium to turn NOx back into plain nitrogen, arrived with the 1981 model year. The converter mandate is what forced unleaded petrol across America. The last country selling leaded petrol was Algeria, which stopped in July 2021. Sources: UNEP, 'Inside the 20-year campaign to rid the world of leaded fuel'; Grokipedia, 'Catalytic converter'; US Patent 4,372,748 (Ford Motor Co.).

question: Joens Jacob Berzelius gathered a pile of odd results in his 1835 survey of chemistry: acid turning starch into sugar syrup, blood making peroxide foam, platinum lighting gas with no flame. He said these were all one thing and gave it a sharp test. What did he say the mystery agent must do?
answer: Hasten the reaction, yet end unaltered in quantity and quality
choices: Hasten the reaction, yet end unaltered in quantity and quality
Hasten the reaction by giving up heat stored in its own bonds
Hasten the reaction while being consumed in step with the product
Hasten the reaction only while held above its melting point
context: Berzelius named the class CATALYSIS, from the Greek katalysis, 'loosening', defining it as 'the property of exerting on other bodies an action which is very different from chemical affinity', the agent hastening the reaction while emerging unaltered in quantity and quality. He had already called Doebereiner's 1823 platinum result 'the most brilliant' of its year and cited it as the founding example. Berzelius also coined isomerism (1830), protein (1838) and allotropy (1841), introduced the modern element symbols, and published an influential table of atomic weights in 1814. FORGOTTEN FIRST: the British chemist Elizabeth Fulhame got there 41 years earlier. Her 'An Essay On Combustion with a View to a New Art of Dying and Painting' (1794), the fruit of fourteen years of experiments, showed that many oxidations run only when water is present, that the water directly participates, and that it is handed back and detectable at the end -- the exact 'consumed then returned' logic. Wikipedia's article on catalysis says outright that the concept 'was invented by chemist Elizabeth Fulhame'. Earlier observations Berzelius was gathering: Gottlieb Kirchhoff's acid-and-starch syrup (1811) and Louis Jacques Thenard's discovery that blood breaks down hydrogen peroxide (1818). Sources: Grokipedia, 'Joens Jacob Berzelius'; Grokipedia, 'Catalysis'; Wikipedia, 'Elizabeth Fulhame'.

question: Fritz Haber pulled ammonia out of plain air in his lab in 1909, but his catalysts were costly osmium and uranium. Alwin Mittasch, at the German firm BASF (Baden Aniline and Soda Factory), went hunting for a cheaper swap, running thirty small pressure reactors side by side, each packed with a different recipe. Which material came out on top?
answer: Fused iron ore, with alumina and potash added
choices: Fused iron ore, with alumina and potash added
Fused nickel ore, with alumina and potash added
Fused copper ore, with alumina and potash added
Fused tungsten ore, with alumina and potash added
context: The winner was fused magnetite (Fe3O4) promoted with alumina (structural -- it holds the surface area open) and potassium oxide (electronic -- it helps split the tough nitrogen molecule), plus lime and silica. Cheap, abundant, and as good as osmium; it is still in use, nearly unchanged, today. Mittasch's parallel mini-reactor programme, begun in 1909, was arguably the first high-throughput catalyst screen (Grokipedia says over 20,000 formulations by 1912; Wikipedia's Mittasch article says roughly 10,000). Credit splits two ways: on 2 July 1909 Haber and his English collaborator Robert Le Rossignol ran off roughly a pint of liquid ammonia over five hours at about 200 atmospheres and 500-600 C -- that was the demonstration. Carl Bosch made it industrial: the first carbon-steel reactor tubes burst after about 80 hours as hydrogen attacked the metal, so Bosch designed a double-walled converter with a replaceable soft-steel liner, patented in 1911, its vents still called 'Bosch holes'. Oppau made its first ammonia on 9 September 1913. Vaclav Smil's ESTIMATE, from nitrogen-response curves and not a measured constant, is that the resulting fertiliser underwrites roughly 40-50% of the world's food supply. Haber took the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, Bosch the 1931. Sources: Grokipedia, 'History of the Haber process'; Wikipedia, 'Alwin Mittasch'.

question: A student sprinkles a spoonful of manganese dioxide powder into a bottle of hydrogen peroxide that has sat so quietly a person would wait days to see a bubble. The bottle foams over within seconds. Afterwards she filters the powder out, dries it and uses it on the next bottle just as well. What did the powder change?
answer: The height of the energy barrier the molecules must climb
choices: The height of the energy barrier the molecules must climb
The temperature at which the reaction becomes possible
The amount of energy the reaction gives off in total
The mixture of products the reaction finally settles into
context: This is the rail that kills the magic. A catalyst opens an ALTERNATIVE pathway with a lower activation energy -- a lower pass over the same mountains -- and ends unchanged. It does not touch the destination: the standard Gibbs energy change is identical with or without it, and catalysts have no effect on where a reaction's equilibrium sits. A catalyst that shifted equilibrium would violate the second law of thermodynamics. In a reversible reaction it speeds the forward and reverse rates in proportion, so the system reaches the SAME equilibrium sooner. Two things a catalyst can never do: supply energy, or make a thermodynamically impossible reaction happen. 'It lowers the temperature the reaction needs' is the subtly wrong cousin -- the reaction was always possible at that temperature; it was simply too slow to see. Quantitative comparisons put the manganese-dioxide-catalysed peroxide breakdown at over 2,000 times the uncatalysed rate; potassium iodide does the same job dissolved rather than as a solid, with iodide ions acting as an intermediate. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Catalysis'; Wikipedia, 'Catalysis'.

question: Irving Langmuir of General Electric measured how gases settle onto clean metal and glass, and between 1916 and 1918 he wrote an equation by matching the rate atoms arrive with the rate they leave. His surface chemistry later won a Nobel Prize. What did he find a gas does when it lands on clean metal?
answer: It sticks in a layer exactly one molecule thick
choices: It sticks in a layer exactly one molecule thick
It dissolves inward and spreads through the metal
It gathers into droplets at the coldest points
It drifts across until it finds a crack to fill
context: Langmuir showed that adsorption occurs in MONOMOLECULAR layers on a clean surface, and derived the Langmuir adsorption isotherm, theta = Kp/(1 + Kp), by equating the rates of adsorption and desorption. He separated chemisorption -- strong, site-specific bonding, oxygen on tungsten at about 160 kcal/mol -- from physisorption, the weak van der Waals kind. He won the 1932 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and was among the first scientists from an industrial laboratory to take one; he also coined the word 'plasma' in 1928. The consequence: if only the outermost single layer of atoms can take part, surface area is the entire game -- which is why catalysts are built as sponges, powders and honeycombs rather than solid blocks. A modern converter uses a cordierite ceramic honeycomb with typically 400 to 900 cells per square inch. The catalytic cycle runs adsorption -> surface reaction -> desorption of product -> catalyst regenerated, and the two classic surface mechanisms are Langmuir-Hinshelwood (both reactants adsorb on adjacent sites, then react) and Eley-Rideal (one adsorbs, the other strikes it straight out of the gas). Sources: Grokipedia, 'Irving Langmuir'; Grokipedia, 'Catalysis'; Grokipedia, 'Catalytic converter'.

question: Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland worked out where CFCs finally end up. The refrigerant gases are so unreactive that nothing at ground level touches them, so they drift upward for decades, until ultraviolet light in the stratosphere snaps a single chlorine atom loose. That one atom goes on destroying ozone molecule after ozone molecule and is never used up. What happens to the chlorine atom on each pass?
answer: It takes an oxygen from ozone, then a loose oxygen atom takes that one away
choices: It takes an oxygen from ozone, then a loose oxygen atom takes that one away
It splits an ozone molecule in two, then drifts free of both halves
It bonds to an ozone molecule, then breaks loose when the cold deepens
It swaps places with an oxygen in ozone, then a second chlorine frees it
context: Cl. + O3 -> ClO. + O2, then ClO. + O -> Cl. + O2. Net: two ozone molecules gone per cycle and the chlorine handed back intact, so one atom destroys thousands before it is finally scavenged. This is the purest possible statement of 'changed by nothing, changing everything' -- and here it is a catastrophe rather than a benefit. Catalysts are not automatically the good guys; the same trick that feeds the world through an iron catalyst tears the ozone layer apart through a chlorine atom. Molina and Rowland's seminal work is where the cycle was worked out. Source: Grokipedia, 'Catalysis' (Basic Examples).

question: Anna Radzicka and Richard Wolfenden clocked an enzyme in 1995 at one stubborn job: stripping carbon dioxide from orotidine monophosphate, a step toward the building blocks of RNA and DNA. Unaided, orotic acid, that molecule's core ring, needs 78 million years in plain water for half a sample to shed its carbon dioxide, longer than the span since the last dinosaurs died. How long does the enzyme need?
answer: About 18 milliseconds
choices: About 18 microseconds
About 18 milliseconds
About 18 seconds
About 18 minutes
context: Radzicka and Wolfenden, 'A proficient enzyme', Science 1995, 267(5194):90-93. Their abstract reports orotic acid, the ring of orotidine 5'-monophosphate (OMP) that carries the carbon dioxide, decarboxylating spontaneously with a half-time of 78 million years in neutral water at room temperature; the enzyme orotidine 5'-monophosphate decarboxylase does the job on OMP with a half-time of 18 milliseconds. That is a rate enhancement of about 10^17, one of the largest known for any enzyme. And the enzyme puts in no energy and is consumed by nothing: it simply opens a lower pass over the same mountain. The same paper reports dimethyl phosphate hydrolysing spontaneously with a half-time of 130,000 years. Sources: Radzicka A, Wolfenden R, Science 1995 (PubMed 7809611); Wikipedia, "Orotidine 5'-phosphate decarboxylase".

question: A research group watched single catalase molecules at work in 2025 and asked what really sets the top speed of one working molecule. Catalase, a liver enzyme that tears hydrogen peroxide apart, is one of the fastest enzymes ever measured. What did the group find limits that top speed?
answer: How fast peroxide molecules can drift into its reach
choices: How fast peroxide molecules can drift into its reach
How fast the iron at its core can reset between splits
How fast its products can clear the narrow channel
How tightly the peroxide clings once it has landed
context: Catalase is classed as a diffusion-limited or 'catalytically perfect' enzyme: its bottleneck is physics, not chemistry -- the substrate simply cannot arrive any faster. A 2025 single-entity protein-electrochemistry study confirmed this for individual catalase molecules. A caution on the numbers: the theoretical diffusion ceiling for k_cat/K_m in water is about 10^8-10^9 M^-1 s^-1, while catalase's measured bimolecular rate constant is around 10^7 M^-1 s^-1 -- APPROACHING that ceiling rather than sitting on it. Carbonic anhydrase, triose phosphate isomerase, superoxide dismutase and acetylcholinesterase are the other textbook diffusion-limited enzymes. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Diffusion-limited enzyme'; Grokipedia, 'Catalase'.

question: Henry Cavendish set out in 1797 to measure the tiny gravitational pull between two lead balls, inside a sealed outbuilding in London. If he entered the room, his own body heat would stir the air and swamp the signal. How did he read the result?
answer: through a telescope from outside the room
choices: through a telescope from outside the room
with his ear pressed to a listening tube
by attaching a long paper pointer that stuck out through a slot in the wall
with a mirror rigged to reflect down a chimney
context: The man who had to leave the room to take his own measurement. Cavendish's shed sat in his garden at Clapham Common; he took 17 patient measurements between August 1797 and May 1798. Source: APS News, 'June 1798: Cavendish weighs the world'.

question: John Michell, a Yorkshire rector, designed a twisting balance but died before he could use it, and Henry Cavendish set it up in a garden shed near London in 1797. Cavendish called the project 'weighing the world.' In his paper he shared only one number about the whole planet. What number was that?
answer: its mean density, in multiples of the density of water
choices: its mean density, in multiples of the density of water
its total mass, measured in tons of iron
the gravitational pull at its surface, in units of feet per second
the length of its diameter, measured in English miles
context: Cavendish's 1798 paper in the Philosophical Transactions was titled 'Experiments to determine the Density of the Earth.' From that single number you can get the mass; from the mass and the size, everything else. Michell had spent years planning the experiment; when he died, the balance had never been fired. Cavendish quietly rebuilt it and kept close to Michell's plan. Sources: Grokipedia -- Cavendish experiment; FamousScientists.org -- John Michell.

question: Francis Baily sat down in 1821 and re-averaged Henry Cavendish's tables by hand. Cavendish had measured the density of the whole Earth in a sealed shed, weighing lead spheres against the tiny pulls they exerted on one another, and he had made 29 tries before printing his number. What did Baily find?
answer: a small arithmetic slip in Cavendish's own average
choices: a small arithmetic slip in Cavendish's own average
a systematic bias caused by a warped suspending wire
a transcription error introduced by the printer of the paper
no mistake at all -- the tables checked out perfectly
context: Cavendish had published 5.48; Baily's corrected average of the same 29 measurements was 5.448. As it happens, the slip had flattered him: the printed 5.48 sits nearer today's 5.514 than the corrected figure does. Sources: APS News, June 2008; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavendish_experiment

question: Henry Cavendish never used the letter G or the term, yet physics textbooks usually say his experiment of 1797-98 measured big G, the gravitational constant. Historians of physics point out that this is not quite right. Who actually extracted G from his data, and when?
answer: Alfred Cornu first extracted G from Cavendish's data in 1873
choices: Alfred Cornu first extracted G from Cavendish's data in 1873
Isaac Newton had already extracted G in his 1687 Principia
James Clerk Maxwell first extracted G while editing Cavendish's notebooks in the 1870s
John Henry Poynting first extracted G when re-checking Cavendish's 29 measurements
context: Cavendish never used the letter G or the term 'gravitational constant'. Newton's law of gravity had a constant of proportionality no one had yet measured; Cornu (with Baille) supplied a value in 1873, and the symbol G came into common use in the late nineteenth century. Cavendish's own quarry was density. Source: 'Historical Notes: The Gravitational Constant', arXiv 2306.06411.

question: A long letter reached the Royal Society in November 1783 from John Michell, describing an object no one else would give a proper name to for nearly two hundred years. Michell was a Yorkshire rector and amateur geologist who also designed the torsion balance Henry Cavendish later used to weigh the world. What did Michell propose in that letter?
answer: a star so massive that its escape velocity would exceed the speed of light
choices: a star so massive that its escape velocity would exceed the speed of light
an invisible planet beyond Saturn whose pull would explain cometary orbits
a comet composed entirely of ice that returns every seventy-six years
a moon of Venus that would eventually be detected by improving telescopes
context: Michell called such an object a 'dark star'. He reasoned that if a star were about 500 solar masses, no light could ever leave it. It is the first written black-hole idea in the scientific literature. Source: APS News, November 2009 -- 'John Michell anticipates black holes'.

question: Cecilia Payne sailed to Harvard because Cambridge would not grant degrees to women. At 25 she finished a thesis on the light of hundreds of stars, and its answer flipped the accepted picture of the universe. What did she find the Sun and the other stars are mostly made of?
answer: Mostly hydrogen and helium, the lightest elements
choices: Mostly iron, a hot version of the Earth's core
Mostly hydrogen and helium, the lightest elements
Mostly carbon and oxygen in roughly equal parts
Mostly heavy metals held together by gravity
context: Payne's 1925 Harvard PhD thesis, 'Stellar Atmospheres,' concluded that the Sun and other stars are composed overwhelmingly of hydrogen and helium -- together about 98 percent of a star's mass -- the two lightest elements in the universe. Her doctorate -- the first astronomy PhD ever granted at Harvard -- was formally issued through Radcliffe College because Harvard would not confer a doctorate on a woman. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Payne-Gaposchkin

question: Arthur Eddington lectured at Cambridge in December 1919, just back from an eclipse expedition to the African island of Principe. A first-year student named Cecilia Payne squeezed in and that night switched from botany to physics. What had his Principe trip just done?
answer: Confirmed Einstein's theory of general relativity
choices: Measured the distance to the Andromeda galaxy
Discovered a new planet beyond Neptune
Confirmed Einstein's theory of general relativity
Proved that the Sun rotates on its axis
context: Eddington's May 1919 eclipse expedition to Principe measured starlight bending around the Sun -- the first observational confirmation of general relativity. Payne, born in England in 1900, was so overwhelmed by his December 1919 lecture that she left botany for physics. Source: https://www.chemistryworld.com/features/the-young-female-astronomer-who-worked-out-what-the-sun-is-made-of/4021693.article

question: Cecilia Payne took down glass plates from the shelves at Harvard College Observatory and read hundreds of stellar spectra off them. A team of women 'computers,' led by Annie Jump Cannon, had spent years classifying stars from those same shelves. What property of a star's light were the women sorting stars by?
answer: The pattern of dark lines in the star's spectrum
choices: The pattern of dark lines in the star's spectrum
The star's precise position in the night sky
The distance to the star in light-years
The rate at which the star's brightness pulses
context: Payne applied Saha's ionization equation to hundreds of stellar spectra taken from the Henry Draper Catalogue at Harvard College Observatory, connecting Saha's theory with the spectral classification system built by Annie Jump Cannon and Harvard's women 'computers.' Source: https://astrobites.org/2018/12/03/the-stuff-of-stars/

question: Meghnad Saha, an Indian physicist, published an equation in 1920 that became Cecilia Payne's key tool. Astronomers before her had read the strength of a spectral line as 'how much of this element is present.' Saha showed that reading was mostly wrong: line strength depends mainly on something else about the star. What?
answer: The temperature of the star's outer atmosphere
choices: The rotation speed of the star on its axis
The distance from the star to the Earth
The temperature of the star's outer atmosphere
The strength of the star's surface magnetic field
context: Saha's 1920 ionization equation showed that a spectral line's strength depends mainly on the star's temperature, because heat strips electrons from atoms and changes which lines the atom can even make. Correcting for temperature is what let Payne read hundreds of stellar spectra and see hydrogen's true abundance. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saha_ionization_equation

question: Cecilia Payne applied Meghnad Saha's formula to hundreds of stellar spectra at Harvard, and her hydrogen numbers came out enormous. They dwarfed anything earlier astronomers had guessed for the makeup of stars. Compared to those earlier readings, roughly how much did her result raise the hydrogen count?
answer: About a million times more abundant
choices: About ten times more abundant
About a hundred times more abundant
About a thousand times more abundant
About a million times more abundant
context: Payne's analysis showed hydrogen was about a million times more abundant in stars than had been assumed, and helium about a thousand times more abundant. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2015/01/cecilia-payne-gaposchkin-universe-changed

question: Harlow Shapley, director of Harvard College Observatory, sent Cecilia Payne's PhD draft to Henry Norris Russell of Princeton, the most senior astronomer in the United States, for a check on her startling hydrogen figure. Russell wrote back a short, blunt reply. How did his letter describe her finding?
answer: As a result that was clearly impossible
choices: As a bold but premature conjecture
As a result that was clearly impossible
As a promising line worth further work
As the natural extension of his earlier calculations
context: Russell wrote to Payne that 'it is clearly impossible that hydrogen should be a million times more abundant than the metals.' Arthur Eddington was skeptical as well. Source: https://physicsworld.com/a/cecilia-payne-gaposchkin-the-woman-who-found-hydrogen-in-the-stars/

question: Cecilia Payne read Henry Norris Russell's letter and feared her whole thesis would be thrown out. Pressed by her seniors, she added one hedging sentence, while her calculated numbers stayed in the text. What did that sentence say about her enormous hydrogen figures?
answer: That they were almost certainly not real
choices: That they were almost certainly not real
That the plates had probably overstated them
That a revised temperature scale would shrink them
That they held only for the very hottest stars
context: At Russell's and Shapley's urging, Payne wrote into the published thesis that the enormous abundance she had derived was 'almost certainly not real', but she left the calculated numbers themselves standing. The finding was softened in prose, never in the data. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2015/01/cecilia-payne-gaposchkin-universe-changed

question: Henry Norris Russell of Princeton wrote his own paper on the Sun's atmosphere in 1929, four years after Cecilia Payne's thesis, and listed its make-up by volume. He reached the same hydrogen-heavy answer by a different route. What became of the public credit for the discovery?
answer: Much of it drifted to Russell
choices: Much of it drifted to Russell
Nearly all of it stayed with Payne
Most of it went to Meghnad Saha
Most of it went to Harlow Shapley
context: Russell, 'On the Composition of the Sun's Atmosphere,' Astrophysical Journal vol. 70, p. 11 (1929). He put the solar atmosphere at roughly 60 parts hydrogen by volume to 2 helium, 2 oxygen, 1 metallic vapours and 0.8 free electrons. Coming from the most powerful astronomer in America, the result settled the question, and much of the credit went with it, though Payne had reached the answer four years earlier. Source: https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1929ApJ....70...11R/abstract

question: Cecilia Payne handed physicists a Sun that could shine by fusing hydrogen into helium, and her result lined up with a second great idea as well. One major cosmological theory predicts a universe dominated by those same two lightest elements. Which cosmological theory was it?
answer: A hot Big Bang, with the universe expanding from an early hot dense state
choices: A hot Big Bang, with the universe expanding from an early hot dense state
A steady-state cosmology in which new matter is continuously created
A cold, static Newtonian universe of fixed unchanging size
A cyclic universe endlessly bouncing between crunches and rebirths
context: A hot Big Bang predicts that the young universe emerged overwhelmingly as hydrogen and helium, with heavier elements forged later inside stars. Payne's 1925 result -- stars are made of that same primordial mix -- became load-bearing for both stellar physics (hydrogen fusion) and modern cosmology. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Payne-Gaposchkin

question: James Chadwick fired a strange 'beryllium beam' at a slab of wax at Cambridge early in 1932, and protons flew out fast. After two weeks of nonstop work he saw what the beam was really made of and mailed a note to Nature. What was the particle?
answer: the neutron
choices: the neutron
the positron
the muon
the neutrino
context: Chadwick's letter to Nature was titled 'Possible Existence of a Neutron' and appeared in February 1932. The full paper in the Proceedings of the Royal Society followed. It closed the book on twelve years of hunting inside the Cavendish Laboratory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Chadwick.

question: A mystery beam streamed out of beryllium struck by alpha rays, and James Chadwick turned it on paraffin wax in 1932. Paraffin holds carbon and hydrogen, and he picked it for the hydrogen. What made hydrogen the perfect target?
answer: its nucleus is a lone proton with nothing else attached
choices: its nucleus is a lone proton with nothing else attached
it is the lightest element, so its atoms move fastest at room temperature
its nucleus has the largest cross-section of any element
its electrons are the most loosely bound of any element
context: That is what makes hydrogen the cleanest target imaginable. If the mystery beam kicks a recoiling nucleus out of the wax, and that nucleus is bare, the recoil speed maps straight to the beam without complications from the rest of an atom. That is the trick. It is why Chadwick used it -- and why the Joliot-Curies had used it before him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_neutron.

question: A team in Paris beat James Chadwick to the paraffin-wax test in January 1932 and saw the same recoiling protons he did. These superb experimenters reported that gamma rays were causing them. Who were the Paris researchers?
answer: Irene and Frederic Joliot-Curie
choices: Irene and Frederic Joliot-Curie
Marie and Pierre Curie
Lise Meitner and Otto Hahn
Gerty and Carl Cori
context: Irene Curie (Marie's daughter) and Frederic Joliot published the paraffin result in Comptes Rendus in January 1932. They went on to a Nobel of their own in 1935 for the discovery of induced radioactivity -- they were superb experimentalists. Their miss on the neutron was a wrong prior about what the radiation had to be, not sloppy work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_neutron.

question: James Chadwick knew what he was seeing in 1932 because he had been hunting it for about twelve years: a neutral particle, roughly the mass of a proton, sitting inside the atomic nucleus. His own boss at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge had predicted such a particle in a famous 1920 lecture to the Royal Society. Which physicist gave that lecture?
answer: Ernest Rutherford
choices: Ernest Rutherford
Niels Bohr
Werner Heisenberg
Arthur Eddington
context: Rutherford's 1920 Bakerian Lecture to the Royal Society sketched a neutral particle of roughly proton mass, arguing it would explain how heavy nuclei hold together and could slip past their electric charge. Chadwick took the sketch as a research programme and ran it for a decade -- until the Joliot-Curies handed him the clue by misidentifying it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_neutron.

question: Lise Meitner, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split uranium in 1938 and 1939 with James Chadwick's new particle, moving slowly. A slow proton fired at uranium is turned away long before it reaches the nucleus. What property of Chadwick's particle lets it walk in where the proton cannot?
answer: it carries no electric charge to be repelled by
choices: it carries no electric charge to be repelled by
it is much smaller than a proton in size
it decays into a photon before it arrives
it moves faster than any proton the lab could make
context: A proton fired at a uranium nucleus meets a wall of Coulomb repulsion -- 92 protons pushing back. A slow neutron feels nothing until it is right at the nuclear surface, where the short-range strong force grabs it. Otto Hahn, Fritz Strassmann and Lise Meitner used that fact to split the nucleus in 1938-39, and the world changed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_neutron.

question: A young chemist opened a new science school for Lille in 1854, for students bound for the factories and dye-works of northern France. An alert mind catches what luck offers, he told them, and he put it in one line: 'in the fields of observation, chance favours only the prepared mind.' Who said it?
answer: Louis Pasteur
choices: Louis Pasteur
Jean-Baptiste Dumas
Marcelin Berthelot
Claude Bernard
context: The line is from Pasteur's printed 7 December 1854 inaugural address for the new Lille faculty of sciences, delivered at Douai. Original French: 'dans les champs de l'observation, le hasard ne favorise que les esprits prepares'. Dumas, Berthelot and Bernard were all leading French scientists active in the 1850s. Source: Louis Pasteur, Wikiquote (https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Louis_Pasteur).

question: Ørsted, a Danish scientist, was lecturing in 1820 when a compass needle twitched beside a live wire. Everyone saw the wobble. Only one man knew what it meant, because he had been chasing that question for years. What link did that tiny twitch reveal?
answer: An electric current creates a magnetic field around the wire
choices: An electric current creates a magnetic field around the wire
A moving magnet produces an electric current in a coil
The wire's heat bends the Earth's magnetism near it
A compass needle holds a hidden electric charge
context: Orsted had spent years expecting a link between electricity and magnetism, and in 1820 the anomaly finally arrived: the needle swung because the current wrapped the wire in a magnetic field. A prepared mind is not a lucky mind - it is a mind with an expectation already loaded, waiting for an anomaly to fit. The reverse effect, a moving magnet driving a current through a coil, waited for Michael Faraday in 1831. Source: APS News, 'July 1820: Orsted & Electromagnetism' (https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2008/07/1820-oersted-electromagnetism).

question: William Stukeley set down Newton's falling apple in his 1752 memoir of Newton. Kekule told of his dream of a snake and the benzene ring in an 1890 speech to the German Chemical Society. Careful historians of science rank both stories as the same kind of source. Which kind?
answer: A late self-told anecdote, not a contemporary record
choices: A late self-told anecdote, not a contemporary record
A passage from the discoverer's own contemporary correspondence
A rival chemist's diary written the same year as the discovery
A signed eyewitness deposition taken at the time
context: Stukeley wrote up Newton's story from a conversation about sixty years after the alleged event; Kekule told the snake-dream story roughly twenty-five years after already publishing the benzene structure. Retold discovery stories smooth themselves with age - the older the retelling and the more famous the teller, the tidier the story gets. That does not prove them false; it means treat them as testimony, not evidence. Sources: History.com on Stukeley; contemporary essays on the Kekule dream.  (Legend.)

question: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, aged 19, sailed from India to England in 1930 for a Cambridge scholarship. Between meals he worked out that a burnt-out star above a certain mass cannot settle as a white dwarf. What does such a doomed star do next?
answer: It collapses into something even denser, like a black hole
choices: It collapses into something even denser, like a black hole
It cools quietly into a giant frozen planet
It splits down the middle into two smaller stars
It swells outward forever into a huge nebula
context: Chandrasekhar was on his way to graduate work at Cambridge. Above roughly 1.4 Suns, the squeezed electrons can no longer hold a dead star's core up against its own gravity, so it keeps collapsing, into a neutron star or a black hole. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandrasekhar_limit

question: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar studied the white dwarf, the burnt-out core of a Sun-like star, a body about the size of Earth crammed with roughly the mass of the Sun. With nothing left to burn, heat pressure cannot hold it up against gravity. What does prop it up?
answer: A quantum rule that forbids two electrons from occupying the same state
choices: A quantum rule that forbids two electrons from occupying the same state
The star's rotation, spinning fast enough to fling matter outward
A magnetic field strong enough to counter its own gravity
Gravitational potential energy released as the star gradually shrinks
context: This is the Pauli exclusion principle. Squeeze electrons close and they shove back -- 'electron degeneracy pressure' -- with a push that has nothing to do with temperature. The slow-shrinkage idea (Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction) was the pre-quantum guess for what powers stars, and it fails for white dwarfs.

question: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar added one piece of physics to the theory of white dwarfs on a boat from India to England in 1930. The older theory said these leftover cores of dead stars could grow to any size and still hold steady, but his version put a ceiling on their mass. What had the older theorists left out?
answer: Special relativity
choices: Special relativity
General relativity
The uncertainty principle
Quantum tunneling
context: As the crushed electrons are driven toward light speed, their outward push stops growing fast enough to keep pace with gravity, so support fails above a definite mass -- the ceiling.

question: A white dwarf, the Earth-sized ember a Sun-like star leaves when its fuel runs out, already holds roughly the Sun's mass. Older theory let such embers grow to any mass and stay steady. Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar's 1930 calculation set a ceiling instead. Where did he put it?
answer: About 1.4 suns
choices: About 1.4 suns
About 100 suns
About 3 suns
About 10 suns
context: Chandrasekhar's ceiling sits at roughly 1.4 times the Sun's mass, now usually given as about 1.44. Because a white dwarf already holds about one Sun, the margin is small: add a little more and the electrons, driven toward the speed of light, can no longer push back hard enough. The limit now carries his name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandrasekhar_limit

question: Arthur Eddington rose in London in January 1935, before the Royal Astronomical Society, and attacked Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar's result in public: any dying star above a certain mass cannot settle as a stable white dwarf and must keep collapsing. In The Observatory that year he put his objection in print. What did his printed objection say?
answer: That a law of Nature ought to stop a star from behaving in so absurd a way
choices: That a law of Nature ought to stop a star from behaving in so absurd a way
That Chandrasekhar's arithmetic was sound but his physics not yet settled
That a star above that mass would first shed matter and so save itself
That the equation held, but no real star would ever reach its boundary
context: The consequence Eddington could not accept: above the limit, nothing was left to halt total collapse -- a star crushed to a few kilometers or to a point. He preferred to think the equation itself must be wrong. His words in The Observatory (1935): 'There should be a law of Nature to prevent a star from behaving in this absurd way.'

question: Landau, a Soviet physicist, put a bold idea in print early in 1932: a star's core, squeezed hard enough, would behave like one giant atomic nucleus. Historians now read it as an early forecast of one kind of collapsed star, found only decades later. Which kind?
answer: A neutron star
choices: A neutron star
A white dwarf
A brown dwarf
A red giant
context: Landau wrote the paper in Zurich in 1931, before the neutron was discovered; it appeared in February 1932, the same month Chadwick announced the neutron, and the matching dates later fed a mistaken story that Landau had been answering Chadwick. Historians read his dense stars that look like one giant nucleus as an early anticipation of neutron stars, which Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky proposed by name in 1934 and astronomers first found, as pulsars, in 1967. White dwarfs were already known, a red giant is swollen rather than collapsed, and a brown dwarf is too small ever to fuse ordinary hydrogen. Source: Yakovlev, Haensel, Baym and Pethick, 'Lev Landau and the conception of neutron stars', Physics-Uspekhi 56 (2013), https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.0682

question: Ernst Chladni clamps a square metal plate at its centre, sprinkles fine sand over it and drags a violin bow along one edge until the plate rings. A student repeats it in a kitchen with a baking sheet, a phone speaker and table salt. What does the sand do?
answer: heaps itself into sharp symmetrical lines
choices: heaps itself into sharp symmetrical lines
slides off the plate entirely
vibrates as a fine mist above the plate
clumps into one mound at the bow contact
context: The book was 'Entdeckungen ueber die Theorie des Klanges' ('Discoveries in the Theory of Sound'). You can reproduce it at home with a cookie sheet, table salt, and a phone speaker. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Chladni

question: A presenter at a Chladni demonstration bows a steady note on a metal plate while the sand on top settles into a striking pattern. Halfway through, she presses one fingertip firmly near the centre of the plate. What happens to the sand pattern?
answer: the whole pattern reorganises around the finger
choices: the whole pattern reorganises around the finger
the pattern instantly vanishes
the pattern stays put and the sand ignores the finger
the sand jumps toward the finger and clings there
context: Your finger cannot move up and down, so wherever it presses the plate the plate cannot vibrate. Physicists call that a forced node. The plate settles into the next standing-wave shape that respects the new constraint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chladni_figures

question: Ernst Chladni drew a violin bow across the edge of a clamped metal plate sprinkled with sand or flour, and the powder jumped around, then gathered into stars, six-fold flowers and roses. He made the experiment famous in the 1780s. Why does the powder collect where it does?
answer: It settles on lines where the plate is not vibrating
choices: It settles on lines where the plate is not vibrating
It piles up where the plate vibrates hardest
The bow's rosin makes it stick in loops
Static electricity draws it into curves
context: Hooke recorded the effect and moved on; Chladni turned the curiosity into a research programme with hundreds of catalogued shapes. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2017/07/first-experiments-chladni-figures

question: Michael Faraday redid Ernst Chladni's experiment in 1831 with a dust much lighter than sand, powdered lycopodium spores. The pattern came out the exact inverse of Chladni's: the powder gathered in the regions moving hardest, not the quiet ones. What was sorting the spores the opposite way?
answer: tiny air currents stirred up by the vibration
choices: tiny air currents stirred up by the vibration
static electricity from the friction of the bow
the plate's own magnetic field
the shape of grain in the metal itself
context: This is called acoustic streaming: the vibrating surface pumps circulating air currents that carry the light spores to the antinodes. Repeat the experiment in a vacuum and the inverse pattern does not form -- Faraday's confirming test. Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/279629673_Convection_and_fluidization_in_oscillatory_granular_flows_The_role_of_acoustic_streaming

question: Sophie Germain alone sent a serious entry when the French Academy offered a prize in 1809 for the mathematics of a vibrating plate. The idea came from the sand patterns Ernst Chladni had shown Napoleon. The École Polytechnique would not admit a woman. How did she learn the hard mathematics she needed?
answer: She taught herself from borrowed lecture notes
choices: She taught herself from borrowed lecture notes
A wealthy uncle hired her private tutors
She disguised herself as a boy and enrolled
The Academy trained her secretly for the contest
context: Poisson was elected to the Academy, which made him a judge rather than a contestant, and no one else was willing to try -- Lagrange had said the problem would need a new branch of analysis. Germain, barred from the Ecole Polytechnique for being a woman, worked from smuggled lecture notes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophie_Germain

question: Sophie Germain saw her first entry for the Paris Academy's prize rejected for mathematical errors, and her second earned only an honourable mention. She won the grand prize in 1816, the first woman ever to take one, but the winning memoir was still not entirely correct. Who later supplied the last piece?
answer: Gustav Kirchhoff, who corrected the boundary conditions
choices: Gustav Kirchhoff, who corrected the boundary conditions
Augustin-Louis Cauchy, who redid the derivation from scratch
Simeon Denis Poisson, who withdrew his own competing paper
Pierre-Simon Laplace, who signed off on it as it stood
context: Germain had leaned on an incorrect expression from Euler, and her boundary conditions were wrong. Kirchhoff (later famous for the circuit laws) supplied the correct ones. The Academy did not invite her to the award ceremony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophie_Germain

question: Ernst Chladni made a bold claim in 1794 about the stones country people said had fallen from the sky, and learned men laughed. Then in April 1803 a spectacular shower rained thousands of small stones over a French village in broad daylight, and the physicist Biot investigated. What did that fall finally settle?
answer: That rocks really do fall to Earth from space
choices: That rocks really do fall to Earth from space
That meteors are burning volcanic dust
That shooting stars are optical illusions
That lightning forges stones inside storm clouds
context: More than three thousand fragments fell on L'Aigle in Normandy on 26 April 1803, in broad daylight and in front of hundreds of witnesses. The French Academy sent the young Jean-Baptiste Biot, whose careful fieldwork on the stones and the witnesses convinced the learned world that rocks really do arrive from space, and Chladni's laughed-at claim of 1794 was vindicated. Until then most scholars followed Aristotle, for whom meteors were vapours from the Earth itself that caught fire in the air. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%27Aigle_(meteorite)

question: Clair Patterson tracked the junk results from his rock tests to lead in everything: the air of his lab, the dust, the benches, the glassware. Then he tested one thing that had nothing to do with the study, and it held lead too. What did he test?
answer: The hair on his own head
choices: The ink in his notebook
The snow on the roof outside
The hair on his own head
The coins in his pocket
context: During his doctoral research Patterson found lead contamination pervasive throughout his laboratory -- including in his own hair. The world itself was dirty enough to ruin the measurement, so before he could weigh the age of the old world he had to build a clean one. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: Tuna came into Clair Patterson's lab two ways in the late 1960s. A fresh fish caught at sea carried about 0.3 nanograms of lead per gram of flesh. The same species canned carried 1,400, thousands of times more. Where was the extra lead coming from?
answer: The lead solder sealing the can's seams
choices: The lead solder sealing the can's seams
The lead pipes in the cannery's water
The tin plating flaking off the steel
The lead-based ink printed on the label
context: The official laboratory that had measured the same comparison reported a rise of only 400 to 700 nanograms per gram -- Patterson found 1,400. He was not only catching industry: he was catching the regulators' own numbers running low. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: The lead ruining Clair Patterson's readings came from the room and not the rock, so in 1953 he built one of the first ultra-clean labs at Caltech. He had every tool acid-washed and every door sealed. He also refused to use the chemicals his suppliers sent as they came. What did he do to them first?
answer: Re-distilled every one of them himself
choices: Diluted them tenfold before any use
Filtered them through fresh charcoal
Froze them and poured off the top
Re-distilled every one of them himself
context: Careful with the credit: Patterson built one of the first ultra-clean LABORATORIES in 1953, but the modern laminar-flow cleanroom was invented by the physicist Willis Whitfield at Sandia National Laboratories in 1960, seven years later. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'; Wikipedia, 'Cleanroom'.

question: A tourist in a visitor centre stands beside a 639-kilogram lump of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, the rock Clair Patterson picked to date the Earth. About 30 tonnes of such chunks have been found across northern Arizona. Why is the meteorite scattered rather than whole?
answer: The asteroid exploded on impact and blasted out a crater
choices: The parent body broke apart high in the atmosphere
The asteroid exploded on impact and blasted out a crater
Glaciers dragged the pieces apart over 50,000 years
Collectors sawed the single mass up for museums
context: The roughly 50-metre asteroid blasted out Meteor Crater in Arizona about 50,000 years ago, and the 639-kilogram Holsinger Meteorite sits in the crater's visitor centre. Canyon Diablo also carries three mineral phases -- sulfide, metal alloys and silicates -- with sharply different uranium and lead contents, which is exactly the spread an isotope analysis needs. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Canyon Diablo (meteorite)'; Wikipedia, 'Age of the Earth'.

question: Clair Patterson wanted the lead in the air of 1750, of 1850 and of 1900, and nobody had measured it because the instruments did not exist. So he went hunting for a place that had recorded each year's air and stored it, layer on layer, ever since. Where did he go?
answer: To Greenland, to drill out a core of ice
choices: To California, to core bristlecone pines
To Switzerland, to dredge a lake bed
To Greenland, to drill out a core of ice
To London, to sample old chimney soot
context: Patterson analysed cores from Camp Century in Greenland in 1964 and from Antarctica in 1965. Snow falls, traps the dust and gases of its year, and is buried by the next year's fall -- so a column of ice is a dated archive of the air, read downwards. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'; Wikipedia, 'Ice core'.

question: Clair Patterson set out to measure how long ago the Earth formed, and the obvious material was lying under his feet by the tonne. He ignored it and worked on meteorites instead. What is wrong with using the Earth's own rocks to time the Earth's beginning?
answer: The surface is endlessly remade, so rock records its last reset
choices: The surface is endlessly remade, so rock records its last reset
The core's heat boils lead out of the crust, leaving it unreadable
Earth's magnetic field scrambles the lead isotope ratios in crust
Uranium is far too rare in crustal rock to leave a usable signal
context: The planet separated into core, mantle and crust, and plate tectonics, weathering and hot water circulating through rock have mixed and remade the surface ever since. A meteorite is debris from the same formation event that was never recycled -- so its clock has been running, untouched, from the beginning. Source: Wikipedia, 'Age of the Earth'.

question: Clair Patterson published his answer for the age of the Earth in 1956: 4.55 billion years, give or take 70 million, read out of the lead in meteorites. The textbooks of the day carried roughly 3.3 billion. Decades of sharper instruments have gone by since. What has become of Patterson's figure?
answer: Later work has shifted it by only about ten million years
choices: Later work halved it once radioactive heating was allowed for
Later work doubled it when far older meteorites turned up
Later work dropped it when the Apollo Moon rocks came back
Later work has shifted it by only about ten million years
context: The modern consensus is 4.54 plus or minus 0.05 billion years -- Patterson's 1956 value was 4.55 plus or minus 0.07, and the two should not be blurred. The same lead-lead technique, sharpened, now dates the oldest solids in the Solar System to 4,567.35 plus or minus 0.28 million years. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Age of the Earth'; Wikipedia, 'Lead-lead dating'.

question: Layer by layer, Clair Patterson read the lead in buried snow, down to layers laid long before any industry existed. By 1969 the result was public. Set against those deep pre-industrial layers, what had the lead done in the most recent snow?
answer: Risen more than two-hundredfold
choices: Risen by about a tenth at most
Risen more than two-hundredfold
Fallen to roughly half its level
Held steady the whole way up
context: Lead levels in Greenland ice had increased by a factor of over 200 since pre-industrial times. The same ice carries older spikes matching Roman-era mining and war, alongside industrial-era rises in copper, cadmium and zinc -- human lead pollution is genuinely thousands of years old, which is precisely why fixing the natural baseline mattered so much. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Ice core'; Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: Clair Patterson took on Robert Kehoe, the top expert on lead in the human body. Kehoe's Kettering Lab at Cincinnati held a near-total lock on lead safety research, and its studies were the ones everyone cited on whether leaded petrol was safe. Who paid for that lab?
answer: General Motors, DuPont and the Ethyl Corporation
choices: The Rockefeller, Carnegie and Guggenheim foundations
The Public Health Service, the Army and the Navy
General Motors, DuPont and the Ethyl Corporation
Ford, Firestone and the Goodyear Tire Company
context: Charles Kettering hired Kehoe at General Motors in 1924; Kehoe became chief medical adviser of the Ethyl Corporation, maker of the leaded petrol additive, in 1925 and held the post until he retired, and he directed the Kettering Laboratory from 1930. His scientific position was that lead in humans was normal and low-level exposure harmless. Source: Wikipedia, 'Robert A. Kehoe'.

question: Robert Kehoe argued that the lead in human bodies had always been there. To test it, Clair Patterson compared bone from 1,600-year-old Peruvian burials with modern bone, and found the modern bone carrying between seven hundred and twelve hundred times more lead. One objection was obvious: ancient bone might simply lose what it holds over sixteen centuries. How did Patterson close that hole?
answer: He measured barium and calcium too, and those had not shifted
choices: He measured barium and calcium too, and those had not shifted
He measured a hundred more burials from the same cemetery
He sealed the ancient bone in clean glass for a year first
He compared the burials with Roman bone of the same age
context: Barium and calcium are chemically similar to lead and are taken up by bone in the same way, so if old bone leaked its contents they should have fallen too. They had not. Only lead had moved -- which is what a control is for. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: Clair Patterson had built the ultra-clean lab, measured lead in old bone and the deep ocean, and set numbers everyone used. The National Research Council put together a panel on airborne lead pollution in 1971. What happened to him when the panel was formed?
answer: He was left off it entirely
choices: He was made its chairman
He was asked to review its draft only
He resigned from it after two meetings
He was left off it entirely
context: After criticism from the lead industry Patterson was also refused contracts by several supposedly neutral research organisations, including the United States Public Health Service. When he did reach an NRC panel in 1978 he refused to sign its consensus and filed a 78-page minority report arguing that controls on leaded fuels, water systems, food containers, paints and glazes should start immediately. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: Clair Patterson ran into the weak point of every radioactive clock: to read it, a scientist must know how much of the end product sat in the sample before any decay began, and nobody was there to write it down. He took several samples at once and plotted them as a straight line, an isochron. Which feature of the plot handed him the starting amount?
answer: The point where the line crosses the axis
choices: The steepness of the line across the plot
The point where the line crosses the axis
The average position of the plotted points
The spread between the outermost points
context: Because several samples are plotted together, no assumption is needed about the initial amount of the decay product -- it falls out of the intercept instead of being guessed. Better still, the method grades itself: points on a straight line give you an age, and scatter tells you an assumption has failed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Isochron dating'.

question: Robert Kehoe insisted, in defence of leaded petrol, that human bodies had always carried lead. He went further and held that the human species had biologically adapted to it, the way a body adapts to anything it lives among. Clair Patterson answered him in a single sentence in the 1960s. What did Patterson say?
answer: Humans have worked lead for a few thousand years, an instant on the Darwinian scale
choices: Humans store lead in their bones, which no species adapted to a poison would do
Humans adapted to the lead in their food, never to the lead pouring from engines
Humans have worked lead for a few thousand years, an instant on the Darwinian scale
Humans take up lead exactly as other primates do, showing no special resistance
context: Kehoe's paradigm, laid down at the Surgeon General's conference of May 1925, was that leaded petrol should be stopped only if someone could show that an actual danger resulted from it -- in the absence of clear evidence of risk, no risk of significance. Patterson's counter had two edges. Against the adaptation claim he set the clock: a few thousand years was only an instant on the Darwinian time scale. And he went after the word itself: 'normal' merely means average, so it should be replaced by 'typical' -- what is commonplace is not therefore harmless. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Robert A. Kehoe'; Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: Clair Patterson supplied the crucial measurement and forced the question, but leaded petrol did not leave American pumps because one man won an argument. The phase-out took twenty years of regulation, finishing in 1986. One step mattered more than any argument about health: from the 1975 model year, new American cars had to burn unleaded fuel because lead wrecked a new device they carried. Which device?
answer: The catalytic converter
choices: The catalytic converter
The electronic ignition module
The fuel injector
The turbocharger
context: The EPA issued regulations to reduce lead in petrol from 1973, the accelerated phase-out finished in 1986, and leaded fuel was fully banned for American road vehicles on 1 January 1996. Average blood lead in American children fell from 13.7 micrograms per decilitre in 1976 to 3 by 1991. Patterson died on 5 December 1995, the year he received the Tyler Prize; minor planet 2511 carries his name. Algeria, the last producer, stopped in July 2021, and the UN declared the global end of leaded petrol that August. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Tetraethyllead'; Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: A panel of experts gathered in a Berlin courtyard in September 1904 to watch a horse called Clever Hans tap out sums with his hoof. It included a veterinarian, a circus director, a cavalry officer, schoolteachers and the Berlin zoo's director. What did the panel decide?
answer: That no trickery was involved
choices: That no trickery was involved
That the owner was hiding a hand signal in his sleeve
That an assistant behind the fence tapped answers first
That the horse had memorised a sound cue per number
context: The horse was Clever Hans. The commission was right that no one was cheating -- and the wonder of the story is exactly that: no fraud existed, and everyone (horse, owner, commission, crowd) was honestly baffled. The trick was hidden inside the questioner's own body, and the commission was not designed to look there. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: Clever Hans tapped his hoof to answer a math problem in front of a Berlin crowd. His owner charged no admission, believed every hoof tap and taught the horse in his own backyard. Who was that owner?
answer: A retired gymnasium mathematics teacher named Wilhelm von Osten
choices: A retired gymnasium mathematics teacher named Wilhelm von Osten
A retired cavalry officer named Oskar Pfungst
A circus impresario named Carl Stumpf
A veterinary surgeon named Bernhard Schillings
context: Von Osten was also an amateur horse trainer and a phrenologist -- he genuinely believed animals could be taught to reason, and Hans was his life's project. That earnestness is why the fraud investigators kept coming back empty-handed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: The owner of Clever Hans led the black stallion out before a Berlin crowd around 1904 and asked him arithmetic questions. The horse tapped out each answer and seemed to be truly thinking. The crowds were shown far more than adding small numbers. Which trio of skills was in his advertised repertoire?
answer: Fractions, telling the time, and spelling German
choices: Fractions, telling the time, and spelling German
Reading Latin, naming coins, and identifying flags of nations
Counting audience members, naming days of the week in French, and reciting the alphabet
Recognising written names, solving simple equations, and telling temperature
context: Hans's public act also included multiplication, division, tracking the calendar, and distinguishing musical tones -- all through hoof taps and small head movements. The bigger the repertoire, the harder any single-trick explanation had to work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: Oskar Pfungst, a student at the Psychological Institute at the University of Berlin, redesigned the Clever Hans tests in 1907 around two knobs he could turn independently. The horse had become famous for seeming to solve math problems by tapping his hoof, and between them the two knobs revealed how he was really getting the answers. What were the two things Pfungst varied?
answer: Whether Hans could see the questioner, and whether the questioner knew the answer
choices: Whether Hans could see the questioner, and whether the questioner knew the answer
The size of the audience, and the temperature of the room
The breed of horse used, and the language of the question
The distance to the questioner, and the volume of the crowd
context: Pfungst blindfolded Hans, changed questioners, and quietly slipped some questioners the right answer and others a wrong one. Von Osten's honesty had passed every earlier test for cheating -- but no earlier test had checked the questioner's knowledge, only the questioner's intent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: Clever Hans scored 50 of 56, or 89 percent, in Oskar Pfungst's trials of 1907 when he faced a questioner he could see who knew the right answer. Given a questioner Hans could not see, how did his score change?
answer: It collapsed to 2 of 35 -- about 6%
choices: It collapsed to 2 of 35 -- about 6%
It stayed near 28 of 35 -- about 80%
It fell to roughly 16 of 35 -- about 45%
It rose to 33 of 35 -- about 94%
context: Six percent is roughly what you would expect from a horse tapping until told to stop; the previous 89% had never been about the horse's counting. The score tracked what the human in the room knew, not what the horse knew. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: A questioner stood before Clever Hans as the horse tapped, and Oskar Pfungst watched the man very closely. Pfungst had worked out that Hans could answer only when the person in front of him already knew the answer, so Hans had to be reading the human, not doing the sum. What was the tiny signal Hans was reading?
answer: A small upward jerk of the head on the correct tap
choices: A small upward jerk of the head on the correct tap
A quiet shift of weight from one foot to the other
A whistled note too high for humans to hear
A finger twitch on the reins the horse could feel
context: Posture tension built up as the taps neared the right count and released with that small head jerk. Hans stopped on the release, because the release was what he had learned to look for. All the humans in the room were giving him the answer without knowing they were doing it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: Oskar Pfungst worked out that Clever Hans was reading a tiny cue from his questioners rather than doing sums, and then he tried something braver. He sat in the questioner's chair himself, now fully aware of the cue, and tried hard not to give it. What happened when he ran the trial?
answer: He emitted the cue involuntarily anyway, even while trying to suppress it
choices: He emitted the cue involuntarily anyway, even while trying to suppress it
He suppressed it easily and Hans got every answer wrong
He suppressed it easily and Hans still got most answers right
He emitted a bigger cue than the untrained questioners had
context: This is why Wilhelm von Osten had never been caught by any earlier commission: not because he was hiding a signal, but because the signal was hiding from him. It is also the reason honest people can still bias an experiment, and why sincerity is not a protection. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: Four researchers tested 'facilitated communication' in 1993, a method in which an assistant physically supports a non-speaking client's hand at a keyboard. In some trials the client and the facilitator were shown different pictures. Whose picture did the typed answer name?
answer: The facilitator's picture, essentially every time
choices: The facilitator's picture, essentially every time
The client's picture, essentially every time
Neither, because the typing became unreadable
Both pictures in equal proportion across the trials
context: The trap is Clever Hans's, eighty-nine years later. The facilitators were not lying -- like von Osten, they believed. The test worked because it made the human in the room ignorant of the target answer. That single design idea, born of a horse, still catches the same illusion whenever it reappears. Source: Wheeler et al., 'An experimental assessment of facilitated communication', Mental Retardation 31(1), 1993.

question: Ole Romer logged about 140 eclipses of Io, a moon of Jupiter, in the 1670s. Io ducks into its planet's shadow once every 1.769 days, so those blackouts should tick like a pendulum, but they would not keep to the table. What was the pattern in the drift?
answer: Early when Earth was near Jupiter, late when it was far.
choices: Early when Earth was near Jupiter, late when it was far.
Later and later, by a little more with every orbit.
Early whenever Jupiter stood high in the night sky.
On time for Io, but hours out for the outer moons.
context: Romer and his colleagues timed the eclipses on Christiaan Huygens' new pendulum clocks, good to about fifteen seconds a day. Io's orbit takes 1.769 days, about 42.5 hours, so the eclipses recur like a ticking pendulum -- which is exactly what makes a drift of whole minutes impossible to miss. A moon used as a clock. Source: Grokipedia, 'Romer's determination of the speed of light'.

question: Galileo Galilei tried to time light with two men at night across a valley, each with a covered lantern. One uncovered his, the other answered on seeing the flash, and the first timed the round trip. What did Galileo report?
answer: He could not tell, only that light must be extraordinarily rapid.
choices: He could not tell, only that light must be extraordinarily rapid.
He saw a clear delay, and put light at some ten miles a second.
He saw no delay at all, and declared light plainly instantaneous.
He gave up when the lanterns proved far too dim to see at all.
context: Galileo's own conclusion was that light is, if not instantaneous, extraordinarily rapid -- an honest report of a test that failed. The historian Carl Boyer later calculated that the lantern method at best established a lower limit of about 60 miles per second for light: true, and useless. Isaac Beeckman had proposed a version nine years earlier, watching a cannon flash reflect off a mirror about a mile away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light, citing Galilei, Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences (Crew and de Salvio trans.) p.43, and C. B. Boyer, Isis 33:1 (1941) p.24.

question: Ole Romer went on record before the fact. In September 1676 he named a coming eclipse of Jupiter's moon Io and said the printed tables had its time wrong. On the night, the Paris Observatory logged the eclipse late, exactly as Romer had said. How late had he said it would be?
answer: About ten minutes late.
choices: About ten minutes late.
About half a minute late.
About one hour late.
About four hours late.
context: Romer explained the reason to the Academie Royale des Sciences on 21 November 1676 -- after the event, not before it; the prediction itself was made in September. Sources differ on the day of the eclipse (Grokipedia gives 9 November, Wikipedia 16 November), so the reliable facts are the year, the roughly ten-minute delay, and that he said it first. A prediction made in advance and checked in public is what turns a pattern into science. Source: Grokipedia, 'Romer's determination of the speed of light', cross-checked against en.wikipedia.org.

question: James Bradley went sailing on the Thames in 1728, as the most-told story has it, three years stuck on a puzzle. Hunting for stellar parallax, he had found instead that every star traces a tiny yearly ellipse, and he could not say why. What does the story say he noticed on the boat?
answer: The masthead flag swung round when the boat turned, not the wind.
choices: The masthead flag swung round when the boat turned, not the wind.
The wake stayed dead straight while the boat swung beneath it.
The sails filled harder on one tack than the other in one breeze.
The gulls overhead slid backwards as the boat gathered way.
context: Wikipedia flags the Thames story as famous but possibly apocryphal, so treat it as a story, not a document. What it points at is real and is called aberration: Bradley told the Royal Society in January 1729 that an observer must tilt the telescope forward while Earth moves; teachers now compare it to a runner tilting an umbrella into vertical rain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bradley.  (Legend.)

question: Watchers from Florence's Accademia del Cimento tried Galileo's lantern test again in 1667, with two lanterns about a mile apart. They looked for any gap between one lantern's flash and the other's reply and saw no delay at all. About how long was the delay they were hunting?
answer: About eleven millionths of a second.
choices: About eleven millionths of a second.
About eleven thousandths of a second.
About one fiftieth of a second.
About one tenth of a second.
context: Light covers a mile in about 5.4 millionths of a second, and the lantern protocol needs the round trip, so the lag was near eleven millionths of a second -- eleven microseconds. Human reaction time is tens of thousands of times too slow. The experiment was beaten by biology, not by bad technique, which is why the next real advance came from the sky instead of the hilltop. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light, citing Foschi and Leone, Perception 38(8):1251-1259 (2009).

question: Ole Romer shared his finding at the Paris Academy of Sciences in November 1676, and the next month it reached print in the Journal des scavans. It was the most talked-about measurement of the century. What form did that printed announcement take?
answer: An anonymous six-paragraph notice, written in the third person.
choices: An anonymous six-paragraph notice, written in the third person.
A signed forty-page memoir with his full tables of eclipses.
A letter from Cassini setting out his assistant's claim.
A single engraved plate with a caption and no text at all.
context: Romer never produced a formal mathematical description of his own discovery. The English translation of those six unsigned paragraphs ran in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society in 1677. The most famous measurement of the seventeenth century was announced by an author who did not sign his name to it. Source: Grokipedia, 'Romer's determination of the speed of light'.

question: Ole Romer published no speed for light at all. Textbooks that credit him with a figure like 227,000 kilometres per second are quoting somebody else's arithmetic, done later and with someone else's numbers. What he gave was a duration. What did that time measure?
answer: The time light needs to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit -- about 22 minutes.
choices: The time light needs to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit -- about 22 minutes.
The time light needs to travel from the Sun out to Earth -- about 11 minutes.
The time light needs to cross the whole of Jupiter's shadow -- about 22 minutes.
The time light needs to travel from Jupiter across to Earth -- about 40 minutes.
context: Romer's 22 minutes was generous: light crosses one astronomical unit in 499 seconds, so the full diameter takes about 998 seconds -- roughly 16.6 minutes. Christiaan Huygens is the man who turned the minutes into a speed, in his Traite de la Lumiere: 110,000,000 toises per second, which converts to about 212,000-220,000 km/s, some 27 percent low. Most of the error was in the 22 minutes themselves; the era's Earth-Sun distance added a little more -- Cassini's 1672 figure was about 140 million km against the true 149.6 million. Source: Grokipedia, 'Romer's determination of the speed of light' and 'Speed of light'; en.wikipedia.org for the toises figure.

question: Hippolyte Fizeau ran a light beam in 1849 from his father's house 8,633 metres to a mirror on Montmartre and back, and on both legs it had to slip between the teeth of a wheel carrying 720 of them. He spun that wheel from a crawl up to dozens of turns a second, watching the mirror's answering flash. What happened to that flash as the wheel sped up?
answer: It vanished at one wheel speed, and returned at double that.
choices: It vanished at one wheel speed, and returned at double that.
It dimmed steadily as the wheel sped up, and never returned.
It arrived doubled, as two separate flashes a moment apart.
It broke into a flicker too fast for any eye to follow.
context: At 12.6 turns a second the wheel moved by half a tooth while the light was away, so a tooth stood where the gap had been and the beam was cut off; at 25.2 turns a full tooth passed, a gap stood where a gap had been, and the flash came through. From the wheel's rate and the 17,266-metre round trip Fizeau got about 313,000 km/s, roughly 4 to 5 percent high -- and the first value for light's speed that owed nothing to astronomy. Marie Alfred Cornu reran the same wheel from 1872 to 1876, pushing to the 21st-order extinction and recording the turns electrically: 300,400,000 m/s, 0.2 percent high. Fizeau is one of the 72 names around the Eiffel Tower. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fizeau%27s_measurement_of_the_speed_of_light_in_air.

question: James Bradley pointed a telescope straight up at one star from 1725 to 1728, hunting stellar parallax, a tiny yearly shift that would prove Earth actually moves. Parallax must peak six months apart, in June and December. Bradley did find a yearly shift of about 20 arcseconds either side of the star's true position. What told him it was not parallax?
answer: Its extremes fell in March and September, three months out.
choices: Its extremes fell in March and September, three months out.
Its extremes came six months apart, but swung the wrong way.
Its extremes came eighteen months apart, not twelve months.
Its extremes arrived a month later with each passing year.
context: The effect is aberration, and it has a second signature parallax cannot fake: it does not shrink with the star's distance.
