Sources: Wikipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphry_Davy ; IET Archives, 'Michael Faraday' — https://www.theiet.org/membership/library-and-archives/the-iet-archives/biographies/michael-faraday ; Britannica, 'Michael Faraday' — https://www.britannica.com/biography/Michael-Faraday

question: Humphry Davy told the Royal Society in 1810 that the choking greenish-yellow gas chemists called oxymuriatic gas was an element, and he named it chlorine. With his batteries and everything else he had, he had failed to pull one particle of oxygen out of it. The result demolished a central rule of Antoine Lavoisier's, one Lavoisier had written into the name oxygen itself, from two Greek roots. What do those roots say oxygen does?
answer: It forms acids.
choices: It forms acids.
It forms alkalis.
It forms salts.
It forms water.
context: 'Oxygen' is Lavoisier's coinage from Greek roots meaning acid-former. He was certain that oxygen is what makes an acid an acid, and he wrote the claim straight into the element's name. Davy's chlorine killed the rule: if chlorine is an element, then muriatic acid — the classic screaming-strong acid — is nothing but hydrogen and chlorine, with no oxygen in it at all. The great chemist had named the element after a job it turned out not to do, and chemists have been stuck with the name ever since. Davy proposed instead that hydrogen is the thing acids have in common, which is closer to right, though it never explained why methane, stuffed with hydrogen, is not an acid. (Hydrogen's own name is built the same way: water-former.) Carl Wilhelm Scheele had first made the gas back in 1774 by dripping hydrochloric acid onto manganese dioxide, and Davy wrote in his follow-up paper, read 21 February 1811, 'As I have named that elastic fluid Chlorine...'. Sources: ChemTeam, 'Early acid base theories: Lavoisier and Davy' — https://www.chemteam.info/AcidBase/Early-Acid-Base.html ; ChemTeam, 'Davy on Chlorine' (Davy's 1811 Phil. Trans. text) — https://www.chemteam.info/Chem-History/Davy-Chlorine-1811.html ; Grokipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Humphry_Davy

question: Humphry Davy tested flames through the autumn of 1815, for coal miners whose candles could set off firedamp, the methane that seeps from a cut seam. A flame, he found, will not cross a fine wire gauze at all. So he caged an oil-wick flame in gauze: gas walks in and burns inside, and the fire does not walk back out. Why can the flame not get through the holes?
answer: The wires drain heat from the burning gas faster than the fire can spread.
choices: The wires drain heat from the burning gas faster than the fire can spread.
The wires carry the flame's charge away, and a flame without charge dies.
The mesh splits the flame into threads too thin to keep themselves alight.
The mesh holds a film of moisture that quenches the fire at every hole.
context: Metal carries heat away fast. The gauze pulls heat out of the burning gas quicker than the gas can carry the fire forward, chilling it below the temperature at which methane will ignite — so the flame burns right up to the mesh and stops dead there. The same cooling is why a flame will not run down a metal tube narrower than about a seventh of an inch, roughly 3.6 mm. Davy's gauze cylinders carried something like 625 to 6,400 holes per square inch. He had a working prototype by 9 November 1815 and read the paper to the Royal Society that same day. This is Davy's own test, and it is one you can watch rather than take on trust: with an adult present, hold a piece of fine metal mesh flat over a candle flame and the flame flattens against it instead of climbing through. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Humphry_Davy ; Wikipedia, 'Davy lamp' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davy_lamp

question: Anders Celsius proposed a new temperature scale in 1742, set by two fixed points: the freezing and the boiling of pure water. He did not simply write 'water boils at this mark.' He wrote a fussy little clause into his boiling-point definition, because a bare 'boiling' does not always land on the same mark. What condition did he insist on?
answer: Mean barometric pressure at sea level
choices: Mean barometric pressure at sea level
That the water be freshly distilled
That the thermometer be immersed a full inch
That a rolling boil, not a simmer, be reached
context: Boil the same pot on a mountain top and the water boils cooler; Celsius's fine print protected his scale from that. It was Fahrenheit and Celsius together who turned temperature from a feeling into a number strangers could compare. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anders_Celsius.

question: Fahrenheit perfected a piece of hardware around 1721 that meant two observers in two different cities could take a reading and mean the same thing. His zero is famous, but historians of science treat the numbers as the less important half of what he built. What piece of hardware?
answer: A mercury-in-glass thermometer
choices: A mercury-in-glass thermometer
An alcohol-in-glass thermometer with a fixed bore
A bimetallic-strip thermometer
A linseed-oil-in-glass thermometer
context: Alcohol thermometers of the day drifted and boiled off too easily; Fahrenheit's mercury column was reproducible enough to trade between labs. Consistent instruments are what turn private impressions into shared measurements. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Gabriel_Fahrenheit.

question: A student seals a gas in a rigid vessel, cools it slowly and plots pressure against temperature: a straight line sloping down. She does the same with two other gases and gets three straight lines. Then she extends them all downward on paper. What do the lines do?
answer: They meet at one point on the temperature axis
choices: They meet at one point on the temperature axis
They fan out to three different points
They curve away from each other before crossing
They flatten into three parallel horizontal lines
context: That shared meeting point is where pressure would fall to zero. Every gas that has ever been measured tells the same story, and that is the geometric ghost of absolute zero, showing up in the arithmetic long before anyone got near the temperature itself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_zero.

question: A teacher repeats the schoolbook line that absolute zero, about minus 273 degrees Celsius, is the temperature at which 'all motion stops.' Modern quantum physics says the line is wrong. Even in a substance cooled as close to zero kelvin as any lab can reach, the uncertainty principle guarantees that something stubbornly refuses to shut off. What actually survives at zero kelvin?
answer: A residue of zero-point energy
choices: A residue of zero-point energy
A ghost of chemical bonding heat
A trickle of nuclear decay warmth
A leftover jitter from cosmic rays
context: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle forbids a particle from having a perfectly known position and a perfectly known momentum at the same time, so it cannot sit perfectly still even in principle. Zero kelvin is the point of minimum possible energy, not zero energy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_zero.

question: Walther Nernst worked out the third law of thermodynamics in 1906: absolute zero, at -273.15 degrees Celsius, cannot be reached in a finite number of steps. He was not complaining about weak refrigerators. His law is a statement about the shape of every cooling method ever invented. What do they all share?
answer: Each step removes only a fraction of what is left
choices: Each step removes only a fraction of what is left
Each step removes a fixed number of joules
Each step warms the fridge back up by a degree
Each step is halted by a small quantum leak
context: Halve, halve, halve: you approach the floor as an infinite sequence with a limit. A better fridge cuts a bigger fraction; it still cannot cut down to nothing. This is why the record has kept dropping without ever landing at zero. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_zero.

question: A team in Bremen chilled a cloud of rubidium atoms in 2021 to about 38 trillionths of a kelvin, the lowest temperature then recorded in any laboratory. The cloud was not resting on a lab bench while it was that cold. Where was it?
answer: Falling freely down a 122-metre drop tower
choices: Falling freely down a 122-metre drop tower
Orbiting Earth aboard the space station
Sunk in a mine, shielded from cosmic rays
Floating on a bath of liquid helium
context: The figure was about 38 picokelvin, held for about two seconds in a Bose-Einstein condensate as it fell through the Bremen drop tower. The magnetic trap that held the cloud also served as a lens, focusing the atoms, and once it was switched off the cloud spread and cooled further as it fell. For scale, the coldest known natural place, the Boomerang Nebula, sits around 1 kelvin. Sources: phys.org/news/2021-10-coldest-temperature38-picokelvins.html ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boomerang_Nebula.

question: The world's measurement scientists retired a sealed glass cell of pure water on 20 May 2019. For most of the twentieth century the triple point of that water had defined the kelvin, pinning one number to one physical setup. What sets the size of a kelvin now, in the International System of Units (SI)?
answer: An exact value of the Boltzmann constant
choices: An exact value of the Boltzmann constant
An exact value of the speed of light
An exact value of Avogadro's number
An exact value of Planck's constant
context: 1.380649 x 10^-23 joules per kelvin, exact by decree. Temperature is now defined by a constant of nature rather than by a jar of water: no substance sits between you and the number. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin.

question: Two German Nobel Prize winners in physics set out in the early 1930s, as the Nazi party rose to power, to throw Einstein's theory of relativity out of German schools. They sneered at it as 'Jewish physics', and their movement took root inside German universities as Deutsche Physik, German Physics. Which pair led it?
answer: Philipp Lenard and Johannes Stark
choices: Philipp Lenard and Johannes Stark
Max Planck and Arnold Sommerfeld
Erwin Schroedinger and Peter Debye
Max von Laue and Walther Nernst
context: Lenard (1905 Nobel, cathode rays) and Stark (1919 Nobel, the Stark effect) attacked relativity as 'juedische Physik' and pushed for a 'German' physics rooted in what they called Aryan experimental style. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-2-pro-nazi-nobelists-attacked-einstein-s-jewish-science-excerpt1/

question: Philipp Lenard, a Nobel-winning German physicist who attacked Einstein's relativity as 'Jewish physics', published a four-volume textbook in 1936 and 1937 in Munich. He called its doctrine Deutsche Physik, German Physics, and in the foreword he put that doctrine in one line. What did Lenard claim decides what counts as science?
answer: race and blood
choices: race and blood
mathematical rigour
practical experience
national tradition
context: Lenard wrote that science, like everything man creates, is determined by race and by blood. The textbook Deutsche Physik in vier Baenden was published by J.F. Lehmann in Munich, 1936-1937. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philipp_Lenard

question: Adolf Hitler's new government passed a law on 7 April 1933 that reached straight into German universities and government offices. It began pushing out professors and office-holders with a Jewish grandparent, along with anyone who had politically opposed the Nazis. Which law was it?
answer: the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service
choices: the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service
the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honour
the Law Against the Overcrowding of German Schools
the Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring
context: Enacted two months after Hitler was appointed chancellor. At President Hindenburg's insistence it at first spared front-line veterans of the First World War, officials in service since 1914 and those who had lost a father or son in the war; the Nuremberg Laws swept those exemptions away in 1935. By 1938 roughly a quarter of Germany's physicists had lost their positions, and eleven past or future Nobel laureates -- including Max Born and James Franck -- were among the emigres. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_for_the_Restoration_of_the_Professional_Civil_Service ; https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/scientific-exodus/

question: Johannes Stark, a Nobel-winning German physicist and open supporter of the Nazi Party, set about pushing Jewish physicists out from a post he took in April 1933. It let him decide who was hired and paid across German physics, and he also ran the country's main research-funding body. Which institute did he take over as president?
answer: the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt
choices: the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt
the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics
the Prussian Academy of Sciences
the Fraunhofer Gesellschaft
context: Germany's national standards institute. Stark served as its president 1933-1939 and simultaneously ran the Notgemeinschaft der Deutschen Wissenschaft, the main research grant body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Stark

question: Johannes Stark used the SS newspaper Das Schwarze Korps on 15 July 1937 to smear a non-Jewish German physicist as a 'white Jew', because that physicist taught modern theoretical physics. Family ancestry had never really been the test. Whom did he attack?
answer: Werner Heisenberg
choices: Werner Heisenberg
Max von Laue
Arnold Sommerfeld
Pascual Jordan
context: Stark's article said Heisenberg should be made to 'disappear'. Heisenberg had defended Einstein's relativity in his teaching. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werner_Heisenberg

question: Heisenberg helped organise a petition of German physics professors in 1936 against the Deutsche Physik movement, a Nazi-friendly faction pressing to purge relativity and quantum mechanics from German universities as 'Jewish physics.' He co-signed it with two senior colleagues. Who were his two co-authors?
answer: Hans Geiger and Max Wien
choices: Hans Geiger and Max Wien
Max Planck and Arnold Sommerfeld
Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner
Walther Nernst and Peter Debye
context: Geiger (of the Geiger counter) and Max Wien organised the petition with Heisenberg; it argued that abstract theory is where practical power comes from -- Heisenberg pointed at Maxwell's equations, pure mathematics that produced radio. Source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-0348-9008-3_49

question: Heisenberg's mother appealed to Heinrich Himmler's mother in 1938; the two families knew each other through a Bavarian hiking club. Argument had not saved him, and this connection did. On 21 July 1938 Himmler wrote two letters clearing Heisenberg, on one condition. What was Heisenberg allowed to teach only if he obeyed it?
answer: relativity, so long as he never credited Einstein by name
choices: relativity, so long as he never credited Einstein by name
quantum mechanics, so long as he called it a German discovery
any physics he liked, but only to SS-vetted students
atomic theory, so long as he swore loyalty to Hitler personally
context: The rescue was a family connection, not a triumph of reason: Heisenberg's maternal grandfather and Himmler's father had been fellow rectors in the same Bavarian hiking club. Heisenberg stayed in Germany and led the wartime nuclear effort. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werner_Heisenberg ; https://www.thenewatlantis.com/publications/the-most-dangerous-possible-german

question: A physicist chaired the opening of the German Physical Society meeting at Wurzburg on 18 September 1933. He compared the Nazi rejection of relativity to the Church silencing Galileo and closed his address with the line attributed to Galileo, in Italian. The audience applauded. Which physicist gave that address?
answer: Max von Laue
choices: Max von Laue
Werner Heisenberg
Max Planck
Arnold Sommerfeld
context: Von Laue ended with 'Eppur si muove' -- 'and yet it moves'. He did it in public, in 1933, as chairman of the society, and remained one of the very few senior German physicists to defy the regime openly for the rest of the Reich. Source: https://live-center-for-science-technology-medicine-society.pantheon.berkeley.edu/current-events/max-von-laue-1879-1960-champion-of-freedom

question: Philipp Lenard pressed German universities to reject Einstein's relativity and quantum theory as 'Jewish physics', and the Deutsche Physik campaign allowed only work by 'Aryan' scientists using classical methods. Germany had led the world in theoretical physics before 1933. The verdict on the campaign was written not in argument but in what the physics it demanded could no longer do. Which task fell outside its reach?
answer: compute a nuclear reaction
choices: compute a nuclear reaction
explain the electric motor
predict a planet's orbit
measure the speed of light
context: A physics that rejected relativity and quantum mechanics could not describe the atomic nucleus. The men who could -- Born, Franck, Bethe, Meitner and dozens more -- were the ones the Reich had driven out; that emigration handed the theoretical lead to Britain and the United States. Source: https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/online/5299/The-scientific-exodus-from-Nazi-Germany

question: James Dewar built the first vacuum flask at the Royal Institution in London in 1892: a double-walled glass bottle with the air pumped out from between the walls, to stop heat crossing. He was not thinking about picnics or hot coffee. What was he trying to hold?
answer: Liquefied gases at extremely low temperatures
choices: Liquefied gases at extremely low temperatures
Molten iron for casting laboratory tools
Radioactive salts for glow experiments
Live bacterial cultures at body temperature
context: The flask was cryogenic laboratory kit. Dewar had been forcing gases to their liquid state for years, and it was expensive work -- he needed a way to keep them liquid long enough to study. He first showed the flask at the Royal Institution on Christmas Day 1892. The picnic flask is a spin-off; it was never designed for soup. Source: https://www.rigb.org/explore-science/explore/collection/james-dewars-vacuum-flask

question: With one glass chamber sealed inside another, James Dewar pumped the air out of the gap between them in his Royal Institution lab in 1892. Now heat had almost no way to cross. One way of moving heat still worked, even through the vacuum. Which one?
answer: Radiation
choices: Radiation
Conduction
Convection
Evaporation
context: Conduction hands heat molecule to molecule; convection carries it in a moving fluid. Take the molecules out of the gap and both stop. Radiation is photons -- infrared light -- and it happily crosses a vacuum. That is the road the silvering has to handle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_flask

question: A flask of coffee stands on a kitchen counter, hours after filling, slowly cooling. It is James Dewar's design: two glass walls with a vacuum between them, the inside silvered like a mirror. The vacuum takes out two of heat's roads and the silvering handles the third. Where does most of the leaking heat get out?
answer: Through the neck and stopper
choices: Through the neck and stopper
Straight through the silvering on the inner wall
Along the seam where the glass was blown
Out the base, where the flask sits on the table
context: There is no vacuum at the neck -- the two chambers have to be joined somewhere. That is where conduction and convection get back in. It is why the lid matters more than the walls, and why an open flask empties its heat fast. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_flask

question: Reinhold Burger and Albert Aschenbrenner, two German glassblowers, built a rugged household version of the laboratory flask with a protective outer casing. A resident of Munich won their naming contest in 1904 with 'Thermos', from the Greek word for heat. James Dewar, who saw his flask as a scientific instrument and had never patented it, took them to court to claim the rights. How did the court fight end?
answer: Dewar lost the case outright
choices: Dewar lost the case outright
Dewar won a share of every flask ever sold
The court ordered the Germans to change the name
The two sides settled and split the profits
context: Dewar had never patented the flask -- he viewed it as a scientific instrument, not a product, and had already been through the exhausting Nobel v. Abel & Dewar cordite patent fight in 1893-1895. No patent, no case. It cost him the fortune the Thermos company went on to make. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_flask ; https://gizmodo.com/how-the-thermos-corporation-cheated-the-inventor-of-the-1420505076

question: Diederik Stapel, a famous Dutch social psychologist at Tilburg University, made headlines around the world in September 2011 by claiming that just thinking about meat makes people more selfish. Something about how that claim reached the public was itself a warning sign that other researchers noticed at the time. What was it?
answer: It went out via press release before any journal saw the paper
choices: It went out via press release before any journal saw the paper
It contradicted his own earlier published work on empathy
It was released in six different languages at once
It was posted anonymously on an academic board
context: Tilburg University sent out the press release on the meat finding a day before Stapel's own junior researchers took their concerns to the department head. Sources: 24oranges.nl coverage; Science, Dutch University Sacks Social Psychologist.

question: Diederik Stapel published a study claiming that litter in a train station makes people more racist, one of the eye-catching findings that made him a celebrated Dutch social psychologist. He had been fabricating his data for years. His faked results survived peer review and passed through the hands of many co-authors, none of whom noticed. Who finally caught him?
answer: Three of his own junior researchers
choices: Three of his own junior researchers
A Nature editor filing a records request
A rival lab that failed to replicate the study
A university auditor doing a routine check
context: The three students were the least powerful people in the building. They had noticed he always handed them finished datasets nobody had watched him collect and discouraged questions about where the numbers came from. Source: Scientific American blog, Reluctance to Act on Suspicions.

question: Someone at Tilburg University finally set Diederik Stapel's raw data files side by side, paper against paper, because his results looked suspiciously clean. What turned up made the fraud undeniable, and university officials moved within days. What did the files show?
answer: Identical rows of scores in two different studies
choices: Identical rows of scores in two different studies
Standard deviations mathematically impossible for the sample
Timestamps predating the experiments themselves
Signatures forged in his own handwriting
context: Real data drawn from different people cannot produce byte-identical rows. Duplication is one of the classic tells investigators check for, along with the GRIM test and Benford's law. Source: Levelt Committee report, University of Groningen.

question: Diederik Stapel, confronted in 2011 about where his data really came from, claimed he had special access to Dutch schools that had run his surveys for him. He had published dozens of eye-catching studies about human behaviour. Tilburg's rector, the head of the university, asked him to produce contacts at those schools. What did Stapel admit?
answer: The schools did not exist
choices: The schools did not exist
The teachers had lost the paperwork
The children had answered anonymously
The recordings had been destroyed
context: That admission -- not any statistical test -- ended his career. He had invented the data from scratch, without ever collecting anything. Source: Levelt Committee final report, 28 November 2012.

question: The whistleblowers in Diederik Stapel's department carried their evidence to the department head, Zeelenberg, at a conference in London rather than back at Tilburg University. Stapel was the department's star, and they suspected him of faking his data. Why the foreign trip?
answer: So the accused professor could not be tipped off
choices: So the accused professor could not be tipped off
So the meeting could be recorded legally
So the head could not simply fire them
So they could reach a journalist first
context: They approached Zeelenberg in London so Stapel could not be immediately warned. Zeelenberg took the evidence to Tilburg's rector, Philip Eijlander, and formal investigations opened at three universities within days. Source: Wikipedia, Diederik Stapel.

question: A student with no training in psychology reads the record of Diederik Stapel's lab at Tilburg University: dozens of published papers resting on fabricated data. She can spot the weakness from the outside, without knowing the field, and it is the one that let the lab go rotten unnoticed for years. What structural feature made the fraud possible for so long?
answer: One person was the sole source of every dataset
choices: One person was the sole source of every dataset
The group published only in low-ranked journals
The group refused to preregister its studies
The group used only undergraduate students as subjects
context: Every study ran through Stapel's hands, and no co-author ever met a participant. Any arrangement where one person controls the only copy of reality is a fraud waiting to happen, however trusted that person is. Source: Levelt Committee report; Academia.edu, Changes in Publication Culture.

question: A schoolteacher in Cologne published a book in 1827 with a rule every physics class now uses: the current in a wire scales with the voltage across it. No university offer came, so he quit. His name is now stamped on every resistor. Which man?
answer: Georg Simon Ohm
choices: Georg Simon Ohm
Alessandro Volta
Andre-Marie Ampere
Michael Faraday
context: Ohm's 1827 book 'Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet' was received coldly; he resigned his Cologne post in March 1828 and did not get a chair of physics (Munich) until 1852, less than two years before his death. Sources: Wikipedia Georg Ohm; MacTutor History of Mathematics.

question: Christian Doppler suggested in Prague in 1842 that a wave's pitch depends on whether its source is moving toward a listener or away. In the same paper he applied the idea to something in the night sky, and he was wrong: the real motion was far too slow. Which claim did he get wrong?
answer: the colours of double stars
choices: the colours of double stars
the phases of Venus
the paths of comets
the parallax of Mars
context: Doppler's 1842 paper to the Royal Bohemian Society was titled 'On the coloured light of the double stars and certain other stars of the heavens'. The principle was right; the stellar-colour application was wrong. Source: Wikipedia Christian Doppler.

question: Christophorus Buys Ballot set out in 1845 to disprove Christian Doppler, on the newly opened railway line near Utrecht. He had listeners with trained pitch on the ground write down what they heard as an open railway carriage passed at speed. Who did he put on the carriage to hold the calibrated pitch?
answer: a band of brass players
choices: a band of brass players
a string quartet
a barrel-organ crew
a choir of boy sopranos
context: Christophorus Buys Ballot's test on the Utrecht-Maarssen line, dated 3 June 1845 by KNMI, the Dutch weather institute he later founded, put brass musicians on an open flatcar (horn players in the Dutch accounts, trumpeters in others), and listeners beside the track heard their note drop as it passed. He had aimed to refute Doppler and ended up confirming him. Sources: https://www.knmi.nl/over-het-knmi/nieuws/doppler-experiment-buys-ballot-160-jaar-geleden ; https://muurformules.sites.uu.nl/mural-paintings/christophorus-buys-ballot/?lang=en

question: Hippolyte Fizeau saw in 1848 how to test Christian Doppler's idea in light. Doppler had predicted that motion should shift the frequency of any wave, higher when the source approaches, lower as it moves away. Fizeau proposed that the same shift should appear in the spectral lines of moving stars. Which way do the lines shift when a star is moving away from Earth?
answer: Toward the red end of the spectrum
choices: Toward the red end of the spectrum
Toward the blue end of the spectrum
They vanish from the spectrum entirely
They double in number
context: Fizeau's 1848 proposal is why the shift is sometimes called the Doppler-Fizeau effect. Sources: Wikipedia Hippolyte Fizeau; MacTutor History of Mathematics.

question: Svante Arrhenius argued in his 1884 Uppsala thesis that a salt, once in water, breaks apart into electrically charged ions on its own, without any current. Nineteen years later that idea won him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. What had his examiners at Uppsala done with the thesis?
answer: Passed it, but with a low grade
choices: Passed it, but with a low grade
Failed it, and sent him away
Passed it with the highest honours
Refused to grade it until rewritten
context: Uppsala's professors, the chemist Per Teodor Cleve among them, were not impressed: the thesis was given a fourth-class grade and was raised to third class only at his defence. Outsiders saw its worth first. Wilhelm Ostwald travelled to Uppsala to recruit him, and Ostwald, van 't Hoff and Clausius championed the theory until it won the 1903 prize. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svante_Arrhenius

question: Alec Jeffreys lifted a wet X-ray film from a developing tank in his Leicester University lab at 9:05 a.m. on Monday 10 September 1984. He was five minutes away from seeing that its pattern was a DNA fingerprint. What was his reaction in the first seconds?
answer: Disgust -- he thought the film was a mess.
choices: Disgust -- he thought the film was a mess.
Alarm -- he thought the samples had been swapped.
Boredom -- he thought the film showed nothing new.
Relief -- he thought the probe had finally worked.
context: His exact words were 'God, what a mess.' Then, he says, 'I stared a bit longer -- and the penny dropped... an absolute Eureka moment. It was a blinding flash. In five golden minutes, my research career went whizzing off in a completely new direction.' At 8:55 that morning, by his own account, he had absolutely no idea the work had any practical use at all. (Genetics Unzipped podcast transcript, geneticsunzipped.com/transcripts/2020/3/26/the-accidental-discovery-of-dna-fingerprinting -- direct Jeffreys quotes; time and date corroborated at grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys)

question: A row of samples from other living things ran along the X-ray film that started DNA fingerprinting, because Alec Jeffreys was checking how widely his new DNA probe worked. The human lanes sat in the middle of them. What else was on that film?
answer: DNA from a cow, a grey seal and tobacco.
choices: DNA from a cow, a grey seal and tobacco.
DNA from a rabbit, a mouse and wheat.
DNA from a horse, a herring and barley.
DNA from a dog, a fruit fly and maize.
context: Jeffreys wanted to know whether his probe would pick out the same kind of repeated DNA across wildly different species -- a mammal, a sea mammal, a plant. The human barcode was an accident sitting in the middle of somebody else's experiment. (labxchange.org/library/items/lb:LabXchange:793cf91f:html:1, 'The Eureka Moment That Revolutionized Crime Solving', caption to the original autoradiograph)

question: Jenny Foxon, a technician in Alec Jeffreys's lab, gave a sample of her DNA, and so did her mother and her father. Those three lanes sat on his film, and reading her column of bands against theirs turned a routine morning into a discovery. What did Jeffreys find in her pattern?
answer: It was unlike anyone else's, yet every band showed up in one parent.
choices: It was unlike anyone else's, yet every band showed up in one parent.
It was unlike anyone else's, and no band showed up in either parent.
It matched her mother's pattern band for band, as a daughter's does.
It sat exactly halfway between her mother's pattern and her father's.
context: Unique to her, and visibly inherited: that single combination is what makes a barcode both an identifier and a family record, and it is why the technique could later be used on families as well as on suspects. Jeffreys called the images 'rather fuzzy-looking barcode-like patterns', and admitted the first ones were 'pretty blurry and horrible'. (timeshighereducation.com/features/the-small-scientist/407947.article, 'The small scientist')

question: Victoria Wilson and Alec Jeffreys wrote out a list of jobs for the first DNA barcode within an hour of seeing it, on 10 September 1984. At his first public talk about the discovery, Jeffreys suggested one of those jobs and part of the audience laughed out loud. Which job did they laugh at?
answer: That it could be used to catch criminals.
choices: That it could be used to catch criminals.
That it could settle who a child's father was.
That it could tell whether twins were identical.
That it could track wild animals in the field.
context: In 1984 the idea that a smear of bands on a film could identify a murderer sounded like science fiction; within four years it had convicted one. The list Jeffreys and Wilson wrote that hour covered paternity disputes, crime-scene identification, telling whether twins were identical, and tracking wild animals -- a fingerprint cannot tell one identical twin from the other, because the two carry the same barcode. Jeffreys' wife Sue added the use nobody in the lab had thought of: immigration cases. (timeshighereducation.com/features/the-small-scientist/407947.article; the laughter from theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation, Ian Cobain, 'Killer breakthrough'; the wife's suggestion corroborated at grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys)

question: Alec Jeffreys went hunting at Leicester University around 1980 for stretches of DNA that differ a lot from person to person. He was not after a way to identify people. His old genetic markers barely differed between individuals and were useless for one important medical job. What job?
answer: Tracing an inherited illness through a family.
choices: Tracing an inherited illness through a family.
Matching a transplant donor to a patient.
Working out how common a blood group was.
Telling whether a tumour had spread.
context: Following a disease gene down through a family takes a nearby marker that differs from person to person; Jeffreys' earlier single-letter markers were nearly identical in everybody, so they could not be tracked. He gave up on them and went hunting wildly variable DNA instead -- and the identification barcode fell out as a by-product. The Guardian later described the experiment that produced it as a failed one. (grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys; theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation)

question: Alec Jeffreys's hunt ended at minisatellites, short bits of DNA that repeat in a row: thirty copies at one spot in one person, twenty-five in the next, eighteen in a third. Those counts change up to ten thousand times faster than ordinary DNA. What makes them so unstable?
answer: The copies mis-align when chromosomes pair off, and the pair swaps unequal lengths.
choices: The copies mis-align when chromosomes pair off, and the pair swaps unequal lengths.
The copying enzyme stutters along the row and slips in an extra copy or two.
Repair enzymes patch the row more sloppily than they patch the rest of the DNA.
Radiation and chemicals strike the row far more often than they strike the rest.
context: One person may carry thirty copies at a spot where another carries twenty-five and a third eighteen. Those counts change up to ten thousand times faster than ordinary DNA: when eggs and sperm are made, the identical copies mis-align as the paired chromosomes line up, and the pair then swaps unequal lengths, so a row gains or loses copies. That instability is exactly why the barcodes differ so much between people. (grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys -- 10-15 bp core motifs, mutation rates up to 10,000x baseline via unequal meiotic exchange, myoglobin gene; repeat-count example quoted from Jeffreys at geneticsunzipped.com)

question: British border officials stopped Andrew Sarbah, a boy of fifteen, in April 1985, saying his passport was fake and another boy had been put in his place. His mother and three undisputed brothers and sisters were in Britain, but the father he claimed was in Ghana and out of reach. Alec Jeffreys rebuilt the missing father's barcode without using Andrew at all. From what?
answer: The bands his brothers and sisters had that their mother lacked.
choices: The bands his brothers and sisters had that their mother lacked.
The bands his brothers and sisters shared with their mother.
The bands his mother had that none of her children did.
The bands all three of his brothers and sisters had in common.
context: Any band in a child that is absent from the mother has to have come from the father, so the three undisputed siblings between them rebuilt most of a man who was never tested. Nearly half of Andrew's bands matched that reconstructed profile. The Home Office dropped the case and he stayed; the family's solicitor was Sheona York. This immigration dispute -- not a crime -- was the technique's first real-world use, and Jeffreys credits his wife Sue with spotting that application. (thebiotalkmagazine.com/the-first-immigration-dispute-case-resolved-by-dna-fingerprinting/; corroborated at grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys)

question: Leicestershire police brought Alec Jeffreys samples from two linked murders near the village of Narborough in August 1986. They already had a suspect, a seventeen-year-old who had confessed to one of the killings, and they wanted the DNA to prove he had done the other one too. Jeffreys worked through the night. What did the film show?
answer: One man had committed both crimes, and it was not the teenager.
choices: One man had committed both crimes, and it was not the teenager.
One man had committed both crimes, and that man was the teenager.
Two different men had done them, and one of them was the teenager.
Two different men had done them, and neither one was the teenager.
context: The very first use of DNA in a murder inquiry cleared the only suspect the police had -- a suspect who had confessed. They did not believe it: the test was repeated, then run a third time. The teenager, who had learning difficulties, had been in custody more than three months, and became the first person in the world exonerated by DNA. (theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation; grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys, which dates the exclusion to early 1987, so the exact month is uncertain)

question: Police in the Narborough murder inquiry wrote to every man born between 1953 and 1970 who lived or worked in the villages, asking him to come and give blood. No force anywhere had tried it. Centres in a school and a council office ran morning and evening sessions three days a week, and after eight months 5,511 men had given a sample. How many of the men asked said no?
answer: Just one of them.
choices: Just one of them.
Just over forty.
Nearly two hundred.
More than a thousand.
context: Every man had to bring proof of identity to the session. The screen -- locally nicknamed 'the blooding' -- was the first mass DNA screen anywhere in the world, and after all that it found nobody: 5,511 samples, one refusal, no match. (theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation; 'the blooding' is the title of Joseph Wambaugh's 1989 book on the case, cited at grokipedia.com/page/Colin_Pitchfork)

question: Colin Pitchfork, a 27-year-old cake decorator at a Leicester bakery, handed a workmate 200 pounds to sit the Narborough blood screen in his name. Every man at the test centre had to show proof of identity at the door. How did Pitchfork get the workmate past it?
answer: He put the workmate's photograph into his own passport.
choices: He put the workmate's photograph into his own passport.
He sent the workmate in with his younger brother's passport.
He had the workmate copy his signature onto a bakery works pass.
He gave the workmate a driving licence he had reported lost.
context: The Guardian published a formal correction on 8 June 2016 confirming the doctored passport was Pitchfork's own, not the workmate's -- many retellings get this backwards. The excuse Pitchfork gave the workmate was a lie: that he had already sat the test once as a favour to a friend and could not sit it again. Pitchfork drove the workmate to the school himself and waited outside. On 1 August 1987 the workmate let it slip over a pint with bakery workmates in the Clarendon in Leicester; six weeks later, on 18 September, one of the drinkers, Jackie Foggin, passed it to a local policeman, and both men were in custody within a day. (theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation and its published 8 June 2016 correction; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Pitchfork)

question: Colin Pitchfork faced Leicester Crown Court on 22 January 1988 and left it the first man in the world convicted of murder through DNA. The case made the new technique famous in courtrooms everywhere. Yet no judge and no jury in that trial ever examined the DNA evidence. What kept it out?
answer: Pitchfork pleaded guilty, so the prosecution never leaned on it.
choices: Pitchfork pleaded guilty, so the prosecution never leaned on it.
The judge ruled the technique too new for a jury to weigh.
The defence and the prosecution agreed to leave it aside.
Jeffreys' laboratory films had been damaged before the trial.
context: The courtroom reputation of DNA evidence was built by a case that never argued it. Because Pitchfork pleaded guilty, the prosecution did not have to rely on the science and no court examined it -- the testing, the assumptions and the odds all went unchallenged. (theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation: 'Pitchfork's guilty pleas meant that DNA evidence was not relied upon by the prosecution, and this new science was not tested by the court')

question: A reporter lays three reputable accounts of the Pitchfork match side by side: one in ten million at a single band position, one in 250 million in another telling, one in 700 million in a third, all for the same test on the same man. That spread is not sloppy reporting, because all three quote the same kind of figure. What does a DNA 'match' number actually state?
answer: How rare that band pattern is in the population it is compared against.
choices: How rare that band pattern is in the population it is compared against.
How likely it is that the suspect, and not someone else, left the sample.
How many people in the whole country carry the same repeat counts.
How rarely that band pattern turns up in the police database itself.
context: A match is a probability statement, not a photograph and not a certainty in the way an old ink fingerprint was sold as one. Change the database you compare against, or change what you assume about how many close relatives the suspect has, and the number moves with it -- which is why three careful sources can print three different odds for one man. Jeffreys' original multilocus method was estimated at one in a million million or lower, but that figure rests on the same kind of assumption. (grokipedia.com/page/Colin_Pitchfork, which reports the 1-in-10-million, 1-in-250-million and 1-in-700-million figures in different sections; grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys)

question: A homeless man in San Jose, California, was charged in December 2012 with murdering a millionaire, a charge that could carry a death sentence, because his DNA was under the victim's fingernails. He had spent that entire night in a hospital bed under constant supervision, nowhere near the house. How did his DNA get there?
answer: The paramedics who had treated him that day answered the murder call.
choices: The paramedics who had treated him that day answered the murder call.
A blanket from the hospital ward he was on was taken to the house.
An officer who had searched him earlier searched the house as well.
The victim had handled a bottle the homeless man threw out that morning.
context: The same ambulance crew that had picked the homeless man up earlier that day responded to the murder scene hours later, carrying his cells on their hands and equipment. He spent about five months in jail before anyone worked it out. Modern tests amplify DNA from a handful of cells, and that sensitivity created a brand-new way to be wrong: in a 2016 Journal of Forensic Sciences study, pairs of volunteers shook hands for two minutes and then one of them picked up a knife -- the other person's DNA turned up on 85% of the samples, and in five of them the person who had never touched the knife came out as the only or the major contributor. (scientificamerican.com/article/when-dna-implicates-the-innocent/; firelawblog.com/2013/06/28/dna-transfer-by-ems-personnel-leads-to-wrongful-arrest/; Cale et al., DOI 10.1111/1556-4029.12894)

question: Alec Jeffreys, who invented the technique, told the British government: 'My genome is my property. It is not the state's.' By 2009 its national DNA database held profiles taken from roughly 800,000 people who had been arrested and then never charged with anything, and he said they were being 'branded as criminals'. What became of those profiles?
answer: A European court ruled the retention unlawful and most were destroyed.
choices: A European court ruled the retention unlawful and most were destroyed.
Parliament reviewed the retention rules twice and left them unchanged.
The Home Office kept them and added everyone arrested afterwards.
Police kept them on file but were barred from ever searching them.
context: The European Court of Human Rights ruled the blanket retention of innocent people's profiles unlawful, and the UK's Protection of Freedoms Act 2012 required most of them destroyed; Jeffreys backed the reform. The inventor of the tool spent years arguing publicly about what the state may keep of you -- an argument about power, not about whether the science works. (dailymail.com/news/article-1170130/Drop-innocent-national-database-says-DNA-pioneer.html, 'branded as criminals'; grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys for the quotation, the ~800,000 figure and the ECtHR ruling; theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation)

question: A jury hears a confession and takes it for the end of the argument. The Innocence Project has counted 375 people in the United States freed by DNA testing after a jury had already convicted them, having served an average of fourteen years each. In what share of those 375 cases had the innocent person confessed, or made statements against himself?
answer: Twenty-nine per cent of them.
choices: Twenty-nine per cent of them.
Three per cent of them.
Eleven per cent of them.
Sixty per cent of them.
context: Nearly three in ten. Those 375 exonerations add up to 5,284 years of imprisonment between them; the first was Gary Dotson's in 1989. Confessions are not the only courtroom evidence that failed: in 2015 the FBI and the Justice Department reviewed 268 trials in which FBI examiners had told juries that a crime-scene hair matched the defendant, and found erroneous statements favouring the prosecution in 257 of them -- 96%. Thirty-two of those defendants had been sentenced to death, and 26 of the 28 examiners involved had given flawed testimony or written flawed reports. Bite-mark comparison has been similarly discredited. Both were in routine use while DNA was still the new and doubted thing. (innocenceproject.org/dna-exonerations-in-the-united-states/; fbi.gov press release on microscopic hair analysis; washingtonpost.com, 18 April 2015)

question: David Goeddel and his team at Genentech announced on 24 August 1978 that they had grown real human insulin in a vat. Until 1982 diabetics relied on insulin scraped from slaughterhouses, and eight ounces could take two tons of pig parts. What had Goeddel's team used to make a human hormone?
answer: Escherichia coli, an ordinary gut bacterium
choices: Escherichia coli, an ordinary gut bacterium
Saccharomyces cerevisiae, brewer's yeast
Chinese hamster ovary cells, a mammalian line
Human pancreas cells, taken from donors
context: Bacteria fold the whole hormone badly, so Goeddel and Dennis Kleid chemically synthesized the genes for insulin's A chain and B chain SEPARATELY, expressed each in E. coli, purified both and joined them chemically into bioactive human insulin. A bacterium could read a human gene at all because the codebook of life is shared. The FDA approved the product in October 1982 and Eli Lilly sold it as Humulin, the first recombinant-DNA medicine; by the mid-1990s fermentation yields passed 10 grams per litre. Source: Grokipedia, 'Genentech' and 'History of genetic engineering'; Wikipedia, 'Insulin (medication)'.

question: Axel Holst and Theodor Frolich finally gave scurvy to a lab animal in 1907, after over a century of failure: rats, mice and dogs stayed healthy on the worst diets going. That same animal is how Albert Szent-Gyorgyi went on to isolate vitamin C itself in 1928. Which animal was it?
answer: The guinea pig
choices: The guinea pig
The ferret
The rabbit
The hamster
context: Guinea pigs, unlike rats, cannot make their own vitamin C, and that is the only reason the model worked: Holst and Frolich had the first non-primate animal model of a human deficiency disease. Szent-Gyorgyi's curative experiments on scorbutic guinea pigs let him isolate and characterize ascorbic acid in 1928. James Lind had shown as early as 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury, that citrus cured scurvy - he split twelve sick sailors into six pairs and gave each pair a different remedy, and only the citrus pair recovered fast - but nobody yet knew what was in the fruit. Source: Grokipedia, 'Scurvy', 'Guinea pig', 'Albert Szent-Gyorgyi', 'James Lind'.

question: A sailor's teeth loosened and his old wounds split open on the rotten rations of a long voyage, while the ship's dog, on the same food, never got scurvy. The difference is not the diet: a human simply has to get vitamin C from food. Why can a human not make it?
answer: The gene for the pathway's last enzyme is still there, wrecked
choices: The gene for the pathway's last enzyme is still there, wrecked
The gene was deleted from the human line, leaving no trace
The pathway is intact but a human liver runs it far too slowly
The liver breaks the vitamin down as fast as it builds it
context: The enzyme is L-gulonolactone oxidase, GULO, and it performs the last step of vitamin C synthesis. Nishikimi and colleagues cloned and mapped the dead human copy in 1994: it sits on chromosome 8p21 and is called GULOP - a pseudogene, meaning a gene still present in the genome but disabled. Compared with the working 12-exon rat gene, only about five of the twelve exon counterparts survive in the human copy; the rest are simply gone. Source: Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'L-gulonolactone oxidase'; Nishikimi et al. 1994; Inai, Ohta & Nishikimi 2003.

question: A distant human ancestor lost the ability to build vitamin C in the liver about 63 million years ago, and every primate descended from it went without. Almost every other mammal still builds its own. But one whole branch of the primates split off before the damage was done. Which primates still make their own supply?
answer: The lemurs and lorises
choices: The lemurs and lorises
The gibbons and siamangs
The marmosets and tamarins
The baboons and mandrills
context: Lemurs and lorises belong to Strepsirrhini, which parted from Haplorhini - the branch holding monkeys, apes and us - at about the time the enzyme was lost. Strepsirrhines kept it. The ability has been lost more than once elsewhere on the tree, too: guinea pigs lost theirs separately within the last 20 million years, some bats have lost it while other bats have not, and in several passerine bird lines it appears to have been lost repeatedly and possibly regained. Same handicap, different scars. Source: Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'L-gulonolactone oxidase'.

question: A biochemist sets human cytochrome c beside the same protein from baker's yeast and counts 44 differences among its 104 or so amino acids. This small protein passes electrons down the line inside every breathing thing, from yeast to a blue whale. She then sets the human version beside a chimpanzee's. How many positions differ?
answer: Zero of the 104
choices: Zero of the 104
Six of the 104
Nineteen of the 104
Thirty-one of the 104
context: The human and chimpanzee sequences are identical, letter for letter. A rhesus monkey differs from a human at one amino acid; baker's yeast at 44. Across more than thirty species tested in one study, 34 of the 104 positions were identical in every single species. Counts shift with the alignment method and published sources disagree on the exact figures, so the ORDER of the distances is the sturdier fact, not the numbers. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cytochrome c'; Biology LibreTexts 19.1.1, 'Taxonomy'.

question: Researchers offered human cytochrome oxidase a strange partner: the cytochrome c of a wheat plant, from a different kingdom of life altogether. The enzyme normally takes its electrons from its human partner, and the two must fit each other like a key in a lock. What came of the swap?
answer: The wheat protein worked, as did every other cross-species pairing tested
choices: The wheat protein worked, as did every other cross-species pairing tested
The wheat protein worked, but no other cross-species pairing tested did
The wheat protein worked only after chemists patched its docking surface
The wheat protein did not work, though closer relatives' versions all did
context: Human cytochrome oxidase reacted with wheat cytochrome c in vitro, and the same held true for every pair of species tested. A human enzyme accepted a plant's protein as its working partner across more than a billion years of separation - the same interchangeability that let a bacterium build a human hormone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cytochrome c'.

question: A geneticist reading the human genome counts roughly 98,000 inherited viral elements and fragments. A retrovirus makes its living by pasting its own genes into the DNA of a cell it infects. Now and then it hits a sperm or an egg cell, and the insert is copied into every cell of every descendant forever. What share of human DNA is old virus?
answer: Somewhere between five and eight percent
choices: Somewhere between five and eight percent
Somewhere between one and two percent
Somewhere between thirty and forty percent
Somewhere between fifty and sixty percent
context: Published estimates for endogenous retroviruses run from about five to eight percent of the genome, with some estimates as low as three percent, across roughly 98,000 elements and fragments. About 90% of them are solo LTRs - stripped of every open reading frame, the burnt-out shell of a virus with the engine gone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Endogenous retrovirus'.

question: Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar at the abbey in Brunn, published his pea-plant results in 1866 in the proceedings of the town's natural history society. Years of crossing peas in the monastery garden had shown him that inherited traits are carried by discrete, stable factors, the things now called genes. What became of the paper?
answer: It sat unread for a generation, until three botanists hit on it in 1900
choices: It sat unread for a generation, until three botanists hit on it in 1900
It was reprinted in London in 1875 and fought over by breeders for a decade
It was answered in 1869 by a rival who held that peas were a special case
It was taught in German universities from 1872 as the new law of heredity
context: Mendel ran his pea experiments from 1856 to 1863 and published 'Versuche uber Pflanzenhybriden' in 1866, formulating segregation and independent assortment. Hugo de Vries in the Netherlands, Carl Correns in Germany and Erich von Tschermak in Austria each rediscovered it independently in 1900 - a full generation later, and eighteen years after Darwin's death. Darwin had published On the Origin of Species in 1859 with no account of heredity at all; the answer he needed was already sitting in print. Source: Grokipedia, 'Mendelian inheritance' and 'History of genetics'.

question: A biologist sorts through roughly 98,000 pieces of old retrovirus in the human genome and finds almost all of them inert wreckage. But one retroviral gene, for the envelope protein that fuses a virus into a cell, was kept and put to work, and the proteins it makes are called syncytins. What job does a virus's fusion gene do in a human body today?
answer: It fuses cells into the placental layer that feeds and shields a fetus
choices: It fuses cells into the placental layer that feeds and shields a fetus
It fuses muscle cells into the long fibres that pull on a limb
It joins bone-eating cells into the units that remodel a skeleton
It fuses the egg and the sperm together at the moment of conception
context: Intact retroviral envelope proteins called syncytins are responsible for the formation and function of the syncytiotrophoblast - the placental layer that handles nutrient exchange and separates the fetus from the mother's immune system. A gene an ancient virus carried in now does a job in every human pregnancy. Muscle-fibre fusion and bone-remodelling cell fusion are real processes too; they just are not this gene's work. Source: Wikipedia, 'Endogenous retrovirus'.

question: J. W. IJdo and his colleagues sequenced two cloned stretches of DNA in 1991, taken from midway along human chromosome 2. The puzzle behind them was a count: a person has 23 pairs of chromosomes, while chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans all have 24, and so did the ancestor shared with them. What did the team find sitting there?
answer: Telomere repeats, the caps that finish a chromosome's ends, running head to head
choices: Telomere repeats, the caps that finish a chromosome's ends, running head to head
Centromere repeats, the alpha satellite a spindle grips, in two blocks side by side
Ribosomal gene clusters, the factories that build protein machinery, stacked in rows
Transposons, the sequences that copy themselves about, packed denser than anywhere else
context: IJdo's team cloned two allelic cosmids, c8.1 and c29B, each carrying two inverted arrays of the vertebrate telomere repeat head to head: 5'(TTAGGG)n-(CCCTAA)m 3'. Telomeres cap the ENDS of chromosomes; these were stranded mid-chromosome, at a band that sits near the base of the long arm. Human chromosome 2 also carries the remains of a second, dead centromere - the pinched waist a chromosome is hauled around by - further down the same arm, and a chromosome normally has exactly one. Jorge Yunis and Om Prakash had matched the banding patterns nine years earlier, in 1982, concluding that 18 of the 23 human pairs are virtually identical to the ancestral hominoid ones. Source: IJdo et al. 1991, PNAS 88:9051; Yunis & Prakash, Science 215:1525 (1982); Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'Chromosome 2'.

question: Kachroo, Marcotte and their colleagues ran a brutal test in 2015: they knocked out 414 yeast genes the cell cannot live without, one at a time, and dropped the matching human gene into each empty slot. Yeast and people last shared an ancestor roughly a billion years ago. How many of the 414 human genes kept the yeast alive?
answer: Nearly half of them
choices: Nearly half of them
About one in twenty
Only three of them
All but a handful
context: 47% of the 414 essential yeast genes could be successfully 'humanized', the human version keeping the yeast alive across roughly a billion years of divergence. Sequence similarity only partly predicted which ones would work: replaceability tracked MODULES, with genes serving the same cellular process tending to be similarly replaceable. Source: Kachroo et al., 'Systematic humanization of yeast genes reveals conserved functions and genetic modularity', Science 348:921 (2015).

question: Fleeming Jenkin, an engineer, reviewed On the Origin of Species anonymously in the North British Review in June 1867. Charles Darwin later said Jenkin had done him more service than any of his other critics, and he answered the review at length the following year. What had Jenkin argued?
answer: If a child comes out midway between its parents, a rare advantage is diluted away
choices: If a child comes out midway between its parents, a rare advantage is diluted away
If the Earth cooled from a molten ball, it is far too young for all this to have happened
If selection built the eye, the half-made eye it passed through would have been useless
If species truly change, the rocks should hold intermediates that nobody has dug up
context: Jenkin argued that if heredity blends, a rare beneficial variation is halved in every generation of interbreeding until it is swamped out of existence long before selection can build on it. Darwin conceded the point and offered pangenesis in 1868 - every cell of the body throwing off granules he called gemmules - specifically to give inheritance discrete particles that could resist swamping. He credited Jenkin in correspondence with more service than his other critics. The other three objections are real ones Darwin also faced. Source: Grokipedia, 'Fleeming Jenkin' and 'Blending inheritance'.

question: M. Barbulescu and colleagues checked one retroviral insert in 2001, at a single address in the chromosomes of humans, chimpanzees, bonobos and gorillas. A retrovirus that pastes itself into a sperm or egg cell leaves its DNA at one fixed address, and every descendant inherits it there. This one was a human endogenous retrovirus. Three of the four species carried it. Which one came up empty?
answer: The humans
choices: The humans
The chimpanzees
The bonobos
The gorillas
context: At the human address there was no provirus at all: the locus carries an intact, uninterrupted pre-integration site - the sequence as it reads before any virus lands. So the shared-insertion evidence is not a one-way story, because an absence can be checked against the branching order just as a presence can. For scale, of 211 HERV-W loci examined, 123 are shared by every catarrhine primate from humans to rhesus macaques, and calling a locus truly orthologous required a minimum of 500 matching nucleotides of flanking sequence on each side. Source: Barbulescu et al., Current Biology 2001; Grandi et al., PMC5775608.

question: Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling noticed in 1962 that the amino-acid differences in hemoglobin between two lineages pile up at a roughly steady rate, a molecular clock. It has since been caught running at odd speeds: tube-nosed seabirds tick at about half the rate of many other birds, turtles at an eighth the rate of small mammals or slower. A deeper limit would still hold if every lineage ticked at exactly the same rate. What is it?
answer: Molecular data alone cannot supply an absolute date, only a count of changes
choices: Molecular data alone cannot supply an absolute date, only a count of changes
Molecular data alone cannot tell a selected change from one that merely drifted in
Molecular data alone cannot separate a true mutation from a sequencing error
Molecular data alone cannot be read from a lineage that left no living descendants
context: Molecular data alone contains no information on absolute times: a clock has to be calibrated against independent evidence, in practice a fossil date. Francisco J. Ayala flagged changing generation times as a further limiting factor, and 'relaxed' molecular clocks using Bayesian and MCMC methods were built to cope with the rate variation. Divergence DATES from a molecular clock are statistical inference, not direct evidence; the branching ORDER is far more secure than the numbers hung on it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Molecular clock'.

question: A student adds up one second of the Sun's fusion: about 600 million tons of hydrogen go in, and the helium that comes out is about 4 million tons lighter. Albert Einstein's E=mc-squared says the mass did not simply vanish. Where did those 4 million tons go?
answer: They left the Sun as sunlight.
choices: They left the Sun on the solar wind.
They left the Sun as sunlight.
They sank into the core as heavy ash.
They were carried off as loose neutrons.
context: The other 596 million tonnes are still there, as helium. Only the missing 0.71 percent leaves, and it leaves as light: four hydrogen nuclei weigh 4.03130 atomic mass units, the helium nucleus they make weighs 4.00268, and the 0.02862 that goes missing is the sunshine on a person's arm. Each such reaction pays out 26.7 million electron-volts, in a core running at about 15 million kelvin. Sources: Grokipedia 'Sun' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Sun); OpenStax Astronomy 2e 16.2 (https://openstax.org/books/astronomy-2e/pages/16-2-mass-energy-and-the-theory-of-relativity).

question: Otto Hahn wrote from Berlin to Lise Meitner on 19 December 1938. He and Fritz Strassmann had hit uranium with neutrons, and one thing that came out acted chemically like barium. His chemistry could find that, but not explain it. Why was barium the impossible answer?
answer: Barium is little more than half uranium's weight.
choices: Barium is heavier than uranium, not lighter.
Barium cannot be made radioactive at all.
Barium is a gas that should have boiled away.
Barium is little more than half uranium's weight.
context: Barium is element 56; uranium is element 92. The nucleus had not been chipped or nudged - it had come apart near the middle. Physicists at the time expected neutron bombardment to push uranium up the table into new heavy elements; Enrico Fermi and Irene Joliot-Curie had both read their own results that way. Hahn's chemistry was sound, but he had no physics to explain it, which is why he wrote to Meitner. Sources: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_nuclear_fission); Grokipedia 'Lise Meitner' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Lise_Meitner).

question: Lord Kelvin and Hermann von Helmholtz proposed, before fusion was known, that the Sun is slowly falling in on itself, shrinking 40 metres a year and good for about 100 million years. Coal was the rival answer, but coal that size would burn out in a few thousand years. Which science killed both?
answer: Geology - rock laid in liquid water 4 billion years ago.
choices: Astronomy - stars like the Sun alight for 10 billion years.
Biology - natural selection, needing hundreds of millions of years.
Geology - rock laid in liquid water 4 billion years ago.
Physics - radium's heat warming the Earth for billions of years.
context: The rocks demanded a Sun billions of years old, and neither coal nor collapse could supply one. The squeeze troubled Charles Darwin badly: natural selection needed the longer clock too, and physics was refusing to give it. Both sides were arguing honestly from good arithmetic; the missing piece was a power source nobody had imagined yet. Source: OpenStax Astronomy 2e 16.1 'Sources of Sunshine: Thermal and Gravitational Energy' (https://openstax.org/books/astronomy-2e/pages/16-1-sources-of-sunshine-thermal-and-gravitational-energy).

question: Lise Meitner did the one sum that mattered in the Swedish snow at Christmas 1938: she weighed the two fragments of a split uranium nucleus against the nucleus they had come from. The gap was absurdly small, about one-fifth the mass of a single proton. Put through E=mc-squared, what did that one-fifth of a proton come out as?
answer: About 200 million electron-volts, every split.
choices: About 200 thousand electron-volts, every split.
About 200 million electron-volts, every split.
About 27 million electron-volts, every split.
About 3 billion electron-volts, every split.
context: Anyone can check her arithmetic: a proton is 938 million electron-volts of mass, and 200 divided by 938 is 0.21 - one-fifth, exactly as she said. The picture she and Frisch used was the liquid-drop model, the nucleus as a wobbling charged droplet held by surface tension until the protons' mutual shoving wins and it pinches in two. Sources: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_nuclear_fission); Grokipedia 'Lise Meitner' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Lise_Meitner).

question: An engineer tallies a reactor's run on a whole tonne of uranium-235: the ash left behind weighs 999 kilograms, so a full kilogram of metal has left as energy, and a good enough scale would in principle catch it missing. A power station burns a thousand tonnes of coal. Chemistry loses mass the same way, only far less of it. How much mass goes missing there?
answer: About half a gram.
choices: About half a milligram.
About half a kilogram.
About half a gram.
About fifty kilograms.
context: 0.53 grams, from a thousand tonnes. This is why chemists, weighing reactions from Lavoisier's day on, concluded that mass is exactly conserved - they were wrong, but by an amount no balance on Earth could see. Sources: radioactivity.eu.com 'Nuclear energy: 200 million electronvolts!' (https://radioactivity.eu.com/articles/nuclearenergy/fission_energy); Grokipedia 'Mass-energy equivalence' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Mass%E2%80%93energy_equivalence).

question: John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton fired protons at lithium in 1932 and split it into two alpha particles, which flew apart carrying about 17 million electron-volts. A test of E=mc-squared also needed the weights of the nuclei going in and coming out, measured finely enough to show the tiny shortfall. Whose measurements, published the next year, supplied them?
answer: Kenneth Bainbridge's, from his mass spectrometer
choices: J.J. Thomson's, from his positive-ray plates
Kenneth Bainbridge's, from his mass spectrometer
Arthur Dempster's, from his mass spectrometer
Ernest Rutherford's, from his scattering counts
context: Bainbridge's mass spectrometer, built in 1932, weighed atoms to about one part in ten thousand, and Francis Aston himself credited Bainbridge's 'accurate comparisons of the masses of the light particles concerned in nuclear disintegrations, particularly that of 7Li, discovered by Cockcroft and Walton.' With those masses the energy E=mc-squared predicted from the shortfall matched the energy the alpha particles carried to within about half a percent, in 1933. Cockcroft and Walton shared the 1951 Nobel Prize for the split. A prediction is only a test if its numbers are pinned down independently of the experiment. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Kenneth Bainbridge'; Wikipedia, 'Mass–energy equivalence' (the 1933 test to within 0.5%).

question: A teacher draws one curve for both the Sun, which cashes in mass by sticking small nuclei together, and a reactor, which breaks big ones apart. It shows why both pay out: how tightly a nucleus grips each of its particles climbs as nuclei grow, peaks at about 8.8 million electron-volts per particle, then falls away. Which nucleus sits near the top of that curve?
answer: Iron-56.
choices: Carbon-12.
Lead-208.
Iron-56.
Silicon-28.
context: That grip is called binding energy per nucleon, and its peak around iron-56 decides everything (strictly, nickel-62 edges iron-56 by a hair): below iron, sticking nuclei together pays; above iron, breaking them apart pays. Nothing on either side of the peak can profit by going the other way. Typical nuclei run a mass shortfall of about 0.9 percent against their loose parts. Source: Grokipedia 'Mass-energy equivalence' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Mass%E2%80%93energy_equivalence).

question: A patient given a fluorine-18 tracer lies inside the ring of crystals of a hospital PET (positron emission tomography) scanner. The tracer sends out positrons; each positron meets an electron somewhere in the tissue, and two photons leave that spot back to back. Every photon of every pair reads 511 thousand electron-volts, and never any other value. Why 511?
answer: It is the electron's own mass, written as energy.
choices: It is the electron's own mass, written as energy.
It is the gamma ray fluorine-18 gives off as it decays.
It is the smallest photon energy the vacuum permits.
It is the energy the crystal ring is built to catch.
context: Total conversion - 100 percent of the mass gone, no ash, no residue. An electron is 511 keV of mass; a positron is another 511; annihilate the pair and out comes 1.022 MeV of light and nothing else. A PET scanner is a machine built to catch exactly that pair: a fluorine-18 tracer emits a positron that travels about 0.6 mm through tissue before it finds an electron, and a ring of crystals watches for two 511 keV photons hitting opposite detectors within about 6 to 12 nanoseconds. The annihilation happened somewhere on the line joining them. Sources: Grokipedia 'Positron emission tomography' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Positron_emission_tomography); Grokipedia 'Mass-energy equivalence' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Mass%E2%80%93energy_equivalence).

question: The Apollo 8 astronauts rounded the far side of the Moon on their fourth orbit on Christmas Eve 1968, cameras aimed at the ground for a mapping run. Then something not on the flight plan came into view, and Bill Anders grabbed a fresh roll of color film. What had he seen?
answer: Earth rising over the Moon's horizon
choices: Earth rising over the Moon's horizon
The Sun eclipsing behind the Moon
A meteor shower crossing their orbit
A comet blazing over the horizon
context: Frank Borman was the commander, James Lovell the command module pilot, and Anders the mission photographer, with the title of lunar module pilot although Apollo 8 carried no lunar module. The flight plan had them shooting the lunar surface, not Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthrise.

question: Bill Anders snapped 'Earthrise', the famous photo of blue Earth over grey Moon, in December 1968, from Apollo 8 sixty miles above the Moon's far side. In that frame Earth looks as if it is climbing above a still lunar horizon, but something else was doing the moving. What carried Earth across the crew's window?
answer: The command module's own orbital motion and attitude
choices: The command module's own orbital motion and attitude
The Moon rotating under the spacecraft
Earth's own libration wobble
A tilt in the lunar rotational axis
context: The Moon turns once per lunar month -- far too slow to lift Earth visibly in seconds. Libration is a small wobble of the Moon (not of Earth); the lunar axis tilt is small and irrelevant here. Apollo 8's own sweep around the Moon carried the view across the horizon. From a fixed spot on the near side, Earth does not rise or set at all -- only a moving spacecraft gets an Earthrise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthrise.

question: Ernie Wright of NASA Goddard rebuilt the whole Earthrise scene in 2013 from the onboard voice tape and the spacecraft's motion. For some forty-five years most books had told it this way: Frank Borman took the first black-and-white frame, and only then did Bill Anders scramble for colour film and get the famous shot. What did Wright's reconstruction show?
answer: Anders took all three frames
choices: Anders took all three frames
Lovell had taken the first frame
Borman took two of the three frames
Lovell took the famous colour frame
context: Wright matched the voice loop (Anders spotting Earth, asking Lovell to hand him colour film, exposing the frames) to the spacecraft attitude data. Frank Borman himself later publicly accepted the correction -- even the eyewitnesses had been wrong until the record was re-derived from data. Historian Andrew Chaikin narrated the 2013 video and helped popularise the analysis; Wright refined it again for the fiftieth anniversary in 2018. Source: smithsonianmag.com/who-took-legendary-earthrise-photo-apollo-8; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthrise.

question: Bill Anders photographed Earth from lunar orbit during Apollo 8 in December 1968, but the 'Earthrise' print that later hung on classroom walls is not the frame as he exposed it. That print shows Earth rising 'up' over a level grey landscape, because NASA and the press adjusted the picture before releasing it to the public. What was done to the original?
answer: It was rotated about 90 degrees clockwise
choices: It was rotated about 90 degrees clockwise
It was flipped left-to-right
It was colourised from black-and-white
It was stitched together from two separate exposures
context: In the raw frame the lunar horizon runs VERTICALLY down the side and Earth sits off to the LEFT -- that is what Anders actually saw through the window. Turning the print 90 degrees clockwise gave a familiar 'sunrise' composition. The image was genuine colour Ektachrome, not colourised. Source: planetary.org/space-images/earthrise.

question: Babylonian astronomers went through clay tablets holding centuries of eclipse records and pulled out a hidden rhythm, now called the saros, of a little over eighteen years. They found it long before anyone could explain it. What did the saros let them do?
answer: Tell roughly when a similar eclipse would return
choices: Tell roughly when a similar eclipse would return
Tell which city would lie under the next total shadow
Work out how far away the Sun and the Moon are
Time the next eclipse's start to the very minute
context: The saros is exactly 223 synodic months, about 18 years, 11 days and 8 hours. After that stretch the Sun, Earth and Moon return to almost the same geometry and a very similar eclipse repeats, so a Babylonian astronomer could say when to watch for one. What the saros could not give him was the shadow's path: the narrow track of totality was beyond such counting. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saros_(astronomy) ; https://skyandtelescope.org/astronomy-news/how-did-the-ancients-predicted-eclipses-the-saros-cycle/

question: A Babylonian astronomer records an eclipse and counts out one saros, the cycle that brings the Sun, Earth and Moon back to almost the same lineup. The cycle runs eight hours past its last whole day, and a similar eclipse duly comes round. Where does that eclipse fall compared with the one he recorded?
answer: it lands about a third of the way around the world westward
choices: it lands about a third of the way around the world westward
it lands at the same city, but starts about 8 hours later
it lands at Earth's opposite pole from the previous one
it fails to reach the ground and passes entirely in space
context: The saros is 223 synodic months, but that works out to 18 years, 11 days AND 8 hours -- and 8 hours is a third of a day, so Earth has spun an extra 120 degrees when the geometry lines back up. Each successive eclipse in the same saros lands about 120 degrees westward. Stack three saroses -- an interval called the exeligmos, about 54 years and 33 days -- and the shadow comes back near the same longitude. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saros_(astronomy) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeligmos
