question: A sky-watcher marks a new moon on her calendar, the moment the Moon slips between Earth and the Sun, as it does roughly every 29.5 days. If space were a flat sheet, that alignment would blot out the Sun every single month. Yet astronomers see only a couple of solar eclipses in a whole year, not twelve. What geometric fact of the Moon's orbit is responsible for the shortage?
answer: its orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to the ecliptic
choices: its orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to the ecliptic
its orbit is a near-perfect circle instead of an ellipse
its orbit runs backwards compared to Earth's spin
its orbit passes directly over the Earth's poles
context: The Moon's orbit is inclined about 5.145 degrees to the ecliptic. At most new moons the Moon passes above or below the Sun's disk as seen from Earth. Only when a new moon falls near one of the two nodes -- the two points where the Moon's tilted orbit crosses Earth's -- can its shadow actually reach the ground. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_of_the_Moon ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclipse_season

question: A crowd watches the Moon slide over the Sun at totality, the two discs almost exactly the same size in the sky. On another day the Moon leaves a bright ring of Sun uncovered instead, because totality is a knife-edge. Two numbers about the Sun and the Moon happen to match with remarkable precision, and that coincidence makes totality possible. Which pair?
answer: the Sun is ~400 times wider and ~400 times farther away
choices: the Sun is ~400 times wider and ~400 times farther away
the Sun is ~400 times wider and ~400 times heavier
the Sun is ~400 times farther and ~400 times brighter
the Sun is ~400 times hotter and ~400 times wider
context: The Sun is roughly 400 times wider than the Moon and, by pure accident, roughly 400 times farther from Earth, so the two look almost the same size in the sky. When the Moon is near the far end of its slightly elliptical orbit it looks too small to cover the Sun entirely, and totality becomes an annular ('ring') eclipse. No other moon in the solar system pulls off this trick. Sources: https://earthsky.org/earth/total-solar-eclipses-are-a-coincidence/ ; https://theconversation.com/explainer-what-is-a-solar-eclipse-33019

question: The Apollo 11, 14 and 15 crews left corner-cube arrays sitting on the lunar surface. Observatories on Earth still fire laser pulses at them and time the round trip, now to the millimetre. That decades-long record shows one thing about the Moon with a consequence for eclipses. What does it show?
answer: the Moon is drifting away by about 3.8 cm each year
choices: the Moon is drifting away by about 3.8 cm each year
the Moon is falling closer by about 3.8 cm each year
the Moon's orbit is tightening into a perfect circle
the Moon rotates on its axis faster than once thought
context: Lunar laser ranging (best current value about 3.83 cm per year) shows the Moon slowly retreating -- a consequence of ocean tides on Earth transferring rotational momentum. Total eclipses therefore have an expiry date: eventually the Moon will look too small in the sky to ever cover the Sun completely, and only annular eclipses will remain. Meanwhile a kid with a clock and NASA's published eclipse tables can time contact to the second and check the prediction against the sky personally. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_Ranging_Retroreflector ; https://earthsky.org/tonight/wayward-moon-receding-from-earth/

question: Arthur Eddington, a Cambridge astronomer and a Quaker, stood before a British tribunal in July 1918 for refusing to fight in World War One. It was his last hearing before a labour camp. He walked out free on one condition, proposed by his fellow astronomer Frank Dyson. What was the condition?
answer: That he lead an eclipse expedition the following year
choices: That he lead an eclipse expedition the following year
That he compute tables for the Nautical Almanac
That he join a magnetic survey of the northern isles
That he take farm work of national importance
context: The letter that did it came from Frank Dyson, the Astronomer Royal, who told the tribunal that the total eclipse of 29 May 1919 was of exceptional importance and that Eddington was the right man to lead the British expedition. So the Quaker who would not fight Germans was released on the condition that he go and test a German's theory, six months after the armistice. Sources: Scientific American, 'The 1919 Solar Eclipse and General Relativity's First Major Triumph'; Grokipedia 'Arthur Eddington'.

question: Edwin Cottingham sailed to the African island of Principe in 1919 as Arthur Eddington's only helper, and he was not a scientist at all. Eddington had come to test Albert Einstein's claim that gravity bends starlight, at a total solar eclipse. What was Cottingham's trade?
answer: A clockmaker, to keep the machinery running
choices: A clockmaker, to keep the machinery running
A carpenter, to repair the telescope mountings
A photographer, to develop the plates by night
A surveyor, to fix the site's exact longitude
context: Edwin Turner Cottingham was a clockmaker, brought along because the instruments ran on clock drives that had to track the sky exactly while a plate was exposed. The other party, Charles Davidson and Andrew Crommelin, went to Sobral in northeastern Brazil. Eddington and Cottingham left England on 8 March 1919 aboard the SS Anselm and reached Principe on 23 April, setting up at Roca Sundy, a cocoa plantation about 500 feet above the sea. Before they sailed, Cottingham is said to have asked Frank Dyson what it would mean if they measured twice Einstein's predicted deflection; Dyson answered, 'Then Eddington will go mad, and you will have to come home alone.' That exchange is reported secondhand. Sources: Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'; Royal Observatory Greenwich; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: Frank Dyson, the Astronomer Royal, proposed the starlight test in 1917 and picked his date years ahead. Catching a bend of under two seconds of arc needs a crowd of stars standing close beside the covered Sun, and most eclipses put the Sun in a thin patch of sky. Where would the eclipsed Sun stand on 29 May 1919?
answer: Inside the Hyades, a cluster in Taurus
choices: Inside the Hyades, a cluster in Taurus
Inside the Pleiades, a cluster in Taurus
Inside the Beehive, a cluster in Cancer
Inside the Butterfly, a cluster in Scorpius
context: The Sun sits in Taurus in late May, and on 29 May 1919 it stood in the Hyades, an unusually rich field of BRIGHT stars, promising many measurable points close to the Sun's edge instead of the usual handful. The Pleiades lie in Taurus too, a few degrees off the Sun's yearly path; that day the Sun was among the Hyades. Totality also ran up to 6 minutes 51 seconds along the track, one of the longest of the twentieth century. Dyson had proposed the test in 1917 after failing to find any displacement at all on plates from the eclipse of 1905. Sources: Wikipedia 'Solar eclipse of May 29, 1919'; Royal Observatory Greenwich.

question: Albert Einstein published a first prediction in 1911 for the bending of starlight past the Sun, about 0.87 seconds of arc, before he had finished general relativity. With the full theory in November 1915 he recomputed it and got 1.75, twice as much. The 1911 figure was worse than merely wrong. What was the trouble with 0.87?
answer: It was exactly what Newton's own mechanics gave
choices: It was exactly what Newton's own mechanics gave
It was too small for the cameras of that decade
It held only near the Sun's poles, not its equator
It assumed the ray crossed the Sun's atmosphere
context: Light treated as fast particles with weight, falling under Newtonian gravity, bends by roughly 0.87 seconds of arc. The German mathematician Johann Georg von Soldner had computed a figure of about this size in 1801, more than a century before Einstein - so Einstein's own first answer was Newton's answer, and any measurement of it would have decided nothing. Only the completed field equations of November 1915, which add the curvature of space itself to the falling, doubled the figure and made an eclipse able to choose between three worlds: no bend at all, the Newtonian half-value, or Einstein's. Sources: Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'; Wikipedia 'Eddington experiment'; T. Sauer, 'Soldner, Einstein, Gravitational Light Deflection and Factors of Two', Annalen der Physik (2021).

question: British astronomers photographed a total eclipse in 1919 to see whether the Sun bends starlight passing close by. The test came down to two plates of one star field: one during totality, with the Sun among those stars, and one at night, with the Sun far away. On the eclipse plate each star sat a little off its spot on the night plate. Which way had the stars moved?
answer: Outward, away from the Sun's centre
choices: Outward, away from the Sun's centre
Inward, toward the Sun's centre
All one way, as if the field had slid
Apart, the whole group spread wider
context: Light passing the Sun bends TOWARD it, so the star it came from appears shoved the other way - outward, away from where it really sits. The shift was biggest for stars closest to the Sun's edge and fell off with distance, and it was that falloff, not any single star, that the least-squares fit actually measured. The other three answers are not silly: a uniform slide would mean a mis-set plate, and a general spreading would mean the plate scale had changed with temperature. Those were exactly the objections raised against the result. Source: Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'.

question: Erwin Finlay-Freundlich, a young Berlin astronomer, set out to photograph an eclipse in 1914 and test Albert Einstein's claim that the Sun bends starlight. His own boss would not pay for the trip, so Einstein went out and found the money himself. Who put it up?
answer: Gustav Krupp, an arms and steel magnate
choices: Gustav Krupp, an arms and steel magnate
Carl Duisberg, a dye and drug magnate
Emil Rathenau, an electrical magnate
Robert Bosch, a motor-parts magnate
context: Freundlich's own observatory director had refused to pay for the trip, so Einstein found the money from the arms manufacturer Gustav Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach. Weeks later Krupp's country was at war with Freundlich's host country: he was interned as an enemy alien, his instruments were seized, and he was freed only in a prisoner exchange, leaving them behind. Sources differ on the exact dates. The failure saved Einstein - at that moment his published prediction was still the 1911 value, and a successful 1914 measurement would have contradicted him. Sources: Wikipedia 'Erwin Finlay-Freundlich'; Encyclopedia.com 'Erwin Finlay Freundlich'; St Andrews eclipse-history project.

question: A British team at Sobral in Brazil pointed its main tool, a 13-inch telescope, at the 1919 eclipse to test whether the Sun bends starlight. As the morning warmed, its steel tube stretched, the telescope went out of focus, and its plates came back with stars like fuzzy smudges. The usable Sobral number came from another instrument. What was it?
answer: A 4-inch lens borrowed from a Jesuit astronomer
choices: A 4-inch lens borrowed from a Jesuit astronomer
A 6-inch refractor lent by a Brazilian observatory
A spare astrograph shipped out from Greenwich
A wide-field camera built during the voyage
context: The 4-inch lens had been lent by Father Aloysius Cortie and packed almost as an afterthought. Seven of its plates were usable and gave a deflection at the Sun's edge of 1.98 seconds of arc; Eddington's Principe plates gave 1.61. Both sit near Einstein's figure and far above the Newtonian one - but the error bars were large. Stephen Hawking later remarked that the size of the error was about the size of the effect being measured, so the honest claim is not that the eclipse proved relativity; it is that the half-size Newtonian rival was excluded, and precision came only later. Sources: Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'; Royal Observatory Greenwich; St Andrews eclipse-history project.

question: Charles Davidson and Andrew Crommelin did not sail for home after the eclipse of 29 May 1919: the two Greenwich astronomers stayed at Sobral in Brazil until 22 July. Their big astrograph, a camera built for photographing the sky, had lost focus during totality, and its nineteen plates had come back with smeared stars. What were they staying for?
answer: To re-shoot the same field with the same telescope in the same spot, so its distortion would cancel
choices: To re-shoot the same field with the same telescope in the same spot, so its distortion would cancel
To have the astrograph's mirror reground at an observatory in Rio, so it would hold its focus
To measure the smeared plates in Brazil, so the long voyage home could not disturb them further
To photograph a second eclipse crossing Brazil later that year, so the trip would not be wasted
context: An eclipse plate proves nothing on its own: the shift only shows up when you set it beside plates of the same stars taken with the Sun elsewhere in the sky. Davidson and Crommelin returned to Sobral on 9 July and re-photographed that star field at night, from 11 to 18 July, with the same instrument standing on the same ground - so that whatever distortion the optics introduced would appear in BOTH sets of plates and cancel out in the comparison. That is what good practice looks like when you suspect your own instrument. Eddington had no such luxury: his Principe plates had to be compared against check plates taken at Oxford, a weaker comparison. Sources: St Andrews eclipse-history project; Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'.

question: John Earman and Clark Glymour, philosophers of science, charged Eddington's team with confirmation bias in 1980. Of the three sets of 1919 eclipse photographs, they said, the one set near the Newtonian half-value, about 0.93 seconds of arc, was the set thrown away, and the two near Einstein's were the ones published. The charge was answered from the surviving 1919 material. How?
answer: The plates were re-measured by Harvey and Clements, and the discarded set no longer favoured Newton
choices: The plates were re-measured by Harvey and Clements, and the discarded set no longer favoured Newton
The logbook was re-read by Crommelin's biographers, and it listed those plates as unusable
The referee reports were re-read by historians, and they had urged that the set be dropped
The check plates were re-measured by Woolley's staff, and they showed the astrograph had shifted
context: In 1979 the original 1919 plates were pulled out of storage at the Royal Greenwich Observatory. Geoffrey Harvey and E. D. Clements re-measured the star positions on a modern plate-measuring machine, and Andrew Murray re-reduced the data with new astrometric software. The 4-inch plates came out at 1.90 plus-or-minus 0.11 seconds of arc - and the discarded astrograph plates at 1.55 plus-or-minus 0.34, near Einstein's value rather than Newton's. The exclusion had been justified by a real, measurable instrument fault, not by wishful thinking. That re-measurement was already finished in 1979, the year before Earman and Glymour published; Daniel Kennefick set the two side by side in Physics Today in 2009. This is the honest shape of the story: the accusation was serious, and it was answered by going back to the evidence. Sources: Kennefick, 'Testing relativity from the 1919 eclipse - a question of bias', Physics Today (2009); Kennefick, 'Not Only Because of Theory', arXiv:0709.0685.

question: Daniel Kennefick, a historian, went back to the surviving records of the Sobral data reduction to see who had actually done the measuring and the arithmetic. The bias story has Arthur Eddington, who believed in general relativity, choosing which Sobral plates to keep. Whose hand fills the notebooks?
answer: Frank Dyson's, and Eddington learned the Sobral numbers by letter
choices: Frank Dyson's, and Eddington learned the Sobral numbers by letter
Andrew Crommelin's, with Dyson signing the results at the end
Eddington's, though only after a second measurer had checked
Charles Davidson's, with the plates re-measured later at Oxford
context: Dyson's handwriting runs all through the Sobral reduction notes and Eddington's does not; Eddington first heard the Sobral results in a letter Dyson sent him. And Dyson was the sceptic of the pair - he described the outcome as contrary to his expectations. The man who supposedly wanted the answer was not the man who chose the data. Sources: Kennefick, Physics Today (2009); Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'.

question: A party camped at Wallal on the coast of Western Australia took plates of more than a hundred stars around the covered Sun on 21 September 1922, under a cloudless sky, and measured a deflection of 1.72 seconds of arc. The 1919 plates had carried large error bars, and this was where the number was pinned down. Whose party made that measurement?
answer: William Campbell's party from Lick Observatory
choices: William Campbell's party from Lick Observatory
Charles Perrine's party from Cordoba Observatory
John Evershed's party from Kodaikanal Observatory
Andrew Crommelin's party from Greenwich Observatory
context: Campbell and Robert Trumpler worked with a 16-inch instrument at Wallal and got 1.72 plus-or-minus 0.11 seconds of arc from over a hundred stars - far more stars than 1919 managed, under a clear sky, with no ruined telescope. Campbell had been openly sceptical of relativity beforehand and accepted the finding once the plates were measured. A careful person should say the deflection was nailed down HERE, in 1922, by an independent team that expected a different answer - not in 1919. Sources: Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'; Grokipedia 'Tests of general relativity'.

question: Arthur Eddington chased a total eclipse because the Sun's glare drowns any star close enough to its edge for the bend to show. The same deflection is now measured without waiting for an eclipse at all, and pinned far tighter than any photographic plate managed. What replaced the eclipse?
answer: Radio telescopes tracking quasars as the Sun drifts past them
choices: Radio telescopes tracking quasars as the Sun drifts past them
Space telescopes observing from above the atmosphere's blur
Coronagraphs that mask the Sun's disc inside the telescope
Infrared cameras that see stars through the solar glare
context: Very Long Baseline Interferometry watches compact quasars as the Sun passes near them in the sky. Radio waves are not drowned by the Sun's light, so there is no eclipse to chase, no cloud to fear, and no photographic plate to smudge. Analyses of quasar observations in the early 2000s confirmed the predicted deflection to within 0.03 percent; a 2004 analysis of roughly two million observations of 541 radio sources reached 0.1 percent, and a 2005 Very Long Baseline Array experiment on four quasars gave the curvature parameter as 0.9998 plus-or-minus 0.0003. Sources: Grokipedia 'Tests of general relativity'; Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'.

question: Albert Einstein wrote a short paper for the journal Science in 1936, and only because a Czech engineer named Rudi Mandl kept pestering him. He showed that a star lined up right behind a closer star would have its light bent into a ring. What did Einstein say about the chance of seeing it?
answer: That it was so improbable no one would ever observe it
choices: That it was so improbable no one would ever observe it
That the next total solar eclipse would confirm it decisively
That Palomar's coming 200-inch telescope would find one easily
That radio telescopes might catch it long before optical ones did
context: Einstein's note ('Lens-Like Action of a Star by the Deviation of Light in the Gravitational Field', Science 84, 506) closes with the line that 'there is no great chance of observing this phenomenon'. In a letter to the Science editor he added that the note had little value but he was submitting it to satisfy Mr Mandl. The alignment of two stars needed for a visible ring seemed effectively impossible.

question: Fritz Zwicky of Caltech wrote a two-page reply in 1937 to Albert Einstein's gloomy short paper on gravity bending starlight into a 'lens'. Einstein had looked at one star lined up behind another, and Zwicky said Einstein had missed something obvious. In that note, what did Zwicky point to as the perfect gravity lens?
answer: Entire galaxies, which he called extragalactic nebulae
choices: Entire galaxies, which he called extragalactic nebulae
Close binary stars, whose combined mass would double the deflection
Globular clusters, whose stars share a common velocity
The Milky Way's own bulge, acting on any distant quasar
context: Zwicky's 1937 notes in Physical Review (vol. 51, pp. 290 and 679) argued that a galaxy would lens far more often and far more strongly than any star, and -- his real punchline -- that measuring the bending of background light would let astronomers weigh the lensing galaxy directly, mass included, whether that mass shone or not. The idea was ignored for forty years. Zwicky died in 1974, five years too early to see it confirmed.

question: Dennis Walsh, Robert Carswell and Ray Weymann pointed the 2.1-metre telescope at Kitt Peak at a pair of very close quasars in 1979, and turned Einstein's toy calculation into a working instrument. The pair, Q0957+561, was one quasar seen twice, not two quasars side by side. What told them so?
answer: The two objects had essentially identical optical spectra and matching redshifts
choices: The two objects had essentially identical optical spectra and matching redshifts
The pair was flickering exactly in phase, minute by minute, on both telescopes
One image sat inside the disc of a foreground galaxy at the same distance
A radio survey found no counterparts, which no real quasar pair could explain
context: Two real quasars, being separate objects, would show at least small differences in their spectra and redshifts. Walsh's pair matched to within measurement error at z = 1.41 -- one source, split around an intervening giant elliptical galaxy at z = 0.36. Q0957+561 (the 'Twin Quasar') was the first confirmed gravitational lens. Today astronomers use exactly Zwicky's trick to map dark matter: where the background sky bends and no visible mass is present, invisible mass has to be.

question: Heinrich Hertz was making sparks cross a small metal gap in his Karlsruhe lab in 1887, out to prove that James Clerk Maxwell's waves were real. A second spark gap stood nearby to catch the wave. When light from the first spark hit the metal knobs of that second gap, what did its spark do?
answer: It jumped the gap far more readily
choices: It jumped the gap far more readily
It shrank unless the gap was darkened
It turned from blue-white to deep red
It wandered to the rim of the knob
context: Hertz wrote the effect down, did not measure it and did not try to explain it, and went straight back to his waves - the puzzle then sat for eighteen years. Presenting Einstein's Nobel Prize in 1922, Svante Arrhenius described exactly what Hertz had seen: an electrical spark between two spheres 'does so more readily if its path is illuminated with the light from another electrical discharge.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'Photoelectric effect'; Nobel Prize in Physics 1921 award ceremony speech (S. Arrhenius, 10 December 1922), nobelprize.org.

question: Wilhelm Hallwachs stood a clean zinc plate on an insulating stand in 1888, wired it to a gold-leaf electroscope so that the two leaves hung apart, and gave the plate a negative charge. Then he shone ultraviolet light on the zinc. A school lab can still repeat it. What did the leaves do?
answer: They fell shut as the charge drained away
choices: They fell shut as the charge drained away
They spread even further apart
They held still until the lamp was moved
They fluttered in time with the lamp
context: Now charge the same plate POSITIVELY and the ultraviolet does the opposite - the leaves spread FURTHER apart, because the plate keeps losing negative charge and grows more positive still. That asymmetry is the whole clue: light is knocking negative things out of the metal. This is a demo a school can still run with a zinc plate, a bit of sandpaper, an electroscope and a UV lamp. Between 1888 and 1891 the Russian physicist Alexander Stoletov took the effect apart with proper instruments and built the first photoelectric cell out of it - an ancestor of the solar cell. Sources: Nobel Prize in Physics 1921 award ceremony speech, nobelprize.org; Wikipedia, 'Photoelectric effect'; Grokipedia, 'Photoelectric effect'.

question: Philipp Lenard shone a bright lamp on a metal plate inside a glass tube in 1902, and electrons flew off the plate. He used a reverse voltage to measure how fast they flew away. Then he simply turned the lamp brighter. What did the extra brightness change?
answer: The number of electrons leaving, but never their top speed
choices: The number of electrons leaving, but never their top speed
The top speed of the electrons, but never their number
Both the number leaving and their top speed, in step
Neither, until the lamp's colour was changed as well
context: The reversal in one line: brightness sets HOW MANY electrons come out; frequency - the colour - sets HOW FAST. A wave should do exactly the opposite, since cranking up a wave ought to shove harder. That is why a feeble blue lamp can free electrons from a metal a blazing red lamp cannot touch. The reverse voltage that just turns back the fastest electron has a name worth keeping - the stopping voltage - and it becomes the key measurement later in this story. Source: Grokipedia, 'Photoelectric effect'.

question: Albert Einstein wrote to Conrad Habicht, a friend, in May 1905, opening 'you frozen whale, you smoked, dried, canned piece of soul', and promised him four papers. One, on moving bodies, is now called special relativity. Einstein rated all four and called just one of them 'very revolutionary.' Which one?
answer: The one on radiation and light
choices: The one on radiation and light
The one on the size of atoms
The one on jittering particles
The one on moving bodies
context: Not relativity. In the letter Einstein said the first paper 'deals with radiation and the energy properties of light and is very revolutionary'; of relativity he said only that 'the fourth paper is only a rough draft at this point, and is an electrodynamics of moving bodies which employs a modification of the theory of space and time.' The one he thought would overturn physics was the light paper - and he was right, though it took twenty years and a man trying to destroy it. Source: Einstein to Conrad Habicht, May 1905, quoted in Walter Isaacson, 'Einstein: His Life and Universe' (Simon & Schuster, 2007), p. 93.

question: Robert Millikan sealed a miniature workshop inside a vacuum tube to test Einstein's equation for the photoelectric effect. He needed a clean face of sodium or potassium, soft alkali metals that rust the second air touches them. He built the tube from quartz, not from ordinary glass. Why quartz?
answer: Ordinary glass blocks ultraviolet light
choices: Ordinary glass blocks ultraviolet light
Ordinary glass glows under a strong beam
Ordinary glass leaks gas into a vacuum
Ordinary glass melts near an arc lamp
context: 'A machine shop in vacuo' was Millikan's own phrase for the thing. The knife was worked from outside by a magnet precisely so nothing ever had to be opened to the air, and the wheel then presented the fresh, unoxidised face to the beam. Quartz was not a luxury: ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet, and ultraviolet was the light Millikan needed to reach the metal. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Robert Millikan'; Rick Dower, 'Millikan Photoelectric Analysis', QuarkNet.

question: A physicist turned a lamp down as dim as it would go and watched a metal plate for the first electron. The old wave theory said an electron in a faint light wave should soak up energy little by little, which with a dim enough lamp should take seconds or even hours. What did the test show?
answer: Electrons came out at once, with no measurable wait at all
choices: Electrons came out at once, with no measurable wait at all
Electrons came out instantly from warm metals, later from cold ones
Electrons came out after a wait that shrank as the lamp was brightened
Electrons came out after a wait, but far shorter than predicted
context: Emission begins within about 10^-9 second - a billionth of a second - of the light arriving, even at very faint intensities, and no measurable lag has ever turned up. The missing time lag is one of the four empirical facts the wave picture could not survive, alongside the sharp threshold colour below which nothing happens at all no matter how bright the lamp. This is what a good test looks like: the theory named a number, someone went and looked for it, and it was not there. Source: Grokipedia, 'Photoelectric effect' ('Key Characteristics' and 'Classical Wave Theory Failure').

question: Albert Einstein took up a puzzle in 1905 that Heinrich Hertz had stumbled on in 1887 and left unexplained: light lands on a metal plate and electrons come flying out. Einstein's paper on it was titled 'On a Heuristic Viewpoint Concerning the Production and Transformation of Light'. What did he propose light was doing?
answer: Arriving in countable packets, each swallowed whole by one electron
choices: Arriving in countable packets, each swallowed whole by one electron
Riding the ether in a steady stream that pushes on electrons inside
Travelling as tubes of electric force with its energy bunched in front
Spreading as a wave whose energy an electron gathers until it escapes
context: In Einstein's own words, the energy of a spreading light ray is 'not distributed continuously over ever-increasing spaces, but consists of a finite number of energy quanta' which 'can be absorbed or generated only as a whole.' That 'only as a whole' is the entire mechanism: one packet, one electron, no part payments. Every metal charges a fixed toll to release an electron - its work function - and whatever the packet has left over becomes the electron's speed: K_max = hv - phi. Below the threshold frequency phi/h a packet simply cannot pay the toll, and a brighter lamp sends only MORE packets, never bigger ones - which is why below that threshold colour a metal gives up no electrons at all, not at twice the brightness, not at a thousand times. Two footnotes: the 'tubes of electric force' choice is real science - J. J. Thomson, who had found the electron, proposed 'tubes of electric force' in 1903 to save the classical field, an honest attempt that still could not produce a sharp threshold. And Einstein never once wrote the word 'photon'; he said 'light quanta'. The American chemist Gilbert N. Lewis coined 'photon' in a letter to Nature on 18 December 1926, from the Greek phos, light. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Photoelectric effect' and 'Photon'; Einstein 1905 quoted at kathylovesphysics.com.

question: Philipp Lenard argued from 1902 that the light was not the source of the escaping electron's energy at all. Until about 1911 most physicists in Europe agreed with the picture he built on that idea. In Lenard's picture, where did the electron get the energy to fly out?
answer: It took the energy from inside the atom, where it already sat waiting
choices: It took the energy from inside the atom, where it already sat waiting
It took the energy from the metal's heat, gathered to a point by the light
It took the energy from the ether, stirred into motion by the light
It took the energy from the charge on the plate, unlocked by the light
context: Lenard's trigger hypothesis, in his own words: in emission 'the light plays only the role of triggering [the release of] a motion which already exists with full velocity inside the atoms of the body' - light as 'the fuse in firing a loaded gun.' It was not a stupid idea; it followed from what he had actually measured, and serious people believed it for a decade. That is the point worth carrying away: the consensus of expert physicists was the wrong answer, and only a better test settled it. Sources: M. Niaz et al., 'Reconstruction of the history of the photoelectric effect...', Science Education (2010), Wiley; kathylovesphysics.com.

question: Robert Millikan shone one colour of light after another on fresh metal. For each colour he measured the stopping voltage, the reverse voltage just big enough to turn back the fastest electron, and he plotted it against frequency: a straight line. He already knew the electron's charge from his oil-drop experiment, so the slope gave him a second number to about half a percent, one from a totally different corner of physics. Which constant?
answer: Planck's constant
choices: Planck's constant
Boltzmann's constant
The electron's mass
The speed of light
context: The slope of stopping voltage against frequency is h/e. Millikan's own oil-drop value for the electron's charge was 1.592x10^-19 coulombs, good to 0.2%, which turned that slope into h = 6.57x10^-27 erg-second (6.57x10^-34 joule-second), accurate to about 0.5%; the modern value is 6.626x10^-34. Planck's constant, first pulled out of a completely different phenomenon, measured all over again from a straight line on a graph of light knocking electrons out of sodium. Two unrelated windows onto nature giving the same number is about the strongest evidence physics ever offers. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Robert Millikan'; Rick Dower, 'Millikan Photoelectric Analysis', QuarkNet.

question: Robert Millikan published a paper in January 1916 that confirmed Einstein's 1905 light-quantum equation to about half a percent. He had thought the equation would fail, and he had spent ten years testing it, colour by colour, on clean faces of sodium and potassium inside a sealed vacuum. What did that same paper say about the light-quantum idea behind it?
answer: That the theory behind the equation seemed at present wholly untenable
choices: That the theory behind the equation seemed at present wholly untenable
That his own results had converted him to it, against his expectations
That the measurements left the theory neither proved nor disproved
That the whole question should be left to the theorists to sort out
context: Millikan printed the confirmation and refused the picture in the same breath - and the honest record matters more than a tidy conversion story. He had gone in hostile on stated grounds, calling Einstein's hypothesis 'bold, not to say reckless': a lump of light that stays put in one place violates the very idea of an electromagnetic disturbance, and the picture 'flies in the face of the thoroughly established facts of interference.' Of Einstein's equation he wrote that it 'cannot in my judgment be looked upon at present as resting upon any sort of a satisfactory theoretical foundation,' even though 'it actually represents very accurately the behavior' of the effect; and flatly, 'Yet the semi-corpuscular theory by which Einstein arrived at his equation seems at present to be wholly untenable.' He accepted the EQUATION and rejected the PHOTON. At Einstein's seventieth-birthday celebration in 1949 he summed it up: 'I spent ten years of my life testing that 1905 equation of Einstein's, and, contrary to all my expectations I was compelled in 1915 to assert its unambiguous experimental verification in spite of its unreasonableness since it seemed to violate everything that we knew about the interference of light.' His 1950 autobiography went softer, saying his data 'scarcely permits of any other interpretation than that which Einstein had originally suggested' - a kinder account of himself than what he actually printed in 1916. Arrhenius credited him at the 1922 Nobel ceremony all the same: 'Einstein's law of the photo-electrical effect has been extremely rigorously tested by the American Millikan and his pupils and passed the test brilliantly.' Einstein's citation reads 'for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect' - relativity is not in it, and Einstein was not in the room ('Being too remote from Sweden, Professor Einstein could not attend the ceremony'). Millikan received his own Nobel Prize in 1923. Sources: Millikan, Physical Review, January 1916, and Phys. Rev. 7 (1916) 355-388, quoted in the National Academies biographical memoir chapter 'Bold, Not to Say Reckless'; Nobel Prize in Physics 1921 award ceremony speech, nobelprize.org; Grokipedia, 'Robert Millikan'.

question: Arthur Compton fired sharp X-rays at a thin block of graphite in 1923, when most physicists still would not swallow the packet, and read the scattered beam angle by angle. Beside the line at the original wavelength sat a second line that had no business existing: on the wave picture, bouncing light off an electron cannot change its colour. What had become of that second line's wavelength?
answer: It was longer, and longer still at wider scattering angles
choices: It was longer, and longer still at wider scattering angles
It was shorter, and shorter still at wider scattering angles
It was longer at narrow angles and shorter at wide ones
It was shifted by the same amount at every angle
context: The shift followed delta-lambda = (h / m_e c)(1 - cos theta) exactly - about 0.041 angstrom at 135 degrees - which is precisely what you get by treating the X-ray as a particle carrying momentum and letting it bounce off an electron like one billiard ball off another. Longer wavelength means less energy: the packet came away poorer because it had paid the electron, which recoiled with the difference. Compton used a Coolidge tube with a molybdenum target (the K-alpha line at 0.71 angstrom), a calcite crystal and an ionisation chamber, and shared the 1927 Nobel Prize with C. T. R. Wilson. Source: Grokipedia, 'Compton scattering'.

question: Niels Bohr, Hendrik Kramers and John Slater made one last try in February 1924 to keep light a pure wave, and they paid a huge price for it. One of the deepest rules in physics would hold only on average across many events, and could break in any one clash between light and an electron. Which rule were they giving up?
answer: The conservation of energy
choices: The conservation of energy
The conservation of charge
The constancy of light's speed
Newton's third law of motion
context: Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger killed the Bohr-Kramers-Slater theory in April 1925 with a test aimed straight at its weak point: put one counter on the scattered X-ray and another on the recoiling electron, and see whether they fire together. If energy is conserved in each individual collision, they must. They did. The price of 1925 precision: a timing resolution near a millisecond, 66 coincidences logged over five hours of which 46 were expected as accidents, an excess with about a 1-in-400,000 chance of being luck, and more than a year spent hand-reading over 3 kilometres of 1.5-centimetre film. Their conclusion: 'One must therefore probably assume that the light quantum concept possesses a high degree of validity.' Bohr took the loss cleanly, writing to Fowler that 'there is nothing else to do than to give our revolutionary efforts as honourable a funeral as possible.' Max von Laue's verdict: 'Physics was saved from being led astray.' Bothe won the 1954 Nobel Prize for inventing the coincidence method. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Bothe-Geiger coincidence experiment'; Walther Bothe, 'The Coincidence Method', Nobel Lecture 1954, nobelprize.org.

question: The colonial government of India watched the summer monsoon, the great rain system that feeds most of the country each year, almost totally fail in 1877. Crops withered, wells ran dry, and the famine that followed took more than ten million lives. What did the disaster drive the government to seek?
answer: A way to forecast the monsoon
choices: A way to forecast the monsoon
A railway to carry grain south
A ban on rice exports to Britain
A census of the famine villages
context: The 1877 monsoon failure was the trigger; British relief policy made it worse. The scale of the disaster is what drove the Government of India to demand a way of predicting the monsoon in advance. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_of_1876%E2%80%931878

question: A Peruvian fisherman watched a strange warm current drift in from the west, chasing away the cold-water anchovies and killing the fishing for months, as it had for centuries. The fishermen's name for it, El Nino, means the Christ Child. Why that name?
answer: It usually arrived around Christmas
choices: It usually arrived around Christmas
It started out weak, like a newborn
A mission priest first wrote it down
It came back every seventh year
context: El Nino is Spanish for 'the boy' and specifically for the infant Christ, because the warm water usually shows up around Christmas. Peruvian fishermen named the phenomenon centuries before oceanographers connected it to anything larger. See https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/elnino/what-is-el-nino

question: Gilbert Walker, a Cambridge mathematician who had never worked a day in weather, went out to India for the British in 1904. He put a room full of Indian clerks to work by hand, looking for which places rose and fell together. What pattern fell out of the arithmetic?
answer: A pressure see-saw across the Pacific: when Tahiti is high, Darwin is low, and back
choices: A pressure see-saw across the Pacific: when Tahiti is high, Darwin is low, and back
A twenty-two-year cycle in monsoon rainfall matching the double sunspot cycle
A three-year lag between North Atlantic hurricanes and Bay of Bengal cyclones
A drift in the Himalayan snowline that predicted the following summer's rain
context: Walker named this see-saw the Southern Oscillation and published it through the 1920s. He could describe it in exquisite statistical detail but could never explain WHY it happened, and for decades most meteorologists treated it as a numerical curiosity rather than a real physical thing. The other choices are all patterns that were seriously proposed at the time. See https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gilbert-Walker

question: Jacob Bjerknes set two old mysteries side by side in 1969. One was the Southern Oscillation that Gilbert Walker had found in the air over the Pacific. The other was El Nino, the warm current that killed off the Peruvian fishermen's catch every few years. For forty years they had sat in separate books, and no one could explain either. What did Bjerknes argue?
answer: The two are one coupled system: the tropical air and the tropical ocean drive each other
choices: The two are one coupled system: the tropical air and the tropical ocean drive each other
The two are downstream signals of the eleven-year sunspot cycle acting on the tropics
The two are triggered by large tropical volcanic eruptions in the preceding year
The two are seasonal responses to the Himalayan snowpack melting in early summer
context: Bjerknes showed that Walker's pressure see-saw in the air and the warm water off Peru are two faces of the same event: the trade winds and the ocean push each other. He named the great east-west overturning of the equatorial atmosphere the WALKER CIRCULATION, after the man whose numbers no one had trusted. The other three options are real hypotheses that had been floated for either the Southern Oscillation or the fishermen's current before 1969. See https://www.moodys.com/web/en/us/insights/insurance/the-el-nino-southern-oscillation-enso-discovery-and-dynamics.html

question: A fisherman off Peru works cold, rich water in a normal year with no El Nino, while along the equator the trade winds blow steadily from east to west and drag warm surface water toward Indonesia. The wind is holding one whole side of an ocean higher than the other. Roughly how much higher does the sea surface stand at Indonesia than off Peru?
answer: About half a metre
choices: About half a metre
About twelve metres
About four centimetres
About five metres
context: Half a metre is the standing tilt maintained by the trade winds alone. Cold, nutrient-rich water wells up along the South American coast to replace what the winds have blown west, and that upwelling is what feeds the anchovy fishery. See https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/elnino/what-is-el-nino

question: Jacob Bjerknes noticed that whenever the equatorial trade winds slackened, the sea off Peru also warmed. He argued this was no coincidence but a loop that drives itself, now called the Bjerknes feedback. How does the loop close?
answer: Weaker winds let warm water slide east, and the extra warmth in the east weakens the winds further
choices: Weaker winds let warm water slide east, and the extra warmth in the east weakens the winds further
Stronger winds pile warm water in the west, and the cooling east strengthens the winds further
Volcanic aerosols cool the tropics, which strengthens the winds and cools the east further
Melting polar ice freshens the Pacific surface, which stalls the winds and warms the east further
context: That runaway is why the system FLIPS between states instead of drifting: cause and effect chase each other around the loop until it saturates. The Bjerknes feedback remains the cornerstone of El Nino theory today. See https://www.moodys.com/web/en/us/insights/insurance/the-el-nino-southern-oscillation-enso-discovery-and-dynamics.html

question: Emily Rosa, aged nine, put a cardboard screen between herself and each Therapeutic Touch practitioner in 1996, with holes for the hands. Such healers claimed to feel invisible energy. She flipped a coin and held her hand above one of the two. What did she ask each practitioner to do?
answer: say which hand felt her energy field
choices: say which hand felt her energy field
guess the outcome of the coin flip in advance
diagnose a hidden illness through the screen
match a pulse to a metronome she tapped
context: Emily Rosa was nine when she designed the test after seeing a video of practitioners claiming to sense a Human Energy Field. Each practitioner ran ten trials. Source: Wikipedia Emily Rosa; Washington Post, 7 April 1998.

question: Emily Rosa ran 280 trials behind her cardboard screen, holding her hand over one of a healer's two hands each time. Twenty-one Therapeutic Touch practitioners took her test in 1996, ten trials at a time, and some came back for a second round. Blind guessing would score 5 out of 10, and anyone who could truly feel the hand should have scored well above that. What did they average?
answer: 4.4 out of 10
choices: 4.4 out of 10
8.7 out of 10
9.6 out of 10
6.3 out of 10
context: The correct-hand count was 123 of 280, an average of 4.4 out of 10; chance alone would give an expected 5. Source: 'A close look at therapeutic touch', JAMA, 1 April 1998.

question: Emily Rosa was eleven in April 1998 when her paper on Therapeutic Touch came out in a leading American medical journal, which had never printed so young an author. Its editor, George Lundberg, knew how unusual that was. What did he say about it?
answer: That age did not matter; good science did
choices: That age did not matter; good science did
That it ran as a classroom example, not research
That the journal would wait for a repeat study
That young readers were its intended audience
context: The paper, 'A close look at therapeutic touch', ran in the Journal of the American Medical Association on 1 April 1998, with her mother Linda Rosa as lead author and Larry Sarner and Stephen Barrett as co-authors. Lundberg's answer: 'Age doesn't matter. It's good science that matters, and this is good science.' Sources: PubMed 9533499; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Rosa

question: Stephan Grupp's team drew an immune cell out of six-year-old Emily Whitehead's blood in Philadelphia in 2012, rewired it in a lab and put it back to hunt her leukemia. The cancer had come back twice and stopped answering chemotherapy. No child had ever had this treatment, and she has been cancer-free ever since. Which immune cell did they rewire?
answer: T cells
choices: T cells
B cells
NK cells
Macrophages
context: Emily was infused on 17 April 2012 by Dr Stephan Grupp's team at CHOP, using the CTL019 construct developed by Carl June's group at the University of Pennsylvania. All four choices are real immune cells that kill or target other cells - the trick is that CAR-T uses T cells specifically because of their targeting receptor. B cells make antibodies; NK cells are natural killers with broad targets; macrophages engulf debris and pathogens. Source: chop.edu Emily Whitehead 10-year celebration.

question: Carl June's group fitted the killer cells drawn from Emily Whitehead's blood with a receptor, built in the lab, that grabs a protein found on every B cell, the cells her leukemia grew from. The rewired cells cleared her cancer. What do they do to a patient's healthy B cells?
answer: Destroy them too, so many patients need antibody replacement
choices: Destroy them too, so many patients need antibody replacement
Spare them, since healthy B cells carry too little of the protein
Turn them cancerous in the years after the treatment
Retrain them to make antibodies against the cancer
context: The protein is CD19, which sits on the surface of B cells at every stage of development, so the rewired T cells clear healthy B cells along with the cancer. B cells make antibodies, so many patients receive regular infusions of donated antibodies, called immunoglobulin, to guard against infection. Sources: FDA tisagenlecleucel approval, Aug 2017; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tisagenlecleucel

question: Bellerophon rode Pegasus against a beast with a lion's head, a goat's body and a snake for a tail, the terror of Lycia, and killed it. That same beast gives the 'C' to the three-letter name of the lab-built receptor that lent Emily Whitehead's cells new eyes for sick B cells. Which mythical creature is the 'C' named after?
answer: Chimera
choices: Chimera
Hydra
Cerberus
Minotaur
context: CAR = Chimeric Antigen Receptor. The word 'chimeric' comes from the Chimera of Greek myth, a creature stitched together from a lion, a goat, and a snake - which is exactly what the receptor is: an antibody head fused to a T-cell signalling tail. Hydra was the many-headed serpent killed by Heracles; Cerberus the three-headed dog guarding the underworld; the Minotaur the bull-headed man of the Cretan labyrinth - all Greek monsters, but only the Chimera gave English the word for mismatched parts spliced into one. Source: pubmed 29451276 tisagenlecleucel review.

question: Emily Whitehead's fever spiked days after her infusion, her blood pressure crashed, and she was moved onto a ventilator in the intensive care unit (ICU). The new cells were working, but so hard that her body was flooded with immune signals called cytokines. Doctors ran blood tests, and one cytokine stood out at very high levels. Which one?
answer: Interleukin-6
choices: Interleukin-6
Tumor necrosis factor alpha
Interleukin-2
Interferon gamma
context: This is now called cytokine release syndrome (CRS), and IL-6 is its signature - the specific cytokine measured off the charts in Emily's blood and the one the team decided to target. TNF-alpha, IL-2 and interferon gamma are all real immune cytokines, released in various inflammatory conditions, but IL-6 was Emily's runaway signal. Source: Penn Medicine 'A Port in the Storm'.

question: Carl June, the lead scientist, knew of an existing antibody drug that blocked the very signal running wild in Emily Whitehead's blood. She lay on a ventilator with a runaway immune reaction, and her team had no time to design a new drug. Within hours of the dose her fever broke. How did June know about the drug?
answer: His own daughter took it for juvenile rheumatoid arthritis
choices: His own daughter took it for juvenile rheumatoid arthritis
He had personally tested it in an earlier study
He read a case report the week before
A colleague at the ICU suggested it on the spot
context: Tocilizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds and blocks the IL-6 receptor. It had been approved for rheumatoid arthritis; nobody had ever given it to a child in a CAR-T crisis before Emily. The FDA later formalised its emergency role by approving it for CAR-T-associated CRS on the same day it approved Kymriah in 2017. Source: AACR interview with Carl June, 2020.

question: Emily Whitehead was still cancer-free when the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the treatment that saved her, on August 30, 2017. Doctors at the University of Pennsylvania had built it, and Novartis brought it to market. It was the first therapy of its kind ever cleared in the United States. What made it historic?
answer: It was the first approved therapy that inserts a new gene into a patient's own cells
choices: It was the first approved therapy that inserts a new gene into a patient's own cells
It was the first cancer drug ever approved by the FDA
It was the first drug tested first on a child
It was the first therapy licensed to Novartis
context: Kymriah (tisagenlecleucel) was approved for patients up to age 25 with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia; the pivotal trial showed an 83% remission rate within 3 months. Source: FDA tisagenlecleucel approval, 30 Aug 2017.

question: Rudolf Clausius wrote down what became the second law of thermodynamics in 1854 as a single plain sentence, using no mathematics at all, just words. His sentence names one thing that never happens on its own. What is it?
answer: Heat passing from a colder body to a warmer one.
choices: Heat passing from a colder body to a warmer one.
Heat being turned entirely into work by an engine.
A wheel turning forever with no fuel at all.
Energy vanishing entirely as two surfaces rub.
context: Clausius's sentence: heat can never pass from a colder to a warmer body 'without some other change, connected therewith, occurring at the same time.' That last clause is why a refrigerator is legal - it drives heat the wrong way only by running a compressor and dumping heat out the back. He published the statement in German in 1854 and in English in 1856, and only coined the word 'entropy' in 1865. Turning heat entirely into work is also impossible, but that is Lord Kelvin's version of the second law, not Clausius's. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf Clausius'; Wikipedia, 'Second law of thermodynamics'.

question: A cook scrambles an egg for good, yet it is nothing but molecules bumping into each other. Suppose you film one collision between two of them and run the film backwards. What do Newton's laws of motion say about that film?
answer: They allow it, since a reversed collision is just as legal.
choices: They allow it, since a reversed collision is just as legal.
They forbid it, since the equations pick out one direction.
They allow it, but only for perfectly elastic collisions.
They forbid it, since momentum runs one way through time.
context: At the level of single collisions the laws of motion are time-symmetric: run any one of them backwards and it is still a legal collision. Nothing in the forces forbids an egg unscrambling. What stops it is the statistics of enormous numbers - the chance of a system stumbling back into a low-entropy condition falls off exponentially as the system gets bigger, and everyday objects hold something like a million million million million particles. The arrow is a matter of odds, not of law. Source: Grokipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'; Wikipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'.

question: Rudolf Clausius went looking for a name in 1865, for a strange quantity his work on heat had turned up. He kept a standing rule for naming important new scientific quantities, and he followed it here. What was the rule?
answer: Go to the ancient languages, so the name means one thing everywhere.
choices: Go to the ancient languages, so the name means one thing everywhere.
Build it from plain German, so any careful reader could follow it.
Ask a classical scholar for a fresh term each time one is needed.
Borrow from the engine shop, so engineers would know it at once.
context: Clausius's rule, in his own words: 'I prefer going to the ancient languages for the names of important scientific quantities, so that they may mean the same thing in all living tongues.' So he built 'entropy' from Greek en, 'in', plus trope, 'transformation' - literally transformation-content, which is nearly what he had been calling the quantity all along in German: Verwandlungsinhalt, transformation content. He shaped the new word to echo an older one too, and said so in the same 1865 memoir: 'I have intentionally formed the word entropy so as to be as similar as possible to the word energy, since both these quantities are so nearly allied in their physical significance that they might be called twins.' The word reached English by 1868, through Peter Guthrie Tait's 'Sketch of Thermodynamics', the first English textbook on the subject. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf Clausius'; Grokipedia, 'Entropy'.

question: Rudolf Clausius ended his 1865 paper, the one that gave the world the word 'entropy', with just two bare sentences. One is about the universe's total energy, the other about its total entropy. What do they say?
answer: The energy of the universe is constant; the entropy of the universe tends to a maximum.
choices: The energy of the universe is constant; the entropy of the universe tends to a maximum.
The energy of the universe is constant; the entropy of the universe tends to zero.
The energy of the universe is falling; the entropy of the universe is rising.
The entropy of the universe is constant; the energy of the universe tends to a maximum.
context: In the German: 'Die Energie der Welt ist constant. Die Entropie der Welt strebt einem Maximum zu.' The first sentence is the first law of thermodynamics - energy is never created or destroyed - and the second is the second law. Clausius delivered the paper as a lecture on 24 April 1865, then printed it as his ninth memoir in Poggendorff's Annalen der Physik. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf Clausius'; pro-physik.de, 'Der Geburtstag der Entropie'.

question: A student opens a textbook and finds entropy glossed as 'disorder': a messy bedroom, a jumbled sock drawer. Physicists who actually use the quantity say that gloss misleads, because entropy is no judgement about tidiness. It is a number reached by counting. In a box of gas, what does it count?
answer: The particle arrangements that match the readings taken from outside.
choices: The particle arrangements that match the readings taken from outside.
The particles moving faster than the average speed inside the container.
The collisions the particles make against the container walls each second.
The units of energy already lost from the gas into its surroundings.
context: What can be measured from outside - energy, volume, temperature, particle number - is called the macrostate. One exact set of positions and momenta for every particle is a microstate. The multiplicity W is how many microstates would look identical from outside, and entropy is S = k ln W, with k about 1.38 x 10^-23 joules per kelvin. The fundamental assumption is that every available microstate is equally likely, so a system drifts to whichever macrostate owns the most of them. That is why 'disorder' is the wrong word: entropy is a count, not a verdict on how something looks. Source: Grokipedia, 'Entropy', section 'Statistical Mechanics Formulation'.

question: A cook leaves a hot frying pan on the kitchen counter and, all by itself, it slowly cools to room temperature. Its heat spreads out into the kitchen and never gathers itself back into the pan, as Rudolf Clausius's second law says it must not. What has become of the energy the pan held?
answer: All of it is still there, but hardly any could now be turned into work.
choices: All of it is still there, but hardly any could now be turned into work.
All of it is still there, and any of it could still be turned into work.
Most of it was used up, and the remainder went into the kitchen air.
Most of it turned into entropy, which is the thing the cooling made.
context: Clausius stated the first law in the very same 1850 paper that started all this: energy is conserved through every irreversible process. Entropy does not track energy going missing; it tracks energy becoming unavailable, heat that can no longer be turned into mechanical work. That is also why 'entropy means things wear out' is subtly wrong - nothing is lost, it is only spread. Source: Grokipedia, 'Entropy'; Grokipedia, 'Rudolf Clausius'.

question: Arthur Stanley Eddington brought a working test to his 1927 Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh: a way to look at any physical process and say which end of it is the future. With it came a new phrase, 'arrow of time.' Anyone who follows the arrow, he wrote, finds one thing increasing. What does the follower find?
answer: More and more of the random element in the state of the world.
choices: More and more of the random element in the state of the world.
More and more heat gathered into fewer and hotter places.
More and more of the world's mass converted into radiation.
More and more separation between the fast and the slow molecules.
context: Eddington's sentence: 'If as we follow the arrow we find more and more of the random element in the state of the world, then the arrow is pointing towards the future.' By 'random element' he meant what statistical mechanics counts - the drift towards the vastly more numerous configurations - not untidiness. He also ranked the second law above every other law of nature, saying it holds the supreme position among them: a theory that disagrees with Maxwell's equations, he argued, may just be bad news for Maxwell's equations; a theory contradicted by observation may only mean the experimentalists bungled it; but a theory found to be against the second law has no hope at all. He restated the passage in New Pathways in Science (1935), so some books date it to 1935. Source: Wikipedia, 'Arrow of time'; JILA, University of Colorado, Eddington quotation page.

question: Ludwig Boltzmann lies in Vienna under one carved line of physics: S = k log W. That formula ties entropy to W, the count of tiny states. But in 1877 Boltzmann said only that entropy was proportional to that count. He never supplied k and never wrote the equation down. Who first wrote it in the form now carved on his stone?
answer: Max Planck.
choices: Max Planck.
Rudolf Clausius.
Josef Loschmidt.
Ernst Zermelo.
context: Planck introduced the constant and wrote S = k log W in a paper presented on 14 December 1900, 'On the theory of the law of the energy distribution in the normal spectrum' - and then named the constant after Boltzmann. So the equation on Boltzmann's grave is Planck's. Boltzmann lies in Group 14C, grave 1, in the same cemetery as Beethoven, Brahms, Schubert and the Strauss family. Source: Grokipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'; Atlas Obscura, 'Boltzmann's Grave in Vienna'.

question: Ludwig Boltzmann believed in 1872 that he had derived one-way time from mechanics alone. He defined a quantity H from the spread of molecular speeds in a gas and proved that H can only fall, never rise. Four years later Josef Loschmidt, a Vienna colleague and a close friend, published the objection that has bothered physicists ever since: do one thing to the gas, he said, and H would have to climb. What was the one thing?
answer: Reverse the velocity of every molecule all at once.
choices: Reverse the velocity of every molecule all at once.
Remove every molecule travelling faster than the average.
Halve the volume of the container in a single stroke.
Heat one wall of the container while cooling the other.
context: In German it is the Umkehreinwand, the 'reversal objection'. Boltzmann answered in two parts. First, odds: states with falling entropy do exist, but the probability of a drop shrinks exponentially with the size of the drop, which for anything of everyday size crushes it to nothing - he conceded that some starting points behave improperly, and claimed only that by far most do not. Second, beginnings: the arrow exists because the system started in a low-entropy condition, which is a fact about initial conditions rather than about the equations. Ernst Zermelo raised the other great objection in 1896 - a bounded system must eventually return close to where it began - and Boltzmann answered with the waiting time, on the order of 10^(10^23) years for an ordinary quantity of gas. Loschmidt was no enemy: his measurements of molecular sizes helped draw Boltzmann into kinetic theory in the first place. Source: Wikipedia, 'Loschmidt's paradox'; Grokipedia, 'Ludwig Boltzmann'; Grokipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'.

question: Sean Carroll counts Earth's trade with the Sun in photons: for every visible photon the Sun delivers, Earth radiates about twenty infrared ones back into space. A freezer makes ice and breaks no law of physics, and Earth pulls off something comparable on a planetary scale. What does that photon trade amount to?
answer: More entropy leaves than arrives, and the surplus pays for order down here.
choices: More entropy leaves than arrives, and the surplus pays for order down here.
More energy leaves than arrives, and the shortfall is what drives the winds.
Less energy leaves than arrives, and the surplus is stored in the deep ocean.
Less entropy leaves than arrives, and the deficit is taken up by living things.
context: Carroll's line: 'the Earth needs to radiate twenty low-energy (long-wavelength, infrared) photons for every one high-energy (short-wavelength, visible) photon it receives.' The Sun runs at about twenty times Earth's average temperature, which is what sets that exchange rate. Earth radiates back into space exactly as much energy as it receives, so the energy books balance and the first law is untouched - but roughly twenty times as much entropy leaves as arrives. Sunlight is energy in a low-entropy, useful form; infrared radiated back to space is the same energy at much higher entropy. That outgoing entropy is what pays for local order on the planet. The freezer runs on the same accounting: it is not a closed system, and it pumps more heat out through the coils at the back than it ever took out of the box, so the compressor's waste heat pays for the ice. Source: Sean Carroll, 'Evolution and the Second Law', Preposterous Universe, 7 May 2009; Energy Education, University of Calgary, 'Second law of thermodynamics'.

question: Roger Penrose has put numbers on how strange the beginning was. Measured in units of Boltzmann's constant, the entropy of the universe today runs to something like 10^103, most of it locked inside black holes. At the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago, the estimate is around 10^88, fifteen orders of magnitude lower. The forward direction of time traces back to that fantastically improbable start. Why did the universe begin with entropy that low?
answer: No accepted explanation exists, only an assumed starting condition.
choices: No accepted explanation exists, only an assumed starting condition.
Inflation flattened the early universe and drove its entropy down.
Gravity gathered the first matter and held its entropy down.
The Big Bang's heat erased whatever entropy came before it.
context: Physicists call it the past hypothesis, and it is a boundary condition put in by hand rather than a result derived from anything. Wikipedia lists it among the unsolved problems in physics: why did the universe have such low entropy in the past, giving us the distinction between past and future? Inflation is the near-miss answer - it does explain the early universe's smoothness, but not its low entropy, and why the pre-inflationary state was so extraordinarily ordered remains unresolved. Today's total is dominated by black holes through the Bekenstein-Hawking area formula. Source: Wikipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'; Grokipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'.

question: William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, took the rules of the engine room out to the whole cosmos in 1852: everything, he foresaw, would in the end even out to one warm temperature with nothing left to drive anything. Lee Smolin is one of several physicists who doubt this heat death, and his reason is gravity. No one yet knows how the cosmos ends. Take energy away from a clump held together by gravity, a star radiating into empty space. What does the clump do?
answer: Its parts speed up, so it draws tighter and grows hotter still.
choices: Its parts speed up, so it draws tighter and grows hotter still.
Its parts slow down, so it settles into an even, cooling calm.
Its parts speed up, but the clump swells outward as it does.
Its parts drift apart, so the clump thins out and fades away.
context: Physicists call it negative specific heat: take energy out of a gravitationally bound system and its components speed up, which is the reverse of what a gas in a box does. Gravity gathers matter into stars and galaxies rather than smoothing it out, so Smolin's point is that a gravitating universe does not even out - it fragments into ever more structured and heterogeneous pieces. He is not alone in doubting the heat death. Max Planck wrote that the phrase 'entropy of the universe' has no meaning, because it admits of no accurate definition. Laszlo Tisza wrote that if an isolated system is not in equilibrium, we cannot associate an entropy with it. Hans Buchdahl objected to 'the entirely unjustifiable assumption that the universe can be treated as a closed thermodynamic system.' Heat death also assumes the expansion continues indefinitely, which depends on dark energy behaving as expected. Hermann von Helmholtz had carried Thomson's idea to the cosmos in an 1854 lecture, 'On the Interaction of the Natural Forces.' Nobody knows how this one ends. Source: Wikipedia, 'Heat death of the universe'; Grokipedia, 'Heat death of the universe'.

question: A passer-by stops on the pavement beside a patchwork cat, orange and black, and runs a genetics test without touching the animal. Roughly 99.9% of calico cats share one trait, and the exceptions turn up about once in 3,000 cats. What does the patchwork coat let the passer-by predict?
answer: That the cat is female
choices: That the cat is female
That the cat is male
That the cat is deaf
That the cat is long-haired
context: About one calico in 3,000 is male, and he is almost always XXY -- carrying two X chromosomes plus a Y (Klinefelter syndrome) -- and usually sterile. The orange-and-black patchwork needs two X chromosomes to be a patchwork at all, which is why the coat doubles as a sex test anyone can run from twenty feet away. To try it, find a calico or a tortoiseshell, predict 'female', then ask the owner. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Calico_cat

question: Mary Lyon bred female mice in 1961 carrying a different version of the same coat-colour gene on each of their two X chromosomes, then looked at how their fur turned out. What she read off those coats became the rule for every female mammal. What did Lyon propose each cell does early on?
answer: Shuts down one of its two X chromosomes at random
choices: Shuts down one of its two X chromosomes at random
Discards one of its two X chromosomes at random
Reads its two X chromosomes in alternating turns
Halves the output of both of its two X chromosomes
context: From 'Gene Action in the X-chromosome of the Mouse', Nature 190:372 (1961). Lyon's rule: the choice is made once, early, and every daughter cell of that cell keeps the same X switched off forever. So the coat is a map of which X won where -- each patch is the descendants of one embryonic cell. She was not working on cats at all; the calico is simply the version anyone can see from the street. Sources: nature.com/articles/190372a0; grokipedia.com/page/X-inactivation

question: A neuron fires electrical signals in a girl's brain while a liver cell strips poisons out of her blood and a beta cell in her pancreas makes insulin, the hormone that lets her body take up sugar. All three grew by division from the one fertilised egg she started as. What actually differs between her neuron and her liver cell?
answer: Which genes are held shut by a chemical tag
choices: Which genes are held shut by a chemical tag
Which genes were cut out as the cell specialised
Which chromosomes the cell kept as it divided
Which genes were rewritten into a new sequence
context: This is what the machinery is actually for -- not inheritance, but memory inside one body. A neuron and a liver cell from one body carry the same DNA: nothing was thrown away and nothing was rewritten. What differs is which genes carry a chemical tag holding them shut, and that annotation is copied every time the cell divides. It is why the insulin gene runs in the beta cells of the pancreas and nowhere else. The mark is how a cell remembers what it is. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Epigenetics

question: Conrad Waddington published what he had instead of a mechanism in 1957, and it turned out to be right. He had coined 'epigenetics' in 1942 for the machinery running between the genes an animal inherits and the body it grows, before anyone knew what a gene was made of. What did he publish?
answer: A drawing of a ball rolling down a valleyed hill
choices: A drawing of a ball rolling down a valleyed hill
A drawing of a switchboard wiring one gene to another
A drawing of a clock whose gears turn each tissue
A drawing of a ladder each cell climbs rung by rung
context: Waddington's 'epigenetic landscape' (1957): a hilly terrain scored with branching valleys, down which a cell rolls toward its fate. Nudge it early and it takes a different valley; once it is deep in one, it stays. He had a metaphor and no chemistry whatsoever -- the methyl tags that fill in the picture were not proposed as the heritable off-switch until the 1970s. The word arrived a generation before the mechanism. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Epigenetics

question: A calico cat crosses a yard in orange, black and white, and only two of those colours are the X-chromosome story. Orange versus black is settled on the X, patch by patch, in the way Mary Lyon described in mice. The white comes from an ordinary gene, piebald spotting, on a chromosome that has nothing to do with sex. Why is a white patch white?
answer: Pigment cells never migrated into that patch of skin
choices: Pigment cells never migrated into that patch of skin
The pigment cells there lack the enzyme that makes colour
The pigment is made but never reaches the hair shaft
The pigment bleached out of those hairs before birth
context: The orange-versus-black choice does sit on the X: a deletion of about 5,000 letters inside the gene ARHGAP36, found by two teams in 2025, flips a pigment cell from making black eumelanin to orange phaeomelanin, and X-inactivation decides which cell gets which. The white is a second system stacked on top -- the autosomal piebald spotting gene (S) blocks pigment cells from migrating into parts of the skin while the embryo is forming, so hair grows there with no pigment cells beneath it at all. Two independent systems on one cat, and only the orange-and-black mosaic is the X-inactivation story. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Calico_cat; Kaelin et al. and Toh et al., Current Biology 2025 (eurekalert.org/news-releases/1083537)

question: Robert Waterland and Randy Jirtle changed one thing in 2003 for a mouse strain whose pups are normally born yellow, fat and prone to diabetes and tumors: what the pregnant mothers were fed. The strain's trouble is a jumping gene stuck next to the coat-colour gene, which nothing ever switches off. Litters moved toward pups that were brown, lean and healthy, and not one letter of the pups' DNA changed. What went into the food?
answer: Folic acid, vitamin B12 and choline
choices: Folic acid, vitamin B12 and choline
Vitamin D, calcium and phosphate
Vitamin C, zinc and magnesium
Extra protein, iron and fish oil
context: Waterland & Jirtle, Molecular and Cellular Biology 23:5293 (2003). Folic acid, vitamin B12, choline chloride and betaine are methyl donors -- raw material for the tags that hold a gene shut. Loading the pregnant mothers' diet with them shifted the pups toward brown pseudoagouti (P = 0.008; 39 supplemented pups against 30 unsupplemented) -- a shift in the odds across the litters, not a switch that turned every pup brown. The jumping gene is an intracisternal A particle retrotransposon, and when its hidden promoter goes untagged it drives agouti protein everywhere. Even untreated, genetically identical littermates in one cage vary widely in coat colour, waistline, glucose tolerance and tumour risk -- because the tag landed differently in each embryo. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC165709/

question: A student at a microscope watches a liver cell get ready to divide, some of its genes switched off by methyl tags: one carbon and three hydrogens parked on the letter cytosine, with not one letter of the DNA altered. The cell unzips its double helix and builds a fresh strand beside each old one, and the fresh strand comes out bare. Both daughter cells still end up with the same genes switched off. How does the pattern survive the copying?
answer: An enzyme reads the old strand and tags the new one to match
choices: An enzyme reads the old strand and tags the new one to match
An enzyme re-tags the whole helix from scratch each division
Small RNAs guide the tags back onto the bare new strand
Proteins packed around the DNA carry the pattern instead
context: The enzyme is DNMT1, the maintenance methyltransferase. After replication it finds a half-tagged double helix -- old strand marked, new strand bare -- and writes the matching tags onto the new strand, so the annotation survives division while the letters stay identical. The tag itself is 5-methylcytosine, a methyl group on the fifth carbon of cytosine; about 1% of all bases in a vertebrate body cell carry one, spread across roughly 28 million CpG sites in the human genome. Rollin Hotchkiss spotted 5-methylcytosine in calf thymus DNA in 1948, five years before anyone knew DNA's shape. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Epigenetics

question: German forces sealed about 4.5 million people inside a blockade of the occupied western Netherlands in the hunger winter of 1944-45, and some 20,000 died. Official adult rations ran between about 500 and 900 calories a day from late November, falling to 400 by late April 1945. Later scientists could tell how deep the hunger ran in each month of a pregnancy. Where do those month-by-month figures come from?
answer: The Dutch ration ledgers kept through the occupation
choices: The Dutch ration ledgers kept through the occupation
German ration decrees issued for the occupied west
Diaries that Dutch families kept through the winter
Red Cross surveys carried out after the liberation
context: The ledgers survived the war, and they are why that winter is a laboratory and not only a tragedy. Official adult rations ran about 1,800 calories a day for most of the occupation, fell to roughly 1,400 by October 1944, dropped below 1,000 in November, and bottomed out at about 400 in late April 1945 -- every figure written down as it happened. The famine also had a sharp start and a sharp end, and the Wilhelmina Gasthuis hospital in Amsterdam never stopped recording the course of each pregnancy and the size of each baby and placenta.
