Out of that paperwork came the Dutch Famine Birth Cohort: 2,414 people born there between November 1943 and February 1947 -- some exposed in early, mid or late pregnancy, some conceived after the food came back as built-in controls -- followed in six waves from about age 50 to age 74. Nobody would ever be allowed to run this experiment. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Dutch_famine_of_1944-1945; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7934722/

question: Bastiaan Heijmans and colleagues drew blood in the 2000s from Dutch adults who had been in the womb during the hunger winter of 1944-45, sixty years after the food ran out, and measured the chemical tags on one gene, IGF2. The tags change no letter of the DNA. The team compared 60 people whose mothers were starving when they were conceived with 62 who met the famine only in the last months before birth. Which group's tags still showed a difference?
answer: Only those conceived during the famine
choices: Only those conceived during the famine
Only those who met it late in pregnancy
Both groups, to about the same degree
Both groups, but only in the men
context: Heijmans et al., PNAS 2008: the periconceptional group carried about 5.2% LOWER methylation at the IGF2 differentially methylated region than their own brothers and sisters. The late-gestation group showed no difference at all. Keep the claim its true size -- one imprinted gene, a roughly 5% shift, measured in blood. This is not 'the famine rewrote their DNA'; the sequence was never touched. What it does show is a window: a few weeks around conception, while the embryo is setting its annotations, left a chemical trace still readable six decades later. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2579375/

question: Ravelli, Stein and Susser pulled the military records of about 300,000 nineteen-year-old Dutch men in 1976. They sorted them by when in the womb the hunger winter had caught them, a winter when rations fell to about 500 calories a day. Men whose mothers had starved in early pregnancy were more likely than the rest to be obese at nineteen. What about the men whose mothers had starved in the last months and just after birth?
answer: They were significantly less likely to be obese
choices: They were significantly less likely to be obese
They were about as likely to be obese as the rest
They were more likely to be obese, but only slightly
They were even more likely to be obese than the rest
context: Ravelli GP, Stein ZA, Susser MW, New England Journal of Medicine 295:349 (1976). Early exposure raised obesity rates significantly; late exposure lowered them significantly. One famine, two opposite answers, decided entirely by which weeks of development the hunger hit -- which is why 'starvation makes you thin' is the wrong lesson to draw from the Dutch winter. Followed into old age, the exposed cohort shows raised rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and coronary heart disease, and accelerated biological ageing on epigenetic clocks -- yet cognitive function at 18 looked unaffected. The damage was specific, not global. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/934222/

question: Carl Linnaeus described a toadflax whose flowers came out radially symmetric, like a star, instead of the usual two-lipped snapdragon shape, and the odd form has bred true ever since, for 250 years. In 1999 Pilar Cubas, Coral Vincent and Enrico Coen examined Lcyc, the gene that sets flower symmetry in that plant. What did they find at Lcyc?
answer: An intact gene, drenched in methyl tags and silent
choices: An intact gene, drenched in methyl tags and silent
An intact gene, blocked by a protein clamped over it
A single changed letter, halfway along the gene
A missing gene, deleted from one chromosome
context: Cubas, Vincent & Coen, Nature 401:157 (1999). The sequence of Lcyc in the peloric toadflax is fine; the gene is simply methylated into silence. The methylation is heritable, it travels with the odd flower, and plants occasionally revert to normal flowers as Lcyc quietly loses its tags. An epimutation -- a heritable change with no change in the letters -- passing down since before the American Revolution. Plants do this; so do nematode worms, where small RNAs carry silencing for at least three generations and, under continuous reinforcement, for as many as eighty. Mammals mostly do not. Source: nature.com/articles/43657

question: Bastiaan Heijmans's team went looking for a chemical mark, one that changes no letter of the DNA, left on Dutch adults by the famine they had been carried through. The team did not compare them with the Dutch population at large, or with a matched sample of strangers. Each exposed person was set against a brother or sister of the same sex, born to the same two parents. What made a sibling the necessary comparison?
answer: How heavily that gene is tagged runs strongly in families
choices: How heavily that gene is tagged runs strongly in families
Brothers and sisters share the same adult diet and habits
Only siblings could be traced through the hospital records
Blood drawn on the same day gives a fairer measurement
context: Methylation at the IGF2 control region is strongly heritable, so two unrelated people can differ for reasons that have nothing to do with any famine. Only a sibling holds the family background steady while the exposure varies. That choice is what makes the 2008 result worth anything: the control group was picked to kill the most obvious rival explanation before a single measurement was taken. Sixty exposed adults, each set against a brother or sister of the same sex. The design is the finding. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2579375/

question: Veenendaal and colleagues followed the children of the Dutch famine babies, a second generation who never went hungry, from their weight at birth into their adult health, testing whether the hunger winter of 1944-45 had reached one generation further down. The team reported in 2013. What did the two measurements show?
answer: No change in birth weight, and none in adult health
choices: No change in birth weight, and none in adult health
Lower birth weight, and more diabetes in adulthood
Lower birth weight, but no change in adult health
Normal birth weight, but more diabetes in adulthood
context: Veenendaal et al., BJOG 2013: no transgenerational effect of prenatal famine exposure on the birth weight of the F2 generation, and no differences in adult health between the F2 groups. A few scattered signals exist -- children of famine-exposed fathers ran somewhat heavier -- but nothing that establishes a mark being handed down, and anyone who tells a child otherwise is ahead of the data. Notice too how the counting works, because it deflates most grandchild claims: when a pregnant woman is exposed, her fetus is exposed directly, and the egg or sperm cells already forming inside that fetus are exposed directly too. Three generations touched at once. Genuine inheritance only begins in the generation after that. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23346894/

question: A biologist checks a mammal embryo a few days old, at the blastocyst stage, and finds most of the methyl tags on its genome gone, with no letter of its DNA changed. Mammals wipe their tags twice each generation: after fertilisation, and later in the cells that will become eggs and sperm. In the wipe after fertilisation, how is the father's DNA treated, and the mother's?
answer: An enzyme scrubs the father's genome; division dilutes the mother's
choices: An enzyme scrubs the father's genome; division dilutes the mother's
An enzyme scrubs the mother's genome; division dilutes the father's
A single enzyme strips both genomes, at the same rate and moment
Division alone dilutes both genomes over the embryo's first days
context: In the mouse zygote the enzyme TET3 actively strips up to about 90% of the methylation from the father's genome before the first division. The mother's genome loses its tags a different way, passively: the maintenance enzyme DNMT1 is shut out of the nucleus, so the tags are simply not copied onto the new strands and thin out as the cell divides. Imprinted regions are the deliberate exception -- about 150 genes, IGF2 among them, where only one parent's copy runs and the marks are protected from the wipe. That exception is exactly why a famine mark could still be read at IGF2 sixty years on, and why, at most other genes, a mark in a grandmother has no obvious road to a grandchild in mammals. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Transgenerational_epigenetic_inheritance

question: The people of Syene, the story goes, looked down a deep stone well far up the Nile, near what is now Aswan, at noon on the summer solstice, the longest day. Something happened at the bottom of it that happened on no other day of the year. What did they see?
answer: Sunlight reached the water at the very bottom
choices: Sunlight reached the water at the very bottom
The water level dropped by exactly one hand
Stars could be seen reflected in the water
The water grew too warm to drink at noon
context: At the summer solstice at Syene (near modern Aswan) the Sun stood so nearly overhead that light reached straight down to the water and a vertical rod cast no shadow at all. That observation is the seed of the whole measurement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_circumference; newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Eratosthenes.

question: Eratosthenes set a vertical rod in Alexandria at noon on the summer solstice, when the Sun stood nearly overhead at Syene, far to the south. His rod threw a shadow. He measured the angle the sunbeam made with the rod at about 7 degrees and 12 minutes. What did he do with that angle?
answer: He recognized it as one-fiftieth of a full circle
choices: He recognized it as one-fiftieth of a full circle
He doubled it to get the tilt of the Earth's axis
He subtracted it from ninety to get the latitude of Syene
He divided it by the height of the rod to get the Sun's distance
context: 7 degrees 12 minutes goes into 360 degrees exactly fifty times. That single ratio is the whole trick: the arc between the two cities is one-fiftieth of the Earth's meridian. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_circumference.

question: Eratosthenes needed one more number around 240 BC to work out the size of the Earth from shadows and geometry: the distance from Alexandria up the Nile to Syene. The figure he used was 5,000 stadia, and it did not come from a surveying chain. Who was actually paid to produce it?
answer: Bematists, professional pacers trained to walk with an even step
choices: Bematists, professional pacers trained to walk with an even step
Priests of Isis who counted temple flagstones between shrines
Naval crews rowing a measured barge up the Nile
Astronomers timing sunrise from paired hilltops
context: Bematists were paid step-counters used across Alexander's world; caravan-day estimates filled in where they did not walk. It is one of history's great answers built on a foot count. Source: aps.org/apsnews/2006/06/eratosthenes-measures-earth.

question: Eratosthenes wrote up his shadow-and-well method for measuring the whole Earth around 240 BC, in a book called On the Measurement of the Earth. Every copy of that book was lost centuries ago. How do historians still know how he did it?
answer: Cleomedes summarized the method centuries later in a surviving textbook
choices: Cleomedes summarized the method centuries later in a surviving textbook
The original scroll was recovered from the ashes of Herculaneum in 1752
Ptolemy quoted the full derivation in the opening of his Almagest
A stone-carved copy still stands in the ruins of Syene
context: Cleomedes' handbook On the Circular Motions of the Celestial Bodies preserves the simplified account. That is why some historians treat the famous well detail with caution: it is Cleomedes, not Eratosthenes, telling us. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eratosthenes; newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Eratosthenes.

question: A teacher sets her class to rerun Eratosthenes, who measured the whole Earth from sunlight, a well and the distance between Alexandria and Syene. She has no boat and no caravan, only a partner school far away. What is the minimum kit the two schools need to reproduce the whole result?
answer: A vertical stick at each school and a phone call at local noon on the same day
choices: A vertical stick at each school and a phone call at local noon on the same day
A telescope at each school and a shared observation of the same star at midnight
One weather balloon released simultaneously from each school
A GPS receiver at each school and a stopwatch
context: Each school records its shortest noon shadow, converts the ratio to an angle, and the difference in angles times the north-south distance gives the whole planet's circumference. Every summer the eratosthenes-project.eu network runs it in hundreds of classrooms. Source: school-education.ec.europa.eu; astro.princeton.edu/~dns/teachersguide/MeasECAct2.html.

question: The noon Sun on the summer solstice cast no shadow at Syene, far to the south, but still cast one in Alexandria, and from that gap and the road distance between the two cities Eratosthenes worked out the size of the Earth. His geometry works cleanly only if the Sun sits exactly over Syene on the solstice and Syene lies exactly due south of Alexandria. Neither is true. What do the two errors do to his answer?
answer: The two mistakes push the answer in opposite directions and partly cancel
choices: The two mistakes push the answer in opposite directions and partly cancel
The two mistakes both shrink the answer, and only luck kept him near the truth
The two mistakes both grow the answer, and later scholars had to divide it down
Only the second matters; the first has no effect on the geometry
context: Syene sits about 37 km north of the Tropic of Cancer (so the Sun is not truly overhead) and roughly 3 degrees of longitude east of Alexandria's meridian. The errors partly offset, and that lucky cancellation is a large part of why the number came out so respectable. Source: geo.hunter.cuny.edu/~jochen/gtech201/lectures/lec6concepts/datums; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_circumference.

question: A schoolchild reads in her textbook that Eratosthenes, using nothing but shadows and geometry around 240 BC, measured the Earth's circumference to within one percent of the true value. Serious historians of ancient science are much more careful with that claim. What is the honest reason his exact accuracy cannot be pinned down today?
answer: Scholars do not know which length of stadion he was using
choices: Scholars do not know which length of stadion he was using
Alexandria's ancient position on the coast has since moved a full degree
The Earth's true circumference was only nailed down after 1990
His original numerical result was scrubbed by later editors
context: Estimates of one stadion run from about 157 metres to about 185 metres. That range gives Earth circumferences from roughly 39,375 km up to 46,100 km, against a true value near 40,075 km. The honest claim is 'within a few percent,' not 'he nailed it.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_circumference; home.adelphi.edu/~bradley/HOMSIGMAA/Walkup.pdf.

question: Posidonius sized the Earth from the bright star Canopus grazing the horizon at Rhodes, after Eratosthenes had used shadows between Alexandria and Syene around 240 BC. Ancient thinkers proposed at least one more sizing method, one that leaned on the sky itself as a clock. Which method was it?
answer: Timing a single lunar eclipse from two widely separated cities
choices: Timing a single lunar eclipse from two widely separated cities
Counting the days a caravan needed to circle a fixed mountain
Comparing the depth of a well dug at the coast against one dug inland
Watching how a star's rising point shifted along the horizon each dawn
context: That is one of the real ancient sizing methods: two cities note the moment a lunar eclipse begins, and the time difference between their local clocks gives the longitude arc between them, a fragment of the whole planet. The other real ancient approaches were Posidonius' Canopus star method from two ports and the simple horizon geometry of a distant ship's hull sinking before its mast. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_circumference; aps.org/apsnews/2006/06/eratosthenes-measures-earth.

question: A girl pours a glass of water at the table, an oxygen atom at the heart of every molecule. Most are plain oxygen-16; about one in 500 is a rarer kind, oxygen-18, which acts the same in chemical reactions. What makes oxygen-18 different from oxygen-16?
answer: It carries two extra neutrons, so it is heavier
choices: It carries two extra neutrons, so it is heavier
It carries two extra protons, so it is a different element
It carries two extra electrons, so it is negatively charged
It is missing two neutrons, so it is lighter
context: That is the definition of an isotope: same element (protons unchanged), different neutron count, so different mass but the same chemistry. Oxygen-16 has 8 neutrons; oxygen-18 has 10. This whole story rests on that tiny mass difference. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_isotope_ratio_cycle.

question: A walker catches the rain as a cloud drifts inland, its first rain richest in oxygen-18 and its later rain poorer. What property of H2-18O, water with that oxygen, drives this?
answer: H2-18O is heavier, so it evaporates less readily and condenses more readily
choices: H2-18O is heavier, so it evaporates less readily and condenses more readily
H2-18O carries a small electric charge, so it clings to airborne dust and salt ions
H2-18O forms a stronger hydrogen bond, so it clumps into larger droplets
H2-18O absorbs sunlight more strongly, so it warms up and rises before H2-16O
context: Fractionation, driven by mass. The two extra neutrons in oxygen-18 make H2-18O slightly harder to lift into the air and slightly easier to pull back out of a cloud. Result: vapour is isotopically light, first rain is isotopically heavy, and what remains in the cloud gets lighter and lighter as it rains itself out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_core.

question: Willi Dansgaard collected the rain right through a two-day Copenhagen storm in June 1952, measuring its ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 hour by hour. When he plotted his numbers, the ratio was tracking one thing about the cloud each drop had fallen from. What was he reading?
answer: The temperature of the cloud the rain fell from
choices: The temperature of the cloud the rain fell from
The altitude the raindrop had started falling from
The distance the storm had travelled inland
The age of the water vapour in the cloud
context: A thermometer you could pour into a bottle. Because the sorting is sharper the colder it gets, the isotope ratio in a raindrop encodes the temperature at which it condensed. Dansgaard later extended the idea to Greenland snow -- the same reading, frozen and stacked layer by layer. The rapid climate flickers he and Hans Oeschger later found in those cores are named Dansgaard-Oeschger events. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willi_Dansgaard.

question: Harold Urey saw in the late 1940s that the oxygen-isotope sorting in rain is locked in again when a sea creature grows its shell. Urey had found deuterium, hydrogen with an extra neutron, in 1931, and won the 1934 Nobel in Chemistry for it. What did his insight turn a fossil shell into?
answer: An instrument recording the temperature of the sea it grew in
choices: An instrument recording the temperature of the sea it grew in
A radioactive clock giving the year the animal died
A pressure gauge showing how deep the seafloor was
A magnetic compass pointing to the ancient pole
context: A dead animal becomes an instrument. Calcium carbonate crystallising in seawater takes up oxygen-18 slightly more readily when the water is cold, so the ratio fossilised in the shell is a paleothermometer. Urey's insight seeded the whole field of stable-isotope paleoclimatology and set up his student Cesare Emiliani's foraminifera work a few years later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Urey.

question: Ötzi the Iceman grew up on water that carried his own valley's signature, because rain gets isotopically lighter the farther inland it falls and the higher up the mountain it lands. Researchers read that signature from his body and named his childhood village, Feldthurns, in South Tyrol. Which body tissues keep such a record of the water a person drinks?
answer: Tooth enamel and hair keratin
choices: Tooth enamel and hair keratin
Bone marrow and spleen tissue
Liver tissue and stomach lining
Muscle fibre and lymph nodes
context: Enamel locks in the oxygen isotopes of childhood drinking water and never remodels; hair records the last few months. When researchers analysed the tooth enamel of Otzi the Iceman, the signature pointed to the South Tyrol village of Feldthurns just north of Bolzano as where he grew up, with later years in valleys about 50 km farther north. The water in you is signed by the clouds over the place you grew up. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope_hydrology; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otzi.

question: Willi Dansgaard argued that snow is rain's archive, each winter's layer freezing in its own isotope ratio, so a drill can read climate back through time. The US Army's Camp Century project pulled the first long ice core to bedrock in 1966, 1,387 metres down. The European Project for Ice Coring in Antarctica (EPICA) later reached bedrock at Dome C, about 3,260 metres down. Roughly how far back in time does that core's climate record reach?
answer: About 800,000 years
choices: About 800,000 years
About 8,000 years
About 80,000 years
About 8 million years
context: Camp Century in 1966 was the first bedrock-reaching ice core, 1,387 m of Greenland ice read layer by layer. The polar deeps went further: Vostok reached about 3,769 m and roughly 420,000 years; EPICA Dome C reached about 3,260 m and pulled a usable climate record extending back roughly 800,000 years -- nearly a million winters of stacked snow, each layer's isotope ratio a temperature reading. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_core.

question: A driller hauls up a polar ice core, and it holds more than oxygen isotopes in frozen water. Tiny bubbles sit in the ice at every depth, literal samples of ancient air, sealed as each year's snow packed down. What did those bubbles show about the air at the last ice age's coldest point, compared with pre-industrial air?
answer: Carbon dioxide was about 30 percent lower
choices: Carbon dioxide was about 30 percent lower
Oxygen was about 30 percent lower
Nitrogen was about 30 percent higher
Water vapour was about 30 percent higher
context: A bubble in a polar ice core is a literal sample of Ice Age air. Direct measurement, no model in between: CO2 at the Last Glacial Maximum was roughly 30 percent below its pre-industrial value. The isotopes of the surrounding ice give the temperature at the same layer, so the two records sit side by side. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_core.

question: Cesare Emiliani, a student of Harold Urey, measured oxygen-18 in 1955 in tiny shells from deep-sea cores, left by sea creatures called foraminifera. He read the ratio just as Urey had taught him. By roughly how much did he report that Caribbean sea temperatures had swung across the great ice-age cycles?
answer: About 6 degrees Celsius
choices: About 6 degrees Celsius
About 2 degrees Celsius
About 10 degrees Celsius
About 15 degrees Celsius
context: Emiliani turned a jar of microscopic shells into a record of glacial cycles -- the first quantitative paleotemperature curve for the deep sea. The interpretation was not the whole story (see another question), but the measurement itself opened a new era of paleoclimatology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesare_Emiliani.

question: Cesare Emiliani had read the oxygen-18 signal in the shells of tiny sea creatures as a direct thermometer of ancient ocean water. Nicholas Shackleton went back to the same kind of data in 1967, and in a Nature paper he said the signal was really driven by something else. Same numbers, different meaning. What did Shackleton say the shells were actually tracking?
answer: How much light water was locked up in continental ice sheets
choices: How much light water was locked up in continental ice sheets
The salinity of the surface ocean during each glacial
The abundance of plankton food across each cycle
The pH of the deep ocean over the last million years
context: When a glacial cycle locks huge volumes of isotopically light water into ice sheets, the ocean left behind gets heavier -- and every shell crystallising in it does too. Shackleton showed that effect dominates Emiliani's signal. Same measurement, wrong interpretation, fixed by a better one -- and it made the record MORE useful, tying the deep-sea shells directly to global ice volume. Source: nature.com/articles/215015a0 (Shackleton, Nature 215:15-17, 1967).

question: A hydrologist looks back to around 1960, when open-air nuclear tests sent tritium into the sky and rain worldwide carried it down. Natural rain holds only about 5 to 10 tritium units (TU); the tests of the late 1950s and early 1960s spiked it by two to three orders of magnitude, with peaks near 1,000 TU. In the decades since, what have hydrologists most commonly done with that global spike?
answer: Used it to date whether a well's water fell as rain before or after the bomb era
choices: Used it to date whether a well's water fell as rain before or after the bomb era
Used it to map how quickly rainwater from the 1960s reaches deep aquifers today
Used it to check whether a glacier's youngest ice was laid down after 1963
Used it to trace bomb-era fallout patterns from the prevailing winds
context: The bomb pulse. A weapons-test scar turned into a hydrologist's dating tool: tritium is radioactive hydrogen with a half-life of about 12.3 years, so water coming out of a well with essentially no tritium fell before about 1953; water carrying a clear bomb-pulse signal fell after, and the decay of the spike puts a decade-scale age on it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritium.

question: Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley launched in May 2020 aboard SpaceX's Dragon Endeavour, bound for the International Space Station. Inside was a small shiny toy dinosaur named Tremor, on a string and doing a real scientific job. What does Tremor show them?
answer: It lifts off its string the instant they go weightless.
choices: It lifts off its string the instant they go weightless.
It swings toward the nose when the thrusters fire.
It presses flat to the wall as the g-force peaks.
It spins on its string if the capsule starts rolling.
context: Tremor was a Ty Flippables apatosaurus chosen by Behnken's and Hurley's sons, Theodore, 6, and Jack, 10. It began floating the moment Dragon Endeavour reached orbit, and at the station it met the crew's own plush 'Little Earth'. Yuri Gagarin is credited with starting the tradition in 1961, releasing a pencil inside Vostok 1 to catch the exact instant; Snoopy flew as the indicator on Artemis I. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Zero-gravity indicator'; Space.com, 'SpaceX "stowaway" revealed by crew as sons' dinosaur toy "Tremor"'.

question: An astronaut on the International Space Station, about 400 kilometers up, gently releases a pen beside her. No string or magnet touches it, yet it hangs there as if it had no weight. Why does it stay beside her instead of dropping to the ground below?
answer: Everything around it falls toward Earth at the same rate.
choices: Everything around it falls toward Earth at the same rate.
There is no gravity in space to pull it downward.
The station's speed cancels out the pull of gravity.
It is far too distant for Earth's gravity to reach.
context: NASA puts it plainly: 'The spacecraft, its crew and any objects aboard are all falling toward but around Earth. Since they are all falling together, the crew and objects appear to float.' The station never hits the ground because the curve of its fall matches the curve of the Earth. What is missing up there is not gravity but WEIGHT — the space journalist James Oberg defined weight as 'the resistance of gravitational attraction by an anchored structure or a counterforce'. Take away the floor's push and you feel nothing, even while gravity keeps pulling at nearly full strength. Sources: NASA, 'What Is Microgravity? (Grades 5-8)'; Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'Weightlessness'.

question: An astronaut floats through the International Space Station about 400 kilometres up, the London-to-Paris distance straight overhead, and people call it 'zero gravity.' Yet Earth's pull fades only slowly with distance. Compared with the pull on a kitchen floor, how strong is Earth's gravity up where she works?
answer: About 90 per cent as strong.
choices: About 90 per cent as strong.
About 50 per cent as strong.
About 10 per cent as strong.
About 1 per cent as strong.
context: Gravity at that altitude measures about 8.69 metres per second squared, against 9.81 at the surface. The Open University states it directly: 'The gravitational field on the ISS is approximately 89% of that on the Earth's surface.' NASA rounds it to 'about 90 percent of what it is on the planet's surface.' So the popular phrase 'zero gravity' is not a small exaggeration — it is wrong about the one thing it names. Sources: Open University OpenLearn, 'Is there any gravity on the ISS?'; NASA, 'What Is Microgravity? (Grades 5-8)'.

question: Isaac Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain so tall its summit rose above the atmosphere, aimed dead level at the horizon. He imagined packing in more and more powder, so each ball flew farther before landing: one mile, two, five, ten, a hundred, a thousand. Then one ball never came down at all, and Newton drew its path. Where did it finish?
answer: Back at the mouth of the cannon it was fired from.
choices: Back at the mouth of the cannon it was fired from.
A quarter turn short of the cannon, and still climbing.
Stalled high above the far side of the turning Earth.
Far beyond the cannon, spiralling wider on every lap.
context: The diagram on page 6 puts the cannon at point V and labels three paths: VD, which falls back almost at once; VE, a longer ellipse that loops partway round before striking the ground; and VF, the circle that carries the ball the whole way round and home to the muzzle. Newton's own words run: 'We may therefore suppose the velocity to be so encreased, that it would describe an arc of 1, 2, 5, 10, 100, 1000 miles before it arrived at the Earth, till at last exceeding the limits of the Earth, it should pass quite by without touching it.' That escape case is described in the text but is NOT drawn on the diagram. ACCURACY RAIL: the scene is from A Treatise of the System of the World, drafted about 1685 and published posthumously in 1728, a year after Newton's death — not in the Principia proper. Voltaire retold the whole scenario for general readers in his Letters Concerning the English Nation (1733), using it to demolish the rival Cartesian vortex theory across Europe. Source: Grokipedia, 'Newton's cannonball'.

question: An astronaut at a window of the International Space Station watches the Sun climb over the horizon, and soon watches it climb again. The station races around the whole planet at roughly 17,500 miles per hour, about ten times the speed of a rifle bullet. How many sunrises does she see in a single 24-hour day?
answer: Sixteen.
choices: Sixteen.
Forty.
Four.
Two.
context: One lap takes about ninety minutes — Wikipedia's figure is 92.9 minutes, or 15.5 orbits a day — at roughly 7.66 kilometres per second, 28,000 km/h, on an orbit running from a perigee of 413 km to an apogee of 422 km. Human bodies cannot run on a ninety-minute clock, so the station keeps Greenwich time and the crew pull the window shades down in order to sleep on a normal twenty-four-hour schedule. Sources: NASA, 'What Is Microgravity? (Grades 5-8)'; NASA Earth Observatory, 'Sunset from the International Space Station'; Wikipedia, 'International Space Station'; Grokipedia, 'Free fall'.

question: A rider on the first steep plunge of a big rollercoaster is, for a second or two, exactly as weightless as an astronaut aboard the space station. No rocket is needed. What else puts an ordinary person into that same real weightlessness?
answer: A lift racing down its shaft with the cable cut.
choices: A lift racing down its shaft with the cable cut.
A submarine sinking fast with its ballast tanks flooded.
A parachutist descending under a fully open canopy.
An airliner holding a shallow, perfectly steady dive.
context: A cut cable leaves the lift and everyone inside it accelerating downward together with nothing pressing back — the identical condition an astronaut is in, except that the astronaut's never ends. Orbit is simply free fall that does not stop; NASA's point is that the crew are not floating in an absence of gravity but falling in it. The other three descents all have something still holding the body up: the open canopy's drag, the water around the submarine's hull, and the wings of the steadily diving airliner each push back, so the people inside still weigh what they always did. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Free fall'; Grokipedia, 'Weightlessness'.

question: Riders aboard Blue Origin's New Shepard rocket climb past 100 kilometers, float weightless for about three minutes, then strap back in and return home. The crew of the International Space Station, at 400 kilometers, float for months on end. What would New Shepard need before its passengers could float that long?
answer: Enough sideways speed to keep missing the ground.
choices: Enough sideways speed to keep missing the ground.
Enough thrust to climb four times higher than it does.
Enough altitude to leave the last of the air behind.
Enough fuel to keep its engine burning far longer.
context: Virgin Galactic's SpaceShipTwo gives four to five minutes of floating near 100 kilometres, and neither vehicle goes fast enough sideways to orbit, so both simply fall back down — Newton's cannonball fired with too little powder. There are clean numbers for how much sideways speed is enough: circular orbital speed just above the surface is about 7.9 kilometres per second, and escape speed is about 11.2 — exactly the square root of two times as fast. Same cannon, same mountain; only the muzzle speed differs. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Weightlessness'; Grokipedia, 'Newton's cannonball'.

question: A pilot climbs the Vomit Comet, a weightlessness trainer flown by the American space program, at a forty-five degree angle, with everyone aboard pressed down at nearly twice normal weight. The pilot then cuts thrust entirely and pushes over the top about eight kilometers above the ground. For the next twenty-five seconds every person and every loose tool inside floats freely. What path is the aircraft tracing through the atmosphere during that stretch?
answer: The exact arc a stone would follow if it were thrown.
choices: The exact arc a stone would follow if it were thrown.
A circle of one fixed radius, held all the way over.
A curve flattened at the top to hold one steady speed.
A curve steepened at the top to match the cabin's weight.
context: The pilot flies the aircraft along the path a thrown object would take on its own, so the aeroplane and everyone inside it fall together and nothing presses on anybody. The pull-out at the bottom costs another twenty seconds at about 1.8 g. The original was a modified KC-135 military tanker flying thirty to forty parabolas per sortie over the Gulf of Mexico from the 1960s until it retired in 2004; NASA then flew a C-9B Skytrain II from 2005 to 2014. ESA's Airbus A310 Zero-G, flown by Novespace out of Bordeaux-Merignac since 2015, does thirty-one parabolas a mission. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Weightlessness'.

question: An engineer at Germany's ZARM (Center of Applied Space Technology and Microgravity) tower in Bremen drops a sealed experiment down the airless shaft, and the plain drop lasts 4.74 seconds. NASA's 155-metre shaft at the Glenn Research Center in Cleveland yields 5.18. The ZARM tower is much the same height, yet it can deliver 9.3 seconds. How does it do that?
answer: It fires the capsule upward first, so it floats going up too.
choices: It fires the capsule upward first, so it floats going up too.
It pumps the shaft to a harder vacuum, cutting the drag.
It releases the capsule from a cradle already moving downward.
It brakes the capsule magnetically, stretching out the fall.
context: A thrown ball is weightless on the way up exactly as it is on the way down, so catapulting the capsule from the bottom of the shaft buys the rise as well as the fall — nearly double the time from the same building. The capsules come to rest in polystyrene granules that hold the impact to about 30 g. NASA's Zero Gravity Research Facility has been running since 1966. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Weightlessness'.

question: An astronaut floats aboard the space station with nine-tenths of Earth's pull still reaching her, and NASA's word for her condition is microgravity, never zero gravity. The word is not only about the pull that remains. That pull is also not quite the same at every point inside the station. Which effect chiefly accounts for the difference?
answer: Her feet sit nearer Earth than her head, so the feet are pulled harder.
choices: Her feet sit nearer Earth than her head, so the feet are pulled harder.
The station's metal hull shields its innermost modules from part of the pull.
The station's own mass tugs loose objects toward its heaviest section.
The Sun pulls hardest on whichever end of the station is turned toward it.
context: That head-to-feet difference is a tidal, or gravity-gradient, effect, and it has been measured: about 0.384 microgravities per metre at 400 kilometres. Add the drag of the thin air and the nudges of astronauts pushing off the walls, and the leftover acceleration on a quiet day comes to roughly one millionth of Earth's gravity (10^-6 g) — small, but not nothing, and that is where the 'micro' comes from. NASA flags the popular error by name: microgravity 'is sometimes called zero gravity, but this is misleading.' Gravity cannot be screened off by any hull; the station's own mass and the distant Sun do pull as well, but the measured gradient that gives 'microgravity' its name is the head-to-feet one. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Weightlessness'; Grokipedia, 'Weightlessness'; NASA, 'What Is Microgravity? (Grades 5-8)'.

question: The crew of the International Space Station wait while a docked Progress freighter runs its engines to shove the station back up, one of six to twelve such boosts a year. Four hundred kilometres up is not a true vacuum: enough thin gas remains to drag on the station, and it sinks about two kilometres lower every month. That sinking is not steady, though. What makes the station fall fastest?
answer: The Sun reaching the peak of its activity cycle.
choices: The Sun reaching the peak of its activity cycle.
The Moon swinging closest to Earth at perigee.
The station gaining mass as freighters and modules dock.
The station passing over the tropics twice each orbit.
context: At solar maximum the upper atmosphere heats and puffs outward, so the station runs into thicker gas at the same altitude and the drag can double or triple. Day to day the loss runs roughly 50 to 100 metres of altitude; the station's own thrusters can perform the reboost when no freighter is docked. Sources: Wikipedia, 'International Space Station'; The Planetary Society, 'How NASA plans to deorbit the International Space Station'.

question: A struggling London blacksmith's son left school at thirteen, knowing only reading, writing and basic arithmetic. At fourteen Michael Faraday was apprenticed to George Riebau on Blandford Street. Where did the boy first pick up the science that made him a chemist?
answer: From the books brought into the shop to be bound.
choices: From the books brought into the shop to be bound.
From evening classes at a London hospital.
From a tutor his master hired for him.
From a chemist's shop where he swept at night.
context: The tradesman was the bookbinder George Riebau of Blandford Street, and Faraday was fourteen when the seven-year apprenticeship began in 1805. Everything he learned came off the workbench: he read the volumes that passed through his hands to be bound. Source: Grokipedia, Michael Faraday (Early Life and Education); Wikipedia, Michael Faraday.

question: Michael Faraday stuck a magnet upright in a lump of wax at the bottom of a deep basin in September 1821. He filled the basin with mercury and hung a wire so its tip dipped into the mercury beside the magnet. Then he sent a current down the wire. What did the wire do?
answer: It travelled round and round the magnet, endlessly.
choices: It travelled round and round the magnet, endlessly.
It sprang upright and stood there, quite rigid.
It glowed red and melted the wax beneath it.
It leapt clear of the mercury and hung still.
context: It was the first device ever built that turned electricity into continuous motion. His notebook for 3 September 1821, describing a cruder first attempt, records only: 'Very satisfactory, but make more sensible apparatus.' He built the basin version the next day. He later mailed pocket-sized working models to colleagues across Europe, where the little motors became fashionable novelty gifts; his own original apparatus does not survive. Source: Royal Institution, 'The birth of electric motion'; IEEE Spectrum, '200 Years Ago, Faraday Invented the Electric Motor'.

question: A visitor stops at a small iron ring wound with copper wire in the Royal Institution's basement museum in London. Michael Faraday made it in 1831. The wire was plain stuff from an everyday London shop, not from a scientific supplier. What had it originally been made for?
answer: Wire made for ladies' bonnets.
choices: Wire made for ladies' bonnets.
Wire made for corset stays.
Wire made for umbrella ribs.
Wire made for fishing tackle.
context: Bonnet wire, wound by hand onto a lump of soft iron in a basement, was the first electric transformer ever built, and the object itself survives in the Royal Institution's collection. Source: Royal Institution collection, 'Michael Faraday's ring-coil apparatus'.

question: A London shop apprentice with no laboratory of his own opened Jane Marcet's 'Conversations on Chemistry,' a book written as a chat for young readers. The boy, Michael Faraday, said long after that it 'came as the full light in my mind.' What did he do with the chemistry in it?
answer: He tested her chemistry with his own cheap experiments.
choices: He tested her chemistry with his own cheap experiments.
He checked her chapters against the other books in the shop.
He set her chemistry to memory and recited it nightly.
He copied the whole book out by hand for his own shelf.
context: Writing to Auguste De La Rive on 2 October 1858, Faraday set out the rule he had taught himself as a boy: he would 'trust a fact' but 'always cross examined an assertion'. When his own cheap experiments agreed with Marcet's book, he said, 'I felt that I had got hold of an anchor in chemical knowledge.' Source: Faraday to Arthur-Auguste De La Rive, 2 October 1858, Epsilon letter archive.

question: Michael Faraday, a twenty-year-old bookbinder's apprentice who had never been to university, sat through four public lectures given by Humphry Davy at the Royal Institution in 1812, taking careful notes on every word. He copied the notes out neatly, expanded them, and sent the finished work to Davy with a letter asking to be hired. What landed on Davy's desk?
answer: A hand-bound volume of three hundred-odd pages.
choices: A hand-bound volume of three hundred-odd pages.
A printed pamphlet of some forty-odd pages.
A leather case of sixty numbered cards.
A fair copy on twenty large folded sheets.
context: He bound his own lecture notes into a book, because binding books was his trade. It worked: Faraday was appointed chemical assistant at the Royal Institution on 1 March 1813. The post was open because Davy's eyesight had been damaged by an exploding sample of nitrogen trichloride and because the previous assistant had been dismissed after a fight. Sources disagree on the page count -- Bence Jones, describing the surviving volume, says 386 small quarto pages, Grokipedia says 313, Wikipedia says 300. Source: Bence Jones, 'The Royal Institution' (Project Gutenberg); Grokipedia, Michael Faraday.

question: Michael Faraday stood inside a wooden cube twelve feet on a side in January 1836, holding lighted candles, while a machine charged the outside until it threw sparks. He had set the cube on glass insulators and covered it with copper netting and bands of tin foil. What happened to the candle flames?
answer: They stood perfectly still.
choices: They stood perfectly still.
They bent towards the netting.
They flared up and burned blue.
They guttered out at once.
context: A gold-leaf electrometer left inside never twitched either, although the outside of the cage reached a potential high enough to ignite alcohol. Charge spreads over the outside of a conductor and leaves the inside untouched. Faraday wrote the work up in the Eleventh Series of 'Experimental Researches in Electricity', received by the Royal Society on 30 November 1837. Source: Grokipedia, Faraday cage (Early Experiments); Wikipedia, Michael Faraday.

question: Michael Faraday turned down a knighthood, twice turned down leading the Royal Society, and refused burial in Westminster Abbey. A Sandemanian, he felt the Bible forbade heaping up riches or worldly honor. Where does he lie instead?
answer: In the dissenters' section of Highgate Cemetery.
choices: In the dissenters' section of Highgate Cemetery.
In the churchyard of his Sandemanian meeting house.
In the vault beneath the Royal Institution.
In the parish ground at Hampton Court Palace.
context: Dissenters were Christians who worshipped outside the Church of England, and Highgate Cemetery keeps a section for them; that is where Faraday lies. He had said he would rather remain 'plain Mr Faraday to the end', and the Royal Society first asked him to be its President in 1857. Westminster Abbey carries only a memorial plaque for him, near Isaac Newton's tomb. Queen Victoria did persuade him to accept one thing: a rent-free grace-and-favour house at Hampton Court in 1858, where he died on 25 August 1867. Source: Wikipedia, Michael Faraday; Grokipedia, Michael Faraday (Later Years; Advisory Roles and Honors).

question: William Wollaston had tried the same trick and failed when Michael Faraday rushed his rotation experiment into print in 1821, in a journal he edited himself, naming nobody else. Soon Humphry Davy, Faraday's own mentor, was calling it plagiarism. Faraday went to see Wollaston. What did Wollaston tell him?
answer: That what others thought of Faraday's conduct was Faraday's affair.
choices: That what others thought of Faraday's conduct was Faraday's affair.
That the credit was his, and he would say so at the Royal Society.
That what Davy had said of the business he would not contradict.
That he wanted his own name added to the paper's next printing.
context: Wollaston's reply ran: 'As to the opinion which others may have of your conduct, that is your concern, not mine; and if you fully acquit yourself of making any incorrect use of the suggestions of others, it seems to me that you have no occasion to concern yourself much about the matter.' Davy was less generous. At a Royal Society meeting on 6 March 1823 he said publicly that 'we owe to the sagacity of Dr. Wollaston, the first suggestion of electro-magnetic rotation', and that Wollaston would have found it himself had his apparatus not failed. Faraday was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1824 with exactly one vote against him, believed to be Davy's; the other Fellows overruled him. Source: Frank James, Davy Notebooks Project, Lancaster University; MacTutor, Michael Faraday.

question: Michael Faraday wound two separate coils of insulated copper onto opposite halves of a soft iron ring on 29 August 1831. One coil ran to a battery of ten pairs of plates. The other, with no battery in its circuit at all, ran to a sensitive galvanometer. When did that galvanometer's needle move?
answer: Only as the battery was joined or broken.
choices: Only as the battery was joined or broken.
Only while the battery current ran steadily.
Steadily at first, then fading away slowly.
Only once the iron ring had grown warm.
context: That 'only at make and break' behaviour is the law itself: a steady magnetic field induces nothing, and only a changing one drives a current. Faraday's earlier attempts had all used static arrangements -- a magnet sitting near a closed loop, a steady current in a neighbouring wire -- which is much of why the hunt took him about ten years. He was not alone in seeing it: Joseph Henry, teaching at the Albany Academy in New York, observed induction independently and had some results earlier, but published only in July 1832, after Faraday's paper of 24 November 1831. Today mutual induction is credited to Faraday, self-induction to Henry, and the unit of inductance is the henry. Source: Grokipedia, Faraday's law of induction; Smithsonian Institution Archives, 'Electromagnetism'.

question: Michael Faraday mounted a copper disc a foot across on a brass axle in the autumn of 1831 and set it spinning between the poles of the Royal Society's great magnet. Sliding contacts touched the disc at its rim and at its centre and ran to a galvanometer. What did the needle do?
answer: It swung right over and held there, turn after turn.
choices: It swung right over and held there, turn after turn.
It kicked once and dropped straight back to zero.
It trembled in time with each turn of the disc.
It crept over slowly and then sank back again.
context: This came only weeks after the two-coil iron ring of 29 August 1831. The needle swung ninety degrees or more, and unlike every earlier result the current did not die away: keep turning the handle and it keeps flowing. Reverse the spin, or flip the magnet, and the current reverses. That disc is the ancestor of every generator in every power station. Faraday's induction law also runs every transformer on every pole and every electric motor from a hairdryer to a locomotive. Source: IEEE Milestones Wiki, 'Faraday's Discovery of Induction'; Joseph Henry Project, Princeton, 'Faraday Unipolar Generator'.

question: A girl at her kitchen table seals a switched-on mobile phone in a plastic bag, wraps the bag completely in aluminium foil and rings the number: nothing. She is testing Michael Faraday's 1836 finding that charge sits on the outside of a conductor and leaves the inside untouched. Then she leaves the bag out, so the foil lies straight against the phone, and the call gets through. Why does the bare-foil version fail?
answer: The foil then acts as an extension of the phone's antenna.
choices: The foil then acts as an extension of the phone's antenna.
The foil then earths itself through the phone's metal case.
The foil then heats slightly and stops blocking the signal.
The foil then carries too little charge to shield anything.
context: The same principle is why a microwave oven's door carries a metal mesh with holes smaller than the microwaves it must hold in, and why a car body protects the people inside it during a lightning strike. Source: University of Iowa Physics instructional demonstrations 5B20.35 'Faraday's Cage - Radio' and 'Cell Phone and Aluminum Foil'; Wikipedia, Faraday cage.

question: Michael Faraday, the son of a poor London blacksmith, worked out how invisible magnetic and electric forces surround wires and magnets, with mathematics that never got past the simplest algebra: no trigonometry, no calculus at all. With no equations to write out, what did he put on paper instead to record what he saw?
answer: Curved lines of force, drawn through empty space.
choices: Curved lines of force, drawn through empty space.
Tables of measured forces, to four decimal places.
Scale drawings of every piece of his apparatus.
Geometric figures built with a compass and rule.
context: Faraday treated those lines as physically real -- tensile lines of stress distributed continuously through space -- not as a bookkeeping trick. That is the idea of the FIELD: space itself carries the action, instead of a magnet reaching across a void. Do not inflate the story into 'no education' -- he read constantly and lectured for over thirty years, giving nineteen series of the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures between 1827 and 1860. Source: Wikipedia, Michael Faraday; Grokipedia, Michael Faraday (Field Theory).

question: James Clerk Maxwell took the diagrams Michael Faraday had drawn of magnetic and electric action and recast them as the equations physicists still use today. Faraday himself could manage only the simplest algebra and had never reached trigonometry. What was Maxwell's own written verdict on him?
answer: That he was in reality a mathematician of a very high order.
choices: That he was in reality a mathematician of a very high order.
That he was a superb observer who left the mathematics to others.
That his drawings were a useful crutch for an untrained mind.
That his instinct had outrun his training at every single step.
context: Maxwell titled his first great electromagnetic paper, in 1855, 'On Faraday's Lines of Force', and wrote of Faraday that he was 'in reality a mathematician of a very high order -- one from whom the mathematicians of the future may derive valuable and fertile methods.' Source: Wikipedia, Michael Faraday (Maxwell quote); Grokipedia, Faraday's law of induction.

question: The best-loved story has Michael Faraday showing his electrical apparatus to the prime minister, William Gladstone, who asks what use it could possibly be. 'One day, sir, you may tax it,' Faraday answers. No letter, newspaper or biography from Faraday's own lifetime carries the tale. Which checkable date shows it cannot be true as told?
answer: Gladstone took that office only in the year after Faraday died.
choices: Gladstone took that office only in the year after Faraday died.
The same exchange appears in a French almanac printed in 1789.
Britain had already been taxing electricity since the year 1852.
Faraday's electrical work was all done before Gladstone was born.
context: Faraday died on 25 August 1867, and William Gladstone did not become Prime Minister until December 1868 -- so the favourite casting breaks on a date anyone can look up. Gladstone had been Chancellor of the Exchequer for years while Faraday lived, so only the prime-minister version is impossible. The earliest known telling, in W. E. H. Lecky's Democracy and Liberty (1899), more than thirty years after Faraday's death, names no office for Gladstone and never mentions electricity; the tidy line 'One day, sir, you may tax it' turns up later still. Snopes can find the tale in no account by Faraday or any contemporary. Faraday is worth loving without it -- and checking a beloved story against a date is exactly what he would have done. Sources: Wikiquote, 'Michael Faraday' (Disputed); Snopes, 'Long Ago and Faraday'.  (Legend.)

question: Michael Faraday stood before the children at London's Royal Institution in December 1860, beginning his last Christmas course: six lectures on one burning candle. He told them why he had chosen so plain an object. What did he tell them a candle was?
answer: The open door into the study of natural philosophy.
choices: The open door into the study of natural philosophy.
The oldest instrument that natural philosophy ever had.
The little sun that every household keeps indoors.
The one machine a child could take wholly to pieces.
context: Six lectures -- two in December 1860, four in January 1861 -- to houses averaging 650 children, the biggest, 740, at the fifth. He opened the first one with 'And now, my boys and girls, I must first tell you of what candles are made.' Faraday's reason for giving a whole course to one object: there is 'no better, there is no more open door by which you can enter into the study of natural philosophy, than by considering the physical phenomena of a candle.' It was his last Christmas series; he had run a candle course before, and gave nineteen series in all. He did not start the tradition either -- the Royal Institution's Managers founded it in 1825, and John Millington gave the first course. Source: Faraday, The Chemical History of a Candle, Lecture I (en.wikisource.org; Project Gutenberg pg14474); Homerton College Library, 'Faraday and the Christmas Lectures'; Royal Institution, '200 years of the Christmas Lectures'.

question: Divers reached the wreck of the warship Royal George fifty-seven years after it sank in 1782, and up came a cracked tallow candle that had lain all that time in salt water. Michael Faraday lit it in front of the children. What did it do?
answer: It lit and burned as steadily as a new one.
choices: It lit and burned as steadily as a new one.
It guttered out in a cloud of steam and smoke.
It burned with a green flame from the sea salt.
It crumbled into a wet powder as it warmed.
context: The Royal George went down on 29 August 1782; Colonel Pasley's salvage operations began in August 1839. Faraday: 'It has been sunk in the sea for many years, subject to the action of salt water... though it is cracked about and broken a good deal, yet, when lighted, it goes on burning regularly, and the tallow resumes its natural condition as soon as it is fused.' His prop table also held a plaited wick that never needs snuffing, paraffin candles made from paraffin out of the Irish bogs, and a wax sent to him from Japan. Source: Faraday, Lecture I and its footnote (en.wikisource.org).

question: Michael Faraday pointed the children to the flame at the top of a candle's wick: every scrap of fuel was down in the solid stick below, and nobody carried it up by hand. The fuel travels, he told them, 'not in a careless way, but very beautifully in the very midst of the centre of action.' What carries it up to the flame?
answer: Capillary attraction, drawing melted wax up the wick.
choices: Capillary attraction, drawing melted wax up the wick.
The wick burning steadily downward into the wax.
Hot air from below, pressing the melted wax up.
The flame boiling wax off the open pool's surface.
context: Capillary attraction is the same pull that walks water up the corner of a paper towel or into a lump of sugar -- try it in a saucer tonight. The wick is a pump, not the fuel: the flame's heat melts a pool, the pool climbs the wick, and only at the top does it turn to vapour and burn. Nothing solid ever burns in a candle. Source: Faraday, Lecture I (en.wikisource.org).

question: Michael Faraday closed the last of his candle lectures with a wish that had nothing to do with chemistry. He hoped his young listeners might, in their own generation, 'be fit to compare to a candle,' and then he said exactly what he meant by it. In what way were they to be like one?
answer: By shining as lights to those about them.
choices: By shining as lights to those about them.
By burning steadily and wasting nothing.
By giving warmth to the house that keeps them.
By making light from the plainest stuff there is.
context: The documented closing words: 'all I can say to you at the end of these lectures (for we must come to an end at one time or other) is to express a wish that you may, in your generation, be fit to compare to a candle; that you may, like it, shine as lights to those about you; that, in all your actions, you may justify the beauty of the taper by making your deeds honourable and effectual in the discharge of your duty to your fellow-men.' He was sixty-nine, and this was the last Christmas course he ever gave. Source: Faraday, Lecture VI, closing paragraph (en.wikisource.org); Homerton College Library.

question: Michael Faraday set a candle burning where nothing disturbed it, and a neat cup formed at its top: a pool of liquid wax inside a solid rim that never let the pool spill over. He made the children look hard at that rim, because something shapes it every second the candle burns. What keeps the rim solid?
answer: Rising air, which cools the outer edge fastest.
choices: Rising air, which cools the outer edge fastest.
The wick, drawing wax hardest from beneath it.
The flame, whose heat is weakest at the edges.
The wax skin, setting as soon as it stops moving.
context: Faraday: 'As the air comes to the candle it moves upwards by the force of the current which the heat of the candle produces, and it so cools all the sides of the wax, tallow, or fuel, as to keep the edge much cooler than the part within.' Spoil the symmetry and the cup fails: 'If I made a current in one direction, my cup would be lop-sided, and the fluid would consequently run over'; 'there will be a guttering round about it because of the irregularity of the stream of air and the badness of the cup which is formed thereby.' That is all guttering is -- a broken cup. Source: Faraday, Lecture I (en.wikisource.org).

question: Michael Faraday gave the children at his 1860 Christmas Lectures a simple experiment that still works at home with one lit candle. A child holds a strip of white paper flat, pushes it straight through the middle of the flame, keeping it perfectly level, and pulls it out after a moment. Where has it burnt?
answer: In two bands, with the middle barely marked.
choices: In two bands, with the middle barely marked.
In one solid black band right across it.
In a single burnt line down the centre.
In an even brown scorch from edge to edge.
context: Two scorch marks mean two hot zones, and that means the flame is hollow -- a dark cone of unburnt vapour sits down the middle of it. Faraday: 'put the piece of paper right across the middle of the flame... you will find that it is burnt in two places, and that it is not burnt, or very little so, in the middle.' Run it with a grown-up, in still air, and pull the paper straight out. Source: Faraday, Lecture II (en.wikisource.org).

question: A fourth-grade teacher in Japan handed a boy named Akira Yoshino a copy of Michael Faraday's candle course, which became a book in 1861, has never been out of print and has been turned into at least nineteen languages. Yoshino has said it taught him why a candle burns and why it has a wick. What did he grow up to invent?
answer: The lithium-ion battery.
choices: The lithium-ion battery.
The blue light-emitting diode.
The flash memory chip.
The quartz wristwatch.
context: Faraday spoke the candle lectures; he never wrote them out as a book. We have the exact words because a young chemist in the audience, William Crookes, took them down: Crookes serialised the 1860-61 course in his own weekly, Chemical News, in early 1861, and Griffin, Bohn and Company issued it as a book that March: 'A Course of Six Lectures on the Chemical History of a Candle... delivered before a juvenile auditory at the Royal Institution of Great Britain during the Christmas holidays of 1860-1. Ed. by William Crookes.' (Faraday had given a candle course earlier as well, but the book everyone reads is the 1860-61 one -- it is never dated 1848.) Crookes's preface opens: 'From the primitive pine torch to the paraffin candle, how wide an interval!' The book has been translated into at least nineteen languages. Akira Yoshino shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing the lithium-ion battery, and has said the book made him understand why a candle burns and why it has a wick. Sources: Grokipedia, The Chemical History of a Candle; Homerton College Library; NobelPrize.org interview material; Japan Times, 12 Nov 2019.

question: Michael Faraday blew a candle out gently, so that a white trail rose off the smoking wick and hung there in the still air. He then brought up a lighted taper, a thin candle, to within two or three inches of the wick, close but nowhere near touching it. What did the children see?
answer: A train of fire ran down the trail and relit the wick.
choices: A train of fire ran down the trail and relit the wick.
The trail flared once and died, the wick staying cold.
The trail blew apart and snuffed out the taper itself.
The trail bent toward the taper and glowed faintly.
context: Faraday: 'you will observe a train of fire going through the air till it reaches the candle.' What the fire runs down is wax vapour -- which is the proof that a candle burns vapour, not the wick and not the solid wax. This is the trick to run at the dinner table: blow the candle out gently so the white trail stays whole, hold still air, and have a grown-up carry the flame. Source: Faraday, Lecture I (en.wikisource.org; Project Gutenberg pg14474).

question: Michael Faraday pushed a bent glass tube into the dark space just above a candle's wick at his 1860 Christmas Lectures, and ran the far end a foot out into the room, well clear of the candle. That dark centre of the flame is cooler than the burning yellow ring around it and full of unburnt wax vapour. What did he show the children next?
answer: He lit the far end, and a second flame burned there.
choices: He lit the far end, and a second flame burned there.
He led the far end into lime-water, which turned milky.
He caught a cold white smoke there that would not light.
He found the tube choked with soot within a minute.
context: Faraday's own words: 'I will arrange another tube carefully in the flame... where we will light it, and obtain absolutely the flame of the candle at a place distant from it.' Then the punchline to the children: 'Talk about laying on gas -- why, we can actually lay on a candle!' The dark centre is fuel that has not yet reached enough air; pipe it away and it will burn wherever you choose to light it. Source: Faraday, Lecture II (en.wikisource.org).

question: Michael Faraday held a cold dry glass over a burning candle and it fogged. He collected those drops and told the children the candle had made water, 'nothing but water,' and then refused to let them take his word for it. He dropped a lump of potassium, Humphry Davy's metal, onto the liquid he had caught. What did the potassium do?
answer: It caught fire on the surface and burned away.
choices: It caught fire on the surface and burned away.
It sank through the liquid and lay there unchanged.
It fizzed quietly and left a white crust behind.
It clouded the liquid to a milky white.
context: Faraday on the drops: 'we find that that part of the product is just water -- nothing but water.' Potassium takes fire on water, so the test settled it in front of the audience: 'See, it takes fire, and burns in just the same manner.' The scale is the startling part -- 'A pint of oil, when burnt fairly and properly, produces rather more than a pint of water' -- because the hydrogen locked in the wax leaves as water vapour. In a later lecture Faraday took that same water apart again on the bench with a battery and two platinum plates, collecting twice the volume of hydrogen as oxygen. Never handle potassium; the cold spoon held over a flame is the safe half of this experiment, and it fogs every time. Source: Faraday, Lectures III and IV (en.wikisource.org).

question: 'In every one of us there is a living process of combustion going on very similar to that of a candle,' Michael Faraday told the children in the last of his six lectures. A slow burning, he meant, inside every child in the room, and he would not leave it there as a fine saying. He proved it at the bench, using his own breath. What did he do?
answer: He breathed through clear lime-water until it turned milky.
choices: He breathed through clear lime-water until it turned milky.
He breathed on a cold glass until it fogged with water.
He breathed into a jar and the candle inside it went out.
He breathed on a glowing splint until its ember flared up.
context: Faraday at the bench: 'you see how white and milky the water is getting' -- the very same change the candle's own product had made earlier in the course, when he bubbled the gas off the flame through lime-water. Carbonic acid, he called it; we call it carbon dioxide, and the flame and the children watching it were both pouring it into the room. His arithmetic: a man converts 'as much as seven ounces of carbon into carbonic acid' in a day, while 'a milch cow will convert seventy ounces, and a horse seventy-nine ounces, solely by the act of respiration.' For the whole city his printed page reads '5,000,000 pounds, or 548 tons, of carbonic acid... in twenty-four hours' -- do that division yourself and the two figures do not agree, since five million pounds is about 2,200 tons. The 548 tons looks to be the weight of the carbon inside the gas rather than the gas itself. Check a printed number when you can, even one of Faraday's. Source: Faraday, Lecture VI (en.wikisource.org).

question: A student reads by a candle's soft yellow light, while a gas jet in a laboratory can burn hotter than that candle and still light almost nothing, its flame pale and nearly colourless. Michael Faraday told the children the difference is not the temperature. What is actually glowing in a candle flame?
answer: Grains of solid carbon, glowing white-hot.
choices: Grains of solid carbon, glowing white-hot.
Sodium from the burning wick, glowing yellow.
Droplets of unburnt wax, glowing as they rise.
Grains of ash off the wick, glowing yellow.
context: Faraday: 'All bright flames contain these solid particles.' The heat inside the flame decomposes the wax vapour and sets carbon free; the grains rise, glow white-hot, give the light, and then mostly burn away. Where air mixes with the gas BEFORE it burns, no grains ever form: 'you see how pale and blue the flame is... the difference is solely due to the solid particles not being separated before the gas is burnt.' Hold a cold spoon in the flame and you catch those same grains as soot -- the light and the black smudge are the same stuff. Source: Faraday, Lecture II (en.wikisource.org); Grokipedia flame-structure section.

question: Astronauts on the Space Shuttle Columbia burned candles in a sealed glovebox in June 1992, about seventy tests in all. On Earth a candle flame is always a teardrop: hot air rises, cool air rushes in below, and the stream stretches the burning gas into a point. In orbit the spacecraft and everything in it are falling together, nothing feels its own weight, and hot air has no reason to rise. What did the flames look like?
answer: A small blue ball, standing off the wick.
choices: A small blue ball, standing off the wick.
A small yellow ball, sootier than on Earth.
A thin blue ring circling the wick.
A teardrop as always, only dimmer.
context: NASA states it plainly: 'Gravity-driven buoyant convection causes a candle flame to be teardrop-shaped' on Earth, whereas in microgravity 'the flame is spherical, soot-free and blue.' The candles burned in the glovebox on Columbia's USML-1 mission in June 1992 -- about seventy tests -- and the report found the flame 'becomes and remains hemispherical and blue (apparently soot-free)' with a large standoff distance from the wick, concluding 'that a candle can burn indefinitely in a large enough ambient of air in microgravity.' The strangest detail: as such a flame died, its TIP was the last part to survive -- the exact opposite of a candle on Earth, where the base is the most reactive part. Sources: NASA, 'Candle Flame - 1g vs Microgravity' (nasa.gov); Ross & Dietrich, 'Candle Flames in Microgravity: USML-1 Results' (ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20030075810).

question: Matthew Kluger's group at the University of Michigan gave desert iguanas a shot of killed bacteria in 1974 and set each one in a long test chamber. An iguana is cold-blooded and cannot warm itself from inside. Yet the injected lizards' body temperature climbed above its normal setting. What had they done to raise it?
answer: Moved to the chamber's hotter end
choices: Moved to the chamber's hotter end
Curled into a tight ball to trap heat
Panted rapidly to draw in warmer air
Buried themselves under the sand
context: A lizard cannot heat itself from the inside; if it wants to be warmer it has to go and find heat. The first report, by Linda Vaughn, Harry Bernheim and Kluger, appeared in Nature in December 1974: one end of the chamber was heated past 50 degrees C and the other kept at room temperature, so each lizard chose its own warmth. The follow-up, 'Fever and survival', appeared in Science on 11 April 1975: infected lizards held at fever temperatures, about two degrees above normal, survived far better than those held cool. Sources: Vaughn, Bernheim and Kluger, Nature 252:473 (1974), epublications.marquette.edu/biomedsci_fac/58; Kluger, Ringler and Anver, Science 188:166 (1975), pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1114347/.

question: Richard Feynman pulled something out of a glass of ice water on the witness table on February 11, 1986, live on television. It was his most famous piece of evidence in the Rogers Commission's inquiry into the Challenger disaster, and a humble one. What was it?
answer: a scrap of rubber from the shuttle booster's O-ring
choices: a scrap of rubber from the shuttle booster's O-ring
a thin foil sample from the external tank's insulation
a slice of the ceramic tile from the orbiter's underside
a shard of the mirror from the crew cabin's periscope
context: Feynman had asked for the ice water in advance and brought the sample himself. Foil, tile and mirror are all real shuttle components, but the failure was in the rubber seal between two segments of the right solid rocket booster.

question: Engineers photographed icicles hanging from the launch tower at Kennedy Space Center on the morning of 28 January 1986, as Challenger waited through Florida's hard freeze. Every earlier shuttle flight had lifted off in air above 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 Celsius). About what was the outside temperature when Challenger finally lifted off?
answer: about 36 degrees Fahrenheit
choices: about 36 degrees Fahrenheit
about 45 degrees Fahrenheit
about 22 degrees Fahrenheit
about 42 degrees Fahrenheit
context: The air at liftoff was 36 F, about 15 F colder than any previous launch by the Rogers Commission's count; the coldest booster seals on any earlier flight, in January 1985, had been at a calculated 53 F. Overnight pad temperatures had bottomed out in the 20s and the right booster joint, sitting in shade, is estimated to have been near 28 F. Sources: Rogers Commission report, Vol. II, Appendix M (nasa.gov/history/rogersrep/v2appm.htm); Wikipedia, 'Space Shuttle Challenger disaster'; AccuWeather retrospective.

question: Engineers at Morton Thiokol, a Utah company working for NASA, held a telephone conference the night before the Challenger launch. They pushed hard against launching in freezing weather, and their first written call was 'no launch.' What part were they afraid the cold would hurt?
answer: The rubber O-rings that sealed the booster segments
choices: The rubber O-rings that sealed the booster segments
The fuel injectors on the main engines
The heat-shield tiles under the wings
The parachutes for booster recovery
context: Morton Thiokol built the Solid Rocket Boosters in Utah; the teleconference of 27 January 1986 pitted Thiokol engineers Roger Boisjoly and Arnold Thompson against senior managers in a caucus that eventually reversed the no-launch call. The other three are real shuttle contractors of the era -- Rockwell International built the orbiter, Aerojet made rocket motors, Martin Marietta built the giant external tank -- each of which could plausibly have been the one to object.

question: Roger Boisjoly, a contractor's engineer, spoke first and hardest against launching Challenger in the freezing cold, on a teleconference the night before. He showed photographs of soot from earlier cold flights. In freezing weather, he warned, the seals would be what?
answer: hard as rocks and would not seal in time
choices: hard as rocks and would not seal in time
several sizes too small to close the joint
brittle enough to shatter on the first vibration
slippery with condensation and unable to hold
context: Boisjoly showed photographs of grease blow-by from earlier cold-weather flights and argued that a stiff O-ring cannot spring back into a flexing joint fast enough to keep hot gas contained. Thiokol management overruled him in a caucus the engineers were shut out of.

question: Richard Feynman asked NASA's managers and its engineers, separately, how likely a shuttle mission was to end in disaster. Management said about 1 in 100,000 launches, which would mean one shuttle a day for some three hundred years with none lost. What did the engineers say?
answer: between 1 in 50 and 1 in 200
choices: between 1 in 50 and 1 in 200
between 1 in 500 and 1 in 1,000
between 1 in 2,000 and 1 in 5,000
between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 25,000
context: Feynman himself put the odds near 1 in 100. Management's 1-in-100,000 number implied a shuttle a day for 300 years without an accident -- a public-relations figure, not an engineering one. This factor-of-a-thousand gap between the two decks of the same building is the deeper finding Feynman was after.

question: General Donald Kutyna, a fellow member of the Rogers Commission, gave Richard Feynman the key hint about cold, but wrapped it in a story to protect the person who had really given him the data. By Kutyna's account, what everyday object did he say had leaked on him in cold weather?
answer: the carburetor of a car he was restoring in his garage
choices: the carburetor of a car he was restoring in his garage
the door seals of the refrigerator on his back porch
the rubber gaskets of the garden hose he had left outside
the front tire of the bicycle he kept in the garage
context: Kutyna's later telling: he showed Feynman a car engine, mentioned that its little O-rings leaked when the weather turned cold, and asked whether the same thing could happen on a shuttle. The BBC's 2013 film 'The Challenger' revealed that Sally Ride had quietly passed Kutyna NASA test data showing the shuttle rings stiffened when chilled -- her role kept secret to protect her source, and made public only after her death in 2012.

question: Richard Feynman insisted that his own dissent be published as Appendix F of the Rogers Commission report. Its final sentence is one of the most quoted lines in modern engineering: 'For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for...' How does the sentence end?
answer: nature cannot be fooled
choices: nature cannot be fooled
the numbers cannot be argued
the hardware cannot be persuaded
the sky itself keeps the score
context: The full Appendix F line: 'For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled.' It belongs to Feynman's minority appendix, not to the commission's main report. The other three choices are plausible-sounding alternates invented for this question -- none of them is Feynman's line.

question: Diane Vaughan, a sociologist, dug through the records asking how careful people at NASA and Morton Thiokol had talked themselves into launching Challenger. Flight after flight had come home with scorched O-rings, and none had ended in disaster. By her 1996 account, what had those safe returns done?
answer: Each pushed the line of acceptable damage a little further out
choices: Each pushed the line of acceptable damage a little further out
Each convinced the engineers that the cold played no part
