Each was kept from the managers by engineers afraid to speak
Each led NASA to set a stricter rule for launching in cold
context: Vaughan's name for that slow drift is normalization of deviance, now standard usage wherever engineers study failure. She traced how each flight that came back with singed rubber and did not blow up nudged the acceptable damage line a little further out; the joint was 'flying', so the damage must be tolerable. Source: Diane Vaughan, The Challenger Launch Decision (University of Chicago Press, 1996); Wikipedia, 'Normalization of deviance'.

question: Challenger vanished into a huge white plume seventy-three seconds after leaving Florida on 28 January 1986, and all seven astronauts were killed. Nearly everyone who watched still calls it an explosion. The Rogers Commission traced the start to a cold-hardened O-ring that let hot gas burn into the external fuel tank, but it was more exact about what destroyed the orbiter. What destroyed it?
answer: aerodynamic forces tore the orbiter apart after the external tank ruptured
choices: aerodynamic forces tore the orbiter apart after the external tank ruptured
the main engines detonated when the fuel line ruptured in the joint failure
a chain reaction in the solid rocket booster's own propellant blew the stack apart
an internal cabin fire ignited by the electrical system consumed the orbiter first
context: The failed joint sent a jet of hot gas that burned through a strut and ruptured the external tank. The tank's hydrogen and oxygen burned in the open air -- the bright cloud viewers remember -- and the orbiter itself, still intact for a moment, tumbled sideways at high speed and was torn apart by aerodynamic loads of about 20 g. The crew cabin survived intact through breakup and fell more than two minutes to the ocean. Told soberly because the truth is grimmer than 'it exploded'.

question: Some island villagers, after the war, built fake runways with fires along the sides, a wooden hut, and a man in it wearing wood headphones with bamboo antennas, and they waited for planes that never came. Richard Feynman told this story at Caltech in 1974. What did he name that kind of failure?
answer: cargo cult science
choices: cargo cult science
pathological science
the Dunning-Kruger effect
publication bias
context: Feynman: they 'follow all the apparent precepts and forms of scientific investigation, but they're missing something essential, because the planes don't land.' Source: Caltech, 'Cargo Cult Science' (1974). Langmuir's 'pathological science' (1953) is a real, closely related idea covered in the questions on N-rays; Dunning-Kruger and publication bias are real but distinct.

question: Richard Feynman stood in front of the graduating class at Caltech in Pasadena on 14 June 1974 and named one rule as the first principle of scientific thought. Everything else honest in science, he said, follows from getting that one principle right. What did he say the first principle is?
answer: You must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.
choices: You must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.
You must state, up front, what would prove your own theory wrong.
You must never rest a claim on an authority bigger than the evidence.
You must weigh a bold new claim against the weight of ordinary practice.
context: The line lives in the address's core section on integrity: after you've stopped fooling yourself, 'it's easy not to fool other scientists.' The other choices are Popper-flavored, Sagan-flavored and Bacon-flavored paraphrases -- adjacent to Feynman's line but not it.

question: Richard Feynman warned the new graduates at Caltech in June 1974 about work that copied the outward form of science, its instruments and jargon, but skipped the honesty at its heart. The name he gave that failure escaped into ordinary English about a decade later. How did most readers first meet it?
answer: as the closing chapter of Feynman's 1985 memoir 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!'
choices: as the closing chapter of Feynman's 1985 memoir 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!'
as the opening chapter of his 1963 undergraduate lecture volumes
as a 1979 essay in Physics Today under Feynman's byline
as a segment of the 1983 BBC television series 'Fun to Imagine'
context: The 1974 address was reprinted as the final chapter of the memoir (Norton, 1985), and the book's bestseller run is what carried the phrase into common use. 'The Feynman Lectures on Physics,' Physics Today, and 'Fun to Imagine' are all real Feynman venues, but not where 'cargo cult science' broke out.

question: Richard Feynman studied the history of electron-charge measurements after Millikan. Each new value came out a bit larger than the one before, creeping upward instead of jumping to the true answer, and nobody cheated. Feynman blamed a habit of the honest experimenters themselves. What was that habit?
answer: They hunted hard for errors only when a value strayed far from the previous one.
choices: They hunted hard for errors only when a value strayed far from the previous one.
They quietly discarded any drop whose fall time did not fit the pattern.
They let the lead experimenter review every data sheet before it was written up.
They sent papers with unusual values back for a second round of measurements.
context: Feynman's exact diagnosis: 'When they got a number that was too high above Millikan's, they thought something must be wrong -- and they would look for and find a reason why something might be wrong. When they got a number closer to Millikan's value they didn't look so hard.' Not fraud, he stresses -- honest people, one-sided error-hunting. The three other choices are real bad-lab habits, but not what Feynman named here.

question: A man named Young ran rats down a corridor of doors, and Richard Feynman praised him for what came next. The rats kept picking the right door long after the food was moved, so Young hunted the hidden cue. It turned out to be something the rats could sense as they ran. What did Young change to kill the cue?
answer: He rebuilt the whole corridor floor out of loose sand.
choices: He rebuilt the whole corridor floor out of loose sand.
He repainted the doors in identical shades of grey.
He rebuilt the corridor without any right-angle turns.
He wiped every wall with a fresh solvent before each trial.
context: Feynman: 'He finally found that they could tell by the way the floor sounded when they ran over it. And he could only fix that by putting his corridor in sand.' Painting doors, straightening the maze, and neutralizing scent are real controls in real rat studies -- but the SOUND cue is the one Young caught and killed.

question: Richard Feynman told the story of Young's rat corridor for a specific reason. He was not praising Young for finishing a good study; he was pointing to what happened to it afterward in the rat-research literature. What was Feynman's actual complaint?
answer: Later rat experiments neither cited Young nor used the controls he had proved were needed.
choices: Later rat experiments neither cited Young nor used the controls he had proved were needed.
Later reviewers re-ran the numbers and the sound cue vanished as a statistical fluke.
Young's own follow-up paper walked back the finding after his department head objected.
The journal that had accepted Young's paper was shut down within a year of printing it.
context: Feynman: 'The subsequent experiment, and the one after that, never referred to Mr. Young. They never used any of his criteria of putting the corridor on sand, or being very careful.' The FIELD went on running rat experiments without the one control Young had proved was needed -- the bamboo-antenna failure in a lab coat.

question: The makers of Wesson cooking oil boasted in a print advertisement that their oil did not seep into anything fried in it. Richard Feynman quoted the boast in his 1974 Caltech commencement speech to show that a claim can be technically true and still dishonest. He said the statement was literally true and yet completely misleading. Why?
answer: At that temperature no oil soaks through food, so Wesson has claimed no real advantage.
choices: At that temperature no oil soaks through food, so Wesson has claimed no real advantage.
The test was run on baked, not fried, food, so no oil was hot enough to soak in.
The word 'food' in the test meant a strip of blotting paper, not any real food.
The company had rewritten the ad after the FDA required a factual correction.
context: Feynman: 'The fact that should be added to that advertising statement is that no oils soak through food, if operated at a certain temperature.' A true sentence framed to imply Wesson is unusual -- when the whole category behaves the same way -- is exactly the dishonesty scientists must avoid, even when every word they publish is technically correct.

question: The graduating class at Caltech in 1974 heard Richard Feynman warn that real scientific integrity means going out of one's way to state what would prove a claim wrong, and telling the whole truth even when it is inconvenient. He closed the address with a single wish for them. What did he wish them?
answer: the good luck to be somewhere free enough to keep that integrity
choices: the good luck to be somewhere free enough to keep that integrity
the patience to keep testing a claim long after their first result
the humility to publish a negative result as loudly as a positive one
the discipline to state up front what would prove them wrong
context: Feynman's closing sentence: 'May you have the good luck to be somewhere where you are free to maintain the kind of integrity I have described.' The word 'luck' concedes what the rest of the address had already implied -- that the freedom to be honest is not a guaranteed feature of a job in science; institutions can and do punish it. The three other wishes are Feynman-adjacent virtues (patience with replication, publishing null results, pre-registering falsifiers) but none are what he actually chose to end on.

question: Villagers in Melanesia built airstrips and mock control towers around the time of the Second World War, hoping to call the American cargo planes back. Their movements came to be called cargo cults, and Richard Feynman borrowed the name. One, a serious anti-colonial religion centred on a figure called John Frum, is still practised today. On which South Pacific island did it take root?
answer: Tanna, in southern Vanuatu
choices: Tanna, in southern Vanuatu
Guadalcanal, in the Solomons
Bougainville, in Papua New Guinea
New Britain, in Papua New Guinea
context: The John Frum movement on Tanna (in what is now Vanuatu) grew in the 1930s and swelled after the wartime American presence -- villagers still march every February 15, John Frum Day. Feynman's telling is a stylized parable, not fieldwork; the real religion is a serious anti-colonial movement, not the joke his metaphor sometimes suggests. Guadalcanal (Solomons) and New Britain (PNG) were major WWII Pacific sites; Bougainville is another Solomons island where cargo-style movements also arose.

question: A shell bursts red high above a watching crowd, and the next one bursts green. Its maker loaded the first with strontium salts and the second with barium salts, and those two loads give those two colours every single time. What is producing the colour up there?
answer: The metal atoms themselves giving off light
choices: Heat-proof dyes surviving the burn
Glowing soot particles tinted by the salts
The metal atoms themselves giving off light
Coloured smoke off the paper casing
context: The colouring compounds are no side ingredient - they can be 10 to 60 percent of a firework composition. The salt takes in heat from the burning star and gives light back out at the wavelengths that belong to that particular metal ion: strontium red, barium green, copper blue, sodium yellow. Nothing survives the fire as a pigment; the element itself is the colour. (Grokipedia: Pyrotechnic colorant.)

question: A boy at a kitchen gas stove sprinkles a few grains of table salt onto a clean wire, a test any kid can run at home. He holds the wire in the burner's blue flame, and the flame changes colour at once. What does the flame do?
answer: Flares yellow-orange
choices: Flares lilac-violet
Flares yellow-orange
Flares apple green
Flares brick red
context: That colour is almost the whole of the light: sodium's pair of lines at 589.0 and 589.6 nanometres. The other three answers are real flame colours of real elements - potassium gives lilac-violet, barium apple green, calcium brick red - which is exactly what makes the test useful. Try it on a gas hob with a clean nichrome wire, and clean the wire between samples, or the last thing you touched shows up instead of the thing you meant to test. (Grokipedia: Flame test.)

question: A woman stands at midnight in a car park under the deep orange of an old low-pressure sodium street lamp. Such lamps were among the most efficient ever built, up to 200 lumens per watt, through the same physics that makes a pinch of salt flare in a gas flame. What has the lamp taken away?
answer: Colour - every surface can only give back that one orange
choices: Colour - every surface can only give back that one orange
Sparkle - nothing under it glints the way it does by day
Depth - everything looks flattened against the tarmac
Detail - fine print and sharp edges blur into a haze
context: Colour is reflected light, and that lamp gives a surface nothing to reflect but 589-nanometre yellow, so everything can only come back as some shade of it. It is the chemistry bench's own sodium fingerprint, running over a car park all night. White LED lamps have nearly finished replacing them - if an orange street still survives near you, go and stand in it before it goes. (Wikipedia: Sodium-vapor lamp.)

question: Robert Bunsen wanted to see the faint colours that different salts add to a flame, but the gas lamps of the 1850s burned with a luminous yellow glow that swamped them. His new burner beat that glow and still reached about 1500 degrees Celsius. How did it get rid of the yellow?
answer: It mixed air into the gas before the gas burned
choices: It burned the gas at a much lower pressure
It fed the flame pure oxygen from a side tap
It passed the gas through charcoal first
It mixed air into the gas before the gas burned
context: A luminous flame is yellow because it is full of glowing soot - carbon specks that never met enough air. Bunsen's tube takes air in through adjustable slits at the base, so gas and air arrive at the top already mixed: the carbon burns completely, the soot never forms, and the flame goes almost invisible in daylight. The instrument was designed around the obstacle. (Wikipedia: Bunsen burner; Grokipedia: Robert Bunsen.)

question: Peter Desaga, the university's mechanic at Heidelberg, took Robert Bunsen's written design rules late in 1854, while the new lab was still half-built. The burner on every school lab bench still carries Bunsen's name. What was waiting when the lab opened a few months later?
answer: Fifty finished burners, ready for his students
choices: Fifty finished burners, ready for his students
One prototype, made for Bunsen's own bench
A patent for the burner in Desaga's own name
A crate of parts for the students to build
context: Desaga was the Heidelberg university mechanic, and he turned a page of design principles into fifty working instruments in a few months, ready for the opening in early 1855. Bunsen specified it, Desaga built it, and neither of them invented the premixed gas burner outright - Michael Faraday had already worked on similar principles in an earlier burner. Bunsen refused to patent his inventions, including his carbon-zinc battery, so that anyone could use them. (Wikipedia: Bunsen burner; Grokipedia: Robert Bunsen.)

question: A single shell bursts high above a crowd with red stars from strontium salts, green stars from barium salts, and among them brilliant white stars and trailing gold sparks. The stars in that one shell do not all make their light in the same way. What is producing the white and the gold?
answer: Hot solid particles glowing across every colour at once
choices: Hot solid particles glowing across every colour at once
A second metal emitting so many lines they blur together
Burning gases fluorescing above the coloured stars
Smoke scattering the burst's light back in all colours
context: Two entirely different mechanisms burn inside the same shell. Strontium and barium give line emission - a few sharp wavelengths belonging to the ion. The white stars are magnesium and aluminium powder giving incandescence: they simply get hot enough to glow, throwing out a smooth continuous spectrum with no lines in it at all, which the eye reads as white. The gold sparks are specks of charcoal incandescing at around 1000 degrees C. (Grokipedia: Pyrotechnic colorant.)

question: A chemist tests a salt for potassium, and a trace of sodium from a fingerprint floods the flame with a glare that buries potassium's fainter signature. Sodium hides in dust, sweat and tap water too. What does he hold between his eye and the flame?
answer: A square of cobalt blue glass
choices: A square of cobalt blue glass
A square of ruby red glass
A square of amber brown glass
A square of bottle green glass
context: Cobalt glass swallows sodium's yellow at 589 nanometres and passes potassium's faint violet line at 404, so the colour a chemist actually came for steps out from behind the contamination; didymium glass does the same job more selectively. The lesson underneath is the one textbooks skip - a test sensitive enough to name an element from an invisible trace is also sensitive enough to be wrecked by a fingerprint. (Grokipedia: Flame test; Wikipedia: Cobalt glass.)

question: Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff burned 3 milligrams of a sodium salt at the far corner of a room of sixty cubic metres, to show that their spectroscope could catch a quantity far too small to weigh. Then they watched a flame burning at the opposite end of the room. What happened at that far-off flame?
answer: It turned yellow and held that colour for minutes
choices: It flickered yellow for a second as the blast passed
It turned yellow and held that colour for minutes
It stayed clear until they fanned the air towards it
It dimmed slowly as the sodium smoke thickened
context: After a few minutes the flame turned yellow, showed a strong sodium line, and did not fade for ten minutes - meaning air carrying less than one twenty-millionth of its weight in sodium was enough to see. They ran it again with 0.3 grams of barium chlorate, stirring the room's air, in the paper's own words, by means of an open umbrella. The same paper puts the limit at less than one three-millionth of a milligram of sodium salt. (Kirchhoff and Bunsen, 'Chemical Analysis by Observation of Spectra', 1860.)

question: A pyrotechnician pushes a blue copper star hotter, hoping for a brighter burst, and gets a washed-out whitish tint instead of a deeper blue. The blue comes from copper(I) chloride, emitting in bands at 420 to 450 nanometres, and it is the hardest firework colour of all. What has the extra heat done?
answer: Torn the copper chloride apart into copper and chlorine
choices: Torn the copper chloride apart into copper and chlorine
Boiled the copper chloride out of the star as vapour
Shifted the copper chloride's bands across into green
Fused the copper chloride into a copper oxide instead
context: The blue comes from a molecule, not an atom, and that is the whole problem: copper(I) chloride falls apart above roughly 1500 degrees C. So blue lives in a narrow window - the star must burn hot enough to glow brightly but cool enough to leave the emitter intact. Lose that balance and what is left is incandescent white with a hint of blue in it. A deep saturated blue is the mark of a maker who found the window. (Grokipedia: Pyrotechnic colorant.)

question: Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen read the sharp bright lines of one substance after another through a prism at Heidelberg in 1859. Nobody could say what those lines really belonged to: the metal in the sample, the compound holding it, the mineral it was dug from, or the fire itself. The two men spent two years changing everything they could. What did their 1860 paper report?
answer: The lines belonged to the metal alone, unmoved by the rest
choices: The lines belonged to the metal alone, unmoved by the rest
The lines belonged to the metal, but shifted with its compound
The lines belonged to the metal, but shifted with the flame used
The lines belonged to the mineral more than to the metal in it
context: In their words, the compound the metal came in and the kind of flame used 'had no influence on the position of the spectral lines corresponding to the individual metals.' That negative result is what turns a colour into a name: if the lines never move, the pattern identifies the element and nothing else about the sample. It is the logic of a fingerprint - useless unless it is the same fingerprint every time. (Kirchhoff and Bunsen, 1860.)

question: Gustav Kirchhoff stood at the prism on 10 May 1860 as Robert Bunsen carried a small residue of mineral water from the Maxquelle spring at Bad Dürkheim to his gas flame. The prism let the two men read chemical elements by their coloured lines. What did Kirchhoff see in that spa-water residue?
answer: Two blue lines no catalogued element could claim
choices: Two blue lines no catalogued element could claim
Two red lines no catalogued element could claim
A green line no catalogued element could claim
A violet line no catalogued element could claim
context: Between them Bunsen and Kirchhoff had already catalogued the line patterns of every element then known, and this pair matched nothing in it: 455.5 and 459.3 nanometres, sitting near a blue line of strontium. Bunsen named the new element caesium, from the Latin caesius, the word the ancients used for sky-blue. It was the first element in history discovered by its light - it existed as two blue lines long before it existed as anything a chemist could hold. Carl Setterberg, working under Bunsen at Heidelberg, finally got beads of the metal in 1882, twenty-two years later. (Grokipedia: Caesium; Bunsen and Kirchhoff, 1861.)

question: Robert Bunsen boiled 44,000 litres of Bad Dürkheim mineral water, about forty tonnes, down to 240 kilograms of brine, then worked that down further. No chemist in 1860 would accept a colour as proof of a new element, so he had to put the salt itself on a balance. What weight of caesium chloride did the forty tonnes finally yield?
answer: About 7 grams
choices: About 70 kilograms
About 7 kilograms
About 700 grams
About 7 grams
context: 7.3 grams of caesium chloride, with 9.2 grams of rubidium chloride alongside it: two teaspoons of salt out of forty tonnes of spa water. This is the half of discovery nobody puts on the poster - the instrument found the element in an evening, and then Bunsen spent months boiling a tanker-load of water to satisfy the chemists. From crumbs like these they still estimated atomic weights, and their rubidium figure of 85.36 sits within a tenth of a percent of the modern 85.47. (Wikipedia: Caesium; Bunsen and Kirchhoff, 1861.)

question: Niels Bohr published his model of the atom in 1913, and it answered a question that chemists and mineralogists had left open for roughly fifty years. They named elements every day from the sharp coloured lines each one painted in a flame through a prism, and nobody could say why a given element gives those lines and no others. What did Bohr say the lines were?
answer: Electrons dropping between fixed energy levels
choices: Atoms vibrating at their own natural frequencies
The ether ringing around the atom like a bell
Electrons dropping between fixed energy levels
Electrons orbiting at speeds set by atomic weight
context: Each drop releases a photon of one definite energy, and energy fixes frequency, so one drop means one exact colour. Different elements have differently spaced levels, which is the whole reason the pattern is a fingerprint at all. Shown Balmer's formula for hydrogen's lines, Bohr said that everything became clear. Notice the order: the test was in daily industrial use for half a century before anyone understood it. A method can be reliable long before it is explained. (Wikipedia: Bohr model.)

question: Alexander Fleming came back to his London lab in September 1928 after some five weeks away and worked through a stack of forgotten staph plates. On one, a fuzzy blue-green mould had grown. What had happened to the staph nearest the mould?
answer: They had dissolved into a clear ring
choices: They had dissolved into a clear ring
They had grown thicker than the rest
They had turned blue-green like the mould
They had spread right over the mould
context: He did not wash the plate. He kept it, subcultured the mould, and photographed it. In that photograph the mould colony is about 20 mm across with a band of wrecked staph around it, and the colonies further out are only stunted (0.8-1.7 mm) rather than killed (0.4-0.8 mm near the mould) -- a gradient, not a clean on/off line. Fleming's caption was simply 'Photograph of a culture-plate.' Date note: Fleming's most-quoted line puts the moment on 28 September 1928, but the laboratory record points to 3 September; his first surviving notebook entry on the mould is 30 October 1928. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'; Asimov Press, 'The Penicillin Myth'.

question: Howard Florey needed penicillium mould by the gallon at Oxford in 1940 to test on patients, but wartime Britain had no drug factory to build him one. His biochemist Norman Heatley found the answer on the wards of the Oxford hospital. What did Heatley grow the mould in?
answer: Hospital bedpans
choices: Hospital bedpans
Hospital kettles
Hospital washbasins
Hospital specimen jars
context: Porcelain bedpans turned out to be near-perfect shallow culture vessels -- but bedpans were scarce in wartime, so Heatley designed a stackable rectangular ceramic version and had J. Macintyre and Company of Burslem, in the Staffordshire potteries, make 500 of them; the first 174 were collected on 22 December 1940 and seeded three days later. He tested sugars, salts, malts, alcohol and even Marmite in the growth broth before brewing yeast turned out to cut incubation time by a third. Two women factory hands were hired at two pounds a week to tend the vessels. Sources: Wikipedia, 'History of penicillin'; University of Oxford Medical Sciences Division, 'The lasting legacy of Norman Heatley'.

question: Alexander Fleming kept a spoiled plate of staphylococcus in September 1928, but it could not tell him what had done the damage around a stray blue-green mould: he could not isolate the substance or measure it. Over the next months he did the work that let him name it in a paper of 1929. What did he do?
answer: He filtered the mould out of the broth and tested the liquid alone
choices: He filtered the mould out of the broth and tested the liquid alone
He crushed the mould colony and rubbed the paste across fresh plates
He injected the mould broth into infected mice and watched them recover
He crystallised the substance out and weighed the doses he needed
context: He grew the mould on the surface of nutrient broth for five or six days at room temperature, then poured the broth through filter paper. What came through was a clear, straw-coloured liquid with no mould in it at all -- he called it 'mould juice'. It still destroyed staphylococci, streptococci and pneumococci; subcultures taken from inside the clear zone came back sterile; his 1929 paper reports it still strongly inhibiting staph and strep when watered down eight hundredfold, while leaving human white blood cells unharmed in the dish. So the killer was a SUBSTANCE the mould leaked into the liquid, not the mould itself -- and in 1929 he named that substance penicillin. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'; Fleming, Br J Exp Pathol 10(3):226-236 (1929).

question: Alexander Fleming tested his mould broth against many different bacteria in his London hospital lab, then wrote it up in the British Journal of Experimental Pathology in June 1929. The paper put the name penicillin into print for the first time, and its title announced the job he thought it best for. What use did the title suggest?
answer: Clearing a plate of rivals so the fussy influenza bacillus could grow
choices: Clearing a plate of rivals so the fussy influenza bacillus could grow
Keeping stored laboratory cultures from spoiling on the shelf
Sterilising surgical instruments between one operation and the next
Treating patients whose throats were crowded with streptococci
context: The full title was 'On the Antibacterial Action of Cultures of a Penicillium, with Special Reference to their Use in the Isolation of B. influenzae'. Penicillin barely touches Gram-negative bacilli, the influenza bacillus among them -- so adding it to a plate wipes out the staph and strep that would otherwise smother that fussy organism and lets it grow alone. This is the forgotten half of the story: the headline use Fleming proposed was penicillin as a LABORATORY TOOL, with antiseptic possibilities mentioned only in passing. The paper ran in a specialist journal read by bacteriologists rather than by clinicians, and drew few citations in its first decade. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'; paper text at PMC2048009.

question: Harold Raistrick, a London biochemist, pulled a crude extract from Fleming's mould in 1932, then quit when it kept falling apart. Almost nobody else chased penicillin through the 1930s, and it sat unused for a decade. What had medicine turned to instead?
answer: Gerhard Domagk's Prontosil and the sulfa drugs
choices: Gerhard Domagk's Prontosil and the sulfa drugs
Paul Ehrlich's Salvarsan and the arsenic compounds
Selman Waksman's streptomycin and the soil antibiotics
Joseph Lister's carbolic acid and the phenol antiseptics
context: Raistrick worked with P. W. Clutterbuck and R. Lovell and had every reason to succeed; crude penicillin simply lost its potency within about ten to fourteen days at room temperature and was destroyed by the heat of evaporation. Surface fermentation on shallow trays yielded micrograms per litre at purities often under 0.001%, and nobody knew penicillin's chemical structure until 1945 -- so all anyone could do was measure zones on agar and guess. Prontosil and the sulfa drugs that followed from 1932 were stable, synthesisable and reliable, and medicine's attention went to them. Penicillin's other rivals were real medicines too: Salvarsan (1909) cured syphilis but was arsenic and worked on one bug; Lister's carbolic acid (1860s) cut deaths after amputation from around 45% to about 15% but was far too toxic to inject; streptomycin arrived in 1943, after penicillin. Source: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'.

question: Albert Alexander, an Oxford policeman, received the first real course of penicillin in February 1941. Most tellings make him a gardener who scratched his face on a rose thorn and could not stop the infection that followed, but his own family told it differently. What did they say opened the wounds on his face?
answer: A German air raid on a police station
choices: A German air raid on a police station
A fall from a roof while chasing a thief
A kick from a horse in the police stables
A crash of his police car in the blackout
context: Alexander had been sent to help the Southampton police during the Blitz. At 5:50 p.m. on 30 November 1940 a German air raid hit the police station, killing a sergeant and injuring two constables -- one of them Alexander, whose facial lacerations came from the blast. His family later called the rosebush version 'a bit of wartime propaganda': a gentler story to tell than 'the Luftwaffe did it' while the bombing was still going on. The rose thorn is the legend; the blast is the documented record. Sources differ on his exact age (43, 44 or 45) and even on which force he served in. Sources: The Conversation, 'Guns, not roses -- here's the true story of penicillin's first patient'; Hektoen International, 'Albert Alexander: Unsung hero of penicillin'.

question: Howard Florey's Oxford team injected eight mice with a dose of Streptococcus certain to kill them on Saturday 25 May 1940, and gave penicillin to only four. Norman Heatley stayed at the bench all night, and his diary records that by 3:45 a.m. every untreated mouse was dead and all four treated ones alive. They ran it again on the Tuesday with sixteen mice. What did that bigger run show about the treated mice?
answer: They lived several days, but all were dead by day nineteen
choices: They lived several days, but all were dead by day nineteen
They lived only if the first dose came within an hour
They lived, but passed the infection on to healthy mice
They lived, and stayed healthy for the rest of their lives
context: Heatley's diary: 'I stayed at the lab until 3:45 a.m., by which time all four control animals were dead.' Two of the treated mice got a single 10 mg dose and two got 5 mg at intervals; one of those four died two days later, and in the larger Tuesday run the treated mice survived several days but were all dead within nineteen. The honest reading is that the DOSE, not the principle, was the limit -- and the team said so. What made any of it possible was Ernst Chain's alumina adsorption column, which concentrated the active substance roughly a hundredfold, plus Heatley's assay for measuring potency and his 'reverse extraction' -- flipping the acidity to pull penicillin back out of an organic solvent into water, first with ether and then with the less flammable amyl acetate. Sources: Wikipedia, 'History of penicillin' and 'Norman Heatley'; Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'.

question: Charles Fletcher, a research student under Howard Florey, began the first real course of penicillin on 12 February 1941 on Albert Alexander, an Oxford policeman dying of infection at the Radcliffe Infirmary. Within a day the fever fell and the wounds began to dry, but the Oxford team's whole stock was running out. What did they do to keep the doses coming?
answer: They recovered penicillin from his urine and re-injected it
choices: They recovered penicillin from his urine and re-injected it
They recovered penicillin from the mould trays a week early
They cut every dose in half and stretched the stock further
They gave him raw mould broth once the pure stock was gone
context: Alexander got an initial 200 mg (about 10,000 units) intravenously, then 100 mg every three hours; his temperature fell, the discharge from his wounds declined, his appetite returned, and by 17 February his remaining eye had normalised. Fletcher recorded 'obvious resolution of the abscesses... importantly, there had been no sort of toxic effect during the five days.' Penicillin passes out of the body largely unchanged, so the team recovered unprocessed drug from his urine and re-dosed him -- and still ran out after about five days. He relapsed in early March and died on 15 March 1941. The drug worked; there was not enough of it. (Dose figures vary by source: Wikipedia's page on Alexander gives 160 mg.) Sources: Wikipedia, 'History of penicillin'; Hektoen International, 'Albert Alexander: Unsung hero of penicillin'.

question: Howard Florey and Norman Heatley brought the problem of too little penicillin to a US Department of Agriculture lab in Peoria, Illinois, in 1941. There Andrew Moyer boosted the yield about tenfold by feeding the mould corn-steep liquor, a sludge left from milling corn. The lab still needed a Penicillium strain that made more drug from the start, and in 1943 it found one growing on something mouldy in Peoria itself. On what?
answer: A cantaloupe melon
choices: A cantaloupe melon
A rye bread loaf
A sack of onions
A leather work boot
context: The strain was catalogued as NRRL 1951, a Penicillium chrysogenum (now Penicillium rubens); grown in deep tanks it produced up to about a hundred times more penicillin than Fleming's original mould, and essentially all industrial penicillin since descends from it. The team then broke its DNA on purpose and screened the survivors: X-rays gave mutant X-1612 at about 300 mg per litre, ultraviolet light gave Q-176, and feeding the culture phenylacetic acid switched output to penicillin G at about 550 mg per litre -- directed evolution with a lamp and a filing system, years before anyone could read a gene. WHO found the cantaloupe, and where, is genuinely unsettled: a Peoria fruit market appears in some accounts and a garbage can in the USDA's own timeline, and the local credit to lab technician Mary K. Hunt, 'Moldy Mary', is lab lore the primary record does not confirm. Sources: The Scientist; USDA Agricultural Research Service, 'Penicillin: Opening the Era of Antibiotics'; Wikipedia, 'History of penicillin'.

question: A researcher drops penicillin into a flask of staphylococci dividing hard, and within hours the cells swell and burst. The same dose in a flask where growth has stalled does almost nothing. The drug blocks the last step in building a bacterium's wall, the cross-links that lock it together as the cell divides. What tears the growing cells apart?
answer: The cell's own wall-chewing enzymes carry on demolishing from inside
choices: The cell's own wall-chewing enzymes carry on demolishing from inside
The cell's dividing membrane pinches through the softened wall
The cell's wall-building enzymes pile material on until it splits
The cell's water pumps race as it divides and force the wall open
context: With no new cross-links going in, the cell's own wall-remodelling autolysins keep chewing, water floods in, and a GROWING bacterium bursts under its own internal pressure -- which is why penicillin does almost nothing to a colony that has already stopped growing. The enzyme it jams is DD-transpeptidase, one of the penicillin-binding proteins; the beta-lactam ring mimics the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of the wall's building block, and once it snaps open onto the enzyme's active-site serine it is welded there permanently. Human cells have no peptidoglycan at all -- no wall of that kind to sabotage -- which is exactly why penicillin can be injected into a person. Bacteria counter-punch with beta-lactamase, an enzyme that hydrolyses the ring open first; Edward Abraham and Ernst Chain described it in E. coli in 1940, before penicillin had ever been given to a human being. Nobody knew the drug's shape until Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin confirmed the four-membered ring by X-ray crystallography in 1945. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Penicillin'; Wikipedia, 'Penicillin'.

question: Norman Heatley built the assay that measured a penicillin batch's strength, found the vessels to grow the mould in and worked out how to pull the drug back out of solvent, all inside Howard Florey's Oxford department, on work the war kept quiet. When the 1945 Nobel Prize for penicillin was announced in Stockholm, his name was not on the list. What kept it off?
answer: The prize's rules cap a single award at three winners
choices: The prize's rules cap a single award at three winners
The prize's rules bar work still sealed as a war secret
The prize's rules allow just one winner from any laboratory
The prize's rules pass over anyone without a medical degree
context: A Nobel Prize may be split at most three ways, so once Fleming, Chain and Florey were on it there was no fourth place left to give Heatley -- a rule of the prize, not a judgement on his work. The Assembly announced it on 25 October 1945 and the ceremony followed on 10 December in Stockholm, the three men sharing it equally. Oxford's own answer came in 1990: an honorary Doctorate of Medicine, the first the university had awarded in its 800-year history to someone who was not medically qualified -- given to the bench chemist who never treated a patient. Heatley called it 'an enormous privilege since I am not medically qualified' and described himself as 'a third rate scientist whose only merit was to be in the right place at the right time'. Henry Harris summed the whole story up in one line: 'Without Fleming, no Chain or Florey; without Florey, no Heatley; without Heatley, no penicillin.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'; Wikipedia, 'Norman Heatley'; Engines of Our Ingenuity No. 601.

question: Alexander Fleming was leaning over a plate of yellow bacteria late in 1921 when a drop from his own body fell on it by accident. Days later a wide clear circle showed where the bacteria had melted into jelly, a sight that would make him keep a mould plate in 1928. Which of his body fluids had fallen on the plate?
answer: his own nasal mucus
choices: his own nasal mucus
his own tears
his own saliva
his own sweat
context: The clear halo Fleming saw was the body's own germ-killer at work. Later he and his assistant V.D. Allison would find the same enzyme in tears, saliva, blood serum and human milk - so all three other choices are real body sources of lysozyme, not fake. But the accidental drop that day in 1921 came from Fleming's nose. Sources: Scientific American, Penicillin Wasn't Alexander Fleming's First Major Discovery; Wikipedia, Lysozyme.

question: Alexander Fleming and his assistant V. D. Allison spent months hunting a bacteria-dissolving enzyme through tears, saliva, blood serum and other body fluids, finding small amounts. One everyday kitchen substance turned out to be packed with it in far greater concentration than any human fluid. Which substance was it?
answer: egg white
choices: egg white
olive oil
honey
vinegar
context: Egg white is one of the richest natural sources of lysozyme known - a hen packs the enzyme around her yolk to defend the embryo from bacteria. Fleming named the enzyme itself 'lysozyme' (from Greek lyso, to dissolve, plus zyme, enzyme) and gave the sensitive yellow test bacterium the name Micrococcus lysodeikticus - 'the one that shows the dissolving'. Source: Scientific American; Wikipedia, Lysozyme.

question: Alexander Fleming tried for seven years to turn lysozyme, the body's own bacterium-killer, into a medicine that could cure infections. Concentrating it did not help; injecting it did not help. One fundamental biological reason doomed it as a broad antibiotic. What was it?
answer: It dissolved only harmless bacteria and left the ones that cause serious human disease alone
choices: It dissolved only harmless bacteria and left the ones that cause serious human disease alone
It broke down human tissues just as easily as it broke down bacterial cells
It survived in the bloodstream for only a few seconds before being destroyed
It only worked when combined with an acid the human body could not produce
context: Lysozyme cuts a specific sugar bond in peptidoglycan - the mesh that makes up the cell wall of many gram-positive bacteria - but the truly dangerous pathogens (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus and most others that kill people) either have walls it cannot crack or protective outer layers that block it. Seven years of chasing a natural germ-killer and coming up short is exactly why, in 1928, when Fleming saw another clear halo - this time around a mould contaminant on a Staphylococcus plate - he did NOT reach for the wash bucket. Sources: Science History Institute, Alexander Fleming; Wikipedia, Lysozyme.

question: A boy drops a steel paperclip point-first into a glass of water and it plunges straight down, being nearly eight times denser than water. He lays a second one gently flat on the still surface, and it stays, the water dipping beneath it. What is holding it up?
answer: The water's top layer, pulled taut like a skin
choices: Buoyancy, shoving aside its own weight of water
A bubble of air caught in the bend of the wire
The water's top layer, pulled taut like a skin
An oily coating on the steel that water avoids
context: This is surface tension, and it is not buoyancy: steel runs 7.75-8.05 g/cm3 against water's 1.00 g/cm3, so displacement is nowhere near enough. Water molecules cling to each other so hard that the top layer behaves like a stretched elastic sheet, about 0.0728 newtons per metre at 20 degrees C. The clip sits in a shallow dimple the surface makes under its weight. Break that surface and it drops at once. Grokipedia uses a steel razor blade as the same example, floating because careful placement avoids breaking the surface. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Steel'; Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Floating and Immersed Objects').

question: A girl lays a small steel paperclip gently flat on a glass of water and leaves it resting there a full minute. Then she touches a toothpick dipped in dish soap to the water at the far side of the glass, well away from the clip. What happens next?
answer: It sinks to the bottom almost at once
choices: It sinks to the bottom almost at once
It drifts to the far rim and floats on
It stays put until the water is stirred
It dips under, then bobs back up flat
context: One drop, and it is gone. The soap does not make the water heavier and does not attack the steel - it destroys the surface. Surfactant molecules gather at the interface and cut surface tension by 50-90%: pure water measures about 72 mN/m, a typical dish-soap solution about 30-40 mN/m. Halve the tension and the surface can no longer hold up eight-times-denser steel. Run it yourself with a glass of water and one drop on a toothpick. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Role of Surfactants'); Vedantu, 'Detergents and Surface Tension'.

question: A girl blows a soap bubble off its wand, a film of liquid closed around a puff of air, and nothing holds it in shape now: no mould, no frame, no hand. Still it settles into a ball, the same shape every time. Why does a free bubble end up a sphere?
answer: No other shape wraps that air in less film
choices: No other shape wraps that air in less film
Air outside presses on it evenly from all sides
The charge on the film spreads out and rounds it
The film's own weight settles it into a ball
context: A sphere is the smallest possible surface around a given volume, and a liquid skin pulls until nothing smaller is on offer - which is why a free drop of water and a soap bubble are round for the same reason. A bubble has TWO surfaces, inner and outer, so its inside is over-pressurised by 4*gamma/r - exactly double a plain droplet's 2*gamma/r. The relation is Young-Laplace, from Thomas Young (1805) and Pierre-Simon Laplace (1806). Source: Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Pressure Differences and Curvature', 'Soap Films and Bubbles').

question: A boy tips a wet glass and a drop gathers on the rim instead of spreading into mist, because water molecules cling to each other. Yet those at the very surface act nothing like those deep in the glass. What makes the ones at the top different?
answer: Nothing tugs at them from above, so their pull runs down and out
choices: Nothing tugs at them from above, so their pull runs down and out
The weight of the whole atmosphere squeezes them flat from above
They move far faster than the molecules below and barely cling
They sit colder than the water below, so they cling much harder
context: A molecule down in the bulk is pulled equally in every direction by its neighbours, and the forces cancel to nothing. A molecule at the top has neighbours only below and beside it, so the pull is unbalanced and the whole surface is dragged inward, contracting like stretched elastic. Water's version is anomalously strong for so small a molecule, about 0.0728 N/m at 20 degrees C, because hydrogen bonds grip far harder than the van der Waals forces holding oils and hydrocarbons together. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Basis in physics: cohesion'); Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Molecular Causes').

question: A cook dips one corner of a paper towel into a saucer of water, and the water climbs up into the dry paper against gravity. She stands a narrow glass tube in the same saucer and the water climbs that too, higher the narrower the tube. Why does the water rise?
answer: Water grips the glass more strongly than it grips itself
choices: Water grips the glass more strongly than it grips itself
Air pressing on the saucer squeezes water into the tube
Evaporation at the top drags the column along behind it
The narrow tube walls pinch the water and force it upward
context: Capillary action. Water wets glass, sticking to the wall harder than to itself, and the surface drags a column up behind it. James Jurin established the law experimentally in 1712: h = 2*gamma*cos(theta)/(rho*g*r), so the rise is inversely proportional to the tube's radius. Halve the tube and you double the climb; a tube of 0.1 mm radius lifts water about 15 cm. Test it tonight with a paper-towel corner in a saucer of coloured water. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Capillary action'; Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Capillary Rise in Tubes').

question: Benjamin Franklin carried a teaspoon of olive oil out to Mount Pond on Clapham Common in London, where the wind had the whole pond rough, and poured it on. He set down what happened in a letter of 7 November 1773 that was read to the Royal Society. What did that one teaspoon do?
answer: It spread until half an acre lay smooth as a looking-glass
choices: It spread until half an acre lay smooth as a looking-glass
It drew the ripples into a ring of ridges around one spot
It gathered into a single lens about the size of a plate
It broke into ribbons and sank out of sight in a minute
context: Franklin wrote it up to William Brownrigg on 7 November 1773; the letter was read to the Royal Society and printed in Philosophical Transactions in 1774 as 'Of the Stilling of Waves by Means of Oil'. He hedged the size himself - perhaps half an acre - and he never did the arithmetic. Do it with his own numbers: half an acre is 2,420 square metres, a teaspoon about 2 x 10^-6 cubic metres, and the division gives 9.9 x 10^-10 metres, a thickness that would wait more than a century for anyone to explain. Sources: Royal Society of Chemistry Education, 'Franklin's teaspoon of oil'; Founders Online, 'Benjamin Franklin to William Brownrigg, 7 November 1773'; Grokipedia, 'Langmuir-Blodgett film'.

question: A boy touches dish soap to a glass of water, and the water's surface tension, the pull along its top layer, falls from about 72 millinewtons per metre to nearer 35. The soap has not made the water heavier. It has crowded up into the very top layer and shouldered the water molecules apart. What drives a soap molecule up into the surface in the first place?
answer: One end of it loves water and the other cannot stand it
choices: One end of it loves water and the other cannot stand it
It weighs far less than water and simply floats to the top
It carries a charge the water shoves away from itself
It is a coil that unwinds where the water meets the air
context: Soap molecules are amphiphilic: a water-loving head and a water-hating tail. The tails cannot stand being surrounded by water, so the molecules pile up at the surface with the tails sticking out, wedging between the water molecules and breaking their grip on one another. Surface tension falls by 50-90%. It is also why soapy water WETS things that plain water beads off. Source: Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Role of Surfactants').

question: A teacher scatters ground pepper across a plate of water, and the flecks sit where they land. She touches one drop of dish soap to the middle of the plate, and the pepper does not drift: it is flung to the rim in an instant, even the flecks already a hand's width out. What flings them?
answer: The untouched water around them, pulling the surface outward
choices: The untouched water around them, pulling the surface outward
The soap spreading beneath them and shoving them ahead of it
A current rising in the middle of the plate and pushing out
The pepper's own oils, loosened the moment the soap arrives
context: The Marangoni effect: liquid flows FROM low surface tension TOWARD high. The soap makes a weak patch in the middle, and the strong untouched water all round it wins the tug-of-war and hauls the surface - and the pepper - outward. James Thomson, Lord Kelvin's brother, first spotted the effect in 1855 watching the 'tears of wine' crawl up a wine glass; it is named for Carlo Marangoni, whose 1865 doctoral thesis at Pavia was on a drop of liquid spreading over another liquid. Build the raft version: a notched card with a dab of soap in the notch shoots forward, pulled by the higher tension in front of it. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Marangoni effect'; Scientific American, 'Surface Tension Science: Build a Raft Powered by Soap'.

question: Agnes Pockels finished building her own instrument by 1882, at the age of twenty, after German universities refused her a place for no reason but her sex. The instrument, for measuring the pull of a water surface, was a metal trough about seventy centimetres long, filled to the brim, with a sliding metal strip to sweep it clean. How did she read the strength of that pull?
answer: A button hung from a balance, weighed as it tore free of the water
choices: A button hung from a balance, weighed as it tore free of the water
A narrow tube stood in the trough, read for how high water climbed
A dropper tip watched closely, timed for how long a drop hung on
A small float set on the surface, watched for how deep it sank in
context: The 'Schieberinne', or slide-trough: a rectangular metal trough about 70 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2 cm deep, filled to the brim; a movable metal strip laid across the surface to sweep it clean and squeeze a film into a measured area, its position read off a ruler; and a disc about 6 mm across hung from an apothecary's balance and lifted until the water film tore free. Pockels dated her own start in a note: '1882: I have developed the Schieberinne.' Sources: Wikipedia, 'Agnes Pockels'; TU Braunschweig, 'Who was Agnes Pockels?'; Europa-Universitat Flensburg, 'The slide trough on the model of Agnes Pockels'.

question: Agnes Pockels wrote in German to Lord Rayleigh in England in January 1891, asking pardon for troubling him with a German note on a scientific subject. He was one of the most respected physicists alive; she had no university post and no way to publish. What did Rayleigh do with her letter?
answer: Had his wife translate it and sent it on to Nature to be printed
choices: Had his wife translate it and sent it on to Nature to be printed
Repeated all of her measurements for two years before naming her
Wrote back urging her to apply to a German university at once
Published her findings himself, with a footnote of thanks to her
context: Rayleigh's wife translated the letter, and he forwarded it to Nature with a covering note asking the editor to find space for the work of a German lady who, with very homely appliances, had arrived at valuable results on the behaviour of contaminated water surfaces. It ran as 'Surface Tension', Nature vol. 43, pp. 437-439, 1891. He later asked her to build him a trough of his own. (TU Braunschweig dates the letter 1890 and Wikipedia 10 January 1891; the Nature volume year is firm.) Sources: A. Pockels, 'Surface Tension', Nature 43, 437-439 (1891); Wikipedia, 'Agnes Pockels'; Chemistry World, 'Pockels' trough'.

question: Brigitte Van Tiggelen, a historian of chemistry, has said she never heard anyone explain Irving Langmuir's interest in surface films by his washing-up. Yet the story usually told of Agnes Pockels makes her a lucky housewife at the sink. Pockels worked a purpose-built trough for years. When a step in her own procedure began skewing her readings, what did she do?
answer: Wrote to Lord Rayleigh herself to report her own mistake
choices: Wrote to Lord Rayleigh herself to report her own mistake
Set the flawed run aside and began the whole series again
Rebuilt her trough to a new design before measuring again
Asked her brother Friedrich to check the figures over first
context: The kitchen-sink story is a distortion worth naming. Van Tiggelen's point is that nobody explains Rayleigh's or Langmuir's interest in surface films by their washing-up, and Pockels deserves the same reading: she worked a purpose-built instrument, published fourteen papers, and policed her own work - she caught her own procedural oversights and wrote to Rayleigh to correct them. She was also the one who established that apparatus cleanliness governs whether surface measurements replicate at all, the rule every later worker in the field had to obey. Rayleigh thought enough of her to ask her to build him a trough of his own. Source: Science History Institute, 'Agnes Pockels and the Kitchen Sink Myth'.

question: Mary Ellen Avery, a young Harvard researcher, ran lung washings from nine infants through a balance in 1959, one descended from Agnes Pockels's trough and built to measure the pull of a liquid's surface. The babies had been born more than eight weeks early and had died of hyaline membrane disease, their lungs stiffening and refusing to stay open, and nobody understood the cause. What did the washings reveal?
answer: The washings did nothing at all to the water's pull
choices: The washings did nothing at all to the water's pull
The washings cut the pull to almost nothing at once
The washings cut the pull, then lost it within minutes
The washings pulled far harder than plain water did
context: The foam simply was not there. Healthy lung washings are strongly surface-active; these were not active at all, which identified the missing substance and pointed straight at replacement therapy. Avery had learned to build the balance after visiting John Clements at the US Army Chemical Center in Maryland, and worked with the experimental biologist Jere Mead; the pull-a-plate-off-the-water measurement is a direct descendant of Agnes Pockels's trough. Published in the American Journal of Diseases of Children, 1959. Sources: Harvard Countway Library, 'The Story of Surfactant'; Harvard Magazine, 'Brief life of Mary Ellen Avery'; 'Historical perspective on surfactant therapy', Seminars in Fetal and Neonatal Medicine.

question: Agnes Pockels poured a trace of oil onto clean water in her trough, then slid the strip across to squeeze it into a smaller and smaller patch, reading the area off a ruler as she went. For a long way the surface pull barely shifted. Then, at one particular area, it changed abruptly. What did she work out had happened to the oil?
answer: It had been pressed down to a single molecule in thickness
choices: It had been pressed down to a single molecule in thickness
It had been squeezed out past the ends of the sliding strip
It had rolled up into visible lenses riding on the surface
It had stiffened into a solid skin under the strip
context: Divide the volume of oil by the area at which the pull jumps and you have the room one molecule takes up. Pockels put it near 20 square angstroms; modern Langmuir monolayers of fatty acids give a limiting area per molecule of 20-25 square angstroms. She was right. Lord Rayleigh ran the same idea from the other end in 1890, dropping a known volume of olive oil on a clean tray and dividing by the area it spread to, and got a film 1.6 nanometres thick. In 1932 Irving Langmuir won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for surface chemistry built on a trough refined from her design; that same year Technische Hochschule Braunschweig gave Agnes Pockels an honorary doctorate in engineering, the first woman it ever so honoured. The Colloid Society had given her the Laura R. Leonard Prize in 1931. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Agnes Pockels'; Grokipedia, 'Langmuir-Blodgett film'.

question: A swimmer draws a deep breath, and the air ends in millions of microscopic sacs, each lined with a film of liquid. The pressure inside a wet sac works out as twice the surface tension of its lining divided by the sac's radius. If that lining were plain water, pulling at about 70 millinewtons per metre, her breathing would fail within minutes. What would happen to the air sacs?
answer: The smallest sacs would empty themselves into the larger ones
choices: The smallest sacs would empty themselves into the larger ones
The largest sacs would burst and tear their neighbours open
Every sac would swell until the lung could not be emptied
Liquid would be pulled out of the sacs and flood the airways
context: Work the law through: halve the radius and you double the pressure, so the smallest sac carries the HIGHEST pressure and would blow its air into its bigger neighbours until the lung was a few slack bags. Pulmonary surfactant, roughly 40% DPPC, drops the alveolar lining from water's ~70 mN/m to about 25 mN/m at equilibrium and below 1 mN/m when the sac is small and its molecules are crowded together. Tension that falls as the sac shrinks is exactly what stops the small sacs draining into the big ones. Babies born before about 28-32 weeks have not made enough of it yet, which is what made hyaline membrane disease a killer. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pulmonary surfactant'; Young-Laplace P = 2*gamma/r.

question: A girl with a blacklight and no lab redoes George Stokes's 1852 experiment on quinine water in five minutes, aiming the light along a row of drinks from the store. One of them glows electric blue. Which drink is it?
answer: Tonic water
choices: Tonic water
Milk
Apple juice
Coca-Cola
context: Tonic water contains quinine (originally as a malaria treatment; the classic gin-and-tonic came out of British India). A cheap UV torch and a bottle of tonic water give the eerie blue Stokes saw. Source: mindat.org David Carter, 'George Gabriel Stokes and the phenomenon of fluorescence'.

question: George Stokes noticed that the glow in his quinine glass ran only one way, and he wrote a rule for it. A blacklight shows the same thing today: its ultraviolet makes a highlighter blaze on paper, while a red lamp cannot make anything glow blue, however bright. Light comes in particles called photons. Why does the trick run one way and not the other?
answer: The re-emitted photon always carries less energy than the absorbed photon
choices: The re-emitted photon always carries less energy than the absorbed photon
The re-emitted photon always carries more energy than the absorbed photon
The re-emitted photon carries exactly the same energy as the absorbed photon
The re-emitted photon carries a random fraction of the absorbed photon's energy
context: This is Stokes's rule, and the energy gap is now called the Stokes shift. The excited molecule sheds a little energy as vibration (heat) before re-emitting, so the outgoing photon is redder (longer wavelength, lower energy) than the incoming one. UV can push electrons hard enough to give off visible light; red light cannot push them hard enough to give off blue. Source: edinst.com 'What is the Stokes shift?'.

question: A boy switches off his bedroom light, and the glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling keep glowing for hours. He switches off an ultraviolet torch aimed at a highlighter, and the highlighter goes dark that instant. The two glows share the same physics up to a point, then split. Which names do they go by?
answer: The bedroom stars are phosphorescent, the highlighter is fluorescent
choices: The bedroom stars are phosphorescent, the highlighter is fluorescent
The bedroom stars are fluorescent, the highlighter is phosphorescent
Both are fluorescence, but at different temperatures
Both are phosphorescence, but at different brightnesses
context: Fluorescence releases the absorbed energy within nanoseconds; phosphorescence traps the energy in a spin-forbidden 'triplet' state that leaks slowly, so the glow can persist for seconds, minutes or hours. Modern glow-in-the-dark toys use doped strontium aluminate, much brighter than the older zinc sulphide, and no longer any radium (a story that cost the Radium Girls their lives). Source: sciencenotes.org and patsnap eureka on phosphorescence.

question: A clerk flicks the switch on a fluorescent tube over her office desk, beside a modern white LED bulb, and the two are the same trick twice. In each, light of one kind is made inside and a coating turns it into visible white light. What light does the coating in that tube actually convert?
answer: Ultraviolet from excited mercury vapour
choices: Ultraviolet from excited mercury vapour
Infrared from a heated tungsten filament
X-rays from a tiny built-in Geiger tube
Microwaves from a low-power magnetron
context: An electric discharge inside a fluorescent tube excites mercury vapour, which emits at 254 nm in the deep ultraviolet; the phosphor on the glass absorbs those UV photons and re-emits visible light (Stokes's rule, again). A common white LED does the same with a blue InGaN chip under a yellow Ce:YAG phosphor -- the leftover blue plus the phosphor's yellow mixes to white. Sources: rp-photonics.com; digikey.com on Ce:YAG.

question: Osamu Shimomura gathered jellyfish by the tens of thousands off Washington state and isolated their glowing green protein. Martin Chalfie then spliced the protein's gene beside another gene in living cells, and Roger Tsien later coaxed new colours from it. What did Chalfie's splice let biologists do?
answer: See where and when the other gene is at work in a living cell
choices: See where and when the other gene is at work in a living cell
Make the cell shine in total darkness, with no lamp on it
Make the other gene work far harder than it did before
Kill off every cell that was carrying the other gene
context: The jellyfish's own protein is green fluorescent protein, GFP. Chalfie showed in 1994 that it works as a genetic tag: spliced beside another gene, it glows wherever that gene is switched on, and later fusions let biologists watch a neuron fire, a tumour spread or a virus enter a cell. Like any fluorescent molecule it glows only while light shines on it. Tsien engineered a rainbow of variants (cyan, yellow, red) so several processes could be tracked at once, and the three men shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Source: nobelprize.org chemistry 2008.

question: Ignaz Semmelweis, a Hungarian doctor, cut deaths on his Vienna hospital birth ward in 1847 by making the doctors wash their hands in chlorine water. Other doctors mocked him instead of thanking him, and he lost his job. Where did he die in 1865, at age forty-seven?
answer: In a lunatic asylum outside the city
choices: In a private surgery in Budapest
On a ship bound for New York
In a lunatic asylum outside the city
At his family estate in the countryside
context: Semmelweis was committed to the asylum at Oberdoebling, outside Vienna, and died on 13 August 1865, two weeks after admission, of an infected wound. His hand-washing conclusion was correct and it did not save him. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/ignaz-semmelweis/

question: Alfred Wegener, a German weather scientist, said in 1912 that the continents, once joined, had drifted apart, matching coastlines and fossils across the Atlantic. Geologists said no for about fifty years, and their one solid objection was a legitimate one. What could he not tell them?
answer: Any force strong enough to move a continent
choices: Any force strong enough to move a continent
Any rock layers that matched across the ocean
Any sign that ancient climates had shifted
Any era in which the continents had split
context: Wegener proposed tidal effects and centrifugal forces from Earth's rotation as the drivers, and geophysicists showed those forces were orders of magnitude too weak. He did bring matching rock formations, evidence of ancient climates and an order of events for the break-up; what he lacked was the engine. The objection was scientifically legitimate; the personal ridicule was not. Vindication came in the 1960s with symmetrical seafloor magnetic stripes -- decades after Wegener died on the Greenland ice sheet in November 1930. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2019/01/alfred-wegener-theory-continental-drift

question: Barry Marshall hit the same wall as Ignaz Semmelweis and Alfred Wegener before him: a right conclusion, rejected for a stretch of years. Calling the critics stupid is tempting, but the pattern is more useful than that. What did each man lack in his own moment that gave his critics a genuine reason to hold back?
answer: A complete argument for WHY his conclusion had to be true
choices: A complete argument for WHY his conclusion had to be true
The willingness to publish his findings in a real journal
The support of at least one working colleague in his field
A method for gathering the data that he had presented
context: Semmelweis had no germ theory and could not say what invisible thing hand-washing removed. Wegener could name no force that could move continents. Marshall's bacteria contradicted the established acid-and-stress model of the stomach. In each case the dissenter had the right conclusion and an incomplete argument -- and that is what real dissent usually looks like from inside. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_reaction_to_Ignaz_Semmelweis

question: Ignaz Semmelweis took mockery in the 1840s for telling doctors to wash their hands between the morgue and the delivery room. Alfred Wegener took it in the 1910s for saying the continents drift across the globe, and Barry Marshall in the 1980s for insisting a common bacterium, not stress, causes most stomach ulcers. All three lonely fights ended the same way, yet mockery alone proves nobody right. In that tradition, what actually settles a science fight?
answer: A test that could lose for either side, and someone willing to run it
choices: A test that could lose for either side, and someone willing to run it
A prediction that matches whatever the later data turn out to be
A mechanism that only the original lab has managed to reproduce
A theory elegant enough that a counter-example seems unlikely
context: The mark of a real dispute is that somebody proposes an experiment that could lose. Franklin's 1784 blindfolded trial killed Mesmerism; Marshall's beaker settled the ulcer question in his own body; Eddington's 1919 eclipse gave general relativity a way to fail on the sky. A prediction that can be reshaped after the data, a result no other lab can reproduce, or a theory whose beauty is treated as evidence -- none of these can settle a real dispute. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Report_of_the_Commissioners_charged_by_the_King_with_the_Examination_of_Animal_Magnetism

question: Stalin's police arrested the botanist Nikolai Vavilov in August 1940, under Trofim Lysenko's rising influence. Vavilov had built in Leningrad the world's first great collection of crop seeds, so that whatever else happened his country would keep its food supply. How did he die?
answer: Of hunger in a Soviet prison at Saratov
choices: Executed by firing squad in a Moscow courtyard
Killed in a bombing raid on Leningrad
Of hunger in a Soviet prison at Saratov
Of typhus in a Siberian labour camp
context: Vavilov died on 26 January 1943 in the NKVD prison at Saratov, on a diet of mashed cabbage and mouldy flour. The seed bank in Leningrad survived the siege because his colleagues starved to death guarding the stocks rather than eat them. Lysenkoism remained official Soviet science until 1965. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-tragedy-of-the-worlds-first-seed-bank/

question: Léon Foucault hung a 28 kg lead bob on a 67-metre wire under the Panthéon's dome on 26 March 1851. Astronomers had reasoned out the Earth's daily spin, but nobody had ever watched it in a room. What did the crowd see the swing do?
answer: The plane crept round and knocked over pegs set in a floor ring
choices: The plane crept round and knocked over pegs set in a floor ring
The bob slowed to a halt despite no visible source of friction
The swing held one line over the same pegs from dawn to dusk
The bob swung higher on one side, flung by the spinning Earth
context: The pendulum swung in a fixed plane, but the floor and the whole city rotated underneath it, so the plane appeared to sweep round the ring hour by hour and topple pegs one by one. It was the first time a person could walk into a room and watch the Earth turn -- until then, Earth's rotation had only been inferred from astronomy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foucault_pendulum

question: Léon Foucault worried that critics could explain his Panthéon pendulum away. So in 1852 he built a second proof that needed no swinging: a heavy wheel spun fast inside a frame free to turn any way. He named it the gyroscope, from Greek for 'to see the turning.' How did the wheel show the Earth turning?
answer: Its axis held one direction in space while Paris turned round it
choices: Its axis held one direction in space while Paris turned round it
Its spin slowed and quickened in step with the Earth's turning
Its frame crept round, dragged by the slowly turning room air
Its wheel spun on for days, driven by the Earth's own spin
context: Foucault felt his pendulum was too easily explained away, so he built a spinning-wheel apparatus whose axis stayed fixed in space while the Earth rotated beneath it; watched against the room, the axis seemed to drift, just as the pendulum's swing had crept round its pegs. He named it 'gyroscope' from Greek gyros (circle) and skopein (to see) -- literally 'a device to see the turning.' Its descendants now sit inside every phone, drone and spacecraft. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foucault's_gyroscope

question: Frances Oldham, a young Canadian pharmacologist, applied to E. M. K. Geiling's laboratory at the University of Chicago in 1936, and the reply offering her the post began 'Dear Mr. Oldham.' She wrote to her McGill supervisor, Dr. Stehle, asking whether she should correct the mistake before accepting. What did Stehle tell her to do?
answer: Sign her name, add 'Miss' in brackets, and go.
choices: Sign her name, add 'Miss' in brackets, and go.
Write back correcting the error, then accept.
Turn it down and apply again under her full name.
Say nothing about it until she reached Chicago.
context: Stehle's exact words were 'Don't be ridiculous. Accept the job, sign your name, put Miss in brackets afterwards, and go!' She did. Kelsey never learned whether the mix-up mattered: 'to this day, I do not know if my name had been Elizabeth or Mary Jane, whether I would have gotten that first big step up. My professor at Chicago to his dying day would never admit one way or the other.' That Chicago training is what put her, twenty-four years later, at the FDA desk where the thalidomide application landed. Source: Frances O. Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.12-13 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: Frances Kelsey held up Richardson-Merrell's thalidomide file for more than a year after the firm filed it to sell the drug in America. Normal drug files, she later said, ran 150 to 200 volumes each, and a volume was 'the size of a city phone book.' How many volumes was the whole thalidomide file?
answer: Four.
choices: Four.
Fourteen.
Forty.
Ninety.
context: Four volumes, for a drug already being swallowed nightly across Europe. Thin files were normal in 1960: under the law then in force a company had to show only that a drug would not poison you, so there was not much to file. Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), p.48 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: Frances Kelsey's supervisors at the Food and Drug Administration handed her two easy files to break her in gently, barely a month into the job. One was the sleeping pill thalidomide, which she held up for over a year. The other was a rectal enema called Lavema. What did she do with that one?
answer: She approved it, and it went on sale.
choices: She approved it, and it went on sale.
She held that file up too, for months.
She passed it to another reviewer instead.
She turned it down for want of animal data.
context: 'It did get marketed, so I must have approved it,' Kelsey said. She was not a reflexive no-sayer: handed two files the same month, she cleared one and stopped the other, and the difference was the evidence in front of her. She had started at the FDA on 1 August 1960; thalidomide reached her in early September, only her second assignment. Her comment on the supervisors' prediction: 'I never got another one quite like that one.' Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), p.49 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: The contact man from Richardson-Merrell stopped arguing about the science on one of his many calls to Frances Kelsey, she said, and stated outright why the company was in such a hurry. She had already held its thalidomide file open for a year. What reason did he give?
answer: Christmas was its best sales season for sedatives.
choices: Christmas was its best sales season for sedatives.
A rival American firm was about to file the same drug.
Its European patent was close to running out.
Its whole stock of tablets was close to expiring.
context: Kelsey's account: 'There was, for example, the time they kept calling me, and they just came right out and said, "We want to get this drug on the market before Christmas, because that is when our best sales are."' They had aimed at the 1960 season, missed it, and were watching a second Christmas go by. She did not move. Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.63 and 74 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: A Scottish doctor sent the British Medical Journal a letter dated 31 December 1960 and headed 'Is Thalidomide to Blame?' It described four patients who had taken the drug nightly for over a year and developed prickling numbness spreading from their feet. Frances Kelsey found it herself, browsing at her desk weeks later. What had held it up?
answer: A mail strike had delayed the FDA's journals.
choices: A mail strike had delayed the FDA's journals.
Her supervisors had routed it to another officer.
The journal had printed it in a late supplement.
The FDA library bound issues before circulating them.
context: Kelsey: 'Although this issue had been published on 31 December 1960, there was a problem with delivery of our journals - I think it was a mail strike - and the journal did not reach us until late January or early February.' The letter was written by Dr. A. Leslie Florence, a Scottish general practitioner (BMJ 1960;2(5217):1954). A mail strike delayed the clue that stopped the drug - and it reached her at all only because she read the journals herself, through no official channel. Sources: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), p.55 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download; Florence AL, BMJ 1960 - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2098660/

question: Frances Kelsey went through the drug maker's reports on patients already given thalidomide and judged that they could not carry the claims the company had built on them. Her first objection was not about a symptom or a dose but about the kind of evidence in the file. What did she say was wrong with those reports?
answer: They were testimonials rather than well-executed studies.
choices: They were testimonials rather than well-executed studies.
They counted patients but never followed them past a month.
They came from doctors the company itself had paid.
They described European patients only, never Americans.
