context: In her words the reports 'were more in the nature of testimonials rather than well-designed, well-executed studies,' and 'the claims made in the NDA for thalidomide were too glowing for the support in the way of clinical back-up.' A doctor vouching for a drug is not the same as anyone measuring it - which is exactly the distinction Congress would write into American law two years later. Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.52-54 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: 'All three of us found problems,' Frances Kelsey said of the thalidomide file, and she spent the rest of her life correcting the story that she had stood alone. Jiro Oyama had read it as pharmacologist at the Food and Drug Administration, and Lee Geismar as chemist. What did Geismar find?
answer: Mistakes in the company's translations of the German data.
choices: Mistakes in the company's translations of the German data.
An impurity in the sample tablets the company had sent.
A dose in the file ten times the one used in Europe.
A German study the application had quietly left out.
context: Geismar had trained in Germany and could read the original German submissions, so she caught errors in Richardson-Merrell's translations. The lone-heroine version of this story is the legend, and Kelsey never told it that way: accepting the President's Award in 1962 she said she was taking it 'on behalf of a lot of different federal workers. This was really a team effort.' Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.51-52 and p.79 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: Frances Kelsey kept the American application for thalidomide open in early 1961, against its makers' years of European sales. The drug was a sedative already taken nightly across Europe, and she had a British report of four patients left with prickling numbness spreading from their feet to their hands. She could not say what it was doing inside the body. What was her reason for holding on?
answer: Nerve damage is not what a simple sleeping pill should do.
choices: Nerve damage is not what a simple sleeping pill should do.
Four cases from one practice outweighed Europe's sales record.
The numbness matched a known reaction to other sedatives.
A drug taken nightly for years needed years of testing.
context: Her own sentence is the hinge of the whole review: 'the peripheral neuritis did not seem the sort of side effect that should come from a simple sleeping pill.' Peripheral neuritis is damage to the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. Kelsey did not know what thalidomide did. She knew it was doing something a sleeping pill has no business doing, and that was enough to keep asking. The report was Dr. A. Leslie Florence's letter in the British Medical Journal of 31 December 1960. Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), p.55 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: Frances Kelsey faced a sixty-day clock on the thalidomide application under the 1938 law: if the Food and Drug Administration raised no objection, or simply forgot the deadline, the drug became approved on its own. She had no power to reject it outright, but one procedural move restarted those sixty days, and she used it from November 1960 onward for over a year. What was the move?
answer: Declaring the application incomplete.
choices: Declaring the application incomplete.
Referring the file to an outside panel.
Demanding a fresh set of animal tests.
Objecting in writing to her division chief.
context: Kelsey: 'if we had no objection or if we forgot that the 60 days had elapsed, the drug automatically became approved.' Ruling the file incomplete restarted the clock, and she did it over and over for fourteen months. She never had the power to say no to thalidomide - only the power to keep saying not yet. Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.49-50 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download; corroborated at https://grokipedia.com/page/Frances_Oldham_Kelsey

question: Frances Kelsey and a colleague ran their own experiment on quinine in rabbits during the war, hunting for a malaria drug, and measured how a pregnant mother and her embryos each handled it. Years later Richardson-Merrell assured the Food and Drug Administration that thalidomide never reached an unborn child, so a pregnant woman could take it safely. What had Kelsey's rabbits actually shown her?
answer: The mother rabbits broke quinine down poorly, and the embryos not at all.
choices: The mother rabbits broke quinine down poorly, and the embryos not at all.
Quinine crossed into the embryos, which cleared it as fast as adults.
Pregnancy sped the breakdown of quinine in mother and embryo alike.
Quinine gathered in the embryos' bones and leaked out after birth.
context: 'We found that during pregnancy there was less ability in the mother to break down the quinine and that the embryo rabbits had no ability at all to do so until after birth.' The work came out of the WWII antimalarial program - with the Dutch East Indies lost, about 90 percent of the Allies' quinine supply had vanished, and a crash program screened over 14,000 candidate compounds. Note how fast Kelsey deflates her own result: 'This is not something we discovered. In fact, after we thought that we had done so, we found that it had been discovered after the First World War.' Her one-sentence principle: 'When you give a drug to a pregnant woman you are exposing, in fact, two people to the drug, the mother and the child.' Sources: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.25-29 and p.61 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: President Kennedy signed the Kefauver-Harris amendments in October 1962. Under the 1938 law Frances Kelsey had worked with, a drugmaker needed to show just one thing before selling a new drug: that it would not poison anyone. The amendments added a second thing every maker had to prove. What was it?
answer: That the drug actually did what the label claimed.
choices: That the drug actually did what the label claimed.
That the drug had been tested on pregnant animals.
That the drug had been approved abroad already.
That the drug could not be taken in a fatal dose.
context: Public Law 87-781 demanded 'substantial evidence' of effectiveness, and the statute spelled out what would count: 'adequate and well-controlled investigations, including clinical investigations, by experts qualified by scientific training and experience.' Testimonials were explicitly no longer enough. Richardson-Merrell had withdrawn its application on 8 March 1962, and Kelsey was careful about the credit: 'There is nothing that would lead me to think we had requested the withdrawal. I think Merrell withdrew it of their own accord when they were finally convinced that there really was a problem.' Sources: Grokipedia 'Kefauver-Harris Amendment' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Kefauver%E2%80%93Harris_Amendment; Kelsey (FDA), p.68 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: The drug company's own contact man telephoned the Food and Drug Administration on 30 November 1961 with the news that the German maker was withdrawing thalidomide. A Hamburg pediatrician named Widukind Lenz had tied it to babies born with severely shortened limbs. Frances Kelsey said she was very surprised: in more than a year of holding the file she had never predicted that particular harm. On what, then, had her objections rested?
answer: That no one had yet produced evidence the drug was safe.
choices: That no one had yet produced evidence the drug was safe.
That the German safety reports covered too few patients.
That the drug's chemistry resembled a known poison.
That nobody had followed the numbness cases to the end.
context: Kelsey: 'I remember very well when he called... I was - I admit it - very surprised. This was what we had been wanting to make sure would not happen with the drug and it appeared it had.' And then the honest note the whole story turns on: 'Our objections... were really on theoretical grounds, largely based on the fact that there was no evidence that it was safe.' She was not clairvoyant. She refused to assume safety, which is a different and repeatable thing. Lenz first suspected the drug on 11 November 1961, telephoned Chemie Grunenthal on 16 November demanding withdrawal, and presented at a Dusseldorf conference on 18 November, having found that 41 of 46 mothers of affected babies had taken it early in pregnancy. The Australian obstetrician William McBride reached the same conclusion independently; his letter ran in The Lancet on 16 December 1961, two weeks after this phone call. Sources: Kelsey (FDA), p.66 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download; Widukind Lenz, 'The History of Thalidomide,' 1992 UNITH Congress - https://www.thalidomide.ca/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Dr-Lenz-history-of-thalidomide-1992.pdf; James Lind Library, McBride WG (1961) - https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/mcbride-wg-1961/

question: An American doctor accepted 'investigational' samples of thalidomide from Richardson-Merrell, though the drug was never approved for sale in the United States. The firm had been shipping it this way for over a year, through a channel the 1938 law barely covered, and the list of investigators it filed named some thirty or forty doctors. How much of the drug had actually gone out?
answer: About 2.5 million tablets, to more than a thousand doctors.
choices: About 2.5 million tablets, to more than a thousand doctors.
About 90,000 tablets, to roughly three hundred doctors.
About 250,000 tablets, to roughly six hundred doctors.
About 12 million tablets, to some eight thousand doctors.
context: The tablets reached an estimated 15,000-20,000 patients, over 600 of them pregnant. Seventeen affected babies were confirmed born in the United States; in about half of those cases the drug had come from overseas, and the FDA could tie ten to the American samples. Kelsey later described what the other doctors had been told: that the drug 'was about to come to market and that they need not bother much about keeping records.' The 'clinical trial' was a sales program, and the FDA learned its real scale only after the withdrawal. America's win here was scale, not perfection - say it plainly. Sources: Kelsey (FDA), pp.58, 71-72, 75 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download; Grokipedia 'Frances Oldham Kelsey' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Frances_Oldham_Kelsey; Smithsonian Magazine - https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/woman-who-stood-between-america-and-epidemic-birth-defects-180963165/

question: Sam Peltzman, an economist, counted the genuinely new drug compounds introduced in the United States each year, before and after the law of 1962 that raised the proof a drugmaker had to show before selling. Demanding proof had kept thalidomide out of American shops. What did his count show?
answer: A fall from about 43 a year to about 16.
choices: A fall from about 43 a year to about 16.
A rise from about 16 a year to about 43.
A steady rate of about 40 a year throughout.
A fall from about 90 a year to about 60.
context: Peltzman's count is the second edge of this story, and both edges are true. Demanding proof is what kept thalidomide away from American mothers. Demanding proof also costs time that sick people do not always have: critics of the 1962 amendments point to a 'drug lag' in which new therapies reached European patients years before American ones. The point is not that the regulator is always right - Kelsey herself said her objections were theoretical. The point is that a claim with no evidence behind it is not yet knowledge, whoever is making it and whichever answer its hearer was hoping for. Source: Grokipedia 'Kefauver-Harris Amendment', Criticisms and Controversies - https://grokipedia.com/page/Kefauver%E2%80%93Harris_Amendment

question: Benjamin Franklin wrote out a plan for a storm kite in Philadelphia in June 1752: two light cedar strips tied in a cross, a sharp wire rising a foot above the wood, and a cover picked to hold up through an hour of hard rain. What did he stretch across the cross?
answer: A large thin silk handkerchief.
choices: A large thin silk handkerchief.
A light square of oiled canvas.
A thin sheet of dressed calfskin.
A fine panel of woven linen.
context: Franklin's own recipe, printed in the Pennsylvania Gazette of 19 October 1752: 'a small Cross of two light Strips of Cedar' with 'a large thin Silk Handkerchief' tied to the four corners, and 'a very sharp pointed Wire, rising a Foot or more above the Wood.' Silk rather than the paper of a child's kite, because paper tears apart once a storm soaks it and this kite had to survive the whole downpour. The instrument that asked the sky a question was a handkerchief, two sticks and a wire. Sources: Franklin, Pennsylvania Gazette, 19 Oct 1752, quoted at the Benjamin Franklin Historical Society (benjamin-franklin-history.org/kite-experiment/); Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment.

question: Benjamin Franklin told the flier of his 1752 storm kite what to watch for as a thundercloud rolls in. Before the rain even reaches the kite, the plain hemp twine gives the first clue of electricity gathering above. What does the twine do?
answer: Its loose fibres stand out from it in every direction.
choices: Its loose fibres stand out from it in every direction.
It glows faintly with a pale light along its length.
It grows warm enough to feel through a glove.
It stiffens and draws itself taut as a bar of iron.
context: Franklin's words: when a thundercloud comes over, 'the loose Filaments of the Twine will stand out every Way, and be attracted by an approaching Finger.' The order matters and is usually retold backwards. The fibres separate BEFORE the rain arrives; only afterwards, once 'the Rain has wet the Kite and Twine,' does the fire 'stream out plentifully from the Key on the Approach of your Knuckle.' Sources: Franklin, Pennsylvania Gazette, 19 Oct 1752, quoted at The Franklin Institute (fi.edu) and the Benjamin Franklin Historical Society.

question: An engraver drew Benjamin Franklin flying his kite with a helper at his elbow, holding the string. There really was an assistant that day, named William, and he and Franklin were the only people present. What did engravers like that one get wrong about William?
answer: He was a grown adult, not a small boy
choices: He was a grown adult, not a small boy
He was Franklin's servant, not his son
He was holding a different tool, not the string
He was standing far away, not at Franklin's elbow
context: William Franklin was twenty-one, a grown man, and he and his father were the only witnesses — no independent observer ever attested to the experiment. In 2023 the Brazilian researcher Breno Arsioli Moura examined seven nineteenth-century illustrations of the kite flight and catalogued their errors, among them lightning shown striking the kite, Franklin shown gripping the conducting string with his bare hand, and William drawn as a young child. The picture is the myth's delivery vehicle. Sources: Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment; Moura, 'Picturing Benjamin Franklin's Kite Experiment in the Nineteenth Century,' Science & Education (2023).

question: Benjamin Franklin stood under shelter as fire streamed from a key to a knuckle held near it, the charge drawn off the cloud down rain-soaked hemp twine. Every picture shows a bolt hitting the kite, but no bolt came, and the Franklin Institute says a real strike would probably have killed him. The charge stopped at the key, because what he held beyond it was not twine. What was it?
answer: A dry silk ribbon.
choices: A dry silk ribbon.
A waxed leather strap.
A short glass rod.
A dry cedar stick.
context: Franklin's instructions put the flier 'within a Door, or Window, or under some Cover, so that the Silk Ribbon may not be wet.' The conducting hemp twine ended at the key, and past the key he held nothing but that ribbon: wet twine carries a charge, dry silk does not, so the storm stopped at the key. Silk, glass, wax and dry wood were the insulators every electrician of the century reached for — Franklin chose the one that could be tied to a line and held in a fist. The rest of the famous picture is wrong too. The Franklin Institute states it flatly: 'Franklin's kite was not struck by lightning. If it had been, he probably would have been electrocuted, experts say.' There was no strike and no flash at the kite at all — the sharp wire above it drew charge silently off a passing thundercloud, and the whole safety of the thing rested on one dry ribbon. Sources: Franklin, Pennsylvania Gazette, 19 Oct 1752, quoted at the Benjamin Franklin Historical Society (benjamin-franklin-history.org/kite-experiment/); The Franklin Institute (fi.edu); Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment.

question: Johann Fischer of Munich counted in 1784 what one European custom had cost over thirty-three years: bell towers struck 386 times, 103 ringers killed at the ropes. Towns had been meeting each thunderstorm by sending men up the towers to haul on the bells. What did the towns believe the peal did to the storm?
answer: That its sound broke the thunderstorm apart over the town.
choices: That its sound broke the thunderstorm apart over the town.
That its sound drove the hail out of the cloud before it fell.
That its sound turned the storm aside toward open country.
That its sound drew the lightning safely into the bell metal.
context: Fischer's 1784 Munich study was titled 'A Proof that the Ringing of Bells during Thunderstorms may be more Dangerous than Useful.' Across the thirty-three years from 1750 to 1783 he counted bell towers struck 386 times and 103 ringers killed on the ropes. The belief was cast into the metal itself: many church bells carry the motto fulgura frango, 'I break the lightning' — the peal was thought to shatter the storm overhead, so the worse the sky looked, the harder the men pulled. Bans on storm-ringing followed in France. This is the world Franklin's rod walked into: a remedy against lightning that reliably killed the men who worked it. Sources: Fischer (Munich, 1784), as reported at The History Blog (thehistoryblog.com/archives/43119) and campaners.com.

question: Benjamin Franklin ran the charge off his kite line into a Leyden jar, the glass bottle electricians used for storing a charge, because a spark at a key proved little by itself: electricians drew sparks from rubbed glass globes in drawing rooms all over Europe. Then he spent the storm's charge on an ordinary laboratory demonstration. What did the charge do?
answer: It set a dish of alcohol alight.
choices: It set a dish of alcohol alight.
It swung a compass needle aside.
It boiled a spoonful of water.
It melted a thin lead wire.
context: Franklin charged a Leyden jar from the key and used the collected charge to run ordinary bench demonstrations, including igniting spirits — alcohol — exactly as electricians did with charge from a rubbed glass globe. That identity, not the spark, was the discovery: the fire from the sky behaved in every way like the fire made on a laboratory bench. Source: Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment.

question: Benjamin Franklin sent Peter Collinson in London a way to find out whether storm clouds carry electricity, two years before any kite flew. He printed the plan without ever trying it, leaving the risk to whoever built it first. What did the 1750 letter describe?
answer: A sentry box on a high tower, a man inside on an insulating stand under an iron rod.
choices: A sentry box on a high tower, a man inside on an insulating stand under an iron rod.
A copper wire on an arrow shot up into a cloud base and traced to a jar below.
A ring of iron posts round a field, wired together to catch the storm as it crossed.
A tall mast raised out at sea, where ships were struck far oftener than buildings.
context: Franklin to Peter Collinson, 'Opinions and Conjectures,' 29 July 1750: a sentry box on a high tower or steeple, a man standing inside on an insulating stand of wood and glass, and a sharp-pointed iron rod 20 to 30 feet long rising from the roof; the observer would present a key or an electroscope to the rod's wire to see whether the cloud was charged. He published the dangerous design two years before anyone ran it. It reached France because Buffon demonstrated Franklin's electrical experiments to King Louis XV in March 1752 and Dalibard translated Franklin's book into French — which is how a Philadelphia printer's design ended up standing in a field outside Paris. Sources: Founders Online (Franklin to Collinson, 29 July 1750); Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment; Physics Today, 'Benjamin Franklin and lightning rods.'

question: Jacques de Romas flew his own kite at a storm at Nérac in France on 7 June 1753. Instead of waiting for rain to make plain hemp conduct, he had woven a metal wire into the string. Benjamin Franklin's line gave sparks a man could draw with his knuckle. What did de Romas record from his?
answer: Sparks about ten feet long, heard cracking across the town.
choices: Sparks about ten feet long, heard cracking across the town.
Sparks about a hand's breadth, hissing on and off for a minute.
A single spark that burned a hole clean through his wooden reel.
A steady blue glow that ran along the wire as the cloud passed.
context: De Romas recorded sparks roughly three metres long, with explosions loud enough to be heard in the town. He and Franklin devised the kite version independently, and only one of them is remembered. The figures come from de Romas's own report. Sources: Wikipedia, Jacques de Romas; Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment.

question: Thomas-François Dalibard built Benjamin Franklin's published design at Marly-la-Ville, north of Paris: a 40-foot iron rod sharpened at the top, on a wooden platform insulated by wine bottles. He was away when the storm broke on 10 May 1752, with the kite still a full month off. Someone else stood at the rod that afternoon and drew the sparks, the first any human hand had pulled from a thundercloud. Who was it?
answer: Coiffier, a retired dragoon.
choices: Coiffier, a retired dragoon.
Raulet, the village priest.
Buffon, the royal naturalist.
Nollet, an abbé and electrician.
context: Dalibard's assistant Thomas-François Coiffier, a retired dragoon, drew the crackling sparks between two and three in the afternoon of 10 May 1752. The village priest, Father Raulet, was fetched to confirm it with an electroscope and reported bluish flames, a sulfurous smell, and shocks like a Leyden jar; Dalibard reported the result to the Académie Royale des Sciences three days later, on 13 May. The design had reached France because Buffon demonstrated Franklin's electrical experiments to King Louis XV in March 1752 and Dalibard translated Franklin's book into French. The first human being ever to pull sparks out of a thundercloud was not a scientist but a retired soldier standing in for one, and it happened a month before Franklin's kite: the proposal had outrun the proposer. Sources: Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment; Physics Today, which calls him 'a retired French dragoon.'

question: Georg Wilhelm Richmann stood a foot from the iron bar he had wired to his roof in St Petersburg on 6 August 1753, repeating Benjamin Franklin's storm experiments, when a globe of blue and whitish fire about four inches across struck his forehead and killed him. Franklin's rod recipe insisted on one thing Richmann's apparatus did not have. What was it?
answer: A conductor carrying the charge down into damp earth.
choices: A conductor carrying the charge down into damp earth.
A copper chain looping from the bar across to the chimney.
A pane of glass set between the bar and the roof timbers.
A silk cord held between the observer and the metal.
context: Franklin's recipe in Poor Richard's Almanack for 1753, 'How to secure Houses, &c. from LIGHTNING,' specifies an iron rod 'of such a Length, that one End being three or four Feet in the moist Ground, the other may be six or eight Feet above the highest Part of the Building.' The damp earth is the load-bearing part: the charge must be given a path that is not the building, and not the man. Richmann's bar had none. Franklin printed the Academy's account of the death in his own Pennsylvania Gazette on 5 March 1754. The autopsy is worth knowing because the usual retelling is wrong: there was no burn on him at all and his hair was 'not in the least burned' — only an oval red mark on the forehead 'about the Bigness of a Rouble' and his left shoe torn in two places. The Academy's engraver, Sokolov, was thrown to the floor by the blast, his clothes burned by flying wire fragments, and survived; his description of the four-inch glowing globe is the first reliable scientific report of ball lightning. Nothing in this story is a thing to try. Sources: Pennsylvania Gazette, 5 March 1754 (todayinsci.com); Grokipedia /page/Georg_Wilhelm_Richmann; Poor Richard's Almanack 1753 via the Pennsylvania Center for the Book.

question: Benjamin Wilson, a painter and electrician, said blunt round rods were safer after lightning damaged the gunpowder store at Purfleet in May 1777, even with Franklin's pointed rods on top. He staged a show at the Pantheon on Oxford Street, a 47-metre spark machine of foil and paper fired at a scale model of the arsenal. King George III watched, in the middle of Britain's war with Franklin's America. What did the King do next?
answer: He had blunt knobs fitted to the roof of his own palace.
choices: He had blunt knobs fitted to the roof of his own palace.
He had blunt knobs fitted to every powder magazine in England.
He had the Royal Society withdraw its report on Purfleet.
He had Wilson appointed his adviser on the whole question.
context: George III had the pointed conductors on the Queen's House (Buckingham House) replaced with blunt knobs, and the Dictionary of National Biography records the king declaring that Wilson's experiments were enough to convince 'the apple-women in Covent Garden.' A question about the shape of a metal tip had become a loyalty test in the middle of the American Revolution. The best-known line of the affair is probably apocryphal: the President of the Royal Society, Sir John Pringle, is said to have answered his king, 'Sire, the prerogatives of the President of the Royal Society do not extend to altering the laws of nature,' and resigned — the Institute of Physics presents that as 'one version of the story' and the Whipple Library calls it likely untrue. London wits put the quarrel in verse: 'Whilst you, great George, for knowledge hunt, / And sharp conductors change for blunt, / The nation's out of joint: / Franklin another plan pursues, / And all your thunder useless views, / By sticking to his point.' Sources: IOP Spark, 'When lightning conductors were political' (citing Heilbron, Elements of Early Modern Physics, 1982); Dictionary of National Biography 1885-1900, 'Wilson, Benjamin'; Whipple Library Books Blog.

question: Benjamin Franklin printed only a short third-person notice about the kite at the time, in the Pennsylvania Gazette of 19 October 1752, with instructions for building one and no word that he had flown it. His autobiography never mentions it. The vivid version, with the key and the spark and the storm-soaked twine, reached print fifteen years afterwards. Whose account was it?
answer: Joseph Priestley's history of electricity, written from talks with Franklin.
choices: Joseph Priestley's history of electricity, written from talks with Franklin.
William Franklin's sworn recollection, set down long after the event.
Peter Collinson's published memoir of his American correspondents.
Thomas-François Dalibard's preface to his French edition of Franklin.
context: The vivid version first appears in Joseph Priestley's History and Present State of Electricity (1767), fifteen years later, from conversations with Franklin; Priestley dated the flight 15 June 1752, while other accounts say 10 or 24 June. How far the doubt goes, and where it stops: Tom Tucker's Bolt of Fate (2003) argues the flight was a hoax staged for scientific reputation, and Carl Van Doren called the story 'dim and mystifying in fact.' Michael Brian Schiffer answers that 'It is doubtful that Franklin would have crafted a piece of fictional science, for he appreciated the penalty that the gentlemanly establishment of natural philosophy would have meted out had the fraud been exposed.' Most historians accept that some version happened. The rod, by contrast, is documented, dated and installed — on his own Philadelphia house in the autumn of 1752, and on Christ Church's spire and the Academy of Philadelphia by early 1753. It is unquestionably his, and it unquestionably worked. Sources: Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment ('Modern Skepticism'); National Constitution Center, 'The great debate about Benjamin Franklin and his kite.'

question: A Munich workshop roof fell in on fourteen-year-old Joseph Fraunhofer on 21 July 1801, and he lay buried for hours while others beside him died. His master, a mirror-polisher, had underfed him and forbidden him candlelight to read by. Being dug out alive made the boy famous. What did that fame win him?
answer: A prince who bought out his contract
choices: A prince who bought out his contract
A guild that named him master early
A professor who hired him as helper
A parish fund that paid for school
context: Prince-Elector Maximilian IV Joseph of Bavaria personally oversaw the rescue, and his help was concrete rather than ceremonial: money, textbooks on mathematics and physics, funds to buy an optical grinding machine, cash to buy out the remainder of the six-year apprenticeship, and an annual allowance to live on while he studied. He also forced the employer to allow the boy time to read. Fraunhofer had been orphaned in 1798 — his mother died of malnutrition and hardship, his father later the same year from the effects of his trade. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Joseph von Fraunhofer' (Birth and Family Background; Apprenticeship and Early Hardships) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Joseph_von_Fraunhofer ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_von_Fraunhofer

question: A girl at home tilts one ordinary object in a sunbeam and throws a full rainbow across a white wall, with no need of the prisms of the finest glass in Europe that Joseph Fraunhofer used around 1814. Which object is it?
answer: The shiny side of a CD
choices: The shiny side of a CD
The bowl of a steel spoon
A pane of window glass
A magnifying glass lens
context: An ordinary pressed CD or DVD is a diffraction grating: a spiral of microscopic pits under a thin metal layer, ruled so finely that light of different wavelengths bounces off at different angles. Fraunhofer built the first grating in 1821 by stretching about 260 fine parallel wires across a frame, then moved to ruling grooves with a diamond point on a screw-driven dividing engine — spacings near 0.003 mm, over 8,000 lines to the inch, the finest around 10,000. He gave gratings away to leading scientists across Europe and was the first person to measure the wavelength of a spectral line with one. Go further: the strongest solar dark lines — his A, B and C groups near the red end — are visible to the naked eye through even a basic spectroscope. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Fraunhofer lines' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Fraunhofer_lines ; Grokipedia, 'Joseph von Fraunhofer' (Development of the Diffraction Grating); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffraction_grating

question: Joseph Fraunhofer sent sunlight through a narrow slit and a prism of his own flint glass in 1814 and examined the band of colour closely. The usual picture of that band was a smooth run from red to violet, each colour melting into the next. His was not smooth. What did he find in it?
answer: Hundreds of sharp dark lines
choices: Hundreds of sharp dark lines
A doubled band, one above the other
Bright lines standing out along it
A violet end that faded out early
context: Fraunhofer mapped roughly 574 of them and lettered the strongest A through K, ordered from the red end toward the blue, publishing an engraved plate of the spectrum in his 1817 memoir in the Annalen der Physik after first presenting the work to the Munich Academy in 1815. Contemporaries said the lines were simply flaws in his glass — streaks or bubbles casting shadows; he killed that objection by getting the identical lines out of several different instruments. And he was not the first to glimpse dark bands: William Hyde Wollaston saw some in 1802 but read them as natural boundaries separating one region of colour from the next. Fraunhofer's contribution is the systematic, measured map, not first sight. On what caused the lines he said plainly that he could not explain them, and the cause stayed unknown for the rest of his life. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Fraunhofer lines'; Grokipedia, 'History of spectroscopy' (Early 19th-Century Solar Spectrum Observations); Grokipedia, 'Joseph von Fraunhofer'

question: Joseph Fraunhofer set up a narrow slit, a prism of flint glass and a small eyepiece on a surveyor's stand in 1814, so that he could measure the angle of anything he saw. He was not an astronomer and had no question about the sky. The apparatus served his trade. What was his trade?
answer: Making telescope lenses for observatories
choices: Making telescope lenses for observatories
Grinding spectacles for Munich's opticians
Casting mirrors for Bavaria's lighthouses
Surveying the roads and borders of Bavaria
context: Fraunhofer was measuring how sharply each batch of his own glass bent each colour — its refractive index and its dispersion — so that he could grind lenses that brought all the colours to one focus. The marks he found in the Sun's spectrum that day became exactly what he needed: fixed, unmoving reference colours to calibrate instruments against. The fingerprint hidden in sunlight was found during quality control. His own summary of himself: 'In all my experiments I could, owing to lack of time, pay attention to only those matters which appeared to have a bearing upon practical optics.' The stand was a modified surveyor's theodolite. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Joseph von Fraunhofer' (Invention of the Spectroscope); Grokipedia, 'History of spectroscopy'; quotation from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_von_Fraunhofer

question: Robert Bunsen wanted a laboratory flame he could control exactly, and about 1854, with the Heidelberg instrument-maker Peter Desaga, he built the burner that still carries his name: a metal tube with sliding collars near the base to let in air. What does the flame do when those collars slide open?
answer: It turns hotter and almost invisible
choices: It turns hotter and almost invisible
It turns cooler and bright yellow
It turns hotter and bright orange
It turns cooler and thick with soot
context: Open collars give a sootless, non-luminous flame reaching about 1,500 °C. That mattered enormously. An ordinary gas or oil flame glows yellow with light of its own and drowns out whatever you drop into it; a flame with almost no light of its own finally let a chemist see the sample's colours instead of the fire's. You can watch the same change on a gas hob at home — the lazy yellow flame that sooties a pan versus the near-invisible roaring blue one. Source: Grokipedia, 'Robert Bunsen' (Laboratory Inventions) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Bunsen

question: Joseph Fraunhofer lettered the strongest dark gaps in the Sun's spectrum from A through K, measuring each one's position more finely than anyone before him. The pair he called D sat in the yellow, at exactly the colour one element blazes when a chemist drops a pinch of it into a flame. Which element?
answer: Sodium
choices: Sodium
Potassium
Lithium
Calcium
context: The D pair sits at 589.0 nanometres (D2) and 589.6 nanometres (D1) — precisely where neutral sodium in a laboratory flame emits its bright yellow doublet. Nobody could shake the coincidence, and for decades nobody could explain it. Test it yourself: table salt is sodium chloride, and a few grains dropped into a gas flame will pull that same hard yellow out of it. Source: Grokipedia, 'Fraunhofer lines' (Prominent Lines and Associations) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Fraunhofer_lines

question: Joseph Fraunhofer admitted he could not say whether his dark lines were made inside the Sun or in Earth's air on the way down. Both happen. The two broad bands he lettered A and B, far out at the red end, are not solar at all: one gas in the air overhead cuts them into sunlight in its last few seconds of travel. Which gas?
answer: Oxygen
choices: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide
Water vapour
context: The A band at 759.4 nm and the B band at 686.7 nm are telluric — 'of the Earth' — produced by molecular oxygen in our own atmosphere, and they are broad molecular bands rather than the sharp atomic lines the Sun contributes. Nitrogen dominates the air by volume but stays almost silent in the visible spectrum. Water vapour leaves telluric bands of its own elsewhere, which is part of why astronomers put telescopes on dry mountaintops and in orbit. Source: Grokipedia, 'Fraunhofer lines' (Naming Conventions; Prominent Lines and Associations table) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Fraunhofer_lines

question: Gustav Kirchhoff heated a platinum wire white-hot in a flame until it glowed with a perfectly smooth band of colour, no lines in it anywhere. Then he put a cool, thin gas between that wire and his prism — a gas whose own bright lines, when it was made to glow, he already knew by heart. What did the gas do to the smooth band?
answer: Cut dark lines exactly where its bright ones fall
choices: Cut dark lines exactly where its bright ones fall
Added its bright lines on top of the smooth band
Dimmed the band evenly, from the red to the violet
Left the band smooth but pushed it toward the red
context: The same element that had thrown bright lines in a flame now cut dark ones in the identical places: a gas absorbs exactly the wavelengths it emits. Kirchhoff set that out as three laws of spectroscopy — a hot solid, liquid or dense gas radiates at all wavelengths and gives a continuous spectrum; a thin gas excited to glow emits at specific wavelengths only, giving bright lines; and continuous light passed through a cooler thin gas comes out with dark lines cut in exactly those places. Apply it to the Sun — a blazing dense body shining up through the thinner, cooler gas above it — and Fraunhofer's hundreds of dark lines become a roll-call of the elements in the Sun's outer layers, readable from a bench in Germany. Kirchhoff presented the underlying thermodynamic principle, that a body absorbs at each wavelength as well as it emits, to the Berlin Academy on 15 December 1859, and showed the same year that the Sun contains sodium — the answer to a coincidence chemists had puzzled over for decades. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Kirchhoff (three laws); Grokipedia, 'Gustav Kirchhoff' (Laws of Spectroscopy; Law of Thermal Radiation)

question: Gustav Kirchhoff's banker asked what earthly use a metal in the Sun could be if nobody could ever fetch it down, or so a well-attested story goes. The Royal Society awarded Kirchhoff its Rumford Medal in 1862, and the prize money reached him from London. He carried the coins to the bank. What did he say as he handed them over?
answer: That here, at last, was gold from the Sun
choices: That here, at last, was gold from the Sun
That the Sun had made him a rich man
That London had fetched it down for him
That he would spend it all on new prisms
context: The Rumford Medal money arrived from London as gold sovereigns. The telling on record has the banker ask 'of what use is gold in the Sun if it cannot be brought to Earth?' and Kirchhoff deposit the sovereigns with the words 'here is gold from the Sun.' This is a well-attested anecdote rather than a minuted fact — the usual account names neither the banker nor the original recorder. There was a cost on the other side of that work: Kirchhoff's eyes were damaged by years of staring into bright spectra, and a fall left him on crutches or in a wheelchair for much of his life. He lectured until he retired in 1886 and died on 17 October 1887. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Kirchhoff ; Grokipedia, 'Gustav Kirchhoff' (Later Appointments and Retirement)  (Legend.)

question: Auguste Comte went looking for an example of knowledge forever out of human reach, in the nineteenth lesson of his Cours de philosophie positive of 1835, and settled on the stars. One question about them, he wrote, could never be answered by any means whatever. He died in 1857 sure of it, and the answer began to arrive two years later. Which question had he closed forever?
answer: What the stars are made of
choices: What the stars are made of
How far away the stars lie
How the stars first formed
Whether stars have planets
context: Comte died on 5 September 1857. Kirchhoff showed that the Sun contains sodium in 1859 — the man who called the question permanently unanswerable missed the answer by two years. His claim is usually reported as allowing that we may determine the stars' forms, distances, sizes and motions while holding their chemical composition beyond reach, though the exact wording varies between translations; a widely circulated English rendering runs 'We shall never be able by any means to study their chemical composition.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Comte ('Other views'); English rendering via https://libquotes.com/auguste-comte ; death date from Grokipedia, 'Auguste Comte' (Later Years and Death); sodium in the Sun 1859 from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Kirchhoff

question: William Huggins lined up Sirius's dark lines in 1868 against the lines of the same elements burning in his own laboratory. The star's lines sat slightly off, displaced a little toward the red. From that small displacement he pulled out a number nobody had ever measured for a star. What had he measured?
answer: Its speed toward or away from Earth
choices: Its speed toward or away from Earth
Its distance from Earth in light-years
The temperature of its glowing surface
The age of the star since it first lit
context: This was the first radial-velocity measurement from a stellar spectrum. Sources disagree sharply on the figure Huggins reported — Grokipedia gives about 9 km/s, Wikipedia's Huggins article records only a redshift in 1868 with no number, other historical accounts differ, and Huggins revised his own value later — so the method and the date are the solid facts, not the speed. The same trick later handed Edwin Hubble an expanding universe, and today it finds planets by the tiny wobble they impose on their star. Be honest about the limits: a spectrum still cannot give you a star's distance or its age, and a single line is read three ways at once — Doppler broadening from heat and turbulence, Stark broadening from charged particles' electric fields, Zeeman splitting in a magnetic field. Reading a spectrum is a chain of inference, not a photograph. Sources: Grokipedia, 'History of spectroscopy' (1860s–1890s); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Huggins ; Grokipedia, 'Fraunhofer lines' (Spectral Properties; Solar and Stellar Analysis)

question: Readers of the New York Times met the headline 'Einstein Attacks Quantum Theory' on 4 May 1935. The article behind it, by Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen, was still eleven days from print. How had the newspaper got the story?
answer: Podolsky had given the contents to a reporter
choices: Podolsky had given the contents to a reporter
Rosen had described the work in a public lecture
Bohr had mentioned the argument in Copenhagen
The journal's own office had tipped off a reporter
context: Boris Podolsky also drafted the published English text, and Albert Einstein never saw it before it was submitted. On 19 June 1935 Einstein complained to Erwin Schrodinger that the essential thing had been, so to speak, smothered by formalism. The most famous paper with Einstein's name on it is therefore one he neither wrote nor approved, and he was annoyed at Podolsky for handing the contents to the press. Sources: plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-epr/ (authorship and the 19 June 1935 letter); 'The Advent and Fallout of EPR', ias.edu/ideas/2013/epr-fallout; New York Times, 4 May 1935.

question: Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen wrote in Physical Review on 15 May 1935 about two particles made together and then carried apart. Measure the first, they said, and the second can be predicted without touching it. From that, what did the three of them decide about quantum mechanics?
answer: It was incomplete, with something missing from it
choices: It was incomplete, with something missing from it
It was inconsistent with its own mathematics
It described crowds of particles, never single ones
It was correct but could never be tested at all
context: Their criterion of reality, verbatim: 'If, without in any way disturbing a system, we can predict with certainty (i.e., with probability equal to unity) the value of a physical quantity, then there exists an element of reality corresponding to that quantity.' The paper's title asks the question outright: 'Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?' Their answer was no. The picture they preferred was of particles leaving the source already carrying their answers, like twins setting out from home with sealed envelopes. Sources: Physical Review 47, issue 10, 777-780, 15 May 1935; plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-epr/.

question: John Stewart Bell showed in 1964 how to test the fight over linked particles, twenty-nine years after Einstein's challenge, when it still looked like a matter of taste. He wrote the paper on a year off from his day job. What was that day job?
answer: Accelerator theory at CERN in Geneva
choices: Accelerator theory at CERN in Geneva
Radio astronomy at Jodrell Bank
Low-temperature physics at Leiden
Reactor engineering at Chalk River
context: Bell submitted the paper in November 1964, during a year's leave spent at Stanford, the University of Wisconsin-Madison and Brandeis. His paid work was accelerator and particle theory, first at Harwell on machines like the synchro-cyclotron and then at CERN from 1960; quantum foundations was the hobby he kept up on the side for years. The paper appeared in Physics Physique Fizika, volume 1, issue 3, pages 195-200. Sources: Grokipedia 'John Stewart Bell' and 'Bell's theorem'; physicsworld.com, 'John Bell and the most obscure journal in physics'.

question: John Clauser switched on the first machine that could decide the quarrel over linked particles at Berkeley in the early 1970s. Einstein said such particles must carry their properties with them all along; quantum theory says they have no fixed answer until one is measured. Years later Clauser said openly which side he had been rooting for. What had he been hoping for?
answer: Einstein's side of the argument to come out right
choices: Einstein's side of the argument to come out right
Niels Bohr's side of the argument to come out right
A third answer neither side had thought to predict
A violation stronger than quantum mechanics allows
context: Clauser, verbatim: 'Before Stu Freedman and I did the first experiment, I also personally thought that Einstein's hidden-variable physics might actually be right, and if it is, then I wanted to discover it.' His own data refuted his own hope, and he reported it anyway - which is what the method asks of you. He later titled his Nobel lecture, delivered on 8 December 2022 at Stockholm University, 'Experimental Proof That Nonlocal Quantum Entanglement is Real'. Sources: caltech.edu/about/news/proving-that-quantum-entanglement-is-real (Caltech Q&A with Clauser); Grokipedia 'John Clauser'.

question: Turning a matter of taste into arithmetic, John Stewart Bell showed in 1964 that any theory in which each particle leaves the source already carrying its own answers must obey a strict limit on how strongly two detectors' results can match. Quantum mechanics predicts breaking that limit. The two pictures do not disagree everywhere, though. When does the gap between them open?
answer: When the two detectors are turned to different angles
choices: When the two detectors are turned to different angles
When the two particles are more than a metre apart
When the same pair is measured over and over again
When both detectors are read at the very same instant
context: Bell's 1964 inequality reads |P(a,b) - P(a,c)| <= 1 + P(b,c), where P is the correlation between two detector settings. Quantum mechanics predicts the singlet correlation E(a,b) = -cos(theta) between the angles, and that curve breaks the bound for some angle choices. Set both detectors to the SAME angle and both pictures predict perfect matching, which is precisely why the argument had gone nowhere for twenty-nine years. The version experimenters actually use is the CHSH inequality of 1969, |E(a,b) + E(a,b') + E(a',b) - E(a',b')| <= 2, written by John Clauser, Michael Horne, Abner Shimony and Richard Holt. Quantum mechanics tops out at 2 times the square root of 2, about 2.828 - a ceiling proved by Boris Tsirelson in 1980, and nobody yet knows why nature stops at that particular number. Sources: Bell, Physics Physique Fizika 1, 195-200 (1964); Clauser, Horne, Shimony and Holt, Physical Review Letters 23, 880 (1969); Cirel'son, Letters in Mathematical Physics 4, 93-100 (1980); Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem'.

question: Two editors at Bell Labs printed John Stewart Bell's 1964 paper in their small magazine, Physics Physique Fizika, and it is now called the most important ever written on the roots of quantum theory. They personally read every paper and shut the magazine down after four years. What did it give its authors that no physics journal gives now?
answer: Ten cents for every word they got in print
choices: Ten cents for every word they got in print
A share of what the issue earned in sales
A decision on the paper within one week
The right to print the work elsewhere too
context: Physics Physique Fizika ran three volumes and folded in 1968. Anderson recalled that Bell's paper simply 'came in', unsolicited. Almost nobody thought the subject was worth working on: Abner Shimony's first reaction to Bell's paper, in his own words, was 'I thought, "Here's another kooky paper that's come out of the blue"', and when he and Michael Horne missed a conference abstract deadline Shimony told him, 'It doesn't matter. Nobody is working on this sort of thing. This is so far out.' Sources: physicsworld.com, 'John Bell and the most obscure journal in physics'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics,_Physique,_Fizika; American Institute of Physics oral history, 'Entanglement and experiment, part 2'.

question: John Clauser built his machine even though his older bosses at Columbia had warned him that testing quantum physics would wreck his career. Richard Feynman said that trying the test was the same as not believing quantum theory. The 1972 Berkeley result sided with quantum theory. By Clauser's own account, what did the Columbia faculty say then?
answer: That he had wasted money and should do real physics
choices: That he had wasted money and should do real physics
That the result was surely a fluke and must be rerun
That he should now chase the loopholes still open
That the gamble had paid off and he should press on
context: Clauser's verbatim account: 'My faculty at Columbia told me that testing quantum physics was going to destroy my career'; 'Caltech's Richard Feynman was highly offended by my impertinent effort and told me that it was tantamount to professing a disbelief in quantum physics'; and afterwards, 'When I reconnected with my Columbia faculty, they all said, "We told you so! Now stop wasting money and go do some real physics."' Not everyone discouraged him: Charles Townes, the maser and laser laureate, backed the Berkeley project, and Eugene Commins freed up his graduate student Stuart Freedman to build it. On 4 October 2022 the Royal Swedish Academy awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics to John Clauser, Alain Aspect and Anton Zeilinger 'for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science'. Sources: caltech.edu/about/news/proving-that-quantum-entanglement-is-real; AIP oral history, 'Entanglement and experiment, part 2'; Grokipedia 'John Clauser'.

question: Stuart Freedman and John Clauser built their own source of entangled light at Berkeley, because in 1972 no such thing could be bought. It threw off two photons at a time, one green at 551.3 nanometres and one violet at 422.7, flying back to back with the tilt of their light waves locked together. What was doing the throwing?
answer: Calcium atoms falling down a two-step cascade
choices: Calcium atoms falling down a two-step cascade
A crystal splitting single photons into pairs
Sodium vapour excited by a pulsed flashlamp
Mercury atoms struck by a beam of electrons
context: Stuart J. Freedman and John F. Clauser, 'Experimental Test of Local Hidden-Variable Theories', Physical Review Letters 28, 938-941, published 3 April 1972. The calcium atoms ran a J=0 to J=1 to J=0 radiative cascade; polarizers were set at angles including 22.5 and 67.5 degrees, and the two ends stood a few metres apart in one room (Clauser has described them as about ten feet apart, and published figures for the separation disagree, so 'a few metres' is the safe statement). The measured violation was delta = 0.050 plus or minus 0.008 against a local-hidden-variable limit of delta <= 0, about six standard deviations. Honest caveat: the photomultipliers caught well under one pair in a hundred, so the conclusion still leaned on the assumption that the pairs they caught were representative of the ones they missed. Sources: link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.28.938; Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem' and 'John Clauser'; caltech.edu Q&A with Clauser.

question: Alain Aspect's team at Orsay had to change each analyser's setting in 1982 while the photons were still in flight: a flip every ten nanoseconds, a hundred million times a second, across a twelve-metre baseline. The switch they built had no moving parts at all. What did the deflecting?
answer: An ultrasonic standing wave inside water
choices: An ultrasonic standing wave inside water
A high voltage applied across a crystal
A magnetic field wrapped round a glass rod
A second laser crossing the photon's path
context: Alain Aspect, Jean Dalibard and Gerard Roger, Physical Review Letters 49, 1804 (December 1982), Institut d'Optique at Orsay. The acousto-optic switches - ultrasonic standing waves in water - redirected each beam roughly every 10 nanoseconds, while a photon needed about 40 nanoseconds to fly the 12-metre separation, so each setting was fixed after the photons had already left the source. The two switches were run at deliberately mismatched frequencies, near 40 and 48 MHz, so the two ends could never fall into step. The run gave a 5-sigma violation. Aspect's earlier 1982 result with fixed two-channel polarizers (Aspect, Philippe Grangier and Gerard Roger, PRL 49, 91) had already measured S = 2.697 plus or minus 0.015 against the local-realist ceiling of 2, a violation of more than 40 standard deviations. Source: Grokipedia 'Aspect's experiment'.

question: A Vienna-led team on La Palma handed the choice of detector settings in 2018 to two telescopes aimed at quasars on opposite sides of the sky, whose light had been travelling for 7.8 and 12.2 billion years. By 2015 the other escapes were nearly all shut, but one worry remained: whatever picks the settings might itself be correlated with the particles about to be measured. What property of that ancient light chose the settings?
answer: The colour of each photon
choices: The colour of each photon
The brightness of each photon
The polarization of each photon
The arrival time of each photon
context: Rauch and colleagues, 'Cosmic Bell Test Using Random Measurement Settings from High-Redshift Quasars', Physical Review Letters 121, 080403 (August 2018). The William Herschel Telescope and the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo read each arriving photon's wavelength, red or blue of a dividing line, and used that to set the detector. Any local-realist conspiracy would have had to be arranged at least 7.8 billion years before the Earth existed. A 2017 forerunner (Handsteiner and colleagues, PRL 118, 060401) used light from Milky Way stars about 600 light-years away, and on 30 November 2016 the BIG Bell Test let more than 100,000 volunteers worldwide tap over 90 million unpredictable bits into phones and computers to set entangled atoms, photons and superconducting devices in 12 laboratories on five continents; every platform showed a violation. The 2015 loophole-free runs came first: Ronald Hanson's Delft group entangled electron spins in diamond 1.3 kilometres apart, Krister Shalm's NIST team ran detectors 184 metres apart with roughly 90 per cent efficient superconducting nanowires, and Marissa Giustina and Anton Zeilinger's Vienna team reached a local-realism probability of 3.74 x 10^-31. NIST even reran its test with setting-bits drawn from popular movies, television shows and the digits of pi, so nobody could claim its random-number generator was in on the conspiracy. Sources: iqoqi-vienna.at, Cosmic Bell Experiments; nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0085-3; nist.gov news release, November 2015; Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem'.

question: Suppose you hand one crew the partner particles of a linked set, fly them to Mars, and try to signal home the instant you measure. Two distant results really do match more often than any theory in which each particle left the source carrying its own answers can allow, and that has tempted people to sketch such a telephone. What does a single crew's own column of results look like, whatever the far crew does?
answer: Pure coin flips, with no pattern in them at all
choices: Pure coin flips, with no pattern in them at all
Pure coin flips until the far crew starts measuring
A bias that tracks the angle of the far crew's dial
A faint bias, identical in every run ever done
context: This is the hard limit, and nothing in any Bell experiment sends anything faster than light. Each side's own statistics are completely unchanged by what the distant experimenter chooses to measure - formally, they are the partial trace over the other subsystem - so no message can ride the entanglement. The correlation becomes visible only when the two lists of outcomes are brought together and compared, and that comparison has to travel over an ordinary channel at light speed or slower. The first rigorous proof is Philippe Eberhard's 1978 paper 'Bell's Theorem and the Different Concepts of Locality'; Eberhard and Ronald Ross extended it to quantum field theory in 1989. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-communication_theorem; Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem', no-signaling assumption.

question: David Bohm published a pilot-wave theory in 1952, twelve years before John Stewart Bell's paper, that gives every particle a definite position at every moment and still reproduces every quantum prediction. So the common one-line summary of Bell's theorem, that particles cannot be carrying hidden instructions after all, is too strong, and Bell knew it. What lets Bohm's theory slip past the theorem?
answer: Its guiding wave answers to the whole arrangement at once
choices: Its guiding wave answers to the whole arrangement at once
Its guiding wave can run backwards in time to the source
Its particles learn the detector settings in advance
Its particles each carry a copy of the wave with them
context: Stated precisely: Bell's theorem rules out LOCAL hidden variables, not all hidden variables. Bohm's guiding wave depends instantaneously on the whole configuration, so the theory is openly nonlocal, reproduces every quantum prediction including the Bell violations, and the theorem leaves it standing. Bohm's 1952 spin reformulation of the EPR setup is also the version Bell actually analysed. The field had earlier lost about two decades to a wrong proof: John von Neumann published a theorem in 1932 claiming that no hidden-variable theory could reproduce quantum statistics, and it discouraged the whole line of inquiry until it was shown to rest on a false assumption about how such a model must handle non-commuting observables. Sources: Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem', Impact on Local Hidden Variable Theories and Nonlocality sections; plato.stanford.edu/entries/qm-bohm/; Bub, 'What is wrong with von Neumann's theorem on no hidden variables'.

question: Paul Davies asked John Stewart Bell on British Broadcasting Corporation radio in 1985 about the one escape from his theorem that no experiment can ever close: a local theory can still match quantum mechanics exactly if a single assumption Bell had taken for granted is given up. Bell named the price of that escape and said he would not pay it. What did Bell say it costs?
answer: The complete absence of free will
choices: The complete absence of free will
A separate physics for living matter
A world that splits at each measurement
An influence running backwards in time
context: Physicists call this escape superdeterminism. Bell, in the 1985 BBC Radio 3 interview with Paul Davies, said it 'involves absolute determinism in the universe, the complete absence of free will', describing a world in which 'our behavior, including our belief that we are free to choose to do one experiment rather than another' is 'absolutely predetermined, including the "decision" by the experimenter to carry out one set of measurements rather than another'. Gerard 't Hooft's cellular-automaton interpretation is its main modern defence, so the position still has serious holders. Meanwhile the violation has become a working tool rather than a curiosity: because a violation certifies that two boxes are not running on pre-set instructions, it underpins device-independent quantum key distribution - Dominic Mayers and Andrew Yao proposed self-testing apparatus in 1998, and Umesh Vazirani and Thomas Vidick published the first unconditional security proof in Physical Review Letters in 2014 - along with certified randomness generation. Sources: Davies and Brown, 'The Ghost in the Atom' (1986), edited transcript of the 1985 BBC Radio 3 interview with Bell; Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Device-independent_quantum_cryptography.

question: Edward Stone, an English country pastor, sent a careful letter to the Royal Society, England's top science club, in 1763. He had tried a simple bitter fever remedy on about fifty parishioners in his village, he wrote, and it had worked. Where did he say he had got the medicine from?
answer: From the bark of a willow tree
choices: From the bark of a willow tree
From dried mint leaves and honey
From the roots of a common nettle
From boiled rowan berries
context: Stone's letter, dated 25 April 1763 and printed in Philosophical Transactions, described drying the bark, powdering it, and dosing it every four hours until the fever broke. Source: Royal Society, 'From plant extract to molecular panacea: a commentary on Stone 1763'.

question: A doctor in the 1870s gave a rheumatism patient salicylic acid, the fever-and-pain compound drawn from willow bark and one of the first drugs that actually worked on that painful joint disease. It had just one fault, so bad that many patients quit the drug rather than go on taking it. What was the fault?
answer: It burned the stomach lining
choices: It burned the stomach lining
It turned the skin bright yellow
It tasted so sweet it caused vomiting
It stopped working after a single dose
context: The bare acid was harsh going down and harsh coming back up. Improving that side effect, not inventing the painkiller, is what Bayer's chemists set out to do in the 1890s. Source: McGill OSS, 'Forget the Willow Bark Extract - Go For Aspirin'.

question: Felix Hoffmann, a 29-year-old chemist at the Bayer laboratory in Elberfeld, Germany, tacked a single small chemical group onto salicylic acid on 10 August 1897. It muzzled the harsh acid, which now released its pain-killing form only once digestion set in. Bayer would sell the result under the name Aspirin. What group did Hoffmann add to the acid?
answer: An acetyl group
choices: An acetyl group
A hydroxyl group
A chloride ion
A sulphate group
context: The result was acetylsalicylic acid, sold from 1899 as Aspirin. The 'a' in Aspirin marks the added group, 'spir' comes from the meadowsweet Spiraea ulmaria (also a source of salicin), and '-in' was a standard drug suffix. Bayer registered the trademark on 6 March 1899. Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'Aspirin'.

question: Arthur Eichengrun, head of Bayer's pharmaceutical laboratory, said afterwards that he had directed the aspirin bench work, though Bayer's own history names Felix Hoffmann. Eichengrun's name was written out of that official history around 1934, and his own account appeared only in 1949. Why was he erased from Bayer's story?
answer: He was Jewish, and the Nazis were purging Jewish names from science
choices: He was Jewish, and the Nazis were purging Jewish names from science
His records of the bench work had been lost in a lab fire
Later chemists had shown that his method was badly flawed
He had retired and signed away any claim to the discovery
context: Eichengrun was a Jewish chemist; a 1999 re-examination by the historian Walter Sneader argued he was the true director of the aspirin project. Bayer's official history still names Hoffmann. Source: Wikipedia, 'Arthur Eichengrun'.

question: John Vane, a British pharmacologist, worked out in 1971, over a single weekend, why aspirin stops pain, fevers and swelling. The drug had sat on shelves everywhere for some seven decades with nobody knowing how it worked. What did he find it does inside the body?
answer: It jams an enzyme the body needs to make its pain signals
choices: It jams an enzyme the body needs to make its pain signals
It numbs the nerves that carry pain up to the brain
It locks onto the brain's own receptors for pain
It kills the germs that inflame and swell a sore spot
context: Vane showed aspirin blocks the enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX), which manufactures prostaglandins - the local chemical signals of pain, fever and inflammation. He shared the 1982 Nobel with Bergstrom and Samuelsson. Source: Nobel Prize 1982 in Physiology or Medicine.

question: A man swallows a tiny 81 mg aspirin against a heart attack, and that one tablet keeps his blood from clotting for about ten days. A normal-size headache aspirin wears off in hours. What quirk of the cells aspirin acts on explains this?
answer: Platelets have no nucleus and cannot rebuild the disabled enzyme
choices: Platelets have no nucleus and cannot rebuild the disabled enzyme
Platelets store the drug in granules and leak it out over days
Platelets divide only once every ten days regardless of dose
Platelets absorb aspirin faster than any other cell in the body
context: Aspirin acetylates a serine in cyclooxygenase and shuts it off for good. Most cells simply build fresh enzyme; platelets, having no DNA, cannot. So the antiplatelet effect lasts a platelet's ten-day life, while a headache dose fades as the body clears the drug. Source: Tulane, 'Antiplatelet Drugs'.

question: A mother reaches for the aspirin for her feverish son and stops at the label. It warns that the drug is not for children and teenagers with a fever or a viral illness, though adults take it freely. What danger is the warning about?
answer: A rare but savage illness of the liver and brain
choices: A rare but savage illness of the liver and brain
Bleeding in a stomach too young to bear the acid
A dose too strong for a child's smaller body
An allergy that strikes the young far more often
context: It is Reye's syndrome, first described in 1963. After the FDA required a warning label in 1986, US cases dropped from hundreds a year to a handful. Adult aspirin is common; children with a fever get paracetamol or ibuprofen instead. Source: American Family Physician, 'Aspirin Use in Children for Fever or Viral Syndromes'.

question: In 2011 two virus labs took H5N1 bird flu and changed it. Ron Fouchier's lab in Rotterdam and Yoshihiro Kawaoka's lab in Wisconsin wanted to know what changes would let the virus jump between mammals through the air. H5N1 kills people but almost never spreads between them. Which animal did both teams use as the mammal test?
answer: Ferrets
choices: Ferrets
Rhesus monkeys
Guinea pigs
Cotton rats
context: Ferrets are the standard model for human influenza: their airways and their sneeze produce a virus-transmission pattern very close to a human's. Both teams passed H5N1 repeatedly through ferrets until it spread cage-to-cage through the air. The exercise deliberately built the thing everyone was afraid of in order to study it. Source: cidrap.umn.edu Fouchier H5N1 study.

question: In late 2011 the papers on the airborne H5N1 work were sent to Science and Nature. The US federal panel that reviews dual-use biology took a rare step. It said the papers could run only with key steps blacked out, so no one could rebuild the exact virus. What is that panel called?
answer: NSABB
choices: NSABB
NIAID
FDA
NAS
context: NSABB = National Science Advisory Board for Biosecurity. On 30 March 2012 the NSABB reversed its recommendation and the papers were published in full, but the redaction request itself was a milestone. NIAID is Fauci's institute inside NIH; the FDA regulates drugs and devices; the NAS is the National Academy of Sciences, an honorary body. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov H5N1 Moratorium Controversy.

question: The bank's answer to that steel-man is that the benefit is speculative but the risk is well documented. Laboratory escapes of dangerous germs have happened many times. In 1978 smallpox escaped a lab in Birmingham, England, and killed a medical photographer named Janet Parker. The wild virus had already been wiped out. How did the virus travel to reach her office?
answer: An air duct
choices: An air duct
A shared coffee mug
A contaminated needle
A door handle
context: Janet Parker's darkroom was connected to Henry Bedson's smallpox lab on the floor below by an air duct. The Shooter Inquiry concluded that was the most likely route, though the exact transmission mechanism is still debated. Parker died on 11 September 1978 - the last recorded smallpox death. A pathogen only has to get out once, and the people who bear the cost were never asked. Source: en.wikipedia.org 1978 smallpox outbreak.

question: Galileo Galilei wanted the law of falling, but no clock in 1600 could time a falling rock, down before a man could say 'now.' So he weakened the fall itself, stretching a one-second drop into many. What did he build?
answer: A grooved wooden beam propped up at one end
choices: A grooved wooden beam propped up at one end
A water tank with a wax ball sinking through it
A well shaft with a bell sounding at the bottom
A silk cord with weights knotted along it
context: Galileo gives the recipe in Two New Sciences: a piece of wooden moulding 'about 12 cubits long, half a cubit wide, and three finger-breadths thick' (roughly 5.5 m), with a channel 'a little more than one finger in breadth' cut along its edge, made 'very straight, smooth, and polished' and lined with parchment 'as smooth and polished as possible.' Down it he rolled 'a hard, smooth, and very round bronze ball,' with one end of the beam raised one to two cubits. The ramp changes none of the physics — it only dilutes gravity until a human being can watch it happen. Which means anyone can run his experiment tonight with a marble, a tilted board and a phone stopwatch. Source: Galileo, Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences, Third Day (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — en.wikisource.org/wiki/Dialogues_Concerning_Two_New_Sciences/Third_Day.

question: David Scott stood on the airless Moon on 2 August 1971, in front of a live television camera, and said one reason Apollo 15 got there was 'a gentleman named Galileo, a long time ago.' He held out one object in each hand and let both go at the same instant. What was he holding?
answer: A geology hammer and a falcon feather
choices: A geology hammer and a falcon feather
A wrench and a strip of gold foil
A rock sample and a nylon flag scrap
A drill bit and a paper checklist page
context: The aluminium geology hammer weighed 1.32 kg and the falcon feather 0.03 kg, and Scott released them from about 1.6 m. They hit the dust together. Scott: 'Which proves that Mr. Galileo was correct in his findings.' CapCom Joe Allen, over applause in Houston: 'How about that!' Modern versions are brutally finer: the MICROSCOPE satellite (2016-17) compared two test masses of different composition falling in orbit and found no difference to about one part in 10^15 — a hundred trillion times finer than anything Galileo could see. Sources: Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Journal, EVA-3 close-out — apollojournals.org/alsj/a15/a15.clsout3.html; NASA Science, 'The Apollo 15 Hammer-Feather Drop'.

question: Vincenzo Viviani, the old Galileo's assistant, wrote that his master sat in Pisa Cathedral at nineteen, around 1583, watching a hanging lamp swing, and thought its wide swings and its small ones took the same time. No clock of that day could mark seconds. What does Viviani say Galileo timed the swings against?
answer: His own pulse, felt at the wrist
choices: His own pulse, felt at the wrist
The chant of the priests at the altar
A candle burning down past its marks
A count whispered under his breath
context: Careful: Viviani's Racconto istorico is the ONLY source for this scene, and he wrote it some seventy years after the date he gives — so treat it as his telling, not as Galileo's own record. The idea itself went somewhere real. Late in life, blind and under house arrest, Galileo described a pendulum clock to his son Vincenzo, who partly built it in 1649; it was never completed. Anyone can test the claim with a weight on a string: pull it far, pull it a little, and count. Sources: Museo Galileo, 'Pisa — Following the path of Galileo'; grokipedia.com/page/Galileo_Galilei; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pendulum_clock.  (Legend.)

question: Galileo needed to compare each roll down the ramp more finely than any clock of 1600 could. He set a large vessel of water above the bench, with a thin pipe soldered into its bottom, and caught the jet in a small glass for exactly the length of each descent. What did he then do with each glassful?
answer: Weighed it on a very accurate balance
choices: Weighed it on a very accurate balance
Poured it into a tube marked in degrees
Counted the drops it had caught
Set it beside the last glass and eyed the level
context: In his own words: 'the water thus collected was weighed, after each descent, on a very accurate balance; the differences and ratios of these weights gave us the differences and ratios of the times.' Notice what he never does — he never measures a second. He measures weights of water, and lets the RATIOS carry the physics. That is the trick worth stealing: when a quantity cannot be measured directly, measure something strictly proportional to it. Source: Galileo, Two New Sciences, Third Day (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — en.wikisource.org/wiki/Dialogues_Concerning_Two_New_Sciences/Third_Day.

question: David Scott wanted a real feather to carry to the Moon, since Apollo 15's lunar module was named Falcon. He, Jim Irwin and Al Worden went and collected two falcon feathers in person in January 1971. Where did the feathers come from?
answer: The mascot falcon of the US Air Force Academy
choices: The mascot falcon of the US Air Force Academy
A peregrine falcon project at Cornell University
A falconry ranch outside Houston, Texas
The raptor collection of the Smithsonian Institution
context: The crew visited the Academy at Colorado Springs; the bird is reported to have been a falcon named Baggin. Two feathers went to the Moon and only one came back into the story — Irwin accidentally stepped on the other, to Scott's annoyance. The feather Scott dropped is still lying on the lunar surface where it fell in 1971, undisturbed, with no air to stir it. Sources: Royal Museums Greenwich, 'The strange things humans have left on the Moon'; Atlas Obscura, 'Object of Intrigue: The Falcon Feather on the Moon'.

question: Galileo Galilei rolled his bronze ball from rest down the parchment-lined groove, measuring each descent against the water caught from his jet clock. Then he cut a single descent into four equal stretches of time and asked how far the ball had travelled during each stretch on its own. The four distances were not equal — they grew as four whole numbers. What were they?
answer: 1, 3, 5, 7 — the odd numbers in order
choices: 1, 3, 5, 7 — the odd numbers in order
1, 2, 3, 4 — the counting numbers in order
1, 2, 4, 8 — the doubling numbers in order
1, 4, 9, 16 — the square numbers in order
context: This is Corollary I of the Third Day. Add those four stretches up and the TOTAL distance runs 1, 4, 9, 16 — the square of the elapsed time. Double the time, quadruple the distance; triple the time, nine times the distance. The speed grows as the plain counting numbers while the distance grows as their squares, and the pattern is the same whatever the ball weighs and whatever the tilt of the beam. Galileo: 'in such experiments, repeated a full hundred times, we always found that the spaces traversed were to each other as the squares of the times, and this was true for all inclinations of the plane.' Source: Two New Sciences, Third Day, Corollary I (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — en.wikisource.org.

question: Antonio Favaro, who edited Galileo's complete works, went to the records of Pisa Cathedral to check a claim: that the hanging lamp shown to tourists is the very one whose swinging the teenage Galileo studied. Guides still tell them so. What did Favaro find?
answer: The lamp on show was hung in 1587, after the date claimed
choices: The lamp on show was hung in 1587, after the date claimed
The lamp on show was recast from an older one in 1650
The cathedral hung no lamps at all before the year 1600
The records name a different church across the square
context: The story puts the scene around 1583, so the lamp visitors are shown had not yet been hung. It is the wrong lamp. Museo Galileo notes that a smaller, plainer votive lamp that DID hang in the cathedral in Galileo's day survives, kept now in the Aulla Chapel of the Monumental Cemetery next door. So the famous object is legend even if the observation behind it may still be his — which is exactly the habit worth learning: check the date on the exhibit, not just the label. Sources: Museo Galileo, 'Pisa — Following the path of Galileo'; grokipedia.com/page/Galileo_Galilei.

question: Galileo quotes Aristotle's rule for falling weights in Two New Sciences and spells out what it means. A 100-pound iron ball and a 1-pound ball drop together from 100 cubits, and the heavy one lands first. By Aristotle's rule, how far has the 1-pound ball fallen at the moment the heavy ball hits the ground?
answer: One cubit
choices: One cubit
Ten cubits
Fifty cubits
Ninety cubits
context: A hundredfold weight meant a hundredfold speed, so the small ball has barely started when the big one is finished. Salviati's reply is one flat line: 'I say that they arrive at the same time.'
