Galileo also doubted the rule had ever been checked: 'I greatly doubt that Aristotle ever tested by experiment whether it be true that two stones, one weighing ten times as much as the other... would so differ in speed.' Aristotle had reached the rule by deduction from his theory of the elements — reasoning downward from a system, rather than dropping anything. Source: Two New Sciences, First Day (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — galileoandeinstein.phys.virginia.edu/tns_draft/tns_061to108.html.

question: Vincenzio Renieri, who took over Galileo's mathematics chair at Pisa, dropped wood against lead from the leaning bell tower in March 1641 and sent his numbers to Galileo, by then blind, who had the letter read aloud to him. Every school book shows Galileo himself dropping two balls from that tower, yet his own works, letters and manuscripts never mention it once. What did Renieri report?
answer: The lead beat the wood down by nearly two metres
choices: The lead beat the wood down by nearly two metres
The wood beat the lead down by nearly two metres
The lead beat the wood down by about a hand's breadth
The lead and the wood struck the pavement together
context: About three braccia, in Renieri's own measure — and in the other pair he dropped, a cannonball against a musket bullet, the bigger lead ball beat the smaller by about one palmo, roughly 25 cm. Wood loses badly to lead in air; nothing here looks like the storybook picture of two balls landing as one. And the tower is the famous one: the Leaning Tower IS the bell tower of Pisa's cathedral, one building under two names — so the documented Pisa drop was made from the very tower the legend borrows, fifty years too late and with the wrong answer for the story. The tower legend itself rests on a single source: Vincenzo Viviani, who became Galileo's assistant in 1639, some fifty years after the supposed event, drafted his life of Galileo in 1654, and it was printed only in 1717, after his own death — sixty-three years after he wrote it, seventy-five after Galileo died. Viviani's line: Galileo 'showed this by repeated experiments made from the height of the Leaning Tower of Pisa in the presence of other professors and all the students.' One suggestion is that the story was born in 1641 itself, in a blind old man's reminiscence prompted by Renieri's letter, and Viviani wrote it down thirteen years later. The scholarly fight is live: Alexandre Koyré (Études galiléennes, 1939) called the drop a myth and held that Galileo's real method was mathematics plus inclined planes; Stillman Drake (Galileo at Work, 1978) thought a Pisa demonstration plausible and in character. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Galileo's_Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa_experiment; 'Vincenzio Renieri and the Law of Falling Bodies,' KCKCC e-Journal 7:1 (2013).

question: Simon Stevin and the Delft lawyer Jan Cornets de Groot climbed the Nieuwe Kerk in 1586, before Galileo ever taught at Pisa, and released two lead balls together, one ten times heavier than the other, from about thirty feet up. Theirs is the drop test that is documented: Stevin wrote up the result that same year, and the light ball did not lag. How did the two men judge that the balls arrived together?
answer: They listened for one impact sound or two
choices: They listened for one impact sound or two
They timed each ball against a swinging pendulum
They counted the beats of their own pulses
They lined the fall up against a nearby window frame
context: Partly by ear, from the sound of the strikes on the boards — a single knock, not two. Stevin's own words in De Beghinselen der Weeghconst (1586): 'Let us take... two lead balls, one ten times heavier than the other, and let them fall together from 30 feet high. That will show that the light ball does not take longer to fall than the heavy one, but they fall together at the same time. This proves that Aristotle was wrong.' His partner was no physicist: Jan Cornets de Groot was a Delft lawyer and burgomaster — and the father of Hugo de Groot (Grotius), who grew up to found modern international law. Stevin called him 'the highly educated and diligent researcher of the mysteries of nature.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_tower_experiment; grokipedia.com/page/Galileo's_Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa_experiment.

question: Giovanni Battista Riccioli, a Jesuit astronomer in Bologna, set out to disprove Galileo's law of fall. He dropped balls from the Torre degli Asinelli, nearly a hundred metres of tower. His timer was a pendulum, but a man watching a falling ball cannot also watch a swinging weight. How did Riccioli get the pendulum's beat to his observers?
answer: A chorus of his fellow Jesuits chanted in time with it
choices: A chorus of his fellow Jesuits chanted in time with it
A brother by the pendulum struck a bell at each swing
A row of novices on the stair passed each count down
A priest at the window tapped a drum at every swing
context: Human beings as a metronome. Francesco Maria Grimaldi and Cassiani stood at the summit and Riccioli on the pavement below, each separately writing on his own sheet the number of pendulum strokes a fall took — a blind-comparison habit worth copying. Riccioli set out to refute Galileo and confirmed him instead, then published the confirmation anyway in the Almagestum Novum (1651): about 15 Roman feet in the first second, 60 in two, 135 in three. He also printed the runs that did NOT flatter the theory. A wooden ball and a lead ball of the same weight (2.5 ounces each) fell together, and when the lead had covered 280 Roman feet the wood had made only 240; two clay balls of the same size, one 10 ounces and one 20, were released together and the lighter was still at least 15 feet up when the heavier struck the pavement. He named air resistance and density as the cause rather than quietly binning the data. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Battista_Riccioli; Christopher M. Graney, 'Anatomy of a fall,' Physics Today 65(9), 36 (2012).

question: Stillman Drake, a historian, argued that Galileo had an instrument finer than any clock of 1600: his own ear. On Drake's reconstruction Galileo tied movable gut frets across the ramp, so that the bronze ball gave a small bump as it crossed each one. What does Drake say Galileo was listening for?
answer: The bumps falling into an even rhythm
choices: The bumps falling into an even rhythm
The bumps crowding closer as the ball ran on
The gaps between the bumps stretching out
The bumps coming in pairs, two close then a gap
context: Once the frets are set right, the marks on the beam ARE the distances at equal times — the ball times itself. Be careful with this one: it is Drake's reconstruction, not a procedure Galileo ever describes. What makes it plausible is the household. Galileo's father, Vincenzo Galilei, was a professional lutenist and music theorist who ran his own experiments on string tension and pitch, and Galileo played the lute well; a trained musician's sense of beat resolves differences far finer than any 1600 clock, which could not split a second at all. And there is hard evidence he really ran the ramps: his surviving motion folios carry raw measured numbers, not just polished prose — 107v on naturally accelerated motion, 114 and 116v on the inclined plane, groove and ball, including a setup on folio 116 where a deflection at the foot of the ramp launched the ball horizontally. Try it: tape pencils across a tilted board and slide them until the clicks come evenly. Sources: Stillman Drake, Galileo at Work (1978); 'Reconstructing Galileo's Inclined Plane Experiments for Teaching Purposes'.

question: Salviati, Galileo's spokesman in Two New Sciences, offers to break Aristotle's rule without dropping anything at all. Suppose, he says, a large stone falls with a speed of eight and a small one with a speed of four, and the two are tied together to fall as a single body. What does Salviati say Aristotle's rule is forced to say about the pair?
answer: It must fall slower than eight, yet it outweighs the eight-stone
choices: It must fall slower than eight, yet it outweighs the eight-stone
It must fall faster than eight, yet its parts each fall slower
It must fall at four, yet nothing has been taken from it
It must fall at twelve, yet no stone was seen to fall so fast
context: Verbatim: 'if a large stone moves with a speed of, say, eight while a smaller moves with a speed of four, then when they are united, the system will move with a speed less than eight; but the two stones when tied together make a stone larger than that which before moved with a speed of eight. Hence the heavier body moves with less speed than the lighter.' The slow stone must drag on the fast one, so the pair is slower than eight; but the pair is heavier than either, so on the same rule it must be faster than eight. Aristotle's physics contradicts itself before anyone climbs a tower — cost of apparatus: nothing. Source: Two New Sciences, First Day (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — galileoandeinstein.phys.virginia.edu/tns_draft/tns_061to108.html.

question: Galileo Galilei has his spokesman Salviati grant, in Two New Sciences, that when a hundred-pound ball and a one-pound ball drop together from a great height the heavy one really does win, by about two finger-breadths. It is exactly the admission an Aristotelian would seize on. How does Salviati answer it?
answer: He asks why two fingers should hide Aristotle's ninety-nine cubits
choices: He asks why two fingers should hide Aristotle's ninety-nine cubits
He asks why two fingers should outweigh a rule Aristotle never tested
He asks why two fingers in air should settle what a void would show
He asks why two fingers should be charged to weight and not to the air
context: Verbatim: 'you find, on making the experiment, that the larger outstrips the smaller by two finger-breadths... now you would not hide behind these two fingers the ninety-nine cubits of Aristotle, nor would you mention my small error and at the same time pass over in silence his very large one.' Aristotle's rule had the small ball one cubit down out of a hundred; Galileo's own error is two finger-breadths. Sagredo reports his own trial in the same dialogue: a cannon ball of one or two hundred pounds beat a half-pound musket ball by less than a span over a 200-cubit drop. Naming one's own error out loud, in print, and then measuring it honestly against the rival's, is the move the whole book is built on. Source: Two New Sciences, First Day (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — galileoandeinstein.phys.virginia.edu/tns_draft/tns_061to108.html.

question: Galileo Galilei dropped a wooden block against a lead ball from a height around 1590, newly holding the mathematics chair at Pisa, and recorded it in a treatise he never published, De motu antiquiora. There he sets out the model that in his view explained what he had recorded, a model it would take him decades to abandon. What did that model say?
answer: That a body sinks through air by its density, as through water
choices: That a body sinks through air by its density, as through water
That each body hurries to the natural place of its element
That a falling body carries a force impressed on it at the start
That the air closing in behind a body keeps driving it down
context: The lead landed first, and the young Galileo believed his eyes: denser bodies, he concluded, genuinely do fall faster through a medium like air. The model is Archimedean — a body sinks through air much as it sinks through water, according to its density in the medium — and it is still half-Aristotelian, because the medium is still doing the deciding. His law of fall first shows up in a letter to Paolo Sarpi in 1604, and the mature claim, that all bodies fall alike where there is nothing to resist them, waits for Two New Sciences in 1638, nearly fifty years after the treatise. The man who broke Aristotle's physics started out believing a version of it, and needed decades and a ramp to talk himself out of it. His Pisa post was no prize either: the mathematics chair from 1589 on a renewable three-year term, poorly paid beside the medical chairs, and he left in 1592 for a better post at Padua. Sources: J. D. Norton, 'Galileo's fall' (sites.pitt.edu/~jdnorton/papers/Galileo_fall_final.pdf) on the 1604 letter; grokipedia.com/page/Galileo's_Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa_experiment; grokipedia.com/page/Galileo_Galilei.

question: Galileo Galilei aimed his homemade tube at Jupiter from Padua on the night of 7 January 1610 and saw three faint points strung in a neat line beside it. He took them for ordinary fixed stars. Over the next nights they shifted their places, and on 13 January a fourth joined them. What were they?
answer: Four bodies circling Jupiter itself
choices: Four bodies circling Jupiter itself
Four stars that Jupiter was drifting past
Four small planets sharing Jupiter's path
Four comets drawn in toward the planet
context: His own words for the first night: 'three little stars, small but very bright, were near the planet.' On 8 January he wrote, 'I found a very different state of things, for there were three little stars all west of Jupiter' -- and fixed stars do not rearrange themselves overnight. By 15 January he had settled it. The whole discovery took about one week of clear nights, and these were the first moons ever seen circling another world. (Wikisource, 'The Sidereal Messenger of Galileo Galilei'; NASA, '415 Years Ago: Astronomer Galileo Discovers Jupiter's Moons')

question: Turning his magnifying tube on the Milky Way in the winter of 1609-10, Galileo Galilei looked at a soft smear of light that the old catalogues could compare only to milk. What did the tube show the band to be?
answer: A mass of countless separate faint stars
choices: A mass of countless separate faint stars
A vast cloud lit by the stars inside it
A trail of fine vapour high in the air
A gap in the sphere of stars, glowing beyond
context: Galileo's line: 'the Galaxy is nothing else but a mass of innumerable stars planted together in clusters.' The same trick worked on every smudge the old catalogues called a 'nebulous star' -- Praesepe, the Beehive, turned out to be 'not a single star but a mass of more than forty starlets.' And the sky got crowded overnight: the Pleiades, six stars to the naked eye, showed more than forty through the tube, and around Orion's belt and sword he added eighty stars nobody had ever recorded. Good binoculars pointed at the Pleiades on a dark night repeat the whole experiment. (Wikisource, 'The Sidereal Messenger of Galileo Galilei'; Wikipedia, 'Sidereus Nuncius')

question: Galileo Galilei watched four faint points shuffle from one side of Jupiter to the other and back in January 1610, night after night, never straying far from it. Educated Europe had been taught several rules about the heavens, and the astronomers who trusted his report saw at once that this sight had destroyed one of them. Which rule?
answer: That every body in the heavens turns about the Earth
choices: That the heavens never alter from one age to the next
That every body in the heavens turns about the Earth
That every body in the heavens keeps one steady pace
That each planet rides on a crystal sphere of its own
context: Here was a second centre of motion -- four objects visibly going round something that was plainly not the Earth -- and no mathematics was needed to see it, only a tube and a clear night. That is why four faint dots detonated a worldview. (Grokipedia, 'Sidereus Nuncius'; Grokipedia, 'Copernican Revolution')

question: Galileo Galilei pointed his new telescope at the crescent Moon on the night of 30 November 1609. He sketched it night after night for weeks, then turned the drawings into watercolour paintings. Old textbooks claimed the Moon was a smooth, perfect ball. How did his drawings really show it?
answer: Rugged and pitted, like the surface of the Earth
choices: Rugged and pitted, like the surface of the Earth
Smooth and polished, like a ball of clear crystal
Flat and still, like a wide sheet of water
Bright and stained, like a disc of beaten silver
context: His own words: the Moon is 'full of inequalities, uneven, full of hollows and protuberances, just like the surface of the Earth itself.' Those watercolours were among the earliest pictures of the Moon drawn through a telescope (Thomas Harriot in England had sketched it that summer) -- and they were made the hard way. His design showed a patch of sky only about fifteen arcminutes across, against the full Moon's thirty, so he could see roughly a quarter of the Moon at a time and had to build the drawings up patch by patch, through a keyhole. (Wikisource, 'The Sidereal Messenger of Galileo Galilei'; Linda Hall Library, 'Mapping the Moon: Early Telescopic Observations'; Rice University Galileo Project, 'Making a Galilean Telescope')

question: Cosimo II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, repaid a piece of flattery in the summer of 1610. His old mathematics tutor, Galileo Galilei, had named four new points of light the Medicean Stars, after Cosimo's family. What did Cosimo hand Galileo?
answer: A salaried court post in Florence with no teaching at all
choices: A salaried court post in Florence with no teaching at all
A teaching chair at Pisa with a seat in the Medici household
A lifetime pension from Venice with a printing licence attached
A share of every tube sold across the Medici lands
context: Court mathematician and philosopher in Florence, at 1,000 florins a year -- double his Padua salary -- and free of lecturing entirely. The discovery doubled as a job application, and the naming was the covering letter. This is told straight rather than tidied away: patronage was how science got paid for in 1610. (Grokipedia, 'Sidereus Nuncius')

question: Hans Lipperhey, a Dutch spectacle-maker, asked for a 30-year patent in October 1608 on a tube he called a kijker, or 'looker.' Less than a year later Galileo Galilei was showing his own tube to Venetian officials at 8 or 9 times power, and he pushed it to about 20 for the Jupiter nights. How did Galileo get his tube?
answer: He heard a description of it and worked out the optics himself
choices: He heard a description of it and worked out the optics himself
He bought one from a Dutch merchant and copied its lens spacing
He was sent a finished kijker by a friend in the Netherlands
He read the patent drawings, which the Dutch had printed in full
context: Galileo did not invent the telescope, and he never claimed to have invented the lens arrangement -- he heard in 1609 that such a thing existed, reasoned out how it had to work, and ground his own lenses. He eventually reached about thirty times. Correcting this one matters: the myth of a lone inventor hides the real skill, which was making a rumour into a working instrument better than anyone else's. (Grokipedia, 'Hans Lipperhey'; Grokipedia, 'Refracting telescope'; Wikipedia, 'Galileo Galilei')

question: A girl looks up at a thin crescent Moon on a clear night and sees the whole dark disc faintly filled in, a dim ashen glow where there should be nothing but night. Galileo Galilei set down an explanation for it, and it has held up ever since. What lights the Moon's dark side?
answer: Sunlight bounced off the Earth
choices: Sunlight bounced off the Earth
Sunlight bent around the Moon's edge
A faint glow of the Moon's own
Starlight gathered from the whole sky
context: It is called earthshine, and the consequence is the striking part: the Earth shines in the Moon's sky exactly the way the Moon shines in ours. The Earth is behaving like one more heavenly body, not a different kind of thing altogether. The next young crescent will show it -- the ashen glow is easy to see with no instrument at all. (Wikipedia, 'Sidereus Nuncius'; Kitchin et al., 'On the Earthshine depicted in Galileo's watercolors of the Moon', arXiv:1707.05314)

question: Galileo Galilei wrote Jupiter's four moons into his notes as plain I, II, III and IV, counted outward from the planet, and called the group the Medicean Stars. Yet every modern chart prints them as Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, and everyone assumes he chose those. Where did the mythological names come from?
answer: Simon Marius, a rival, prompted by Johannes Kepler
choices: Simon Marius, a rival, prompted by Johannes Kepler
Johannes Kepler alone, in a letter printed at Prague
Cosimo II de' Medici, over Galileo's own objection
The astronomers of Rome, a century after Galileo's death
context: Marius printed the names in Mundus Iovialis in 1614, following Kepler's suggestion. They did not become the standard scientific designations until the middle of the twentieth century -- more than three hundred years later. Until then, working astronomers wrote Jupiter I, II, III and IV, exactly as Galileo had. (Grokipedia, 'Galilean moons'; Grokipedia, 'Simon Marius')

question: Johannes Kepler puzzled over a scrambled anagram that Galileo Galilei mailed him after seeing Saturn with two smaller companions in July 1610. Galileo, unsure of his discovery, had hidden the claim that Saturn was triple-bodied. Kepler tried to unscramble it himself before Galileo shared the key. What did Kepler conclude Galileo had found?
answer: Two moons circling the planet Mars
choices: Two moons circling the planet Mars
Two moons circling the planet Venus
A fifth moon circling the planet Jupiter
A pair of stars circling each other
context: Kepler's misreading was 'Salve umbistineum geminatum Martia proles' -- hail, twin offspring of Mars. Mars does have two small moons, though nobody would actually see them for another two and a half centuries. Saturn beat Galileo in the end: in December 1612 the two companions were simply gone, and he wrote, 'Has Saturn devoured his own sons?' (The rings had turned edge-on; Earth crossed the ring plane on 17 February 1613.) He sketched Saturn again in 1616 and never solved it. Christiaan Huygens did, in 1655, with a telescope he ground himself. (Springer, 'The scientific significance of planetary ring systems'; Mental Floss, 'How A Misinterpreted Anagram Predicted The Moons of Mars'; The Oikofuge, 'Galileo, Disappearing Rings, And The Seasons Of Saturn')

question: Galileo Galilei watched bright specks kindle in the darkness along the creeping line of lunar sunrise, points already lit while the ground around them was still in night. He worked out that they were mountain peaks catching the Sun early, and he put a number on their height: more than four Italian miles, when no mountain on Earth, he wrote, reaches even one. What did he measure to get that number?
answer: The distance from a lit peak to the shadow line
choices: The distance from a lit peak to the shadow line
The time from a peak's first light to full sunrise
The width of the notch a peak cut in the Moon's rim
The brightness of a peak against the dark around it
context: His own words: 'more than 4 Italian miles; but in the Earth there are no mountains which reach to the perpendicular height even of one mile.' Geometry, performed on a world he could never visit, from a shadow. Modern measurement says he was close to right. The same investigation can start tonight: any decent binoculars show the ragged sunrise line and the specks kindling ahead of it, and the Moon looks best not when it is full but when that line is crossing the middle of the disc. (Wikisource, 'The Sidereal Messenger of Galileo Galilei'; Wikipedia, 'Sidereus Nuncius')

question: Christoph Scheiner, a Jesuit writing under the pen name 'Apelles hiding behind the painting,' argued that the dark blotches crossing the Sun were swarms of tiny planets passing in front of it, leaving the Sun itself spotless. Everyone agreed the Sun was perfect and unchanging. Galileo Galilei answered that they were marks on its own surface, and pointed to one thing the blotches did. What did they do?
answer: They squashed into thin slivers near the Sun's edge
choices: They squashed into thin slivers near the Sun's edge
They came back darker after each trip across the face
They always crossed along one single straight path
They kept exactly the same spacing from one another
context: That squashing is called foreshortening, and it is the giveaway: a mark painted on a turning sphere gets compressed as it swings toward the edge, while a body floating in front of the Sun would keep its shape all the way across. Galileo published the argument as Istoria e dimostrazioni intorno alle macchie solari in Rome in 1613. So the last perfect thing in the sky both turns and blemishes. WARNING: a telescope, binoculars or the naked eye must never be pointed at the Sun -- solar observation is done by projecting the image onto paper. (Wikipedia, 'Letters on Sunspots'; Linda Hall Library, 'Optics: Telescopes and Technological Change')

question: King Philip III of Spain offered a lifetime pension to anyone who could tell a captain how far east or west he had sailed. In the 1610s Galileo offered the Spanish court a solution: Jupiter's moons slip into the planet's shadow on a schedule predictable years ahead, so a sailor at sea and an astronomer at home could each watch the same eclipse. What were the two men to compare?
answer: The local clock times at which each of them saw the eclipse begin
choices: The local clock times at which each of them saw the eclipse begin
The lengths of time for which each of them saw the eclipse last
The heights above the horizon at which each of them saw Jupiter
The background stars against which each of them saw Jupiter sit
context: Two people anywhere on Earth can watch the same eclipse of the same moon at the very same instant; compare the local time each of them reads off, and the difference gives the difference in longitude. The moons are a clock hung in the sky where everybody can see it. Spain said no, and kept saying no to his later attempts. In 1636 -- old, going blind and under house arrest after his trial -- Galileo petitioned the Dutch States General instead. Their committee reached the same verdict as Spain's but sent him a gold chain anyway, and the Inquisition forbade him to accept it. (Wikipedia, 'History of longitude', which dates his application to Spain to 1616; Grokipedia, 'Celatone'; Grokipedia, 'History of longitude'; Grokipedia, 'Longitude rewards')

question: Galileo Galilei pointed a homemade 20-power scope at Jupiter for the first time in January 1610. Night after night he saw something no one had recorded before, and he wrote it up in a short book that sold out across Europe. What was he watching?
answer: Four small points of light that shifted position
choices: Rings of ice and rock encircling the planet
A great red spot as wide as three Earths
Four small points of light that shifted position
A trail of comets sweeping past the planet
context: Galileo first observed Jupiter on 7 January 1610 and saw three points; a fourth appeared soon after. He watched them almost nightly through March 1610. Sidereus Nuncius (March 1610) announced Jupiter's four largest moons -- now called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. He named them the 'Medicean stars' to court Medici patronage. Source: https://www.loc.gov/collections/finding-our-place-in-the-cosmos-with-carl-sagan/articles-and-essays/modeling-the-cosmos/galileo-and-the-telescope/

question: Galileo Galilei watched through his telescope as one bright planet cycled from a thin crescent to a full round disk and back to a crescent again, from September 1610 through February 1611. Ptolemy's Earth-centred system could not produce that pattern, though Tycho Brahe's compromise system could. Which planet was it?
answer: Venus
choices: Mercury
Venus
Mars
Saturn
context: In the Ptolemaic arrangement Venus rides on an epicycle roughly between Earth and Sun, so it can never show more than a narrow sickle. Galileo saw a FULL cycle of phases, from crescent through gibbous to full and back. That result is incompatible with Ptolemy -- though it is consistent with Tycho Brahe's geo-heliocentric compromise as well as with Copernicus. Source: https://www.cabinet.ox.ac.uk/galileos-most-decisive-telescopic-observation-phases-venus-1610-23-0

question: Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, the Catholic Church's leading theologian, called Galileo Galilei in for a private meeting in Rome on 26 February 1616. Galileo had been publicly championing Copernicus's idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, and the cardinal gave him a formal warning about it. What did Bellarmine say Galileo could and could not do with that idea?
answer: He could treat it as a mathematical hypothesis but not hold or defend it as physically true
choices: He could treat it as a mathematical hypothesis but not hold or defend it as physically true
He could publish only in Latin and only outside the Papal States
He could hold it privately but not teach it to any student under thirty
He could defend it only if he first submitted every draft to the Inquisition
context: Two days earlier, on 24 February 1616, the Inquisition's eleven theologian-qualifiers had graded the proposition that the Sun stands still at the centre of the world 'formally heretical.' Bellarmine's admonition, on 26 February, told Galileo he could use heliocentrism as a calculating device (hypothesi) but could not claim it was physically true. Source: https://www.tau.ac.il/education/muse/museum/galileo/prohibition_helioce.html

question: Galileo Galilei staked his main physical case for the Earth's motion on one everyday thing, in Book Four of the Dialogue, and the case turned out to be wrong. He argued that it proved both the Earth's daily spin and its yearly orbit at once, and he tossed out the old star-based story of it as a myth. Which everyday thing was it?
answer: The ocean tides
choices: The ocean tides
The passage of the trade winds
The scouring of river valleys
The great earthquakes of Sicily
context: Galileo argued that ocean tides were water sloshing in the basins as Earth's daily rotation and yearly orbit combined -- his headline proof of motion. He waved off the Moon's gravitational pull on the seas as astrology. Newton would later show the Moon's pull was in fact the main driver. The heretic on trial was right about his conclusion (Earth moves) and wrong about his best argument for it. Source: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/galileo/

question: Pope Urban VIII gave Galileo Galilei a favourite theological argument while the two were friends: God can produce any effect on Earth by any means He chooses. Galileo's Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems came out in Florence in February 1632. In the finished book, whose mouth did Galileo put that argument into?
answer: Simplicio, the slow-witted Aristotelian
choices: Salviati, the sharp Copernican character
Sagredo, the intelligent Venetian layman
Simplicio, the slow-witted Aristotelian
An anonymous narrator addressing the reader
context: The Dialogue is a three-way conversation among Salviati (the Copernican), Sagredo (the open-minded layman) and Simplicio (the Aristotelian whose name suggests 'the simpleton'). Urban VIII, reading his own favourite argument in Simplicio's mouth, took it as personal mockery, and the Inquisition machinery moved against Galileo shortly after. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialogue_Concerning_the_Two_Chief_World_Systems

question: Kneeling before the Roman Inquisition on 22 June 1633, Galileo Galilei abjured the idea that the Earth moves, and the Dialogue was placed on the Index. The formal wording of the verdict was more specific than simple 'heresy.' What was he actually convicted of?
answer: Vehement suspicion of heresy
choices: Formal heresy of the first degree
Vehement suspicion of heresy
Contempt of the Inquisition's officers
Blasphemy against the Pope himself
context: The sentence of 22 June 1633: 'we pronounce, judge, and declare, that you, the said Galileo ... have rendered yourself vehemently suspected by this Holy Office of heresy, that is, of having believed and held the doctrine (which is false and contrary to the Holy and Divine Scriptures) that the sun is the center of the world, and that it does not move from east to west, and that the earth does move, and is not the center of the world.' He was made to abjure on his knees the same day. Source: https://hti.osu.edu/sites/default/files/documents_in_the_case_of_galileo.pdf

question: Going blind under house arrest at his villa at Arcetri, outside Florence, Galileo Galilei wrote his greatest work in physics, Discourses on Two New Sciences. Newton would build his mechanics on that book. Where was it actually printed in 1638?
answer: At Leiden in the Dutch Republic
choices: In Rome, quietly, with a Papal licence
In Florence, by his own students
At Leiden in the Dutch Republic
In Venice, under a false author's name
context: The manuscript was smuggled out of Italy and printed in 1638 at Leiden by Louis Elzevir, safely beyond the Inquisition's reach. Galileo went completely blind that same year and died at Arcetri on 8 January 1642. The Church's ban on heliocentric books was only slowly un-written: the general prohibition dropped in 1758, Pius VII allowed printing in Rome in 1822, and the Dialogue itself was struck from the Index in 1835. Source: https://www.biography.com/scientists/galileo

question: Pope John Paul II addressed the Pontifical Academy of Sciences on 31 October 1992, closing a commission he had convened in 1980 to re-examine the Galileo trial. He conceded that the theologians of 1633 had made a mistake about Scripture and natural science. Newspapers around the world reported the address inaccurately the next morning. What did the address not do?
answer: It did not annul the 1633 sentence or declare Galileo innocent
choices: It did not annul the 1633 sentence or declare Galileo innocent
It did not reopen any other Index of Forbidden Books rulings
It did not apologise on behalf of Pope Urban VIII by name
It did not lift ecclesiastical review of astronomy texts in seminaries
context: John Paul II acknowledged that the theologians had erred about the relationship of Scripture to natural science, and called for the old misunderstanding between science and faith to be put in the past. He did NOT formally annul the 1633 sentence and did NOT declare Galileo innocent -- a caveat many contemporary press reports missed and still miss. Source: https://www.pas.va/en/magisterium/saint-john-paul-ii/1992-31-october.html

question: Leonard Coatsworth crawled to a tower of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge on 7 November 1940, thrown against the curb as a steady 40 mph wind twisted the road to pieces. He had to leave something behind in his car. What did he leave?
answer: A cocker spaniel named Tubby
choices: A cocker spaniel named Tubby
His leather briefcase
His press camera
His portable typewriter
context: Coatsworth drove onto the bridge around 10:00 a.m. with the family dog. Professor Frederick Farquharson tried to rescue Tubby around 10:55 a.m. but the terrified dog bit him and he had to back away; Tubby went down with the deck. Source: WSDOT, https://www.wsdot.wa.gov/tnbhistory/collapse.htm

question: Leonard Coatsworth was out on the Tacoma Narrows Bridge on the morning of 7 November 1940, the deck heaving up and down as it had for four months, when the motion suddenly changed character. Within an hour the bridge was gone. What did the deck begin doing that morning that it had not done before?
answer: Twisting so hard the two lanes went in opposite directions
choices: Twisting so hard the two lanes went in opposite directions
Sagging in the middle under its own weight
Whipping side to side against its cables
Swaying gently in long slow arcs
context: The standard account is that a cable band slipped at midspan and unbalanced the deck; the new mode was torsional, with one lane rising while the other fell. Photographs show tilt angles reaching about 45 degrees before the suspenders let go around 11:00 a.m. Source: WSDOT, https://www.wsdot.wa.gov/tnbhistory/collapse.htm

question: K. Yusuf Billah and Robert Scanlan published a paper in the American Journal of Physics in 1991 naming the physics textbooks that had the Tacoma Narrows collapse wrong. For half a century those books had reprinted the film as their classic example of one specific concept. Which concept did the textbooks wrongly attach to the collapse?
answer: Classical forced resonance
choices: Classical forced resonance
Metal fatigue in the cables
The Bernoulli effect on the deck
Thermal expansion of the steel
context: The paper was titled 'Resonance, Tacoma Narrows Bridge Failure, and Undergraduate Physics Textbooks'. It named the actual books and showed that the bridge's failure was not the swing-being-pumped kind of resonance most students were taught. Source: Billah and Scanlan 1991, American Journal of Physics, https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Resonance,-Tacoma-Narrows-bridge-failure,-and-Billah-Scanlan/937cd56aca1ebe07044f87f96630cda82f723d0c

question: Robert Scanlan and K. Yusuf Billah pointed to the wind at the Tacoma Narrows on 7 November 1940: it blew steadily from one direction, yet each twist of the deck grew larger than the last until the suspender cables snapped near a 45-degree tilt. Engineers now call the mechanism aeroelastic flutter. How does it feed a steady wind into a bigger and bigger twist?
answer: Air peeled off the tilted deck and locked in step with the twist
choices: Air peeled off the tilted deck and locked in step with the twist
The wind's push simply grew past what the deck could bear
Long ocean swell shoved the roadway upward in bursts
Suspender cables stored and released energy like rubber bands
context: Instead of bleeding energy away, the structure's own motion pumps itself out of a steady flow: as the deck tilts, the way the air separates from its solid flanks changes and shoves harder on the next twist. Above roughly 35 mph the amplitude grew without limit. Some engineers (e.g., Larsen 2000) argue vortex shedding locked onto the torsional mode, so the settled claim is 'self-excited aeroelastic instability, not classical forced resonance', not one tidy equation. Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma_Narrows_Bridge_(1940)

question: Humphry Davy pulled a new metal out of sodium hydroxide in 1807: silver, soft enough to slice with a knife, and needing to be kept under oil. A small lump of this sodium dropped into a bowl of water hisses and fizzes at once. Where in the bowl is the lump while it reacts?
answer: Riding on the surface of the water
choices: Riding on the surface of the water
Resting on the bottom of the bowl
Hovering halfway down in the water
Pinned against the side of the bowl
context: Sodium's density at 20 C is 0.9688 g/cm3 - just under water's - so a lump of it FLOATS while it reacts, skating on the gas it makes. It melts at only 98 C, which is why the racing lump often turns into a molten ball. Davy isolated it in 1807 by electrolysis of sodium hydroxide; because it tarnishes in air by combining with oxygen, sodium is stored under oil or inert gas. Source: Wikipedia 'Sodium' - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium

question: A chemist brings together sodium, a metal that catches fire the moment it touches water, and chlorine, a yellow-green gas heavy enough to sink into low ground. The two dangerous elements react, and the result is a harmless white powder found in every kitchen. Which one?
answer: Table salt
choices: Table salt
Baking soda
Icing sugar
Corn starch
context: The two elements: sodium, a silvery metal soft enough to cut with a knife, isolated by Humphry Davy in 1807; chlorine, a gas with a density of 3.2 g/L against air's ~1.2 g/L, which Davy named in 1810 from the Ancient Greek chloros, 'pale green', for its colour. Carl Wilhelm Scheele made the first detailed study in 1774 by reacting manganese dioxide with hydrochloric acid, recording 'the bleaching effect on litmus, the deadly effect on insects, the yellow-green colour'. At the Second Battle of Ypres on 22 April 1915 the German army released 168 long tons of chlorine from 5,730 cylinders along a 6.5 km front - a 'strange green cloud of death' that tore a 6 km gap in the French line; Fritz Haber proposed using the heavier-than-air gas and supervised the cylinder installation. Sources: Wikipedia 'Sodium', 'Chlorine', 'Second Battle of Ypres'.

question: A girl tips a spoonful of salt onto a dark plate and looks at the grains through a hand lens. They are not shapeless specks: every grain has grown into the same regular form, the one the mineral takes when miners cut it out of the ground as halite. What form is it?
answer: Tiny cubes
choices: Tiny cubes
Slim needles
Flat plates
Round pellets
context: Halite (rock salt / table salt) forms isometric crystals whose habit is 'predominantly cubes', with perfect {001} cleavage in three directions at right angles and a Mohs hardness of only 2.0-2.5 - softer than a copper coin. Its unit cell measures a = 5.6404 A, so the cube you can see on the plate is the inner arrangement enlarged roughly ten million times. Bonus for the lens: 'hopper crystals', cube skeletons, form when the edges grow faster than the faces during rapid crystallisation. Source: Wikipedia 'Halite' - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halite

question: A boy shakes a white seasoning over his dinner without a thought, and it is nothing but sodium, a metal that bursts into flame on water, and chlorine, a gas that kills what breathes it. Nothing was added and nothing was taken away: the same two kinds of atom are all that is there. What did the sodium and the chlorine do to each other?
answer: One electron moved from each sodium to a chlorine
choices: One electron moved from each sodium to a chlorine
One pair of electrons ended up shared between them
All the outer electrons pooled into a common sea
Each atom kept its own and they clung together weakly
context: The give-away in one line: a sodium atom hands over its single outer electron (Na -> Na+ + e-) and a chlorine atom takes it (Cl + e- -> Cl-). What sits in the shaker is not sodium and chlorine ATOMS at all but sodium and chloride IONS - same nuclei, one electron moved, and every property changes. The three wrong options are all real bonding pictures, just not this one: the shared pair is the covalent bond, the common sea is metallic bonding, and weak clinging is van der Waals attraction. Source: Grokipedia 'Ionic bonding' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Ionic_bonding

question: Lawrence Bragg and his father aimed X-rays at a crystal of common salt, NaCl, in 1913. That formula reads like a recipe for a couple: one sodium locked to one chlorine, that pair repeated over and over through the grain. The X-rays found no couples anywhere. What is the real arrangement?
answer: An endless grid, every sodium ringed by six chlorines
choices: An endless grid, every sodium ringed by six chlorines
Chains of four atoms repeating, laid side by side
Flat sheets of sodium alternating with sheets of chlorine
Linked rings of eight atoms with hollow gaps between
context: Solid sodium chloride is a face-centred cubic array of chloride ions with sodium ions filling every octahedral hole - coordination number 6 for BOTH ions, each sodium ringed by six chlorides and each chloride by six sodiums, repeating to the edge of the grain. Wikipedia states it flatly: there are 'no discrete NaCl molecules' in the solid. Chloride ionic radius 167 pm, sodium 116 pm, lattice constant a = 564.02 pm. Sources: Wikipedia 'Sodium chloride' - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chloride ; Grokipedia 'Ionic bonding'.

question: A cook drops a salt crystal into a litre of water and it comes to pieces within seconds; 360 grams of salt will vanish into that one litre. The crystal is a rigid block of charged particles, ions, clamped together by an enormous electrical grip. Yet a water molecule carries no net charge at all. What lets water get hold of those ions and haul them apart?
answer: Each molecule is lopsided: one end negative, one end positive
choices: Each molecule is lopsided: one end negative, one end positive
Water molecules link into chains that pull by hydrogen bonding
Water molecules are small enough to wedge in between the ions
Water's own molecules split into charged pieces that swap places
context: Water does it the other way from salt, and unfairly. Oxygen's Pauling electronegativity is 3.44 against hydrogen's 2.20 - a difference of 1.24 - so oxygen SHARES the electrons but pulls harder, leaving oxygen partially negative and each hydrogen partially positive. The molecule is bent, which stops the two pulls cancelling: the gas-phase H-O-H angle is 104.48 degrees, the O-H bond length about 0.96 A, and the net dipole moment 1.8546 D. Salt's solubility is 360 g/L at 25 C. Sources: Wikipedia 'Properties of water', 'Electronegativity', 'Sodium chloride'; Grokipedia 'Chemical polarity'.

question: Gilbert N. Lewis filled his lecture notes from about 1902 with atoms drawn as little cubes, an electron possible at each corner, and he kept the sketch to himself for fourteen years. When he finally published 'The Atom and the Molecule' in 1916, he set down what a chemical bond between two atoms actually is. What did he propose a bond to be?
answer: A pair of electrons shared between the two atoms
choices: A pair of electrons shared between the two atoms
A single electron passed from one atom to the other
An attraction between the two atoms' opposite poles
A set number of affinity units each atom must satisfy
context: Lewis's cubes were a teaching doodle in unpublished notes, 'in which the corners of the cube represented possible electron positions'; in that picture a single bond is two cubes sharing an EDGE (two shared electrons) and a double bond two cubes sharing a FACE (four). Walther Kossel, son of the Nobel laureate Albrecht Kossel, published the rival give-and-take (ionic) picture independently in the same year, 1916 - both men reaching the octet from opposite ends. Irving Langmuir coined the term in 1919, not 1916, and the word was 'covalence': in the Journal of the American Chemical Society of 1 June 1919 he wrote, 'we shall denote by the term covalence the number of pairs of electrons that a given atom shares with its neighbors.' Merriam-Webster dates the exact phrase 'covalent bond' to 1939. Lewis's shared pair had no physics under it until Walter Heitler and Fritz London worked out the hydrogen molecule in 1927 - 'the first successful quantum mechanical explanation of chemical bonding', eleven years after the drawing. Lewis himself was nominated for the Nobel Prize 41 times and never won one; he coined the word 'photon' in 1926 and produced the first pure sample of heavy water in 1933. On 23 March 1946 a graduate student found his body under a laboratory workbench at Berkeley; he had been working with liquid hydrogen cyanide and had returned from lunch with his old rival Langmuir 'in a dark mood'. Sources: Wikipedia 'Gilbert N. Lewis', 'Cubical atom', 'Covalent bond', 'Walther Kossel'; Grokipedia 'Gilbert N. Lewis'.

question: Henry E. Armstrong, an old-guard chemist, fired back in Nature in 1927 with a one-page piece headed 'Poor Common Salt!' Lawrence Bragg, who had read the crystal with X-rays, had announced that salt holds no NaCl molecules at all: the equal numbers of the two atoms fall out of how the crystal packs, not from atoms pairing off. How is Armstrong reported to have swatted the physicists' picture aside?
answer: By insisting that chemistry is neither chess nor geometry
choices: By insisting that chemistry is neither chess nor geometry
By insisting X-rays could see only the crystal's outer faces
By insisting the salt in the experiment must have been impure
By insisting the molecules were hiding inside the pattern
context: Sodium chloride was the first crystal structure ever determined by X-ray diffraction, published in 1913 by W. Lawrence Bragg with his father W. H. Bragg ('The Structure of Some Crystals as indicated by their Diffraction of X-rays', Proc. Roy. Soc.); it showed crystals are repeating ATOMIC lattices, not stacks of molecules. Von Laue, Friedrich and Knipping had only discovered X-ray diffraction by crystals in April 1912. Father and son shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics; Lawrence was 25 and remains the youngest science laureate ever. Bragg had written: 'In sodium chloride there appear to be no molecules represented by NaCl... it is a result of geometry and not of a pairing-off of the atoms.' Armstrong's furious reply protested 'the unjustified aspersion of the molecular character of our most necessary condiment'. Flagged as legend because the exact wording of his chess-and-geometry line is corroborated through a secondary source rather than the Nature page itself. Sources: H. E. Armstrong, 'Poor Common Salt!', Nature 120, 478 (1927) - https://www.nature.com/articles/120478b0 ; wording corroborated via RSC Chem. Educ. Res. Pract. accepted manuscript; OUPblog centenary piece; Wikipedia 'William Lawrence Bragg'.

question: A student turns a tap down to a thread-thin stream and holds beside it a comb he has just dragged through his hair, and the stream bends toward the comb. Rubbing loaded the comb with extra electrons, so a friend explains the bend at once: water must carry a positive charge, and opposite charges attract. The student rubs a glass rod until it carries a positive charge and holds it beside the stream instead. Which way does the stream go?
answer: It bends toward the rod, just as it did toward the comb
choices: It bends toward the rod, just as it did toward the comb
It bends away from the rod, the opposite way to before
It runs dead straight, unmoved by the positive rod
It bends toward the rod only while the tap runs fast
context: The stream is attracted either way. Water molecules simply rotate, turning whichever end suits toward whatever charge is nearby, so a negatively charged comb and a positively charged glass rod both pull the stream over. A kid who reasons 'the comb is negative, so it pulls the positive water' has the wrong model, and the glass rod is the test that exposes it - which is exactly what a second, opposite trial is for. You can run both tonight with a comb, a glass rod and a wool sleeve. Sources: Saint Mary's University Physics Demos, 'Bending Water with Static Electricity' - https://demos.smu.ca/demos/e-n-m/62-bending-water ; Rutgers Chemistry demo, 'Polarity - Bending of a Liquid Stream'.

question: Philip Mason and Pavel Jungwirth filmed a drop of a sodium-potassium alloy hitting water in 2015, at 10,000 frames per second. For a hundred years textbooks had explained sodium in water one way: the metal makes hydrogen, the heat lights the hydrogen, and the piece bangs. In the first millisecond, before any flame, the film showed something that story cannot explain. What happened to the drop in that first millisecond?
answer: Metal spikes shot out of the drop in all directions
choices: Metal spikes shot out of the drop in all directions
A shell of steam lifted the drop clear of the water
The drop flattened into a thin disc before it burned
A blue glow spread through the water round the drop
context: Electrons leave the metal into the water almost instantly, leaving positive metal ions packed side by side; they repel one another past the Rayleigh instability limit and the drop tears itself apart in a 'Coulomb explosion', which then exposes fresh metal and makes the whole thing worse. The camera ran at 10,000 frames per second - 400x slow motion. A demonstration performed in schools for over a century was not fully explained until 2015, which is a standing reminder that 'everyone knows why' is not the same as 'somebody checked'. Source: Mason, Uhlig, Vanek, Buttersack, Bauerecker & Jungwirth, 'Coulomb explosion during the early stages of the reaction of alkali metals with water', Nature Chemistry (2015) - https://www.nature.com/articles/nchem.2161 ; corroborated at Chemistry World and C&EN.

question: Linus Pauling proposed electronegativity in 1932, a single number for how hard an atom pulls on the electrons it shares. Sodium and chlorine differ by 2.23, and the bond is filed as ionic; oxygen and hydrogen in water differ by 1.24, and the bond is filed as covalent. The cut-off between the two names sits at 1.7. Where does 1.7 come from?
answer: From agreement among chemists; nothing in nature changes at 1.7
choices: From agreement among chemists; nothing in nature changes at 1.7
From a jump in bond behaviour; measurements cluster right at 1.7
From Pauling's X-ray work; salt crystals fixed the line at 1.7
From molten-salt experiments; current flows only above 1.7
context: Pauling's scale 'characterizes a bond along the continuous scale from covalent to ionic bonding' - it is a spectrum, not two boxes. Fluorine is the highest at 3.98 and caesium the lowest at 0.79. Textbooks 'generally' call a difference above 1.7 predominantly ionic and above 2.0 near-complete transfer, but those cut-offs are conventions, not nature. Covalent character is greatest between atoms of similar electronegativity: H-H is the perfectly even case, H-Cl the lopsided one, water sits at 1.24 and sodium chloride off the end at 2.23. The honest words are 'mostly ionic' and 'mostly covalent'. Sources: Wikipedia 'Electronegativity', 'Covalent bond'; Grokipedia 'Ionic bonding'.

question: James Cloyd Downs patented a cell in 1924 that runs common salt backwards: a current pushed through molten sodium chloride between a carbon rod and an iron shell, with chlorine gas bubbling off one and molten sodium running off the other. To keep the bath liquid near 600 C instead of 801 C, two-thirds of it by weight is calcium chloride, so there is more calcium in the pot than sodium. Yet almost none of that calcium comes out as metal. Why?
answer: Calcium ions take up electrons less readily than sodium ions
choices: Calcium ions take up electrons less readily than sodium ions
Calcium ions carry two charges and barely move in the melt
Calcium metal dissolves back into the melt as fast as it forms
Calcium ions cannot reach the iron shell where the metal forms
context: In the Downs cell (invented 1923, patented 1924) the reactions are 2Cl- -> Cl2(g) + 2e- at the carbon anode and 2Na+ + 2e- -> 2Na(l) at the iron cathode: green gas out one side, molten silvery metal out the other, the two lethal elements pulled back out of the seasoning. The bath runs at about 33.2% NaCl to 66.8% CaCl2, which drops the melting point to roughly 600 C. Calcium's standard reduction potential (-2.87 V) is more negative than sodium's (-2.71 V), so the sodium ions collect the electrons first and the calcium mostly stays in the melt; the little calcium that does come out is the main impurity in Downs-cell sodium and is removed afterwards. Source: Wikipedia 'Downs cell' - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downs_cell

question: A New York Times editorial writer sneered at Robert H. Goddard on 13 January 1920. Goddard, who taught physics at Clark College, had suggested a rocket could reach the Moon. That sneer became the most-quoted line in science reporting. What did it say Goddard lacked?
answer: the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools
choices: the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools
the training given freely in technical colleges
the patience learned in any working laboratory
the arithmetic taught in first-year engineering
context: The piece was unsigned, ran in the 'Topics of the Times' column, and was titled 'A Severe Strain on Credulity'. The same paper had run a straight, respectful news story the day before, on 12 January 1920, headed 'Believes Rocket Can Reach the Moon' -- it reported the claim, then ridiculed it twenty-four hours later. The editorial also jabbed that doubting the professor would mean denying 'a fundamental law of dynamics, and only Dr. Einstein and his chosen dozen, so few and fit, are licensed to do that.' The press called Goddard the 'Moon man' and the 'rocket man' for years afterward. Sources: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?' (Air & Space Quarterly, Summer 2026); Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard'.

question: Robert H. Goddard flew the world's first liquid-fuel rocket on his Aunt Effie's snowy farm at Auburn, Massachusetts, on 16 March 1926. With no ignition switch, one assistant had to set it going by hand and get clear fast. How did the assistant light it?
answer: he held up a blowtorch on the end of a long pole
choices: he held up a blowtorch on the end of a long pole
he touched a burning taper down through the frame
he fired a signal flare at the base from cover
he dropped a lit rag onto the launch stand and ran
context: The assistant then, in historian Kevin Schindler's phrase, 'ran like heck.' Esther Goddard was filming, but her camera could shoot only seven seconds at a time and the rocket sat roaring on its frame so long that the film ran out before it lifted -- there is no film of the first liquid-fuel rocket flight. Goddard's diary the next day: 'It rose 41 feet & went 184 feet, in 2.5 secs., after the lower half of the nozzle burned off,' and 'It looked almost magical as it rose.' Roughly 60 mph. The launch site is now the ninth fairway of the Pakachoag Golf Course, marked by a four-foot granite obelisk. Sources: Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?'; Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard'; Clark University Goddard Collection.

question: Editors at the New York Times printed a short item titled 'A Correction' on 17 July 1969, the morning after Apollo 11 lifted off. Their paper had mocked Robert Goddard forty-nine years earlier. Experiment had proved Isaac Newton right, the notice said, and it closed 'The Times regrets the error.' What did it say was now known?
answer: that a rocket can work in a vacuum as well as in air
choices: that a rocket can work in a vacuum as well as in air
that a rocket can carry a man beyond Earth's gravity
that a rocket can be steered across hundreds of miles
that a rocket can lift more than its own weight in fuel
context: The correction in full: 'Further investigation and experimentation have confirmed the findings of Isaac Newton in the 17th Century, and it is now definitely established that a rocket can function in a vacuum as well as in an atmosphere. The Times regrets the error.' Watch the date: Apollo 11 launched on 16 July 1969 and landed on 20 July, so the paper corrected itself the morning after the LAUNCH, not after the landing. Goddard did not live to see it; he had died decades earlier. Sources: Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?'; Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard'.

question: Reporters passed over the sober mathematics that filled nearly all of Robert H. Goddard's 69-page Smithsonian paper of 1919 and seized on about eight lines on the next-to-last page. There he sketched a way to prove a rocket had actually reached the Moon. What did those eight lines propose?
answer: setting off flash powder on the Moon's dark face for a telescope
choices: setting off flash powder on the Moon's dark face for a telescope
bouncing a wireless signal off the Moon and timing its return
sending a mirror to catch sunlight and flash it back to Earth
sending a camera around the Moon and bringing the film back
context: Goddard's own wording: 'The only reliable procedure would be to send the smallest mass of flash powder possible to the dark surface of the moon in such a way that it would be ignited on impact. The light would then be visible in a powerful telescope.' Eight lines at the back of a technical monograph -- and they produced years of ridicule. The paper was 'A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes', Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections Vol. 71 No. 2 (1919). Sources: Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?'; Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard'.

question: Robert H. Goddard sealed something inside a chamber at Clark in 1915, drew out the air, set it off and watched which way it moved. Five years later a New York Times editorial charged that he did not grasp action and reaction and needed 'something better than a vacuum against which to react.' What had he sealed in there?
answer: a loaded pistol
choices: a loaded pistol
a firecracker
a signal flare
a flash-powder charge
context: When the pistol fired inside the vacuum chamber, the escaping gases pushed it the opposite way -- exactly as they would in open air. In a second 1915 experiment Goddard fired small rockets inside a vacuum tube he had bent into a ring; they worked perfectly well. The editorial of 1920 was written against an experiment that already existed and was five years old. Source: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?', quoting NASA historian James Anderson.

question: The writer who mocked Robert H. Goddard in the New York Times in 1920 applied to rockets something genuinely true of a different engine. A jet airliner really cannot operate above the atmosphere; put a jet engine in a vacuum and it stops dead. Why does a jet engine need the air it flies through?
answer: it scoops the oxygen it burns straight out of that air
choices: it scoops the oxygen it burns straight out of that air
it needs the air outside for its exhaust to push against
it relies on air rushing past to keep its blades cool
it depends on outside air pressure to hold its flame steady
context: A jet is air-breathing: no air, no oxygen, no fire. A rocket carries its own oxidiser along with its fuel, which is exactly why it works where a jet cannot. The 1920 writer took a true fact about one kind of engine and applied it to the wrong kind. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rocket engine' -- 'Rocket vehicles carry their own oxidiser, unlike most combustion engines such as pulse engines or jet engines, so rocket engines can be used in a vacuum.'

question: Neighbours at Auburn thought an aeroplane had come down in 1929, when Robert H. Goddard's rocket climbed about ninety feet, nosed over, crashed and set the grass alight. They called for help, and the state fire marshal banned him from launching there again. The flight was still a first in the history of science, because of what it carried. What was aboard?
answer: a camera, a thermometer and a barometer
choices: a camera, a thermometer and a barometer
a compass, a stopwatch and a hygrometer
a clock, a magnetometer and a spectroscope
a thermometer, a hygrometer and an electroscope
context: They were the first scientific instruments ever launched by a rocket. The crash also put Goddard back in the papers -- the next day's headline read 'MOON ROCKET MISSES TARGET BY 238,799 1/2 MILES' -- and that coverage caught Charles Lindbergh's attention. Lindbergh met Goddard at Clark on 23 November 1929, and the Guggenheim grant approved in July 1930 funded the rest of his career. Sources: Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?'; Grokipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard'; TIME, 'Rocket Scientist Robert Goddard' (headline).

question: The Times writer of 1920 took it for granted that a rocket must shove against something in the world around it: Robert H. Goddard, he wrote, needed 'something better than a vacuum against which to react.' Goddard's sealed-chamber test had already shown thrust surviving with nothing around it. What does a rocket shove against?
answer: the hot gas it throws backwards out of its own nozzle
choices: the hot gas it throws backwards out of its own nozzle
the walls of the chamber where its own fuel burns
the Earth's gravitational field, which it pushes away
the shock front its burning fuel drives out ahead of it
context: This is Newton's third law, stated in the Principia of 1687: 'to every action there is always opposed an equal reaction.' The engine shoves hot exhaust backwards and the exhaust shoves the rocket forwards, just as hard. The propellant is the partner, not the atmosphere -- which is why the editorial's demand for 'something better than a vacuum' was asking for something a rocket never needed. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Newton's laws of motion' (third law and the rocket-propulsion worked example); Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?'.

question: Robert H. Goddard took his readings from the sealed chamber at Clark in 1915, and they answered more than the question 'does a rocket still work with no air around it?' They also settled what the surrounding atmosphere actually does to an engine's push. What did his measurements show?
answer: thrust rose in the chamber -- the air had been cutting it
choices: thrust rose in the chamber -- the air had been cutting it
thrust fell in the chamber -- the air had been adding to it
thrust held steady -- the air made no measurable difference
thrust varied -- the air helped some fuels and hurt others
context: A rocket's performance actually decreases under atmospheric pressure. The thrust equation carries a pressure term, A_e(p_e - p_amb): as the outside pressure falls, thrust rises. At the Earth's surface that pressure thrust can be reduced by up to 30 percent, depending on engine design. Air is not the rocket's partner -- air is in the way. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard' ('his experiment demonstrated that a rocket's performance actually decreases under atmospheric pressure') and Wikipedia, 'Rocket engine'.

question: A student at a blackboard writes that momentum is mass times velocity, and that in a closed system the total never changes. Newton's third law, she adds, is that same bookkeeping seen as forces: every push comes with an equal push the other way. So the two pushes on a rocket should cancel, she reasons, and leave nothing to move. Yet the rocket accelerates. Where does her argument go wrong?
answer: the two forces act on two separate bodies, the gas and the rocket
choices: the two forces act on two separate bodies, the gas and the rocket
the two forces act at two separate moments, one just after the other
the two forces act along two separate lines, so they never truly oppose
the two forces act on two separate parts of the same rocket body
context: A common misconception is that action and reaction cancel one another; because they act on distinct bodies, their effects are independent and each body accelerates on its own. One force acts on the exhaust gas, the other on the rocket. It is the same bookkeeping that makes a rifle recoil into your shoulder and lets a swimmer who shoves water backwards travel forwards. Source: Grokipedia, 'Newton's laws of motion'.

question: Robert H. Goddard put a formula for the top speed a rocket can reach in the early pages of his 1919 Smithsonian paper, the very document the New York Times was reviewing when it declared he did not understand reaction. Only two things fix that ceiling: the share of the rocket's mass that is fuel, and one property of the engine. Which property?
answer: how fast the gas leaves the nozzle
choices: how fast the gas leaves the nozzle
how much thrust it makes at lift-off
how much fuel it burns each second
how long the engine keeps firing
context: Goddard's formula was v = c(1-k) ln(M/(M-m)): c is the speed of the exhaust gas, k the inert, non-propellant share, and M and M-m the rocket's mass before and after the burn. Thrust never appears in it, nor burn time -- and neither does the air. He built the whole derivation from conservation of momentum alone: the forward impulse on the rocket equals the backward momentum of its exhaust, with no atmosphere anywhere in it. The proof the editorial said he lacked was sitting inside the document the editorial was reviewing. He was also not the first to get there: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, a deaf Russian schoolteacher who taught himself physics in Moscow's public libraries after scarlet fever took his hearing at about nine, had derived the same rocket equation in 1903 and analysed rocket propulsion specifically in vacuum conditions. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard' and 'Konstantin Tsiolkovsky'; Goddard, 'A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes', Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections Vol. 71 No. 2 (1919).

question: A child eats a bowl of white rice, and it gives her almost no beta-carotene, the orange pigment the body turns into vitamin A. The same plant makes plenty in its green leaves. Children raised on a rice-only diet can go blind from that gap. Why does the grain end up with almost none?
answer: The pathway is switched off in the endosperm
choices: The pathway is switched off in the endosperm
The pathway is destroyed when the outer bran is milled away
The pathway runs only in green tissue that sees sunlight
The pathway is blocked by phenolic compounds in the husk
context: The endosperm never expresses the enzymes that would carry the carotenoid chain to completion, so a food that dominates half the world's plates carries almost no provitamin A. This is why children living mainly on white rice go blind. Source: goldenrice.org/Content2-How.

question: Two European plant scientists published their finished result in the journal Science in January 2000, after about eight years on one problem. They had added a genetic pathway to rice so that its grains would produce beta-carotene. Who were the two authors?
answer: Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer
choices: Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer
Norman Borlaug and M. S. Swaminathan
Marc Van Montagu and Jeff Schell
Mary-Dell Chilton and Robert Fraley
context: Potrykus (ETH Zurich) and Beyer (Freiburg) began the work in the early 1990s and finally succeeded in 1999; the paper was Ye et al., Science 287:303-305 (2000). All four pairs are real names from twentieth-century crop and plant-genetics work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingo_Potrykus; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11880581.

question: The original Golden Rice team borrowed exactly two enzyme genes from outside rice to finish the beta-carotene pathway inside the grain. One came from a soil bacterium, Erwinia uredovora. The other, a phytoene synthase, came from a common European garden flower. Which flower?
answer: Daffodil
choices: Daffodil
Marigold
Sunflower
Tulip
context: The daffodil gene (Narcissus pseudonarcissus) supplied phytoene synthase; the bacterial crtI carried the intermediate on to beta-carotene. Together they wake the pathway back up inside the endosperm. Marigold and sunflower are real carotenoid-rich plants -- honest wrong picks. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11880581.

question: A German plant scientist stood among yellow rice plants on the front cover of Time magazine on 31 July 2000. The rice had been genetically engineered to carry beta-carotene, the orange nutrient the body turns into vitamin A, and it was aimed at children in poor countries who go blind from lacking it. What did the cover line above him promise?
answer: This rice could save a million kids a year
choices: This rice could save a million kids a year
The grain that will end world hunger forever
One seed that could feed a billion people
A modified crop that could beat malnutrition
context: The kids in the headline were the roughly 250,000-500,000 children the WHO estimated go blind each year from vitamin A deficiency, about half of whom die within twelve months. Source: time.com/archive/6598226; who.int/data/nutrition/nlis.

question: Critics of the 1999 prototype made one fair, specific charge: its beta-carotene dose, about 1.6 micrograms per gram, was too low for rice alone to meet a child's daily vitamin A need. A team at Syngenta answered in 2005 with a second-generation line that produced roughly 23 times more carotenoid. What one change did the trick?
answer: They replaced the original psy gene with the maize version
choices: They replaced the original psy gene with the maize version
They added a third enzyme borrowed from the carrot pathway
They increased the copy number by growing the line in polyploid rice
They fortified the milled grain with synthetic beta-carotene after harvest
context: Maize (Zea mays) phytoene synthase massively outperformed the original in tissue-culture screens. Golden Rice 2 reached about 37 micrograms/g of carotenoid (~84% beta-carotene). The dose objection was answered nearly two decades before the plant was allowed to be grown. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15793573.

question: Government researchers were a few weeks from harvesting a field trial of Golden Rice at Pili, in Camarines Sur province in the Philippines, on 8 August 2013. The yellow rice was engineered to carry vitamin A for children at risk of going blind, and the crop stood ready to be measured and studied. What ended the trial before it could be harvested?
answer: Roughly four hundred protesters uprooted the plot by hand
choices: Roughly four hundred protesters uprooted the plot by hand
A typhoon flattened the plot the day before harvest
Regulators quietly pulled the permit and had it plowed under
A rice-blast fungal outbreak wiped the trial out
context: Data collection was set back months. Field reports differ on exactly who was in the crowd, so the record simply says protesters. This was one of a handful of GM trials destroyed by direct action worldwide that decade. Source: science.org, 'Activists Destroy Golden Rice Field Trial'.

question: Sir Richard Roberts published an open letter in late June 2016, signed by Nobel prize winners, urging one campaign group to stop opposing Golden Rice, the rice engineered to carry vitamin A to poor children. The group fought all patented engineered crops and warned that Golden Rice would pave the way for more. Which group was it, and about how many laureates signed at launch?
answer: Greenpeace, about 107 laureates
choices: Greenpeace, about 107 laureates
Friends of the Earth, about 80 laureates
IFOAM Organics International, about 50 laureates
ETC Group, about 40 laureates
context: The launch press event was held June 30, 2016 at the National Press Club in Washington; more laureates added their names over the following months. Greenpeace's public reply was that Golden Rice had 'failed' after 20 years -- the letter's point was that 20 years of blocking was what produced the delay. The other three groups are real organizations that have campaigned against GM crops. Source: sciencealert.com, '107 Nobel Laureates Just Signed a Letter Slamming Greenpeace'.

question: Judges of the Philippine Court of Appeals revoked the commercial permit for Golden Rice in April 2024, three years after the Philippines had become the first country to approve it for growing. They ruled under a special writ for large environmental cases. What reason did they give?
answer: Conflicting scientific views on its long-term safety
choices: Conflicting scientific views on its long-term safety
Its vitamin dose was too low to help any child
Its seed patents belonged to a foreign company
It had failed the country's own food-safety tests
context: The writ was the Writ of Kalikasan, 'kalikasan' being Filipino for 'nature', a remedy the Philippine Supreme Court created in 2010 for large-scale environmental cases. The court cited a lack of full scientific certainty about the rice's effects on health and the environment, found no scientific consensus on its safety, and leaned on the constitution's precautionary principle. The low-dose objection had been answered by Golden Rice 2 back in 2005. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Golden rice'; phys.org, 'Philippine court blocks GMO golden rice production over safety fears'.

question: Charles Goodyear had mixed rubber with anything he could beg. Every batch still turned to sticky goo in the summer heat. In 1839, at a Woburn factory he was closing, a scrap of his rubber-and-sulphur mix touched a hot stove. What did it do?
answer: It charred and stiffened like a piece of leather.
choices: It melted into a bright pool across the iron.
It puffed up and gave off a choking white smoke.
It charred and stiffened like a piece of leather.
It cracked apart into small brittle black flakes.
context: Goodyear's own 1853 memoir gives the moment in one quiet sentence, written of himself in the third person: 'He was surprised to find that the specimen, being carelessly brought in contact with a hot stove, charred like leather.' What made that astonishing was that gum-elastic 'always melted when exposed to a high degree of heat.' Note what is NOT in his account: no rage, no flung sample, no general store, no frying pan. The popular retellings added those and they contradict each other (Lemelson-MIT has locals mocking him in a store until an animated gesture lands the sample on a potbellied stove; Wikipedia's own vulcanization article has him 'accidentally drop the mixture in a hot frying pan'). It happened at the old Eagle India Rubber works at Woburn, Massachusetts, which Goodyear was visiting for the purpose of shutting the manufacturing down. Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), pp. 117-119, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good; myth versions at lemelson.mit.edu/resources/charles-goodyear and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcanization.

question: Frank Seiberling founded a rubber works in Akron, Ohio, in 1898 and named it after a dead stranger: Charles Goodyear, who had died deep in debt in 1860 and whose family had no stake in the firm. What did the firm make?
answer: Horseshoe pads, poker chips and bicycle tires.
choices: Raincoats, boot soles and surgical tubing.
Horseshoe pads, poker chips and bicycle tires.
Automobile tires, inner tubes and rubber floor mats.
Fire hoses, drive belts and printing rollers.
context: Frank Seiberling founded the Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company in Akron on 29 August 1898. He simply borrowed the name; the firm had no connection to Charles Goodyear or to his family, and cars barely existed yet, so before there were automobiles to sell to it made bicycle and carriage tires, rubber horseshoe pads and poker chips. Goodyear himself had earned nearly $163,000 from the patent but owed far more. He died on 1 July 1860, aged 59, at the Fifth Avenue Hotel in New York: he had been travelling to see a dying daughter and was told on arrival that she was already dead, and collapsed. His estate stood at roughly $200,000 in debt, and his son Charles Jr. untangled the books and paid the creditors. Five years before that he had managed both extremes in a single year: debtors' prison in England and again in France, over debts run up staging lavish rubber displays at the Paris Exposition Universelle, and induction into the French Legion of Honour while he was imprisoned. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodyear_Tire_and_Rubber_Company; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Goodyear (citing Charles Slack, 'Noble Obsession', 2003, pp. 210, 213, 226, 230, 234-5); connecticuthistory.org, 'Charles Goodyear and the Vulcanization of Rubber'.

question: Rubber men at a works in Woburn, Massachusetts, watched Charles Goodyear hold up a scrap of his mixture in 1839, his own brother among them. It had just refused to melt on a hot stove, and he saw at once that it mattered. How did they take it?
answer: They shrugged it off as one more of his experiments.
choices: They demanded he repeat it in front of a chemist.
They offered to buy the mixture from him on the spot.
They put it down to the stove, not to the mixture.
They shrugged it off as one more of his experiments.
context: Goodyear's memoir is blunt about the reception: 'The occurrence did not at the time appear to them to be worthy of notice; it was considered as one of the frequent appeals that he was in the habit of making, in behalf of some new experiment.' The men in that room knew the rubber trade, and they had watched Goodyear cry wolf over promising scraps for years. It is one of the sharpest lessons in the history of discovery: the most important moment in rubber happened in front of witnesses who were qualified to judge it, and they judged it worthless.
