Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), p. 119, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good.

question: Neighbours took in Charles Goodyear's wife and children while he sold the family furniture and went on mixing rubber with every powder and liquid he could get. Two of his small sons died in those five years. In the worst of it, what were the Goodyears living on?
answer: Frogs they caught and half-frozen potatoes they dug.
choices: Clams they raked at low tide and greens they boiled.
Frogs they caught and half-frozen potatoes they dug.
Salt fish and beans bought on credit at the village store.
Acorns they gathered and eels they speared in the creek.
context: Goodyear was jailed for debt repeatedly, on both sides of the Atlantic, and came close to killing himself with his own chemistry: while secretly running his nitric-acid process he 'came near being suffocated by generating a large quantity of gas in a close room; he, however, escaped with a course of fever.' The frogs-and-potatoes winter is the low point of a five-year stretch in which he had no laboratory, no chemical training, and no income, and it is the reason the stove is not really a story about luck. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Goodyear (citing Diana Ross McCain, 'It Happened in Connecticut', 2008, p. 82); Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), p. 107.

question: Mr. Chaffee had stirred sulphur into rubber at the Roxbury company years before Charles Goodyear's stove, and neither he nor the company thought the result worth a second look. Goodyear names one plain practical thing that had kept sulphured rubber out of the shops. What was it?
answer: The goods themselves gave off a strong sulphur smell.
choices: The sulphur cost more than the rubber it went into.
The goods themselves gave off a strong sulphur smell.
The goods stained everything they touched bright yellow.
The sulphur crumbled back out of the rubber in weeks.
context: Goodyear's wording: 'the obnoxious odor of sulphur in the goods was an effectual barrier to their reception in the market.' Of Chaffee's earlier trial at Roxbury he writes that 'the effects were not deemed worthy of notice, either by that company or himself.' Half the answer to the greatest materials problem of the age was already lying around in the industry, and the trade had walked past it because the product smelled bad. What was missing was heat, and someone still looking. Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), pp. 113-114, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good.

question: Charles Goodyear wrote his recipe into his 1844 patent: twenty-five parts rubber to five parts sulphur, held near 270 degrees Fahrenheit. Raw rubber is a tangle of very long molecule chains, wound around one another but each chain a separate strand, and rubber like that turns to goo in summer heat. He could not account for why so little sulphur cured it. What was the sulphur doing to those chains?
answer: Building short bridges from one chain across to another.
choices: Welding the chains end to end into far longer chains.
Coiling each chain into a spring that grips its neighbours.
Wedging fine hard grains into the gaps between the chains.
Building short bridges from one chain across to another.
context: Chemists call such a bridge a CROSS-LINK. The reactive spots on a rubber chain are its allylic C-H bonds, hydrogens on carbons sitting next to a C=C double bond; vulcanization swaps some of those for short chains of one or several sulphur atoms running across to a cure site on a DIFFERENT chain, with hundreds or thousands of carbons between one bridge and the next. The segments between bridges can still stretch and recoil, so the rubber stays springy, but whole chains can no longer slide past one another and flow. It also runs one way only: vulcanized rubber is a thermoset, so you cannot melt it down and recast it the way you can a plastic. Goodyear's actual recipe is in the patent: 'I take twenty-five parts of india-rubber, five parts of sulphur, and seven parts of white lead,' heated between 212 and 350 degrees Fahrenheit but 'for the best effect approaching as nearly as may be to 270.' Nobody then could say what the white lead was doing; it was acting as what chemists now call an activator. Turn the sulphur far up instead, to somewhere between 25 and 80 percent, and the springy solid becomes rigid black ebonite, the hard rubber Charles's brother Nelson Goodyear developed in 1851 for combs, bowling balls, clarinet mouthpieces and car battery cases. Same reaction, different dial setting. Sources: US Patent 3,633 (15 June 1844), patents.google.com/patent/US3633A/en; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcanization; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur_vulcanization; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebonite; Akiba, 'Vulcanisation and crosslinking in elastomers', Progress in Polymer Science 22(3):475-521 (1997).

question: Admirers as far away as Europe praised the finish Charles Goodyear gave his rubber goods by boiling them in quicklime and water, which tanned the gum and killed its stickiness. He thought he had already won, before the stove ever came into it. Then he found the flaw himself, and it wiped the process out. What had he found?
answer: A drop of weak acid turned the rubber soft again.
choices: A night of hard frost cracked the goods right through.
A week in strong sun bleached and powdered the surface.
A drop of weak acid turned the rubber soft again.
A rag soaked in lamp oil lifted the finish clean off.
context: The quicklime bath 'appeared to have the effect of tanning the gum, and destroying its viscous property' -- and then a drop of weak acid neutralised the alkali and the rubber went soft again. Goodyear broke his own triumph, which is the first scientific virtue: the first person an experimenter must doubt is himself. The graveyard of his other fixes is just as instructive. Magnesia, up to a pound of it to a pound of gum, gave him rubber that came out WHITE, a genuine novelty since 'no India rubber goods except black had before that time been made in the United States,' but it did not last. Quicklime stirred straight into the gum was 'too powerfully caustic to be worked by hand.' And his nitric-acid 'acid gas' process cured only the skin: a US Government mail-bag order made with it was treated across the trade as the test of the invention, and the bags rotted in the warm season because the acid had 'not changed far below the surface.' The compound he happened to test on the stove was the same one that had decomposed in those mail-bags. Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), pp. 100-110, 115-118, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good.

question: Charles Goodyear held a piece of rubber-coated cloth in front of an open fire to test what the stove had done, since a charred scrap looks like a ruined one. The cloth blackened again. One detail in that scorched cloth told him he was right after all. What was it?
answer: A narrow band at the burn's edge, firm and springy and whole.
choices: A round patch at the very centre, firm and springy and whole.
A narrow band at the burn's edge, firm and springy and whole.
A thin skin across the whole face, firm and springy and whole.
A scatter of small spots in the char, firm and springy and whole.
context: In his own words: 'The same effect, that of charring the gum, followed; but there were further and very satisfactory indications of ultimate success... as upon the edge of the charred portions of the fabric, there appeared a line, or border, that was not charred, but perfectly cured.' That thin band is the whole discovery. It proved heat had a RIGHT amount, not only a wrong one, which turned the remaining problem from 'what should I add?' into 'how hot, and for how long?' He also established that 'India rubber could not be melted in boiling sulphur at any heat ever so great, but always charred.' And the stove did not hand him a process: he moved his family to Lynn to get at the steam power of Messrs. Baldwin & Haskins, then moved back to Woburn, where 'he now pursued his inquiries and experiments for some months quite alone, until the desired result was obtained.' Months more, working by himself, before he 'felt himself amply repaid for the past.' Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), p. 119, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good.

question: A reader of Charles Goodyear's memoir finds him blunt that the sulphur in his 1839 stove mixture was not his idea. He had bought the right to it, on paper, in February 1839, months before the stove. Who had he bought it from?
answer: Nathaniel Hayward, the foreman of the Woburn works.
choices: Mr. Chaffee, a manufacturer at the Roxbury company.
William Brockedon, an English painter and inventor.
Nathaniel Hayward, the foreman of the Woburn works.
Nelson Goodyear, his own brother and partner.
context: Hayward had been putting sulphur into the solvent and drying the goods in the sun, a trick he called solarizing. Goodyear: 'It was through him that the writer received the first knowledge of the use of sulphur as a drier of gum-elastic.' He bought Hayward's claim and the patent issued on 24 February 1839, months before the stove -- and then drew the line himself, in print: 'It should be remarked that this claim was for the use of sulphur, and not for the heating or vulcanizing process, subsequently discovered by the writer.' Hayward had even warned him not to use sulphur crude, 'because its effects were so powerful when used in a minute quantity.' This is the honest shape of the story: Goodyear did not invent the ingredient, he bought it, and what he added was the heat and the years of looking. Sources: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), pp. 112-114, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_Hayward.

question: Outsiders saw a failed hardware seller with no chemical training, rescued by a hot stove, and Charles Goodyear knew it. In his memoir he grants the no-training part but flatly refuses the word 'accident,' reaching instead for one famous story to explain the difference. Which story?
answer: Isaac Newton and the falling apple.
choices: Archimedes and the overflowing bath.
Isaac Newton and the falling apple.
James Watt and the boiling kettle.
Benjamin Franklin and the storm kite.
context: His sentence: 'Like the falling of an apple, it was suggestive of an important fact to one whose mind was previously prepared to draw an inference from any occurrence which might favor the object of his research. While the inventor admits that these discoveries were not the result of scientific chemical investigations, he is not willing to admit that they were the result of what is commonly termed accident; he claims them to be the result of the closest application and observation.' Elsewhere he states the principle flat out: what cannot be found by research 'will most likely be discovered by accident, if at all, and by the man who applies himself most perseveringly to the subject, and is most observing of every thing relating thereto.' He had the receipts, too. Years earlier he had daubed nitric acid on a piece of rubber drapery only to strip bronze decoration off it, threw the discoloured piece away as worthless, and later found it cured; he calls the two episodes 'parallel cases.' The same man having the same kind of luck twice is the tell that it was not luck. (Newton's apple is itself an anecdote Newton told late in life, not a documented event -- which makes Goodyear's borrowing of it a story about a story.) Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), pp. 96, 104, 119-120, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good.

question: Thomas Hancock, an English rubber manufacturer, was handed a few small scraps of a marvellous new American rubber by an agent of its inventor in the autumn of 1842. He turned the scraps over and caught a faint smell of sulphur on one of them. What did he decide the smell meant?
answer: That someone had dusted sulphur on to send him the wrong way.
choices: That the sulphur had rubbed off the packing on the voyage.
That the sulphur was a preservative to stop the gum rotting.
That sulphur had been mixed in as a filler to save money.
That someone had dusted sulphur on to send him the wrong way.
context: The scraps reached Hancock through his friend William Brockedon. Hancock's own 1857 narrative: 'Some time in the early part of the autumn of 1842, Mr. Brockedon showed me some small bits of rubber that he told me had been brought by a person from America, who represented himself as the agent of the inventor.' The agent's story was that the secret lay in a cheap new solvent, which was a blind alley. Then came the sentence that matters: 'The first named had a slight smell of sulphur, and I thought that a little sulphurous powder had been rubbed on to mislead.' The one real clue was literally under his nose and he filed it as a deliberate decoy -- then spent months getting there the hard way anyway. He melted sulphur in an iron vessel, noting its melting point 'was only about 240 [F], which I knew would not be injurious to the rubber,' and dipped in half-inch slips of sheet rubber; by the third immersion the tan colour had gone right through, and on the fourth one slip came out 'perfectly changed,' while the ends of the others nearest the fire were 'turning black, and becoming hard and horny.' His verdict on how unguessable it all was: 'I believe I may confidently affirm that it was not previously known even that rubber would absorb sulphur, and no degree of chemical knowledge, no analogy of reasoning on the relative nature of the two substances would ever have suggested or anticipated the possibility of such a result.' Source: Thomas Hancock, 'Personal Narrative of the Origin and Progress of the Caoutchouc or India-Rubber Manufacture in England' (1857), pp. 91-92, 102-104, archive.org/details/personalnarrati00hancgoog.

question: Charles Goodyear cooked his first vulcanized rubber at Woburn in 1839. Thomas Hancock, in England, did not see a scrap of the American material until the autumn of 1842, and worked backwards from it to a sulphur-and-heat process of his own. Both men then filed patents within months of each other, Goodyear in the United States on 30 January 1844. Who was first onto the register, and by how much?
answer: Hancock, by about ten weeks: he filed on 21 November 1843.
choices: Hancock, by nearly a year: he filed on 15 February 1843.
Goodyear, by about six weeks: Hancock filed on 13 March 1844.
Hancock, by about ten weeks: he filed on 21 November 1843.
Goodyear, by only three days: Hancock filed on 2 February 1844.
context: Hancock filed on 21 November 1843 and enrolled his full specification on 30 May 1844; Goodyear filed in the United States on 30 January 1844 and was granted US Patent 3,633 on 15 June 1844. So the Briton's claim genuinely precedes the American's ON PAPER, while the American's working discovery in 1839 precedes both -- which is why the honest answer to 'who invented vulcanization?' is not a single name. Goodyear refused to fight it out in print: he 'has intentionally omitted all mention of the English patent for the vulcanization of caoutchouc, enrolled by Thomas Hancock on the 30th May, 1844, and also from expressing any views or opinions in relation to the circumstances under which this patent was taken out, lest he might possibly do some injustice to Mr. Hancock or his partners.' An English court tested the question in 1855 (Hancock v. Moulton); Goodyear attended, chemists testified that a sample could not have revealed how it was made, and Hancock prevailed. Hancock also had what Goodyear never did -- a factory. He had invented the rubber 'masticator' in 1820 and ran Charles Macintosh & Co.'s works, and by 1857 could report that 'solid twelve-inch cubes have been done at our works, vulcanized throughout,' while Goodyear worked in attics and borrowed mills with his wife and children helping. One last honesty: neither man knew WHY it worked. Goodyear conceded the results 'have not yet been satisfactorily accounted for,' and cross-linking as an explanation arrived decades later. The word itself was an afterthought too: Hancock had been calling it merely 'the change' until Brockedon, a painter and not a chemist, proposed 'vulcanization' after Vulcan. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hancock_(inventor); patents.google.com/patent/US3633A/en; Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic' (1853), pp. 88, 119-120; Hancock, 'Personal Narrative' (1857), pp. 11-12, 107-108, 112.

question: The team at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) caught, on 14 September 2015, the first gravitational wave anyone had ever seen. That day did not sit in the middle of a science run. When did the wave arrive?
answer: Four days before it began, with the machines in shakedown
choices: Four days before it began, with the machines in shakedown
Four days after it began, with the machines fully calibrated
Four months in, during the run's most sensitive stretch
On its last night, hours before a planned shutdown
context: The upgraded detectors had begun engineering run ER8 on 17 August 2015, and the formal O1 science run was not due to start until 18 September. The first gravitational wave ever detected arrived on 14 September - four days before the observatory was officially open for business. Source: Wikipedia, 'First observation of gravitational waves' (GW150914): the detectors were operating in 'engineering mode'; LIGO/Virgo, arXiv:1602.08492, 'Localization and broadband follow-up of GW150914' (ER8 began 17 August; O1 scheduled for 18 September).

question: Marco Drago, a young Italian physicist in Hannover, saw an email pop up on 14 September 2015 with two matching graphs from twin detectors in Louisiana and Washington state: the first gravitational wave ever detected. About an hour later, what did he do about it?
answer: Emailed the collaboration asking if anything could have faked it
choices: Emailed the collaboration asking if anything could have faked it
Phoned Hanford to have the mirrors re-locked and rechecked
Logged the trigger as noise and went back to his own work
Sent the graphs to an astronomer to hunt for the source
context: Each link opened a graph that looked like the traces ornithologists use to record birdsong. Drago's first move was not celebration but suspicion - he asked the whole collaboration whether anyone knew of anything that could have produced a false signal. The automatic trigger had already fired within about three minutes of the wave passing, at 09:54 UTC. Source: INFN Scienza per Tutti, interview with Marco Drago ('Onde Gravitazionali | Intervista a Marco Drago'); Wikipedia, GW150914.

question: The builders of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) hung mirrors at the ends of two arms, each 4 kilometres long, in every detector. When the wave passed on 14 September 2015, the arms stretched and squeezed by turns. How big was the change in an arm's length?
answer: About a thousandth of the width of a proton
choices: About a thousandth of the width of a proton
About a tenth of the width of a hydrogen atom
About a hundredth of the width of a human hair
About a thousandth of the width of a red blood cell
context: The peak strain was 1.0 x 10^-21, a fraction, not a fixed length: over 4 km it makes a difference of about 4 x 10^-18 metres between the two arms, one stretching as the other shrinks, so each arm changed by about 2 x 10^-18 metres, roughly a thousandth of a proton's width. Mirrors fold the laser back and forth until its light covers about 1,120 km, but the folding boosts the signal; it is the arm that changes. As a proportion it is like the distance to the nearest star outside the Solar System changing by one hair's width. Sources: LIGO/Virgo discovery paper, arXiv:1602.03837 / Phys. Rev. Lett. 116, 061102 (peak strain 1.0 x 10^-21); LIGO science summary, 'GW150914: The Advanced LIGO detectors in the era of first discoveries' (arm-length difference about 4 x 10^-18 m); Wikipedia, GW150914.

question: Rainer Weiss was teaching at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1967 when his students wanted to know how Joseph Weber's bar detectors could catch a gravitational wave. Weber had wrapped a huge aluminium cylinder in sensors and claimed several hits, and Weiss could not explain the bars. What did Weiss do about it?
answer: Set the class the problem of designing the simplest possible detector
choices: Set the class the problem of designing the simplest possible detector
Invited Joseph Weber to MIT to explain the bars to the class himself
Dropped the subject from the course until the claims were settled
Wrote to Joseph Weber asking for the raw data behind his detections
context: Weiss's own answer to his own homework problem was an L-shaped laser interferometer with free-hanging mirrors. He wrote it up in 1972 in an internal MIT report, 'Electromagnetically Coupled Broadband Gravitational Antenna', and LIGO grew out of that report; he shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics with Barry Barish and Kip Thorne. Source: MIT News, 'Q&A: Rainer Weiss on LIGO's origins'; Science/AAAS, 'Meet the college dropout who invented the gravitational wave detector'; Wikipedia, 'Rainer Weiss'.

question: Physicists added up the masses behind the signal of 14 September 2015. Two black holes, one about 36 times the mass of the Sun and one about 29, had merged 1.3 billion light-years from Earth into a hole of about 62. But 36 and 29 make 65. Roughly three Suns' worth of mass had gone somewhere. Where did it go?
answer: It left as ripples in spacetime, spreading outward through space
choices: It left as ripples in spacetime, spreading outward through space
It was blasted out as a burst of gamma rays and hard X-rays
It went into the spin of the new hole, which whirls faster for it
It became heat in the gas and dust swirling around the pair
context: This was GW150914, heard by LIGO on 14 September 2015. About 3.0 solar masses were radiated away as gravitational waves in a fraction of a second - mass turned directly into the energy of the wave. The pair lay roughly 1.3 billion light-years off, so that wave had been on its way for 1.3 billion years before it reached the mirrors. Source: LIGO/Virgo discovery paper, arXiv:1602.03837 (36 and 29 solar masses, final mass 62, 3.0 solar masses radiated, luminosity distance 410 Mpc).

question: Physicists compared the traces from two identical machines on 14 September 2015, one in Livingston, Louisiana, and one in Hanford, Washington, 3,002 kilometres apart. The same trace had shown up at Livingston 6.9 milliseconds before Hanford. What did that tiny lag prove?
answer: Something had swept in from the sky, crossing both sites at light speed
choices: Something had swept in from the sky, crossing both sites at light speed
A tremor had travelled through the crust from Louisiana to Washington
The two sites' atomic clocks had drifted apart over the summer
A storm front had crossed the country, hitting each detector in turn
context: Light needs about 10 milliseconds to cross 3,002 km, so a 6.9 ms offset is exactly what a wavefront arriving at an angle from the sky produces. Nothing local can imitate that: a truck, a quake or a storm cannot show up at two sites separated by less than the light-travel time between them. Source: Wikipedia, GW150914 (time delay 6.9 (+0.5, -0.4) ms; sites 3,002 km apart; peaks seen at Livingston first).

question: About 300 gravitational-wave physicists packed into a room in Arcadia, California, on 14 March 2011 and opened a sealed envelope. They had studied a strong signal from the constellation Canis Major, which they called the Big Dog, for six months, written the paper and voted to send it in. The signal was a fake, known in advance to only four people. How had it been planted?
answer: By shaking the detectors' mirrors
choices: By shaking the detectors' mirrors
By writing it into the recorded data
By modulating the laser's frequency
By seeding it in the analysis code
context: A hundred more watched the envelope opening by video link. Only four LIGO scientists were ever allowed to know when such a blind injection had been made - which is why, when a real signal arrived in September 2015, the very first thing the collaboration did was run a chain of internal emails confirming that no injection, scheduled or unscheduled, had been made that morning. Source: LIGO Scientific Collaboration, 'Blind injection stress-tests LIGO and Virgo's search for gravitational waves' (ligo.org/news/blind-injection.php); Wikipedia, GW150914.

question: A physicist takes the 2015 merger of two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses, whose peak output reached about 3.6 x 10^49 watts for a few thousandths of a second. She sets that against every star in the observable universe shining at once. How did the merger compare?
answer: It was greater than all of that starlight put together
choices: It was greater than all of that starlight put together
It was about equal to one large galaxy's starlight
It was a millionth of that starlight, but concentrated
It was about what the Sun radiates in its lifetime
context: And not one photon of it was light. The wattage is agreed across sources; the multiple is not - LIGO's own science summary says more than ten times all the starlight in the observable universe, Wikipedia says fifty times, Grokipedia says about two hundred. So the honest claim is the one all three support: greater. Source: Wikipedia, GW150914 (3.6 x 10^49 W); LIGO Scientific Collaboration science summary for GW150914; Grokipedia, 'First observation of gravitational waves'.

question: Albert Einstein had predicted gravitational waves in 1916, working them out of his own field equations. Twenty years later, in June 1936, he and Nathan Rosen mailed Physical Review a manuscript titled 'Do Gravitational Waves Exist?'. What answer did the two of them give to their own title?
answer: That the waves are not physically real at all
choices: That the waves are not physically real at all
That the waves cannot escape the body that makes them
That the waves are real but far too weak to detect
That the waves form only near very dense stars
context: Working with the full nonlinear field equations, Einstein and Rosen ran into what looked like a singularity and read it as proof that the waves were not physically real - twenty years after Einstein had predicted them himself. The manuscript reached Physical Review on 1 June 1936. He had already corrected himself once on this subject: an error in the 1916 derivation was fixed in a 1918 paper, which produced the quadrupole radiation formula. Source: Daniel Kennefick, 'Einstein Versus the Physical Review', Physics Today; Grokipedia, 'Sticky bead argument'; Einstein 1916 (SPAW 688-696) and 1918 (SPAW 154-167).

question: John Tate, the editor of Physical Review, thought the ending of Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen's 1936 paper on gravitational waves was odd, and he sent it to a reviewer, the cosmologist Howard Percy Robertson, who wrote back ten pages of criticism. The two authors had hit a place where their math blew up, a singularity, and had built their whole point on it. What did Robertson show they had gotten wrong?
answer: They had read a quirk of their own coordinates as a feature of spacetime
choices: They had read a quirk of their own coordinates as a feature of spacetime
They had used an approximation where the blow-up demanded the full equations
They had dropped a factor of two from the formula for radiated energy
They had assumed a spherical source, which radiates nothing at all
context: Tate returned the manuscript with Robertson's report on 23 July 1936. A coordinate singularity is a bookkeeping artefact: choose different coordinates and it vanishes, because nothing physical is happening at that point. Robertson was right, and the paper's conclusion did not survive it. Source: Daniel Kennefick, 'Einstein Versus the Physical Review', Physics Today ('Einstein and Rosen mistook a coordinate singularity for a physical one').

question: Albert Einstein was furious when Physical Review's editor sent his 1936 paper to a referee. He wrote back on 27 July, called the reviewer's comments wrong and withdrew the paper. That October his assistant Leopold Infeld talked the same problem over at Princeton with Howard Percy Robertson, who turned out to be the referee, and the two found the mistake. When Infeld brought the correction back to him, what did Einstein do?
answer: Said he had found an error himself the night before - then reversed the paper
choices: Said he had found an error himself the night before - then reversed the paper
Thanked Infeld for the correction - then pulled the paper from print entirely
Disputed the correction for years - then published the paper word for word
Handed the whole problem to Infeld - then never wrote on the waves again
context: Einstein rewrote the paper to the opposite conclusion, retitled it 'On Gravitational Waves', and published it in the Journal of the Franklin Institute in January 1937. He later thanked Robertson for his help. Apart from a single letter to the editor in 1952, he never published in Physical Review again. Source: Daniel Kennefick, 'Einstein Versus the Physical Review', Physics Today (Einstein's letter to Tate of 27 July 1936 quoted verbatim; Infeld's October 1936 discussions with Robertson).

question: Joseph Weber built the first gravitational-wave detector, a resonant aluminium bar, and announced in 1969 that he was catching waves, which for a while made him one of the most famous scientists alive. Nobody else could reproduce it: Richard Garwin's bar gave one probable-noise pulse in six months. David Douglass went through Weber's analysis program and found the flaw. What was it?
answer: It allowed for noise of random amplitude but not of random phase
choices: It allowed for noise of random amplitude but not of random phase
It counted every coincidence twice, once for each end of the bar
It compared the bars against a clock that drifted through the night
It discarded the quietest hours, when the bar was most sensitive
context: Weber's specific detections did not hold up; the claims were discredited through the 1970s, he lost his main funding in 1987, and he argued for them to the end. He also founded the entire field - it was a student's question about Weber's bars that sent Rainer Weiss looking for a better instrument. Source: Wikipedia, 'Joseph Weber'; Aeon, 'How Joe Weber's gravity ripples turned out to be all noise'; Science/AAAS, 'Remembering Joseph Weber, the controversial pioneer of gravitational waves'.

question: Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor used the 305-metre Arecibo dish in 1974 to find a pulsar orbiting another neutron star every 7.75 hours - a natural clock in a binary system. Timing its pulses year after year gave physics the first indirect evidence that gravitational waves exist, and won the two men the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physics. What in the timing was the evidence?
answer: The orbit winding tighter, the two stars falling closer every year
choices: The orbit winding tighter, the two stars falling closer every year
The pulses running early and late as passing waves stretched the gap
The pulses reddening as they climbed out of the companion's gravity
The pulsar's beam bending as it swept past the companion each orbit
context: Their timing showed the 7.75-hour orbit tightening - the period dropping 76.5 millionths of a second a year, the orbit's long radius shrinking about 3.5 metres - as the pair steadily loses energy. The rate matches Albert Einstein's quadrupole radiation formula of 1918 to within 0.2%. Hulse and Taylor never detected a wave - their 1993 Nobel citation reads 'for the discovery of a new type of pulsar, a discovery that has opened up new possibilities for the study of gravitation'. They watched a binary bleed energy at precisely the predicted rate; PSR B1913+16's two stars will merge in about 300 million years. Source: Wikipedia, 'PSR B1913+16'; Grokipedia, 'First observation of gravitational waves'.

question: Richard Feynman answered Nathan Rosen at the Chapel Hill meeting of 1957 with a thought test: two beads threaded on a stiff rod, free to slide along it. Rosen had co-written a 1936 paper on gravitational waves with Albert Einstein, yet he insisted the waves carried no energy and could do nothing. What did Feynman say a passing wave would do to that rod?
answer: Rub the beads along it and warm it by friction
choices: Rub the beads along it and warm it by friction
Ring it at its own resonant note, like a struck bell
Slide the beads to one end and leave them there
Stretch it lengthwise while the beads stayed put
context: Feynman's own phrasing, from his 1962-63 Caltech Lectures on Gravitation: the mass 'in accelerating up and down will rub the stick, and therefore by friction make heat.' Heat means work was done, and work done means the wave carries real energy. Hermann Bondi later published a version of the argument. Rosen never gave way - he was still publishing objections to the bead argument in 1979. The Chapel Hill conference (18-23 January 1957) was organised by Bryce DeWitt and Cecile DeWitt-Morette and paid for by the industrialist Agnew Bahnson. Source: Grokipedia, 'Sticky bead argument'; Wikipedia, 'Chapel Hill Conference' and 'Sticky bead argument'.

question: Operators of the Fermi telescope caught a gamma-ray burst on 17 August 2017, 1.74 seconds behind a gravitational wave from the same patch of sky. The wave came from two neutron stars colliding about 140 million light-years off, and it had rolled through the detectors for about 100 seconds; more than 70 observatories swung around to look. What did comparing those two arrival times establish?
answer: That gravity and light travel at the same speed
choices: That gravity and light travel at the same speed
That gravity outruns light across open space
That gamma rays are slowed by the gas they cross
That gravity acts instantly, with no travel time
context: The event was catalogued as GW170817, the burst as GRB 170817A. Set a 1.74-second gap against 140 million years of travel and the two speeds match to about one part in 10^15: the measured difference lies between -3 x 10^-15 and +7 x 10^-16 of the speed of light. The wave itself ran about 100 seconds, some 3,000 cycles. Source: Wikipedia, 'GW170817' (detection 17 August 2017 at 12:41:04 UTC; GRB 170817A 1.74 +/- 0.05 s later; ~100 s signal, ~3,000 cycles; host galaxy NGC 4993 at about 140 million light-years; more than 70 observatories).

question: Albert Einstein, a 28-year-old clerk at the patent office in Bern, was at his desk in 1907 when, by his own later telling, a simple idea struck him. He called it 'the happiest thought of my life,' the seed of his general theory of relativity. What was the thought?
answer: That a man falling freely would not feel his own weight.
choices: That a man falling freely would not feel his own weight.
That a moving clock must tick slower than a resting one.
That mass and energy are two names for one thing.
That light travels at the same speed for everyone.
context: Einstein put the insight into print that same year, in 'On the Relativity Principle and the Conclusions Drawn from It' (Jahrbuch der Radioaktivitaet und Elektronik, 1907). The famous phrase is his own later retelling, not a 1907 notebook entry — the same way Newton's apple comes from Newton's late-life anecdote. In an unpublished 1920 manuscript he wrote that 'for an observer in free-fall from the roof of a house there is during the fall — at least in his immediate vicinity — no gravitational field,' and in a 1922 lecture in Kyoto he said, 'If a man falls freely, he would not feel his weight. I was taken aback. This simple thought experiment made a deep impression on me.' Source: Grokipedia, 'Equivalence principle'; Wikipedia, 'Einstein's thought experiments'.

question: David Scott, the Apollo 15 commander, stood on the Moon on 2 August 1971 with a TV camera running, a hammer in one hand and a falcon feather in the other. He said he was testing what Galileo had claimed about falling things, and let them go. What happened?
answer: The feather struck the dust with the hammer.
choices: The feather struck the dust with the hammer.
The feather floated for a full minute first.
The feather landed a clear half-second later.
The feather drifted sideways out of the shot.
context: Scott's words on live television: 'Well, in my left hand, I have a feather; in my right hand, a hammer. And I guess one of the reasons we got here today was because of a gentleman named Galileo, a long time ago, who made a rather significant discovery about falling objects in gravity fields. And we thought where would be a better place to confirm his findings than on the Moon.' At 167:22:43 mission elapsed time he said 'How about that!' — CapCom Joe Allen answered 'How about that!' to applause in Houston — then 'Which proves that Mr. Galileo was correct in his findings.' NASA logs the objects as a 1.32-kg aluminium geological hammer and a 0.03-kg feather, 'observed to undergo the same acceleration and strike the lunar surface simultaneously.' The same equality has been tested far more finely than a Moon drop: Lorand Eoetvoes's torsion balance found no difference between materials to about one part in a billion by 1908, and the French MICROSCOPE satellite, letting cylinders of two different alloys fall side by side in orbit, pushed that to about one part in 10^15 in 2022. Source: Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Journal, 'EVA-3 Close-out'; NASA Science, 'The Apollo 15 Hammer-Feather Drop'; Grokipedia, 'Lorand Eoetvoes'; Wikipedia, 'MICROSCOPE (satellite)'.

question: A giant hauls a small windowless box upward by a rope, far from any star or planet, in a thought experiment Albert Einstein set his readers. The box picks up speed evenly, at exactly the rate a stone falls on Earth. What does everything inside the box feel like to the man sealed in it?
answer: Exactly like a room standing still in a gravitational field.
choices: Exactly like a room standing still in a gravitational field.
Exactly like a room falling freely toward a distant planet.
Exactly like a room spinning slowly about its own axis.
Exactly like a room where every object has gained mass.
context: This is the equivalence principle: inside a sealed box, being hauled along at a steady acceleration and standing at rest in a gravitational field give identical results, so no experiment performed inside can tell them apart. The equivalence is only local, and Einstein knew it. Make the box big enough and the difference shows: objects falling in a real planet's field are all aimed at its centre, so their paths slowly converge, while under a rope's uniform pull they stay parallel. That converging is the tidal effect — and it is exactly what the curvature of spacetime means. Source: Wikipedia, 'Einstein's thought experiments'; Grokipedia, 'Equivalence principle'.

question: A teacher tells her class that Galileo Galilei climbed the Leaning Tower of Pisa around 1590 and dropped two cannonballs of different weight to prove they fall together. Yet when historians hunt for a first-hand record of the drop, every account traces back to one single source. What is that source?
answer: A life of Galileo written by his student Vincenzo Viviani.
choices: A life of Galileo written by his student Vincenzo Viviani.
A passage in Galileo's own book Two New Sciences (1638).
The transcript of Galileo's trial before the Inquisition.
A letter from the astronomer Johannes Kepler in Prague.
context: Viviani wrote it in 1654, twelve years after Galileo died, and it was not published until 1717. Galileo never described doing the drop himself. What he did publish were his inclined-plane experiments, which slowed falling down enough to time it, and in Two New Sciences (1638) his thought experiment about two stones tied together. Most historians treat the tower drop as a thought experiment rather than a physical test — which is exactly why David Scott repeating it on the Moon in 1971, in front of a television camera, mattered. Source: Wikipedia, 'Galileo's Leaning Tower of Pisa experiment'; Grokipedia, 'Equivalence principle', which calls the cannonball account 'legendary and unverified'.

question: David Scott carried two falcon feathers to the Moon on Apollo 15 and had meant to try the hammer-and-feather drop privately first, before doing it for a live television audience. He ran out of time and, as he later put it, 'we just winged it.' What had he been worried about?
answer: That static charge would stick the feather to his glove.
choices: That static charge would stick the feather to his glove.
That the hammer would bounce up and tear his suit open.
That the feather would be crushed flat inside its pouch.
That the camera would be aimed the wrong way entirely.
context: Scott told the Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Journal: 'I had a friend who was a professor at the Air Force Academy. Their mascot's the Falcon. And we had the (LM) Falcon. So that was indeed, a falcon feather from an Air Force Academy bird. In fact, I had two of them. I was going to try it, first, to see if it worked — because of static charge... Didn't have time, so we just winged it. And it worked!' The lunar module was named Falcon, so the feather was, as Scott said on air, 'appropriately, a falcon feather for our Falcon.' The demonstration was CapCom Joe Allen's idea. Analysts later identified the bird as a small gyrfalcon and the feather as a primary flight feather about 30.5 cm long. One of the two feathers is still lying on the Moon. Source: Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Journal, 'EVA-3 Close-out'.

question: Albert Einstein used the sealed-box argument in 1911 to squeeze out a testable number. His claim was that a box speeding up and a box in gravity cannot be told apart. Starlight passing the Sun, he calculated, should be bent by about 0.83 arcseconds. He finished his general theory in November 1915 and ran the math again. What became of the prediction?
answer: It doubled, to about 1.75 arcseconds.
choices: It doubled, to about 1.75 arcseconds.
It stayed put, at about 0.83 arcseconds.
It halved, to about 0.42 arcseconds.
It grew tenfold, to about 8.3 arcseconds.
context: The 1911 paper was 'On the Influence of Gravitation on the Propagation of Light' (Annalen der Physik), and its number came from the equivalence of gravity and acceleration alone, with no curvature of space in it at all. The finished theory added that curvature and doubled the answer — which is what made the 1919 eclipse a genuine three-way test: no deflection at all, about 0.87 arcseconds if light were simply a Newtonian particle falling, or 1.75 if Einstein's full theory held. Sobral's four-inch backup telescope returned 1.98 plus or minus 0.18 arcseconds, and Eddington's Principe plates 1.61 plus or minus 0.45. The result was announced on 6 November 1919. Source: Grokipedia, 'General relativity' and 'Eddington experiment'; Wikipedia, 'History of general relativity'.

question: Albert Einstein bolted two identical clocks, in thought, inside his sealed chamber in 1911, one to the floor and one to the ceiling, while a rope hauled the chamber so that it steadily gathered speed. The chamber had already given him a prediction about light; this one was about clocks. What did he conclude they must do?
answer: The floor clock must run slow against the ceiling clock.
choices: The floor clock must run slow against the ceiling clock.
The ceiling clock must run slow against the floor clock.
Both must run slow against a clock left outside the box.
Both must keep perfect step until the hauling stops.
context: He reasoned it from light. A beam sent up from the floor arrives at a ceiling that has been picking up speed away from it the whole time the light was in flight, so it arrives shifted down in frequency — fewer waves arriving each second, which is a slower clock. If acceleration and gravity truly cannot be told apart, gravity must do the same thing: a clock deeper in a gravitational field runs slow. Einstein published this four years before general relativity existed. One consequence, worked out much later: because clocks run slower deeper in the well, the Earth's core is in effect about 2.5 years younger than its surface, accumulated over 4.5 billion years. Source: Grokipedia, 'Tests of general relativity'; Wikipedia, 'Gravitational time dilation'.

question: Kelly Foyle and Philip Freeman put a blunt question to the bowling-ball-on-a-rubber-sheet demonstration of general relativity: what makes the sheet sag in the first place? Earth's gravity pulls the ball down, so the demonstration explains gravity by using gravity. They did not throw the fabric away; they published a repair that takes Earth's gravity out of the job. Which repair is theirs?
answer: Stretch the fabric upward over a laboratory flask.
choices: Stretch the fabric upward over a laboratory flask.
Blow air up from beneath to hold the fabric domed.
Pull the fabric down with a magnet instead of a weight.
Freeze the sagged fabric solid and lift the ball out.
context: Foyle and Freeman's words: 'what causes the fabric to sag? The massive ball at the centre of the fabric is being pulled down, but by what? ... gravity in the analogy is being caused by gravity outside the analogy. We are explaining gravity using gravity.' Bending the fabric upward over a flask or funnel gives the same curvature with Earth's gravity no longer doing the work, and they recommend laying strips of tape on it rather than rolling marbles, since a rolling marble is being accelerated by its own weight and the slope — 'this use of a bent fabric is in fact a demonstration of force and potential, not of the effect of geometry.' The sheet is not worthless, and this is the honest part: a sagging trampoline really is curved, and you can measure it yourself. Tape out a triangle and its interior angles no longer add to 180 degrees; trace a circle with a pin and string and its circumference is no longer 2 x pi x r. Source: K. Foyle & P. Freeman, 'General Relativity: Beyond the Bowling Ball and the Trampoline', OAPT Newsletter, 23 November 2020.

question: A boy throws a ball, and it arcs back down to the grass. General relativity swaps gravity's pull for bent spacetime with two halves: a mass curves nearby space, so a passing radio signal has further to travel, and it stretches nearby time, so a clock ticks slower. Kelly Foyle and Philip Freeman weigh the two halves. For an everyday arc like that ball's, which does the work?
answer: The warping of time, while the warping of space adds very little.
choices: The warping of time, while the warping of space adds very little.
The warping of space, while the warping of time adds very little.
The warping of time and of space, in roughly equal measure.
The warping of space when a body moves, of time when it rests.
context: The classroom rubber sheet, dented into a funnel by a bowling ball, is a picture of bent space — and Kelly Foyle and Philip Freeman call that the analogy's worst failure, because the sheet shows the small effect and hides the big one: 'almost all our everyday experiences of gravity (i.e. throwing a ball or being stuck to the Earth) are due to the warping of TIME in general relativity and not the warping of space. The warping of time gives us essentially Newton's gravity, while the effect of curvature of space is quite small and makes a difference only in extreme cases, such as the discrepancy in the precession of Mercury's orbit.' Nor does the split depend on whether the object happens to be moving: an object sitting still is still travelling through time, and that is the direction the curvature bends. The space curvature is real, though, and it has been caught: a radio signal from the Cassini spacecraft passing close to the Sun in 2002 arrived late, because there was genuinely further to go, pinning the space-curvature parameter to general relativity's value within about 20 parts per million. Source: K. Foyle & P. Freeman, OAPT Newsletter, 23 November 2020; Grokipedia, 'Tests of general relativity'.

question: A diver steps off the board and, with air resistance set aside, follows a geodesic: the straightest track available through curved spacetime, travelled with no force acting and no acceleration at all. Suppose you sit watching her from a poolside chair. What is happening to you?
answer: You are being shoved off that straightest path by the chair.
choices: You are being shoved off that straightest path by the chair.
You are following an even straighter path through spacetime.
You are held motionless by the Earth's gravitational pull.
You are being pulled down and pushed up in perfect balance.
context: Foyle and Freeman put it plainly: 'Setting aside air friction, a falling object experiences no forces at all and follows a straightest line path through curved spacetime,' while 'the chair is constantly pushing you away from a straightest line path through spacetime.' That is why the falling person feels nothing at all — the sensation you call your weight is the chair, the floor or the ground interrupting a free fall. It is also why the curvature has to be in spacetime and not in space alone. Drop three balls off a cliff, one released from rest and two thrown horizontally at different speeds: the two thrown balls start off in the same direction in space but land at different distances, and the dropped ball has no direction of motion at all yet still falls. One strip of tape on a curved sheet cannot produce three different paths. Only a spacetime picture can, because even the ball released from rest is still travelling through time. Source: K. Foyle & P. Freeman, OAPT Newsletter, 23 November 2020.

question: Isaac Newton was uneasy about his own gravity: a force reaching instantly across empty space, touching nothing on the way. In a 1690 letter to Christiaan Huygens, Nicolas Fatio de Duillier proposed a replacement, and Georges-Louis Le Sage arrived at the same idea independently in 1748. Physicists took it seriously for two hundred years. How did Fatio and Le Sage say gravity worked?
answer: Unseen corpuscles stream in from all sides, and bodies shade one another.
choices: Unseen corpuscles stream in from all sides, and bodies shade one another.
Whirlpools of fine matter sweep bodies along, and planets ride the swirl.
An ether presses on all bodies, and thins in the gap between any two.
The distant stars fix each body's inertia, and heaviness follows from it.
context: Le Sage called the streams 'ultramundane corpuscles' — arriving from beyond the known world, from every direction at once. Two bodies each block a little of the rain falling on the other, so each is pushed into the other's shadow: gravity as a shove from outside rather than a tug from within. Serious people argued over it for two centuries. James Clerk Maxwell, and later Henri Poincare, killed it by working out that the collisions would heat the Earth by something like 10^26 degrees every second. The rival accounts were real too. Isaac Newton's Principia (1687) made gravity a force acting instantly across any distance — which sits badly with a universe where nothing outruns light. Mach's principle held that inertia is defined relative to all the mass in the universe. What finally replaced them all is the sentence John Archibald Wheeler wrote with Kenneth Ford in Geons, Black Holes, and Quantum Foam: A Life in Physics (1998, p. 235): 'Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve.' Nothing in that sentence pulls on anything. Source: Grokipedia, 'General relativity' and 'Equivalence principle'; Wikipedia, 'Le Sage's theory of gravitation'; J. A. Wheeler with Kenneth Ford, Geons, Black Holes, and Quantum Foam: A Life in Physics (1998), p. 235.

question: John Cutler's team of US Public Health Service doctors ran a secret study in Guatemala from 1946 to 1948. Their subjects were 1,308 prisoners, soldiers, mental-hospital patients and sex workers, and the diseases were syphilis and gonorrhea. The Tuskegee study in Alabama, from 1932 to 1972, watched already-infected black sharecroppers go untreated for decades. What set the Guatemala study apart?
answer: The researchers gave the subjects the disease on purpose, through infected partners and inoculation
choices: The researchers gave the subjects the disease on purpose, through infected partners and inoculation
The researchers withheld a working cure from subjects who already had the disease
The researchers paid the subjects to hide a positive diagnosis from their own families
The researchers recorded symptoms in secret and never admitted subjects to a hospital
context: Tuskegee (1932-1972) followed 399 Black men in Alabama who ALREADY had syphilis and were left untreated. Guatemala INFECTED healthy people on purpose - through arranged contact with infected sex workers, scarification of the skin, and direct injection. The distinction is the whole point: withheld vs. gave. Source: Presidential Commission for the Study of Bioethical Issues, 'Ethically Impossible: STD Research in Guatemala from 1946 to 1948' (September 2011).

question: John Cutler's US Public Health Service doctors, working with Guatemalan officials, deliberately infected roughly 1,300 Guatemalan prisoners, soldiers and mental-hospital patients with syphilis and other diseases from 1946 to 1948, testing the new drug penicillin in the years when judges at Nuremberg tried Nazi doctors. The whole file stayed hidden for 62 years after the last subject was inoculated. It came to light in 2010. Who opened the box, and where was it sitting?
answer: A Wellesley medical historian, reading the director's own donated papers at the University of Pittsburgh
choices: A Wellesley medical historian, reading the director's own donated papers at the University of Pittsburgh
A Justice Department lawyer, subpoenaing sealed Public Health Service records in Washington
A Guatemalan journalist, tracing a survivor's family medical file back to the original clinic
A State Department archivist, cataloguing declassified 1940s diplomatic cables from Central America
context: Susan M. Reverby was researching Tuskegee. John C. Cutler had directed the Guatemala study AND later worked on Tuskegee; he donated his papers to the University of Pittsburgh, where he was a faculty member, and died in 2003. Reverby read the Guatemala records in his own file, presented findings in January 2010, and the story broke that autumn. President Obama and Secretary Clinton apologized to Guatemala on 1 October 2010; the 2011 Bioethics Commission report was titled 'Ethically Impossible.' The record survived because a dead man donated his own crime to a university library, and a scholar with a library card opened the box.

question: Edmond Halley published a book on comets in 1705, carefully comparing the paths of the bright comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682. From that comparison he reached one bold conclusion. What did he claim about those three separate appearances?
answer: They were the same object returning about every 76 years
choices: They were the same object returning about every 76 years
They were three fragments of a single shattered world
They were harmless streaks in the upper atmosphere
They were signals sent by a nearby unseen star
context: Halley's Synopsis Astronomia Cometicae (1705) compiled 24 comet observations; he used Newton's gravity to argue the 1531, 1607, and 1682 comets shared an orbit, and predicted the next return for 1758. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

question: Edmond Halley boldly predicted in 1705 that a bright comet would come back in the year 1758. The comet did return as he had said, but Halley himself never saw his prediction confirmed. Why not?
answer: He had died in 1742, sixteen years before it came back
choices: He had died in 1742, sixteen years before it came back
He had gone blind by the year of his prediction
He was on a ship and clouds hid the sky for weeks
He was exiled to Prussia and forbidden to observe
context: Halley died in 1742, well before the 1758-9 return. The French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille later attached his name to the comet in 1759. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

question: Nicole-Reine Lepaute, with Clairaut and Lalande, told the Paris Academy in November 1758 how long Jupiter and Saturn would delay Halley's comet. They named mid-April 1759 for its pass round the Sun and openly stated a margin of error. When did it actually round the Sun?
answer: In mid-March, a month early and inside their margin
choices: In mid-March, a month early and inside their margin
In mid-April, the very week their sums had named
In late June, two months late, outside their margin
In spring 1760, nearly a year behind their forecast
context: Clairaut reported to the Academy on 14 November 1758 that the giant planets would delay the comet by about 618 days, giving a perihelion of mid-April 1759 with a stated month of uncertainty. It arrived 13 March 1759 -- a month early, and inside the declared error. Source: cosmosmagazine.com/science/mathematics/the-comet-calculator-nicole-reine-lepaute/

question: Johann Georg Palitzsch, an amateur living near Dresden, spotted Halley's comet on Christmas night 1758. Astronomers all over Europe had been watching for it, and he beat every professional with a big observatory telescope. What did Palitzsch do for his living?
answer: He was a farmer with a homemade telescope
choices: He was a farmer with a homemade telescope
He was a Lutheran organist and part-time engraver
He was a schoolmaster's assistant in a village outside Dresden
He was a wandering surveyor for the Saxon mines
context: Johann Georg Palitzsch (1723-1788) recovered the comet on the night of 25 December 1758 -- the first sighting of a comet whose return had been predicted. Charles Messier picked it up independently in January 1759. Source: blogs.otago.ac.nz/emxphi/halleys-comet-and-christmas-day/

question: Controllers at the European Space Agency flew their Giotto probe close enough to the nucleus of Halley's comet to photograph it in March 1986. The bright thing in the sky is gas and dust boiled off a lump of ice and rock about 15 by 8 by 8 kilometres. How reflective is that lump?
answer: It reflects only about 4 per cent of the light hitting it -- darker than coal
choices: It reflects only about 4 per cent of the light hitting it -- darker than coal
It reflects about 60 per cent -- close to fresh snow
It reflects about 25 per cent -- roughly the colour of dry sand
It reflects almost none, because the surface glows red-hot
context: Giotto's cameras showed a peanut-shaped nucleus roughly 14.4 x 7.4 x 7.4 km with an albedo near 0.04. The glowing 'comet' is the coma -- sunlight scattering off gas and dust the dark nucleus sheds when the Sun warms it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

question: A girl marks 28 July 2061 on a calendar, the day Halley's comet next reaches perihelion, its closest swing past the Sun. The 1986 pass was a poor show from Earth, and this one is expected to be far brighter. What geometry makes the 2061 pass a good one?
answer: Earth will be on the same side of the Sun as the comet at perihelion, close and lit
choices: Earth will be on the same side of the Sun as the comet at perihelion, close and lit
A close pass by Jupiter has shortened the comet's period by several years
The nucleus has grown by accreting material in the outer solar system
The comet will pass inside Earth's orbit for the first time on record
context: In 1986 the comet reached perihelion on the far side of the Sun from Earth, making it one of the poorest apparitions on record. On 28 July 2061 Earth will be on the same side of the Sun as the comet, so the fully sunlit coma will be much closer and much brighter. The nucleus does not grow between passes -- it loses mass each perihelion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

question: Yuval Noah Harari earned his Oxford doctorate in 2002. He still teaches at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem. The world knows him for his books Sapiens (2011) and Homo Deus (2016), which sold tens of millions of copies. What field was he actually trained in?
answer: Medieval and military history
choices: Medieval and military history
Molecular neuroscience
Development economics
Comparative literature
context: His doctoral thesis was on Renaissance military memoirs, c. 1450 to 1600, and he won the Society for Military History's Moncado Award for outstanding articles in 2011. A historian became a futurist; the distinction is worth keeping. Source: Wikipedia 'Yuval Noah Harari'; Hebrew University faculty page.

question: Readers opened an essay by Yuval Noah Harari on 24 February 2017, drawn from his best-selling book Homo Deus. In his telling, artificial intelligence and automation would create a coming category of human beings, not merely without jobs but without any possibility of ever having one. What did Harari call them?
answer: The useless class
choices: The useless class
The surplus workers
The idle citizens
The forgotten majority
context: Harari's essay 'The rise of the useless class' ran at ideas.ted.com and paraphrased a passage from Homo Deus. He presented it as a danger to head off, not a policy to enact. Source: ideas.ted.com, 24 February 2017.

question: Yuval Noah Harari wrote in his 2016 book Homo Deus of a coming class of people whom the economy simply does not need and who cannot compete with machines. He defines that class in one exact sentence, listing three kinds of worth it will lack. Which three does he name?
answer: Economic, political or artistic
choices: Economic, political or artistic
Personal, familial or spiritual
Genetic, moral or educational
Cognitive, physical or emotional
context: Full quote: 'people devoid of any economic, political or even artistic value, who contribute nothing to the prosperity, power and glory of society.' Every noun measures output, and the sentence stands on the record for any reader to weigh. Source: Homo Deus (2016).

question: An economist opens Homo Deus, the 2016 book in which Yuval Noah Harari writes that one problem may be the most important question in 21st-century economics. It arises if artificial intelligence and robots become better than humans at almost every kind of work. What is the problem he names?
answer: What to do with all the people whose work is no longer needed
choices: What to do with all the people whose work is no longer needed
How to stop thinking machines from becoming conscious
How to tax the corporations that own the smartest machines
How to teach machines to obey human values and laws
context: The sentence in Homo Deus: 'The most important question in twenty-first-century economics may well be what to do with all the superfluous people.' The language of surplus applied to human beings. Harari says he is warning; his critics answer that the choice of word is itself the turn, whatever the intent. Source: Yuval Noah Harari, Homo Deus (2016), as quoted in Goodreads author-blog review, 'Homo Deus by Yuval Harari (part 2 of 3)'.

question: Readers of the Guardian on 14 September 2018 found Yuval Noah Harari arguing that the belief in free will had suddenly become dangerous, since the easiest people to manipulate are those who hold it. In the same essay he said what free will itself is. What did he call it?
answer: A myth inherited from Christian theology
choices: A myth inherited from Christian theology
A tale told by kings to keep subjects docile
A legal fiction first written by the courts
A fact that brain science has now proved
context: Harari's words: 'Unfortunately, "free will" isn't a scientific reality. It is a myth inherited from Christian theology.' Then: 'now the belief in "free will" suddenly becomes dangerous', because 'the easiest people to manipulate will be those who believe in free will.' Critics dispute the premise; the sentences, venue and date are on the record. Source: Yuval Noah Harari, 'The myth of freedom', The Guardian, 14 September 2018; quoted at whyevolutionistrue.com, 16 September 2018.

question: Yuval Noah Harari says his warnings about people shut out of work by artificial intelligence describe a danger as a historian sees it, not a policy he endorses. On the record, his critics answer that the decisive turn lies not in his stated conclusions but in his word choices, the very vocabulary he reaches for to name what is happening. Which family of words do those critics point to as the tell?
answer: The vocabulary of surplus inventory
choices: The vocabulary of surplus inventory
The language of technocratic determinism
The framing of humans as data
The rhetoric of inevitability
context: Both readings are on the record for any reader to judge. Critics argue that words like 'superfluous' and 'useless' pre-decide how the reader learns to see the people so labelled, however the framing is presented. Source: reviews and criticism collected on Harari's Wikipedia page and Brownstone Institute article.

question: Sir Cloudesley Shovell's fleet struck the Scilly rocks on an October night in 1707, and some 1,400 to 2,000 sailors drowned. The famous telling blames a navy that could not find its longitude. A captain whose ship survived wrote down where the fleet had really been. What did he report?
answer: Farther north than expected, and farther east too
choices: Farther north than expected, and farther east too
Farther south than expected, and farther west too
Farther west than expected, on the right latitude
Farther south than expected, on the right longitude
context: The captain of the Torbay wrote: 'We were much to ye Northward of what was expected, and likewise more to the Eastward.' Modern study of the logs points to errors in latitude as well as longitude, faulty charts and pilot books, and compasses in poor repair: at Portsmouth only four of 112 wooden-cased compasses from nine returning ships proved serviceable. The longitude problem was real, and the wreck gave weight to the campaign for the 1714 Longitude Act, but it was not the whole story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scilly_naval_disaster_of_1707.

question: Members of Parliament put a 20,000-pound bounty on the longitude problem in 1714, a sum that would make a working man rich for life. To earn all of it, how close did a method have to be?
answer: Within half a degree, tested by a voyage to the West Indies
choices: Within half a degree, tested by a voyage to the West Indies
Within one degree, tested by a voyage across the English Channel
Within one minute of arc, tested by any voyage in European waters
Within one nautical mile, tested by a voyage around the world
context: The 1714 Longitude Act set 20,000 pounds for a method accurate to half a degree after a West Indies voyage, with smaller graduated prizes for coarser methods. The full 20,000-pound sum was never officially paid out to anyone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harrison.

question: A captain sails with a clock still set to home port and watches the Sun climb to noon where he is now. The difference between that noon and the clock tells him how far east or west he has come around the world. How many degrees of longitude does one hour of that difference equal?
answer: 15 degrees of longitude
choices: 15 degrees of longitude
1 degree of longitude
60 degrees of longitude
24 degrees of longitude
context: The Earth turns 360 degrees every 24 hours, so 15 degrees an hour, or one degree every four minutes. A kid with a wristwatch left on home time and a stick's shortest shadow can find her own longitude by this rule. Source: explorersweb.com/longitude-john-harrison.

question: A clockmaker bolted one of the finest pendulum clocks of 1720 to a ship, hoping to carry the exact time of the home port across the ocean and so fix the ship's east-west position. On land it kept time perfectly. Like every other taken to sea, it failed as soon as it left the harbour. What ruined the pendulum?
answer: A pitching deck disturbed its swing on every wave
choices: A pitching deck disturbed its swing on every wave
Salt air rusted the case shut within one Atlantic crossing
Sailing near the poles weakened gravity below what the pendulum needed
The iron of the ship's hull magnetized the escape wheel
context: A pendulum needs a still, level base and a constant swing length; a ship offers neither. Christiaan Huygens' 1660s sea-going pendulum trials had failed for exactly this reason two generations earlier. Source: hautehorlogerie.org/en/watches-and-culture/watchmaking-knowledge/encyclopedia/john-harrison.

question: John Harrison, a self-taught Yorkshire joiner from a village with no watchmaking tradition at all, built his earliest clocks almost entirely of wood. Clock oils of his day went thick in winter and thin in summer, yet his wooden clocks ran without a drop of oil. What did he cut their hard-wearing parts from?
answer: Lignum vitae, a dense tropical hardwood
choices: Lignum vitae, a dense tropical hardwood
Ebony, a dense black tropical hardwood
Walnut, a dense brown European hardwood
Holly, a dense white European hardwood
context: His wooden movements were built of oak and lignum vitae, a tropical wood so oily that it lubricates itself, so the rubbing parts needed no added oil and the rate did not drift as oils thickened and thinned. Three of his early wooden longcase clocks survive, and his wooden turret clock at Brocklesby, in Lincolnshire, built in the early 1720s, still works. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harrison ('a wooden movement of oak and lignum vitae').

question: The crew of HMS Deptford carried H4, John Harrison's fourth try at a sea clock, to Jamaica in 1761 for its official trial. It was meant to keep time well enough to fix a ship's longitude, and the voyage took 81 days. When the watch was checked against local astronomical time on arrival, how far off had it run?
answer: About five seconds slow, roughly one nautical mile of longitude
choices: About five seconds slow, roughly one nautical mile of longitude
About five minutes fast, roughly seventy-five nautical miles of longitude
About one full hour fast, roughly 900 miles of longitude
About one minute slow, roughly fifteen nautical miles of longitude
context: The rules demanded accuracy to half a degree, about 30 nautical miles at the equator. H4's 5 seconds came to an error of about 1.25 minutes of longitude, more than twenty times better than that. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harrison.

question: John Harrison came to the Board of Longitude expecting his prize after some thirty years of building sea clocks. His fourth attempt, H4, a large silver pocket watch, had crushed its 1761 trial to Jamaica. What did the Board actually do?
answer: They called the result a lucky one and demanded a second sea trial
choices: They called the result a lucky one and demanded a second sea trial
They paid the prize but forbade the design to be copied
They awarded the money to the astronomer Nevil Maskelyne
They referred the whole question to the French Academie des Sciences
context: A second trial to Barbados in 1764 was as good or better. The Board still balked, arguing that one handmade watch, six years in the building, was not yet a reproducible method. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harrison; barringtonwatchwinders.com.

question: John Harrison hunted the 20,000-pound Longitude Prize for decades with his sea chronometers H1 through H4. The Board of Longitude held out, arguing that a single handmade watch did not yet amount to a method others could repeat. The story is often told wrong, as if he simply collected the money in the end. What actually happened to that particular sum?
answer: It was never officially awarded to anyone
choices: It was never officially awarded to anyone
It was paid to Harrison in full in 1765 after the Barbados trial
It was split between Harrison and Maskelyne in 1773
It was awarded to Larcum Kendall for his working copies of H4
context: In 1773, at age 80, Harrison received 8,750 pounds by a separate act of Parliament, after his son's appeal reached King George III, who had personally tested H5 at Kew for ten weeks. The original Longitude Act prize went unclaimed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harrison.

question: A boy at the table ties a band around his upper arm and lets the arm hang. His forearm veins stand up in ropes, and along each rope sit small firm knots. William Harvey put this trick in his book so any reader could run it on himself. What is each knot?
answer: A valve set inside the vein
choices: A valve set inside the vein
A gland that filters the blood
A muscle that pinches the vein
A swelling where two veins join
context: Harvey's next step, Chapter 13: press a finger on the vein just below a knot and stroke the blood away toward your hand. That stretch stays empty, while above the knot the vein is well distended; lift the finger and it refills at once. He chose this demonstration because a reader needed no corpse and no scalpel to check him. Source: Robert Willis translation of De Motu Cordis ch. XIII (1628 text).

question: Galen of Pergamon taught that blood was never reused, and Europe's doctors followed him for fourteen centuries. The body made it fresh, all day long, from food, sent it out through the veins, and the flesh soaked it up. Which organ did he name as the factory?
answer: The liver
choices: The liver
The heart
The spleen
The stomach
context: In Galen's picture the liver turned chyle absorbed from the gut into blood and charged it there with 'natural spirit', and the veins carried it one way to the parts, which used it up. That is why a Galenist felt no need for a return trip: nothing came back, because nothing was left. Source: 'Galen and the beginnings of Western physiology', Am. J. Physiol. Lung Cell Mol. Physiol.

question: Galen's followers had to get blood across the middle of the heart, from the right chamber into the left, with a thick wall of muscle standing between the two. For fourteen centuries anatomists taught one confident answer to that difficulty. How did they say the blood made the crossing?
answer: Seeped through pores in the wall too fine to see
choices: Seeped through pores in the wall too fine to see
Travelled out through the lungs and back again
Was carried across by the beating of the wall
Was made fresh in the left chamber out of air
context: Nobody ever saw those pores, because the wall (the interventricular septum) is solid. Blood really does cross by going out through the lungs and back — the pulmonary transit, described by Ibn al-Nafis in the 13th century, by Michael Servetus in 1553 inside a book of theology, and by Realdo Colombo in 1559. None of the three saw the full body-wide circuit. Sources: Am. J. Physiol. Lung Cell Mol. Physiol., 'Galen and the beginnings of Western physiology'; J. Appl. Physiol., 'Ibn al-Nafis, the pulmonary circulation, and the Islamic Golden Age'.

question: William Fitzer, a Frankfurt bookseller, took William Harvey's 72-page Latin manuscript to a licensed printing shop in 1628. It came back so badly set that the shop bound in an errata leaf, a printer's list of his own misprints, running to 126 corrections. The craftsmen were mediocre, but Harvey had made it worse. What was his share of the fault?
answer: His handwriting, cramped and atrocious
choices: His handwriting, cramped and atrocious
His Latin, crammed with new coinages
His revisions, sent in after typesetting
His hurry, pressing the shop to finish
context: Fitzer had eight licensed shops in Frankfurt to choose from, and by one historian's judgement all of them were mediocre craftsmen; the book came out on thin, unsightly paper in poor type. But the misprints came chiefly from Harvey's hand, which the same historian calls 'atrocious, crabbed' — cramped, jammed together, hard for a compositor to read. The result: 126 corrections for 72 pages, nearly two to a page. The book that ended Galen's fourteen centuries came into the world as a cheap, typo-riddled pamphlet. Sources: 'William Harvey's Anatomy Book and Literary Culture', PMC2175066; Worcester College Library, 'One of the two greatest books of seventeenth-century science'.

question: William Harvey named the creatures that taught him the most: 'toads, frogs, serpents, small fishes, crabs, shrimps, snails, and shell-fish.' Their hearts beat slowly enough for him to follow one whole beat with the naked eye, and he caught a change a warm-blooded heart moves far too fast to show. What did the heart do at the instant it squeezed?
answer: It turned paler than when it lay at rest
choices: It turned paler than when it lay at rest
It turned a deeper red than when at rest
It swelled a little but held its colour
It darkened only where the great veins entered
context: In fishes and other cold-blooded animals Harvey saw the heart go paler as it moved and deepen to blood-red as it rested. The slow beat gave him something else as well: he could separate the squeeze of the small upper chamber (the auricle, today called the atrium) from the squeeze of the big lower one (the ventricle) — in a warm-blooded animal the whole sequence is gone in an instant. Source: Robert Willis translation of De Motu Cordis ch. II.

question: William Harvey opened the left ventricle of a corpse and found it held two or three ounces when full. He allowed that only a fraction of that leaves with each beat — a fourth, a fifth, perhaps only an eighth. Then he counted the pulse: more than a thousand beats in half an hour. He multiplied the ounces by the beats. What did his half-hour total come to?
answer: More blood than the entire body contains
choices: More blood than the entire body contains
About a tenth of what the body contains
Rather less than the liver makes in a day
About what a man loses in a mortal wound
context: Harvey's own line, in Willis's translation: 'Multiplying the number of drachms propelled by the number of pulses, we shall have either one thousand half ounces, or one thousand times three drachms... sent from this organ into the artery — a larger quantity in every case than is contained in the whole body!' The Latin gives five hundred ounces in half an hour. CORRECTION WORTH KNOWING: the famous '540 pounds an hour' in modern textbooks is NOT Harvey's figure. It comes from later writers assuming two ounces a beat at 72 beats a minute; Harvey used about thirty-three beats a minute and half an ounce at most, and his punchline was a comparison, not a weight. Sources: Willis translation of De Motu Cordis ch. IX (Fordham Modern History Sourcebook); Latin text, Truman State University.

question: William Harvey bound a band around a volunteer's upper arm, as tight as the man could bear: below it the pulse died away and the hand went cool and pale. Then Harvey eased the band to a middling tightness, snug now but no longer choking the arm, and watched. What did the forearm and hand below it do?
answer: They swelled and turned warm to the touch
choices: They swelled and turned warm to the touch
They swelled harder but stayed cold and pale
They stayed slack while the swelling rose above
They stayed cold and slack until the band came off
context: The tight band shut everything, deep arteries included, so the hand below it went cool and pale while the arm above stayed warm and full. The middling band still let the arteries — which lie deeper and push harder — force blood in, while the surface veins stayed pinched shut, so blood piled into the forearm and could not get out: warm, swollen, the veins engorged.
