Blood arrives by artery and leaves by vein, and release the band and the veins empty in the direction of the heart, not the hand. Sources: De Motu Cordis ch. XI; James Lind Library review of Harvey's experimentation.

question: Hieronymus Fabricius, William Harvey's own teacher at Padua, published life-size engravings of the valves in the veins in 1603, a quarter of a century before De Motu Cordis. He had even shown that a finger pressed on a bound vein made them act, yet he read them as doing a different job. What did Fabricius think the valves were for?
answer: Holding the blood back so each part got an even share
choices: Holding the blood back so each part got an even share
Squeezing the blood onward, like pumps in the wall
Straining impurities out of the blood as it passed
Sealing the vein shut wherever it had been wounded
context: Fabricius published them as De Venarum Ostiolis (Padua, 1603), with copperplate engravings, and read their purpose as retarding the blood so it would be distributed evenly to the parts. Harvey asked the different question — not what they do, but what they are FOR — and saw that a one-way gate only makes sense if the traffic is one-way, toward the heart. Sources: Britannica, 'De Venarum Ostiolis'; Nature 135, 567 (1935) review of Franklin's facsimile.

question: A living snake lay open before William Harvey in the 1620s, a cold-blooded creature whose heart beat slowly enough to watch stroke by stroke. He took hold of the great trunk vein feeding the heart, the vena cava, and pinched it shut. What did he see in the seconds that followed?
answer: The heart and the aorta both drained and went pale
choices: The heart and the aorta both drained and went pale
The heart swelled dark while the aorta went pale
The heart and the aorta both swelled and darkened
The heart paled while the aorta stayed full and dark
context: The vena cava is the trunk that carries blood back to the heart; the aorta is the great artery leading out of it. Harvey then moved the pinch to the aorta instead and got the opposite result: the heart swelled and became engorged. Two pinches, two opposite results — blood comes in by one door and leaves by the other. Source: De Motu Cordis ch. X, summarised in Revista Argentina de Cardiologia, 'William Harvey (IV) De Motu Cordis'.

question: William Harvey needed one link he could never point to: somewhere in the body's tissue, blood had to pass from the smallest arteries into the smallest veins. He faced that gap in Chapter 7 of De Motu Cordis and spent a single phrase on it. What did he write?
answer: That it passed through hidden porosities, as fluid seeps through a kidney
choices: That it passed through hidden porosities, as fluid seeps through a kidney
That vessels too fine for the eye must join the arteries to the veins
That the flesh drank the blood up and then passed it on to the veins
That the heart's force drove the blood clean through the solid tissue
context: His Latin is 'pulmonum caecas porositates' — the hidden porosities of the lungs — with 'the minute inosculations of vessels', compared to fluid seeping through a kidney or a liver. He did not predict the capillaries and did not name them; he marked the hole in his own argument and left it open, which is what an honest case looks like. Sources: Willis translation of De Motu Cordis ch. VII; J. Appl. Physiol., 'Historical Perspective: Harvey's epoch-making discovery of the Circulation'.

question: Marcello Malpighi turned a microscope on the lung of a living frog four years after William Harvey died with the last link of his circuit still unfound. The living lung defeated him: he could see blood moving through vessels far finer than the eye can resolve, but he could not follow them to their ends. What did Malpighi do next?
answer: He dried the lung and traced the network in the dead tissue
choices: He dried the lung and traced the network in the dead tissue
He injected coloured wax and cut the dried lung into slices
He ground a stronger lens and watched the living lung again
He compared the frog's lung against the lung of a drowned dog
context: What he mapped were the capillaries — thin-walled vessels joining the smallest arteries to the smallest veins — published in 1661 as De pulmonibus observationes anatomicae. Harvey's circuit was closed four years after his death, by an instrument he never owned. Sources: 'Marcello Malpighi and the Discovery of the Pulmonary Capillaries and Alveoli' (Thoracic Key / Int. J. Cardiol.); '1661 in science'.

question: John Aubrey heard William Harvey tell of the years after his 1628 publication, and he later recorded the account. The short Latin treatise, De Motu Cordis, had argued that the same blood keeps coming back to the heart it left. What did Aubrey record that publishing it cost Harvey?
answer: His patients left him, and men thought him crack-brained
choices: His patients left him, and men thought him crack-brained
His fellow physicians barred him from the College's lectures
His pupils deserted him, and studied under a rival
His rivals printed a book naming him a butcher
context: Aubrey, in Brief Lives: 'I have heard him say, that after his book of the circulation of the blood came out, that he fell mightily in his practice, and that 'twas believed by the vulgar that he was crack-brained; and all the physicians were against his opinion.' Physicians of the period were long reported to have said they would 'rather err with Galen than proclaim the truth with Harvey' — a saying repeated for centuries with no named speaker behind it, so take it as tradition, not as testimony. General acceptance took roughly twenty years; Thomas Hobbes remarked that Harvey was the only modern author whose doctrine was established in his own lifetime. Sources: John Aubrey, Brief Lives (Internet Archive); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Harvey.

question: William Harvey could not measure exactly how much blood the left ventricle throws out with each squeeze, and he said so plainly. In Chapter 9 he offered a range, a fourth of the chamber, a fifth, a sixth, 'or even but the eighth part,' and then ran the whole calculation on the smallest figure, and on a stingy guess for the chamber's size as well. Why build the argument on his own lowest numbers?
answer: Because a total impossible even at the lowest guess cannot be argued down
choices: Because a total impossible even at the lowest guess cannot be argued down
Because the lowest guess was the one Galen's followers already granted
Because a lower total stayed within what the liver was thought to make
Because the lowest guess was the only figure he had actually weighed
context: Harvey ran the same sum on animals with the same deliberate stinginess: allow only a single scruple per beat in a sheep or a dog, and half an hour still throws about three and a half pounds into the aorta — while the whole animal holds not above four pounds. An argument built on your opponent's most favourable assumptions is one he cannot rescue by haggling over the measurement. Source: Robert Willis translation of De Motu Cordis ch. IX (Fordham Modern History Sourcebook).

question: He Jiankui announced in November 2018 that he had used a new gene-editing technique to alter the DNA of human embryos, and that two of them had been born as healthy baby girls. He said he had switched off a gene to try to make them resistant to the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). To protect the twins' real identities he gave them pseudonyms. What are those pseudonyms?
answer: Lulu and Nana
choices: Lulu and Nana
Lily and Rose
Yin and Yang
Ada and Grace
context: A third gene-edited child, given the pseudonym Amy, was born the following year. The researcher was He Jiankui of Southern University of Science and Technology in Shenzhen. Source: sciencealert.com, 'China Quietly Confirms a Third CRISPR-Edited Baby'.

question: He Jiankui aimed his gene-editing tool at one gene. Its product sits on the surface of a T cell and acts as the door most strains of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) use to get in. Some people are born with a mutation that turns the gene off, and they resist HIV very well. Which gene was the target?
answer: CCR5
choices: CCR5
CXCR4
TP53
BRCA1
context: He was copying the natural CCR5-delta-32 variant. Even a perfect knockout only blocks R5-tropic HIV strains; X4-tropic strains use a different co-receptor (CXCR4) and would go around the edit entirely. Source: academic.oup.com/jlb/article/6/1/111.

question: He Jiankui said he had to edit the twin girls because their father had HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus). Bioethicists and IVF (in vitro fertilization) doctors pushed back. A simple method already stopped HIV going from father to child for these couples. Which method?
answer: Sperm washing before fertilization
choices: Sperm washing before fertilization
PrEP for the mother during conception attempts
Timed intercourse during the father's undetectable viral load
IVF using donor sperm from an HIV-negative donor
context: Sperm washing separates HIV particles from the sperm before IVF and has been standard practice for decades in HIV-serodiscordant couples. He was editing healthy embryos against a risk ordinary medicine had already solved. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperm_washing.

question: Outside researchers sequenced the DNA of the twin girls He Jiankui had secretly edited as embryos and implanted in 2018. He had said he was copying delta-32, a natural mutation many healthy people inherit that helps block the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). What actually appeared in their genes?
answer: Brand-new mutations no one had ever studied in humans
choices: Brand-new mutations no one had ever studied in humans
A clean copy of the delta-32 deletion in both girls
The delta-32 deletion in one girl, no edit in the other
No detectable edit at all in either girl
context: Lulu ended up heterozygous: one normal CCR5 and one carrying a 15-base-pair in-frame deletion. Nana had a 4-base-pair deletion on one allele and a single-base insertion on the other. Those variants are not found in nature; their consequences are unknown -- and the girls can pass them on. Source: Kiran Musunuru thread; journals.plos.org, 'Gene-edited babies: what went wrong'.

question: About seven hundred colleagues watched He Jiankui defend his experiment onstage at the international gene-editing summit in Hong Kong in November 2018, three days after his video announcing twin girls born from edited embryos. How did the summit's own organizers describe what he had done?
answer: Unexpected and deeply disturbing
choices: Unexpected and deeply disturbing
A courageous first step in a hard field
Regrettable but scientifically defensible
Consistent with international norms
context: The condemnation was near-universal, but the language mattered: the objection was not to gene editing as such, it was to secrecy, invalid consent, and untested edits on healthy embryos who cannot consent for themselves or their descendants. Source: hongkongfp.com, 'Hong Kong conference slams deeply disturbing baby gene-editing claim by Chinese scientist'.

question: Judges of the Nanshan District People's Court in Shenzhen sentenced He Jiankui on 30 December 2019 to three years in prison and a three-million-yuan fine. The Chinese state did not need to invent a new gene-editing statute for the conviction. Under what existing charge did the court actually convict him?
answer: Illegal practice of medicine
choices: Illegal practice of medicine
Endangering public safety by dangerous means
Fraud in scientific research grants
Producing counterfeit pharmaceuticals
context: He and two colleagues, Zhang Renli and Qin Jinzhou, were also banned for life from reproductive medicine. He was released from prison around April 2022. Source: science.org, 'Chinese scientist who produced genetically altered babies sentenced to 3 years in jail'.

question: The couples in He Jiankui's project signed a consent form that struck bioethicists as a warning sign in itself. What did the form threaten them with if they tried to withdraw after embryo implantation?
answer: Repayment of all project costs, with fines for late payment
choices: Repayment of all project costs, with fines for late payment
Loss of legal custody of any resulting children
Public disclosure of their HIV-positive status
A ten-year ban from all fertility clinics in China
context: The form also described the study as an 'AIDS vaccine development project' rather than as germline editing. The people who could not consent at all, of course, were Lulu, Nana and Amy -- no future form can fix that. Source: scienceretractions.wordpress.com, 'Why is He Jiankui in real trouble'; PMC, 'Informed Consent for Human Embryo Genome Editing'.

question: He Jiankui's fellow scientists condemned him, but not with the slogan that gene editing is evil. They laid out specific charges instead, and keeping those charges separate let them tell his case apart from legitimate therapeutic editing. Which set of four charges did they make?
answer: Untested, medically unnecessary, no real consent, heritable
choices: Untested, medically unnecessary, no real consent, heritable
Illegal in China, illegal in the US, unprofitable, unpublished
Wrong gene, wrong strain of HIV, wrong clinic, wrong country
Off-target cuts, mosaicism, viral contamination, cell death
context: Therapeutic gene editing on consenting adults -- Casgevy for sickle-cell in 2023, CAR-T therapies, Luxturna for inherited blindness -- meets exactly the tests He failed: real disease, real consent, tested first, not heritable. That distinction is why the field could praise those treatments in the same decade it condemned him. Source: theconversation.com, 'Tension as scientist at centre of CRISPR outrage speaks at genome editing summit'.

question: Jerry Ehman was reading a paper printout from the Big Ear radio telescope at Ohio State University in August 1977 when he found a short burst far stronger than the normal noise. He circled it in red pen and wrote one word next to it. What word did he write?
answer: Wow!
choices: Wow!
Bingo!
Aha!
Voila!
context: Ehman was working on a SETI survey and had gone home for the weekend when the burst came in; the paper was already several days old when he saw it. His marginalium is still on the original printout at the Ohio History Connection. See https://www.bigear.org/wow.htm

question: A magazine writer calls the string '6EQUJ5' a coded message from whatever sent it. Jerry Ehman had circled those six characters on a printout of a strong 72-second burst, picked up by the Big Ear radio telescope from empty sky near Sagittarius on 15 August 1977. What is the string actually?
answer: A record of how loud the signal was, one character every 12 seconds as it rose and fell
choices: A record of how loud the signal was, one character every 12 seconds as it rose and fell
A frequency stamp, six numbers reading the tuning of the receiver over the burst
A sky coordinate, giving the right ascension and declination of the source in the printout
A checksum the Big Ear computer produced to certify the burst was not receiver noise
context: Big Ear rated the signal in each 12-second window on a scale where numerals and then letters climb: '1' was the smallest bin above the background, 'U' was near the top. The 'U' in '6EQUJ5' marks a peak about thirty times the background noise. The string carries no content whatsoever. See https://academics.uccs.edu/rtirado/PES_1100/wow.pdf

question: A radio astronomer tunes her receiver to 1420 megahertz and points it at the night sky. The Big Ear telescope picked up its famous burst of 1977 at almost exactly that number. For years before it, searchers for alien radio had argued that a smart broadcaster would pick that frequency, a natural landmark on the dial. Why 1420?
answer: It is the natural radio emission line of neutral hydrogen, the most common atom in the universe
choices: It is the natural radio emission line of neutral hydrogen, the most common atom in the universe
It is the low-noise centre of Earth's atmospheric radio window for ground-based receivers
It is the resonance frequency at which a laboratory maser cavity built by Charles Townes rings
It is the frequency at which the Sun's quiet corona happens to be nearly silent as seen from Earth
context: The 1420 MHz line (21 cm wavelength) is produced by a hyperfine flip in the hydrogen atom. Any species anywhere in the galaxy that studies radio astronomy will know this frequency and will listen there, so it is often called the 'universal calling channel'. That the Wow! sat on it made the coincidence unbearable. See https://www.bigear.org/wow.htm

question: Antonio Paris published a claim in 2017 that hydrogen clouds around comets 266P/Christensen and P/2008 Y2 had made the strong burst Ohio State's Big Ear telescope logged in 1977. That burst has never repeated: Ohio State and other observatories, including the Very Large Array in New Mexico, have listened to that patch of sky roughly fifty times since and heard nothing. Why did the Ohio State observatory staff reject the claim?
answer: Neither comet was anywhere near the beam's position on 15 August 1977
choices: Neither comet was anywhere near the beam's position on 15 August 1977
Neither comet ever comes closer to the Sun than the orbit of Neptune
The Big Ear beam could not have detected an object as cold as a comet
The Ohio State original data logs had been destroyed and could not be checked
context: The Ohio State observatory staff pointed out that Paris's follow-up observations were taken in 2017 near the modern position of the Wow! source, whereas the comets in question were on very different orbits back in 1977. The honest verdict on this signal: it is UNEXPLAINED. It is neither evidence of aliens nor debunked. See http://naapo.org/WOWCometRebuttal.html

question: Duncan Lorimer and his student David Narkevic went back through 2001 tapes from Australia's Parkes telescope in 2007 and found a five-millisecond radio blast that briefly outshone almost every other object in the sky. Parkes then caught sixteen more brief bursts, nicknamed perytons. Emily Petroff's team traced the perytons to their source in 2015. Where did they come from?
answer: The observatory's own microwave ovens, leaking a burst when a staff member yanked the door open
choices: The observatory's own microwave ovens, leaking a burst when a staff member yanked the door open
A satellite in geostationary orbit that swept the antenna field at roughly the same time each afternoon
The observatory's electric perimeter fence, arcing whenever a kangaroo touched the wire in summer
A defective magnetron in the telescope's own receiver, misfiring intermittently at 1.4 gigahertz
context: Petroff's team installed a real-time radio-interference monitor at Parkes and caught three perytons in January 2015, each coincident with a signal at 2.3-2.5 GHz, exactly the band used by domestic microwave ovens. Yanking the door open shut the magnetron down mid-cycle, and the shut-down transient leaked out near 1.4 GHz. Feynman's rule earned its keep: check your own kitchen before you announce the universe. See https://skyandtelescope.org/astronomy-news/microwave-ovens-spark-radio-signals-peryton-05122015/

question: Duncan Lorimer's 2007 burst survived the check that sank the perytons. Its lower frequencies had lagged behind its higher ones, and the size of that lag counts the loose electrons the signal crossed on the way, a figure called the dispersion measure. Lorimer's was huge. What did that huge figure let the Parkes team argue about the source?
answer: That the burst had come from outside our galaxy, from cosmological distances
choices: That the burst had come from outside our galaxy, from cosmological distances
That the burst had come from a compact object less than a kilometre across
That the burst had been beamed straight at Earth by a rotating source
That the burst had passed through the magnetic field of a nearby neutron star
context: As a radio pulse travels, its lower frequencies drag through the sparse plasma of interstellar space slightly slower than its higher frequencies. Adding up all the electrons crossed gives the 'dispersion measure', which can be turned into a rough distance. Lorimer's burst had a dispersion far higher than any line of sight inside the Milky Way could deliver, so the Parkes team argued the source had to be extragalactic. The perytons, being local, showed no such delay. See https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19106

question: Astronomers caught a fast radio burst inside the Milky Way on 28 April 2020 and traced it to a known object. That was enough to prove that at least some such bursts can be made by a particular type of star, though not that all of them are. What type of star made this one?
answer: A magnetar, a neutron star with an extreme magnetic field, catalogued as SGR 1935+2154
choices: A magnetar, a neutron star with an extreme magnetic field, catalogued as SGR 1935+2154
A young pulsar, a rapidly spinning neutron star of the kind Jocelyn Bell Burnell found in 1967
A T Tauri star, a young low-mass star still contracting toward the main sequence
A red dwarf flare star, of the kind that periodically brightens by orders of magnitude
context: SGR 1935+2154 lies about 30,000 light-years away in the Milky Way. Its burst was picked up in the 1.28-1.47 GHz band by the STARE2 array and coincided with an X-ray flare. The result showed magnetars CAN make fast radio bursts. It did not show that magnetars make ALL of them; more than one source population may be out there. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SGR_1935+2154

question: A coach pulls an instant cold pack from a first-aid kit and gives it a firm squeeze. It holds no ice, no batteries and no coolant, yet it plunges to near zero degrees Celsius in seconds. Inside, a sealed bag of water has burst over crystals of one chemical. Which one?
answer: Ammonium nitrate
choices: Ammonium nitrate
Sodium chloride
Calcium chloride
Sodium bicarbonate
context: Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water endothermically, absorbing about 25.7 kilojoules per mole; the dissolving pulls heat out of the surroundings (including the hand holding it) fast enough to drop the pack near 0 C. Calcium chloride is the opposite: dissolving it in water releases heat. Source: Wikipedia, Ice pack.

question: A skier tears the outer plastic wrapper off a disposable hand warmer, and only then does it start to warm. Tearing the wrapper does nothing exotic. It simply lets air get in, so a specific slow process can run on the powder sealed inside. Which process is it?
answer: Iron powder oxidising to ordinary rust
choices: Iron powder oxidising to ordinary rust
Sodium powder reacting with air moisture
Charcoal powder slowly smouldering to ash
Aluminium powder reacting with the oxygen
context: The pouch contains iron powder plus salt, water, activated charcoal, and vermiculite; when oxygen enters, the iron oxidises to rust and gives off heat (about 1.7 kilocalories per gram of iron) for hours. The mix reaches around 74 C in about twenty minutes. Source: Wikipedia, Hand warmer.

question: A nurse hands a patient a squeezed instant cold pack, and it drops toward zero degrees within seconds. A common story is that the pack somehow creates cold. Suppose you held one. What is a physicist's more accurate description of what is happening between the pack and your palm?
answer: Heat flows out of your palm into the pack, where dissolving crystals absorb it
choices: Heat flows out of your palm into the pack, where dissolving crystals absorb it
Cold rays radiate outward from the pack's crystals into your skin
A tiny refrigerator cycle inside the pack pumps heat away from your palm
A supercold liquid inside the pack seeps out against your bare skin
context: Cold is not a substance; nothing 'makes' cold. Whenever something feels cold, heat is FLOWING OUT OF YOU into a colder thing (or, as here, into a chemical process that absorbs it). This one reframe unlocks half of chemistry-in-the-kitchen. Source: Wikipedia, Endothermic process.

question: A hiker presses and releases the small metal disc floating in a reusable heat pad, a clear liquid in a plastic pouch. Within seconds a wave of change races through the pouch, and it turns hot to hold. What is releasing the heat?
answer: A liquid solidifying and giving off its stored energy
choices: A liquid solidifying and giving off its stored energy
A salt reacting chemically with the plastic lining
A tiny lithium battery buried in the metal disc
A slow oxidation of iron flecks in the disc
context: The clear liquid is a supersaturated solution of sodium acetate, sitting far below the temperature at which it OUGHT to have crystallised, held there by having no seed to start on. The click creates a nucleation site; the wave you see is crystallisation, which is exothermic. Reset by boiling until every crystal redissolves. Source: Wikipedia, Hand warmer.

question: Hans Goldschmidt patented a reaction in 1895, lit with a bit of magnesium ribbon. Dry aluminium powder is mixed with iron-oxide powder, and once it starts, the mix climbs past 2,500 degrees Celsius. Since about 1899 rail crews around the world have used it out on the track, with no power supply. For what specific job?
answer: Welding one steel rail to the next steel rail
choices: Welding one steel rail to the next steel rail
Hardening rail-ends by localised heat treatment
Cutting through a snapped rail so it can be lifted out
Casting replacement wheel bearings on the spot
context: Aluminium 'wants' oxygen more than iron does, so it simply takes it, releasing enormous heat and depositing molten iron exactly where the small clay crucible is aimed: the rail-end joint. The reaction needs no power supply and no external heat once ignited, which is why the same chemistry Goldschmidt patented in 1895 still welds rails outdoors on remote track today. Source: Wikipedia, Hans Goldschmidt; Britannica, Thermit.

question: A sound engineer gets an odd order from a musician: a beep of exactly 440 hertz, the note A that orchestras tune to, one pure frequency and nothing else, lasting only one thousandth of a second. He says it cannot be done. Why not?
answer: No such sound exists — a tone that starts and stops spreads across frequencies
choices: No such sound exists — a tone that starts and stops spreads across frequencies
No such purity exists — a speaker's cone never holds one frequency steady
No speaker can start and stop its cone cleanly in one millisecond
No microphone can sample a millisecond burst without smearing it
context: Engineers call this the Gabor limit: a signal's duration times its bandwidth, both measured as standard deviations, can never drop below 1/(4*pi). Improve the localization in one and the spread in the other necessarily widens. There is no quantum mechanics anywhere in it — it falls straight out of the Fourier transform, and it governs ocean waves and radio signals just as strictly. Test it tonight: pluck a guitar string, let it ring, and a phone tuner locks onto a note; pluck it and clamp it dead, and the tuner finds nothing, because a click is not a pitch. Source: Grokipedia 'Uncertainty principle', Applications > Signal Processing — https://grokipedia.com/page/Uncertainty_principle

question: Werner Heisenberg, twenty-one, was failing his doctoral oral at Munich in 1923. Wilhelm Wien asked him about an interferometer, a telescope and a microscope, and he could solve none of them. Wien tried one last question with no optics in it, and Heisenberg was still stuck. What had Wien asked?
answer: How a storage battery works
choices: How a storage battery works
How a telephone carries speech
How a thermometer is calibrated
How a compass needle finds north
context: Arnold Sommerfeld graded him top marks; Wien failed him outright. The compromise left the future Nobel laureate with a III — roughly a C — in physics and for the doctorate overall. Four years later the argument that made his name was built on an imaginary microscope, the very instrument he had fumbled that afternoon. Source: AIP Center for History of Physics, Heisenberg exhibit, 'The Sad Story of Heisenberg's Doctorate' — https://history.aip.org/exhibits/heisenberg/sad-story.html ; APS News, January 1998.

question: Dennis Gabor, an electrical engineer, got stuck in 1946 on a problem that sounds simple: describing a siren whose pitch slides steadily upward. Fourier analysis, the standard method for breaking a sound into pure tones, kept failing on it. What was the flaw?
answer: It builds from tones that run forever, so it cannot say when a pitch happened
choices: It builds from tones that run forever, so it cannot say when a pitch happened
It handles only tones a human ear can hear, and a siren climbs past them
It assumes the signal repeats exactly, and a siren's sweep never repeats
It requires the loudness to hold steady, and a siren swells and fades
context: Gabor published it as 'Theory of communication. Part 1: The analysis of information' in the Journal of the Institution of Electrical Engineers Part III, vol. 93 no. 26 (1946), pp. 429-441 — importing Heisenberg's trade-off wholesale into radio and sound engineering. His fix was to analyse a signal in short windowed chunks instead of all at once, which is the ancestor of every spectrogram you have ever seen. Source: Wikipedia 'Gabor atom', citing Gabor 1946 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabor_atom ; corroborated by Grokipedia 'Uncertainty principle' > Signal Processing.

question: Werner Heisenberg sat writing in Copenhagen in March 1927, and his whole argument rested on a device nobody could build: a microscope that locates a single electron by bouncing gamma rays off it. Short wavelengths would give a sharp position. His paper named the price of that sharpness. What was it?
answer: The photon would kick the electron's momentum to an unknown value
choices: The photon would kick the electron's momentum to an unknown value
The gamma rays would strip the electron from its atom before imaging
The lens would need to be wider than any laboratory to catch the rays
The exposure would last so long the electron had already moved on
context: His own words: 'At the instant of time when the position is determined, that is, at the instant when the photon is scattered by the electron, the electron undergoes a discontinuous change in momentum.' The paper was 'Ueber den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik', March 1927, written at Niels Bohr's institute. Note the constant: Heisenberg estimated the product as roughly Planck's constant h; the sharper h-bar/2 that textbooks print belongs to Earle Kennard's proof, not to the microscope story. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Uncertainty Principle', quoting Heisenberg 1927 pp. 174-175 — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-uncertainty/

question: A lab technician chills helium toward absolute zero at ordinary atmospheric pressure, and it simply stays liquid. Every other substance on Earth freezes if made cold enough, but helium has to be squeezed past about twenty-five atmospheres before it will form a solid at all. Why does helium alone hold out?
answer: Its atoms can never come fully to rest, and that motion beats their feeble attraction
choices: Its atoms can never come fully to rest, and that motion beats their feeble attraction
Its atoms fill their outer shell, and a filled shell leaves no bonds for a lattice
Its atoms turn superfluid as they cool, and a superfluid cannot hold a rigid lattice
Its atoms are all bosons, and bosons crowd into a single state instead of a lattice
context: Helium-4 boils at 4.222 K and needs pressures above about 2.5 MPa — roughly 25 atmospheres — before it will solidify near 1 K. Its van der Waals attraction is simply too weak to overcome the zero-point energy of atoms that are not permitted to be at rest. Below the lambda-point at 2.17 K the liquid instead turns into a superfluid. This is the one entry in the phase tables you can point at and say: that blank space is the uncertainty principle. Source: Grokipedia 'Helium', Physical and Chemical Properties > Phase Transitions and States of Matter — https://grokipedia.com/page/Helium

question: Niels Bohr returned from skiing in Norway in 1927, read Werner Heisenberg's gamma-ray microscope paper and told him the argument was misleading. They argued hard and did not agree, and the paper was already submitted. What did Heisenberg do?
answer: He added a last-minute note crediting Bohr and left the argument standing
choices: He added a last-minute note crediting Bohr and left the argument standing
He withdrew the paper and rewrote the whole argument along Bohr's lines
He published it unchanged and answered Bohr in a separate paper that autumn
He cut the microscope out entirely and kept only the mathematical relation
context: Bohr had been working out complementarity on that holiday. Heisenberg's addition is titled 'Nachtrag bei der Korrektur' — Addition in proof — and it grants Bohr's point that what matters is not that the momentum changes but that the change cannot be measured in the same experiment. He did not withdraw the microscope, which is one reason the picture outlived the objection to it. (No primary source supports the popular story that Bohr reduced Heisenberg to tears; the record says only that they discussed intensely and disagreed.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Uncertainty Principle' (Hilgevoord & Uffink) — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-uncertainty/

question: Ernst Abbe demonstrated in the 1870s that a microscope's resolving ability depends on more than the light it uses. Werner Heisenberg's 1927 paper set resolution equal to the wavelength and stopped there. Niels Bohr's complaint about the gamma-ray microscope was partly this plain mistake in the optics. What had Heisenberg ignored?
answer: The width of the lens's opening, which sets the range of angles it gathers
choices: The width of the lens's opening, which sets the range of angles it gathers
The thickness of the lens, which bends edge rays differently from central ones
The brightness of the source, which fixes how many photons form the image
The distance from specimen to lens, which sets the image's magnification
context: Abbe's theory shows that the directions along and across the optical axis behave differently, so the lens's half-angle has to enter the resolution. Put it back in and the position blur is about the wavelength divided by the sine of that half-angle, while the momentum kick goes as Planck's constant over the wavelength times that same sine — the wavelength and the angle cancel and the product comes out around h. Bohr's deeper objection was conceptual, and he later wrote that 'the uncertainty in question is not simply a consequence of a discontinuous change of energy and momentum.' Source: Werner & Farrelly, 'Uncertainty from Heisenberg to Today', arXiv:1904.06139 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06139 ; Bohr quote via Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Bohr 1985: 93).

question: Earle Hesse Kennard published the strict version of the famous inequality in 1927, the one every physics textbook prints under Werner Heisenberg's name. Using Erwin Schroedinger's wave mechanics, he showed that delta-x times delta-p is at least h-bar over two, where each delta means a standard deviation, a spread. What does Kennard's inequality say?
answer: Which quantum states can exist: none holds a sharp position and a sharp momentum
choices: Which quantum states can exist: none holds a sharp position and a sharp momentum
How hard a probe must hit: no photon is gentle enough to leave momentum sharp
How good instruments can get: no detector will ever pin both quantities at once
What a particle secretly holds: both values are sharp but no test reveals them
context: This is the load-bearing distinction in the whole subject. Kennard's relation — and Howard Robertson's 1929 generalization of it to any pair of observables, with Schroedinger's 1930 sharpening on top — are PREPARATION relations: they describe the spreads of the probability distributions belonging to a given quantum state. In the Stanford Encyclopedia's words, they 'do not address simultaneous measurement accuracy or disturbance from the act of measuring itself.' No quantum state of any particle, however gently anyone handles it, has both a sharp position and a sharp momentum. It is a statement about which states exist, not about how carefully you look. Equality holds exactly for Gaussian wave packets, and it is a floor rather than a value: the nth state of a harmonic oscillator sits at h-bar(n + 1/2), so only the ground state touches the bound. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Uncertainty Principle' — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-uncertainty/ ; Grokipedia 'Uncertainty principle' > Kennard Inequality.

question: A student runs the classical physics of the 1890s on a single atom and finds it should fall apart in a nanosecond. An electron circling a nucleus is an accelerating charge, and accelerating charges radiate away their energy, so the electron ought to spiral into its nucleus almost instantly. Atoms have held together for billions of years instead. What holds the electron out?
answer: A kinetic energy that squeezing the electron into a small space forces on it
choices: A kinetic energy that squeezing the electron into a small space forces on it
A centrifugal push from the orbit that grows stronger as the radius shrinks
A short-range repulsion from the nucleus that outmuscles the electric pull
A radiating-and-reabsorbing balance that keeps the orbit's energy books even
context: Confine an electron closer to the nucleus and its momentum spread must grow, which forces a minimum kinetic energy that no cooling can remove. That zero-point kinetic energy is what balances the attractive Coulomb pull and sets the size of the atom. The bookkeeping is checkable: minimizing h-bar^2/(8m<x^2>) plus (1/2)m*omega^2*<x^2> for a harmonic well returns exactly the true ground-state energy, (1/2)h-bar*omega. The same effect shows up in chemistry — hydrogen's zero-point energy of about 0.27 eV is why its measured dissociation energy is 4.48 eV while the well itself is 4.75 eV deep. The molecule can never sit at the bottom of its own well. Source: Grokipedia 'Zero-point energy', Theoretical Foundations > Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle and Atomic Physics Phenomena — https://grokipedia.com/page/Zero-point_energy

question: Aya Furuta wrote a Scientific American piece on 8 March 2012 under the headline 'One Thing Is Certain: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle Is Not Dead.' Yuji Hasegawa's group in Vienna had sent neutron spins through an interferometer and broken a limit that had carried Werner Heisenberg's name since 1927, and the result stood. She explained why nothing had died: two different statements had been sharing that one name, and only one of them fell. Which statement fell?
answer: The claim that observing something must inevitably disturb what is observed
choices: The claim that observing something must inevitably disturb what is observed
The claim that no particle can hold a sharp position and a sharp momentum at once
The claim that the same limit covers every pair of incompatible quantities
The claim that states with correlated spreads obey a still tighter bound
context: Furuta separated the two statements cleanly: what the Vienna team violated was Heisenberg's 1927 measurement-disturbance claim that 'in observing the world, we inevitably disturb it', while the Kennard-Robertson relation, which describes a state's own fluctuations in position and momentum, 'does not say anything about what happens when a measurement is performed'. The Vienna paper was Erhart, Sponar, Sulyok, Badurek, Ozawa and Hasegawa, 'Experimental demonstration of a universally valid error-disturbance uncertainty relation in spin-measurements', Nature Physics 8, 185-189 (2012), posted as arXiv:1201.1833 on 9 January 2012. Two independent confirmations followed the headline rather than preceding it: Rozema, Darabi, Mahler, Hayat, Soudagar and Steinberg in Toronto used weak measurements on single photons, Physical Review Letters 109, 100404, published 6 September 2012; and Baek, Kaneda, Ozawa and Edamatsu at Tohoku reported flatly that 'Ozawa's relation always holds, whereas Heisenberg's relation fails for all measurement strengths', Scientific Reports 3, 2221 (2013). All three matched Masanao Ozawa's corrected 2003 relation, which carries three terms where the naive version had a single product, so the first term alone can dip below the old bound. Kennard's preparation relation was never in danger and was never tested by any of it. Source: Aya Furuta, Scientific American, 8 March 2012 — https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/heisenbergs-uncertainty-principle-is-not-dead/ ; arXiv:1201.1833 ; arXiv:1208.0034 ; Scientific Reports 3, 2221 (2013).

question: An experimenter at a particle collider plots the energies of what the rho meson decays into and gets a broad bump about a hundred and fifty million electron-volts across. She fits that width straight off the data and prints it beside the mass. The fuzziness is a measured property of the particle, not a shortcoming of the apparatus. What is that width telling her?
answer: How briefly the particle exists before it decays
choices: How briefly the particle exists before it decays
How fast the particle was moving when it formed
How many different ways the particle can decay
How much energy the collision that made it carried
context: A state that decays with lifetime tau has a spectral width Gamma = h-bar/tau. The rho meson lives about ten to the minus twenty-three seconds, which is exactly why its width comes out around 150 MeV — its mass is a Breit-Wigner bump rather than a number. Be careful with the energy-time version, though: it is not the same kind of statement as position-momentum, because time in quantum mechanics is a parameter rather than an observable, and Pauli's theorem shows no self-adjoint time operator conjugate to a bounded-below Hamiltonian can exist. The usable form is Mandelstam and Tamm's 1945 relation, in which delta-t means the time an observable's expectation value takes to shift by about its own uncertainty — not the duration of a measurement. Source: Grokipedia 'Uncertainty principle', Energy-Time Uncertainty > Time in Quantum Mechanics and > Mandelstam-Tamm Relation — https://grokipedia.com/page/Uncertainty_principle

question: Henrietta Lacks, a tobacco farmer and mother of five, lay unconscious at Johns Hopkins on 8 February 1951, radium about to go in for her cervical cancer. Before it did, Dr. Lawrence Wharton Jr did something her treatment did not require. What did he do?
answer: He cut two dime-sized pieces from her cervix.
choices: He cut two dime-sized pieces from her cervix.
He scraped cells from her cervix with a wooden spatula.
He drew two large vials of blood from her arm.
He took a swab of cells from inside her cheek.
context: One piece was healthy tissue, one was tumour; neither was needed for her treatment, and nobody asked her. George Gey, whose lab received the sample, did not take it himself - the popular retelling that puts him in the room is wrong. She was dead by 4 October 1951, aged 31, with tumours through nearly every organ. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HeLa ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_Lacks ; grokipedia.com/page/HeLa

question: Mary Kubicek, George Gey's young lab assistant, had never seen a corpse when she was sent to Henrietta Lacks's autopsy on 4 October 1951. Keeping her eyes away from the dead woman's face, she caught sight of one small detail and nearly fainted. What had she seen?
answer: Her chipped red toenail polish.
choices: Her chipped red toenail polish.
Her plain gold wedding ring.
Her tight hospital wristband.
Her cracked and callused hands.
context: Kubicek later told the writer Rebecca Skloot: 'When I saw those toenails, I nearly fainted. I thought, Oh jeez, she's a real person.' Kubicek was the one who had labelled the culture tubes 'HeLa', two letters from each of her names, to keep the donor anonymous. For twenty-five years the public was told the cells came from a woman called Helen Lane, sometimes Helen Larson; a 1976 Rolling Stone article by Michael Rogers first brought the real woman behind the cells to a wide public. Source: Johns Hopkins Magazine, 'Immortal Cells, Enduring Issues' (2010), quoting Rebecca Skloot's 'The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks'.

question: George Gey packed vials of HeLa in sawdust and cardboard boxes and mailed them free to anyone who asked, with no patent and no penny for himself. They reached Texas, Amsterdam, India and Chile in the pockets of airline pilots. What carried one shipment part of the way?
answer: A mule's saddlebag.
choices: A mule's saddlebag.
A fisherman's ice chest.
A beekeeper's crate.
A dogsled's supply pack.
context: Gey shipped the line free for the rest of his life and died without earning anything from it. Later, companies sold HeLa products for decades; the estate's suit against Thermo Fisher Scientific settled in 2023. Source: Cathy Gere, 'Dying and Not Dying: Henrietta Lacks', London Review of Books v32 n11 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Otto_Gey

question: Margaret Gey and Mary Kubicek minced Henrietta Lacks's tumour tissue and fed it a homemade broth, in a lab where every human sample so far had died within weeks. They rotated the tubes in a roller drum George Gey had built himself. What was in the broth?
answer: Chicken plasma, calf embryo extract and umbilical cord serum.
choices: Chicken plasma, calf embryo extract and umbilical cord serum.
Beef bouillon, powdered egg white and distilled rainwater.
Horse serum, evaporated milk and dried brewer's yeast extract.
Sheep blood, boiled potato starch and warm glucose syrup.
context: The roller drum was Gey's own invention, built to keep every cell bathed as the tubes turned. In the tube beside the tumour, Henrietta's own healthy cervical tissue withered and died, exactly as human cells always had. The tumour cells doubled every 20 to 24 hours instead. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/HeLa ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Otto_Gey

question: George Gey and two colleagues, William Scherer and Jerome Syverton, found in 1953 that a single tube of HeLa could give a plain yes-or-no answer. Jonas Salk's polio vaccine went into a field trial on more than 1.8 million children the next year, and laboratories had to test batch after batch of virus and vaccine first, which was slow, costly work. What made HeLa work as the test?
answer: Poliovirus infects HeLa and visibly destroys it.
choices: Poliovirus infects HeLa and visibly destroys it.
Poliovirus makes HeLa clump into visible strands.
Poliovirus makes HeLa glow under ultraviolet light.
Poliovirus turns the broth around HeLa bright red.
context: Dead cells in the tube meant live virus; healthy cells meant none. Scherer, Syverton and Gey demonstrated poliovirus typing in HeLa in 1953, and the vaccine was licensed on 12 April 1955. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/HeLa ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HeLa

question: George Gey watched demand for HeLa swamp his lab by 1953. To supply the labs testing Jonas Salk's polio vaccine, the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis built a big center that shipped twenty thousand tubes every week, about six trillion cells. Where was that center built?
answer: At the Tuskegee Institute, a college in Alabama.
choices: At the Tuskegee Institute, a college in Alabama.
At the Wistar Institute, a lab in Philadelphia.
At the University of Minnesota, a school in Minneapolis.
At the Rockefeller Institute, a lab in New York.
context: Charles Bynum, the foundation's first Black executive, recommended the site, and Dr. William Scherer shipped the seed culture there in April 1953. Six Black scientists and technicians ran the centre at the start and about 35 staff at its peak, many of them women; they supplied the laboratories that ran the tests on the Salk vaccine. This HeLa factory is a completely different thing from the Tuskegee syphilis study, an unrelated U.S. Public Health Service experiment that withheld treatment from Black men in the same town from 1932 to 1972. Sources: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7484676/ ; Scientific American, 'Hidden Black Scientists Proved the Polio Vaccine Worked'

question: George Gey had surgery for pancreatic cancer in 1970, after nineteen years of growing Henrietta Lacks's cells and mailing them around the world. The surgeons found it had spread to his lymph nodes, lungs and heart, and they closed him again without doing the one thing he had asked of them beforehand. Gey woke from the anaesthetic furious. What had he asked for?
answer: To cut a piece of his tumour for a new cell line.
choices: To cut a piece of his tumour for a new cell line.
To inject HeLa cells into the tumour as a treatment.
To photograph every organ the cancer had reached.
To try an experimental drug first tested in HeLa.
context: He wanted a line called 'GeGe' grown from his own cancer. The surgeons judged that cutting would kill him on the table and took nothing. Gey died on 8 November 1970. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Otto_Gey ; Rebecca Skloot, 'The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks', ch.22

question: A lab worker watches a dish of normal human cells stop dividing after about fifty rounds. Each division shortens the telomeres, the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes, and once the caps are worn away a cell stops for good. In the next dish, HeLa has been dividing since 1951 and has never stopped. How did Henrietta Lacks's tumour cells escape the fifty-division limit?
answer: Viral DNA in the tumour keeps the enzyme telomerase switched on, so fresh caps are built after every division.
choices: Viral DNA in the tumour keeps the enzyme telomerase switched on, so fresh caps are built after every division.
Her radium treatment fused the chromosome ends into closed rings, leaving no caps that could wear away at all.
The tumour cells divide so quickly that the caps have no time to wear down between one division and the next.
The cells pull spare caps off the chromosomes of their dying neighbours each time they are about to divide.
context: A human papillomavirus had spliced its DNA into her tumour; its E6 and E7 proteins disable p53 and Rb, which leaves telomerase permanently on, so the countdown never starts. Switch E6 and E7 back off in a HeLa culture and the telomeres shorten, the cells age, and they stop - which is how the causal link was proven. Human telomerase itself was first caught and characterised in 1989 in extracts of HeLa: the immortal cells were the tool used to find the enzyme that made them immortal. Source: grokipedia.com/page/HeLa (Mechanism of Immortality and Telomerase Expression)

question: Stanley Gartler stood before some seven hundred researchers at a cell-culture meeting in Bedford, Pennsylvania, in the mid-1960s. He told them that eighteen of the world's most-used human cell lines, said to come from different patients, different organs and different countries, were all Henrietta Lacks's HeLa. One single clue had caught all eighteen. What was it?
answer: All eighteen carried G6PD-A, an uncommon variant of a human enzyme.
choices: All eighteen carried G6PD-A, an uncommon variant of a human enzyme.
All eighteen carried an extra chromosome 21, the marker of Down syndrome.
All eighteen typed as blood group AB, the rarest of the four human groups.
All eighteen doubled in exactly twenty-four hours in an identical broth.
context: Henrietta Lacks was a Black tobacco farmer from Virginia, and G6PD-A is found almost exclusively in Black Americans - one woman's rare marker turned up in eighteen laboratories at once. Gartler published the finding in 1968 as 'Apparent HeLa Cell Contamination of Human Heteroploid Cell Lines'; scientists called it the HeLa bomb. Walter Nelson-Rees then spent the 1970s using chromosome banding to document roughly 240 misidentified lines - HEp-2, published for years as a laryngeal cancer line, was HeLa. Modern surveys still find 20-36% of cell lines in active use contaminated or misidentified. Labs now check identity by short tandem repeat profiling at 8-21 genetic loci, standardised in 2012, and by a nested PCR that can spot five HeLa cells hiding in a culture. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/HeLa ; Gartler, Nature 217 (1968) ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HeLa

question: Victor McKusick sent a young researcher, Susan Hsu, to draw blood from Henrietta Lacks's husband and children in 1973. He needed the family's genetic markers to tell HeLa apart from the lines it had taken over, yet for twenty-two years the family had known nothing about her cells. Hsu gave them almost no explanation. What did they think the blood was for?
answer: To test them for the cancer that had killed her.
choices: To test them for the cancer that had killed her.
To screen them for an inherited blood disease.
To sign them up as donors of a rare blood type.
To give them a free check-up from the hospital.
context: They were not told that the blood was for cell-line identification, and no result ever came back to them. The irony runs deep: the family learned of HeLa at all only because HeLa had contaminated so many other laboratories that researchers needed her relatives' DNA to sort the mess out. Sources: Rebecca Skloot, 'The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks', ch.23 ; grokipedia.com/page/HeLa

question: Dr Lawrence Wharton Jr cut tissue from Henrietta Lacks at Johns Hopkins in 1951 without asking her, and the charge is made again and again that the hospital broke the law. Her family was in fact shut out of every decision and every dollar for decades afterwards. On the narrow question of the law, what did an American hospital in 1951 have to do about leftover surgical tissue?
answer: Nothing: no American law and no Hopkins rule required asking the patient.
choices: Nothing: no American law and no Hopkins rule required asking the patient.
Nothing in law, though Hopkins' own written rules required the patient's consent.
Get a signed tissue-release form from the patient, as federal law required.
Obey the Nuremberg Code of 1947, which bound American hospitals directly.
context: Taking leftover surgical tissue was routine practice, and nothing then-illegal happened. The Nuremberg Code of 1947 existed but was not binding on American hospitals and had almost no effect on the practice. Both halves of the honest statement hold at once: no crime was committed in 1951, and the family was shut out of every decision and every dollar for decades. Source: grokipedia.com/page/HeLa (Consent Practices in 1950s Medical Research)

question: A team at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory published HeLa's full genome on 11 March 2013. Much of it was the inherited information of Henrietta Lacks's children and grandchildren, and the team had not asked them. The family objected, and by that August the National Institutes of Health had worked out an agreement with them. What did the agreement give the family?
answer: Two seats on the board that reviews every request for the data.
choices: Two seats on the board that reviews every request for the data.
A share of the fee charged to laboratories that download the data.
The right to have the genome erased from every public database.
A veto over any paper that names Henrietta Lacks as the donor.
context: Announced 7 August 2013: the data went behind controlled access in dbGaP, two Lacks family members joined the working group reviewing every application, and resulting publications must acknowledge Henrietta Lacks. On 1 August 2023 - what would have been her 103rd birthday - the estate settled its unjust-enrichment suit against Thermo Fisher Scientific; terms are confidential and the company admitted no liability. A further suit against Novartis and Viatris followed in August 2024. No court has ever ruled on whether the family owns the cells. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HeLa ; NIH, 'The NIH-Lacks Family Agreement' ; CNN and NPR, 1 August 2023

question: Harald zur Hausen cloned two cancer-causing types of papillomavirus in 1983 and 1984, proved that papillomaviruses cause cervical cancer, and took the 2008 Nobel Prize for it. The Gardasil vaccine, approved in 2006, blocks both of those types. Henrietta Lacks had been dead for more than thirty years before the first was cloned. What does Gardasil have to do with the cells taken from her?
answer: The virus in her tumour is one of the two types it blocks.
choices: The virus in her tumour is one of the two types it blocks.
The virus proteins in every dose of it are grown in HeLa.
The safety test for every batch of it is run in HeLa cells.
The tumour that killed her is where the virus was first seen.
context: The two types zur Hausen cloned were HPV-16 in 1983 and HPV-18 in 1984, both out of cervical tumours; the virus in Henrietta Lacks's own tumour was HPV-18. The cells taken from Henrietta Lacks helped build the vaccine against the exact cancer that killed her. The rest of the ledger: HeLa appears in over 110,000 publications and roughly 11,000 patents, by 2009 at a rate of over 300 new papers a month, and it flew in the early American satellite programme to see what weightlessness does to a dividing human cell. One scientist estimated that all the HeLa ever grown would weigh more than 50 million metric tons - from a woman who weighed about a hundred pounds at the end. In 2021 the WHO gave her a posthumous Director-General's award, accepted in Geneva by her 87-year-old son Lawrence. Sources: nobelprize.org, 2008 Medicine press release ; grokipedia.com/page/HeLa ; who.int, 13 October 2021

question: Pierre Janssen aimed his spectroscope at a bright red loop rising from the Sun's edge in August 1868, during a total solar eclipse in southern India. He recorded a yellow line at 587 nanometers, right beside but not on the sodium lines, and it matched no substance known on Earth. What element had he just met in the Sun?
answer: Helium
choices: Helium
Neon
Argon
Coronium
context: Janssen had crossed the Indian Ocean to catch totality. The 'red loop' was a solar prominence -- an arch of glowing gas held up by the Sun's magnetic field. The mystery yellow line became the D3 line of a new element. Source: aps.org 'August 18 and October 20, 1868: Discovery of Helium'.

question: Pierre Janssen looked through his spectroscope at Guntur and saw the eclipse's prominence lines glare so brightly that he spotted a way to record them without another eclipse. Solar eclipses are brief and rare, chased across the globe by ships. What was his shortcut?
answer: Reading them out of the ordinary daytime sky
choices: Reading them out of the ordinary daytime sky
Bouncing sunlight off the full Moon at night
Waiting for the annual dust haze after monsoon
Flying a hydrogen balloon above the weather
context: Norman Lockyer in London worked out the same daylight method independently within weeks. Their letters reached the French Academy within minutes of each other, and the Academy later struck a single medal carrying both their faces. Source: aps.org; britannica.com Lockyer.

question: Norman Lockyer gave a name to an element known only from a yellow line seen in the Sun's light in 1868, and the profession accepted it. Many chemists thought it reckless to name a thing nobody had ever held, and for nearly thirty years nobody did. What finally put the gas in a chemist's hands?
answer: William Ramsay found it inside a uranium mineral
choices: William Ramsay found it inside a uranium mineral
Lord Rayleigh found it left over in purified air
James Dewar boiled it off a flask of liquid air
Henri Moissan split it from a salt with a current
context: Lockyer built the name from the Greek helios, the Sun. In March 1895 William Ramsay treated cleveite, a uranium-rich mineral, with acid and collected a gas whose spectral lines matched the line seen in the Sun: the Sun's element, at last in a bottle on Earth. For nearly thirty years before that, helium had been a line on a chart and nothing more. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Helium; sciencemuseum.org.uk 150-years blog; aps.org discovery-of-helium-1868.

question: Ira Bowen solved the puzzle of nebulium, the new element astronomers had blamed for odd green lines in the nebulae, in 1927. The lines were 'forbidden' transitions from a familiar element in a state Earth labs cannot make, with too few collisions and too little pressure. Which familiar element, stripped of two of its electrons, had been posing as nebulium all along?
answer: Oxygen
choices: Oxygen
Carbon
Nitrogen
Hydrogen
context: In extremely thin nebular gas an oxygen atom stripped of two electrons can sit for seconds in a metastable state before it slowly relaxes -- a 'forbidden' transition. Coronium was cracked a decade later: Grotrian and Edlen (around 1939-41) showed the coronal green line came from IRON with thirteen electrons ripped off, at temperatures of millions of degrees. Not new elements, familiar elements under exotic conditions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebulium.

question: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes liquefied the last common gas still holding out, at Leiden on 10 July 1908, at 4.2 kelvin. Three years later, using a bath of that new liquid, he cooled a thread of mercury, and it abruptly did something no metal had ever been known to do. What did the mercury do?
answer: Its electrical resistance fell to zero
choices: Its electrical resistance fell to zero
Its electrical resistance climbed to infinity
It emitted a bright yellow light
It crept up the glass walls on its own
context: Kamerlingh Onnes had discovered superconductivity, and won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Physics for the low-temperature work. Below 2.17 K, liquid helium-4 does its own trick: it becomes a superfluid, with zero viscosity, and creeps up and over the walls of its container. Both effects only became reachable because Onnes had learned how to keep helium liquid. Sources: ethw.org superconductivity 1911; wmi.badw.de on liquid helium.

question: Hennig Brand began a project in Hamburg in 1669. The alchemist was sure that a common body fluid, if boiled down long enough, would let him turn base metal into one metal he could sell. Which metal was he hunting for?
answer: Gold
choices: Gold
Silver
Copper
Iron
context: The old doctrine of signatures said 'like reveals like': the deep yellow of urine, Brand thought, must hide gold. He was wrong about the goal and stumbled onto something better. Source: Science History Institute, Hennig Brandt and the Discovery of Phosphorus.

question: Hennig Brand had saved a huge store of urine in Hamburg, fifty buckets by one account, and left it to putrefy. He was chasing the same prize every serious alchemist wanted. Isaac Newton spent years hunting for it too. What was that prize called?
answer: The philosopher's stone
choices: The philosopher's stone
The alkahest
The elixir of life
A homunculus
context: The philosopher's stone was said to transmute lead into gold and confer long life; every serious alchemist in Europe wanted one. The alkahest was a hypothetical universal solvent; the elixir was for long life alone; the homunculus was a made-in-a-flask miniature person. Source: Wikipedia, Hennig Brand.

question: Johann Kunckel, a German alchemist who had only ever seen samples of the finished substance, worked out his own urine route by about 1678, after Hennig Brand sold his secret recipe to a Dresden merchant, Johann Daniel Kraft, for 200 thalers. What finally made it public science was a London man's own recipe, lodged sealed with the Royal Society in 1680 and printed after his death. Who?
answer: Robert Boyle
choices: Robert Boyle
Robert Hooke
Christopher Wren
Isaac Newton
context: Boyle worked out his own preparation, lodged it sealed with the Royal Society on 14 October 1680, and it was opened and printed in 1692, just after his death; unlike Brand's secret it was now anyone's to repeat, which is what turned a fairground marvel into a reproducible experiment; Lavoisier only classified phosphorus as an element more than a century later. Sources: Wikipedia, Hennig Brand; John Emsley, New Scientist (johnemsley.com/articles/new_scientist/ns_phosphorus.html); encyclopedia.com on Kunckel.

question: Edward Pickering hired a whole room of women around 1900 to measure stars on the glass photo plates at Harvard's observatory. He paid Henrietta Swan Leavitt about 30 cents an hour. What did Pickering call each of these women?
answer: computer
choices: computer
librarian
secretary
draftsman
context: Long before the machines took the name, a 'computer' was a person who computed. Leavitt joined as a volunteer in 1895 and was formally hired in 1902 at roughly 30 cents an hour -- about $10.50 a week -- measuring star images on glass plates with a magnifying glass at a light table. Source: lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/henrietta-swan-leavitt/

question: A kid with a notebook steps outside and finds Delta Cephei, a star in Cepheus bright enough to see with the naked eye. She logs it brightening and dimming against its neighbors on a repeating schedule. About how long is one full cycle?
answer: 5.4 days
choices: 5.4 days
90 minutes
48 hours
27 days
context: John Goodricke first noticed Delta Cephei was variable in 1784. It cycles between magnitudes 3.48 and 4.37 every 5.366 days -- the naked-eye prototype for the whole class of Cepheid variable stars. Test it yourself: pick a clear-sky week and log its brightness against the nearby fixed stars each night. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Cephei

question: Henrietta Swan Leavitt sat at a light table in Cambridge, Massachusetts, measuring stars on a glass plate of the southern sky. She herself never used a telescope. A distant Harvard observing station had captured the plate and shipped it north. On which continent was that station?
answer: South America
choices: South America
Africa
Australia
Antarctica
context: Harvard ran a southern-sky outpost called the Boyden Station in Arequipa, Peru. Plates were exposed there and shipped back to Cambridge, where Leavitt measured star brightness with a magnifying glass. The Magellanic Clouds -- her hunting ground -- are only visible from the southern hemisphere. Source: fords.org/solving-the-unknown-what-astronomer-henrietta-swan-leavitt-accomplished/

question: With a print of one night's Harvard plate laid over another, Henrietta Leavitt hunted for variable stars, stars whose brightness changes on a schedule. Her landmark catalog of 1908 listed every one she had discovered in two small nearby galaxies of the southern sky. About how many did it list?
context: Her paper was titled '1777 Variables in the Magellanic Clouds' and appeared in the Annals of the Astronomical Observatory of Harvard College. Source: fords.org/solving-the-unknown-what-astronomer-henrietta-swan-leavitt-accomplished/

question: Working from a sample of 25 Cepheid variables inside the Small Magellanic Cloud in 1912, Henrietta Leavitt plotted each star's brightness against how long it took to complete one bright-dim-bright cycle. The dots fell into a strikingly simple pattern. What did she find?
answer: the longer the cycle, the brighter the star
choices: the longer the cycle, the brighter the star
the shorter the cycle, the brighter the star
brightness swung wildly with no relation to cycle length
every star in the cloud shared the same cycle length
context: This is Leavitt's period-luminosity relation. Time a Cepheid's cycle and you know how bright it truly is; compare that to how bright it looks and you know how far away it is. It became astronomy's first honest yardstick for anything beyond parallax range -- the bottom rung of the cosmic distance ladder still in use today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_Swan_Leavitt

question: Henrietta Leavitt set down one hard limit of her own law in the 1912 paper itself. She had timed 25 Cepheids and compared them, and she left that piece of the problem for other astronomers to solve. What was the honest limit she named?
answer: her law gave only relative distances, not absolute ones
choices: her law gave only relative distances, not absolute ones
her sample of 25 Cepheids was too small to trust
the relation held only for Cepheids inside the Milky Way
the same relation would not hold for fainter Cepheids beyond her sample
context: She had no measured distance to any single Cepheid, so she could sort stars by true brightness but could not convert those sorts into miles or light-years. A ruler with no zero mark is still a ruler once someone marks the zero. Ejnar Hertzsprung supplied the first calibration in 1913 using Milky Way Cepheids; Harlow Shapley refined it in 1918. Leavitt named the gap in her own paper rather than paper over it. Source: lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/henrietta-swan-leavitt/

question: Gosta Mittag-Leffler mailed a letter to Henrietta Leavitt at Harvard in 1925. The Swedish mathematician planned to nominate her for the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics for her period-luminosity work. What did the observatory's reply tell him?
answer: she had died of stomach cancer about three years earlier
choices: she had died of stomach cancer about three years earlier
she had retired and moved away from Cambridge
she had already declined all prize nominations on principle
she was now the head of the Harvard College Observatory
context: Leavitt died on December 12, 1921, at age 53, and is buried in Cambridge Cemetery beneath a hexagonal monument topped by a globe. The Nobel is not awarded posthumously, so the nomination went nowhere. Harlow Shapley wrote back to Mittag-Leffler suggesting the real credit for interpreting her findings belonged to him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_Swan_Leavitt

question: Daniel Elmer Salmon, head of the US Bureau of Animal Industry, wrote an article in 1894 about well-fed livestock that fought off disease as a group. The idea of protection by the herd began on a farm. Which livestock did his article describe?
answer: hogs
choices: hogs
sheep
goats
horses
context: Daniel Elmer Salmon, a veterinary scientist, was writing about hog nutrition and disease resistance; by 1916 the same Bureau was using 'herd immunity' about cattle recovered from brucellosis. It was a farmer's observation before it was ever an equation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herd_immunity ; vaxopedia.org/2020/02/19/on-the-origins-of-herd-immunity/

question: Topley and Wilson, two British scientists, ran outbreaks through cages of a small animal in 1923 and turned a farm saying into a real experiment. Their goal was to show that not every animal has to be immune to stop the spread. Which animal did they use?
answer: mice
choices: mice
rabbits
guinea pigs
pigeons
context: Topley and Wilson published in the Journal of Hygiene in 1923: they added susceptible newcomers to a stable cage, watched a fresh wave of infection rise, and watched it fade as immune numbers grew. This was the moment 'herd immunity' was first used in a human-medicine context. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34111938/ ; sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673620319243

question: A boy with measles walks into a crowd where no one is immune. R-nought is the average number of new cases one sick person causes in such a crowd. Measles is the classic tough case for stopping an outbreak. Which range is its R-nought thought to sit in?
answer: about 12 to 18
choices: about 12 to 18
about 2 to 3
about 5 to 6
about 25 to 30
context: A 2017 Lancet Infectious Diseases systematic review put measles R0 in the 12-to-18 range, which is why the classical threshold for measles is 92 to 95 percent immune. Flu, with R0 near 1.3, has a classical threshold near 23 percent. Source: thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(17)30307-9/abstract

question: Two Scottish researchers proved a threshold theorem in 1927: below a certain fraction of susceptible people in a population, a large epidemic simply cannot take off. Their theorem is the mathematical parent of every modern herd-immunity number. Whose theorem is it?
answer: Kermack and McKendrick
choices: Kermack and McKendrick
Ross and Hudson
Reed and Frost
Snow and Farr
context: William Ogilvy Kermack and Anderson Gray McKendrick, working in Edinburgh, published the 1927 paper that also introduced what is now called the SIR (Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered) model. Their threshold theorem is why an epidemic can peak and then die out even when many people never catch it. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02464422

question: A student at a blackboard wants the herd-immunity threshold, the share of a crowd that must be immune to stop new outbreaks. She starts from R-nought, the number of new cases one sick person sparks in a crowd where nobody is immune yet. In the simple textbook version, where everyone mixes evenly, which expression gives the threshold?
answer: 1 - 1/R-nought
choices: 1 - 1/R-nought
1/R-nought
R-nought / (R-nought + 1)
the square root of R-nought
context: Plug in: measles at R0 = 15 gives 1 - 1/15 = about 93 percent; flu at R0 = 1.3 gives 1 - 1/1.3 = about 23 percent. One fraction explains why measles is the hard case and flu is not. Source: historyofvaccines.org/vaccines-101/what-do-vaccines-do/how-herd-immunity-works/

question: Britton and his colleagues rebuilt a model disease in 2020. Its R-nought, the average new infections per case in a fully susceptible crowd, equals 2.5, and the tidy classroom formula puts its herd-immunity threshold at 60 percent immune. They set it inside an age-structured population where people mostly mix with their own age group. About what figure did the disease-induced threshold reach in their model?
answer: 43 percent
choices: 43 percent
18 percent
72 percent
85 percent
context: The classical formula quietly assumes homogeneous mixing - everyone equally likely to meet everyone else. Real people cluster by age, workplace, and neighbourhood; when a model respects that, its threshold falls sharply. The same math also warns the other way: a 95 percent national average can hide a 60 percent local pocket where measles tears through. Source: Britton, Ball, Trapman, Science 2020 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abc6810); pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7236739/

question: Kreck and Brauner put a ceiling in 2023 on the tail of an outbreak in the standard SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered) model. New cases keep landing after the peak, because those already sick keep spreading it, and modelers call this extra tail 'overshoot.' At most, about what portion of a crowd can still get infected past the peak?
answer: 30 percent
choices: 30 percent
5 percent
50 percent
70 percent
context: The Royal Society Interface paper (Kreck and Brauner, 2023) fixed the bound at roughly 0.30 of the population, occurring near R-nought = 2.15. The herd-immunity threshold marks the turning point of the curve, not where it stops - which is why 'let it burn to herd immunity' quietly comes with a large added bill. Source: royalsocietypublishing.org/rsif/article/20/209/20230322/90454/Fundamental-bound-on-epidemic-overshoot-in-the-SIR

question: William Herschel stopped his backyard telescope at a small greenish object over Bath on 13 March 1781. It did not look quite like a star. He ran a test any kid with a telescope can copy on Jupiter tonight. What did he do?
answer: He cranked up the magnification and watched it swell into a disk
choices: He cranked up the magnification and watched it swell into a disk
He waited for it to twinkle the way stars do at the horizon
He timed how long it took to cross the eyepiece
He held a candle behind a card to compare its colour
context: Stars stay stubborn points however hard you magnify -- they are too far to resolve. Planets and comets show a real disk that grows with the eyepiece. Any kid comparing Jupiter and a bright star through binoculars sees the same effect. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus

question: Anders Johan Lexell worked out the path around the Sun of the object William Herschel had reported as a comet in 1781. The shape of that orbit told the world it was no comet at all but a new planet, the one now called Uranus. What did Lexell find about the orbit?
answer: A nearly circular orbit far beyond Saturn
choices: A nearly circular orbit far beyond Saturn
A tightly stretched orbit diving inside Mercury
A short two-year orbit crossing Mars
A wildly wobbly orbit fitting no known shape
context: Uranus orbits at about 19 AU, roughly twice Saturn's 9.5 AU -- Lexell's near-circular orbit beyond Saturn proved the object was a new planet, not a comet, and roughly doubled the known solar system. It was the first planet added in recorded history; the other five had been known since antiquity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus

question: John Flamsteed wrote William Herschel's future planet into his 1690 star catalogue without noticing what it was. Others logged it too, at least twenty times in all, as an ordinary star, and no one noticed that it moved. What entry did Flamsteed give it?
answer: 34 Tauri, an ordinary star in the constellation Taurus
choices: 34 Tauri, an ordinary star in the constellation Taurus
78 Ceti, an ordinary star in the constellation Cetus
12 Leonis, an ordinary star in the constellation Leo
56 Orionis, an ordinary star in the constellation Orion
context: Flamsteed's 1690 entry as '34 Tauri' was one of the earliest known pre-Herschel sightings; Pierre Charles Le Monnier logged the same object a dozen times between 1750 and 1769 without noticing it wandered. Evidence in plain sight, filtered out by what people expected to see. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus

question: Johann Titius and Johann Bode published an arithmetic recipe that reproduced the spacing of the known planets and put a slot at about 19.6 astronomical units (AU). Uranus turned out to fit at 19.2 AU, and confidence in the rule sent astronomers hunting in another of its slots, the gap between Mars and Jupiter. Who found something there on 1 January 1801, and what was it named?
answer: Giuseppe Piazzi found a body he named Ceres
choices: Giuseppe Piazzi found a body he named Ceres
Heinrich Olbers found a body he named Pallas
Karl Harding found a body he named Juno
Franz von Zach found a body he named Astraea

Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titius%E2%80%93Bode_law

question: A student runs the Titius-Bode rule one step past Uranus on a sheet of paper and lands near 39 astronomical units. The rule had matched the spacing of the known planets and slotted Uranus at about 19, so the next planet out should sit there. Where does Neptune actually orbit?

A recipe that fits the data you already have, with no mechanism underneath it, is a curve fit and not a law of nature. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titius%E2%80%93Bode_law

question: William Herschel slid a blackened-bulb thermometer along a prism's band of sunlight at home in Slough in 1800. One step further, in a strip where nothing showed, it read higher than in any visible colour. What kind of light had he found?

context: Herschel published his results in 1800. He called the new rays 'calorific rays' -- the word 'infrared' (Latin infra, 'below') came in decades later, once physicists had a wavelength picture. Source: Cool Cosmos / IPAC-Caltech.

question: William Herschel stood at his telescope with a real problem. He needed a coloured-glass filter that would cut the Sun's glare and heat enough to let him safely do one kind of solar work. What was he trying to do more safely?
