question: Spreading a prism's rainbow of sunlight across a table in 1800, William Herschel laid out three mercury thermometers with blackened bulbs to measure the heat in each colour. He placed only one of them in the coloured band at a time. Why did he insist on the other two?
answer: as controls, to catch the room itself drifting warmer

as replicates, to average out reading noise on the middle bulb
as calibration checks, to confirm all three agreed at room temperature
as before/after tests, warmed by breath to check each bulb's response
context: This is why the discovery stands. A rising reading in the beam meant nothing if the whole room was drifting warmer. The two extra thermometers, kept out of the sunlit spectrum, isolated the real effect from any background warming. The classic home version needs only a prism, a sunny window and three blackened-bulb thermometers: catch the rainbow on a table, run one bulb from violet to just past red, and the space beyond the red reads warmest. Sources: Cool Cosmos -- Herschel Backyard Experiment; InterNACHI -- History of Infrared Thermography.

question: William Herschel found in 1800 that sunlight carries a light no eye can see: in the dark strip just past the red, his blackened thermometer still warmed up. The James Webb Space Telescope hunts that same light from distant galaxies, and engineers chilled its detectors to about 40 kelvin and one camera to under 7. Why must a telescope hunting Herschel's light be run so cold?

choices: the telescope itself glows in the infrared and would drown the signal

the sunshield only holds its taut shape at cryogenic temperatures
the detectors would lose their gold anti-reflection coating above 100 kelvin
context: Every warm object radiates infrared -- a human body, the walls, the telescope tube. To see faint infrared from a distant galaxy, the instrument must be cold enough that its own glow stays fainter than that light, or the glow swamps what it is trying to see. Herschel's discovery is why the whole 10-billion-dollar architecture of Webb is a giant refrigerator. Source: NASA -- How Does Webb Stay Cold.

question: Heinrich Hertz cranked an induction coil in a dark Karlsruhe laboratory on 13 November 1886 until a spark jumped between two brass balls. Yards away, a plain copper loop with a small gap sparked in sympathy, wired to nothing. What had he built the first working example of?

A Tesla coil
context: A transmitter and a receiver, coupled only by an invisible wave crossing empty air. Maxwell had died in 1879, seven years before Hertz's experiments, and never saw his equations confirmed with hardware. Source: ethw.org Milestones - First Generation and Experimental Proof of Electromagnetic Waves.

question: To prove his invisible waves behaved in every way like ordinary light, Heinrich Hertz reflected them off metal mirrors and polarised them with a grid of parallel wires. To refract them, bending a beam by passing it through a transparent block, he built a large 1.5-metre prism. What unlikely-looking material did he use?

Sulphur
context: Pitch (asphalt) is opaque to visible light but transparent to radio waves; Hertz's prism bent the beam by 22 degrees, giving an index of refraction of 1.69 for pitch at those wavelengths. Source: Wikimedia commons file Hertz radio wave experiments - refraction.

question: Ultraviolet light fell on the tiny spark gap of Heinrich Hertz's receiver in 1887, and he noticed something odd. He wrote the observation up in Annalen der Physik and moved on to other things. Einstein would explain the phenomenon in a March 1905 paper. What is the effect Hertz stumbled on and never pursued?
answer: The photoelectric effect

The Compton effect
The Doppler effect
context: Ultraviolet light on the gap knocked electrons out of the metal, easing the spark's leap. Einstein's March 1905 paper explained it by proposing that light comes in QUANTA (photons); the Nobel Committee awarded him the 1921 Prize specifically for that paper, not for relativity. Source: aps.org Einstein and the Photoelectric Effect; spark.iop.org Hertz's photoelectric effect.

question: A student once asked Heinrich Hertz what practical use his beautiful new waves could possibly have. By his students' later recollection, Hertz answered that they were of no use at all; he had only wanted to prove Maxwell right. The quotation is second-hand, not from any Hertz manuscript. Within seven years, whose attic experiments would prove him wrong about that?
answer: Guglielmo Marconi

Alexander Graham Bell
Nikola Tesla
context: Marconi read Augusto Righi's 1894 memorial article on Hertz's work and began his experiments at Villa Griffone near Bologna in 1895, aged 21. Hertz himself had died of granulomatosis on New Year's Day 1894, aged 36. Source: en.wikipedia.org Augusto Righi.

question: Oliver Lodge, an English physicist, showed wireless signaling at the Royal Institution in June 1894, a year before Marconi's attic work near Bologna. What best explains why Marconi, not the Englishman, became the famous name?
answer: Marconi turned the discovery into a business

Marconi's waves travelled faster than Lodge's
Marconi had the deeper training in physics
Marconi supplied the theory behind the waves
context: Lodge's Royal Institution lecture on 1 June 1894 memorialised Hertz and demonstrated wireless transmission across a few metres. He also improved the coherer detector Branly had invented. Other contemporaries: Jagadish Chandra Bose in Calcutta, and Nikola Tesla in the United States. Source: en.wikipedia.org History of radio receivers.

question: Royal Navy crews at Sheerness cut down HMS Challenger's spars and pulled 15 of her 17 guns. She sailed in December 1872, bound for three and a half years at sea. What filled the gun deck when she left?
answer: laboratories
choices: laboratories
coal bunkers
extra marines' quarters
casks of fresh water
context: HMS Challenger was a working warship stripped for science; the gun deck was fitted out with chemistry, biology and sounding labs before she left Portsmouth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_expedition

question: Edward Forbes dredged the Aegean aboard HMS Beacon in 1843 and came away with the theory of the deep sea that still reigned when Challenger sailed. From what his nets brought up, he made a bold claim about the ocean below a certain depth. What did he claim?
answer: no animals could survive down there
choices: no animals could survive down there
the water was fresh, not salt
a single warm current ran through it northward
the seabed was heated from below by volcanoes
context: This was the azoic hypothesis (Greek a- + zoe, 'without life'), the reigning consensus. Challenger's dredges kept coming back with living animals from thousands of fathoms and finished the idea off. Norwegian zoologist Michael Sars had already dented it before the voyage, pulling 427 species from 450 fathoms off Norway. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azoic_hypothesis

question: HMS Challenger's men watched their sounding line go down and down at Station 225, near the Mariana Islands in the west Pacific, on 23 March 1875. When the reading came back they sounded a second time in the same spot to check it. What did the doubled sounding read?
answer: 4,475 fathoms
choices: 4,475 fathoms
1,200 fathoms
2,340 fathoms
6,900 fathoms
context: 4,475 fathoms is about 8,184 m, the deepest sounding anyone had made; the place still carries the ship's name as the Challenger Deep. Modern multibeam sonar now puts the same spot at about 10,935 m -- a rope can only underestimate a drifting depth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep

question: Thomas Huxley opened an old bottle of Atlantic mud in 1868, four years before Challenger set sail, and found a translucent gelatinous slime laced with veins. The mud had been dredged in 1857. He announced the slime to the scientific world as a living organism and named it Bathybius haeckelii, after Ernst Haeckel. What did Huxley claim this slime was?
answer: a primordial protoplasm bridging non-living matter and life
choices: a primordial protoplasm bridging non-living matter and life
the larval stage of the giant squid
a new kind of colonial deep-sea coral
the eggs of an unknown abyssal fish
context: Haeckel had already theorized an Urschleim, a primordial slime out of which life arose; Huxley believed Bathybius was the thing itself, dredged up from the seabed. Source: https://bigthink.com/the-past/primordial-slime-huxley/

question: John Murray took up the unfinished Report on the Scientific Results of the Voyage of H.M.S. Challenger when Charles Wyville Thomson died, and he saw it through to 1895, nineteen years after the ship docked. Roughly how big was the finished Report?
answer: 50 volumes and over 29,500 pages
choices: 50 volumes and over 29,500 pages

a single 400-page monograph
context: It is still the largest publication ever produced from a single scientific expedition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_expedition

question: John Young Buchanan, the young ship's chemist aboard HMS Challenger, set out to check Thomas Huxley's celebrated Bathybius haeckelii on fresh samples right out of the dredge. He came away certain that Huxley had been fooled. What did Buchanan show Bathybius actually was?
answer: a chemical precipitate thrown down in the sample bottle
choices: a chemical precipitate thrown down in the sample bottle
a colony of abyssal bacteria feeding on iron in the mud
shredded protoplasm from surface plankton that had sunk
amoebae released only under the pressure of the deep
context: Buchanan traced it: the alcohol used to preserve the mud met dissolved salts in the seawater and threw down a gelatinous white precipitate -- calcium sulfate -- that looked like protoplasm; fresh samples with no alcohol never produced it. Charles Wyville Thomson sent Huxley a courteous letter with the finding; Huxley published part of it in the journal Nature and formally recanted Bathybius at the 1879 meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, publicly killing his own celebrated discovery. Ernst Haeckel, however, refused to give it up and was still defending Bathybius into the 1880s. Source: https://www.realclearscience.com/blog/2022/11/09/the_great_primordial_slime_affair_863783.html

question: John Murray sorted the dredged mud into a map of the seabed by what each patch was made of. Across the barren deep, shells had dissolved before reaching the bottom, and the dredges came back full of one material, with black lumps on top from marble-size to potato-size. What was the seabed made of in those deepest, most barren stretches?
answer: red clay from volcanic dust
choices: red clay from volcanic dust
white sand from ground coral
black basalt gravel
sheets of frozen methane
context: Murray also mapped globigerina ooze and radiolarian ooze -- carpets of microscopic shells -- across the shallower abyss. The black lumps were nearly pure manganese oxide; Murray and Renard's 1891 Deep-Sea Deposits volume named them manganese nodules, and they are still commercially and scientifically argued over today. Source: https://doi.pangaea.de/10.1594/PANGAEA.849073

question: HMS Challenger's crew lowered a thermometer to the seabed, read the temperature, and did it again in the next ocean, and the next. The ship is remembered for sounding the ocean's depth, but her quiet triumph was the thermometer, not the rope. What global pattern did those deep-water readings first hint at?
answer: cold polar water sinks and creeps along the seabed worldwide
choices: cold polar water sinks and creeps along the seabed worldwide
warm surface water descends in the tropics and rises at the poles
the deep ocean is heated from below by seabed volcanism
the deep ocean sits in still, layered basins that never mix
context: Challenger found the deep water uniformly cold in every ocean, tropics to poles -- the earliest empirical hint of what is now called the global overturning circulation, the conveyor of cold, dense polar water that keeps the abyss cold and moves heat around the planet. Source: https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/maritime-history/hms-challenger-expedition-oceanography-trailblazer

question: A sailor on HMS Challenger watched the weighted rope drift, catch and stretch on its way down, and no one aboard could verify the number it gave. The answer, when it came in the 1920s, was not more rope but different physics. What replaced the weighted line?
answer: timing the echo of a sound pulse off the seabed

context: A ship pings the seabed and times the return of the echo; because a rope can only underestimate a drifting depth, the modern Challenger Deep figure of about 10,935 m by multibeam sonar is well below the ship's own 8,184 m rope reading. Source: https://tos.org/oceanography/article/implosion-in-the-challenger-deep-echo-sounding-with-the-shock-wave

question: Robert Hooke sharpened a penknife 'as keen as a Razor' and shaved off a sliver thin enough to see light through. Under his microscope lay row on row of tiny hollow boxes, and biology still uses his word for them. What had he sliced?
answer: A shaving of cork
choices: A shaving of cork
A curl of birch bark
A paring of ox horn
A leaf of dried moss
context: Observation XVIII of Micrographia (1665). Hooke laid the slice "on a black object Plate, because it was it self a white body" and cast light onto it through a deep plano-convex glass - the black backing is the trick that made the pale cork readable. His sentence coined the word: the pores, "or cells," were "a great many little Boxes, separated out of one continued long pore, by certain Diaphragms." He knew he was first: "the first microscopical pores I ever saw, and perhaps, that were ever seen." The unit of all life got its name from a bottle-cork - dead bark, with nothing living in it. (Micrographia, Observ. XVIII, primary text.)

question: Robert Hooke bent over his lens to draw an ant that would not hold still. It kept twisting and winding its body, and he complained it was more troublesome to draw than anything else in Micrographia. What did he do to it?

choices: Dosed it with brandy until it dropped
Pinned it through the body to a board
Chilled it on ice from the cellar
Glued its feet down with tree gum
context: Hooke gave the ant "a Gill of Brandy, or Spirit of Wine" - a gill is about a quarter-pint - "which after a while e'en knock'd him down dead drunk, so that he became moveless." It stayed "moveless about an hour," long enough for him to finish the drawing, and then, "upon a sudden, as if it had been awaken out of a drunken sleep, it suddenly reviv'd and ran away." (Micrographia, "Of an Ant or Pismire," Observ. XLIX.)

question: Under the lens, Robert Hooke tallied the little boxes lying end to end in his cork slice, multiplied the rate outward, and printed the total in Micrographia: 1,259,712,000 of them. How much cork held that many?

choices: One cubic inch, a lump about the size of an ice cube
One paper-thin slice, the size of a thumbnail
One square foot of sheet cork, the size of a mat
One cubic foot, a hatbox packed full of the stuff
context: Hooke's own arithmetic: "there were usually about threescore of these small Cells placed end-ways in the eighteenth part of an Inch in length, whence I concluded there must be neer eleven hundred of them... in the length of an Inch, and therefore in a square Inch above a Million, or 1166400. and in a Cubick Inch, above twelve hundred Millions, or 1259712000. a thing almost incredible." Sixty boxes in one-eighteenth of an inch, and he did the rest with a pen. The same move works on anything that repeats: count a short measured row, then multiply outward. (Micrographia, Observ. XVIII.)

question: A reader of Robert Hooke's 1665 book Micrographia unfolds a plate bigger than the book itself, about 17 by 10 inches, and a single creature covers the whole table. Of the book's sixty observations, readers loved two such fold-outs best. Which two creatures got them?

choices: The flea and the louse
The ant and the bee
The fly and the gnat
The spider and the moth
context: The Royal Society describes the louse plate as unfolding to nearly twice the size of the book; Wikipedia says four times - the sources disagree on the multiple. The ant, the fly and the spider are all really in there too; only the flea and the louse got the monster fold-outs. Of the sixty observations, fifty-seven were microscopic and three telescopic. The Royal Society also notes that Hooke drew the flea's recessed antennae with a precision that "could not have been visible to Hooke with the degree of magnification afforded by his microscope" - his eye and hand outran his instrument. (Royal Society blog, "Micrographia online," 2020.)

question: Samuel Pepys carried home his copy of Robert Hooke's Micrographia on 20 January 1665, and the next night his diary called it 'the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life.' How had Pepys spent that evening?
answer: Sat up in his chamber reading until two in the morning
choices: Sat up in his chamber reading until two in the morning
Read it aloud to his wife and her maid after supper
Took it to the coffee-house to show it to the company
Sent it out to be rebound in finer calfskin and gilt
context: Pepys, 21 January 1664/65: "Before I went to bed I sat up till two o'clock in my chamber reading of Mr. Hooke's Microscopicall Observations, the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life." He had bespoken it at the bookbinder's on 2 January, before it was even bound: "so pretty that I presently bespoke it." Micrographia sold out fast and is usually called the first science bestseller; it sent Antonie van Leeuwenhoek off to grind his own lenses and made Christopher Cock's microscope business boom. (The Diary of Samuel Pepys, 2 / 20 / 21 January 1664-65.)

question: Beside his drawing of a cork slice in Micrographia, Robert Hooke printed the answer to an old puzzle. Cork had been in daily use for centuries, and everyone knew it floats high in water, but nobody could say why. What did his lens show was the reason?
answer: It is mostly air, sealed inside tiny closed boxes
choices: It is mostly air, sealed inside tiny closed boxes
It is soaked through with a light oil that repels water
It is threaded with hollow tubes open to the air
It is built of a substance lighter than water itself
context: Hooke concluded cork's substance is "altogether fill'd with Air, and that that Air is perfectly enclosed in little Boxes or Cells," which makes it "a very small quantity of a solid body, extended into exceeding large dimensions" - hardly any matter at all, spread over a large volume, so it rides high. The same boxes, he went on, explain why cork will not drink in water, why it can stop the air in a bottle, and why it springs back when squeezed. Worth holding on to: the word that now names the unit of every living thing was coined for a piece of dead bark. (Micrographia, Observ. XVIII.)

question: Without leaving his house, Robert Hooke found the specimen for the first published picture of a microorganism, a growth whose structure no unaided eye can resolve. Under the lens he drew slender transparent stalks, not quite straight, each bending under the weight of a round white knob at its top. What was the blue mould growing on?

choices: The sheepskin covers of a small book
The whitewashed plaster of a wall
The crust of a loaf gone stale
The rind of a cheese in the larder
context: Observation XX, drawn as Figure 1 of Scheme XII. Hooke's specimen was mould on "the red covers of a small book, which, it seems, were of Sheeps-skin, that being more apt to gather mould, even in a dry and clean room, then other leathers." He drew "small long cylindrical and transparent stalks, not exactly streight, but a little bended with the weight of a round and white knob that grew on the top of each of them." Careful with secondary sources here: Grokipedia labels this Observation XII, but XII is the scheme number - the observation is XX. (Micrographia, Observ. XX; Royal Society print archive RS.5095.)

question: Christopher Cock, a London instrument maker, built Robert Hooke a compound microscope that was not a great instrument: about thirty to fifty times magnification, with coloured fringes smearing every edge. Hooke openly admitted in print that a single lens gave a clearer image than his own multi-lens tube. His real advantage over everyone else lay elsewhere. Where did he put his ingenuity?
answer: Into the light: a lamp beamed through a glass globe of brine
choices: Into the light: a lamp beamed through a glass globe of brine
Into the stage: a screw mount that gripped the specimen still
Into the eyepiece: smoked glass ground to kill the colour fringe
Into the mirror: a polished steel dish throwing sun up the tube
context: From the Preface: "I procur'd me a small Pedestal... on the undermost of these I plac'd a pretty large Globe of Glass G, fill'd with exceeding clear Brine... on the upper Arm was placed a small Lamp K," with "a deep plain Convex glass" to steer the beam. He had conceded that "the fewer the Refractions are, the more bright and clear the Object appears" - his own compound tube lost to a single lens - so he built a light he could summon "at any time," and drew at night. His discipline followed: "I never began to make any draught before by many examinations in several lights, and in several positions to those lights, I had discover'd the true form." Any magnifier shows it: better lighting usually beats more magnification. (Micrographia, Preface.)

question: Robert Hooke laid a piece of petrified wood beside a piece of ordinary wood under the same lens and found the two built alike inside. From that match he argued the stone had once been a living tree, against the learned view of his day that such stones had never been alive at all. What did that view say had made their shapes?
answer: A shaping power latent in the Earth, growing stone into lifelike forms
choices: A shaping power latent in the Earth, growing stone into lifelike forms
A stray influence of the stars, pressing shapes into the rock below
A craft of ancient peoples, moulding clay that later turned to stone
A seed of stone, sprouting in the rock as a seed sprouts in soil
context: Observation XVII. Under the same lens the petrified wood's structure matched ordinary wood's, and from that match Hooke argued that fossils are the remains of things that were once alive, against the prevailing view that they were "Stones form'd by some extraordinary Plastick virtue latent in the Earth itself." Micrographia was never only biology: in Observation IX, on the colours in thin plates of Muscovy glass, Hooke argued that light travels as pulses or vibrations in a subtle medium rather than as flying particles - a wave picture of light well over a century before Fresnel formalised one. (Micrographia, Observ. XVII; roberthooke.org.uk, "Fossils"; Grokipedia: Micrographia.)

question: Robert Hooke went on cutting after the cork that gave him the word "cell": elder pith, fennel, carrots, burdocks, teasels, ferns and reeds, every one of them laid under the lens. What did he report finding inside those plants?
answer: Cells full of juices, sweating them out by degrees
choices: Cells full of juices, sweating them out by degrees
Walls as dry and bare as the ones in the cork
No cells at all, only long unbroken fibres
Boxes far larger and more regular than the cork's
context: The plant biologist Winfried Peters went back to Observation XVIII in 2024 to correct a line repeated in classrooms - that Hooke only ever saw dead, empty walls. "It is incorrect that Hooke only saw dead cell walls," Peters writes; Hooke had reported "these Cells or Pores fill'd with juices, and by degrees sweating them out." What does stay true is narrower and stranger: the word "cell" was coined for boxes of air in dead bark, and Hooke had no idea he had named the unit every living thing is built from. That took another 173 years - Matthias Schleiden on plants in 1838 and Theodor Schwann on animals in 1839 turned the word into cell theory. Hooke named the brick long before anyone knew there was a building. (Winfried S. Peters, "Will the real Robert Hooke please stand up?", The Plant Cell 36(11):4680, 2024.)

question: Robert Hooke finished his drawing of a blue mould growing on leather: the slender stalks, the round white knob bending each one over. Beneath the drawing he wrote down his account of where such growth comes from in the first place. What did Hooke conclude?
answer: That mould needs no seed, arising from rotting matter kept moist and warm
choices: That mould needs no seed, arising from rotting matter kept moist and warm
That invisible seeds drift in the air and settle wherever a surface is damp
That the leather's own substance was slowly changing form into a new plant
That the mould had been alive in the sheep's skin before the beast was killed
context: Hooke's words: "Mould and Mushroms require no seminal property, but the former may be produc'd at any time from any kind of putrifying Animal, or Vegetable Substance, as Flesh, &c. kept moist and warm." That is spontaneous generation - the very claim Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flasks would later have to kill, and the rival idea, seeds drifting in the air, is far closer to what is now known. The first published picture of a microorganism arrived with the wrong account of where microorganisms come from. That is not a mark against Hooke; it is what the record shows, and it is why a published drawing and a published explanation have to be judged separately. (Micrographia, Observ. XX.)

question: Winfried Peters, a plant biologist, searched Robert Hooke's writings in 2024 for a comparison found in almost any textbook: that the boxes in his cork reminded him of the bare little rooms where monks slept. He reported that no monk, no monastery, and not even the Latin word cellula appears anywhere in those writings. What comparison did Hooke actually put on the page?

choices: A honeycomb with irregular pores
A sponge riddled through with holes
A froth of bubbles on new ale
A pomegranate packed with seeds
context: Hooke's actual sentence: the cork was "all perforated and porous, much like a Honey-comb, but that the pores of it were not regular." Peters calls the monastic version "the monastic myth" - and Grokipedia, Britannica and National Geographic all repeat it, which is exactly why a famous story is worth checking against the original text. Micrographia is free to read online; the cork passage is Observation XVIII. Popularity is not evidence. (Winfried S. Peters, "Will the real Robert Hooke please stand up?", The Plant Cell 36(11):4680, 2024; Micrographia, Observ. XVIII.)

question: Ray Owen tested the blood of fraternal twin cattle in Wisconsin in 1945. Each pair came from two eggs, no more alike than ordinary siblings, and genetics said one red-cell type per calf. Owen found two. Where did the second come from?
answer: From its twin, through blood vessels fused in the womb.
choices: From its twin, through blood vessels fused in the womb.
From its twin, through cells taken in with milk after birth.
From its mother, through her blood crossing the placenta.
From its own marrow, through a second line starting late.
context: Owen published it in Science in 1945 — 'Immunogenetic consequences of vascular anastomoses between bovine twins' — reporting red-cell types 'usually identical, contrary to genetic expectation.' The calves' blood vessels had fused across a shared placenta before birth, so each animal grew up a permanent mosaic of two cell populations and never attacked the borrowed half. It also explained the freemartin, the sterile heifer born twinned to a bull calf: she carries her brother's blood-forming cells for life. Tolerance, it turned out, is not inherited — it is learned, and it is learned before birth. Source: Science 102(2651):400 (1945); Royal College of Surgeons of England Bulletin, 'Observations from the farmyard: cattle, chimerism and a Nobel prize.'

question: A ten-year-old is diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, a disease that, unlike type 2, has nothing to do with weight or diet. Her own immune system has singled out one population of cells in her body and destroyed them. Which cells did it kill?
answer: The insulin-making beta cells of her pancreas.
choices: The insulin-making beta cells of her pancreas.
The liver cells that store sugar as glycogen.

The muscle cells that pull sugar from her blood.
context: Type 1 diabetes is the self-or-other checkpoint failing on exactly one cell type — the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas. Grokipedia states plainly that, unlike type 2 diabetes, it 'is not linked to lifestyle factors like obesity.' Source: Grokipedia, 'Type 1 diabetes'.

question: Hugh Donald, an Edinburgh cattle researcher, asked the zoologist Peter Medawar in 1948 for a way to tell identical calf twins from non-identical ones. Medawar suggested skin grafts: identical twins should keep each other's skin, and fraternal pairs should throw it off within days. At Donald's farm the test was useless. Why?
answer: Fraternal twins kept each other's grafts as readily as identicals.
choices: Fraternal twins kept each other's grafts as readily as identicals.
Identical twins threw off each other's grafts within a few days.
Every graft on every calf, twin or not, sloughed away.
The grafts healed so slowly that no result could be read.
context: Medawar went to Donald's farm expecting a quick diagnostic and watched it break: the freemartin accepted skin from the bull calf she had shared a womb with, and he accepted hers. The useless test was the evidence — anything present while the immune system is being built gets filed as 'self'. Five years later Medawar turned that failure into the mouse experiment that won him a Nobel Prize. Source: Royal College of Surgeons of England Bulletin, 'Observations from the farmyard: cattle, chimerism and a Nobel prize.'

question: Hakaru Hashimoto, a Japanese surgeon, described four thyroid glands in 1912 that he had cut out of his patients. Each was swollen and turning to fibrous scar, yet he found no infection in them and no cancer. What filled the gland tissue instead?
answer: The patient's own white blood cells, packed in crowds.
choices: The patient's own white blood cells, packed in crowds.
Hardened crystals of iodine, gathered in clumps.
Fat from the neck, pushed in as smooth sheets.
Small cysts of clear fluid, in scattered nests.
context: Hashimoto called it struma lymphomatosa — a goitre full of lymph cells — working from just four surgical cases. He was describing an immune attack on the body's own tissue decades before anyone could demonstrate in a laboratory that such a thing was possible; the disease still carries his name. Source: Grokipedia, 'Autoimmunity'.

question: A mother learns that her child has type 1 diabetes, in which a child's own immune system attacks a body tissue, and she searches the family tree for someone else who had it. Parents almost always do. About what share of people with type 1 diabetes have no family history of it at all?
answer: About 80 to 90 percent.
choices: About 10 to 20 percent.
About 30 to 40 percent.
About 55 to 65 percent.
About 80 to 90 percent.
context: Roughly 80–90% of people diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have no family history of it. Genes load the dice across autoimmune disease without deciding the outcome: identical-twin concordance is only about 15% for rheumatoid arthritis and 20–25% for multiple sclerosis, and HLA-B27 is carried by 5–8% of the general population while only about 1–5% of carriers ever develop ankylosing spondylitis. Something outside the genome has to pull the trigger. Source: Grokipedia, 'Type 1 diabetes' and 'Autoimmunity'.

question: Paul Ehrlich named a law at the start of the 1900s that he thought the body obeyed: horror autotoxicus, Latin for the body's dread of self-poisoning. A body arming itself against its own tissues, he argued, would make no sense. The idea then stalled the study of self-attacking disease for fifty years. What did Ehrlich claim about antibodies aimed at a body's own tissue?
answer: The body can make them, but safeguards stop them doing harm.
choices: The body can make them, but safeguards stop them doing harm.
The body can make them, but only against dying tissue.
The body clears them out of its blood within hours of making them.
The body cannot make them at all, in health or illness.
context: In Collected Studies on Immunity (1906) Ehrlich named the safeguards himself: 'the organism possesses certain contrivances by means of which the immunity reaction, so easily produced by all kinds of cells, is prevented from acting against the organism's own elements.' He allowed that self-directed attacks could occur; he held that innate protections would stop them ever becoming pathological. The textbook one-liner — that a body simply cannot make antibodies against itself — is a flattening of what he wrote, and it cost the field decades: when Julius Donath and Karl Landsteiner showed in 1904 that serum from patients with paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria destroyed red cells after being chilled and then warmed, the first human autoantibody ever shown to cause disease was filed away as a curiosity. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Horror autotoxicus' / 'Paul Ehrlich'; IUPAC Gold Book, 'horror autotoxicus' (which dates the term to Ehrlich, 1902).

question: Jacques Miller cut the thymus out of newborn mice in 1961 and raised them to adulthood. Until then that soft lump of tissue behind the breastbone had been written off as a leftover organ, a graveyard where worn-out lymph tissue collected. What could those mice no longer do?
answer: Throw off a skin graft, even one from another species.
choices: Throw off a skin graft, even one from another species.
Clot their blood after even the smallest cut.
Put on anything close to a normal adult weight.
Clear ordinary bacteria out of the gut wall.
context: Miller's thymectomised mice also could not make antibodies to ordinary antigens. He published a preliminary communication in The Lancet in 1961 and the full account in Proceedings of the Royal Society B in 1962, and the 'vestigial' organ became the training school of the immune system. Source: Nature, Cell Death & Differentiation, 'The early work on the discovery of the function of the thymus, an interview with Jacques Miller'; Science, 'The function of the thymus and its impact on modern medicine'.

question: Rupert Billingham, Leslie Brent and Peter Medawar injected cells from one mouse strain into the embryos and newborn pups of another in 1953. Grown up, those mice wore skin grafts from the donor strain indefinitely, where an untreated mouse tears such a graft off within days. A critic could answer that the injections had simply crippled the animals' defences. Which finding in the same paper met that objection?
answer: Skin from a third, unrelated strain was still rejected on schedule.
choices: Skin from a third, unrelated strain was still rejected on schedule.
The treated mice cleared injected bacteria as fast as untreated ones.
Their blood destroyed foreign red cells normally in a test tube.
Their lymph nodes held normal numbers of cells at autopsy.
context: '"Actively acquired tolerance" of foreign cells,' Nature 172:603–606 (1953). The third-strain graft is what makes the result mean something: the mice were not defenceless, they had learned a specific list of what counts as 'me'. Frank Macfarlane Burnet and Frank Fenner had written the prediction in 1949 in The Production of Antibodies — implant foreign cells during embryonic life and the grown animal should mount no antibody response against them — and other people's mice proved it. In Prague, Milan Hašek reached the same conclusion by a stranger route, surgically joining two chick embryos of different strains so their blood mixed; he was left out when Burnet and Medawar shared the 1960 Nobel Prize, though Medawar credited the chicken experiments in his Nobel lecture. Source: Nature 172:603–606 (1953); WEHI history, 'Publication of Burnet's Nobel Prize-Winning Immune Tolerance Theory'; Nature Reviews Immunology, 'Milan Hašek and the discovery of immunological tolerance'.

question: Ernest Witebsky refused to believe the young researcher in his own lab. Noel Rose had spent months injecting rabbits with purified thyroid protein, and Witebsky, raised inside Paul Ehrlich's own scientific line, twice sent him back to the bench to run it again more carefully. Each time the result held. Then Witebsky named the single version of the experiment he would accept as proof. What did he demand?
answer: Take the protein from a rabbit and inject it back into that same rabbit.
choices: Take the protein from a rabbit and inject it back into that same rabbit.
Take the whole series through a second species before publishing it.
Show the same damage with no adjuvant added to the protein at all.
Prove the protein came from thyroid tissue and from no other organ.
context: Witebsky's first objection was the reasonable one — the thyroglobulin must have been denatured in purification, so the rabbits were reacting to a mangled protein rather than a real self-protein. Gentler handling gave the same result. So he demanded the version no objection could survive: a protein taken out of an animal's own body and returned to that same body, which then destroyed its own thyroid. Note the record precisely — the published 1956 paper used homologous (other-rabbit) thyroid extract; the same-animal version was the confirmation Witebsky insisted on. He was not an outsider attacking a doctrine but a protégé of one of Ehrlich's own trainees, which is exactly why he fought the result so hard. Source: The Scientist, 'The Father of Autoimmunity: A Profile of Noel Rose'.

question: A child sits in a doctor's office, weeks past a strep throat, with no fever and no strep bacteria left in her body. The doctor hears something new: a soft murmur, the sound of blood slipping past a heart valve that is quietly scarring over. No bacteria can be found inside the valve itself. What is doing the damage?
answer: Antibodies raised against the bacterium that also stick to heart tissue.
choices: Antibodies raised against the bacterium that also stick to heart tissue.
A toxin left behind by the bacteria that slowly stiffens the valve.
White cells drawn to the valve during the illness that never left.
A clot thrown during the infection that hardened onto the valve.
context: Molecular mimicry: the streptococcus wears an alpha-helical coiled-coil M protein and a group A carbohydrate (N-acetylglucosamine) that structurally resemble cardiac myosin. Antibodies against the carbohydrate bind valve endothelium and switch on VCAM-1; activated T cells then push into the avascular valve and a Th1 response scars it. The murmur of rheumatic carditis is friendly fire. HONEST CAVEAT, stated plainly: 'Although rheumatic fever has been attributed to molecular mimicry for half a century no antigen has been formally identified.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Autoimmunity' (caveat verbatim); Microbiology Spectrum, 'Molecular Mimicry, Autoimmunity, and Infection: The Cross-Reactive Antigens of Group A Streptococci and their Sequelae'.

question: A teacher sketches the thymus on a blackboard for her class. Every T cell must pass an audition there: it is shown fragments of the body's own proteins, and if it grips them too tightly it is killed. But the thymus, behind the breastbone, never sees the pancreas, so a trainee should meet no insulin, and a T cell that would attack insulin should stroll out alive. It does not. How does the thymus stop that cell?
answer: Thymus cells switch on thousands of genes belonging to other organs.
choices: Thymus cells switch on thousands of genes belonging to other organs.
Thymus cells display protein fragments built at random, shape after shape.
Thymus cells show trainees proteins left over from the embryo's tissues.
Thymus cells release a hormone that bars trainees from entering organs.
context: The gene is AIRE, found in 1997 by positional cloning on human chromosome 21 at band 21q22.3. In medullary thymic epithelial cells it forces 'promiscuous gene expression' — thymus cells switch on thousands of tissue-restricted antigens borrowed from organs all over the body, so trainees can be shown insulin, eye protein and adrenal protein, and killed if they react. Roughly 95% of thymocytes never leave the thymus alive; cells with intermediate self-affinity are not killed but diverted into regulatory T cells, the body's own suppression squad. When AIRE breaks — over 150 pathogenic variants are known — the result is APECED, autoimmunity striking several organs at once. Source: Grokipedia, 'Autoimmune regulator' and 'Immune tolerance'.

question: A woman opens a lab report and finds a positive test for antinuclear antibodies, antibodies aimed at a cell's own nucleus. It sounds like proof of autoimmune disease, yet 20 to 30 percent of healthy people carry them at low levels. Every healthy body also makes self-binding antibodies of the IgM class. In a healthy body, what job do those antibodies do?
answer: They stick to damaged and dying cells and mark them for clearance.
choices: They stick to damaged and dying cells and mark them for clearance.
They soak up loose iron spilled by cells that have burst open.
They plug tears in cell membranes until the cell repairs itself.
They coat newly made cells so the body registers them as its own.
context: A little self-recognition is normal and useful. Healthy people carry natural autoantibodies, mostly germline-encoded IgM, that bind damaged and dying cells and tag them for clean-up; germ-free mice have markedly less of this natural autoreactivity than ordinary mice. The line between health and disease is a threshold of affinity and persistence, not the mere presence of self-recognition. Source: Grokipedia, 'Autoimmunity' (Low-Level Autoimmunity).

question: Howard Chang's team went after the best clue available in 2024: Xist, a long RNA that only females make, which coats one of a female's two X chromosomes to switch it off. About 78 percent of Americans living with an autoimmune disease are women, and nobody has explained why. To find out whether Xist itself was part of the answer, what did the team do?
answer: Engineered male mice to make a non-silencing form of Xist.
choices: Engineered male mice to make a non-silencing form of Xist.
Deleted Xist from female mice before they reached puberty.
Transplanted marrow from female mice into male littermates.
Bred female mice carrying only one X chromosome instead of two.
context: The engineered males produced autoantibodies, their T and B cells shifted to resemble wild-type females', and SJL/J males carrying the transgene developed markedly worse disease in a pristane-induced lupus model; human autoimmune patients carry autoantibodies against components of the XIST protein complex. It is the best clue anyone has — it is not the answer. Wikipedia states the puzzle flatly: 'Being female is the single greatest risk factor for developing autoimmune disease than any other genetic or environmental risk factor yet discovered.' Hashimoto's thyroiditis runs roughly 10:1 female, systemic lupus erythematosus 9:1, Graves' disease 7:1 — and no one yet knows why. Source: Cell (2024), 'Xist ribonucleoproteins promote female sex-biased autoimmunity'; Nature Reviews Rheumatology commentary; Wikipedia, 'Autoimmunity'.

question: Peter Buxtun, a 27-year-old investigator in the US Public Health Service, filed a written objection against the Tuskegee syphilis study in 1966. He was overruled. He argued it in person in Atlanta in 1967 and was overruled again. In 1972 he did the one thing that closed the study within months. What did he do?
answer: He handed the file to a reporter
choices: He handed the file to a reporter
He resigned in a public protest
He mailed the file to a Senator
He filed a suit against the Service
context: The chain ran Peter Buxtun to AP's Edith Lederer to Jean Heller, whose story broke on July 25, 1972 in more than 100 newspapers. The Service ended the study inside a few months. The chain was employee, then journalist; the institution was never in it. Source: cnn.com/2024/07/16, uclawsf.edu.

question: Harrison Martland, medical examiner for Essex County, New Jersey, took a single exhalation from a living radium-dial painter in the 1920s. Her employers denied any link to the paint she had licked to point her brush, and he could not X-ray her whole body. What did he capture from her breath to prove the paint was still inside her?
answer: A trace of radon gas
choices: A trace of radon gas
A trace of mercury vapour
A trace of luminescent dust
A trace of vaporised lead
context: Radon is the daughter product of radium decay; it drifts out through the lungs. Detecting it in exhaled breath was direct forensic proof the women's own bodies had become radium sources. Source: environmentalhistory.org.

question: Harrison Martland laid bones of dead radium-dial painters on unexposed photographic film and left them there. The bosses had controlled the payroll, the medical records and the courtroom, but not the women's own bodies. When developed, the film showed a soft image printed into the emulsion. Where had the image come from?
answer: The bones themselves were radioactive
choices: The bones themselves were radioactive
A weak lamp above the storage shelf
The developer bath used on the film
Bacteria feeding on residues in the bone
context: The dial-painters' bones were so contaminated with radium that they took their own picture - a jaw, a spine, a hand, printed by their own decay. When a company controls the records, the physical evidence in the victim IS the record. Source: environmentalhistory.org, history.com.

question: Susan Reverby, a historian, brought a buried story to light in 2010: the US Public Health Service (PHS) had on purpose infected hundreds of people in Guatemala with syphilis and gonorrhoea during the late 1940s. It came out sixty-two years after it happened. Where, exactly, was the evidence found?
answer: In the personal papers of a dead PHS doctor
choices: In the personal papers of a dead PHS doctor
In a declassified batch of State Department cables
In court exhibits from a settled civil lawsuit
In transcripts of a Congressional subcommittee
context: Susan Reverby, a Wellesley College medical historian, was reading John Cutler's own donated notes in the University of Pittsburgh archives while researching Tuskegee. Perpetrators keep files. Files outlive them. Source: neh.gov, oah.org.

question: Henri Pitot built an instrument in 1732 that faced an oncoming flow, let the fluid pile up inside and read how high it climbed. Its descendant juts from an airliner's nose today and gives the pilot his airspeed. The first thing Pitot pushed his instrument into was not the sky. What was it?
answer: The current of the Seine, to learn how fast the river ran
choices: The current of the Seine, to learn how fast the river ran
The rush of a Loire mill-race, to learn how fast the water ran
The blast of a Rouen forge bellows, to learn how fast the air ran
The updraught of a Lyon chimney, to learn how fast the smoke ran
context: Henri Pitot (1695-1771) was a French hydraulic engineer, and the Academie he served sat in Paris, on the Seine. His machine was two glass tubes fixed in a wooden triangular-prism frame - one bent to face the current, one straight and side-on - with a movable copper scale for reading the two heights. He published it in the Memoires de l'Academie Royale des Sciences for 1732 as 'Description d'une machine pour mesurer la vitesse des eaux courantes, et le sillage des vaisseaux': a machine for measuring the speed of running water, and the wake of ships. Henry Darcy, from 1856 with Henri Bazin, added the second, side-facing opening that makes the modern pitot-static tube. Source: Grokipedia, 'Pitot tube'.

question: A crew took off from Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic, on 6 February 1996 in a Boeing 757 whose pitot tubes, which read airspeed, had stood uncovered for two nights. The captain's dial showed 350 knots at a true 220. The autopilot believed it, and all 189 aboard died. What most likely blocked his tube?
answer: A mud dauber wasp's nest, built of mud and grit
choices: A mud dauber wasp's nest, built of mud and grit
A plug of sea salt crusted from the coastal air
A strip of masking tape left on by a cleaner
A wad of straw dropped in by a nesting bird
context: None of the tubes was ever recovered, but investigators concluded that mud dauber wasps (Sceliphron caementarium) had most likely packed the captain's tube with mud and debris. The autopilot, trusting the false reading, pulled the thrust back to idle and raised the nose, and the crew mistook the stick shaker for a configuration warning. Ice does the same thing: on 1 June 2009 the Thales pitot probes of Air France 447, an Airbus A330 crossing the Intertropical Convergence Zone at 35,000 feet, iced over in cumulonimbus and all three air-data units lost airspeed at 02:10:05 UTC. The autopilot dropped out, the pilots held persistent nose-up inputs, and the aircraft fell in a stall at more than 10,000 feet per minute into the Atlantic; all 228 aboard died and the wreckage lay about 3,900 metres down. The BEA's 2012 final report issued 25 safety recommendations. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Birgenair Flight 301' and 'Air France Flight 447'.

question: A student holds a strip of paper to her lower lip and blows across the top, and the far end rises. Teachers call this Bernoulli's principle: the fast air above is low-pressure air that lifts the paper. She turns the strip over and blows along its underside, with nothing moving above it. What does the strip do?
answer: It rises again, just as it did before
choices: It rises again, just as it did before
It swings downward instead of rising
It flutters hard but stays where it is
It curls up at the far end and droops
context: Anyone can try it both ways. What lifts the strip is not a comparison between its two sides at all. The air leaving the mouth is at exactly the pressure of the room around it - moving air is not automatically low-pressure air - and 'it is false to make a connection between the flow on the two sides of the paper using Bernoulli's equation since the air above and below are different flow fields.' What does the work is the curving of the blown jet: the paper bends the jet, and the bent jet pushes back. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle', 'Misunderstandings about the generation of lift'.

question: A physics class pumps water through a glass pipe on the bench. It narrows to a throat and widens again, with liquid-filled side tubes tapped into its wall. The same amount passes every point, so at the pinch the water must hurry. Each side tube reports the pressure at its spot. What do they show?
answer: The liquid stands lowest at the throat
choices: The liquid stands lowest at the throat
The liquid stands highest at the throat
The liquid stands level along the whole pipe
The liquid climbs steadily toward the outlet
context: This is a Venturi tube, and it is what a genuine demonstration of Bernoulli's principle looks like: a pressure drop measured directly where the flow is measured to be fastest. Daniel Bernoulli published the principle in Hydrodynamica in 1738 and it has never been in doubt - it lets a Venturi meter read a pipe's flow rate off nothing but that drop, draws petrol into the airstream at a carburettor's throat, drives an aspirator and a scent atomiser, and gives a pilot his airspeed through a pitot tube. Keep this straight: when the schoolbook explanation of a wing fails, the principle is not the part that fails. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle'; Wikipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle'.

question: An audience listens as Holger Babinsky, a Cambridge aerodynamics professor, asks who was taught this story of how a wing lifts. The air splits at the nose. The top is the longer path. The two streams meet again at the back edge, so the top air must hurry. Faster air runs at lower pressure, so the wing is sucked up. About 95% of hands go up. Which of those four steps is the invention?
answer: That the two halves rejoin at the trailing edge
choices: That the two halves rejoin at the trailing edge
That the flow divides at the wing's leading edge
That the upper surface is the longer of the two paths
That faster-moving air runs at lower pressure
context: Note which step survived the audit: Bernoulli's. The principle is sound physics; what fails is the equal-transit assumption bolted onto it. Wikipedia's 'Lift (force)' is blunt: 'There is no physical principle that requires equal transit time in all situations and experimental results confirm that for a body generating lift the transit times are not equal.' There is a second, quieter error too: 'No difference in path length is needed, and even when there is a difference, it is typically much too small to explain the observed speed difference.' Babinsky's own verdict on the story 95% of every audience raises a hand to: 'But this is wrong.' Sources: University of Cambridge, 'How wings really work'; Wikipedia, 'Lift (force)'; Grokipedia, 'Lift (force)'.

question: Holger Babinsky mounted an aerofoil in a Cambridge wind tunnel and released pulses of smoke into the airflow, filming what became of them. Each pulse split at the wing's nose, half riding over the humped top and half running along underneath; he published the frames in 2003. In a single frame, where have the two halves of one pulse got to?
answer: The top half is past the trailing edge; the bottom half is not
choices: The top half is past the trailing edge; the bottom half is not
The bottom half is past the trailing edge; the top half is not
Both halves reach the trailing edge together, side by side
Both halves meet again a little past the trailing edge
context: The smoke over the top arrives early and has already left the wing behind. Babinsky published the physics in 'How do wings work?', Physics Education 38(6), page 497, 2003; the abstract says the popular explanation 'is common, quick, sounds logical and gives the correct answer, yet also introduces misconceptions.' The numbers convict the story too: if the parcels really had to meet, the top air would need to run only about 3-5% faster than the air underneath, yet measurements show it running as much as 50% or more above the freestream speed. David Anderson of Fermilab and Scott Eberhardt of the University of Washington did the arithmetic for a Cessna 172, whose upper surface is only 1.5-2.5% longer than its lower: on the equal-transit story 'a Cessna 172 would have to fly at over 400 mph to generate enough lift.' It cruises at about 110 knots. The historian J. A. D. Ackroyd adds that Babinsky was not the first - 'over the years, photographs and films have consistently shown the same behaviour' - the evidence was there and simply went unbelieved. Sources: Babinsky, Physics Education 38 497 (2003); Ackroyd, Journal of Aeronautical History Paper No. 2015/01; Grokipedia, 'Lift (force)'; Anderson & Eberhardt, 'How Airplanes Fly'.

question: A stunt pilot rolls onto his back at an airshow and holds steady inverted flight. On the schoolbook story he should not be able to: the wing's humped surface is now the lower one, so the longer path is underneath and the wing ought to be pressed toward the ground. What keeps the upside-down wing lifting?
answer: The pilot holds the nose up, and the wing's tilt alone makes the lift
choices: The pilot holds the nose up, and the wing's tilt alone makes the lift
The pilot flies faster, and the extra speed alone carries the weight
The engine angles its thrust up, and that push alone holds the plane
The propeller blasts the wing's underside, and that wash alone lifts it
context: The tilt has a name: the angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air. 'When a cambered airfoil is upside down, the angle of attack can be adjusted so that the lift force is upward.' The same point kills the shape story outright, since it 'does not explain how flat plates, symmetric airfoils, sailboat sails, or conventional airfoils flying upside down can generate lift.' Thin-aerofoil theory gives a flat plate - no hump at all - a lift coefficient of CL = 2 x pi x alpha, with alpha the angle of attack in radians: a plain plate lifts perfectly well the moment it is tilted. Babinsky on a sail, whose two faces are exactly the same length: 'here the distance on each side is the same but it is slightly curved when it is rigged and so it acts as an aerofoil.' A flat balsa glider thrown across a room tests this at home. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Lift (force)'; Grokipedia, 'Lift (force)'; University of Cambridge, 'How wings really work'.

question: A teacher points a hairdryer straight up, rests a ping-pong ball in the jet, and the ball hovers there and will not fall out. Bernoulli, says the teacher: the fast air of the jet is low-pressure air, so the ball sits in a pocket of suction. Measure the plume, though, and its pressure is exactly the room's. What holds the ball in the jet?
answer: Off-centre, the ball meets lopsided flow that shoves it back inward
choices: Off-centre, the ball meets lopsided flow that shoves it back inward
Spinning, the ball drags air around itself and steers itself inward
Charged, the rushing air builds static that pins the ball inward
Warmed, the plume thins and the ball slides down into its core
context: 'The air in the plume has the same pressure as the surrounding air. The ball remains in the plume since as it moves away from the center of the plume it experiences an asymmetric air flow which pushes it back toward the center.' A charming demonstration with a wrong caption. A genuine Bernoulli demonstration is a Venturi tube read with a liquid gauge, where the pressure at the throat is measured directly. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle'; Grokipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle', 'Common Demonstrations and Errors'.

question: Paul Bowen, shooting for Cessna, caught an aeroplane a moment after it had passed low over a flat bank of fog. Where the machine went by, a huge hole stood open in the grey deck. Aerodynamicists reprint the frame whenever they argue about lift. What punched the hole?
answer: The wing had thrown a whole column of air downward as it passed
choices: The wing had thrown a whole column of air downward as it passed
The engine's hot exhaust had burned a trench through the droplets
The low pressure above the wing had drawn the fog up after it
The propeller's swirl had wound the fog into a rope and flung it
context: 'A huge hole is punched through the fog by the downwash from the airplane that has just flown over it' (Fig. 6, photograph by Paul Bowen, courtesy Cessna Aircraft Co.). By Newton's third law, air pushed down pushes the wing up - and the downward turning 'is not produced solely by the lower surface of the airfoil'; the flow above the wing does much of it. Anderson and Eberhardt estimate that a Cessna 172 at 110 knots, with an average downwash of about 9 knots, must pump 'a whopping 2.5 ton/sec of air' downward to make its 2,300 lb of lift, accelerating essentially all the air within about nine feet above the wing - and they note their own estimate 'may be as much as a factor of two too low.' The same tight downward column shows under a helicopter's rotors, behind a propeller and below a household fan, all of which are rotating wings. 'If a plane were to fly over a very large scale, the scale would register the weight of the plane.' Sources: Anderson & Eberhardt, 'How Airplanes Fly'; Wikipedia, 'Lift (force)'.

question: A pilot eases the nose up and the wing lifts harder; further still, and harder still. Then, near fifteen degrees of tilt, the lift does not merely level off, it collapses while the drag surges. This is the moment pilots call a stall. What has happened to the air flowing over the wing's upper surface?
answer: It has torn away from the surface instead of following it round
choices: It has torn away from the surface instead of following it round
It has slowed to a standstill and settled into a still cushion
It has been squeezed to a higher pressure than the air beneath
It has run faster than sound and thrown a shock wave across it
context: Past the critical angle of attack - roughly fifteen degrees - the boundary layer, the thin sheet of air right against the wing's skin, separates from the upper surface, and with the flow no longer following the wing round the lift collapses while drag surges. Recovery shows hysteresis: the pilot must lower the nose further than the angle at which it broke before the flow will reattach. Leading-edge slats and vortex generators can delay the stall by a few degrees. Source: Grokipedia, 'Lift (force)', 'Boundary Layer, Drag, and Stalling'.

question: An engineer writes down the ideal-flow equations for air streaming past a wing, and they refuse to give a single answer. They allow an infinity of solutions, each with a different circulation, a different strength of spin running round the wing, and each satisfies the mathematics perfectly. Only one of them describes a real wing in real air. What one physical requirement picks it out?
answer: That the flow must leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly, not whip round it
choices: That the flow must leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly, not whip round it
That the flow must close up smoothly behind the wing, leaving no vortex
That the flow's spin must add up to zero on a loop around the wing
That the flow must reach its lowest pressure at the wing's thickest point
context: This is the Kutta condition: 'A body with a sharp trailing edge which is moving through a fluid will create about itself a circulation of sufficient strength to hold the rear stagnation point at the trailing edge.' Mathematically it 'enforces a specific choice among the infinite allowed values of circulation' - and it is why aerofoils are built with sharp trailing edges even though sharp edges are awkward to make. The circulation it fixes IS the lift, by the Kutta-Zhukovskii theorem: L = rho x V x Gamma, with rho the air density, V the flow speed, and Gamma the circulation - the sum, round any imaginary loop enclosing the wing, of the flow's speed along that loop. How anyone knows this is true: in the 1920s British researchers measured airflow velocities all round wind-tunnel aerofoils and then did the laborious hand-summation of the circulation round a loop. Bryant and Williams (results published 1924, a thick cambered aerofoil) got a lift from L = rho V Gamma within 6% of the lift computed from the measured pressures; Tanner (1930, an RAF 30 symmetrical section at 7 degrees incidence) got within 2%. And because a vortex cannot simply end, the trailing vortices behind a wing 'can be traced right back to the airfield at which the wing first generated lift', where the loop is closed by the starting vortex shed the instant the wing first took up lifting incidence. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Kutta condition'; Ackroyd, Journal of Aeronautical History Paper No. 2015/01.

question: Two engineers argue about a wing at a blackboard. One says lift is a pressure difference: lower pressure above, higher pressure below. The other says lift is Newton's third law: the wing turns air downward and the air shoves back. Each calls the other's account a mere by-product. The Euler equations, which govern the flow itself, settle the quarrel. What do those equations say about which of the two comes first?
answer: Neither is primary; pressure and turned flow produce each other together
choices: Neither is primary; pressure and turned flow produce each other together
Pressure is primary; the turning of the flow is only its visible after-effect
Flow turning is primary; the pressure difference is only its book-keeping
Neither is primary; both follow from the air's friction against the skin
context: 'Changes in velocity induce pressure gradients that, in turn, cause streamline curvature and further alterations in velocity... neither pressure nor velocity can be considered primary; instead, they evolve together in a self-consistent manner throughout the flow field.' The concrete grip: a curved streamline needs a centripetal force to bend it, and the pressure gradient across the streamlines supplies it - sharper curvature over the top is exactly why the pressure there is lower. Babinsky's positive statement of the mechanism: 'What actually causes lift is introducing a shape into the airflow, which curves the streamlines and introduces pressure changes - lower pressure on the upper surface and higher pressure on the lower surface.' Viscous skin friction contributes less than 5% of the total lift, so lift really is a pressure phenomenon, even though viscosity is what sets the circulation up in the first place. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Lift (force)', 'Pressure-Velocity Interactions and Limitations of Simpler Models'; University of Cambridge, 'How wings really work'.

question: Jeremiah Horrocks became the first person ever to predict and observe Venus crossing the Sun, at Much Hoole in England in 1639. An eye put to his telescope would have been blinded in an instant. He watched for half an hour and kept his sight. How?
answer: He cast the Sun's image out of the telescope onto paper.
choices: He cast the Sun's image out of the telescope onto paper.
He capped the eyepiece with a disc of smoked glass.
He caught the Sun's reflection in a basin of still water.
He waited for thin cloud to dim the Sun enough to look.
context: Horrocks threw the Sun through the telescope onto a sheet of paper on which he had already drawn a circle, so he could measure Venus against it. He watched from about a quarter past three until sunset at about ten to four, and wrote: 'I then beheld a most agreeable spectacle, the object of my sanguine wishes, a spot of unusual magnitude and of a perfectly circular shape.' You can do exactly this yourself: hold a white card behind binoculars or a small telescope and let the Sun's image fall on it -- and never, ever look through them at the Sun. Source: Wikipedia, '1639 transit of Venus'; tide-and-time.uk, 'Local heroes: Jeremiah Horrocks'.

question: Aristarchus of Samos set out around 280 BC to learn how much farther the Sun is than the Moon. He had only his eyes and a plan of pure geometry: wait for one particular moment, then take a single measurement. Which moment did he wait for?
answer: When the Moon showed exactly half lit.
choices: When the Moon showed exactly half lit.
When the Moon slid fully into Earth's shadow.
When the Moon blotted out the Sun entirely.
When the full Moon rose exactly at sunset.
context: At the instant the Moon is exactly half lit, the angle at the Moon between Earth and Sun must be a right angle -- so the angle between Moon and Sun as seen from the ground fixes the whole triangle. Aristarchus measured that angle as 87 degrees. It is really 89.853, and no naked eye can catch a difference that fine, so he put the Sun at 18 to 20 times the Moon's distance instead of about 390. His geometry was sound; his instrument was not. Go out at a half Moon and try to judge how far around the sky the Sun sits from it, and you will feel how brutal the measurement is. (Eratosthenes' famous stick-and-shadow trick, often muddled with this one, sizes the Earth -- it says nothing about the Sun's distance.) Two thousand years later the true distance was still unknown, which is why a black dot creeping across the Sun was worth crossing oceans for. Source: Wikipedia, 'Astronomical unit' (Aristarchus, 87 degrees against 89.853; 18-20 times).

question: Edmond Halley printed his method for measuring the Sun's distance in the Philosophical Transactions of 1716. It depended on a transit of Venus, and the next two would not occur until 1761 and 1769. He knew he would live to see neither one. What did Halley put in the closing lines of that paper?
answer: A plea to strangers not yet born to make the observation.
choices: A plea to strangers not yet born to make the observation.
A table of the exact hours the 1761 crossing would fall.
A challenge to the Paris Observatory to attempt it first.
A warning that his own arithmetic might hide an error.
context: The paper was 'A new Method of determining the Parallax of the Sun, or his Distance from the Earth' (Philosophical Transactions, 1716); Halley had read an early version to the Royal Society back in 1691, and wrote in Latin on purpose, so astronomers all over Europe could use it. One common English rendering of his closing words: 'I recommend it therefore again and again to those curious astronomers who, when I am dead, will have an opportunity of observing these things.' He died nineteen years before the first of the two transits he had planned. Source: classicalastrologer.com, 'Edmund Halley: Admonition of 1716'; Grokipedia, 'The Transit of Venus'; skyandtelescope.org, 'Transits of Venus in history, 1631-1716'.

question: Two observers on far-apart parts of Earth time one planet crossing the Sun in Edmond Halley's way of measuring the Sun's distance. Each sees it cut a slightly different line, so each records a slightly different crossing time, and that difference is the whole measurement. Mercury crosses the Sun too, and more often. Why did Halley insist on Venus?
answer: Venus passes far nearer Earth, so its shift is far bigger.
choices: Venus passes far nearer Earth, so its shift is far bigger.
Venus crosses far more slowly, so the timings are easier.
Venus shows a far bigger disc, so its edge is sharper.
Venus rides nearer the Sun's centre, so its line is longer.
context: The difference between the two timings gives what astronomers call the Sun's parallax, and that number is the whole point. Kepler's laws had already fixed the spacing of the solar system perfectly -- Venus at 0.723 of Earth's distance from the Sun, Mars at 1.524, Jupiter at 5.203 -- but in relative units only: nothing anywhere said how many miles one unit was. Measure a single real distance and every other one follows. Halley's arithmetic promised that if observers could time the moments of contact to within two seconds, the Sun's distance would come out good to one part in 500. That promise is what persuaded governments to pay. Source: Grokipedia, 'The Transit of Venus'; Wikipedia, "Kepler's laws of planetary motion"; Ohio State Astronomy 161 notes, 'Venus and the Sun'.

question: Guillaume Le Gentil left Paris in March 1760 to time the transit of 6 June 1761 from Pondicherry in India. The British took the town before he arrived, and on transit morning he was still at sea, where a shipboard timing is worthless. Rather than go home, he stayed in the Indian Ocean for the eight years to the next transit. What survey did he carry out?
answer: He charted the east coast of Madagascar.
choices: He charted the east coast of Madagascar.
He mapped the reefs of the Coromandel coast.
He surveyed the volcanoes of the Java coast.
He measured the tides of the Persian Gulf.
context: Le Gentil sailed from Paris on 26 March 1760, reached Mauritius that July, and was still aboard ship when Venus crossed the Sun on 6 June 1761 under a clear sky. He filled the eight years with work: he charted Madagascar's east coast, went to Manila in 1766, was driven out by a Spanish governor-general who insisted his royal letters were forgeries, and reached Pondicherry -- French again after the 1763 peace -- in March 1768, where he built himself a small observatory on a ruined fort. Source: Wikipedia, 'Guillaume Le Gentil'; armaghplanet.com, 'The unluckiest astronomer in history'.

question: Jeremiah Horrocks, barely in his twenties, sat at Much Hoole in Lancashire with a single telescope, watching the Sun on 24 November 1639 by the old Julian calendar England still used. Kepler's Rudolphine Tables, the best star tables in Europe, promised no transit of Venus before 1761. What had put him there?
answer: He had reworked Kepler's own numbers and found the crossing himself.
choices: He had reworked Kepler's own numbers and found the crossing himself.
He had a letter from a Dutch astronomer predicting the crossing.
He had watched the Sun daily for sunspots and caught it by luck.
He had followed a rival set of tables printed that year in Paris.
context: Kepler's tables had Venus passing just above the Sun that day -- a near miss. Horrocks recomputed them, found the near miss was really a hit, and had under four weeks to prepare. England was still on the Julian calendar; that date was 4 December 1639 on the Gregorian calendar used across the Channel. Only one other human being saw it: his friend William Crabtree at Broughton near Manchester, who got a glimpse through a cloud gap and sketched fast -- and whose rushed estimate of Venus's size beat Horrocks's careful one by an arcsecond. Horrocks's figure for the Sun's distance came out near 60 million miles, about two-thirds of the truth, but ten times larger than the value astronomers had inherited from Ptolemy. He died on 3 January 1641, aged 22; his account 'Venus in sole visa' sat unpublished for 22 years until Hevelius printed it in 1662. Source: Wikipedia, '1639 transit of Venus' and 'Jeremiah Horrocks'; Grokipedia, '1639 transit of Venus'.

question: Jean-Baptiste Chappe d'Auteroche hauled his instruments across a continent to Tobolsk in Siberia for the 1761 transit. That spring the rivers there flooded worse than anyone could remember. He timed the whole crossing successfully from a hilltop, with armed Cossacks standing round him. Why did he need the guard?
answer: Peasants blamed that spring's floods on his meddling with the Sun.
choices: Peasants blamed that spring's floods on his meddling with the Sun.
Flood refugees had been looting the town for anything portable.
The governor suspected him of mapping the frontier for France.
A rival Russian party had threatened to seize his instruments.
context: Chappe got the entire 1761 transit despite the hostility. For 1769 he travelled to the mission at San Jose del Cabo in Baja California and again got a clean observation -- and then an epidemic swept the settlement. He caught it while nursing the sick and died on 1 August 1769, aged 47. Only one member of his party survived to carry his notebooks back to Paris. Source: Wikipedia, 'Jean-Baptiste Chappe d'Auteroche'; IMCCE (Paris Observatory), promenade.imcce.fr.

question: Guillaume Le Gentil crossed back into France in October 1771, after eleven years, six months and thirteen days away. He had lost the 1761 transit at sea, and on the morning of the 1769 transit a cloud had covered the Sun over Pondicherry. What had French law done with him in the meantime?
answer: It had declared him dead and let his heirs divide his estate.
choices: It had declared him dead and let his heirs divide his estate.
It had seized his estate to repay the crown's outlay on him.
It had granted him a pension against his eventual return.
It had held his estate in trust under a court's appointed man.
context: His seat at the Academy of Sciences had also been filled, and it took lengthy litigation and the intervention of the king to get it back. He later married, had a daughter, and died in Paris on 22 October 1792. His own published verdict on the whole affair: 'That is the fate which often awaits astronomers. I had gone more than ten thousand leagues...' Sources differ on whether the Pondicherry cloud fell on 3 or 4 June 1769, and the often-repeated claim that his wife had remarried is disputed -- the losses above are the ones the records agree on. Source: Wikipedia, 'Guillaume Le Gentil'; armaghplanet.com, 'The unluckiest astronomer in history'; IMCCE, promenade.imcce.fr.

question: James Cook took the Endeavour to Matavai Bay in Tahiti for the transit of 3 June 1769. That day, he wrote, 'not a Cloud was to be seen the whole day and the Air was perfectly clear.' Cook, Charles Green and Daniel Solander each timed the instants when Venus's edge met the Sun's, and their three sets of times disagreed far more than anyone had expected. What did Cook's journal blame?
answer: A dusky shade clinging round the body of the planet.
choices: A dusky shade clinging round the body of the planet.
A tremor in the sandy ground beneath the telescopes.
A fault in the clock the Royal Society had supplied.
A dispute over which edge marked the first contact.
context: The Royal Society got 4,000 pounds from King George III for the voyage, and Cook built an earthwork-and-palisade camp he called Fort Venus; the headland at Matavai Bay is still called Point Venus today. Cook wrote that the three of them 'differ'd from one another in observeing the times of the Contacts much more than could be expected', and that they 'very distinctly saw an Atmosphere or dusky shade round the body of the Planet which very much disturbed the times of the Contacts.' Astronomers came to call it the black drop. Perfect weather was not enough; the limit was in the light itself. Source: Wikipedia, '1769 transit of Venus observed from Tahiti' (quoting Cook's journal); aaa.org, 'History of the transit of Venus'.

question: Mikhail Lomonosov watched the 1761 crossing from St Petersburg and noticed something at the two instants when Venus sat half on and half off the Sun's face. The transit campaigns had been mounted to measure a single distance, and nobody had sailed anywhere to look for that detail. He interpreted it correctly on the spot. What had Lomonosov become the first human being to detect?
answer: An atmosphere on another planet.
choices: An atmosphere on another planet.
A moon orbiting another planet.
A ring of dust round another planet.
A mountain range on another planet.
context: Lomonosov saw a luminous arc standing around the part of Venus still hanging off the Sun, at entry and again at exit, and read it as sunlight bent through the planet's own air. It is the first detection of an atmosphere on any world beyond Earth -- found by a man who had come to measure a distance and got a planet's weather instead. Source: Wikipedia, 'Transit of Venus'; arXiv:1206.3489, "Lomonosov's discovery of Venus atmosphere in 1761".

question: An observer at a transit of Venus watched the planet's disc meet the Sun's inner edge and seem to stretch a dark thread back to that edge, like a drop refusing to fall. This black drop smeared the timings by around ten seconds; Halley's arithmetic had needed two. Astronomers argued for a century about the cause, and most blamed something belonging to Venus itself. Which observation ruled that out?
answer: Mercury's transits show the same thread, and Mercury has no air.
choices: Mercury's transits show the same thread, and Mercury has no air.
The Moon's edge shows the same thread at a partial eclipse.
The ligament appeared on the Sun's far edge, well away from Venus.
Ships' observers saw it, while mountain observers saw none at all.
context: Friedrich Bessel and Friedrich Argelander made the point with Mercury's transits in 1832: the same dark thread appears, and Mercury has essentially no atmosphere at all. The modern explanation is not the planet -- it is the extreme darkening of the Sun's own disc near its edge, combined with the limited resolving power of the telescope and the shimmer of Earth's air. A method that needed two-second precision was being asked for it by eyes looking through a wobbling atmosphere. Source: Wikipedia, 'Black drop effect'; Grokipedia, 'black drop effect'.
