question: Carl Littrow, who had inherited Maximilian Hell's papers at Vienna, went through the original data sheets from Hell's 1769 transit at Vardo, inside the Arctic Circle. He found figures scraped out and written over in ink of a slightly different shade, and he published the charge that Hell had faked his results. The charge stood for decades. In 1883 Simon Newcomb examined the very same sheets. What did Newcomb discover?
answer: Littrow was colour-blind, and the two inks were one ink.
choices: Littrow was colour-blind, and the two inks were one ink.
The darker ink was added at Vienna years after Hell died.
The ink had faded unevenly where the sheets were kept damp.
Littrow's own hand had made the changes while cataloguing.
context: Newcomb first showed that the smudges had been made with a wet finger while the ink was still fresh -- corrections made on the spot by an observer fixing his own numbers, not a forger's later work. Then he found that Littrow, who had convicted Hell on the evidence of colour, could not distinguish colours. Hell's Vardo data were sound. The lesson generalises: when a charge rests on one man's observation, check the observer. Source: faculty.fairfield.edu/jmac/sj/hell.htm; Wikipedia, 'Maximilian Hell'; Newcomb's 1883 paper "On Hell's alleged falsification of his observations of the transit of Venus in 1769".

question: Johann Encke reworked every 1761 and 1769 transit timing in 1824 and put the Sun at 153.3 million kilometres, against a true 149.6 million, an error of two and a half per cent. Then in 1961 teams in the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain each got the figure independently, and none of them watched Venus cross anything. How did the three teams get their figure?
answer: They bounced radio pulses off Venus and timed the returning echo.
choices: They bounced radio pulses off Venus and timed the returning echo.
They photographed Venus from opposite poles on the same night.
They timed starlight grazing the Sun's edge during an eclipse.
They weighed the Sun's pull with pendulums at three latitudes.
context: Muhleman and colleagues, using 12.5 cm radar, published 149,598,845 km give or take 250 km; Millstone Hill got 149,597,700 and Jodrell Bank 149,601,000. That is a few hundred kilometres of uncertainty, not metres -- the metre-level figures came later, from tracking spacecraft, and in 2012 the IAU simply defined the astronomical unit as exactly 149,597,870,700 metres. The transits were not wasted, either: Thomas Hornsby's reduction of the 1769 data gave 93,726,900 miles against a true 92,955,000 -- an error of 0.8 per cent, from men timing a black dot by pendulum clock on a Pacific beach. Source: Muhleman et al., Astronomical Journal 67, 191 (1962); IEEE, 'The 1961 JPL Venus radar experiment'; Wikipedia, 'Astronomical unit' and '1769 transit of Venus observed from Tahiti'.

question: A student lays one of her hairs under a microscope, a strand about 70 micrometres wide, or 70 millionths of a metre. Most of her cells measure only about 10 to 30 micrometres across. How many of them, side by side, would span the hair?
answer: About two to seven
choices: About two to seven
About sixty to eighty
About five hundred
About ten thousand
context: A typical human cell runs 10-30 micrometres, and 70 divided by 30 is about two. Laid end to end, a few dozen E. coli bacteria, each about 2 micrometres long, would span the same hair, and a bacterium holds a thousandth of a human cell's volume or less. Sources: Medical News Today, 'How many cells are in the human body?'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escherichia_coli (about 2 micrometres long, 0.6-0.7 cubic micrometres).

question: Ron Sender and Ron Milo counted a human body's cells in 2016 and got about 30 trillion; Eva Bianconi's 2013 count reached about 37 trillion. Both found most of those cells, 84 percent in the 2016 count, belong to one tiny kind making up only a few percent of the body's mass. Which kind?
answer: Red blood cells
choices: Red blood cells
Skin cells shed from the outer layer
Fat cells stored under the skin
Muscle cells in the heart and gut
context: Each red blood cell is about 8 micrometres across and jettisons its nucleus before entering circulation -- which is why it stays small and fast and is thrown away after ~120 days. Bianconi's team counted about 26 trillion red cells, some 70 percent of its total; the 2016 recount found about 25 trillion, 84 percent of a smaller total. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016.

question: Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo simply redid the arithmetic in 2016 on a line textbooks and talks had repeated for forty years: 'you are only 10 percent human -- bacteria outnumber your own cells ten to one.' What ratio did the fresh count give?
answer: Roughly 1.3 bacteria to 1 human cell
choices: Roughly 1.3 bacteria to 1 human cell
Roughly 100 bacteria to 1 human cell
Roughly 1 bacterium to 10 human cells
Roughly 1,000 bacteria to 1 human cell
context: The 10:1 line traced back to a single 1972 back-of-the-envelope estimate by microbiologist Thomas Luckey and had never been checked. The whole microbiome weighs about 0.2 kg, not the widely repeated 1-2 kg. A myth killed by careful counting -- no new instrument needed. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016.

question: Olivier Gros, a marine biologist, pulled sunken mangrove leaves from the shallow seafloor of Guadeloupe in the Caribbean in 2009 and saw long white threads on them. Each thread turned out to be a single bacterial cell, though almost every bacterium ever known has been tiny. When his team measured one, how big was that single cell?
answer: Up to about 2 centimetres long -- visible without a microscope
choices: Up to about 2 centimetres long -- visible without a microscope
Up to about 100 micrometres -- just visible in a hand lens
Up to about 5 micrometres -- typical bacterial size
Up to about 2 millimetres -- the size of a pinhead
context: Thiomargarita magnifica -- 'magnificent' -- can be picked up with tweezers, roughly 5,000 times larger than a normal bacterium and 50 times larger than the previous record-holder. Gros first spotted the threads in 2009; the species was formally described in Science in June 2022. Sources: Guinness World Records, Largest bacterium; Natural History Museum (UK), 'World's largest bacteria are visible to the naked eye'.

question: Biologists described Thiomargarita magnifica, from a mangrove swamp in Guadeloupe, in 2022: a bacterium thousands of times bigger than the usual 5 micrometres. A cell's surface must be big enough for its volume, so by the usual rule it should starve, its middle too far from its skin. It does not. What cheat lets the giant get around that trap?
answer: A vast internal vacuole pins its living cytoplasm to the outer skin
choices: A vast internal vacuole pins its living cytoplasm to the outer skin
It streams its cytoplasm round and round to stir food in
It grows a second, inner surface to double its intake area
It slows its metabolism to about a hundredth of normal
context: The central vacuole fills 65-80% of the cell, so the living, hungry cytoplasm sits as a thin shell against the outside -- and its DNA is packed into membrane-bound sacs called 'pepins' rather than floating loose. Bacteria are supposed not to have membrane-bound organelles; this one does. Source: Natural History Museum (UK), 2022.

question: A runner wiggles her toe, at the far end of the longest cell in her body, which starts at the base of her spine roughly a metre away. The surface-to-volume rule says a cell that grows too big starves in the middle. How does this one get away with it?
answer: It is a thin thread, so every point is still close to its surface
choices: It is a thin thread, so every point is still close to its surface
It draws all its food from the fluid around the spinal cord
It survives on stored food and dies after a few weeks
It is actually thousands of small cells fused end to end
context: A motor neuron running from the lumbar spinal cord to the foot is a single cell -- but a wire, not a ball. The surface-to-volume trap punishes SPHERES; stretch the same volume into a thread and the surface stays generous. The rule bends where the shape bends. Source: Interesting Engineering, 'How many cells are in the human body?'

question: A first-year microbiology student sets a single E. coli cell on a warm dish of nutrient jelly with all the food it can eat. The rod-shaped bacterium, the workhorse organism of biology labs, splits into two roughly every 20 minutes. What is the consequence of that little number?
answer: One invisible cell becomes a visible colony overnight
choices: One invisible cell becomes a visible colony overnight
The population level stabilises within a few hours
Individual cells grow steadily larger for a day
Only every tenth cell on the dish stays alive
context: 20 minutes is the ideal-broth doubling time; nothing in nature ever gets ideal broth for long, or the biosphere would be one enormous petri dish. Source: Medical News Today, 'How many cells are in the human body?'

question: A biology student labels a diagram of the retina: red cone, green cone, blue cone, each tuned to a different range of light wavelengths. Researchers have carefully measured each cone's response to every wavelength across the rainbow. Where does the so-called red cone actually peak?
answer: In greenish-yellow, just past the green cone's peak
choices: In greenish-yellow, just past the green cone's peak
In deep red, far past the green cone's peak
In orange, roughly midway between green and red
In blue-green, just short of the green cone's peak
context: The measured peaks: S about 420 nm, M about 534 nm, L about 564 nm — and the L and M pigments overlap broadly right through the yellow-green. Wikipedia is blunt: 'while the L cones have been referred to simply as red receptors, microspectrophotometry has shown that their peak sensitivity is in the greenish-yellow region of the spectrum.' Red is not the wavelength the L cone likes best. Red is what you see when L outruns M. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Color_vision (checked first); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_vision; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cone_cell.

question: A teenager fills her phone screen with a solid patch of yellow and presses a magnifying loupe against the glass. A screen is built from pixels, and each pixel from a few smaller subpixels, small enough for the loupe to pull apart. What is actually sitting under the glass where the yellow looks solid?
answer: Red and green dots firing together, with no yellow dot
choices: Red and green dots firing together, with no yellow dot
Yellow dots packed in between the red and green ones
White dots shining up through a thin yellow filter
Orange and green dots blurring together at this size
context: Wikipedia: 'A single pixel on a color display is made of several subpixels, typically three arranged left-to-right as red, green, and blue (RGB),' and 'the components are readily visible with a small magnifying glass, such as a loupe.' The screen fires red and green so that a viewer's three cones receive the same three numbers real yellow light would produce. Two physically different spectra a human cannot tell apart are called METAMERS, and because the eye samples the whole spectrum at only three points they are unavoidable — Grokipedia notes that human vision 'samples the spectrum at only three points, ignoring finer variations that might distinguish the stimuli physically.' Photography, television and printing are all built on that blind spot. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subpixel_rendering; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamerism_(color); grokipedia.com/page/Color_photography.

question: James Clerk Maxwell stacked three projected plates on one screen at a Royal Institution talk in London on 17 May 1861, one lantern and one filter for each. Thomas Sutton had shot one object three times, through a red filter, a green filter and a blue-violet filter, for this first lasting colour photograph. What was the object?
answer: A tartan ribbon
choices: A tartan ribbon
A bowl of oranges
A vase of roses
A stained-glass panel
context: Maxwell had predicted the whole trick in a paper read to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in March 1855 — six years before anyone made the picture. The surviving 1861 photograph is held at the Science Museum in London. Sutton patented the world's first single-lens reflex camera that same year: a wooden sliding box with a movable mirror, so a photographer could see exactly what the lens saw. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sutton_(photographer); grokipedia.com/page/James_Clerk_Maxwell; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell. (Grokipedia's separate Color photography page says Royal Society of London; two other sources say Royal Institution, which is used here.)

question: Ewald Hering put a test to Hermann von Helmholtz in 1870s Germany that needed no laboratory, only the imagination. Helmholtz taught that colours mix freely in the head; Hering said some pairs of colours fight each other and refuse to blend. Which of these four colours does ordinary seeing never show?
answer: A reddish green
choices: A reddish green
A greenish blue
A reddish yellow
A bluish red
context: Greenish blue is teal, reddish yellow is orange, bluish red is purple — but a reddish green is nothing at all, and neither is a bluish yellow. Wikipedia puts it exactly: 'In the same way that there cannot exist a "slightly negative" positive number, a single eye cannot perceive a bluish-yellow or a reddish-green.' Three independent sensors predict no such hole, so Hering proposed instead that colour rides on OPPOSING pairs — red set against green, blue against yellow — which makes a reddish green a colour that cancels itself. In ordinary viewing the rule holds, though in 1983 Hewitt Crane and Thomas Piantanida reported volunteers seeing 'forbidden' reddish greens when an image was held perfectly still on the retina, a claim still argued over. Sources give the year as 1872, 1878 and 1892, so 'the 1870s' is the safe framing. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_vision; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewald_Hering; webvision.pitt.edu (colour perception); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impossible_color.

question: A reader stops and stares at a strong solid red book cover, eyes fixed on one point, for a full half-minute. Then she turns to a blank white wall. A shape floats there. What colour is it?
answer: A green shape
choices: A green shape
A blue shape
A grey shape
A red shape
context: Around 25 to 30 seconds of fixation is the standard figure. Grokipedia describes the mechanism: 'prolonged fixation on a color like red fatigues the red-excitatory channel, leading to rebound excitation in the green-inhibitory counterpart when viewing a white field, resulting in a green afterimage.' The afterimage always arrives as the opponent partner — a green square gives magenta, blue gives yellow. The blank wall shows the retina's own wiring at work. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Color_vision; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opponent_process; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afterimage.

question: Thomas Young spoke to the Royal Society about colour vision in November 1801. He had no anatomy to show, since cones would not be found for generations, so his argument rested on reasoning alone. He rejected one theory of the retina. Which theory did he reject?
answer: A separate nerve for each of the thousands of tints the eye can tell apart
choices: A separate nerve for each of the thousands of tints the eye can tell apart
A separate kind of nerve for each of the seven hues Newton had named in sunlight
A single kind of nerve, reporting each hue by the rate at which it vibrates
A pair of nerves for every hue, one to report it and one to report its opposite
context: Young reasoned his way to three receptors before anyone could see a cone. His Bakerian Lecture 'On the Theory of Light and Colours' was delivered on 12 November 1801 and published the following year, and he argued from impossibility rather than anatomy: as one summary of the paper puts it, 'perception of colour can be coded by three principal colour receptors rather than thousands of colour receptors coding for individual colours.' A separate nerve for every wavelength was not a thing a retina could plausibly carry. Hermann von Helmholtz took the idea up around 1850, which is why it is called the Young-Helmholtz theory. (The famous verbatim Young quote about 'each sensitive point of the retina' could not be checked against the primary text, so it is not quoted here.) Sources: webvision.pitt.edu (colour perception); grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Young_(scientist); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young–Helmholtz_theory.

question: Thomas Sutton shot three filtered plates for James Clerk Maxwell's first colour photograph, outdoors in bright sunlight, one exposure through each filter. Wet collodion plates responded far better to blue light than to red. The blue-filtered plate was finished in about six seconds. How long did the red-filtered plate take?
answer: About eight minutes
choices: About eight minutes
About twenty seconds
About ninety seconds
About forty minutes
context: Grokipedia's figures for that session: roughly 6 seconds for the blue-filtered image, 8 minutes for red, and 12 minutes for green, all in bright sunlight. The red exposure ran about eighty times as long as the blue one, under the same sun and on the same subject. Wikipedia's history of the process explains why: collodion was 'for all practical purposes totally insensitive to red light and only marginally sensitive to green.' The exposure figures are single-sourced to Grokipedia's Sutton page; treat the exact numbers as that source's. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sutton_(photographer); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_color_photography.

question: A teacher sends sunlight through a prism and it fans out into a band running from about 700 nanometres at the red end to about 380 at the violet end. She holds a magenta card up against that band and searches all along it without finding a match. Why is magenta not in there?
answer: Magenta needs long and short wavelengths together, with the middle silent
choices: Magenta needs long and short wavelengths together, with the middle silent
Magenta lies past violet, where a prism cannot bend light far enough
Magenta needs more light than a prism throws into one narrow band
Magenta is a printing colour, and inks subtract light instead of adding
context: Magenta is a NON-SPECTRAL colour. It appears when long-wave light around 650-700 nm and short-wave light around 450-500 nm fire the L and S cones together while the M cone stays quiet, and the brain 'interpolates the gap between the spectrum's red and violet ends.' The visible spectrum is a straight line that never closes into a loop; magenta is the stitch the brain invents to join the two ends. Browns and pinks are non-spectral too. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Color_vision (Hue Detection and Non-Spectral Colors).

question: Ralph M. Evans took up a question in 1961 that nobody had asked for a hundred years. Wet collodion plates were, for practical purposes, blind to red light, so the red-filtered plate in Maxwell's 1861 demonstration had no business recording anything at all. It did, and the projection worked. According to Evans in Scientific American, what had got through?
answer: Ultraviolet the red dyes reflected, which the red filter passed
choices: Ultraviolet the red dyes reflected, which the red filter passed
Infrared from the sunlight, which the plate registered as heat
Green light leaking around the edge of the red filter
Blue light bouncing off the bright sky into the lens
context: Ralph M. Evans, 'Maxwell's Color Photograph', Scientific American Vol. 205 No. 5, November 1961: 'many red dyes also reflect ultraviolet light, coincidentally transmitted by Sutton's red filter,' and 'the three images were probably due to ultra-violet, blue-green and blue wavelengths, rather than to red, green and blue.' The founding demonstration of three-colour photography worked by luck — and it took a century before anyone checked the claim instead of repeating it. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_color_photography; scientificamerican.com/article/maxwells-color-photograph/.

question: Ewald Hering insisted colour runs on opposing pairs, each hue cancelling its partner, against Thomas Young and Hermann von Helmholtz, who had the retina holding a few kinds of receptor. For a century the two accounts were treated as rivals; then it turned out both were right, describing the same wire at different points along it. Where does the opponent stage sit?
answer: In the retina's own ganglion cells, before the signal leaves the eye
choices: In the retina's own ganglion cells, before the signal leaves the eye
In the visual cortex, after the signals cross at the optic chiasm
In the cone pigments themselves, as they bleach and regrow
In the optic nerve, where fibres from the two eyes interleave
context: Wikipedia states it exactly: 'trichromacy arises at the level of the receptors, and opponent processes arise at the level of retinal ganglion cells and beyond.' The retina rewrites three cone signals into three channels before they ever reach the brain — L versus M, S versus L plus M, and a plain light-versus-dark luminance channel. That re-encoding is why an afterimage comes back in the opposite colour. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_vision; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opponent_process.

question: A doctor holds up a colour chart for a boy and his sister. Red-green colour blindness turns up in about one man in twelve and about one woman in two hundred, while blue-yellow deficiency, under one person in ten thousand, strikes men and women at the same rate. The difference is genetic architecture, not pigment chemistry. What makes the red-green case so lopsided between the sexes?
answer: Its two genes sit side by side on the X and trade segments easily
choices: Its two genes sit side by side on the X and trade segments easily
Its two genes sit on chromosome 7, which men copy less faithfully
Its two genes are switched off in one of a woman's two X copies
Its two genes lie next to the sex-determining gene on the Y
context: OPN1LW and OPN1MW — the long-wave and medium-wave opsin genes — sit in a TANDEM ARRAY at Xq28 on the X chromosome, governed by a shared locus control region. Near-identical neighbours swap segments during recombination, so the array scrambles easily, and a man with one X has no spare copy to fall back on. The blue-yellow gene OPN1SW sits on chromosome 7 instead — not sex-linked — which is why that deficiency hits both sexes equally, at under 1 in 10,000. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Color_vision; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_blindness.

question: Caitlin McNeill posted a photograph to Tumblr on 26 February 2015 asking whether a dress was white and gold or blue and black, and within a day the argument had swallowed the internet. Roman Originals settled the object question: the dress is royal blue and black. Everyone arguing was looking at exactly the same pixels. What were the two camps' visual systems disagreeing about?
answer: What colour the light falling on the dress had been
choices: What colour the light falling on the dress had been
How many cone types their own retinas carried
How bright their screens were set at the time
Which part of the picture their eyes landed on first
context: Cecilia Bleasdale, the bride's mother, took the photograph in a shop at Cheshire Oaks near Chester, for a wedding on the Scottish island of Colonsay; McNeill's caption read 'guys please help me - is this dress white and gold, or blue and black?' Roman Originals confirmed the real colours on 27 February 2015. Lafer-Sousa, Hermann and Conway surveyed about 1,400 people (Current Biology 25(13):R545, 2015): 57 percent saw blue and black, 30 percent white and gold, 11 percent blue and brown, 2 percent something else. The name for what the brain is doing is COLOUR CONSTANCY — subtracting the colour of the light so an object keeps its identity from noon to lamplight. Bevil Conway described the brain as trying to 'discount the chromatic bias of the daylight axis.' When the researchers simulated yellow room lighting, nearly everyone saw blue and black. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/The_dress; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_dress.

question: Hanne Thoen and her colleagues trained mantis shrimps in 2014 and measured, for the first time, how finely the animals could tell two wavelengths apart. The mantis shrimp is famous for the richest colour equipment on Earth: twelve to sixteen photoreceptor types against the human three. What did the test find?
answer: They failed below about 25 nanometres apart, where humans manage a few
choices: They failed below about 25 nanometres apart, where humans manage a few
They beat humans by roughly ten times across the whole visible range
They matched humans closely, but only inside the ultraviolet band
They beat humans in the red and fell well behind them in the blue
context: Thoen, How, Chiou and Marshall, 'A different form of color vision in mantis shrimp', Science 343:411 (2014), reported 'a surprisingly poor performance': the animals could not discriminate wavelengths less than about 25 nm apart, where a human with three cones manages 1-4 nm. The authors posed the puzzle themselves: 'Why use 12 color channels when three or four are sufficient for fine color discrimination?' The likely answer is that the shrimp compares photoreceptor outputs directly, like scanning a barcode, instead of running them through opponent channels. More sensors turned out to mean less discrimination — and a decade of popular claims had to be rewritten. Sources: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458639/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantis_shrimp; grokipedia.com/page/Mantis_shrimp.

question: Gabriele Jordan's team tested a woman logged as cDa29 in 2010, one of the roughly 12 percent of women who carry the genetic recipe for a fourth cone type. Very few carriers show any measurable gain, only a handful have passed stringent testing, and her case is still debated. By the team's report, what could she do that a three-cone eye cannot?
answer: Tell apart yellows and reds that look identical to everyone else
choices: Tell apart yellows and reds that look identical to everyone else
See a band of ultraviolet beyond the violet end of the spectrum
Pick out colours in light far too dim for anyone else to see
Match a colour from memory weeks after seeing it just once
context: X-inactivation gives a carrier a mosaic retina, so the extra pigment — peaking somewhere around 535-545 nm, between the standard green and red cones — can genuinely be present. Jordan's subject cDa29 discriminated along a fourth dimension in the 546-670 nm range, the stretch running from green-yellow out to deep red (Jordan et al., Journal of Vision 10(8):12, 2010). But Grokipedia notes that 'no new confirmed functional cases have been reported since the early 2010s,' and the finding is still contested — a real claim, not an established one. (Sources disagree on Jordan's institution, so it is left unnamed.) Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Tetrachromacy; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrachromacy.

question: A reader opens a short unclassified summary that the Office of the Director of National Intelligence released on 27 August 2021. It sets out how America's intelligence elements and the National Intelligence Council (NIC) split on how COVID-19 began, each judgement with its confidence word. How does it describe the split?
answer: Four plus the NIC leaned spillover at low confidence; one leaned lab at moderate; three undecided
choices: Four plus the NIC leaned spillover at low confidence; one leaned lab at moderate; three undecided
Six leaned lab at moderate confidence; two leaned spillover at low; the CIA was undecided
The FBI and CIA leaned lab at high confidence; five leaned spillover at low; one undecided
Four plus the NIC leaned lab at low confidence; one leaned spillover at high; three undecided
context: The one element leaning laboratory-related was the FBI, at MODERATE confidence; the four elements plus the National Intelligence Council leaned natural spillover at LOW confidence. Publishing an open, itemised disagreement was the newsworthy thing -- most intelligence products speak as one voice. Source: ODNI unclassified summary (dni.gov / odni.gov).

question: A student reading a report from the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) stops at a set phrase: 'we assess with low confidence.' Every analyst is trained to use the exact words, high, moderate or low confidence. In official intelligence tradecraft, what do those confidence words actually measure?
answer: The quality and consistency of the evidence backing the judgement
choices: The quality and consistency of the evidence backing the judgement
How strongly the analyst personally feels about the conclusion
The share of analysts in the agency who voted for the finding
How much money and manpower the agency put into the report
context: 'Low confidence' does not mean 'we do not believe our conclusion' -- it means 'the underlying evidence is thin, inconclusive, or contradictory, and a reasonable person might read it another way'. Reading assessments without this vocabulary is why headlines routinely mangle intelligence findings. Source: ODNI declassified assessment methodology note.

question: American intelligence analysts put a divided judgement before the public in 2021 on how the COVID-19 pandemic began. Some leaned toward a natural spillover from animals, at low confidence; the lean toward an accidental leak from a laboratory in Wuhan, China, came at moderate confidence. Every intelligence element in the report agreed on one thing about SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes the disease. What was it?
answer: That the virus was not developed as a biological weapon
choices: That the virus was not developed as a biological weapon
That the virus had not been genetically engineered at all
That Chinese officials knew of the virus before the outbreak
That the virus originated in a bat cave in Yunnan province
context: All IC elements agreed the virus was not developed as a bioweapon; most also assessed with low confidence that it was probably not genetically engineered, though two elements said the evidence was too thin to judge either way. The community also judged that China's officials had no foreknowledge of the virus before the outbreak. The bioweapon hypothesis was ruled out early; the argument was over natural spillover versus a research-related accident. Source: ODNI unclassified summary (odni.gov).

question: Analysts at one American agency changed their judgement in February 2023 on how COVID-19 began. From the start scientists had split over the cause: a natural spillover in a wet market, or a leak from the nearby Wuhan Institute of Virology. This agency had been publicly undecided, and now it came down on the side of a lab-related origin, at 'low confidence'. Which agency was it?
answer: The Department of Energy
choices: The Department of Energy
The Central Intelligence Agency
The National Security Agency
The Defense Intelligence Agency
context: The Wall Street Journal broke the DOE shift in February 2023. The CIA did not report a lean until January 2025, when it too came in for a research-related origin at LOW confidence, explicitly noting no new intelligence had driven the change. Sources: NPR 2023-02-27; CBS 2025-01-25.

question: Members of the House Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic released a 520-page final report on December 2, 2024, saying COVID-19 most likely came from a Wuhan lab. One central argument was a biological feature of SARS-CoV-2 that the report said is not seen in nature among the virus's close cousins. What was that feature?
answer: A furin cleavage site in the spike protein
choices: A furin cleavage site in the spike protein
A double-stranded DNA genome instead of single-stranded RNA
A protein coat modelled on the polio virus's capsid
A missing envelope layer typical of ebolavirus
context: The subcommittee argued that the furin cleavage site -- a short stretch that lets the spike protein be cleaved by a common human enzyme, boosting infectivity -- has not been found in any close bat sarbecovirus. The report also cited the star-like early phylogeny (consistent with a single introduction into humans) and reported illness among Wuhan Institute of Virology researchers in autumn 2019. Source: oversight.house.gov COVID Select final report.

question: Chinese investigators swabbed the stall surfaces at the Huanan Seafood Market in Wuhan on 1 January 2020, hours after it was closed. Alongside the virus's RNA they detected DNA from live animals of one particular kind at the wildlife stalls. That co-location, no smoking gun, is the strongest specific evidence for natural spillover. Which animal was it?
answer: Raccoon dogs
choices: Raccoon dogs
Palm civets
Pangolins
Dromedary camels
context: Raccoon dogs -- SARS-CoV-2-susceptible mammals known to have been sold live at Huanan -- had their DNA co-located with viral RNA on the wildlife stall surfaces. That is short of proof any of the raccoon dogs were infected, and no infected intermediate host has ever been identified in years of animal sampling (SARS-CoV-1's civets and MERS's camels were pinned down comparatively fast). WHO's SAGO panel in June 2025 still leaned zoonosis on the weight of such evidence, while stating explicitly that a laboratory incident must remain on the table -- the honest scientific answer at this point is that no one yet knows. Sources: Nature Crits-Christoph et al. 2023; SAGO report 2025-06-27.

question: With the letter N, for nova, Edwin Hubble marked three suspected new stars on his 1923 Andromeda plate. Older plates of the same patch of sky showed one of them getting brighter and dimmer on a regular schedule. What did he do to that mark?
answer: Crossed out the N and wrote VAR! in red ink
choices: Crossed out the N and wrote VAR! in red ink
Circled it and labelled it Nova I
Erased it and drew a red star
Underlined the N three times in pencil
context: Plate H335H still carries the red-ink annotation. The 'VAR!' star is now catalogued as M31-V1, the first Cepheid variable ever identified beyond the Milky Way -- and one word in red ink multiplied the known size of the universe. Source: https://carnegiescience.edu/about/history/archives/plate-archives/m31var

question: Edwin Hubble spotted a Cepheid inside the fuzzy Andromeda nebula in 1923, a star whose brightness pulses on a clock. Henrietta Leavitt had found that the pulse gives such a star's true brightness, so comparing that with how bright it looks gives its distance. Hubble got about 900,000 light years. How far away does today's better answer put Andromeda?
answer: About 2.5 million light years
choices: About 2.5 million light years
About 250,000 light years
About 25 million light years
About 250 million light years
context: The modern number is 2.54 million light years (765 kiloparsecs) -- about 2.8 times Hubble's original 1923 figure. His answer was wrong by nearly a factor of three, but it was already vastly bigger than any then-imagined Milky Way, so the qualitative conclusion held: Andromeda is another galaxy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andromeda_Galaxy

question: Two leading American astronomers faced off on the size of the universe in a public showdown at the U.S. National Museum in Washington, D.C., on 26 April 1920, three years before Hubble's Cepheid settled the question. Who were the two men on stage?
answer: Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis
choices: Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis
Edwin Hubble and Harlow Shapley
Heber Curtis and Vesto Slipher
George Ellery Hale and Edwin Hubble
context: It became known simply as 'the Great Debate.' Shapley put the Milky Way at roughly 300,000 light years across and argued the spiral nebulae were objects inside it; Curtis put the Milky Way at only about 30,000 light years across and argued the spirals were separate 'island universes.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Debate_(astronomy)

question: Harlow Shapley played his strongest card in the Great Debate: a set of photographic measurements by Adriaan van Maanen, who had compared plates of spiral nebulae like the Pinwheel taken years apart. Van Maanen claimed the plates showed the spirals doing something that would be impossible at any great distance. What did they seem to be doing?
answer: Visibly rotating over a few years
choices: Visibly rotating over a few years
Drifting sideways across the sky
Splitting into pairs of stars
Shrinking as they cooled
context: If a spiral really was turning by measurable arc in a few years, its outer edges would be moving faster than light unless it was near enough to sit inside the Milky Way. The measurements were later shown to be spurious -- an artefact of how van Maanen compared plates. Curtis was right about the spirals; Shapley was right that the Milky Way is very large and the Sun is far from its centre. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Debate_(astronomy)

question: Vesto Slipher, a quieter astronomer at the Lowell Observatory, began measuring spiral spectra in 1912, and the redshifts later plotted with Hubble's distances were his data, not Hubble's. He found Andromeda moving toward Earth at about 300 km per second. Of 25 other spirals he measured by 1917, what were almost all of them doing?
answer: Racing away from Earth
choices: Racing away from Earth
Approaching Earth like Andromeda
Standing still relative to Earth
Orbiting the Milky Way
context: Slipher's spectrograph work at Flagstaff was the first hint that the universe was in motion on the largest scale. Hubble and Milton Humason later supplied the distances that turned Slipher's velocities into a straight line on a graph. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesto_Slipher

question: Milton Humason put his name beside Edwin Hubble's on the 1929 distance-velocity paper, an unusual place for a man who had hauled supplies up the mountain as a mule driver and then worked as the observatory janitor. He was hired to the scientific staff in 1919. What formal schooling did he ever have?
answer: None past the eighth grade
choices: None past the eighth grade
Two years of high school
A night-school high-school diploma
A year at a teachers' college
context: Humason turned out to be one of the finest observers of his generation. He took the exquisitely long exposures needed to catch the redshifts of faint, distant galaxies -- exactly the data Hubble's distance ladder needed to make its case. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Humason

question: Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist, met Albert Einstein in Brussels to explain in person what he had worked out in 1927: that Einstein's own equations of general relativity pointed to a growing universe with a beginning. Einstein's reply, in French, became famous. By Lemaitre's own memory, what was Einstein's verdict?
answer: That the calculations were correct but the physics abominable
choices: That the calculations were correct but the physics abominable
That the calculations were wrong, so the universe stayed static
That the physics was sound but the calculations careless
That the idea was elegant but beyond any telescope's test
context: In the original French: 'Vos calculs sont corrects, mais votre physique est abominable.' Einstein had earlier added his 'cosmological constant' to general relativity precisely to keep the universe static; by George Gamow's later account, Einstein called it his greatest blunder. The exact wording of the Lemaitre exchange is by Lemaitre's later recollection, so it is preserved here as testimony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Lema%C3%AEtre  (Legend.)

question: Walter Baade told a stunned International Astronomical Union meeting in Rome in 1952 about a fix that roughly doubled every extragalactic distance overnight. Hubble's 1929 slope had given a Hubble constant of about 500 km/s per megaparsec, which meant a universe only about 2 billion years old, younger than rocks already dated on Earth. What had Baade found?
answer: Cepheid variables come in two populations with different luminosities
choices: Cepheid variables come in two populations with different luminosities
Andromeda contains a supermassive black hole distorting the distances
Interstellar dust dims Cepheids by a factor of two
The Milky Way itself is drifting toward Andromeda at 300 km/s
context: Baade had used Mount Wilson during the wartime Los Angeles blackouts to resolve individual stars in Andromeda's core. Hubble had been reading Population II Cepheids against a Population I calibration -- his photography was fine; the standard candle was miscalibrated. Correcting the populations doubled the distance scale, pushed the age of the universe past the age of the Earth, and dissolved the paradox. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Baade

question: The SH0ES team read the Hubble constant from its local ladder of Cepheids and supernovae and got about 73 km/s/Mpc, confirmed by the James Webb Space Telescope in 2023. The Planck satellite, fitting the cosmic microwave background, reads 67.4. The two answers now disagree by more than chance can explain. Where does the field stand on why?
answer: Nobody yet knows -- it may be a hidden systematic, or genuinely new physics
choices: Nobody yet knows -- it may be a hidden systematic, or genuinely new physics
The Planck value is confirmed; the local ladder has a known dust bias
The local ladder is confirmed; Planck missed a foreground galaxy
The two are being averaged into a single accepted value of 70
context: This is the 'Hubble tension' -- one of the sharpest live disagreements in cosmology, and one told honestly here rather than papered over. If the tension survives further tests, it points at unknown physics in the early universe (extra radiation, evolving dark energy, or something stranger); if it dies, someone will have found a subtle systematic in one of the two pipelines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_tension

question: The makers of the 1991 comedy Naked Gun 2½: The Smell of Fear dressed a bar-room scene with framed photographs of history's most famous disasters. Among them hung the year-old Hubble Space Telescope and its flawed mirror. Which pair did the joke put Hubble between?
answer: The Hindenburg and the Titanic
choices: The Hindenburg and the Titanic
The Tacoma Narrows Bridge and the Teton Dam
Chernobyl and the Andrea Doria
The Maginot Line and the Spruce Goose
context: Hubble launched aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery on 24 April 1990; on 21 June the project manager announced that it could not be properly focused. America turned it into a joke. Humorist Dave Barry called it the 'Orbiting Space Punch Line,' and Senator Barbara Mikulski -- one of the telescope's strongest defenders in Congress -- called it a 'techno-turkey' with a 'cataract.' On 13 January 1994, after the repair, that same senator stood beside NASA Administrator Dan Goldin, showed the first sharp pictures, and announced: 'The trouble with Hubble is over.' Sources: NASA Science, 'Hubble's Comeback Story'; NASA History, 'Lewis Experts Supported a Critical Repair on Hubble in the 1990s'; NASA Goddard SVS, 'Senator Mikulski Celebrates Hubble Success'; NASA, 'Hubble Space Telescope Optical Systems Failure Report' (Allen Commission, Nov 1990), Executive Summary.

question: Astronomers aimed both of Hubble's high-resolution cameras at a single star in 1990, and each sent back the same photo. The mirror's outer rim was a bit too flat, a flaw opticians call spherical aberration. What did that photo of the star show?
answer: A small bright core drowned in a wide halo
choices: A small bright core drowned in a wide halo
A short comet-like tail flaring to one side
A line stretched one way, squeezed the other
A sharp point fringed with red and blue
context: Rim light and centre light never met at one point, so a star arrived not as a point but as a bright spot wrapped in a halo holding most of its light. Both high-resolution cameras -- the Wide Field/Planetary Camera and the Faint Object Camera -- showed the same signature, which is how investigators knew the trouble lay in the mirrors themselves. Other optical faults leave other signatures: a comet-tail smear is coma, a stretched line is astigmatism, and colour fringes are chromatic aberration -- which a mirror cannot produce at all, because reflection does not depend on the colour of the light. That is exactly why Isaac Newton, having concluded that a colour-free lens telescope could not be built, made his telescope out of a mirror. Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Executive Summary and Appendix C; Wikipedia, 'Newton's reflector.'

question: Perkin-Elmer's polishers left the outer edge of Hubble's 2.4-metre mirror too flat, and the telescope, launched in April 1990, sent back fuzzy first images and became a national joke. The whole blunder lay in that one edge. By how much was it too flat?
answer: About 2.2 micrometres, roughly 1/450 of a millimetre
choices: About 2.2 micrometres, roughly 1/450 of a millimetre
About 22 micrometres, roughly 1/45 of a millimetre
About 0.22 millimetres, roughly 1/5 of a millimetre
About 2.2 millimetres, roughly 1/450 of a metre
context: About 2,200 nanometres -- 2.2 micrometres, or roughly 1/11,000 of an inch. That was the whole error. The contract asked Hubble to put 70 percent of a star's light inside a circle 0.1 arcsecond in radius; what it delivered was 70 percent inside 0.7 arcsecond, ten times wider. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Hubble Space Telescope'; Physics Today, 'Hubble's blurry years'; NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter V 'The Failure.'

question: Lew Allen's board opened Perkin-Elmer's Danbury file in 1990, since Hubble's 2.4-metre mirror was already in orbit and out of reach. The file held the tests on the finished glass against its template, the target shape the polishers had been told to work to. How closely did the glass match that template?
answer: It beat the contract tolerance across the whole disc
choices: It beat the contract tolerance across the whole disc
It met the contract tolerance exactly, edge to centre
It beat the contract tolerance at the centre but not the rim
It fell just short of the contract tolerance everywhere
context: The fit was better than 0.014-wave rms at 632.8 nanometres -- in the Board's words, 'better than the contract specification.' The grinding was superb; the shape they had been aiming at was not. That is the distinction this whole story exists to teach: precision means landing in the same spot every time, accuracy means landing in the right spot, and Hubble had one without the other. It went unnoticed partly because no end-to-end test of the assembled telescope was ever made -- checking the finished optics at full accuracy would have needed a large flat mirror plus a spherical one about 15 percent larger, two more mirrors as big as Hubble's own, at roughly the cost of the entire optical telescope assembly. The Board noted that in hindsight 'a much less severe test could have been done to check for a gross' error. NASA formed the investigating board on 2 July 1990 under Lew Allen, director of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory; it found the mirror 'made in the wrong shape, being too much flattened away from the mirror's center,' an error 'ten times larger than the specified tolerance.' Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter IV sections D and E, and Executive Summary.

question: Perkin-Elmer's opticians polished Hubble's mirror against a null corrector, a rig of two small mirrors and a field lens that shows a featureless pattern only when the glass has reached the shape wanted. In 1990 Lew Allen's board measured the rig. What was wrong with it?
answer: Its field lens sat about a millimetre out of position
choices: Its field lens sat about a millimetre out of position
Its field lens had been ground to the wrong curvature
One of its two mirrors was tilted a fraction of a degree
One of its two mirrors had been polished a shade too flat
context: The reflective null corrector's internal spacings had to be right to 10 micrometres. Its field lens was sitting about 1.3 millimetres too far from the lower mirror -- roughly 130 times the allowed tolerance -- and nobody at Perkin-Elmer ever re-verified the corrector's dimensions after it was first assembled. The rig was a novel design of Perkin-Elmer's own, and one of the things that won the firm the Hubble contract. In 1990 the Board found that corrector and its interferometer still standing in the test chamber, unused and unchanged since 1982, measured the lens spacing in place, and reported that 'the measured amount, 1.3 mm, accounts in detail for the amount and character of the observed image blurring.' The murder weapon was still on the table. Mismark a ruler and every length measured with it comes out wrong -- and this was the ruler. Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Executive Summary and Chapters IV and VII.

question: Jim Crocker, the engineer leading the design, stood in a hotel room in Germany, stuck. Ten small corrective mirrors had to reach into Hubble's light beams, yet the package holding them had to slide into a bay about the size of a telephone booth. What did he notice in that room?
answer: A showerhead on a rod, folded flat to the wall
choices: A showerhead on a rod, folded flat to the wall
A reading lamp on a hinged arm above the bed
A shaving mirror swung out beside the basin
A luggage rack that dropped from the wardrobe
context: This is Crocker's own account of where the idea came from. At a meeting in Germany in late 1990 he noticed that his hotel showerhead rode on a vertical rod and could be clamped at any height and angle -- and the maid had left it folded flat against the wall, taking up almost no space. Fold the mirrors flat, slide them in, then deploy them on arms into the beam. COSTAR (Corrective Optics Space Telescope Axial Replacement) cost roughly $50 million, was built by Ball Aerospace, and carried ten mirrors about 18 to 24 millimetres across on swing-out arms, feeding corrected light to the Faint Object Camera, the Faint Object Spectrograph and the Goddard High Resolution Spectrograph. To make room for it, the High Speed Photometer -- judged the least important of the four axial instruments -- was pulled out and brought home. Sources: 'Life With Hubble: An insider's view of the world's most famous telescope' (IOP), ch. 3; Georgia Tech AE seminar bio of James Crocker; Wikipedia, 'COSTAR.'

question: Lew Allen's board set up one of Perkin-Elmer's alignment tools in July 1990 and took a fresh interferogram, a picture of the mirror's shape written in light and dark fringes. It showed the flaw plainly. Then the board went looking for an older interferogram to compare it with. Where did the matching 1982 photo turn up?
answer: In the personal notebook of a Perkin-Elmer employee
choices: In the personal notebook of a Perkin-Elmer employee
In the sealed quality-assurance file at NASA headquarters
In the launch-readiness review submitted to Congress
In the microfilmed test records at the Danbury plant
context: The Board's fresh interferogram was taken on 22 July 1990; the one in the notebook was dated 22 June 1982. The two were virtually identical, both clearly showing spherical aberration. The proof had been sitting in a private notebook for eight years. The mirror's own timeline explains how there was time for that: rough grinding began in December 1978 at Wilton, Connecticut, polishing was finished at Danbury in April 1981, the final post-coating test was made in February 1982 -- and then the mirror waited eight years for a launch, already the wrong shape, with every test saying it was perfect. Hence the report's central sentence, and the reason this story is taught: 'The most unfortunate aspect of this HST optical system failure, however, is that the data revealing these errors were available from time to time in the fabrication process, but were not recognized and fully investigated at the time.' Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter I, Chapter VI (Figure 6-2), and Executive Summary.

question: Sandra Faber and her team helped pin Hubble's blur down as spherical aberration, and soon it was measured exactly. The telescope spent three and a half years with the wrong mirror, so observers ran deconvolution, a procedure that starts from a known blur and works back through it, on pictures already taken. What did the restored pictures show?
answer: One blob came apart into a group of separate stars
choices: One blob came apart into a group of separate stars
One star's halo drew in to a hard, bright ring
One star's halo vanished, its core left as it was
One galaxy came out finer than the mirror could record
context: Richardson-Lucy iterations, and rival methods such as maximum entropy, put photons back where they belonged, and could pull apart what had looked like one blob into individual stars. The Space Telescope Science Institute ran workshops on 'The Restoration of HST Images and Spectra'; the second, on 18-19 November 1993, drew 126 participants and 55 papers -- two weeks before the repair crew launched. Hubble was never useless in the meantime. Roughly 40 percent of the planned observing programmes went ahead with the aberrated telescope, project scientist Robert O'Dell's own figure: about 15 percent of a star's light still landed in a sharp core while the other 85 percent smeared into a halo several arcseconds across, so compact bright objects came through, the spectrographs worked whenever the field was not crowded, and ultraviolet observations were precious because almost nothing else could make them. Blurry-era results include the proplyds -- the dusty disks around newborn stars, picked out in 1992 images of the Orion Nebula -- and SN 1987A's thin tilted ring with debris moving at 6,000 km/s. Hubble also had a second, unrelated problem: crossing the day/night line each 94-minute orbit, the solar arrays' booms expanded and contracted in the temperature swing and shook the telescope. Sources: Physics Today, 'Hubble's blurry years'; Astronomical Society of the Pacific, 'The New and Improved Hubble Space Telescope'; STScI, 'The Restoration of HST Images and Spectra II'; ESA, 'How Hubble got its wings.'

question: Astronauts carried two new instruments up to Hubble in December 1993: Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, and COSTAR (Corrective Optics Space Telescope Axial Replacement), a package of ten small mirrors on swing-out arms. Nobody could regrind the 2.4-metre primary mirror in orbit, so the fix had to work on the light after it left that mirror. What did the new optics do to the beam?
answer: They carried the equal and opposite error, cancelling the mirror's
choices: They carried the equal and opposite error, cancelling the mirror's
They cropped the beam down to the mirror's well-shaped centre
They split the beam and recombined it to average the blur away
They steered each colour of the beam to a detector of its own
context: Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 carried relay mirrors with the inverse aberration ground into them, correcting the light before it reached its four CCDs; COSTAR swung its ten small mirrors into the beams of the three older instruments. The telescope's own bad data had specified its own prescription. Servicing Mission 1 flew as STS-61 on Endeavour, launched 2 December 1993 with a crew of seven -- Richard Covey, Ken Bowersox, Kathryn Thornton, Claude Nicollier, Jeffrey Hoffman, Story Musgrave and Thomas Akers -- and two alternating spacewalk pairs made five EVAs totalling 35 hours 28 minutes, a record at the time, installing WFPC2 and COSTAR and fitting new solar arrays, gyroscopes and a computer upgrade. It landed on 13 December 1993. Sources: NASA Science, 'Hubble's Mirror Flaw'; Wikipedia, 'COSTAR' and 'STS-61'; NASA History, '30 Years Ago: STS-61, the First Hubble Servicing Mission.'

question: An operator at Perkin-Elmer set the spacings inside a null corrector, two small mirrors and a field lens stacked along one beam, by bouncing a laser onto the polished end of an Invar metering rod. A small cap sat over the rod's end. The laser came back clean, and the operator wrote down a number wrong by more than a millimetre. What had the laser reflected off?
answer: The cap's own metal, bared around its central hole
choices: The cap's own metal, bared around its central hole
The rounded end of a second rod, one place over
The polished underside of the field lens above it
The lower mirror of the corrector, down the beam
context: The top of the field cap was coated with non-reflecting material -- and in the Board's words, 'some of this material had, apparently inadvertently, broken away from a small area around the field cap aperture,' so the operator's laser auto-reflected off that exposed metal instead of the rod end. One wrong reflecting surface, and the field lens ended up 1.3 millimetres out. Invar is a metal that barely expands with temperature, which is why the rods were made of it. The Board rebuilt the setup in 1990 and tried the measurement itself: 'A test performed in 1990 with the equipment showed that it was quite easy, even probable, to make this error with the configuration used.' The mistake was designed in, not merely careless. Note that the popular retelling differs from the official finding: in September 1990 the Baltimore Sun reported strong evidence that a technician had put the flat end of the rod, rather than the finely polished rounded end, into the cap, and quoted board chairman Lew Allen calling the error 'painful and tragic' and saying 'adequate prudence was not taken.' The published report settles on the field-cap reflection. Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter VII and Figure 7-5; Baltimore Sun, 'Upside-down rod blamed as cause of Hubble flaw,' 14 Sept 1990.

question: Technicians at Perkin-Elmer brought the field lens of Hubble's null corrector toward the end of rod B and ran out of travel in the positioning screws. The rig of two small mirrors and a field lens, held on long metal rods, projected the test pattern the 2.4-metre mirror was polished to match. The lens would not go where their measurement said it belonged. What did they do next?
answer: Slipped extra spacers in behind the lens
choices: Slipped extra spacers in behind the lens
Reground the rod ends until it seated
Swapped in the spare rod and started over
Logged the shortfall for the designers
context: 'There was no adjustment left in the screws used for this positioning,' the Board found. Rather than ask why the lens would not reach, the technicians made the extra room by inserting spacers between the field lens and the lower mirror mounting plate -- and the adjustment mechanism was then never staked, that is, secured against movement, even though staking was a specified procedure. The apparatus had physically resisted the wrong setting, and the resistance was engineered around. Source: NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter VII, p. 7-7.

question: Opticians in Perkin-Elmer's optical division discounted two warnings at Danbury, one as early as 1982. An inverse null corrector, built to mimic the reflection of a perfect mirror, and a refractive corrector made only of lenses ran alongside the reflective one, and both showed something was wrong. Lew Allen's board asked why the division set them aside. What did the board find?
answer: That the division trusted no instrument but the reflective corrector
choices: That the division trusted no instrument but the reflective corrector
That the division blamed the odd readings on chamber vibration
That the division's report of them reached NASA too late to matter
That the division's managers overruled the staff who flagged them
context: The Board was blunt: because Perkin-Elmer had concluded the reflective corrector was the only device accurate enough, it refused to consider any less-accurate independent measurement, and 'such independent data were obtained incidental to other measurements and were rationalized away due to this mindset.' It also found that the Optical Operations Division ran a 'closed-door' environment 'which permitted discrepant data to be discounted without review,' and that some technical staff there 'were deeply concerned at the time that the discrepant optical data might indicate a flaw' but never raised it outside the division -- nobody overruled them, because nobody outside ever heard. Then the Board checked the instruments that had been dismissed: an analysis 'verified that the RvNC was accurate to better than 0.02 wave rms,' and of the inverse corrector the report says it 'was quite accurate enough to detect the gross error, and indeed did so.' The witnesses nobody believed had been telling the truth. The Board also found the failure to press 'particularly surprising since the members were aware of the history of manufacture of other Ritchey-Chretien telescopes, where spherical aberration was known to be a common problem.' Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Executive Summary, Chapter VI, and Chapter IX 'Judgmental Statements' items 2, 4, 7 and 9.

question: Eastman Kodak's opticians polished and tested a 2.4-metre mirror of their own, a spare Hubble primary that NASA had directed Perkin-Elmer to order from its rival. Lew Allen's board listed that subcontract among the opportunities NASA let slip. What check did the subcontract make available that NASA never ran?
answer: Having Kodak's finished mirror checked against Perkin-Elmer's
choices: Having Kodak's finished mirror checked against Perkin-Elmer's
Having Kodak weigh the two finished mirrors against each other
Having Kodak's polishers audit Perkin-Elmer's polishing logs
Having Kodak's opticians witness Perkin-Elmer's final mirror test
context: Kodak polished its mirror against a refractive and a reflective null corrector of completely different design, matched both templates to better than 0.014-wave rms, and the Board 'has every reason to believe it is the correct hyperboloidal shape.' A correct Hubble mirror existed on Earth the whole time. The two firms were fierce competitors, and the Board wrote that 'NASA did not utilize the opportunity offered by this directed subcontract to validate, and gain confidence in, the P-E approach to the primary mirror manufacture.' Two independent answers existed and were never put side by side -- which is the cheapest test in science and the one nobody ran. Kodak's mirror was never aluminised; it sat in storage at Danbury until the end of 2000 and is now in the collection of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter IV section D and Chapter IX item 5; Smithsonian NASM object record, 'Mirror, Primary Backup, Hubble Space Telescope.'

question: John Playfair resigned in 1782, at age 34, from a job he had held for nine years, so he could tutor students in Edinburgh and study mathematics and science full time. In 1788 he sailed to Siccar Point with the geologist James Hutton. What job had he given up?
answer: Minister of two country parishes in Scotland
choices: Minister of two country parishes in Scotland
Surveyor of harbours for the Royal Navy
Physician at the Edinburgh public infirmary
Engineer at a coal mine in Lanarkshire
context: Playfair was ordained in the Church of Scotland in August 1773 and served the united parishes of Liff and Benvie until he resigned in 1782 to tutor and pursue mathematics. By 1785 he was joint Professor of Mathematics at the University of Edinburgh - the post he held when he stepped into Hutton's boat three years later. Source: Grokipedia, 'John Playfair'; Wikipedia, 'John Playfair'.

question: A crew hung off the cliff at Siccar Point, on the few metres of rock James Hutton pointed at in 1788. The American Museum of Natural History in New York wanted its guests to stand before that same exposure. What did the crew do?
answer: They painted it with thick liquid latex and lifted the mould
choices: They painted it with thick liquid latex and lifted the mould
They cut a slab from the cliff with a diamond-toothed saw
They photographed it and printed it life-size on a wall
They quarried matching stone and rebuilt it by hand
context: Research Casting International hung on scaffolding off the cliffs at Siccar Point and painted a large section of the rocks with thick liquid latex to make the mould; the resulting cast of Hutton's Unconformity stands in the Gottesman Hall of Planet Earth at the American Museum of Natural History. In October 2022 the International Union of Geological Sciences put Siccar Point first on its list of 100 global geological heritage sites. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siccar Point'.

question: James Hutton hired a boat down the Berwickshire coast in the spring of 1788 and landed at Siccar Point. Grey rock layers stand there almost on end, with red-brown layers flat across their tops. He told his two companions the grey rock had a long history before any red sand settled on it. What had it been through?
answer: Laid down flat, hardened, tilted on end, worn down, then drowned
choices: Laid down flat, hardened, tilted on end, worn down, then drowned
Settled from one universal ocean that afterwards drained away
Buckled upright by a great flood that then laid down the sand
Folded upright while still soft, then buried by blowing sand
context: Hutton called what the sea had exposed there 'a beautiful picture of this junction washed bare by the sea.' The grey rock is greywacke: laid down flat on a sea floor, hardened into stone, folded and lifted until it stood on end, worn off to a flat stump, and drowned again before the red sand ever arrived. The two men with him were the mathematician John Playfair and Sir James Hall of Dunglass, from whose family estate the boat had set out. Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton' and 'Siccar Point'.

question: 'The mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far back into the abyss of time,' John Playfair wrote of the Siccar Point trip. The line is usually staged as something he gasped while standing on the rock. Where did that sentence actually first appear?
answer: In his account of Hutton's life, printed eight years after Hutton died
choices: In his account of Hutton's life, printed eight years after Hutton died
In a letter Sir James Hall wrote home from Dunglass that same evening
In a footnote Hutton himself added to his own printed paper of 1788
In a speech Playfair gave with Hutton himself sitting there listening
context: The line comes from Playfair's biographical memoir of Hutton, printed in Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, vol. V, pt. III, 1805 - eight years after Hutton's death in 1797. Nobody wrote it down at the outcrop. The full sentence runs: 'The mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far back into the abyss of time; and whilst we listened with earnestness and admiration to the philosopher who was now unfolding to us the order and series of these wonderful events, we became sensible how much further reason may sometimes go than imagination may venture to follow.' The 'philosopher' is Hutton himself. Note that some reference sites wrongly place the line in Playfair's 1802 Illustrations of the Huttonian Theory; the 1805 Transactions citation is the one Wikipedia carries in two separate articles. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siccar Point' and 'James Hutton'; full text on the Geological Society of London Siccar Point Geosite page.

question: James Hutton's party sailed on along the coast after Siccar Point and found more of the grey beds standing on end. On the upright surfaces of those beds was something that told Hutton exactly how they had formed and gave him, he said, 'great satisfaction.' What was on them?
answer: Ripple marks, like the ones on a sandy sea bed
choices: Ripple marks, like the ones on a sandy sea bed
Burrows dug by worms living in the mud
Beds of shells broken and packed together
Trails left by snails crawling over the floor
context: Ripples form on sand under water and are preserved when the sand hardens to stone, so finding them on beds now standing on end proved those beds had been laid down flat under water before anything tilted them - a confirmation Hutton had only supposed until that afternoon. Of the whole day he said: 'we never should have dreamed of meeting with what we now perceived.' Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton'.

question: A geologist runs her hand along the bottom of the red sandstone at Siccar Point and finds no clean sand at all. For up to six metres it is a jumble of rounded pebbles and sharp broken chunks cemented together. Geologists call a junction like this an angular unconformity. Where did the chunks come from?
answer: From the grey rock lying directly beneath them
choices: From the grey rock lying directly beneath them
From a coral reef growing on that same sea floor
From lava erupted onto that same stretch of coast
From a desert lying inland from that same coast
context: The basal Devonian conglomerate and breccia - up to about six metres thick - carries rounded pebbles and angular fragments derived from the greywacke directly under it: the worn-down older rock's own wreckage, recycled into the rock that buries it. That is the erosion step proved by the rock itself rather than argued from a diagram, which is why the outcrop settled the question and a drawing could not. An unconformity is defined as a buried surface of erosion or non-deposition representing a significant gap in the record - a real old ground surface you can lay a hand on. Source: Grokipedia, 'Siccar Point' and 'Unconformity'; Wikipedia, 'Siccar Point'.

question: Sir James Hall, who had sailed with James Hutton to Siccar Point, packed limestone into a sealed gun barrel and heated it hard. In an open fire limestone burns to quicklime, its gas escaping into the air, and Hall wanted to know what it does when cooked deep underground, where nothing can escape. What came out of the barrel?
answer: A block of crystalline marble
choices: A block of crystalline marble
A cake of powdered quicklime
A lump of clear green glass
A crust of hardened ash
context: Sealing the carbonate of lime kept its gas from escaping, so under pressure it did not burn to quicklime at all - it came out crystalline marble. Between 1798 and 1805 Hall ran more than 500 separate experiments, reaching over 1000 degrees C and pressures equal to a column of seawater 2,720 metres deep. He is described as the first geologist directly to apply the test of laboratory experiment to geological hypotheses; his motto, borrowed from Paracelsus, was that 'Vulcan is a second nature, imitating concisely what the first takes time and circuit to effect.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Sir James Hall, 4th Baronet'; Dictionary of National Biography 1885-1900, 'Hall, James (1761-1832)'; Encyclopedia.com, 'Hall, Sir James'.

question: John Playfair judged that 'the great size of the book, and the obscurity which may justly be objected to many parts of it' had probably kept James Hutton's 2,138-page Theory of the Earth from being received as it deserved. Hutton died in 1797. What did Playfair spend nearly five years doing after that?
answer: Rewriting Hutton's whole theory as a book of his own
choices: Rewriting Hutton's whole theory as a book of his own
Translating the book into French for the Paris academies
Cutting the book down into a short pamphlet for miners
Hunting the Scottish coast for more of Hutton's junctions
context: Playfair spent almost five years, from Hutton's death in 1797 until 1802, writing Illustrations of the Huttonian Theory of the Earth; Charles Lyell then carried the ideas the rest of the way in Principles of Geology (1830-33). The ideas had also been attacked as dangerous, not merely unreadable - the chemist Richard Kirwan called them atheistic and illogical, which is what pushed Hutton to expand the theory into his 1795 volumes. One historian's verdict on the irony: 'It is ironic that Hutton, the man whose prose style is usually dismissed as unreadable, should have coined one of the most memorable, and indeed lyrical, sentences in all science.' Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton'; MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'James Hutton'; Keith Stewart Thomson, American Scientist 89(3): 212 (2001).

question: A student lays two fingers across the seam at Siccar Point. Modern radiometric dating gives the grey rock below an age of about 440 million years and the red sandstone above about 375 million, so roughly 65 million years are missing under her fingers. James Hutton had no way to measure these numbers, though he was certain the time was beyond imagining. What happened during the missing time?
answer: An ocean closed and Himalayan-sized mountains rose, then wore away
choices: An ocean closed and Himalayan-sized mountains rose, then wore away
A deep sea covered the whole region and never once drained away
A desert basin filled with dune sand and dried out again and again
Ice sheets ground across the region and scraped it flat again
context: The Iapetus Ocean, which had lain between what is now Scotland and what is now England, closed during those missing years, throwing up mountains of Himalayan scale to the north-west. The Devonian sand that buries the greywacke washed south off those very mountains as they wore down - so the younger rock is made of the older range's remains. The lower unit is early Silurian (Llandovery) greywacke at c.440 Ma; the flat-lying unit above is late Devonian sandstone at c.375 Ma. Hutton knew the time was unimaginably vast; he had no method that could give him a number. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siccar Point'; Grokipedia, 'Siccar Point'.

question: James Hutton went up Glen Tilt in the Scottish Highlands in the summer of 1785 to study granite in place for the first time. Abraham Werner taught that every rock on Earth, granite included, had settled out of one universal ocean that once covered the whole planet and then receded. What were the granite veins doing to the layered schist around them?
answer: Cutting clean across its layers and breaking through them
choices: Cutting clean across its layers and breaking through them
Lying in flat sheets neatly between each of its layers
Wrapping around it in smooth rounded lumps of stone
Crumbling to loose sand everywhere along its edges
context: Granite that cuts across the layers it sits among must have arrived molten and been forced in, which makes it younger than the rock it invades - and a chemical sediment settling out of water can never cut across the layer it settled onto. Glen Tilt was Hutton's first geological field trip, taken as a guest of the Duke of Atholl at Forest Lodge; he hauled a 400-pound granite-veined boulder out of the River Tilt and carted it back to Edinburgh. Werner taught his theory, Neptunism, at the Freiberg Mining Academy in Saxony and never published a complete treatise on it - it spread almost entirely through his lectures. He also insisted basalt was a water-laid sediment containing fossils; Hutton answered that basalt never contains fossils and is always insoluble, hard and crystalline, and one of Werner's own star students, Leopold von Buch, defected after fieldwork among the volcanic cones of the Auvergne. Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton' and 'Neptunism'; Grokipedia, 'James Hutton' and 'Abraham Gottlob Werner'.

question: James Hutton found tilted rock lying under flat rock for the first time on the Isle of Arran, at Lochranza in 1787, in an exposure too poor to show what the rock did below the surface he could see. He is remembered for reading rock correctly, but here he got it wrong. What did he wrongly conclude about the rock down there?
answer: That the two sets ran parallel again further down
choices: That the two sets ran parallel again further down
That the upper set was the older of the two down there
That both sets had settled out of one and the same sea
That an earthquake had cracked the two sets apart below
context: The Lochranza exposure was too limited to show the deeper strata, and Hutton incorrectly decided that the two sets were conformable - running parallel - below the outcrop he could see. Siccar Point mattered precisely because there the sea had already dissected the junction and laid it open, leaving nothing to guess at. He had also found granite veins at Glen Tilt in 1785, another such junction at Jedburgh on the Jed Water later in 1787, and a magma intrusion at Salisbury Crags in Edinburgh now called Hutton's Section. He was hunting on purpose: at Jedburgh he wrote that he 'rejoiced at my good fortune in stumbling upon an object so interesting in the natural history of the earth, and which I had been long looking for in vain.' Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton'.

question: Sir James Hall set out to test James Hutton's theory by melting rock in a furnace, after arguing with Hutton for three years before accepting it. Hutton disapproved, objecting one could not 'judge of the great operations of the mineral kingdom from having kindled a fire and looked into the bottom of a little crucible.' What did Hall do about his friend's objection?
answer: He held back every result until Hutton died in 1797
choices: He held back every result until Hutton died in 1797
He published anyway and the two men never spoke again
He rebuilt the experiments at the scale of a hillside
He put his results out under another man's name instead
context: Hall postponed publishing any of his results until after Hutton's death in 1797, then melted whinstone and lava collected from fifteen British and foreign localities and showed that a melt cooled quickly turns to glass while the very same melt cooled slowly turns stony and crystalline - basalt and even ordinary bottle-glass both did it. Hall also drew the Siccar Point outcrop in 1788, and the rock is still much as he sketched it; he ran the first analogue model of rock folding in 1815 and served as President of the Royal Society of Edinburgh. He was fallible too: he attributed the erratic boulders scattered across the Jura to a great sea-flood or 'debacle', following de Saussure and Pallas and against Hutton and Playfair, where we now recognise glaciers. Source: Dictionary of National Biography 1885-1900, 'Hall, James (1761-1832)'; Wikipedia, 'Sir James Hall, 4th Baronet' and 'Siccar Point'.

question: Nicolas Steno had described junctions where tilted rock lies under flat rock a full century before James Hutton reached Siccar Point, and the naturalist Horace-Benedict de Saussure had found them in the Alps. Hutton was the first man to read one as an enormous stretch of time. What had those earlier observers taken the very same rock for?
answer: Primary formations left by a retreating universal ocean
choices: Primary formations left by a retreating universal ocean
Broken wreckage dumped by one violent worldwide flood
Mountain roots heaved upward by fire beneath the crust
New formations raised by a second, separate creation
context: Steno and de Saussure had both looked at angular unconformities and read them in Neptunist terms, as 'primary formations' left by the universal ocean. Hutton was the first to read one as a quantity of time. The observation was available to anyone standing on the ledge; what changed was the question asked of it - which is why the outcrop is remembered under his name and not theirs. Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton'; Grokipedia, 'Unconformity'.

question: James Hutton closed his 1788 paper with the words 'we find no vestige of a beginning, - no prospect of an end.'
