He meant that the rocks keep no record of a starting point, not that the Earth never had one. Clair Patterson fixed the age of the Earth at 4.55 billion years in 1956. What did Patterson measure to get it?
answer: The lead built up inside a handful of fallen meteorites
choices: The lead built up inside a handful of fallen meteorites
The salt building up in the water of the world's oceans
The thickness of every sedimentary rock layer known
How long a molten ball the size of Earth needs to cool
context: Patterson established the figure in 1956 by lead-lead dating of several meteorites, including the Canyon Diablo meteorite; his own figure was 4.55 billion years, give or take 70 million, and today's accepted age is 4.54 plus or minus 0.05 billion years, on a clock built from radioactive decay that Hutton had no way to imagine. His closing sentence came out of an engine with no starting line - land wears to sediment, sediment is buried and cemented into rock, and the Earth's internal heat lifts that rock back up as new land, which wears down again. Note the honest limit: Hutton's picture of endless identical cycles is not modern geology, which has a definite time of formation and directional change through time. Earlier estimates fell far short - Archbishop James Ussher had put the creation of the world at 4004 BC in his Annales Veteris Testamenti of 1650, and Lord Kelvin's 1862 calculation gave only 20 to 400 million years because he did not know about radioactive heat. Source: Wikipedia, 'Age of the Earth', 'James Hutton', 'Ussher chronology'.

question: Hwang Woo-suk, a veterinarian at Seoul National University, announced in 2004 and 2005 that he had cloned human embryos and grown eleven stem-cell lines matched to individual patients. Independent investigators later showed the stem-cell work had been faked. Of all his headline 2005 claims, only one result survived close review. What was it?
answer: Snuppy, an Afghan hound - the first cloned dog
choices: Snuppy, an Afghan hound - the first cloned dog
eleven patient-matched embryonic stem-cell lines
a human embryo cloned from an adult skin cell
a paralysed dog walking again after a stem-cell graft
context: Snuppy was born April 24, 2005 at Seoul National University; his name is a portmanteau of SNU and puppy. He was made from ear tissue of a 3-year-old male Afghan hound named Tai, and out of 1,095 implanted embryos across 123 surrogate mothers he was the only survivor. When the fraud investigation was over, Snuppy was the one thing the panel confirmed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snuppy

question: A government bodyguard walked beside Hwang Woo-suk, the cloning scientist celebrated across South Korea in 2004 and 2005 as the country's greatest living researcher. Before the fraud in his stem-cell papers came out at the end of 2005, the state honoured him with something ordinary scientists never receive. What was it?
answer: his own commemorative postage stamp
choices: his own commemorative postage stamp
a statue outside the Blue House
a public holiday in his home province
his face on the 10,000-won banknote
context: He was called the 'Pride of Korea'. The national post office pulled the stamp from sale on January 11, 2006, the day after the Seoul National University panel reported that his stem-cell lines were fabricated. He had also been given a government bodyguard and free first-class Korean Air travel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwang_Woo-suk

question: Anonymous scientists on a Korean biology research website did something in December 2005 that no one at the journal had thought to do. Hwang Woo-suk's paper in Science claimed eleven separate patient-matched stem-cell colonies, and their check broke the story. What did they do?
answer: compared the photographs and spotted the same colony printed twice
choices: compared the photographs and spotted the same colony printed twice
ran the DNA sequences and found none matched the patients
grew the cell lines themselves and got different chromosome counts
checked the hospital records and found the patients did not exist
context: On December 5, 2005 an anonymous poster on BRIC laid the images side by side and showed that photos of the supposedly eleven different colonies had been duplicated and Photoshopped. Ordinary readers, on a message board, with nothing but the printed figures - that was the first crack. Source: https://www.science.org/content/article/korean-university-will-investigate-cloning-paper

question: A Seoul National University panel had already exposed Hwang Woo-suk's human-embryo results as faked when it turned to Snuppy, the Afghan hound he had announced as the world's first cloned dog. One straightforward check would show whether the puppy was faked too. What did the panel compare?
answer: Snuppy's DNA with that of the donor dog, Tai
choices: Snuppy's DNA with that of the donor dog, Tai
Snuppy's photographs with the papers' figures
Snuppy's birth records with the kennel's logs
Snuppy's blood type with that of every lab dog
context: Snuppy's DNA matched Tai's, so the cloning was real. Two independent DNA analyses appeared in Nature in 2006. Nuclear microsatellite markers plus mitochondrial DNA confirmed Snuppy was a genuine genetic clone of the ear-tissue donor, an adult male Afghan hound named Tai. Amid the wreckage of the human stem-cell claims, the dog was real. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04686

question: Reporters at the Korean television programme PD Notebook went after the cloning scientist Hwang Woo-suk on November 22, 2005, and they did not attack his science first. They attacked the ethics of where he had got the human eggs he used in his experiments. What did PD Notebook report about the source of those eggs?
answer: they came from his own junior researchers and from paid donors
choices: they came from his own junior researchers and from paid donors
they came from unclaimed IVF embryos at a Seoul fertility clinic
they came from illegal cross-border shipments out of China
they came from cadavers taken without family consent
context: The 2004 paper had claimed 16 unpaid volunteers. PD Notebook's reporting - which the public initially rejected, forcing sponsors to pull ads - turned out to be accurate. On November 21 co-author Roh Sung-il admitted he had paid women US$1,400 each; junior female staff, unable to freely refuse, had also donated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwang_Woo-suk

question: Investigators at Seoul National University reported on January 10, 2006 that all eleven claimed stem-cell lines were fabricated. Their panel also totted up how many human eggs Hwang Woo-suk's team had actually consumed between November 2002 and December 2005. What number did it reach?
answer: at least 2,061 eggs
choices: at least 2,061 eggs
roughly 185 eggs
roughly 427 eggs
at least 12,400 eggs
context: The 2005 paper had reported 185 eggs. The panel's audit put the real figure at over ten times that. It was the scale of the waste - human eggs harvested from paid strangers and coerced juniors - that made the ethical failure inseparable from the scientific one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwang_Woo-suk

question: Hwang Woo-suk claimed he could take an ordinary cell from a sick patient, clone it into an embryo, and harvest stem cells able to grow into any tissue the patient needed, with no immune rejection. The medical problem was real, and his papers were exposed as fraud in late 2005. One year later a different scientist solved it by a different route. Who, and how?
answer: Shinya Yamanaka - reprogrammed ordinary adult cells with four genes
choices: Shinya Yamanaka - reprogrammed ordinary adult cells with four genes
Ian Wilmut - refined the Dolly nuclear-transfer technique
James Thomson - isolated cells from unused IVF blastocysts
Jennifer Doudna - edited embryonic cells with CRISPR-Cas9
context: In 2006 the Japanese researcher Shinya Yamanaka showed that four transcription factors delivered into an ordinary adult skin cell could dial it back to a pluripotent state - induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPS cells. He shared the 2012 Nobel for it. The lesson: the real answer to Hwang's question did not need a shortcut, or a lie, or a single human egg. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Induced_pluripotent_stem_cell

question: Karl Lashley put a rat that had memorised a maze under anaesthetic and cut a piece out of its cortex, the brain's wrinkled outer layer. He kept at it for about thirty years, hoping to find the exact spot the memory lived in. What did he find where he expected it to be?
answer: Nothing -- the memory was never in the piece he removed
choices: Nothing -- the memory was never in the piece he removed
A dense knot of neurons that glowed under stain
A cluster of cells just behind the eyes in every rat
A ring of scar tissue that formed only in trained rats
context: Karl Spencer Lashley (1890-1958) ran this programme from the 1920s to about 1950 at Harvard and elsewhere. He would train the rats, cut, then re-test. The maze memory was never in the piece he removed. He wrote up the search under the title 'In Search of the Engram' in 1950 and admitted, half seriously, that his own evidence had begun to make him wonder whether learning was even possible.

question: Karl Lashley cut different pieces of cortex, the brain's wrinkled outer layer, out of rats that had learned a maze, then ran them through it again. Rat after rat, one measure predicted how badly each one now did. What was it?
answer: How much cortex he took, wherever he cut it
choices: How much cortex he took, wherever he cut it
Which part of the cortex he cut away
How long before surgery the rat had learned it
How old the rat was when he operated
context: Lashley's 1929 book Brain Mechanisms and Intelligence reported that the rats' errors grew with the AMOUNT of cortex removed, not with its location. From that he proposed two principles: MASS ACTION, impairment scales with the amount of cortex lost, and EQUIPOTENTIALITY, other cortical areas can take over a missing part's role. Together they paint memory as distributed across the cortex rather than filed in one drawer. Lashley did NOT prove memory has no physical trace -- he showed the maze memory is distributed, at least for the tasks he tested.

question: Karl Lashley bent over one more rat's cortex, hunting for an 'engram,' the physical trace a memory leaves behind in the brain. He never found one. The word had already been coined years before he started looking, back when no tool existed to hunt for one. Who invented it?
answer: Richard Semon, a German biologist, in his 1904 book Die Mneme
choices: Richard Semon, a German biologist, in his 1904 book Die Mneme
Sigmund Freud, in his 1900 book The Interpretation of Dreams
Ivan Pavlov, in his lectures on conditioning in the 1920s
William James, in his 1890 Principles of Psychology
context: Semon (1859-1918) also named the encoding step (engraphy) and the retrieval step (ecphory), and argued that memory must leave a physical modification in the nervous tissue. He was ignored for most of the twentieth century -- the term 'engram' outlived his other coinages -- and rediscovered in the modern engram-cell literature.

question: A team in Susumu Tonegawa's lab at MIT tagged, in 2012, the exact hippocampus neurons that lit up while a mouse learned to fear one box, using a light-sensitive protein called channelrhodopsin. Then the team moved the mouse into a completely different, completely safe box and fired a pulse of blue light down a fibre-optic into the tagged cells. What did the mouse do?
answer: It froze in place, as if the shock were about to come
choices: It froze in place, as if the shock were about to come
It reared up on its hind legs and vocalized
It darted to the far corner and defecated
It groomed itself calmly in place
context: Liu, Ramirez, Pang and colleagues, Nature 484:381, April 2012. The tagged cells were in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus. The technique is OPTOGENETICS -- installing a light-operated switch (a light-sensitive channel from a green alga) into chosen neurons so that a pulse of blue light through a fibre-optic turns just those cells on. Reactivating that specific set of cells REPLAYED the fear memory those cells had helped store. Freezing is the standard rodent fear response, but rearing, darting, and defecation are all real defensive/arousal behaviors -- the point is that the tagged cells drove the SPECIFIC learned response.

question: Susumu Tonegawa's lab at MIT made a mouse freeze in fear in 2013 inside a box where nothing bad had ever happened to it. The year before, the same team had used optogenetics, inserting light-sensitive proteins into brain cells so that a fibre-optic flash can switch those cells on, to make a mouse remember a box on cue. This time the fear was real and specific to that box. How had the team done it?
answer: They reactivated the tagged cells for that box while shocking the mouse in a different box
choices: They reactivated the tagged cells for that box while shocking the mouse in a different box
They tagged fear cells in the amygdala and reactivated those instead of hippocampus cells
They gave a drug that erased the memory of the shock box so the safe box took its place
They surgically joined two mice so one felt the other's shock through shared blood
context: Ramirez, Liu, Redondo, Tonegawa and colleagues, Science 341:387, July 26, 2013. The mouse first explored a neutral box (box A) and the neurons that lit up were tagged. Then in a second box (box B), the tagged A-cells were reactivated by light AT THE SAME MOMENT the mouse got a foot-shock. Back in box A, unshocked, the mouse froze -- the shock had been welded to the tagged memory of A rather than the memory of B. A false memory, implanted.

question: John Ioannidis, a Stanford doctor, put out a short essay in PLoS Medicine in August 2005, with no data tables and a title like a charge sheet. He and David Chavalarias later found nearly every medical paper citing a p-value under 0.05, impossible unless failures stayed hidden. What did the title say?
answer: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
choices: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
The End of Certainty in Modern Biology
How Statistics Lie in the Medical Age
A Manifesto for Reproducible Science
context: PLoS Medicine 2(8): e124, August 30, 2005. Widely reported as the most-downloaded article in the history of open-access publishing. Ioannidis was at Stanford; the paper is one of the founding documents of the metascience movement. Chavalarias, Wallach, Salem, Ioannidis, JAMA 2016. Ioannidis: 'It's impossible that 96 percent of all the hypotheses being tested would be significant.' What you are seeing is a shelf, filtered -- the null results were strained out before print. The publication-bias mechanism has a name: the file-drawer problem.

question: With no new experiment of his own, John Ioannidis worked out one equation from probability theory in 2005 and applied it to the medical papers already in print. When a paper marks a finding 'statistically significant', what number does his equation give?
answer: the positive predictive value of the finding
choices: the positive predictive value of the finding
the Bayes factor comparing the two rival hypotheses
the statistical power of the test that produced the finding
the false discovery rate across the whole journal issue
context: PPV = (1 - beta) * R / (R - beta*R + alpha), where alpha is the false-positive rate and (1 - beta) is the study's power. The whole paper is arithmetic applied to the shape of the existing literature -- no new experiments, no data tables. TEST-IT-YOURSELF: you can work the equation on paper.

question: To show how far a reader can trust a study reporting 'p < 0.05', the cutoff scientists use to call a result 'significant', John Ioannidis built a simple mathematical model in 2005. In his model one number decides how trustworthy that finding really is. What mostly sets that number high or low?
answer: the true-hypothesis ratio, times the study's power
choices: the true-hypothesis ratio, times the study's power
the study's chosen p-value threshold, all on its own
the study's sample size multiplied by its effect size
the number of prior independent replications
context: Ioannidis's core inequality: a research finding is more likely true than false only when (1 - beta) * R > alpha -- power times the true-hypothesis ratio has to beat the false-positive rate. A field testing thousands of long shots at low power will publish mostly noise, no matter how strict the p-value threshold looks.

question: John Ioannidis drew several corollaries from his 2005 model, short logical rules that follow from its arithmetic. The first took a whole research field that mostly runs small studies with weak statistical power, and asked what ends up on its journal pages. What did he say fills them?
answer: noise that will not replicate
choices: noise that will not replicate
settled truth that other labs will confirm
null results that quietly correct the field
effects too small for journals to print
context: Corollary 1 verbatim: 'The smaller the studies conducted in a scientific field, the less likely the research findings are to be true.' Small samples swing wildly and only the lucky swings clear p < 0.05, so the shelf that survives publication is the shelf of lucky swings.

question: John Ioannidis imagined a lab testing 100,000 gene sites for a link to schizophrenia, when in truth only about 10 of those sites are linked to the disease. The example sits in Box 1 of his 2005 PLoS Medicine essay, which listed six numbered corollaries, rules of thumb about when a positive finding is most likely to be wrong. Which one does it best show?
answer: the greater the number and the lesser the selection of tested relationships, the less likely the findings are to be true
choices: the greater the number and the lesser the selection of tested relationships, the less likely the findings are to be true
the smaller the studies conducted in the field, the less likely the findings are to be true
the greater the flexibility in designs, definitions, outcomes, and analytical modes, the less likely the findings are to be true
the hotter a scientific field, with more scientific teams involved, the less likely the findings are to be true
context: Corollary 3 verbatim. In Box 1, at 60% power and p < 0.05 the post-study probability of any single significant SNP-schizophrenia hit being real is only about 12/10,000 -- and any bias in the pipeline drops it further. Firing 100,000 shots at 10 real targets means most of your 'hits' are noise.

question: At number six on his list of corollaries, John Ioannidis set down a paradox: the more scientific teams pile into a hot question, the worse the published record on that question gets. What mechanism makes a crowded field manufacture false positives?
answer: the first team to hit p < 0.05 publishes, so racing selects the lucky noisy runs out of the pack
choices: the first team to hit p < 0.05 publishes, so racing selects the lucky noisy runs out of the pack
the labs share equipment and contaminate each other's samples with each hand-off
hot fields recruit dishonest researchers who go on to fabricate data on purpose
peer reviewers cannot keep up with the submission rate and wave more mistakes through
context: Corollary 6: 'The hotter a scientific field (with more scientific teams involved), the less likely the research findings are to be true.' Twenty teams testing the same shaky hypothesis at 5% false-positive rate expect one to hit significance by chance -- and that team goes to print first, while the nulls stay in drawers.

question: Leah Jager and Jeffrey Leek took on John Ioannidis in print in 2014, with a reanalysis in the journal Biostatistics. They estimated the science-wise false-discovery rate across top medical journals, a direct test of his headline claim, and the argument goes on. What figure did they reach?
answer: about 14%
choices: about 4%
about 14%
about 31%
about 42%
context: Jager and Leek, Biostatistics 15(1), 2014. Their estimate, about 14 per cent, sat far below the 'most' of Ioannidis's title. Steven Goodman and Sander Greenland separately argued Ioannidis's model rested on plausible-but-chosen assumptions rather than measured ones. Ioannidis replied in the same issue; the argument is live. Feynman's rule applied even to a favorite paper: 'you must not fool yourself.'

question: John Ioannidis argued in 2005 that small studies, weak effects and publication pressure together mean a big share of what medical journals print will not replicate. The paper became one of the most cited in modern science, and what it is wrongly said to claim matters as much as what it says. Which of these does it not actually claim?
answer: that science is worthless and its published findings should be ignored
choices: that science is worthless and its published findings should be ignored
that small studies chasing small effects are especially vulnerable to false positives
that pre-registration and larger studies would help repair the filter
that financial interests raise the false-positive rate in a field
context: Ioannidis explicitly named the repairs: better-powered evidence (larger studies), low-bias meta-analyses, and upfront pre-registration of studies such as randomized trials. The claim is that the FILTER is weak, not that inquiry is worthless.

question: John Ioannidis argued in his 2005 paper that scientists, journalists and even fellow researchers routinely misread 'p < 0.05' as a much stronger claim than it makes. What does that p-value actually mean, in the strict technical sense?
answer: under a true null, data at least this extreme would appear less than 5% of the time
choices: under a true null, data at least this extreme would appear less than 5% of the time
there is less than a 5% chance that the finding itself is wrong
there is at least a 95% chance the finding will replicate in future studies
the researcher's underlying hypothesis is at least 95% likely to be true
context: The p-value is a statement about the data under the null hypothesis, not about the hypothesis itself. Ioannidis's paper attacks exactly the three misreadings listed here -- readers see 'significant' and hear 'true,' 'unlikely to be wrong,' or 'will replicate.' Feynman's rule for your own favorite paper: 'you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.'

question: James Lind took twelve sailors sick with scurvy aboard HMS Salisbury in 1747 and split them into six pairs, each to get a different suspected remedy. Before the first dose he did one thing with all twelve. What was it?
answer: Put them in one sick berth on one identical diet.
choices: Put them in one sick berth on one identical diet.
Sent them back to their normal watch and rations.
Let each pair eat whatever it could keep down.
Moved each pair to a different part of the ship.
context: In Lind's own words the twelve lay together in 'a proper apartment for the sick in the fore-hold' and had 'one diet in common to all': water-gruel sweetened with sugar in the morning, fresh mutton broth for dinner, light puddings and boiled biscuit with sugar, and barley, raisins, rice, currants, sago and wine for supper. Same room, same food, one thing changed between the pairs. That is the whole idea of a controlled trial, and Lind built its shape roughly two centuries before anyone had the phrase. 20 May is now marked every year as International Clinical Trials Day in honour of this experiment. Sources: Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753), quoted at sportsci.org/news/history/lind/lind_sp.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind; jameslindlibrary.org/articles/james-lind-aboard-salisbury/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_trial.

question: James Lind handed one pair of his scurvy patients two oranges and a lemon a day aboard HMS Salisbury in 1747. So little fruit was aboard that it ran out after six days. Where did those six days leave the two men?
answer: One was fit for duty; the other nursed the rest.
choices: One was fit for duty; the other nursed the rest.
One had improved a little; the other was unchanged.
Both had stopped bleeding; neither could stand yet.
Both could walk the deck; neither could work yet.
context: Lind wrote that 'the most sudden and visible good effects were perceived from the use of the oranges and lemons; one of those who had taken them, being at the end of six days fit for duty.' The second man was 'the best recovered of any in his condition' and Lind put him to work as nurse to the other sick. All twelve had begun the trial the same way - putrid gums, the spots, lassitude and weak knees - and Lind's opening sentence is the founding line of clinical trials: 'On the 20th May, 1747, I took twelve patients in the scurvy on board the Salisbury at sea. Their cases were as similar as I could have them.' Sources: Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753), quoted at hekint.org/2017/01/29/the-mysteries-of-james-lind-and-scurvy/ and renalrounds.substack.com/p/twelve-patients-on-the-salisbury; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind.

question: George Anson set sail in 1740 with about 1,854 men aboard six ships, bound to raid Spain's Pacific colonies. He took a Spanish treasure galleon in a fight that killed one man, but the voyage was a slaughter, mostly by scurvy. How many of the 1,854 came home on his flagship, the Centurion?
context: Roughly 500 of the squadron's 1,854-1,900 men survived the voyage at all, and 188 came home in the Centurion. Disease - overwhelmingly scurvy - did nearly all the killing, while the richest sea-fight of the age cost one life. Shipowners of the period simply budgeted for a 50% death rate on long voyages; between Columbus's crossing and the mid-1800s scurvy killed more than two million sailors, more than storms, shipwreck, combat and every other disease combined. Anson's losses are what made the Admiralty care, and Lind dedicated his 1753 Treatise of the Scurvy to him. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Anson%27s_voyage_around_the_world; sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-age-of-scurvy/; nzgeo.com/stories/a-scurvy-business/.

question: James Lind gave each of six pairs of scurvy patients a different remedy, every one a treatment top doctors pushed on the fleets. The pair on oranges and lemon recovered. Four pairs gained nothing at all. One pair improved a little. Which remedy gave that slight improvement?
answer: A quart of cider a day.
choices: A quart of cider a day.
A quart of malt wort a day.
A quart of spruce beer a day.
A quart of tamarind water a day.
context: The cider pair improved slightly and no one else did. The seawater, the vinegar and the elixir of vitriol - twenty-five drops of dilute sulphuric acid, taken three times a day - produced nothing, and neither did the sixth pair's electuary: a lump the size of a nutmeg made of garlic, mustard seed, balsam of Peru, dried radish root and gum myrrh, taken three times a day and washed down with barley water acidulated with tamarinds. None of the six was a joke. Every one was a remedy serious physicians of the day pressed on the fleets, which is exactly why a fair comparison was worth running. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind; sportsci.org/news/history/lind/lind_sp.html; sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-age-of-scurvy/.

question: A sailor chews salt beef and hard biscuit on a long passage, with nothing fresh aboard. The food is almost impossible to convict of scurvy, because a crew eating it stays perfectly well for a stretch before the gums begin to bleed. How long is that stretch?
answer: At least a month.
choices: At least a month.
About a week.
Three or four months.
The better part of a year.
context: It takes at least a month of little or no vitamin C before symptoms appear. That delay is why the cause was so hard to trace: the meal that starts the damage and the bleeding gums that announce it are separated by weeks of open ocean, and by then the ship is a thousand miles from the port where the fresh food ran out. Any effect that lags its cause by a month is a punishing thing to spot without a deliberate test - which is what makes Lind's six-pair comparison so much more powerful than shipboard experience. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scurvy.

question: James Lind recommended a fix for fresh oranges, which rot in weeks and could not last aboard a ship bound for the Indies: a 'rob', citrus juice held near boiling for hours until it cooked down to a sixth. What did those hot hours do to the vitamin C in the juice?
answer: Destroyed most of it, leaving a syrup that could not cure.
choices: Destroyed most of it, leaving a syrup that could not cure.
Concentrated it sixfold, exactly as Lind had hoped.
Left it intact, but only for a few weeks in cask.
Left it intact, so the rob cured as well as fresh fruit.
context: Vitamin C is ascorbic acid, and heat destroys it - cooking alone can cut the vitamin C in a food by around 60%, and hours near boiling takes far more than that. So Lind's practical recommendation, the one piece of his work built for real ships, was the version of the medicine that did not work. It is a hard, honest lesson about engineering a cure without knowing the mechanism: the man who ran the best test of the century then shipped the broken version of the answer. Sources: jameslindlibrary.org/articles/james-lind-and-scurvy-1747-to-1795/ ('a process that destroyed much of the ascorbic acid, rendering it ineffective'); Jeremy Hugh Baron, 'Sailors' scurvy before and after James Lind - a reassessment', hekint.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/sailors_scurvy-final.pdf; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C.

question: A sailor lies deep in scurvy, gums bleeding, knees too weak to hold him, as two-thirds of an ounce of lemon juice goes into his grog, the Royal Navy's tiny daily ration. That works out to only about ten milligrams of vitamin C. What does ten milligrams a day do to a man that far gone?
answer: Reverses every obvious symptom of the disease.
choices: Reverses every obvious symptom of the disease.
Slows the disease but cannot turn it back.
Protects the healthy but cannot cure the sick.
Helps only alongside fresh meat and vegetables.
context: Ten milligrams a day is enough to completely reverse all the obvious symptoms of scurvy. The whole catastrophe - fleets emptied, voyages ended, a 50% death rate budgeted in advance, more than two million sailors dead between Columbus's crossing and the mid-1800s - turned on about a spoonful of juice a day. For scale: oranges and lemons carry roughly 53 mg of vitamin C per 100 g of fruit. You can check how fragile the stuff is in a kitchen, since cooking alone can cut a food's vitamin C by around 60%. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind (the Suffolk ration); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C ('All obvious symptoms of scurvy could be completely reversed by supplementation of only 10 mg a day'); sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-age-of-scurvy/.

question: James Lind sat down after the voyage to write up his trial of twelve sick sailors, and his book A Treatise of the Scurvy came out in 1753 at some 400 sides of print. The whole book is remembered today for that trial alone. How much of it did Lind give the trial?
answer: About five paragraphs, two hundred pages in.
choices: About five paragraphs, two hundred pages in.
The opening chapter and the dedication.
A third of the book, with all the case notes.
Roughly a quarter, spread across the text.
context: The most influential experiment in the history of medicine sits about five paragraphs long, roughly two hundred pages into a four-hundred-page book - and by the third edition in 1772 Lind had added disclaimers that further undercut his own finding. He did not know what he had. A reader in 1753 hunting for the cure would have had to wade two hundred pages to find the five paragraphs that contained it. Source: sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-age-of-scurvy/ (page and paragraph counts are that account's; treat them as approximate).

question: James Lind saw the two men on citrus make the only clear recovery of his 1747 trial. Yet when he wrote it up six years later in A Treatise of the Scurvy, he did not name citrus as the cure for scurvy. What did he argue instead?
answer: That scurvy had several causes at once, so needed several remedies.
choices: That scurvy had several causes at once, so needed several remedies.
That the fruit worked only on scurvy caught in its first weeks.
That the sick berth's warmth, not the fruit, had done the healing.
That the men would have mended in time with no remedy at all.
context: Lind held that scurvy had many causes acting together and therefore needed many remedies, leaning on damp, cold and blocked perspiration: moisture, he wrote, 'concurring with other peculiar circumstances, as a gross diet, cold etc. disposes in a particular manner to the scorbutic corruption.' He treated the fruit as one remedy among several. He was also not the first to suspect citrus - John Woodall, first Surgeon-General of the East India Company, wrote in The Surgeon's Mate (1617) that 'the use of the juyce of Lemmons is a precious medicine and well tried... let it have the chiefe place, for it will deserve it', and Sir Richard Hawkins had called oranges and lemons 'our chief refreshing and the most fruitful remedy' after his 1593 voyage. Lind's contribution was never the idea. It was the test - and he then read his own test wrong. Sources: hekint.org/2017/01/29/the-mysteries-of-james-lind-and-scurvy/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind; rmg.co.uk/stories/maritime-history/library-archive/surgeons-mate-john-woodall; Baron, hekint.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/sailors_scurvy-final.pdf.

question: On Anson's Centurion, a sailor had taken a wound at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690. More than fifty years after it healed, he watched it break open again. The chaplain wrote that a long-mended broken bone was found 'dissolved, and the fracture seemed as if it had never been consolidated'. Why does scurvy undo a body's oldest repairs?
answer: Scar and bone callus are collagen, which scurvy stops the body rebuilding.
choices: Scar and bone callus are collagen, which scurvy stops the body rebuilding.
Scar and knitted bone are calcium, which scurvy leaches slowly back out.
Scurvy thins the blood until old scars are forced open from beneath.
Damp and cold rot the flesh inward, and old scar tissue gives way first.
context: Collagen is the fibre that stitches a body together, and the body is always tearing old collagen down and building new. Vitamin C is the required cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, the enzymes that convert proline and lysine inside collagen into hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine - and those are what let collagen strands cross-link into a stable triple helix. Without vitamin C the demolition continues and the rebuilding cannot, so scar tissue and bone callus come apart and the body literally comes unstitched. The Boyne case comes from Richard Walter's A Voyage Round the World (1748), the chaplain's own account of Anson's voyage. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scurvy; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Anson%27s_voyage_around_the_world; nzgeo.com/stories/a-scurvy-business/.

question: Rear Admiral Alan Gardner had lemon juice issued on HMS Suffolk for a twenty-three-week run to Madras, while Gilbert Blane pressed the case from inside the Navy's Sick and Hurt Board. That board had turned down fruit-juice proposals the year after James Lind published in 1753. How long after Lind's 1747 trial did the Admiralty issue lemon juice to the whole fleet?
answer: Forty-eight years.
choices: Forty-eight years.
Eleven years.
Twenty-two years.
Ninety-one years.
context: The fleet-wide order came in 1795 - forty-eight years after the twelve men in six pairs, and forty-two years after the book. The Suffolk had reached Madras in 1794 with no serious scurvy aboard, and that voyage, not the Treatise, is what moved the Admiralty. Lind himself had seen the problem coming: before the subject could be set right, he wrote, it was necessary to remove 'a great deal of rubbish' from what was already believed. The evidence existed for half a century and did not implement itself. Sources: jameslindlibrary.org/articles/james-lind-and-scurvy-1747-to-1795/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Blane.

question: A Royal Navy sailor in the 1860s found lime juice in his ration where Mediterranean lemon juice had been: the Admiralty had switched. Lime carries about a quarter of the scurvy-fighting power, and by 1875 scurvy was back in the fleet. Polar expeditions met it for decades after. What drove the switch?
answer: Limes came from Britain's own colonial plantations.
choices: Limes came from Britain's own colonial plantations.
Limes kept their strength far better in tropical casks.
Limes had tested stronger than lemons in Navy trials.
Limes replaced lemons after Mediterranean crops failed.
context: A solved problem, un-solved by a purchasing decision. Limes carry about 30 mg of vitamin C per 100 g against 53 mg for lemons, and processing takes more still. There is a darkly funny wrinkle: the 1867 Merchant Shipping Act made a daily citrus ration a legal requirement on British ships - and the legally required juice was the one that did not work, which is where the nickname 'limey' comes from. When a laboratory finally analysed the Navy's lime juice in 1918, it found virtually no antiscorbutic power at all, after more than half a century of issue. (A widely repeated claim adds that the juice was pumped through copper piping, which would degrade it further; the chemistry is solid - copper and iron salts do accelerate vitamin C loss - but the piping detail itself is contested, so treat it as an unproven anecdote.) Sources: idlewords.com/2010/03/scott_and_scurvy.htm; psychiatrymargins.com/p/how-the-citrus-cure-for-scurvy-was; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scurvy; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C; thevintagenews.com/2018/08/24/limey/.

question: Malcolm Beasley of Stanford chaired Bell Labs' outside inquiry into its star physicist, Jan Hendrik Schön, in 2002, after outside physicists noticed the same random noise in graphs from different experiments. That September his committee found sixteen of twenty-four misconduct charges proven. What did one of them establish?
answer: Some curves came from mathematical formulas, not instruments
choices: Some curves came from mathematical formulas, not instruments
Some devices were bought in and passed off as his own
Some results were copied from a rival group's papers
Some samples were grown by students and never credited
context: The Beasley report established misconduct in 16 of 24 allegations, including whole datasets reused across unrelated experiments and 'measurements' generated from mathematical functions rather than any real instrument. Of the remaining eight allegations, two had no clear tie to a publication and six were 'troubling' but did not rise to conclusive misconduct. Source: Beasley Committee report, Sept 2002; UCLA-hosted PDF.

question: Jan Hendrik Schön put about twenty other scientists' names on his fake papers as co-authors between 1998 and 2002, people at Bell Labs itself and at universities on two continents. Malcolm Beasley's committee ruled on those co-authors in September 2002. What did its report say?
answer: All co-authors were formally cleared of scientific misconduct
choices: All co-authors were formally cleared of scientific misconduct
About half the co-authors were found complicit
Every named co-author was dismissed alongside Schon
Only the most senior co-authors were exonerated
context: The Beasley report explicitly stated that all of Schon's co-authors were completely cleared of scientific misconduct and that no co-author's laboratory practices lay outside accepted norms. This matters: Schon's collaborators trusted samples and figures he produced alone, and were themselves victims of the fabrication. Source: Beasley Committee report, Sept 2002.

question: Edward Jenner made two shallow cuts in a boy's arm on 14 May 1796, in the English village of Berkeley. The boy was James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of Jenner's own gardener. Jenner rubbed matter into the cuts. Where had he taken it from?
answer: A milkmaid's blistered hand
choices: A cow's diseased udder
A milkmaid's blistered hand
A smallpox patient's ripe pustule
A horse's inflamed heel
context: The donor was Sarah Nelmes, a dairymaid at a farm near Berkeley who had caught cowpox from her master's cows that same May. Jenner's Case XVI names her; Case XVII records the boy: 'I selected a healthy boy, about eight years old... the matter was taken from a sore on the hand of a dairymaid... and it was inserted, on the 14th of May, 1796, into the arm of the boy by means of two superficial incisions.' Source: Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae (1798), Cases XVI-XVII (gutenberg.org/files/29414); grokipedia.com/page/Edward_Jenner.

question: Edward Jenner left one name out of his 1798 pamphlet on cowpox: the cow's. Tradition has called her Blossom, and part of her still hangs on the library wall at St George's medical school in London. What part?
answer: Her hide
choices: Her horns
Her skull
Her hide
Her bell
context: The hide is at St George's in Tooting; the horns are at Dr Jenner's House museum in Berkeley. Flagged as tradition, not testimony: the NAME Blossom is an attribution attached to the surviving hide long afterwards — Jenner names no cow anywhere in the Inquiry. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Jenner; Jenner, An Inquiry (1798).  (Legend.)

question: James Phipps, eight years old, stayed perfectly well after Edward Jenner deliberately gave him cowpox, the mild disease of the dairy herds, on 14 May 1796. That proved nothing about whether the boy could now resist smallpox. Jenner came back to him on 1 July. What did he do to the boy that day?
answer: He scratched matter from a smallpox sore into the boy's arm
choices: He scratched matter from a smallpox sore into the boy's arm
He sent the boy to sleep beside a smallpox patient
He wrapped the boy in blankets from a smallpox sickbed
He walked the boy through a ward full of smallpox cases
context: Jenner's own words: 'In order to ascertain whether the boy... was secure from the contagion of the Small-pox, he was inoculated the 1st of July following with variolous matter... no disease followed.' He deliberately gave a child real smallpox — that was variolation, the standard immunising method of the day, which killed roughly one or two in every hundred who took it against about thirty in a hundred for natural smallpox. Jenner repeated the challenge; over his life Phipps was inoculated with smallpox more than twenty times and never caught it. Sources: Jenner, An Inquiry (1798), Case XVII; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Phipps; grokipedia.com/page/Variolation.

question: Edward Jenner rubbed cowpox matter into the arm of his own gardener's boy, eight-year-old James Phipps, in 1796, and he never forgot the child who had trusted him with that test. He also inoculated the poor for free from a rustic hut in his own garden. What did Jenner give Phipps as thanks?
answer: The lease of a cottage for his family
choices: A place as his apprentice in medicine
The lease of a cottage for his family
A pension paid from his own practice
A share of his parliamentary award
context: Jenner called the hut at his house, The Chantry, the TEMPLE OF VACCINIA, and vaccinated the poor there free. Phipps got the lease of a cottage in Berkeley, rent-free, for himself, his wife and their two children. He attended Jenner's funeral on 3 February 1823 and died in 1853, buried at St Mary's, Berkeley — the church where he had been baptised. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Edward_Jenner; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Phipps.

question: Aged about eight, Edward Jenner went through the old smallpox protection himself, in Gloucester around 1757. The procedure was the least of it: the six weeks of preparation beforehand wrecked his health for years. What did those six weeks consist of?
answer: Repeated bleeding, purging and near-starvation on a vegetable drink
choices: Repeated cold baths, mercury rubs and a course of hot cupping
Daily blistering plasters, sweating powders and forced bed rest
Six weeks of quarantine at home on beef broth and fortified wine
Repeated bleeding, purging and near-starvation on a vegetable drink
context: 'He was bled until pale, then purged and fasted repeatedly, until he wasted to a skeleton. He was denied solid food in favor of a vegetable drink that was supposed to sweeten the blood; after the inoculation itself — the least traumatic event of the entire experience — he was removed to an "inoculation stable," and, according to an early biographer, "haltered up with others in a terrible state of disease, although none died."' It matters for reading everything he did later: Jenner was not hunting a FIRST method of protection, he was hunting a SAFER one. Sources: Jenner On Trial, ch.2 (bioethicscourse.info/jotsite/jot-chp2.html); EBSCO Research Starters, 'Edward Jenner'.

question: Edward Jenner wrote up his cowpox test on an eight-year-old boy in 1797 and sent it to the Royal Society in London, the most respected scientific body in Britain. The Society refused to print it. What did Jenner get back instead?
answer: A warning not to risk his reputation on it
choices: An invitation to demonstrate before the Fellows
A warning not to risk his reputation on it
A referral to the Royal College of Physicians
A demand for a dozen more cases first
context: Jenner 'was given to understand that he should be cautious and prudent, and that he ought not to risk his reputation by presenting anything, which appeared so much at variance with established knowledge.' Not a refutation — a career warning. He paid a printer himself the next year: An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae (1798), a slim pamphlet of 23 numbered cases with four engraved plates of cowpox sores by William Skelton so that doctors could recognise the real thing, posted to physicians across Britain and Europe at his own expense. Sources: 'Edward Jenner, Benefactor to Mankind', in Artenstein (ed.), Vaccines: A Biography (Springer); grokipedia.com/page/Edward_Jenner.

question: Benjamin Jesty, a Dorset cattle farmer with no medical training, walked his wife Elizabeth and their two small boys about seven miles to a farm with sick cows in 1774, with smallpox loose in his village. There he scratched matter from the cows into all three of their arms. What did he scratch it in with?
answer: A darning needle
choices: A surgeon's lancet
A butcher's knife
A darning needle
A sharpened quill
context: His neighbours did not applaud. Jesty 'was labelled inhuman, and was "hooted at, reviled and pelted whenever he attended markets in the neighbourhood"' — some genuinely feared his family's 'metamorphosis into horned beasts' for having a cow's disease put into them. It nearly went badly, too: the two boys had mild local reactions, but Elizabeth's arm 'became very inflamed and for a time her condition gave cause for concern', though she recovered fully. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Jesty; grokipedia.com/page/benjamin_jesty.

question: Twelve medical officers of the Original Vaccine Pock Institution in London sat down Benjamin Jesty, a Dorset cattle farmer with no medical training, in August 1805. They asked about the cowpox he had scratched into his wife and two sons thirty-one years before. What happened in front of the officers?
answer: His eldest son Robert took an inoculation of live smallpox
choices: His eldest son Robert took an inoculation of live smallpox
His younger son Benjamin took a fresh scratch of cowpox matter
His wife Elizabeth bared the scar left by the 1774 cut
His wife Elizabeth swore a statement about the 1774 scratching
context: The son took the risk in public, and showed only mild inflammation and no disease. Jesty went home with a signed testimonial affirming the experiment's success over 31 years, a pair of gold-mounted lancets, and a portrait painted by Michael William Sharp, later engraved by William Say. He never got money. Dr George Pearson had put Jesty's 1774 case before a House of Commons committee in 1802 — before Jenner's first award — and the committee granted Jesty nothing; in Pearson's own pamphlet the farmer's name came out as 'Justins'. Parliament paid Jenner £10,000 in 1802 and a further £20,000 in 1807, £30,000 in all. Jesty's gravestone at St Nicholas of Myra, Worth Matravers, Dorset still makes the claim in stone: he was 'particularly noted for having been the first Person (known) that Introduced the Cow Pox by Inoculation, and who from his great strength of mind made the Experiment from the (Cow) on his Wife and two Sons in the Year 1774.' Elizabeth was buried beside him in 1824; both headstones are Grade II listed. THE HONEST ACCOUNTING, stated exactly as the sources state it: Jenner was not the first to put cowpox into a person — Jesty (1774), John Fewster and Peter Plett all preceded him. What Jenner did first was the scientific act: 'he was the first to publish his evidence and distribute vaccine freely, provide information on selection of suitable material, and maintain it by arm-to-arm transfer.' Jesty 'did not publicise his findings made some twenty years earlier in 1774.' Sources: grokipedia.com/page/benjamin_jesty; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Jesty; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox_vaccine; grokipedia.com/page/Edward_Jenner; Pead, 'Benjamin Jesty: the first vaccinator revealed', The Lancet.

question: In his Inquiry Edward Jenner wrote that the dairy disease did not start in the cow at all. He traced it to a sore on a different farm animal, and he blamed farmhands who dressed that sore and then went to the milking without washing their hands. Which sore did he blame?
answer: A horse's diseased heel
choices: A pig's ulcerated snout
A sheep's rotting hoof
A dog's running ear
A horse's diseased heel
context: Jenner's text: 'There is a disease to which the Horse, from his state of domestication, is frequently subject. The Farriers have termed it the Grease... One of the former having been appointed to apply dressings to the heels of a Horse affected with the Grease, and not paying due attention to cleanliness, incautiously bears his part in milking the Cows, with some particles of the infectious matter adhering to his fingers.' And the kicker: the virus in the vaccine that eventually wiped out smallpox is not cowpox at all. Allan Watt Downie showed in 1939 that it was serologically distinct from cowpox, and it was recognised as its own species, vaccinia; whole-genome sequencing since has found vaccinia's closest relative is HORSEPOX — a smallpox vaccine manufactured by Mulford in 1902 turned out to be 99.7% similar to horsepox. Jenner's horse hunch may have been nearer the mark than his cow. Sources: Jenner, An Inquiry (1798); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox_vaccine; grokipedia.com/page/Edward_Jenner.

question: To sell the new method to a skeptical medical establishment, Edward Jenner wrote his 1798 Inquiry and made big promises in print about how well it would work. Doctors kept repeating one of them for decades, and his own century of use proved it false. What had he promised?
answer: That one course of cowpox protected a person for life
choices: That a vaccinated mother passed her protection to her children
That one course of cowpox protected a person for life
That no vaccinated person could carry smallpox to another
That the matter could pass arm to arm without ever weakening
context: Jenner wrote that 'the person who has been thus affected is for ever after secure from the infection of the Small Pox' — he 'rashly claimed that the protective effect was lifelong. This last proved to be incorrect.' 'Late in the 19th century, it was realized that vaccination did not confer lifelong immunity and that subsequent revaccination was necessary.' The man who found the effect got the duration of his own discovery wrong, inside his own century — and it was testing, not his authority, that settled it. Sources: Jenner, An Inquiry (1798); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox_vaccine; Riedel, 'Edward Jenner and the history of smallpox and vaccination', Proc Bayl Univ Med Cent (PMC1200696).

question: A leading scientist proposed in 1881, in Edward Jenner's honour, that Jenner's Latin cow-word should cover the shots labs across Europe were making for many other diseases. Jenner had meant only cowpox: Variolae vaccinae, from vacca, a cow. The word spread by that proposal, which is why a flu shot is called a vaccine today, though each new shot still had to bring its own evidence. Who made the proposal?
answer: Louis Pasteur
choices: Louis Pasteur
Robert Koch
Joseph Lister
Paul Ehrlich
context: Pasteur made the proposal in his 1881 'Address on the Germ Theory' (The Lancet 118 (3024), pp. 271-272), and he made it as a tribute: he asked that 'vaccine' and 'vaccination' be extended from Jenner's cowpox procedure to every protective inoculation then being developed. So Jenner's one Latin cow-word, minted for one 1796 result, was generalised forward by a proposal rather than by a result — the name spread across the new products, while the trials and the safety record behind each of them stayed separate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccine, citing Pasteur, 'Address on the Germ Theory', The Lancet 118 (3024), 1881, pp. 271-272.

question: John Snow, a London doctor who had studied cholera for years, walked Soho to find the cause after the disease struck on 31 August 1854 and killed 127 people within three days. What did he do?
answer: He marked every death as a black bar at the address where it happened.
choices: He marked every death as a black bar at the address where it happened.
He measured how high each street stood above the level of the Thames.
He sampled the air in the worst courts, morning and night.
He counted the dead parish by parish in the weekly returns.
context: The bars were short, and stacked where several had died in one house — and the pile-up sat around a single object: the public water pump on Broad Street. 616 people were dead by the end of the outbreak. Snow had doubted for years that bad air carried cholera, but doubt is not evidence. Plotting each death at the address where it happened, rather than counting by parish or by height above the river, is the move that started epidemiology. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak; grokipedia.com/page/John_Snow (Grokipedia checked first).

question: Edwin Lankester, a local doctor, drew a glass from the Broad Street pump in Soho while cholera was killing people around it in 1854. The pump stood among outdoor toilets and leaking cesspits. What did he find when he examined the water?
answer: It was clear, odourless and pleasant to the taste.
choices: It was clear, odourless and pleasant to the taste.
It was clear but bitter, tasting of chalk and iron.
It was cloudy with white flecks and smelled of the drains.
It was yellowish and oily, with a taste of coal tar.
context: Lankester, inspecting while the outbreak was running, found the water clear, odourless and palatable — and residents widely regarded it as the purest water in the neighbourhood. That is the trap: the killer water looked and tasted better than the safe water, so people carried it home on purpose. No eye or tongue can tell a poisoned well; only the pattern of who fell ill could. Source: grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak ('Edwin Lankester's Assessment').

question: Hunting the ones who had escaped, John Snow called on Mr Huggins, owner of a brewery in the middle of the dying around Broad Street in September 1854. Not one of the seventy-odd workmen there had died of cholera. What did Huggins tell him?
answer: They were allowed a daily ration of beer and drank no water at all.
choices: They were allowed a daily ration of beer and drank no water at all.
They worked all day in the heat rising off the boiling coppers.
They were dosed with brandy and quinine at the start of each shift.
They lodged out beyond the parish and only came in to work.
context: Snow's own words in 1855: 'There is a Brewery in Broad Street, near to the pump, and on perceiving that no brewer's men were registered as having died of cholera, I called on Mr. Huggins... He informed me that there were above seventy workmen employed in the brewery, and that none of them had suffered from cholera, — at least in a severe form, — only two having been indisposed... The men are allowed a certain quantity of malt liquor, and Mr. Huggins believes they do not drink water at all.' A quiet irony: Snow signed the abstinence pledge around 1836 and had been a vegetarian since seventeen, and the cleanest piece of evidence he ever found was seventy men saved by their beer ration. (Beware retellings that say '500 employees' — that figure belongs to the Poland Street workhouse, not the brewery.) Sources: epi-snow.ph.ucla.edu/Stream2_BSPoutbreak_c.html (verbatim Snow 1855); grokipedia.com/page/John_Snow.

question: Inside the Poland Street workhouse, where the parish housed its poor, John Snow went looking for what it had that the streets around it did not. Houses where people were dying ringed it on three sides, yet of the 535 people packed inside, five died of cholera. What did he find?
answer: A well of its own, sunk in the yard behind the wards.
choices: A well of its own, sunk in the yard behind the wards.
A rainwater cistern, fed from the roofs of the wards.
A floor of quicklime, laid down at the end of August.
A rule against going out, kept while the cholera lasted.
context: Snow in 1855: 'The Workhouse in Poland Street is more than three-fourths surrounded by houses in which deaths from cholera occurred, yet out of five hundred and thirty-five inmates only five died of cholera, the other deaths which took place being those of persons admitted after they were attacked. The workhouse has a pump-well on the premises, in addition to the supply from the Grand Junction Water Works, and the inmates never sent to Broad Street for water.' Notice the second half of that sentence: Snow refused to count people who arrived already sick as cases the house had produced. Deciding who counts as a case is half of an epidemiologist's work. Source: epi-snow.ph.ucla.edu/Stream2_BSPoutbreak_d.html (verbatim Snow 1855).

question: Henry Whitehead, a curate at St Luke's in Berwick Street, went door to door through Soho late in 1854. He talked to 497 of the 896 people who had lived on the stricken streets and wrote to those who had moved away, the deepest survey anyone made of the outbreak. Why had he begun it?
answer: He believed in bad air himself and meant to break Snow's water theory.
choices: He believed in bad air himself and meant to break Snow's water theory.
He had been hired by the parish to price the rebuilding of the sewers.
He was collecting names for a memorial to be raised in the churchyard.
He had been sent out by Snow to canvass the streets he could not reach.
context: Whitehead ended up convinced by the evidence he had gone looking to destroy, and became one of Snow's defenders. His door-to-door work is what turned up the outbreak's first case: five-month-old Frances Lewis at 40 Broad Street, daughter of the police constable Thomas Lewis and his wife Sarah. The baby died on 2 September 1854. A hostile investigator who follows his own data wherever it goes is worth more to a theory than ten friendly ones. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak ('Henry Whitehead's Field Inquiry'); choleraandthethames.co.uk/cholera-in-london/cholera-in-soho/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Whitehead_(priest).

question: Sarah Lewis rinsed her five-month-old baby's soiled nappies into the cesspit, the household waste pit, sunk in front of 40 Broad Street. The baby was the outbreak's first case, and the Broad Street pump drew its water from a well a short way off. How did the pit's filth reach that well?
answer: The cesspit's brick lining had rotted, and the well stood in loose gravel.
choices: The cesspit's brick lining had rotted, and the well stood in loose gravel.
The cesspit had been sluiced out into the sewer that ran past the well.
The cesspit stood uphill of the well, on ground that sloped sharply.
The cesspit had been emptied into the gutter above the well's shaft.
context: The well, some twenty-eight feet deep by the government inspectors' account, was sunk in loose gravel and sand with no layer of impermeable clay to stop seepage, and the cesspit's brick lining had rotted through. Sources genuinely disagree on how far apart the two stood — Wikipedia gives about three feet, Grokipedia about twenty — so the decayed brickwork and the porous ground are the solid parts of the story. Frances Lewis died on 2 September 1854; the reported dates for when she first fell ill vary across sources. Sources: Fraser, Hughes and Ludlow, report to the General Board of Health (johnsnow.matrix.msu.edu, Document 28); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak; grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak.

question: A widow of 59 fell ill with cholera on a Friday evening at West End in Hampstead, miles north of Soho, in a quiet district where nobody else had the disease. She was dead by Saturday, 2 September 1854. John Snow tied her death to the outbreak around Broad Street. What had come to her from there?
answer: A cart brought her a large bottle of the pump's water each day.
choices: A cart brought her a large bottle of the pump's water each day.
Her son had come up from the street to sit with her that week.
A basket of fruit had been sent up to her from the market there.
Her washing went down to a laundress in the street and came back.
context: Snow: 'A cart went from Broad Street to West End every day, and it was the custom to take out a large bottle of the water from the pump in Broad Street, as she preferred it.' The water went out on Thursday 31 August; she drank it that evening and again on Friday. Then the knockout line — 'A niece, who was on a visit to this lady, also drank of the water; she returned to her residence, in a high and healthy part of Islington, was attacked with cholera, and died also,' and 'There was no cholera at the time, either at West End or in the neighbourhood where the niece died.' Bad air does not travel in a cart. Snow's register calls her the widow of a percussion-cap maker; other accounts name her Susannah Eley, whose sons ran the Eley Brothers works in Broad Street and sent the water out to her. Sources: epi-snow.ph.ucla.edu/Stream1_introduction_d9.html (verbatim Snow 1855); choleraandthethames.co.uk/cholera-in-london/cholera-in-soho/.

question: John Snow argued his case to the parish board of St James's on 7 September 1854, and the next day the board had the handle taken off the Broad Street pump so nobody could draw from it. When Snow wrote the outbreak up in a book the following year, what did he say about that removal?
answer: He could not decide whether the well still held the poison by then.
choices: He could not decide whether the well still held the poison by then.
He could not doubt that the removal had cut the outbreak short.
He could not find a single death that had begun after that day.
He could not trust the water again while the cesspit stood beside it.
context: Snow's actual words: 'There is no doubt that the mortality was much diminished... but the attacks had so far diminished before the use of the water was stopped, that it is impossible to decide whether the well still contained the cholera poison in an active state, or whether, from some cause, the water had become free from it.' The reason deaths were already falling is that Soho had emptied — panic set in from 31 August and by 1 September the local streets were largely stripped of inhabitants, so there was hardly anyone left to catch it. Henry Whitehead wrote in 1867 that the outbreak 'had already reached its climax, and had been steadily on the decline for several days before the pump-handle was removed.' The schoolbook version — handle off, epidemic over — is not Snow's claim; he argued against his own best story, which is what a scientist is supposed to do. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak (quoting Snow 1855); grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak; epi-snow.ph.ucla.edu/Stream2_BSPoutbreak_e.html (Whitehead 1867).

question: John Snow drew a single line on his 1855 map of the Soho cholera, one most people never notice among the marks for each death. It turned the map from a picture into a test. What does that line enclose?
answer: Every spot that lay nearer to the Broad Street pump than to any other.
choices: Every spot that lay nearer to the Broad Street pump than to any other.
Every spot that lay within two hundred yards of the Broad Street pump.
Every spot that lay above the new sewers driven under the parish.
Every spot that lay lower than thirty feet above the level of the river.
context: Snow plotted every public pump in the district first, then drew the boundary enclosing all the points closer to the Broad Street pump than to any other. Wikipedia describes the method plainly: 'He mapped the individual water pumps and generated cells representing all the points on his map that were closest to each pump.' Mathematicians now call that partition a Voronoi diagram; Snow drew one in 1855, long before it had a name, and the deaths sat inside his line. It is widely reported that the second map measured distance by the nearest road on foot through the alleys rather than in a straight line — treat that refinement as reported rather than nailed down. The exceptions are the best part: only ten deaths fell in houses decidedly nearer some other pump, and in five of those ten 'the families of the deceased persons informed me that they always sent to the pump in Broad Street, as they preferred the water to that of the pumps which were nearer.' People walked past a safe pump because the deadly one tasted better. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak; epi-snow.ph.ucla.edu/Stream2_BSPoutbreak_f.html.

question: Donald Fraser, Thomas Hughes and John Ludlow went house to house through Soho for the General Board of Health in September 1854. Residents pressed two culprits on them: the Broad Street pump, and a new sewer dug through an old plague burial ground. What did the three conclude?
answer: Neither culprit could account for the outbreak
choices: Neither culprit could account for the outbreak
The pump water alone had caused the outbreak
The disturbed burial ground alone had caused it
The pump and the sewer had caused it together
context: Their orders had framed the inquiry around 'the condition of the atmosphere'. Their verdict, in their own words: 'Neither of these causes, we believe, affords a satisfactory reason for the outbreak,' and they suspected both stories had been 'prominently put forth by interested persons' wanting to turn anger away from their own nuisances, such as a slaughterhouse owner who loudly blamed the sewer. Yet the same report admits 'some cases of disease and death which we find ourselves unable to explain upon any other hypothesis than that of the deleterious influence of this water', the Hampstead widow among them, and notes that the workhouse and the brewery, whose people escaped, had wells of their own. The evidence was in their hands; their orders pointed them at the air. Source: Fraser, Hughes and Ludlow, report to the General Board of Health, printed 1855 (johnsnow.matrix.msu.edu/documentUploads/15-78-2B3/15-78-2B3-22-Doc28-F,H,L-RptToHall.pdf).

question: Edmund Parkes, a physician, reviewed John Snow's 1855 book On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, which laid out the case that the disease travelled in water: the Soho map, the Hampstead widow, a comparison of two London water companies. Parkes named the weakness Snow's critics had all felt. What could Snow not produce?
answer: Any impurity in the pump water itself that his own analysis could show.
choices: Any impurity in the pump water itself that his own analysis could show.
Any record of where each victim had gone in the days before falling ill.
Any animal made ill by a dose of water drawn from the Broad Street pump.
Any case of the cholera passing from one person to another under his eye.
context: Parkes pointed out that Snow's own examination of the pump water had found 'so little impurity... of an organic nature' — no visible filth, no demonstrated sewage, and certainly no microbe. Snow never saw a cholera germ and never claimed to; he inferred a self-multiplying poison that was swallowed and multiplied in the gut. He won on pattern, not on a specimen. The specimen already existed on paper, unread: in that same year, 1854, the Italian anatomist Filippo Pacini examined victims during an outbreak in Florence, saw a comma-shaped organism he called a vibrio in their intestinal contents, and published it. Italian medicine was committed to bad air and ignored him; Robert Koch re-found the same comma bacillus in Egypt and India in 1883-84 and got the credit. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak ('Contemporary Objections from Miasmatists'); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filippo_Pacini.

question: House by house, John Snow counted the cholera deaths over the first seven weeks of the 1854 epidemic in south London, where two water companies ran their pipes down the same streets. Lambeth had moved its intake upriver to Seething Wells in 1852; Southwark and Vauxhall still drew from the sewage-fouled tidal Thames, and that company's 40,046 houses lost 1,263 people. How much deadlier was cholera in those houses than in Lambeth's?
answer: About eight and a half times as many deaths per house.
choices: About eight and a half times as many deaths per house.
About two and a half times as many deaths per house.
About four and a half times as many deaths per house.
About sixteen and a half times as many deaths per house.
context: Lambeth's 26,107 houses lost 98 people against Southwark and Vauxhall's 1,263. That is 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 houses against 37 — neighbours on one street, breathing the same air, eating the same food, working the same trades, drinking different rivers and dying at about eight and a half times the rate. Snow called it a grand experiment, and it is as close to a controlled trial as a city ever offers: the only thing that differed between the two groups was which company's pipe reached the house. Careful with the famous numbers — Snow separately reported that over the first FOUR weeks cholera was 'between thirteen and fourteen times' as fatal in the Southwark and Vauxhall population, and 'nearly eight times as great' over the next three weeks. The '14 times' and the per-house figures cover different periods; name the period, never blend them. Sources: smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/cholera-john-snow-and-the-grand-experiment-33494689/; archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson1/section2.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Snow.

question: William Farr, the government's statistician, followed the death returns through London's eastern parishes in 1866, after cholera came back and killed more than 5,000 Londoners. He had built the best case bad air ever had: a real and repeatable link between cholera deaths and how low a district lay above the Thames. What did he trace the deaths to?
answer: The reservoir belonging to one of the water companies.
choices: The reservoir belonging to one of the water companies.
The low ground lying nearest the river below the city.
The clothing carried away from the beds of the sick.
The fruit sold cheap in the streets of those parishes.
context: Farr followed the deaths to the water supply, and the trail ran to the Old Ford Reservoir of the East London Water Company. Note what his elevation correlation had been: real, reproducible, and still not the cause — low ground near the river is also where the fouled water was. A correlation can be perfectly solid and still point at the wrong thing, which is exactly why Snow's two-company comparison mattered. Snow never saw the vindication: he had a stroke in his office on 10 June 1858 and died six days later, on 16 June 1858, aged 45 — eight years before the man who had opposed him used his method to shut a reservoir. Sources: ph.ucla.edu/epi/snow/farr/farr_eastlondon_a.html (Halliday, 'William Farr: campaigning statistician'); sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/medicine/cholera-victorian-london; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Snow.

question: Joseph Black, chemistry professor at Glasgow, asked in the late 1750s why a snowdrift took days to vanish once the spring thaw came. If warm air simply added heat, the drift should have melted in minutes. Where was all that heat going?
answer: Into melting the ice without raising its temperature
choices: Into melting the ice without raising its temperature
Down through the soil and lost to the bedrock
Straight back into the air by reflection
Sideways into the surrounding puddles
context: The heat was pouring in and the thermometer refused to move -- because the incoming energy was busy turning ice into water, not warming anything up. Black had found the biggest missing entry in the heat-books. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Black

question: Joseph Black set a lump of ice at 0 C in a warm room in December 1761 and clocked how long it took to melt. Then he took the same weight of water at 0 C and clocked how long it took to warm up to the temperature the melted ice had reached. Which took longer?
answer: The ice, by many times over
choices: The ice, by many times over
The water, by many times over
The two took almost exactly the same time
The ice took slightly less because ice is thinner
context: The ice sat there absorbing heat with no reading on the thermometer -- Black measured the hidden intake as enough to raise the same water by about 143 F. Heat was going IN with no temperature going up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Black

question: Joseph Black caught heat pouring into melting ice and boiling water in the late 1750s without the thermometer moving at all: present in the substance, invisible to the instrument. The name he gave that heat is still the one every physics student learns. What did he call it?
answer: Latent heat
choices: Latent heat
Specific heat
Sensible heat
Radiant heat
context: From the Latin latens, hidden. Physicists set it against sensible heat, the kind a thermometer registers. The name has stuck: latent heat of fusion (ice to water) and latent heat of vaporisation (water to steam) are still the terms every physics student meets. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latent_heat

question: A student tests Joseph Black's discovery about boiling at her kitchen stove. She stands a thermometer in a pot of vigorously boiling water, cranks the burner to maximum and watches the numbers. What does the reading do?
answer: Stays stuck at about 100 C
choices: Stays stuck at about 100 C
Climbs steadily as long as you leave the burner on
Drops slightly because the steam takes heat away
Spikes to about 130 C at the surface
context: Every extra joule you push in goes into ripping liquid molecules apart into vapour -- the same latent heat Black had seen in his melting ice, this time hiding in the steam. The thermometer will not move off 100 C until all the water is gone. Source: https://www.tec-science.com/thermodynamics/heat/why-steam-burns-are-more-dangerous-than-water-burns/

question: Joseph Black warmed equal weights of different things by the same amount and found they needed very different amounts of heat, a property now called specific heat. One common substance had an unusually big appetite: ounce for ounce it soaked up more heat than almost anything else Black tested. Which was it?
answer: Water
choices: Water
Iron
Sand
Mercury
context: Water's high specific heat is why the sea moderates coastal climate, why radiators use water, and why the human body -- mostly water -- is thermally stable. Black called the property a capacity for heat, and noted that mercury, in contrast, has a very small appetite for heat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Black

question: James Watt, instrument maker at Glasgow and the friend of the chemistry professor Joseph Black, set to repairing a model Newcomen atmospheric engine in 1763. He saw it wasting most of its coal on one thing, every cycle. He solved the problem on a Sunday walk on Glasgow Green in May 1765. What was the engine's ruinous waste?
answer: Reheating the cylinder after chilling it with cold water
choices: Reheating the cylinder after chilling it with cold water
Pumping the same water up and down forever
Blowing steam straight out of the exhaust valve
Turning the flywheel against a slipping belt
context: Newcomen's design shot cold water into the working cylinder every stroke to condense the steam -- then had to reheat the whole cold cylinder from scratch. Watt's answer was the SEPARATE CONDENSER: condense the steam in a chamber next door, keep the working cylinder always hot. It roughly quartered fuel consumption. (Black taught the friendship and lent money; historians treat the design as Watt's own invention.) Source: https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co50928/watts-second-separate-condenser-1765

question: A cook reaches across a pot boiling at ordinary kitchen pressure, where the water stands at 100 C and the steam coming off it is at exactly the same temperature. The steam burns her arm far worse than the boiling water would. By what Joseph Black showed about the heat hiding in a phase change, why?
answer: The steam condenses on the skin and dumps its latent heat there
choices: The steam condenses on the skin and dumps its latent heat there
The steam clings to the skin longer than water does
Water vapour is chemically more corrosive than liquid water
The steam pushes heat in faster because it is under pressure
context: Water's latent heat of vaporisation is about 2260 J/g -- a huge reservoir. When steam at 100 C touches cooler skin it condenses back into water AT 100 C, unloading all that hidden energy in an instant, roughly five times what the same mass of boiling water would deliver. It is also why sweating cools you: evaporating water carries latent heat OFF your skin the same way. Source: https://www.tec-science.com/thermodynamics/heat/why-steam-burns-are-more-dangerous-than-water-burns/

question: A girl mixes vinegar and baking soda in a jug, and carbon dioxide fills it. She tilts the jug over a lit candle, no liquid leaving it, and the flame dies. What property of the gas is at work?
answer: It is denser than ordinary air and displaces the oxygen the flame needs
choices: It is denser than ordinary air and displaces the oxygen the flame needs
It is lighter than ordinary air and rises past the flame in an updraft
It reacts chemically with the candle wax and smothers the wick
It cools the wick below the temperature a flame can sustain
context: CO2 is about 1.5 times as dense as ordinary air, so it flows out of the tilted jug like an invisible liquid and slides down over the candle, pushing the oxygen away. The flame goes out because it is starved, not chilled or chemically attacked. Source: https://sensidyne.com/application/brewery-gas-detection/
