But he had taught physics at Caltech since 1975 and been its provost from 1995 to 2004. From May 2009 to November 2011 he also held a Senate-confirmed post under President Obama. Which post was it?
answer: Under Secretary for Science at the Department of Energy
choices: Under Secretary for Science at the Department of Energy
Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency
Director of the National Science Foundation
Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy
context: Koonin was confirmed to the post under Energy Secretary Steven Chu, winner of the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics, and oversaw an annual science budget of more than $5 billion and the stewardship of ten national laboratories, Argonne and Lawrence Berkeley among them. Before that he was chief scientist at BP from 2004 to 2009. He left Stuyvesant High School at 16, took a Caltech physics B.S. in 1972 and an MIT Ph.D. in 1975, joined the Caltech faculty the same year with no postdoc, and made full professor in 1981. Critics note that his later home, Stanford's Hoover Institution, has taken fossil-fuel money; his own answer is that his claims are checkable against the published reports, which is the whole point. Source: Grokipedia, 'Steve Koonin' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Steve_Koonin); Wikipedia, 'Steven E. Koonin'.

question: Often waved off as a physicist who distrusts computer models, Steven Koonin wrote the 1986 textbook 'Computational Physics' and won the Energy Department's E.O. Lawrence Award in 1998 for his simulation work. One Energy Department program leaned on simulations like his for its main job. What were those computers checking?
answer: that America's nuclear warheads would still work
choices: that America's nuclear warheads would still work
that buried nuclear waste would stay sealed for millennia
that a fusion reactor's plasma could reach ignition
that the national power grid could survive a solar storm
context: That is stockpile stewardship: once the United States stopped setting off test explosions, the confidence that its weapons still functioned had to come out of a computer. Koonin also built numerical methods for nuclear many-body problems and was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2010. It matters for the rest of his story: his complaint about climate models is a model-builder's complaint about how models are tuned, not a layman's suspicion of computers. Source: Grokipedia, 'Steve Koonin' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Steve_Koonin), with the DOE Office of Science Lawrence Award citation.

question: Steven Koonin published an essay in the Wall Street Journal on 19 September 2014, 'Climate Science Is Not Settled'. Later he shared an annotated version with twelve notes, which a newspaper column does not usually carry. What do the twelve notes point to?
answer: numbered figures and sections of the IPCC's own report
choices: numbered figures and sections of the IPCC's own report
temperature datasets that NASA and NOAA publish monthly
peer-reviewed papers that contradict the IPCC's findings
chapters of the federal National Climate Assessment
context: The notes cite the Fifth Assessment Report by address: 'AR5 WG1 Figure 2.11', 'AR5 WG1 3.6.6', 'AR5 WG1 9.4.1.4.2', 'AR5 WG1 Table 9.1'. Every one of those pages is free to download from ipcc.ch, so a reader with nothing but a library card can go and check whether Koonin quoted the report honestly. That is the transferable move in this whole topic: not 'trust him', but 'open the document he is pointing at'. Source: Koonin, 'Climate Science Is Not Settled', WSJ 19 Sept 2014, annotated version with all twelve notes (https://www.sfu.ca/~palmer/Koonin.pdf).

question: Standing up at the American Physical Society meeting in Baltimore on 1 May 1989, Steven Koonin, a Caltech theorist, told the session what he made of the Utah result. Six weeks earlier the chemists Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons had announced from Utah nuclear fusion in a jar of water on a laboratory bench. The room rose and applauded him. What did he say the result was the product of?
answer: the incompetence and delusion of Pons and Fleischmann
choices: the incompetence and delusion of Pons and Fleischmann
the wishful arithmetic and haste of Pons and Fleischmann
the inexperience and stubbornness of Pons and Fleischmann
the miscalibration and optimism of Pons and Fleischmann
context: The New York Times carried it on 3 May 1989 under the headline 'Physicists Debunk Claim Of a New Kind of Fusion'. Koonin then served on the Energy Department's Cold Fusion Panel, whose November 1989 final report found the evidence unconvincing. The episode matters here because it is the same move performed a quarter-century earlier against a claim nobody could call political: check the measurement, say what you find. Source: Grokipedia, 'Steve Koonin'; LENR-CANR archive of the APS Baltimore meeting, 1-2 May 1989 (https://lenr-canr.org/acrobat/APSinformatio.pdf); New York Times, 3 May 1989.

question: Writing in the Wall Street Journal on 19 September 2014, Steven Koonin argued that the certainty in climate headlines is badly overstated. He took up human influence on the climate directly in the essay's fourth paragraph, in a single sentence. What did he write there?
answer: That is no hoax: greenhouse gases from fossil fuels are influencing the climate
choices: That is no hoax: greenhouse gases from fossil fuels are influencing the climate
That is not in dispute: human emissions are the main driver of today's warming
That is still open: no instrument has cleanly separated our signal from nature's
That is doubtful: our influence is dwarfed by the climate's own natural swings
context: Verbatim: 'Nor is the crucial question whether humans are influencing the climate. That is no hoax: There is little doubt in the scientific community that continually growing amounts of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, due largely to carbon-dioxide emissions from the conventional use of fossil fuels, are influencing the climate.' The paragraph before it is just as flat: 'The climate has always changed and always will.' The essay is routinely summarised as an argument that man-made warming is fake, and that summary is simply false about what Koonin wrote - he concedes the greenhouse effect in the opening column inches and then argues about certainty, about how much confidence the models earn, and about what follows for policy. Source: Koonin, WSJ 19 Sept 2014 (https://www.sfu.ca/~palmer/Koonin.pdf).

question: Working from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment, Steven Koonin annotated his 2014 essay. His note [9], on Antarctic sea ice, carries out in a single paragraph the reading technique the whole essay is recommending. What does note [9] do?
answer: sets the summary's sentence beside the chapter's own sentence
choices: sets the summary's sentence beside the chapter's own sentence
sets the chapter's sentence beside the cited paper's sentence
sets the summary's sentence beside the previous report's sentence
sets the press release's sentence beside the summary's sentence
context: Note [9] quotes the Summary for Policymakers on Antarctic sea ice, then says: 'It is interesting to compare the last sentence to the wording in the WG1 report itself (9.4.3.1)' - and prints that one too. The summary is the layer officials and journalists actually read; the chapters underneath it are the layer almost nobody opens. The essay's thesis sentence explains why Koonin bothers: 'Yet a public official reading only the IPCC's "Summary for Policy Makers" would gain little sense of the extent or implications of these deficiencies.' And: 'These and many other open questions are in fact described in the IPCC research reports, although a detailed and knowledgeable reading is sometimes required to discern them.' You can run this yourself on any report that has a summary. Source: Koonin, WSJ 19 Sept 2014, note [9] (https://www.sfu.ca/~palmer/Koonin.pdf).

question: Steven Koonin, who had spent his career writing computer simulations, compared the roughly fifty-five climate models behind the Fifth Assessment of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Each one tried to match a century of temperatures already on record. What did he report about how they described that century?
answer: they differ from one another by over three times the measured warming
choices: they differ from one another by over three times the measured warming
they cluster within a few hundredths of a degree of one another
they agree with one another but miss the measured record entirely
they differ from one another only for the years before 1950
context: Verbatim: 'The models differ in their descriptions of the past century's global average surface temperature by more than three times the entire warming recorded during that time... Since they disagree so markedly, no more than one of them can be right.' Koonin also notes that model grid cells are 'no finer than 60 miles', so that 'the distance from New York City to Washington, D.C., is thus covered by only four grid cells', and that everything smaller than a cell - clouds above all - must be fitted with numbers that are, in his words, 'tuned, in the jargon of modelers'. He cites AR5 WG1 Figure 9.8. Source: Koonin, WSJ 19 Sept 2014, main text and notes [5] and [6] (https://www.sfu.ca/~palmer/Koonin.pdf).

question: Steven Koonin sat Richard Lindzen, John Christy and Judith Curry across from Isaac Held, Bill Collins and Ben Santer in Brooklyn on 8 January 2014, and he grilled all six for a day. He was chairing the panel for the American Physical Society, three years before he called for climate reports to face tough debate. What did the Society do with that day?
answer: posted the full transcript of the day on its website
choices: posted the full transcript of the day on its website
published a two-page consensus summary of the day
sent its recordings of the day to the IPCC's authors
sealed the proceedings until its own panel reported
context: The workshop met at New York University's Center for Urban Science and Progress; Koonin's subcommittee was Phillip Coyle, Scott Kemp, Tim Meyer, Robert Rosner and Susan Seestrom. The transcript ran to more than 500 pages and went up on the APS policy-statements site with the presenters' slides embedded, so a curious kid can read the actual argument between Held, Santer, Collins, Lindzen, Christy and Curry rather than somebody's report about the argument. In April 2017 Koonin proposed formalising this in the Wall Street Journal: a Red Team of scientists writes a critique of an assessment and a Blue Team rebuts it - a practice he said came from intelligence analysis and spacecraft design, and one 'more rigorous than traditional peer review, which is usually confidential and always adjudicated, rather than public and moderated', leaving behind 'a traceable public record'. Sources: Judith Curry, 'APS reviews its Climate Change Statement', 19 Feb 2014 (https://judithcurry.com/2014/02/19/aps-reviews-its-climate-change-statement/); transcript mirror https://geoffstuff.com/koonin_2014.pdf; Koonin, WSJ 20-21 April 2017.

question: Five scientists handed Energy Secretary Chris Wright a review of how greenhouse gases affect the United States climate on 23 July 2025: John Christy, Judith Curry, Steven Koonin, Ross McKitrick and Roy Spencer. The report said plainly that carbon dioxide warms the climate. It also said U.S. records do not show a clear long-term rise in extreme weather. What happened next?
answer: more than eighty climate scientists published a joint rebuttal
choices: more than eighty climate scientists published a joint rebuttal
the Energy Department withdrew it within a week of release
no organised scientific response to it ever appeared
the IPCC cited it in a special report on extreme weather
context: Edited by Andrew Dessler of Texas A&M and Robert Kopp of Rutgers, the 'Climate Experts' Review of the DOE Climate Working Group Report' appeared on 2 September 2025, ran to hundreds of pages, and charged cherry-picking, overstated uncertainty and misquotation of peer-reviewed work. Carbon Brief catalogued over 100 statements it called false or misleading; an Associated Press survey found 53 of 64 responding experts reviewed the report negatively; the American Meteorological Society issued its own statement of objections. The Union of Concerned Scientists and the Environmental Defense Fund sued on 12 August 2025 under the Federal Advisory Committee Act; DOE dissolved the Climate Working Group on 3 September 2025; and on 30 January 2026 a federal judge ruled that DOE had 'failed to hold open meetings or assemble a balance of viewpoints, as the law requires'. The report's own Preface says the group worked 'on the condition that there would be no editorial oversight by the Secretary, the Department of Energy, or any other government personnel'. Koonin defended it in the Wall Street Journal on 8 September 2025. This is a defensible minority position that was contested hard, and both halves of that sentence are true. Sources: DOE, 'A Critical Review of Impacts of Greenhouse Gas Emissions on the U.S. Climate', 23 July 2025; Dessler and Kopp (eds.), https://sites.google.com/tamu.edu/doeresponse/home; AMS response statement.

question: Beside one range in his 2014 essay, Steven Koonin added a note on where it came from: the range the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) gives for climate sensitivity, the warming once the carbon dioxide in the air has doubled. What does his note say produced that range?
answer: the assessment panel's own expert judgment
choices: the assessment panel's own expert judgment
an average over the fifty-five model runs
a fit to the past century's temperature record
a calculation from satellite radiation budgets
context: Note [12], verbatim: 'IPCC's latest assessment (AR5 WG1 TS.5.3) of ECS is 1.5-4.5 C (66% CI). It is notable that this estimate is not derived from hard science, but rather from "expert assessment" (AR5 WG1, p. TS-56).' In the main text he adds that the estimate was 'no different, and no more certain, than it was 30 years ago... despite an heroic research effort costing billions of dollars.' Expert assessment is not nothing - it is trained people weighing evidence - but it is a different kind of thing from a measurement, and the report says so on its own page. Source: Koonin, WSJ 19 Sept 2014, main text and note [12] (https://www.sfu.ca/~palmer/Koonin.pdf).

question: Steven Koonin complained in 2014 that the quoted range for climate sensitivity, 1.5 to 4.5 degrees Celsius, was no narrower and no more certain than it had been thirty years and billions of dollars earlier. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) took the question up again in its Sixth Assessment in August 2021, four months after his book 'Unsettled' appeared. What did it report?
answer: a best estimate of 3 degrees, likely range 2.5 to 4
choices: a best estimate of 3 degrees, likely range 2.5 to 4
the same range of 1.5 to 4.5, with no best estimate
a best estimate of 3.5 degrees, likely range 2 to 6
a best estimate of 1.8 degrees, likely range 1 to 3
context: AR6 WG1 Summary for Policymakers A.4.4, verbatim: 'The very likely range of equilibrium climate sensitivity is between 2C (high confidence) and 5C (medium confidence). The AR6 assessed best estimate is 3C with a likely range of 2.5C to 4C (high confidence), compared to 1.5C to 4.5C in AR5, which did not provide a best estimate.' So Koonin's 'no different than thirty years ago' was true through the Fifth Assessment and was overtaken in the same year his book came out. Anyone still quoting 1.5 to 4.5 as the current range is quoting a superseded number - and checking that is exactly the habit worth having, applied to Koonin himself. Source: IPCC AR6 WG1 SPM A.4.4 (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/summary-for-policymakers/).

question: Steven Koonin read to the very end of the one paragraph the 2021 Summary for Policymakers of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) gives to tropical cyclones. Its confidence is uneven: 'low confidence' in long-term trends in how often cyclones of any kind form, and 'likely' that the share of the strongest storms, Categories 3 to 5, has risen over the past forty years. One other finding there gets the report's strongest rating, 'very likely'. Which finding is it?
answer: the latitude at which north-west Pacific cyclones peak has moved north
choices: the latitude at which north-west Pacific cyclones peak has moved north
the speed at which Caribbean hurricanes cross the open sea has slowed
the season in which Bay of Bengal cyclones form has stretched longer
the distance Gulf Coast hurricanes drive inland before dying has grown
context: AR6 WG1 SPM A.3.4, verbatim, all of it one paragraph: 'It is likely that the global proportion of major (Category 3-5) tropical cyclone occurrence has increased over the last four decades, and it is very likely that the latitude where tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific reach their peak intensity has shifted northward; these changes cannot be explained by internal variability alone (medium confidence). There is low confidence in long-term (multi-decadal to centennial) trends in the frequency of all-category tropical cyclones.' Three findings, three different confidence labels, one paragraph. A careless alarmist quotes the first sentence and stops; a careless sceptic quotes the last one and stops; the finding the report is surest about is the one almost nobody quotes at all. Reading to the end of the paragraph is the whole method, and it costs nothing but the click that opens the report. Source: IPCC AR6 WG1 SPM A.3.4 (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/summary-for-policymakers/).

question: In his book 'Unsettled', Steven Koonin pointed hard at one stretch of the temperature record: from 1940 to 1970, greenhouse gas emissions climbed sharply but the global temperature did not rise. Climate models can match that flat stretch, but only by adding a second human effect that pushes the other way. What is that cooling effect?
answer: aerosols, the haze of particles that industry emits
choices: aerosols, the haze of particles that industry emits
ozone loss, the thinning that refrigerant gases caused
irrigation, the water that new farmland evaporates
contrails, the ice clouds that aircraft leave behind
context: The IPCC states the size of the term itself. AR6 WG1 SPM A.1.3, verbatim: 'The likely range of total human-caused global surface temperature increase from 1850-1900 to 2010-2019 is 0.8C to 1.3C, with a best estimate of 1.07C. It is likely that well-mixed GHGs contributed a warming of 1.0C to 2.0C, other human drivers (principally aerosols) contributed a cooling of 0.0C to 0.8C.' The aerosol term runs from zero to more than half the total warming - room enough to absorb an awkward thirty years. Aerosol cooling is real physics, measured and not invented; Koonin's argument is about how much freedom that uncertainty gives a model that has to hit a known answer. Sources: BenBella Books page for 'Unsettled' (https://benbellabooks.com/shop/unsettled/); IPCC AR6 WG1 SPM A.1.3.

question: For most of his September 2014 Wall Street Journal essay, Steven Koonin argued that the climate's future is far less certain than the headlines and computer models suggest. He closed by saying what should follow from that uncertainty. What did he call well-justified prudence?
answer: accelerating low-emissions technology and energy efficiency
choices: accelerating low-emissions technology and energy efficiency
postponing energy decisions until the models converge
moving coastal infrastructure inland ahead of the sea
funding a decade of new satellite measurement first
context: Verbatim: 'That uncertainty need not be an excuse for inaction. There is well-justified prudence in accelerating the development of low-emissions technologies and in cost-effective energy-efficiency measures.' And the sentence that names both errors at once: 'Policy makers and the public may wish for the comfort of certainty in their climate science. But I fear that rigidly promulgating the idea that climate science is "settled" (or is a "hoax") demeans and chills the scientific enterprise.' He puts 'hoax' in the same sentence as 'settled' and refuses both. He has serious published critics who say he is wrong anyway - Raymond Pierrehumbert in Slate on 1 October 2014, Gary Yohe in Scientific American on 13 May 2021, and his own former student Mark Boslough in Yale Climate Connections on 25 May 2021 - and he answered them in print. In August 2025 he summed up his own position to The Free Press as 'the truth about climate change lies somewhere in the middle.' Source: Koonin, WSJ 19 Sept 2014 (https://www.sfu.ca/~palmer/Koonin.pdf); Wikipedia, 'Steven E. Koonin' for the named critics.

question: Stephanie Kwolek mixed a fresh polymer batch one morning in 1964 at the DuPont laboratory in Wilmington, hunting a new fiber stiff enough to reinforce car tires. Every batch before it had come out clear and syrupy, like molasses. This one looked like nothing she had ever made. How did it look?
answer: Cloudy and thin, like buttermilk
choices: Cloudy and thin, like buttermilk
Cloudy and stiff, like cold mayonnaise
Clear and thin, like plain tap water
Amber and stiff, like set jelly
context: Kwolek's own words, from a 1993 speech: 'The solution was unusually [low viscosity], turbid, stir-opalescent and buttermilk in appearance. Conventional polymer solutions are usually clear or translucent and have the viscosity of molasses, more or less.' By the lab's ordinary standards the batch was ruined; a solution that cloudy was normally thrown out. The story is often retold as though someone ordered her to bin it - what the record actually shows is only that such batches were routinely discarded, and that Kwolek asked for hers to be spun anyway. Sources: Kwolek 1993 speech quoted at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek; lemelson.mit.edu/resources/stephanie-kwolek

question: Starting at DuPont in 1946, Stephanie Kwolek set herself a plan: work a few years, save the money and leave for what she really wanted to do. She stayed forty years, invented Kevlar and never went. What had she been saving up for in the first place?
answer: Medical school, to become a doctor
choices: Medical school, to become a doctor
Graduate school, to earn a doctorate
Teacher training, to run a classroom
Law school, to become a patent lawyer
context: Kwolek joined DuPont in 1946 meaning to bank a few years' salary for medical school. At the interview she asked W. Hale Charch to decide sooner than the two weeks he had quoted, because another company was waiting on her answer; Charch called in his receptionist and dictated her offer letter on the spot. She never left, retiring in 1986 with 17 US patents. She later said she knew 'that because I had only a bachelor's degree, it would not be easy, that there would be prejudice... but especially because I was a woman.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek; sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/stephanie-l-kwolek

question: Stephanie Kwolek's group got its orders from DuPont in 1964: replace the steel cord buried inside every car tire with a new fiber. The order came out of a worry about what the next decade would bring, nothing to do with soldiers or armor. What was DuPont worried about?
answer: A gasoline shortage - lighter tires stretch a gallon further
choices: A gasoline shortage - lighter tires stretch a gallon further
A steel shortage - the mills could not meet tire demand
A rubber shortage - natural latex supplies were tightening
A rust problem - steel cords corroding inside the tires
context: Kevlar was born out of a fuel-economy problem, not a weapons program: DuPont expected a gasoline shortage, and lighter tires mean better mileage, so the target was the steel cord inside the tire. The irony is that tire makers balked at the cost of retooling their plants, so the application Kevlar was invented for is not the one that made it famous. It reached the market in 1971. Sources: Invention & Technology Magazine, Jim Quinn, 'Kevlar' (Fall 2010), inventionandtech.com/content/kevlar; grokipedia.com/page/Stephanie_Kwolek

question: Stephanie Kwolek asked to have her strange new batch spun into fiber. Charles Smullen, the DuPont man who ran the spinning machine, said no. It was not stubbornness. The liquid was nothing like the batches he fed the machine every day, and he had a real worry. What did Smullen think was in her batch?
answer: Grit that would clog the machine
choices: Grit that would clog the machine
Water that would weaken the fiber
Acid that would corrode the machine
Air bubbles that would snap the thread
context: Smullen's reasoning was sound: cloudiness normally means particulate matter, and particles would clog the fine holes of the spinneret; on top of that, the water-thin liquid behaved nothing like a normal polymer dope. Kwolek argued that her polymer was chemically dissolved in the solvent, not suspended in it. After what the accounts call 'considerable discussion' he relented, and it spun without incident. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek; Invention & Technology Magazine, Jim Quinn, 'Stephanie Kwolek, Kevlar' (Winter 2020); grokipedia.com/page/Stephanie_Kwolek

question: Without waiting for the testing lab, Stephanie Kwolek took up the first fiber spun from her strange batch, unlike anything she had drawn before, and ran the first test herself, right there at the machine. What did she do, and what happened?
answer: She pulled it in her hands, and it did not break
choices: She pulled it in her hands, and it did not break
She held a flame to it, and it did not catch
She knotted it round a weight, and the knot held
She rubbed it between her fingers, and it did not fray
context: Her words: 'Unlike ordinary nylon, this fiber was very difficult to break by hand. At that moment I knew we had a most unusual fiber.' Her first instrument was her own two hands - the same test anyone can run on a thread, which is exactly why the moment is so easy to picture. The machines confirmed it afterward. Source: Invention & Technology Magazine, Jim Quinn, 'Stephanie Kwolek, Kevlar' (Winter 2020), inventionandtech.com/content/stephanie-kwolek-kevlar

question: Looking at her cloudy batch, Stephanie Kwolek faced the obvious verdict: she had contaminated it, since a cloudy liquid almost always means something solid is drifting in it, undissolved. She settled that at the bench with one simple test, and the result was flat: whatever was scattering the light, it was not floating solids. What was the test?
answer: She pushed the batch through a fine filter, and none was caught
choices: She pushed the batch through a fine filter, and none was caught
She spun the batch in a centrifuge, and nothing settled out
She left the batch standing overnight, and nothing sank down
She shone a lamp through the batch, and saw no glinting specks
context: Kwolek's words: 'The solution that I prepared looked like a dispersion but was totally filterable through a fine pore filter.' Every drop went through, so the cloudiness could not be suspended solids - she had ruled out the dirty-beaker explanation before she ever asked for the batch to be spun. She added that she did not yet understand what she was actually looking at. This one test is the cleanest answer to anyone who says she simply got lucky with a contaminated batch: she tested it. Source: Kwolek 1993 speech, quoted at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek

question: Stephanie Kwolek read strength numbers on her new fiber so far above anything DuPont had ever spun that a scientist hunting a reputation would have run down the hall with them. She did not. What did she do before she would let herself say she had discovered anything?
answer: Had the strength tests repeated over and over again
choices: Had the strength tests repeated over and over again
Sent a sample to an outside lab for a second opinion
Asked a second chemist to make the polymer again
Checked the machine against a fiber of known strength
context: Her account: 'I had the tests repeated a number of times before I became convinced that I had made a significant discovery.' Tensile strength, elongation and stiffness, run again and again, because the numbers were too good and she suspected herself first. Skepticism of your own result is the first scientific virtue and the hardest to practise - the extraordinary measurement you want to be true is exactly the one to re-run. Source: Invention & Technology Magazine, Jim Quinn, 'Stephanie Kwolek, Kevlar' (Winter 2020), inventionandtech.com/content/stephanie-kwolek-kevlar

question: Stephanie Kwolek and Paul Morgan published a beaker demo in 1959 that teachers still perform. It is called the Nylon Rope Trick. Two liquids go into one beaker, with no heat. A solid nylon strand can be lifted out and reeled off like thread from a spool. Where in the beaker is the nylon being made?
answer: At the line where the two liquids meet
choices: At the line where the two liquids meet
Throughout the beaker, wherever they have mixed
At the top, where the liquid meets the air
At the bottom, where the beaker is coolest
context: The strand forms at the boundary line where the two liquids meet, and it can be drawn out of the beaker continuously - a rope of nylon at room temperature, with no heat needed. Morgan and Kwolek's 1959 paper 'The Nylon Rope Trick' (Journal of Polymer Science 40(137):299-327) won an American Chemical Society publication award and is still standard in classrooms; Kwolek performed it for schoolchildren herself after retiring in 1986. Worth asking a chemistry teacher to run it: the woman who discovered Kevlar also wrote the demonstration. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek; grokipedia.com/page/Stephanie_Kwolek

question: In her cloudy batch Stephanie Kwolek found nothing solid floating, and yet it scattered light like milk. Ordinary polymer solutions stay clear because their molecules are floppy tangles, tumbling every which way past one another. Her molecules were doing something else in that flask, and that was what threw the light back. What were they doing?
answer: Lining up side by side into liquid-crystal patches
choices: Lining up side by side into liquid-crystal patches
Cross-linking into one loose three-dimensional net
Curling into tight coils packed like small springs
Splitting into microscopic droplets of a second liquid
context: This is the whole discovery. Kwolek's para-aramid molecules are stiff rods, not floppy coils, and above a critical concentration rods can no longer tumble freely past one another - they snap into parallel domains, a lyotropic liquid crystal. Those aligned domains scatter light, which is why the batch looked cloudy: the reason it looked wrong is the reason it was strong. Rods already lined up in the beaker come out of the spinneret still lined up, and alignment is strength. The Science History Institute records the team's surprise - 'Though their liquidity was initially a cause of technical concern, to everyone's surprise, these liquid crystalline solutions spun beautifully.' Kwolek's poly-p-benzamide and PPTA solutions were the first liquid crystal polymers ever prepared. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Stephanie_Kwolek; sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/stephanie-l-kwolek; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek

question: A police officer straps on a vest of twenty to thirty layers of woven Kevlar, rated for handgun rounds, a 9mm or even a .44 Magnum. The word for it is bullet-resistant, not bulletproof, and the gap between those two words is real: a rifle round punches straight through. What has to be added to stop one?
answer: A hard ceramic plate slid into the vest
choices: A hard ceramic plate slid into the vest
A steel mesh sewn between the layers
A thicker stack of the same woven layers
A rubber backing to spread the impact
context: Soft Kevlar vests are rated NIJ Level II or IIIA - handgun rounds, including 9mm full metal jacket and .44 Magnum. Rifle rounds need hard ceramic or UHMWPE plates. A second honest limit: a vest that stops bullets does not reliably stop a knife or a spike, because edged and pointed threats defeat soft armor and need different construction entirely. What the fabric does do is real - the National Institute of Justice credits Kevlar armor with saving more than 3,000 officers' lives, and an officer wearing a vest is about 76% less likely to die of a torso gunshot wound. The first documented life saved by a Kevlar vest was in Seattle in 1975. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Kevlar, citing NIJ Standard-0101.06; grokipedia.com/page/Stephanie_Kwolek

question: Stephanie Kwolek had spun a fiber whose molecules lie stretched out and parallel along its length, which is why pulling on it is so hard: weight for weight it beats steel about five to one. But a single chain on its own would simply slide past its neighbors, and the fiber would come apart like a handful of loose threads. Something grips neighboring chains together sideways. What holds them?
answer: Hydrogen bonds, each N-H reaching the next C=O
choices: Hydrogen bonds, each N-H reaching the next C=O
Covalent bridges, one carbon welded to the next
Ionic bonds, metal ions bridging chain to chain
Sulfur cross-links, the trick that hardens rubber
context: Each amide's N-H reaches across to the neighboring chain's C=O, building the parallel chains into hydrogen-bonded sheets; pull along the fiber and a colossal number of those bonds have to resist at once (Kevlar 29 modulus about 70.5 GPa, Kevlar 49 about 112 GPa; tensile strength about 2,900-3,000 MPa at a density of 1.44 g/cm3 against steel's 7.8). The honest other side is that this strength runs one way only. Push or bend Kevlar instead of pulling it and it fails by kink bands - the fiber buckles and folds. It is a rope, not a pillar. It does not stretch to save itself either: elongation at break is only 2.4% (Kevlar 49) to 3.6% (Kevlar 29), a nearly straight line to fracture with no warning. And unprotected Kevlar keeps only about 60% of its strength after 1,000 hours of sunlight, because ultraviolet snaps the chains - which is why it is rarely used outdoors uncovered. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Kevlar; 'Compressional behaviour of Kevlar fibres' (1981) and 'Compressive properties of aramid fibres' (1997), ScienceDirect

question: Stephanie Kwolek saw her name go on a United States patent as the inventor of Kevlar in 1974. The fiber had reached the market in 1971, and it has since made several billion dollars. What became of that patent?
answer: She signed it over to DuPont and earned nothing from it
choices: She signed it over to DuPont and earned nothing from it
She licensed it to DuPont and drew a royalty per pound
She held it jointly with DuPont and shared the profits
She sold it to DuPont and took a single lump payment
context: Kwolek was a DuPont employee, so the patent went to the company: she signed over US Patent 3,819,587, 'Wholly Aromatic Carbocyclic Polycarbonamide Fiber,' granted 1974. The discovery earned DuPont several billion dollars; she never benefited from it financially. She held 17 US patents in all, and had already handed DuPont a second fiber: she worked out the conditions for the meta-aramid released in 1961 as Nomex, the flame-resistant one. Nomex and Kevlar are the same chemistry with one difference - meta linkages put a permanent bend in the chain, so Nomex stays flexible and heat-resistant but never reaches Kevlar's strength. During the week Kwolek died, in June 2014, the one-millionth bullet-resistant vest made with Kevlar was sold. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek (citing Jeremy Pearce, New York Times obituary, June 21, 2014, and Alyssa Newcomb, Good Morning America, June 20, 2014); invent.org/inductees/stephanie-louise-kwolek; lemelson.mit.edu/resources/stephanie-kwolek

question: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck gave his famous example in 1809 in Philosophie Zoologique, the first serious book-length theory of how living species change. He took a giraffe feeding at a tall tree. How did he say it got its long neck?
answer: each giraffe stretched for high leaves, and its calves inherited the longer neck
choices: each giraffe stretched for high leaves, and its calves inherited the longer neck
each parent shed tiny gemmules from every organ that gathered in the seed to shape the calf
calves were an average blend of the two parents' necks, with the blend fixed at birth
giraffes descend from a much taller ancestor, and their necks have been shrinking
context: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck published this in his 'Philosophie Zoologique' (1809). The idea is called the inheritance of acquired characteristics: a trait a parent worked into its own body during life is handed down to its offspring. One other choice is Charles Darwin's own later heredity guess, pangenesis (1868); another is blending inheritance -- both were seriously held by working scientists of the era and both turned out wrong. Sources: Britannica 'August Weismann'; sciencereader.com on Lamarckian evolution.

question: August Weismann cut the tails off 68 white mice in the 1880s, then off their pups and their pups' pups, for five generations. He was testing Lamarckism, the old claim that a trait an animal picks up during its life, like a scar or a lost tail, can pass to its young. What did he find?
answer: zero shortened tails, not one single mouse across all 901 offspring
choices: zero shortened tails, not one single mouse across all 901 offspring
a handful of pups with shortened tails, all clustered in the fifth generation
one litter with kinked tails in the third generation, then none after
no shortened tails, but a steady rise in coat-color anomalies by the fifth generation
context: Weismann's own words: '901 young were produced by five generations of artificially mutilated parents, and yet there was not a single example of a rudimentary tail or of any other abnormality in this organ.' Weismann himself was careful about the scope; he said the result settled the specific claim about inherited MUTILATIONS, and used the outcome to argue his broader germ-plasm theory (published as 'Das Keimplasma' in 1892), which held that body cells cannot write back to the cells that make the next generation. Source: Wikipedia, 'August Weismann'.

question: Karl Landsteiner, a young pathologist in Vienna, set drops of his colleagues' blood together on a plate in 1900 and watched some pairs clump. Until then a transfusion was a coin flip: some patients rallied within the hour, others burned with fever and died. What did his plate reveal?
answer: Blood types
choices: Blood types
White blood cells
Germs in the blood
Red blood cell size
context: Landsteiner (1868-1943) trained as a physician in Vienna and turned to serology when the clinical mystery of transfusion killings caught his interest. His 1900 note and 1901 paper opened the field. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Landsteiner

question: Karl Landsteiner sorted the pattern of clumped and smooth squares from his six-donor grid, and the donors did not fall into a random tangle. Their blood sorted cleanly into three categories, and he gave each one a short label. Which labels did he choose?
answer: A, B and C
choices: A, B and C
I, II and III
alpha, beta and gamma
plus, minus and neutral
context: Landsteiner's original three-group scheme was A, B and C. The C group was renamed O in 1910 by Ludwik Hirszfeld and Emil von Dungern, and that is the name it still carries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABO_blood_group_system

question: Two of Karl Landsteiner's students went back to his blood groups in 1902 with a far larger set of samples. His six donors had been enough to reveal three groups but not a fourth, rarer one. The students pulled out the missing group, later named AB. Who were they?
answer: Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli
choices: Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli
Emil Behring and Paul Ehrlich
Robert Koch and Friedrich Loeffler
Jules Bordet and Octave Gengou
context: The lesson buried in the discovery story is a lesson about sample size: rare types show up only when you test enough people. Decastello and Sturli found AB in 1902; Hirszfeld and von Dungern gave it its modern name in 1910. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABO_blood_group_system

question: Karl Landsteiner mixed drops of blood from different people on a glass plate in 1900 and watched some pairs clump into red flecks while other pairs stayed smooth. The clumping was not the red cells themselves misbehaving. It was a real chemical fight between two invisible partners. What were they?
answer: sugar antigens attacked by matching antibodies
choices: sugar antigens attacked by matching antibodies
iron atoms attacked by digestive enzymes
cholesterol patches attacked by cell walls
clotting factors attacked by platelets
context: A-type plasma carries anti-B antibodies, B-type carries anti-A, O carries both, AB carries neither. The antibodies grip the mismatched sugar markers on the donor red cells and pull them into visible clumps, which is why an incompatible transfusion can kill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABO_blood_group_system

question: A nurse reaches into an emergency room's small stock of one particular donor blood for a patient there is no time to type. Since Karl Landsteiner's 1900 work, doctors have known that a mismatched transfusion can kill, but this stock can be given to almost anyone. Which donor blood is it?
answer: O-negative red cells
choices: O-negative red cells
AB-positive red cells
A-negative red cells
B-positive red cells
context: O-negative red cells lack A, B and Rh(D) surface markers, so almost no recipient's antibodies bind them. For PLASMA the picture is opposite: AB plasma carries no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so AB is the universal plasma donor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABO_blood_group_system

question: Jean-Baptiste Denys, a young physician in Paris, transfused a 15-year-old boy with the blood of another creature on 15 June 1667, one of the first attempts to put an animal's blood into a human. The boy survived. A later patient, Antoine Mauroy, died. Whose blood had Denys given the boy?
answer: a lamb's
choices: a lamb's
a horse's
a dog's
a calf's
context: Denys used lamb's blood on the boy and calf's blood on Mauroy. After the deaths, the Royal Society and French government banned the practice in 1668 and the Vatican condemned it in 1670; human transfusion stayed nearly untouchable for a century and a half. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_transfusion

question: A girl sets a wad of steel wool on one pan of a kitchen balance and levels the beam. She touches a lit match to the wool, and it glows orange, spreads and crumbles into a dark, brittle crust. What does the beam do?
answer: It tips down on the burnt side; the crust outweighs the wool.
choices: It tips down on the burnt side; the crust outweighs the wool.
It tips up on the burnt side; the crust weighs less than the wool.
It stays level; burning rearranges matter but never adds any.
It tips down, then rises back level once the crust cools.
context: The burnt side sinks: burnt steel wool weighs MORE than the wool did, which is exactly the result that broke chemistry open in the 1770s. Burn a candle in an open jar instead and mass seems to vanish. Neither one breaks the law of conservation of mass; both show that you cannot keep the books unless you count the gases too -- which is why Antoine Lavoisier did his burning inside sealed vessels. Closed-system version you can run at home: put baking soda and vinegar in a bottle with a balloon stretched over the neck. The balloon inflates, and the whole apparatus weighs exactly what it did before. Sources: RSC Education, 'The combustion of iron wool' (edu.rsc.org/experiments/the-combustion-of-iron-wool/717.article); Grokipedia, Conservation_of_mass.

question: Joseph Priestley focused sunlight through a big burning lens onto a red mercury powder on 1 August 1774 and caught the strange new gas that came off in a glass jar. He lowered a lit candle down into it. What did the candle do?
answer: It blazed up, five or six times brighter than in ordinary air.
choices: It blazed up, five or six times brighter than in ordinary air.
It shrank to a small blue bead and burned on without smoke.
It went out at once, as though it had been smothered.
It burned exactly as it would have in ordinary air.
context: It blazed. A mouse sealed in the same gas lived roughly four times as long as in an equal volume of ordinary air, and Joseph Priestley breathed it himself, reporting a feeling of lightness and ease in his lungs. He called it 'dephlogisticated air' -- air emptied of fire-stuff and therefore hungry for more -- and he never gave the theory up: in 1800, exiled in Northumberland, Pennsylvania, he published 'The doctrine of phlogiston established, and that of the composition of water refuted,' and died a phlogistonist on 6 February 1804. Priestley was not first, either. Carl Wilhelm Scheele, a self-taught Swedish apothecary, had made the same gas around 1771-72 and called it 'fire air,' but published only in 1777. Lavoisier came last of the three: he did not discover this gas -- he weighed it, showed it was a distinct element, and named it. Sources: Grokipedia, Oxygen and Carl_Wilhelm_Scheele; archive.org scan of Priestley (1800).

question: Antoine Lavoisier kept four ounces of mercury simmering in a sealed glass vessel of air for twelve days, until red particles crusted the silver surface and the air inside had shrunk by about a sixth. He lowered a lit taper into what was left of that air. What did the flame do?
answer: It went out instantly, as though plunged into water.
choices: It went out instantly, as though plunged into water.
It flared white, then guttered down and smoked.
It burned steadily, a little dimmer than in open air.
It burned brighter and faster than in open air.
context: In Lavoisier's own words, the leftover air killed the taper 'as if it had been immersed into water,' and animals put into it 'were suffocated in a few seconds.' The sixth that had gone missing was the part of the air that does the burning; what stayed behind is what we now call nitrogen. His numbers for the run: four ounces of mercury and about 50 cubical inches of air, twelve days of simmering, 45 grains of red crust collected, and the air down to 'between 42 and 43 cubical inches; consequently it had lost about 1/6 of its bulk.' (His better-known 'about a fifth' figure for the respirable part of air comes from a different memoir; this twelve-day run never went to completion.) Source: Lavoisier, Elements of Chemistry, trans. Robert Kerr (1790), Part I ch. III -- gutenberg.org/files/30775/30775-h/30775-h.htm.

question: A smelter heated a dull grey calx, the powder a roasted metal leaves, with charcoal, and shiny metal came back out. Before Antoine Lavoisier, every chemistry student in Europe learned to explain that trick with phlogiston, a fire-stuff said to be locked inside anything that burns. What did the theory say the charcoal was doing?
answer: Handing over its own phlogiston to the starved calx.
choices: Handing over its own phlogiston to the starved calx.
Drawing the last phlogiston out of the calx.
Shielding the calx from the phlogiston in the air.
Splitting the calx into two simpler earths.
context: Charcoal was reckoned almost pure phlogiston, so it could restock a calx that had lost its own -- and the theory got the direction right every time, which is why competent men held it for eighty years. It also explained the small pile of ash left when wood burns: the fire-stuff had gone, and only the earthy residue stayed. Georg Ernst Stahl renamed Johann Joachim Becher's 'terra pinguis' (fatty earth) to phlogiston in 1703, from the Greek phlogistos, 'burnable'; he taught at the University of Halle from 1694 to 1716, and his 1723 Fundamenta Chymiae carried the theory across Europe. Source: Grokipedia, Phlogiston_theory.

question: Jean Rey, a French doctor, took up a puzzle in 1630. An apothecary named Brun had melted two pounds and six ounces of tin in a furnace for six hours, and the powder he poured out weighed seven ounces more than the tin had. What did Rey say had added the weight?
answer: Air, thickened by the long heat, had attached itself to it.
choices: Air, thickened by the long heat, had attached itself to it.
Fire-matter from the furnace had soaked into it.
A heavy earth had risen out of the crucible into it.
Water in the metal had been baked to a denser stuff.
context: Rey published it as 'Essays ... on an Enquiry into the Cause Wherefore Tin and Lead Increase in Weight on Calcination' (1630). Brun had repeated the trial with six pounds of lead and gained six ounces. Rey's idea was that air, thickened and made adhesive by the long furnace heat, attached itself to the metal -- substantially the right answer, a hundred and forty-four years before Lavoisier's sealed vessels, and it sank without trace. It was dug up again only during the eighteenth-century arguments over calcination weight. Being right is not enough; you also have to be heard. Sources: Wellcome Collection scan of Rey's 1630 Essays (wellcomecollection.org/works/grnfnfwy); 'The Essays of Jean Rey,' Popular Science Monthly vol. 44 (Dec 1893); revival noted at Grokipedia, Phlogiston_theory.

question: Antoine Lavoisier sealed eight ounces of tin inside a glass vessel with about fifteen grains of air, weighed the whole thing, and heated the tin until it crusted over. Weighed again with the seal unbroken, the vessel came out at exactly its old weight, not a tenth of a grain different. He then broke the seal and weighed the crusted metal by itself. What had happened to the tin, and to the air shut in with it?
answer: The tin gained 3.12 grains; the air lost the same 3.12.
choices: The tin gained 3.12 grains; the air lost the same 3.12.
The tin lost 3.12 grains; the air gained the same 3.12.
Tin and air both lost grains; the glass had taken them up.
Neither had changed; the tin had only changed its colour.
context: The tin came out 3.12 grains heavier, and the air sealed in with it had lost 3.12 grains -- the same figure to the last decimal. The extra weight had come from inside the jar, not from the fire outside it, and the sealed vessel as a whole never changed at all. This is the experiment the memoir is named for: 'Memoir on the calcination of tin in closed vessels and on the cause of the gain in weight which this metal acquires in the operation,' in the Memoires de l'Academie Royale des Sciences for 1774, published 1777. Lavoisier's whole method is in that one run -- weigh everything, before and after, and let nothing escape, on balances sensitive to about a tenth of a grain, what Grokipedia calls his 'scrupulous exactitude.' Robert Boyle had run nearly the same trial in 1673 and drew the opposite conclusion for one procedural reason: he broke the seal BEFORE weighing again, found the calx heavier, and decided that corpuscles of fire had passed through the glass into the metal. Lavoisier's advance was not a new idea but a new order of operations. Sources: Le Moyne 'Classic Chemistry' on Lavoisier's 1774 tin memoir (web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/classicalcs/lavoisier.html); Grokipedia, Antoine_Lavoisier; sethi.org/phlogiston timeline (Boyle).

question: Jean-Baptiste Chardenon, a French chemist, offered a rescue in 1764 that kept phlogiston alive another twenty years. The theory said a burning body gives off fire-stuff, so a roasted metal ought to come out lighter, yet on the balance the ashy calx came out heavier every single time. What was his rescue?
answer: Phlogiston has negative weight, so losing it adds weight.
choices: Phlogiston has negative weight, so losing it adds weight.
Phlogiston drags off a lighter earth than the one it leaves.
Furnace soot is driven into the metal while it roasts.
The metal's pores shut, trapping water the fire cannot expel.
context: Chardenon proposed in 1764 that phlogiston has levity -- negative weight -- so that a body which loses it must end up heavier. Louis-Bernard Guyton de Morveau argued the same repulsive-levity idea in his 1772 'Digressions academiques,' where he also confirmed that the weight gain happens across metals generally. Critics answered that negative weight flatly contradicts Newton's gravitation. This is what a theory looks like in its last years: it stops predicting and starts being patched. Source: Grokipedia, Phlogiston_theory.

question: Antoine Lavoisier reached for two Greek words in 1777 to record something he was convinced the new gas did, a conviction most chemists of the 1780s shared with him. The name he built from them is still in use. What did he think the gas was?
answer: The substance that makes every acid an acid.
choices: The substance that makes every acid an acid.
The substance that gives every flame its colour.
The substance that makes every metal a metal.
The substance that gives a living body its warmth.
context: He built the name from the Greek oxys, 'sharp' or 'acid,' and genes, 'producer': the acid-maker. Lavoisier proposed 'oxygine' in 1777, and it was formally fixed as 'oxygene' in the 1787 'Methode de nomenclature chimique,' written with Guyton de Morveau, Berthollet and Fourcroy; it entered English as 'oxygen' in 1790. He did not discover the gas -- Carl Wilhelm Scheele made it first, around 1771-72, and Joseph Priestley published first, in 1774-75. What Lavoisier supplied, between 1775 and 1777, was the quantitative evidence that it was a distinct element. Sources: Grokipedia, Oxygen and Antoine_Lavoisier.

question: Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier put the whole of Richard Kirwan's 'Essay on Phlogiston' into French the year after it appeared in 1787. It was the strongest defence of the theory ever written. She already helped in the lab and had translated Priestley, Black and Cavendish. What did the Paris edition of 1788 carry that Kirwan's original did not?
answer: The French chemists' refutation, running in notes underneath.
choices: The French chemists' refutation, running in notes underneath.
The experiments Kirwan had described but never actually run.
The names of the French chemists Kirwan had quoted uncredited.
Lavoisier's own memoirs on the gases, bound in behind it.
context: The Paris 1788 title page says it outright: 'Essai sur le phlogistique, et sur la constitution des acides ... avec des notes de MM. de Morveau, Lavoisier, de La Place, Monge, Berthollet, & de Fourcroy.' The best case anyone had made for phlogiston was printed in French with the refutation running underneath it, note by note -- the opposition steel-manned and answered on the same page. Marie-Anne added a preface and notes of her own, and Nicholson translated the whole thing back into English. She also engraved the thirteen folding copperplates of apparatus in the 1789 Traite -- the drawings that let chemists across Europe rebuild the sealed vessels and check the results for themselves -- having learned to draw for the purpose under the painter Jacques-Louis David. Sources: Smithsonian Libraries record si.edu/object/siris_sil_335133; Grokipedia, Marie-Anne_Paulze_Lavoisier.

question: Antoine Lavoisier stood trial as a tax farmer with twenty-seven others on 8 May 1794 and went to the guillotine that afternoon, at age fifty. He had paid for his lab by buying into the Ferme générale, a group that collected France's taxes on salt, tobacco and goods coming into cities. One charge accused him of a fraud he had spent years catching himself. What was it?
answer: Watering the tax farm's tobacco to inflate its weight.
choices: Watering the tax farm's tobacco to inflate its weight.
Debasing the coin struck for the tax farm's accounts.
Short-weighting the salt sold under the royal monopoly.
Forging the seals on goods entering the city gates.
context: He was condemned as a tax farmer, not as a chemist: the verdict was 'conspiracy against the people of France,' and among the charges was watering tobacco to inflate its weight -- a fraud Lavoisier had personally spent years devising tests to catch. Twenty-eight men were tried that day, including his own father-in-law Jacques Paulze. His widow Marie-Anne was imprisoned for over two months, and the family's instruments and notebooks were inventoried and seized the very next day. In 1796 the French government formally exonerated him and returned the property, declaring the charges false. Lagrange's remark on hearing of the execution -- reported through the astronomer Delambre, and not traceable to a primary source -- was that it took the mob only a moment to remove his head, and a century would not suffice to reproduce it. Sources: Grokipedia, Antoine_Lavoisier and Marie-Anne_Paulze_Lavoisier; MacTutor, Lagrange quotations.

question: Antoine Lavoisier put a red crust alone into a fresh vessel and heated it hard. It had formed on his mercury over twelve days of simmering in a sealed jar of air, and the air in the jar had lost several cubic inches of its bulk. What came off the crust?
answer: Running mercury, and the very air the jar had lost.
choices: Running mercury, and the very air the jar had lost.
Running mercury, and no trace of any gas at all.
A white ash, and far more air than the jar had lost.
Nothing at all, until charcoal was added to restock it.
context: From 45 grains of red crust Lavoisier recovered '41 1/2 grains of running mercury' and '7 or 8 cubical inches of elastic fluid' -- and 7 to 8 cubical inches is exactly what the air in the jar had lost (50 down to 42 or 43). The mercury came back, the air came back, and the books balanced in both directions. That is the step phlogiston could not match: a fire-substance that escapes when something burns can never be poured back in. Source: Lavoisier, Elements of Chemistry, trans. Robert Kerr (1790), Part I ch. III -- gutenberg.org/files/30775/30775-h/30775-h.htm.

question: Humphry Davy took apart muriatic acid in 1810, the fuming acid that ate through metals in every lab in Europe, and he weighed every piece that came out of it. His result showed Antoine Lavoisier's name for oxygen to be wrong. What is muriatic acid made of?
answer: Hydrogen and chlorine.
choices: Hydrogen and chlorine.
Oxygen and chlorine.
Hydrogen and sulphur.
Chlorine and sulphur.
context: Davy found no oxygen in it whatever: hydrogen, and a green gas he named chlorine, a new element. Oxygen is not the acid-maker; hydrogen is. Davy recognised that around 1815, but the argument dragged on -- a dozen oxygen-free acids were known by 1830, and the hydrogen theory of acids was not generally accepted until about 1840. Muriatic acid is what we now call hydrochloric acid. The word 'oxygen' has meant 'acid-former' and been wrong about it for over two hundred years: the man who destroyed one wrong theory carved his own mistake into a word we still say every day. Sources: Grokipedia, Oxygen; chemteam.info/AcidBase/Early-Acid-Base.html.

question: 'Nothing is lost, nothing is created, everything is transformed.' Chemistry books everywhere print that line under the name of Antoine Lavoisier, as the sum of conservation of mass: matter is never destroyed by fire or reaction, only rearranged. Where does the sentence actually come from?
answer: A later French summing-up, found in nothing he wrote.
choices: A later French summing-up, found in nothing he wrote.
The closing sentence of his Traite elementaire de chimie.
The eulogies read over him after the Revolution killed him.
A maxim of the Greek atomists that he liked to repeat.
context: It is a later French paraphrase. 'Rien ne se perd, rien ne se cree, tout se transforme' has not been found in the Traite or in the sourced collections of his quotations -- the most famous sentence Lavoisier ever gets credited with, he never wrote. What he did write, in the 1789 Traite elementaire de chimie (Robert Kerr's 1790 translation), he called an incontestible axiom: 'We may lay it down as an incontestible axiom, that, in all the operations of art and nature, nothing is created; an equal quantity of matter exists both before and after the experiment; the quality and quantity of the elements remain precisely the same; and nothing takes place beyond changes and modifications in the combination of these elements. Upon this principle the whole art of performing chemical experiments depends.' That closing line turns a piece of bookkeeping into the foundation of a craft. If you are going to quote him, quote the axiom. Sources: gutenberg.org/files/30775/30775-h/30775-h.htm; en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Antoine_Lavoisier.

question: Antoine Lavoisier printed the first modern table of elements in his 1789 Traité élémentaire de chimie: thirty-three substances he judged could not be broken down into anything simpler. He set two entries at the very top of that list, ahead of oxygen itself. What were they?
answer: Light, and caloric -- the fluid he believed heat was.
choices: Light, and caloric -- the fluid he believed heat was.
Air, and water -- the survivors of the four elements.
Gold, and mercury -- the metals the alchemists ranked first.
Fixed air, and inflammable air -- the two newly caught gases.
context: Light and caloric -- caloric being the weightless fluid Lavoisier believed heat was made of. Both are classed in his table as imponderable: unweighable. The man whose entire case against phlogiston was that nobody could ever put it on a balance printed two unweighable substances at the head of his own list of elements, and caloric turned out to be just as wrong as phlogiston was. Reformers carry their own ghosts. Sources: Grokipedia, Phlogiston_theory; Lavoisier's table of simple substances, Traite (1789) p.192, transcribed at chem125-oyc.webspace.yale.edu.

question: Suppose you burn one gram of carbon inside a sealed vessel and weigh the whole apparatus again, to push on Antoine Lavoisier's law of equal matter before and after. The total really has dropped, by about three ten-billionths of a gram, though no balance ever built could catch it. Where did that missing mass go?
answer: It left with the heat and light; energy has mass.
choices: It left with the heat and light; energy has mass.
It leaked out; no glass vessel is perfectly tight.
It was destroyed; a few carbon atoms ceased to be.
It left as light alone; heat carries no mass at all.
context: It left with the heat and light. Energy has mass, so a reaction that pours energy out really does end up lighter: burning graphite loses about 3.6 x 10^-10 grams per gram of carbon, roughly a third of a part per billion, or about eight millionths of an electron's mass for each carbon atom burned. No balance ever built could see it, which is why Lavoisier's law is exactly right for every purpose a chemist has. Nuclear reactions show the same effect tens of thousands of times bigger, atom for atom: the decay of one mole of carbon-14 loses 0.000168 g, and in uranium fission the loss reaches about 0.1 per cent, at last a change a balance could weigh. Conservation of mass is a superb approximation, not a law of the universe. Sources: Chemistry LibreTexts, 'Converting Mass to Energy: Mass Defect and Nuclear Binding Energy'; Grokipedia, Conservation_of_mass.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, with no college and no lab behind him, picked up his first little magnifying glasses in Amsterdam, learning a shop trade from 1648. They made things three to five times bigger, no more. Which trade were they tools of?
answer: Selling cloth, where a glass counted threads per inch
choices: Grinding spectacles, where a glass checked the curve
Testing coin, where a glass read the mint's stamp
Selling cloth, where a glass counted threads per inch
Engraving seals, where a glass guided the cutting tip
context: Leeuwenhoek apprenticed from 1648 to 1653 under William Davidson, a Scottish cloth merchant in Amsterdam, then opened his own draper's shop in Delft in 1654. The shop glass was called a thread counter -- three to five times magnification, just enough to count threads per inch and check a weave. The man who would open the microbial world met his first lens over a bolt of fabric. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antonie van Leeuwenhoek' (Early Life / Transition to Scientific Pursuits); The American Scholar, 'A Kingdom of Little Animals'.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek put a drop of water under his lens in September 1674, from Berkelse Mere, the lake outside Delft that turned whitish every midsummer with 'little green clouds.' The clouds were green streaks wound like serpents. But another thing in that drop made his letter famous. What was it?
answer: Very many little animals, swimming
choices: Very many little animals, swimming
A fine white mould, spreading fast
Small green seeds, sprouting open
Thin red worms, coiled up tight
context: The green spirals were Spirogyra, a freshwater alga. The letter describes the lake as clear in winter but turning 'whitish, and there are then little green clouds floating in it,' and the streaks inside as 'spirally wound serpent-wise, and orderly arranged.' Then the line that changed biology: 'among these streaks there were besides very many little animalcules.' The first sighting of the microbial world happened at a lake, not in a laboratory. Source: Nick Lane, 'The unseen world: reflections on Leeuwenhoek (1677) Concerning little animals', Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (PMC4360124).

question: Writing to readers in London in 1674 who had no lens like his, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek knew a bare number would tell them nothing. He said some of the creatures he saw were 'above a thousand times smaller' than one every reader had seen at home. Which creature did he name?
answer: A mite on the rind of a cheese
choices: A gnat on a summer windowpane
A flea on a dog's winter coat
A nit in a child's braided hair
A mite on the rind of a cheese
context: 'I judge that some of these little creatures were above a thousand times smaller than the smallest ones I have ever yet seen, upon the rind of cheese.' Cheese mites were the smallest creature most people in 1674 had ever laid eyes on. He kept doing this all his life -- sizing microbes against a grain of coarse sand, a millet seed, a hair from his own beard -- so a reader who owned no lens could still picture the scale. Source: Nick Lane, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (PMC4360124); Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'Counting the Little Animals'.

question: Never having learned Latin, the working language of European science, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek wrote to the Royal Society in Dutch about the tiny things he saw in a drop of lake water. He made up no fancy term, only a plain word a Delft shopkeeper might use for anything small. What did translators make of his word in English?
answer: Little animals
choices: Little animals
Tiny worms
Little seeds
Dust motes
context: In Dutch he wrote diertjes, dierkens or diertgens -- diminutives of dier, 'animal,' meaning roughly 'little beasties.' 'Animalcule' is the word every textbook puts in his mouth, and he never wrote it: 'animalcule' and 'little animals' are what his English and Latin translators made of him. He was embarrassed enough by his lack of Latin that he hesitated to approach the Royal Society at all; his physician friend Reinier de Graaf forwarded his first letter for him on 28 April 1673. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antonie van Leeuwenhoek' and 'Animalcule'; Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'How many letters did Leeuwenhoek write?'

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek wrote to Francis Aston at the Royal Society on 17 September 1683 about a sample from a place nobody had thought to look, one he carried about with him all day. The drawings sent with that letter are the earliest known pictures of bacteria. Where did the sample come from?
answer: The soft white matter between his own teeth
choices: The wax taken from inside his own ear
The sweat scraped from the crook of his arm
The soft white matter between his own teeth
The grit washed from between his own toes
context: Letter L-135, 17 September 1683, to Francis Aston: he scraped the soft white matter from between his own teeth, mixed it with clean rainwater, and found it swarming with living animalcules. Published in Philosophical Transactions Vol. 14 (1684), pp. 568-574, it is the first documented observation of bacteria, and the drawings that went with it are the first pictures of bacteria ever made. Getting a sample took planning -- 'I am in the habit of rubbing my teeth with salt in the morning, and then rinsing my mouth with water,' he wrote, so he deliberately stopped cleaning for three days to collect enough. For contrast he also sampled an old man who 'had never washed his mouth all his life.' Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, Letter L-135 of 1683-09-17 to Francis Aston.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek riveted two thin metal plates, about 5 cm by 2.5 cm, around a single tiny lens, with the specimen skewered on a brass pin and shifted by two fine screws. Robert Hooke's microscope was nothing like it: a tall tube on a stand with several lenses inside. How did Leeuwenhoek use his?
answer: He held the plate to his eye and aimed it at a candle flame
choices: He held the plate to his eye and aimed it at a candle flame
He held the plate at arm's length and squinted past the pin
He held the plate to his eye and turned his back to the window
He laid the plate on his knee and bent his eye down to the lens
context: You held the whole instrument in your fist, pressed the plate flat against your eye, and aimed it at a candle flame or a window; a sharp brass pin carried the specimen and two fine screws moved it. ACCURACY RAIL: he did not invent the microscope. Compound instruments had existed in the Netherlands since about 1590 (credited to Zacharias and Hans Janssen, with Hans Lippershey a rival claimant), and Hooke's illustrated Micrographia appeared in 1665, before Leeuwenhoek ground his first lens around 1670. His innovation was a far better SIMPLE (single-lens) microscope plus the screw rig that held and focused the specimen. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antonie van Leeuwenhoek' (Lens Grinding and Microscope Design / Operational Techniques); Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'Leeuwenhoek's Microscopes'.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek found the numbers of his new creatures hard to say in his letter of 17 September 1683, so he reached for a comparison, the line of his still quoted three centuries later. He added, dryly, 'especially in those who don't ever clean their teeth.' What was the comparison?
answer: More animals in one man's mouth than men in a whole kingdom
choices: More animals in one man's mouth than stars in a clear sky
More animals in one man's mouth than grains in a sack of wheat
More animals in one man's mouth than drops in the Delft canal
More animals in one man's mouth than men in a whole kingdom
context: 'There are more animals living in the scum on the teeth in a man's mouth, than there are men in a whole kingdom' -- and then the dry addition, 'especially in those who don't ever clean their teeth.' A common alternate translation runs: 'there are more living animals in the unclean matter in the teeth in one's mouth than there are men in a whole Kingdom.' Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, Letter L-135 of 1683-09-17 to Francis Aston; The American Scholar, 'A Kingdom of Little Animals'.

question: Not content to look at the creatures he had found, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek went after them, trying hot coffee and vinegar to see what would still them: one of the first kill-tests anyone had run on a microbe. The vinegar result, printed in London, had an effect on readers he can hardly have intended. What did it do to them?
answer: Some were so disgusted they swore off vinegar for good
choices: Some wrote in demanding he test the wine trade next
Some were so disgusted they swore off vinegar for good
Some accused him of killing creatures he had invented
Some began selling vinegar as a guard against plague
context: He attacked his mouth animalcules with vinegar and with hot coffee to see what would still them -- an early kill-test on microbes, and one of the first times anyone tried to do something TO a microbe rather than merely watch it. The published account of the vinegar work had a side effect on readers: some 'were so disgusted at the spectacle, that they vowed they would never use vinegar again.' Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, Letter L-135 of 1683-09-17 to Francis Aston.

question: Johan Hoogvliet sat turning the last letters of his friend Antonie van Leeuwenhoek into Latin in Delft in August 1723, with the old man ninety and dying of pneumonia, 'being already in the throes of death,' Hoogvliet wrote, 'though none the less mindful of his art.' Thirty-six hours before the end, his limbs already going numb, Leeuwenhoek was still dictating. What was he dictating about?
answer: Sand an East India Company director had brought him, to test for gold
choices: Sand an East India Company director had brought him, to test for gold
A bee's eye dried onto a flake of mica so it would not distort
Blood moving in the tail of a live eel, held still in a glass tube
Tartar from an old man who had never once washed out his mouth
context: His publisher friend Reinier Boitet recorded that 'six-and-thirty hours before his death, when his limbs were already growing numb,' Leeuwenhoek was still dictating -- about sand samples a director of the East India Company had brought him, asking whether they contained gold. For the last two letters he summoned Johan Hoogvliet to translate them into Latin for James Jurin, editor of Philosophical Transactions; Hoogvliet wrote that Leeuwenhoek was 'being already in the throes of death, though none the less mindful of his art.' In that final letter he defended his spermist theory and described the palpitations of his own diaphragm, along with a glass device of his own design he had built to treat them. He died of bronchial pneumonia on 26 August 1723 in his house in the Hippolytusbuurt, aged 90, and was buried in the Oude Kerk; the letter was read aloud at a Royal Society meeting on 21 November 1723, three months after he was in the ground. The condition he described in himself is now called 'Leeuwenhoek's disease' -- respiratory myoclonus, or diaphragmatic flutter: he wrote up his own symptoms so precisely that the illness carries his name. Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'Leeuwenhoek's Death' and Letter L-588 of August 1723 to James Jurin.

question: Henry Oldenburg, secretary of the Royal Society, faced twelve more letters from Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft tradesman whose notes he had been printing in Philosophical Transactions within months. Now the letters claimed that living creatures swam in a drop of water, too small for any eye to see. What did Oldenburg do with the twelve?
answer: He printed three, and none of those touched the creatures
choices: He printed nine, and cut the animalcule passages out of them
He printed all twelve, with a note distancing the Society
He printed three, and none of those touched the creatures
He printed one, and asked Delft for sworn witnesses first
context: Oldenburg had been printing Leeuwenhoek within months of receipt. Once the animalcule claims arrived, he went quiet: of the next twelve letters, only three were published, and not one of those touched the animalcules. An extraordinary claim had stalled at the editor's desk -- not refuted, not answered, just not printed. Source: Nick Lane, 'The unseen world: reflections on Leeuwenhoek (1677) Concerning little animals', Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (PMC4360124).

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek sent the Royal Society a bundle of sworn statements from Delft in 1677. A notary, a lawyer, a physician and several ministers swore that they had put their own eyes to his lens and seen the swimming creatures. The Fellows in London were not satisfied by testimony, however solemn. How did they settle the matter?
answer: They had Robert Hooke reproduce the observation himself
choices: They sent Nehemiah Grew to Delft to watch Leeuwenhoek at work
They asked Christopher Wren to design a lens of equal power
They ruled the claim unproven and stopped reading his letters
They had Robert Hooke reproduce the observation himself
context: The Society had already asked Robert Hooke, its Curator of Experiments, in October 1677 to reproduce the observation, and the Delft affidavits were read at the very November meeting where his first attempt failed. Once Hooke succeeded, the affidavits ceased to matter. That is the whole difference between science and testimony: eight men under oath is still eight men saying so, and the Society trusted the repeat instead, a test run by someone with nothing invested in Leeuwenhoek being right. Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, chronology of the Royal Society (lensonleeuwenhoek.net/timeline/tax/Royal%20Society), '1677: To confirm his observations' and 'Hooke's Three Tries'.

question: Robert Hooke tried in front of the Fellows and failed twice. On 1 November 1677 pump-water in glass pipes gave 'no discovery'; on 8 November, with a better mount, better lighting and pepper-water, 'nothing of Mr. Leeuwenhoek's animals could be seen.' On 15 November he tried once more and saw 'great numbers of exceedingly small animals swimming to and fro,' with Christopher Wren, John Aubrey and Nehemiah Grew watching. What had he changed?
answer: He had let the pepper-water steep nine or ten days
choices: He had ground a finer lens for the third attempt
He had let the pepper-water steep nine or ten days
He had warmed the pepper-water over a small flame
He had drawn his water from a canal instead of a pump
context: Two public failures, then patience. The pepper-water Hooke brought on 8 November had steeped only two or three days; for the third try he let it stand nine or ten, and that alone was the difference between nothing and 'great numbers.' Birch's History of the Royal Society records the verdict after 15 November: 'there was no longer any doubt of Mr. LEEWENHOECK's discovery... there could be no fallacy.' John Hoskyns and Jonas Moore were in the room too. The lesson is sharper than the story: a failed replication is not automatically a refutation -- sometimes it means the protocol was not run long enough. Hooke's first failure also owed something to his instrument and a badly lit room. Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'Hooke's Three Tries' and 'Hooke finally succeeded in replicating Leeuwenhoek's observations'.

question: Tiemen Cocquyt and a Delft team fired neutrons through two sealed Leeuwenhoek instruments in 2021 to image the lenses without prising them apart. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek had told the Royal Society in 1676 that his method for seeing the smallest creatures he kept 'for myself alone,' and for three centuries people assumed a lost lens-making secret. What was the high-power lens?
answer: A blown glass globule, by a method Robert Hooke had published
choices: A ground biconvex lens, by the method Christiaan Huygens used
A polished rock-crystal bead, by the method Delft jewellers used
A blown glass globule, by a method Robert Hooke had published
A stacked pair of thin lenses, by the method the Janssens used
context: Tiemen Cocquyt of Rijksmuseum Boerhaave with Zhou Zhou, Jeroen Plomp and Lambert van Eijck of TU Delft published the neutron tomography in Science Advances on 14 May 2021.
