Producing speech and understanding speech turned out to be separate jobs in separate places. Source: Grokipedia, Paul Broca ('Localization of Brain Function'); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Broca

question: An epileptic patient lay awake on Wilder Penfield's operating table in Montreal, talking and answering questions while the surgeon touched a small electrode to the bare cortex. What made staying awake for brain surgery possible?
answer: The brain has no pain receptors of its own
choices: The brain has no pain receptors of its own
Local anaesthetic soaks down into the cortex
The electrode's current numbs whatever it touches
Pain fibres shut down once the skull is opened
context: Penfield numbed only the scalp and the dura. The brain itself feels nothing, which is exactly why the Montreal Procedure worked: a fully conscious patient could report what each touch produced, and Penfield could map the cortex while he operated on it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilder_Penfield; psywww.com, 'Brain Stimulation' ('The brain has no pain receptors itself, so the patient did not feel any pain from the electrical stimulation.')

question: A student repeats the old claim that a person uses only ten percent of the brain. A 2013 Michael J. Fox Foundation survey found sixty-five percent of Americans still believed it. Researchers treat it as long dead. Which finding kills it most directly?
answer: Damage to almost any patch of brain costs the patient an ability
choices: Damage to almost any patch of brain costs the patient an ability
Every neuron in the cortex fires nonstop, awake or asleep
Electrode mapping drew a response out of every point on the cortex
Every region of the cortex burns fuel at one steady rate
context: Neurologist Barry Gordon puts it plainly: 'there is almost no area of the brain that can be damaged without loss of abilities.' The brain is about two percent of your body weight and burns up to twenty percent of your energy — evolution does not pay that bill for idle tissue. The myth traces back to a misreading of William James's 1907 essay 'The Energies of Men', popularised by Lowell Thomas in his 1936 foreword to Dale Carnegie. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ten_percent_of_the_brain_myth; Grokipedia, Ten-percent-of-the-brain myth

question: Wilder Penfield touched an electrode to the temporal lobe of an awake secretary. She said, 'I hear music.' He touched the same spot again without warning her, and she heard it again -- humming along with an orchestra no one else could hear. What did she do about the tune later?
answer: She tracked down the sheet music and played it on the piano
choices: She tracked down the sheet music and played it on the piano
She asked him never to touch that part of her brain again
She could not recall a single note of it by that evening
She insisted a radio had been playing somewhere nearby
context: She wrote afterwards that it was not even a song she liked — she simply wanted to hear properly what her own temporal lobe had handed her. Other patients under the electrode reported a tingling thumb, a smell, a flash of light, or the feeling of someone stroking the back of a hand. Source: TIME archive, 'Medicine: The Brain as Tape Recorder'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilder_Penfield

question: A surgeon cut through a patient's corpus callosum, the thick cable of nerves between the brain's two halves, because her epilepsy had answered to nothing else. A seizure on one side could no longer cross, and the surgery worked. What did such patients say about themselves afterward?
answer: That they felt exactly the same as they always had
choices: That they felt exactly the same as they always had
That the left half of their body would no longer obey
That they could no longer recognise their own family
That their voice had gone flat and toneless ever after
context: W.J., the first West Coast split-brain patient, reported feeling no different except for being free of seizures. Two halves of a brain, no longer talking to each other, and the person notices nothing — the strangeness only appears under laboratory conditions that feed information to one hemisphere alone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_callosum; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Gazzaniga

question: Paul Broca had staked his 1861 case for a speech centre on one patient's brain. Months later Lazare Lelong, an eighty-four-year-old grounds worker at the same Paris hospital, died, a man worn down over the years to five words: his own name, 'yes', 'no', 'always' and the number 'three'. Broca now had a second case. What did he do next?
answer: Collected twelve more autopsies over the following two years
choices: Collected twelve more autopsies over the following two years
Published both cases at once and dared anyone to disprove them
Asked two rival anatomists to re-examine the brains themselves
Spent the next two years hunting a living patient to test
context: One case is an anecdote; the REPEAT is what turned a story into evidence. Every one of the new lesions landed in essentially the same small patch of the left frontal lobe. On 15 June 1865 Broca ended a paper to the Société d'Anthropologie with the line that made the case: 'Nous parlons avec l'hémisphère gauche' — 'We speak with the left hemisphere.' It was the first serious claim that the two halves of the brain do not do identical jobs. Sources give Lelong's first name inconsistently; Wikipedia records him as Lazare. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Broca; academic.oup.com/brain, 'Paul Broca: from fame to shame?'

question: 'Yes, Doctor! Yes, Doctor! Now I hear people laughing: my friends in South Africa,' called a patient recorded only as J.T., with Wilder Penfield's electrode on his right temporal lobe. Time magazine ran the story under the headline 'The Brain as Tape Recorder'. Penfield and Phanor Perot went back through every patient whose temporal lobe had been stimulated, 520 in all. What did the tally show?
answer: 40 of the 520 ever relived anything
choices: 40 of the 520 ever relived anything
95 of the 520 ever relived anything
240 of the 520 ever relived anything
460 of the 520 ever relived anything
context: In their 1963 final summary in the journal Brain, Penfield and Phanor Perot found experiential responses, the sense of reliving a past moment, in 40 of the 520 patients whose temporal lobes had been stimulated: under one in twelve. The electrode did not replay memories on demand; the tape-recorder headline was always the rare exception, not the result. Most of what the electrode produced was far simpler: a tingling thumb, a smell, a flash of light, the feeling of someone stroking the back of a hand. Sources: Penfield & Perot, Brain 86:595-696 (1963), as cited at arxiv.org/pdf/1408.7073; psywww.com, 'Brain Stimulation' (patient J.T.); TIME archive, 'Medicine: The Brain as Tape Recorder'

question: Wilder Penfield and Edwin Boldrey used tiny electric shocks on the cortex of 126 awake patients. From what those patients felt, they drew a map of the body along a groove called the central sulcus. The drawing came out weird -- some parts huge, others tiny. Which parts came out huge?
answer: The lips, tongue, hands and fingers
choices: The lips, tongue, hands and fingers
The chest, back, shoulders and neck
The thighs, knees, shins and feet
The scalp, ears, jaw and eyelids
context: The distorted little figure is called the homunculus. Cortical territory is handed out according to how richly a body part is wired for sensation and fine control — not according to how big the part is. Penfield and Boldrey published it on 1 December 1937 in a 55-page paper in the journal Brain, built from patients operated on between 1928 and 1936; the drawing was made for them by an illustrator, Mrs. H. P. Cantlie. The map also runs upside down, with the toes at the very top of the hemisphere. Source: academic.oup.com/brain, 'A little man of some importance'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cortical_homunculus

question: William Beecher Scoville removed about eight centimetres of tissue from each side of twenty-seven-year-old Henry Molaison's brain on 1 September 1953, hoping to stop seizures no drug could touch. The seizures stopped. Molaison's IQ tested higher afterwards than before, his grammar and conversation stayed fine, and he kept his sense of humour. What had the operation destroyed?
answer: His ability to turn new experiences into memories he could keep
choices: His ability to turn new experiences into memories he could keep
His ability to recognise the faces of people he had known
His ability to feel fear, pain or any strong emotion
His ability to picture a place or an object in his mind
context: Scoville took the medial temporal lobes from both sides — both hippocampi, both amygdalae, the entorhinal cortex. Molaison's Wechsler IQ went from 104 the day before surgery to 112 afterwards, and his digit span was a normal six or seven. He was not brain-damaged in any general sense; one specific machine had broken. He described it himself: 'like waking from a dream — every day is alone in itself.' Source: Grokipedia, Henry Molaison; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Molaison

question: Brenda Milner sat Henry Molaison down to trace a star he could see only as a reflection in a mirror, so every stroke of his hand went the wrong way. On day one he made about thirty errors; by the third day he made almost none. And every single time Milner set the paper in front of him, he told her the same thing. What did he say?
answer: That he had never tried this task before in his life
choices: That he had never tried this task before in his life
That the mirror had been shifted since the last time
That his drawing hand had gone numb during the night
That he had already done this one far too many times
context: Milner's own verdict: 'To see that H.M. had learned the task perfectly but with absolutely no awareness that he had done it before was an amazing dissociation.' He was down from about thirty errors to five or six by the tenth trial on day one. Milner first met Molaison in 1955 and travelled from Montreal to Hartford to test him for more than thirty years; he never once remembered her name. Every visit, she was a stranger who had just walked in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Molaison; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brenda_Milner

question: Roger Sperry and his graduate student Michael Gazzaniga flashed a picture into the left visual field of a patient whose corpus callosum had been cut, so that only the silent right half of his brain saw it. Asked what he had seen, the man answered truthfully that there had been nothing. Then they let him reach into a bag he could not see into. What happened?
answer: His left hand pulled out exactly the object he had just denied seeing
choices: His left hand pulled out exactly the object he had just denied seeing
His left hand searched the bag and came up empty every single time
His right hand found the object but he could not put a name to it
Both of his hands seized the same wrong object and would not let go
context: One person, two answers, both sincere. The speaking left hemisphere never received the image, so its denial was honest; the right hemisphere had it and could act on it through the left hand. Testing on the first West Coast split-brain patient, W.J. — a World War II paratrooper whose seizures began after a German soldier struck him with a rifle butt — started in 1962 with a tachistoscope flashing images to one visual field at a time. Sperry took half the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work; the other half went to David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Split-brain; Grokipedia, Roger Wolcott Sperry

question: Michael Gazzaniga showed a patient whose corpus callosum had been cut two pictures at once: a chicken's claw where only the speaking left hemisphere could see it, and a snow scene where only the silent right could. The patient's right hand pointed at a chicken and his left at a shovel. Asked why he had picked the shovel, his speaking half answered at once, inventing a story for a choice it had not made. What did the patient say?
answer: That you need a shovel to clean out the chicken shed
choices: That you need a shovel to clean out the chicken shed
That the shovel was for scooping out the chicken's feed
That he was digging worms with the shovel to feed the chicken
That the shovel was for turning the dirt in the chicken run
context: The speaking half had never seen any snow. It invented a reason anyway, and believed it. Gazzaniga called this the left-hemisphere INTERPRETER: the talking half of the brain is a full-time narrator that never admits it does not know. Flash the word 'walk' to the right hemisphere and the patient stands up; ask him why and he says, 'I'm going to get a Coke.' Accounts differ over which patient gave the chicken-shed answer, so it is told here without initials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Gazzaniga; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-brain_interpreter; Grokipedia, Michael Gazzaniga

question: Brenda Milner split memory in two at her mirror-drawing table. Henry Molaison had lost the kind he could state out loud, facts and events, which psychologists call declarative memory; it depended on the hippocampi William Beecher Scoville had cut out. Yet Molaison's hand kept getting better at the tracing, so the skill kind of memory was running on structures Scoville never touched. Which ones?
answer: The basal ganglia and the cerebellum
choices: The basal ganglia and the cerebellum
The motor strip and the central sulcus
The frontal lobes and the corpus callosum
The insula and the white matter beneath it
context: Declarative memory — facts and events, the kind you can state out loud — is hippocampus-dependent, and Scoville had taken both hippocampi. Procedural memory, the skill kind that lives in the hands, runs through the basal ganglia and the cerebellum, and it went on learning without him. Memory is not one thing. Molaison died on 2 December 2008 and gave his brain to science; on 4 December 2009 Jacopo Annese's team at UC San Diego cut it into 2,401 wafer-thin slices, losing only two, so that anyone, forever, can check exactly what Scoville took out. Source: Grokipedia, Henry Molaison; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Molaison

question: A teacher sorts his class into 'left-brained' logical types and 'right-brained' creative types, an everyday claim that traces back to Roger Sperry's Nobel-winning split-brain work. Scanners have since watched ordinary people read a sentence, work through sums and listen to music. What did the scans show?
answer: Both halves lighting up, the two working the same task as one network
choices: Both halves lighting up, the two working the same task as one network
Both halves lighting up, each one taking a different part of the task
Both halves lighting up, the left one always a beat ahead of the right
Both halves lighting up, the pattern running backwards in left-handers
context: A narrow clinical finding about one function in a few dozen surgical patients, stretched into a personality test for everybody. Split-brain work showed that language is usually handled on the left in those patients; it never showed that people come in logical and creative types. Modern imaging finds ordinary tasks lighting up integrated networks across both halves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Split-brain

question: A girl at the dinner table closes one eye, stares at a pen mark on a napkin and slides the napkin until a nearby dot vanishes. A patch of each eye is truly blank, yet what she sees looks like a seamless picture, not a picture with a hole punched in it. Something behind her eye is doing the covering. What is her brain doing?
answer: interpolating from the surrounding pattern
choices: interpolating from the surrounding pattern
swapping in a memory of the last thing seen there
hallucinating a plausible object to fill the gap
borrowing signal from the ear's balance nerves
context: The technical term is filling-in. Place your blind spot over striped wallpaper and the stripes run unbroken across a region no eye ever detected -- the brain smooths the surrounding texture across the missing patch, stripes over stripes, blue over blue. Crucially it does NOT invent new objects: a lone red spot dropped into your blind spot simply disappears, replaced by whatever surrounds it, not by an imagined new thing. Part of what you are looking at right now is a construction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_spot_(vision).

question: Mariotte, a French priest and founding member of the Paris Academy of Sciences, tested his own eyes with little circles of white paper in 1668. With one eye shut, he stared at one circle and found that another, in plain view off to the side, vanished completely. Where in his eye was that vanished circle's image falling?
answer: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye
choices: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye
On the fovea, the retina's sharp centre
On the far outer rim of the retina
On the lens, just behind the pupil
context: The vanished circle's image had landed on the optic disc, where the optic nerve leaves the back of the eye: the one patch of retina with no light-sensitive cells at all. Mariotte reported it in 1668 in a letter titled 'New Discovery Concerning Vision'. The popular telling that he amused King Charles II by placing courtiers in his blind spot so their heads appeared to vanish is an anecdote that has grown in the retelling, not solidly documented, so it is told as story rather than record. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_spot_(vision); Encyclopedia, Edme Mariotte.

question: Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer were studying how electrons bounce off metal at Bell Labs in New York in April 1925, firing a beam at a hot nickel target in a vacuum tube. One afternoon something above the apparatus broke, cracked their charcoal trap and coated the clean nickel with rust. What was it that broke?
answer: A bottle of liquid air
choices: A bottle of liquid air
A mercury manometer tube
A cathode-ray glass envelope
A quartz spectrograph window
context: The broken bottle is what turned a routine scattering study into the first proof matter is a wave. Air rushed into the vacuum tube and oxidized the hot nickel. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davisson-Germer_experiment ; construction-physics.com/p/how-bell-labs-won-its-first-nobel

question: Louis de Broglie handed in a doctoral thesis in Paris in 1924 with one bold idea: every particle, even an electron, must also travel as a wave, the way light already did. His examiners were unsure what to make of it, and his adviser Paul Langevin mailed it to Albert Einstein in Berlin for a second opinion. What did Einstein write back on 16 December 1924?
answer: That de Broglie had lifted a corner of the great veil
choices: That de Broglie had lifted a corner of the great veil
That the argument was mathematically ingenious but physically empty
That such waves would violate the equivalence principle
That the young man should try again after ten years of experiment
context: Einstein's endorsement is what got the thesis taken seriously; Erwin Schrodinger read it in 1925 and it fed straight into his wave equation the year after. Source: institucional.us.es/blogimus/en/2019/10/the-great-veil-is-lifted-what-if-everything-is-nothing-but-waves/

question: Suppose you run yourself through Louis de Broglie's single formula: wavelength equals Planck's constant divided by momentum. Planck's constant is about 6.6 x 10^-34 joule-seconds, and a walking person's momentum is roughly a hundred kilogram-metres per second, so the answer is about 10^-35 metres. What does that tiny number explain about you?
answer: Why you never notice yourself bending around a door frame
choices: Why you never notice yourself bending around a door frame
Why your body warms a room by radiating infrared light
Why you cast a soft-edged shadow instead of a knife-sharp one
Why you feel weight even when nothing pushes back on your skin
context: The wave nature is universal but the wavelength has to be comparable to a slit for diffraction to bend a beam. Electrons work because they are light and slow; you do not. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matter_wave

question: Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer baked a block of nickel in a furnace for weeks at Bell Labs in 1925 to drive off the oxygen, after a vacuum accident let air rush in and wrecked the target with a coating of oxide. When they restarted the machine, the scattered electrons came off in sharp, orderly peaks, a pattern nobody had seen before the accident. What had the long heating done to the metal to make those peaks show up?
answer: Fused many tiny grains into a few large single crystals
choices: Fused many tiny grains into a few large single crystals
Deposited a mirror-smooth layer of pure carbon on the surface
Magnetized the block so the electrons curved in flight
Boiled off a hidden copper impurity that had been blurring the beam
context: Before the accident their nickel was polycrystalline mush; the long bake left a few big crystal facets. Only those ordered planes could act as the diffraction grating that made the wave nature of the electron visible. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davisson-Germer_experiment

question: William Henry Bragg and his son Lawrence published a rule in 1913 for a very different kind of wave scattering off crystal planes, and Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer found that their sharp new electron peaks fit it. With Louis de Broglie's electron wavelength in that rule, the angles matched. What kind of wave had the Braggs originally been aiming at crystals?
answer: X-rays
choices: X-rays
Radio waves
Ultraviolet light
Sound waves in metal
context: The Braggs won the 1915 Nobel for X-ray crystallography. That the same geometric rule fit electrons ten years later is what proved the electrons were arriving as waves, not just as recoiling billiard balls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davisson-Germer_experiment

question: George Paget Thomson scattered electrons through thin metal films at Aberdeen, got diffraction rings and shared the 1937 Nobel Prize in Physics with Clinton Davisson. His father, J. J. Thomson, had won the 1906 Nobel for a Cavendish experiment on cathode rays. What had those cathode-ray measurements established about the electron?
answer: That it is a corpuscle with a definite charge-to-mass ratio
choices: That it is a corpuscle with a definite charge-to-mass ratio
That it is a standing vibration in the luminiferous ether
That it carries exactly one third of a hydrogen atom's charge
That it can never be pulled free of an atom
context: J. J. Thomson bent cathode rays with electric and magnetic fields and measured e/m, arguing the beam was a stream of tiny charged corpuscles. Thirty-one years later his son showed that same corpuscle diffracts like a wave. Both were right; wave-particle duality is why. Source: chemistryworld.com/culture/a-history-of-the-electron-jj-and-gp-thomson/6090.article

question: A student peers at a speck of dust through a light microscope, and green light, at about 550 nanometres, sets her limit: no light microscope can ever resolve anything much finer than about half of that. An electron at 100 kilovolts has a de Broglie wavelength of about 3.9 picometres, roughly a hundred thousand times shorter. What does that short wavelength let a modern electron microscope do that no light microscope can?
answer: Photograph individual atoms in a crystal
choices: Photograph individual atoms in a crystal
See straight through solid lead as if it were glass
Read writing on a coin buried under a metre of soil
Freeze the motion of light itself for later playback
context: The rule that resolution is limited to about half a wavelength was known before de Broglie; his formula turned it into an invitation. The wave nature of matter is why we can see the things atoms are made of. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_microscope ; advanced-microscopy.utah.edu/education/electron-micro/

question: A young Austrian physicist read Louis de Broglie's thesis in 1925 and came to believe that particles really were waves. That winter he wrote down the equation for the wave itself, and the equation he finished the next year is still the heart of chemistry today. Who was he?
answer: Erwin Schrodinger
choices: Erwin Schrodinger
Werner Heisenberg
Wolfgang Pauli
Max Born
context: Schrodinger's wave mechanics and Heisenberg's matrix mechanics turned out to be the same theory in different dress. de Broglie's single line lambda = h/p is the seed of both. Source: ias.ac.in/article/fulltext/reso/031/01/0063-0082

question: A student in a dark room points an ordinary TV remote at the selfie camera on a phone and presses a button. Her eyes see nothing at the front of the remote, but the phone screen shows a bright flash at its tip. What is the camera picking up that her eyes cannot see?
answer: a pulse of infrared light
choices: a pulse of infrared light
a pulse of ultraviolet light
a pulse of radio waves
a pulse of microwaves
context: That is the remote's infrared LED -- the same mechanism as visible light, only a longer wavelength, and a sensor built for visible light registers it anyway because to the sensor there is no difference. Rear cameras more often carry an infrared-blocking filter, which is why the selfie camera works better. Radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are one phenomenon at different wavelengths, all moving at the same speed in vacuum -- and that is Maxwell's claim, not a later addition to it. Sources: IOP Spark, 'Invisible Wavelengths'; Sony support, 'Test if your remote control sends an infrared (IR) signal'; Carolina Knowledge Center, 'Detecting IR Light with a Smart Phone'; NASA Imagine the Universe, 'Electromagnetic Spectrum'.

question: Heinrich Hertz drove two metre-long copper wires hard with an induction coil at Karlsruhe in 1887. Metres away sat a plain wire loop with a narrow slit cut in it, joined to no wire and no battery. Hertz watched that slit. What did he see?
answer: a tiny spark jumped across it
choices: a tiny spark jumped across it
a bead of metal formed across it
its cut edges slowly blackened
a compass needle beside it swung
context: A tiny spark, metres away, with nothing whatever connecting the two -- that was the entire result, and it was the first electromagnetic wave anyone had made on purpose. The induction coil was driving a discharge across a gap of about 7.5 mm between the inner ends of the two copper wires; the loop had no source of its own at all. Hertz went on to bounce the waves off metal sheets to build standing waves and read their length off the node spacing: 0.7 to 6 metres, roughly 50-450 MHz. They reflected, refracted and polarised exactly like light. Published as 'Uber elektromagnetische Wellen im Raume', Annalen der Physik, 1888. Source: Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations', section 'Experimental Confirmation by Hertz (1880s)'.

question: Michael Faraday made his curved lines of magnetic force show up by tapping iron filings on a card, but he could not write an equation for them. Young James Clerk Maxwell put numbers on those lines in two Cambridge essays in 1855 and 1856. What did he treat each one as?
answer: a tube of incompressible fluid
choices: a tube of incompressible fluid
a chain of magnets, pole to pole
an orbit traced by one particle
a ridge on a stretched sheet
context: 'On Faraday's Lines of Force', read to the Cambridge Philosophical Society in December 1855 and February 1856. Faraday had almost no mathematics; what he had was a picture. By modelling each line as a tube of incompressible fluid, Maxwell could carry the whole machinery of fluid mechanics across to magnetism -- flow rates, pressures, tube cross-sections -- and so put arithmetic on a drawing its own author could not calculate with. In the same essays he went after the reigning action-at-a-distance theories of Coulomb and Ampere for demanding instantaneous forces with nothing in between. Source: Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations' and 'James Clerk Maxwell'.

question: James Clerk Maxwell read 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field' to the Royal Society of London in December 1864. Every physics classroom today prints four short vector equations under his name, but those four are not in that paper. What is actually written on its pages?
answer: twenty simultaneous equations in twenty variables
choices: twenty simultaneous equations in twenty variables
eight simultaneous equations in eight variables
twelve simultaneous equations in six variables
three simultaneous equations in twelve variables
context: Twenty, written out component by component; they can be grouped as eight lettered relations, A through H -- law of total currents, magnetic potential, Ampere's circuital law, electromotive force, electric elasticity, Ohm's law, Gauss's law, continuity of charge. The four compact vector equations everyone recites were a later compression by another hand entirely. Maxwell's own summing-up in that paper: 'The agreement of the results seems to show that light and magnetism are affections of the same substance, and that light is an electromagnetic disturbance propagated through the field according to electromagnetic laws.' Sources: IEEE Spectrum, 'The Long Road to Maxwell's Equations'; Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations'; Wikipedia, 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field'.

question: James Clerk Maxwell printed two numbers side by side in the Philosophical Magazine in January 1862. One was 310,740 km per second, the speed he had figured for a ripple in his medium. The other was 314,858, Fizeau's measured speed of light. Every number in his calculation came from one 1856 experiment by Wilhelm Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch in Germany, with no lamp, no mirror and no spinning toothed wheel in it. What were those two men measuring?
answer: the charge in a Leyden jar, gauged by force and by current
choices: the charge in a Leyden jar, gauged by force and by current
the spark from a Leyden jar, timed as it leapt an air gap
the pull between two magnets, gauged at fixed distances
the current in a coil, gauged as its iron core withdrew
context: Weber and Kohlrausch were after the ratio between the electrostatic and the electromagnetic unit of charge -- the same charge in a foil-lined glass jar, weighed once by the force it exerts and once by the current it makes. The ratio came out carrying the units of a velocity: 3.107 x 10^8 metres per second. No lamps, no mirrors, no light of any kind. Weber had even labelled the constant 'c' in an 1846 paper with no thought of light, and neither man made much of the coincidence. Maxwell saw what it was, and set the punchline in italics: '...we can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations' and 'Leyden jar'; Wikisource scan of Philosophical Magazine, series 4, vol. 23 ('On Physical Lines of Force', Part III, Prop. XVI).

question: A student takes the turntable out of a microwave oven so nothing can spin, lays a flat bar of chocolate on the oven floor and runs it until the first patches soften. The melted patches come out in a neat row, about six centimetres apart, with firm chocolate between them, because the oven's waves are standing still inside the box. What does that six-centimetre spacing equal?
answer: half of one wavelength
choices: half of one wavelength
one full wavelength
two full wavelengths
a quarter of a wavelength
context: Neighbouring hot spots sit half a wavelength apart, so double the six centimetres and multiply by the frequency printed on the oven -- almost always 2450 million cycles per second -- and you get about 3 x 10^8 metres per second. You have just measured the speed of light on a countertop, with an invisible wave made purely by electricity: Maxwell's whole claim, tested in an afternoon with a chocolate bar. A tray of marshmallows works too. Sources: Science Buddies, 'Measuring the Speed of Light with a Microwave Oven'; Open University OpenLearn; University of Georgia Extension, 'Cooking at the Speed of Light'.

question: Richard Feynman told his Caltech students to look back on the 1860s from ten thousand years in the future. From that distance, he said, one event of the decade would stand as the most important of the 1800s: James Clerk Maxwell working out the laws of electrodynamics. Another famous event of the same decade would 'pale into provincial insignificance' next to it. Which event did he name?
answer: the American Civil War
choices: the American Civil War
the unification of Italy
the opening of the Suez Canal
the freeing of the Russian serfs
context: Verbatim, from The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II, Lecture 1, section 1-6: 'From a long view of the history of mankind -- seen from, say, ten thousand years from now -- there can be little doubt that the most significant event of the 19th century will be judged as Maxwell's discovery of the laws of electrodynamics. The American Civil War will pale into provincial insignificance in comparison with this important scientific event of the same decade.' Einstein made a similar claim at the 1931 centenary of Maxwell's birth, calling the change in the conception of physical reality that Maxwell brought about 'the most profound and the most fruitful that physics has experienced since the time of Newton'. Sources: Wikiquote, Richard Feynman, citing The Feynman Lectures Vol. II ch. 1 (1964); James Clerk Maxwell Foundation, for Einstein's centenary essay.

question: Faced with a charging capacitor, James Clerk Maxwell saw a hole in the law. Current runs up the wire and stops dead at the gap between the plates, which no charge crosses. Ampere's law, tying the magnetic field around a loop to the current threading it, then gives two answers for one circuit: a field where a surface is pierced by the wire, nothing where it crosses the gap. Maxwell ruled that something else in the apparatus counts as a current too. What was it?
answer: a changing electric field in the gap
choices: a changing electric field in the gap
a magnetic current between the plates
a charge piling on the plate faces
a slow warming of the air in the gap
context: He named it the displacement current, and in 'On Physical Lines of Force' he pictured it physically, as a 'displacement of the rows of particles' in the ether. Do the arithmetic and the displacement current through the gap comes out exactly equal to the conduction current in the wires: the circuit closes. That one term is also why light exists in the equations at all -- a changing electric field sources a magnetic field, whose change sources an electric field, and the disturbance regenerates itself outward with nothing to wave in. Delete the term and the equations support no self-sustaining oscillation in free space, and sunlight could not cross the vacuum. Source: Grokipedia, 'Displacement current' (the two-surface paradox, the continuity violation, the derivation, and the 'Electromagnetic Waves' section).

question: Oliver Heaviside cut Maxwell's equations down to the four every textbook now prints, over the summer of 1884. Scarlet fever had left him partly deaf, he had left school at sixteen because his family had no money, and he had quit telegraph work to do physics alone at his parents' house. Maxwell wrote in fields and potentials, a potential being a quantity a field is worked out from. Heaviside said one drastic move let him do it. Which move?
answer: he threw out the potentials and kept the fields
choices: he threw out the potentials and kept the fields
he threw out the fields and kept the potentials
he threw out the ether and worked in empty space
he threw out the vectors and worked in quaternions
context: His own words: 'I never made any progress until I threw all the potentials overboard.' Heaviside insisted on writing the theory in the measurable fields themselves, and Maxwell's twenty simultaneous equations in twenty variables collapsed into four vector equations over the summer of 1884, published in 1885. He was no dullard for all his missing schooling: he had ranked fifth out of five hundred pupils in 1865, the year before the money ran out. On first getting hold of Maxwell's 1873 Treatise he wrote, 'I saw that it was great, greater and greatest... I was determined to master the book.' Even the name is his: the phrase 'Maxwell's equations' first appears in his 1885 series 'Electromagnetic Induction and its Propagation' in The Electrician, where he wrote 'Maxwell's equations of propagation' -- before that people said 'Maxwell's theory', and Oliver Lodge's 1888 lectures pushed the new phrase into general use. Heaviside died on 3 February 1925 in a Torquay nursing home after a fall, on a civil-list pension of 220 pounds a year, and was buried in an unmarked plot beside his parents in Paignton Cemetery; admirers added his name and 'F.R.S.' to the stone years later. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Oliver Heaviside' and 'History of Maxwell's equations'; IEEE Spectrum, 'The Long Road to Maxwell's Equations'.

question: James Clerk Maxwell drew a full mechanical picture behind his 1861 calculation of how fast a ripple would run through his medium. Spinning molecular vortices packed space, and between them tiny round particles rolled without slipping, like the idle wheels in a gear train; an electric current was those particles on the move. Then, in the same paper, he wrote about his own gear train. What did he say about it?
answer: that he did not offer it as existing in nature
choices: that he did not offer it as existing in nature
that only the vortices, not the particles, were real
that he had built a brass model to test it
that Faraday had described the same gearing
context: His exact words: the conception of a particle connected to a vortex by perfect rolling contact 'may appear somewhat awkward', and 'I do not bring it forward as a mode of connexion existing in nature, or even as that which I would willingly assent to as an electrical hypothesis.' He built a machine he did not believe in, turned the crank, and the speed of light came out of it. Three years later he threw the vortices away and rebuilt the theory abstractly in 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field'. Note the scope of the doubt: it was this gear-train machinery Maxwell disowned, not the ether itself, which he never doubted was there. Sources: Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations'; Bruce J. Hunt, 'Maxwell, Measurement, and the Modes of Electromagnetic Theory' (2015), for both verbatim hedges.

question: At Glenlair, his family estate in Galloway, James Clerk Maxwell worked out his electromagnetic equations in the summer of 1861 with none of his reference books to hand. He carried the result back to London late that year, looked up the lab figures, changed them into his own units and got 310,740 kilometres per second. Three rival measurements of the speed of light were around then. How did his number sit among those three?
answer: they disagreed with each other by more than any did with his
choices: they disagreed with each other by more than any did with his
they agreed with each other more closely than any did with his
they clustered tightly together, and all three sat above his
they fell either side of his, each about equally far off
context: The rival optical values then in circulation were Fizeau's 314,858 km/s, Foucault's 298,000, and roughly 308,000 from stellar aberration. Maxwell's 310,740 landed inside that spread: the measurers of light stood further apart from each other than any of them stood from a figure he had got out of electricity and magnetism alone, with no light in it anywhere. The order of events matters as much as the closeness. He made the equations out at Glenlair before he had any suspicion of the nearness between the two velocities, and said so to William Thomson in his December 1861 letter -- a number that falls out of a theory before its author has looked the measurement up cannot have been fitted to that measurement, which is the whole working difference between a prediction and a curve fit. The modern value is 299,792,458 metres per second, exact by definition. Sources: Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations', for the rival figures; Wikipedia, 'On Physical Lines of Force'; Instituto de Matematicas, Universidad de Sevilla, 'Maxwell sees the light' (Glenlair, the missing books, the December 1861 letter to Thomson).

question: James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny being in an 1867 letter, posted at a trapdoor between the two halves of a box of gas. If it passed fast molecules in one direction and slow ones in the other, the gas would sort itself into a hot side and a cold side without any work being done. That would cheat one of physics' most important laws. Which law does the imaginary creature seem to break?
answer: The second law of thermodynamics
choices: The second law of thermodynamics
The first law of thermodynamics
The law of conservation of mass
Newton's third law
context: Energy is never created in the sorting, so the first law, the conservation of energy, survives; it is the second law, which says heat does not flow from cold to hot by itself, that the demon seems to cheat. The name was Kelvin's, not Maxwell's: he coined it in 'Kinetic Theory of the Dissipation of Energy' (Nature, 9 April 1874), meaning it in the Greek sense of a helpful attendant spirit, not an evil one. Source: Wikipedia, Maxwell's demon.

question: James Clerk Maxwell used his trapdoor gatekeeper to teach a subtle point about what kind of rule one great law of physics really is. The story is almost always mistold as Maxwell trying to overthrow that law; he was doing the opposite. What deeper truth about that law was he illustrating?
answer: that it holds only statistically for bulk gas, not as a ban on any single molecule
choices: that it holds only statistically for bulk gas, not as a ban on any single molecule
that it can be broken outright by a clever enough sorting machine
that it is not a real physical law but a bookkeeping convention
that it applies to heat as a fluid substance stored inside each molecule
context: Maxwell's point: any single molecule is free to move the 'wrong' way; the second law of thermodynamics wins only because there are Avogadro-many of them. The demon was a teaching device, not a proposed perpetual-motion machine. Source: Wikipedia -- Maxwell's demon.

question: Leo Szilard sharpened the puzzle of Maxwell's demon in 1929, shrinking it to a cylinder holding just one molecule. He argued that the demon's engine could not run for free: one specific step in the process had to cost entropy. Which step did he name?
answer: finding out which half of the cylinder the molecule was in
choices: finding out which half of the cylinder the molecule was in
inserting the partition into the middle of the cylinder
letting the trapped molecule push the piston outward
resetting the piston to its starting position
context: Szilard, 'Uber die Entropieverminderung...', Zeitschrift fur Physik 53, 1929. Reducing the gas to a single particle stripped the puzzle to its skeleton: no measurement, no engine. He was the first to link information to entropy in a quantitative way. Source: Wikipedia -- Maxwell's demon.

question: Antoine Berut and colleagues in Lyon, Augsburg and Kaiserslautern finally measured Rolf Landauer's limit in 2012, after it had sat as pure theory for fifty-one years. That limit is the minimum heat bill for erasing one bit of memory. What did they actually hold and watch in their tabletop experiment?
answer: a single 2-micrometre silica bead trapped between two laser wells
choices: a single 2-micrometre silica bead trapped between two laser wells
a swarm of hydrogen atoms held in a magnetic bottle
a single trapped calcium ion cooled by a radio-frequency cage
a nitrogen-vacancy centre inside a chilled diamond chip
context: Berut et al., Nature 483, 187-189 (2012). Left-well and right-well encoded the two possible bit values; tilting the trap forced the bead into one well regardless of where it started -- an erasure. The released heat matched Landauer's floor. A 19th-century thought experiment was closed by a measurement in the 21st.

question: Rolf Landauer, a physicist at International Business Machines, proved a strange lower limit in 1961: erasing a single bit of information must release at least a tiny minimum amount of heat, no matter how cleverly the machine is built. How do today's real computer chips stand next to that floor?
answer: they dissipate orders of magnitude more heat per bit than the limit demands
choices: they dissipate orders of magnitude more heat per bit than the limit demands
they already run right at the limit, so no further cooling is possible
they run below the limit because transistors are quantum devices
they cheat the limit by using reversible logic in every operation
context: Modern CMOS erases a bit with roughly a million times Landauer's minimum, so the limit is not today's engineering bottleneck -- it is a floor no future chip can pass. In principle a fully REVERSIBLE computer would dodge it, since only bit-destruction pays; no one has built a practical one. Source: Wikipedia -- Landauer's principle.

question: Julius Robert Mayer, ship's doctor on a Dutch three-master sailing to Java, bled several sick sailors on deck in the summer of 1840 and got a shock. The venous blood coming out of them, which had already run through their tissues, looked wrong to him. In what way?
answer: It was nearly as bright red as arterial blood
choices: It was nearly as bright red as arterial blood
It ran black instead of the usual dark red
It came out watery and thin
It was noticeably cooler than blood back in Europe
context: Venous blood back home was dark because tissues had stripped most of the oxygen out of it on the way. In the tropics the crew's bodies were burning far less oxygen to keep warm, so the returning blood still glowed red. Mayer stood on deck holding a bucket and puzzled about it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_von_Mayer

question: Anchored off Java in 1840 on a Dutch trader, the ship's doctor Julius Robert Mayer opened a sailor's vein to bleed him. Very little oxygen had been stripped out of the blood on its trip through the tissues. He worked back to why. What internal process were the sailors' bodies running less of in the tropical heat?
answer: Burning food to make their own heat
choices: Burning food to make their own heat
Sweating salt out through the skin
Pumping blood through the lungs
Storing sugar in the liver
context: Less internal fire meant less oxygen consumed, so less oxygen taken out of the venous blood. To Mayer this was a clue that heat, food-energy and work were all the SAME quantity in different forms -- warmth pouring in from outside could stand in for warmth burned from within. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_von_Mayer

question: To put a number on how much mechanical work a given amount of heat is worth, what physicists now call the mechanical equivalent of heat, Julius Robert Mayer built no apparatus of his own. He did not measure it himself at all. Where did his number come from?
answer: Published heat-capacity data for gases
choices: Published heat-capacity data for gases
A paddle wheel he built and stirred water with
Steam-engine coal-burn records from the Ruhr
The temperature rise in bent iron bars
context: Mayer used the difference between the specific heat of air at constant pressure and at constant volume (Cp minus Cv) -- the extra heat needed when a gas is allowed to expand and do work against the atmosphere -- to compute about 365 kilogram-metres per kilocalorie. Because he had never actually done an experiment, the English experimentalists found him easy to dismiss. Source: https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/mayer-julius-robert

question: Johann Christian Poggendorff, editor of Annalen der Physik, the leading German physics journal, received a first physics paper from the young ship's doctor Julius Robert Mayer in June 1841. Mayer was an outsider with no physics degree, and the paper was rough in places but essentially right. What did Poggendorff do with it?
answer: Filed it away without reply and never printed it
choices: Filed it away without reply and never printed it
Sent it back with a page of demolishing corrections
Forwarded it to Helmholtz for a second opinion
Printed a short version, then a retraction three months later
context: The paper was neither published nor returned. Mayer had to work up a second version essentially from memory. Poggendorff's copy of the original turned up in his papers 36 years later, long after the priority fight was over. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_von_Mayer

question: Julius Robert Mayer, the ship's doctor who had read the conservation of energy in his sailors' bright red blood, lost two children in rapid succession in 1848, while Joule's supporters in England openly denied that he had got there first. The double blow broke him. Where did the years that followed take him?
answer: Into a series of asylum confinements
choices: Into a series of asylum confinements
Into voluntary exile in Paris and London
Into a monastery in the Black Forest
Into private practice as an army surgeon
context: Mayer spent the early 1850s in and out of the asylums at Goppingen, Kennenburg and Winnenthal; his own circle described him as a broken man when he emerged. He lived on to 1878. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_von_Mayer

question: John Tyndall stood up at London's Royal Institution in 1862 to lecture on the discovery of energy, with a punchline prepared. After crediting his ideas to 'a man of whom you have scarcely ever heard,' whom did he name?
answer: A German physician named Mayer
choices: A German physician named Mayer
A Prussian steam engineer named Krupp
A Danish civil servant named Colding
An Alsatian brewer named Reiss
context: Tyndall had rediscovered Mayer's buried 1842 paper while preparing his own lectures on heat and made rescuing Mayer a personal cause. The Royal Society finally handed Mayer its Copley Medal -- its highest honour -- in 1871; Joule had received the same medal only the year before. Even Joule eventually conceded the IDEA to Mayer while keeping the experimental proof. Source: https://skullsinthestars.com/2023/07/31/john-tyndall-rescues-julius-mayer-1862/

question: Barbara McClintock studied maize kernels in the late 1940s that should have been plain yet were freckled with colour. She traced the freckles to two chromosome pieces working as a team, and showed that each freckle was a family of cells descended from a single cell. What had happened in that founding cell?
answer: One piece had popped the other out of a colour gene
choices: One piece had popped the other out of a colour gene
A virus had carried in a working copy of a colour gene
A colour gene had repaired itself by chance mutation
A pollen grain had brought a colour gene into that cell
context: Ds (Dissociation) lands inside a pigment gene and shuts it off; Ac (Activator) can pop Ds back out partway through kernel development, and every cell descended from THAT one cell restarts the pigment. The colour patch is that family made visible. McClintock named the pair Dissociation and Activator and called such pieces controlling elements; the word transposon came later. Source: Ac/Ds transposable controlling elements, Wikipedia.

question: Barbara McClintock published results from her maize plants in 1950 that broke a picture biologists had held for fifty years: genes as beads strung on a wire, fixed units in a fixed order along the chromosome. Mapping a chromosome meant nailing down exactly where each gene sat. What was so shocking about her 1950 claim?
answer: Some of those units get up and move
choices: Some of those units get up and move
The chromosome itself was chemically misidentified
Mapping distances were pure statistical luck
Every unit was really two units fused together
context: Fixed-order mapping was the crown jewel of Morgan's fly-room and every classroom since. McClintock did not reject it -- she added an exception the model could not accommodate. Source: PMC 3528533, 'Barbara McClintock and the discovery of jumping genes'.

question: George Beadle and Salvador Luria sat in the room at the Cold Spring Harbor Symposium on Long Island in the summer of 1951 when Barbara McClintock laid out her evidence for jumping genes in maize. According to people who were there, how did her talk actually go over?
answer: Puzzlement rather than argument
choices: Puzzlement rather than argument
Immediate applause and unanimous acceptance
An organised campaign to have her fired
A demand that she rerun the crosses at scale
context: By the mid-1950s she had stopped giving talks on controlling elements and largely stopped publishing on them. Not shunned; simply not followed. Source: MCB140 lecture notes (Berkeley) on McClintock.

question: When Barbara McClintock announced in 1950 that pieces of chromosome could physically pick themselves up and jump to new places inside a corn cell, most biologists refused to believe it. Proof strong enough to convert them did not come from corn. It came in 1968, from a bacterium, when small mobile pieces of DNA called 'insertion sequences' were spotted jumping around its chromosomes in the lab. Which bacterium?
answer: Escherichia coli
choices: Escherichia coli
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Bacillus subtilis
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
context: Through the 1970s transposons were cloned and sequenced across many species, McClintock's picture was vindicated, and in 1983 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to her ALONE -- still the only unshared prize a woman has held in that category. Source: PMC 3528533.

question: Nathaniel Comfort showed in his 2001 book The Tangled Field that Barbara McClintock was no shunned, jobless genius found again by a Nobel committee in 1983. She held major posts even during her supposed wilderness years. Which of these did she actually hold in the 1940s?
answer: President of the Genetics Society of America
choices: President of the Genetics Society of America
Director of the Carnegie Department of Genetics
Editor-in-chief of the journal Genetics
President of the American Society of Naturalists
context: She took the GSA presidency in 1945 -- its first woman president -- and had been elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1944, only its third woman. What her colleagues resisted was her CLAIM about jumping genes, not her STANDING as a geneticist. A more useful lesson than martyrdom. Source: Comfort, 'The Tangled Field'; Wikipedia, 'Barbara McClintock'.

question: A geneticist goes through the human genome, the roughly three billion letters of DNA in each human cell, and adds up how much of it is built out of transposons and their broken, worn-out leftovers. Those are the mobile pieces Barbara McClintock found jumping in corn. Roughly what fraction does the count reach?
answer: About half
choices: About half
About one percent
About five percent
Essentially all of it
context: Roughly 40-80% of many plant genomes too. Whether those elements are cellular machinery, cellular garbage or cellular parasites is the honest next question. Source: Current Biology, 'C-value paradox, junk DNA and ENCODE'.

question: Leslie Orgel and Francis Crick published a paper in Nature in April 1980, back to back with a companion by W. Ford Doolittle and Carmen Sapienza, that gave transposons an unflattering new reading, the opposite of Barbara McClintock's own view of them as controllers. What did the two papers argue transposons mostly are?
answer: Freeloaders replicating themselves at the cell's expense
choices: Freeloaders replicating themselves at the cell's expense
Relics of ancient viruses reawakened by stress
The primary drivers of new species forming
Sequences inherited only through the mother
context: Orgel and Crick titled theirs 'Selfish DNA: the ultimate parasite'; Doolittle and Sapienza's companion piece ran in the same issue. McClintock had read her elements as controllers doing something useful for the plant; the 1980 papers said no, they are propagating at the host's expense. The honest modern answer is that BOTH happen, and telling which is which in any given case is unfinished work. Source: Nature 288, 645 (1980), 'Selfish DNA'.

question: Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Mechain set out in 1792 to survey a long slice of the Paris meridian, because the Academy could not just declare a fraction of the planet to be the metre. The job took until 1798. Between which two coastal cities did their survey run?
answer: Dunkirk and Barcelona
choices: Dunkirk and Barcelona
Calais and Cadiz
Le Havre and Lisbon
Ostend and Marseille
context: Jean-Baptiste Delambre took Dunkirk south to Rodez; Pierre Mechain took Rodez through the Pyrenees to Barcelona. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_measurement_of_Delambre_and_Mechain.

question: A suspicious villager watched Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Mechain haul brass instruments up a bell tower in the middle of the French Revolution. The two astronomers were measuring the arc of a meridian to define the new unit called the metre. Again and again the locals had them arrested on the same charge. Of what were they accused?
answer: spying for the royalists
choices: spying for the royalists
practising forbidden witchcraft
hiding smuggled gold in the instrument cases
trespassing on private church land
context: Locals could not imagine a peaceful reason for strangers with polished brass and telescopes on their roofs; both men were detained more than once during the survey. Source: frieze.com/article/walking-dunkirk-barcelona-measure-curvature-earth.

question: Jean-Baptiste Delambre hauled the survey's key sighting instrument up the church towers of France: a brass circle built in 1784 that shrank the random error of a measured angle to a level no earlier instrument had reached. How did it do that?
answer: It measured the same angle again and again around its ring
choices: It measured the same angle again and again around its ring
It magnified each target through a far longer telescope
It took the average of two observers sighting at once
It sat on a heavy stone base that kept it from trembling
context: It was Borda's repeating circle, made by Etienne Lenoir in 1784 while he was Jean-Charles de Borda's assistant, and later improved by Borda. Its trick was to observe the same angle again and again around the ring; stacking N sightings divided the reading error by roughly N. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_measurement_of_Delambre_and_Mechain.

question: The French commission of 1791 looked at a rival plan already used across Europe before it picked the meridian: set a pendulum ticking once per second, measure its length and call that the metre. It tossed the plan out. What was the deciding objection?
answer: its length depends on local gravity and would differ from town to town
choices: its length depends on local gravity and would differ from town to town
wooden pendulums swell and shrink with the weather
no clock in France was accurate enough to time the ticks
the Church claimed pendulums as its own liturgical property
context: Jean Richer had discovered the gravity-with-latitude effect on his 1671-1673 Cayenne expedition. Talleyrand had proposed the pendulum standard in 1790; the commission - Borda, Lagrange, Laplace, Legendre, Lavoisier - rejected it in March 1791. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_metre.

question: Pierre Mechain measured the latitude of Barcelona from two different stations, the Mont-Jouy fortress and a rented inn. The two figures should have agreed to a whisker; they disagreed by about three arcseconds, roughly a hundred metres on the ground, and he could not explain it. What did he do with the second set?
answer: concealed it and altered his notebooks to shrink the gap
choices: concealed it and altered his notebooks to shrink the gap
blamed the Spanish military and demanded a new site
burned the papers and wrote a public confession
handed both sets to Delambre to arbitrate
context: The concealment tormented him for the rest of his life. He avoided returning to Paris to meet Delambre and produced almost no work for two years, and refused to share his raw data. Source: mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Mechain.

question: Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Mechain measured the meridian with great care, yet the legal metre came out about 0.2 millimetres short of its own definition, one part in ten million of the pole-to-equator arc. Modern analysis traces most of that shortfall to a real physical effect nobody in the 1790s had allowed for. What was it?
answer: Nearby mountains pulled the plumb line sideways
choices: Nearby mountains pulled the plumb line sideways
Warm air near the ground bent the starlight
The Earth's axis wobbled during the sightings
Summer heat stretched the brass of the circle
context: Massive nearby terrain pulls a plumb line sideways, so 'straight down' does not point at the Earth's centre, and a latitude taken from star sightings, which are measured against the plumb line, is thrown off. Geodesists call it deflection of the vertical. About 95% of the missing length of the legal metre traces to it; roughly 3% comes from a wrong assumption about the Earth's flattening, and less than 2% from the measured arc itself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_measurement_of_Delambre_and_Mechain.

question: Otto Frisch arrived at Kungalv in Sweden at Christmas 1938 to find his aunt, Lise Meitner, puzzling over a letter from her old partner Otto Hahn. They argued it out in the snowy woods, Frisch on skis, Meitner at sixty on foot. What did the two do when it came to arithmetic?
answer: Sat on a tree trunk and calculated on scraps of paper
choices: Sat on a tree trunk and calculated on scraps of paper
Turned back and telephoned Niels Bohr in Copenhagen
Waited until Frisch reached Bohr's institute
Posted the problem back to Otto Hahn in Berlin
context: Frisch's own memoir: 'we both sat down on a tree trunk... and started to calculate on scraps of paper.' Meitner was spending Christmas with the von Bahr family and had asked Frisch to come; there was nowhere else to go. She was a refugee sharing bench space in Manne Siegbahn's Stockholm institute, with no funding and no research group of her own; she called it her exile from physics. The physics of the atomic age got worked out sitting on a log. Source: Wikipedia 'Lise Meitner', quoting O. R. Frisch, What Little I Remember.

question: Otto Frisch picked the words cut into his aunt Lise Meitner's gravestone in St James's churchyard at Bramley, in Hampshire. He was the nephew who had argued nuclear physics with her in the snow. The words call her a physicist who never lost one particular thing. Which?
answer: Her humanity
choices: Her humanity
Her curiosity
Her nerve
Her country
context: The full inscription: 'Lise Meitner: a physicist who never lost her humanity.' She had lost her country, her laboratory, her name on papers she helped write, and the prize. The man who knew her best thought this was the thing worth carving. Source: De Gruyter Conversations, 'Lise Meitner: A physicist who never lost her humanity'; Atomic Heritage Foundation profile. (Grokipedia's Meitner page instead claims a Bible verse; that is unsupported elsewhere.)

question: Otto Hahn wrote to Lise Meitner in December 1938 about something that made no sense. He and Fritz Strassmann had been firing neutrons at uranium in Berlin, and now the 'radium' they had been catching would not act like radium. He named the element it was acting like instead, one far too light to come from uranium. Which element?
answer: Barium
choices: Barium
Lanthanum
Cerium
Strontium
context: Hahn to Meitner: 'more and more we come to the frightful conclusion: our Ra-isotopes do not behave like Ra but like Ba.' He could not explain it, and asked whether she could suggest some fantastic explanation. They had been partners on the uranium problem since 1907. Source: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'; APS News, 'December 1938: Discovery of Nuclear Fission'.

question: Lise Meitner boarded a train for the Dutch border with two small suitcases and no exit visa in July 1938, after thirty-one years in Berlin. The Nazi regime had forbidden her to leave Germany legally, and the Dutch physicist Dirk Coster rode with her to see her across. Otto Hahn gave her one thing to take with her. What was it?
answer: A diamond ring from his mother, to sell if she ran short
choices: A diamond ring from his mother, to sell if she ran short
A letter of introduction to Niels Bohr in Copenhagen
A packet of banknotes sewn into the lining of a case
The key to an account he had opened for her in Zurich
context: Hahn and Paul Rosbaud packed the two suitcases; Coster travelled down from the Netherlands to ride the train out with her; they crossed on 13 July 1938 at the lightly used Bad Nieuweschans station and were not stopped. She was fifty-nine, and the ring was Hahn's inheritance from his own mother. Source: Wikipedia 'Lise Meitner'; Sime, 'Lise Meitner's escape from Germany', American Journal of Physics.

question: The British group heading to Los Alamos asked Lise Meitner to join the bomb project. Her nephew Otto Frisch was already going. The physics they meant to use was hers. She was a refugee with no lab, no funding, and no steady job, so the offer was everything she lacked. What did she answer?
answer: That she would have nothing to do with a bomb
choices: That she would have nothing to do with a bomb
That she would go only if the bomb were never used
That she would send the bomb team her calculations only
That she would wait to see what Germany built first
context: Her recorded reply: 'I will have nothing to do with a bomb!' She never worked on a nuclear weapon for any country. Grokipedia and the Atomic Heritage Foundation date the invitation to 1943, the US National Park Service to 1942; the refusal itself is not in dispute. Source: Ruth Lewin Sime, 'Lise Meitner: A Life in Physics' (1996), p. 305, quoted by the National Park Service and the Atomic Heritage Foundation.

question: Lise Meitner recalled the formula for the mass of a nucleus, out in the snow at Kungalv at Christmas 1938, and added up the two fragments Otto Hahn's chemistry had produced. Together they were lighter than the uranium nucleus they came from, by about one-fifth the mass of a proton. Otto Frisch put that missing bit through E=mc-squared. Compared with burning, how much energy per atom was it?
answer: About a hundred million times as much
choices: About a hundred million times as much
About a hundred thousand times as much
About a thousand times as much
About a million times as much
context: One-fifth of a proton mass works out to roughly 200 million electron-volts, 200 MeV, for every single atom that splits; a chemical reaction such as burning releases a few electron-volts per atom. That factor is the whole difference between a bonfire and a reactor, and it came off a scrap of paper. Source: Wikipedia 'Lise Meitner' (Frisch's account); Wikipedia 'Nuclear fission'.

question: Lise Meitner wrote back to Otto Hahn on 21 December 1938. His letter of 19 December had asked her to make sense of a light element his chemistry kept catching where only radium should have been, and hinted that she might suggest some fantastic explanation. Nothing in the physics of 1938 allowed a heavy nucleus to come apart like that. What position did she take in the reply?
answer: She told him she doubted it but would not rule it out yet
choices: She told him she doubted it but would not rule it out yet
She told him the light element had to be contamination
She told him she had been expecting exactly this for years
She told him to publish nothing until she saw the raw data
context: Her exact words: 'At the moment the assumption of such a thoroughgoing breakup seems very difficult to me, but in nuclear physics we have experienced so many surprises, that one cannot unconditionally say: It is impossible.' She did not yet believe it. She refused to declare it impossible. That single sentence is what an open mind looks like in practice. Source: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'.

question: Otto Frisch, back at Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen in January 1939, had to name a nuclear process no one had a name for: a uranium nucleus coming apart into two pieces. He asked a colleague from another science what that science called such a split, and he borrowed the word. Which field did 'nuclear fission' come from?
answer: From biology: it is what a living cell does when it divides in two
choices: From biology: it is what a living cell does when it divides in two
From geology: it is what a crystal does when it cleaves in two
From engineering: it is what a loaded cable does when it parts in two
From metallurgy: it is what a hot billet does when it shears in two
context: Frisch asked what biologists call it when a living cell splits in two, was told 'binary fission', and borrowed the word. Sources disagree about the colleague: Wikipedia's fission-discovery page calls William A. Arnold a biologist, its nuclear-fission page calls him a physicist. The borrowing from biology is not in dispute. Source: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'; Wikipedia 'Nuclear fission'.

question: Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Munzenberg's team at Darmstadt fired iron-58 at bismuth-209 on 29 August 1982 and made a single atom of element 109. Ten years later they proposed a name, and in 1997 the naming body agreed on meitnerium. Among all named elements, meitnerium holds one distinction. Which?
answer: The only element named for a real woman and no one else
choices: The only element named for a real woman and no one else
The only element named for a person who held no doctorate
The only element named for a person who never saw it exist
The only element named for a person honoured while alive
context: Curium honours Pierre and Marie Curie together, which is why meitnerium stands alone as the one element named specifically after a woman who is not a figure out of myth. The whole basis for the honour was a handful of single atoms, made fifteen years before the name was approved. Source: Grokipedia 'Meitnerium'; Wikipedia 'Meitnerium'.

question: Niels Bohr pictured a heavy nucleus as a droplet of liquid: like a water drop, it is pulled into a ball by a kind of surface tension. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch imagined a captured neutron setting such a drop wobbling until it stretched out into a dumbbell. At that stretched moment, what finally pinches the drop in two?
answer: The protons' electric repulsion overpowers the surface tension
choices: The protons' electric repulsion overpowers the surface tension
The surface tension gathers each end into a ball of its own
The wobble itself builds until the stretched neck shakes apart
The thinned neck sheds an alpha particle and parts there
context: A uranium nucleus is crowded with protons, every one of them pushing on all the others. Stretching the drop pushes the two ends further apart, which loosens surface tension's grip while the electrical push between the halves keeps working; past a certain elongation the repulsion wins and the drop ruptures. The two positively charged fragments then hurl each other apart, and that is where the energy goes. Source: Grokipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'.

question: Otto Frisch went back to Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen in January 1939 to check his aunt's arithmetic against an instrument, but his uranium sample threw out alpha particles by the million, drowning the rare splits in a constant crackle of counts. Each split should hurl its two halves apart with enormous energy. What did he do to the counter on 13 January so the answer could not be mistaken?
answer: Raised its trigger threshold until alpha particles were too weak to register
choices: Raised its trigger threshold until alpha particles were too weak to register
Put a foil in front of it thick enough to stop the alpha particles dead
Ran it for hours and subtracted the average alpha background afterwards
Packed it in paraffin so that slow neutrons would show up in the count
context: He set the threshold above anything an alpha could produce, so a fission fragment would give a pulse enormously bigger than any background. He switched it on and the giant pulses were there, exactly as predicted. A prediction that says 'you will see something far larger than this instrument has ever shown' is about as testable as physics gets. Source: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'.

question: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann sent their uranium paper to a journal on 22 December 1938. They had expected to find radium, actinium or thorium. Instead their tests kept finding elements that weigh just over half as much as uranium. What did the printed paper say about the result?
answer: It gave the chemistry and said they could not bring themselves to believe it
choices: It gave the chemistry and said they could not bring themselves to believe it
It gave the chemistry and announced that the uranium nucleus had broken in two
It gave the chemistry and blamed a contaminant somewhere in the apparatus
It gave the chemistry and appealed in print for a physicist to explain it
context: Their own sentence: 'As chemists... we should substitute the symbols Ba, La, Ce for Ra, Ac, Th. As "nuclear chemists" fairly close to physics we cannot yet bring ourselves to take this step which contradicts all previous experience in physics.' They had the fact and refused to claim the explanation, and they printed the refusal rather than hide it. Published 6 January 1939. Source: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'.

question: The Royal Swedish Academy held the 1944 Chemistry prize back until November 1945, three months after the war ended. It was to go for the discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei. Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann had done the chemistry in Berlin; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, both driven into exile, had sent the explanation to Nature in January 1939. What did the Academy's slim majority decide?
answer: To give it to Otto Hahn alone, for discovering fission
choices: To give it to Otto Hahn alone, for discovering fission
To give it to Lise Meitner alone, for explaining fission
To give it jointly to Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann
To give it jointly to Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner
context: Hahn collected it in Stockholm on 10 December 1945, 'for his discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei'. Neither Meitner nor Strassmann was included. Get the date right: the 1944 prize was decided in November 1945. Grokipedia's fission page gives 16 November 1944, which contradicts its own Meitner page and the archival study. Source: Crawford, Sime & Walker, 'A Nobel Tale of Postwar Injustice', Physics Today 50(9), Sept 1997; NobelPrize.org.

question: Enrico Fermi said in 1934 that firing neutrons at uranium had made brand-new transuranics heavier than uranium. That same year, German chemist Ida Noddack raised an objection: the products need not be uranium's neighbours at all, because the nucleus might break up into several large pieces. Fermi brushed her point aside. What did Otto Hahn, Lise Meitner, and Fritz Strassmann do about Fermi's supposed transuranics over the next four years?
answer: They published seven papers of their own hunting the same new elements
choices: They published seven papers of their own hunting the same new elements
They left uranium alone for four years and stayed with older work
They wrote to Ida Noddack and worked the fragment idea up with her
They set the chemistry aside to hunt for the missing energy first
context: Hahn, Meitner and Strassmann themselves published seven papers between 1935 and 1938 on transuranic elements that were not there, and the Joliot-Curies in Paris reported the same. Noddack had the idea four years early, with no mechanism and no energy calculation to go with it, so nobody took it up. Being right is not enough to move a field; the mechanism and the numbers are what Meitner and Frisch supplied four years later. Source: Wikipedia 'Nuclear fission'; Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'.

question: Elisabeth Crawford, Ruth Lewin Sime and Mark Walker read the file on the 1944 Chemistry prize once the Nobel committees' fifty-year seal lifted, and published it in 1997. They found no considered judgement against Lise Meitner at all. Evaluators could not handle a discovery straddling chemistry and physics; the committees knew little theoretical physics; wartime Sweden was cut off. One cause was uglier: the published record itself had been bent against her. What had bent it?
answer: Nazi rules had forced her name off the German papers she helped produce
choices: Nazi rules had forced her name off the German papers she helped produce
Wartime censors had held the Berlin journals back until after the war
Her Stockholm host had published her Swedish results under his own name
The Nature letters she wrote with Otto Frisch had been printed unsigned
context: Crawford, Sime and Walker found four causes, none of them a weighed rejection of her work: the evaluators' inability to handle a cross-disciplinary discovery, the committees' thin competence in theoretical physics, Sweden's wartime isolation, and nobody allowing for the fact that Nazi persecution had distorted the published record itself. The failure belongs to the Academy's committees, not to Hahn. Source: Crawford, Sime & Walker, 'A Nobel Tale of Postwar Injustice', Physics Today 50(9), Sept 1997.

question: To know exactly which pea plant fathered each seed, the friar Gregor Mendel had to stop the flower pollinating itself. At St Thomas's Abbey in Brno he pried each young bud open with fine tweezers. What did he do before he brushed on the pollen from his chosen father plant?
answer: Cut out its anthers before they could shed
choices: Cut out its anthers before they could shed
Snipped its petals off so no bee would land
Brushed its own pollen away with a feather
Tied the young bud shut until he was ready
context: He then bagged the blossom so no insect could interfere. Every cross in the whole eight-year run, 1856-1863, was made by hand this way, in the vegetable garden of St Thomas's Abbey - roughly 28,000 plants, seven either/or traits, one at a time. The pea's habit of fertilising itself inside the closed flower is exactly why its lines breed true, and exactly why Mendel had to open every single blossom himself. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Hybridization Methods and Observations; Methodological Innovations).

question: In his abbey garden at Brno, the friar Gregor Mendel crossed a pea line whose seeds were always round with a line whose seeds were always wrinkled. Every naturalist of his day expected the hybrids to look like a mixture of the two. Mendel grew the whole first generation and opened the pods. What was inside?
answer: Every seed round, and not one wrinkled anywhere
choices: Every seed round, and not one wrinkled anywhere
Every seed faintly dimpled, halfway between them
Round seeds and wrinkled seeds in equal numbers
Round seeds in some pods, wrinkled in others
context: The wrinkled form was not weakened and not averaged away.
