It was simply gone - and Mendel could only find out what had become of it by letting these hybrids pollinate themselves and counting the generation after, seed by seed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Quantitative Data; Hybridization Methods and Observations).

question: Gregor Mendel bred mice in his own room at St Thomas's Abbey in Brno, grey crossed with white, to watch how coat colour passed from parent to young, before he ever touched a pea plant. The story goes that the mice had to go. What ended the mouse experiment?
answer: His bishop objected to a monk breeding animals that mate
choices: His bishop objected to a monk breeding animals that mate
His abbot claimed the room back for the abbey library
The town council feared mice loose in the granaries
His physician judged the cages a risk to his health
context: Mendel switched to plants, and is said to have remarked, with some amusement, that the objection had overlooked the fact that plants have sex lives too. The tale reaches us through later tellings rather than Mendel's own papers, so treat it as a good story with a plausible core - the mouse work itself is well attested. Sources: Asimov Press, 'Origins of the Lab Mouse'; PNAS 119 (2022), 'Behavioral genetics and genomics: Mendel's peas, mice, and bees'.  (Legend.)

question: Seed by seed, Gregor Mendel counted the whole next generation of his round-by-wrinkled pea hybrids, 7,324 seeds, after letting those hybrids pollinate themselves. Nothing yet told him what had become of the wrinkled parent's form. How did that harvest come out?
answer: 5,474 round to 1,850 wrinkled - near three to one
choices: 5,474 round to 1,850 wrinkled - near three to one
7,324 round to none wrinkled - the form was gone
3,662 round to 3,662 wrinkled - a dead even split
6,591 round to 733 wrinkled - near nine to one
context: Never exactly three to one: seed shape came out at 2.96, the seed interior at 3.01 (6,022 yellow to 2,001 green), stem height at 2.84 (787 tall to 277 dwarf), and the remaining four traits between 2.82 and 3.15. Mendel got a law out of numbers that never landed clean by counting until the wobble stopped mattering. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Quantitative Data); remaining four traits per OpenStax Biology 2e, ch.12.

question: Gregor Mendel stood in front of over 300 boys at the Brunn technical school as a substitute teacher, even after his abbey had sent him to Vienna to study physics under the famous Christian Doppler. He stayed a substitute for all thirteen of his years there. What kept him off the full permanent staff?
answer: He twice failed the teaching-certificate examination
choices: He twice failed the teaching-certificate examination
His abbey forbade him any salaried post outside it
He refused the loyalty oath the state demanded
His weather station for Moravia ate half his week
context: He flunked the oral portion in 1850, then failed again in 1856 after two years at the University of Vienna under Doppler in physics and Franz Unger in botany. The man who founded the study of heredity was never certified to teach school science. He did also run the abbey's official weather station for Moravia, log sunspots, and keep the abbey's bees - the peas were the side project of a man with no spare time. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (University of Vienna; Daily Life and Responsibilities).

question: Gregor Mendel put an old doctrine of inheritance to the test in his abbey garden at Brno, counting the seeds and offspring of pea plants from 1856 to 1863. Every naturalist of his day simply assumed the doctrine, and nobody thought it even needed checking. His tallies broke it. Which doctrine was he overturning?
answer: Blending: the parents' traits mix like paints and cannot be unmixed
choices: Blending: the parents' traits mix like paints and cannot be unmixed
Pangenesis: every organ sheds tiny particles that gather in the seed
Use-inheritance: traits a parent strengthens in life pass to its young
Preformation: a whole miniature lies folded in the seed already
context: Under blending inheritance, a wrinkled form crossed into a round-seeded line should have been thinned away for good. Instead it vanished for one whole generation and came back undiluted - heredity travels in units that can hide without being watered down. The other three were real rival doctrines held by serious people: pangenesis was Darwin's own proposal, use-inheritance was Lamarck's, and preformation had ruled the previous century. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Factors Hindering Immediate Recognition; Foundational Role in Genetics).

question: Gregor Mendel let 34 varieties of pea pollinate themselves in his abbey garden at Brno through 1856 and 1857, before he crossed a single flower, and simply watched what came up. Only 22 of the 34 went forward into the experiment proper. What was he checking about each variety in those two years?
answer: Whether each gave identical offspring, generation after generation
choices: Whether each gave identical offspring, generation after generation
Whether each could ripen inside the short Moravian summer
Whether each flowered early enough to be crossed with the rest
Whether each threw enough seed to be counted in thousands
context: Those 22 bred true: left to pollinate themselves, they gave back the same form year after year, which is the only thing that makes a hybrid's behaviour readable at all. The screening came first and the experiment came second - two of Mendel's eight years went into testing his own materials before he tested a single idea. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Rationale for Pea Plants).

question: Three botanists, Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak, each dug Gregor Mendel's pea paper out of the proceedings of a small Brno society within a few months of 1900. What had happened to all three?
answer: Each had hit the same ratios himself, in his own experiments
choices: Each had hit the same ratios himself, in his own experiments
Each had been handed a copy by a teacher who knew Mendel
Each was combing old journals for forgotten Austrian science
Each had been sent the paper by the abbey after Mendel died
context: De Vries found the ratios in evening primrose and published in French in June 1900 without citing Mendel, then amended his German report to acknowledge Mendel's priority; Correns had them in four-o'clocks and credited Mendel outright in April 1900; von Tschermak was working on peas and published in July. Three plants, three laboratories, one forgotten friar - sixteen years dead. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Key Rediscoverers in 1900).

question: Round or wrinkled, yellow or green: Gregor Mendel ran a cross with two traits at once, using peas that differed in both seed shape and seed colour. Out of 556 seeds he counted 315 round-and-yellow, 108 round-and-green, 101 wrinkled-and-yellow and 32 wrinkled-and-green. What did that four-way split show him?
answer: Shape and colour are dealt out independently of each other
choices: Shape and colour are dealt out independently of each other
Shape and colour travel together, inherited as one package
Colour comes from the pollen parent and shape from the other
Each trait halves the other's chance of showing at all
context: That is the 9:3:3:1 pattern - two independent near-three-to-one splits multiplied together. The two middle classes are easy to swap: 101 is the wrinkled-yellow class and 108 the round-green one, per Mendel's own tabulation. Independence does not hold for every pair of traits in nature; ones riding close together on the same chromosome are handed down as a set, which nobody would understand until long after Mendel died. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (dihybrid tabulation, N=556).

question: Carl Naegeli, the most eminent botanist Gregor Mendel could reach, wrote his private verdict on the friar's pea paper in the margin: 'only empirical and not rational'. Mendel had posted it to him on New Year's Eve 1866. Ten letters passed between them over seven years and Naegeli never once engaged with the counts, but he did give Mendel one piece of advice. What was it?
answer: Run the whole experiment again in hawkweed, his own speciality
choices: Run the whole experiment again in hawkweed, his own speciality
Run the whole experiment again in beans, an easier flower to open
Rewrite the paper for a Vienna journal with a far wider reach
Hand his seed to a professional breeder who could check it
context: Naegeli did write back, two months later: 'It seems to me that the experiments with Pisum, far from being finished, are only a beginning.' Then he steered Mendel into Hieracium, the genus Naegeli had made his own. It cost Mendel four years and very nearly his eyesight, and it produced nothing. Sources: The Scientist, 'The Mendel-Naegeli Letters, circa 1866-73'; grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel.

question: Gregor Mendel did not stop at the counts of round and wrinkled peas in his 1866 paper 'Experiments on Plant Hybrids'. Having set out which trait masks which, and how often the hidden trait comes back a generation later, he told his readers what he thought actually passes physically from parent to offspring. What did he say the inherited thing was?
answer: Differing elements inside the cell
choices: Differing elements inside the cell
Genes strung along the chromosomes
Gemmules shed by every organ
Pangens gathered in the cell
context: Mendel wrote in German of differirende Zellelemente - differing cell elements - and of Merkmale, traits. He could not have written 'gene': Wilhelm Johannsen coined it in 1909, and William Bateson coined 'genetics' in 1905, both more than twenty years after Mendel's death. He never saw a chromosome identified as the carrier, and never wrote a word about DNA. Two of his own words did survive intact into that vocabulary assembled long after he was dead: 'dominant' and 'recessive' are his. Sources: Hereditas (2023), 'Mendel's terminology and notation reveal his understanding of genetics'; genome.gov, '1909: The Word Gene Coined'; historyofinformation.com, 'William Bateson Coins the Term Genetics'.

question: Gregor Mendel turned from peas to hawkweed in 1869, a daisy whose flower head is a crowd of florets so tiny that he dissected them under a plain hand lens, often in poor light, until 'a peculiar fatigue and exhaustion of the eyes' set in. Past 5,000 florets later he had no clean ratios at all, and he blamed his own clumsy hands. What had really defeated him?
answer: Much hawkweed seed forms with no fertilisation at all, so nothing is shuffled
choices: Much hawkweed seed forms with no fertilisation at all, so nothing is shuffled
Hawkweed traits all ride on one chromosome, so nothing ever separates
His hawkweed stocks had never been screened, so none of them bred true
Hawkweed hybrids are sterile, so the second generation never arrived
context: The trick is apomixis: many Hieracium build a seed with no meiosis and no fertilisation, so the offspring are clones of the mother and nothing is ever dealt out afresh. In H. piloselloides and H. aurantiacum only about 2.0% and 2.4% of seeds formed sexually. Mendel read his clone-like offspring as his own botched handiwork and blamed his hands for a plant that had simply skipped sex. His verdict, July 1870: 'the hybrids of Hieracium show a behaviour exactly opposite to those of Pisum.' He had the right law and the wrong organism, and no way in 1870 to tell which. Sources: PMC5121183, 'Seeds of doubt: Mendel's choice of Hieracium to study inheritance'; J. Exp. Botany 62(5):1699, 'Apomixis in hawkweed: Mendel's experimental nemesis'.

question: R. A. Fisher checked Gregor Mendel's tables in 1936 with chi-square tests, the standard measure of how far a set of counts strays from the theory it is meant to fit. His complaint was not that the counts missed. They hugged theory too tightly, with joint odds of fits that good near one in twenty thousand. Fisher stopped short of accusing Mendel, and the laws survived the audit. What did Fisher offer instead?
answer: That an assistant who knew what was expected had deceived him
choices: That an assistant who knew what was expected had deceived him
That the Brunn printers had tidied the tables before setting them
That the rediscoverers of 1900 had recopied the figures wrongly
That peas themselves ripen too unevenly ever to be counted well
context: Fisher's own words were blunt - the data 'have been falsified so as to give a closer fit to expectations than would have been likely to occur by chance' - but he added that 'it remains a possibility among others that Mendel was deceived by some assistant who knew too well what was expected.' And the laws stood. Modern replications of Mendel's crosses reproduce his patterns, and a 2020 Monte Carlo fact-check of his two-trait data found the goodness-of-fit well inside what honest experiment can produce: differential seed viability, pollen-tube competition and aggregated replicates can all tighten a ratio with nobody's thumb on the scale. Science audited its own founder in public, and the finding survived the audit. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Mendelian Paradox; Defenses Based on Empirical Rigor), citing Fisher 1936, Annals of Science 1:115-137; Franklin et al., 'Ending the Mendel-Fisher Controversy'.

question: Gregor Mendel counted wrinkled peas for years without ever learning what wrinkles them. In 1990 researchers found the recessive form of his seed-shape factor: a piece of DNA had jumped into the middle of a gene and killed it, and that gene's job had been to lock loose sugar away as starch. Why does a broken copy leave the ripe seed wrinkled?
answer: The unpacked sugar pulls in water, and the swollen seed collapses on drying
choices: The unpacked sugar pulls in water, and the swollen seed collapses on drying
The unused sugar hardens the seed coat, which then cracks into deep ridges
The seed runs short of food, shrivels early and never fills out its pod
The jumped DNA also breaks the gene that smooths the growing seed coat
context: The gene is starch-branching enzyme SBEI, broken by a transposon-like insertion of about 0.8 kb (Bhattacharyya, Smith et al., Cell 60, 1990). With the enzyme dead the seed makes far less starch, leaves nearly twice as much sucrose sitting in the cell, draws in extra water as it grows fat, then collapses into wrinkles as it dries - answered 124 years after Mendel counted them. The last of his seven traits was pinned to DNA only in 2025: a roughly 100,000-base deletion upstream of the chlorophyll-synthase gene ChlG makes yellow pods, an Ogre retrotransposon in a MYB gene plus a premature stop in a CLE peptide gene make constricted pods, and a five-base deletion moves the flowers to the tip of the plant. Every one turned out to be a single locus, exactly as the counting had said. Sources: Cell 60 (1990); Nature (2025), 'Genomic and genetic insights into Mendel's pea genes'.

question: Alexandre-Emile Beguyer de Chancourtois, a French geologist, sorted every known chemical element by its atomic weight in 1862, with chemical cousins, elements that behaved alike, right next to each other. The Paris academy printed his paper but left out the picture, and no reader could follow his argument. What did the missing picture show?
answer: The elements wound in a spiral round a cylinder
choices: The elements wound in a spiral round a cylinder
The elements stacked in a staircase of eight steps
The elements linked in rings of three by family
The elements plotted as a rising and falling curve
context: Beguyer de Chancourtois called his 1862 arrangement the 'telluric screw': the elements wound round a cylinder in order of atomic weight, so that ones with similar properties came out above one another. The paper went to print without its diagram, so nobody could follow the argument, and the work sank. The rival schemes of those years were all real and clever - Johann Doebereiner's 1817 'triads', John Newlands' 1865 'law of octaves', Lothar Meyer's 1870 atomic-volume curve - and every one of them sorted the elements. Not one of them bet on a hole. Mendeleev did: conclusion 6 of his 1869 paper reads, 'One can predict the discovery of many new elements, for example analogues of Si and Al with atomic weights of 65-75.' He was too ill to present that paper himself - his colleague Nikolai Menshutkin read it to the Russian Chemical Society in St Petersburg on 6 March 1869 (22 February, Old Style). Sources: Grokipedia 'Dmitri Mendeleev'; Mendeleev 1869, English translation in Carmen Giunta's Classic Chemistry archive; Chemistry World, 'Ordering the elements'.

question: A student closes a bare hand around a lump of gallium, a soft silver metal that looks a lot like aluminium and sits solid on the shelf. Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran teased it out of zinc ore in 1875. She holds it a minute or two. What happens to the lump?
answer: It melts into a silvery puddle at body heat
choices: It melts into a silvery puddle at body heat
It tarnishes to a dull black crust in seconds
It grows cold enough to numb the fingers
It crumbles into brittle grey flakes
context: Gallium melts at 29.8 degrees C. That was on the shopping list: in 1871 Mendeleev specified for the square under aluminium an atomic weight of about 68, an oxide of formula E2O3, a chloride ECl3, salts more basic than aluminium's, and a notably LOW melting point. Gallium's atomic weight is 69.72 and its oxide is Ga2O3. Boisbaudran announced it on 27 August 1875, having caught two violet lines at about 417.2 and 403.1 nanometres in the spark spectrum of sphalerite from the Pierrefitte mine in the Hautes-Pyrenees, and named it after Gallia, the Latin name for France. Sources: Grokipedia "Mendeleev's predicted elements"; Wikipedia 'Gallium'; Grokipedia 'Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran'.

question: Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran built his own spectroscopes and found three new elements, the first of which dropped straight into one of Mendeleev's empty squares. He worked in a lab on the second floor of his family's house in western France, and the family business paid for it all. What was that business?
answer: Distilling brandy for the export trade
choices: Distilling brandy for the export trade
Smelting zinc and lead from mountain ore
Grinding optical glass for instrument makers
Milling flour for the towns along the river
context: The laboratory sat on the second floor of the family house on Rue de Lusignan in the town of Cognac, and cognac paid for it. Boisbaudran never held an academic post of any kind. A rumour later went round that he had quietly named gallium after himself - 'le coq' is French for 'the rooster', and the Latin for rooster is gallus - and he denied the conjecture in print in an 1877 article. Treat that one as a story, not a fact. Sources: Grokipedia 'Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran'; Wikipedia 'Gallium'.

question: Dmitri Mendeleev laid out his periodic table in 1869 with several squares left empty, for elements he was sure existed but nobody had yet isolated. He needed to call those squares something before the real tenants turned up, and he did not improvise: every one got its placeholder name by exactly the same rule. What was the rule?
answer: Name it for the element directly above, plus a counting word
choices: Name it for the element directly above, plus a counting word
Name it for the atomic weight its tenant was expected to have
Name it for the mineral its tenant was expected to hide in
Name it for a planet, taken in order outward from the Sun
context: The counting words were Sanskrit: eka- ('one'), dvi- ('two'), tri- ('three'), attached to the element sitting directly above the hole. 'Eka-aluminium' therefore meant simply 'one row below aluminium', and 'eka-silicon' meant 'one row below silicon'. Mendeleev knew Otto von Boehtlingk, the Sanskrit scholar at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, and the neutral, numerical naming had a diplomatic advantage: it favoured no living language and staked no national claim on an element nobody had yet found. Source: Grokipedia "Mendeleev's predicted elements".

question: Dmitri Mendeleev fell asleep tired at his desk in St Petersburg, the most famous story goes, saw the whole layout of the elements in a dream, then woke up and wrote it down. His own notebooks and drafts tell a very different story about the real work behind the table. How did he actually work the pattern out?
answer: He shuffled element cards, like a game of patience
choices: He shuffled element cards, like a game of patience
He built a wooden model with rows that slid on rails
He sorted them by the colours of their burning salts
He read the pattern off a graph of atomic volumes
context: The record shows years of sorting element cards 'in a way similar to playing a game of patience' - solitaire - not a vision. The dream story, with its night of drinking and card-playing, is not supported by the evidence; nor is the related claim that Mendeleev set Russian vodka at 40% alcohol, a figure that comes from 18th-century tax law and predates his thesis on alcohol and water. One of the wrong answers is a real chemist's real method: the graph of atomic volumes is Lothar Meyer's 1870 curve, a rival system to Mendeleev's table rather than a way of building it. Sources: Grokipedia 'Dmitri Mendeleev'; RSC Education, 'Mendeleev - the man and his legacy'; Chemistry World, 'Ordering the elements'.

question: Clemens Winkler, at the Freiberg Mining Academy in Saxony, was handed a new silver mineral called argyrodite in 1886 and asked to say what was in it. He took it apart with care and weighed each part: silver, sulfur, a trace of mercury, specks of iron and arsenic. Something in the work told him a brand-new element was sitting in that rock. What told him?
answer: His weighed parts came to only about nine-tenths of the sample
choices: His weighed parts came to only about nine-tenths of the sample
A pair of unfamiliar violet lines showed in its spark spectrum
The crystals would not dissolve in any acid on his shelf
The mineral weighed far more than its formula allowed
context: Winkler's analysis of argyrodite from the Himmelsfuerst mine came to only 93-94%: silver 73-75%, sulfur 17-18%, mercury about 0.21%, traces of iron and arsenic. Six to seven percent of the rock was an element nobody had ever seen. He isolated it pure on 6 February 1886. A missing few percent is exactly the kind of thing a chemist could blame on his own sloppy work; Winkler trusted his weighing instead, and went hunting. Sources: Wikipedia 'Clemens Winkler'; ChemTeam, 'Discovery of Germanium'.

question: Dmitri Mendeleev read the news in St Petersburg, 2,000 miles away: on 27 August 1875 Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran had announced a new metal from a Pyrenees zinc mine, with the properties he had measured. Mendeleev had never seen the sample, but four years earlier he had written a spec, with numbers, for the element he expected in that square. He published a note correcting the discoverer. What did the note say?
answer: His sample was still impure; the density should read 5.9
choices: His sample was still impure; the density should read 5.9
His atomic weight of 69.7 was a full unit too high
His two violet lines belonged to zinc, not a new metal
His metal belonged under silicon, not under aluminium
context: The note, 'Remarques a propos de la decouverte du gallium', appeared in Comptes Rendus on 22 November 1875: the sample must be impure, and the density should be 5.9 - the figure Mendeleev had published in 1871 for the tenant of that square. Boisbaudran had measured 4.7, working from a speck of metal (the RSC gives almost 600 milligrams, won from some 450 kilos of ore) obtained by electrolysing gallium hydroxide in potassium hydroxide solution. He repurified it and got 5.9. His first reaction had not been gratitude: he read the note as an attempt to claim his discovery, fired back in the same journal, and even suggested Mendeleev had lifted the system from earlier French work - then had to publish the correction anyway. Sources: Wikipedia 'Gallium'; RSC Periodic Table, 'Gallium'; Slate, 'Gallium: It Proved That Dmitri Mendeleev Wasn't a Crackpot'.

question: Clemens Winkler had his new element pure in the crucible on 6 February 1886, drawn out of a silver-bearing ore from Saxony called argyrodite. Mendeleev's periodic table had predicted this exact element fifteen years before, marking its empty slot 'eka-silicon'. The first name Winkler proposed for the metal was neptunium, after the planet, and the choice was deliberate. Why Neptune?
answer: Neptune had been predicted on paper before any telescope found it
choices: Neptune had been predicted on paper before any telescope found it
Neptune was the newest planet in the sky when he was a boy
Neptune's blue-grey colour matched the lustre of the metal
Neptune's discovery had been claimed by two rival astronomers
context: Neptune had been worked out from the wobbles in Uranus's orbit and then found where the mathematics said it would be. An element written down on paper and afterwards dug out of an ore was the same trick performed in a crucible. The name was already taken: another chemist had claimed 'neptunium' for a supposed element that turned out to be a niobium-tantalum alloy, so Winkler named his after his homeland instead - germanium. His own verdict: 'The quadrivalency of germanium has by now become an incontrovertible fact, and there can be no longer any doubt that the new element is no other than the eka-silicium prognosticated fifteen years ago by Mendeleev.' Sources: Wikipedia 'Germanium'; ChemTeam, 'Discovery of Germanium'.

question: Clemens Winkler had the new element from argyrodite in his hands in 1886 and still could not say which of Mendeleev's empty squares it belonged in. Winkler argued it sat between antimony and bismuth. Mendeleev, consulted about his own table, said it was the missing element under cadmium. Both of them were wrong. Who named the right square, the one under silicon?
answer: Lothar Meyer, who had published a rival table of his own
choices: Lothar Meyer, who had published a rival table of his own
John Newlands, who had sorted the elements in eights
Bohuslav Brauner, who weighed atoms for Mendeleev in Prague
Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, who hunted by spectrum
context: Meyer's 1870 paper plotted atomic volume against atomic weight and produced a beautiful sawtooth curve - the peaks the soft, violently reactive alkali metals, the troughs the dense transition metals. It was the first graphical proof of periodicity, and it left no blanks; Meyer and Mendeleev shared the Royal Society's Davy Medal in 1882. Once the square was settled, Winkler measured the metal against the fifteen-year-old spec: predicted density 5.5 against his measured 5.469; oxide density 4.7 against 4.7; chloride density 1.9 against 1.887; a chloride boiling 'under 100 C' against 86 C for GeCl4; atomic weight 72 against his 72.32. Sources: ChemTeam, 'Discovery of Germanium'; Science History Institute, 'Julius Lothar Meyer and Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev'.

question: Lars Fredrik Nilson boiled two rare minerals down to a small quantity of pure oxide of a new metal at Uppsala University in 1879, and he named the metal scandium, after Scandinavia. He seemed unaware that Mendeleev, working in St Petersburg eight years earlier, had already predicted a metal for exactly that slot, calling its placeholder 'eka-boron'. Who first spotted that scandium and eka-boron were the same element?
answer: Per Teodor Cleve, a colleague in the same building
choices: Per Teodor Cleve, a colleague in the same building
Mendeleev himself, reading the paper in St Petersburg
Lothar Meyer, matching the oxide against his own curve
Clemens Winkler, comparing it with the predicted figures
context: Cleve recognised Nilson's oxide as eka-boron and wrote to Mendeleev in August 1879. The 1871 spec had called for atomic weight 44 and density about 3.0, with a weakly basic oxide sitting chemically between calcium oxide and titanium dioxide. Scandium's atomic weight is 44.96 and its density 2.99 - the density prediction was off by 0.3 percent, for a substance that did not yet exist on any shelf in the world. Sources: Wikipedia 'Scandium'; Grokipedia "Mendeleev's predicted elements".

question: Charles Augustus Young and William Harkness each saw a green line at 530.3 nanometres in the Sun's corona at the total eclipse of 7 August 1869, a line no laboratory on Earth had ever produced. Astronomers named the ghost behind it coronium, and Mendeleev took the ghost seriously enough to write it into his own work. It took sixty years to catch. Walter Grotrian and Bengt Edlen showed in the 1930s what was making the line. What was it?
answer: Iron, with 13 of its 26 electrons torn away
choices: Iron, with 13 of its 26 electrons torn away
Calcium, with 14 of its 20 electrons torn away
Nickel, with 12 of its 28 electrons torn away
Argon, with 9 of its 18 electrons torn away
context: The corona runs to millions of degrees, hot enough to strip 13 of iron's 26 electrons away; an atom that badly stripped glows at wavelengths its ordinary form never shows, which is why no laboratory on Earth had matched the line. Helium is why coronium was a reasonable guess rather than a foolish one: helium really was found in the Sun first, in 1868, from a line no earthly laboratory could match, and it really did turn out to be a new element. This time the ghost was an old metal in an extraordinary state. Sources: Wikipedia 'Coronium'; IFLScience, 'Coronium: The Strange Story Of The Eclipse Element That Didn't Exist'.

question: Dmitri Mendeleev had specified gallium so exactly that the metal matched his blank almost perfectly. The same instinct produced his outright failure. Physicists of his day held that light travelled through an invisible medium filling all space, the ether, and Mendeleev thought his table ought to account for it. He set out his answer in a 1902 book, An Attempt Towards a Chemical Conception of the Ether. What did he propose the ether was made of?
answer: Elements lighter than hydrogen, set ahead of it in the table
choices: Elements lighter than hydrogen, set ahead of it in the table
An element between hydrogen and helium, too thin to weigh
Hydrogen itself, thinned until it weighed almost nothing
Vapours given off by every element alike, kept off the table
context: He called them newtonium (element x, atomic weight about 0.17) and coronium (element y, 0.4), and put them before hydrogen to be the stuff of the ether. A single proton weighs more than twice 0.4, so nothing could ever be that light. The English edition appeared in 1904 (Longmans, Green). Sources split on newtonium's weight - Grokipedia gives about 0.17, Wikipedia 0.14. This is the honest caveat on the whole story: the same table, the same man, the same confidence, and this time the blanks were imaginary. Sources: Grokipedia "Mendeleev's predicted elements"; Wikipedia 'Newtonium'.

question: Mendeleev said tellurium's chemistry put it before iodine. But its measured weight was heavier, which should have placed it later. He kept his order and said the weighing must be wrong. He had won that bet before with four other elements. What happened when chemists weighed tellurium again?
answer: The weighing held: tellurium really is heavier than iodine
choices: The weighing held: tellurium really is heavier than iodine
Tellurium came down to 125, close to where he had put it
The iodine samples proved to be contaminated with bromine
Both weights shifted once purer samples were prepared
context: Tellurium is 127.6 and iodine 126.9. The weights were right; the ordering rule was wrong. Mendeleev made his own assistant chase the error: Bohuslav Brauner spent years measuring the molecular weight of a volatile tellurium halide, trying to drive the number down, and when it kept coming out too high he concluded he must have failed to remove some heavy impurity. He hadn't. Mendeleev's instinct about the ORDER was right - iodine really does belong after tellurium - but the reason has nothing to do with atomic weight, and running it down belongs to a later chapter of this story. Sources: Mendeleev 1869, English translation, Giunta's Classic Chemistry; RSC Education, 'Mendeleev - the man and his legacy'; Grokipedia 'Dmitri Mendeleev'.

question: Urbain Le Verrier turned from Neptune to a stranger puzzle: Mercury's elongated orbit slowly rotated around the Sun a little faster than Isaac Newton's gravity said it should. The extra shift was less than the Moon's width in a hundred years, too tiny to watch. In 1859 he pinned it down from old records. What records?
answer: Timings of Mercury crossing the Sun's face, back to 1697.
choices: Timings of Mercury crossing the Sun's face, back to 1697.
Timings of Mercury slipping behind the Moon, back to 1660.
Timings of Mercury at widest from the Sun, back to 1677.
Timings of Mercury crossing a bright star, back to 1720.
context: Le Verrier presented the work to the Academie des Sciences on 12 September 1859: transit data from 1697 to 1848, fourteen transits in all, plus meridian observations. A single transit gives a timing good to seconds, and timings stacked over 150 years reveal a drift no eye could ever catch directly. He found about 38 arcseconds per century that nothing accounted for; Simon Newcomb, with more data, refined the leftover to about 43 in 1882. An arcsecond is 1/3600 of a degree: 1,296,000 of them fill a full circle, and the full Moon is about 1,800 across. Forty-three of them, piled up over a hundred years, is roughly a fortieth of the Moon's width -- and that scrap is what eventually broke Newton's gravity. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Tests of general relativity'; MacTutor, 'Urbain Le Verrier'.

question: Star-watchers turned to the Sun in December 1860 on dates Urbain Le Verrier had named. He claimed a hidden little planet, Vulcan, circled inside Mercury's orbit and tugged on it, and he had announced exactly when it should slide across the Sun's face. What did they see?
answer: Nothing crossed the Sun on any date he had named.
choices: Nothing crossed the Sun on any date he had named.
Nothing crossed in December, but a dot crossed in March.
A dot crossed on time, and proved to be a sunspot.
A dot crossed, but only one observatory saw it.
context: The orbit was not vague. Le Verrier computed a period of 19 days 17 hours, a distance of 0.143 AU from the Sun (about 21 million km), an inclination of 12 degrees 12 minutes, and a mass around one-seventeenth of Mercury's -- precisely the mass needed to produce the missing motion. Every predicted transit failed. Naming dates is what made the claim testable, and a claim that names dates can be killed by the sky itself, which is exactly what makes it science. Source: Grokipedia, 'Vulcan (hypothetical planet)'.

question: Edmond Lescarbault, a country doctor at Orgeres in France, watched a small black dot creep across the face of the Sun in March 1859, from a small observatory built onto his roof. It was exactly what a tiny planet inside Mercury's orbit would look like from Earth. He knew he needed an accurate timing before any astronomer in Paris would believe him. What did he use to time it?
answer: The pendulum he took his patients' pulses with, and an old clock.
choices: The pendulum he took his patients' pulses with, and an old clock.
The pocket watch he carried on his rounds, and a village sundial.
A marine chronometer borrowed from a naval officer at Brest.
A metronome lent by the village schoolmaster, and a sand-glass.
context: He made the crossing last 1 hour, 17 minutes and 9 seconds, and noted that the dot carried no bright fringe, which is why he judged it was not a sunspot. His telescope was a 3.75-inch refractor. Then he sat on the sighting for nine months, wanting to catch it a second time before he said anything to anyone. Note for accuracy: Grokipedia's page calls him a veterinary surgeon named Joseph; Wikipedia and MacTutor both give a medical doctor named Edmond Modeste Lescarbault (1814-1894). Sources: Wikipedia, 'Vulcan (hypothetical planet)' and 'Edmond Modeste Lescarbault'.

question: Urbain Le Verrier took a train out to see a country doctor, Edmond Lescarbault, who had written in 1859 to say he had watched a dark dot cross the Sun. Le Verrier grilled the doctor for an hour, and days later he stood before the French Academy declaring his hidden planet Vulcan confirmed. What happened to the doctor next?
answer: Napoleon III made him a Chevalier of the Legion d'honneur.
choices: Napoleon III made him a Chevalier of the Legion d'honneur.
Le Verrier hired him at the Paris Observatory as an aide.
The Academie asked him to repeat the sighting before printing it.
The Academie sent two observers to watch the next transit with him.
context: A village doctor was knighted for observing a planet that does not exist, and learned societies across France invited him to come and describe it. Le Verrier named the planet Vulcan, for the Roman god of fire. His opening line at the door is traditional rather than archival, but as the story is always retold he accused Lescarbault on the spot of claiming a planet inside Mercury's orbit and then keeping the observation secret for nine months -- which he called a grave offence. Note that the charge was the secrecy, not the sighting. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Vulcan (hypothetical planet)'; Wikipedia, 'Edmond Modeste Lescarbault'.

question: James Craig Watson, in Wyoming, reported a reddish object close to the Sun during the total solar eclipse of 29 July 1878, and Lewis Swift, near Denver, reported one too. Both men were hunting a planet said to orbit inside Mercury, and Vulcan seemed confirmed twice over. What undid the claim?
answer: Both objects turned out to be ordinary stars in Cancer.
choices: Both objects turned out to be ordinary stars in Cancer.
Both men had in fact watched Mercury itself, low and red.
Both objects were moving, which marked them out as comets.
Both sightings were reflections inside their own eyepieces.
context: Watson put his object about 2.5 degrees south-west of the Sun, Swift about 3 degrees -- close enough to sound like agreement, far enough apart that they could not be the same body. Both were eventually identified as ordinary stars, theta and zeta Cancri. Across more than fifty years Vulcan was 'seen' perhaps ten to twenty times, and never twice in the same place, which is the signature of a thing that is not there. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Vulcan (hypothetical planet)'.

question: Workmen cut a long slanting shaft into a Wisconsin hillside for James Craig Watson, who had claimed a glimpse of the planet Vulcan during the total solar eclipse of 1878 and wanted to hunt it again in ordinary daylight. He set a mirror at the top of the shaft and a telescope at the bottom. What old idea was his shaft built on?
answer: An old belief that stars show in daylight from the bottom of a well.
choices: An old belief that stars show in daylight from the bottom of a well.
A finding that cold air in rock steadies a mirror against shimmer.
A theory that solid rock screens out the Sun's scattered heat glare.
A claim that smoked glass reveals faint objects near the Sun's rim.
context: The well belief is ancient and false: a deep shaft does not make daylight stars visible, because what hides them is the sky's own scattered light, and that fills the shaft too. Watson never got to test it. He died on 23 November 1880, aged 42, after a week's illness, and the shaft was left unfinished. Sources: WisContext, 'Discovering Double Stars And Debunking The Planet Vulcan'; Popular Science Monthly, 'Sketch of James Craig Watson' (1881).

question: Urbain Le Verrier refused to drop his tiny planet Vulcan even when, by the mid-1870s, the searches for it had failed and every claimed daytime sighting had fallen apart. He had staked his reputation on one planet inside Mercury's orbit. What did he do with the idea?
answer: He broke the one planet into a swarm of bodies too small to see.
choices: He broke the one planet into a swarm of bodies too small to see.
He moved the one planet closer in, where the Sun's glare hides it.
He kept the planet but blamed the Sun's bulge for the rest of it.
He blamed the observers' small telescopes and called for new ones.
context: The swarm got a name of its own -- 'Vulcanoids' -- and the move is worth learning to spot, in others and in yourself: when a testable claim fails, it can be quietly reshaped into one that is harder to test. Le Verrier died on 23 September 1877 still convinced something was in there, exactly thirty-one years to the day after Neptune was found where his arithmetic said it would be. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Vulcan (hypothetical planet)'; Wikipedia, 'Urbain Le Verrier'.

question: Albert Einstein plugged the orbit of Mercury into his brand-new general relativity on the afternoon of 18 November 1915 in Berlin, and his equations gave the number for the tiny drift astronomers had puzzled over for fifty years. He later wrote to his friend Paul Ehrenfest about what the moment did to him physically. What did he say?
answer: It had given him heart palpitations.
choices: It had given him heart palpitations.
It had kept him awake for three nights.
It had left him unable to hold a pen.
It had made him weep at his desk.
context: He also wrote to Paul Ehrenfest that he had been beside himself with joyous excitement for days. His biographer Abraham Pais judged it by far the strongest emotional experience of Einstein's scientific life, perhaps of his whole life. Einstein added a wry note: the pedantic accuracy of astronomy, which he had been in the habit of laughing at, had turned out to be rather useful. English translations of the German letters vary, so the wording here is paraphrase, not quotation. Sources: Janssen & Renn, 'Einstein and the Perihelion Motion of Mercury' (Max Planck Institute); Advanced Science News.

question: Albert Einstein tried Mercury before he was ready. In June 1913, across about fifty pages of scratch calculation with his friend Michele Besso, he ran the orbit through a draft version of his gravity theory. A first pass gave an absurd 1,821 arcseconds per century. He found the error. Cleaned up, how much of the 43 arcseconds per century did the draft theory deliver?
answer: About 18 arcseconds per century.
choices: About 18 arcseconds per century.
About 43 arcseconds per century.
About 5 arcseconds per century.
About 58 arcseconds per century.
context: Eighteen out of forty-three: the draft 'Entwurf' theory was wrong, and Mercury said so first. Einstein kept working for two more years. Those scratch pages, now called the Einstein-Besso manuscript, sold at Christie's in Paris on 23 November 2021 for about $11.5 million -- roughly a quarter of a million dollars a page for a calculation that failed. Sources: Janssen & Renn, 'Einstein and the Perihelion Motion of Mercury' (arXiv:2111.11238); Advanced Science News.

question: Einstein handed his Mercury paper to the Prussian Academy on 18 November 1915, a week before he sent in the final field equations. For fifty years, astronomers had tried to explain Mercury's 43 arcseconds per century. They tried an unseen planet, a dust belt, a flattened Sun, or a slight tweak to the inverse-square law. Why did physicists find Einstein's 43 much harder to dismiss?
answer: It contained no adjustable quantity that could be fitted to the 43.
choices: It contained no adjustable quantity that could be fitted to the 43.
It rested on Newcomb's fresh timings rather than Le Verrier's older ones.
It matched Venus's and Earth's leftovers before anyone had tried Mercury.
It used the same arithmetic that had already turned up Neptune in 1846.
context: The relativistic term depends only on the Sun's mass, the size of Mercury's orbit and the shape of its ellipse, and it gives 42.98 arcseconds per century with no dial to turn. Every rival could be adjusted -- pick the mass of your hidden planet, pick the flattening of your Sun -- and a hypothesis you can tune to any answer is not really being tested by that answer. Einstein's number was fixed before it was compared. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Tests of general relativity' and 'Vulcan (hypothetical planet)'.

question: An astronomer charts the advance of Mercury's perihelion, the point where it swings closest to the Sun, against the equinox and gets roughly 5,600 arcseconds per century. The leftover that no known planet can explain is only 43. Nearly 5,025 arcseconds of that 5,600 is not Mercury moving at all. What is that 5,025?
answer: The wheeling of Earth's own axis, dragging the reference point with it.
choices: The wheeling of Earth's own axis, dragging the reference point with it.
The drift of the observatory's own meridian, remeasured each decade.
The Moon's pull on Earth, slowing the clocks the timings used.
The bending of the Sun's light in Earth's air, low on the horizon.
context: The 5,600 figure is measured against the equinox, the crossing point of Earth's equator and its orbit, and that point slides steadily as Earth's axis wheels round in a 26,000-year cone. This is the precession of the equinoxes: Earth's own coordinate frame turning, not Mercury moving. Subtract it (about 5,025) and the pull of the other planets (about 532) and 43 is what remains. Measured instead against the fixed stars, the entire advance is only about 574 arcseconds per century, 532 planetary plus the same 43. Both totals are correct, but they are different measurements, not two figures for the same thing. Sources: MathPages, 'Anomalous Precession'; Wikipedia, 'Tests of general relativity'.

question: Park and colleagues fixed the size of the Sun's bulge at last in 2017, settling one rival to Einstein that never had to be argued away, only measured. A Sun that bulges at its equator would twist Mercury's orbit on its own and could claim part of the 43 arcseconds for itself, but a bulge that slight had defeated astronomers for decades. What measurement did they use?
answer: Radio ranging to the MESSENGER orbiter as it circled Mercury.
choices: Radio ranging to the MESSENGER orbiter as it circled Mercury.
Timings of Mercury transits watched from the SOHO observatory.
Radar echoes bounced off Venus from Arecibo across three decades.
Laser ranging to the retroreflectors Apollo left on the Moon.
context: MESSENGER circled Mercury from 2011, and radio ranging to the spacecraft let Park and colleagues (2017) measure Mercury's total perihelion precession at 575.3100 +/- 0.0015 arcseconds per century and the relativistic part at 42.9799 +/- 0.0009, while pinning the Sun's flattening at J2 = 2.25 x 10^-7 -- far too small to hide inside the anomaly. The radar echoes of 1966 to 1990 had already confirmed the relativistic precession to 0.1%; the spacecraft ranging tightened it by several more decimal places and measured the bulge at the same time. The last rival did not lose an argument. It was measured, and found too small. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Tests of general relativity'; Park et al., Astronomical Journal 153, 121 (2017).

question: Urbain Le Verrier built his fame on one rule: an unexplained wobble means an unseen body. Applied to Uranus in 1846 it produced Neptune, found almost exactly where he said it would be. Applied to Mercury in 1859 it produced Vulcan, and fifty years of searching turned up nothing. Why did the same rule turn up nothing at Mercury?
answer: The law of gravity used to do the subtracting was itself incomplete.
choices: The law of gravity used to do the subtracting was itself incomplete.
The body responsible was too small and too near the Sun to be seen.
The old transit timings were too crude to trust at that precision.
The Sun's outer atmosphere was dragging on the planet's orbit.
context: The same move, twice, with opposite results: an anomaly can mean a missing object or a broken law, and the reasoning itself cannot tell you which -- only going and testing can. That is why Le Verrier's failure is worth more than a silly mistake would be. His method was not foolish, it was proven. Grokipedia's own summary draws the moral, that Vulcan underscores the importance of considering modified physics rather than positing ad-hoc unseen bodies. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Vulcan (hypothetical planet)'; Wikipedia, 'Urbain Le Verrier'.

question: Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl set out at Caltech in 1958 to test how DNA copies itself in a living cell. They needed to tell old DNA from newly made DNA without cutting the strands up, so they grew E. coli on food in which one common element was swapped for an isotope, a heavier form of the same element. Which heavy isotope did they feed the bacteria?
answer: Nitrogen-15
choices: Carbon-13
Nitrogen-15
Oxygen-18
Deuterium
context: A version of an element with a different number of neutrons is called an isotope; nitrogen-15 has one more neutron than ordinary nitrogen-14 and so weighs slightly more. After roughly fourteen generations in nitrogen-15 ammonium chloride medium every nitrogen atom in the bacterial DNA was heavy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meselson%E2%80%93Stahl_experiment

question: Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase used radioactive phosphorus and sulfur tags in 1952 to follow which part of a virus, its DNA or its protein, entered the bacteria it infected. Six years later Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl used a tag that was not radioactive at all, so their ultracentrifuge could not sort DNA by any glow. What property of the DNA did it sort by?
answer: Its density in a spinning column of salt
choices: Its electrical charge in a salt bath
Its melting temperature under mild heat
Its density in a spinning column of salt
Its size, by how fast it sank in the tube
context: Nitrogen-15 is a stable heavy isotope, not radioactive. The heavier isotope makes the DNA molecule literally weigh slightly more per unit length, and it was that tiny density difference the experiment resolved. Confusing this with Hershey-Chase (which did use radioactive labels on a phage) is the standard student error. Source: https://www.pearson.com/channels/genetics/asset/af7bec45/describe-the-role-of-n-in-the-meselson-stahl-experiment

question: To catch a tiny gap in DNA's weight, Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl spun it for 20 hours in a tube of thick salt water. The salt settled thicker at the bottom, and each piece of DNA floated to the depth that matched its density. Which salt did they use to build that gradient?
answer: Caesium chloride
choices: Sodium chloride
Potassium bromide
Ammonium sulphate
Caesium chloride
context: Caesium chloride is heavy enough that at high centrifugal force it forms a stable density gradient inside the tube, right through the range where DNA molecules band. Meselson had helped invent this equilibrium density gradient technique the year before the replication experiment; DNA absorbs ultraviolet light, so a UV camera above the spinning tube captured the bands. Source: https://thebumblingbiochemist.com/365-days-of-science/meselson-stahl-seized-the-opportunity-to-use-a-cesium-chloride-gradient-to-show-the-semiconservative-nature-of-dna-replication-earn-a-place-in-the-history-books/

question: Franklin Stahl and Matthew Meselson washed their fully tagged bacteria into ordinary medium and allowed them to divide exactly once. The photograph came out with a single dark band, exactly halfway between the pure-heavy and pure-light spots, with no heavy band left on the film. Which of the three replication models could not survive that one photograph?
answer: The conservative model
choices: The conservative model
The semiconservative model
The dispersive model
The rolling-circle model
context: Conservative replication requires the original heavy double helix to survive intact through every round of copying, so a fully heavy band should have persisted forever. One photograph with no heavy band and a single intermediate band ruled it out. Both dispersive and semiconservative still fitted the picture at this stage. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meselson%E2%80%93Stahl_experiment

question: Elie Metchnikoff stared down his microscope at Messina in 1882, at a starfish larva so clear he could see through it. Cells drifted inside its body, and he wondered whether they were guards hunting anything that did not belong. How did the zoologist test the idea?
answer: Pushed a small garden thorn in under its skin
choices: Pushed a small garden thorn in under its skin
Dropped bacteria from a rotting fish in its dish
Smeared a drop of another animal's blood on it
Left it overnight in unfiltered harbour water
context: Metchnikoff told this story himself, decades later: the family had gone to see performing apes, 'I remained alone with my microscope... when a new thought suddenly flashed across my brain.' His reasoning was an analogy -- 'if my supposition was true, a splinter introduced into the body of a star-fish larva, devoid of blood-vessels or of a nervous system, should soon be surrounded by mobile cells as is to be observed in a man who runs a splinter into his finger.' The larva having no vessels and no nerves was the whole point: nothing else could have summoned the cells. Sources disagree on the plant -- the memoir mentions thorns fetched from a garden where the children's 'Christmas tree' had been set up on a little tangerine tree; later writers say rose, or citrus. The memoir chapter is headed 1883, while most reference works date the experiment 1882. Source: Olga Metchnikoff, 'Life of Elie Metchnikoff, 1845-1916' (1921), Ch. XVIII -- gutenberg.org/files/44194/44194-h/44194-h.htm  (Legend.)

question: Carl Claus, the zoologist, knew ancient Greek, so Elie Metchnikoff called on him in Vienna on his way home to Russia. Metchnikoff's new idea was a cell that hunts down germs, and it needed a proper scientific name. What did he ask Claus for?
answer: The Greek for 'devouring cells'
choices: The Greek for 'devouring cells'
The Greek for 'wandering cells'
The Greek for 'soldier cells'
The Greek for 'guard cells'
context: The room's answer was PHAGOCYTE -- from Greek phagein, to eat, and kytos, cell -- and nobody has improved on it since. Claus then asked Metchnikoff for the memoir and printed it in the review he edited, in 1883. Metchnikoff's wife credits the whole room with the coinage; Wikipedia credits Claus himself with suggesting the term. Source: Olga Metchnikoff, 'Life of Elie Metchnikoff' (1921), Ch. XVIII -- gutenberg.org/files/44194/44194-h/44194-h.htm ; Wikipedia, 'Elie Metchnikoff'

question: Too excited to sleep, Elie Metchnikoff bent over his dish at Messina very early one morning. The day before he had pushed a garden thorn under the skin of a see-through starfish larva, to learn whether its drifting cells were the body's soldiers. What did he find at the thorn?
answer: Wandering cells massed on it in clumps visible unaided
choices: Wandering cells massed on it in clumps visible unaided
A hard clear capsule sealed smoothly over the whole thorn
Nothing -- the cells had drifted off to the far end
The skin had closed and pushed the thorn back out again
context: 'I was too excited to sleep that night in the expectation of the result of my experiment, and very early the next morning I ascertained that it had fully succeeded.' The amoeba-like cells had heaped onto the foreign body in clumps large enough to see without the microscope he had been staring through all evening. He closed the account: 'That experiment formed the basis of the phagocyte theory, to the development of which I devoted the next twenty-five years of my life.' He also marked what that night did to him -- 'A zoologist until then, I suddenly became a pathologist.' Source: Olga Metchnikoff, 'Life of Elie Metchnikoff' (1921), Ch. XVIII -- gutenberg.org/files/44194/44194-h/44194-h.htm

question: A water flea lay under Elie Metchnikoff's microscope, a daphnia clear enough to see through, and he watched a whole fight run its course. A fungus's needle-shaped spores, swallowed with food, pierce the gut wall and reach the body cavity. Some fleas recover; some die. What decides which?
answer: Whether its mobile cells digest the spores before they sprout
choices: Whether its mobile cells digest the spores before they sprout
Whether the pierced gut wall closes before more spores pass
Whether the flea stops feeding while the spores are still few
Whether its blood carries the spores back out through the gut
context: The fungus is Monospora bicuspidata. Its needle-shaped spores are swallowed with food and drive through the gut wall into the body cavity, where the phagocytes attack them singly or in groups. If the cells digest the spores the daphnia recovers; if not, the spores germinate, the fungus spreads, and it dies. In Metchnikoff's words, 'the recovery or death of the daphnia depends therefore on the issue of the struggle.' This one is checkable: daphnia live in most still fresh water, and they are transparent enough that a cheap microscope shows the heart beating -- an immune battle a patient person can sit and watch. Source: Olga Metchnikoff, 'Life of Elie Metchnikoff' (1921), Ch. XVIII -- gutenberg.org/files/44194/44194-h/44194-h.htm ; Grokipedia, 'Elie Metchnikoff'

question: Ralph Steinman fought pancreatic cancer with treatments built on his own discovery, the dendritic cell. He died in 2011, three days before the Nobel Assembly named him. Its rules bar a prize to the dead, but nobody there had known. What happened to his prize?
answer: The prize stood; his family collected it in December
choices: The prize stood; his family collected it in December
The prize went to the two living laureates instead
The prize was held over and re-awarded the next year
The prize was withdrawn; only the medal was sent
context: Diagnosed at 64, Steinman had the tumour cut out and then joined experimental dendritic-cell immunotherapies designed around his own research -- his own cells harvested, loaded with tumour antigens and put back into him. The Nobel statutes bar a posthumous award only when the death is known before the announcement; the Nobel Foundation ruled that the award should stand. His family accepted it in Stockholm on 10 December 2011, and his colleague Michel Nussenzweig gave the lecture. The press release put it plainly: 'Sadly, Ralph Steinman passed away before the news of his Nobel Prize reached him.' Source: Nobel Prize press release, 3 October 2011 -- nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2011/press-release/ ; Grokipedia, 'Ralph M. Steinman'

question: Elie Metchnikoff said something new and unpopular in 1883 about the red, hot, swollen skin around a wound. Doctors read it as the disease itself, a thing to be fought, cooled and driven back with poultices. He then spent 25 years defending his answer against Europe's leading pathologists. What did he say inflammation really was?
answer: The visible signs of the body's mobile cells fighting microbes
choices: The visible signs of the body's mobile cells fighting microbes
The blood rushing in to wash the microbes out of the wound
The nerves raising an alarm so the animal guards the hurt part
The microbes' own poison being burned off by the body's heat
context: His chain of reasoning ran: pus is made of leucocytes; leucocytes are mobile mesodermic cells; and the same kind of cell had swarmed a thorn in a larva that had no blood vessels and no nerves at all. Therefore 'the essence of inflammation consists in the reaction of the mobile cells, whilst vascular and nervous intervention has but a secondary significance,' and 'morbid symptoms are no other than the signs of the struggle between the mesodermic cells and the microbes.' Reading his first paper to a congress of physicians and naturalists at Odessa in the autumn of 1883, he compared the phagocytes to an army hurling itself upon the enemy -- the standing-army image is his own. Kleinenberg, the German professor of zoology at Messina, called the theory 'an Hippocratic thought' and told him to publish at once. Source: Olga Metchnikoff, 'Life of Elie Metchnikoff' (1921), Ch. XVIII -- gutenberg.org/files/44194/44194-h/44194-h.htm

question: Rudolf Virchow, Germany's top pathologist, came through Messina and looked down Elie Metchnikoff's microscope. The slides were convincing, he said, and then he warned Metchnikoff to be careful. The textbooks of 1883 taught a very different job for white cells. What did those books say white cells did with germs?
answer: Carried them around the body and helped them multiply
choices: Carried them around the body and helped them multiply
Ignored them, leaving the work to the blood's own fluid
Sealed them into the wound under a crust of dried fluid
Poisoned them with an acid squeezed out into the tissue
context: 'It was believed that the leucocytes, far from destroying microbes, spread them by carrying them and by forming a medium favourable to their growth.' The white cell was taken for the germ's taxi, not its executioner -- so a man claiming the reverse was contradicting the settled teaching of his field, and Virchow knew what that costs. Metchnikoff 'always preserved a deep gratitude towards Virchow and Kleinenberg for the moral support which they gave him at that time,' and published his 1884 immunity work in Virchow's Archiv, where it passed unnoticed. (Note the source conflict: Grokipedia's page lists Virchow among the early sceptics; the family memoir and Wikipedia both make him a key defender.) Source: Olga Metchnikoff, 'Life of Elie Metchnikoff' (1921), Ch. XVIII -- gutenberg.org/files/44194/44194-h/44194-h.htm ; Wikipedia, 'Elie Metchnikoff'

question: Elie Metchnikoff wanted proof, as cholera swept France in 1892, that the comma-shaped Vibrio germ alone caused the disease. He was by then at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, and no lab animal would catch it: rats, guinea pigs and rabbits all shrugged the germ off. What did he do instead?
answer: Swallowed a whole flask of the living culture himself
choices: Swallowed a whole flask of the living culture himself
Compared the wells of a struck town and a spared one
Hunted the vibrio in the guts of people who recovered
Sent cultures to five laboratories for parallel trials
context: He drank the vibrios and stayed well. A worker in his laboratory, M. Latapie, volunteered and repeated it, also unharmed. Then a second volunteer, M. Jupille, swallowed an older culture that Metchnikoff suspected had weakened in the flask -- he even hoped it might work as a vaccine. Jupille developed textbook cholera, severe enough that a doctor who knew the disease said so, and 'Metchnikoff was in mortal anxiety, and even said to himself that he could not survive a fatal issue.' Jupille recovered. Later Metchnikoff swallowed harmless-looking 'choleriform' vibrios from Versailles, a town no epidemic had ever touched, and gave them to several other people; one, an incurable epileptic, sickened, recovered, then died a short time afterwards of a cause never established. Metchnikoff thought his experiment might have contributed, and resolved to perform no further experiments on human beings. The compulsion that drove him back to the beaker a second time he named, in his own word, a 'psychosis.' Two other men drank cholera on purpose: Max von Pettenkofer of Munich, to argue that the vibrio alone was not enough -- and, ninety years later, Barry Marshall with his H. pylori. Source: Olga Metchnikoff, 'Life of Elie Metchnikoff' (1921), Ch. XXIV -- gutenberg.org/files/44194/44194-h/44194-h.htm

question: Elie Metchnikoff told the humoral school that mobile cells, not the blood's fluid, beat an infection by eating the invaders. The quarrel ran twenty-five years. The fluid's champions were Emil von Behring, whose diphtheria antitoxin was its triumph, and Paul Ehrlich, its leading theorist. The Nobel committee ruled on it in 1908. What did the committee do?
answer: Divided the prize between Metchnikoff and Paul Ehrlich
choices: Divided the prize between Metchnikoff and Paul Ehrlich
Divided the prize between Metchnikoff and von Behring
Gave the whole prize to Metchnikoff for the eating cells
Gave the whole prize to Paul Ehrlich for the serum school
context: The 1908 prize in Physiology or Medicine went jointly to Elie Metchnikoff and Paul Ehrlich 'in recognition of their work on immunity' -- the cell man and the serum man on one platform. Behring's antitoxins had genuinely shaken Metchnikoff: 'this discovery was a shock to Metchnikoff, for it was in apparent contradiction with the cellular theory of immunity,' and Behring had taken the very first medicine Nobel in 1901. The humoralists were not cranks; they were half right, and so was he. Out of that refusal to choose grew the modern division: INNATE immunity -- fast, general, built from genes you are born with, acting within minutes to hours -- and ADAPTIVE immunity -- T cells, B cells and antibodies, exquisitely specific, days to build, and it remembers, so the second attack is met faster and harder. Metchnikoff joked afterwards that it was the Nobel Prize which, 'like a magic wand,' had revealed to the public the value of his researches. Source: Olga Metchnikoff, 'Life of Elie Metchnikoff' (1921), Ch. XXIII and XXIX -- gutenberg.org/files/44194/44194-h/44194-h.htm ; Wikipedia, 'Elie Metchnikoff'

question: Hans Buchner filtered every cell out of fresh blood serum at Munich late in the 1880s and found that the clear fluid still killed anthrax bacilli on its own. He warmed a batch just past 56 degrees Celsius and tested it again, then tipped a splash of unheated serum into the same batch. What did the two tests show?
answer: Heat destroyed the fluid's power; fresh serum restored it
choices: Heat destroyed the fluid's power; fresh serum restored it
Heat destroyed the fluid's power; fresh serum did not revive it
Heat left the fluid's power intact; fresh serum doubled it
Heat left the fluid's power intact; fresh serum added nothing
context: Buchner named the fragile killer ALEXIN, Greek for 'to ward off'; Paul Ehrlich renamed it COMPLEMENT in 1899 and that name stuck. It is a cascade of blood proteins that finishes by punching holes in a bacterium's membrane -- heat-sensitive because proteins unfold when warmed, which is exactly why a few degrees abolished the killing and a splash of fresh serum brought it straight back. Note where complement sits: it is humoral, in the fluid, and yet it is innate -- fast, general, born with you, needing no previous exposure. So the cell-versus-serum quarrel had a third answer neither side had named. Jules Bordet, working in Metchnikoff's own laboratory at the Pasteur Institute, carried the work further and won the 1919 Nobel Prize. Buchner succeeded Max von Pettenkofer at Munich in 1894; his brother Eduard won the 1907 Nobel in Chemistry. Source: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Hans Ernst August Buchner'

question: Ralph Steinman and Zanvil Cohn sorted through mouse spleen and lymph nodes in 1973 and found a rare cell with long branching arms, just 0.1 to 1.6 per cent of the cells there. Unlike the big eaters beside it, it barely swallowed anything. They tried it on naive T cells, the specific fighters yet to meet a target. How did it compare with ordinary spleen cells?
answer: 100 to 300 times better at rousing them
choices: 100 to 300 times better at rousing them
20 to 30 times better at rousing them
2 to 3 times better at rousing them
30 to 50 times worse at rousing them
context: Steinman and Cohn named them DENDRITIC CELLS, after the branches -- Greek dendron, tree. They are the bridge between the two armies: a dendritic cell at the front line captures a fragment of an invader, travels to a lymph node, and shows that fragment to the adaptive specialists, which is how a cell type making up barely one per cent of the tissue can start so large a response. The paper: Steinman and Cohn, 'Identification of a novel cell type in peripheral lymphoid organs of mice. I. Morphology, quantitation, tissue distribution,' Journal of Experimental Medicine, 1 May 1973, 137(5), 1142-1162 -- which notes that unlike macrophages these cells 'do not appear to engage in active endocytosis.' Steinman was awarded half the 2011 Nobel Prize for the discovery. Source: PubMed 4573839 -- pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/4573839/ ; Grokipedia, 'Ralph M. Steinman'

question: Jules Hoffmann's team in Strasbourg broke one gene in fruit flies in 1996, and the flies died of a mould that healthy flies shrug off. A fly has no antibodies and no T cells; this gene, Toll, was a switch behind its antifungal defence. Yet Toll had been famous since 1985 for a job with no connection to disease. What was it already known to do?
answer: Set which side of a fly embryo becomes its underside
choices: Set which side of a fly embryo becomes its underside
Control how fast a fly larva grows into an adult
Give the adult fly its bristles and its wing veins
Decide the colour pattern of the fly's compound eye
context: The paper: Bruno Lemaitre, Emmanuelle Nicolas, Lydia Michaut, Jean-Marc Reichhart and Jules Hoffmann, 'The dorsoventral regulatory gene cassette spatzle/Toll/cactus controls the potent antifungal response in Drosophila adults,' Cell, 20 September 1996, 86:973-983. Flies with the pathway broken could not switch on the antifungal peptide DROSOMYCIN and died of the mould Aspergillus fumigatus; the Nobel Committee's summary was blunt -- 'Toll mutants died because they could not mount an effective defense.' The gene's name comes from an exclamation: as the story is told, Christiane Nusslein-Volhard, screening fly mutants with Eric Wieschaus in 1985, saw a larva with a bizarrely underdeveloped underside and said 'Das ist ja toll!' -- roughly 'That's amazing!' The name stuck, and their work on the genes that shape the embryo won the 1995 Nobel Prize. Toll was a body-plan gene for eleven years before anyone suspected it had a second job in defence. Source: PubMed 8808632 -- pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8808632/ ; Nobel Prize press release, 3 October 2011 ; Wikipedia, 'Toll-like receptor'

question: Charles Janeway Jr. opened a 1989 symposium with 'the immunologist's dirty little secret'. A pure protein injected into an animal raises almost no antibodies, but stirred into a slurry of crushed microbes it draws a strong response. Nobody could say why the dirt was needed. His explanation called for something nobody had yet found. What did he say the immune system must be carrying?
answer: Receptors that match patterns shared by whole germ families
choices: Receptors that match patterns shared by whole germ families
Cells that read the tissue damage crushed microbes leave
Cells that hold the debris and leak the protein out for weeks
Receptors that fire only when a protein arrives clumped on debris
context: Janeway called them PATTERN RECOGNITION RECEPTORS: not one receptor per microbe -- there are far too many microbes for that -- but a small, ancient set of sensors for molecular signatures shared by whole classes of germ and never made by us. Those signatures were later named PAMPs, pathogen-associated molecular patterns. It also explains the dirty little secret: the crushed-microbe slurry is full of patterns, so the adjuvant is what tells the immune system that the clean protein arrived in dangerous company. Janeway predicted the receptor before anyone had one in hand -- first the argument, then the hunt. Source: Cell, 'Bridging Innate and Adaptive Immunity' (2011) -- cell.com/fulltext/S0092-8674(11)01430-9 ; 'A Bitter Sweet Nobel -- Beutler, Janeway, and the Dawn of Innate Immunity', ScienceBlogs, 6 October 2011

question: Bruce Beutler published in Science in 1998 why one laboratory mouse strain, C3H/HeJ, was deaf to bacterial endotoxin. That molecule throws a body into septic shock and floors almost any other mouse. He had spent years walking the strain's chromosomes to find the difference. What had gone wrong in those mice?
answer: One swapped letter in Tlr4, a receptor gene
choices: One swapped letter in Tlr4, a receptor gene
A deletion in Cd14, the toxin's docking gene
An extra copy of Aoah, a toxin-chewing gene
A silencing change in Tlr2, a bacterial-sensor gene
context: Poltorak et al., 'Defective LPS signaling in C3H/HeJ and C57BL/10ScCr mice: mutations in Tlr4 gene,' Science 1998;282(5396):2085-2088. The change swapped one amino acid -- proline for histidine -- at position 712 of Tlr4; a second strain, C57BL/10ScCr, had lost the gene's function outright. The predicted pattern receptor had been found, and it was a relative of the fruit fly's Toll gene: the same ancient sensor family, running in a mouse. On 3 October 2011 the Nobel Assembly gave one half of the prize jointly to Bruce Beutler and Jules Hoffmann 'for their discoveries concerning the activation of innate immunity,' and the other half to Ralph Steinman 'for his discovery of the dendritic cell and its role in adaptive immunity' -- Metchnikoff and Ehrlich's 1908 truce restated 103 years later. (Accuracy note: Grokipedia's Toll-like receptor page wrongly names Shizuo Akira as a 2011 laureate; the Nobel record does not.) Source: PubMed 9851930 -- pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9851930/ ; Nobel Prize press release and summary, 3 October 2011

question: Ronald Ross, a British army doctor, tracked the real carrier of malaria in India in 1897, and it too thrives near still water. The disease's name is old Italian for 'bad air', and for centuries Europeans had blamed marsh vapours, since people near wetlands did catch it. What gives a person malaria?
answer: A mosquito's bite
choices: A mosquito's bite
A river worm's egg
A grain mould's spore
A bedding louse's bite
context: 'Malaria' entered English in 1740, credited to the Italian physician Francisco Torti, and for more than a century it meant the marsh air itself; only around 1866 did it replace the older English word 'ague' as the name of the disease. The marshes were the right place to look and the wrong thing to blame. Every hospital on Earth still uses a word that quietly carries a theory nobody believes. Sources: etymonline.com/word/malaria; grokipedia.com/page/Miasma_theory (Etymology and Terminology); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miasma_theory

question: Michael Faraday rowed out on the Thames in July 1855 to see how filthy it had become, with no tools, just a plain thing to drop over the side. His warning to The Times that the river was a real sewer was ignored. A student on a bridge can repeat his test today, counting seconds. What did Faraday drop in?
answer: Scraps of white paper
choices: Scraps of white paper
Handfuls of chalk dust
Knotted lengths of string
Corks cut from bottles
context: Faraday was measuring how murky the water was: he dropped the white scraps in from the boat and watched how fast they disappeared from sight. They vanished almost at once, and in the same letter he described the filth rolling in dense clouds near the bridges. His letter ran in The Times on 9 July 1855, three years before the Great Stink drove Parliament to act, and nothing was done about the river in the meantime. You can run Faraday's test this weekend with a scrap of paper, a bridge and a count of seconds. Sources: The Times, 9 July 1855 (Faraday's letter on the state of the Thames); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Stink (Background)

question: Benjamin Disraeli fled a committee room in June 1858 with his handkerchief pressed to his nose. London sat at 34 to 36 degrees in the shade, and the Thames beside Parliament had become an open sewer. Every member there had been taught to fear bad air, so the House took the precaution its theory called for. What did it do?
answer: Hung its windows with lime-soaked curtains
choices: Hung its windows with lime-soaked curtains
Moved its committees a mile from the river
Burned tar barrels along the corridors
Packed its window sills with wet clay
context: The curtains were soaked in chloride of lime, a disinfectant, and hung at the river-side windows. Disraeli, tabling the sewer bill on 15 June, called the Thames 'a Stygian pool, reeking with ineffable and intolerable horrors'. Parliament had refused to fund a London sewer for years; the smell moved it in weeks, and on 2 August 1858 the Metropolitan Board of Works was authorised to borrow three million pounds for Joseph Bazalgette's intercepting sewers. The money was voted to carry away the smell. It carried away the cholera. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Stink; grokipedia.com/page/Great_Stink (Onset in June 1858; Legislative Action and Funding)

question: Edwin Chadwick refused to argue about disease in the abstract, so his investigators went out and counted. His 1842 report set an average life of 45 years in rural Rutland beside one of 26 in the new industrial towns. Parliament passed the Public Health Act of 1848. What did that Act create?
answer: Local boards that could build sewers
choices: Local boards that could build sewers
Parish officers that could fumigate houses
Town furnaces that could burn street refuse
River wardens that could fine polluters
context: The Act created local boards of health, with power to build sewers and pipe in clean water. Chadwick's Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population had documented an average age at death of about 26 years in the industrial towns against 45 in rural Rutland, in the same country in the same decade, and argued that reform could cut deaths by as much as two thirds. Chadwick's explanation of WHY people were dying was flatly wrong. Almost every action he demanded was right, because filth and germs genuinely travel together, so the cleaning hit the real cause by a different route. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Miasma_theory (Sanitary Reforms and Engineering)

question: Edwin Chadwick stood before a House of Commons committee in 1846, while it looked into London's overflowing sewage. He was leading Britain's sanitary reforms, in filthy industrial cities that many blamed for spreading fever and cholera. The MPs asked him plainly how bad smells were linked to disease. What did Chadwick tell them?
answer: That all smell, if intense, is itself disease
choices: That all smell, if intense, is itself disease
That smell warns of disease but never causes it
That smell only harms those already weakened
That smell matters less than the water below it
context: His exact words: 'All smell is, if it be intense, immediate acute disease; and eventually we may say that, by depressing the system and rendering it susceptible to the action of other causes, all smell is disease.' Not a metaphor, and not stupidity either. In the mid-century city the air was visibly and overwhelmingly filthier than the water, so blaming what you could smell was the rational reading of what a man could actually observe. The link between stink and death was real. Only the direction of cause was wrong. Sources: Metropolitan Sewage Committee proceedings, Parliamentary Papers 1846;10:651, reproduced at victorianlondon.org/disease/miasma.htm; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1121911/

question: Londoners in one narrow band of the East End, between Aldgate and Bow, did nearly all of the dying in 1866, in the city's last great cholera outbreak: 5,596 in all. The rest of London was barely touched. About 93 per cent of the dead had lived in districts that shared a single feature. What did those districts have in common?
answer: They sat outside the new sewer network
choices: They sat outside the new sewer network
They stood lowest above the river's high water
They held the most crowded lodging houses
They lay nearest the river's foulest reach
