context: Joseph Bazalgette's system, 82 miles of main intercepting sewers feeding 1,100 miles of street sewers and 318 million bricks of it, was still being connected district by district, and the East End was last in line. Built to remove a smell, it removed the cholera with it. The honest caveat that cannot be skipped: those same districts differed from the rest of London in more ways than one at the same time, and untangling which difference was doing the killing is exactly what took the argument decades. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Stink; sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/medicine/cholera-victorian-london

question: Florence Nightingale told nurses to attack one thing in the building rather than shut the patient away. She had run the British army's hospital at Scutari during the Crimean War, and she did not believe disease passed from one sick person to the next: a house, she thought, made its own. Which household source did she blame for measles, smallpox and scarlet fever alike?
answer: Air rising out of the house's own drains
choices: Air rising out of the house's own drains
Water standing in the house's own cistern
Damp breathed out by the ground beneath the floors
Soot from the fires burning in its own grates
context: Nightingale blamed the house drains for all three. Holding the wrong mechanism did not make her useless. In Notes on Nursing (1860) she defined nursing itself as 'the proper use of fresh air, light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet, and the proper selection and administration of diet', a miasmatist's checklist that is still good nursing today. Fresh air, light, cleanliness and clean water all attack filth, and filth is where the germs are, so her regimen worked for reasons she rejected. At Scutari the death rates fell sharply only after a Sanitary Commission arrived in March 1855, six months behind her, and flushed the sewers and improved the ventilation. That is the whole point, and it cuts both ways. A treatment that works is not proof that the theory behind it is true. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Nightingale; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1121911/; en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Florence_Nightingale (Notes on Nursing, 1860)

question: William Farr, a statistician, spotted a pattern in the cholera figures that looked like hard proof of bad air: district by district, deaths fell as the ground rose above the Thames high-water mark. He trusted the curve enough to add about 13 feet to every district's height to make it fit tighter. The gradient was real, but height was standing in for something else. What was the elevation actually tracking?
answer: Which company's pipes supplied that ground
choices: Which company's pipes supplied that ground
Which streets lay nearest the sewer outfalls
Which districts had been built up most thickly
Which valleys held the morning fog longest
context: The low districts drew their water from the polluted stretch of the river and the high ones did not, so the height was quietly reporting the water. A hidden third factor was driving both the elevation and the deaths at once; that is called a confounder, and it is why a strong, repeatable correlation is never by itself a cause. Note on the numbers: sources give conflicting mortality-per-elevation figures for Farr's 1852 table, so only the gradient is stated here and no rate is quoted. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/William_Farr (Elevation and Environmental Factors Analysis; Criticisms of Farr's Interpretations); J. Eyler, 'William Farr on the cholera', J Hist Med Allied Sci

question: Max von Pettenkofer built a test at Munich, where he held the world's first chair of hygiene, and it stayed the standard until 1958. He started the first Institute of Hygiene in 1879, and his drainage reforms cut disease in his city. A teacher can carry the test's cheap descendant into her classroom today. What did his test measure?
answer: The carbon dioxide in a room's air
choices: The carbon dioxide in a room's air
The soot suspended in a street's air
The damp held in a building's walls
The lead dissolved in drinking water
context: Pettenkofer's carbon-dioxide method became the standard test of indoor air quality and held that place until 1958, the ancestor of the cheap CO2 meter you can buy today and carry into a stuffy classroom to watch the number climb. This is why the bad-air theory deserves a fair hearing instead of a laugh: the man who got cholera wrong was not a crank on the fringe, he was the founder of the field, working with the best instruments and the best intentions of his day. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/max_joseph_von_pettenkofer (Founding of Hygiene Institutions); grokipedia.com/page/Carbon_dioxide_sensor

question: Max von Pettenkofer took a dose of sodium bicarbonate on 7 October 1892, aged 73, with witnesses watching. Then he swallowed a broth of live cholera bacteria from Robert Koch's own laboratory, to settle whether Koch's germ alone caused the disease. Why did he take the bicarbonate first?
answer: So his stomach acid would not kill the bacteria
choices: So his stomach acid would not kill the bacteria
So the broth would not curdle before he drank
So the witnesses would not doubt the dose was full
So his nerves would not turn his stomach first
context: He was making the test harder on himself, not easier. Stomach acid destroys swallowed bacteria, so Pettenkofer deliberately disarmed his own best defence to give the germ its fairest possible chance to do its worst. That is real scientific courage, and he did not get cholera. Careful with the popular version: 'he felt nothing at all' is the legend, not the record. The BMJ report of 19 November 1892 describes colic and diarrhoea, so the defensible statement is that he did not get cholera. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/max_joseph_von_pettenkofer (Cholera Research and Self-Experiment); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_von_Pettenkofer; BMJ, 'Pettenkofer on Cholera', 19 November 1892

question: Witnesses watched Max von Pettenkofer, Munich's professor of hygiene, swallow a broth of live cholera bacteria in 1892, at the age of 73. He did not get cholera, and he announced that he had beaten germ theory. Researchers today can account for his survival without granting him a single point of his argument. What do they think probably spared him?
answer: A partial immunity from an earlier, milder infection
choices: A partial immunity from an earlier, milder infection
A culture gone weak in the days before he drank it
A dose he had sipped slowly across a whole day
A protective serum, taken from a recovered patient
context: Modern accounts credit a low infecting dose together with a probable partial immunity from an earlier, milder infection, and Pettenkofer himself credited a possible earlier, milder bout in childhood. The lesson here is the hard one. He was brave, he was sincere, he tested his own claim on his own body rather than demanding that others take his word, and he was still wrong. Barry Marshall would later drink a beaker of bacteria to make a point and turn out to be right; the two beakers looked identical from the outside, and the difference was not courage and it was not sincerity. Consensus is not evidence. The lone dissenter is not evidence either. One body is a sample of one. Source: grokipedia.com/page/max_joseph_von_pettenkofer

question: Max von Pettenkofer granted that Robert Koch's cholera germ was real. Alone, he insisted, it was never enough to cause an outbreak: a further condition had to be met first. When he swallowed the live germ in 1892 and stayed well, he said that condition had simply been missing. What condition did his theory demand?
answer: The soil had to ferment the germ as the ground water fell
choices: The soil had to ferment the germ as the ground water fell
The air had to ferment the germ into a specific poison
The ground had to lie low beside the river's high water
The season had to turn the marsh air foul at night
context: Pettenkofer called the germ factor X, the soil condition factor Y, and a susceptible person factor Z, and he read his own survival as proof that factor Y had simply been missing that day. Look at what that means in working practice: his theory carried a spare part that could absorb any result at all, so no experiment could ever count against it. A claim that fits every possible outcome has stopped predicting anything, and a claim nothing could refute is not a strong claim but a weak one. What finally ended the cholera argument was not eloquence on either side. It was tests that could have gone either way. Source: grokipedia.com/page/max_joseph_von_pettenkofer (Advocacy of Miasma Theory; Cholera Research and Self-Experiment)

question: Albert Michelson and Edward Morley set up an optical experiment in a Cleveland basement in 1887. It had to turn by hand with no jolt at all, so they built it on a heavy sandstone slab, and the slab floated on a pool. What filled the pool?
answer: Liquid mercury
choices: Liquid mercury
Chilled water
Whale oil
Molten wax
context: Mercury is heavy enough to float a stone slab and slick enough that the slab could be turned by hand without vibration. Modern museums keep the mercury behind glass; in 1887 it was open in the basement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment.

question: Maxwell and Kelvin assumed that light must ride on something, as sound rides on air and ocean waves on water. Physicists of their century were nearly unanimous: light waves had an invisible substance to travel through, filling all of space and staying perfectly still as the planets moved. What did they call this imagined medium?
answer: The luminiferous ether
choices: The luminiferous ether
The celestial phlogiston
The primal caloric
The universal magnetic fluid
context: Maxwell, Kelvin and virtually every serious physicist of 1880 took the ether for granted. Phlogiston, caloric and magnetic fluids were invisible substances that earlier science had seriously believed in and then given up; by the 1880s the ether was the one still standing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment; sciencenotes.org.

question: Albert Michelson set out to catch a wind nobody could feel. Earth races round its orbit at about 30 km per second, so if the ether, the unseen medium of light, stands still, the planet should sail through a headwind of it. He meant to rotate his apparatus and watch for a change. What change was he hoping to catch?
answer: A shifting pattern of bright and dark bands where two beams meet
choices: A shifting pattern of bright and dark bands where two beams meet
A gentle push on a suspended weight at the centre of the room
A slow chill on a thermometer aligned along the wind
A hiss on a sensitive microphone facing forward
context: Michelson's interferometer split a single light beam in two, sent each half down a perpendicular arm to a mirror, and recombined them. If the two half-beams took even a slightly different time to return, the recombined light would show a shifted pattern of bright and dark fringes. That fringe pattern is the ether wind's fingerprint. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment.

question: Alfred Potier and Hendrik Lorentz spotted a math slip in Albert Michelson's write-up of 1881. He had taken his new interferometer to Potsdam, near Berlin, to hunt the ether, the invisible sea light was thought to swim through. Two light beams sent along and across Earth's motion should finish at slightly different times, shifting a striped pattern of fringes. What had Michelson gotten wrong?
answer: He had overestimated his expected fringe shift by a factor of two
choices: He had overestimated his expected fringe shift by a factor of two
He had confused fringes of interference with fringes of diffraction
He had corrected for Earth's spin twice
He had used the wrong speed of light in the calculation
context: Once the correction was applied, Michelson's Potsdam sensitivity was barely at the level of the effect he was hunting for. He needed a bigger apparatus. That is what he built with Morley six years later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment.

question: Edward Morley, a chemist, joined Albert Michelson at Cleveland, Ohio, in 1887 to rebuild the ether hunt, after Potsdam gave no clear answer. The idea was the same: split a light beam, send the halves down two arms at right angles, and watch for a shift in the stripes. This time mirrors bounced each beam back and forth across a slab a few feet wide. About how long was each arm now?
answer: About 11 metres
choices: About 11 metres
About 11 centimetres
About 110 metres
About 1.1 kilometres
context: The physical stone was only a few feet across; the mirrors folded the light path roughly tenfold. That tenfold jump in path length is why the 1887 rebuild could see an effect the 1881 attempt could not. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment.

question: Edward Morley and Albert Michelson turned their sandstone slab slowly through the ether wind in a Cleveland basement in 1887. The ether theory made a specific prediction: the stripes where their two crossed light beams met, called fringes, should shift by about four-tenths of one fringe. That was the target. What did they actually measure?
answer: Less than one-twentieth of a fringe, well below the predicted shift
choices: Less than one-twentieth of a fringe, well below the predicted shift
About half of the predicted shift, ambiguously above the noise
Roughly the predicted shift, then withdrew the paper as spurious
Nothing at all; the fringes vanished entirely under rotation
context: The measured upper bound was less than 0.02 fringes against a predicted 0.4. That is a factor-of-twenty ceiling on any ether wind, not zero. The precision of the ceiling is what mattered. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment.

question: Albert Michelson built the most sensitive optical instrument on the planet, aimed it with Edward Morley at a precise prediction about the ether at Cleveland in 1887, and after months of runs came up with almost nothing. Physics textbooks today call that a triumph that helped clear the way for relativity. In his own letters and papers, Michelson described it quite differently. What did he call it at the time?
answer: A failure that he might have botched somehow
choices: A failure that he might have botched somehow
The single greatest achievement of his career
A stepping stone toward Einstein's theory
A confirmation of Fresnel's partial ether drag
context: Michelson spent years afterwards suspecting the null result was his own instrumental error and returned to the problem more than once. That the most celebrated experiment in physics was, to the man who ran it, a failure is the punchline of the whole story. Source: aps.org/apsnews/2007/11/november-1887-michelson-uminiferous-ether.

question: George FitzGerald offered a strange rescue for the ether in 1889, and Hendrik Lorentz did the same independently in 1892. Michelson and Morley had found almost no ether wind, yet physicists were reluctant to give up an invisible medium for light. The rescue took that result seriously and still let the medium exist. What did the two men propose?
answer: Moving objects shorten along the direction of motion by exactly the amount needed to hide the effect
choices: Moving objects shorten along the direction of motion by exactly the amount needed to hide the effect
The Earth drags a thin layer of ether along with it, so surface instruments see no wind
Light speeds up in the direction of motion, precisely cancelling any expected delay
The ether flows through solid matter, so laboratory walls never enclose a still sample
context: The Lorentz-FitzGerald contraction was serious, quantitative, and testable. It is also, mathematically, exactly the contraction that survives inside special relativity. The other choices echo real rival ideas, among them George Stokes's ether dragged along by the Earth, but none of them was FitzGerald's rescue. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment; ebsco.com/research-starters/mathematics/lorentz-contraction.

question: Albert Einstein, a young Swiss patent clerk, cut the knot in 1905 with a move so bold it took a generation to feel natural. Physicists had piled on ever-cleverer patches to explain why the ether, the invisible medium of light, could not be found: maybe clocks slowed, maybe Earth dragged it along. Instead of explaining why the ether hid, he did something simpler. What did he do?
answer: He threw the ether out and made the constancy of the speed of light a starting postulate
choices: He threw the ether out and made the constancy of the speed of light a starting postulate
He replaced the ether with a static gravitational field permeating space
He proposed that light is a stream of particles with mass and needs no medium
He argued that Earth carries the ether with it perfectly, saving the theory
context: The 1905 paper on the electrodynamics of moving bodies took c-is-constant as an axiom, not a mystery to be explained. From that one postulate, together with the principle of relativity, the Lorentz contraction dropped out as a consequence. Einstein was inconsistent later in life about how much the 1887 experiment had actually influenced him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment; arxiv.org/pdf/2407.12960.

question: A student reads that Albert Michelson and Edward Morley hunted Earth's motion through the invisible ether in 1887 and got a 'null' result, with their interference fringes barely moving. She shrugs and writes in her notebook: 'They saw nothing, so they know nothing.' Why is that reading wrong?
answer: It is a measured upper limit, and a limit that tight rules out whole families of theories
choices: It is a measured upper limit, and a limit that tight rules out whole families of theories
It proves the ether does not exist at all, and proof of absence is knowledge too
It proves the ether was there but hidden, since the beams' timing cancelled out
It pinned down the speed of light to a new accuracy, ether or no ether
context: The distinction between 'we measured nothing' and 'we did not measure' is one of the most abused points in popular writing on physics. A null result carries as much information as a positive one, provided the error bar is quoted: the 1887 run put the fringe shift below about a twentieth of what the ether demanded. It did not prove the ether absent, though; George FitzGerald and Hendrik Lorentz kept it alive with their contraction, and the experiment never measured the speed of light itself. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/1810.10071.

question: Dayton Miller ran thousands of Michelson-style light-beam tests high up on Mount Wilson in California in the 1920s, and he claimed to see a small but steady 'ether drift'. If real, the signal would have overturned Einstein's special relativity, and physicists took him seriously for years. What finally settled his signal?
answer: Modern reanalysis traced his drift to temperature gradients in the apparatus
choices: Modern reanalysis traced his drift to temperature gradients in the apparatus
He was found to have falsified his data ledgers
Enrico Fermi repeated the experiment in a vacuum and got zero
The signal is still unexplained and treated as an open anomaly
context: Miller himself was a careful and honest observer; his apparatus was simply not thermally isolated. The Miller episode is a useful reminder that a positive signal can be as much an artefact as a null one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment.

question: Milutin Milankovic, a Serbian astronomer and engineer, married in June 1914 and took his new wife back to his home village of Dalj, then inside the Austro-Hungarian empire. Weeks later Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and the Austrian police arrested the 35-year-old scientist at his door. What made him worth arresting?
answer: He held a commission in the Serbian army reserve
choices: He had signed a petition against Austrian rule
He was carrying survey maps of the Danube frontier
He held a commission in the Serbian army reserve
He taught at Belgrade's university, in the enemy capital
context: Milankovic held a reserve commission in the Royal Serbian Army, which turned a professor on his honeymoon into an enemy officer the moment Austria-Hungary moved against Serbia. He never got back to Belgrade: roughly six weeks under house arrest, then a train to the internment camp at Nezsider in Hungary, today Neusiedl am See in Austria. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic'; Smithsonian Magazine, 'This World War I Prisoner of War Solved the Mystery of the Ice Ages', 26 August 2024.

question: Austrian police locked Milutin Milankovic in a jail cell in 1914, and he opened his one small suitcase that first night. Inside lay his printed papers and his notes on what he called the cosmic problem, how Earth's slow wobbles and tilts change its climate. By his own memoir, what did he do with the rest of that night?
answer: He started writing, and stopped long past midnight
choices: He read one paper over and over until the light failed
He started writing, and stopped long past midnight
He hid the notes where the guards would not find them
He wrote to his old Vienna professor asking for help
context: His memoirs, word for word: 'In the suitcase I had my printed works and my notes on the cosmic problem, there was clean paper too and I started writing. It was far past midnight when I stopped.' Smithsonian describes the container as a briefcase holding a few scientific papers and some of his notes. Flagged as testimony because the only witness to that night is Milankovic himself, writing years later. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic', quoting the memoirs; Smithsonian Magazine, 26 August 2024.  (Legend.)

question: Szily, who ran the Academy of Sciences library in Budapest, heard that a prisoner had come to town. Milutin Milankovic had left the internment camp on Christmas Eve 1914, but not into freedom: he was told not to leave the city, and he had to check in with police each week. What did Szily do?
answer: Gave him a desk in the library and left him to work
choices: Found him paid work cataloguing the library's maps
Set him to translating papers for the Academy's journal
Had the library's clerks copy his notes for the Academy
Gave him a desk in the library and left him to work
context: Szily 'eagerly accepted Milankovic and enabled him to work undisturbed in the Academy's library and the Central Meteorological Institute' -- for the remaining four years of the war. The release itself was arranged by his old Vienna professor Emanuel Czuber, pressed by Milankovic's wife Kristina and his uncle Vasa. Kristina, an amateur opera singer, crossed a war to join him, and their only child Vasilije was born in Budapest on 25 December 1915 -- in the city his father was forbidden to leave. Milankovic on those years: 'I was her prisoner of war, and in her my four-year longing for freedom would have drained my core, if I had not found refuge in scientific work.' Sources: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic'; European Geosciences Union portrait; Grokipedia; Smithsonian Magazine, 26 August 2024.

question: With no calculating machine in the room, Milutin Milankovic finished another line with his pen at a desk in Budapest during the war. He was doing the same calculation over and over, a hundred days of it for one set of tables, and every finished line gave him one number. What was that number?
answer: The sunlight arriving at one latitude of Earth in one ancient season
choices: The sunlight arriving at one latitude of Earth in one ancient season
The hours of daylight at one latitude of Earth in one ancient season
The height of the noon Sun at one latitude of Earth in one ancient season
The snow left unmelted at one latitude of Earth in one ancient season
context: The quantity has a name: insolation, the sunlight arriving on a patch of Earth. Those hundred days produced a graph of solar radiation at 55, 60 and 65 degrees north reaching back about 600,000 years, computed line by line without a machine. The same problem filled roughly 27 years and four works: 'Theorie mathematique des phenomenes thermiques produits par la radiation solaire' (1920), the curve printed by Wladimir Koppen and Alfred Wegener in 1924, 'Mathematische Klimalehre' (1930), and the 1941 Canon. A laptop now redoes the whole calculation in a fraction of a second. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic'; Grokipedia; European Geosciences Union portrait.

question: James Croll, a Scot, blamed the ice ages on Earth's orbit in a top journal in 1864, fifty years before Milutin Milankovic took up the sums. His byline listed him at Anderson's University in Glasgow. He had been a wheelwright and a tea seller, he had taught himself physics, and he wrote to Charles Darwin. What was his job at the University?
answer: The janitor, who swept and locked up
choices: The porter, who carried and fetched
The clerk, who shelved the journals
The janitor, who swept and locked up
The technician, who mended the instruments
context: James Croll (1821-1890) worked as a wheelwright, a tea merchant, a temperance-hotel manager and an insurance agent before becoming janitor at Anderson's University in 1859 -- and then taught himself physics and astronomy out of the library he was employed to keep. His orbital ice-age theory ran in the Philosophical Magazine in 1864. By the end of the century it was discredited, partly because estimates of how fast Niagara Falls was cutting back its gorge did not fit his chronology. Some scholars now argue the cycles should be called Croll-Milankovitch cycles. Source: Wikipedia, 'James Croll'.

question: Milankovic sent the manuscript of his life's work, the 626-page 'Canon of Insolation and the Ice-Age Problem', to a Belgrade printing house on 2 April 1941. Four days later, on Hitler's order to destroy the city from the air, German bombers levelled the printing house. What became of the book?
answer: The printed sheets survived in the warehouse and it appeared that year
choices: A set of proofs reached Vienna and was printed there after the war
The printed sheets survived in the warehouse and it appeared that year
He rewrote it from his surviving notes and published it in 1948
Only the first hundred pages survived, issued later as a pamphlet
context: 'The manuscript was submitted to print on 2 April 1941 -- four days before the attack of Nazi Germany and its allies on the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. In the bombing of Belgrade on 6 April 1941, the printing house where his work was being printed was destroyed; however, almost all of the printed sheet paper remained undamaged in the printing warehouse.' The raid was German, not Allied: the Luftwaffe's Operation Retribution, first bombs at 06:30 on a Sunday morning, after Hitler ordered that Belgrade be destroyed from the air by continual day and night attack. The National Library of Serbia burned to the ground in the same raid. The 626-page 'Kanon der Erdbestrahlung und seine Anwendung auf das Eiszeitenproblem' was published that same year by the Royal Serbian Academy. (Grokipedia's article calls it Allied bombing; for 6 April 1941 that is wrong.) Sources: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic'; EGU portrait; RFE/RL, 'Operation Punishment: The Nazi Bombing Of Belgrade 80 Years Ago'.

question: Milutin Milankovic ran his figures season by season at 65 degrees north, hunting the one condition that lets an ice sheet thicken year after year until it covers a continent. Putting a number on that condition turned an old hunch into a theory anyone could test. By his arithmetic, which condition is it?
answer: A summer too cool to melt off the winter's snow
choices: A spring thaw that comes weeks late in the year
A summer too cool to melt off the winter's snow
A first autumn snow that falls weeks early
A winter cold enough to bury the ground in snow
context: James Croll had argued in the 1860s that glacials begin when winters are long and cold -- more snow, more ice. Milankovic turned the argument around: what matters is not winter but summer. Snow that survives one weak summer reflects sunlight back to space and helps keep the next summer cool, so the ice compounds; melting is the lever, not snowfall, which is why he computed summer sunlight at 65 degrees north. He did not invent the idea: Joseph John Murphy proposed in 1869 that ice ages need a long, cool summer and a short, mild winter, and Milankovic adopted it. His own contribution was to make it calculable -- an actual sunlight number for a given latitude in a given epoch -- which is what turned a hunch into something testable. Sources: CliMA/Caltech, 'Sunlight and the pace of ice ages', 4 August 2026; Encyclopedia of the Environment, 'Astronomical theories of climate'.

question: Two German officers knocked at Milutin Milankovic's house in occupied Belgrade on 15 May 1941, a month after German bombers flattened his printer. They were geology students in uniform, bringing greetings from Professor Wolfgang Soergel of Freiburg. Milankovic sent something back to Soergel with them. What did he put in their hands?
answer: The only complete printed copy of his Canon
choices: The only complete printed copy of his Canon
The hand-drawn plates of his insolation curves
His wartime notebooks from the Budapest library
The manuscript pages he had kept from the printer
context: Wikipedia records it plainly: the two officers 'brought greetings from Professor Wolfgang Soergel of Freiburg. Milankovic gave them the only complete printed copy of the Canon to send to Soergel, to make certain that his work would be preserved.' The man whose printer had just been bombed handed his only finished book to two soldiers of the army that bombed it -- because they were geology students, and they would keep it safe. Flagged as testimony: the scene comes down from the Milankovic side rather than from an independent record. Source: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic'.  (Legend.)

question: A geologist reportedly called Milutin Milankovic's ice-age theory rubbish a year before Milankovic died in 1958. J. D. Hays, John Imbrie and Nicholas Shackleton tested it in the journal Science eighteen years after that death. Checking a curve of ancient sunlight meant finding somewhere the climate of the past 450,000 years had left a readable record. Where did they read it?
answer: In the mud collecting on the floor of the deep ocean
choices: In the moraines left by the four Alpine glaciations
In the mud collecting on the floor of the deep ocean
In the gorge Niagara Falls has cut back since the ice
In the ice sheet standing over the middle of Greenland
context: Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton read three indices of global climate over the past 450,000 years out of Southern Hemisphere ocean-floor sediments. The record gave 'three discrete spectral peaks at periods of 23,000, 42,000, and approximately 100,000 years', holding about 10, 25 and 50 percent of the climatic variance, and the three authors concluded that 'changes in the earth's orbital geometry are the fundamental cause of the succession of Quaternary ice ages'. Milankovic had died on 12 December 1958 -- eighteen years, almost to the day, before the paper appeared. His own answer to obscurity: 'As many scientific discoveries, far greater than mine, had remained unrecognized for years, I knew that, if my work was to become a real contribution to science, it would find its way without any help, recommendation or praise.' Sources: Science, 10 December 1976, vol. 194 no. 4270, pp. 1121-1132, DOI 10.1126/science.194.4270.1121; Smithsonian Magazine, 26 August 2024.

question: J. D. Hays, John Imbrie and Nicholas Shackleton matched Milutin Milankovic's orbital cycles to the climate record in 1976. The feeblest of his three wobbles alters the sunlight Earth receives by less than a fifth of a watt per square metre, yet for the last million years the ice has kept its roughly 100,000-year beat. Why the weakest push moves the most ice, no one yet knows. What shorter rhythm did the ice keep before that?
answer: About 41,000 years, the beat of the axis tipping
choices: About 26,000 years, the beat of the axis wheeling
About 41,000 years, the beat of the axis tipping
About 23,000 years, the beat of the seasons drifting
About 19,000 years, the beat of the orbit swiveling
context: The switch is called the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, roughly 1.25 to 0.7 million years ago: before it, the ice ages followed the 41,000-year tipping of Earth's axis between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees; after it, the ~100,000-year beat took over, and nobody has explained either the switch or why the feeblest forcing dominates. The numbers that make it bite: eccentricity moves the global annual mean by under 0.2 watts per square metre, precession swings midsummer sunlight at 65 degrees north by 3 to 5, obliquity by roughly 0.5 to 1 in high-latitude annual means. Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton flagged the puzzle in their own 1976 abstract -- explaining the eccentricity correlation 'probably requires an assumption of nonlinearity'. The most recent major attempt, Stephen Barker and colleagues in Science on 28 February 2025, still says the 100,000-year problem 'remains unresolved'. One prediction from the 1941 Canon has not expired: this warm interglacial holds, and the next glacial advance begins in roughly 50,000 years. Sources: Grokipedia, '100,000-year problem'; Science 1976 and 2025.

question: Stanley Miller, a 22-year-old graduate student in Chicago, sealed four gases and hot water into a closed glass loop in 1952. He shot electric sparks through the mix for a week, imitating lightning storms over a young Earth ocean. What had formed in the water?
answer: Amino acids
choices: Amino acids
Cell membranes
Living bacteria
Table salt crystals
context: Miller was working under Harold Urey at the University of Chicago. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Miller ; nasonline.org (Miller memoir).

question: Charles Darwin wrote to his botanist friend Joseph Hooker in 1871 with a guess at how life on Earth might have begun. He pictured a spot with ammonia, phosphoric salts, light, heat and electricity, where a protein compound could form and start reacting. He never published the guess. What did he call that spot?
answer: a warm little pond
choices: a warm little pond
a deep sea trench
a lightning-struck peak
a fresh volcanic crater
context: Darwin never published on the origin of life; the phrase survives only because Hooker kept the letter. Source: darwinproject.ac.uk letter DCP-LETT-7471.

question: Harold Urey, a Nobel Prize-winning chemist at Chicago, had shaped his student's sealed gases around his own picture of a young Earth with no free oxygen. When Stanley Miller's paper on the spark loop was ready, Urey made a choice about the byline. What did he do?
answer: Kept his own name off it so Miller would get the credit
choices: Kept his own name off it so Miller would get the credit
Put his own name first, as the senior chemist on the work
Held the paper back until another lab repeated the run
Added the glassblower who built the loop as a co-author
context: Urey won the 1934 Nobel for discovering deuterium. When the paper was ready he refused co-authorship, fearing his name would drown out Miller's, and Miller published alone in Science in 1953. The work is still called the Miller-Urey experiment all the same. Source: nasonline.org memoir; wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Urey.

question: Stanley Miller looked at the murky water left in his spark loop and could name the exact chemistry behind his amino acids. His electric sparks had broken the sealed gases into two small, highly reactive intermediate molecules, and those two had then combined with more ammonia. Which pair of intermediates was doing the building?
answer: hydrogen cyanide and formaldehyde
choices: hydrogen cyanide and formaldehyde
carbon monoxide and nitric oxide
acetylene and ethylene
urea and glucose
context: The pathway is called Strecker synthesis after Adolph Strecker's 1850 amino-acid recipe; Miller had rediscovered it running on lightning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Urey_experiment.

question: A student sets aside the sunny poster version of the story and tallies the carbon in Stanley Miller's flask. Of all the carbon that started as methane, only a few percent ended up in amino acids. Where did much of the rest end up?
answer: into an intractable brown tar
choices: into an intractable brown tar
into proteins strung from those amino acids
into sugars dissolved in the water
into the building blocks of DNA
context: Miller himself estimated that half or more of the methane's carbon had turned into organic matter, most of it complex polymer: the tar that coated the inside of the glass. The small molecules he could pick out and name came to only about fifteen percent of the carbon. No sugars and no nucleotides appeared, and the amino acids never linked up into proteins: the flask made building blocks, not the things built from them. Sources: Jeffrey Bada, 'One of the foremost experiments of the 20th century', Metode (metode.org); Miller and Urey, Science 130 (1959).

question: A geologist reads ancient rock for what the young Earth's air was made of. Stanley Miller's flask assumed a strongly reducing mix of methane and ammonia. Reruns with the mix geologists now favour yield far fewer amino acids. What do the rocks now suggest that air was?
answer: mostly carbon dioxide and nitrogen
choices: mostly carbon dioxide and nitrogen
mostly oxygen and helium
mostly ozone and chlorine
pure water vapor
context: The chemistry Miller demonstrated is real; the recipe he used may just not match the young planet. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18204914 (Cleaves et al. 2008).

question: A chemist reruns Stanley Miller's flask at an alkaline vent, on iron-sulfur minerals and on clay, and each time the amino acids come out fifty-fifty left-handed and right-handed. Living things do something this chemistry does not, and no one yet knows how they came to it. What does living protein use?
answer: only the left-handed forms
choices: only the left-handed forms
only the right-handed forms
a fifty-fifty mix
a random mix per organism
context: This still-open puzzle is called the homochirality problem. Meteorite amino acids show a small left-hand excess, and autocatalytic amplification is one candidate mechanism; no one yet knows how nature picked a hand. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/2012.12850.

question: A biology teacher tells her class that every B cell owes its letter to a small lymph pouch near a chicken's tail, the bursa of Fabricius, named for a 1500s anatomist. Mammals have no bursa. Where then does a human B cell finish growing up?
answer: bone marrow
choices: bone marrow
the thymus
the spleen
the tonsils
context: The letter survived the organ: the 'B' still stands for bursa but human B cells mature in the marrow of long bones. T cells still mature in the thymus. The naming accident is the reason immunology owes chicken farms a footnote. Source: sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/bursa-of-fabricius ; fortislife.com/resources/antibody-resources/b-is-for-bursa

question: Bruce Glick, a poultry student at Ohio State, cut a small organ called the bursa from young chicks in 1955 and saw nothing wrong. Then another student borrowed the birds for a routine class vaccine demonstration. The vaccine failed in the birds without a bursa, and most of them died. What did the accident show the bursa was needed for?
answer: Making antibodies
choices: Making antibodies
Making T cells
Making red blood cells
Raising fevers
context: The failed class demo WAS the experiment. Chang immunised the borrowed chicks with Salmonella O antigen; the bursectomised birds could not raise antibodies and died, and Glick, checking his notes, realised the intact-bursa chicks were the survivors. A teaching lab uncovered a whole lineage of the immune system. T cells, the other line of targeted defence, mature in the thymus instead. Source: popsci.com/chickens-bursa-immune-award/ ; academic.oup.com/cei/article/145/1/1/6458731

question: Jacques Miller, an Australian-born PhD student in London, made an immune-system discovery in 1961 that changed how doctors see the body's defences. He went on to an accolade so specific it is almost eerie. Historians of medicine describe him as the last living scientist to have discovered the function of what?
answer: a human organ
choices: a human organ
a mammalian hormone
a childhood disease
a vitamin
context: The great organ hunts - liver, pancreas, spleen, kidneys, thyroid - were finished by the mid-20th century. The thymus was the last one left with 'unknown' next to its function line, and Miller settled it in 1961. There is no organ left in the human body whose function is still up for discovery. Source: thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(11)61565-1/fulltext

question: Robert Millikan sprayed a fine mist of oil between two flat metal plates at Chicago in 1909. Each droplet picked up its own tiny electric charge as it fell through the air. He watched one through his microscope and held it hanging motionless in the gap. What did he adjust to hold it still?
answer: The voltage on the plates
choices: The voltage on the plates
The temperature of the chamber
The tilt of the plates
The pressure of the surrounding air
context: The upward electric pull on the charged droplet grew or shrank with the voltage across the plates; at the right setting the pull exactly balanced the droplet's weight and it hung motionless. Millikan then read off that voltage to work out the charge the drop was carrying. Source: Wikipedia, Oil drop experiment.

question: Robert Millikan and Harvey Fletcher, his student, set out at Chicago to measure the charge of a single electron, and they deliberately chose oil for their suspended droplets. J. J. Thomson and H. A. Wilson had used water a few years earlier at Cambridge. Why did water fail?
answer: The drops evaporated as they were watched, changing mass mid-measurement
choices: The drops evaporated as they were watched, changing mass mid-measurement
The drops carried too little charge to respond to any manageable voltage
The drops froze solid in the cool laboratory air within a few seconds
The drops broke apart into finer droplets whenever the field was turned on
context: Oil has an extremely low vapor pressure, so a droplet held in view for minutes barely shrinks. Source: Wikipedia, Oil drop experiment.

question: Robert Millikan peered through a microscope around 1910 at single oil droplets rising and falling between two metal plates. From the way each drop moved he could work out the exact electric charge riding on it. He measured hundreds of drops and wrote down all the charges. What did the numbers look like when he laid them out?
answer: Every drop's charge was a whole-number multiple of one base amount
choices: Every drop's charge was a whole-number multiple of one base amount
The charges spread smoothly across every value with no gaps
Half the drops carried the same charge and half carried none
The charges doubled from drop to drop in a geometric sequence
context: That pattern -- one, two, three, seven times a single lump, never one-and-a-half -- is what showed electric charge is quantized. The base lump is the charge on one electron. Source: Wikipedia, Oil drop experiment.

question: Richard Feynman went back decades later through Robert Millikan's 1913 value for the charge of a single electron, the number that won Millikan a Nobel. It sat about 0.6 percent below what modern measurements give, and Feynman traced that small offset to one input Millikan had used and gotten slightly wrong. What was that input?
answer: The viscosity of air
choices: The viscosity of air
The mass of the electron
The density of the oil
The strength of Earth's gravity
context: The formula turning a drop's fall speed into its size uses the air's viscosity; a slightly wrong tabulated value fed straight into the answer. Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science,' Caltech commencement 1974.

question: Richard Feynman took up the measurements of the electron's charge published after Robert Millikan's original 1913 value, in his 1974 Caltech commencement speech 'Cargo Cult Science'. He wanted to show his graduating students how badly a first result from a famous scientist can bias every measurement that follows. What did the successive numbers actually do?
answer: Crept upward from Millikan's value in small steps until they settled near the modern answer
choices: Crept upward from Millikan's value in small steps until they settled near the modern answer
Jumped immediately to the modern answer within a year of Millikan
Swung wildly above and below Millikan with no trend at all
Stayed exactly at Millikan's value for fifty years, then corrected in a single 1959 paper
context: Feynman's point was psychological, not arithmetic: an experimenter who got a number much higher than Millikan's went hunting for what was wrong with his own apparatus, and stopped hunting once the number sat near Millikan's. Big physics teams now guard against that pull with blind analysis.

question: A young physicist joins a big particle-physics team and learns about the 'Millikan effect'. Robert Millikan came up a touch too low on the charge of the electron, and later physicists, knowing his published number, unconsciously nudged their own answers toward it. To keep that from steering her result, her team uses a discipline called blind analysis. What does the team actually do to the data?
answer: Hide the signal region or add a secret offset until the analysis method is frozen, then unblind
choices: Hide the signal region or add a secret offset until the analysis method is frozen, then unblind
Run the entire experiment twice and average the two answers together
Have the theorists compute the expected answer first and use it as a check on every cut
Rotate lab shifts each night so no single person sees more than a few hours of data
context: Common tricks include a hidden numerical shift added to every measurement, a scrambled sample, or a covered 'signal box.' Once the selection cuts and the analysis code are locked in, the collaboration unblinds -- and whatever comes out is what gets published. Source: Klein & Roodman, Blind Analysis in Nuclear and Particle Physics, Ann. Rev. Nucl. Part. Sci. 55.

question: Felix Ehrenhaft insisted in Vienna, from 1910 on, that charges smaller than an electron's rode on his drops. Every other laboratory's drops showed the same single lump. Half a century later physics did find particles carrying a third or two-thirds of an electron's charge, the quarks. Why do quarks not rescue Ehrenhaft's drops?
answer: They stay locked inside protons and neutrons, never free
choices: They stay locked inside protons and neutrons, never free
Their charge is too small for any oil drop to show
They turned up only in particle beams, never in matter
They decay away long before they could reach a drop
context: Quarks carry a third or two-thirds of an electron's charge, but they are confined: no free quark has ever been caught on its own, so a lone quark could never ride an oil drop. Ehrenhaft, at the University of Vienna, never conceded. Einstein wrote in 1940 that he did not believe Ehrenhaft's numbers but that nobody had a clear explanation for what Ehrenhaft was actually seeing. Sources: Wikipedia, Felix Ehrenhaft; Wikipedia, Quark.

question: Harvey Fletcher wrote a memoir and asked that it stay unpublished until he had died. He had been Robert Millikan's graduate student at the University of Chicago during the oil-drop experiments, and in it he told what happened when it came time to publish the key 1913 paper. What did Fletcher say Millikan did?
answer: Took sole authorship of the main paper, invoking a Chicago rule that a thesis had to be single-authored
choices: Took sole authorship of the main paper, invoking a Chicago rule that a thesis had to be single-authored
Listed Fletcher as first author of the main paper and put himself second, as Fletcher had done the bench work
Removed his own name from the main paper entirely so his graduate student could have full credit
Split the byline exactly evenly with Fletcher on every paper the two of them ever published together
context: Fletcher's memoir 'My Work with Millikan on the Oil-Drop Experiment' appeared in Physics Today in June 1982, after Fletcher had died -- he had asked that it be held. Source: Physics Today, 1982.

question: Thomas Midgley Jr. stood before the American Chemical Society in 1930 to prove his brand-new refrigerator gas, Freon, was completely safe to breathe and would not catch fire. He wanted a live demonstration no one in the room would forget. What did he do on the spot?
answer: He inhaled a lungful of it and exhaled it onto a candle, snuffing the flame.
choices: He inhaled a lungful of it and exhaled it onto a candle, snuffing the flame.
He sealed himself in a chamber flooded with the vapor for ten minutes.
He poured a beaker of the liquid across a lit Bunsen burner.
He drank a full glass of the liquid in front of the audience.
context: Freon (dichlorofluoromethane, a CFC) really was non-toxic and non-flammable at ordinary exposures -- exactly the properties that let it drift intact into the stratosphere fifty years later and cause the problem Molina and Rowland would predict in 1974. Sources: Chemistry World 'Life-changing chemistry'; Smithsonian Magazine 'One Man Invented Two of the Deadliest Substances of the 20th Century'.

question: Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina put a plain question in 1974 about chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, the refrigerants people thought were harmless: where do the gases end up? They said the gases drift up into the stratosphere, and there something finally breaks them and frees a chlorine atom. What breaks them up there?
answer: ultraviolet light from the Sun
choices: ultraviolet light from the Sun
cosmic rays from deep space
lightning inside stratospheric clouds
collisions with high-energy oxygen atoms
context: Above roughly 20 km altitude the atmosphere lets through the short-wavelength UV that lower down is filtered by the ozone itself. That UV finally breaks the C-Cl bond in an intact CFC molecule and liberates a chlorine atom into the stratosphere. Molina and Rowland won a share of the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this line of reasoning. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mario Molina' and 'Ozone depletion'.

question: Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland, two University of California chemists, warned in 1974 that chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, the safe-seeming refrigerant gases, were drifting up into the stratosphere and quietly destroying the ozone layer. DuPont sold more of those gases than anyone. How did the chair of DuPont's board react in public?
answer: outright ridicule as a science fiction tale and utter nonsense
choices: outright ridicule as a science fiction tale and utter nonsense
a call for a decade of confirming atmospheric measurements first
a pledge of voluntary CFC production cuts pending further study
a commissioning of DuPont scientists to test the calculation themselves
context: The direct quotation is preserved on the Wikipedia 'Ozone depletion' article and in the contemporary press: 'a science fiction tale ... a load of rubbish ... utter nonsense.' It is the classic case of an industry chairman ridiculing a calculation that turned out to be right, and it is also why Molina and Rowland's later vindication became one of the founding stories of atmospheric chemistry. Source: Wikipedia 'Ozone depletion' (direct quotation).

question: Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland saw what made a tiny bit of chlorine so dangerous to the ozone layer: a chlorine atom is a catalyst. It is not used up, so it comes out the other side ready to strike again. About how many ozone molecules does one atom destroy before it is finally removed?
answer: around 100,000
choices: around 100
around 10,000
around 100,000
context: The number 100,000 is stated exactly on Wikipedia's Ozone depletion article and traces back to standard atmospheric-chemistry reviews. It is why a few million tonnes of a supposedly inert refrigerant could plausibly matter to a planet-sized shield -- the multiplier is the whole story. Source: Wikipedia 'Ozone depletion'.

question: Another atmospheric chemist showed in 1970 that a different family of gases could eat ozone the same catalytic way, four years before Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland took up chlorine. The Nobel Prize in Chemistry went jointly to all three men in 1995. Who was the earlier chemist, and what family of gases did he name?
answer: Paul Crutzen, nitrogen oxides from nitrous oxide
choices: Paul Crutzen, nitrogen oxides from nitrous oxide
James Lovelock, bromine compounds from sea spray
Sydney Chapman, atomic oxygen from oxygen photolysis
Gordon Dobson, sulfur oxides from volcanic eruptions
context: Crutzen's 1970 work on the NOx catalytic cycle gave Molina and Rowland the template they applied to chlorine four years later. The 1995 Nobel in Chemistry went jointly to Crutzen, Molina and Rowland 'for their work in atmospheric chemistry, particularly concerning the formation and decomposition of ozone.' The other three names among the choices are real atmospheric scientists -- Lovelock actually invented the electron-capture detector that measured CFCs in the air; Chapman worked out the classical gas-phase ozone cycle; Dobson invented the ground-based spectrophotometer used at Halley. Sources: Wikipedia 'Paul J. Crutzen' and 'Mario Molina'.

question: Farman and two fellow British scientists published the numbers from Halley Bay in the journal Nature in 1985. Their station on the Antarctic coast had been tracking ozone since the 1950s, and October levels kept falling. How big a drop did their paper report over Antarctica each southern spring?
answer: up to 70 percent of the ozone column
choices: up to 30 percent of the ozone column
up to 50 percent of the ozone column
up to 70 percent of the ozone column
up to 95 percent of the ozone column
context: The paper -- 'Large losses of total ozone in Antarctica reveal seasonal ClOx/NOx interaction', Nature vol. 315 issue 6016 p. 207 -- was the moment the abstract 1974 prediction became a measured emergency, and it came from a hand-calibrated ground instrument the satellite community had almost forgotten. Shanklin's specific contribution was calibrating the Dobson instrument itself. Sources: Wikipedia 'Jonathan Shanklin' and 'Ozone depletion'.

question: British scientists at the Halley Bay station in Antarctica reported a huge seasonal hole in the ozone layer in 1985. Two years later 43 nations signed the Montreal Protocol, freezing and halving production of chlorofluorocarbons, the chemicals in fridges and spray cans. Among all United Nations environmental treaties, what honour does Montreal alone still hold?
answer: It is the only one every UN member state has ratified.
choices: It is the only one every UN member state has ratified.
It is the only one with a binding global carbon-price mechanism.
It is the only one to have set legally binding species-recovery targets.
It is the only one requiring signatories to submit annual satellite verification.
context: The Montreal Protocol is the only UN environmental treaty ever ratified by every member state -- and the enforcement mechanism turned out to be the measurement itself: atmospheric chlorine peaked in the late 1990s and has been falling since. The 2023 UN scientific assessment projects a return to 1980 ozone values by around 2040 globally, 2045 over the Arctic, and 2066 over Antarctica. Source: Wikipedia 'Ozone depletion'.

question: A teacher tells her class the old story that NASA's Total Ozone Mapping Spectrometer satellite spotted the Antarctic ozone hole first, but its computer 'threw the data away.' A 1993 NASA report shows that story is a myth. What did the software actually do with ozone readings below 180 Dobson units?
answer: It flagged them as suspected sensor error for later human review.
choices: It deleted them permanently as digital noise.
It flagged them as suspected sensor error for later human review.
It auto-corrected them upward to match a physical model.
It overwrote them with monthly averages from surrounding grid cells.
context: The NASA team had checked the very low TOMS values against other data, which showed around 300 Dobson units, and reasonably assumed the sensor was malfunctioning. The British Halley ground data was not available to them. After Farman et al. 1985 the entire TOMS archive was reprocessed (Version 6, released November 1990) and confirmed the hole had been sitting in the data all along. The real lesson is sharper than the myth: a filter that encodes what you expect to be normal can hide the abnormal. Sources: robjhyndman.com 'The ozone hole and the anomaly detector' (citing Fleig et al. 1986 GRL and NASA Reference Publication 1323, 1993).

question: Susan Solomon flew south with her team in 1986 to face a puzzle. The 1974 chemistry of Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland predicted a slow, worldwide thinning of ozone through reactions in the gas of the stratosphere, and what appeared each September was a huge hole over Antarctica alone. She argued the chlorine reactions were not happening in the gas at all. Where were they taking place?
answer: on the surfaces of ice crystals in polar stratospheric clouds
choices: on the surfaces of ice crystals in polar stratospheric clouds
inside supercooled droplets of liquid nitric acid
on the underside of the Antarctic ice sheet itself
in the plumes of erupting Antarctic volcanoes
context: The winter polar vortex chills the Antarctic stratosphere to around or below -80 C, cold enough to form clouds that almost never form anywhere else. On the ice surfaces of those clouds, harmless chlorine reservoir compounds are converted into active chlorine that then waits, storing up, until the September sun returns. Then the destruction happens all at once. Solomon, about 30 years old at the time, was the sole leader of the 1986 and 1987 National Ozone Expedition to McMurdo and the only woman on the team; her group measured chlorine oxide roughly 100 times higher than expected. Sources: Wikipedia 'Susan Solomon' and 'Ozone depletion'.

question: James Anderson's team flew instruments out of Chile late in 1987 aboard NASA's ER-2 (Earth Resources 2), a research plane based on the U-2 spy plane, crossing right into and out of the Antarctic polar vortex. Susan Solomon's idea needed a real test inside the vortex itself. What did the team's 'smoking gun' plot show as the aircraft crossed the vortex edge?
answer: chlorine monoxide climbing exactly where and when ozone crashed
choices: chlorine monoxide climbing exactly where and when ozone crashed
nitric oxide and ozone rising and falling together in step
carbon dioxide climbing steadily on both sides of the vortex
methane concentrations doubling inside the vortex core
context: The ClO-versus-ozone anti-correlation from the Airborne Antarctic Ozone Experiment (AAOE) is the plot people mean when they say a single graph ended a scientific debate. Anderson himself: 'That anti-correlation between ClO and ozone was a dramatic clue to what was happening.' Rival explanations that serious atmospheric scientists had proposed -- a natural dynamical cycle lifting ozone-poor air, solar-cycle nitrogen oxides, volcanic emissions -- were all tested and rejected against this measurement. Sources: NOAA CSL 'AAOE overview'; Smithsonian Magazine 'The Ozone Problem is Back'.

question: Henry Moseley, a young Oxford physicist, put one pure metal after another inside a vacuum tube in 1913. He fired a beam at each sample and photographed the sharp lines it threw back onto a strip of film. What was he firing at the metals?
answer: A beam of electrons
choices: A beam of electrons
A beam of neutrons
A beam of visible light
A jet of hot mercury vapour
context: Electrons knocked deep-shell electrons out of the target atoms; when outer electrons fell in to fill the holes, each element emitted its own characteristic X-rays. Moseley diffracted those X-rays off a crystal and let them expose photographic film, using Bragg's law to read off the wavelength. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Moseley

question: Henry Moseley caught the X-rays each element gave off in 1913 and found a signature frequency that stepped up cleanly from element to element, like a staircase. He gave each step a whole-number label. In a 1914 paper he said that number was not just a label but a real count inside the atom. What was he counting?
answer: The positive charges in the nucleus
choices: The positive charges in the nucleus
The layers of electrons around the atom
The neutrons inside the nucleus
The isotopes of the element known so far
context: Ernest Rutherford's 1911 experiment had already shown the atom has a small, dense, positively charged core (its nucleus). Moseley measured how much charge sits in that core for each element. The Dutch amateur van den Broek had guessed as much in 1911; Moseley supplied the proof. The particle carrying one unit of that charge (the proton) was not named by Rutherford's group until 1920. Source: chemteam.info/AtomicStructure/AtNum-Moseley.html

question: Dmitri Mendeleev had put tellurium before iodine and cobalt before nickel on chemical grounds, even though the weighing scale disagreed each time. He blamed the odd weights on sloppy laboratory work. Henry Moseley's X-ray staircase, one step per element, showed the chemistry was right, but for a reason Mendeleev had never guessed. What was that reason?
answer: Tellurium and cobalt each carry fewer nuclear charges than their lighter neighbour
choices: Tellurium and cobalt each carry fewer nuclear charges than their lighter neighbour
Tellurium and cobalt each hold an extra outer electron shell
Tellurium and cobalt each occupy two boxes on the table at once
Tellurium and cobalt are each really mixtures of two undiscovered elements
context: The extra weight comes from neutrons (isotopes), not from more protons. Mendeleev had the elements in the right order for the right chemical reason and the wrong stated reason. After Moseley, the table stopped being ordered by mass and started being ordered by nuclear charge, an idea we now call the atomic number. Source: ck12.org/flexi/physical-science/Mendeleevs-Periodic-Table

question: Henry Moseley pointed straight at the gaps in his staircase of whole numbers, which allowed no missing step, and predicted that certain undiscovered elements had to exist. Nothing else could be squeezed between the steps. Which set of specific holes did he name in the periodic table?
answer: Elements 43, 61, 72 and 75
choices: Elements 43, 61, 72 and 75
Elements 3, 11, 19 and 37
Elements 84, 86, 88 and 92
Elements 2, 10, 18 and 36
context: The four holes were filled later as technetium (43), promethium (61), hafnium (72) and rhenium (75). Moseley also settled a running argument by proving that the rare-earth (lanthanide) row must contain exactly fifteen members, no more and no less. The table stopped being a matter of judgement and became a matter of counting. Source: nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/02/henry-moseley-and-periodic-table-elements

question: A Turkish sniper killed Henry Moseley at Gallipoli on 10 August 1915, aged 27. He had volunteered for the British Army in 1914, after about two years of work on his X-ray staircase. Robert Millikan called his loss one of the heaviest costs of the war to science. Which rule kept his name off the Nobel roll?
answer: The Nobel Prize could not go to anyone already dead when nominated
choices: The Nobel Prize could not go to anyone already dead when nominated
The Nobel Prize was suspended for the whole of the First World War
British officers were barred from Swedish scientific honours
Only work published after 1915 was eligible for the physics prize
context: Svante Arrhenius had nominated him for both the 1915 physics and chemistry prizes, but that year they went to the Braggs and to Richard Willstatter. After his death no fresh nomination could count, because the statutes of the day barred a prize for the work of someone already dead; the flat rule against posthumous prizes was written only in 1974. The physics prize for 1917 went to Charles Barkla, who had done earlier X-ray work. Rutherford summed up Moseley's discovery by saying the X-ray wavelength changes could be explained by supposing the charge on the nucleus increases from one element to the next by exactly one unit. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Moseley; nobelprize.org nomination archive; aps.org/apsnews/2012/08/henry-moseley-killed-action-1915

question: Rene Blondlot of Nancy said in 1903 that he had found a new kind of ray, the N-ray, and other labs confirmed it. An American visitor quietly tested Blondlot's apparatus during a demonstration in 1904. What were the N-rays finally shown to be?
answer: Imaginary rays that never existed
choices: Imaginary rays that never existed
A disguised form of X-rays
Cosmic rays from deep space
Radiation from radioactive rocks
context: Blondlot named the rays N-rays (N for Nancy) in the spring of 1903 while trying to polarize X-rays. They were imaginary: when Robert W. Wood secretly pocketed the prism that was supposed to spread them into a spectrum, the observer went on reading off the same spectrum. Becquerel had found radioactivity in 1896 and Villard gamma rays in 1900, so in that decade a new kind of ray did not sound strange at all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N_ray.

question: A seated observer stared through the dark at Nancy at a small electric spark and a strip of paint that glowed faintly. That was the whole detector for Rene Blondlot's N-rays: the watcher judged by eye whether the paint got brighter. What made this way of reading the fatal weakness of the entire N-ray program?
answer: The observer knew when the apparatus was supposedly 'on'.
choices: The observer knew when the apparatus was supposedly 'on'.
The phosphor decayed after only a few minutes of use.
The spark could not be photographed on the plates of the day.
The apparatus lost calibration whenever the room warmed up.
context: Nobody was ever blinded to the setup: the observer knew which trials were the 'on' trials, the effect sat at the very threshold of detection, and expectation itself became the instrument. All three other choices are real worries for a dim optical detector, but the fatal one is that the human doing the seeing knew what he was supposed to see, and when.

question: Rene Blondlot claimed in 1903 to have found a new radiation, N-rays, coming from iron, from wood, even from the human brain. Other French labs quickly reported the same thing, and a full-blown field grew up between 1903 and 1906. About how many papers on N-rays appeared before it collapsed?
answer: about 300
choices: about 300
about 30
about 3,000
about 30,000
context: Roughly 300 papers by about 120 scientists, with 26 papers from Blondlot himself. The scale is the whole point of the story: this was not one crank -- it was normal, credentialed physics running for three years without a hitch.

question: Robert W. Wood, an American physicist, travelled to Nancy in 1904 to see the N-ray demonstration for himself. In the dark he palmed one small piece of the apparatus into his pocket, and the readings carried on unchanged. Which piece did he remove?
answer: the aluminium prism from the spectroscope
choices: the aluminium prism from the spectroscope
the phosphorescent thread from the detector
the electrical filament from the discharge tube
the copper collimator from the front of the apparatus
context: The prism was the piece that supposedly separated the incoming N-rays into their spectrum; without it there could be no reading at all. The demonstrator went on calmly reading off exactly the same spectrum after Wood pocketed it.

question: An American visitor to Nancy, Robert W. Wood, ran a quiet test of his own on the N-ray apparatus. He was told that a steel file was one of the objects emitting the rays, so he substituted something on the sly to see if the demonstrator noticed. What did Wood swap for the steel file?
answer: a plain piece of wood
choices: a plain piece of wood
a heavy bar of lead
a small slab of copper
a length of glass rod
context: Green wood, in Blondlot's own catalogue, did NOT emit N-rays. When Wood substituted wood for the file, the readings kept coming anyway -- which no consistent N-ray theory could allow. Lead, copper and glass are real materials Wood might plausibly have grabbed, but wood was the specific test-case, and it was the substance N-rays were said NOT to emit.

question: Rene Blondlot won the Prix Leconte and its 50,000 francs from the French Academy of Sciences in December 1904, three months after Robert W. Wood's letter exposed his N-rays. The Academy was not willing to abandon its own, so it kept the prize but rewrote the citation. For what did it now honour him?
answer: the totality of his work
choices: the totality of his work
his measurement of the speed of radio waves
his long service to the University of Nancy
his defence of French science against attack
context: The rewording was a bureaucratic finesse: the prize was announced, but the citation quietly dropped the N-rays and pointed back at Blondlot's career as a whole, which did include real earlier work.

question: Irving Langmuir gave a talk at General Electric's Knolls laboratory on December 18, 1953, half a century after the N-rays vanished. In it he named the whole family of failures they belonged to, from N-rays through mitogenetic rays to the Davis-Barnes effect. What name did he give to the pattern?
answer: pathological science
choices: pathological science
cargo cult science
the tyranny of expectation
the observer effect
context: Langmuir called it 'the science of things that aren't so.' The Knolls talk survived only on a microgroove disk transcript and was finally published in Physics Today in October 1989 (edited by Robert Hall). 'Cargo cult science' is Feynman's later, related name for a slightly different failure mode -- both belong on any bookshelf about self-deception in the lab.

question: Denis Rousseau of Bell Labs ended a decade-long chase in 1971 after a supposed new form of water, polywater, said to freeze at -40 C and boil at 150 C. He compared its infrared spectrum with a fluid he had collected from his own body. What was the fluid?
answer: his sweat, collected after a handball game
choices: his sweat, collected after a handball game
his saliva, taken after breakfast in the lab
his blood plasma, drawn during a routine physical
his tears, produced during a wind test on the roof
context: The two spectra matched: polywater was ordinary water contaminated with the ionic soup of a sweaty athlete. First reported by Nikolai Fedyakin in Kostroma in 1961 and pushed by Boris Derjaguin, polywater fits every one of Langmuir's symptoms -- the effect never grew when the apparatus was scaled up, and every failed replication met a fresh excuse.

question: Thucydides watched the plague sweep through Athens in 430 BC. Most people fled the sick for fear of catching it, yet some still sat with the dying and nursed them without fear. The historian wrote down what all those nurses had in common. What was it?
answer: They had already been through the disease and recovered
choices: They had already been through the disease and recovered
They had been given a physician's protective mixture
They came from families the priests judged favoured
They had grown up in the villages outside the city
context: Thucydides' own words, in the Crawley translation: "Yet it was with those who had recovered from the disease that the sick and the dying found most compassion. These knew what it was from experience, and had now no fear for themselves; for the same man was never attacked twice - never at least fatally." This is the first written record of immunity in any language, and the man who wrote it was a general and a historian, not a physician - and he had caught the plague himself and survived it. Sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 2 ch. 51 (Crawley translation), MIT Internet Classics Archive - http://classics.mit.edu/Thucydides/pelopwar.2.second.html ; Grokipedia, 'Plague of Athens' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Plague_of_Athens

question: A young Dane, Peter Ludvig Panum, went looking through the Faroe Islands in 1846 for the people a measles epidemic had passed over. It had landed at Thorshavn in April, and about 6,000 of the 7,782 islanders fell ill within half a year. Who were the ones it spared?
answer: The old people who had gone through measles in their youth
choices: The old people who had gone through measles in their youth
The people who had come through smallpox or scarlet fever
The families that had scrubbed their homes clean of filth
The households that kept fires burning against the bad air
context: Panum's own sentence: "In this connection it is quite remarkable, however, that of the many aged people still living on the Faroes who had had measles in 1781, not one, as far as I could find out by careful inquiry, was attacked the second time. I myself saw ninety-eight such old people, who were exempt because they had had the disease in their youth." Measles had last visited the islands in 1781 - a gap Panum states as "sixty-five years" - so almost everybody under sixty-five was meeting it for the first time. One traveller brought it back: a Faroese man who had visited someone ill with measles in Copenhagen, felt perfectly well through the nine-day crossing, and broke out about a week after landing. Source: P. L. Panum, 'Observations Made During the Epidemic of Measles on the Faroe Islands in the Year 1846' (English translation, Delta Omega archive) - https://s3.amazonaws.com/aspphwebassets/delta-omega/archives/PanumFaroeIslands.pdf

question: The churchwarden's daughter at a Faroe Islands farmhouse had just recovered from measles when Peter Ludvig Panum called in 1846. The nine others in the house felt fine and hoped they had escaped. He asked when her rash had appeared, checked the almanac and drew a black line under one later date. What was he predicting?
answer: That measles would strike the rest of the house that day
choices: That measles would strike the rest of the house that day
That the daughter would stop being infectious that day
That the family could safely rejoin the village that day
That the last of her rash would have faded by that day
context: Panum had pinned the gap between catching measles and the rash at about a fortnight: "thirteen to fourteen days intervene between the reception of the contagion and the eruption of the exanthem," and "the latent stage of measles of about fourteen days was so conspicuously constant, that many laymen had already made this observation." The isolated villages were his laboratory - in a city nobody could ever say a patient had been exposed once, on one known day. In his own words on what followed: "In Fuglefjord, on Osteroe, on account of my observations, I acquired the reputation of being able to prophesy." A falsifiable prediction, written on a calendar, in front of witnesses - which is the whole method in miniature, and something you can still do yourself with a household outbreak and a wall calendar. Source: Panum 1847 treatise (English translation) - https://s3.amazonaws.com/aspphwebassets/delta-omega/archives/PanumFaroeIslands.pdf

question: Thucydides survived the plague that struck Athens in 430 BC and wrote a careful account of what he saw in the others who came through it. In the joy of their own survival, he said, those Athenians half-hoped for something he called foolish. What did they hope?
answer: That they would never fall ill of anything again
choices: That they would never fall ill of anything again
That the plague would leave the city before winter
That their children would be born proof against it
That the gods had marked them out for something
context: The sentence runs straight on from his immunity observation: survivors "not only received the congratulations of others, but themselves also, in the elation of the moment, half entertained the vain hope that they were for the future safe from any disease whatsoever." In one breath Thucydides records the correct fact - you are not struck twice by THIS disease - and the wrong inference drawn from it. It is the first written case of over-reading a true finding, and it is 2,400 years old. Source: Thucydides, Book 2 ch. 51 (Crawley translation) - http://classics.mit.edu/Thucydides/pelopwar.2.second.html

question: Peter Ludvig Panum wanted to know, in the Faroe Islands measles of 1846, whether great age itself could shield a person from the disease. He found his test in villages the previous epidemic, in 1781, had never reached, where even the oldest had never had measles. What happened to the old people there?
answer: Every one of them caught measles
choices: Every one of them caught measles
Most of them escaped it
About half of them caught it
They caught it, but only mildly
context: Panum's own sentence is what turns an anecdote into a measurement: "a high age by no means lessened the susceptibility to measles, since, as far as I know, all the old people who had not gone through with measles in earlier life were attacked when they were exposed to infection; whereas certain young persons, although constantly exposed, were exempt." He found the same thing village by village: "there were, however, several houses and small villages that had not been invaded in 1781 and in these the older folk were attacked just as the others." Age did nothing. Having had the disease did everything. Panum was twenty-five, had qualified only the year before, and his title page reads "Candidate in Medicine and Surgery"; he stayed almost five months and personally treated about 1,000 of the roughly 6,000 cases. Source: Panum 1847 treatise (English translation) - https://s3.amazonaws.com/aspphwebassets/delta-omega/archives/PanumFaroeIslands.pdf

question: A girl catches a germ for the first time, and her body takes four to seven days to make any antibody, a protein built to lock onto that one germ. The first batch grips only loosely. When the same germ comes back, antibody arrives in one to three days and grips hard. How much of it does her body make the second time, compared with the first?
answer: A hundred to a thousand times as much
choices: A hundred to a thousand times as much
A thousand to ten thousand times as much
Ten to a hundred times as much
Two to ten times as much
context: A primary response is dominated by low-affinity IgM and peaks at seven to ten days - which is roughly how long you feel ill. A secondary response has a lag of only one to three days, switches straight to high-affinity IgG, and reaches antibody titres 100- to 1,000-fold higher. That is why you never notice the second attack: the fight is finished before the symptoms would have started. Source: Grokipedia, 'Immune system' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Immune_system

question: An old man beat an infection as a boy, and some of his plasma cells are still making antibody, the protein that locks onto one germ and marks it to be destroyed, at up to ten thousand molecules per second. The plasma cells from the illness itself lived only three to five days. How do these ones keep going for decades?
answer: They moved into survival niches in the bone marrow and never left
