choices: He had paired two kinds of glass whose colour errors cancel out.
He had ground the lens far thinner so the colours had less to cross.
He had stopped the lens down to a small hole at its very centre.
He had curved the two faces of the lens to quite different radii.
context: Hall built the first achromatic doublet by pairing crown glass with flint glass so that their colour errors cancelled. To hide it he sent the two lenses to different opticians, Edward Scarlett and James Mann — who both quietly subcontracted the same man, George Bass. Bass spotted what he was making, mentioned it to John Dollond in the late 1750s, and Dollond patented it in 1758. Newton's most famous wrong call came out of the very work that made his name: even he could declare a thing impossible and be beaten by a hobbyist with two sorts of glass. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achromatic_lens

question: Robert Hooke and Francis Bacon lent Isaac Newton the name experimentum crucis, 'the crucial experiment', and Newton used that very test to tear down Hooke's own account of light. What had Hooke argued light is, in his 1665 book Micrographia?
answer: pulses spreading through an ether that fills all space
choices: pulses spreading through an ether that fills all space
hard particles shot out in straight lines from bright bodies
a pressure pushed through a world packed solid with matter
thin films peeled off bodies and flying to the eye
context: Hooke argued in Micrographia (1665) that light is vibrations or pulses travelling through an ethereal medium, and in his 1672 critique he insisted colour arises from modifications of those waves during refraction, and that Newton's prism demonstrations did not disprove an undulatory account. It was a live, serious position, not a strawman — and the irony is that Hooke is credited with coining the Latin 'experimentum crucis' (after Francis Bacon's instantia crucis in Novum Organum), which Newton then hung on the experiment built to dismantle Hooke's own account of colour. Descartes' La Dioptrique (1637), for its part, treated light as pressure in a medium and assumed every ray refracts by the same amount. Christiaan Huygens and Ignace Pardies also wrote critiques of the 1672 letter. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimentum_crucis ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Hooke ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Opticks

question: Robert Hooke answered Isaac Newton's 1672 letter on colour the same week: he had performed such experiments himself years before, and they fitted his own account of light just as well. Newton was twenty-nine, with a book on light nearly finished. What did the quarrel make him do with that book?
answer: He shelved it for over thirty years, until Hooke was dead.
choices: He shelved it for over thirty years, until Hooke was dead.
He rushed it into print to answer Hooke within the year.
He rewrote it as a reply addressed to Hooke by name.
He handed it to the Royal Society to publish for him.
context: Stung, Newton withdrew from public debate and sat on his optical book. Hooke died on 3 March 1703; Newton was elected President of the Royal Society on 30 November 1703; Opticks appeared in 1704, published anonymously in London by Samuel Smith and Benjamin Walford with 19 folding plates engraved from Newton's own drawings. He wrote it in English rather than the Latin every European natural philosopher used — a deliberate choice to reach instrument makers and craftsmen, not just university men. A Latin edition, Optice, translated by Samuel Clarke under Newton's supervision, followed in 1706. LEGEND, and thinner than it sounds: it is widely repeated that Newton had Hooke's portrait removed or destroyed once he took the chair. What is documented is only that no authenticated portrait of Hooke survives, that a visitor saw portraits of Boyle and Hooke at the Society in 1710, and that when the Society moved house that year Hooke's was the only portrait to go missing. Sources: https://grokipedia.com/page/Opticks ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opticks ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hooke

question: A child names the colours of the rainbow and gets seven, in Isaac Newton's order. Newton first wrote down six bands, red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet, and then added indigo, between blue and violet, to make the count seven. Why did he want that seventh name?
answer: To make the colours match the notes of a musical scale.
choices: To make the colours match the notes of a musical scale.
To mark a seam he could see that other men had missed.
To answer a rival who had already published only six.
To give the dyers a name for the shade they worked in.
context: Newton thought seven a perfect number, tying the colours to the notes of a scale, the known planets and the days of the week. The spectrum itself is continuous, with no boundaries at all between one colour and the next — the seven names are a human labelling laid over a seamless band. Isaac Asimov later grumbled: 'it has never seemed to me that indigo is worth the dignity of being considered a separate color. To my eyes, it seems merely deep blue.' Gary Waldman has argued that Newton's 'indigo' is what we would call blue and his 'blue' what we would call blue-green or cyan; other scholars reject that reading, but nobody disputes that the count of seven was a choice. The same taste for harmony shows in the first colour wheel in history, in Opticks: Newton bent the spectrum into a circle with white at the centre and sized the segments unequally, to the intervals of a Dorian scale. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visible_spectrum ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigo ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_wheel

question: 'I was astonished, as I looked at a white wall through the prism, that it stayed white!' wrote Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, the poet. Colour, he argued against Isaac Newton for twenty years, is born at the boundary where light meets dark. A girl can test the quarrel by aiming a blue lamp and a yellow lamp at one white wall. What shows where the beams overlap?
answer: White, the two together looking like plain daylight.
choices: White, the two together looking like plain daylight.
Green, exactly as blue and yellow paint would give.
Grey, the two colours cancelling one another out.
Orange, the shade lying halfway between the lamps.
context: Mixing blue and yellow PAINT gives green; mixing blue and yellow LIGHT gives white, and this is exactly where Goethe's scheme fails. Wittgenstein judged the book to contain 'no experimentum crucis' and said 'nothing can be predicted by means of it.' But Goethe kept something real: his work on physiological colours — afterimages, simultaneous contrast, colour constancy and complementary pairs — anticipated Hering's opponent-process theory. He lost the physics and was doing perception, which Newton's spectrum never claimed to cover. TEST IT YOURSELF with two torches and coloured cellophane, or with the red, green and blue channels of any phone screen under a magnifier. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_Colours

question: Florence Nightingale added up the dead of the Crimean War, after her years at the British hospital at Scutari. Out of about 18,000 British deaths across the whole war, she showed, roughly 16,000 came from a single cause. What was that cause?
answer: Preventable disease
choices: Preventable disease
Bayonet and sabre wounds
Frostbite in the trenches
Starvation during the siege
context: Typhus, cholera and dysentery in the wards did the killing. The wounded and the frostbitten filled a fraction of the mortuary; the disease dead filled most of it. Source: Hektoen International, 'Scutari Crimean War Hospital'.

question: Florence Nightingale came back to London from the army hospital at Scutari wanting ministers and Queen Victoria to face the numbers, and she knew a plain table would put them to sleep. So in 1858 she drew a bold picture for people not used to figures. What was it?
answer: A colored circle divided into twelve monthly wedges
choices: A colored circle divided into twelve monthly wedges
A hand-drawn bar chart of monthly deaths at Scutari
A map of the hospital wards color-coded by ward
A lithograph of the Scutari mortuary at dawn
context: Her Diagram of the Causes of Mortality in the Army in the East was drawn as two polar-area charts, one per year, with blue for disease, red for wounds and black for other causes. Source: The Radiant Diagrams of Florence Nightingale, Friendly & Wainer.

question: A student checks Florence Nightingale's first polar chart, printed in 1858. Each month's line runs out from the centre in step with that month's death rate, yet the shading invites a reader to judge each month by its area. Nightingale soon caught the problem herself. What did the design do to the picture?
answer: It made the worst months look far worse, since area grows as the square of the length
choices: It made the worst months look far worse, since area grows as the square of the length
It made the worst months look milder, since area grows more slowly than the length
It made every month look the same size, since each kept the same slice angle
It muddled the order of the months, since the circle had no marked start
context: Hugh Small, the historian of her diagrams, found that in this first chart, which he calls the bat's wing, the length of each month's radial line was proportional to the death rate, while both the text and the look of the chart implied that the shaded area was. Area grows with the square of the length, so the bad months looked far worse than they were. Nightingale recognised the error, inserted an erratum slip, and in later documents replaced the chart with her famous wedge diagram, in which areas carry the counts. A student with graph paper can test the rule: draw one wedge twice as long as another at the same angle and it covers four times the paper. Source: Hugh Small, 'Florence Nightingale's Statistical Diagrams' (1998), york.ac.uk/depts/maths/histstat/small.htm.

question: Nightingale took what her Scutari numbers had taught her and turned it on Britain in peacetime. Her figures argued that a young man was safer as a civilian than in the army, because home barracks were killing men at nearly twice the civilian rate. What did her campaign win from the government?
answer: A Royal Commission on the Health of the Army
choices: A Royal Commission on the Health of the Army
A knighthood and a lifelong pension
A private audience with the Queen only
A ban on her further publications
context: Sidney Herbert chaired the 1857 commission; it reported in 1858 and produced sanitary construction codes, a military medical school and an army statistics office. She got the reform out of a diagram. Source: Rutgers, 'Florence Nightingale's Bar Chart'.

question: Ventilation, drainage, scrubbing, lime-washed walls, plenty of light: Florence Nightingale prescribed the right things at Scutari and in the barracks. Yet she held to the end of her active career to a theory of disease that a modern textbook does not endorse. Which theory did she trust?
answer: Foul air rising from filth and decay
choices: Foul air rising from filth and decay
An imbalance of the four bodily humours
A hereditary weakness in enlisted men
A curse settling on unlucky regiments
context: She distrusted contagion and championed the miasma theory. The ventilation and drainage she prescribed happened to be exactly what the (then unknown) bacteria hated. She got the right prescription from the wrong mechanism, and trusted the numbers over the theory. Source: Harvard 'Contagion' collection, Florence Nightingale 1820-1910.

question: William Farr, who ran Britain's death records and had built its first real system for sorting causes of death, worked the sums of Florence Nightingale's famous charts with her. Together they used their numbers to push for one specific change in hospitals. What change did their data call for?
answer: Better hygiene and sanitation
choices: Better hygiene and sanitation
More surgeons
Anaesthesia during surgery
Longer hospital stays
context: Farr, at the General Register Office, supplied the statistical technique; Nightingale supplied the political campaign and the pictures. The diagrams were as much his numbers as hers. Source: Science Museum Journal, 'A statistical campaign: Florence Nightingale and Harriet Martineau'.

question: Twelve science-lovers met at Gresham College in London in November 1660 and founded what became the Royal Society, the world's oldest science club still going today. In the 1660s its Fellows took up a short Latin motto, Nullius in verba, which the Society still uses on its coat of arms. What does that motto mean in plain English?
answer: Take nobody's word for it
choices: Take nobody's word for it
Knowledge itself is power
Nothing comes without effort
For the greater glory of God
context: The Royal Society was founded on 28 November 1660 after a lecture by Christopher Wren; its motto is 'Nullius in verba', which the Society itself renders as 'take nobody's word for it'. That instruction is roughly three and a half centuries old. Sources: https://royalsociety.org/about-us/who-we-are/history/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nullius_in_verba

question: Fellows of the young Royal Society lifted their motto in the 1660s from a Roman poet's book of Epistles, where the poet declares himself 'not bound to swear by the words of any master.' They cut it down to three Latin words: Nullius in verba. Which Roman poet wrote the line?
answer: Horace
choices: Horace
Virgil
Ovid
Catullus
context: The line is from Horace's Epistles, Book I, Epistle I, addressed to his patron Maecenas: 'Nullius addictus iurare in verba magistri'. John Evelyn was among the Fellows who chose it in the 1660s. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nullius_in_verba

question: A Latin student sets the Royal Society's motto beside its source, a Roman poet's line that reads literally 'not bound to swear by the words of a master.' The English version most people know today, 'take nobody's word for it,' is something else again, not a straight translation at all. What is that English version?
answer: An idiomatic English gloss written by the Society itself
choices: An idiomatic English gloss written by the Society itself
A tightened King James rendering of the same Latin line
The next line down in the same Horace epistle
The wording carved on the Society's original mace
context: A story about rigour cannot afford to blur its own translation: the Latin says one thing, the modern English is the Society's own paraphrase. Both are honest; they are not the same sentence. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nullius_in_verba

question: The Royal Society's Fellows set out in the 1660s what their Latin motto meant. Nullius in verba, 'on the word of no one,' said they would never just take a great man's word for a claim, however noble or learned or high-ranking he was. Every claim, they said, would be settled 'by an appeal to' what?
answer: Facts determined by experiment
choices: Facts determined by experiment
Consensus of the learned
Plain reading of scripture
Unaided light of reason
context: The Society's own formulation, written down in the 1660s -- roughly three and a half centuries before anyone was told to trust the science. Source: https://royalsociety.org/about-us/who-we-are/history/

question: Richard Feynman gave the commencement speech at Caltech in 1974, on scientific integrity. He named the first principle in one blunt line, and it pointed at the easiest person in the world for a scientist to fool. Who is that person?
answer: The scientist himself
choices: The scientist himself
The scientist's rivals
The scientist's critics
The scientist's sponsors
context: Feynman: 'The first principle is that you must not fool yourself -- and you are the easiest person to fool.' Nullius in verba turned inward: the first authority to distrust is one's own. Source: https://calteches.library.caltech.edu/51/2/CargoCult.htm

question: Hans Christian Oersted sent a current through a wire at an evening lecture in Copenhagen in April 1820, and a nearby compass needle swung away from north. No one had ever seen a current move a magnet before. How did the audience react?
answer: They barely reacted; the twitch was too feeble to impress.
choices: They barely reacted; the twitch was too feeble to impress.
They applauded, and the news left Copenhagen that week.
They accused him of hiding a magnet under the table.
They demanded he do it again before believing him.
context: Oersted, writing about himself in the third person: 'The magnetical needle, though included in a box, was disturbed; but as the effect was very feeble, and must, before its law was discovered, seem very irregular, the experiment made no strong impression on the audience.' The most consequential twitch in nineteenth-century physics went over in the room as a dud. Source: Oersted, The Edinburgh Encyclopaedia (1830), quoted in the Niels Bohr Institute's 'H. C. Oersted and the Discovery of Electromagnetism' (2019).

question: Writing up his live wire in 1820, Hans Christian Oersted had to coin a name for whatever filled the space around it, because the words 'magnetic field' did not exist. The Latin title of his pamphlet is built on that name. What did he call it?
answer: the conflict of electricity
choices: the conflict of electricity
the electric atmosphere
the galvanic effluvium
the imponderable fluid
context: His own words: 'To the effect which takes place in this conductor and in the surrounding space, we shall give the name of the conflict of electricity.' In Latin, conflictus electricus -- which is why the pamphlet is titled Experimenta circa effectum conflictus electrici in acum magneticam. Source: Oersted, 'Experiments on the Effect of a Current of Electricity on the Magnetic Needle', Annals of Philosophy 16 (Oct 1820), p. 273.

question: Wanting to know whether anything could stop the new effect, Oersted stacked barrier after barrier between his live wire and the compass needle, and the needle kept swinging every time. Then he shut it inside the most extreme shield he could rig, and it still swung. What was the shield?
answer: a brass box filled with water
choices: a brass box filled with water
a hollowed block of marble
a case packed with dry sand
a sealed jar of thick oil
context: 'The effect of the uniting wire passes to the needle through glass, metals, wood, water, resin, stoneware, stones; for it is not taken away by interposing plates of glass, metal or wood.' Oersted knew how strange this was: 'It is needless to observe that the transmission of effects through all these matters has never before been observed in electricity and galvanism.' His control run: needles of brass, glass and gum-lac did not move at all -- only magnetic ones did. Source: Oersted, Annals of Philosophy 16 (Oct 1820).

question: With a far stronger battery in July 1820, Hans Christian Oersted held a live wire above a compass needle and watched one pole swing west. He moved the same wire underneath the needle, with the current running the same way. What did that same pole do?
answer: It swung east, the opposite way.
choices: It swung east, the opposite way.
It swung west again, only further.
It swung west again, but half as far.
It settled back onto north and held.
context: Oersted gave readers a memory formula for it: 'the pole above which the negative electricity enters is turned to the west; under which, to the east.' Reverse the battery leads and everything reverses too -- the swing is bolted to the direction of the current. From the above-and-below opposition alone he reasoned his way to the shape of the force: 'we may likewise infer that this conflict performs circles; for it is the nature of a circle that the motions in opposite parts should have an opposite direction.' Source: Oersted, Annals of Philosophy 16 (Oct 1820).

question: Francois Arago told the Paris Academie des Sciences on 4 September 1820 what Hans Christian Oersted had done with a wire and a compass, and the room answered with open disbelief. Arago was back before the same members on 11 September. What did he do?
answer: He performed the experiment himself, there in the room.
choices: He performed the experiment himself, there in the room.
He handed a wire and a compass to his loudest critic.
He read Oersted's Latin pamphlet aloud in French.
He had the Academie appoint a commission to test it.
context: The French Physical Society's record of the 4 September session says Arago's report was met with 'incredulite et scepticisme'. A week later he stopped arguing and simply built the thing in front of the doubters. In November he went further and scattered iron filings around a live wire, where they arranged themselves into circles -- the invisible made visible. Source: Societe Francaise de Physique ephemeris, '4 septembre 1820'; Niels Bohr Institute, 'H. C. Oersted and the Discovery of Electromagnetism' (2019).

question: Hans Christian Oersted defended a doctoral dissertation in Copenhagen in 1799 with not one experiment in it. The whole thing argued over a philosopher's system of nature, one he had first met in lectures he sat through as a teenager. Twenty-one years later the same man swung a compass needle with a live wire. Whose system was it?
answer: Immanuel Kant, on the metaphysics that natural science rests on
choices: Immanuel Kant, on the metaphysics that natural science rests on
Friedrich Schelling, on the one world-soul that all nature shares
Rene Descartes, on the vortices that whirl the planets around
Gottfried Leibniz, on the monads that every material body contains
context: The dissertation was on Kant's Metaphysical Foundations of Natural Science. Oersted had sat through Professor Borge Riisbrigh's Kant lectures as a teenager, and the conviction never left him. In 1803 he wrote: 'Our physics, therefore, will no longer be a collection of fragments on motion, on heat, on air, on light, on electricity, on magnetism, and who knows what else, but with one system we shall embrace the entire world.' His own account in 1830 says he was led there not by experimental hints but 'by the philosophical principle, that all phenomena are produced by the same original power'. Source: Oersted, Materials for a Chemistry of the Nineteenth Century (1803) and The Edinburgh Encyclopaedia (1830), both quoted in the Niels Bohr Institute's 2019 study.

question: By his own account, Hans Christian Oersted had the needle test ready on his bench before he lectured one evening in April 1820, put there on purpose. The famous story has him stumble on it by chance, mid-lecture. What had he decided to do with it that evening?
answer: Skip it, and try the test another day.
choices: Skip it, and try the test another day.
Open with it, before touching the theory.
Save it for the end of the evening's lecture.
Let a student run it while he talked.
context: Oersted's own words, written of himself in the third person: 'The preparations for the experiments were made, but some accident having hindered him from trying it before the lecture, he intended to defer it to another opportunity; yet during the lecture, the probability of its success appeared stronger, so that he made the first experiment in the presence of the audience.' The only accident in the whole story is that he never got to rehearse -- so a man who had been predicting this result for years set the gear up, lost his nerve, then changed his mind in front of the class and did it live. He had put the demand into print back in 1813: 'it must be determined whether electricity in its most latent state has any action upon the magnet as such.' The lucky-accident version has a traceable pedigree: a 1913 article by Philip E. B. Jourdain was titled 'An Accident that Led to a Notable Discovery', and the historian R. C. Stauffer complained in 1957 that accounts were still marred by 'unwarranted emphasis on the role of chance'. Source: Oersted, The Edinburgh Encyclopaedia (1830), quoted in the Niels Bohr Institute's 'H. C. Oersted and the Discovery of Electromagnetism' (2019); Wikipedia, Hans Christian Oersted.

question: Oersted saw his compass needle stir beside a live wire in April 1820, and his printed pamphlet announcing it to Europe is dated 21 July. Textbook accounts often fill those three months with patient, systematic testing. His own later account says otherwise. What did he do between April and July?
answer: He set the experiment aside and did not touch it.
choices: He set the experiment aside and did not touch it.
He wrote to Paris asking Ampere to repeat it for him.
He toured German laboratories showing the effect off.
He drafted the pamphlet and sat on it until July.
context: In his own words: 'It may appear strange, that the discoverer made no further experiments upon the subject during three months; he himself finds it difficult enough to conceive it; but the extreme feebleness and seeming confusion of the phenomena in the first experiment, the remembrance of the numerous errors committed upon this subject by earlier philosophers, and particularly by his friend Ritter... may have determined him to delay his researches.' The friend was Johann Wilhelm Ritter, whose failures on this exact question had made Oersted gun-shy. In July he came back with a far bigger battery. Source: Oersted, The Edinburgh Encyclopaedia (1830), in the Niels Bohr Institute's 2019 study; Wikipedia, Hans Christian Oersted.

question: A battery of twenty copper troughs made the needle's swing unmistakable when Oersted rebuilt the experiment in July 1820. Before he printed a word of it, he took one precaution that put his critics' likeliest objection out of reach. What did he do?
answer: He repeated every result in front of six invited observers.
choices: He repeated every result in front of six invited observers.
He had the university seal his apparatus in a locked cabinet.
He wrote the whole procedure out as numbered instructions.
He tested three separate compasses from three makers.
context: He printed their names in the pamphlet: his friend Esmarck, Mr Wleugel (head of the Pilots), Mr Hauch, Professor Reinhardt of Natural History, Professor Jacobsen of Medicine, and the chemist Dr Zeise. His line: 'I had often made experiments by myself; but every fact which I had observed was repeated in the presence of these gentlemen.' He built his own replication into the paper. Source: Oersted, Annals of Philosophy 16 (Oct 1820); Niels Bohr Institute (2019).

question: Andre-Marie Ampere stood before the Paris Academie des Sciences on 25 September 1820, three weeks after it first heard of Oersted's needle, with no compass and no lodestone anywhere on the bench. His result turned one twitching needle into a whole new science. What did he show the members?
answer: Two live wires, side by side, pulling on each other.
choices: Two live wires, side by side, pulling on each other.
A live wire dragging an uncharged wire toward itself.
A live wire pulling a copper coin across the table.
A live wire twisting a second wire into a tight coil.
context: Run the two currents the same way and the wires attract; run them opposite and they repel. Magnetism with no magnet in it. Accuracy note: Ampere did not coin the word 'electrodynamics' that September, as many accounts say -- it arrives in the title of his 1826-27 memoir on the mathematical theory of electro-dynamic phenomena. The rest of that autumn: Biot and Savart announced how the force falls off with distance on 30 October, and in November Arago made the field visible with iron filings. Source: Niels Bohr Institute (2019); Wikipedia, Andre-Marie Ampere; Wikipedia, Ampere's force law.

question: Hans Christian Oersted slid his live wire from the east side of the compass needle across to the west side, keeping it parallel to the needle the whole way, and compared what the needle did from each position. He wrote that this single move ruled one explanation out for good. Which one?
answer: That the wire and the needle simply pull on each other.
choices: That the wire and the needle simply pull on each other.
That the wire turns the needle toward its battery end.
That the wire makes the needle lie along its own length.
That the wire drags the needle toward its thicker end.
context: Oersted's sentence: 'Hence the effect cannot be ascribed to attraction; for the same pole of the magnetic needle, which approaches the uniting wire, while placed on its east side, ought to recede from it when on the west side, if these declinations depended on attractions and repulsions.' The same pole swung the same way from both sides. A pull would have reversed when he crossed over; this did not -- which is the fingerprint of a force that runs in circles around the wire instead of pointing at it. He killed the other suspects with other tests: barriers of glass, metal, wood and water did not block the effect, and needles of brass, glass and gum-lac never moved at all. Source: Oersted, Annals of Philosophy 16 (Oct 1820).

question: A student runs Hans Christian Oersted's experiment at home one evening. She lays a compass flat, holds a straight wire just above it, lined up north-south, and touches the wire briefly across an AA cell through a resistor: the needle swings aside. Then she turns the wire a quarter turn so it lies east-west, straight across the needle, and touches the cell again. What does the needle do?
answer: Nothing at all -- it stays where it is.
choices: Nothing at all -- it stays where it is.
It swings the opposite way from before.
It swings aside twice as far as before.
It turns to lie along the wire above it.
context: Parallel gives the biggest swing; square across gives nothing at all, because the field circles the wire. Physicists at the Niels Bohr Institute point out the oddity that a single AA cell today produces 'a dramatic effect' while Oersted's twenty-trough acid battery produced a feeble one, and suspect his April geometry was simply off. Even at his best the needle turned only about 45 degrees with the wire three-quarters of an inch away -- it settles where the wire's circling field balances the Earth's. Keep the contact to a second or two: a bare wire across a cell gets hot. Source: Niels Bohr Institute (2019); Oersted, Annals of Philosophy 16 (Oct 1820).

question: A friend asked Andre-Marie Ampere in February 1821 how nobody had thought to hold a compass near a live wire in the twenty years since Volta built the first battery. Ampere named the thing that had made the test unthinkable, and said the prohibition was so total that Arago's news was rejected 'just as was the idea of stones falling from the sky'. What had blocked everyone?
answer: Coulomb's hypothesis about what magnetism is.
choices: Coulomb's hypothesis about what magnetism is.
Volta's rule about how long a pile can last.
Gilbert's claim that only iron can be magnetic.
Newton's law of forces acting at a distance.
context: Ampere's letter, in full on the point: 'I believe we can determine the reason which was Coulomb's hypothesis as to the nature of the magnetic action; we believed that this hypothesis was a fact; it absolutely excluded any idea of interaction between electricity and the so-called magnetic wire.' A hypothesis mistaken for a fact, in one line of 1821 handwriting. The irony: Ampere himself had declared in 1802 that electricity and magnetism were two different fluids acting independently -- he was defending the wall he would later tear down. Source: Ampere to Jacques Roux-Bordier, 21 February 1821, reproduced and translated in the Niels Bohr Institute's 2019 study.

question: Oersted wrote in his pamphlet that celebrated natural philosophers, scientists in the language of the day, had tried the same test years before him and got nothing at all: their needles never moved. In a single clause he named what had gone wrong for them. What was it?
answer: Their circuit was left open, so no current flowed.
choices: Their circuit was left open, so no current flowed.
Their needle was pinned in its case, so it could not swing.
Their wire lay far across the bench, so nothing reached it.
Their battery had run flat, so the wire carried nothing.
context: The clause: 'the galvanic circle must be complete, and not open, which last method was tried in vain some years ago by very celebrated philosophers.' Before Volta built his pile in 1800, 'electricity' meant static electricity -- charge sitting still on a conductor, which does nothing whatever to a compass. You need a current. And the wall this broke was two centuries old: William Gilbert's De Magnete (1600) had carefully separated magnetism, which he found in iron and lodestone, from the amber-rubbing effect he named 'electric', after the Greek elektron. Source: Oersted, Annals of Philosophy 16 (Oct 1820); Niels Bohr Institute (2019); Grokipedia, Electromagnetism.

question: Georg Simon Ohm set out in the early 1820s to measure exactly how much current a given push of voltage sends through a wire. He was a schoolteacher at a Jesuit school in Cologne with no lab budget at all, and no money for delicate equipment. What did he do about it?
answer: He built his own apparatus and drew his own wire.
choices: He built his own apparatus and drew his own wire.
He borrowed a full electrical laboratory from the University of Berlin.
He was granted a state research fund by the Prussian government.
He inherited the instruments of the recently deceased Alessandro Volta.
context: Ohm arrived at the Jesuit Gymnasium of Cologne on 11 September 1817 as a math and physics teacher. There was no grant and no lab; every measurement in his 1825-26 papers was made on instruments he built himself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Ohm .

question: Georg Ohm's readings would not settle as he tried, in the 1820s, to pin down the relation between electrical push (voltage) and current. The problem was not the wire. It was the power source itself. Which kind of source was letting him down?
answer: A voltaic pile whose output sagged noticeably as it ran.
choices: A voltaic pile whose output sagged noticeably as it ran.
A friction machine that only sparked when the room was dry.
A Leyden jar that discharged the moment he closed the circuit.
An electrophorus that lost its charge with each spark drawn.
context: Volta's stack of copper and zinc discs was the standard current source of the 1820s, but the chemistry drifted as it ran and no two readings taken an hour apart agreed. Ohm's friend Johann Christian Poggendorff pointed him at a way out. Source: hackaday.com/2021/07/20/the-story-behind-ohms-law .

question: Johann Poggendorff told Georg Ohm to try a steadier source: a bar of bismuth soldered to a bar of copper, a pair Thomas Seebeck had shown could drive a steady current. What did Ohm do with the two junctions to keep the source rock-steady all day?
answer: He held one junction in boiling water and the other in melting ice.
choices: He held one junction in boiling water and the other in melting ice.
He rubbed one junction with amber and left the other in the dark.
He wrapped both junctions in silk and shielded them from any draught.
He kept both junctions in the same beaker of warm mercury.
context: The Seebeck effect gave a voltage that depended only on the temperature difference between the two junctions. With one held at 100 C and the other at 0 C by physics itself, Ohm's source drifted no more than the freezing point of water did. The instrument is why the law was findable at all. Source: egr.msu.edu/~wierzba/ohm.pdf .

question: Georg Ohm borrowed the mathematics for his rule of current in a wire, in the 1820s, straight from a problem Joseph Fourier had solved a few years earlier in a completely different corner of physics. He did not build the rule from first ideas about electric charge. What problem had Fourier solved?
answer: The flow of heat along a metal bar.
choices: The flow of heat along a metal bar.
The vibrations of a plucked violin string.
The orbit of a comet returning to the Sun.
The refraction of light through a glass prism.
context: In Fourier's picture, temperature difference drove heat and the length of the bar resisted the flow. Ohm swapped temperature for voltage and heat for current and got the same shape of equation -- his 1827 book Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet is Fourier's method wearing an electrical hat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Ohm .

question: Georg Ohm stated in his 1827 book, in words, that current is proportional to the driving voltage and inversely proportional to the resistance, so that doubling a wire's length halves the current. Critics in Germany were not impressed. What sneering phrase did they famously use for the book?
answer: A web of naked fancies.
choices: A web of naked fancies.
A curious little algebra of sparks.
The dream of a Cologne schoolmaster.
An arithmetic unworthy of Newton.
context: The idealist school of German physics considered a mathematical treatment of electricity un-physical, and 'a web of naked fancies' is the standard rendering of their verdict. Ohm's own Cologne gymnasium did not value the work; he resigned and spent years tutoring in Berlin before the Royal Society awarded him the Copley Medal in 1841 and Munich finally gave him a chair in 1852. He died two years later. Source: hackaday.com/2021/07/20/the-story-behind-ohms-law .

question: Georg Ohm showed that the current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it, and generations of students have been told this is a law of nature. It is not: it holds only for some materials, only under some conditions. The coloured stripes on every resistor are still read in the unit named after him. On which of these does the relation hold cleanly?
answer: A length of copper wire held at steady temperature.
choices: A length of copper wire held at steady temperature.
The tungsten filament of an incandescent lamp as it heats.
A semiconductor diode with voltage applied both ways.
The neon gas inside a glowing discharge tube.
context: Ohm's relation is an empirical description of ordinary metals at fixed temperature, and it is a very good one. It fails for a filament (resistance climbs sharply as the wire glows), for a diode (current flows in one direction and almost nothing the other way), and for gas in a discharge tube (a hard-to-strike arc that then runs at almost fixed voltage). Knowing where it breaks is knowing more than the law. Source: phys.libretexts.org University Physics II ch. 9.5 .

question: Investigators chasing uranium-235 missing from ore dug at Oklo, in Gabon, suspected theft in 1972, and learned instead that pockets of the ore had run as natural nuclear reactors about 1.7 billion years ago, with no human help. Nothing like it could start up on Earth today, because the fuel itself has changed. What was different about natural uranium 1.7 billion years ago?
answer: It was about 3 percent U-235, the same level a modern power reactor is fuelled with
choices: It was about 3 percent U-235, the same level a modern power reactor is fuelled with
It was purer than any uranium found on Earth today, at nearly 100 percent U-235
It came bound to a rare isotope of water that no longer exists on Earth
It contained plutonium as a natural admixture, which today has entirely decayed
context: U-235 (half-life ~704 million years) decays faster than U-238 (~4.47 billion). Over the last two billion years the U-235 fraction of natural uranium has fallen roughly fivefold, from ~3 percent to today's ~0.72 percent. The planet has simply run out of the right fuel. Source: mragheb.com, Natural Nuclear Reactors: The Oklo Phenomenon.

question: A geochemist reads the ruthenium in a sample from the Oklo ore zones and finds that 27 to 30 percent of it is ruthenium-99, more than double the natural share of about 12.7 percent. What extra source of ruthenium-99 does that surplus record?
answer: Technetium-99 produced by fission, which decayed to ruthenium-99
choices: Technetium-99 produced by fission, which decayed to ruthenium-99
A rare form of platinum from a comet impact enriching the local rock
Slow neutron capture by ordinary ruthenium already present in the ore
Cosmic-ray spallation of molybdenum atoms in exposed rock
context: Technetium-99 is one of fission's characteristic products; it decays into Ru-99. Neodymium in the same rock also gives it away - Oklo neodymium is under 6 percent Nd-142, where ordinary Nd is about 27 percent. No hypothesis except natural fission produces both patterns. Source: mragheb.com, Natural Nuclear Reactors: The Oklo Phenomenon.

question: Modellers reconstructed a pulse rhythm for the Oklo reactors: roughly 30 minutes on, then 2.5 hours off, repeated for a few hundred thousand years. Nobody observed it. They read it from something specific still held in the rock, and only one geochemical clock preserves that kind of timing over a billion years. Which one?
answer: Xenon isotopes trapped in aluminium phosphate minerals in the reactor zones
choices: Xenon isotopes trapped in aluminium phosphate minerals in the reactor zones
Argon-40 accumulated in muscovite mica flakes above the ore
Helium bubbles in quartz veins cutting through the deposit
Uranium-lead ratios read from zircon crystals in the host rock
context: Xenon-136 forms fast and diffuses out while the reactor is hot; other xenon isotopes arrive later from iodine decay, once the water and heat are gone, and get frozen in. The isotope mix in the aluminium phosphates records the on-off cycle directly. Source: sciencedirect.com, Modelling the Short-Term and Long-Term Behaviour of the Oklo natural reactor.

question: A student holds a diamond in one hand and a pencil in the other. The diamond scratches every other mineral on Earth; the pencil's grey core smears off on her thumb. Atom by atom, both are one element, differently arranged. Which element is it?
answer: Carbon
choices: Carbon
Silicon
Boron
Sulfur
context: Diamond and graphite are allotropes — the chemists' word for one element built into different structures. In diamond every carbon is covalently bonded to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement; in graphite, to only three. Nothing else is present in either. Carbon's allotrope family also includes graphene (a single sheet), carbon nanotubes, fullerenes, amorphous carbon (charcoal, soot, carbon black), lonsdaleite and carbyne. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Diamond' and 'Allotropes of carbon'.

question: Miners at Borrowdale in Cumbria cut a soft black mineral in the 1560s, and its first name was plumbago, lead ore. English still says 'pencil lead', German Bleistift, Irish peann luaidhe: all three still name the metal. What is a pencil core made of?
answer: Graphite powder, mixed with clay and fired.
choices: Graphite powder, mixed with clay and fired.
Powdered lead, bound with soft beeswax.
Charcoal, ground fine and set in resin.
Soot, pressed into rods with gum arabic.
context: No pencil has ever contained a single atom of lead; the 400-year-old error is fossilised in half of Europe's languages. The Borrowdale find, around 1565, is still the only large deposit of graphite pure and solid enough to saw into sticks. When it ran short, Nicolas-Jacques Conté in 1795 mixed powdered graphite with clay, formed rods and fired them in a kiln — and found that varying the graphite-to-clay ratio varied the hardness. That ratio is what the H and B grades on a pencil still record. Abraham Gottlob Werner named the mineral 'graphite' in 1789, from the Greek graphein, to write or draw. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Pencil' and 'Graphite'.

question: A chemist heats a diamond past about 800 °C. The stone sits alone at the top of the mineral hardness scale, and for centuries people took that to mean indestructible, yet at that heat it stops being a diamond. What happens to it?
answer: It catches fire and burns, leaving no ash behind.
choices: It catches fire and burns, leaving no ash behind.
It melts into a clear liquid, leaving a glassy bead.
It crumbles into grey grit, leaving a small heap.
It shatters into shards, leaving a fine white dust.
context: Hardness and durability are different properties. Diamond resists scratching better than anything else in nature, and it is also flammable: in pure oxygen its ignition point runs from 690 °C to 840 °C, and even in ordinary air, above roughly 400 °C at atmospheric pressure the surface structure begins to change into graphite. Burning carbon leaves nothing behind to sweep up — it all departs as gas. This is the fact every experiment on the nature of diamond was built on: you cannot analyse what you cannot take apart. Source: Wikipedia, 'Diamond'.

question: A teacher draws one carbon atom from deep inside a diamond on the board. Carbon builds a whole family of allotropes, one element in many structures with nothing else present, and the structure decides everything about the stuff. How is that atom held in place?
answer: It grips four neighbours at once, in a three-dimensional cage.
choices: It grips four neighbours at once, in a three-dimensional cage.
It grips three neighbours at once, in flat stacked sheets.
It grips two neighbours at once, in long unbranched chains.
It grips no fixed neighbour, in a sea of roaming electrons.
context: Each carbon in diamond is bonded to four others at the corners of a tetrahedron, 0.1545 nm apart, in a lattice that repeats in all three directions with no easy plane to slide along. That is where the hardness comes from: diamond stands alone at 10 on the Mohs scale, and in nature nothing scratches it but another diamond — yet the carbon atom itself has nothing to do with it, since the same atom makes the soft grey stuff in a pencil. The three rejected options are all real chemistry: graphite lays its carbons in flat stacked sheets of three, carbyne is a chain of carbons, and metals do share a sea of roaming electrons (amorphous carbon — charcoal, soot — has no long-range order at all). That same four-bond capacity, plus carbon's unusual willingness to bond to itself in chains and rings, is why over ten million carbon compounds are known and why life is built on carbon rather than silicon. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Diamond'; Grokipedia, 'Diamond cubic', 'Carbon-based life', 'Catenation'.

question: A boy drags a pencil across a page and grey stays behind on the paper. The core is graphite, a form of pure carbon in which every atom bonds to just three neighbours. At the atomic scale, what has just moved from tip to page?
answer: Whole flat layers of atoms, sliding off intact.
choices: Whole flat layers of atoms, sliding off intact.
Single atoms, torn loose from the crystal.
Fine dust, crumbled from broken crystal edges.
The clay binder, softened by the hand's warmth.
context: Three bonds per atom lay the carbons out in flat hexagonal sheets — a honeycomb lattice — stacked one above the next. Within a sheet the carbons are locked tight. Between the sheets there is only a feeble van der Waals attraction across a 0.335 nm gap, so the layers glide past one another and transfer wholesale onto the fibres of the paper. The same gliding is why graphite works as a dry lubricant — and why writing is, physically, just sheets of carbon changing address. Source: Wikipedia, 'Graphite'.

question: Richard Smalley and Harold Kroto aimed a laser at a spinning graphite disc at Rice University in Texas in 1985, trying to copy a chemistry seen far out in space. Their machine kept giving back the same striking signal: 60 carbon atoms stuck together in one neat piece. What shape did the 60 carbons form?
answer: A hollow cage of hexagons and pentagons, like a football.
choices: A hollow cage of hexagons and pentagons, like a football.
A long straight chain, like a string of glass beads.
A flat single sheet, like a scrap of chicken wire.
A rolled-up tube, capped off at both of its ends.
context: Twenty hexagons and twelve pentagons — a truncated icosahedron about 1.01 nm across, average bond length 0.14 nm. Harold Kroto named it buckminsterfullerene after Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes had given him the clue to the structure. 'C60: Buckminsterfullerene', by Kroto, Heath, O'Brien, Curl and Smalley, ran in Nature on 14 November 1985; Curl, Kroto and Smalley took the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. For five years C60 existed only as a peak on a chart — nobody had enough of it to hold — until Wolfgang Krätschmer, Konstantinos Fostiropoulos and Donald Huffman struck an electric arc between graphite electrodes in helium in 1989–90 and produced the soot by the gram. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Buckminsterfullerene', 'Harold Kroto'.

question: Antoine Lavoisier and his fellow chemists turned a great burning lens, about 89 cm across, on diamonds under a glass bell jar over water in Paris in 1772, and the stones at the focus shrank away. Lavoisier then tested the air inside the jar with limewater. What had the air gained?
answer: Fixed air, the gas a burning coal gives off
choices: Fixed air, the gas a burning coal gives off
Inflammable air, the gas iron gives off in acid
Vital air, the gas that keeps a candle burning
Marine acid air, the gas from salt and vitriol
context: The limewater turned cloudy, the classic sign of fixed air, the gas now called carbon dioxide. Lavoisier's 1772 report to the Academy concluded that 'the air in which one has evaporated diamond acquires at least in part the properties of fixed air', and the water level inside the bell jar had risen. Fixed air was already known from burning charcoal and from breath, so the diamond had turned into the same gas a glowing coal gives off. The test is easy to repeat: breathe out through a straw into limewater and it clouds the same way. The 1772 burning-lens campaign ran 192 experiments between 14 August and 17 October. Sources: Gemmological Association of Australia, 'The early history of synthetic diamond' (gem.org.au); Sztejnberg, 'Priestley, Scheele, Lavoisier, and the Burning Lenses', Revista CENIC 2019; Wikipedia, 'Diamond'.

question: A girl draws one thick dark pencil line at the kitchen table, clips a coin cell to it at one point and a light-emitting diode (LED) at another, then slides one clip along the line to change the gap. Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon; only the bonds differ. What does she see?
answer: The LED lights, and dims as the gap between the clips grows.
choices: The LED lights, and dims as the gap between the clips grows.
The LED lights, and brightens as the gap between the clips grows.
The LED lights just as brightly at every gap she tries.
The LED stays dark at every gap she tries: graphite blocks current.
context: Graphite's fourth electron is delocalised across the whole sheet — the same roaming that chemists call aromaticity — so each sheet conducts, and a pencil line is simply a resistor whose resistance grows with its length. Conduction perpendicular to the sheets is about a thousand times worse than within them. Diamond, with every electron tied into a bond, has a 5.47 eV band gap and a resistivity of 10^13–10^16 ohm-cm. Practical note: on a 9 V battery, put a small resistor in series to protect the LED, and press hard enough to lay down a really dark line. Sources: Science Museum Group Learning, 'Graphite Circuits'; University of Washington Clean Energy Institute, 'Draw a Circuit: Fun with Graphite'; Grokipedia, 'Material properties of diamond'.

question: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov lifted a single sheet of carbon, one atom thick, off a crystal of laboratory graphite in Manchester in 2004 and set it down on a silicon wafer. It was graphene, the first single sheet anyone had isolated, and a Nobel Prize in Physics came six years later. The tool that did it cost almost nothing. What was it?
answer: Ordinary sticky tape, pressed on and peeled off again and again.
choices: Ordinary sticky tape, pressed on and peeled off again and again.
A rubber eraser, rubbed over the crystal until flakes lifted.
A razor blade, drawn along the crystal at a very shallow angle.
A jet of compressed air, played across the crystal's edge.
context: Formally it is micro-mechanical cleavage; everyone calls it the Scotch tape technique. The flakes came off highly oriented pyrolytic graphite onto a thin silicon-dioxide layer on a silicon wafer, and the paper — Novoselov, Geim, Morozov and colleagues, 'Electric Field Effect in Atomically Thin Carbon Films' — ran in Science, volume 306, page 666, in October 2004. It was not funded work. Geim's lab spent about ten percent of its time on 'Friday evening experiments', long shots unrelated to any grant; in the four years leading to graphene those sessions produced exactly one other success, gecko tape in 2003, and before that the levitation of a live frog in a 16-tesla magnet, which won Geim the 2000 Ig Nobel Prize. He is the only person alive holding both an Ig Nobel and a Nobel. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of graphene', 'Andre Geim'; Wikipedia, 'Graphene'.

question: Smithson Tennant sealed powdered diamond in a gold tube in 1797 with nitre, a salt that gives off oxygen when it is heated, fired the tube and measured the gas that came off. Nobody had yet proved what a diamond is, and that measurement on its own proved nothing. What did he do next?
answer: He ran the whole procedure again on an equal weight of charcoal.
choices: He ran the whole procedure again on an equal weight of charcoal.
He ran the whole procedure again on an equal weight of powdered glass.
He ran the whole procedure again with twice the quantity of nitre.
He ran the whole procedure again with the gold tube left empty.
context: Equal weights of diamond and charcoal, run through the same apparatus, gave exactly the same quantity of exactly the same gas. Tennant's verdict, in 'On the Nature of the Diamond', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London vol. 87, pp. 123–127, read in 1797: diamond 'consists entirely of charcoal, differing from the usual state of that substance only by its crystallized form.' Note what turned a suspicion into a measurement — not the burning, but the second run. Burning one substance tells you little; burning it beside a known substance of equal weight, in the same apparatus, is a comparison, and comparison is what settles arguments. Source: Royal Society, Philosophical Transactions.

question: James Hone of Columbia was on the team that measured graphene, a single sheet of carbon, as the strongest material ever tested, at 130 gigapascals. He put that number into a picture anyone could hold. What did he say it would take to break through a graphene film as thick as kitchen cling wrap?
answer: An elephant, balanced on the point of a pencil.
choices: An elephant, balanced on the point of a pencil.
A whale, resting on the flat of one hand.
A locomotive, standing on a single dinner plate.
A church bell, set down on the head of a nail.
context: Hone's exact line: 'It would take an elephant, balanced on a pencil, to break through a sheet of graphene the thickness of Saran Wrap.' The measurement — Lee, Wei, Kysar and Hone, Science, 2008 — also gives graphene a Young's modulus of about 1 TPa. It is absurdly light with it: one square metre weighs 0.762 mg, so the Nobel Foundation's illustration has a one-square-metre graphene hammock supporting a 4 kg cat while weighing about as much as one of that cat's whiskers. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Graphene'; Scientific American, 'Balancing Act'.

question: Harold Kroto came from Sussex to Rice University in September 1985 to borrow a machine that vaporised solids with a laser. He was not hunting a new form of carbon; he was chasing a puzzle from space. He had built long carbon-chain molecules in the lab, and skywatchers had found those same chains, in surprising amounts, somewhere out there. Where?
answer: In the outer atmospheres of ageing red giant stars.
choices: In the outer atmospheres of ageing red giant stars.
In the ice particles that make up the rings of Saturn.
In the polar caps of Mars, beneath the frozen surface.
In the tail of a comet, sampled as it rounded the Sun.
context: Kroto and Walton had synthesised long linear carbon chains at Sussex; radio-astronomy work with Canadian astronomers then found those same unusual carbonaceous species in large abundances in interstellar space and around carbon-rich red giants. Kroto went to Rice to reproduce that stellar chemistry in a machine — and the machine handed him something nobody had gone looking for at all. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Harold Kroto', 'Buckminsterfullerene'.

question: A copywriter named Frances Gerety wrote 'A Diamond Is Forever' late one night in 1947 for De Beers. At everyday temperature and pressure, though, graphite is carbon's lower-energy form, so every diamond is on its way to becoming pencil lead. The trip takes millions to billions of years. What holds it up that long?
answer: Rebuilding every bond in the lattice needs a huge push of energy.
choices: Rebuilding every bond in the lattice needs a huge push of energy.
Diamond's surface oxidises to a graphite skin that seals it.
The pressure that formed it is still locked inside the stone.
Nitrogen atoms trapped inside the lattice pin the structure.
context: At 298 K the standard free-energy change for diamond → graphite is about −2.9 kJ/mol, so graphite is the stable phase at everyday conditions and diamond is merely metastable. It never arrives because the kinetic barrier is enormous: every atom's four bonds would have to break and re-form into three, which puts the conversion on a timescale of millions to billions of years. Only above about 4,500 K does diamond convert rapidly. Gerety wrote the line at N. W. Ayer & Son in Philadelphia; it first ran in 1948, and Advertising Age crowned it slogan of the century in 1999. A diamond is not forever — it is just very, very slow. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Diamond', 'Mary Frances Gerety'; Chemistry LibreTexts, 'Gibbs Free Energy and Work, Kinetic Metastability'.

question: A jeweller touches a heated probe to a stone and tells a real diamond from a good imitation in about a second. Diamond carries heat away faster than any other solid known, over five times copper's rate. In a metal, heat rides on loose electrons, but diamond has none at all and is one of the finest electrical insulators there is. What carries the heat through a diamond?
answer: Vibrations of the whole lattice, racing along the bonds.
choices: Vibrations of the whole lattice, racing along the bonds.
Infrared light, bouncing from one atom to the next.
Ripples running through the atoms' magnetic spins.
The atoms themselves, drifting slowly through the crystal.
context: Those travelling lattice vibrations are called phonons. Diamond's stiff, light, near-perfectly ordered bond network gives them high velocities, very little anharmonic scattering and long mean free paths, so heat crosses the crystal faster than it crosses copper — while every electron stays locked in a bond, leaving the crystal an insulator. Single-crystal values run roughly 900–2,320 W/m·K against copper's 400. Splitting the two carriers apart is the whole trick: in a metal they are the same particles, in diamond they are not. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Material properties of diamond', 'Diamond cubic'; Wikipedia, 'Diamond'.

question: A chemist lays a pencil beside a diamond. Diamond scratches every mineral on Earth and graphite gives way against a sheet of paper, and bond length is a fair guide to bond strength: the shorter the bond, the stronger the grip. Each carbon bond in diamond measures 0.154 nanometres. What do the same measurements give for two carbons inside a single graphite sheet?
answer: 0.142 nanometres — shorter than diamond's, and stronger.
choices: 0.142 nanometres — shorter than diamond's, and stronger.
0.154 nanometres — precisely the same as diamond's.
0.168 nanometres — longer than diamond's, and weaker.
0.335 nanometres — far longer, and far weaker.
context: This is the fact that kills the obvious explanation. Graphite is NOT soft because its bonds are weak — inside a sheet they are the stronger of the two, and one such sheet is described as probably the strongest two-dimensional network structure known. Bonding to three neighbours instead of four puts 33% s-character into each bond against diamond's 25%, contracting it, and a shared cloud of electrons stabilises it further; the length lands between a pure single bond (0.1544 nm) and a double bond (0.1334 nm). Graphite is soft because the sheets are held to each other by nothing stronger than van der Waals attraction across a 0.335 nm gap, and so they slide. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Graphite'; Britannica, 'Carbon — Structure of carbon allotropes'; Asbury Advanced Materials, 'Graphite 101'.

question: James Herrick, a Chicago doctor, took in a twenty-year-old dental student from Grenada, Walter Clement Noel, in December 1904. Noel was pale, out of breath and sore with leg ulcers. Herrick handed the case to his resident, Ernest Irons, who put Noel's blood under the microscope and saw a shape no textbook of the day showed. What did Irons see on the slide?
answer: Red cells drawn out into long curved sickle shapes
choices: Red cells with no nucleus and no shape at all
Red cells drawn out into long curved sickle shapes
Red cells clumped tightly around dark specks of parasite
Red cells swollen to twice their normal round diameter
context: Noel was admitted to Chicago's Presbyterian Hospital in December 1904, and Herrick published the case in 1910 in the Archives of Internal Medicine as Peculiar Elongated and Sickle-Shaped Red Blood Corpuscles in a Case of Severe Anemia. It named a disease by the shape of the cell, four decades before anyone could say why the shape appeared. The resident Ernest Irons drew the sickles at the microscope; the attending Herrick wrote the paper. Sources: https://scinfo.org/2016/06/14/early-history-of-sickle-cell-disease/ ; Wikipedia, 'Sickle cell disease'.

question: Linus Pauling and his Caltech team pushed haemoglobin from healthy people and from sickle-cell patients across a gel with an electric field in 1949. The two proteins drifted at different speeds, because the sickle version carried a slightly stronger positive charge. It was the first time a human illness had been tied to one faulty protein. What did Pauling call the illness in the title of his paper?
answer: A molecular disease
choices: A proteinopathy
A molecular disease
A charge-defect anaemia
An isoform disorder
context: The paper, 'Sickle Cell Anemia, a Molecular Disease', appeared in Science on 25 November 1949 (Pauling, Itano, Singer, Wells) and coined the term: a whole human illness traced to a single wrong molecule. It was the first time anyone had causally linked a specific abnormal protein to a specific disease. Vernon Ingram narrowed the defect to the single amino-acid swap in 1956. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sickle_Cell_Anemia,_a_Molecular_Disease

question: Spots of chopped haemoglobin spread across a paper sheet in Vernon Ingram's Cambridge laboratory in 1956, driven one way by an electric flow and the other by chemistry. Ingram, working under Max Perutz, was hunting the exact place where sickle haemoglobin differed from normal, and the two patterns matched except for one spot in the wrong place. What did he call his grid of spots?
answer: A fingerprint
choices: A signature
A fingerprint
A profile
A snapshot
context: Ingram's technique, still called peptide fingerprinting, treats each spot as one small piece of the protein; two proteins that differ anywhere show a different spot somewhere on the sheet. Normal and sickle haemoglobin gave identical fingerprints except for one spot. The whole illness was traced to a single peptide, then within that peptide to a single amino acid. Source: https://www.genome.gov/25520257/online-education-kit-1956-cause-of-disease-traced-to-alteration

question: Vernon Ingram traced sickle-cell disease to one changed link in 1956: position 6 of the beta chain of haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein of the blood. In the DNA behind that link, a single letter had shifted, and the code GAG had become GTG. Which amino acid swap does that base change make?
answer: Valine has replaced glutamic acid
choices: Lysine has replaced arginine
Glutamic acid has replaced valine
Valine has replaced glutamic acid
Serine has replaced threonine
context: The codon GAG codes for glutamic acid, a water-loving amino acid with a negative side chain; the codon GTG codes for valine, a greasy amino acid with no charge at all. One letter out of three billion in the human genome, at position six of the beta chain, is the whole molecular basis of sickle-cell disease. Sources: http://mama.indstate.edu/users/stuart/cmb/ch11a/tsld005.htm; Wikipedia, 'Sickle cell disease'.

question: A red blood cell moves through a sickle-cell patient's tissues, its haemoglobin carrying one greasy patch where a healthy cell has a water-loving link. That single swap is enough to bend the whole cell into a sickle. Under what condition, and how, does the greasy patch deform the cell?
answer: In low oxygen, the greasy patches lock haemoglobin molecules into stiff fibres that warp the cell from inside
choices: In low oxygen, the greasy patches lock haemoglobin molecules into stiff fibres that warp the cell from inside
In high oxygen, the greasy patches let each haemoglobin molecule float loose so the cell wall collapses
In cold blood, the greasy patches attract calcium that crystallises into needles inside the cell
In acidic blood, the greasy patches pull water out of the cell so it shrinks to a curved sliver
context: When haemoglobin has released its oxygen (in exercising muscle, high altitude, or the tissues generally), the beta-6 valine patch on one molecule sticks to a matching pocket on the next, and the molecules stack into long stiff polymer fibres. Those fibres physically push the red cell into the curved sickle shape Ernest Irons had drawn from Walter Noel's blood. That is why exercise, illness or altitude can trigger a crisis. Sources: https://homs.concord.org/sickle4.html; Wikipedia, 'Sickle cell disease'.

question: Anthony Allison worked in East Africa in the mid-1950s on a puzzle J. B. S. Haldane had set in 1949. If two copies of a gene are often lethal in childhood, natural selection should drive that gene down to nearly zero, yet the sickle-cell gene stayed common along a scattered band of the Old World. What did the children who carried just one copy gain from it?
answer: Substantial protection against severe falciparum malaria
choices: Substantial protection against severe falciparum malaria
Full immunity to yellow fever and dengue infections
Faster wound healing after cuts and burns
Improved night vision in dim conditions
context: Allison, working in Kenya and Uganda in 1954, found that children with one copy of the sickle-cell allele carried lower parasite loads and survived falciparum malaria at higher rates than children with two normal copies. The same allele that is often lethal in two doses is protective in one; the arithmetic is fully visible and fully cruel. Source: https://iubmb.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/bmb.2002.494030050108

question: An eye doctor examines a small boy whose two copies of a gene called RPE65 are both broken, so his eyes cannot recycle vitamin A properly after each flash of light. As he grows, he will first lose sight in one setting. Which setting?
answer: In dim light
choices: In dim light
In bright sunshine
In moving vehicles
In direct eye contact
context: Night vision goes first because RPE65 is central to the retinal-recycling step (11-cis-retinal regeneration). Daytime vision fades later. The disease is called Leber congenital amaurosis. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voretigene_neparvovec

question: A surgeon readies a needle for a child born with two broken copies of the RPE65 gene. It holds Luxturna, which the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved in December 2017: a modified virus carrying a working copy, bound for one exact spot in the eye. Where does the needle go?
answer: Beneath the retina at the back of the eye
choices: Beneath the retina at the back of the eye
Into the vitreous jelly at the centre of the eye
Into the cornea at the front of the eye
Into the optic nerve behind the eye
context: The subretinal injection puts the AAV2 vector right where the retinal pigment epithelium cells that need RPE65 sit. Developed at Penn and Children's Hospital of Philadelphia by Jean Bennett and Albert Maguire and marketed by Spark Therapeutics. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voretigene_neparvovec ; https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-a-vision-restoring-gene-therapy-proved-that-we-can-treat-inherited-diseases/

question: A doctor prepares Zolgensma, approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in May 2019, for a baby with spinal muscular atrophy type 1. His motor nerve cells are dying because both his SMN1 genes are broken, and most such babies never sit up on their own. By which route does the drug deliver a working gene?
answer: A single infusion into a vein
choices: A single infusion into a vein
A daily pill through the first year of life
A monthly injection into a leg muscle
A weekly injection into the spinal fluid
context: One IV drip through a peripheral vein, dose set by body weight. Approved 24 May 2019 for children under two, including babies treated before symptoms appear. The spinal-fluid option describes the real rival treatment nusinersen (Spinraza), which IS given by lumbar puncture. Source: https://www.drugs.com/history/zolgensma.html

question: A doctor explains Zolgensma to a baby's parents: its working gene has to get from the blood into motor neurons inside the spinal cord. The whole plan depends on the coat protein of the adeno-associated virus (AAV) that carries it, and each AAV type, or serotype, wears its own. Which AAV serotype does Zolgensma use?
answer: AAV9
choices: AAV9
AAV2
AAV5
AAV1
context: AAV comes in 'serotypes' whose capsid (coat) proteins act like tissue address labels. AAV9 is the serotype that can cross out of the bloodstream through the blood-brain barrier and reach central-nervous-system cells -- so a needle in a vein reaches motor neurons in the spinal cord. Luxturna, by contrast, uses AAV2 injected directly at its target. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8599021/

question: A doctor tells a family that Zolgensma, a gene therapy for babies with spinal muscular atrophy, is 'one shot for life': a second infusion of the same drug would largely fail. Zolgensma ferries a corrected gene into the baby's cells inside a harmless virus, adeno-associated virus (AAV). What is the biological reason a second dose bounces off?
answer: The immune system makes antibodies against that virus's coat
choices: The immune system makes antibodies against that virus's coat
The delivered genes silence themselves by DNA methylation
The blood-brain barrier permanently thickens after the first crossing
A second dose is toxic to the liver at the tested concentrations
context: The first infusion trains the immune system to recognise that specific AAV capsid, so neutralising antibodies destroy a second dose before it can reach the target cells. Getting around this is one of the biggest open problems in AAV gene therapy. Source: https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/advances/fulltext/S2329-0501(17)30123-7

question: Scientists set out in 2011, about 270 of them, to re-run 100 famous psychology studies from three top journals, a four-year job. Of the 100, 97 had first reported a real effect. When the re-runs were counted, how many of the 100 came out with the same real effect?
context: Open Science Collaboration, Science, August 2015. The pair 97-in / 36-out is the number that broke psychology open -- and the field itself put it in the pages of its own flagship journal.

question: A University of Virginia psychologist led the Reproducibility Project, which tried to re-run 100 published psychology studies and reported in 2015. In 2013 he had co-founded a nonprofit in Charlottesville to make more of these replication tests happen. Who is he?
answer: Brian Nosek
choices: Brian Nosek
Daniel Kahneman
John Ioannidis
Amos Tversky
context: Brian Nosek of the University of Virginia co-founded the Center for Open Science in January 2013 with Jeffrey Spies. The Open Science Collaboration coordinated 270 authors across the four-year effort; Science named the result among the top scientific achievements of 2015.

question: Researchers on the 2015 Reproducibility Project split their re-runs of 100 published psychology studies by subfield, and the numbers came out very uneven. Memory and cognition studies re-ran fine about half the time. One branch of psychology hit only about 25 percent. Which branch did the worst?
answer: social psychology
choices: social psychology
developmental psychology
neuropsychology
clinical psychology
context: The closer a finding sat to a stopwatch and the further from a story about human nature, the better it held. Cognitive psychology hit about 50%; social psychology about 25%. The lesson: methodology matters more than domain.

question: Some original authors of famous psychology studies argued that their effects, which had failed when others tried to reproduce them, were real but delicate, needing exactly the right lab, the right undergraduates, the right country. The Many Labs 2 project put that defence to the test in 2018, running 28 well-known effects across 125 samples on some 15,000 people in dozens of countries. What pattern showed up in the results?
answer: when an effect replicated it replicated nearly everywhere, and when it failed it failed nearly everywhere
choices: when an effect replicated it replicated nearly everywhere, and when it failed it failed nearly everywhere
American labs replicated most effects, but foreign laboratories replicated only a small fraction
the effects replicated well in laboratories established more than twenty years, but not in newer ones
the effects replicated much better when the original author was consulted on the protocol
context: Klein et al., Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 2018. Only 15 of the 28 effects (54%) reached significance in the replication. Fragility was NOT the explanation -- the failures were uniform, which killed the hidden-moderators defense.

question: Monya Baker sent a survey for the journal Nature to 1,576 working scientists across many fields, asking how often they had failed to reproduce another researcher's experiment. She published the result in May 2016. What was the headline number?
answer: more than 70% had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment
choices: more than 70% had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment
about 22% had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment
about 8% had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment
roughly 40% had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment
context: Nature 533, 452-454, May 2016. More than half had also failed to reproduce their OWN experiments. By field the failure-to-reproduce-others rates were: chemists 87%, biologists 77%, physicists and engineers 69%. This was not a psychology problem.

question: Researchers in one field reported the most failures when Monya Baker broke her 2016 Nature survey of 1,576 working scientists out by discipline. Ranked by how often they had tried and failed to reproduce someone else's published result, that field topped the list at 87 percent. Which field was it?
answer: chemistry
choices: chemistry
physics
biology
engineering
context: Chemists: 87%. Biologists: 77%. Physicists and engineers: 69%. Nature, 2016. The reproducibility crisis is not a soft-science problem -- benchwork with fussy reagents is where the reagent problem bites hardest.

question: Opportunity rolled across Mars for more than fourteen Earth years after it landed in January 2004. The team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California had built the six-wheeled rover for a far shorter job. How long was it designed to last?
answer: About 90 sols, roughly three months
choices: About 90 sols, roughly three months
About 360 sols, roughly one Earth year
About 900 sols, roughly two and a half years
About 1,800 sols, roughly five Earth years
context: It was built for 90 sols, or Martian days of about 24 hours 40 minutes each, and it ran for 5,111 sols, about 14 years and 4 months. The team planned a three-month field trip and got a career. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover).

question: Mission controllers added up Opportunity's drive after a storm silenced the rover in 2018. It had rolled across Mars, crater to crater, for more than fourteen Earth years, and its total matched one famous distance from Earth sports. What was it?
answer: A full marathon distance
choices: A full marathon distance
A sprint 100-metre stretch
A city road-race half distance
A cross-country ultra distance
context: 45.16 km, edging past the 42.195 km of the Olympic marathon: the first marathon driven on another world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover).

question: Opportunity's team landed the rover on Mars in January 2004 expecting fine red Martian dust to settle on its solar panels and starve them of sunlight within months. Something on Mars kept undoing that damage, and the rover kept working for over 14 years. What kept the panels going far longer than planned?
answer: Wind gusts sweeping the panels
choices: Wind gusts sweeping the panels
CO2 frost sublimating off the panels at dawn
Electrostatic self-cleaning by the panels
Seasonal axial tilt exposing new cell area
context: The design model only let the covering accumulate. The margin came from what mission engineers later called cleaning events -- passing gusts that periodically scoured the array. Honest engineering told the story that way: Mars turned out to be luckier than the arithmetic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover).

question: The mission team studied the bedrock in the walls of Eagle, a small Martian crater, after Opportunity bounced down there in early 2004. Thousands of tiny grey mineral spheres sat in the rock and lay loose on the crater floor. The team gave them a food-based nickname that stuck for good. What was the nickname?
answer: Blueberries
choices: Blueberries
Peppercorns
Coffee beans
Fish eggs
context: They looked bluish against the rust-red Martian soil in false-colour panoramas, though the mineral itself is grey haematite. Sizes ran from under 1 mm up to about 8 mm. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martian_spherules.

question: Geologists back on Earth saw what Opportunity found in a small Martian crater in 2004: tiny grey spheres of the iron mineral haematite, sitting right next to bright yellow sulfate salts in the same rock. They knew that exact pair of minerals as a fingerprint of one particular kind of past environment. What environment on ancient Mars did the pair point to?
answer: Standing acidic water
choices: Standing acidic water
Freshly cooled basalt lava
Wind-drifted volcanic ash
Constant deep-freeze dry ice
context: Haematite concretions and sulfate salts on Earth form in shallow, salty, chemically active pools. Opportunity was a field geologist, and its verdict on Meridiani Planum was that this ground had once been soaked. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martian_spherules.

question: NASA landed twin golf-cart-sized rovers on opposite sides of Mars three weeks apart in January 2004. Opportunity kept rolling until 2018. Its twin, Spirit, stopped roving for good in 2009, at a spot nicknamed Troy. What ended Spirit's driving days?
