answer: It sank into soft soil and never drove free
choices: It sank into soft soil and never drove free
A dust storm smothered its panels for good
It slid into a crater too steep to climb
A rock fall from a cliff crushed its mast
context: Spirit landed on 4 January 2004 and bogged down in soft sand in May 2009; months of attempts to drive it out failed, and on 26 January 2010 NASA made it a stationary science platform. It fell silent on 22 March 2010, and its mission was declared complete in May 2011. A dust storm, not sand, ended Opportunity nine years after Spirit stuck. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_(rover).

question: Engineers on Earth heard the last radio signal from the solar-powered rover Opportunity on 10 June 2018, more than fourteen years after it landed on Mars. The same Martian weather that had kept it alive finally killed it: a storm went planet-encircling, blacking out the sky over the rover for weeks and starving its panels of sunlight. What was the storm made of?
answer: Dust lifted off the surface
choices: Dust lifted off the surface
Fine ice crystals from the poles
Volcanic ash from Tharsis vents
Salt aerosols off ancient seabeds
context: Martian global dust storms recur every few years and can blanket the whole planet. NASA declared the mission over on 13 February 2019. The wind that had cleaned the panels, then blocked the Sun. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover).

question: The engineers who built Ingenuity had to fly a helicopter in Martian air, only about one per cent as dense as Earth's at sea level. Martian gravity, 38 per cent of Earth's, helps but does not close the gap. They closed it by making the 1.21-metre rotors spin unusually fast. At what speed did those rotors spin during flight?
answer: Around 2,400 rpm
choices: Around 2,400 rpm
Around 240 rpm
Around 400 rpm
Around 24,000 rpm
context: Roughly ten times a terrestrial helicopter's rotor speed. Lift scales with air density and with the square of blade tip speed, so if you cannot have the density you spin harder to make up for it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingenuity_(helicopter).

question: Ingenuity's team flew the little helicopter for the last time on 18 January 2024, and it came down on featureless ground its navigation camera could not read, snapping all four rotor blades. They had funding for 5 flights in 30 sols and had flown it 72 times over nearly three years, covering 17.2 km. Bolted underneath, on its belly, was a small souvenir cut from an aviation artefact on Earth. What was it a piece of?
answer: The 1903 Wright Flyer's wing cloth
choices: The 1903 Wright Flyer's wing cloth
The Spirit of St Louis's fuselage skin
The Bell X-1's cockpit lining
Amelia Earhart's flight-jacket leather
context: A scrap of the muslin that had covered the Wrights' wings at Kitty Hawk, flown to Mars and back into flight there. The gesture echoes the fragment of Wright cloth Apollo 11 carried to the Moon in 1969. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingenuity_(helicopter).

question: Joseph Priestley set up a big magnifying lens in his workshop on 1 August 1774 and focused summer sunlight onto a small heap of bright red powder in a sealed glass jar. A gas hissed out, and he caught it. What was that red powder?
answer: Red mercuric oxide
choices: Red mercuric oxide
Powdered iron rust
Dried cochineal beetle
Cinnabar ore from Almaden
context: Priestley called his new gas 'dephlogisticated air' because he still believed the old phlogiston theory, that burning things released a substance called phlogiston into the air. His own words, written up in 'Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air' (1775), were that it was 'an air five or six times as good as common air'. Source: aps.org/publications/apsnews/201008/physicshistory.cfm

question: A mouse went first: Joseph Priestley sealed it in a jar of the strange new gas he had drawn off a red powder in 1774, and watched. Weeks later he breathed some himself and wrote down what he felt. What did he record about his own chest?
answer: It felt 'peculiarly light and easy' for some time afterwards
choices: It felt 'peculiarly light and easy' for some time afterwards
It felt heavier and slower than after ordinary breathing
It burned as though he had inhaled hot vinegar
It gave him a stabbing headache and blurred sight for hours
context: The mouse lived far longer in the sealed jar than it should have in that volume of ordinary air. Priestley's own written line was: 'The feeling of it to my lungs was not sensibly different from that of common air; but I fancied that my breast felt peculiarly light and easy for some time afterwards.' Source: azquotes.com/quote/789511

question: Joseph Priestley sealed a candle in a jar in 1771, three years before he ever turned a burning lens on a red powder, and let it burn out. Then he placed a living sprig of mint in the used-up jar for several days. What did that let him do a few days later?
answer: Relight a candle in the same jar
choices: Relight a candle in the same jar
Make the flame of a fresh candle burn with a steady blue light
Turn a piece of iron placed inside noticeably rustier
Cause dew to gather on the inside of the glass overnight
context: Priestley had accidentally seen photosynthesis without the concept: the mint had 'restored' the exhausted air. The Royal Society gave him the Copley Medal in 1773 for the paper describing this and other airs. Source: bio.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Botany/Introduction_to_Botany_(Shipunov)/03:_Photosynthesis/3.01:_Discovery_of_Photosynthesis

question: Carl Wilhelm Scheele, a Swedish apothecary, made a gas two or three years before Joseph Priestley made the same one, using different starting materials, and he gave it a vivid name of his own: 'fire air'. His manuscript sat with the printer while others published, and by the time his book appeared in 1777 the credit had already been handed elsewhere. What common gas had he made?
answer: Oxygen
choices: Oxygen
Hydrogen
Nitrogen
Chlorine
context: Scheele called the gas 'fire air' (Feuerluft) and its counterpart 'foul air' (verdorbene Luft), which we now call nitrogen. His 'Chemische Abhandlung von der Luft und dem Feuer' finally appeared in 1777. In science, priority is not about who knew first; it is about who publishes first. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_air

question: A French chemist sat at dinner in Paris one evening in October 1774, hearing about a gas from Joseph Priestley, who had come with his patron Lord Shelburne. Priestley had drawn it off a red powder, and next day he repeated the experiment at the Frenchman's bench. That chemist then ran the same reaction over again on a precision balance and drew the conclusion Priestley never would. Who was the host at that dinner?
answer: Antoine Lavoisier
choices: Antoine Lavoisier
Claude Berthollet
Pierre Macquer
Jean Chaptal
context: Lavoisier's balance let him track the weights of everything going in and coming out. He concluded the new gas was an element in its own right and renamed it 'oxygene' (from the Greek for 'acid-maker', because he wrongly thought it was in every acid). His new theory of combustion and respiration displaced phlogiston. Source: britannica.com/biography/Antoine-Lavoisier/Oxygen-theory-of-combustion

question: A historian of chemistry sets three men's claims to the discovery of one common gas side by side: a Swede's, an Englishman's and a Frenchman's. She settles the three-way fight as her field does, by giving each man a different verb, because each did one part of the discovery first. Which pairing of who-did-what-first does she give?
answer: Scheele made it first, Priestley published it first, Lavoisier understood it first
choices: Scheele made it first, Priestley published it first, Lavoisier understood it first
Priestley made it first, Scheele published it first, Lavoisier understood it first
Lavoisier made it first, Scheele published it first, Priestley understood it first
Priestley made it first, Lavoisier published it first, Scheele understood it first
context: Scheele's laboratory work in 1771-72 came earliest but was buried by his publisher until 1777. Priestley's 1774 experiment reached print in 1775. Lavoisier saw that combustion, calcination and respiration were the same kind of reaction and named the element. Source: journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajplung.00310.2013

question: Pamphlet after pamphlet came from Joseph Priestley to the end of his life in 1804, defending an older framework that had just been overthrown. He never accepted what his own gas actually was, and he kept the old name for it. Which discarded scientific theory did he defend to the grave?
answer: The phlogiston theory
choices: The phlogiston theory
The caloric theory of heat
Van Helmont's gas theory
The four-element doctrine of earth, water, air and fire
context: In 1791 a Church-and-King mob burned Priestley's Birmingham house and laboratory over his religious and political views, and he emigrated to Pennsylvania in 1794. Consensus is not truth: the man who made the gas rejected what it meant, and the man who never made it was the one who understood it. Source: sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/joseph-priestley

question: Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn ran a deliberately absurd experiment in 2011. It showed a certain Beatles song making 20 college students about a year and a half younger: not feeling younger, but younger by birth date. Which song did they use?
answer: 'When I'm Sixty-Four'
choices: 'When I'm Sixty-Four'
'Yesterday'
'Hey Jude'
'Let It Be'
context: Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn, 'False-Positive Psychology,' Psychological Science 22(11), 2011. ANCOVA controlling for father's age: Beatles listeners adjusted M = 20.1 years, Kalimba listeners adjusted M = 21.5, F(1,17) = 4.92, p = .040. The paper disclosed the demonstration as intentional in the same pages.

question: Three American psychologists published a paper in 2011 that appeared to 'prove' a Beatles song made adults literally younger. It was not fraud. Joe Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn had built the fake finding on purpose from the tiny everyday choices any lab makes: what to test, when to stop, which control song to use. What memorable name did they give those choices?
answer: researcher degrees of freedom
choices: researcher degrees of freedom
the file-drawer problem
publication bias
the Rosenthal effect
context: Simmons Nelson Simonsohn 2011 coined the phrase. The paper's punchline: 'It is unacceptably easy to publish statistically significant evidence consistent with any hypothesis.' The remedy they proposed was disclosure -- list every variable measured, every condition run, every choice made.

question: Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn ran a test using four common tricks: pick the best outcome, add more people after a peek, test an extra control, drop a group. The false-positive rate was supposed to be 5%. When all four tricks were used, what rate did the test report?
context: Table 1, Simmons Nelson Simonsohn 2011: 15,000 simulated samples, all four researcher degrees of freedom combined, false-positive rate 60.7% at p<.05. 'A researcher is more likely than not to falsely detect a significant effect by just using these four common researcher degrees of freedom.'

question: Thirty University of Pennsylvania students sat through a deliberately silly kids' song in the first study of the famous 2011 'Beatles' paper by Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn. The authors reported that people felt older after it than after a control track, a result as fake as the Beatles one. Which song did they play?
answer: 'Hot Potato' by The Wiggles
choices: 'Hot Potato' by The Wiggles
'Baby Beluga' by Raffi
'Rubber Duckie' by Sesame Street's Ernie
'Yellow Submarine' by The Beatles
context: Study 1, Simmons Nelson Simonsohn 2011. Adjusted M = 2.54 vs 2.06 on a 1-5 subjective age scale, F(1,27) = 5.06, p = .033. Same ordinary analytic choices, second bogus 'finding' -- showing the Beatles result was not a one-off fluke but the predictable output of the flexibility itself.

question: Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken wrote in 2014 about a sincere researcher who runs just one test and thinks it was the right one. He can still be fooled, because the test was picked only after looking at the data. What image did the two men give this problem?
answer: the garden of forking paths
choices: the garden of forking paths
the funnel-plot asymmetry
the file-drawer effect
the Texas sharpshooter
context: Gelman and Loken, American Scientist, November 2014. Their point: even a sincere researcher who never runs a second analysis is still making the same category of error, because the analysis was chosen post hoc. No cheating occurred and the p-value is still not what it says. Funnel-plot asymmetry, the file-drawer effect and the Texas sharpshooter fallacy are all real adjacent problems -- none is what Gelman and Loken named.

question: Raphael Silberzahn and colleagues, Brian Nosek among them, handed 29 independent teams the same football dataset in 2018 with one question: do referees show more red cards to dark-skinned players? Same data, one question, twenty-nine analyses. How did the answers come back?
answer: 20 teams found a significant positive effect and 9 did not, with odds ratios from 0.89 to 2.93
choices: 20 teams found a significant positive effect and 9 did not, with odds ratios from 0.89 to 2.93
all 29 teams found a significant positive effect, with odds ratios from 1.21 to 1.44
none of the 29 teams found a significant effect in either direction, with all odds ratios near 1.00
the 29 teams split evenly at 14-14, with odds ratios scattered from 0.35 to 3.10
context: Silberzahn et al., Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 2018. Twenty-one different combinations of covariates were used across the 29 analyses. Same data, opposite headlines, everyone competent. The paper is the sharpest empirical evidence that analysis choice can dominate the answer.

question: A scientist writes down exactly what she expects before an experiment, runs the test and looks at the real data. Then she quietly changes her written prediction so it matches what she saw. The published paper now looks like a clean, successful call, even though she picked the prediction after seeing the answer. Why is that dishonest, even when the data itself is real?
answer: It hides a lucky guess behind a made-up prediction
choices: It hides a lucky guess behind a made-up prediction
It steals another researcher's idea
It uses too few test subjects
It publishes the same data twice
context: HARKing = Hypothesizing After the Results are Known, coined by Norbert Kerr in 1998. A test you design after seeing the result is not a test. Cherry-picking, outcome switching (changing which endpoint you report after seeing the trial) and salami slicing (splitting one study into multiple papers) are all real sibling QRPs; HARKing is the specific one for retro-fitting the hypothesis. The only remedy that survives every objection is writing the prediction down BEFORE the data exists -- pre-registration.

question: Joseph Simmons and his two co-authors simulated optional stopping: start with 10 subjects per condition, check the p-value after each new subject, and stop the moment it dips under 0.05, the line of significance. The advertised false-positive rate was 5%. What rate did the simulation report for that practice alone?
answer: about 22%
choices: about 22%
about 6%
about 55%
about 88%
context: Figure 1, Simmons Nelson Simonsohn 2011. 22.1% false positives from optional stopping alone, starting at n=10 and testing every additional observation until n=50. Even a 'small' interim-checking habit multiplies the advertised error rate more than fourfold.

question: Brian Wansink, a famous Cornell food researcher, published a blog post in November 2016 praising a graduate student who 'never said no', and described how he had sent her back into a failed pizza-buffet dataset again and again until multiple papers came out of it. Outside statisticians read the post as a confession and went looking. What did they find in his published papers?
answer: Many errors and manipulated data
choices: Many errors and manipulated data
A few typos and nothing worse
Sound numbers but overstated claims
Honest data but a weak control group
context: Tim van der Zee, Jordan Anaya and Nick Brown went through four of the pizza papers in 2017 and counted some 150 numbers that could not fit the reported design. Cornell's own committee confirmed academic misconduct on 20 September 2018; more than twenty Wansink papers were retracted or corrected and he resigned, effective mid-2019. Wansink admitted method failures but denied fraud. He ran Cornell's Food and Brand Lab and had earlier headed the USDA office that produced the 2010 Dietary Guidelines.

question: A researcher quietly tries dozens of ways to slice one dataset until one looks like a real finding, then writes the paper as if that was the plan the whole time. That is p-hacking. Proposed cures sound sensible, but most still leave an outside reader unable to tell a genuine prediction from a story told after the fact. Which reform truly closes that loophole?
answer: the hypothesis and analysis plan are filed before the data is collected
choices: the hypothesis and analysis plan are filed before the data is collected
the paper reports every measure the study collected
an independent team reproduces the analysis on the same data
the raw data and analysis code are posted publicly at submission
context: Pre-registration. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn (2011) also pushed full disclosure of every measure collected; Nosek's Center for Open Science built independent reanalysis and open data and code into standard practice. All four are real reforms of the replication crisis and each helps, but only pre-registration lets an outside reader tell a prediction made in advance from a story told after the fact. The Registered Reports format built around it makes the plan public before data collection begins.

question: Blaise Pascal thought in 1647 that the weight of the open air held up the mercury in the new glass tube. Months before anyone climbed a mountain, he wrote down where the mercury would stand at a summit, and said his idea was dead if it stood anywhere else. Where did he say it would stand?
answer: Lower at the summit than at the foot
choices: Lower at the summit than at the foot
Higher at the summit than at the foot
Exactly the height it stood at the foot
Emptied back into the dish entirely
context: Pascal's reasoning: if the mercury is held up by the weight of the air stacked above the dish, then carrying the tube up a mountain leaves less air overhead, and the column must fall. He set that down in advance and named it as the result that would kill the idea if it failed to appear -- a falsifiable prediction rather than a demonstration staged to impress. He had learned of the mercury tube through Marin Mersenne and had repeated it himself in 1646. Source: Grokipedia, 'Blaise Pascal' ('Pascal hypothesized that the barometer's mercury height resulted from the weight of the overlying air column, predicting it would decrease at higher altitudes... Pascal's altitude tests provided falsifiable predictions upheld by the Puy de Dome data').

question: One man carried Blaise Pascal's mercury tube up the Puy de Dome, an extinct volcano in central France, on 19 September 1648, and took the reading. Pascal himself was too ill to climb a staircase, let alone a volcano. Who made the climb?
answer: Florin Perier, his brother-in-law, a judge at Clermont
choices: Florin Perier, his brother-in-law, a judge at Clermont
Michelangelo Ricci, the Roman friend of Torricelli
Marin Mersenne, the Paris friar who sent him the news
Etienne Noel, the Jesuit who had once taught Descartes
context: Florin Perier was a councillor at the Cour des Aides, the tax court of Clermont-Ferrand, and had married Pascal's older sister Gilberte. The legwork for the most famous prediction of the century was done by a provincial tax-court judge doing a favour for his wife's brother. The Puy de Dome is a lava dome 1,465 m high, one of the youngest volcanoes of the Chaine des Puys, about 10 km from the city; it last erupted around 10,700 years ago. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Blaise Pascal' ('Unable to perform the test himself due to health issues, he instructed his brother-in-law Florin Perier'); Linda Hall Library, 'Florin Perier'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Blaise Pascal'; Wikipedia, 'Puy de Dome'.

question: Florin Perier came down off the Puy de Dome on 19 September 1648 and three days later sent his brother-in-law Blaise Pascal a letter setting out the whole day -- the readings, the weather, the witnesses he had named. Pascal was the famous one, and the idea under test was his. What did Pascal do with the letter?
answer: Printed it whole inside a pamphlet of his own
choices: Printed it whole inside a pamphlet of his own
Rewrote it as his own summary of the results
Held it back until a second mountain was climbed
Kept it private and published the numbers alone
context: Perier's letter is dated 22 September 1648, three days after the climb, and Pascal printed it in full inside his own pamphlet, Recit de la grande experience de l'equilibre des liqueurs, published that same year. He gave readers the other man's raw report rather than his own summary of it, so anyone who doubted the result could read the day as the man who spent it had written it down. The figures in that letter: 26 inches 3 and a half lines in the friars' garden at the foot of the mountain, 23 inches 2 lines at the summit, a fall of 3 inches 1 and a half lines -- 711 mm down to 627 mm in modern units, about the width of a man's palm. Worth knowing: several reputable-looking sources round the base figure to 'about 27 inches', which is simply wrong, and a good reminder to check a number against the original report rather than the retelling. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Blaise Pascal' (base 26" 3.5 lines, summit 23" 2 lines); Grokipedia, 'Blaise Pascal' ('Perier detailed these results in a letter to Pascal dated September 22, 1648, which Pascal publicized'); gbenthien.net, 'Pascal: Scientific Contributions' (711 mm and 627 mm); American Physiological Society, 'Torricelli and the Ocean of Air'.

question: Father Chastin watched a mercury tube all day in a garden at the foot of a French mountain, while Florin Perier carried a matching tube up to the summit. The weather that day kept shifting, from calm to rainy to foggy to windy. What did the garden tube do?
answer: Held at exactly the height it had started at
choices: Held at exactly the height it had started at
Fell steadily all morning, then went no lower
Rose and fell by half an inch as the rain passed
Dropped once when the wind got up, and stayed down
context: Father Chastin's report survives inside Perier's own account of the day: through rain, fog, wind and calm by turns, the tube in the garden never moved. That is what made the fall at the summit impossible to blame on the weather. What Perier had built is what we would now call a control -- an untouched twin of the instrument being tested, watched all day by a named man, so that the mountain was left as the only thing that had changed. Doing that in 1648 is what makes this experiment read as modern. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Blaise Pascal' (the friar's quoted report); Wikipedia, 'Blaise Pascal'.

question: A woman rides a lift to the top of a tall tower, and her ears go stuffy. Behind each eardrum sits a small sealed pocket of gas; as she rises the outside push weakens, the trapped gas presses outward and the eardrum bulges. A moment later the drum snaps flat with an audible click. What has just happened?
answer: A vent from the middle ear down to the throat opened
choices: A vent from the middle ear down to the throat opened
A pore in the eardrum itself opened, then closed
The ear canal widened and let outside air inward
A passage from the middle ear to the sinuses opened
context: The vent is the Eustachian tube, running from the middle ear down to the back of the throat; a swallow or a yawn opens it and the trapped gas equalises with the pop you hear. Push the difference too far and the system defeats you: at a difference of about 90 mmHg (12 kPa) the tube becomes functionally locked shut and cannot be opened voluntarily at all, which is why divers and pilots equalise early and often rather than waiting. This is the same physics Perier carried up a volcano -- felt from the inside. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ear clearing'.

question: Blaise Pascal wrote to Florin Perier on 15 November 1647 and spent most of the letter on how to take the mercury readings, not on the mountain itself. He told Perier to run the test again and again, at the foot of the Puy de Dome volcano and again at the summit. Beyond repeating the reading in both places, what else did he insist on?
answer: Using the very same tube and the very same mercury throughout
choices: Sealing the tubes in Paris and breaking the seals up there
Using a fresh tube at the summit, so no valley air crept in
Taking every reading at dawn, before the day's heat built
Using the very same tube and the very same mercury throughout
context: Pascal's letter spelled out method rather than hope: the same tube, the same mercury, several runs on the same day, sometimes at the bottom and sometimes at the summit. If two different tubes gave two different readings, a critic could blame the glassware or the metal; by nailing down the instrument, the altitude was left as the only thing free to vary. Change one thing at a time -- here the one thing was the mountain. Sources: Bibliotheques Clermont Metropole, Blaise Pascal collection ('experience du Puy de Dome'); MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Blaise Pascal'.

question: Five named witnesses watched Florin Perier on top of the Puy de Dome try to break his own successful result before he would trust it. He did not simply write down the summit number and start back down. What did he do to the tubes?
answer: Tilted and shook them, to see if a hidden bubble was at work
choices: Warmed them against his coat, to see if the cold had acted
Tilted and shook them, to see if a hidden bubble was at work
Turned them out of the sun, to see if the light was heating
Emptied and refilled them from a flask carried up for it
context: The height did not change when he tilted or shook them, which ruled out a trapped bubble doing the work. He also read the mercury repeatedly on the way down, watching it climb back step by step until, in the garden, it matched the tube that had never left the bottom -- the effect was reversible, and a reversible effect is far harder to fake than a single lucky reading. Perier named his witnesses in the report as well: Father Bannier of the Minims, Mosnier a canon of the cathedral, La Ville and Begon, councillors of the Court of Aides, and La Porte, a doctor of medicine. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Blaise Pascal' ('no change upon tilting or shaking... ruling out instrumental artifacts'); Linda Hall Library, 'Florin Perier'; Bibliotheques Clermont Metropole.

question: Etienne Noel brought out an entire book against Blaise Pascal in 1648, Le Plein du Vuide, 'The Fullness of the Void'. A Jesuit who had taught the young Descartes and ran the College de Clermont in Paris, he would not grant that the space at the top of the mercury tube was empty. What did he say was up there?
answer: A fine air that seeps in through the pores of the glass
choices: A vapour boiled off the mercury by the warmth of a hand
A thin smoke left behind as the heavy metal sank away
A fine air that seeps in through the pores of the glass
A fire-stuff pulled down out of the sky by the gap itself
context: Etienne Noel (1581-1659) argued that a fine air passes through the pores of the glass and fills the space, so the 'void' is no void at all -- a serious position held by a serious man, and exactly the kind of alternative a good test has to close off. A note for the careful reader: some sources, including Grokipedia's own page on Pascal, name 'Jesuit Denis Papin' as the critic here. Papin was born in 1647, was an infant in 1648, and was a Huguenot rather than a Jesuit; the real Jesuit critic was Noel. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Etienne Noel'; Wikipedia, 'Denis Papin'.

question: Blaise Pascal wanted the Puy de Dome result checked against a climb any Parisian could make, so he ran the test again up the bell tower of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie: fifty metres of stonework, against most of a kilometre of volcano in Auvergne. He read the tube in the street, then again at the parapet. How far had the mercury fallen?
answer: About two lines, four and a half millimetres
choices: About two lines, four and a half millimetres
About half a line, a single millimetre
About twelve lines, a full French inch
About thirty lines, two and a half inches
context: A French line is a twelfth of a French inch, about 2.26 mm, so two lines is roughly four and a half millimetres -- and that feeble drop is what turned the Puy de Dome from an anecdote into a rule. Check the arithmetic yourself, the way Pascal would have: the volcano cost the column 84 mm over about 900 m of climb, so 50 m of tower should cost about 4.6 mm -- two lines, almost exactly. A tiny climb gives a tiny fall, a big mountain a big fall: the drop keeps step with the height. Because pressure tracks height that faithfully, a barometer is also an altitude gauge. The altimeter on an airliner's instrument panel is an aneroid barometer with its dial marked in feet instead of millibars, and the pilot dials a reference pressure -- 1013 hPa, or 29.92 inches of mercury -- into the small Kollsman window on its face. Pressure falls roughly one inch of mercury per 1,000 feet climbed, so a plane at 30,000 feet is finding its height by exactly what Perier found on a French volcano in 1648. The tower still stands, 52 m tall, with a statue of Pascal at its foot. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Blaise Pascal' ('about 50 metres... the mercury dropped two lines'); Wikipedia, 'Tour Saint-Jacques'; Grokipedia, 'Barometer'; Wikipedia, 'Altimeter'.

question: A crowd at Rouen had to call it in advance, early in 1647: Blaise Pascal had the town glassworks draw tubes some forty-five feet tall, filled one with water and one with wine, and asked which would stand higher. The Aristotelians chose the water: wine gives off more vapour, they argued, which would fill the space above and press its column down. The wine stood higher. Why did it?
answer: Wine is less dense, so more of it is needed to weigh the same
choices: Wine is less dense, so more of it is needed to weigh the same
Wine wets glass better, so the tube's sides help carry it
Wine holds more dissolved air, which buoys it from within
Wine is thinner, so it climbs the tube more freely than water
context: The air presses down on the open dish with a fixed push, and the column standing in the tube must weigh exactly as much as that push. Wine is less dense than water, so a taller column of wine is needed to weigh the same -- the wine stood higher, the opposite of what the room had predicted. What makes this a test rather than a show is that Pascal made the crowd commit BEFORE the tubes were raised. A prediction stated in advance can be killed by the result; a demonstration explained afterwards cannot. Sources: Revue d'histoire des sciences 2015-1 via Cairn.info, 'How Did Blaise Pascal Conceive and Carry out his Experiment on Liquids in Rouen?' ('the column of wine was higher because... the density of wine is lower than that of water'); gbenthien.net, 'Pascal: Scientific Contributions' (tubes about 45 feet high); Siemens Simcenter, 'The Inflowencers' (the Rouen glassworks and the audience's prediction).

question: A teacher pours a few cups of water down a long thin pipe rammed through the lid of a sealed barrel, and the barrel bursts its staves. The French call it the creve-tonneau, the barrel-buster; textbooks date it to 1646 and put Blaise Pascal behind it. The physics is real and the demonstration genuinely works. What is wrong with the story?
answer: Pascal never mentions it anywhere in his surviving works
choices: Perier ran it at Clermont, and Pascal only reported it
Pascal never mentions it anywhere in his surviving works
It was staged a century later, with wine instead of water
Pascal tried it and the barrel merely leaked, never bursting
context: The barrel appears nowhere in Pascal's preserved works. It seems to have been attached to his name by nineteenth-century French schoolbook authors, around 1863, who gave it the name creve-tonneau -- so it is folklore, and it is told here as folklore. The physics behind it is entirely real: pressure at the bottom of a liquid depends only on the DEPTH of the column, never on how much liquid there is, so a thin pipe of water a metre tall presses on its base exactly as hard as a metre-deep lake presses on its bed. Simon Stevin proved that in 1586 in De Beghinselen des Waterwichts, sixty years before Pascal. A true story about physics can still be a false story about history. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Pascal's barrel'; Grokipedia, 'Pascal's law'.  (Legend.)

question: Rene Descartes spent two days in Paris in September 1647 arguing with the young Blaise Pascal about whether the space at the top of a mercury tube was empty at all, and afterwards wrote to Christiaan Huygens that Pascal 'has too much vacuum in his head'. Descartes had no rival experiment to offer; his physics ruled the vacuum out before any tube was raised. On what ground?
answer: Matter is nothing but extension, so empty space is a contradiction
choices: Matter is nothing but extension, so empty space is a contradiction
Nature abhors a vacuum, and rushes to close any gap that opens
Motion in a void would be infinitely fast, so no void can exist
Place is the shell of a surrounding body, so empty place is nothing
context: Descartes identified matter with extension: to be a body just IS to be stretched out in length, breadth and depth, so a stretch of space with nothing in it would be a body that is not a body. The vacuum was ruled out by the definition, before anyone climbed anything. He visited Pascal in Paris on 23 September 1647 and stayed two days arguing exactly that, and afterwards sent Huygens the line about too much vacuum in the young man's head. He also claimed the mountain test as his own idea -- to Marin Mersenne in December 1647, and twice more to Pierre de Carcavi in 1649: 'It was I who two years ago advised him to do it, for although I have not performed it myself, I did not doubt of its success.' Pascal's circle denied it flatly, and historians have argued the priority ever since. Who first thought of the climb is still disputed. Who actually went and made it, with an untouched instrument at the base and five witnesses named in the report, is not. Sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Blaise Pascal' (the Carcavi quotation and the Huygens line); Encyclopedia.com, 'Blaise Pascal' (letters of 13 Dec 1647, 11 June and 17 Aug 1649).

question: A mechanic presses the thin handle of a car jack and two tonnes of car rises. Pascal's law makes it work: pressure applied anywhere in a trapped liquid is passed on undiminished to every part of it, so a much wider piston turns a small push into a large lift. Nothing is created for free, though, and the machine takes its payment somewhere. Where?
answer: In distance: the handle moves a metre to lift the car a couple of centimetres
choices: In distance: the handle moves a metre to lift the car a couple of centimetres
In heat: the oil warms by several degrees with each stroke of the handle
In friction: the seals swallow about a fifth of every push he gives it
In time: the car creeps up over fifty slow strokes, one after another
context: The relation is F2/F1 = A2/A1: fifty times the area gives fifty times the force, but the small piston must travel fifty times as far -- 100 cm of stroke under the mechanic's hand for 2 cm of lift under the car, which is exactly why a jack needs so many pumps to raise a car a few centimetres. Force is bought with distance, and no energy is manufactured anywhere in the machine. Pascal set the principle out in his Traite de l'equilibre des liqueurs, published after his death in 1663, and the SI unit of pressure now carries his name: 1 pascal = 1 newton per square metre, made official by the 14th General Conference on Weights and Measures in 1971. Standard sea-level pressure is 101,325 Pa, or 760 mm of mercury -- the ocean of air, weighed. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Pascal's law' (the 50x piston worked example, 100 cm for 2 cm); Grokipedia, 'Pascal's law'.

question: A researcher aims Cas9, a molecular tool for cutting DNA at a chosen spot, at one wrong letter in a cell's genome. Classic Cas9 slices right through both strands of the double helix, and the cell's fast emergency repair rushes in to mend the break. If the goal is to swap the wrong letter for the right one, that quick repair turns out to be a bad fit. Why?
answer: It rejoins the ends sloppily and leaves random insertions or deletions
choices: It rejoins the ends sloppily and leaves random insertions or deletions
It refuses to work on any single-letter mutation
It disables the immune system for several weeks afterward
It always inserts the same wrong letter at every repair site
context: The cell's stopgap is called non-homologous end joining -- it patches the ends because an unrepaired double-strand break is fatal, but it does not restore the exact original sequence. That is fine when you want to BREAK a gene: Casgevy (2023) uses classic Cas9 to disrupt the BCL11A switch so fetal hemoglobin comes back on in sickle cell disease. It is terrible when you want to fix one wrong letter. Source: Nature Protocols review of base editing, 2020.

question: David Liu set out at the Broad Institute in Massachusetts in 2016 to fix a single-letter typo in DNA without cutting both strands of the double helix. Ordinary gene editing uses a short guide RNA to steer an enzyme called Cas9 to an exact address, and Cas9 snips right through. Liu's team kept the guide RNA and the address-finding, crippled the cutter and bolted a new piece on. What was the new piece?
answer: A deaminase, a chemistry enzyme that swaps one base for another on the spot
choices: A deaminase, a chemistry enzyme that swaps one base for another on the spot
A second guide RNA that hunts for the mistake and marks it with a fluorescent tag
A stretch of donor DNA that the cell has to copy in over several days
A protein pump that pulls the wrong base out of the double helix
context: The Cas9 in a base editor is disabled or a nickase -- it can find the address but cannot cut across both strands. A deaminase is a small enzyme that strips a chemical group off the base, converting it into a different letter in place. The cytosine base editor (CBE) turns C into T (Komor, Kim, Packer, Zuris, Liu; Nature, 2016); the adenine base editor (ABE) turns A into G (Gaudelli et al., Nature, November 2017).

question: The Liu lab went past single letters in 2019. A base editor can only swap C to T or A to G; the new tool could insert or replace a longer stretch of DNA, still without breaking both strands. The trick was to fuse a new enzyme to a Cas9 nickase, which cuts only one strand, and add a much longer guide, a pegRNA, that carries the desired edit. What is the new enzyme it writes with?
answer: A reverse transcriptase, which copies the new sequence off the pegRNA into the DNA
choices: A reverse transcriptase, which copies the new sequence off the pegRNA into the DNA
A DNA ligase, which glues together fragments the cell has already made
A CRISPR-Cas12a nuclease, which trims the strand into shorter pieces
A telomerase, which extends the natural cap at the end of chromosomes
context: This is prime editing (Anzalone et al., Nature, 2019). The pegRNA parks the machine on the target and carries the edit with it as an extra tail. The reverse transcriptase, an enzyme first discovered in retroviruses, reads that RNA tail and writes DNA off it, polymerising the replacement text directly onto the nicked strand. No double-strand break, no separate donor template.

question: Kiran Musunuru and Rebecca Ahrens-Nicklas raced to help a baby boy of the Muldoon family, born in Philadelphia in August 2024 with a rare urea-cycle disorder. His liver could not clear ammonia. About one in a million babies get it, and most die young. What made the therapy their team gave him a real first?
answer: It was built from scratch for one child's exact mutation, then given only to him
choices: It was built from scratch for one child's exact mutation, then given only to him
It was the first CRISPR therapy the FDA had ever approved
It was the first gene medicine delivered inside the body by a lipid nanoparticle
It was the first gene edit performed inside the body instead of on cells removed first
context: The therapy is called k-abe (kayjayguran abengcemeran), named after the patient. It is a modified adenine base editor plus a guide RNA matched to KJ's specific CPS1 mutation, packaged in a lipid nanoparticle that homes to the liver. The other choices are real firsts that already belonged to other therapies: Casgevy in 2023 was the first FDA-approved CRISPR therapy; patisiran (2018) and the COVID mRNA vaccines had already delivered payloads by lipid nanoparticle; in-vivo editing itself was not new (EDIT-101 for a form of Leber congenital amaurosis had already been dosed). What was new was 'bespoke' -- a therapy designed for one patient's exact mutation. KJ got his first infusion on February 25, 2025, with follow-ups in March and April. Musunuru et al., New England Journal of Medicine, June 12, 2025.

question: The Muldoon baby in Philadelphia got his first dose of a custom base editor far sooner than the usual road allows. That road takes years: pick the target, test in cells, mice and monkeys, build to clinical grade, and get a yes from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). About how long did his take from diagnosis to first dose?
answer: About six months
choices: About six months
About four weeks
About four years
About twelve years
context: Within one month the lab had cell models carrying KJ's mutation; by two months they had chosen the best editor; by five months the therapy was tested in non-human primates; at six months it was manufactured to clinical grade and cleared by the FDA. The speed is the point: when the system chooses to move, it can. Source: Science, May 2025; CHOP press release.

question: Kiran Musunuru and Rebecca Ahrens-Nicklas led the team behind the Muldoon baby's therapy, and the team hopes to have built more than one baby's medicine: a reusable kit, a base editor packed in a tiny fat bubble, that can be re-aimed at the next patient's mutation. If that hope holds, which slow step of the usual drug pipeline does the kit shrink with each reuse?
answer: The target-finding and manufacturing steps, because only the guide RNA changes from patient to patient
choices: The target-finding and manufacturing steps, because only the guide RNA changes from patient to patient
The clinical-trial phase, because an n-of-1 case legally replaces the usual Phase 1, 2, and 3 trials
The FDA review, because bespoke therapies for one patient no longer need regulatory approval
The cost of the raw enzymes, because deaminases are much cheaper to make than nucleases
context: The reused pieces are the base-editor protein, the lipid-nanoparticle delivery, and the safety work that has already been done on that chassis; the swap for each new patient is the short guide RNA that aims the editor at that person's specific mutation. What the platform does NOT bypass is regulatory oversight -- KJ's therapy was FDA-cleared, and how regulators, insurers, and manufacturers will treat future n-of-1 swaps (as one approval or many) is the open policy question. The biology has shown it is possible; the political economy is still being worked out.

question: Louis Pasteur set two flasks of boiled broth on a bench, both open to the air. The straight-necked one clouded in days. The one with its neck drawn into a long downward S stayed clear until he tipped it, so the broth ran up into the curve and back. Within a day it swarmed. What had the tilt carried in?
answer: Dust settled in the bend
choices: Air trapped in the curve
Moisture left on the glass
Dust settled in the bend
Soot from shaping the neck
context: Pasteur put the puzzle to his own Sorbonne audience: "What difference is there, then, between those two vases? They contain the same liquid, they both contain air, both are open! Why does one decay and the other remain pure?" The slow-moving air lets its dust fall out and lodge on the curved neck. He then ran the ruin deliberately: "if I shake the vase violently two or three times, in a few days it contains animalculae or mouldiness. Why? because air has come in violently enough to carry dust with it." This is one of the rare famous experiments a kitchen can copy -- two jars of the same boiled broth, one left straight-mouthed, one fitted with a long bent tube for a neck. Source: Rene Vallery-Radot, 'The Life of Pasteur' (trans. R. L. Devonshire), Project Gutenberg #60956; corroborated at grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_generation.

question: Francesco Redi left some jars of meat wide open in 1668 and stretched fine gauze over the mouths of others, to test the old belief that maggots simply appear out of rotting meat. Flies gathered around both sets. On the covered jars, where did the maggots hatch?
answer: On the gauze itself
choices: In the meat below it
On the rim of the jar
In the juice beneath
On the gauze itself
context: Redi published it as 'Esperienze intorno alla generazione degl'insetti' (1668): the flies, drawn by the smell, laid their eggs on the cloth, and the maggots hatched there -- not in the flesh. It did not end the argument. Microscopes soon showed swarming life in sealed liquids no fly could reach, and the question moved from maggots to microbes, where it stayed stuck for another two centuries. Source: Vallery-Radot, 'The Life of Pasteur', Gutenberg #60956; grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_generation; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_generation.

question: Lazzaro Spallanzani sealed his flasks of broth in 1765, then boiled them for up to an hour. Nothing ever grew inside. John Needham, who had grown life in his own briefly boiled flasks twenty years before, would not give in. What did he say the long boil had killed?
answer: The vital force in the trapped air
choices: The oxygen dissolved in the broth
The vital force in the trapped air
The nourishment the meat had held
The freshness of the sealed-in air
context: Needham (1745) had boiled mutton broth only a few minutes and stoppered his vessels with cork and paper; life appeared, and he credited a 'vegetative force'. Spallanzani (1765) sealed first and boiled for 30 to 60 minutes; nothing grew. Needham's reply -- that so long a boil had killed the vital force in the trapped air -- could not be tested, and the argument sat in stalemate for a century, because neither man had found a way to leave a flask OPEN to the air and still keep the dust out. That gap is exactly the one a drawn-out swan neck fills. Source: Vallery-Radot, 'The Life of Pasteur', Gutenberg #60956; dates and boiling times from grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_generation.

question: Louis Pasteur and Félix Pouchet led rival camps in France by 1860, trading experiments over whether tiny living things could pop up out of dead matter on their own, the doctrine of spontaneous generation. The French Academy of Sciences was tired of the fight. What did the Academy do to force a decision?
answer: Hung a cash prize on a decisive experiment
choices: Sent inspectors into both men's laboratories
Barred the question from its published memoirs
Put the matter to a vote of its members
Hung a cash prize on a decisive experiment
context: It was the Alhumbert Prize, 2,500 francs, worded: "To attempt to throw some new light upon the question of so-called spontaneous generation by well-conducted experiments." A prize is a device for forcing a test rather than a debate -- and it worked. Pasteur's memoir 'Memoire sur les corpuscules organises qui existent dans l'atmosphere' (Organized Corpuscles Existing in the Atmosphere, 1861) was unanimously preferred, and he took the prize in 1862. Source: prize wording and the unanimous vote from Vallery-Radot, Gutenberg #60956; sum and year from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Pasteur; the 1860 offer date from grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_generation.

question: Félix Pouchet said a litre of air from anywhere on Earth would breed swarms of life in broth, and he travelled to prove it. He ran the Rouen natural history museum and was no crank: his 1859 book of tests was why the French Academy took up the question. Where did he collect air?
answer: On the plains of Sicily, up Etna, and out at sea
choices: In the sewers of Paris, a hospital, and a coal mine
On the plains of Sicily, up Etna, and out at sea
On the Baltic coast, in a mill, and in a marsh
Over the Channel, in a shipyard, and in a cathedral
context: Pouchet's own boast: "With a cubic decimetre of air, taken where you like, I affirm that you can ever produce legions of microzoa." His side's slogan ran: "everywhere, strictly everywhere, air is constantly favourable to life" -- and every sample he took gave him growth. Felix Archimede Pouchet (1800-1872) directed the Rouen Museum of Natural History from 1828 and published 'Heterogenie, ou traite de la generation spontanee' in 1859. The educated public was leaning his way, too: in 1860 a science writer in the Paris paper La Presse told Pasteur in print, "I am afraid that the experiments you quote, M. Pasteur, will turn against you.... The world into which you wish to take us is really too fantastic...." Source: Vallery-Radot, 'The Life of Pasteur', Gutenberg #60956; biography from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Archimede_Pouchet.

question: Near Arbois, on the valley road, Louis Pasteur opened twenty sterile flasks and eight of them grew life. It was the start of his answer to Félix Pouchet. On Mont Poupet, 850 metres up, he opened twenty and five grew life. Then he crossed to the Mer de Glace, a glacier at about 2,000 metres, and opened twenty there. How many of those spoiled?
answer: One of the twenty
choices: None of the twenty
One of the twenty
Two of the twenty
Three of the twenty
context: Exactly one -- and that single flask matters. Popular summaries of the mountain trip (Grokipedia's among them) say none of the glacier flasks spoiled; Pasteur's own report to the Academie says one did, and he reported it instead of tidying it away. The gradient is the argument: 8 of 20 in the valley, 5 of 20 at 850 m, 1 of 20 on the ice. He had set out for Arbois carrying seventy-three flasks and opened twenty on the old road to Dole near his father's tannery, kneeling in the dust while vine labourers wondered what a holiday tourist wanted with all those little phials -- his old friend Jules Vercel told them, "What would you have? it amuses him!" The Mont Poupet summit above Salins is still marked as the spot. Source: Vallery-Radot, 'The Life of Pasteur', Gutenberg #60956; site confirmation terredelouispasteur.fr; the 'none spoiled' error at grokipedia.com/page/Louis_Pasteur.

question: High on the Mer de Glace, a glacier in the French Alps where the air should be at its cleanest, Louis Pasteur stood with sterile broth flasks in 1860. Each flask had to be opened to catch the air, then instantly melted shut in the jet of a spirit lamp. On his first day on the ice he did not manage to seal a single one. Why not?
answer: Glare off the ice made the flame invisible
choices: The thin mountain air would not let it light
The cold had frozen the alcohol to a jelly
Glare off the ice made the flame invisible
His guide had left the lamp down in Chamonix
context: In Pasteur's words to the Academie, "the dazzling whiteness of the ice in the sunlight was such that it was impossible to distinguish the jet of burning alcohol" -- and the wind kept blowing the flame he could not see off the glass. He could think of no way to make it visible without scattering strange dust into the air, so he carried thirteen unsealed, open flasks back down to the little Montanvert inn, "a sort of hut, letting in wind and rain," where they stood overnight in the dust of the room he slept in. Nearly all of them spoiled. He sent his guide down to Chamonix, a tinker rebuilt the lamp overnight, and the famous twenty were opened properly the next morning. He had reached Chamonix on 20 September 1860; a mule carried the case of thirty-three flasks up to the Montanvert while Pasteur walked right behind it along the precipices with one hand on the case so it would not be shaken. Source: Vallery-Radot, 'The Life of Pasteur', Gutenberg #60956, quoting Pasteur's own report.

question: Félix Pouchet refused to be settled by Louis Pasteur's mountain flasks. He took his own into the Pyrenees with two friends and hired guides, and opened the first at 8 in the evening at 2,083 metres, 83 metres higher than the spot where Pasteur had opened his. What did Pouchet do next?
answer: Slept out on the mountain and climbed to a glacier at dawn
choices: Slept out on the mountain and climbed to a glacier at dawn
Sent his guides back down the mountain for more phials
Opened the rest of his phials at that same height that night
Sealed his remaining phials to carry back to Rouen unopened
context: Pouchet judged eighty-three metres too small a margin to settle anything, so the party slept out in bitter cold and pushed on at first light to a glacier of the Maladetta at 3,000 metres -- a full kilometre above the ice where Pasteur had worked. In a very deep narrow crevasse they opened four phials, filled with a decoction of hay. Coming down, Joly slipped and a guide caught him above a precipice. Every one of the four phials grew life, and Pouchet reported it plainly: "therefore the air of the Maladetta, and of high mountains in general, is not incapable of producing alteration in an eminently putrescible liquor." He was not cheating and he was not careless; he really did see what he reported, and it would take another fifteen years to find out why. The party -- Pouchet with his colleagues Joly and Musset, and their guides -- had set out from Bagneres-de-Luchon. Source: Vallery-Radot, 'The Life of Pasteur', Gutenberg #60956, quoting Pouchet's own report.

question: Four phials opened in a Pyrenean crevasse all grew life for Félix Pouchet, while Louis Pasteur's flasks, opened lower down on a glacier, had almost all stayed clear. Pouchet was neither cheating nor careless, and the answer was not in the mountain air: it was in what the two men had put inside their glass. Pouchet used a decoction of hay; Pasteur used yeast water. What did that difference hide?
answer: Hay carries tough spores that live through boiling
choices: Hay water holds far more dissolved air than yeast water
Hay carries tough spores that live through boiling
Hay leaves an oily film that seals the phial's mouth
Hay water is too acid for a short boil to clean it
context: Hay water carries the spores of Bacillus subtilis -- dormant, armoured forms that survive a boil that kills ordinary bacteria. They stay inert while air is shut out and develop the moment oxygen returns, so Pouchet's 'sterilised' phials really did breed life. Nobody knew this at the time; the explanation surfaced about fifteen years later out of Pasteur's dispute with Henry Bastian (c. 1876-77), and Ferdinand Cohn independently proposed heat-resistant endospores after growing B. subtilis on boiled cheese. Sterilising liquids at 120 degrees C dates from that same quarrel -- which is Vallery-Radot's point: "A chapter might well have been written by a moralist On the use of certain opponents." Pouchet's side had put it in writing to the Academie -- "If one only of our flasks remains pure, we will loyally own our defeat" -- but when the commission (Flourens, Dumas, Brongniart, Milne-Edwards and Balard) ruled that one experiment would decide it, they withdrew, and Joly called the trial a 'circus competition'. Source: Vallery-Radot, 'The Life of Pasteur', Gutenberg #60956; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endospore.

question: Louis Pasteur stood before the Académie des Sciences in Paris in 1860 and reported on the sterile broth flasks he had carried into the Alps to test whether air carries living microbes. Popular books credit his swan-neck flasks with proving that germs cause disease. He was more careful about what he claimed. What did he himself say about disease in that report?
answer: That he hoped it might prepare the road for research into disease
choices: That he doubted the same dust had any part in human illness
That he would say nothing of disease until the flasks were repeated
That he hoped it might prepare the road for research into disease
That disease was work for physicians rather than for chemists
context: His actual words were a hope, not a claim: "What would be most desirable would be to push those studies far enough to prepare the road for a serious research into the origin of various diseases." The flasks had answered a narrower question -- where the life in spoiled broth comes from -- and Pasteur's explicit linking of microbes to contagion came much later, in 'Les Microbes organises' (1878). He also refused to let the flask result be used as a weapon by anyone: "There is here no question of religion, philosophy, atheism, materialism, or spiritualism... It is a question of fact; when I took it up I was as ready to be convinced by experiments that spontaneous generation exists as I am now persuaded that those who believe it are blindfolded." The physiologist Pierre Flourens had given the Academy the short version in November 1863: "M. Pasteur's experiments are decisive. If spontaneous generation is real, what is required to obtain animalculae? Air and putrescible liquor. M. Pasteur puts air and putrescible liquor together and nothing happens. Therefore spontaneous generation is not." Source: Vallery-Radot, 'The Life of Pasteur', Gutenberg #60956; 1878 dating from grokipedia.com/page/Louis_Pasteur.

question: Louis Pasteur, twenty-five, saw in 1848 that the crystals of a wine-cask salt came in two mirror-image shapes, like a left hand and a right hand. He decided to sort them into two piles. How did he separate them?
answer: He picked them apart one at a time with tweezers and a lens.
choices: He picked them apart one at a time with tweezers and a lens.
He seeded a fresh solution so that only one kind grew in it.
He boiled the heap down and drew off the crystals formed first.
He passed a polarized beam through the dish and read each one.
context: The tell was a hemihedral facet - a small extra face that shows on one side of a crystal and, on its mirror twin, on the other side. Wikipedia's 'Racemic acid' records that Pasteur was 'able in 1848 to isolate each of the two enantiomers by laboriously separating the two kinds of crystals using delicate tweezers and a hand lens'; Grokipedia's 'Louis Pasteur' describes the same work as sorting them into two piles under magnification. He was a year out of the Ecole Normale. His apparatus was patience. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racemic_acid ; grokipedia.com/page/Louis_Pasteur

question: Rene Vallery-Radot, Louis Pasteur's son-in-law, told in the family biography what Pasteur did in the minutes after his 1848 crystal sort worked. Only that book has it. What does it claim Pasteur did?
answer: He seized a curator in the corridor and dragged him to the gardens.
choices: He shut himself in the laboratory and answered nobody for a day.
He carried the two piles across Paris in his hat to his father.
He seized a curator in the corridor and dragged him to the gardens.
He stood on a bench in the courtyard and shouted at the students.
context: Vallery-Radot's The Life of Pasteur has the young man bolt from the laboratory, seize a curator in the corridors of the Ecole Normale and haul him into the Luxembourg Gardens to explain what he had found. The scene reaches us only through the family biography - Pasteur's notebooks say nothing of it - so it is filed here as legend, the same shelf as Newton's apple and Kekule's snake. Source: Rene Vallery-Radot, The Life of Pasteur (archive.org/details/lifeofpasteur00vall ; gutenberg.org/files/47505/47505-h/47505-h.htm)

question: Jean-Baptiste Biot, seventy-four, whose own tool for measuring how a solution twists light had made the question askable, would not trust a twenty-five-year-old on a crystal claim. He called Louis Pasteur to his lab to do it all again. By Pasteur's later telling, what did Biot insist on supplying?
answer: The acid, the soda and the ammonia that went in.
choices: The tweezers, the lens and the bench to work at.
The witnesses, the clerk and the written record.
The cask, the tartar and the water to dissolve it.
The acid, the soda and the ammonia that went in.
context: Pasteur's own recollection: 'He handed over to me some paratartaric acid which he himself had previously studied with particular care, and which he had found to be perfectly indifferent to polarised light. I prepared the double salt in his presence, with soda and ammonia which he had likewise desired to provide.' Biot supplied the acid, the soda and the ammonia; he would trust nothing of Pasteur's. Source: Pasteur's 1860 lecture on molecular asymmetry, English translation, web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/pasteur60.html

question: Louis Pasteur tipped out his dish of wine-cask salt and saw the crystals were not all built alike: the small extra facet each one carried sat on one corner in some of them and on another in the rest. A chemist in a hurry would have called the batch spoiled and thrown it out. Pasteur read the split heap as a finding instead. What in his earlier work made the split so startling?
answer: He had checked nineteen other compounds, and in each the facets all agreed.
choices: He had checked nineteen other compounds, and in each the facets all agreed.
He had grown this salt a dozen times, and never once seen a split heap.
He had read the whole tartrate literature, and found no split reported.
He had been taught from the start that such facets never vary at all.
context: Before the wine-cask salt, Pasteur had surveyed nineteen compounds, and in every one the small hemihedral facets all leaned the same way and the dissolved crystals all twisted a beam of polarized light the same way. A batch carrying both leans at once had never turned up. That perfect run is why the split heap struck him as an anomaly worth hours of sorting rather than as dirt in the flask. Source: whonamedit.com/doctor.cfm/2994.html (Louis Pasteur, on the 22 May 1848 Academy paper)

question: Eilhard Mitscherlich told the Paris Academy in 1844 about a puzzling acid, 'paratartaric'. It matched tartaric acid in every way: same recipe, same crystals, same weight. Yet tartaric acid twists a light beam and paratartaric did nothing. Chemists shrugged. Louis Pasteur found the answer in 1848. What was paratartaric acid?
answer: Two mirror-image forms in equal amounts, their opposite turns cancelling.
choices: Two mirror-image forms in equal amounts, their opposite turns cancelling.
Two unrelated acids mixed together, neither able to turn the light alone.
One acid holding an impurity that quenched the turn it would show alone.
One acid whose turn is far too small for any polarimeter to catch.
context: Pour the two sorted piles back together and the rotation vanishes to zero: the opposite turns cancel exactly, which is why Mitscherlich's polarimeter had read nothing. Paratartaric acid had never been one substance. Mitscherlich's 1844 note - read to the Academy by Biot himself - insisted that in the two salts 'the nature, the number, the arrangement, and the distance of the atoms are the same', and that sentence was the wall the young Pasteur refused to walk away from. This is where the idea of a racemic mixture begins. Sources: xray-exhibit.scs.illinois.edu/books/pasteur.php ; grokipedia.com/page/Racemic_mixture ; web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/pasteur60.html

question: Louis Pasteur told how Jean-Baptiste Biot, seventy-four and unconvinced, made him repeat the crystal experiment under his eye at the College de France. Biot put the more surprising of the two solutions into his instrument first and saw from the colours alone, without taking a measurement, that Pasteur was right. He took the young man by the arm and began, 'My dear child...'. How did Biot finish?
answer: '...I have loved science so much throughout my life that this makes my heart throb.'
choices: '...you have given an old man the finest morning he has known in fifty years.'
'...I have waited half a century for someone to bring me a result like this.'
'...I would give every honour I hold to have found this myself at your age.'
'...I have loved science so much throughout my life that this makes my heart throb.'
context: Pasteur's telling: 'He first placed in the apparatus the more interesting solution, that which ought to deviate to the left. Without even making a measurement, he saw by the appearance of the tints of the two images, ordinary and extraordinary, in the analyser, that there was a strong deviation to the left.' Then: 'Very visibly affected, the illustrious old man took me by the arm and said: My dear child, I have loved science so much throughout my life that this makes my heart throb.' In French: 'Mon cher enfant, j'ai tant aime les sciences dans ma vie que cela me fait battre le coeur.' The whole scene survives only through Pasteur's own 1860 lecture, twelve years after the fact, so it is flagged here as testimony rather than record. Sources: web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/pasteur60.html ; French original in Vantomme & Meijer, Chirality 2021 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291139/)  (Legend.)

question: About thirty to forty grams of crystals formed while Jean-Baptiste Biot waited at the College de France, because he had Louis Pasteur grow them in front of him. Then he called Pasteur in to pick out the right-hand crystals and the left-hand crystals by their shape, and imposed one more condition on him. By Pasteur's own later telling, what did Biot require?
answer: That Pasteur say which pile would turn the light which way, in advance.
choices: That Pasteur sort the whole batch twice and show the two runs agreed.
That Pasteur say which pile would turn the light which way, in advance.
That Pasteur do the sorting with Biot's own tweezers and no others.
That Pasteur hand both piles over and never touch the instrument himself.
context: Pasteur's account: 'When it had furnished about 30 to 40 grams of crystals, he asked me to call at the College de France in order to collect them and isolate before him, by recognition of their crystallographic character, the right and the left crystals, requesting me to state once more whether I really affirmed that the crystals which I should place at his right would deviate to the right, and the others to the left.' Biot made Pasteur call the shot before the instrument spoke - a pre-registered prediction, 1848 style, and the reason the result could not be talked into shape afterwards. Told by Pasteur himself in 1860, so flagged as testimony. Source: web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/pasteur60.html  (Legend.)

question: Louis Pasteur set down one working rule for the crystal separation: it had to be started in the morning. He was not being romantic about early hours - by afternoon the Paris laboratory had made the sorting impossible. What went wrong later in the day?
answer: The warmth partly redissolved the crystals and erased the small facets.
choices: The dust of the working day settled and hid the small facets from view.
The crystals went on growing until the small facets were overgrown.
The warmth partly redissolved the crystals and erased the small facets.
The daylight shifted and the small facets stopped catching the light.
context: Pasteur's working note: the crystallization 'must be undertaken in the morning, because the temperature elevation during the day makes the crystals partly redissolve, which makes the small hemihedral facets disappear.' The single feature he sorted by could be wiped out by an afternoon in a warm room. His apparatus really was patience. Source: Vantomme & Meijer, 'Pasteur and chirality: A story of how serendipity favors the prepared minds', Chirality 2021 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291139/)

question: A student tries Louis Pasteur's crystal sort with sodium ammonium paratartrate above about 28 degrees Celsius, and her tweezers have nothing to sort. The salt parts into left-handed and right-handed grains only when the room is cool, so Pasteur got lucky. What happens above that temperature?
answer: The two forms grow together into one crystal that holds both hands.
choices: The two forms grow together into one crystal that holds both hands.
The two forms grow as separate crystals far too small to be handled.
The two forms stay dissolved and never crystallize however long you wait.
The two forms keep swapping hands, each becoming its own mirror image.
context: The measured line: 'At 20 C, the sodium-ammonium tartrate crystallizes as a conglomerate and at 30 C as a racemate due to the dehydration of the conglomerate occurring at 28 C.' Above 28 C the two hands grow together into a single crystal and no tweezers on earth would separate them; Pasteur's laboratory happened to sit below the line. The wider luck: 'Less than 10% of racemic species can be resolved spontaneously by crystallization in the form of conglomerates.' Nine times in ten the trick simply does not work. The luck was real - what made him a scientist is that he knew what he was looking at. Sources: Vantomme & Meijer, Chirality 2021 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291139/) ; grokipedia.com/page/Louis_Pasteur

question: Louis Pasteur told his two kinds of crystal apart by a facet on the outside of each one, then dissolved the two piles and measured the liquids. The crystal shapes were gone, dissolved away, and each liquid kept its own effect on the light anyway. From that, Pasteur drew a conclusion he had no way to prove in 1848. What did he conclude?
answer: The twist must be built into the shape of the molecule itself.
choices: The crystal must leave a lasting imprint on the water it dissolves in.
The twist must come from a subtle fluid carried into the water.
The twist must come from how the molecules pack as they dissolve.
The twist must be built into the shape of the molecule itself.
context: Because the twist survived the destruction of the crystal, it had to live in the molecule. But nobody could say what shape a molecule even was until Jacobus van 't Hoff and Joseph Le Bel independently proposed the tetrahedral carbon atom in 1874 - twenty-six years after 1848. Pasteur's own image for what he had found: substances that 'resemble each other like the right and left hands'; he called the property dissymetrie, decades before the word chirality existed. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Asymmetric_carbon ; grokipedia.com/page/Jacobus_Henricus_van_'t_Hoff ; grokipedia.com/page/Stereochemistry ; web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/pasteur60.html

question: Louis Pasteur filled a flask with ammonium paratartrate in 1860, added a little phosphate and dropped in the common blue-green mould Penicillium glaucum. The salt held equal amounts of the right-handed and left-handed forms, which cancel each other out, so the flask turned polarized light, light vibrating in a single plane, not at all. Weeks later he read the flask in the polarimeter again. What had the mould done?
answer: It ate the right-handed form and left the left-handed one untouched.
choices: It ate neither form and lived instead on the phosphate he had added.
It ate the right-handed form and left the left-handed one untouched.
It ate both forms at the same rate and left the reading still at zero.
It ate the left-handed form first and then finished the right-handed one.
context: A flask that started optically dead ended up turning light to the left, because the mould had eaten one hand and left the other behind. Pasteur had seen the effect first in 1857, when microorganisms fed ammonium tartrate consumed the (+) form in strong preference to the (-) form; the 1860 mould experiment made it unmistakable. Living chemistry can tell left from right. Published as 'Note relative au Penicillium glaucum et a la dissymetrie moleculaire des produits organiques naturels', Comptes Rendus, session of Monday 20 August 1860. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Penicillium_glaucum ; the 1860 note as listed at lynge.com/en/chemistry/48139

question: A chemist makes an amino acid in a flask, and the reaction, left to itself, turns out a 50/50 mixture of both hands, exactly as Louis Pasteur's wine-cask salt did. Yet nearly every amino acid in a human body's proteins is the left-handed form, and nearly every sugar in its nucleic acids is the right-handed one. Why is life one-handed?
answer: No one yet knows - several explanations are live and none has won.
choices: Starlight of a single twist set the bias before life ever began.
A tiny early excess amplified itself until the other hand vanished.
No one yet knows - several explanations are live and none has won.
Meteorites delivered amino acids already biased toward one hand.
context: Said plainly: the origin of homochirality is still unknown. Live proposals include circularly polarized starlight driving asymmetric photochemistry; delivery by meteorites (some meteorite amino acids do show a small excess of the same hand life uses, though recent analysis challenges the link); autocatalytic amplification of a tiny initial excess, demonstrated in the laboratory but silent on where the first excess came from; and spin-polarized electrons or polarized muons from radioactive decay. None is settled. Pasteur's tweezers separated two hands that chemistry had made in equal numbers; life, somehow, did not. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Homochirality ; 'Life's homochirality: Across a prebiotic network' (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12403148/)

question: Wolfgang Pauli had a fix for a crisis in nuclear physics, but when the radioactivity experts gathered in Tubingen to argue it out, he did not go. He posted them an open letter from Zurich on 4 December 1930 and gave his reason in the letter itself. What kept him at home?
answer: A ball he was going to that week
choices: A ball he was going to that week
A concert he had promised to attend
A lecture course he could not miss
An illness his doctor warned of
context: Pauli's own words in the letter: 'Unfortunately, I cannot personally appear in Tubingen since I am indispensable here in Zurich because of a ball on the night from December 6 to 7.' He sent a colleague to carry the letter and answer questions for him, calling him 'the bearer of these lines', and signed off 'your humble servant, W. Pauli'. FOR THE RECORD: the dramatic confession popularly attached to this letter, about having done a terrible thing by postulating a particle that cannot be detected, is in no version of it. Two independent full translations have been read start to finish and it is not there. Source: Symmetry Magazine, English translation of the 4 December 1930 letter by Kurt Riesselmann, https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/sites/default/files/legacy/pdfs/200703/logbook_letter_translation.pdf ; second independent translation in Los Alamos Science No. 25 (1997), 'Detecting the Poltergeist', https://www.roma1.infn.it/~maiani/corso-fermi/letture-consigliate/letture-consigliate3/Detecting-the-Poltergeist.pdf

question: Worried by energy going missing when certain atoms spat out beta particles, Wolfgang Pauli wrote to a physics meeting in December 1930, suggesting that a tiny invisible particle was carrying it away. He was not proud of the idea, and he gave his own scheme a two-word nickname. What did he call it?
answer: A desperate remedy
choices: A desperate remedy
A convenient fiction
A hopeless conjecture
A necessary evil
context: The full phrase: his invention was 'a desperate remedy to save the exchange theorem of statistics and the law of conservation of energy'. He added, 'But so far I do not dare to publish anything about this idea, and trustfully turn first to you, dear radioactive people.' The letter, headed 'Physics Institute of the ETH Zurich', is addressed 'Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen'. Pauli did not just wave at a ghost either: he gave the particle spin one-half, made it obey his exclusion principle, denied it the speed of light, and capped its mass at 'in any event not larger than 0.01 proton mass'. His private name for it was 'my foolish child'. Sources: Symmetry Magazine translation of the letter, https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/sites/default/files/legacy/pdfs/200703/logbook_letter_translation.pdf ; C. Jarlskog, 'Birth of the neutrino, from Pauli to the Reines-Cowan experiment', https://inspirehep.net/files/277b3a60e9d5496069cb9077b2827f98

question: A girl lies asleep at midnight while neutrinos from the Sun come up through her bed from below, after crossing the whole planet. About 65 billion cross each square centimetre of her skin every second. Fermilab says only a tiny handful will ever actually strike anything inside her. Over her whole lifetime, how many?
answer: About one or two
choices: About one or two
About a thousand
Roughly a million
Several every day
context: Fermilab, flatly: despite the trillions passing through you every second, 'in your entire lifetime only one or two will stop and interact.' The flux is about 65 billion (6.5 x 10^10) solar neutrinos per square centimetre per SECOND, not per year, a figure popular accounts often garble. The same ghostliness is why they are such good messengers: when SN 1987A exploded, about two dozen neutrinos were caught within 12 seconds by detectors on opposite sides of the planet, machines that normally expect about one event a day. Frederick Reines on that work: 'It's like listening for a gnat's whisper in a hurricane.' Sources: Fermilab, 'What are neutrinos?', https://neutrinos.fnal.gov/faq/what-are-neutrinos/ ; Wikipedia 'Neutrino', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrino ; Los Alamos Science No. 25 (1997), 'Detecting the Poltergeist', pp.14, 16, https://www.roma1.infn.it/~maiani/corso-fermi/letture-consigliate/letture-consigliate3/Detecting-the-Poltergeist.pdf

question: James Chadwick measured the electrons from beta decay in 1914, hoping for the neat picture of alpha decay, where every alpha particle from a given atom comes out with the same energy. What he saw broke the math for sixteen years. What did those electron energies look like?
answer: A smooth spread from near zero to a sharp maximum
choices: A smooth spread from near zero to a sharp maximum
A single sharp line at the full decay energy
A cluster of three lines, one per decay path
A single line that drifted lower as the sample aged
context: Los Alamos Science: 'in 1914, to the great consternation of many, James Chadwick showed definitively that the electrons emitted in beta decay did not have one energy or even a discrete set of energies.' Only at the sharp upper end did the accounts balance; every decay below it looked like a theft.
