The problem was so ugly that physicists dodged it: Pauli's 1930 letter quotes Peter Debye, who had held Pauli's Zurich chair before him and who told him in Brussels, 'Oh, it's better not to think about this at all, like new taxes.' Source: Los Alamos Science No. 25 (1997), 'Detecting the Poltergeist', p.2, https://www.roma1.infn.it/~maiani/corso-fermi/letture-consigliate/letture-consigliate3/Detecting-the-Poltergeist.pdf ; Debye remark from the Symmetry Magazine translation of the letter, https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/sites/default/files/legacy/pdfs/200703/logbook_letter_translation.pdf

question: Frederick Reines and Clyde Cowan widened a narrow test well in their neutrino detector at the Hanford reactor in 1953 until a person would fit, on a team member's suggestion. They trussed up and lowered in everyone they could talk into it, the secretary included. All of them set the counters going. What in the human body was making those counts?
answer: Potassium-40 sitting naturally in their tissues
choices: Potassium-40 sitting naturally in their tissues
Carbon-14 built up from the food they ate
Radon gas breathed in and held in the lungs
Strontium-90 from fallout, lodged in bone
context: Cowan's account: 'a number of people, including our secretary, were trussed up and lowered into the 18-inch hole. We found quite a detectable counting rate from everyone. It was due to the radioactive potassium-40 naturally present in the body.' You are, right now, faintly radioactive, and so is every banana in the kitchen. The accident grew into the Los Alamos whole-body counter, used through the 1950s to measure how much fallout people had taken up. The idea came from team member Robert Schuch. Source: Los Alamos Science No. 25 (1997), 'Detecting the Poltergeist', pp.6, 8, quoting Cowan (1964), 'Anatomy of an Experiment', Smithsonian Institution Annual Report: 409, https://www.roma1.infn.it/~maiani/corso-fermi/letture-consigliate/letture-consigliate3/Detecting-the-Poltergeist.pdf

question: Wolfgang Pauli lost the name of his invisible particle within two years of his 1930 letter. He had called it a 'neutron', but something else entirely took the word, and Enrico Fermi's circle in Rome settled on 'neutrino', the little neutral one. What had taken the original word away?
answer: James Chadwick found a heavy neutral particle in the nucleus
choices: James Chadwick found a heavy neutral particle in the nucleus
Carl Anderson photographed a neutral track in cosmic rays
Paul Dirac predicted a neutral partner for the electron
Ernest Rutherford isolated a neutral form of hydrogen
context: The same James Chadwick who had opened the whole crisis in 1914 by measuring the beta spectrum closed off Pauli's name for the cure in 1932. Fermi first heard about Pauli's particle at a congress he organised in Rome in October 1931; Wikipedia credits Edoardo Amaldi with 'jokingly' coining 'neutrino' in conversation with Fermi at the Institute of Physics on via Panisperna, while Jarlskog's account credits Fermi himself. In a 1958 letter to Max Delbruck, Pauli traced the idea's real starting point back to Lise Meitner's long fight over the beta-decay spectrum. Sources: Wikipedia 'Neutrino', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrino ; C. Jarlskog, 'Birth of the neutrino, from Pauli to the Reines-Cowan experiment', https://inspirehep.net/files/277b3a60e9d5496069cb9077b2827f98

question: Norris Bradbury, the Los Alamos director, approved a plan in 1951 to catch a neutrino in the flash of a 20-kiloton bomb test. Frederick Reines and Clyde Cowan would hang their detector in a vacuum tank 75 feet long, in a shaft 150 feet deep near ground zero. The ground shock would arrive right behind the blast, and Cowan had an answer for that. What was the detector to do at countdown zero?
answer: Cut loose and fall freely down the tank
choices: Cut loose and fall freely down the tank
Set spinning on a gimbal to ride the shock
Lower fast onto a bed of liquid mercury
Drop onto a stack of heavy steel springs
context: Cowan, describing it in 1964: 'break the suspension with a small explosive, allowing the detector to fall freely in the vacuum' so that the earth shock passed harmlessly by an object already falling; then 'the detector would reach the bottom of the tank, landing on a thick pile of foam rubber and feathers', to be dug back out days later. They nicknamed the one-cubic-metre detector 'El Monstro' and the whole hunt 'Project Poltergeist'. Reines on how it ever got approved: 'Life was much simpler in those days - no lengthy proposals or complex review committees.' In autumn 1952 J. M. B. Kellogg, head of the Los Alamos Physics Division, talked them into trying a fission reactor instead. Source: Los Alamos Science No. 25 (1997), 'Detecting the Poltergeist', pp.4-6, quoting Cowan (1964) and Reines's Los Alamos talk notes, https://www.roma1.infn.it/~maiani/corso-fermi/letture-consigliate/letture-consigliate3/Detecting-the-Poltergeist.pdf

question: Hans Bethe and Robert Bacher calculated in 1936 that a neutrino would have to cross several light-years of solid matter before being stopped, and most physicists thought it impossible to catch. But their paper named one reaction a neutrino could definitely produce, and Frederick Reines and Clyde Cowan walked through that same door twenty years later. What was that process?
answer: Striking a proton and turning it into a neutron
choices: Striking a proton and turning it into a neutron
Knocking an electron clean out of its atom
Jolting an alpha particle out of a heavy nucleus
Sending a whole nucleus recoiling intact
context: Bethe and Bacher, 1936: 'it seems practically impossible to detect neutrinos in the free state... There is only one process which neutrinos can certainly cause. That is the inverse beta process.' Inverse beta decay is ordinary beta decay run backwards. In beta decay a neutron inside a nucleus turns into a proton and flings out an electron; run the other way, an arriving neutrino strikes a proton and turns it into a neutron. That grudging second sentence is the one door the pessimists left open, and it is the door Reines and Cowan walked through twenty years later. Source: Los Alamos Science No. 25 (1997), 'Detecting the Poltergeist', p.3, quoting Bethe & Bacher (1936), Reviews of Modern Physics 8:184, https://www.roma1.infn.it/~maiani/corso-fermi/letture-consigliate/letture-consigliate3/Detecting-the-Poltergeist.pdf

question: Clyde Cowan wrote of the 1953 run at Hanford, Washington, that they had the neutrino by the coattails but their evidence would not stand up in court. He and Frederick Reines had buried their detector under six feet of paraffin and eight inches of lead beside a working reactor, expecting a fifth of a count per minute. The counters ran at about five a minute whether the reactor was at full power or shut down cold. What was drowning them?
answer: Cosmic rays raining down through the roof
choices: Cosmic rays raining down through the roof
Potassium-40 in the concrete of the building
Radon seeping up through the floor of the room
Electrical noise inside the photomultipliers
context: Cowan's line, and it is the reason the next detector went into a basement: 'It is easy to shield out the noise men make, but impossible to shut out the cosmos... We felt we had the neutrino by the coattails, but our evidence would not stand up in court.' At Savannah River from late 1955 they took the only room that would fit the apparatus - a cramped basement with 11 metres of concrete between them and the reactor core and 12 metres of earth and building overhead, which is what finally killed the cosmic-ray rate. Source: Los Alamos Science No. 25 (1997), 'Detecting the Poltergeist', pp.7-9, quoting Cowan (1964), https://www.roma1.infn.it/~maiani/corso-fermi/letture-consigliate/letture-consigliate3/Detecting-the-Poltergeist.pdf

question: Niels Bohr refused to add any new particle to explain the energy leaking out of beta decay in 1930, while Wolfgang Pauli invented an unseen one to carry it quietly away. Bohr was willing instead to weaken the rule that energy is always conserved. What weakened version did he propose?
answer: Energy is conserved on average, not in each event
choices: Energy is conserved on average, not in each event
Energy is conserved in the nucleus, not on the way out
Energy is conserved for matter, not for radiation
Energy is conserved at low speeds, not near light speed
context: Pauli would not have it. On a postcard to Bohr in March 1929 he asked, in a literal translation from the German, 'Do you intend to continue with maltreatment of the poor energy law?' When Bohr sent him a draft note on the beta spectrum that July, Pauli's verdict was brutal: he doubted whether 'with such lack of knowledge one can at all justify publishing a note. In any case, let the note rest for a long time. And let the stars shine in peace.' The 1924 Bohr-Kramers-Slater paper ran nearly twenty pages and contained exactly one equation. Pauli later told C. S. Wu that Bohr had been his 'great opponent' while Enrico Fermi had sided with him - and that 'Bohr and I were accustomed to this kind of struggles in all friendship.' Source: C. Jarlskog, 'Birth of the neutrino, from Pauli to the Reines-Cowan experiment', https://inspirehep.net/files/277b3a60e9d5496069cb9077b2827f98

question: A fingerprint was what Frederick Reines and Clyde Cowan wanted at Savannah River in 1956, one that a single event either carried or did not and that no stray particle could forge. Background counts had outnumbered the neutrino signal at Hanford by more than twenty to one, and no shielding they could afford would fix it. What did they demand before an event counted as a neutrino?
answer: Two flashes microseconds apart, in a fixed order
choices: Two flashes microseconds apart, in a fixed order
One flash of exactly 1.8 million electron-volts
A flash seen by all 110 tubes in the same instant
A brightness that matched the neutrino's energy
context: THE TRICK: an antineutrino hits a proton in the water and makes a positron plus a neutron. The positron annihilates against an electron almost instantly - two gamma flashes at 0.51 MeV each. The neutron blunders about slowing down for a few microseconds, then is swallowed by one of the cadmium nuclei they had dissolved in the water (about 40 kg of cadmium chloride), which drops to a lower energy and releases roughly 9 MeV of gamma rays: a second, far brighter flash. Two flashes, in that order, 0.75 to 30 microseconds apart, each in its own energy window. Nothing else fakes it. The rate was about three such events an hour. Then they attacked their own signal: they dissolved a copper-64 positron source in the water to check the first flash; DOUBLED the cadmium and watched the delay shorten exactly as predicted; half-filled the tank with heavy water to halve the target protons and watched the signal halve; and piled four feet of sawdust bags, donated by a local sawmill and soaked for density, around the whole thing. On 14 June 1956 they wired Pauli: 'We are happy to inform you that we have definitely detected neutrinos from fission fragments by observing inverse beta decay of protons.' Pauli, at a CERN symposium in Geneva, interrupted the meeting to read it out - 'I make this announcement because otherwise everybody would ask me separately' - and wired back: 'Thanks for message. Everything comes to him who knows how to wait.' Reines wrote that Pauli and friends then got through a case of champagne. Published in Science, 20 July 1956; the Nobel came in 1995, to Reines alone, Cowan having died in 1974. Source: Los Alamos Science No. 25 (1997), 'Detecting the Poltergeist', pp.6-14, 22, https://www.roma1.infn.it/~maiani/corso-fermi/letture-consigliate/letture-consigliate3/Detecting-the-Poltergeist.pdf ; C. Jarlskog, https://inspirehep.net/files/277b3a60e9d5496069cb9077b2827f98

question: A physicist watches a detector deep underground for one decay nobody has ever recorded: two neutrons inside a germanium-76 or xenon-136 nucleus turning into two protons and two electrons, with nothing else leaving the atom. The searches have only pushed its minimum half-life past 10^26 years. Physicists still cannot answer a basic question about the neutrino, and they say so plainly. What would a single such decay prove about the neutrino?
answer: That the neutrino is its own antiparticle
choices: That the neutrino is its own antiparticle
That the neutrino's mass comes from the Higgs
That energy is not conserved in the nucleus
That a fourth, sterile neutrino exists
context: In ordinary double-beta decay two neutrons turn into two protons, two electrons AND two antineutrinos. If a neutrino were its own antiparticle - the Dirac-versus-Majorana question - the two could annihilate each other inside the nucleus and never come out, leaving the electrons to carry the whole energy. No one has seen it: GERDA has pushed the germanium-76 half-life limit past 1.8 x 10^26 years, KamLAND-Zen past 2.3 x 10^26 years for xenon-136. Nor does anyone know what a neutrino weighs. Cosmology (DESI, 2025) caps the sum of all three masses below 0.064 eV/c-squared at 95% confidence, and the best direct laboratory limit, from tritium beta decay, puts the electron neutrino below 0.45 eV/c-squared. Pauli's ghost is still not fully caught. Source: Grokipedia 'Neutrino', 'Basic Characteristics' and 'Majorana Nature' sections, https://grokipedia.com/page/Neutrino

question: Kary Mullis was driving up Highway 128 toward his cabin one Friday evening in 1983 when a way to copy any piece of DNA over and over popped into his head. He pulled over at mile marker 46.7 to check it. What did he work it out on?
answer: paper he found in the glove compartment
choices: paper he found in the glove compartment
the back of a road map from the door
a napkin from a diner in Cloverdale
the margins of a journal on the seat
context: Mullis in his own Nobel lecture: 'I stopped the car at mile marker 46,7 on Highway 128. In the glove compartment I found some paper and a pen.' Two accuracy notes for anyone who looks this up. First, secondary accounts often move the drive to Highway 17 or Highway 101, and Grokipedia's page on Mullis manages both in the same article; the man who was in the car says 128, toward Mendocino. Second, he never names the month. What he describes is California buckeye 'heavily in blossom' leaning over the road, which puts it in late spring. Source: Kary B. Mullis, Nobel Lecture, 8 December 1993, 'The Polymerase Chain Reaction' (nobelprize.org).

question: Jennifer Barnett, a chemist herself, rode beside her boyfriend Kary Mullis on Highway 128 one Friday night in 1983. He pulled over twice, and at the second stop, realizing his new scheme could copy any stretch of DNA he chose, he said out loud, 'Dear Thor!' What was Barnett doing through the whole invention?
answer: sleeping in the passenger seat
choices: sleeping in the passenger seat
reading the map by the dome light
telling him it could not work
writing the scheme down for him
context: Mullis shook her: 'Jennifer, wake up. I've thought of something incredible.' His own four words for what happened next: 'She wouldn't wake up.' Barnett was a chemist herself, and she slept through the invention of PCR. The realization at that second stop was the one that mattered: the two short primers did not have to sit close together, so he could pick any stretch of DNA he liked and copy that. Source: Kary B. Mullis, Nobel Lecture, 8 December 1993 (nobelprize.org).

question: Too wound up to sleep, Kary Mullis reached his mountain cabin very late one night in 1983 with a way to copy DNA in his head. The cabin had no phone, and no biochemist lived anywhere nearby to tell him whether it would work. What did he do until dawn?
answer: covered every flat surface with diagrams
choices: covered every flat surface with diagrams
wrote the scheme out as a patent claim
worked back through his graduate notes
walked the road below the cabin for hours
context: 'We got to my cabin and I starting drawing little diagrams on every horizontal surface that would take pen, pencil or crayon until dawn.' He was still hunting for the flaw all the next day, while Barnett sunned herself by the pond 'taking no interest in the explosions that were rocking my brain.' Source: Kary B. Mullis, Nobel Lecture, 8 December 1993 (nobelprize.org).

question: On a California roadside in 1983, Kary Mullis worked out what doubling could do. Ten doublings made a thousand. Twenty made a million. Thirty made a billion. He stopped at a billion, because it landed close to a number he knew about human beings. What did a billion land near?
answer: the base pairs in a human genome
choices: the base pairs in a human genome
the cells in a human body
the genes in a human genome
the neurons in a human brain
context: His words: 'close to the number of base pairs in the human genome.' The real figure is about three billion base pairs. For scale, the other three answers are real numbers too and none of them is near a billion: a human body runs to tens of trillions of cells, a brain to roughly 86 billion neurons, and the genome to only about 20,000 protein-coding genes. Source: Kary B. Mullis, Nobel Lecture, 8 December 1993 (nobelprize.org).

question: Kary Mullis set up his first PCR (polymerase chain reaction) near midnight in early September 1983: human DNA, two short primers aimed at a 400 base-pair target, one heating and cooling, then the enzyme. Next day it went on a gel, where DNA of one length makes a band. What did the gel show?
answer: no band at 400 base pairs
choices: no band at 400 base pairs
a clean band at 400 base pairs
a faint band at 400 base pairs
a band at half that length
context: Mullis's own report of the result is exact: there was no 400-base-pair band at all. The tube was 'a little screw-cap tube with an O-ring and a purple top,' and he added about 10 units of polymerase. He had been hoping to dodge the tedious part: heating and cooling the same tube over and over by hand. The missing band told him he could not. The first run that worked came on 16 December 1983, after he retreated from human DNA to a short piece of the bacterial plasmid pBR322, with a young mathematician on his staff, Fred Faloona, helping set it up. Source: Kary B. Mullis, Nobel Lecture, 8 December 1993 (nobelprize.org).

question: A student in a genetics lab starts a tube of polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which doubles its target every cycle: heat splits the double helix, two short synthetic pieces of DNA called primers settle onto the ends of the target, and a polymerase fills in the rest. In theory forty cycles from a single molecule would make over a trillion copies. Her real tube climbs hard for about twenty-five or thirty cycles and then flattens out. What stops the climb?
answer: the primers and loose bases run out
choices: the primers and loose bases run out
the finished copies begin to break apart
the enzyme starts miscopying every strand
the strands grow too long to come apart
context: This is called the plateau, and it arrives after roughly 25 to 30 cycles as the reagents are consumed. The standard cycle: about 94 to 98 C for 20 to 30 seconds to pull the strands apart, 50 to 65 C for 20 to 40 seconds so the primers latch on, then about 72 C for the polymerase to fill in, repeated 20 to 40 times. Thirty cycles turns one molecule into roughly a million to a billion copies. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polymerase_chain_reaction.

question: A whole weekend of hunting the flaw in his own DNA-copying scheme sent Kary Mullis to the library on Monday morning. It looked far too easy: if the method really worked, somebody must already have tried it and he would have heard about it. He searched for any earlier paper using two primers to copy DNA over and over. What did he find?
answer: nothing on it at all, success or failure
choices: nothing on it at all, success or failure
several groups already racing toward it
a report that it had been tried and failed
a description buried in a Cetus memo
context: 'There was nothing in the abstracted literature about succeeding or failing to amplify DNA by the repeated reciprocal extension of two primers.' Nobody had tried it. Mullis credits the gap in his own training for letting him see it at all: 'My ignorance served me well.' The reason it felt too easy was that every single step in the scheme was already routine, which is exactly why his Cetus colleagues shrugged when he described it at an in-house seminar that August. Source: Kary B. Mullis, Nobel Lecture, 8 December 1993 (nobelprize.org).

question: A technician in the first years of PCR (polymerase chain reaction) carried one tube between hot and cool water baths twenty or thirty times over, and a single run tied her up for the entire day. At every cycle she unscrewed the cap and pipetted in a fresh dose of enzyme. Why did the enzyme have to be replaced every time?
answer: the heat that split the strands destroyed it
choices: the heat that split the strands destroyed it
the enzyme was used up building each copy
the cooling step washed it off the strands
each new copy locked one enzyme in place
context: The enzyme in the 1983-84 experiments was the Klenow fragment of E. coli DNA polymerase I, and the 90 to 95 C denaturation step cooked it every round. Mullis: 'This also meant adding the thermally unstable polymerase after every cycle.' Cetus engineers built a robot to take over the pipetting, a prototype nicknamed Mr. Cycle, cobbled together from a liquid-handling instrument the company already owned with a sliding sample tray on the front; it is now in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. The first thermal cycler sold commercially, the Perkin-Elmer Cetus TC1, followed in 1987. Sources: Mullis Nobel Lecture 1993; grokipedia.com/page/Taq_polymerase; americanhistory.si.edu collection record for Mr. Cycle.

question: Two Cetus scientists purified an enzyme from a yellow rod-shaped bacterium, Thermus aquaticus, late in 1985. Dropped into PCR (polymerase chain reaction) the next year, it let a sealed tube be cycled and then left alone. Thomas Brock and his student Hudson Freeze had scooped that bacterium up 19 years earlier, chasing a question that had nothing to do with DNA. Where did they find it?
answer: a hot spring in Yellowstone National Park
choices: a hot spring in Yellowstone National Park
a hydrothermal vent in the deep Pacific
a compost heap on a Wisconsin farm
the outflow of an Illinois power station
context: Strain YT-1 came out of Mushroom Spring in the Lower Geyser Basin of Yellowstone in 1966, water at about 73 C, and Brock and Freeze formally described the species in 1969. Cetus never had to go to the park: Brock had deposited the culture with the American Type Culture Collection, where anyone could order it, and it is still listed as ATCC 25104, 'Thermus aquaticus Brock and Freeze.' Neither Brock nor Yellowstone ever collected a cent of royalty on Taq polymerase. Taq holds up for 40 to 50 minutes at 95 C and works best at 75 to 80 C, but it has no proofreading, so it miscopies about one base in every 10,000. Sources: nps.gov thermophile article; grokipedia.com/page/Thermus_aquaticus and /Taq_polymerase; atcc.org product 25104.

question: Thomas Brock set out in the 1960s with a National Science Foundation grant and a plain question: how hot can water get before life gives out? He sampled water hot enough to scald, and put his answer into a single sentence in a 1967 paper in Science. What did he conclude?
answer: that no upper temperature of life can be fixed
choices: that no upper temperature of life can be fixed
that growth stops a little short of boiling
that only spores, not growing cells, hold on
that the water's minerals set the real limit
context: The scientific literature of Brock's day held that water that hot could support nothing at all. His sentence: 'It is thus impossible to conclude that there is any "upper temperature of life."' Brock later said, 'I am very lucky to have been able to spend 10 years doing research in Yellowstone, one of the most exciting places on the planet.' In 2013 he and Hudson Freeze received the Golden Goose Award, which exists to honor odd-sounding federally funded research that pays off enormously, described as 'two scientists with an NSF grant [who] followed their insatiable curiosity to a hot spring.' Curiosity-driven microbiology in a hot spring paid off two decades later in every crime lab on Earth. Sources: nps.gov thermophile article, quoting Brock's 1967 Science paper; goldengooseaward.org.

question: Dan Koshland, who had sat on Kary Mullis's PhD qualifying committee at Berkeley, was editing the journal Science when it proclaimed PCR (polymerase chain reaction) its Molecule of the Year. Three years earlier, Mullis had sent that same journal the paper he had written himself setting out the method. What had Science done with it?
answer: rejected it outright
choices: rejected it outright
run it as a cover story
held it two years in review
asked for more experiments
context: Mullis notes the pairing in his Nobel lecture: Koshland 'would be the editor of Science when my first PCR paper was rejected from that journal and also the editor when PCR was three years later proclaimed Molecule of the Year.' The same journal did publish the first applied PCR paper, by Saiki, Scharf, Faloona, Mullis, Horn, Erlich and Arnheim in 1985, using PCR to diagnose sickle cell anemia; the version using the heat-proof enzyme followed in 1988 and could find a single target molecule among 100,000 genomes. Peer review is a filter, not a truth detector. Sources: Mullis Nobel Lecture 1993; Science 230:1350-1354 (1985); Science 239:487-491 (1988).

question: Detectives got the profile of the woman they had hunted for sixteen years back from the burned remains of a male asylum seeker in March 2009. Her DNA had surfaced at more than forty crime scenes across Germany, Austria and France, among them a half-eaten biscuit, a burned-out car and the 2007 murder of a young police officer, Michele Kiesewetter. The hunt had run to about two million euros. Where had the DNA been coming from?
answer: a worker on the line making the police swabs
choices: a worker on the line making the police swabs
a technician who had handled every one of the files
a fault that copied one profile across records
an officer who had attended all the scenes
context: The Phantom of Heilbronn was a woman on the production line at Greiner Bio-One in Austria, which manufactured the sterile cotton swabs the police used to collect their evidence. The swabs were genuinely sterile: bacteria, fungi and viruses had all been killed. Sterile is not the same thing as DNA-free, and PCR copies a stray molecule as faithfully as the one you wanted. Baden-Wurttemberg alone had burned more than 16,000 hours of police overtime and posted a 300,000-euro reward. The case produced ISO 18385 in 2016, the first international standard requiring forensic swabs and tubes to be manufactured free of human DNA. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Phantom_of_Heilbronn; iso.org news release, July 2016.

question: A worker in a hospital PCR (polymerase chain reaction) laboratory mixes reagents in one room, opens patient samples in a second and cycles the sealed tubes in a third. She, her racks and her paperwork move through those rooms in one direction only. Which stray DNA is that whole layout built above all to keep out of a fresh tube?
answer: the copies made by an earlier run
choices: the copies made by an earlier run
sample DNA from the patient before
shed skin cells from a technician
template DNA in the reagent stock
context: The dangerous contaminant is not the patient, it is yesterday's success: a finished reaction holds billions of copies of exactly the sequence tomorrow's reaction is looking for, so traffic runs clean to dirty and never back. Every run also carries a negative control, a tube given everything except a sample; if that one comes up positive, the run is thrown out. Many labs go further and build each new copy using uracil in place of thymine, then open the next reaction with an enzyme that chews up anything carrying uracil, destroying last week's product before this week's cycling starts. It is worth being precise about what a positive result claims: 'detected' is a statement about molecules present in a tube, not a statement that an infection is live. Sources: WHO laboratory quality guidance on separated PCR areas; US EPA QA/QC guidance for PCR.

question: Kary Mullis left Cetus Corporation in 1986 with a few months' salary and a one-time bonus that the company called the largest it had ever paid a scientist for an invention. Cetus, not Mullis, owned the two patents on PCR (polymerase chain reaction), and on 23 July 1991 it sold PCR to Hoffmann-La Roche for $300 million in cash. What was the bonus?
choices: $2 million
context: Ten thousand dollars, reported as the largest bonus Cetus had ever paid a scientist for an invention, against a sale price of $300 million plus royalties reported at up to $30 million more. The patents were U.S. 4,683,195 and 4,683,202. Ron Cook, who had built the first commercial DNA synthesis machine, gave Mullis the advice at his own dinner table in 1983: quit, patent it yourself, get rich. Sources: Mullis Nobel Lecture 1993; grokipedia.com/page/Kary_Mullis; nationalgeographic.com on Mullis and the PCR test.

question: Kary Mullis shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for one piece of work, the polymerase chain reaction. Later he wrote that HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) does not cause AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome), saying he could not find the paper that proved it. The evidence for the link is overwhelming, and the strongest answer was a count. The Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study tracked the immune cells whose loss defines AIDS in men without HIV. In more than 22,000 tests, how many showed the collapse?
context: Exactly once, out of more than 22,000 determinations. The rest of the count runs the same way: in NIH cohort data, people who were HIV-positive were about 1,100 times more likely to develop an AIDS-defining illness than people who were not; AIDS turned up in heterosexual men and women, homosexual men and women, hemophiliacs, transfusion recipients, drug users and infants, groups sharing almost nothing except HIV infection; drugs designed to block specific HIV enzymes work; and people carrying certain CCR5 mutations resist infection. The Institute of Medicine concluded that 'the evidence that HIV causes AIDS is scientifically conclusive.' Mullis, who also rejected human-caused climate change and died at home in Newport Beach on 7 August 2019, is the reason this question exists. A Nobel Prize is awarded for a piece of work; it is not a certificate that its holder is right about everything afterwards. Note that the rule cuts both ways: an authority's credentials are not evidence, and neither are a dissenter's. What settles it is the count. Sources: NIAID fact sheet, 'The Evidence That HIV Causes AIDS'; grokipedia.com/page/Kary_Mullis.

question: Arthur Smith Woodward, the British Museum's chief geologist, stood with the amateur fossil hunter Charles Dawson before a room of geologists in London in 1912. They claimed to have solved the biggest puzzle in human origins: the missing link between ape and man. What had they brought to show?
answer: A skull dug from a Sussex gravel pit
choices: A skull dug from a Sussex gravel pit
A tooth found in a cave on Java
A footprint cast from an Ethiopian bed
A rib fossil dug from a German quarry
context: They named it Eoanthropus dawsoni, the 'Piltdown Man', after the Sussex village nearby. It sat in the textbooks as the first Englishman for forty-one years. Source: Natural History Museum (nhm.ac.uk).

question: Kenneth Oakley ran a chemistry test in 1953 on the Piltdown skull and its jaw, celebrated for forty years as the missing link between ape and man. Buried bones absorb fluorine from the surrounding soil over time, so two bones from one body should carry similar amounts. What did his numbers show?
answer: Wildly different fluorine levels in the two pieces
choices: Wildly different fluorine levels in the two pieces
Identical fluorine levels in the two pieces
No fluorine absorption at all in either piece
Fluorine levels older than any known human fossil
context: They could not be from one creature. Oakley's follow-up chemistry with Weiner then blew the case wide open. Source: Science History Institute.

question: A student assumes that anonymous outside experts have always read scientific papers before they were printed. The modern system, where two or three referees judge a paper before publication, is far younger than she guesses: the famous British journal Nature began requiring outside referees only in 1973. Before that year, what did Nature require of the scientists submitting papers?
answer: No outside referees; the editor decided alone
choices: No outside referees; the editor decided alone
Two outside referees and a statistical check
A public seminar before submission was allowed
A signed affidavit of methods from every author
context: Newton, Darwin and Einstein published without a modern peer-review system. Henry Oldenburg's Philosophical Transactions (1665) used trusted Royal Society members informally. Nature made external refereeing a requirement only in 1973, under editor David Davies. Source: Baldwin, Notes and Records of the Royal Society (PMC).

question: Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen sent a paper on gravitational waves to Physical Review in 1936. The editor, John Tate, did something unusual for the day. Einstein wrote back furiously and pulled the paper. In his letter, what did he say Tate had done wrong?
answer: Shown his manuscript to specialists before it was printed
choices: Shown his manuscript to specialists before it was printed
Refused to pay him the standard author's fee that year
Insisted the paper be co-signed by an American physicist
Demanded he remove Rosen's name from the byline entirely
context: The sting in the tail: the referee, Howard Percy Robertson, had spotted a real error -- Einstein's paper had claimed gravitational waves do not exist. Einstein quietly fixed it, republished in the Journal of the Franklin Institute, and never sent to Physical Review again. Source: Kennefick, Physics Today; Weinstein 2016 (arXiv).

question: An editor slips several deliberate method errors into a paper and sends it out to reviewers, testing them the way a metal detector is tested: plant known objects and count how many the machine finds. Roughly what fraction of those planted errors do reviewers catch on average?
answer: About one in three
choices: About one in three
About nine in ten
Essentially all of them
Essentially none of them
context: Godlee (1998) and Schroter et al. (2008) both put the average detection rate at roughly 20 to 33 percent. Two or three busy strangers reading your write-up, with no access to your raw data. Useful. Not a truth-detector. Source: Schroter et al., JRSM 2008 (PubMed).

question: John Bohannon, a journalist writing in Science, ran a ten-month sting in 2013. He wrote a fake paper about a cancer drug from a lichen, with errors any competent reviewer should have caught, and sent 304 versions to open-access journals. What happened?
answer: 157 of the 304 journals accepted it
choices: 157 of the 304 journals accepted it
All 304 correctly rejected it
Only 3 of the 304 accepted it
Only 10 of the 304 accepted it
context: Elsevier and Sage titles were among the acceptors. Bohannon's sting had no subscription-journal control group and was criticised for that; the fair reading is 'lax review is common', not 'open access is worse'. Source: Bohannon, Science 342:60 (2013).

question: Jan Hendrik Schön published a solid-state physics paper roughly every eight days at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey in 2001, most of them in Nature or Science, and he was widely tipped for a Nobel Prize. Peer reviewers waved every one of them through without complaint. What eventually gave him away as a fraud?
answer: Other physicists spotted the same noise curve in different experiments
choices: Other physicists spotted the same noise curve in different experiments
A whistleblower inside his own lab reported him to police
An automated image-forgery scanner flagged duplicated figures
The journal editors ran a routine statistical audit that year
context: Julia Hsu and Lynn Loo noticed the anomaly first while checking his papers for a patent; Lydia Sohn confirmed it. The Beasley committee reported on 25 September 2002, and about 25 papers were withdrawn -- seven from Nature and eight from Science. The catch came from readers, not reviewers. Source: American Physical Society, APS News 2022.

question: Outside readers poked at the numbers in a study The Lancet printed in May 2020, on 96,032 COVID-19 patients from 671 hospitals worldwide, supplied by a company called Surgisphere. The World Health Organization (WHO) had paused a hydroxychloroquine trial arm on the strength of it. What did they spot that really killed the paper?
answer: Surgisphere had about eleven employees and impossible Australian figures
choices: Surgisphere had about eleven employees and impossible Australian figures
The lead author had been previously convicted of research fraud
None of the 671 hospitals named in the paper actually existed
The statistical software used had been discontinued a decade earlier
context: Retracted on 4 June 2020, three weeks after publication. Peer review at The Lancet had cleared it; a handful of readers with a spreadsheet did not. Source: Wikipedia (Surgisphere); The Lancet retraction notice 2020.

question: A reader goes through the cases of Jan Hendrik Schön at Bell Labs and Diederik Stapel at Tilburg, who both invented their data for years while peer review, anonymous experts reading a paper before a journal prints it, waved every fake through. It would be tempting to conclude that peer review is worthless. Controlled studies say something more interesting. What has it, at its best, been shown to be reliably good at?
answer: Improving how a paper's methods and writing are reported
choices: Improving how a paper's methods and writing are reported
Detecting outright invented raw data before publication
Predicting which studies will replicate ten years later
Ranking papers by their eventual future citation count
context: Peer review is a smell test performed by two or three busy strangers who never see the raw data. Useful. Not the same thing as true. The catch, when it comes, tends to come from outside review -- from a reader with a ruler, a chemist with a spreadsheet, a graduate student who wouldn't let it go. Source: Schroter et al., JRSM 2008.

question: Eighteen-year-old William Perkin was trying to build a malaria drug from coal-tar chemicals in a small lab at the top of his London house over Easter 1856. His test gave a thick black sludge. Instead of throwing it out, he poured alcohol on it. What did the alcohol pull out?
answer: a brilliant purple solution
choices: a brilliant purple solution
a colourless oily liquid
a stiff olive-green paste
a cloudy yellow-brown oil
context: Perkin called the colour 'strangely beautiful'. Purple crystals settled out of the solution as it cooled. He was eighteen, on a school holiday - and what he had made had nothing whatever to do with quinine, the malaria drug he was chasing; nobody built quinine in a flask until the twentieth century. What makes him a scientist rather than a boy who spilled something is that he investigated the failure instead of rinsing it down the sink. Source: Grokipedia 'William Henry Perkin' §Synthesis and Identification; Grokipedia 'Mauveine' §Perkin's Accidental Synthesis; Chemistry World, 'Mauveine'.

question: Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge was distilling coal tar in 1834, the sticky black waste left by making coal gas, when he drew off a clear oily liquid that nobody had a name for yet. On a hunch he dripped bleaching powder into a fresh sample. What did the liquid do?
answer: It flashed a strong blue
choices: It flashed a strong blue
It clouded a milky white
It turned a deep blood red
It settled to a straw yellow
context: Runge's liquid flashed a strong blue, and he named the substance 'kyanol', the Greek for blue; the chemical he had added was bleaching powder, calcium hypochlorite. Carl Julius Fritzsche gave the compound the name we still use, aniline, in 1840, and Otto Unverdorben had already isolated the same thing from indigo in 1826, calling it 'crystallin'. Runge's route is the one that mattered, because coal tar was piling up by the ton at every gasworks and nobody wanted it. Twenty-two years later a schoolboy made the first synthetic dye out of that same liquid. Source: McGill Office for Science and Society, 'From Black Goo to Blue Dye and Beyond'; Grokipedia 'William Henry Perkin' §Attempt to Synthesize Quinine.

question: A doctor at St Thomas's Hospital in London admitted a malaria patient in 1853, one of roughly a quarter of all admissions there, 237 patients in every thousand. One substance, and only one, reliably treated the disease, and it grew nowhere in Europe. What was the drug drawn from?
answer: the bark of the South American cinchona tree
choices: the bark of the South American cinchona tree
the seed of the East Indian nutmeg tree
the resin of the Arabian frankincense tree
the root of the West African kola tree
context: Quinine came from cinchona bark, shipped across the Atlantic, and by the 1850s overharvesting plus a Spanish commercial monopoly had made it scarce and ruinously expensive - the East India Company alone was spending about £100,000 a year on bark in the 1850s and still could not get enough. That price is why chemists wanted to build quinine from scratch in a flask. Source: Grokipedia 'William Henry Perkin' §Attempt to Synthesize Quinine.

question: The head of London's Royal College of Chemistry put an idea into print in 1849. Tons of coal tar were piling up at the city's gasworks, and out of it came a cheap stuff called aniline. Could quinine, the only malaria drug, be built from that? In 1855 he handed the problem to a 17-year-old lab assistant, William Perkin. Which chemist ran the college?
answer: August Wilhelm von Hofmann
choices: August Wilhelm von Hofmann
Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge
Carl Julius Fritzsche
Hermann von Fehling
context: August Wilhelm von Hofmann had come from Germany to run the Royal College of Chemistry, and his 1849 proposal is what pointed a laboratory at cheap gasworks aniline in the first place. Aniline was available at all because Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge had distilled it out of coal tar in 1834, and Carl Julius Fritzsche gave it its modern name in 1840. Perkin enrolled in October 1853, aged fifteen, and Hofmann made him a laboratory assistant by 1855, aged seventeen. The proposal was chemically hopeless - nobody built quinine in a flask until the twentieth century - but it is the reason a teenager was heating aniline at Easter in 1856. Source: McGill Office for Science and Society, 'From Black Goo to Blue Dye and Beyond'; Grokipedia 'William Henry Perkin' §Schooling and Apprenticeship, §Attempt to Synthesize Quinine.

question: A stoker at a London gasworks cooked a batch of coal for the city's street lamps, lit by coal gas since 1813, and was left with a thick black tar. For forty years nobody in the country had any use for the stuff, and the works made tons of it. What did the gasworks do with it?
answer: Ran it straight into the river beside the works
choices: Ran it straight into the river beside the works
Burned it off in open pits behind the retort houses
Buried it in trenches at the edge of the city
Mixed it into mortar for the London building trade
context: Gasworks were built beside rivers partly so they could dump their liquid waste: tar, ammonia and sulfuric acid went straight into the Thames. The dumping only tailed off in the 1850s, when chemists began pulling useful compounds out of the tar instead - and Perkin's purple, in 1856, is what turned that trickle into an industry. The rubbish became the raw material. Source: The Chemical Engineer, 'Old King Coal Part 3: Coal Chemicals'; Greater London Industrial Archaeology Society, 'Chemicals from Coal', Part 1.

question: William Henry Perkin, eighteen, dyed scraps of silk with his new colour and sent them to J. Pullar & Son of Perth, an established Scottish dyeing house, to hear what a professional would make of them. Robert Pullar wrote back calling the discovery one of the most valuable to come out in a very long time - and attached one condition to the praise. What was the condition?
answer: That the dye must not make the finished goods too expensive
choices: That the dye must not make the finished goods too expensive
That the dye must hold its colour in strong summer sunlight
That the dye must take on wool and cotton as well as silk
That the dye must be supplied by the ton, not the sample bottle
context: Robert Pullar wrote: 'if your discovery does not make the goods too expensive, it is decidedly one of the most valuable that has come out for a very long time.' Perkin filed his patent shortly afterwards. The condition was shrewd - mauveine sold at around £120 a kilogram in 1857, and Perkin's process gave a yield of only about 1-2% after purification. Source: Selvedge Magazine, 'Maverick Mauveine'; Grace's Guide, 'William Henry Perkin (1838-1907)'; Grokipedia 'Mauveine' §Initial Recognition and Patenting.

question: Empress Eugenie of France was wearing William Perkin's new colour by 1857, and within three years of his accident London had gone mad for it. Queen Victoria would appear in a gown of it at the London International Exhibition of 1862. The satirical magazine Punch gave the craze a mocking name in August 1859, a disease name. What did Punch call it?
answer: the mauve measles
choices: the mauve measles
the aniline itch
the dyers' fever
the purple pox
context: Punch's joke ran that the epidemic began with a rash of ribbons and ended with the whole body covered in mauve. Perkin had first called the colour 'Tyrian purple', after the ancient dye wrung out of murex sea snails - roughly 10,000 shellfish for a single gram, by the historian B. Caseau's reckoning, and Diocletian's price edict of 301 CE valued a pound of it at about three pounds of gold. Perkin's colour was renamed mauveine, from the French mauve, the mallow flower, and the short name took hold around 1859. Purple had been the most expensive colour on Earth for three thousand years; a teenager made it out of gasworks tar. The Science Museum holds fabric samples supplied to Queen Victoria around 1860. Source: Grokipedia 'Mauveine' §Cultural and Fashion Significance, §Initial Recognition and Patenting; Science Museum, 'Mauve Mania'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Tyrian Purple'.

question: An eighteen-year-old chemistry student, William Henry Perkin, set out in 1856 to make artificial quinine, the precious drug that was the only cure for malaria, from cheap chemicals fished out of coal tar. By the standards of his day the plan was perfectly respectable, and his professor approved it. It was also doomed from the start. What kind of reasoning was the plan built on?
answer: Counting atoms: if the formulas balance, the molecules should follow
choices: Counting atoms: if the formulas balance, the molecules should follow
Copying nature: concentrating the natural drug down step by step
Fitting shapes: assembling the atoms into the right arrangement
Brute trial: mixing coal-tar compounds until one of them worked
context: Perkin's arithmetic ran: two molecules of allyltoluidine (C10H13N) plus three oxygens should give quinine (C20H24N2O2) plus water. The atoms balance exactly - and that means nothing, because the same atoms can be arranged into completely different molecules. In 1856 chemists knew molecular formulas but not molecular shapes; structural theory, from Kekule, Couper and Butlerov, arrived roughly a decade later. Perkin's first attempt used allyltoluidine and gave a red-brown precipitate; he simplified to plain aniline and got the black sludge. Nobody made quinine in a flask until the twentieth century. Source: Resonance (Indian Academy of Sciences), 'Perkin's Mauve: The History of the Chemistry'.

question: A chemist repeats William Henry Perkin's 1856 experiment today with clean, laboratory-pure aniline and gets no mauve. The aniline Perkin started from was distilled out of coal tar, and it was dirty with toluidines, aniline molecules carrying an extra methyl group. The dirt was not bad luck that Perkin got away with; it was a requirement. Why was it required?
answer: The methyl groups end up built into the dye molecule itself
choices: The methyl groups end up built into the dye molecule itself
The methyl groups are stripped off and drive the reaction forward
The methyl groups shield the ring so only one linkage can form
The methyl groups seed the crystals that pure aniline never forms
context: Mauveine A is C26H23N4+ and mauveine B is C27H25N4+. The product you get from pure aniline alone - pseudomauveine, C24H19N4+ - carries no methyl groups at all, and it is not mauve. Chemistry World puts it flatly: 'If Perkin had employed pure aniline for his experiment, he would not have obtained the dye.' So this is not an anecdote about luck; it is a structural requirement. Modern replications using controlled 1:2:1 aniline / p-toluidine / o-toluidine ratios reach yields of 4-9%. Source: Chemistry World, 'Mauveine'; Grokipedia 'Mauveine' §Molecular Composition, §Original Perkin Process; Imperial College, 'Mauveine: The First Industrial Organic Fine-Chemical'.

question: The professor who had set William Henry Perkin on the quinine problem in the first place told him plainly not to abandon academic chemistry for trade. Perkin was nineteen. He held a patent on a purple dye and had neither money nor a factory. How did he raise the capital?
answer: Talked his carpenter father into staking the family's savings
choices: Talked his carpenter father into staking the family's savings
Sold the patent outright to a Manchester printing house
Licensed the process to the Scottish firm that had praised it
Borrowed against his salary as a college laboratory assistant
context: Perkin's father George, a carpenter and builder, put up the money; his elder brother Thomas came in on construction and the business. The Science History Institute records the decision plainly - it was taken 'Against Hofmann's recommendation.' Perkin had filed on 26 August 1856, aged eighteen: British Patent No. 1984, 'Manufacture of Certain New Colouring Matters from Aniline', granted 20 February 1857, the first legal protection for a synthetic organic dye. Ground was broken in June 1857 at Greenford Green near Harrow - about six acres on the Grand Junction Canal, chosen for water and transport - and the works were producing by December 1857. Source: Science History Institute, 'William Henry Perkin'; Grokipedia 'William Henry Perkin' §Patenting and Production; Grokipedia 'Mauveine' §Industrial Production.

question: Gerhard Domagk fed compounds off the shelves of the German chemical combine IG Farben (Interessengemeinschaft Farben) to mice infected with streptococcus, chasing what Paul Ehrlich had called a magic bullet, a substance that attacks germs inside a patient without harming the patient. One of them cured the mice in 1932, and by 1935 it was on sale as Prontosil, the first drug that ever cured a bacterial infection. What had Domagk taken down from the shelf?
answer: a red dye for cloth
choices: a red dye for cloth
an extract of mould
an arsenic compound
a quinine derivative
context: Domagk, at IG Farben's Elberfeld laboratories, took down a red azo dye carrying a sulfonamide group: the first drug in history that could cure a bacterial infection was a cloth dye, and he took the 1939 Nobel Prize for it. The idea behind it started at a microscope. Paul Ehrlich spent his 1878 doctoral work at Leipzig staining tissue with the new coal-tar dyes and kept noticing that a dye would fasten onto one kind of cell and ignore the cell lying beside it; if a colour could find its target that precisely, he reasoned, a drug could be built to do the same. His cousin Carl Weigert had pioneered aniline dyes as biological stains, and Ehrlich had earlier tried methylene blue against malaria parasites. Compound 606, an arsenic compound sold as Salvarsan, was the first successful targeted antimicrobial, and Ehrlich coined a word for the whole approach: chemotherapy. Bayer itself had been founded in 1863 as a coal-tar dye firm, opened a pharmaceutical department in 1888 and patented aspirin in 1899. Source: Hektoen International, 'Paul Ehrlich: From aniline dyes to the magic bullet'; Science History Institute, 'Paul Ehrlich' and 'Gerhard Domagk'; Britannica, 'Gerhard Domagk'; Bayer corporate history, 'History 1863-1881'.

question: William Henry Perkin patented mauveine in 1856, built a factory on it, dressed an empress in it and made a fortune out of it. The answer to what the stuff actually was did not arrive until 1994, a hundred and thirty-eight years later. What had nobody realised about the purple in Perkin's own vats?
answer: It is a mixture of a dozen or more chemically related salts
choices: It is a mixture of a dozen or more chemically related salts
It is a single molecule built around a ring of six nitrogens
It is the same molecule the ancients wrung out of sea snails
It is a close chemical relative of the quinine he was chasing
context: Mauveine is a mixture of a dozen or more related phenazinium salts. Its principal component was identified in 1994 as 3-amino-2,9-dimethyl-5-phenyl-7-(p-tolylamino)phenazinium salt; the 1994 work moved an aminotolyl group to position 7, changed the 5-substituent from tolyl to phenyl, and moved a methyl to position 9. Perkin made it, sold it and never knew its formula. He sold Perkin & Sons in 1874, aged thirty-six, worn down by German competition, and spent the rest of his life on research, publishing around ninety papers. He was knighted in 1906, fifty years after the accident, and the Perkin Medal was founded that same year and first awarded to him. Source: Imperial College, 'Mauveine: The First Industrial Organic Fine-Chemical'; Grokipedia 'Mauveine' §Molecular Composition; Grokipedia 'William Henry Perkin' §Retirement and Challenges, §Honours and Awards.

question: Ludwig Rehn, a Frankfurt surgeon, read a paper called Urinary Bladder Tumours Among Fuchsine Workers at a German surgeons' meeting in April 1895. Using a lighted tube for looking inside the bladder, he had checked forty-five men from the magenta room at the Hoechst dyeworks, and he found cancer in three of them. How did the dyeworks reply?
answer: The company's own surgeon disputed him then and there
choices: The company's own surgeon disputed him then and there
The company shut the magenta department within a year
The company paid the three men and said nothing publicly
The company funded Rehn to examine its whole workforce
context: Rehn kept going. By 1904 he had reported twenty more cases among men making aniline, fuchsine, benzidine and naphthylamine. He was right: the aromatic amines that made the brilliant new colours also caused the tumours, and dye work became one of the first occupational cancers ever identified. The honest version of Perkin's story has to carry this too - the same chemistry that gave the world cheap colour, aspirin and the first antibacterial drug also killed the men in the magenta department. Source: Frontiers in Bioscience (Elite), 'Bladder tumours and aromatic amines - historical milestones from Ludwig Rehn to Wilhelm Hueper'; Urology, 'Workers Died of Dyes: The Discovery of Occupational Bladder Cancers'.

question: Charles Redheffer charged admission in New York in 1813 to a machine he claimed would spin forever with no fuel. Robert Fulton, the steamboat engineer, watched it and, without touching a part, called it a fraud. What had he noticed?
answer: Its motion staggered unevenly instead of running steady
choices: Its motion staggered unevenly instead of running steady
Its wheel turned too smoothly for its rough old bearings
Its main wheel was far larger than the load it lifted
Its parts were painted over to hide the joins between them
context: Fulton said the machine's motion was unsteady and wobbling, as though a person were driving it by hand, irregularly. A machine running on its own steady power does not stagger. He announced the fraud before he laid a finger on anything -- the entire diagnosis came from watching. Source: Wikipedia, 'Charles Redheffer' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Redheffer).

question: Robert Fulton offered to bet he could expose what really turned Charles Redheffer's New York machine. He knocked boards off the wall next to it and traced a catgut cord out of sight. What, in every telling, sat at the other end?
answer: An old man turning a hand crank, eating a crust of bread
choices: An old man turning a hand crank, eating a crust of bread
A stable boy walking a treadmill wheel behind a screen
A hired workman pumping a foot treadle out of sight
A servant winding a clockwork spring behind a curtain
context: The cord -- catgut is tough cord spun from dried animal gut, the same material as violin strings -- ran up to the floor above, where an old bearded man sat turning a hand crank with one hand and eating a crust of bread with the other. He had been cranking all day for the paying customers below. The crowd destroyed the machine and Redheffer fled the city. The bread is the detail carried in every telling of the story and cannot now be independently verified. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Charles Redheffer' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Redheffer); Museum of Hoaxes, 'Redheffer's Perpetual Motion Machine (1812)' (https://hoaxes.org/archive/permalink/redheffers_perpetual_motion_machine).  (Legend.)

question: Nathan Sellers brought his grown son Coleman in January 1813 when eight Philadelphia officials came to inspect Charles Redheffer's machine before voting him public money. Redheffer let them look through a barred window but not touch. Coleman spotted the fraud from where he stood. What did he see?
answer: Cog teeth worn on the side only a driving gear wears
choices: Cog teeth worn on the side only a driving gear wears
A rope groove cut into the rim of the main wheel
Sawdust heaped below one bearing but not the others
Floorboards flexing in time with the wheel's turning
context: A gear that receives power and a gear that delivers it wear on opposite faces of their teeth. The wear on the gear Redheffer called the 'output' showed that it was the one pushing -- power was coming IN through it. Coleman Sellers worked that out through a barred window, having touched nothing at all. (Popular retellings call him a boy; Coleman Sellers, son of the inspector Nathan Sellers, was born in 1781 and was about 31 that day.) Redheffer had been charging admission at a house near the Schuylkill River on the edge of Philadelphia -- a reported $5 for men, women admitted for less or free -- and had asked the city for funds to build a larger version. That is what the commissioners came to assess. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Charles Redheffer' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Redheffer); Live Science, 'Perpetual Motion Machines' (https://www.livescience.com/55944-perpetual-motion-machines.html).

question: Isaiah Lukens, an engineer, set a machine down in front of Charles Redheffer, who had been caught once already in Philadelphia. Nathan Sellers, who wanted the point made in public, had hired Lukens: the machine looked as if it ran forever, but clockwork inside drove it. What did Redheffer do?
answer: He offered to buy the machine on the spot
choices: He offered to buy the machine on the spot
He denounced Lukens as a thief before the crowd
He challenged Lukens to a public trial of both
He smashed the counterfeit with a hammer
context: Redheffer was so impressed by the fake that he wanted to own it -- he could not tell someone else's fraud from his own. He then left Philadelphia for New York and built his machine again there. A strange coda: in 1816 he built yet another and refused to demonstrate it to officials, and on 11 July 1820 the U.S. Patent Office granted him a patent for 'machinery for the purpose of gaining power.' After that his fate is unknown. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Charles Redheffer' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Redheffer); Museum of Hoaxes (https://hoaxes.org/archive/permalink/redheffers_perpetual_motion_machine).

question: A girl sets a drinking-bird toy beside a glass of water on the kitchen table. It dips its beak, rises and bobs down again for hours, with nothing wound and nothing plugged in. Something is feeding it, and one minute of kitchen work stops it dead. What kills it?
answer: Trapping it under a jar until the air around it is saturated
choices: Trapping it under a jar until the air around it is saturated
Standing it on a thick cork mat to insulate its base
Filling its glass with water straight from the kettle
Turning it to face away from the window's daylight
context: The bird's head is wrapped in felt, and water evaporating from that felt chills the top bulb, so the warmer base pushes the liquid inside (dichloromethane) up the neck until the bird tips forward and drinks -- rewetting the felt. Saturated air is air already holding all the water vapour it can, so nothing more can evaporate: seal the bird in a jar and the chilling stops, and so does the bird. Letting the felt head dry out does the same job. Take away the evaporation and you have taken away the engine. That is the test that names the input. Source: Wikipedia, 'Drinking bird' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drinking_bird).

question: Bhaskara II, a twelfth-century Indian mathematician, drew a wheel with curved hollow spokes carrying mercury. On the way down, the liquid would slide outward, farther from the axle, and drag the wheel around forever. Every real version stops. Why do the two sides come out exactly even?
answer: The side reaching farther out carries fewer weights
choices: The side reaching farther out carries fewer weights
The mercury's own friction eats the extra turning force
The mercury slides back inward before reaching the bottom
The rising spokes hold their mercury pressed to the rim
context: This is the overbalanced wheel, the design that never dies. Brahmagupta described a mercury-spoke wheel in 7th-century India, and around 1230 the French master mason Villard de Honnecourt drew a wheel hung with swinging hammers -- the earliest known Western attempt. They all fail on the same arithmetic: turning force is reach multiplied by weight. The falling side's weights hang farther out, but there are fewer of them; the rising side has more weights sitting closer in. The two products match and the wheel settles. Leonardo da Vinci sketched overbalanced wheels around 1490-1500 and then mocked the whole pursuit in his notebooks: 'Oh ye seekers after perpetual motion, how many vain chimeras have you pursued? Go and take your place with the alchemists.' Robert Fludd tried a different route in 1618 -- falling water turning a wheel that drove an Archimedes screw that lifted the same water back to the top tank -- which cannot run because raising the water costs exactly what letting it fall returns. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Perpetual motion' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetual_motion); Grokipedia, 'Perpetual motion' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Perpetual_motion).

question: Arthur Beverly built a clock in 1864 that still runs in the Physics Department at the University of Otago in New Zealand, and nobody has ever wound it. It is not perpetual: something feeds it, about enough to lift a one-pound weight one inch. What goes in?
answer: The rise and fall of air temperature inside a sealed box
choices: The rise and fall of air temperature inside a sealed box
The slow discharge of a buried sulphur-and-zinc pile
Vibration carried up through the building's foundations
Condensation gathering and dripping from its glass case
context: One cubic foot of air, sealed airtight, expands and contracts with a daily temperature swing of about 6 degrees Fahrenheit, and that breathing box winds the clock -- roughly enough each day to raise a one-pound weight an inch. The proof of the input is that the clock has stopped several times, including during spells when the temperature simply did not swing enough. It sits in the third-floor lift foyer of the Physics Department at Otago, in Dunedin. Its cousin is the Oxford Electric Bell at the Clarendon Laboratory, ringing almost continuously since 1840 -- roughly 10 billion times, a Guinness World Record for battery durability -- and it is not perpetual either: it runs on two sulfur-coated dry piles, each ring carrying a sliver of charge across, and it will stop when the piles equalise, unless the clapper wears through first. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Beverly Clock' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Clock); Wikipedia, 'Oxford Electric Bell' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Electric_Bell).

question: Johann Bessler asked 100,000 reichsthalers for the secret of his 3.7-metre wheel. It was locked and sealed inside a room at Weissenstein Castle on 12 November 1717, and two weeks later, with the seals broken, it was still turning. Sealed in again until 4 January 1718, it was found running at 26 revolutions a minute. How did the truth come out in November 1727?
answer: His maid swore in testimony that she had turned it by hand
choices: His maid swore in testimony that she had turned it by hand
A carpenter admitted building a false wall around the room
An inspector found a clockwork spring hidden in the axle
His brother sold the drawings to a rival German court
context: Anne Rosine Mauersbergerin testified under oath that she had turned the machine by hand from an adjoining room, taking shifts with Bessler's wife, his brother, and Bessler himself. A sealed room stays sealed; the crank simply lives next door. Bessler had asked 100,000 reichsthalers -- about 20,000 pounds, a fortune -- for his secret, and he had already smashed the wheel himself after the mathematician Willem 's Gravesande inspected its axle, accusing 's Gravesande of trying to steal the secret without paying. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bessler wheel' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessler_wheel).

question: An inventor proposes a ship that needs no fuel: its engine draws heat out of the seawater it floats in and turns that heat into motion. Nothing comes from nowhere here, since the ocean's store of heat is real and enormous. Physicists rule such a ship out before anyone builds one. Why can it never work?
answer: An engine running on heat must always pass some on to a colder place
choices: An engine running on heat must always pass some on to a colder place
Heat can never travel from a colder body into a warmer one
Water's heat is locked inside its molecules and cannot become motion
No machine can take in heat and give out motion over and over
context: Engineers sort impossible machines by which law they break. A perpetual motion machine of the FIRST kind produces work with no energy input at all: it breaks the first law of thermodynamics, which says energy is conserved. The ship is the SECOND kind -- it takes heat from a single reservoir and turns all of it into work with no cold sink, which breaks the second law, stated exactly by Kelvin and Planck: no engine working in a cycle can take heat from one reservoir and convert all of it into work without dumping some into a colder place. Even a perfect frictionless Carnot engine is capped at an efficiency of 1 - (Tc/Th), so the ocean-heat ship is ruled out before anyone builds it. Most modern 'over-unity' claims are the second kind, the sneakier one, because nothing appears to come from nowhere. There is an honest THIRD kind too: a machine that merely tries to remove all friction so motion never decays. It breaks no law -- vacuum-sealed flywheels on superconducting magnetic bearings spin at 20,000-60,000 rpm at 85-90% efficiency and coast for hours or days -- but eddy currents and material imperfections always take the last of it. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Perpetual motion' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Perpetual_motion); Wikipedia, 'Perpetual motion' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetual_motion).

question: John Keely of Philadelphia fired his so-called vaporic gun for War Department officials at Sandy Hook Proving Ground on 20 September 1884. A five-ounce lead ball smashed through spruce planking and travelled 300 yards, driven, Keely claimed, by an etheric force liberated from just six drops of water. Lieutenant Edmund Zalinski, an ordnance officer who had designed experimental guns himself, gave a flat one-sentence verdict. What did he say?
answer: Plain compressed air would give exactly the same result
choices: Plain compressed air would give exactly the same result
A small powder charge could throw that ball just as far
The ball was too light for the test to prove anything
The planking had been cut thin before the officials came
context: Zalinski built pneumatic dynamite guns for a living -- artillery driven by air pressure rather than gunpowder -- so he knew the signature on sight, and he named Keely's input fourteen years before anyone proved it. The ball left the gun at about 523 feet per second. Keely told investors that four drops of water could yield 27,000 pounds per square inch, and described his own method in 1884: 'I take water and air, two mediums of different specific gravity, and produce from them by generation an effect under vibrations that liberates from the air and water an inter atomic ether.' On 17 November 1888 Judge Finletter held Keely in contempt and sent him to Moyamensing Prison for refusing a court order to explain how the motor worked; the Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed the contempt order on 28 January 1889. Sources: Grokipedia, 'John Ernst Worrell Keely' (https://grokipedia.com/page/John_Ernst_Worrell_Keely); Wikipedia, 'John Ernst Worrell Keely' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ernst_Worrell_Keely).

question: Engineers and physicists from the University of Pennsylvania took John Keely's workshop apart for the Philadelphia Press after he died of pneumonia in November 1898. For twenty-five years he had started and stopped his motor on command, with investors only a few feet away, and credited an etheric force liberated from a few drops of water. Their January 1899 report named the hidden control he had worked all along. What was it?
answer: Foot valves under the floorboards, worked with his shoe
choices: Foot valves under the floorboards, worked with his shoe
Brass taps in the machine's frame, turned with his thumb
Silk cords in his sleeve, pulled to signal a man next door
Weighted levers in the doorway, tripped as he stepped past
context: He worked the valves with his shoe -- often while playing his violin, which gave the audience something else to look at. The investigators traced hidden tubing threaded through walls, ceilings and solid beams, and found a hollow iron sphere weighing three tons buried in the cellar; two floors below the laboratory a silent water motor was keeping that sphere charged. Of the etheric force there was no trace at all. The Keely Motor Company had been capitalised at $5,000,000 -- roughly $159 million in today's money -- with about 3,000 stockholders; in more than twenty-five years it never paid a dividend, never sold a working engine and never delivered a product. His greatest patron, the Philadelphia philanthropist Clara Jessup Bloomfield-Moore, gave him over $100,000 across nearly two decades, wrote a book defending him in 1893 and read a paper on his work at the University of Pennsylvania in January 1891; it was her own son Clarence who helped set the exposing investigation in motion, and she died less than two months after Keely, still believing. Keely reportedly told a friend shortly before his death that his epitaph should call him the greatest humbug of the nineteenth century. Sources: Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'John Ernst Worrell Keely' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ernst_Worrell_Keely ; https://grokipedia.com/page/John_Ernst_Worrell_Keely).

question: The Irish company Steorn dared scientists in The Economist in 2006 to test its 'free energy' machine, Orbo. Within 36 hours, 420 scientists wrote in, and a jury was set up under a retired professor. Steorn ran a public demo at a London museum in July 2007. What happened there?
answer: The device never ran, and Steorn blamed heat from the lighting
choices: The device never ran, and Steorn blamed heat from the lighting
The device ran ten minutes, and Steorn blamed a seized bearing
The device ran all week, but the jury declined to inspect it
The device ran only while Steorn's own engineer stood by it
context: The demonstration was cancelled. Steorn carried on for nine more years; in June 2009 the jury concluded unanimously that Steorn's attempts had not shown the production of energy. The company raised about 23 million euros, shut down in November 2016, and was liquidated in May 2024. Notice the part of the story that is easy to miss: 420 scientists volunteered within a day and a half to TEST the claim rather than wave it away. Source: Wikipedia, 'Steorn' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steorn).

question: An inventor files for a patent on a perpetual-motion machine, and his papers land on a desk at the U.S. Patent Office. The office's manual names perpetual motion as its one special case and sets a single condition, a standing public bet open to anyone on earth: meet it and the patent is his. Nobody has ever collected. What does the manual demand of him?
answer: A working model, set running in front of the examiner
choices: A working model, set running in front of the examiner
A sworn affidavit from a disinterested expert witness
Certified test data from an independent laboratory
A complete set of stamped engineering drawings
context: The manual says it in one sentence: 'With the exception of cases involving perpetual motion, a model is not ordinarily required by the Office to demonstrate the operability of a device.' All other inventors are taken at their written word; the perpetual-motion applicant is asked to bring the machine in and let it run. Nobody ever has -- which is why the rule is a test rather than a decree. Britain does it the other way and refuses on paper alone: 'Processes or articles alleged to operate in a manner which is clearly contrary to well-established physical laws, such as perpetual motion machines, are regarded as not having industrial application.' The European Patent Office likewise refuses on the description alone under Article 52(1) EPC. The American wall is not perfect either: U.S. Patent 4,151,431 was granted in 1979 to Howard R. Johnson for a 'permanent magnet motor', slipping through because the claims described arrangements of magnetic fields and never actually asserted more power out than in. Examiners judge the wording in front of them, not the inventor's hopes. Sources: MPEP 608.03 (USPTO), quoted at BitLaw (https://www.bitlaw.com/source/mpep/608-03.html); UK IPO Manual of Patent Practice and Wikipedia, 'Perpetual motion' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetual_motion); Grokipedia, 'Perpetual motion' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Perpetual_motion).

question: Joseph Newman took the Patent Office to court after it rejected his 'Energy Machine' in 1983. The U.S. District Court then did something unusual with a free-energy claim: instead of dismissing it, the judge ordered the National Bureau of Standards to test the device. The Bureau reported its measurements in June 1986. What had it found?
answer: In every test the output was less than the batteries supplied
choices: In every test the output was less than the batteries supplied
The output matched what the battery pack supplied, near exactly
The output rose above the input in two runs out of forty
The device drew no current at all once it was fully spinning
context: The Bureau, now called NIST, reported that in every single test the output power was less than the power drawn from the battery pack -- efficiency under 100%. It did not wave Newman off; it measured him, and then named the input: batteries. That is the whole skill these questions teach. Do not ask 'can it run forever' -- ask 'what goes IN?' Every device ever examined has turned out to be drawing on something ordinary. Two related traps are worth knowing. First, magnet-ramp videos: if the magnets and the iron are bolted to the same cart, the forces between them are INTERNAL, and Newton's third law pairs each with an equal and opposite partner, so the net external force is zero and the centre of mass cannot accelerate even on a frictionless surface. Second, 'tapping the zero-point energy of the vacuum': zero-point energy is the ground state, the lowest rung there is, and extracting work requires a difference -- a hot side and a cold side, a high place and a low place -- so a uniform floor with nothing below it offers nothing to fall. There are honest cousins that merely look like magic: a radioisotope thermoelectric generator ran Voyager for decades on the decay heat of plutonium-238, and betavoltaic batteries using nickel-63 are being built for 50-year lifespans. Each has a named, depleting fuel. Believers reply that working free-energy machines exist but are suppressed by oil companies and governments, and the case usually offered is Stanley Meyer's 'water fuel cell' dune buggy of the 1990s, his sudden death in 1998 attributed to industry agents; the part usually left out is that a court had convicted Meyer of fraud in 1996 and ordered him to repay investors $25,000 over misleading demonstrations. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Joseph Newman (inventor)' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Newman_(inventor)); Grokipedia, 'Perpetual motion' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Perpetual_motion).

question: Phineas Gage's men put him in an ox cart on a Vermont railroad job in 1848, after a blasting charge went off early and drove a 13-pound iron bar through his skull. He rode three-quarters of a mile to his hotel. An hour after they set him down, what was he doing?
answer: Walking up a long flight of stairs to his bed
choices: Walking up a long flight of stairs to his bed
Being carried up to his room on a door
Sleeping under laudanum in a downstairs room
Retching into a basin while his men held him
context: His doctor, John Harlow, wrote that Gage 'was thrown upon his back by the explosion, and gave a few convulsive motions of the extremities, but spoke in a few minutes.' His men — 'with whom he was a great favorite' — carried him to the road and put him in an ox cart, in which he rode three-quarters of a mile to his hotel sitting upright. He got out of the cart himself, and AN HOUR LATER WALKED UP A LONG FLIGHT OF STAIRS and got onto the bed where he was dressed. Source: John M. Harlow, 'Recovery from the Passage of an Iron Bar Through the Head' (1868), read to the Massachusetts Medical Society, 3 June 1868.

question: Edward Williams, the first doctor to reach Phineas Gage, saw the wound from his carriage, half an hour after a blasting charge drove a thirteen-pound iron bar through the foreman's skull. Gage was sitting up, awake, and spoke first. What did Williams later recall him saying?
answer: Doctor, here is business enough for you.
choices: Doctor, here is business enough for you.
Doctor, I am afraid I shall lose my place.
Doctor, do not send word to my mother yet.
