Polonium-212 is the same physics at the sprinting end: its 8.78 MeV alpha faces a 26.4 MeV wall, three times taller than the alpha's whole energy; it hammers on that wall 1.1 x 10^21 times a second and gets through with a probability of about 2.47 x 10^-15 per attempt. Multiply those two numbers and the model predicts a half-life of 0.25 microseconds. The measured value is 0.3. Two numbers, one multiplication, and the impossible comes out right — and that is what finally settled what Geiger and Nuttall had left on the table. Nothing classical turns a tenfold change in energy into a twenty-odd-order-of-magnitude change in lifetime. An exponential does. SOURCE: Physics LibreTexts, '7.A: Alpha Decay (Project)' — U-238 emits 4.2 MeV alphas against a barrier as high as 25 MeV, half-life about 4.5 billion years; Grokipedia 'Alpha decay' (Coulomb barriers of order 20-30 MeV vs alpha energies of 4-9 MeV). HyperPhysics (Georgia State University), 'Modeling Alpha Particle Tunneling for Polonium-212' (hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Nuclear/alptun2.html) — 8.78 MeV alpha, 26.4 MeV barrier, assault frequency 1.1 x 10^21 /s, probability 2.47 x 10^-15, calculated 0.25 us vs measured 0.3 us. Geiger–Nuttall: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geiger%E2%80%93Nuttall_law and Grokipedia 'Geiger-Nuttall law'.

question: A teacher follows one proton through the Sun's core on the blackboard. Tunnelling brings it close enough to touch another, yet fusion does not follow: a given proton waits on the order of billions of years. That slowness is why the Sun has lasted so long. Something in that first step is far less likely than the tunnelling. What has to happen?
answer: One of the two protons must turn itself into a neutron
choices: One of the two protons must turn itself into a neutron
One of the two protons must first swallow an electron
The pair must absorb a photon of exactly the right energy
The pair must be struck by a third proton at that instant
context: The first step of the proton–proton chain needs one of the two protons to flip into a neutron by beta-plus decay during the brief instant the pair is jammed together — a weak nuclear force event, and so improbable that it, not tunnelling, is the real bottleneck. (Sources give the average proton's wait as anywhere from about one billion to nine billion years, so treat it as an order of magnitude: billions.) Once that step finally fires, the rest is a stampede: the newborn deuterium nucleus lasts only a few seconds before becoming helium-3, and the helium-3 a few hundred years. Billions of years, then seconds. Which is why the Sun is a spectacularly BAD reactor — fusion at the very centre generates about 276.5 watts per cubic metre, a power density closer to reptile metabolism or an active compost heap than to a bomb, and lower than what your own body produces per unit volume. The Sun is not intense. It is merely enormous. SOURCE: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton%E2%80%93proton_chain (first step is 'the rate-limiting reaction and is extremely slow due to it being initiated by the weak nuclear force'; average proton waits 9 billion years) and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_core (~1 billion year timescale; deuterium ~4 seconds, helium-3 ~400 years; 276.5 W/m3, 'more nearly approximates reptile metabolism than a thermonuclear bomb').

question: Joseph Meister, nine, arrived from Alsace at Louis Pasteur's laboratory in Paris on 6 July 1885, at his mother's insistence. Two days earlier something had happened to him on the walk to school that, at the time, meant an almost certain death sentence. What had happened to him?
answer: A rabid dog had mauled him
choices: A rabid dog had mauled him
A viper had bitten his ankle
He had swallowed cleaning lye
A horse had kicked him in the head
context: Meister had been bitten fourteen times by a dog his neighbours had already killed and cut open, finding straw and hay in its stomach: a classic sign of rabies. Source: Pasteur Institute, 'The history of the first rabies vaccination in 1885'.

question: Jacques-Joseph Grancher held the syringe in July 1885 when nine-year-old Joseph Meister got the experimental rabies treatment Louis Pasteur had tested on rabbits and dogs. Pasteur stood and watched. Why did he not give the shots himself?
answer: He held no medical license and would have broken the law
choices: He held no medical license and would have broken the law
He was too ill that week to hold a syringe steady
He was in Marseille the day the injections began
The Meister family had refused to let him touch their son
context: Pasteur was a chemist, not a physician. A doctor named Jacques-Joseph Grancher gave all thirteen injections over about ten days. Source: Wikipedia, 'Joseph Meister'.

question: Joseph Meister took thirteen injections in the belly over about ten days at Louis Pasteur's Paris laboratory in July 1885. Each new syringe was a little stronger than the one before, so his body could build up defenses step by step. What was actually inside those syringes?
answer: Emulsions of dried spinal cord from rabbits that had died of rabies
choices: Emulsions of dried spinal cord from rabbits that had died of rabies
A clear filtered serum drawn from cured dogs
A boiled extract of the brain of the dog that bit him
A tincture of cinchona bark and morphine
context: Pasteur passed rabies through rabbit after rabbit and then air-dried the spinal cords. Longer drying meant a weaker preparation; each successive dose used cord dried for fewer days, so virulence climbed daily. Source: PNAS, '1885, the first rabies vaccination in humans'.

question: Louis Pasteur had a way by 1885 to treat rabies after a bite: a series of injections, given day by day, that could stop the disease before symptoms ever began. That sounds too late to help, and yet the method worked, because of one particular thing the rabies agent does inside the body, which buys the treatment time. What does the agent do?
answer: It creeps slowly along the nerves toward the brain
choices: It creeps slowly along the nerves toward the brain
It hides in the bloodstream for months without moving
It waits in the liver until the next fever
It lingers in the lymph glands for half a year
context: The nerve journey typically takes weeks to months. A vaccine started after a bite can still teach the immune system in time. Modern rabies post-exposure prophylaxis works on exactly this principle. Source: Utah Poison Control, 'Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis'.

question: Louis Pasteur beat rabies without ever seeing what caused it, unlike his earlier enemies, anthrax and fowl cholera. This one had never been seen, grown or photographed by anyone alive, and the microscopes of the 1880s could not resolve it. Why not?
answer: Rabies is caused by a virus, far smaller than any bacterium
choices: Rabies is caused by a virus, far smaller than any bacterium
Rabies is caused by a toxin, not a living thing at all
Rabies is caused by a parasite that only appears after death
Rabies is caused by a chemical released only by dog saliva
context: The word 'virus' would not carry its modern meaning until Ivanovsky and Beijerinck in the 1890s. Pasteur beat something he could not culture on any plate, could not stain, and could not photograph; he kept it alive only by passing it from rabbit to rabbit. Source: ScienceDirect, 'Rabies Vaccine' overview.

question: Jean-Baptiste Jupille, a shepherd of fifteen, reached Louis Pasteur a few months after Joseph Meister, and it was his case, not Meister's, that made the rabies treatment famous around the world. He had done something heroic before he was bitten. What did he do?
answer: He fought a rabid dog off younger children with his whip and bare hands
choices: He fought a rabid dog off younger children with his whip and bare hands
He carried a plague-stricken child three miles to the nearest town
He pulled two men out of a burning stable at night
He dived into an icy river to save a drowning shepherd
context: Jupille was treated and lived. A bronze statue by Emile-Louis Truffot of him wrestling the dog stands to this day at the Institut Pasteur. Source: Pasteur Institute, '130 years ago, the Institut Pasteur opened its doors for the first time'.

question: Gerald Geison read Louis Pasteur's sealed laboratory notebooks and reported in 1995 that the moment with Joseph Meister had been riskier than Pasteur ever admitted. For a century the rabies work had looked like a clean triumph. What did Geison say the notebooks revealed?
answer: He had already tried the treatment on two patients before Meister and one had died
choices: He had already tried the treatment on two patients before Meister and one had died
He had used a completely different vaccine never tested on any animal
He had done the injections himself in secret before Grancher arrived
He had known Meister was not actually bitten by a rabid dog
context: The notebooks record an elderly man named Girard, who survived, and an eleven-year-old girl, who did not. Geison also found the specific Meister protocol had been tested on only about eleven dogs, fewer than Pasteur implied at the time. He gambled harder than he told anyone. Source: 'The Private Science of Louis Pasteur', Gerald Geison, Princeton 1995.

question: The Russian tsar and the emperor of Brazil were among the foreign heads of state who sent donations to Paris once news of the treatment spread. Thousands of bitten patients arrived too. In 1888 the French president opened what all that money had built. What was it?
answer: A brand-new research institute in Paris devoted to infectious disease
choices: A brand-new research institute in Paris devoted to infectious disease
A new rabies wing added to the Ecole Normale Superieure
A charity hospital on the grounds of the Hotel-Dieu
A public vaccination bureau inside the Sorbonne medical faculty
context: The building was the Institut Pasteur, inaugurated 14 November 1888. Meister himself later worked there as the concierge. Source: Pasteur Institute, 'History'.

question: Lord Rayleigh put a litre of nitrogen he had made in a chemical reaction on his scales in 1892, and it came to 1.2505 grams. A litre stripped out of ordinary air came to 1.2572 grams. The gap was only about half a percent, but he took it seriously. What did it actually mean?
answer: The air sample was hiding an unknown gas
choices: The air sample was hiding an unknown gas
His scales had drifted between measurements
One sample had absorbed extra moisture
Air-nitrogen and lab-nitrogen were different isotopes
context: The gap was argon, about 1% of the atmosphere. Rayleigh could have written the difference off as experimental error; instead he treated it as a signal. Source: Giunta, 'The Discovery of Argon' (Le Moyne College).

question: 'I am much puzzled by some recent results as to the density of nitrogen,' Lord Rayleigh wrote in 1892, opening a short letter to the journal Nature. It was an unusual step for a man stuck on an odd result. What was he doing?
answer: Asking anyone at all for an explanation
choices: Asking anyone at all for an explanation
Asking other labs to repeat his weighings
Withdrawing an earlier density figure
Warning chemists off a faulty method
context: The letter is Nature vol. 46, p. 512 (1892). A Nobel-caliber physicist openly saying 'help' is a small piece of the scientific method most textbooks skip.

question: William Ramsay ran nitrogen from the air across red-hot magnesium, over and over, until only a small residue was left. He and Lord Rayleigh announced a new gas in August 1894 that made up roughly one part in a hundred of the air. They named it 'argon' from an ancient Greek word. Which Greek word did they pick, and why?
answer: 'Lazy' -- it refused to combine with anything
choices: 'Lazy' -- it refused to combine with anything
'Hidden' -- it lay unseen in every breath
'Stranger' -- it belonged to no known family
'New' -- it had never been isolated before
context: Ramsay had passed air-nitrogen over red-hot magnesium until only ~290 cubic centimetres of residue was left; it reacted with nothing he offered. Four years later Ramsay and Travers would use the other three Greek names -- kryptos ('hidden'), xenos ('stranger'), neos ('new') -- on the three gases they teased out of liquid argon. Source: Giunta, 'The Discovery of Argon'.

question: Henry Cavendish, working alone in his London laboratory in 1785, sparked ordinary air with an excess of oxygen until nothing more would combine. A small stubborn bubble was left, no more than one part in a hundred and twenty of the original air, and it refused to react with anything he tried. What did he do about it?
answer: Recorded it honestly and left it unexplained
choices: Recorded it honestly and left it unexplained
Claimed it as a new element on the spot
Concluded his glassware was leaking
Assumed it was ordinary water vapour
context: That bubble was argon; Cavendish's honest note sat in the literature for 109 years before Rayleigh and Ramsay explained it. He did NOT claim a new element -- which is precisely why the credit belongs to 1894, not 1785. Source: Chemicool, 'Composition of Air'.

question: William Ramsay had argon in his hands but nowhere to put it on the periodic table. In March 1895 he boiled the mineral cleveite in weak sulfuric acid, and William Crookes read the spectrum of the gas that came off. What did the spectrum turn out to match?
answer: Helium, previously known only from the Sun
choices: Helium, previously known only from the Sun
Radon, streaming out of the cleveite ore
Hydrogen, freed by the acid attack
Chlorine, released as a green vapour
context: Helium had been seen in the solar spectrum by Janssen and Lockyer in 1868. Ramsay's 27 March 1895 announcement brought it down to Earth. Two inert orphans in one year -- not an anomaly, a whole missing column. Source: chemistry.unt.edu, Ramsay biography.

question: Morris Travers and William Ramsay liquefied argon in the summer of 1898 and let it boil off in stages, catching each fraction as it came. Travers wrote later of one moment: 'the blaze of crimson light from the tube told its own story, and it was a sight to dwell upon and never to forget.' Which of the three gases they netted that summer was he watching?
answer: Neon
choices: Neon
Krypton
Xenon
Radon
context: In 42 days the pair added krypton in May, neon in June and xenon in July. The crimson glow is neon's discharge signature and is now the entire aesthetic of a city street. Source: Science History Institute, 'A Blaze of Crimson Light'.

question: Dmitri Mendeleev insisted at first that William Ramsay's argon was really a triatomic form of an old gas: N3, mass 42. He came round only in 1902. Why did that idea feel less crazy to him than accepting argon as it stood?
answer: Adding a whole new group had no precedent in his table
choices: Adding a whole new group had no precedent in his table
Nitrogen was known to form N3 in the atmosphere
The measured density of argon exactly matched 42
N3 had already been isolated by French chemists
context: Mendeleev came round and formally added Group 0 to the periodic table in 1902. The lesson is not that he was foolish -- it is that even the man who INVENTED the periodic table preferred a small fix to a big rewrite. Source: 'Rediscovery of the Elements: The Noble Gases'.

question: A grade-10 chemistry student holds up a sealed tube of argon and says in one sentence why it almost never combines with anything, just like the other noble gases. For a long time chemists had no clue why. What is her sentence?
answer: Their outermost electron shell is already full
choices: Their outermost electron shell is already full
Their nuclei carry no net electric charge
Their atoms are unusually small and dense
Their atoms are heavier than air molecules
context: A full outer shell means nothing to gain, lose or share -- so no bonds. This is why the whole column is called 'noble'. Later chemists forced xenon into a few compounds (Bartlett, 1962), but the rule holds. Source: chemistry.unt.edu, 'Noble Gases'.

question: Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay announced together in 1894 that they had discovered a new colourless, unreactive gas in the air, and called it argon, the first of the noble gases. Nobel recognition came ten years later, in 1904. How was the credit split?
answer: Rayleigh took Physics, Ramsay took Chemistry
choices: Rayleigh took Physics, Ramsay took Chemistry
Both shared the Chemistry prize equally
Rayleigh took Chemistry, Ramsay took Physics
Ramsay took the Chemistry prize alone
context: The paired 1904 Nobels are the receipt on shared credit. Ramsay went on to isolate radon in 1910. Source: nobelprize.org, Chemistry 1904.

question: William Buckland toured Scotland in autumn 1840 with Louis Agassiz, who blamed vanished glaciers for the scratched bedrock and stray boulders Buckland had made his name reading as wreckage from Noah's Flood. Buckland then chaired the meeting where Agassiz read his glacier case. What did Buckland do that day?
answer: Rose after Agassiz with a paper backing him
choices: Asked the Society to wait for more fieldwork
Read a rebuttal defending his Flood account
Rose after Agassiz with a paper backing him
Left the chair to Charles Lyell and went home
context: Buckland had been Britain's foremost diluvialist, reading erratics, moraines and scratched bedrock as the wreckage of a Noah-style global flood. In the field that October he wrote, 'We have found abundant Traces of Glaciers round Ben Nevis' - in country with no glacier in it today. As President of the Geological Society he changed his mind in the most public place available to him: Agassiz, Buckland and Lyell presented interrelated papers at three successive fortnightly meetings across November and December 1840. Source: Journal of Glaciology, 'Early Discoverers XXVII: Announcement of Glaciation in Scotland, William Buckland (1784-1856)'; Grokipedia, 'William Buckland' and 'Diluvium'.

question: A. E. Douglass began measuring the widths of tree rings in the pine forests of Arizona in 1901. He was an astronomer at Lowell Observatory, no botanist, and the rings were his instrument. He believed the widths recorded something that lived not in the tree but in the sky. What was he hunting in them?
answer: The Sun's cycle of sunspots
choices: The Sun's cycle of sunspots
The drift of the magnetic pole
The dates of ancient eclipses
The track of a lost comet
context: Douglass was after the Sun's rhythm written into wood. Along the way he proved the tight link between a tree's radial growth and rainfall, published in 1909, and in 1914 he turned the method on wood from Puebloan ruins. The archaeology, not the astronomy, is what made him famous - and the Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research he founded at Arizona, voted into existence by the Board of Regents in December 1937, still runs. Source: University of Arizona Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research, 'History of the LTRR'; Grokipedia, 'Dendrochronology'.

question: Claude Lorius was chilling a glass of whisky with chunks of ice cut from the ice sheet at the French Antarctic station Dumont d'Urville in 1965. The old ice fizzed as it melted. By his own account, what did Lorius realise the escaping bubbles were?
answer: Ancient air, sealed in when that snow fell
choices: Gas driven out of the ice by the alcohol
Cracks popping open as the old ice relaxed
Sea spray blown inland and buried by storms
Ancient air, sealed in when that snow fell
context: Lorius told this as the moment ice-core chemistry began. Air is sealed off when firn compacts to about 830 kg per cubic metre, capturing the composition of the atmosphere at the time the ice formed. A modern lab melts a sample in a tank evacuated for at least an hour and a half, recirculates the freed gas through the meltwater, then runs it into an isotope-ratio mass spectrometer. That recovered ancient air holds about 180 parts per million of CO2 during ice ages and about 280 ppm during warm intervals, right across the last 800,000 years. Told here as Lorius's own anecdote. Source: Grokipedia, 'Claude Lorius' and 'Ice core'; Wikipedia, 'Ice core'.  (Legend.)

question: A driller slices a long polar ice core down its length and can often see banding, one pair of layers for each year the snow fell. To count years back down the core, she has to tell summer from winter in each pair. What marks out the layer laid down in summer?
answer: Its bubbles are noticeably bigger
choices: It is stained darker with fine dust
Its bubbles are noticeably bigger
It is the thinner band of the pair
It is threaded with salt crystals
context: Verbatim: 'The layers corresponding to the summer snow will contain bigger bubbles than the winter layers.' The counting has an end, though. At roughly 1,500 metres the ice crystal structure changes from hexagonal to cubic, the air molecules migrate into the crystals as clathrate, the bubbles disappear and the ice turns transparent. Below that the annual banding can no longer be read this way. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ice core'.

question: Russian drillers at Vostok Station in Antarctica drove a borehole to 3,623 metres by 1996, recovering more than 400,000 years of climate and four earlier glacial cycles. Then they stopped, with the drill sound and ice still beneath them. Why did they stop?
answer: A sealed lake lay below and the drill fluid would foul it
choices: A sealed lake lay below and the drill fluid would foul it
The bottom ice was too churned to be read as layers
Clathrate had swallowed the bubbles the work needed
Four glacial cycles was all the project was funded for
context: The halt came at the request of the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research, over fears of contaminating Lake Vostok, which lies sealed beneath the ice. Usable proxy information runs down to 3,310 metres, about 414,000 years. The deeper record came later from EPICA Dome C, which reached 3,260 metres and about 800,000 years - roughly eight glacial cycles. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vostok Station'; Wikipedia, 'Ice core'.

question: A glaciologist at the Allan Hills in Antarctica holds up a core taken in 2016, with ice dated to 2.7 million years, by far the oldest yet dated from a core. It sat near the surface. Antarctic ice much older than a few hundred thousand years normally lies deep under kilometres of newer ice. What puts the ancient ice on top there?
answer: The sheet flows up against buried hills while wind strips the surface
choices: Meltwater refreezes each summer and welds old ice into the surface
The sheet flows up against buried hills while wind strips the surface
Almost no snow falls, so a whole century leaves barely a hand's depth
The sheet cracks open there and deep layers are shoved up the walls
context: This is what glaciologists call a blue-ice area: the flow lifts old ice against an obstacle while wind removes the fresh snow, so a person can walk up and sample ice that would otherwise sit under three kilometres of newer ice. The same conveyor concentrates meteorites - about 1,800 have been recovered from the Allan Hills blue-ice area. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ice core'; Grokipedia, 'Blue-ice area' and 'Allan Hills'.

question: A glaciologist digs into the Antarctic snow and finds it still porous near the top, with the atmosphere circulating through it. Only 50 to 120 metres down does the weight above squeeze the passages shut, so the gas in a bubble is younger than the ice holding it. At Vostok, how old can the ice be by the time its bubbles finally close?
answer: About 6,000 years old
choices: About 300 years old
About 800 years old
About 60,000 years old
About 6,000 years old
context: Caillon and colleagues state that at a low-snowfall site like Vostok the ice at that sealing depth 'may be 6000 years old', and that the gas-age/ice-age difference 'may be uncertain by 1000 years or more'. Every claim about what came first at a deglaciation has to fight through that gap - which is exactly why later teams went hunting for ways around it. Source: Caillon et al., Science 299:1728-1731 (2003); Parrenin et al. 2013 for the 50-120 m lock-in depth; Wikipedia, 'Ice core'.

question: James Croll, a self-taught Scot, published the first serious answer in 1864 to a question Louis Agassiz had left open. Agassiz had persuaded geologists that great glaciers once buried Europe, but he could not say what brought the ice or took it away. Shifts in Earth's orbit, Croll argued, could cut the summer sunlight falling on the north and start the ice building. Then Croll named a weakness in his own idea. What was it?
answer: The orbital push was far too feeble on its own to build ice sheets
choices: The orbital push was far too feeble on its own to build ice sheets
The orbital cycles ran far too slowly to match the ice ages' timing
The orbital figures rested on planet paths still poorly measured
The orbital idea offered no rock or fossil that could ever test it
context: Croll recognised from the start that the orbital nudge would need amplifying feedbacks inside the climate system to do the job. Milankovitch later redid the calculations properly. Agassiz's gap is the part worth holding onto: he could show that ice had been there and could not say why it came or why it left, and geologists lived with that for decades. Source: Grokipedia, 'James Croll' and 'Orbital forcing'; Wikipedia, 'History of climate change science'.

question: Nicolas Caillon and colleagues read argon isotopes in the air trapped in the Vostok core, so that their temperature signal and their CO2 came out of the very same gas. They were timing the CO2 rise against the warming at a thaw roughly 240,000 years ago, and they published in Science in March 2003. By how much did the two events miss each other?
answer: CO2 rose about 800 years after Antarctic warming began
choices: CO2 rose about 80 years after Antarctic warming began
CO2 rose about 800 years after Antarctic warming began
CO2 rose about 2,500 years after Antarctic warming began
CO2 rose about 8,000 years after Antarctic warming began
context: Their abstract, verbatim: 'The sequence of events during Termination III suggests that the CO2 increase lagged Antarctic deglacial warming by 800 +/- 200 years and preceded the Northern Hemisphere deglaciation.' Reading argon in the gas phase let them take temperature from the same sample as the CO2, sidestepping the age gap between a bubble's air and the ice around it. Fischer and colleagues had earlier, in 1999, put the lag at 600 +/- 400 years across the last three terminations. This is the single most misquoted number in climate argument - and the authors' own reading of it is a separate matter from the number. Source: Caillon, Severinghaus, Jouzel, Barnola, Kang, Lipenkov, Science 299:1728-1731 (2003).

question: Nicolas Caillon and his colleagues closed their 2003 paper on an ancient thaw by turning to the rise in CO2 under way today. At that thaw, roughly 240,000 years ago, they had found the warming came first and the CO2 rise followed, and they read the CO2 as amplifying a warming that Earth's orbit had begun. How did they describe today's rise?
answer: As a rise imposed first, driven by human activity
choices: As a rise the ocean has been releasing since the 1800s
As a rise imposed first, driven by human activity
As a rise pushed along by feedbacks the ice ages lacked
As a rise humans began but the ocean now sustains
context: Verbatim from the Discussion: 'The sequence of events during this Termination is fully consistent with CO2 participating in the latter ~4200 years of the warming. The radiative forcing due to CO2 may serve as an amplifier of initial orbital forcing, which is then further amplified by fast atmospheric feedbacks that are also at work for the present-day and future climate.' And their distinction, in their words: the deglacial rise was an internal response, whereas the modern rise 'has clearly been imposed first, as a result of anthropogenic activities'. A lag at an ancient thaw shows CO2 was not the trigger there; it does not show that CO2 fails to warm. Source: Caillon et al., Science 299:1728-1731 (2003), Discussion.

question: Parrenin's team went at the timing of CO2 and warming with a better clock in 2013, ten years after Nicolas Caillon's Vostok result. They used nitrogen isotopes to fix how deep each core's bubbles had sealed, then stacked a temperature record from five Antarctic cores tied together. For the start of the most recent thaw, what did they find?
answer: No real gap: CO2 leading by 10 years, give or take 160
choices: A firm gap: warming leading CO2 by some 400 years
A firm gap: CO2 leading warming by some 900 years
No real gap: CO2 leading by 10 years, give or take 160
No real gap inland, but 300 years in the coastal cores
context: Their abstract, verbatim: 'We find no significant asynchrony between them, indicating that Antarctic temperature did not begin to rise hundreds of years before the concentration of atmospheric CO2, as has been suggested by earlier studies.' The honest picture is not one tidy number, and they said so. Their four break points: onset of Termination I, 10 +/- 160 years with CO2 leading; onset of the Bolling oscillation, -260 +/- 130 with temperature leading; onset of the Younger Dryas, 60 +/- 120 with CO2 leading; onset of the Holocene, -500 +/- 90 with temperature leading. They also noted that the earlier result was for a different deglaciation entirely: 'We cannot exclude the possibility that the aCO2-AT phasing is different for TI and TIII.' Source: Parrenin, Masson-Delmotte, Kohler, Raynaud, Paillard, Schwander, Barbante, Landais, Wegner, Jouzel, Science 339:1060-1063 (2013).

question: Keith Briffa's team reported in Nature in 1998 that tree-ring density and measured summer temperature had pulled apart after about 1960. Across hundreds of sites in the far north the two had tracked each other closely before that, with correlations running as high as 0.7. What had the rings done?
answer: Their density fell while the thermometers showed temperature rising
choices: Their density stopped varying at all, flattening into a straight line
Their density fell while the thermometers showed temperature rising
Their density rose while the thermometers showed temperature falling
Their density began following rainfall instead of anything thermal
context: Briffa et al., 'Reduced sensitivity of recent tree growth to temperature at high northern latitudes', Nature 391:678 (1998). Correlations that had run as high as r = 0.7 before 1960 drop to near zero or negative after it, and reconstructions built on maximum latewood density are commonly truncated at 1960 to avoid the mismatch. The unsettling part is the logic: this is a proxy failing in the one stretch where we have thermometers to check it against - which is worth remembering for every century where we have none. Source: Briffa et al., Nature 391:678 (1998); Grokipedia, 'Divergence problem'.

question: A girl chops a red cabbage, boils the leaves and strains off the deep purple water: an instrument in a glass. It runs red-pink in acid, purple near neutral, then blue, green and yellow as things turn more alkaline. She stirs in a heaped spoonful of baking soda. Where does the colour stop?
answer: Blue, and no further
choices: Blue, and no further
Green, and no further
Yellow, the top of the range
Purple — it does not move
context: Baking soda is only mildly alkaline — a sodium bicarbonate solution sits at about pH 8.3, so it lifts the juice to blue and stops there. Reaching the green and yellow end takes something genuinely caustic, like oven or drain cleaner, which an adult handles and which nobody stirs into a drinking glass. Nothing is being dyed, either: the anthocyanin pigments in the cabbage physically rearrange as hydrogen ions are pulled off or pushed back on — one molecule changing shape, four times over. Treat cabbage juice as an approximate reading rather than a calibrated one; published cabbage charts disagree in their details, but the reliable core is red-pink in acid, purple near neutral, then blue, green and yellow as things turn more basic. Boil one cabbage and check it yourself with lemon juice, milk, soap and baking soda. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Sodium bicarbonate' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Sodium_bicarbonate; Grokipedia, 'pH indicator' (Natural Indicators) — https://grokipedia.com/page/PH_indicator

question: Robert Boyle set out in 1664 to find every thing that turned blue violet syrup green. He worked through the alkalis his lab could supply: wood ashes, pot-ashes, lime-water and salt of tartar. His list did not stop with minerals. Which three animal things did he also boil down and pour on?
answer: Deer horn, urine, and blood
choices: Deer horn, urine, and blood
Egg white, milk, and honey
Fish oil, tallow, and gall
Bone ash, marrow, and hoof
context: Boyle's own words list 'Spirit of Harts-horn, of Urine, of Sal-Armoniack, of Blood' — hart's-horn being distilled deer antler — and he reported that every one of them 'will immediately change the Blew Syrrup, into a perfect Green.' The alkali doing the work in the animal distillates is ammonia. Source: Robert Boyle, 'Experiments and Considerations Touching Colours' (1664), annotation upon the twentieth experiment — https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/14504

question: Robert Boyle gave his 1664 readers a recipe, so that they could try his colour test at home and not just take his word for it. They were to take good violet syrup and drop a little of it. Where did he tell them to put that drop?
answer: On a sheet of white paper
choices: On a sheet of white paper
In a shallow silver dish
On a polished black slate
Into a glass of clear water
context: Boyle's instruction in full: 'Take good Syrrup of Violets, Imprægnated with the Tincture of the flowers, drop a little of it upon a White Paper (for by that means the Change of Colour will be more conspicuous, and the Experiment may be practis'd in smaller Quantities).' That is a test strip. Boyle wrote it more than three centuries before the pH paper sitting in a school drawer: one small drop, a pale background so the change reads clearly, and hardly any of the costly syrup used up. Source: Robert Boyle, 'Experiments and Considerations Touching Colours' (1664), Experiment XX — https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/14504

question: A man preparing medicines around 1300 used litmus to tell an acid from a base, some 360 years before Robert Boyle's 1664 book put plant indicators on a systematic footing. Most textbooks still hand Boyle the litmus test. Who was that man?
answer: Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a Catalan physician
choices: Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a Catalan physician
Paracelsus, a Swiss physician and alchemist
Albertus Magnus, a German bishop and naturalist
Roger Bacon, an English friar and experimenter
context: Arnaldus de Villa Nova is the first person known to have used litmus to tell acids from bases, in medical preparations, roughly three and a half centuries ahead of Boyle. Boyle's contribution was method, not invention, and any source that crowns him litmus's discoverer has it wrong. The word is older than English chemistry too: 'litmus' comes from the Old Norse 'litmosi', dye moss — 'litr' for dye, 'mosi' for moss. Source: Grokipedia, 'Litmus' (Etymology and Early Discovery) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Litmus

question: S. P. L. Sørensen introduced pH in 1909, the hydrogen-ion exponent, so that acidity could be stated as one small number instead of a string of zeros. No university paid for that work: he ran the chemistry department inside a Copenhagen firm's own laboratory, and pH came out of the problems on its factory floor. Whose laboratory was it?
answer: The Carlsberg brewery, with its fermenting vats
choices: The Carlsberg brewery, with its fermenting vats
The Tuborg brewery, with its lager cellars
The Royal Copenhagen works, with its clay slips
The Burmeister & Wain yard, with its pickling baths
context: Sørensen ran the chemistry department at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen, where enzyme and fermentation work demanded exact acidity control; the paper was 'Enzymstudier II'. The 'p' comes from Danish 'potens', power — the power of ten. He was nominated for a Nobel Prize 25 times between 1915 and 1935, eight times in Chemistry and five in Medicine, and never won: the committee praised pH's usefulness but judged it a reformulation rather than a discovery. Every laboratory on Earth now uses his number. Source: Grokipedia, 'S. P. L. Sørensen' — https://grokipedia.com/page/S._P._L._S%C3%B8rensen

question: A boy stands a cup of vinegar on a kitchen scale and tips in a spoonful of baking soda, and the foam climbs while the reading falls. He seals the identical mixture inside a freezer bag first, and the reading does not move at all. What accounts for the difference between the two runs?
answer: The carbon dioxide leaves the open cup; inside the bag it has nowhere to go
choices: The carbon dioxide leaves the open cup; inside the bag it has nowhere to go
Foam is lighter than the liquid it replaced, so the open cup weighs less
The bag's pressure stops the reaction before it can finish
The open cup warms up and boils some of the vinegar away
context: The reaction is NaHCO3 + H+ → Na+ + H2O + CO2, and gas has mass. Antoine Lavoisier settled the principle in 1789 by calcining tin inside sealed glass and weighing everything: the metal's gain exactly matched the air consumed. His rule, from the Traité Élémentaire de Chimie — 'in every operation an equal quantity of matter exists both before and after the operation.' Your stomach lining runs the identical reaction to defend itself, HCl + HCO3− → H2CO3 → CO2 + H2O. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Sodium bicarbonate' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Sodium_bicarbonate; Grokipedia, 'Antoine Lavoisier' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Antoine_Lavoisier

question: A doctor compares two fluids from one hungry patient: stomach juice at a pH of about 1.7, and arterial blood held between 7.35 and 7.45. That is more than five whole steps apart on the pH scale. She counts the free hydrogen ions actually loose in each. How does the stomach's load compare with the blood's?
answer: Hundreds of thousands of times more
choices: Hundreds of thousands of times more
Hundreds of millions of times more
A few thousand times more
About six times more
context: pH is defined as minus the base-ten logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity, so every whole step compresses a factor of ten: a gap of about 5.7 steps means roughly half a million times more free hydrogen ions in the stomach than in the blood, and the ordinary 0-to-14 span covers a hundred-trillion-fold range in fourteen numbers. The stomach does not neutralise its own acid, either — it maintains a cliff. Across the thin mucus gel lining it, pH climbs from about 2 in the open cavity to about 7 at the cell surface, because the surface cells pump bicarbonate outward faster than acid diffuses inward: hydrochloric acid at 0.05–0.1 M sits millimetres from living tissue held at neutral. And do not take 0 and 14 for walls of nature — drainage from the abandoned Iron Mountain Mine in Shasta County, California has been measured at pH −3.6, the most acidic natural water ever documented. Sources: Grokipedia, 'pH' — https://grokipedia.com/page/PH; Grokipedia, 'Gastric acid' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Gastric_acid; Grokipedia, 'Iron Mountain Mine' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Iron_Mountain_Mine

question: Robert Boyle refused in 1664 to take on trust what others said about blue syrup of violets. They had turned it red before him and put the change down to some peculiar quality of the liquors they happened to have poured on. He carried the same trial through every liquid his laboratory could supply. What did he report?
answer: Almost any acid salt will redden the syrup of violets
choices: Almost any acid salt will redden the syrup of violets
Almost any alkali salt will redden the syrup of violets
Almost any strong spirit will redden the syrup of violets
Almost any volatile oil will redden the syrup of violets
context: Boyle's sentence: the change had 'not been unknown to divers Persons who have produc'd the like, by Spirit of Vitriol, or juice of Limmons, but have Groundlessly ascrib'd the Effect to some Peculiar Quality of those two Liquors, whereas ... almost any Acid Salt will turn Syrrup of Violets Red.' The observation was old; the discovery was that it named a CLASS. That is why he headed the experiment 'the use of it for Investigating the Nature of Salts' — the moment a colour change stopped being a curiosity and became a test. He also policed his own claim, running the same trial on cornflower tincture and publishing 'some Restrictions to shew it not to be so general a propriety as one might imagine', and noting that neither acid nor alkali would restore the syrup to 'its native Blew'. Source: Robert Boyle, 'Experiments and Considerations Touching Colours' (1664), Experiments XX–XXI — https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/14504

question: A teacher sets a strip of litmus paper beside a glass of boiled red cabbage juice. The juice climbs a whole staircase of colours, each step reading a different band of acidity. The litmus does far worse: red at the acid end, blue at the alkaline end, and a vague purple across everything between pH 4.5 and 8.3. Why is litmus so much blunter than a vegetable?
answer: It is a mixture of ten to fifteen lichen dyes, each flipping at its own point
choices: It is a mixture of ten to fifteen lichen dyes, each flipping at its own point
The paper backing soaks the sample up unevenly, blurring every reading
Fixing the dye to paper stops the molecule from changing shape freely
Lichen dye keeps drifting in colour for hours after the sample lands
context: Litmus is squeezed out of lichens, chiefly Roccella tinctoria: crush the dried lichen, soak it in ammonia solution — historically urine — with potassium carbonate, and let it ferment in warm air for two to three weeks while the blue-violet develops. The yield is brutal, roughly 1.5–2 kg of dye from 46 kg of lichen. Chlorine bleaches the paper permanently white by oxidation, destroying it as a test. A reading that smears across four pH units is exactly why a single calculated number was worth inventing. Source: Grokipedia, 'Litmus' (Extraction and Preparation; Color Transition Details) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Litmus

question: A student stirs ammonia into water, and the solution reads strongly alkaline. The rule she was taught says a base is a substance containing hydroxide, and hydroxide ions are unmistakably in there, doing everything a base is supposed to do. Where did those hydroxide ions actually come from?
answer: From the water — the ammonia has no hydroxide at all
choices: From the water — the ammonia has no hydroxide at all
From the ammonia — a hidden hydroxide group is freed
From dissolved oxygen — the ammonia combines with it
From the glass — alkali leaks out into any solution
context: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH−. The WATER is the acid in that beaker: it donates the proton, ammonia accepts it, and the hydroxide is left over as a product rather than carried in. In 1923 Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted ('the chemical character of acids and bases is most simply and generally defined by the scheme acid ⇌ base + H+') and Thomas Martin Lowry ('a base is best described as an acceptor of hydrogen nuclei') published this redefinition months apart, in different countries, neither aware of the other. It also means water switches sides depending on company: with hydrogen chloride, H2O + HCl ⇌ H3O+ + Cl−, and the water is now the base. Acid and base are roles, not substances. Source: Grokipedia, 'Brønsted–Lowry acid–base theory' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Br%C3%B8nsted%E2%80%93Lowry_acid%E2%80%93base_theory

question: A girl at a school bench watches phenolphthalein run colourless below about pH 8.2 and pink above 10, and methyl orange go red to yellow between 3.1 and 4.4. Each indicator is a weak acid caught between two forms, one still holding its proton and one having let it go, and the two forms are different colours. Every such window is about two pH units wide. Why can no indicator be sharper than that?
answer: The eye reads a colour cleanly only once one form holds nine parts in ten
choices: The eye reads a colour cleanly only once one form holds nine parts in ten
Impurities left in the dye flip a little later than the main molecule does
The sample consumes the dye itself, and it does so across a range of pH
A tenfold excess of sample is needed before the new colour registers at all
context: Written out, the equilibrium is HIn ⇌ H+ + In−, the protonated form one colour and the deprotonated form another — the indicator is made of the very thing it measures. Across the range pKa ±1 the ratio of the two forms swings from 1:10 to 10:1, and the eye only reads a colour cleanly once one form holds 90% or more of the mixture, so every transition sits centred on that indicator's own pKa and runs about two units wide. It is also why the manufactured version needs several dyes at once: Yamada's 1933 patent (Japanese Patent 99,664) blended thymol blue, methyl red, bromothymol blue and phenolphthalein in ethanol — four staggered pKa values assembled to imitate the staircase that boiling one vegetable hands you free. Source: Grokipedia, 'pH indicator' (Definition and Mechanism; Acid-Base Equilibria; Modern Universal Indicator) — https://grokipedia.com/page/PH_indicator

question: A waiter cracks open a bottle of soda water, and behind the fizz is carbonic acid, H2CO3, formed when carbon dioxide meets water. Chemists wrote equations with it for more than a century without ever holding any, because in water it breaks back into CO2 and water within microseconds. Then someone calculated how long the dry molecule would last, with no water around it. What did that number turn out to be?
answer: About 180,000 years
choices: About 180,000 years
About a tenth of a second
About three weeks
About four hundred years
context: The reversal inside the ghost: it is not carbonic acid that is fragile, it is carbonic acid IN WATER. Calculations for the anhydrous molecule give a half-life of roughly 0.18 million years at 300 K — the surrounding water molecules are what catalyse its own destruction. The first direct experimental evidence of carbonic acid came only in 1991, from irradiating a CO2/water ice at about 10 kelvin and catching its infrared fingerprint. Joseph Black had the first handle on the gas back in 1756, heating magnesia alba and limestone to make 'fixed air', watching it snuff out flames, turn limewater milky, and make water acidic when dissolved. Source: Grokipedia, 'Carbonic acid' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Carbonic_acid

question: Alexander Fleming imagined a day in his 1945 Nobel lecture when penicillin could be bought in any shop. He made up two characters: Mr. X, who takes too little for a sore throat, and Mrs. X, who catches his infection and dies of pneumonia even with penicillin. Whom did Fleming blame for her death?
answer: Mr. X himself
choices: Mr. X himself
Mrs. X's doctor
The shopkeeper
Fleming himself
context: Fleming's exact words: "Who is primarily responsible for Mrs. X's death? Why Mr. X whose negligent use of penicillin changed the nature of the microbe." His moral was five words long -- "If you use penicillin, use enough." The man who found penicillin used his Nobel Prize speech to warn the world how to lose it. Source: Alexander Fleming, 'Penicillin', Nobel Lecture, 11 December 1945 (nobelprize.org).

question: Surveyors for the World Health Organization (WHO) asked about 10,000 people across twelve countries in 2015 what they understood about antibiotic resistance, the trouble where bacteria stop responding to medicines that used to kill them. Three quarters gave the same wrong account of how it works. What did 76% of them believe?
answer: That the patient's body becomes resistant to the drug
choices: That the patient's body becomes resistant to the drug
That the virus causing the illness becomes resistant
That the antibiotic itself weakens with repeated use
That resistance is inherited from a person's parents
context: A patient's body never becomes resistant to an antibiotic -- the bacteria do, and then they travel to other people. The same survey found 66% believed they were personally safe as long as they took antibiotics exactly as prescribed, and 44% thought resistance only threatened people who take antibiotics often. It is a population's germs that change, not one patient's flesh. Source: WHO multi-country survey, 16 November 2015 (paho.org; iris.who.int).

question: Michael Baym and Roy Kishony built a petri dish the size of a tabletop, two feet by four, and poured it in nine bands, the antibiotic ten times stronger at each step inward, with drug-free strips along the outer edges. They released E. coli at those edges and fixed a camera above the dish. What did the time-lapse show each time the bacteria broke into a stronger band?
answer: A fan of growth spreading out from a single point
choices: A fan of growth spreading out from a single point
The whole front creeping forward evenly at once
Colonies dying back, then returning much later
Scattered specks appearing far ahead of the front
context: Every fan is one mutant's descendants claiming territory. The advancing lawn halts at the edge of each new band and sits there until one cell in that stalled front happens on the mutation that lets it grow in the stronger drug -- and only that one cell's offspring push inward, which is why a breakthrough looks like a fan rather than a straight advance. The team called it the MEGA-plate, for Microbial Evolution and Growth Arena. Source: Baym et al., 'Spatiotemporal microbial evolution on antibiotic landscapes', Science 353 (2016); AAAS news, 'Scientists Build Giant Petri Dish to Film Bacteria Resistance'.

question: Roy Kishony and Michael Baym set E. coli with no resistance at all on the drug-free outer edge of a dish the size of a tabletop. The innermost band held trimethoprim at 3,000 times the dose that stops ordinary E. coli, and the bacteria had to conquer three weaker bands to reach it. How long did the crossing take?
answer: About ten days
choices: About ten days
About ten weeks
About ten months
About three years
context: Ten days for trimethoprim, twelve for ciprofloxacin. And they did not stop where the plate did: the strains that finished the trimethoprim run had become 10,000 times harder to kill than their ancestors, and the ciprofloxacin runners 100,000 times -- more resistance than the toughest band on the dish ever demanded of them. Source: Baym et al., Science 353 (2016).

question: A nurse gives a patient penicillin, and one bacterium in the infection walks through the dose unharmed. It makes a beta-lactamase, one of a huge family of bacterial enzymes that attack the one chemical feature penicillin and its many relatives all share. By 2019 more than 2,000 kinds had been catalogued. What do these enzymes do to the drug molecule?
answer: They cut its central ring wide open
choices: They cut its central ring wide open
They wrap it in a sugar that blocks it
They clamp it in a harmless pocket
They flip it into a mirror image
context: That ring is the whole weapon: snap it and what is left is chemically dead before it ever reaches the cell wall. Two thousand variants is not a fluke, it is an arms race with a long history, and these enzymes turn up in bacteria of every kind, Gram-positive and Gram-negative alike. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antimicrobial resistance'.

question: A technician doses the gut bacterium Escherichia coli with fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and beta-lactams, three very different antibiotic families, and it stays hard to kill with all three. One long protein assembly, AcrAB-TolC, reaches from inside the cell all the way out through the outer membrane. What is AcrAB-TolC actually doing for the cell?
answer: It bails each one back out as fast as it comes in
choices: It bails each one back out as fast as it comes in
It shreds all three with one broad-spectrum enzyme
It seals the cell so that none of the three can enter
It hides the targets all three of the drugs aim at
context: AcrAB-TolC is an efflux pump, from the resistance-nodulation-division family, and it runs on the flow of protons across the membrane. The bacterium never destroys the drug -- it simply refuses to keep it, holding the concentration inside the cell below the killing threshold. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antimicrobial resistance'.

question: British doctors saw staph shrug off methicillin only a year after it reached hospitals in 1960 to kill the staph penicillin could no longer defeat. These resistant strains, called methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), carry a borrowed gene named mecA that plain staph never had. What does mecA give the germ?
answer: A replacement protein the methicillin key cannot fit
choices: A replacement protein the methicillin key cannot fit
A pump that throws methicillin back out of the cell
An enzyme that cuts the methicillin molecule apart
A thicker coat that methicillin cannot get through
context: mecA rides on a mobile chunk of DNA called the staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec, and it encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with such low affinity for the drug that the beta-lactam key no longer turns the lock. In the United States, MRSA went from negligible in the 1970s to more than 60% of all S. aureus isolates by the early 2000s. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antimicrobial resistance'.

question: A hospital microbiologist finds one resistance gene in two species that are not close relatives. New resistance mutations are rare, roughly one cell in a million to one in a billion per generation, and the gene has spread far faster than mutation could explain. It sits on a plasmid, a small loop of spare DNA alongside the main chromosome. Which route carries most of that spread?
answer: One cell pushes a plasmid into another through a tube
choices: One cell pushes a plasmid into another through a tube
Dying cells burst and neighbours swallow their plasmids
Viruses ferry plasmids from one infected cell to the next
Each stressed cell rewrites its own plasmid to suit the drug
context: The tube is a pilus and the process is called conjugation, driven by a type IV secretion system: a physical handoff, cell to cell. Riding on those plasmids are transposons that cut and paste themselves and integrons that collect gene cassettes, so a single plasmid can carry a whole toolkit across a species boundary. A modern one you can trace to a farm is mcr-1, the colistin-resistance gene that came out of Chinese pig production and turned up in human patients around the world -- already circulating, waiting for a last-resort drug that doctors had shelved and then brought back. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antimicrobial resistance'.

question: Doctors at a Michigan hospital isolated in June 2002 the thing infection specialists had been dreading: a Staphylococcus aureus that vancomycin, the drug held back for when everything else has failed, could not kill. The patient was a woman of 40, on dialysis since 1999. Sequencing found a resistance gene called vanA inside her staph, a gene staph had never carried. Where had it come from?
answer: From an Enterococcus infecting the same woman at the time
choices: From an Enterococcus infecting the same woman at the time
From a virus that had infected her staph and carried it in
From bacteria living in the dialysis machine's water lines
From a Streptococcus already living in her own throat
context: She was carrying a vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecalis at the same time, and it handed its vanA over. Two different species swapped weapons inside one woman, and the last resort against methicillin-resistant staph fell: her staph's minimum inhibitory concentration ran above 32 micrograms per millilitre. vanA rebuilds the cell-wall building block so that vancomycin has nothing left to grab. Source: Chang et al., New England Journal of Medicine (NEJMoa025025); CDC MMWR, 5 July 2002.

question: Researchers sampled 400 metres down in New Mexico's Lechuguilla Cave, sealed off from the surface for more than four million years, and brought up a bacterium they named Paenibacillus LC231. Nothing growing there has ever met a medicine. They tested 40 modern antibiotics against it. How many did it shrug off?
answer: Twenty-six of them, across fourteen different drug classes
choices: Twenty-six of them, across fourteen different drug classes
Nine of them, all of them penicillin's close relatives
Three of them, all of them made by soil-dwelling fungi
None of them -- every drug on the list killed it outright
context: It could chemically inactivate seven whole classes outright. Inside its chromosome researchers found 18 resistance elements, including five gene families never described before and three mechanisms nobody had previously connected to antibiotics at all. An earlier survey of the same cave screened 93 strains against 26 drugs and found three Streptomyces that resisted 14 of them -- including daptomycin, a drug they could never have met. Source: Pawlowski et al., Nature Communications (2016); Bhullar et al., PLoS ONE 7(4):e34953 (2012).

question: Vanessa D'Costa's team hunted for resistance genes where no prescription was ever written: Beringian permafrost frozen for 30,000 years. They checked hard that the DNA was truly ancient, not modern contamination. They found resistance genes against three drug families. Then they rebuilt one whole gene from the ancient sequence, made the protein, and tested it. What did the 30,000-year-old gene turn out to do?
answer: Defeat vancomycin exactly as its modern version does
choices: Defeat vancomycin exactly as its modern version does
Defeat penicillin, but nothing stronger than penicillin
Break down natural plant poisons rather than medicines
Nothing at all -- the ancient protein no longer folded
context: The reconstructed element was VanA -- the same one that turned up inside that Michigan patient's staph in 2002 -- and it was already sitting in frozen ground 30,000 years before any human made a medicine. D'Costa and colleagues titled the paper exactly what the data said: 'Antibiotic resistance is ancient'. The reason is that antibiotics are ancient too: soil microbes such as Streptomyces have been poisoning their rivals with these chemicals for millions of years. Viable staphylococci resisting tetracycline and chloramphenicol have been pulled from Siberian permafrost dating to the Middle Miocene. We did not start this war -- we walked into it carrying weapons the other side had already seen. Source: D'Costa et al., 'Antibiotic resistance is ancient', Nature 477 (2011); Grokipedia, 'Antimicrobial resistance'.

question: Michael Baym's team reconstructed the family trees of the E. coli that had crossed their giant dish of ever-stronger antibiotic, which let them see both where every lineage sat on the plate and how much drug each one could take. Where did the most resistant mutants of all turn out to be sitting?
answer: Stuck in place just behind the lineages leading each advance
choices: Stuck in place just behind the lineages leading each advance
Out at the very front, leading the break into each new band
Spread evenly through all nine bands of the giant dish
Back at the drug-free edge of the dish where the run began
context: Baym's own summary: "What we saw suggests that evolution is not always led by the most resistant mutants. The strongest mutants are, in fact, often moving behind more vulnerable strains." The paper's phrase is that highly resistant mutants "may be trapped behind more sensitive lineages" -- hemmed in by neighbours, with nowhere to grow. Geography beat fitness. Resistance does usually carry a real cost as well: resistant strains often grow more slowly than their vulnerable cousins when no drug is present, which is why sensitive strains can win ground back -- until compensatory mutations pay that debt off. Source: Baym et al., Science 353 (2016); Michael Baym quoted in AAAS news (2016).

question: Martin Llewelyn and a group of infection specialists took up a familiar rule in the British Medical Journal (BMJ) in 2017, the one children are told: finish the whole course of antibiotics even after feeling better, because stopping early breeds resistance. What did they argue about it?
answer: Nobody has established the right course length for most infections
choices: Nobody has established the right course length for most infections
Stopping early remains the biggest single driver of resistance
Course length matters far less than getting the dose size right
The rule was settled by trials in the 1950s and still holds today
context: Llewelyn and colleagues argued that the evidence for 'always finish the course' is weak, while taking antibiotics for longer than you need does raise resistance risk -- and that for most drugs and most infections nobody has actually run the trials to find the right duration. Read the argument carefully, because it is easy to misuse: their point was that durations are under-studied and should be set by a clinician for each patient, NOT that you should cut your own course short. The safe and true line is still take what your doctor prescribed. What makes this worth knowing is that even the advice everyone repeats is being tested. Source: Llewelyn et al., 'The antibiotic course has had its day', BMJ 358:j3418 (2017).

question: Johann Wilhelm Ritter split sunlight with a prism in a dark room on 22 February 1801. William Herschel had found invisible warmth past red the year before, so Ritter reasoned something invisible must lie past the other end too. A strip of silver-chloride paper laid there darkened faster than any strip in the colours. What had he discovered?
answer: Ultraviolet light
choices: Ultraviolet light
X-rays
Microwaves
Gamma rays
context: Ritter had chosen his detector well: silver chloride blackens when light knocks the chlorine off it, and the chemistry runs faster the more energetic each incoming particle of light. He called the new rays 'chemical rays'; 'ultraviolet' was coined decades later. Source: britannica.com/biography/Johann-Wilhelm-Ritter ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Wilhelm_Ritter.

question: William Herschel laid a thermometer just past the red end of the spectrum in 1800 and watched the mercury climb. Johann Ritter used a different detector when he went hunting past violet: paper soaked in silver chloride. Why did Herschel's thermometer method not work at Ritter's end of the spectrum?
answer: Light past violet carries almost no heat, so a thermometer would barely twitch
choices: Light past violet carries almost no heat, so a thermometer would barely twitch
Rays past violet are absorbed by air before ever reaching the thermometer bulb
The atmosphere refocuses the rays into a spot too narrow for a thermometer to catch
Rays past violet were thought to pass straight through mercury without warming it
context: Each ultraviolet particle of light carries a lot of energy, but sunlight past violet delivers very little total warmth to a surface -- most of the Sun's heat is in the red and infrared. Chemistry is a much more sensitive test for the presence of UV than temperature is. Sources: opencurriculum.org 'Ritter Discovers Ultraviolet Light'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet.

question: Johann Ritter went hunting past the violet edge of sunlight on a hunch, not on a cool test. He belonged to the German Romantic Naturphilosophie circle, and its ideas shaped what he expected to find. What exactly was the hunch?
answer: That an opposite to Herschel's heat rays past red must exist to balance them
choices: That an opposite to Herschel's heat rays past red must exist to balance them
That an eighth colour must exist to complete Newton's seven into a musical octave
That a 'cold ray' predicted by Herschel would chill a thermometer past violet
That an electric ray, Franklin's invisible partner of daylight, must reach the eye
context: Naturphilosophie held that nature was organised in polarities -- positive and negative, north and south, heat and its opposite. Ritter's metaphysical hunch pointed him at a real thing this time; plenty of the same reasoning led his other work nowhere. The hunch is not the evidence. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Wilhelm_Ritter ; danielpatrickcarroll.substack.com/p/johann-wilhelm-ritter.

question: Barry Marshall drank a beaker of Helicobacter pylori in 1984 to prove it caused stomach ulcers, and shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Johann Ritter also experimented on himself, running the two poles of a voltaic pile across his own eyes, tongue, nose and ears for years, with opium to blunt the effects. How did Ritter's story end?
answer: He died in Munich in 1810, at the age of 33, deep in debt
choices: He died in Munich in 1810, at the age of 33, deep in debt
He was blinded in both eyes but lectured on optics until 1854
He recovered his health and shared the 1830 Copley Medal with Volta
He was banned by the King of Bavaria from further self-experiment in 1815
context: Ritter's obituary listed heart failure; his friends laid the blame on the years of shocks, the sleepless nights and the alcohol and opium. He is the same courage as Marshall with the opposite ending -- and the two belong side by side so no one mistakes 'the scientist tried it on himself' for a story that always works out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Wilhelm_Ritter.

question: A boy warms his face at a 250-watt red heat lamp for hours, pleasantly. Twenty minutes in bright noon sunlight can leave him visibly sunburned, though over those hours the lamp puts more total warmth on him. The Sun's ultraviolet does the burning. What sets a single ultraviolet particle of light apart from a red-lamp one?
answer: It carries more energy per particle -- enough to break chemical bonds in skin
choices: It carries more energy per particle -- enough to break chemical bonds in skin
It carries a small electrical charge that ionises skin cells as it passes
It travels through the air far faster than an infrared particle can
It resonates with the water in the skin the way a microwave does
context: The energy of a particle of light (a photon) is set by its wavelength, not by how many arrive. Red photons don't have enough energy to break a DNA bond no matter how many strike; a single ultraviolet photon does. Same reason UV fades curtains, sterilises drinking water in a plastic bottle and blackened Ritter's silver-chloride paper 220 years ago. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet ; epa.gov/radtown/ultraviolet-uv-radiation.

question: A 69-year-old American delivery-truck driver had his face photographed for the June 2012 New England Journal of Medicine. The left half of it looked two decades older than the right, with deep leathery wrinkles reaching down his neck, while the right side stayed smooth. He had driven the truck 28 years with the window at his left shoulder closed. What did the photograph make clear about ordinary window glass?
answer: It blocks the shorter UVB wavelengths but lets the longer-wavelength UVA straight through
choices: It blocks the shorter UVB wavelengths but lets the longer-wavelength UVA straight through
It blocks all ultraviolet completely, so the ageing must be from visible sunlight alone
It blocks visible light on that side but transmits infrared, which is what dried out the skin
It amplifies incoming ultraviolet by focusing the rays through curvature in the glass
context: The case was reported by Jennifer Gordon and Joaquin Brieva of Northwestern (NEJM 366:e25, 2012). UVA penetrates deep into the dermis and breaks down its collagen and elastin -- the mechanism of long-term skin ageing, distinct from the short-term sunburn caused by UVB. Sunscreen does not just prevent burning; a car window will not save you from it. Sources: news.feinberg.northwestern.edu/2012/06/20/sun-damage/; livescience.com/20743-photo-sun-damage-skin-cancer.html.

question: Wilhelm Roentgen sealed his discharge tube in thick black cardboard at Wuerzburg on 8 November 1895, so no light escaped, and darkened the room. He switched it on, and something on a bench two metres away, well outside the tube's path, began behaving oddly. What did he see?
answer: A small coated screen was glowing faint green
choices: A small coated screen was glowing faint green
A magnetised needle was swinging slowly aside
A gold-leaf electroscope was losing its charge
A sealed thermometer was climbing a few degrees
context: The cardboard was there precisely so that no light could leak out; the little screen, painted with barium platinocyanide, lay about two metres away and out of the cathode rays' path. Something invisible was crossing the room. Roentgen never claimed to know what it was, and named it for the unknown, writing in his paper: 'X-rays (as I will call the rays, for the sake of brevity)' -- in the German, X-Strahlen. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Wilhelm Roentgen', section Discovery and Study of X-rays; W. C. Roentgen, 'On a New Kind of Rays' (1895), translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/roentgen.html.

question: Anna Bertha Roentgen held her hand on a photographic plate for about fifteen minutes on 22 December 1895. The developed image, the oldest surviving X-ray, shows her finger bones and wedding ring. But her husband had already watched living bones weeks before. Where had he seen them?
answer: As a live shadow on a fluorescent screen
choices: As a live shadow on a fluorescent screen
As a pale shape on the tube's glass wall
As a grey outline thrown on the far wall
As a dark blur on a sheet of white paper
context: His own sentence in the 1895 paper, written before he ever made a plate: 'If the hand be held before the fluorescent screen, the shadow shows the bones clearly with only faint outlines of the surrounding tissues.' He had been watching living bones move as a shadow on the glowing screen for weeks before he asked his wife, Anna Bertha Ludwig, to hold still on a photographic plate for about fifteen minutes on 22 December 1895. The Germans titled that plate 'Hand mit Ringen' -- hand with rings. One caution about the famous moment: the line often attached to it, 'I have seen my death', appears only in later retellings and in no contemporary document, and the add-on that she never entered his laboratory again is legend too -- so treat both as story, not record. Sources: W. C. Roentgen, 'On a New Kind of Rays' (1895), translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/roentgen.html; Grokipedia, 'Wilhelm Roentgen'; litfl.com/wilhelm-rontgen; the quotation hedged as 'reportedly' / 'according to legend' at caferoentgen.com and hyperallergic.com.

question: Wilhelm Roentgen ruled out light first: his discharge tube sat sealed inside black cardboard, so the invisible thing crossing his darkened laboratory could not be that. He had spent years studying cathode rays and had to prove that this was not simply those. What test does his 1895 paper report as producing no effect whatever?
answer: He brought a strong magnet up and watched for a bend
choices: He brought a strong magnet up and watched for a bend
He sent the rays through a glass prism to split them
He passed the rays by a charged plate to see a pull
He aimed the rays through a pair of narrow slits
context: His own sentence in the paper: 'I have not succeeded in observing any deviation of the X-rays even in very strong magnetic fields.' Cathode rays swerve hard in a magnet; these went dead straight, which meant they carried no electric charge and so were not cathode rays. The cardboard shield had already ruled out ordinary light. That double elimination is what turned a strange glow into a discovery -- and, unable to say what the rays were, he called them X. Source: W. C. Roentgen, 'On a New Kind of Rays' (1895), translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/roentgen.html.

question: Wilhelm Roentgen saw his first glow across a darkened laboratory on the afternoon of 8 November 1895, then announced nothing at all until the very end of December. Seven weeks went by with almost no one outside that room knowing. What was he doing in the gap?
answer: He ate and slept in the laboratory, testing the rays
choices: He ate and slept in the laboratory, testing the rays
He rebuilt the tube from scratch to rule out a fault
He searched the physics journals for an earlier report
He trained two assistants to reproduce the green glow
context: He told almost no one. He worked without assistants and built much of his own apparatus by hand. In those seven weeks he mapped what the rays would go through: the screen still lit up behind 'a book of a thousand pages', and 'printer's ink offers no marked resistance'; the fluorescence showed behind two packs of cards; pine boards two or three centimetres thick 'absorb only very little'; but 'Lead 1.5 mm thick is practically opaque.' A thousand-page book beat a millimetre and a half of lead -- the empirical root of every lead apron since. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Roentgen; Grokipedia, 'Wilhelm Roentgen', section Interests and Personality; Roentgen 1895, translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/roentgen.html.

question: A boy slides his feet into the slot of a wooden cabinet in an American shoe shop, one of roughly ten thousand such shops about 1950. An X-ray tube sits in the base, and a fluorescent screen shows his foot bones wiggling inside a brand-new shoe. What have the makers fitted to the top of the cabinet?
answer: Three viewing ports, for child, parent and clerk
choices: Three viewing ports, for child, parent and clerk
Three timing bells, for men, women and children
Two brass dials, reading each foot in inches
Two tilting mirrors, letting the shop crowd look
context: Trade names included the Adrian, the X-Ray Shoe Fitter, the Foot-O-Scope and the Pedoscope; roughly 3,000 more ran in Britain, 1,500 in Switzerland and 1,000 in Canada. The machines ran at 50 kilovolts through a filter of just 1 mm of aluminium, with settings labelled for men, women and children; a single twenty-second look delivered something like 7 to 14 roentgens to the feet, against a 1946 American standard of 0.1 R per day. A 1948 Detroit survey of 43 machines found 16 to 75 roentgens per minute, and one machine measured 116 R in one 20-second viewing. No study ever showed the cabinet fitted a shoe better than a tape measure and a trained clerk -- the radiation physicist Lauriston Taylor noted in 1950 that the image gave no fitting data at all -- and a 1947 trade journal sold it with the line 'Kiddies love it!'. The people hurt worst were the ones who stood there: a 1957 British Medical Journal report by H. Kopp described a shoe-shop worker of ten years who ran the machine 15 to 20 times a day and would put her own foot in to reassure nervous children; she developed severe radiation damage to her right leg and foot. Pennsylvania banned the machines in 1957; by 1970 thirty-three states had. Sources: ORAU Museum of Radiation and Radioactivity, 'Shoe-Fitting Fluoroscope'; Grokipedia, 'Shoe-fitting fluoroscope'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoe-fitting_fluoroscope; spectrum.ieee.org.

question: Wilhelm Roentgen gave the only public lecture of his life about his discovery at Wuerzburg on 23 January 1896. To close it he took the hand of Albert von Koelliker, the eminent old anatomist, and made a plate of it live in front of the hall. Koelliker then rose to his feet and put a proposal to the audience, which answered with a general cheer. What did Koelliker propose?
answer: That Roentgen's name be given to the rays themselves
choices: That Roentgen's name be given to the rays themselves
That Roentgen be made an honorary doctor of medicine
That Roentgen repeat the plate on a patient's skull
That Roentgen sit for a portrait to hang in the hall
context: Koelliker asked that they be called Roentgen rays, and the hall answered with 'allgemeiner Jubelruf' -- general cheering. In German they are Roentgenstrahlen to this day. Two details worth noticing: this was the one and only public talk Roentgen ever gave on the rays, and the Koelliker plate is markedly sharper than the one of his wife's hand a month earlier -- he had improved his technique fast. Sources: lindahall.org, Scientist of the Day, 'Wilhelm Roentgen'; caferoentgen.com, 'A Tale of Two Hands'; the Koelliker plate at artsandculture.google.com.

question: Physicists in Montreal and in New Hampshire had machines running within six weeks of Wilhelm Roentgen's paper of 28 December 1895, photographing bones inside living patients. Almost no discovery has ever been taken up that fast, and one decision of Roentgen's is why the rays could spread so quickly. What was the decision?
answer: He refused to take out any patent on the rays
choices: He refused to take out any patent on the rays
He printed full tube plans alongside his paper
He shipped ready-made tubes to foreign labs
He handed the whole method to the newspapers
context: He refused a patent because he wanted society as a whole to benefit -- which is exactly why anyone, anywhere, could build a machine within weeks, and why he never earned a penny from the rays. He took no money from the discovery at all, and by the early 1920s German hyperinflation had wiped out his savings and left him nearly bankrupt in a modest country house at Weilheim. The two machines named above were running by February 1896: the McGill physicist John Cox in Montreal, and at Dartmouth in New Hampshire the physics professor Edwin Frost with his physician brother Gilman, who on 3 February imaged the wrist of a schoolboy broken while skating. The honours came later and cost him nothing: IUPAC named element 111 roentgenium (Rg) after him in 2004, and 8 November -- the day the screen glowed -- was made World Radiography Day in 2007. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Roentgen; Grokipedia, 'Wilhelm Roentgen', sections Interests and Personality and Influence on Science and Medicine; home.dartmouth.edu; 'Seeing the bones of things', Canadian Family Physician (PMC3192089); Grokipedia, 'World Radiography Day'.

question: Wilhelm Roentgen travelled to Stockholm in 1901 to accept the very first Nobel Prize in Physics, for the discovery of the remarkable rays, and gave the money away to the University of Wuerzburg. But there was one part of the Nobel week he simply would not do. Which part?
answer: Delivering the Nobel lecture
choices: Delivering the Nobel lecture
Attending the royal banquet
Sitting for the official portrait
Shaking the king's hand on stage
context: The full 1901 citation reads 'in recognition of the extraordinary services he has rendered by the discovery of the remarkable rays subsequently named after him'. Roentgen was so shy of public speaking that he declined to deliver a Nobel lecture -- the first physics laureate in history, and he would not make the speech. On the prize money, the sources agree on the act and disagree on the figure: Wuerzburg's own archive and LITFL say he donated 50,000 crowns, while Grokipedia says he donated the entire 150,782 kronor. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Roentgen; uni-wuerzburg.de university archive; Grokipedia, 'Wilhelm Roentgen'.

question: John Cox, a McGill physicist, held Tolson Cunning under the rays for forty-five minutes in Montreal in February 1896, barely six weeks after Wilhelm Roentgen's paper reached the world. His plate showed the bullet the surgeons had hunted for and failed to find, in Cunning's lower leg. Dr Robert Kirkpatrick then cut it out. Days later that same plate was carried into a place no photograph like it had ever entered. Which place?
answer: Into a courtroom, at the trial of the man who shot him
