choices: Into a courtroom, at the trial of the man who shot him
Into a patent office, with Cox's claim on the method
Into a police station, as the record of a shooting
Into a medical school, as a teaching plate for students
context: The judge accepted the plate -- apparently the first X-ray ever entered as legal evidence anywhere -- and the man who shot Tolson Cunning drew fourteen years. Cox's image showed the bullet lying between the tibia and the fibula. Sources split on the exact day: 3 February per the Canadian Family Physician history, 7 February per others. America's first clinical X-ray was just as quick off the mark: on 3 February 1896 at Dartmouth, the physics professor Edwin Frost and his physician brother Gilman imaged the wrist of the schoolboy Eddie McCarthy, broken skating on the Connecticut River two weeks earlier. Sources: 'Seeing the bones of things: A scan of x-rays' early history', Canadian Family Physician (PMC3192089); auntminnie.com, 'Moments in Radiology History'; home.dartmouth.edu.

question: H. J. W. Dam, an American journalist, interviewed Wilhelm Roentgen for McClure's Magazine in April 1896, in a mixture of German, English and French. Roentgen shunned the fame and gave almost no interviews, so it is very nearly the only record of him describing his own discovery. Dam asked what went through his mind the moment the little screen first glowed. How did Roentgen answer?
answer: That he had not thought, he had investigated
choices: That he had not thought, he had investigated
That he had not guessed, he had waited
That he had not believed it, he had repeated it
That he had not looked away, he had watched
context: His exact words: 'I did not think, I investigated. I assumed that the effect must have come from the tube since its character indicated that it could come from nowhere else.' Dam also asked the obvious question -- what ARE the rays? Roentgen's answer was three words: 'I don't know.' He had found something, named it for the unknown, and refused to pretend he understood it. Sources: H. J. W. Dam interview, McClure's Magazine, April 1896; quotations corroborated at litfl.com/wilhelm-rontgen and web.mit.edu/redingtn/www/netadv/SP20140210.html.

question: A radiographer switches on an X-ray tube, a simple machine. A hot filament boils off electrons, tens of thousands of volts hurl them down the tube, and a slab of tungsten sits at the far end. Nothing inside it is radioactive, and no chemical reaction takes place. What actually makes the X-ray photons?
answer: The electrons losing energy as they are pulled up short
choices: The electrons losing energy as they are pulled up short
The tungsten atoms heated until they glow past violet
The high voltage tearing electrons off the gas inside
The filament shedding light as its wire runs white-hot
context: German physicists named the effect bremsstrahlung -- braking radiation. Electrons accelerated across 20 to 150 kilovolts are deflected and decelerated by the nuclei of the target and shed the lost energy as photons. The harder the stop, the more energetic the ray: the maximum photon energy equals the full accelerating voltage. Roentgen's own tube had no metal target at all -- his rays came from the spot where the cathode rays struck the glass wall. Sources: Grokipedia, 'X-ray', section Production Mechanisms / Electron-Based Production; Grokipedia, 'Wilhelm Roentgen'.

question: A technician aims a modern X-ray tube at a patient's chest, and under one percent of the electricity going in comes back out as X-rays. Over ninety-nine percent turns straight into heat, dumped on a focal spot smaller than a grain of rice, hot enough to pit or vaporise the metal. What do high-power tubes do to the tungsten target?
answer: Spin it as a disc at thousands of revolutions a minute
choices: Spin it as a disc at thousands of revolutions a minute
Flood it from behind with fast-running cooling water
Swap it for a fresh target every few hundred exposures
Slide it a fraction sideways between each exposure
context: High-power tubes use a tungsten-rhenium disc spun at 3,000 to 10,000 revolutions per minute, so the beam burns a ring instead of a hole -- the heat is smeared around a whole circle of metal rather than piling into one spot. It is worth sitting with the headline number: the machine that made radiology possible is a spectacularly bad converter, throwing away more than ninety-nine percent of what it is fed. Source: Grokipedia, 'X-ray', section Electron-Based Production.

question: A doctor holds an X-ray plate up to the light. Bone throws a hard shadow on it, while the flesh around the bone barely dims the beam. The calcium in bone is atomic number 20; the hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen of soft tissue average about 7.4. How does an atom's grip on X-ray photons scale with its atomic number?
answer: It climbs with the cube of the atomic number
choices: It climbs with the cube of the atomic number
It climbs with the square of the atomic number
It climbs with the fourth power of the atomic number
It climbs with the fifth power of the atomic number
context: Photoelectric absorption goes roughly as Z-cubed over E-cubed, where Z is the atomic number and E the photon's energy. Calcium is Z=20; soft tissue -- hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen -- has an effective Z of only about 7.4, a ratio of about 2.7. Cube 2.7 and you get roughly twenty, which is the whole reason a shadow of your own skeleton exists on a plate. (The cube law describes how hard a single atom grabs a photon, not the exact fraction of a beam a whole limb stops -- but it is why bone and flesh look so different.) Lead is Z=82, and cubing that is exactly and only why a lead apron works. Roentgen found the empirical version of this rule in 1895 without any of the theory: the screen still glowed behind a book of a thousand pages, but 'Lead 1.5 mm thick is practically opaque.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'X-ray', section Photoelectric Absorption; Roentgen 1895, translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/roentgen.html.

question: Thomas Edison chased Roentgen's new rays hard in 1896, building a fluoroscope at his New Jersey laboratory. His glassblower, Clarence Dally, tested the beams by holding his own hands in them, day after day. Surgeons took Dally's left hand in 1902, then four fingers of the right, then both arms, and he died in 1904 at thirty-nine, the first American killed by X-rays. What did Edison do about X-ray work after that?
answer: He gave it up and said outright that he feared the rays
choices: He gave it up and said outright that he feared the rays
He carried on from behind a shielded lead cabinet
He put the blame on the tube maker and redesigned it
He took over the testing himself with brief exposures
context: Edison abandoned X-ray work and said in 1903: 'Don't talk to me about X-rays; I am afraid of them.' Clarence Dally died on 2 October 1904, aged thirty-nine, after failed skin grafts and amputations at the wrist, then the elbow, then the shoulder. By 1908 the American Roentgen Ray Society counted forty-seven radiation deaths. And here is the honest correction to the story people usually tell: Roentgen himself died on 10 February 1923 in Munich of intestinal carcinoma, aged seventy-seven, and it is NOT attributed to his rays -- he worked mostly behind photographic plates rather than standing at a live screen. The martyrs of early radiology were the people who watched. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Dally; Grokipedia, 'Wilhelm Roentgen'; spectrum.ieee.org.

question: Howard Scott, an American engineer, set out in the 1930s to abolish money. Every citizen would get energy certificates instead, a share of the continent's power output, and Scott gave them one rule for any certificate its owner left unspent. What was the rule?
answer: It expired at the end of its period
choices: It expired at the end of its period
It lost a little value every month
It could be cashed in for gold
It could be lent out at interest
context: Every citizen's certificates were to be worth an equal share of the year's power output. Unspent certificates would expire so no one could hoard. Scott argued this would settle 'the price problem' by removing prices altogether. See https://www.americanheritage.com/howard-scott-and-his-technocratic-utopia

question: Howard Scott gathered engineers, scientists and technicians in New York in late 1919 to inventory every unit of energy produced and wasted in North America. It was his first attempt; the mass movement of 1932 was his second. What became of that first group?
answer: It dissolved in 1921 without finishing the energy survey
choices: It dissolved in 1921 without finishing the energy survey
It was quietly absorbed into Herbert Hoover's Department of Commerce in 1922
It was outlawed under the 1919 Palmer Raids as suspected Bolshevik infiltration
It became the founding chapter of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers
context: It was called the Technical Alliance. The 'prosperity and conservatism of the 1920s undermined the political orientation of the Technical Alliance', but the more basic problem was arithmetic: the data a planner needs can be bigger than the planner. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_Alliance

question: Garrett Hardin set out a parable in the December 1968 issue of Science. In it, each user of a shared resource rationally captures the whole gain of taking a little more, while sharing the cost with everyone else. What scene did he use to make the argument?
answer: Herdsmen adding cattle to a pasture open to all until the pasture is ruined
choices: Herdsmen adding cattle to a pasture open to all until the pasture is ruined
Coastal captains overfishing an open bay until the boats sit idle at the wharf
Villagers cutting a village woodlot for fuel until only saplings remain
Householders drawing water from a common well until the water table falls
context: Hardin called this 'the tragedy of the commons' and offered it as a general law of shared resources under population growth. The other three scenes are all real cases the literature has since debated, but Hardin's own essay used the pasture. See https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.162.3859.1243

question: Garrett Hardin imagined a pasture open to every herdsman in his 1968 essay 'The Tragedy of the Commons'. Each one, he argued, would keep adding cattle until the grass was destroyed, because each extra animal was pure profit for him while the cost of overgrazing was shared by all. Critics later found an assumption tucked inside the parable. What does it quietly assume about the herdsmen?
answer: That the herdsmen cannot talk to each other, watch each other, or punish each other
choices: That the herdsmen cannot talk to each other, watch each other, or punish each other
That the pasture regrows at the same rate no matter how much has been eaten
That the herdsmen have no idea that too many cattle will ruin the grass
That the price of beef holds steady however many animals go to market
context: Real users of a shared resource often do talk, watch and punish one another, as Elinor Ostrom's fieldwork went on to document, and that changes the arithmetic. Where users truly cannot, on a resource open to all with no rules, Hardin's tragedy can still play out. See https://aeon.co/essays/the-tragedy-of-the-commons-is-a-false-and-dangerous-myth

question: Elinor Ostrom did not argue with Garrett Hardin's parable on paper. Hardin had concluded in 1968 that any resource owned by everyone must inevitably collapse. She and her students took a very different road. What did they spend some twenty years doing?
answer: Walking the actual pastures, forests and irrigation canals and reading the village rulebooks
choices: Walking the actual pastures, forests and irrigation canals and reading the village rulebooks
Running undergraduate volunteers through pasture-and-cattle experiments in the university lab
Building a global computer simulation of every commons on Earth to test Hardin's arithmetic
Petitioning governments to nationalise the commons Hardin's essay had said would collapse
context: Her cases included the Swiss alpine pastures of Torbel, Japanese village forests at Hirano, Nagaike and Yamanoka, and the huerta irrigation canals of Valencia. She kept finding communities that had governed shared resources for centuries without either private ownership or a state. See https://drganghe.github.io/program-evaluation/stories/elinor-ostrom-and-case-studies.html

question: Elinor Ostrom shared the Nobel Prize in Economics with Oliver Williamson in 2009. Her fieldwork had shown that Garrett Hardin's 'tragedy of the commons' was only one possibility, not an iron rule: open resources with no rules really can collapse, and the result turns on the rules people write. What further honor did that prize carry for Ostrom herself?
answer: She was the first woman ever to win the economics Nobel
choices: She was the first woman ever to win the economics Nobel
She was the first political scientist ever to win any Nobel
She was the youngest laureate ever named in the economics category
She was the first American laureate ever named in the economics category
context: The economics prize had been awarded for forty years and never to a woman. Ostrom was trained as a political scientist rather than an economist, but the Nobel committee cited her fieldwork on the governance of commons. See https://csgs.kcl.ac.uk/crises-of-the-commons-elinor-ostroms-legacy-of-self-governance/

question: An Austrian-born economist at the London School of Economics published a short paper in the American Economic Review in September 1945. The question in the air was whether a central planner in Moscow could really run an economy from a desk in a ministry. His answer would ripple through decades of debate about socialism and markets. Who wrote it, and what did the paper say about a central planner?
answer: Friedrich Hayek: the knowledge a planner would need is dispersed, local, and often unwritten
choices: Friedrich Hayek: the knowledge a planner would need is dispersed, local, and often unwritten
John Maynard Keynes: a planner cannot know the animal spirits driving investment decisions
Milton Friedman: a planner underestimates how long monetary policy takes to bite
Joseph Schumpeter: a planner cannot predict which innovations will destroy the old order
context: The essay was 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'. Written in the middle of the socialist-calculation debate, it is Ostrom's canals with a title page: the fieldworkers who walked the Torbel meadows with notebooks were collecting exactly the knowledge Hayek said no central desk could ever hold. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society

question: Benjamin Thompson, Count Rumford, set two horses walking in a slow circle in the Munich arsenal. They turned a brass cannon against a steel borer. The gun sat sealed inside a box of cold water, and no fire burned anywhere in the room. After two and a half hours, what had the water done?
answer: It had come to a full rolling boil.
choices: It had come to a full rolling boil.
It had warmed a little, then held steady.
It had grown hot only around the borer.
It had thrown off steam but never boiled.
context: It boiled. Rumford wrote that it would be “difficult to describe the surprise and astonishment expressed in the countenances of the bystanders, on seeing so large a quantity of cold water heated and actually made to boil without any fire.” The box held 18.77 pounds of water; air, cannon and water all started at exactly 60 degrees F. The borer was pressed against the closed bottom of the bore with about 10,000 pounds of force while the cylinder turned some 32 times a minute. Try the cheap version yourself: rub your palms hard together, or drag a coin fast across a tabletop, and feel heat appear out of nothing but motion. Source: Rumford, “An Inquiry Concerning the Source of the Heat Which is Excited by Friction”, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 88 (1798).

question: Count Rumford stood over the cannon-boring at the Munich arsenal in the 1790s, watching workers drill long brass barrels day after day. It was plain workshop labor. Then one small detail of the daily work hit him hard enough to make him stop and study it. What had he noticed?
answer: The chips off the borer were hotter than boiling water.
choices: The chips off the borer were hotter than boiling water.
The borer's edge wore blunt within a single morning.
The brass rang at a lower note as the work went on.
The grease on the borer smoked off in the first hour.
context: The paper opens with it, in Rumford's own words: “Being engaged, lately, in superintending the boring of cannon, in the workshops of the military arsenal at Munich, I was struck with the very considerable degree of heat which a brass gun acquires, in a short time, in being bored; and with the still more intense heat (much greater than that of boiling water, as I found by experiment) of the metallic chips separated from it by the borer.” Note the habit worth copying — he did not take the workshop's word for how hot the chips were, he checked, and the parenthesis “as I found by experiment” is him saying so. The whole investigation grew out of noticing something everybody else had walked past for years. Source: Rumford, Philosophical Transactions 88 (1798).

question: Neighbors chased Benjamin Thompson out of Boston in 1776 as a suspected Loyalist spy. He raised a troop against his old countrymen, then showed up in Bavaria as Count Rumford, feeding the Munich poor a soup of barley, peas and potatoes. The cannon test was no lucky accident: heat was his lifelong passion. Which daily thing is also his invention?
answer: Thermal underwear
choices: Thermal underwear
The vacuum flask
The pressure cooker
The safety match
context: Thermal underwear. He also designed the Rumford fireplace — a shallow, angled firebox that throws far more heat into the room and far less up the chimney, which Thomas Jefferson had built at Monticello — and a percolating coffee pot. The regiment was the King's American Dragoons, raised in 1781. He endowed the Rumford Medals of the Royal Society and of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and died on 21 August 1814, buried in the small cemetery at Auteuil in Paris. Sources: Wikipedia “Benjamin Thompson”; Royal Society blog, “Rumford — the colourful Count”; Grokipedia “Benjamin Thompson”.

question: Count Rumford had his machine fitted with a steel borer that had been deliberately dulled, before the horses took a step, then pressed it into the bore under some 10,000 pounds of force. The cannon in his box was never going to become a gun. Why dull the tool on purpose?
answer: Dull steel rubs and grinds where sharp steel cuts, so far more of the horses' work turns into heat.
choices: Dull steel rubs and grinds where sharp steel cuts, so far more of the horses' work turns into heat.
Dull steel bites slowly, so the heat would build gently enough to read on a thermometer.
Dull steel sheds fewer chips, so the water in the box stayed clean enough to weigh accurately.
Dull steel wears far more slowly, so a single borer could last through the whole trial.
context: A sharp borer cuts: it slices metal away cleanly, and much of the energy leaves with the chips. A blunt one mostly rubs — and rubbing is friction, which was the entire point. Rumford was not manufacturing a cannon, he was manufacturing friction on an industrial scale, and he wanted as much of the horses' effort as possible to show up as heat in the water. The cylinder he had bored into the gun was 7 3/4 inches across and 9 8/10 inches long, and it turned about 32 times a minute. Source: Rumford, Philosophical Transactions 88 (1798).

question: Count Rumford answered in print the one-sentence reply a caloric chemist could make to his boiling box: the heat was never made at all, it had only leaked into the brass out of the cold water packed around it. He answered from what the trial itself had shown him. What was his answer?
answer: The water was itself growing hotter, and no body gives heat to what it takes heat from.
choices: The water was itself growing hotter, and no body gives heat to what it takes heat from.
The water had begun the day no warmer than the brass, the borer or the arsenal air.
The water sat in wood, and caloric was thought to creep through wood very slowly.
The water grew hot in every corner of the box alike, far from the borer as well as near.
context: His answer was that the water was itself steadily getting hotter — and a body cannot be giving heat to, and receiving heat from, the same body at the same moment. So the water was out. He closed the air off as well by keeping the whole apparatus immersed, where nothing could reach the rubbing surfaces. That is the unglamorous half of a discovery: before you may say where the heat came from, you have to say where it did not come from, and every one of those checks is an invitation to prove yourself wrong. Copy the habit next time somebody tells you what caused something — ask what else could have caused it, and whether anyone bothered to look. Source: Rumford, “An Inquiry Concerning the Source of the Heat Which is Excited by Friction”, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 88 (1798).

question: Count Rumford tested caloric's ready answer: grind solid brass into chips, its defenders said, and the chips hold less caloric than the block, so the surplus comes out as heat. He heated the borer's dust and an equal weight of brass slips to 212 degrees, dropped each into equal cold water and compared how far each warmed it, a test of what is now called specific heat. What did the two thermometers say?
answer: Both portions of water were warmed by exactly the same amount.
choices: Both portions of water were warmed by exactly the same amount.
The chips' water was warmed distinctly less than the slips' water.
The chips' water was warmed distinctly more than the slips' water.
The chips' water warmed in jumps while the slips' water warmed smoothly.
context: Rumford's own words: “the portion of the water into which the chips were put was not, to all appearance, heated either less or more than the other portion.” Specific heat is simply how much heat a substance needs to raise its temperature by one degree — a fingerprint of the material — and the chips' fingerprint was identical to the parent brass. Nothing had been squeezed out of them. Rumford shut the other doors too: the whole apparatus was immersed, so no air could reach the rubbing surfaces, and the surrounding water could not be the source because it was itself steadily getting hotter, and a body cannot be giving heat to and receiving heat from the same body at the same moment. Source: Rumford, Philosophical Transactions 88 (1798).

question: Count Rumford printed a calculation against his own apparatus. Two horses had walked in a circle for two and a half hours to heat eighteen pounds of water in a wooden box, and one horse, he noted, could have turned the machine alone. What did the calculation show?
answer: Simply burning the hay needed to keep a horse alive would have yielded more heat.
choices: Simply burning the hay needed to keep a horse alive would have yielded more heat.
An hour of summer sunlight on the box would have yielded more heat than the horses.
The two horses gave off more heat from their own bodies than the borer ever did.
A single candle under the box would have done the same work in half the time.
context: Verbatim from the paper: “As the machinery used in this experiment could easily be carried round by the force of one horse... more heat might be obtained by using the fodder necessary for the support of a horse, as fuel.” He had built a beautifully convincing and utterly terrible heat engine, and said so in print, in the very paper that made his name. Attacking your own result before anyone else can is the habit that separates a scientist from a salesman — and Rumford does it here in a single sentence, against himself. Source: Rumford, Philosophical Transactions 88 (1798).

question: Humphry Davy, the story goes, rubbed two blocks of ice together by clockwork inside a vacuum in 1799 until they melted: heat made where no caloric could have flowed in. Most textbooks pair that story with Rumford's. The journal Nature has printed corrections to it twice, in 1926 and again in 1935, and it is still reprinted anyway. What is wrong with it?
answer: The ice was rubbed in the open air; the vacuum belongs to a separate trial of his using wax.
choices: The ice was rubbed in the open air; the vacuum belongs to a separate trial of his using wax.
The ice was rubbed by hand rather than by clockwork, and Davy's own breath warmed the jar.
The blocks were not ice at all but frozen brine, which melts well below the freezing point.
Davy never ran the trial himself; a Bristol assistant did, and Davy published the result.
context: Davy did melt ice by rubbing — in the open air. He separately melted wax by rubbing metal in a vacuum. Somewhere in the retelling the two got welded into one perfect experiment, and the perfect version is the one that spread, because it is tidier and it supports a conclusion people already held. Nature ran “Did Davy melt Ice by Friction in a Vacuum?” in 1926 and another correction in 1935, and the false version is still in circulation nearly a century later. Historians also note the real ice experiment was not decisive: caloric's defenders could always point to the surrounding air. Sources: Nature (1926) and Nature (1935); Wikipedia “Caloric theory”.

question: Count Rumford read his thermometer by the clock: 60 degrees at the start, 107 after an hour, 142 after ninety minutes, 178 after two hours. The rise never slackened, and he could keep the water boiling for as long as the horses kept walking. There he stopped measuring and started arguing, and he set the whole case down as one general principle. Which one?
answer: Anything an insulated body can go on furnishing without limit cannot possibly be a material substance.
choices: Anything an insulated body can go on furnishing without limit cannot possibly be a material substance.
Anything a body can furnish for hours on end must be drawn in from the air that surrounds it.
Anything a body gives out without ceasing must lessen its weight, and a balance will find it.
Anything a body can furnish endlessly must be stored in it in a form no balance can detect.
context: Verbatim: “anything which any insulated body, or system of bodies, can continue to furnish without limitation cannot possibly be a material substance.” It is not a measurement, it is a reasoning move — no finite stock of stuff can supply an endless flow. Rumford had already written that “the source of the heat generated by friction, in these experiments, appeared evidently to be INEXHAUSTIBLE”, and the next sentence delivers the verdict in his own capital letters: it seemed to him “extremely difficult, if not quite impossible, to form any distinct idea of any thing, capable of being excited and communicated, in the manner the heat was excited and communicated in these experiments, except it be MOTION.” Source: Rumford, Philosophical Transactions 88 (1798).

question: James Prescott Joule went back to the figures printed in Rumford's paper fifty-two years after the arsenal and worked out the exchange rate they implied between work and heat: about 1,034 foot-pounds of work for every pound of water raised one degree. His own careful value was 772. He did not accuse Rumford of sloppiness; he named the specific thing the old sum had left out. What was it?
answer: The heat that soaked into the wooden box and drained away into the room.
choices: The heat that soaked into the wooden box and drained away into the room.
The heat carried off by the metal chips the borer was shaving loose.
The heat spent turning the machine's own gears, axle and harness.
The heat already stored in the brass before the horses started walking.
context: Joule's own explanation: Rumford “made no estimate of the heat accumulated in the wooden box, nor of that dispersed during the experiment.” Heat leaks. The water was the only thing Rumford counted, so every scrap of heat that went into warming 15 1/4 pounds of wet wood, or wandered off into the Munich air, showed up in the arithmetic as work that had produced nothing — which inflates the apparent price of heat. Even so, he was within about a third of the right answer, fifty years early, with two horses and a thermometer. It was Joule's measurement of the mechanical equivalent of heat, not Rumford's argument, that finally retired caloric as a working theory. Source: Joule, “On the Mechanical Equivalent of Heat”, Philosophical Transactions (1850); corroborated by Wikipedia and Grokipedia “Mechanical equivalent of heat”.

question: A student sets up three jars for a fortnight: a nail in dry air over a drying agent, a nail in boiled water sealed under oil, and a nail in tap water, half in the air. Only the third rusts. What does the experiment show rust needs?
answer: Both oxygen and water together, and either one alone is not enough
choices: Water alone; oxygen has nothing to do with it
Oxygen alone; water only carries the powder away
Both oxygen and water together, and either one alone is not enough
Oxygen, water and a starter of acid, all three together
context: This is the standard schoolroom demonstration of iron corrosion. Jar 1 lacks water; jar 2 lacks dissolved oxygen; only jar 3 has both, and only it rusts. Source: https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/General_Chemistry/Map:_Chemistry_-_The_Central_Science_(Brown_et_al.)/20:_Electrochemistry/20.08:_Corrosion

question: A girl touches a lit match to a tuft of steel wool, and it flares bright orange and throws sparks for a second or two. A garden gate rusts through over a wet winter. A chemist would call those two events the same reaction, running fast in one case and slow in the other. What is the reaction, and why do the two look so different?
answer: Iron joining with oxygen in both cases; rust simply never gets hot enough to glow
choices: Iron joining with oxygen in both cases; rust simply never gets hot enough to glow
Iron joining with hydrogen in both cases; the winter version releases hydrogen more slowly
Iron joining with nitrogen in both cases; the flame version releases stored heat all at once
Iron joining with carbon dioxide in both cases; the flame version drives the reaction visibly
context: Both are iron plus oxygen. Steel wool has such a high surface area that once a spark starts it, the reaction runs away and glows; a solid gate has almost none, so the same reaction crawls along in the cold and dark. Source: https://adamequipment.com/media/education/Documents/education-experiment-burning.pdf

question: A boy weighs a piece of steel wool on a kitchen scale and burns it in a spoon. He guesses, as almost every child does, that the black ashy residue will weigh less. It weighs more. Weighings like this helped Antoine Lavoisier overturn a whole theory of chemistry in the 1770s. Where did the extra weight come from?
answer: From oxygen the iron pulled out of the air and locked into the ash
choices: From soot in the flame settling onto the residue as it cooled
From oxygen the iron pulled out of the air and locked into the ash
From heat itself, which chemists then treated as a weighable substance
From water vapour condensing onto the black residue as it cooled
context: The theory that lost was phlogiston, the supposed substance released by burning things. Careful weighing by Antoine Lavoisier and others showed that burning metals GAIN weight in exactly the amount of oxygen they take from the air, and the ledger balances. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/antoine-laurent-lavoisier/

question: A cook opens a damp kitchen drawer and finds an iron nail slowly rotting into powder, while the aluminium foil beside it is not. Both metals react with oxygen just as fast, so reactivity is not the difference. What makes iron's rust ruinous and aluminium's oxide protective?
answer: The oxide on aluminium is a tight sealing film; the oxide on iron is flaky and porous, so it sheds off and exposes fresh metal
choices: Iron's oxide forms only on the outside surface; aluminium's oxide grows equally throughout the metal
The oxide on aluminium is a tight sealing film; the oxide on iron is flaky and porous, so it sheds off and exposes fresh metal
Kitchen air simply has more chloride ions near iron; chloride ions do not attack aluminium
Iron oxide is electrically conductive and keeps the reaction running; aluminium oxide is an insulator that stops it
context: Fresh aluminium grows an invisible layer of aluminium oxide, roughly 20 angstroms thick, in seconds and it seals the surface. The iron oxides that make up rust are a whole family of hydrated compounds, flaky and porous, so they crumble away and expose fresh metal underneath, and the attack never stops. Source: https://shop.machinemfg.com/understanding-aluminum-oxidation-and-corrosion-a-beginners-guide/

question: A conservator checks the Statue of Liberty's outer skin, copper only 3/32 of an inch (2.4 mm) thick, about two coins stacked, after over a century in salt-laden harbour air. She finds it has lost only a tiny fraction of that skin. Why has the sea air not eaten the statue hollow?
answer: The green patina is a stable sealing layer of copper carbonates and sulfates that protects the copper underneath
choices: The iron frame inside carries her weight, so no copper sheet is under mechanical stress and can crack away
The green patina is a stable sealing layer of copper carbonates and sulfates that protects the copper underneath
New York's harbour air is unusually low in the sulfur compounds that attack copper on other coasts
Bartholdi's alloy blended the copper with a little nickel, which suppresses further corrosion at the surface
context: Copper darkens, then turns brown, then greens over about twenty years. The green layer is basic copper carbonate and copper sulfates, and it is tight and adherent enough that oxygen and moisture do not get through it easily. Conservators in the 1980s deliberately left the patina in place. Source: https://freshscientific.org/lady-liberty-copper-patina-science

question: A gardener leaves an iron spade out in the rain, and its wet surface starts to rust. That rust is not just a chemical reaction but an electrical one, run between one small patch and a neighbouring patch, like a tiny battery set up on the metal itself. What are the two patches doing?
answer: One patch releases iron and electrons; the other consumes those electrons by combining oxygen with water, and the film between carries the ions
choices: Both patches release electrons into the water and the electrons drift off into the air as tiny visible sparks that leave the surface
Both patches soak up electrons from the water and slowly get plated with a fresh layer of pure iron under the wet film
One patch releases iron and electrons; the other consumes those electrons by combining oxygen with water, and the film between carries the ions
One patch is warmed by daylight and one is not; the temperature difference alone drives the whole reaction across the wet metal
context: Every rusting patch of iron is a microscopic battery running on its own surface. The anode dissolves; the cathode consumes oxygen; the water film is the salt bridge. This is why anything that raises the water's conductivity, above all dissolved salt, accelerates rust dramatically. Source: http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Chemical/corrosion.html

question: A shipyard crew bolts blocks of a different metal to the outside of a steel hull. Over the months the blocks slowly corrode away and are replaced on a schedule, while the steel beside them stays sound. What are the blocks, and why do they corrode in place of the steel?
answer: Zinc, because zinc gives up electrons more readily than iron, so the surface battery eats zinc and spares steel
choices: Zinc, because zinc gives up electrons more readily than iron, so the surface battery eats zinc and spares steel
Copper, because copper conducts electricity better than steel and short-circuits any corrosion current along the hull
Lead, because lead's heavy oxide spreads over the nearby hull and seals the steel away from the seawater
Nickel, because nickel resists seawater far better than steel and lends that resistance to the hull it touches
context: They are called sacrificial anodes. Zinc's standard reduction potential, -0.76 volts against iron's -0.44, is the more negative, so in a shared electrolyte the zinc becomes the anode and dissolves while the iron becomes the cathode and is protected. Galvanising is the same bargain applied as a thin zinc coating. Source: https://www.marineinsight.com/understanding-sacrificial-anodes-on-ships/

question: Hans Geiger needed a small job for his student Ernest Marsden at Manchester in 1909, and he asked Ernest Rutherford for one. Rutherford suggested firing alpha particles at thin gold foil and counting how many, if any, bounced straight back, and he took it for routine busywork. What did he later admit he had expected?
answer: He had not believed a single one would come back
choices: He had not believed a single one would come back
He had already worked out how many would return
He had long suspected the atom hid a hard core
He had feared the foil would stop them all dead
context: Rutherford told the story at Cambridge on 15 October 1936. Geiger had asked, 'Don't you think that young Marsden, whom I am training in radioactive methods, ought to begin a small research?' and Rutherford answered, 'Why not let him see if any alpha-particles can be scattered through a large angle?' -- adding in the same lecture that he did not believe they would be. The man who set the task expected nothing. Marsden was twenty and still reading honours physics; he had come to Manchester in 1907 at eighteen, straight from Queen Elizabeth Grammar School, Blackburn. Source: Rutherford's Cambridge lecture of 15 October 1936, published in Background to Modern Science (1938).

question: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden needed to know at Manchester in 1909 which way each single alpha particle flew after it struck a gold foil, one at a time, for hours on end. What did they use to detect them?
answer: A zinc-sulfide screen watched flash by flash under a microscope
choices: A zinc-sulfide screen watched flash by flash under a microscope
A photographic plate developed after every run of the beam
An electrical counter clicking once for every single particle
A cloud chamber photographing the track that each particle left
context: The detector was a human eye. Each alpha striking the screen -- about one square millimetre of it -- made one faint scintillation, and a person sat in a blacked-out room counting them through a low-power microscope. No instrument read out a number. It is often said Geiger built his famous counter to escape this misery, but the dates run the other way: he and Rutherford reported an electrical method of counting alpha particles to the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society on 11 February 1908, a year before the backscatter run, and went back to the eye for the scattering work anyway, because that work needed one chosen angle at a time. The clicking Geiger-Muller tube came twenty years later still, in 1928, built at Kiel with his doctoral student Walther Muller. Sources: Grokipedia, Geiger-Marsden experiments and Hans Geiger.

question: Ernest Rutherford stood at Cambridge in October 1936, twenty-seven years after the gold-foil test, and tried to give the crowd the feeling of hearing that alpha particles had bounced straight back off the foil. He called it the most amazing event of his life. What comparison did he reach for?
answer: Firing a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and having it come back at you
choices: Firing a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and having it come back at you
Firing a 12-pound cannonball at cheesecloth and having it come back at you
Firing a rifle bullet at a soap bubble and having it come back at you
Firing a 6-inch shell at a cobweb and having it come back at you
context: The line in full: 'It was quite the most incredible event that has ever happened to me in my life. It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.' Mind the date -- he said it in 1936, as a reminiscence in a lecture, not shouted at the bench in 1909. And it was Geiger, not Marsden, who carried the news at the time: 'Then I remember two or three days later Geiger coming to me in great excitement and saying, "We have been able to get some of the alpha-particles coming backwards."' Marsden did the looking; Geiger carried the word. Sources: Rutherford's Cambridge lecture of 15 October 1936; Wikiquote, Ernest Rutherford.

question: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at silver, aluminium, copper, lead, tin, iron and other metals. But gold was the one they returned to over and over, and it is gold's name the experiment still carries. What property of gold could no rival match?
answer: It can be beaten into sheets thinner than any other metal
choices: It can be beaten into sheets thinner than any other metal
It carries more positive charge per atom than any other
It stays cleaner in air than any other workable metal
It is the heaviest metal that can be rolled into a sheet
context: Gold is the most malleable of the metals, and that mattered for a reason of logic, not convenience: only in a foil that thin can a single particle's deflection be fairly blamed on one encounter with one atom rather than a pile-up of many small ones. The working foils ran about 0.00004 cm thick -- roughly a thousand atoms deep. The 1909 paper closes on the astonishment of it: 'it seems surprising that some of the alpha-particles, as the experiment shows, can be turned within a layer of 6 x 10^-5 cm. of gold through an angle of 90 degrees, and even more.' Sources: Geiger and Marsden, 'On a Diffuse Reflection of the alpha-Particles', Proc. Roy. Soc. A 82:495 (1909); Grokipedia, Geiger-Marsden experiments.

question: Ernest Rutherford told the room at the Nobel dinner in 1908 that the quickest change he had ever seen had just happened to him. He had spent nearly ten years timing how fast radioactive elements change into other elements, some over centuries, others in seconds. What was the change?
answer: His own change from a physicist into a chemist
choices: His own change from a physicist into a chemist
His own change from a student into a professor
His own change from a bench man into a lecturer
His own change from a New Zealander into a Briton
context: The 1908 prize was in Chemistry -- 'for his investigations into the disintegration of the elements, and the chemistry of radioactive substances' -- and Rutherford was a physicist to his bones. He had in fact drawn twelve nominations in physics against only four in chemistry. A separately attested version of the remark: 'I must confess it was very unexpected and I am very startled at my metamorphosis into a chemist.' Sources: nobelprize.org, Chemistry 1908 facts; C&EN, 'Ernest Rutherford, Nobel Chemist'; Wikiquote citing Dardo, Nobel Laureates and Twentieth-Century Physics (2004), p.69.

question: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden built the whole test again in 1913, when the nuclear atom still rested on just a handful of bounces. Their sealed chamber could turn to catch scattered alpha particles from 5 to 150 degrees. Only two or three flashes came per minute, and each had to be seen and counted by a person sitting in the dark. How many flashes did the check cost the two men?
answer: More than a hundred thousand flashes
choices: More than a hundred thousand flashes
A little over two thousand flashes
Somewhere near twenty thousand flashes
Something close to a million flashes
context: At two or three a minute, a hundred thousand flashes is on the order of a year of nights at the microscope. What it bought was the shape of the curve: the number scattered varied as 1/sin^4 of half the angle -- in their own summary, 'The number of alpha particles scattered in a definite direction varies as cosec^4 phi/2' -- exactly as Rutherford's atom required. They confirmed the predicted dependence on the alphas' speed as well, falling off as the fourth power of velocity. This is what a confirmation costs when nobody has an instrument that can do it for you. Source: Grokipedia, Geiger-Marsden experiments, 1913 confirmation experiments.

question: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden printed one number in 1909 that everybody still quotes: one alpha particle in eight thousand bouncing back. Every retelling ties it to gold foil, but the two men got it from a thicker foil of a different metal. Gold's real rate for large-angle bounces was closer to one in twenty thousand. Which metal gave the famous number?
answer: Platinum
choices: Platinum
Silver
Aluminium
Copper
context: Geiger and Marsden 1909: 'Three different determinations showed that of the incident alpha-particles about 1 in 8000 was reflected, under the described conditions' -- and the described conditions are a platinum reflector. Worth keeping as a habit: Grokipedia's Rutherford-model page splits the two figures correctly (about 1 in 20,000 for large-angle scattering from thin gold, about 1 in 8,000 backscattered above 90 degrees from thicker platinum), while its Hans Geiger page swaps them. Two pages, one contradiction, and the primary paper settles it. Go to the source. Sources: Geiger and Marsden, Proc. Roy. Soc. A 82:495 (1909); Grokipedia, Rutherford model.

question: Ernest Rutherford concluded in 1911, from the tiny fraction of alpha particles that turned right around, that almost all of an atom's mass and all of its positive charge must be packed into a centre far smaller than the atom itself, with the rest of it empty. Take that centre at its measured size and blow one atom up to the size of a hundred-metre football field. What sits on the centre spot?
answer: A half-millimetre grain of sand
choices: A half-millimetre grain of sand
A hundredth-millimetre grain of pollen
A ten-millimetre glass marble
A twenty-millimetre copper coin
context: Rutherford's bound put the centre under 10^-14 m against an atom of about 10^-10 m -- under a ten-thousandth of the atom's radius. By modern figures, with the nucleus nearer 10^-15 m, it is about a hundred-thousandth, and a half-millimetre grain on a hundred-metre field is a ratio near 1:200,000, so the retellable image is fair. Which means the chair you are sitting on is very nearly empty space, and what holds you up is electric repulsion, not solidity. One more thing: the word 'nucleus' does not appear in the 1911 paper at all. Rutherford called it a 'central charge', and only put 'nucleus' into print in 1912. Sources: Grokipedia, Rutherford model and Geiger-Marsden experiments.

question: A schoolchild opens a physics book and meets J. J. Thomson's 1904 atom, a ball of positive charge with the electrons studded through it, as the 'plum pudding' model. The phrase itself has a traceable origin. Where did it first turn up?
answer: A chemists' trade paper, The Chemist and Druggist, in 1906
choices: A chemists' trade paper, The Chemist and Druggist, in 1906
Thomson's own paper in the Philosophical Magazine, in 1904
A lecture Lord Kelvin gave on his earlier atom, in 1902
A jibe in one of Ernest Rutherford's letters, in 1911
context: The first known appearance of the phrase in print is a 1906 article in The Chemist and Druggist, a trade paper for pharmacists. Popular science writers coined it to make the model easy for laymen, and Wikipedia states the rest flatly: neither Thomson nor his colleagues ever used the analogy at all. Two things ride along with that. The picture you were taught may not be the one the scientist actually drew -- so check. And a caricature is easy to knock down, which is worth remembering whenever a textbook makes a superseded idea look stupid: Thomson's atom was the serious, considered work of a Nobel physicist, not a joke. Source: Wikipedia, Plum pudding model.

question: Niels Bohr came to Manchester in 1912 and took on a hard problem in Ernest Rutherford's atom. Classical physics says any accelerating charge radiates energy away, and an electron going round a circle is accelerating every instant. Left to itself it should bleed away its energy and spiral into the centre almost at once, yet atoms plainly last. Bohr published his answer in 1913. What did he add to make the atom stand up?
answer: A rule that only certain orbits exist, and those never radiate
choices: A rule that only certain orbits exist, and those never radiate
A second negative charge at the centre that held electrons out
A drag term that stretched the spiral out over billions of years
A magnetic field from the centre that locked electrons in place
context: Bohr's three-part paper 'On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules' ran in the Philosophical Magazine in July, September and November 1913. The rule he imposed was that an electron's angular momentum can only come in whole multiples of a fixed quantum, L = n times h-bar, so only a discrete set of orbits exists at all, and an electron sitting in one of them simply does not radiate. He gave no classical reason for it; it was a postulate that worked, and it is why hydrogen glows in sharp separate colours rather than a smear. Rutherford's atom was load-bearing for about two years before it needed the quantum patch. Sources: Grokipedia, Rutherford model; Wikipedia, Niels Bohr.

question: Reidun Renstrom and Nils-Erik Bomark went back to Ernest Rutherford's 1911 paper in 2022 and read it line by line. The story every physics textbook tells is that the paper confessed his atom could not be stable, and that Niels Bohr rode in two years later to rescue it. What did the two of them report finding in the paper?
answer: Rutherford never discussed the motion of the electrons at all
choices: Rutherford never discussed the motion of the electrons at all
Rutherford named the problem, then answered it with strong central fields
Rutherford calculated the collapse and found it slow enough to ignore
Rutherford had the electrons sitting still rather than in orbit
context: Renstrom and Bomark, 'Textbook myths about early atomic models' (arXiv:2212.08572, 2022), argue that the radiative-instability problem 'is not there at all' in Rutherford's paper, because 'Rutherford did not even discuss the motion of the electrons' -- the problem was read back into him afterwards by the people telling the story. Now the honest tension: Grokipedia's account says close to the opposite, that Rutherford acknowledged the stability problem and suggested strong fields near the centre might balance it. Two sources, two readings, one paper -- and that paper is old enough to be free and short enough to read yourself. That is not a weakness of the account; it is the invitation. Sources: arXiv:2212.08572; Grokipedia, Ernest Rutherford and Rutherford model.

question: 'A fire-breathing dragon lives in my garage,' Carl Sagan imagines telling a reader in all seriousness. Camera? She's invisible. Flour for footprints? She floats. Infrared for the fire? The fire is heatless. Spray paint? She's incorporeal. What is Sagan's own closing question?
answer: what is the difference between this dragon and no dragon
choices: what is the difference between this dragon and no dragon
why should anyone believe such a claim at all
what test could still catch her out
who else has ever seen this dragon
context: Sagan's exact wording: 'Now, what's the difference between an invisible, incorporeal, floating dragon who spits heatless fire and no dragon at all?' Source: The Demon-Haunted World, 1995.

question: Carl Sagan plays the believer in his own garage-dragon parable, meeting each test with an excuse invented only after the test is proposed. The camera fails, so she is invisible; the flour fails, so she floats; the heat sensor fails, so her fire is cold. A claim rebuilt for each test has done what?
answer: stopped predicting anything at all
choices: stopped predicting anything at all
attracted more scientific attention
become simpler to prove wrong
gained more evidence in its favour
context: A claim that predicts nothing cannot be checked by anyone, including the person making it; that is the whole point of the parable. Source: Carl Sagan, The Demon-Haunted World, 1995.

question: Carl Sagan told a parable in his 1995 book The Demon-Haunted World: an invisible fire-breathing dragon in a garage, and every test a visitor proposes comes back empty. In the same book he laid out a set of plain-spoken rules for spotting bad arguments, and he gave the whole collection its own homespun nickname. What did he call his checklist?
answer: the baloney detection kit
choices: the baloney detection kit
the swindler's index
the crackpot filter
the humbug ledger
context: The kit's nine tools include seeking independent confirmation, encouraging debate from critics, distrusting arguments from authority, spinning multiple hypotheses, not getting attached to your own, quantifying where possible, checking every link, preferring the simpler hypothesis (Occam's razor), and asking if the claim can in principle be falsified. Source: Sagan, The Demon-Haunted World, 1995.

question: Carl Sagan made 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence' famous on Cosmos in 1980. But someone had written almost the same line two years earlier, in the first issue of a journal called Zetetic Scholar. Who wrote it?
answer: the sociologist Marcello Truzzi
choices: the sociologist Marcello Truzzi
the physicist Richard Feynman
the mathematician Kurt Godel
the biologist Edward Wilson
context: Truzzi co-founded the Committee for the Scientific Investigation of Claims of the Paranormal in 1976. The core idea is older still: around 1810-1814 Pierre-Simon Laplace wrote that 'the weight of evidence for an extraordinary claim must be proportioned to its strangeness'. Sources: Quote Investigator; Wikipedia entry on the phrase.

question: Carl Sagan wrote in his 1995 book The Demon-Haunted World that a pair of habits sits at the heart of science, and that the two must be held together. Drop either half, he warned, and science breaks down. Which pair did he name?
answer: openness to new ideas AND ruthless scrutiny of them
choices: openness to new ideas AND ruthless scrutiny of them
reverence for tradition AND appetite for novelty
humility about ignorance AND confidence in method
trust in experts AND respect for laypeople
context: Sagan's point, in paraphrase: openness alone cannot tell a good idea from a bad one, and scrutiny alone lets no new idea in, so a thinker who can manage only one of the two is in deep trouble. The balance is the whole game. Source: The Demon-Haunted World, 1995.

question: A violinist tunes to today's usual A before a concert, 440 vibrations a second. A baroque ensemble tunes near 415, nearly a semitone lower. Where did 440 come from?
answer: An American standards committee recommended it in 1936
choices: An American standards committee recommended it in 1936
A French government decree fixed it for Paris in 1859
Physicists derived it from the resonance of the human ear
Piano makers found it the strongest note on their frames
context: Nothing in physics singles out 440. The American Standards Association recommended it in 1936; ISO adopted it as Recommendation R 16 in 1955 and formalised ISO 16 in 1975. Before that, France used 435 Hz in the 1860s, Austria recommended 435 in 1885, British piano tuners worked at A439 in 1899, classical-period pitch ran 427-430, modern baroque practice uses about 415, and some old German church organs sat near 466. Even today orchestras in continental Europe commonly run between 440 and 444; Leonard Bernstein tuned to A442 and drew complaints from piano tuners. Source: Wikipedia, 'A440 (pitch standard)'.

question: A guitarist tries a ten-second trick on any string. She rests a fingertip on it right at the halfway point, so light it never touches the wood, plucks near the bridge and lifts her finger. What comes out?
answer: A clear note an octave above the usual one
choices: A clear note an octave above the usual one
A clear note two octaves above the usual one
A clear note a fifth above the usual one
A clear note a third above the usual one
context: The fingertip creates a node — a point of the string forced to stay motionless — and every vibration that would have to move there is killed, the lowest one included. What survives is the shape that already has a still point exactly at the middle: the octave. Touch a quarter of the way along instead and the string vibrates with four loops instead of one, at four times the lowest frequency, about two octaves up. Try both. Source: UNSW School of Physics, Joe Wolfe, 'Strings, standing waves and harmonics' and 'Harmonics'.

question: John Shore, trumpeter to the English royal court, bent steel into a two-pronged fork in 1711, and tuners have used one ever since. A plucked guitar string gives the main note plus a stack of fainter ones above it. A struck fork gives almost nothing else. Why does so little ride on top?
answer: Its next possible note sits over six times higher, taking little energy
choices: Its next possible note sits over six times higher, taking little energy
Its two prongs swing opposite ways and cancel each other's extra notes
Its steel is too dense to carry more than one vibration at once
Its stem drains the extra notes into whatever surface it rests on
context: The fork's shape puts its first overtone at roughly 25/4 — six and a quarter — times the fundamental, so hardly any energy goes into it, and what little does die away faster than the fundamental, leaving very nearly a pure sine wave. That is why a fork is the reference and a string is not: almost every other instrument hands you a whole recipe of notes at once. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tuning fork'.

question: A sound engineer records a trumpet and a piano on the same note, and nobody has trouble telling them apart. She cuts away the first fraction of a second of each note, leaving every fainter note that rides above the main note exactly as it was. What do listeners find?
answer: Both become much harder to recognise
choices: Both become much harder to recognise
Both stay as easy to recognise as ever
Both seem to be played far more softly
Both seem to slide slowly out of tune
context: Much of an instrument's identity lives in its attack — the hammer striking the strings, the first blast of the player's lips — not in the steady note that follows. Roughly a 4 dB change in the mid or high harmonics is enough to hear as a change of timbre, and the ear needs on the order of 60 milliseconds to judge tone quality at all. The Acoustical Society of America gave up on a positive definition entirely: timbre is officially defined as whatever lets a listener judge two sounds 'dissimilar' when their pitch and loudness are the same — a definition by elimination. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Timbre'; HyperPhysics (Georgia State University), 'Timbre'.

question: Marin Mersenne, a French friar, printed the rules of a vibrating string in Harmonie universelle in 1636, and unlike Galileo Galilei, who had judged such rules impossible to prove, he measured real strings to check them. One rule catches everyone out: pull a string twice as tight and the pitch does not double. What does it take to double the pitch?
answer: Four times the pull
choices: Four times the pull
Three times the pull
Eight times the pull
Sixteen times the pull
context: Mersenne's laws: frequency is inversely proportional to length, proportional to the square root of the stretching force, and inversely proportional to the square root of mass per unit length — f = (1/2L)·sqrt(F/mu). Because the pull sits under a square root, doubling it raises the pitch by only about 1.4 times; you need four times the pull to double it. Try it with a rubber band and a spring scale. The Galileo detail comes down to us as the tradition around the laws: Mersenne is credited with physically proving by experiment what Galileo considered impossible to prove. Joseph Sauveur (1653-1716) later sharpened the measurements using acoustic beats and metronomes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mersenne's laws'.

question: A student stretches a violin string between two bricks and bows it, and almost nothing comes out: a bare string barely moves any air. Screwed onto a violin, the same string fills a hall, because the bridge feeds its shaking into the carved body. The body is not the only thing here with a resonance of its own. What else answers when the string sounds?
answer: The air shut inside the box, sloshing through the f-holes
choices: The air shut inside the box, sloshing through the f-holes
The air trapped under the strings, above the fingerboard
The soundpost, wedged between the belly and the back
The horsehair of the bow, drawn tight along its stick
context: The air trapped in the body sloshes through the f-holes like the air in a bottle when you blow across the top — a resonance around 300 Hz that props up the violin's low notes. The bridge is especially good at transmitting power to the body between about one and four kHz, exactly where the ear is most sensitive. The soundpost couples the flexible belly to the stiffer back and pins the bridge's treble foot; the bass bar spreads the other foot's motion across the belly. Two violins with identical strings sound different because the boxes do. Source: UNSW School of Physics, 'Violin acoustics: an introduction'.

question: A band kid holds a low note on a clarinet and presses the register key, a check anyone can run. A saxophone's octave key does what its name says, and the note jumps up an octave. The clarinet's pitch leaps much further. Where does it land?
answer: Three times the starting frequency, a twelfth above
choices: Three times the starting frequency, a twelfth above
Four times the starting frequency, two octaves above
Five times the starting frequency, two octaves and a third
Six times the starting frequency, two octaves and a fifth
context: The key sits about a third of the way down the instrument. Opening it disrupts the fundamental while barely touching the higher harmonics, so the clarinet jumps to three times the fundamental — a twelfth, an octave plus a fifth. It can only land there because a clarinet sounds essentially the odd harmonics, 1:3:5:7; with no 2f available, the next rung up is 3f. A saxophone has the whole series, so its octave key gives 2f. On a B-flat clarinet the lowest written note is E3, about 147 Hz, and the register break runs from A#4 to B4, around 440 Hz. Source: UNSW School of Physics, 'Clarinet acoustics'.

question: Hermann von Helmholtz set out to learn exactly which fainter notes were hiding in a violin's tone, decades before machines existed to measure them. He had hollow brass and glass spheres made, each tuned to a different pitch, each with a small neck at one end and a wider opening at the other. Where did the small neck go?
answer: Into his own ear, sphere by sphere
choices: Into his own ear, sphere by sphere
Against his own throat as he hummed
Over the violin's f-hole, facing in
Onto the mouth of an organ pipe
context: In 'On the Sensations of Tone' (1863) Helmholtz described a rigid container of known volume, nearly spherical, with a small neck and hole at one end and a larger hole at the other. You jam the neck into your ear; when the resonator's own tone is present in the sound around you, Helmholtz wrote, it 'brays into the ear most powerfully'. A whole tuned set let him read the ingredient list of a real instrument by ear, with his own hearing as the detector. He began the book in 1854 and finished in 1862; Alexander J. Ellis produced the first English edition in 1875, adding his own extensive translator's notes. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Helmholtz resonance'; 'On the Sensations of Tone'.

question: Joseph Fourier claimed any repeating wave, however jagged, could be built by stacking pure sine waves. He announced the idea to the French Academy in 1807, and he was not working on music or sound at all. What problem had led him to the discovery?
answer: How heat spreads through a solid body
choices: How heat spreads through a solid body
How the tides rise and fall in a harbour
How a cannonball curves in flight
How a planet's orbit shifts over centuries
context: Fourier announced the result in 1807 in a memoir on the propagation of heat in solid bodies and published the full 'Theorie analytique de la chaleur' in 1822. The judges of his 1811 prize essay — Lagrange and Laplace among them — ruled that the way he reached his equations was 'not exempt of difficulties' and that his analysis left 'something to be desired on the score of generality and even rigour'. Dirichlet, around 1829, and later Riemann supplied the missing conditions specifying which functions can actually be represented. So the honest statement is about periodic, well-behaved wiggles — not literally every possible sound. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fourier series'.

question: August Seebeck spun a siren in Dresden, a disc of holes chopping a jet of air, one of the very few sound sources whose frequency he could state exactly. He set the holes so that the sound leaving the disc held no vibration whatever at the low frequency its pattern repeated at, only components well above it. Then he asked listeners what they heard. What did they report?
answer: The low pitch, as clearly as if it were in the air
choices: The low pitch, as clearly as if it were in the air
Only a thin whistle at the highest component present
A rough beating with no definite pitch at all
A pitch an octave above the one the pattern repeated at
context: Seebeck (born 27 December 1805 in Jena, died 19 March 1849 in Dresden) had demonstrated that pitch does not depend on the fundamental frequency component being physically present. His weapon mattered: the siren, of the kind Baron Charles Cagniard de la Tour designed in 1819 — two perforated discs at the outlet of a pneumatic tube, one fixed and one spinning — was among the few sound sources of known frequency, so he could state exactly what he had put into the air. His challenge to Georg Ohm is the scientific instinct in one line: 'How else can the question as to what makes out a tone be decided but by the ear?' Historians record that he forced Ohm to withdraw from the field — then died in 1849, fourteen years before Helmholtz's 1863 book buried the result for most of a century. Sources: Wikipedia, 'August Seebeck'; 'Siren (noisemaker)'.

question: A girl plays a song on her phone, whose speaker, the size of a thumbnail, cannot move enough air to make a deep bass note. Yet phones are sold on their bass, and one processing trick for it has been patented and used on hit records. What does that processing add to the signal?
answer: A stack of the fainter, higher notes above the bass
choices: A stack of the fainter, higher notes above the bass
A gentle lift near one kilohertz, where the ear hears best
A short, sharp click at the front of every bass note
A trace of distortion smeared across the vocals
context: Small speakers fake bass by synthesising the harmonics of a note the driver cannot physically produce, and letting your hearing supply the pitch; Waves Audio patented a bass-enhancement technology of this kind in mid-1999, used on recordings including Christina Aguilera's 'Lady Marmalade'. The same loophole is why telephones, which cannot reproduce anything below 300 Hz, carry a male voice with a fundamental near 150 Hz at the right pitch. Orchestral timpani do it acoustically: tuned to 200, 302, 398 and 488 Hz, they imply a 100 Hz fundamental no part of the drum is producing, and that is the pitch the hall hears. Source: Wikipedia, 'Missing fundamental'.

question: A woodwind student sets a clarinet beside an oboe and a saxophone. The clarinet's register key leaps past the octave where the oboe's octave key stops, and its voice is hollow and woody rather than bright. The easy answer is the reed sealing the player's end, but the oboe and the saxophone have reeds too, and both jump the plain octave and sound the whole stack of fainter notes above. What actually sets the clarinet apart?
answer: Its tube is a straight cylinder, where theirs widen into cones
choices: Its tube is a straight cylinder, where theirs widen into cones
Its tube is narrower than theirs from mouthpiece to bell
Its tube is longer than theirs for the same lowest note
Its tube is thicker-walled than theirs, muffling the bright notes
context: It is the cylinder, not the reed and not the bore width. The longest sine wave that fits an open pipe is twice the pipe's length; in a cylinder stopped at one end it is four times the length — and on a clarinet the stopped end is the tiny aperture between reed and mouthpiece, not the bell. That is why a clarinet sounds about an octave below a flute of similar length (roughly 140 Hz against 280 Hz for a 0.6 m tube) and why it sounds essentially the odd harmonics only, 1:3:5:7 — the hollow, woody voice. Oboes and saxophones have reeds too, but their conical bores give the same harmonics and the same bottom note as an open cylinder of the same length. A clarinettist can play approximately C4 on half the instrument. Sources: UNSW School of Physics, 'Pipes and harmonics'; 'Open vs closed pipes (Flutes vs Clarinets)'; 'Clarinet acoustics'.

question: J. C. R. Licklider set out in 1954 to test Hermann von Helmholtz's explanation of the low pitch listeners hear when no low vibration is present. For a century it had been written off as a distortion cooked up inside the ear, a specific and testable idea. What did Licklider do to find out whether the ear was manufacturing the pitch?
answer: He buried the tones in a noise that would drown anything the ear added
choices: He buried the tones in a noise that would drown anything the ear added
He raised the tones' loudness until the ear could no longer distort them
He played the tones through bone conduction, bypassing the eardrum
He played the tones to one ear at a time and compared the reports
context: Licklider's 1954 experiments showed the pitch persisted even under masking noise that would have eliminated any distortion artefact from inner-ear physics — so the low note was not being made in the ear. Helmholtz deserves respect in defeat: his mechanism was concrete, not hand-waving. Two tones f1 and f2 generate a faint difference tone f2 - f1 in the ear's own non-linearity, so 200 and 300 Hz manufacture a 100 Hz that was never in the air. That phenomenon is real and old — Giuseppe Tartini reported in 1754 that he had heard it as early as 1714, hence 'Tartini tones' — and Lagrange, Chladni and Young had first, wrongly, blamed acoustic beats for it. The modern account is that the brain computes the pitch from the spacing of the harmonics present, apparently from auditory-nerve timing, with the mechanism still debated; J. F. Schouten (1910-1980) at the Philips Natuurkundig Laboratorium had already shown pitch perception does not work as Helmholtz proposed. And the honest verdict on the old fight is split, not a rout: Ohm was right that the ear analyses sound into partials, Seebeck was right that the perceived pitch does not require the fundamental to be there. Listeners even differ from one another in which they report. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Missing fundamental'; 'Combination tone'; 'Jan Frederik Schouten'; 'Ohm's acoustic law'.

question: Erwin Schrodinger imagined sealing a cat in a steel box in 1935, as a thought experiment. Inside he placed a Geiger counter, a bit of radioactive stuff with a 50-50 chance of one decay in an hour, a switch, a hammer and one more thing, which would kill the cat if the atom decayed. What was it?
answer: A flask of hydrocyanic acid
choices: A flask of hydrocyanic acid
A canister of chlorine gas
A pinch of strychnine powder
A jar of venomous spiders
context: The decay would trip the counter, the relay would drop a hammer, the hammer would break the flask, and cyanide vapour would fill the box. The apparatus is deliberately over-designed; Schrodinger wanted the chain from single atom to dead cat to be undeniable. Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6dinger%27s_cat

question: Erwin Schrodinger imagined his cat in a box in a 1935 paper, and people often say he did it to show off how strange quantum mechanics is. The paper itself calls the case ridiculous. He used it to attack one idea in the physics of his day. Which idea?
answer: The Copenhagen interpretation of quantum measurement
choices: The Copenhagen interpretation of quantum measurement
Einstein's insistence that God does not play dice
The steady-state model of the universe
The idea that atoms have solid nuclei at all
context: Schrodinger's charge against the Copenhagen view was that its rules, taken literally, would place a large everyday object in an alive-and-dead smear until someone peeked. The cat is a reductio ad absurdum, not a doctrine. Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6dinger%27s_cat

question: Albert Einstein wrote to Erwin Schrodinger in 1935, before the cat appeared, about a familiar unstable object. Taken at face value, quantum mechanics would show it as a smear of two very different large-scale states. The cat in the box is Schrodinger's sharpened take on this. What object had Einstein described?
answer: A keg of gunpowder
choices: A keg of gunpowder
A candle burning in a draft
A vase teetering on a shelf's edge
A house of cards on a table
context: Einstein wrote that quantum mechanics would describe an unstable keg as a mixture of exploded and unexploded, which he judged plainly absurd. He and Schrodinger egged each other on by letter through 1935; the cat scenario is a domestic pet standing in for the keg. Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6dinger%27s_cat

question: Erwin Schrodinger singled out one feature of quantum theory in 1935, the same year he built his cat. He called it the characteristic trait of quantum mechanics, the one that pulls it entirely away from classical thinking, and he gave it a new name. Today it is the working substance of quantum computing. What did he name?
answer: Entanglement
choices: Entanglement
Superposition
Uncertainty
Complementarity
context: Schrodinger's German word was Verschrankung, and he rendered it himself as 'entanglement'; the 'characteristic trait' line comes from his English paper of 1935 on separated systems. In the same year he built a thought experiment to embarrass the theory, he named its crown jewel; today entanglement is the resource behind quantum cryptography and every serious quantum computer design. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement

question: Erwin Schrodinger imagined a cat sealed in a box in 1935, which one literal reading of the theory left both alive and dead until someone opened it. Take that as a real cat in a real box. Every instant it exchanges countless photons and air molecules with its surroundings. What does that constant contact do to any quantum superposition of the cat that the equations might describe?
answer: The state leaks into the environment in far less than a nanosecond
choices: The state leaks into the environment in far less than a nanosecond
The state slowly cools until it settles after several minutes
The state is preserved as long as the box is dark and sealed
The state grows louder and easier to measure over time
context: This is decoherence: information about the superposition escapes into the surroundings so fast that no laboratory could tell the cat from ordinary alive-or-dead. It explains why we never SEE such states in daily life; it does not by itself explain why one particular outcome actually happens (that is the still-open measurement problem). Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_decoherence

question: Serge Haroche and his Paris group never tested decoherence on a cat. They built a tabletop system small enough to hold in a superposition, then watched that superposition fall apart step by step. What did they actually trap and observe?
answer: A few microwave photons bouncing between two mirrored superconducting walls
choices: A few microwave photons bouncing between two mirrored superconducting walls
A single electron circling a laser-cooled hydrogen atom
A pair of entangled diamond crystals cooled to absolute zero
A neutron held in a magnetic bottle inside a lead shield
context: The cavity was about 2.7 cm long, its curved mirrors superconducting and chilled almost to absolute zero, and rubidium atoms in a quantum superposition were shot through it one at a time to count the photons without destroying them. The bigger the 'cat', the faster it died: exactly what the theory predicted. Haroche shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physics with David Wineland for this work. Source: APS Physics, https://physics.aps.org/articles/v5/114

question: A doctor tests a couple's embryos with preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M), which looks for a single disease gene one or both parents carry, such as cystic fibrosis or Huntington's. PGT-A comes off the same lab bench. What does PGT-A look for instead?
answer: Whether the embryo has the right number of chromosomes
choices: Whether the embryo has the right number of chromosomes
Whether the embryo will be blond or dark-haired
Whether the embryo carries a novel mutation not seen in either parent
Whether the embryo will develop asthma later in life
context: PGT-A stands for Preimplantation Genetic Testing for ANEUPLOIDY. It counts chromosomes: monosomies (a missing chromosome) or trisomies (an extra one) usually cause miscarriage or failed implantation, and Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most familiar surviving case. PGT-A is a common add-on to IVF meant to raise the chance a transfer will take. PGT-M requires the family to already know which gene to look for.

question: Shai Carmi and his team showed in 2019 that a polygenic score, a prediction built on thousands of common variants in DNA, works well on unrelated strangers but loses most of that power when embryos from the same two parents are ranked against one another. The reason is a simple number. On average, what fraction of their variable DNA do full brothers and sisters share?
answer: About one half
choices: About one half
About one quarter
About three quarters
Essentially all of it
context: Full siblings share on average about 1/2 of their variable DNA (identical twins share ~all; first cousins ~1/8). A polygenic score is built on the huge genetic spread between random strangers; between siblings there is only half that spread to sort on, so the expected IQ or height gain from picking the top-ranked embryo out of a normal IVF batch is small and swamped by huge prediction intervals. Karavani et al., Cell, November 2019.

question: An undercover reporter from The Guardian went to a US start-up called Heliospect Genomics in October 2024, for a story done with the group Hope Not Hate. By the paper's account, Heliospect quoted about $50,000 to rank up to 100 of a couple's in vitro fertilization (IVF) embryos on a single headline trait, and framed the service as helping parents pick the best child. Which trait, the paper reported, was Heliospect selling?
answer: Predicted IQ
choices: Predicted IQ
Predicted adult height
Predicted athletic VO2 max
Predicted extraversion
