context: The Guardian / Hope Not Hate investigation, October 2024. Heliospect's pitch to the undercover client was explicitly to rank embryos by predicted IQ; the company also discussed sex, height and 'risk of obesity.' Selecting embryos on predicted IQ is illegal under UK law; in most US states it is unregulated. The Karavani result from another question is the standing scientific reason to doubt the pitch would actually deliver a smarter child.

question: Erwin Mueller and his student cooled a sharp tungsten tip at Penn State in 1955 and let in helium gas. Bright dots filled the screen in a neat pattern. What had they just become the first people to do?
answer: See individual atoms directly for the first time
choices: See individual atoms directly for the first time
Weigh a single atom for the first time
Photograph a virus for the first time
Detect a neutron star for the first time
context: Mueller had invented the field ion microscope in 1951; the 1955 image was the payoff, with the cold tip holding tungsten atoms still enough for the helium image gas to reveal them one by one. Mueller shouted 'Atoms, ja, atoms!' at the screen. Source: https://pubsapp.acs.org/cen/coverstory/83/8348atoms.html

question: Heinrich Rohrer and Gerd Binnig built a microscope in Zurich on a quantum effect. Classical physics says a particle without the energy to climb a wall must bounce back. Quantum mechanics adds a small extra option. What is it?
answer: The particle has a small chance to pass straight through the wall
choices: The particle has a small chance to pass straight through the wall
The particle can borrow energy from a nearby photon and jump the wall
The particle shatters the wall and rides through the pieces
The particle vanishes and reappears at a random distant location
context: This effect is called quantum tunnelling. A wavefunction leaks exponentially into a barrier, so a small but real probability of finding the particle on the far side remains -- and the current made by that leak is astonishingly sensitive to distance, which is what makes single-atom imaging possible. Source: https://chem.tufts.edu/sykes-lab/resources/how-scanning-tunneling-microscope-works

question: Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer, two International Business Machines (IBM) scientists in Zurich, held a metal needle just above a surface in 1981. A tiny current of electrons quietly jumped the gap. What did their new instrument do with that current?
answer: Held it steady while scanning, so the tip's rise and fall traced each atom
choices: Held it steady while scanning, so the tip's rise and fall traced each atom
Amplified it until the surface glowed with the atoms' own light
Sprayed it back at the surface to write atomic-scale patterns
Compared it to a beam of X-rays to build a hologram of the surface
context: This is the scanning tunnelling microscope. Because the tunnelling current shrinks exponentially with distance, holding it constant while scanning turns the tip's height record into an atomic-height map. Binnig and Rohrer won half of the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics for the design; the other half went to Ernst Ruska for the electron microscope. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/rohrer-lecture.pdf

question: Donald Eigler and Erhard Schweizer used the tip of a scanning tunnelling microscope in 1989 to push atoms instead of just looking at them. They took 35 xenon atoms on a cold nickel surface. What did they do with them?
answer: Spelled the three-letter logo IBM by dragging them into position
choices: Spelled the three-letter logo IBM by dragging them into position
Lined them up in a perfect straight row a nanometre long
Fused them into a single blob to prove atoms could combine
Weighed them one by one on the smallest scale ever built
context: It was the first time atoms had been placed precisely on a surface. The result appeared in Nature (April 1990) and remains one of the iconic scientific images of the century. Almaden is IBM's California research campus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_(atoms)

question: Donald Eigler's group at International Business Machines (IBM) arranged 48 iron atoms in a neat ring on a cold copper surface in 1993 and took an image that landed in every physics textbook. What did the image reveal inside that ring?
answer: The ripple pattern of electrons trapped by the ring -- a wavefunction made visible
choices: The ripple pattern of electrons trapped by the ring -- a wavefunction made visible
A shadow cast by the iron atoms in the copper's own atomic glow
A stray helium atom that had crept in from the vacuum
The magnetic field of each iron atom, curling into a spiral
context: This is the 'quantum corral': surface electrons on the copper are confined by the iron ring, and the standing waves predicted by the Schroedinger equation appear as circular ripples inside the corral. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.262.5131.218

question: Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer built their first scanning microscope in 1981. A machine of that kind shows what look like round bumps in a neat grid, the individual atoms of a metal surface. People often say it 'photographs' the atoms, but strictly its pictures are not photographs at all. Why not?
answer: The images are built from a tunnelling current, not light through a lens
choices: The images are built from a tunnelling current, not light through a lens
The images are drawn later by hand from the raw data, in colour for effect
The images are formed by X-rays instead of visible light
The images are actually of the tip itself, mirrored back onto the surface
context: An STM image is a reconstruction from a signal, not an optical photograph. The instrument measures how easily electrons tunnel at each point on the surface, and the 'atoms' seen are bumps in that tunnelling map. Source: http://spiff.rit.edu/classes/phys314/lectures/stm/stm.html

question: Leo Gross's group at International Business Machines (IBM) Zurich cooled an atomic-force microscope to near absolute zero in 2009. They took the sharpest picture yet of a single pentacene molecule, with every carbon-carbon bond visible. What tiny molecule did they stick on the tip to reveal those bonds?
answer: A single carbon monoxide molecule
choices: A single carbon monoxide molecule
A single water molecule
A single hydrogen molecule
A single benzene molecule
context: The CO molecule, held to the tip, is chemically almost inert and acts as a tiny rigid probe. Gross's 28 August 2009 Science paper resolved pentacene's bond skeleton with unprecedented clarity. Source: https://www.chemistryworld.com/features/picture-perfect-pentacene/3004732.article

question: A pregnant woman dropped to her knees in the courtyard of the Vienna General Hospital in the 1840s, begging the porters not to send her into the First Clinic. There the physicians and their students delivered the babies, and childbed fever killed mothers in huge numbers. Some women went even further to stay out. What did they do?
answer: Gave birth in the street, then came in saying it happened on the way
choices: Bribed the porters to enter them on the midwives' register instead
Gave birth in the street, then came in saying it happened on the way
Waited outside the gates until a bed opened on the safer side
Sent their husbands in first to plead their case with the professor
context: Semmelweis described desperate women begging on their knees not to be put in the First Clinic, and Wikipedia records the rest plainly: 'Women began purposefully giving birth in the streets, pretending to have given birth en route to the hospital so they could avoid being admitted to the clinic.' A birth on the pavement really did survive better than a birth in the doctors' ward. The women of Vienna had read the hospital correctly years before its faculty would. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis; grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis

question: A woman arrived in labor at the front gate of the Vienna General Hospital in the 1840s and did not get to pick her clinic. One of the hospital's two clinics, run by physicians and students, buried roughly four times as many mothers to childbed fever as the other, run by midwives. What decided which door she was sent through?
answer: The day of the week: the clinics admitted on alternating days
choices: The fee she could pay: the cheaper clinic took the poorest
The rank of the birth: first-time mothers went to one side
The day of the week: the clinics admitted on alternating days
The luck of the beds: she went wherever a place was free
context: The First Clinic (physicians and medical students) and the Second (student midwives only) sat in the same building, one door apart, and admitted on alternating days -- so the calendar, not the patient and not the doctor, sorted the women. That accident is what makes the comparison so strong: same city, same building, same air, same kind of women, divided by something with no connection to how sick anyone was. A modern trial spends enormous effort to arrange that on purpose; Vienna had it by accident and ignored it for years. Semmelweis was appointed assistant to Professor Johann Klein in the First Clinic on 1 July 1846. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis

question: Ignaz Semmelweis came home from a trip in March 1847 and learned his friend Jakob Kolletschka was dead. The autopsy findings matched what Semmelweis kept finding in mothers dead of childbed fever: the same disease, in a man who had never given birth. How had Kolletschka caught it?
answer: A student's scalpel nicked his finger at a post-mortem
choices: A dying mother's blood soaked his cuff at a delivery
A student's scalpel nicked his finger at a post-mortem
A fever patient's breath reached him on the morning round
A soiled dressing brushed a cut on his wrist in the ward
context: Jakob Kolletschka, professor of forensic medicine, died on 13 March 1847 after a student's scalpel pricked his finger at a post-mortem; Semmelweis had left for Venice on 2 March and learned of it on his return on 20 March. The autopsy showed widespread suppuration and inflammatory infiltration virtually identical to what he kept finding in mothers dead of childbed fever -- the same thing, differing only in where the infection got in: a wound in the hand instead of the birth canal. One friend's death, read carefully, was the clue. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis; sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/ignaz-semmelweis/

question: Ignaz Semmelweis went through the days of both staffs in Vienna's two maternity clinics hour by hour. The clinics stood one door apart and took the same kind of women, yet one buried four times as many. How did that clinic's physicians spend their mornings?
answer: Cutting up the dead in the pathology room, then straight to the delivery beds
choices: Airing the ward at the windows, then straight to the delivery beds
Cutting up the dead in the pathology room, then straight to the delivery beds
Bleeding the women admitted in the night, then straight to the delivery beds
Hauling the dead down to the mortuary yard, then straight to the delivery beds
context: In the First Clinic the students and assistants moved from the pathology room to the delivery beds with nothing washed in between; the student midwives of the Second Clinic never touched a corpse. Grokipedia notes that the monthly mortality peaks 'aligned to periods of heightened dissection activity.' Notice what Semmelweis did not have: he had no idea what was being carried, and would not have believed you if you had said bacteria. He had a difference and the habit of counting. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis

question: Ignaz Semmelweis tested the Vienna faculty's favorite reason for the gap between the two clinics against the hospital's own admission records. That reason was crowding: too many women packed into too few beds. What did the records actually show?
answer: The midwives' clinic, the safer one, was consistently the more crowded
choices: The two clinics ran at almost exactly the same numbers all year
The physicians' clinic filled up only in the coldest winter months
Crowding rose in both clinics in the years the deaths fell fastest
The midwives' clinic, the safer one, was consistently the more crowded
context: The Second Clinic was always the more crowded of the two, so overcrowding could not explain deaths four times higher next door. Semmelweis worked through the others the same way: the climate could not do it, since the clinics stood feet apart; and he altered the position in which mothers gave birth to test that too. This is what a control looks like before anyone had a word for it -- hold everything else the same and see what is left standing. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis; grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis; sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/ignaz-semmelweis/

question: Ignaz Semmelweis ordered every hand scrubbed before an examination in mid-May 1847. Soap and water alone would not do: it had to be a solution of chlorinated lime, worked into the skin and under the nails until the hands felt slippery. He was trying to remove something no one could see. Why chlorine in particular?
answer: Only chlorine removed the smell of the dead, his one test for a clean hand
choices: Chlorine was thought to neutralise the miasma rising off the ward floor
Only chlorine removed the smell of the dead, his one test for a clean hand
The hospital's soap was rationed, and chlorinated lime cost almost nothing
Chlorine stung enough that a man could feel his hands had been cleaned
context: Semmelweis picked chlorinated lime precisely because it destroyed the corpse smell that soap alone left behind: the odour was his only detector for the invisible thing he was trying to remove. PBS records that he made the students wash 'until the smell of the putrid bodies they dissected in the autopsy suite was no longer detectable.' The protocol was roughly a 4% solution -- about one part chlorinated lime to thirty of water -- five minutes of scrubbing hands and nails until the skin went slippery, with basins standing at the clinic entrances. The staff resented it: it ate time and dried out their skin. The First Clinic's monthly mortality ran 18.3% in April 1847, then 2.2% in June, 1.2% in July, 1.9% in August; the 1848 annual rate was 1.27%. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis; pbs.org/newshour/health/ignaz-semmelweis-doctor-prescribed-hand-washing

question: Ignaz Semmelweis set out in the 1840s to work out why so many young mothers were dying of childbed fever on his Vienna maternity ward. The answer he defended for the rest of his life came later. First he blamed something else in the ward entirely, an idea he later dropped. What had he blamed?
answer: The priest crossing the ward to give the last rites, scaring the women
choices: The winter cold striking the women in an unheated delivery room
The priest crossing the ward to give the last rites, scaring the women
The coarse hospital food the women were given after the birth
The bad air rising into the ward from the hospital's old drains
context: Before the chlorine, Semmelweis proposed that the priest passing through the ward to administer the last rites was frightening the mothers into the fever. He was a careful man having a bad idea, which is how most science actually goes. The rivals were not jokes either: the reigning theory was miasma, bad air, and Carl Braun's textbook listed thirty causes of childbed fever including 'conception and pregnancy, uremia, pressure exerted on adjacent organs by the shrinking uterus, emotional traumata, mistakes in diet, chilling, and atmospheric epidemic influences.' Cadaveric infection ranked twenty-eighth of the thirty. (A popular retelling adds a bell to the priest's walk; that detail could not be verified and is left out here.) Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis; grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis

question: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr told the Boston Society for Medical Improvement that doctors were carrying childbed fever from patient to patient, and he published the argument in 1843, four years before Vienna. Charles Meigs of Philadelphia answered him in print in 1854 with a reply that rested on no evidence at all. What was it?
answer: That doctors are gentlemen, and a gentleman's hands are clean
choices: That the fever was God's affliction, and no man's to prevent
That doctors are gentlemen, and a gentleman's hands are clean
That a physician's oath forbade him to suppose he did harm
That the poor took the fever because they lived in filth
context: Holmes read 'The Contagiousness of Puerperal Fever' before the Boston Society for Medical Improvement and published it in April 1843: 'The disease, known as Puerperal Fever, is so far contagious as to be frequently carried from patient to patient by physicians and nurses.' Charles Delucena Meigs answered in his 1854 book on childbed fevers: 'Did he carry it on his hands? But a gentleman's hands are clean.' Meigs and Hugh Hodge ridiculed him. Holmes had argued from clusters, not theory -- in 1821 Dr Campbell attended two fatal childbed cases straight after autopsying an infected patient; in 1842 Dr Warrington saw five cases, two fatal, after a similar post-mortem -- and his prescription was concrete: avoid autopsies of fever cases, wash thoroughly, change clothes, suspend practice for weeks. The evidence existed in 1843; a profession's self-image outvoted it. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Contagiousness_of_Puerperal_Fever; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Delucena_Meigs; grokipedia.com/page/Oliver_Wendell_Holmes_Sr.

question: Ignaz Semmelweis had his rule working in the Vienna clinic with Louis Pasteur's germ theory fourteen years off and Robert Koch's anthrax bacillus nearly thirty. He still had to name the thing he believed was killing the mothers. What did he call it?
answer: Cadaverous particles: decaying matter off the dead
choices: Miasma: a poisonous vapour rising off the ward floor
Contagion: a taint passed from the sick to the well
Cadaverous particles: decaying matter off the dead
Uremia: a waste the mother's own body failed to clear
context: Semmelweis never said 'germs' and did not know bacteria existed. His German phrase was 'an der Hand klebende Cadavertheile' -- cadaver bits clinging to the hand -- and he pictured inert, decaying organic matter, not living, self-replicating organisms. That gap is the honest part of the story, and his critics used it against him: they charged post hoc ergo propter hoc, that deaths falling after the washing did not prove the washing caused it. Wrong conclusion, respectable logic. The rival explanations were serious ones: miasma, bad air, was the reigning theory, and Carl Braun's textbook worked through thirty causes of childbed fever -- uremia and emotional trauma among them -- with cadaveric infection ranked twenty-eighth. The mechanism came later and from other men: Pasteur's germ theory in 1861, Lister's carbolic antisepsis in 1867 (post-operative mortality from over 50% to under 10%), Koch's anthrax bacillus in 1876. Modern bacteriology can finally name the killer in those wards: Streptococcus pyogenes, spread by hand contact. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis; grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis

question: Ignaz Semmelweis imposed his chlorine rule on the maternity ward at St Rokus Hospital in Pest in 1851, unpaid, after Vienna dismissed him. Before the rule, the doctor-run clinic in Vienna had been burying about one mother in every ten. Over the next four years the Pest ward delivered 933 babies. How many mothers did childbed fever take?
answer: 8 mothers
choices: 31 mothers
8 mothers
76 mothers
129 mothers
context: Eight childbed-fever deaths in 933 births between 1851 and 1855 -- about 0.86% -- in a different hospital, with different staff, under the same rule. That is replication, the step that turns one man's result into knowledge. In Vienna the rule had already cut the First Clinic's monthly mortality from 18.3% in April 1847 to 1.2% that July, and Johann Klein terminated Semmelweis's assistantship on 20 March 1849 regardless, handing the post to Carl Braun. Semmelweis ran the St Rókus ward from 21 May 1851; across his 22 months over Vienna's First Clinic the tally had been 142 puerperal deaths in 6,495 admissions (2.19%), against a pre-intervention baseline over 9%. He became professor of obstetrics at the University of Pest on 18 July 1855. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis; semmelweis.hu/english/about-us/ignac-semmelweis/

question: Ignaz Semmelweis finally brought out his book on the cause and prevention of childbed fever in 1861, after fourteen years of publishing almost nothing on the rule he had proved in the Vienna clinic. The profession shrugged it off. What did he do next?
answer: He wrote open letters naming his opponents and calling them murderers
choices: He printed the two clinics' death counts as a public charge against the faculty
He wrote open letters naming his opponents and calling them murderers
He demanded that both clinics be put under his rule for a full year
He petitioned the Emperor to force the washing rule on every ward
context: 'Die Ätiologie, der Begriff und die Prophylaxis des Kindbettfiebers' appeared in 1861 after a fourteen-year silence and landed badly. Semmelweis followed it with open letters naming specific opponents and denouncing them as irresponsible murderers or ignoramuses, framing their resistance as complicity in massacre. Grokipedia's assessment: he 'forfeited opportunities for collaborative validation, as peers recoiled from the ad hominem tone.' Both things are true at once -- he was right, and he was a ruinous advocate for being right, and the mothers paid for the second fact as surely as for the first. His own words survive: 'Most medical lecture halls continue to resound with lectures on epidemic childbed fever and with discourses against my theories.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis; grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis

question: Ferdinand von Hebra lured Ignaz Semmelweis into a Vienna institution on 30 July 1865, saying he wanted to show him one of his new institutes. Semmelweis worked out where he was and tried to leave; the guards beat him and shut him in a darkened cell. He was dead fourteen days later, aged 47. What did the autopsy find had killed him?
answer: Blood poisoning from a gangrenous wound on his right hand
choices: A stroke brought on by the beating the guards gave him
Starvation and exhaustion after refusing all his food
Blood poisoning from a gangrenous wound on his right hand
Tuberculosis of the kind then sweeping the Vienna wards
context: He died on 13 August 1865 of pyaemia -- blood poisoning -- from a gangrenous wound on his right hand, possibly taken in the struggle with the guards, treated with none of the antisepsis he had spent eighteen years demanding; the autopsy found an extensive abscess in the chest wall that had perforated into the chest cavity and reached the sac around the heart. He was killed by the same family of infection that killed his patients, in a hospital that would not wash its hands. A popular retelling has him cutting himself on a cadaver on purpose to prove his point; that is not what the record says. What historians do still argue over is the breakdown that came first -- syphilis, blood poisoning, bipolar illness, early Alzheimer's and sheer exhaustion have all been proposed, and nobody knows. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis; pbs.org/newshour/health/ignaz-semmelweis-doctor-prescribed-hand-washing

question: Colleagues mocked Ignaz Semmelweis and drove him out of Vienna. His name today sits on two things: Hungary's largest medical university, in Budapest, and a phrase the writer Robert Anton Wilson coined in English in 1979, the Semmelweis reflex. What does that phrase name?
answer: Rejecting new evidence out of hand because it contradicts settled belief
choices: Assuming a treatment worked because the patient recovered after taking it
Crediting a discovery to whoever explained it, not whoever found it first
Defending a colleague's known error to protect the standing of a profession
Rejecting new evidence out of hand because it contradicts settled belief
context: Semmelweis University in Budapest, Hungary's largest medical institution, carries his name -- and so does the reflex. Robert Anton Wilson defined it in 'The Game of Life' (1979) as 'mob behavior found among primates and larval hominids on undeveloped planets, in which a discovery of important scientific fact is punished.' The man's name is now the label for the thing that was done to him. The recognition worth keeping: when someone answers evidence with status -- 'a gentleman's hands are clean' -- instead of with a counter-test, that is the reflex, and the reply Semmelweis gave is still the right one: count, and go on counting.  Sources: semmelweis.hu/english/about-us/ignac-semmelweis/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semmelweis_reflex; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Semmelweis

question: Dan Shechtman aimed a beam of electrons at a rapidly cooled aluminum-manganese alloy at a US lab in April 1982. Around the center of the pattern he saw a ring of bright points. The count made him doubt his own microscope. How many points did he see?
answer: Ten
choices: Six
Eight
Ten
Twelve
context: Sample number 1725, prepared by Frank Biancaniello using melt spinning (about 86 percent aluminium, 14 percent manganese). Beside the entry in his notebook Shechtman wrote '10 Fold ???' -- the three question marks are the whole point. Source: NIST, 'The Nobel Moment: Dan Shechtman'.

question: Dan Shechtman fired electrons through a new aluminum-manganese alloy in 1982 and got back a symmetry every textbook said no crystal could show. Any kid can check the rule on a kitchen floor: a crystal repeats the way tiles do. Which of these regular shapes cannot be laid side by side without leaving gaps?
answer: Regular pentagon
choices: Equilateral triangle
Square
Regular pentagon
Regular hexagon
context: Triangles, squares and hexagons each tile a plane with no gaps -- which is why the classical rule allowed 3-fold, 4-fold and 6-fold rotational symmetries in a periodic crystal (plus 2-fold). Pentagons leave gaps, and so do 5-, 7-, 8-, 10- and 12-fold arrangements. Shechtman's tenfold ring was on the forbidden list. Source: Wikipedia, 'Quasicrystal'.

question: Dan Shechtman rushed a strange result to his research-group leader at America's National Bureau of Standards in Maryland in 1982. He had shot electrons through a new aluminum-manganese alloy, and the pattern showed fivefold symmetry, a kind of order crystallography then held impossible in a real crystal. The leader did not congratulate him. What did the leader do instead?
answer: Handed him a textbook and told him to go read it
choices: Handed him a textbook and told him to go read it
Rushed a preprint to Physical Review Letters that week
Called the electron microscope in for realignment
Sent the alloy to a rival lab for confirmation
context: The same leader later asked Shechtman to leave the research group for bringing 'disgrace' on it. It took two more years -- and John Cahn's reluctant conversion -- before the paper was published. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dan Shechtman'.

question: Roger Penrose worked out in 1974 how to tile a floor endlessly with true fivefold symmetry, using just two simple shapes that never fall into a repeating pattern. Only three regular shapes tile a floor on their own: squares, triangles and hexagons. None of them shows fivefold symmetry. Which pair of shapes did one of his best-known versions use?
answer: Two rhombuses, one thin and one thick
choices: Two rhombuses, one thin and one thick
Two trapezoids, one tall and one short
A regular decagon paired with a thin rhombus
A regular pentagon paired with a five-pointed star
context: The thin rhombus has a 36-degree acute angle; the thick one has 72 degrees. Their areas stand in the golden ratio. A quasicrystal is essentially the three-dimensional version of such an aperiodic tiling -- which is why its diffraction spots stay razor-sharp even though the atomic pattern never repeats. Penrose also invented a 'kite and dart' quadrilateral pair that tiles the plane aperiodically in the same way. Source: Wikipedia, 'Penrose tiling'.

question: Luca Bindi and Paul Steinhardt confirmed in 2009 that a tiny grain from a Russian meteorite was a natural quasicrystal. It was exactly the 'forbidden' kind of material the two-time Nobel laureate Linus Pauling had mocked Dan Shechtman for. The parent rock's age told Bindi and Steinhardt how long quasicrystals had been around. How long was that?
answer: About 4.5 billion years, from the birth of the solar system
choices: About 4.5 billion years, from the birth of the solar system
About 66 million years, from the dinosaur-killing impact
About 12,000 years, from the end of the last ice age
About 250 years, from an eighteenth-century meteorite fall
context: The parent body was a CV3 carbonaceous chondrite -- roughly as old as the solar system itself. The specific mineral is called icosahedrite (Al63Cu24Fe13). Nature had been making quasicrystals for billions of years before Shechtman's electron beam. Source: Wikipedia, 'Icosahedrite'.

question: Scientists at the biotech giant Amgen tried around 2011 to redo the results of 53 top cancer papers, wanting to know which biology to build new drugs on. C. Glenn Begley and Lee Ellis wrote up the audit in Nature. Of the 53 papers, how many did Amgen's team report confirming?
answer: Six
choices: Six
Thirty-one
All fifty-three
Forty-seven
context: Six out of fifty-three, roughly 11 percent. Amgen never publicly named the individual papers, so the number is an internal industry audit rather than a hit-list of specific studies. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/483531a

question: Bayer's scientists in Germany went through 67 of the firm's own projects in cancer, heart and women's health around 2011, ahead of a better-known audit by the biotech firm Amgen. About what share fully matched the papers they were built on?
answer: About a quarter
choices: About a quarter
About three quarters
Essentially all of them
None of them
context: Bayer's audit and Amgen's audit were run independently, in different countries, and reached the same broad answer. Two separate drug companies had checked and neither believed the literature was safe to build on. Source: http://blogs.nature.com/news/2011/09/reliability_of_new_drug_target.html

question: Scientists at Amgen and Bayer separately tried in the early 2010s to reproduce dozens of published results before spending years building new drugs on top of them. Both audits found that most of the work would not hold up. These two industry audits carried more weight than most academic replication tries, for a reason that had nothing to do with their numbers. What made them so hard to dismiss?
answer: The companies were spending money hoping the papers would be true
choices: The companies were spending money hoping the papers would be true
The companies were owned by the same parent conglomerate
Both audits were run by former academic critics of pharma
Both audits were commissioned by the same NIH grant
context: Amgen and Bayer had every commercial reason to WANT the published biology to hold up: they were staking drug programmes on it. When the people who wanted the finding to be real cannot reproduce it, the excuse 'the replicators were hostile' evaporates. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/483531a

question: Tim Errington's team lined up 193 target experiments from 53 famous cancer papers for their redo project. The most damaging finding had nothing to do with statistics or effect sizes, and it emerged before a single bench experiment was run. What did the team find when they looked across all 193?
answer: Not one experiment was described in enough detail to repeat from the paper alone
choices: Not one experiment was described in enough detail to repeat from the paper alone
More than half of the papers relied on a single unblinded assay
Most of the papers had used the same cell line without authentication
Nearly every paper reported only the best of multiple runs
context: Zero of 193. Only 2 percent of the papers made their raw data openly available, and 0 percent had complete public protocols; on roughly 70 percent of the experiments the team had to write to the original authors for reagents or protocols. Source: https://elifesciences.org/articles/67995

question: Tim Errington's team ran short of money and lab access early in the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, launched in 2013 to redo 193 key experiments from 53 landmark cancer papers. In the end they finished only about 50 experiments, from just 23 of the 53 papers. Among the ones they did finish, how did the reported effect sizes compare to the originals on average?
answer: About 85 percent smaller
choices: About 85 percent smaller
About the same size
About 15 percent larger
About twice as large
context: In 92 percent of the replicated experiments the effect was smaller than in the original paper; on average, about 85 percent smaller. The direction of the finding often survived; the industrial-strength effect sizes that made the papers famous did not. Source: https://elifesciences.org/articles/71601

question: Leonard Freedman and two colleagues put a dollar figure on the problem in a 2015 Public Library of Science (PLOS) Biology paper. They assumed about half of preclinical spending fails to reproduce. How much did they estimate the United States spends each year on preclinical research nobody can reproduce?
answer: About 28 billion dollars a year
choices: About 28 billion dollars a year
About 280 million dollars a year
About 2.8 trillion dollars a year
About 28 million dollars a year
context: Roughly half of preclinical spending, on their assumptions, is funding results nobody else can reproduce. The point of the paper was not blame; the authors used it to argue for cheap fixes like reagent authentication and reporting standards. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article%3Fid=10.1371%252Fjournal.pbio.1002165

question: Francis Collins, director of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and his deputy Lawrence Tabak rewrote its grant rules after the audits, in a 2014 Nature commentary and then in the 2015 grant forms. They added three new topics every applicant now had to address. Which three did they add?
answer: Scientific rigor, resource authentication and prior-evidence strength
choices: Scientific rigor, resource authentication and prior-evidence strength
Pre-registration, open data and mandatory replication
Blinded analysis, sample-size justification and effect-size reporting
Randomization, sample-size justification and independent audit
context: The rigor-and-reproducibility form language rolled out through 2015 notices NOT-OD-16-011 and its siblings. The Collins-Tabak commentary named the audits by Amgen and Bayer as the reason. Source: https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-16-011.html

question: Ali Maow Maalin broke out in a rash in Merca, Somalia, in October 1977, and became the last person on Earth ever to catch smallpox in the wild. He worked at the town hospital, but not as a doctor or a nurse. What was his real job there?
answer: cook
choices: cook
gardener
electrician
night watchman
context: Maalin caught the milder form of the virus, variola minor, from two sick children he had briefly ridden with in a vehicle from the hospital to the local smallpox office. He lived, and no naturally acquired case of smallpox has been recorded anywhere on the planet since. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Maow_Maalin

question: Ali Maow Maalin stood before wary parents in a Somali village and told them his own story of surviving smallpox in 1977. He walked such villages as a vaccinator until malaria killed him in 2013. Which other disease had he spent those years fighting?
answer: polio
choices: polio
measles
cholera
tuberculosis
context: Maalin joined the polio eradication campaign, and often used his own smallpox story to persuade wary parents to vaccinate their children. The last person on earth to catch one disease spent thirty years trying to end another. Source: polioeradication.org/news/the-world-loses-one-of-the-true-heroes-of-polio-eradication/ ; npr.org/sections/health-shots/2013/07/31/206947581/last-person-to-get-smallpox-dedicated-his-life-to-ending-polio

question: A global health team hunting smallpox in the 1970s faced two forms of the virus. On the skin they looked alike, and their DNA was nearly the same, yet one, variola major, was far deadlier than the other, variola minor. Roughly what share of its victims did each kill?
answer: Major about one in three; minor about one in a hundred
choices: Major about one in three; minor about one in a hundred
Major about one in three; minor about one in ten
Major about one in ten; minor about one in a thousand
Major about two in three; minor about one in five
context: Variola major and variola minor are two strains of one virus, near-identical in their DNA, yet their case fatality rates were about 30 percent and 1 percent or less. The hemorrhagic and flat presentations of major were nearly always fatal. Source: programs.fas.org/bio/factsheets/smallpoxfs.html

question: William Foege, a young American missionary doctor, ran short of vaccine in eastern Nigeria in December 1966. He mapped each case by radio, then vaccinated only the contacts around each outbreak. The worldwide smallpox campaign was not won by vaccinating everyone; it was won by this. What is the method called?
answer: Ring vaccination
choices: Ring vaccination
Mass vaccination
Herd immunity
Cordon sanitaire
context: William Foege's ring approach, later named surveillance-and-containment, worked far better than mass campaigns had done and is the method that actually finished the disease. Donald Henderson led the overall WHO programme; Frank Fenner chaired the certification commission; Edward Jenner had invented the vaccine 170 years earlier. Source: scienceheroes.com/foege ; washington.edu/alumni/columns/top10/calling_the_shots.html

question: William Foege mapped each smallpox case in his districts and vaccinated only the contacts around it, where doctors had thought about 80 percent of a region must be vaccinated. A much smaller share turned out to work. Roughly what fraction of the local people actually stopped the spread?
answer: 7 to 8 percent
choices: 7 to 8 percent
20 to 25 percent
45 to 50 percent
70 to 75 percent
context: The heresy that won: in Foege's affected areas, immunising the ring around each active outbreak - about 7 to 8 percent of the population - was enough. Classical herd-immunity arithmetic demanded roughly ten times that, and the vaccine simply did not exist in those quantities. Source: uchicagomedicine.org/forefront/patient-care-articles/global-health-pioneer-who-helped-eradicate-smallpox-wins-prestigious-maclean-center-ethics-prize

question: Janet Parker, a medical photographer, was working in a University of Birmingham darkroom in 1978 when smallpox escaped from the research lab on the floor beneath her. She died that September, the last smallpox death on record and not a natural case at all. How did the virus reach her?
answer: through an air duct
choices: through an air duct
through a torn glove
through a shared drinking cup
through a discarded slide
context: The Birmingham lab, run by Professor Henry Bedson, connected to Parker's office suite through an unsealed ventilation duct. Parker died on 11 September 1978. A pathogen got out of a laboratory, and it killed someone - a warning worth keeping alongside the eradication triumph. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_smallpox_outbreak_in_the_United_Kingdom ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Bedson

question: Delegates from around the world declared smallpox eradicated in May 1980, so far the only human disease ever wiped out in the wild. It has one companion on that short list of eradicated diseases, finished off in cattle in 2011. Which cattle disease shares the list with smallpox?
answer: rinderpest
choices: rinderpest
brucellosis
anthrax
tuberculosis
context: The World Organisation for Animal Health declared rinderpest eradicated on 25 May 2011 - the second disease ever wiped out worldwide and the first in animals. The name 'rinderpest' is German for 'cattle plague'. Polio, guinea worm and measles are the remaining serious candidates. Source: news.un.org/en/story/2011/06/379902 ; britannica.com/today-in-history/May-8-smallpox-eradicated

question: A boy blows a soap bubble with a wand. The soapy water itself is completely clear, with no dye, no pigment, nothing coloured inside. Yet the surface shimmers in bright rainbow bands that drift slowly downwards as the bubble hangs in the air. Where do the colours actually come from?
answer: Light bouncing off the top of the film and off the bottom reinforce at some colours, cancel at others
choices: Light bouncing off the top of the film and off the bottom reinforce at some colours, cancel at others
Tiny mirror-like bubbles inside the film reflect the sky around it in rainbow order
Soap molecules absorb some wavelengths and re-emit them shifted in colour
Dust and grease in the water scatter sunlight the way a cloud scatters a rainbow
context: This is thin-film interference. The two reflections arrive out of step by roughly twice the film's thickness (in wavelengths), so the colours that reinforce depend on the film thickness at that exact spot. As gravity drains the film, the bands migrate downward and the top thins first. Source: explainthatstuff.com/thin-film-interference.html.

question: A girl blows a fat soap bubble and watches the crown: just before it bursts, a strange dark patch spreads across the top. It looks like a hole in the bubble, and it is a warning that the bubble will pop in the next few seconds. What has happened to the film where that dark patch appears?
answer: It has thinned to well below the wavelength of visible light
choices: It has thinned to well below the wavelength of visible light
It has locally thickened to hundreds of times the wavelength of light
It is boiling off tiny puffs of water vapour into the surrounding air
It has crystallised into a solid transparent skin at that spot
context: When the film is under about 100 nanometres, the two reflections arrive so nearly in step that they cancel across ALL visible wavelengths -- transparent-dark. Even the smallest disturbance will now break it. That black patch is a five-second countdown. Source: sciencenews.org shimmering-soap-bubbles-have-dark-side ; physics.upenn.edu demolab li12.html.

question: Isaac Newton pressed a curved lens against a flat glass plate, and coloured rings appeared in the thin wedge of air trapped between them. He measured them with more care than anyone before, then explained them the wrong way, saying light particles have 'fits of easy reflection.' What was Newton actually looking at?
answer: Interference between light reflecting off the two glass surfaces of the air wedge
choices: Interference between light reflecting off the two glass surfaces of the air wedge
Diffraction of light around the sharp curved edge of the pressed lens
Refraction of light through the varying thickness of the air pocket
Absorption of certain colours by traces of iron impurity in the glass
context: The setup is the classic thin-film experiment done with an AIR film instead of a soap one, and Newton catalogued it so meticulously that his numbers still work. He collected the strongest wave-optics evidence of the 17th century and read it as particles, because his corpuscular commitments were prior. Source: sciencedemonstrations.fas.harvard.edu/presentations/newtons-rings.

question: A natural philosopher described the colours in mica sheets and soap bubbles thirty-nine years before Isaac Newton's Opticks, in a book that became the first scientific bestseller. The priority quarrel fed a long, bitter feud between the two men at the Royal Society. Who was the rival?
answer: Robert Hooke
choices: Robert Hooke
Christiaan Huygens
Robert Boyle
Edmond Halley
context: Hooke's Micrographia (1665) illustrated the colours of thin films of mica and soap and correctly guessed they were wave-like -- a claim Newton would work strenuously to overshadow. Hooke also famously described 'cells' in cork, coined the word, and got the credit for that. The feud was legendary and outlasted them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micrographia ; pubs.aip.org/aapt/pte/article/63/7/539 Newton-Hooke.

question: Thomas Young explained Newton's rings as interference of waves around 1802 and pointed out one detail that seals the wave case. At the very centre, where the curved lens actually touches the flat plate and the air gap goes to zero, everything should reinforce into a bright bullseye. Instead the centre is a dark spot. Why is the centre dark?
answer: Light reflecting off the flat glass gets its phase flipped by half a wavelength -- and cancels
choices: Light reflecting off the flat glass gets its phase flipped by half a wavelength -- and cancels
The direct contact drives all the air out, so the two glass surfaces stop reflecting at all
Newton's own measurements were slightly wrong -- the true centre is actually a bright bullseye
The pressure of contact bends the flat plate into a matching curve, so no wedge remains
context: A light wave reflecting off a denser medium picks up an extra half-wavelength of phase; a wave reflecting off a less-dense one does not. At the centre one reflection has flipped and the other has not, so they arrive exactly out of step and cancel across all colours. The dark centre is the fingerprint of the flip -- and a direct wave-optics prediction Newton's particle theory could never explain. Source: physics.bu.edu/~duffy/semester2/c26_newtons_rings.html.

question: A photographer tilts a modern camera lens in bright light and sees a faint purple sheen on the glass. It is no decoration: the coating is deliberately made a quarter of a wavelength thick. What is the coating engineered to do?
answer: Cancel out the reflection off the glass, so more light passes into the camera
choices: Cancel out the reflection off the glass, so more light passes into the camera
Filter out ultraviolet light that would otherwise damage the camera sensor
Convert incoming sunlight into a small trickle of stored electric power
Harden the glass surface against scratches from a lens cap or a cloth
context: A quarter-wave coating puts the front-surface reflection and the back-surface reflection exactly half a wavelength out of step, so they cancel for the wavelength they are tuned to. Most coatings are tuned for green, where the eye is most sensitive; red and blue get through only partly cancelled, and the leftover reflection reads as purple. The oil slick on a wet road is the same trick, thickness varying colour by colour. Source: hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/phyopt/antiref.html.

question: A teacher holds a Digital Versatile Disc (DVD) up in sunlight, and it throws rainbow flashes across the ceiling, much as a soap bubble glows in rainbow bands. It is tempting to say the same physics runs both, but it does not. The bubble's colour comes from one thin film. What is the disc's rainbow actually doing that a soap film is not?
answer: Splitting sunlight by diffraction off its evenly-spaced data tracks, like a ruled grating
choices: Splitting sunlight by diffraction off its evenly-spaced data tracks, like a ruled grating
Reflecting the ceiling lights of the room in rainbow order off its shiny metal foil
Filtering white light through the coloured plastic dye printed on its top label
Bending sunlight by refraction through the thin transparent polycarbonate cover
context: A CD or DVD is a ruled diffraction grating -- billions of parallel pits and lands, each roughly 1.6 micrometres apart. Sunlight striking the surface diffracts off that spacing: each colour bends by a different angle set by the ratio of wavelength to spacing. Structural colours in a butterfly's wing and the flash of an opal are ALSO not thin-film -- opal is a stack of tiny silica spheres, butterfly wings a stack of many layers. Same family of physics; different mechanisms. Source: spark.iop.org cd-diffraction-grating.

question: Soviet engineers launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957, the first man-made satellite ever to orbit Earth. It was a shiny aluminum ball about 58 centimeters across, made from two thin metal halves bolted together, with four long whip antennas trailing behind. What did they put inside the sealed ball?
answer: A radio transmitter, a thermistor and a pressure gauge
choices: A radio transmitter, a thermistor and a pressure gauge
A radio transmitter, a cosmic-ray counter and a camera
A radio transmitter, a Geiger tube and a dust microphone
A radio transmitter, a spectrograph and a dose meter
context: That was the lot. The entire payload was a 1-watt radio transmitter weighing 3.5 kg, beeping on 20.005 and 40.002 MHz; the thermistor and the pressure sensor were housekeeping, not science. The two hemispheres were sealed with O-rings and thirty-six bolts, and the sphere was pressurised with dry nitrogen. Grokipedia: 'No dedicated scientific instruments were included, reflecting the proof-of-concept focus.' The first satellite was a proof that you could put anything up there at all -- and a signal any stranger could check. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Sputnik 1'; Wikipedia, 'Sputnik 1'.

question: Crowds stood outside at dusk in October 1957 to watch a moving point of light cross the sky and told each other it was Sputnik. But the polished 58-centimetre sphere was only about sixth magnitude, right at the limit of the unaided eye. What were they almost certainly watching?
answer: The spent core stage of the R-7 rocket, in the same orbit
choices: The spent core stage of the R-7 rocket, in the same orbit
The jettisoned nose-cone shroud, drifting on a lower track
Sunlight flashing from the satellite's four trailing antennas
The vented propellant still streaming from the upper stage
context: The bright object was the 26-metre (85 ft) core stage of the R-7 that had lifted Sputnik, tumbling along in orbit behind it -- vastly bigger and brighter than the satellite itself. Almost none of those who said they saw Sputnik saw Sputnik. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sputnik 1'.

question: Soviet officials guarded Sputnik 1's launch as a state secret, yet a small Soviet magazine called Radio ran a technical note about the coming spacecraft in June 1957. Radio Moscow repeated the same detail three days before launch. What had been given away, so that ham radio operators worldwide were ready from the first beep?
answer: The frequencies the transmitters would use
choices: The frequencies the transmitters would use
The exact minute of each pass overhead
The call sign the satellite would send
The Morse pattern the beeps would spell out
context: The June 1957 Radio told amateurs the satellite would carry two transmitters near 20 and 40 MHz radiating about one watt, so they could be ready to monitor it -- the frequencies, but not the launch date. Its 65-degree orbit carried it over virtually the whole inhabited world, so anyone with a shortwave set was in a position to confirm the claim without taking Moscow's word for anything. That is the difference between an announcement and an experiment. Sources: NSA declassified technical journal, 'Soviet Communications Journals as Sources of Intelligence'; Grokipedia, 'Sputnik 1'.

question: William Guier and George Weiffenbach, two Johns Hopkins physicists, learned the Monday after Sputnik went up that nobody had listened for it over the weekend. So they did, with a borrowed receiver and a home tape recorder. To read the beeps, they had to know when each one arrived. How did they stamp the time onto the tape?
answer: They mixed in WWV, the national time station
choices: They mixed in WWV, the national time station
They took time checks from the Naval Observatory
They read the wall clock aloud onto the tape
They clicked a stopwatch into the microphone
context: 'The Monday after the launch of Sputnik I, we met in the cafeteria for lunch... apparently no one had come to the Laboratory over the weekend and attempted to receive the signals. The more we discussed the issue, the more keen we became on listening in.' Nobody assigned them this. The Laboratory happened to sit 12 miles from WWV, the Bureau of Standards station broadcasting the national time and frequency standard -- so close that 'a 2-ft wire hanging from the receiver was an adequate antenna.' Weiffenbach owned a good 20-MHz receiver only because he was finishing a PhD in microwave spectroscopy, and Guier brought in his newly bought home hi-fi tape deck. A borrowed set, a wire and a tape recorder: that was the entire instrument. Source: W. H. Guier and G. C. Weiffenbach, 'Genesis of Satellite Navigation,' Johns Hopkins APL Technical Digest 18(2), 178-181 (1997).

question: Soviet engineers sent Sputnik up with no camera and no telescope, yet the satellite's own shape did real science. Long after its batteries died the sphere kept circling, and the rate its orbit sank gave researchers their first solid figure for the thickness of the air 200 to 300 kilometers up. Why does a sphere make that figure trustworthy when another shape would not?
answer: A sphere pushes aside the same area of air however it tumbles
choices: A sphere pushes aside the same area of air however it tumbles
A sphere meets the thin air with less drag than any other shape
A sphere is slowed evenly on every side, so it cannot be tipped
A sphere's drag climbs smoothly with speed instead of jumping
context: Wikipedia states the shape was chosen 'to help determine atmospheric density from its lifetime in orbit.' From Sputnik's decay, researchers put thermospheric density at roughly 1e-12 to 1e-13 g/cm3 at 200-300 km, refining pre-launch models and exposing how solar activity puffs the whole atmosphere outward. The three silver-zinc batteries -- about 60% of the satellite's entire mass -- died on 26 October 1957 after 22 days and the beeping stopped; the silent sphere flew on until 4 January 1958, 1,440 orbits and some 70 million km later. The silence did not end the experiment. The decay curve was the data. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Sputnik 1'; Grokipedia, 'Sputnik 1'.

question: Sputnik's builders gave it two sensors and no data channel of any kind. Nothing came down but the beep, alternating between two frequencies and transmitting about 21.6 seconds out of every minute. How did those two readings reach the ground?
answer: The length of each pulse was varied to carry them
choices: The length of each pulse was varied to carry them
The pitch of each pulse was shifted to carry them
The loudness of each pulse was stepped to carry them
The order of the two frequencies was swapped to carry them
context: Temperature and pressure were encoded in the DURATION of the pulses; the system was designated DTK-34. Inside, a fan switched on if the interior passed 30 degrees C, and an alert condition was triggered if the pressure fell below 0.35 kg/cm2 or the temperature left the 0-50 C band. Everything the world learned about conditions inside the first satellite, it learned from how long the beeps were. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Sputnik 1' (Power and Telemetry Systems; Telemetry Signals and Data Collection); Wikipedia, 'Sputnik 1'.

question: William Guier and George Weiffenbach ran their tapes of Sputnik's rising and falling tone through a newly delivered Univac computer and proved something nobody had claimed. A single overhead pass holds enough information to fix a satellite's whole orbit. But the proof came with one strict condition attached. What was it?
answer: It needed nearly the whole curve, horizon to horizon
choices: It needed nearly the whole curve, horizon to horizon
It needed the transmitter's exact frequency known beforehand
It needed the satellite's altitude known to a few kilometres
It needed each beep timed to a thousandth of a second
context: Nine unknowns came out of one pass at once: six orbital parameters plus three system parameters -- a correction for the satellite's oscillator frequency, its drift, and a one-parameter model of the electron density of the upper air. That last one they had not gone looking for; the ionosphere fell out of the arithmetic as a free bonus. Source: Guier & Weiffenbach, 'Genesis of Satellite Navigation,' JHU APL Technical Digest. (The machine was a Univac 1200F, not the 1103A that some secondary accounts name.)

question: Frank McClure called William Guier and George Weiffenbach into his office at the Applied Physics Laboratory on Monday 17 March 1958 and asked them to shut the door. For five months the two had been reading a satellite's orbit out of the rising and falling tone of its beep. McClure first checked that they still stood by that claim, then asked one more question. What did he ask?
answer: Could they solve for the listener's position, given a known orbit?
choices: Could they solve for the listener's position, given a known orbit?
Could they fix an orbit from a pass recorded by a ship at sea?
Could they cut the computing down so a fix took minutes?
Could they measure how an orbit drifted over weeks rather than minutes?
context: In their own words: 'Mac asked if we could invert the solution, i.e., determine the station position while assuming the orbit is known.' Guier and Weiffenbach had solved for the SATELLITE; McClure asked for the OBSERVER. That is the birth of satellite navigation -- and the credit is worth getting exactly right: the two physicists did not invent it. Their director's question did. Sources: Guier & Weiffenbach, 'Genesis of Satellite Navigation,' JHU APL Technical Digest (direct quotes); date corroborated by Grokipedia, 'Transit (satellite)'.

question: Frank McClure's Applied Physics Laboratory threw out a Naval Observatory plan in 1958, though its math was sound. The US Navy's Polaris missile would be shot from a submerged sub, which had to fix its own position within a few hundred feet before firing. The plan was a three-foot dish on a stabilised platform, swinging to track a satellite across the sky. What was the laboratory's objection?
answer: The dish would have shown up on an enemy's radar screen
choices: The dish would have shown up on an enemy's radar screen
The dish would have been heard turning by enemy sonar
The dish would have drawn more power than the boat could spare
The dish would have needed a fresh orbit table every week
context: The Naval Observatory plan mounted a three-foot dish on a stabilised platform to take direction measurements, which made 'an easily detectable target for radar.' The Applied Physics Laboratory ruled out active sonar imaging of the ocean bottom for the same kind of reason: it was 'a no-no for Polaris submarines, which were to be undetectable.' What won was the method that gave the boat nothing to give away -- a Doppler fix needs only a simple non-directional antenna, so the boat listens and says nothing. The idea reached Polaris through Frank McClure, the APL department head who had been spending part of his time at the Navy's Special Projects Office, the office building Polaris. On the Friday he learned of Guier and Weiffenbach's progress he phoned his close friend Dick Kershner, and over that one weekend the two of them designed the essentials of Transit: polar-orbiting satellites radiating two ultrastable frequencies encoded with their own orbits, a ground network solving the direct problem, and injection stations uploading fresh orbit parameters back to each satellite. Source: Guier & Weiffenbach, 'Genesis of Satellite Navigation,' JHU APL Technical Digest (direct quotes).

question: Frank McClure asked William Guier and George Weiffenbach to flip their problem, known orbit and unknown listener, and he expected the new problem to be more accurate. He was right: their tests came back with what they called 'unbelievable accuracy'. What made the flipped problem the easier one?
answer: Five unknowns to solve from the same data, not nine
choices: Five unknowns to solve from the same data, not nine
Twice as many minutes of usable curve in the same pass
Two independent checks on the same orbit instead of one
One free parameter dropped from the ionosphere model
context: Solving for the orbit: six orbital plus three system parameters, nine. Solving for the observer: two position plus three system parameters, five -- and with one further trick it could be pushed down to three. 'The very first simulations indicated great accuracy -- unbelievable accuracy! When we reported excitedly back to Mac, he, of course, was not surprised.' Fewer unknowns from the same data is the whole reason satellite navigation works better than satellite tracking. Source: Guier & Weiffenbach, 'Genesis of Satellite Navigation,' JHU APL Technical Digest (direct quote and parameter counts).

question: A Navy navigator tunes in a Transit satellite, the operational descendant of William Guier and George Weiffenbach's work, and finds it sending two signals at once: 150 and 400 megahertz. He needs only one signal to trace a Doppler curve, and a second transmitter on every satellite cost mass, power and money. What did the second frequency buy him?
answer: A way to cancel the bending of the signal by the charged upper air
choices: A way to cancel the bending of the signal by the charged upper air
A way to cancel the drift of the satellite's own crystal oscillator
A way to cancel the error from the ship's uncertain compass heading
A way to cancel the delay introduced by the receiver's own circuits
context: The ionosphere bends radio waves by an amount that depends on their frequency, so comparing the same pass at 150 and 400 MHz lets that error be subtracted out instead of guessed at -- which is what dropped the fix from five unknowns to three. The cost in patience was real: a fix took the whole 10-15 minute horizon-to-horizon pass of ONE satellite, gave about 200 metres, and you waited an hour or two at mid-latitudes for the next pass, several hours near the equator. Transit could not navigate anything moving fast, which is why aircraft never used it. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Transit (satellite)'; Wikipedia, 'Transit (satellite)'; Smithsonian Time and Navigation, 'Transit Satellites'.

question: A cyclist checks her phone, and its GPS receiver times how long signals from several satellites take to arrive. Transit, the ancestor that handed the job over on 31 December 1996, did not work that way. Three satellites are already enough to fix a point on Earth. Why does the receiver need a fourth?
answer: To correct the error in the receiver's own clock
choices: To correct the error in the receiver's own clock
To supply the receiver's height above sea level
To check the other three against a fourth fix
To replace whichever satellite sets first
context: GPS.gov: 'It takes four GPS satellites to calculate a precise location on the Earth... three to determine a position on the Earth, and one to adjust for the error in the receiver's clock.' The satellites carry atomic clocks good to about 40 nanoseconds; the receiver in your pocket does not, so the fourth signal buys the clock correction. Different measurement, same ancestry. And the Transit satellites were never switched off: on 1 January 1997 the survivors were repurposed as dual-frequency beacons for the Navy Ionospheric Monitoring System, and Transit 5B-5, launched in 1964, is still transmitting. Sources: GPS.gov, 'Trilateration' and 'GPS and Telling Time'; Grokipedia, 'Transit (satellite)'.

question: Thales of Miletus rubbed one material with cloth or fur around 600 BC, and it pulled straw across a table. William Gilbert, a physician, built the Latin 'electricus' from its Greek name in 1600. What is the word 'electricity' named after?
answer: Amber, hardened resin of ancient trees
choices: Amber, hardened resin of ancient trees
Jet, fossil wood polished coal-black
Lodestone, a magnetic iron ore
Rock crystal, clear mountain quartz
context: The Greek for amber is 'elektron'. Thales' note, around 600-585 BC, is the oldest recorded electrical observation, and Gilbert's De Magnete (1600) coined 'electricus' from it while separating this rubbing-attraction from magnetism. The whole science is named after a lump of tree resin. [Grokipedia, Triboelectric effect: Historical Development; Key Scientific Milestones]

question: A student drags a plastic comb through her clean dry hair on a winter morning. The strands lift up, fan out and refuse to lie back down against each other. Why do the strands hold apart?
answer: Each strand carries the same charge, and like charges repel
choices: Each strand carries the same charge, and like charges repel
The comb stripped away the oil that weighs each strand down
Rubbing warmed the strands, and warm hair curls up and out
The comb's own charge tugs every strand out behind it
context: The comb comes away negative and the hair positive. Try the same thing in a steamy bathroom and it barely works: humid air carries the charge away as fast as the comb gathers it, which is why static is a dry-weather phenomenon. [Grokipedia, Triboelectric effect: Everyday and Natural Examples; Environmental Influences]

question: A boy rubs a balloon on his dry hair and holds it beside a thin stream falling from a tap, and the water bends toward it. A glass rod rubbed with silk carries the opposite charge, yet the stream bends toward that too. Why does water lean toward either charge?
answer: Each water molecule is lopsided and free to spin, turning an attracting face outward
choices: Each water molecule is lopsided and free to spin, turning an attracting face outward
The stream takes the opposite charge from the air, so it is always pulled in
Falling water holds no charge at all, and simply drifts toward any nearby object
Tap water is full of dissolved salts, and those free ions answer either charge
context: This is polarisation: a water molecule has a positive end and a negative end, and it rotates in place rather than gaining any charge, so a positive rod and a negative rod attract it equally well. That is also why this lovely kitchen test cannot tell you which object ended up positive and which negative -- both do exactly the same thing to the stream. [The Physics Classroom, 'Polarization'; University of Houston Physics Outreach, 'Bending Water with a Balloon']

question: A farmer on his porch sees a flash and starts counting out loud. Lightning and its thunder leave the strike at the same instant, but light travels roughly a million times faster than sound, so his count is really the sound walking toward his ears. How many seconds does that walk take per mile?
answer: About five seconds
choices: About one second
About five seconds
About fifteen seconds
About thirty seconds
context: Five seconds per mile, three per kilometre. NOAA's rule of thumb: if the thunder arrives within 30 seconds of the flash, the strike was inside six miles and you should already be indoors. [NOAA JetStream, 'Determining distance to a thunderstorm']

question: Ewald Georg von Kleist, an amateur electrical experimenter in Pomerania, rigged up a device of his own in October 1745, charged it and touched it. The shock left his whole arm and shoulder numb, the first strong electric jolt anyone had ever stored up. What was the device that hit him?
answer: A medicine bottle of alcohol with a nail through the cork
choices: A medicine bottle of alcohol with a nail through the cork
A glass globe spun against a dry woollen pad on a stand
An iron bar slung from a ceiling beam on silk cords
A cake of hard resin in a dish, rubbed hard with fur
context: Kleist filled a small medicine bottle with alcohol, pushed a nail through the cork and charged it -- the first of the charge-storing jars, able to hold a charge and hand it back all at once. Wikipedia dates the invention 11 October 1745, Grokipedia 15 October; the exact day is not settled across sources. For a while the device was called the Kleistian jar. [Wikipedia, Ewald Georg von Kleist; Grokipedia, Leyden jar: Invention and Independent Discoveries]

question: Pieter van Musschenbroek, a professor at Leiden, tried the new charge-storing trick in his own lab in 1746 and took the full shock. It scared him so much that he wrote to the French naturalist Reaumur, begging him never to try it. The letter was read to the Academy of Sciences that April, and the news raced across Europe. How did Musschenbroek say he would refuse a second shock?
answer: He would not do it again for the whole kingdom of France
choices: He would not do it again for the whole kingdom of France
He would not do it again for all the gold of the Indies
He would not do it again for a place in the French Academy
He would not do it again for the crown of Prussia
context: The letter, in Latin, dated 20 January 1746, opens: 'I would like to tell you about a new but terrible experiment, which I advise you never to try yourself, nor would I, who have experienced it and survived by the grace of God, do it again for all the kingdom of France.' Reaumur passed it to Abbe Nollet, who read it to the Academy on 20 April 1746. Nollet then named the device the Leyden jar after Musschenbroek's city -- though Kleist had built one months earlier in Pomerania, so it is named for the wrong city and the wrong man. [Linda Hall Library, Scientist of the Day: Pieter van Musschenbroek]

question: Abbe Jean-Antoine Nollet, tutor in physics to the French royal family, persuaded about two hundred Carthusian monks in 1746 to stand in a great circle, roughly a mile in circumference, each man joined to the next by a length of iron wire. He discharged a battery of Leyden jars into the ring. What did the monks do?
answer: Every man leapt at the same instant, the whole mile around
choices: Every man leapt at the same instant, the whole mile around
The men nearest the jars leapt, and the rest felt nothing
The jolt ran round the ring slowly enough for Nollet to time it
The shock faded out after some forty men and stopped there
context: The timing was the whole point: the effect crossed a mile faster than anyone could catch by eye, so whatever electricity was, it travelled enormously fast. Nollet ran the same stunt at court, discharging a jar through a chain of 180 royal guardsmen in front of King Louis XV, and the whole line sprang into the air together. Nollet was no showman-crank; he was Franklin's serious scientific opponent. [Wikipedia, Jean-Antoine Nollet; Grokipedia, Leyden jar: Historical Uses]

question: Three men took their places in a demonstration Benjamin Franklin described to Peter Collinson in London in May 1747. One stood on wax and rubbed a glass tube, a second on wax drew a spark off him, and a third on the floor could draw a spark from either. From this Franklin stated a rule about rubbing that physics has kept ever since. What was the rule?
answer: Rubbing does not make electric fire; it collects what matter already holds
choices: Rubbing does not make electric fire; it collects what matter already holds
Rubbing creates fresh electric fire, and the harder you rub the more of it
Rubbing squeezes the electric fire out of glass, which alone stores it
Rubbing opens the pores of a body so an outward stream of fire escapes
context: Franklin to Collinson, 25 May 1747: 'the Electrical Fire was not created by Friction, but collected, being an Element diffused among, and attracted by other Matter.' The same letter coins the words still in use: 'We say B (and other Bodies alike circumstanced) are electrised positively; A negatively: Or rather B is electrised plus and A minus.' The 'pores' choice was no joke either -- that was Abbe Nollet's rival theory of 1746, an electrical atmosphere of effluent and affluent streams, which he defended against Franklin as late as 1760. [Franklin to Collinson, 25 May 1747, Founders Online 01-03-02]

question: A girl crosses a carpet on a dry winter day and reaches for a metal doorknob, and a spark jumps a clear millimetre from her fingertip. Air is one of the better insulators around until the electrical squeeze across it gets steep enough, and then it gives way all at once. Roughly what voltage is she carrying?
answer: About three thousand volts
choices: About thirty volts
About three hundred volts
About three thousand volts
About thirty thousand volts
context: Air stops insulating at roughly three million volts per metre at sea level -- about three kilovolts per millimetre. A spark you can watch jump one millimetre therefore means you were carrying something like three thousand volts across it. [Grokipedia, Lightning: Electric Field Development and Leaders; dielectric-strength reference, getacademy.blog]

question: A hiker watches a thundercloud build over a ridge. Up in its cold middle, roughly minus fifteen to minus twenty Celsius, updraughts drive tiny ice crystals up past graupel, soft hail pellets grown heavy by supercooled droplets freezing onto them. Crystal and pellet touch for an instant and bounce apart, and that contact is where a storm's charge is made. What does the collision leave behind?
answer: The graupel negative and falling, the light crystals positive and rising
choices: The graupel negative and falling, the light crystals positive and rising
The graupel positive and falling, the light crystals negative and rising
Both kinds of ice neutral, with the charge carried by the air between them
Both kinds of ice negative, with the positive charge left on the raindrops
context: That is how a cloud becomes a stacked battery kilometres tall: negative graupel sinking toward the base, positive crystals riding to the anvil. The sign is not fixed, though -- Takahashi's 1978 riming experiments found a charge-reversal temperature between about -20 and -10 C, warmer than which the graupel charges positive instead, which is why real storms carry a lower positive pocket and why the lab physics is still being parameterised. And the folk story is simply wrong: clouds do not rub against each other. [Grokipedia, Lightning: Charge Separation Processes; Saunders & Peck / Takahashi 1978 review, Atmospheric Research]

question: Benjamin Franklin pictured a single electric fluid in the 1740s, when nobody knew what was doing the moving, and he called a body with a surplus of it plus, a body short of it minus. Nearly a hundred and fifty years later the electron was identified, and it proved to be the particle that actually drifts along a copper wire. How is current drawn on a circuit diagram today?
answer: From plus to minus, against the way the electrons drift
choices: From plus to minus, against the way the electrons drift
From minus to plus, following the way the electrons drift
In whichever direction the charge in that wire moves
With the terminals marked but the direction left off
context: Franklin had to guess the direction of the flow before anyone knew what was flowing, and he guessed backwards: the electron carries the negative charge and drifts from minus to plus. Rather than relabel a century and a half of work, physics kept his convention, so conventional current still runs plus to minus in every schematic while the electrons in the copper go the other way. [W. B. Jensen, 'The Origin of Positive and Negative in Electricity'; WHYY on Franklin's nomenclature]

question: A man jumps and swears at a spark from a doorknob while lightning splits a tree outside his window. The two break the air down at the very same field strength, yet one stings and the other kills people. If the breakdown physics is identical, what actually separates them?
answer: The charge behind it: a whole charged person holds about a hundredth of a joule
choices: The charge behind it: a whole charged person holds about a hundredth of a joule
The voltage behind it: a fingertip spark never climbs past about a hundred volts
The path it takes: a bolt drives current through the chest, a spark over the skin
The conductor it meets: dry human skin turns away most of what a spark carries
context: The standard engineering model of a charged person is a 100-picofarad capacitor; even at a brutal 15,000 volts that stores only about 11 millijoules, dumped in well under a microsecond. Lightning at the same volts-per-metre threshold carries tens of coulombs, peak currents near 30,000 amperes and potential differences of hundreds of millions of volts. Same physics, same breakdown field -- the entire difference is how much charge is standing behind it. [Wikipedia, Human-body model; Grokipedia, Lightning: Discharge Dynamics]

question: A pilot flies an armoured aircraft straight through a thundercloud, field meters running, to measure the electric field inside a storm about to fire. Instrumented balloons and rockets have made the same trip for decades. Air breaks down and sparks at about three million volts per metre; below that value it holds as an insulator. What is the strongest field anyone has ever measured inside a thundercloud?
answer: About a third of the breakdown value
choices: About a third of the breakdown value
About equal to the breakdown value
About three times the breakdown value
About ten times the breakdown value
context: Decades of instrumented flights have never found a field strong enough to break air down: ordinary storms sit near a tenth of the critical threshold, and the strongest field ever measured inside a thundercloud reaches only about a third of it. Joseph Dwyer of the University of New Hampshire: 'You have to increase the electric field all the way above the conventional breakdown threshold. But that doesn't seem to happen in nature.' Three candidates are live and none decisive: relativistic runaway electrons cascading near light speed and throwing off gamma rays (NASA's July 2023 ALOFT flights found clouds glowing and flickering in gamma rays with no visible lightning); cosmic-ray air showers as the trigger (Xuan-Min Shao of Los Alamos reported radio evidence in 2025 that David Smith of UC Santa Cruz called 'extremely convincing'); and needle-sharp ice crystals amplifying the local field tenfold. Victor Pasko's 2025 modelling paper was reported in the press as having solved it; the field does not treat it as settled. Dwyer again: 'It just gets more and more bizarre the more we look.' [Quanta Magazine, 'What Causes Lightning? The Answer Keeps Getting More Interesting', 6 May 2026]

question: Juan Carlos Sobarzo and Scott Waitukaitis, in Austria, cut blocks from one batch of silicone and touched them together in pairs, thousands of times over. Same material, same treatment: no block had a reason to prefer a direction. At first the blocks charged each other at random, as expected. After roughly two hundred contacts the behaviour changed, and no one yet knows why. What did the identical blocks start doing?
answer: Sorting into a fixed order set by how many contacts each had already had
choices: Sorting into a fixed order set by how many contacts each had already had
Charging harder with every contact, but still in random directions
Refusing to exchange charge at all, as if the surfaces had worn smooth
Tracking the room's humidity, flipping direction as the air dried out
