context: Published in Nature in February 2025. The block with more contacts in its history reliably charged negative against one with fewer -- contact history, not material identity, set the order. Sobarzo on the moment it appeared: 'I took a set of samples I had at hand... and to my disbelief, I saw that they ordered in a series.' The suspected cause is that repeated contact smooths nanoscale roughness, but the mechanism is not pinned down. Nor is the effect itself: a standard review of contact electrification notes it 'has been studied for more than 2500 years' while 'a fundamental understanding of the mechanism behind contact electrification remains elusive', and physicists still argue whether rubbing two insulators transfers electrons, ions or literal scraps of material. The balloon on your head is not a solved problem. [Sobarzo et al., Nature 638:664-669 (2025); Lacks & Sankaran, J. Phys. D 44 (2011) 453001]

question: James Till and Ernest McCulloch injected bone marrow cells in 1961 into mice they had irradiated to wipe out the animals' own marrow. Days later small raised lumps stood out on the spleens. One thing about those lumps founded a whole field. What was it?
answer: They rose in number with each extra cell injected
choices: They rose in number with each extra cell injected
They always appeared at the same six spots
They formed only after the highest radiation dose
They faded within a week, then came back
context: That steady proportion is the whole trick: it meant each lump grew from one injected cell, so you could COUNT something nobody had ever seen. The test is still called CFU-S, 'colony forming unit - spleen', and the lumps are counted 8 to 12 days after injection: long enough for one cell to build a visible colony, short enough that you can still tell the colonies apart. The paper that founded stem cell biology never says 'stem cell' in its title. It is Till JE & McCulloch EA, 'A direct measurement of the radiation sensitivity of normal mouse bone marrow cells,' Radiation Research 14:213-222, 1961: they were measuring how much radiation marrow could survive, and the spleen lumps were the tool, not the target. Till was a biophysicist who thought in radiation survival curves; McCulloch was a hematologist who knew blood and leukemia. The physicist supplied the counting, the physician supplied the marrow, and neither could have done it alone. They shared the Gairdner Award in 1969 and the Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research in 2005. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Hematopoietic stem cell'; Wikipedia, 'James Till' and 'Ernest McCulloch'; PubMed PMID 13776896.

question: A doctor studies a sample of a patient's bone marrow. That marrow turns out more than 500 billion new blood cells every single day, and every one of them descends from a blood stem cell. How common are blood stem cells inside the marrow itself?
answer: About one marrow cell in ten thousand
choices: About one marrow cell in ten thousand
About one marrow cell in ten
About one marrow cell in three hundred
About one marrow cell in a billion
context: One in ten thousand is the older estimate, and the strict modern markers make it rarer still: as few as one marrow cell in a hundred thousand, or even one in a million, qualifies as a true blood-forming stem cell. Out of that vanishingly thin seed the body rebuilds its entire blood supply, over and over, every day of your life. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Hematopoietic stem cell'; Grokipedia, 'Hematopoietic stem cell'.

question: John Gurdon showed with frog eggs that a mature adult cell could be reprogrammed all the way back into an embryo, and he shared the 2012 Nobel Prize for it. On his office desk at Cambridge he kept exactly one document framed for the rest of his life. Which document was it?
answer: The Eton report judging his hopes of science ridiculous
choices: The Eton report judging his hopes of science ridiculous
The Oxford letter refusing him a place to read zoology
The Eton ruling barring him from the advanced science exams
The Oxford timetable putting him back to school-level science
context: The 1949 Eton biology report reads: 'His small ability has been used to the full... he has ideas about becoming a scientist; on his present showing this is quite ridiculous; if he can't learn simple biological facts he would have no chance of doing the work of a specialist, and it would be a sheer waste of time, both on his part and of those who would have to teach him.' The master was not being unfair. Gurdon ranked LAST out of the 250 boys in his year in biology, sat in the bottom set for every science subject, and Eton barred him from the advanced science exams. He got into Christ Church, Oxford to read CLASSICS, switched to zoology after a term, and had to spend a preliminary year doing school-level physics, chemistry and biology to qualify. On why he kept the report where he could see it: 'When you have problems like an experiment doesn't work, which often happens, it's nice to remind yourself that perhaps after all you are not so good at this job.' Sir John Gurdon died on 7 October 2025, five days after his ninety-second birthday. Sources: Grokipedia, 'John Gurdon'; Wikipedia, 'John Gurdon'.

question: E. Donnall Thomas reported his first six human bone marrow transplants in 1957, and doctors worldwide attempted about 200 through the 1950s and 1960s. A transplant of blood stem cells is the one stem cell treatment that has genuinely saved lives, with about 90,000 done every year. How many of those early patients survived long-term?
answer: None of them
choices: None of them
Two of them
Twenty of them
Fifty of them
context: Thomas's first six patients were all dead within weeks, and across the whole world through two decades the running total of long-term survivors stayed at zero. He kept going for another ten years anyway, and shared the 1990 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Joseph Murray. He had started with DOGS in 1955 at a small hospital in Cooperstown, New York, on money from the US Atomic Energy Commission, which wanted a treatment for radiation exposure and was not thinking about leukemia at all. More than a million of these transplants have now been done, for leukemia, lymphoma and severe aplastic anemia; the first umbilical cord blood transplant was performed in 1988, for a child with Fanconi anemia. Sources: Grokipedia, 'E. Donnall Thomas' and 'Hematopoietic stem cell'.

question: Andy Becker, a graduate student of James Till and Ernest McCulloch, proved in 1963 what the two could only argue in 1961: each spleen lump was the offspring of a single injected cell. He marked the donor marrow cells before injecting them, then looked inside a single lump and found every cell there carrying the same mark. What was the mark?
answer: A random pattern of chromosome breaks made by radiation
choices: A random pattern of chromosome breaks made by radiation
A dye bound into the nucleus and passed to daughter cells
A radioactive atom built into the cell's own DNA
A virus tag dropped at a random point in the genome
context: The mark was chromosome damage. Andy Becker irradiated the donor cells to snap their chromosomes, and because the breaks fall differently in every cell, the pattern works as a private signature: no two cells carry the same one. Every cell inside a single spleen lump carried the identical scar, which meant the lump was one cell's family and nobody else's. Published as Becker, McCulloch & Till, 'Cytological demonstration of the clonal nature of spleen colonies derived from transplanted mouse marrow cells,' Nature 197:452-454, 1963. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Ernest McCulloch' and 'James Till'.

question: Lou Siminovitch joined James Till and Ernest McCulloch in breaking apart a single spleen colony and injecting the pieces into a second irradiated mouse. By 1963 Till and McCulloch could reliably grow such a colony from one injected marrow cell. What did that second mouse show?
answer: The pieces built fresh colonies, just as the first mouse had
choices: The pieces built fresh colonies, just as the first mouse had
The pieces built mature blood cells, a full wave of them
The pieces built colonies in the marrow, deep in the leg bones
The pieces built colonies of red cells, thousands of them
context: Self-renewal. The broken-up colony still contained fresh colony-FORMING cells, able to start the entire process over again in a new animal. Till and McCulloch already knew that one spleen colony held several different kinds of blood cell; what they did not know was whether the colony could restart itself. It was this experiment, not the first, that gave biology its definition of a stem cell: self-renewal, plus many kinds of blood cell from one ancestor. A cell that makes many kinds of offspring and then runs out is not a stem cell; a cell that also copies itself is. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ernest McCulloch'.

question: John Gurdon destroyed the nucleus of an African clawed frog's egg with ultraviolet light at Oxford in 1962 and slid in a nucleus taken from another cell. A normal tadpole hatched and swam. The whole force of the result rested on where that replacement nucleus had come from. Where?
answer: The gut lining of a tadpole already feeding
choices: The gut lining of a tadpole already feeding
The skin of an adult frog's webbed hind foot
The tail muscle of a tadpole already swimming
The heart blood of a fully grown adult frog
context: An intestinal cell of a feeding tadpole has already committed to being gut, and it still carried the complete instructions for building a whole animal. Specialising is not deleting. The odds were brutal: 712 nuclear transfers produced 18 normal, fertile adult frogs, about 1 to 2 percent, with most embryos dying or coming out malformed from incomplete reprogramming. The 18 that worked were enough. Gurdon's supervisor was Michail Fischberg, and a lucky lab accident made the proof possible: Fischberg's frog colony carried a '1-nu' nucleolar mutation, a marker visible inside the nucleus, which let Gurdon show the tadpole had grown from the DONOR nucleus and not from a surviving egg nucleus. No marker, no proof. Sources: Grokipedia, 'John Gurdon'; Wikipedia, 'John Gurdon'.

question: Haruko Obokata of Japan's RIKEN (Institute of Physical and Chemical Research) published two papers in the journal Nature in January 2014, claiming she could reset ordinary mouse cells to an embryo-like state with no added genes at all. Nature's own news page called it an easy path to stem cells, and Obokata, then 30, was on magazine covers within days. What was her treatment?
answer: Half an hour's soak in a mildly acidic bath
choices: Half an hour's soak in a mildly acidic bath
A brief squeeze through a narrow glass tube
A short chill to just above freezing point
A pulse of ultraviolet light across the dish
context: Thirty minutes at pH 5.7, and she called the result STAP cells - stimulus-triggered acquisition of pluripotency. Nature's news headline ran: 'Acid bath offers easy path to stem cells.' It was cheap, it needed no genes, and it was on front pages worldwide within days. Source: Grokipedia, 'Stimulus-triggered acquisition of pluripotency'.

question: A team in Basel repeated John Gurdon's nuclear transfer in 1975. Doubters of his 1962 tadpoles had a fair point: a scraping of tadpole gut might hide a stray unspecialised cell, and if it did, the experiment proved nothing. The team used a donor cell that put the doubt to rest. Which cell did they use?
answer: A white blood cell actively making one antibody
choices: A white blood cell actively making one antibody
A muscle fibre actively pulling a swimming leg
A pigment cell actively making dark melanin
A nerve cell actively firing along the spinal cord
context: A lymphocyte churning out a single specific antibody wears its finished identity as a molecular badge - there is no arguing it might secretly be an unspecialised stray. The group at the Basel Institute for Immunology transplanted that nucleus and got living tadpoles, and the objection died. This is worth sitting with: Gurdon's result was doubted for a GOOD reason, not a stupid one. The critics also pointed out that the egg's own nucleus might not have been fully destroyed by the ultraviolet light. Thirteen years of doubt was the system working, not failing. Sources: Wikipedia, 'John Gurdon'; Grokipedia, 'John Gurdon', section 'Criticisms and Scientific Skepticism Encountered'.

question: Investigators sequenced the DNA of Haruko Obokata's famous cells after labs all over the world had tried her 2014 stem cell recipe and none could make it work. Japan's RIKEN (Institute of Physical and Chemical Research) had found research misconduct in April, and Nature had retracted both papers in July. What did the sequencing show the cells were?
answer: Ordinary embryonic stem cells from that same lab
choices: Ordinary embryonic stem cells from that same lab
Skin cells that had swollen and merely looked reset
Cancer cells that will grow in almost any dish
Cells from a second mouse strain mixed in by mistake
context: The 'STAP cells' were contaminated with embryonic stem cells that were already growing in the laboratory. RIKEN's inquiry, reported on 1 April 2014, also found fabricated Western blot images and duplicated gel lanes; both papers were retracted on 2 July 2014; Waseda University revoked Obokata's PhD in November 2015. A 2015 replication effort run through seven laboratories, led from Harvard Medical School and Boston Children's Hospital, produced nothing at all. Here is the part worth remembering: the STAP manuscripts had already been submitted in 2012 and rejected by Nature, Science AND Cell for insufficient evidence of real reprogramming. They were revised and accepted a year later. The first refusals were right. Exciting is not the same as true, and replication - not fame, not a headline, not a journal's name - is what decides. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Stimulus-triggered acquisition of pluripotency'.

question: Shinya Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi began in 2006 with 24 genes known to be switched on in embryonic cells, loaded all 24 into adult mouse skin cells by virus, and found that a tiny fraction of the cells reset to an embryo-like state. With 24 suspects in the dish, that result singled out no gene. How did the two men work out which genes actually did it?
answer: They removed the genes one at a time and re-tested
choices: They removed the genes one at a time and re-tested
They added the genes back one at a time from none
They read which genes stayed switched on afterwards
They matched the list against human embryonic cells
context: Subtract one, see whether the resetting survives; if it collapses, that gene mattered. Twenty-four came down to four: Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc, published in Cell on 25 August 2006. Only 0.01 to 0.1 percent of the cells reset - but the ones that did reset all the way. Yamanaka named them 'iPS cells' with a deliberate lowercase i, borrowing the naming style of the iPod in the hope the name would spread the way Apple's products had. In November 2007 James Thomson's group and Yamanaka's group independently reported human iPS cells on the same day, Thomson using a different quartet: Oct4, Sox2, Nanog and Lin28. On 8 October 2012 the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institutet gave the Prize in Physiology or Medicine jointly to Gurdon and Yamanaka 'for the discovery that mature cells can be reprogrammed to become pluripotent' - one prize covering an experiment from 1962 and an experiment from 2006, fifty years apart, same idea. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Shinya Yamanaka'; Wikipedia, 'Induced pluripotent stem cell'.

question: Shinya Yamanaka's team published their answer to a deadly problem in 2007. Their four-factor recipe had reset adult mouse cells, and then roughly a quarter of the mice given cells made that way died of tumours. The culprit was one of the four factors, c-Myc, a gene long known to drive cancer. What was the answer?
answer: Drop c-Myc, and accept a far slower, rarer reset
choices: Drop c-Myc, and accept a far slower, rarer reset
Deliver c-Myc as protein rather than as a gene
Swap c-Myc for a factor borrowed from human eggs
Screen the tumour-forming cells out after the reset
context: The three-factor recipe is much less efficient and much safer: the fix cost speed and bought safety, which is what most real fixes do. Yamanaka's reason for wanting a route that did not use embryos at all was personal - looking through a microscope at a frozen human embryo in a fertility clinic, he thought of his own daughters. He has said: 'My position has always been that if we can avoid using human embryos, we should do so.' The first human trial using iPS-derived cells began in Japan in 2014, sheets of retinal pigment epithelium transplanted into patients with wet macular degeneration. It was suspended in 2015 over concerns about the reprogramming protocol, then resumed using donor-derived cells: eight years from bench to a patient's eye, with a stop in the middle. Meanwhile more than 550 unlicensed clinics in the United States alone sell 'stem cell cures' that have never passed a trial, typically for 10,000 to 20,000 dollars with no insurance cover; documented harms include blindness and tumours, and in 2018 the FDA forced roughly 500,000 dollars in refunds from fat-derived stem cell marketers. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Induced pluripotent stem cell' and 'Stem-cell therapy'; Grokipedia, 'Shinya Yamanaka'.

question: Two fishermen dragged a huge sea animal ashore near Livorno in October 1666, and the Grand Duke of Tuscany sent a piece to his anatomist, Nicolas Steno. His dissection told him what the triangular 'tongue stones' of Malta's hillsides really were. What are tongue stones?
answer: the teeth of sharks
choices: the teeth of sharks
the claws of crabs
the beaks of squid
the spines of rays
context: The piece the Grand Duke sent was the head. Steno published the result in 1667, and not as a book about sharks: it was tacked onto a treatise on the geometry of muscle - 'Elementorum myologiae specimen... cui accedunt canis carchariae dissectum caput', 'to which is added the dissected head of a shark'. The stones are teeth from once-living animals, buried in mud and sand that later hardened around them. Some Maltese tongue stones run over 180 mm (7.1 in) from tip to base: megalodon teeth, the largest shark teeth known. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Nicolas Steno' and 'Megalodon'; UCMP Berkeley, 'Nicolas Steno'.

question: A European noble hangs a little triangular tongue stone round his neck as a pendant, long before anyone knows what such stones are. He has paid well for it and will not travel without it. What does he believe the stone has done for him?
answer: protected him from poison
choices: protected him from poison
sharpened his eyes at dusk
kept fever out of his blood
won him favour at court
context: Tongue stones were believed to cure poisons and snakebite, so nobles and royalty wore them as pendants or kept them in their pockets as good-luck charms - a fossil tooth carried as an anti-poison amulet. Pliny the Elder, writing around AD 73, had recorded a different account: he said the triangular stones fell from the sky during lunar eclipses, and thought they resembled petrified human tongues. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Glossopetrae' and 'Megalodon'.  (Legend.)

question: Maltese islanders told a story by the 1100s to explain the small triangular stones that turned up everywhere in their hillside rock. It fastened on the Apostle Paul, shipwrecked on the island in the Book of Acts, and the Maltese still call the stones by his name. What did the story say the stones were?
answer: serpents that Paul turned to stone
choices: serpents that Paul turned to stone
tears that Paul wept, hardened in the rock
nails of the wrecked ship, gone to stone
hailstones of that storm, set hard as flint
context: In Maltese the stones are 'Ilsien San Pawl', Saint Paul's tongue; German calls them 'Natternzungen', adder's tongues. The serpent story is why the stones were credited with power against venom. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Megalodon' and 'Glossopetrae'.  (Legend.)

question: Walking the hills near Florence, Nicolas Steno studied cliffs built of flat bands of rock stacked one on another like the pages of a shut book. Geologists call these bands strata, and the lowest were laid down first. Comparing the lower bands with those above, he noticed something no one had reported. What was it?
answer: the lower bands held no fossils at all
choices: the lower bands held no fossils at all
the upper bands held no fossils at all
the lower bands held the larger fossils
both bands held the very same fossils
context: In the Apennines Steno found lower layers with no fossils at all lying under fossil-rich upper layers - the first geological evidence of distinct periods in Earth's history. Reading a cliff from the bottom up is superposition, his first rule, and it turns a cliff into a stack of time. Steno's own wording: 'At the time when a given stratum was being formed, there was beneath it another substance which prevented the further descent of the comminuted matter.' Sources: Wikipedia, "Steno's laws"; UCMP Berkeley, 'Nicolas Steno'.

question: Fabio Colonna, an Italian botanist, printed a paper in 1616 arguing that tongue stones came from a real living creature. About fifty years later Nicolas Steno, a Dane working in Tuscany, got the famous credit for the idea, though he was not first. What did Steno add that Colonna had not?
answer: rules for reading the order of layers
choices: rules for reading the order of layers
a chemical test for stone and bone
a catalogue of every fossil then known
a measurement of the age of the Earth
context: Fabio Colonna (1567-1640) was one of the first members of the Accademia dei Lincei; his argument for the organic origin of glossopetrae ran in 'De glossopetris dissertatio', an appendix to his 'Ekphrasis altera' (1616; some sources date the demonstration to 1611). Epilepsy stopped him practising law after he graduated in 1589, so he turned to the ancient writers on medicine, botany and natural history. Agostino Scilla, a painter from Messina, made the same case in 1670 in 'La vana speculazione disingannata dal senso' - 'Vain Speculation Undeceived by Sense'. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Fabio Colonna', 'Glossopetrae', 'Agostino Scilla'.

question: Nicolas Steno printed his book on reading time out of rock in Florence in 1669, meaning it as a short preview of the full treatise to come. Its title carried the word 'Prodromus', Greek for forerunner, the runner sent ahead of the main body. What became of that full treatise?
answer: he never wrote it at all
choices: he never wrote it at all
the Inquisition seized it
it burned with his papers
his students finished it
context: The full title is 'De solido intra solidum naturaliter contento dissertationis prodromus' - 'Preliminary discourse to a dissertation on a solid body naturally contained within a solid'. UCMP Berkeley: 'He intended this as merely an introduction to a larger treatise he never completed.' Steno also left a law in a different science: the constancy of interfacial angles, which holds that the angles between corresponding faces of crystals of the same mineral are always the same. It is called the first law of crystallography. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Nicolas Steno', 'Prodromus', "Steno's laws"; UCMP Berkeley.

question: A geologist stops at a cliff where a band of rock stands almost on end, nearly vertical, its layering pointing at the sky. She reads the face the way a reader takes a page, with Nicolas Steno's four rules, and one of them settles what happened to that band. What does the rule say?
answer: it was tilted after it hardened
choices: it was tilted after it hardened
it was laid down on a steep slope
it was dumped by a fast current
it was squeezed while still soft
context: This is original horizontality: 'Layers of sediment are originally deposited horizontally under the action of gravity.' It is the rule that lets a geologist read violence in a cliff face. Honest caveat worth knowing: coarse sediment such as sand can come to rest at angles up to about 15 degrees, its angle of repose - but nothing settles standing on end. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Principle of original horizontality'; UCMP Berkeley, 'Nicolas Steno'.

question: Nicolas Steno asked a stranger question in 1669 than 'what is this stone?': how can one solid body end up sitting inside another? He looked closely at a stone tooth locked in a slab of rock. The rock had taken the exact shape of every ridge and serration of the tooth, while the tooth carried no mark of the rock at all. What did Steno say that one-sided fit proved?
answer: the tooth was hard before the rock
choices: the tooth was hard before the rock
the rock was hard before the tooth
the two of them hardened together
a fluid hardened the tooth in place
context: Steno's rule, in his own words: 'If a solid body is enclosed on all sides by another solid body, of the two bodies that one first became hard which, in the mutual contact, expresses on its own surface the properties of the other surface.' The tooth was buried first; the mud packed around it and only later set into rock. The idea that shapes grew inside rock had a respectable ancestor - Avicenna proposed petrifying fluids, succus lapidificatus, in 1027. Sources: UCMP Berkeley, 'Nicolas Steno'; Wikipedia, 'Nicolas Steno' and 'Fossil'.

question: A hiker stands on the rim of a canyon with a bright band of rock running along the wall below her. On the far wall, a kilometre off, the same band runs at the same height, the same colour, the same thickness. One of Nicolas Steno's four rules settles the matter. What does the band tell her about the canyon?
answer: the canyon was cut later, through a single layer
choices: the canyon was cut later, through a single layer
the canyon was there before the layer was laid
the canyon opened as the layer sagged and split
the canyon divided two basins that filled alike
context: This is lateral continuity. Steno's words: 'At the time when any given stratum was being formed it was either encompassed on its sides by another solid substance, or it covered the entire spherical surface of the earth.' A layer spreads until something stops it - so a band on one wall of a valley is the same band as on the far wall, and the valley was cut through it afterwards. Source: Wikipedia, "Steno's laws".

question: A student sketches three things written over a cliff's layers. A fault, a break where the rock has slipped, runs up through the lower layers but stops dead at an unconformity, a buried, worn-down surface with fresh layers on top. A dike, a sheet of once-molten rock, slices through the fault, the unconformity and everything above them. Steno's rules settle the order without a date. What is the order, oldest first?
answer: the fault, then the unconformity, then the dike
choices: the fault, then the unconformity, then the dike
the dike, then the fault, then the unconformity
the unconformity, then the fault, then the dike
the fault, then the dike, then the unconformity
context: The rule is cross-cutting: 'If a body or discontinuity cuts across a stratum, it must have formed after that stratum.' The fault is truncated by the unconformity, so the fault came first; the dike cuts both, so the dike is youngest. Steno stated the principle in 1669; James Hutton refined it in 'Theory of the Earth' (1795) and Charles Lyell in 'Principles of Geology' (1830). Stack Steno's four rules and you can order an entire cliff - still the working grammar of field geology 350 years on. Sources: Wikipedia, "Steno's laws" and 'Cross-cutting relationships'.

question: The naturalists of Europe watched Nicolas Steno publish his rules for reading time out of rock in 1669, at thirty-one. Then his interest in natural science drained away: he was ordained a priest, consecrated a bishop and sent to the missions of the Protestant north, where he died at Schwerin at forty-eight. What had the bishop done with his ring and cross, the silver marks of his office?
answer: he sold them and gave the money away
choices: he sold them and gave the money away
he had them melted into a chalice
he left them to his Medici patrons
he took them with him into his grave
context: Steno, the son of a Lutheran goldsmith in Copenhagen who worked for King Christian IV, converted to Catholicism on All Souls' Day 1667, influenced among others by Lavinia Cenami Arnolfini, a noblewoman of Lucca. Wikipedia: 'After his conversion, his interest in the natural sciences rapidly waned giving way to his interest in theology.' He was ordained on 13 April 1675, appointed Vicar Apostolic of the Nordic Missions on 21 August 1677 and consecrated titular bishop that September; he sold his bishop's ring and cross to help the needy. He died on 25 November 1686, aged 48, and Cosimo III de' Medici had the body shipped to Florence, where it lies in the Basilica of San Lorenzo. Pope John Paul II beatified him in 1988; his feast day is 5 December. Before any of the geology he had been an anatomist: he found the duct of the parotid salivary gland, still called Stensen's duct, and showed that the heart is an ordinary muscle, against both Galen and Descartes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Nicolas Steno'.

question: Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach fired silver atoms past a magnet at a glass plate in 1922. Old physics said the tiny atomic magnets point every which way, so the beam should land as one smeared blob. What actually landed on the plate?
answer: Two separate spots with a clean gap between them
choices: Two separate spots with a clean gap between them
One perfectly round central bullseye
A vertical rainbow of five bands
A single crescent bent toward the stronger pole
context: Nature refused every value but two. The gap is the whole point: no gradient, no in-between, just the discrete quantum answer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stern-Gerlach_experiment

question: Walther Gerlach was ready to write the run off: the silver film on the plate was so thin it was invisible. The pattern appeared only after Otto Stern leaned over the plate, a man on a junior salary who smoked cheap Frankfurt cigars. What developed the image?
answer: His breath turned the metal into jet-black silver sulfide
choices: His breath turned the metal into jet-black silver sulfide
The overhead gaslight slowly tarnished the film brown
A drop of mercury from the vacuum pump beaded on the deposit
Static from his wool jacket attracted floating soot particles
context: Sulfur in the cheap tobacco was the secret reagent -- clean breath does nothing, but bad-cigar breath converts silver to jet-black silver sulfide. In 2003 Bretislav Friedrich and Dudley Herschbach reconstructed the whole business in the laboratory and confirmed that only cigar smoke, not clean breath, does the developing. Sources: Friedrich & Herschbach, Physics Today, Dec 2003 ; backreaction.blogspot.com/2011/12/advent-calendar-16-sterns-cigar.html

question: Walther Gerlach and Otto Stern announced in 1922 that their two spots had confirmed a theory, the reigning consensus of the day. They turned out to be right about the splitting but wrong about the cause, and the true explanation would not be proposed for another three years. Which older theory did they believe those spots had confirmed?
answer: Bohr-Sommerfeld space quantization of orbital angular momentum
choices: Bohr-Sommerfeld space quantization of orbital angular momentum
Einstein's photon model of the photoelectric effect
Larmor's classical precession of an atomic magnet
The Lorentz-Zeeman splitting of spectral lines
context: A landmark result with a wrong explanation, cheerfully accepted for years. Silver in that state actually has zero orbital angular momentum; the split comes from something else entirely. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09412

question: Two physicists proposed in 1925 that the electron itself carries a built-in spin with just two allowed directions. Silver splits into two beams in a magnet, they said, because its lone outer electron carries this property, one no one had heard of in 1922. Who proposed the idea?
answer: Samuel Goudsmit and George Uhlenbeck
choices: Samuel Goudsmit and George Uhlenbeck
Werner Heisenberg and Max Born
Louis de Broglie and Paul Langevin
Pieter Zeeman and Hendrik Lorentz
context: They were graduate students at Leiden. They called the property 'spin'. Pauli initially thought it was nonsense. It is what the Stern-Gerlach magnet is really sorting, though nobody realized it for another five years. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09412

question: A student works through a sequel to the silver-atom experiment with pencil and paper. He blocks the lower of the two beams and sends only the upper one, 'spin up', into a second magnet rotated ninety degrees, so that its axis is now horizontal. What comes out of that second magnet?
answer: The beam splits again into two spots, left and right
choices: The beam splits again into two spots, left and right
One straight beam continues undeflected through the middle
The beam curves smoothly toward the horizontal south pole
No atoms emerge; the horizontal field extinguishes the beam
context: The 'spin up' atoms are perfectly definite about vertical but completely undecided about horizontal. Ask sideways and you get a fresh coin flip. Source: standard quantum mechanics texts (e.g. Griffiths).

question: David Strachan combed a British study in 1989 that had followed 17,414 children, born in one week of March 1958, up to age 23, hunting for whatever gives a young adult hay fever. One of the sixteen background features he tested stood out far above the rest. Which one?
answer: how many older brothers and sisters he had
choices: how many older brothers and sisters he had
whether he had grown up in a rented home
how long he had been breastfed as a baby
which region of Britain he was born in
context: Strachan's own words: 'Of the 16 perinatal, social, and environmental factors studied the most striking associations with hay fever were those for family size and position in the household.' The staircase he found at age 23: 20.4% reported hay fever among those with no older children at home, then 15.7% with one older sibling, 11.6% with two, 9.6% with three, and 6.5% with four or more. Roughly a threefold drop, and the firstborn is the worst off. The same staircase showed at age 11, 9.6% down to 2.8%. The other factors he adjusted for were father's social class, housing tenure, shared household amenities, breast feeding, region of birth, and cigarette smoking at 23. Source: Strachan DP, 'Hay fever, hygiene, and household size', BMJ 1989;299:1259-60 (PMID 2513902), full scan at researchonline.lshtm.ac.uk/id/eprint/292318/1/bmj00259-0027.pdf

question: Carole Ober compared the Amish and the Hutterites, two farming peoples of the American Midwest. Their children eat similar food, and neither group keeps a dirty home, yet Hutterite children get asthma about four times as often. What did Ober find different on the two groups' farms?
answer: the Amish barn sits next to the house
choices: the Amish barn sits next to the house
the Amish keep chickens loose in the yard
the Amish drink their milk straight from the cow
the Amish nurse their babies far longer
context: Carole Ober, the University of Chicago geneticist who led the study: 'Neither the Amish nor the Hutterites have dirty homes. Both are tidy. The Amish barns, however, are much closer to their homes.' Amish children 'run in and out of them, often barefoot, all day long.' The Hutterites farm industrially, in communal operations of 15 to 25 families, with barns set well away from the houses and young children kept out of them. Measured rates: asthma 5.2% Amish against 21.3% Hutterite; allergic sensitisation 7.2% against 33.3%. The US average for ages 5-14 is about 10.3%, so the Amish sit at half the national rate and the Hutterites at double it. Note what this is NOT: nobody found that dirt protects. Source: Stein MM et al., 'Innate Immunity and Asthma Risk in Amish and Hutterite Farm Children', N Engl J Med 2016;375:411-421 (PMID 27518660); UChicago Medicine, 'Growing up on an Amish farm protects children against asthma', Aug 2016

question: Carole Ober and her team suspected that something on Amish farms, not in the children, was blocking asthma, which Hutterite children got about four times as often. They gathered the same substance from both groups' farms and dripped it into the noses of lab mice. What had they gathered?
answer: dust from inside the houses
choices: dust from inside the houses
dust from inside the barns
soil from the barn floors
straw from the animal bedding
context: Ordinary indoor house dust, not barn muck. The protocol was fourteen instillations of 50 microlitres of dust extract into BALB/c mice that were being sensitised to ovalbumin, the standard laboratory asthma model. The point of going to mice was to strip away everything else two human communities differ in and ask a narrower question: can the dust alone carry the effect? Source: Stein MM et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:411-421, full text at pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5137793/

question: David Strachan wrote the word 'hygiene' just twice in his 1989 report: in the title and in his work address at the school. He never wrote 'hygiene hypothesis'; others pinned the label on him later. What did Strachan suggest might be protecting children who had older brothers and sisters?
answer: infection in early life, passed from child to child at home
choices: infection in early life, passed from child to child at home
the longer breast feeding common in bigger families
fewer house dust mites in the crowded, busy rooms
the cleaner country air of the regions they lived in
context: Strachan's own sentence, and note how hedged it is: allergic diseases might be 'prevented by infection in early childhood, transmitted by unhygienic contact with older siblings, or acquired prenatally from a mother infected by contact with her older children.' Could, however, be explained if - he proposed, he did not declare. 'Unhygienic contact' is as close as the paper ever comes to the word that ended up naming the idea; he never wrote 'hygiene hypothesis' at all. Other people attached that label afterwards, and it has caused trouble ever since, because it invites a reading Strachan never made. His actual closing sentences, hedged twice more: 'Over the past century declining family size, improvements in household amenities, and higher standards of personal cleanliness have reduced the opportunity for cross infection in young families. This may have resulted in more widespread clinical expression of atopic disease.' That is the entire hypothesis as originally written. Source: full text of Strachan DP, 'Hay fever, hygiene, and household size', BMJ 1989;299:1259-60, LSHTM Research Online; Bloomfield SF et al., Clin Exp Allergy 2006, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1448690/

question: Carole Ober's team stopped arguing about cleanliness, since Amish and Hutterite homes are both kept tidy, and measured what was actually floating in the household dust. Amish homes came in at 4,399 units per square metre, Hutterite homes at 648, nearly seven times less. What were they counting?
answer: endotoxin, a molecule from the outer wall of bacteria
choices: endotoxin, a molecule from the outer wall of bacteria
pollen, the grains shed by grasses and trees
mould spores, the seeds thrown off by fungi
dust-mite droppings, the classic indoor allergen
context: Median airborne endotoxin in house dust: 4,399 EU/m2 in Amish homes against 648 EU/m2 in Hutterite homes, 6.8 times as much. The bacterial communities in the dust differed in composition too. The Amish house is not dirtier; it is microbially busier, because the barn is next door. Independent support for the dose idea: Charlotte Braun-Fahrlander's ALEX team measured endotoxin in the mattresses of 812 rural children in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, and the more endotoxin in the child's own bed, the LESS hay fever, atopic asthma and sensitisation. Source: Stein MM et al., N Engl J Med 2016, PMC5137793; Braun-Fahrlander C et al., N Engl J Med 2002;347:869-877 (PMID 12239255)

question: Plotting Amish and Hutterite whole genomes against those of other European populations, Carole Ober's team looked at how near each group sat to the rest. Amish schoolchildren in Indiana report 5.2% asthma, Hutterite schoolchildren in South Dakota 21.3%. Both communities descend from small 16th-century Anabaptist groups, the Amish out of Switzerland, the Hutterites out of the South Tyrol. Where did the two land?
answer: side by side, set apart from the other Europeans
choices: side by side, set apart from the other Europeans
each beside its own homeland, Swiss and Tyrolean
spread evenly through the other European groups
far apart, with the Hutterites the tighter cluster
context: Both are 16th-century Anabaptist founder populations: the Amish trace to Switzerland and emigrated to Pennsylvania, Ohio and Indiana in the 18th and 19th centuries; the Hutterites trace to the South Tyrol and reached South Dakota in the 19th. Principal-component analysis of their genomes clusters the two groups together relative to other European populations, so 'it is genetic' is ruled out before the study begins. The communities also controlled the lifestyle confounders themselves, in the researchers' words sharing 'diets rich in fat, salt, and raw milk, low rates of childhood obesity, long durations of breast-feeding, minimal exposure to tobacco smoke and air pollution, and taboos against indoor pets, TV, and internet.' Source: Stein MM & Ober C, Curr Opin Immunol 2017, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5682224/

question: Carole Ober's team dripped dust extracts, some Amish and some Hutterite, into the noses of mice being made allergic to egg protein, the standard laboratory way to bring on an asthma-like reaction. Fourteen doses later they measured the animals' airways. How did the two groups compare?
answer: the Amish-dust mice had calmer airways and less egg-specific antibody
choices: the Amish-dust mice had calmer airways and less egg-specific antibody
the Hutterite-dust mice had calmer airways and less egg-specific antibody
both groups had calmer airways than mice given no dust at all
neither group's airways differed from mice given no dust
context: Mice given Amish dust showed significantly less airway hyperreactivity, fewer eosinophils in the airway, and suppressed ovalbumin-specific IgE. Mice given Hutterite dust showed none of that protection. Donata Vercelli: 'The results of the mouse experiments conclusively prove that products from the Amish environment are sufficient to confer protection from asthma.' This is the step from correlation to cause, and it is why the Amish-Hutterite comparison is so hard to argue away: the dust itself was doing the work. Source: Stein MM et al., N Engl J Med 2016, PMC5137793; UChicago Medicine, Aug 2016

question: Erika von Mutius set out in the early 1990s to prove that dirty air causes childhood allergy. She compared 9-to-11-year-olds in wealthy West Germany with children in East Germany, whose coal-burning industrial cities left the air far filthier, and she fully expected the East German children to have more allergies. What did she actually find?
answer: West German children were twice as allergically sensitised as East German ones
choices: West German children were twice as allergically sensitised as East German ones
East German children were twice as allergically sensitised as West German ones
the two halves came out level on sensitisation and on asthma alike
East German children had more asthma but far less hay fever
context: Atopic sensitisation ran at 36.7% among 5,030 West German children against 18.2% among 2,623 East German children, an odds ratio of 2.6 (p < 0.0001) - the exact reverse of what the pollution explanation predicts, and von Mutius reported it against her own hypothesis. Then, after reunification, hay fever and sensitisation in Leipzig rose significantly between 1991-92 and 1995-96 as Western living conditions arrived, while asthma and bronchial hyper-responsiveness did not budge. Von Mutius later joined the Amish-Hutterite team. Source: von Mutius E et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 1994 (PMID 8306030); von Mutius E et al., Lancet 1998 (PMID 9525363)

question: Counting the older children in each British household, David Strachan saw eczema in a baby's first year fall steadily as the count rose in his 1989 table: 6.0% where there were none, 2.1% where there were four or more. The same table carried a second count, the younger brothers and sisters in each household. What did that column show?
answer: no association with the eczema rate at all
choices: no association with the eczema rate at all
the same falling staircase as the older children
a rise in eczema with each younger child
a fall, but only in the largest households
context: Strachan's line: 'There was no association between eczema in infancy and younger children of the family (who were not yet born).' Those younger brothers and sisters did not exist when the eczema being counted appeared, so they cannot have caused it - and the column duly shows nothing. That null is the cleanest evidence in the whole paper that the staircase is not simply large families reporting childhood illness differently: if reporting habits were doing the work, the younger-children column would have sloped the same way. A control does not always have to be built. Sometimes the data already holds one, if you go looking for the comparison that SHOULD show nothing. The older-children figures: eczema in the first year fell from 6.0% (308 of 5,096) with none to 2.1% (8 of 381) with four or more. Source: Strachan DP, BMJ 1989;299:1259-60

question: To learn what inside a mouse was picking up the Amish dust that protected it from an asthma-like reaction, Carole Ober's team repeated the experiment in mice engineered to lack one signalling protein at a time. In one such strain the protection largely vanished. Which mice?
answer: mice bred without MyD88, the relay for Toll-like receptor signals
choices: mice bred without MyD88, the relay for Toll-like receptor signals
mice bred without NOD2, the sensor of bacterial wall fragments
mice bred without GPR43, the receptor for short-chain fatty acids
mice bred without VDR, the receptor for the vitamin D signal
context: In MyD88-knockout mice the protection was 'strongly reduced'; in mice lacking both MyD88 and Trif it was 'completely abrogated', gone entirely. Cut the innate signalling and the barn dust does nothing. Ober: 'We also clearly show, in humans and in mice, that this protection requires engagement of the innate immune system.' The innate system is the fast, inherited half that reacts to broad danger signals, as against the adaptive half that learns specific enemies. The Amish children's own blood matched: more and younger neutrophils, fewer eosinophils, suppressive monocytes, median serum IgE of 21 kU/litre against 64 in the Hutterites. Nobody has bottled it. Ober: 'You can't put a cow in every family's house.' Source: Stein MM et al., N Engl J Med 2016, PMC5137793; UChicago Medicine, Aug 2016

question: Nils Sigurs wanted to see what one big early infection leaves behind, so he followed Swedish babies for eighteen years. All had been sent to the hospital with a bad case of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) bronchiolitis, an infection that floods a baby's tiny airways. How did they turn out?
answer: far more asthma - roughly seven times the risk
choices: far more asthma - roughly seven times the risk
far less asthma - roughly seven times lower risk
no measurable difference in asthma either way
less asthma, but far more hay fever and eczema
context: Roughly a 7.2-fold increased risk of asthma eighteen years on. Some early-life microbes protect and some do real damage, which is why 'catching bugs is good for you' is a false reading of Strachan. It is also why Graham Rook proposed a refinement in the early 2000s: the protective organisms are not childhood infections at all but ancient co-evolved companions, in his words 'saprophytic mycobacteria, helminths and lactobacilli' from mud, animals and faeces. Rook is explicit that 'more recently evolved childhood infections are not likely to have evolved this role.' Two findings from the PARSIFAL farm study point the same way against slogans: antibiotics in infancy tracked with MORE allergic disease, while MMR vaccination tracked with LESS rhinoconjunctivitis. Source: Sigurs cohort as reported in Bacharier LB et al., J Allergy Clin Immunol 2012 (PMID 22444510); Rook GA, grahamrook.net; Strachan & Bloomfield, Front Allergy 2022, PMC9731379

question: Yukihiro Furusawa's team in Japan traced one chemical link between gut bacteria and the immune system in 2013. Bacteria fermenting the fibre in food release short-chain fatty acids, one of them butyrate. Furusawa followed butyrate into naive T cells, young immune cells not yet assigned a job, in the wall of the colon. What did he catch it doing there?
answer: loosening the packaging at the Foxp3 gene, so the cell becomes a brake
choices: loosening the packaging at the Foxp3 gene, so the cell becomes a brake
switching on the IL-4 gene, so the cell drives allergic antibody
shredding the cell's own DNA, so it dies before it can react at all
coating the cell's receptors, so it can no longer see the allergen
context: Fibre goes in, gut bacteria make butyrate, butyrate loosens the packaging around the Foxp3 gene, and the cell becomes a regulatory T cell - a brake whose whole job is to say 'stand down, this is harmless'. Technically: butyrate-treated naive T cells showed enhanced histone H3 acetylation at the Foxp3 promoter and its conserved non-coding regions, and NMR metabolome analysis showed luminal short-chain fatty acid concentration correlating with colonic Treg numbers. Short-chain fatty acids reach the cell two ways, which is why the effect is hard to argue away: from inside as histone deacetylase inhibitors, and from outside as agonists at the receptors GPR43 and GPR109A. Source: Furusawa Y et al., 'Commensal microbe-derived butyrate induces the differentiation of colonic regulatory T cells', Nature 2013;504:446-450 (PMID 24226770)

question: David Strachan turned on his own explanation in 2004, fifteen years after the hay-fever paper that made his name. The popular version had recast his finding as a trade-off between two arms of the immune system, Th1 and Th2, one arm rising as the other falls. Strachan and Sheikh called that somewhat simplistic and named one plain observation the trade-off cannot survive. What was it?
answer: allergic and autoimmune disease often strike the same person
choices: allergic and autoimmune disease often strike the same person
babies given antibiotics grow up with more allergy, not less
vaccination against measles tracked with less hay fever
hay fever rose in Leipzig while asthma there did not budge
context: The see-saw sat allergy on the Th2 arm and autoimmune disease on the Th1 arm, so carrying both at once should be rare. It is not: allergic and autoimmune disorders frequently occur in the same people, which a simple reciprocal trade-off cannot explain. Sheikh and Strachan concluded the Th1/Th2 model was 'somewhat simplistic' and suggested regulatory T cells as the more plausible mechanism instead. Strachan publishing against his own famous idea is exactly the behaviour the method asks for. And the honest bottom line thirty-plus years on, from the 2022 review: systematic attempts to identify WHICH specific infections do the protecting have been 'largely inconclusive', and the underlying mechanism remains unexplained. A strong hypothesis, not a closed case. Source: Strachan DP & Bloomfield SF, 'The hygiene hypothesis for allergy - conception and evolution', Front Allergy 2022;3:1051368, PMC9731379, citing Sheikh & Strachan 2004

question: Sally Bloomfield's team, who study household hygiene for a living, went looking in the European data for the claim thirty years of headlines had boiled David Strachan's paper down to: that children are simply too clean. They concluded that relaxing hygiene standards seems neither justified, nor rational. Which finding did they put up against the too-clean story?
answer: bleach use varies thirtyfold across Europe with no matching allergy pattern
choices: bleach use varies thirtyfold across Europe with no matching allergy pattern
soap sales run tenfold higher in the European countries where allergy rose least
hand-washing campaigns in twenty European countries never shifted hay fever rates
allergy kept climbing for two decades after European antibiotic use levelled off
context: Bloomfield's team also found no correlation across European countries between soap and detergent consumption and allergy prevalence, and the largest allergy survey ever run - ISAAC phases I to III, 1991 to 2010 - found no correlation between cleaning activity and atopy anywhere in the world. Whatever changed, it was not scrubbing. Their verbatim conclusion: 'On the basis of current evidence, relaxing hygiene standards seems neither justified, nor rational.' They and others propose renaming the idea outright - 'microbial deprivation hypothesis' (Bjorksten), 'high turnover and diversity hypothesis' (Matricardi), 'biodiversity hypothesis' (Haahtela) - precisely because the current name 'risks discouraging good hygiene practice'. Rival explanations still partly live for the allergy rise include traffic emissions, dust mites in sealed heated homes, dietary change, obesity, shorter breastfeeding, antibiotics, lower vitamin D, and better diagnosis. Source: Bloomfield SF, Stanwell-Smith R, Crevel RWR, Pickup J, 'Too clean, or not too clean', Clin Exp Allergy 2006, PMC1448690; Strachan & Bloomfield, Front Allergy 2022, PMC9731379

question: Sapan Desai, a vascular surgeon, supplied the data for a paper on COVID in The Lancet in May 2020, through a company almost nobody in the field had heard of. The data covered 96,032 patients across 671 hospitals on six continents, and within days the World Health Organization paused an arm of a big trial. What made his company the first thing worth staring at?
answer: It had about eleven employees, fewer than a football team
choices: It had about eleven employees, fewer than a football team
It was based in a country with no COVID cases yet
It had been founded only a few weeks earlier
It was owned by one of the paper's peer reviewers
context: The company was Surgisphere, founded in 2008 by vascular surgeon Sapan Desai and based in Palatine, Illinois. Around eleven employees were supposedly running a live medical-records network spanning six continents. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgisphere; The Lancet retraction, 4 June 2020.

question: Outside readers tested a Lancet paper of May 2020 with a school-book move. The paper claimed the malaria drug hydroxychloroquine raised the risk of death in COVID-19 patients, on records a firm called Surgisphere said it held from hospitals worldwide. The readers took its Australian in-hospital death numbers and compared them to a figure anyone could look up online. What did that first comparison reveal?
answer: The paper's Australian in-hospital deaths exceeded Australia's national COVID toll to date
choices: The paper's Australian in-hospital deaths exceeded Australia's national COVID toll to date
The paper's Australian in-hospital deaths matched Australia's national toll almost exactly
The paper reported far fewer Australian deaths than Australia had recorded
The paper listed no Australian patients at all
context: On 29 May 2020 The Lancet issued a correction saying one hospital assigned to the paper's 'Australasia' group should have been placed in Asia. That fixed the label but not the substance -- the check that broke the paper open was a population figure and a calculator. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgisphere.

question: Mandeep Mehra and Sapan Desai published a huge Surgisphere database study in The Lancet in May 2020, claiming hydroxychloroquine killed COVID-19 patients. The famous flaw was the Australia count, but that was only the door in. Beyond the Australia problem, what wider pattern in the dataset bothered careful readers most?
answer: Patient demographics and drug doses were implausibly uniform across every continent
choices: Patient demographics and drug doses were implausibly uniform across every continent
The dataset only reported patients from teaching hospitals
The dataset used a different definition of death from most countries
Every hospital in the dataset was in a capital city
context: Real hospital records vary wildly in age structure, comorbidity coding, dose units, and reporting fields from country to country -- and Surgisphere's numbers were smooth across six continents. No epidemiologist any signatory could think of had ever seen or heard of a live 1,200-hospital feed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgisphere.

question: James Watson, a statistician at Oxford's Mahidol tropical medicine unit, published an open letter on 28 May 2020 with more than 140 co-signers, addressed to The Lancet and the authors of a study it had run. The study claimed the malaria drug hydroxychloroquine was killing hospitalised COVID patients, on data from a company called Surgisphere that no outsider could verify. What did the letter ask for?
answer: The hospital-level data, an independent validation, and the peer-review comments
choices: The hospital-level data, an independent validation, and the peer-review comments
The removal of Mandeep Mehra from all future medical publications
A retraction on the front page of every major newspaper
A criminal referral to the United States Department of Justice
context: The letter listed the impossibilities and asked, essentially, to see the workings. Watson later said he simply could not believe any organisation had assembled that quantity of African hospital data in the time available. Source: BuzzFeed News, 29 May 2020.

question: A few authors of two COVID-19 drug papers from May 2020, one in The Lancet and one in the New England Journal of Medicine, asked for an independent audit as the numbers came under fire from outside scientists. Both papers drew on a firm called Surgisphere, which claimed hospital data from tens of thousands of patients worldwide. The auditor asked Surgisphere, plainly, for the raw dataset. What did Surgisphere do?
answer: Refused to hand it over, citing client confidentiality agreements
choices: Refused to hand it over, citing client confidentiality agreements
Handed over anonymised data that later checked out
Sued the auditor for defamation and blocked the request in court
Released the data publicly on its own website the same day
context: With no dataset there was nothing to check. Three of the four co-authors -- Mehra (Harvard), Ruschitzka (Zurich) and Patel -- retracted, saying they could 'no longer vouch for the veracity of the primary data sources'. Sapan Desai, the fourth co-author and the source of the numbers, did not sign the retraction. Source: The Lancet retraction, 4 June 2020.

question: Reviewers at The Lancet and the New England Journal of Medicine passed two COVID-19 papers in 2020, both built on data from one hospital-analytics company, Surgisphere. Trials were halted worldwide on the strength of them, and weeks later both were retracted after outsiders showed the dataset was impossible. What does journal peer review, done as journals normally do it, actually inspect?
answer: The manuscript that was submitted, not the raw dataset behind it
choices: The manuscript that was submitted, not the raw dataset behind it
The raw dataset, one row at a time, before publication
The authors' laboratory notebooks, kept on file at the journal
The source-code repository the authors used to run the analysis
context: Reviewers get the write-up. They do not receive medical records, cannot audit a private company's servers, and typically do not re-run the analysis. The correction here came from strangers with a calculator and a population figure -- exactly the outside check the system does not perform for you. Source: The Hospitalist community post; C. Piller commentary.

question: Statisticians took apart a Lancet paper by Mandeep Mehra in 2020, one that used data from a company called Surgisphere to claim hydroxychloroquine was killing hospitalised COVID patients. It was retracted, and many people treated the retraction as proof the drug was fine. What did exposing that paper as worthless prove, by itself, about hydroxychloroquine in hospitalised patients?
answer: Nothing about the drug -- a bad study being wrong is not evidence the drug works
choices: Nothing about the drug -- a bad study being wrong is not evidence the drug works
That the drug clearly worked, since the paper against it had collapsed
That the drug was dangerous for a different reason not covered by the paper
That the drug had never been properly tested in any setting
context: The honest hydroxychloroquine answer came from randomised trials. The UK RECOVERY trial reported on 5 June 2020: 25.7% 28-day mortality on hydroxychloroquine vs 23.5% on usual care (1,542 vs 3,132 patients, HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.98-1.26) -- no benefit in hospitalised patients. The WHO's own Solidarity trial dropped the arm on 17 June 2020 for the same reason. A bad study being exposed tells you about the study, not about the drug. Sources: recoverytrial.net statement, 5 June 2020; WHO Q&A on hydroxychloroquine.

question: The Army Air Forces brought Abraham Wald's Statistical Research Group at Columbia a heap of inspection reports in 1943. Bombers returning from Europe had wings and fuselages pocked with bullet holes, and the Air Forces wanted to know where to add armor. What did Wald tell them?
answer: Reinforce the parts that came back unmarked
choices: Reinforce the parts that came back unmarked
Reinforce the wings and fuselage where the marks cluster
Reinforce every square inch of the plane equally
Reinforce the tail gunner's position most of all
context: Wald's answer was to armour the places where the returning planes showed no damage at all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survivorship_bias

question: Abraham Wald spent World War II in New York at the Statistical Research Group, helping the Army Air Forces decide where to armor bombers returning from Europe. Later writers loved to show him in a briefing room, pointing at a drawn bomber covered in red dots, but that scene is a modern retelling. What did Wald actually turn in during 1943?
answer: A series of eight technical statistical memoranda
choices: A series of eight technical statistical memoranda
A single classified photograph handed to Curtis LeMay
A short training film shown to bomber crews before missions
A one-page telegram fired off to the War Department
context: The SRG issued eight memoranda by Wald on analyzing damage from combat aircraft; memo five gave a method for estimating the vulnerability of each part from the damage pattern on returning planes. They were reprinted by the Center for Naval Analyses in 1980. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survivorship_bias

question: J. B. Rhine's laboratory at Duke University ran card-guessing trials for extrasensory perception (ESP) through the 1930s and reported some subjects with astonishing streaks of correct guesses. Martin Gardner, a magician and skeptic, argued that Rhine had discovered nothing real. What was Gardner's central charge?
answer: Rhine repeated the tests but did not report the failures
choices: Rhine repeated the tests but did not report the failures
Rhine's shuffling was too regular to count as random
Rhine's assistants had marked the backs of the cards
Rhine had used the wrong statistical formula to score hits
context: Gardner: Rhine tried to replicate his own work and produced only failures he never reported. His star subject Hubert Pearce could not score above chance when anyone but Rhine was watching. If you test enough people at guessing 25 shuffled cards, chance alone will produce some subjects with astonishing streaks -- report only those streaks and hide the failures, and you have discovered nothing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Banks_Rhine

question: 'Steve Jobs, Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg all dropped out of college and got rich -- so dropping out helps you get rich.' Statistics students meet this broken argument on their first day. It sounds right until someone asks about the people who dropped out and stayed poor. Which statistical leak is doing the damage?
answer: The losing cases are missing from the sample entirely
choices: The losing cases are missing from the sample entirely
Extreme cases drift back toward the average next time
The target was drawn around the shots after the fact
People count the hits and forget the misses
context: This is survivorship bias, the same shape as Wald's diagram: the sample is only the winners, so the millions of dropouts who stayed poor never appear and the pattern is an illusion. The other three name real, adjacent leaks worth learning to tell apart -- regression to the mean, the Texas sharpshooter fallacy, and confirmation bias. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survivorship_bias

question: A drug trial reports a positive effect only on left-handed women over sixty. The obvious worry: the researchers hunted through the data until they found a subgroup that worked. Modern journals demand a discipline called preregistration to block exactly this move. What does preregistration actually require?
answer: Committing publicly to an analysis plan before seeing the data
choices: Committing publicly to an analysis plan before seeing the data
Hiding which patients got the drug from the doctors running the trial
Assigning patients to treatment or placebo by coin flip
Sending the finished manuscript to two independent expert reviewers
context: Preregistration locks the analysis in advance, so a null result cannot quietly disappear into the file drawer and a subgroup 'finding' cannot be quietly invented. Blinding, randomization and peer review are real, distinct disciplines worth telling apart from it. It is the same rule Wald was reaching for: decide what counts BEFORE seeing who survived. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preregistration_(science)

question: Maurice Hilleman and Ben Sweet described a previously unknown virus late in 1960, Simian Virus 40 or SV40, contaminating the monkey kidney cells used to grow polio vaccine. Nearly every adult rhesus monkey in captivity carried antibodies to it. What was SV40 doing inside those monkeys, long before humans ever came into the story?
answer: Living in their kidneys for life, causing no disease
choices: Living in their kidneys for life, causing no disease
Living in their gut for a season, then clearing away
Scarring their kidneys into a slow, lasting decline
Raising tumours in the lining of their chests
context: SV40's natural host is the rhesus macaque. In a normal monkey it settles into the kidney epithelium as a chronic, silent infection with no described disease -- which is exactly why nobody went looking for it in the vaccine substrate. Seroprevalence in macaque breeding colonies passes 75 per cent by two to three years of age. Sources: IARC Monographs Vol. 104, Simian Virus 40 (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK294242); PMC3122853.

question: Bernice Eddy, a virologist at the National Institutes of Health, took the monkey kidney cells used to grow polio vaccine, made plain extracts of them in the 1950s and injected those into 154 newborn hamsters. This was not the vaccine, just the cells. Over the next few months, what showed up in the animals?
answer: Tumours, in 109 of the 154
choices: Tumours, in 109 of the 154
Paralysis, in 109 of the 154
Kidney failure, in 40 of the 154
Nothing at all, in any of the 154
context: Eddy BE, Borman GS, Berkeley WH, Young RD, 'Tumors induced in hamsters by injection of rhesus monkey kidney cell extracts', Proc Soc Exp Biol Med 1961;107:191-197 (PMID 13725644). About 70 per cent of the injected animals grew subcutaneous tumours over three and a half to nine months. She had injected the vaccine's own substrate rather than a purified virus -- which is exactly what her critics would fasten on. Sources: Europe PMC PMID 13725644; IARC Monographs Vol. 104 (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK294242).

question: Leonard Norkin, a virologist, estimated how much SV40 survived the step that made the Salk polio vaccine safe. The poliovirus was soaked in formaldehyde until it was dead, the soak timed against poliovirus, but SV40 rode in the same fluid, and it is tougher. What fraction of the SV40 particles came through alive, by his reckoning?
answer: About one in 10,000
choices: About one in 10,000
About one in ten
About one in a thousand
About one in a million
context: The one-in-10,000 figure rests on the account of virologist Leonard Norkin and should be read as his estimate; the qualitative point is independently reported -- conditions sufficient to inactivate poliovirus were insufficient to completely inactivate SV40. The safety step was real and it worked. It simply was not aimed at this. Sources: norkinvirology.wordpress.com/2014/07/24/sv40-contaminated-polio-vaccines-and-human-cancer; PMC153983 (Clin Microbiol Rev, 'Simian Virus 40 Infection of Humans').

question: Ben Sweet and Maurice Hilleman of the drug company Merck published a paper in November 1960 on a new monkey virus they had isolated, and they did not soften what they had found. Where did they report the virus had already got to?
answer: Into all three types of Sabin's live polio vaccine
choices: Into all three types of Sabin's live polio vaccine
Into the chick-embryo cultures used for measles work
Into the human cell lines kept for testing vaccines
Into the mouse colonies housed in the same building
context: Sweet BH & Hilleman MR, Proc Soc Exp Biol Med 1960;105:420-427 (PMID 13774265). They described the agent as a common and essentially ubiquitous contaminant of rhesus monkey kidney cultures, reported it in all three types of Sabin's live poliovirus vaccine and in numerous respiratory-virus seed lines already used in human volunteer inoculations, and speculated in print about the possible long-term effects of introducing such a virus into the human population. Sources: Europe PMC PMID 13774265; PMC4675525.

question: Bernice Eddy told a cancer conference in New York in October 1960 what the monkey-kidney material used to make polio vaccine had done to her hamsters. Her boss, Joseph Smadel, had already reviewed the same data. What did Smadel do after the conference?
answer: Forbade her to speak on it in public without clearing her words first
choices: Forbade her to speak on it in public without clearing her words first
Ordered the hamster work repeated in three outside laboratories
Took the data to the licensing board and had suspect lots withheld
Resigned his post rather than approve another season of vaccine
context: Smadel reviewed Eddy's data and dismissed her finding of a tumour-inducing virus in early Salk lots; after the October 1960 conference he required her to clear any public remarks with him first. The honest other half: Maurice Hilleman alleged that her experiments were poorly controlled, and the dispute cut both ways -- which is why the control she published in 1962 matters so much. This account comes from virologist Leonard Norkin's history rather than from a primary document. Sources: norkinvirology.wordpress.com/2014/07/24/sv40-contaminated-polio-vaccines-and-human-cancer; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernice_Eddy.

question: Shah and Nathanson looked back in 1976 at the polio shot that about 98 million Americans, mostly children, had received between 1955 and 1963. That shot is thought to be the main way SV40 got into people in the United States. How much of that vaccine did they think had carried live SV40?
answer: 10 to 30 per cent of it
choices: 10 to 30 per cent of it
Under 1 per cent of it
About 60 per cent of it
Nearly all of it
context: On that arithmetic an estimated 10 to 30 million Americans were actually exposed. The Institute of Medicine's 2002 review used the same figures: 'IPV administered between 1955 and 1963 to about 98 million children and adults is assumed to be the primary source of human exposure to SV40 in the United States'; 'Shah and Nathanson (1976) estimated that 10% to 30% of IPV contained live SV40.' Source: IOM, Immunization Safety Review: SV40 Contamination of Polio Vaccine and Cancer (2002), ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK221118.

question: Cutrone and colleagues tested stored vaccine samples from 13 countries in 2005. From 1961 American rules had required every lot of polio vaccine to test negative for SV40 before release, and other countries were assumed clear after 1962. What did Cutrone's team find?
answer: One eastern European maker's oral vaccine carried live SV40 to 1978
choices: One eastern European maker's oral vaccine carried live SV40 to 1978
Every sample made after 1962 was free of live SV40 everywhere
Only vaccine made before the 1955 licence carried live SV40
American-made vaccine carried live SV40 until about 1970
context: Cutrone R, Lednicky J, Dunn G, Rizzo P, Bocchetta M, Chumakov K, Minor P, Carbone M, 'Some oral poliovirus vaccines were contaminated with infectious SV40 after 1961', Cancer Res 2005;65:10273. The contaminated oral vaccine was produced from the early 1960s until approximately 1978, because that manufacturer's heat-inactivation step did not completely inactivate SV40. The American fix was forward-looking only: already-approved lots were not recalled, and potentially contaminated vaccine from those earlier lots may have been used until early 1963. Sources: aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/65/22/10273; IARC Vol. 104 (NBK294242); IOM 2002 (NBK221112).

question: A student looks down a microscope at a hamster cell carrying SV40. In a hamster, the virus's protein large T antigen is enough to turn a healthy cell cancerous. A cell is held in check by two brakes: p53, which orders a damaged cell to stop or to die, and Rb, which holds back the machinery of division. What does large T antigen do to them?
answer: Clamps onto both of them at once, holding each out of action
choices: Clamps onto both of them at once, holding each out of action
Clamps onto p53 alone, and leaves Rb working normally
Cuts the genes for both of them out of the cell's own DNA
Copies itself into the gene for Rb and silences it there
context: Large T antigen binds p53 through a region at its C-terminal end, and binds Rb and its relatives p107 and p130 through a short motif spelled LxCxE at residues 103 to 107. Holding Rb pries loose the E2F transcription factors that push a cell into dividing; holding p53 blocks the cell's own order to stop or to die. One viral protein, both brakes, released at once -- and no mutation of the cell's own genes required. Sources: PMC153983 (Clin Microbiol Rev, 'Simian Virus 40 Infection of Humans'); EMBO J 2001;20:295, 'Structural basis for the inactivation of retinoblastoma tumor suppressor by SV40 large T antigen'.

question: Maurice Hilleman argued that Bernice Eddy's experiments were poorly controlled. Her hamster tumours proved something in the monkey-kidney extract caused cancer, but not what. In 1962 she pulled virus back out of the tumours and injected it into fresh newborn hamsters, and tumours grew again. What did she do to one batch of that virus so that no tumours grew at all?
answer: Mixed it with rabbit antiserum raised against SV40 before injecting
choices: Mixed it with rabbit antiserum raised against SV40 before injecting
Heated it to sixty degrees for half an hour before injecting
Passed it through a filter fine enough to hold back bacteria
Diluted it a thousandfold in sterile saline before injecting
context: Eddy BE, Borman GS, Grubbs GE, Young RD, 'Identification of the oncogenic substance in rhesus monkey kidney cell culture as simian virus 40', Virology 1962;17:65-75 (PMID 13889129). Block the antibody's target and you block the cancer: the tumours were this virus's doing and not something else in the soup. It is also the answer to the 'poorly controlled' charge -- she supplied the control herself. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/13889129.

question: Lopez-Rios and his colleagues ran 71 frozen mesotheliomas through the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in 2004, because reports of SV40 DNA inside such tumours kept appearing. Their first primer sets, short probes for one stretch of DNA, found SV40 in 56 to 62 per cent of the tumours, matching the earlier positive studies exactly. Then they looked hard at the primers. What had those primers been reading?
answer: SV40 sequence that also sits inside ordinary laboratory plasmids
choices: SV40 sequence that also sits inside ordinary laboratory plasmids
BK virus sequence, a human cousin of SV40 living in the same tissue
Human DNA that happens to spell the same short stretch of letters
Adenovirus sequence left behind in the tumours by an old infection
context: Primers designed to avoid that stretch gave only 4 faint positives out of 71 (6 per cent). All 71 tumours were negative for T-antigen transcripts by RT-PCR and none carried T-antigen-positive tumour cells on immunohistochemistry. The loop is exact: large T antigen is now a routine laboratory reagent for immortalising cells, and SV40's promoter and regulatory sequences are built into an enormous number of ordinary expression plasmids -- the tool made from the virus contaminated the test for the virus. Cross-reaction with the human polyomaviruses BK and JC is a real confounder too, but for antibody tests rather than for this study's primers. Lopez-Rios F, Illei PB, Rusch V, Ladanyi M, The Lancet 2004 (PMID 15451223).

question: A researcher reads the 35-year record of 1,073 people given SV40-contaminated polio vaccine as newborns between 1961 and 1963. Cancer deaths overall stand at 4 against 3.16 expected. One cancer alone breaks the pattern, with 2 deaths against 0.05 expected. Bigger registry studies show no clear excess, and the question stays unsettled. Which cancer is it?
answer: Testicular cancer
choices: Testicular cancer
Brain cancer
Bone cancer
Chest-lining cancer
context: Two testicular-cancer deaths against 0.05 expected gives P = 0.002. The authors called their results 'for the most part, consistent with other negative epidemiologic investigations' while noting that 'further study of testicular cancer may be warranted'. The larger negative stands beside it: Strickler and colleagues (JAMA 1998), using US SEER registry data with more than 30 years of follow-up, found no significant excess of ependymomas and other brain cancers, osteosarcomas or mesotheliomas among the exposed -- osteosarcoma relative risk 0.87 (95% CI 0.71-1.06). The Institute of Medicine's 2002 review put the position in two sentences that point different ways: 'the evidence is inadequate to accept or reject a causal relationship between SV40-containing polio vaccines and cancer', and 'the biological evidence is moderate that SV40 exposure could lead to cancer in humans under natural conditions'. In 2013 IARC placed SV40 in Group 3 -- not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans. The exposure is not in dispute; the consequence is not settled. Sources: Br J Cancer (PMC2375249); JAMA 1998 (PMID 9605895); IOM 2002 (NBK221118); IARC Monographs Vol. 104 (NBK294242).

question: Leo Szilard read Ernest Rutherford's 'moonshine' verdict on atomic power in The Times in September 1933 and went walking.
