By his own later account, the idea of the chain reaction struck him while he stood at a crossing, waiting for a light to change. Which London street corner did Szilard name as the setting?
answer: Southampton Row at Russell Square
choices: Southampton Row at Russell Square
Baker Street at Marylebone Road
Fleet Street at Ludgate Hill
Oxford Street at Marble Arch
context: Szilard told the story decades later; Richard Rhodes's 'The Making of the Atomic Bomb' (1986) is the standard secondary source. He realised that if a nucleus struck by ONE neutron could throw off TWO, the reaction would feed itself. Twenty-four hours after Rutherford's dismissal.  (Legend.)

question: Leo Szilard tried candidates himself at St Bartholomew's Hospital and at Oxford's Clarendon Laboratory in 1934 and 1935. His 1934 patent needed a real substance that would spit out more neutrons than it absorbed, and no one knew of one. Which pair of elements did he actually test and eliminate?
answer: Beryllium and indium
choices: Beryllium and indium
Uranium and thorium
Radium and polonium
Cadmium and boron
context: Neither worked; Szilard concluded indium was incapable of chain-reacting. The idea then sat idle until the 1939 fission papers gave him a candidate he had not thought of - uranium. Source: dannen.com Szilard chronology.

question: Enrico Fermi's team pulled the last long rod out of a stack of graphite and uranium at 3:25 pm on 2 December 1942, under the west stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. They drew it slowly, until the neutron counter stopped falling and began climbing on its own. What material was that final rod made of?
answer: Cadmium
choices: Cadmium
Beryllium
Tungsten
Lead
context: Chicago Pile-1: about 400 tons of graphite and 50 tons of uranium; the first self-sustaining chain reaction ran for 28 minutes. Cadmium was chosen because its nuclei absorb neutrons very effectively, so pulling the rods out lets the multiplication factor rise past 1 - the definition of 'critical' Szilard had coined eight years earlier. Source: aps.org first self-sustained chain reaction.

question: Sivel, Crocé-Spinelli and Gaston Tissandier took the hydrogen balloon Zenith up on 15 April 1875 to study the thin air, and they rose past 8,000 metres. What happened up there?
answer: Two of the three suffocated at altitude; only Tissandier came down alive
choices: Two of the three suffocated at altitude; only Tissandier came down alive
All three came back safe but were struck deaf for life by pressure change
The basket broke free and the men parachuted down from the upper air
A lightning strike lit the envelope and forced an emergency descent
context: Sivel and Croce-Spinelli died of hypoxia (oxygen starvation) at altitudes we now know push into mountaineering's 'death zone'. The men had carried oxygen bags but not nearly enough for the climb they attempted. Tissandier survived but was left partly deaf. Source: Beauchamp, 'Martyrs made in the sky', Notes & Records of the Royal Society 74 (2020).

question: French upper-air scientists drew a hard lesson from the Zenith tragedy of 15 April 1875, when a hydrogen balloon carried three men more than 8 km up. Instead of sending people higher into the thin air, they changed the whole approach. What did they change to?
answer: Small unmanned balloons carrying self-recording thermometers up on their own
choices: Small unmanned balloons carrying self-recording thermometers up on their own
Tall observation towers built in the Alps to reach the same altitudes on foot
Kites tethered to the ground carrying a wire back down to the recording gear
Artillery shells with instruments that recorded during the shell's arcing flight
context: Send the instrument, not the man. From 1898 Leon Teisserenc de Bort ran the first sustained programme of unmanned soundings, at his private observatory in Trappes near Versailles - eventually more than 200 flights. Source: UCAR SciEd, 'The History of Atmospheric Discovery'.

question: Léon Teisserenc de Bort, who first mapped the stratosphere around 1902, insisted on running many of his balloon launches at night. He sent hundreds of thermometers aloft from his own observatory at Trappes, near Versailles. Why did he pick night flights?
answer: So no critic could argue that sunlight had warmed the thermometer and skewed the reading
choices: So no critic could argue that sunlight had warmed the thermometer and skewed the reading
So the balloons would be invisible from the ground and not draw hostile military attention
So he could track the balloons visually against the stars with a fixed transit telescope
So the colder night air let the hydrogen envelopes carry more instrument payload aloft
context: This is a control - a deliberate step to kill an objection before anyone could raise it. Teisserenc de Bort knew that a bright thermometer reading in the upper air would be waved away as 'the sun warmed the instrument'. By running many launches at night, he removed the objection from the argument. Source: Wikipedia; hogback.atmos.colostate.edu, 'Discovery of the Stratosphere'.

question: Léon Teisserenc de Bort sent his thermometers past about 11 km over France and got a report no one expected. For centuries scientists had assumed one obvious thing about the upper air: keep going up and it just keeps getting colder. What did the thermometers report?
answer: The temperature simply stopped falling and stayed nearly flat as the balloons climbed higher
choices: The temperature simply stopped falling and stayed nearly flat as the balloons climbed higher
The temperature dropped abruptly by about 40 degrees in a narrow band a few hundred metres thick
The temperature fluctuated wildly by 20 degrees within each single balloon flight
The temperature fell TWICE as fast as at lower altitudes, then went off the thermometer's scale
context: Teisserenc de Bort announced the finding to the French Academy of Sciences on 28 April 1902, and later coined the name STRATOSPHERE for the calm upper deck and TROPOSPHERE for the churning lower one. Source: Ebsco, 'Stratosphere and Troposphere Are Discovered'; Britannica, 'Leon Teisserenc de Bort'.

question: Léon Teisserenc de Bort announced a new atmospheric layer in 1902, later called the stratosphere, after years of sending unmanned hydrogen balloons into the sky. A finding this odd would usually be blamed on broken instruments. What made other scientists take it seriously?
answer: Richard Assmann in Berlin reported the same layer, from his own separate balloon programme
choices: Richard Assmann in Berlin reported the same layer, from his own separate balloon programme
The Paris Observatory verified it by measuring air temperature from a Himalayan expedition
The French Academy re-flew Teisserenc de Bort's exact balloons under a supervising committee
The King of Belgium personally funded a repeat programme run by a Jesuit meteorological order
context: Assmann announced the same isothermal layer to the Prussian Academy of Sciences on 1 May 1902, three days after Teisserenc de Bort - independently, from a separate programme. Independent confirmation, not the authority of any one man. Source: AMS abstract 269395; Wikipedia, 'Richard Assmann'.

question: A pilot on a long flight north checks the height of the tropopause, the boundary Léon Teisserenc de Bort discovered around 1900 at the top of the churning lower air. It is no shelf at one fixed altitude: it bulges upward over warm regions and sinks down over cold ones. Where does it sit at the equator, and where at the poles?
answer: About 17 km up over the equator, but only about 8 km up over the poles
choices: About 17 km up over the equator, but only about 8 km up over the poles
About 8 km up over the equator, but climbing to about 17 km over the poles
About 12 km up worldwide, varying by less than one kilometre with latitude
About 25 km up over the equator, but pressed all the way down to the ground at the poles
context: Vigorous tropical convection lifts the boundary; cold polar air lets it sag. This is why 'the stratosphere begins at 11 km' is a French average, not a planetary constant. Source: code7700.com, 'Tropopause'; NOAA JetStream.

question: A rocket pilot passes 50 miles, about 80.5 km, and the United States awards him astronaut wings. The Fédération Aéronautique Internationale (FAI), the world sporting body, uses 100 km, the famous Karman line, so the two official edges of space disagree by about 20 km. How did that disagreement come about?
answer: Von Karman's own aerodynamic estimate was closer to 84 km; the FAI rounded up to 100 km for a tidy figure
choices: Von Karman's own aerodynamic estimate was closer to 84 km; the FAI rounded up to 100 km for a tidy figure
The FAI adopted 100 km from a UN treaty on outer-space liability, ratified in 1967
The US Air Force's 80 km figure was chosen to match the ceiling of the X-15 rocket plane
Von Karman himself proposed both numbers and let each nation choose which one to adopt
context: Nobody discovered where space starts. Two committees defined it, differently, and neither number matches Karman's original calculation. When someone in the news claims a rocket 'reached space', ask which line the claim used. Source: McDowell, 'The edge of space: Revisiting the Karman Line', Acta Astronautica (2018), arXiv/planet4589.

question: An airline passenger sets a cup of coffee on her tray as the jet climbs into the stratosphere, the calm deck above Teisserenc de Bort's boundary. That layer is upside down compared to the air below it: warm at the top, cold at the bottom. Why does that inversion exist, and why does it give her such a smooth ride?
answer: Ozone up there absorbs ultraviolet sunlight and heats the air where it sits; warm-over-cold refuses to overturn, so the layer barely mixes
choices: Ozone up there absorbs ultraviolet sunlight and heats the air where it sits; warm-over-cold refuses to overturn, so the layer barely mixes
The atmosphere thins so much that molecules almost never collide, so heat cannot travel downward at all through the layer
The Earth's magnetic field traps solar-wind particles at that height and heats the layer by direct particle bombardment from above
The stratosphere is dominated by dry descending polar air that only sinks and never rises anywhere on Earth
context: Because the stratosphere does not convect, anything injected into it - volcanic sulfate from Pinatubo, CFCs, aircraft soot - lingers for years and drifts sideways instead of rinsing out. That non-mixing is exactly what makes it calm to fly in and what makes it globally consequential when it is polluted. Source: NOAA JetStream, 'Layers of the Atmosphere'; Lumen 'Layers of the Atmosphere'.

question: A doctor in West Germany prescribes Contergan, the sedative Grünenthal began selling in 1957, known abroad as thalidomide. The company says nobody can overdose on it. Doctors hand it out for anxiety, sleep trouble and one particular pregnancy problem that no other drug is helping much. Which pregnancy problem?
answer: morning sickness
choices: morning sickness
back pain
heartburn
swollen ankles
context: Gruenenthal marketed Contergan aggressively to expectant mothers on the strength of the 'cannot overdose' claim, which was based on rodent studies that never tested for effects on a developing fetus. The active ingredient was thalidomide. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide_scandal.

question: Widukind Lenz, a German pediatrician, and William McBride, an Australian obstetrician, each independently linked the sleeping drug thalidomide, late in 1961, to a wave of babies born with severe birth defects, most famously missing or seal-flipper-like limbs. One medical word for that injury pattern came out of the crisis into common use. Which word?
answer: phocomelia
choices: phocomelia
spina bifida
hydrocephalus
clubfoot
context: Phocomelia (from Greek phoke, seal + melos, limb) describes limbs shortened or absent, sometimes leaving hands or feet attached close to the trunk. Between 10,000 and 12,000 children were affected worldwide, with about 40 percent dying at or shortly after birth; Germany was hardest hit. The other three conditions are unrelated birth defects with their own causes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide_scandal.

question: Handa's group in Japan tracked down thalidomide's target in 2010. The drug has two mirror-image forms, and the (S) form fits one particular human protein like a key, jamming cellular machinery that a fetus needs. Which protein is the (S) form binding?
answer: cereblon
choices: cereblon
haemoglobin
insulin
actin
context: Handa's group in Japan identified cereblon as the target in 2010, almost fifty years after the disaster. Cereblon is part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase, a molecular machine that tags other proteins for destruction; thalidomide misdirects that tagging, taking out proteins the developing limb needs. Haemoglobin carries oxygen, insulin regulates blood sugar, actin builds muscle filaments - all correct answers to different questions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide.

question: A nurse counts back to the day a mother took thalidomide, because the injury pattern is oddly narrow: only babies exposed between about day 20 and day 36 after conception are hurt. Different days in that two-week window hit different body parts. The drug disrupts one building process under way only during those two weeks. Which process?
answer: the formation of the limb buds
choices: the formation of the limb buds
the closing of the neural tube
the descent of the kidneys
the fusion of the palate
context: Between days 20 and 36 the limb buds emerge and pattern themselves head-to-tail and thumb-to-little-finger; (S)-thalidomide's binding to cereblon disrupts that pattern. Day 24 exposure hit arms; day 28 hit legs. The neural tube closes earlier, the kidneys migrate later, the palate fuses later still. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide.

question: A student repeats the common moral of the thalidomide story: 'if only they had sold the good (R) hand of the molecule alone, none of this would have happened.' Her teacher says the moral is wrong and that it hides the real chemistry. The carbon at the molecule's centre carries an acidic hydrogen, which lets the molecule do something in a patient that defeats the scheme. What does the molecule do?
answer: the (R) form spontaneously inverts into (S) inside the body
choices: the (R) form spontaneously inverts into (S) inside the body
the (R) form is oxidized by a liver enzyme into (S)
both forms break down to a common toxic metabolite
both forms are metabolized to an achiral intermediate
context: Give a patient pure (R)-thalidomide and the body manufactures (S) anyway - the acidic proton at the chiral centre falls off and re-adds from the other face at random. This spontaneous inversion is called racemization; it happens without any enzyme and is why the tidy 'sell one enantiomer' fix could never have saved thalidomide. Modern chirally-pure medicines have to be checked case by case for in-vivo inversion; it is not the general rule for chiral drugs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide.

question: A leprosy patient swallows thalidomide under strict pregnancy-prevention rules, for a painful problem called erythema nodosum leprosum. The same molecule has come back into medicine a second way: since 2006 the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved it, given with dexamethasone, for one blood cancer. Which cancer?
answer: multiple myeloma
choices: multiple myeloma
Hodgkin's lymphoma
chronic leukaemia
acute leukaemia
context: Thalidomide (with dexamethasone) received FDA approval for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma in 2006. The same cereblon-binding action that once wrecked limb-building in fetuses turns out, in adult multiple-myeloma cells, to degrade proteins those cells depend on to survive. Hodgkin's uses combination chemotherapy; chronic and acute leukaemias have their own targeted regimens (imatinib, ATRA, chemotherapy). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide.

question: Walter Alvarez wanted to know how long a thin clay band in the limestone above Gubbio, Italy, had taken to settle. His father Luis, a Nobel-winning physicist, offered to time it by measuring something that reaches the clay at a steady rate. What did Luis want to measure?
answer: a metal that space dust sprinkles down steadily
choices: a metal that space dust sprinkles down steadily
a gas that seeps out of buried rock steadily
a shell layer that dead plankton leave steadily
a salt crust that drying seawater leaves steadily
context: The metal was iridium, which drifts down in cosmic dust at a slow, fairly steady trickle -- so the amount buried in a layer should say how long the layer took to form. Luis Alvarez had won the 1968 Nobel Prize for the liquid hydrogen bubble chamber and had flown observation missions over Hiroshima and Nagasaki to measure blast yields; here he was offering a physicist's clock for a geologist's problem, with no thought of what killed anything. Walter was at Gubbio in the mid-1970s working on paleomagnetic reversals, and had noticed that the limestone below the 1-2 cm clay band is crammed with the chalky shells of planktonic foraminifera while the limestone above holds almost none. Source: Grokipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (Alvarez research origins; iridium anomaly discovery); Grokipedia, 'Luis Walter Alvarez'.

question: A geologist in Colorado counts fossil pollen just above the clay layer that marks the dinosaurs' end, 66 million years ago. Fern spores flood the count, as much as ninety percent in some spots, and ferns are pioneer plants. What kind of landscape does that fern spike show?
answer: bare ground being colonised from scratch
choices: cool bog thickening into a bed of peat
bare ground being colonised from scratch
old forest closing into deep, wet shade
coastal swamp drowning under a rising sea
context: Charles Orth and colleagues reported the 'fern spike' in 1981, and it has since been documented at over 100 sites: ferns are the pioneers that move first onto scorched, emptied ground, and their spores briefly drown out everything else in the pollen record. The same 1981 study carried a second, quieter blow. Orth's iridium spike sat in rocks laid down in FRESH water, which destroyed the standing objection that seawater chemistry had somehow concentrated the metal at sea-floor boundaries. Source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event research' (1981, Orth et al.); Grokipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (Paleontological correlations).

question: Frank Asaro and Helen Michel, two Berkeley chemists, counted the iridium in clay Walter Alvarez had sampled at Gubbio in 1977. Slow settling should leave the clay a bit richer in the metal than the rock around it, fast settling a bit poorer. What did their count come back as?
answer: about thirty times the iridium in the limestone beside it
choices: about the same iridium as in the limestone beside it
about half the iridium in the limestone beside it
about thirty times the iridium in the limestone beside it
about a thousandth of the iridium in the limestone beside it
context: The Gubbio clay ran roughly 3-9 parts per billion of iridium (peak about 9.1 ppb) against about 0.3 ppb in the limestone on either side. The answer was wrong in the most interesting possible way: no rate of settling produces that. The team then went to the chalk cliffs of Stevns Klint in Denmark and found the same spike about 160 times background, up to 29 ppb. Asaro and Michel measured it by neutron activation analysis -- dissolve away the carbonate, irradiate the residue so iridium-191 becomes radioactive iridium-192, then count its gamma emissions -- good down to about 0.001 ppb. Source: Grokipedia, 'Iridium anomaly' (discovery; initial reports); Grokipedia, 'Walter Alvarez' (neutron activation analysis).

question: A chemist sets a chip of Earth's crust beside a meteorite made from the same material. The crust holds almost no iridium; the meteorite holds plenty. What happened to Earth's iridium while the young planet was still hot and melted?
answer: it sank with the iron that was forming the core
choices: it boiled off with the gases that made the first air
it stayed behind in crystals deep in the mantle
it left with the rock flung out to form the Moon
it sank with the iron that was forming the core
context: Iridium is a siderophile -- an 'iron-lover'. When the young molten Earth separated and its iron sank to build the core, the iridium dissolved in that iron and went down with it, leaving the crust stripped to about 0.02-0.05 parts per billion. Asteroids never differentiated that way, so they kept theirs: carbonaceous chondrite meteorites run about 500 ppb. That single fact is what turns a chemistry reading into a detective's fingerprint. Any iridium spike sitting at Earth's surface is a visitor from outside. Source: Grokipedia, 'Iridium anomaly' (siderophile behaviour, planetary differentiation, CI chondrite abundance).

question: Luis and Walter Alvarez and two colleagues turned an oddity into a number that could be checked, in a 1980 paper. All the iridium spread through boundary clays around the world came to about fifty thousand tonnes. From that mass alone the four of them worked out one thing. What did fifty thousand tonnes of iridium tell them?
answer: the width of the body that fell, about ten kilometres
choices: the width of the body that fell, about ten kilometres
the depth of the sea it fell into, about four kilometres
the time the clay took to settle, about ten thousand years
the age of the boundary itself, about sixty-six million years
context: That number is what made the hypothesis dangerous to its own authors: a body roughly 10 km across leaves a crater of matching age 150-200 km wide, so such a crater had to exist somewhere on Earth and had to be findable. 'Extraterrestrial cause for the Cretaceous-Tertiary extinction' ran in Science on 6 June 1980 (vol. 208, pp. 1095-1108). A rival got there first and almost nobody remembers: the Dutch paleontologist Jan Smit, working the boundary at Caravaca in Spain, published the same conclusion independently with Jan Hertogen in Nature on 22 May 1980, two weeks earlier. The boundary's age, 66.04 million years, was measured much later and by other means. Source: Grokipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (Publication and early reception); Smit & Hertogen, Nature 285:198-200, 22 May 1980.

question: Geologists checked quartz grains from the boundary clay against man-made reference grains. The clay grains had dead-straight glassy lines inside them, and making those lines takes shock pressure far beyond anything volcanoes or mountain-building can supply. Where did the reference grains come from?
answer: quartz dug out from under a buried nuclear test
choices: quartz melted in a furnace and cooled in seconds
quartz dug out from under a buried nuclear test
quartz squeezed between the tips of two diamonds
quartz fired from a gas gun into a steel plate
context: The lamellae are planar deformation features, and it takes shock above roughly 5-10 gigapascals to make them at all. The 1962 Sedan test at the Nevada Test Site -- 104 kilotons, buried -- drove pressures above 30 gigapascals and produced quartz with multiple crossing sets of planar deformation features, which became the calibration standard; the Soviet 140-kiloton Chagan test of 1965 did the same. Slow tectonic squeezing leaves a single, broader, curved set instead, and explosive volcanism generally cannot reach the pressure at all. The boundary grains matched the bomb-crater grains. When Bruce Bohor's team found shocked quartz in boundary claystone in Montana in 1984, it swayed skeptics partly for a sociological reason: Bohor's people were geologists using geologists' methods, so it did not read as outsiders lecturing the field. Source: Grokipedia, 'Shocked quartz' (planar deformation features; Sedan 1962; Chagan 1965); Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event research' (1984, Bohor).

question: Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo flew magnetic surveys for a Mexican oil company in 1978 and spotted a buried half-circle 180 kilometres wide under the Yucatan. Penfield wrote to Walter Alvarez in 1980 and got no reply, and for ten years nobody found the crater the Alvarez paper needed. What finally got Penfield's buried structure to the impact scientists in 1990?
answer: a newspaper reporter told a geologist about it
choices: a satellite image of the Yucatan reached the journals
a graduate student dug out his 1981 conference talk
a newspaper reporter told a geologist about it
a new oil well cut straight through its melt rock
context: Carlos Byars of the Houston Chronicle mentioned Penfield's buried structure to the geologist Alan Hildebrand in 1990. Hildebrand and Penfield then tracked down surviving Pemex drill cores that had sat in storage in New Orleans for decades -- others had burned in a warehouse fire -- found shocked quartz and impact melt in them, and matched the chemistry to boundary tektites from Haiti; Hildebrand and William Boynton published the identification in 1991. Penfield had done everything right: Pemex held the survey data as proprietary so he could not publish it, and when he and Camargo presented the structure to the Society of Exploration Geophysicists in 1981 -- explicitly proposing it as the Alvarez crater -- the conference was under-attended and the report attracted little notice. Argon-argon dating of the crater's melt rock later gave 66.04 +/- 0.05 million years, landing exactly on the boundary. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chicxulub crater' (Initial Discovery; 1990 Critical Connection); Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event research' (1978, 1980, 1981, 1990-91); Grokipedia, 'Chicxulub crater' (Ar-Ar age).

question: Drillers cored the peak ring of the Chicxulub crater in 2016, and the gypsum was the surprise: there was almost none of it left in the shattered rock. Beneath the Yucatan lay three to five kilometres of limestone, and under that a bed of gypsum and anhydrite some three hundred to eight hundred metres thick, sulfur-rich rock left where ancient seas dried out. Where had the gypsum gone?
answer: vaporised outright and flung into the high atmosphere
choices: dissolved away by the seawater that poured back in
pushed far downwards as the crater floor rebounded
melted and refrozen into the glass sheets below
vaporised outright and flung into the high atmosphere
context: The gypsum went up as sulfate aerosol, injected into the stratosphere, where it blocks sunlight far more effectively than dust. This is the asteroid's geological bad luck: had the same rock struck sulfate-poor crystalline bedrock, the chemistry of the aftermath would have been far less lethal. The near-complete absence of gypsum in the peak-ring cores is the physical evidence that it was vaporised rather than merely buried or melted. Source: Grokipedia, 'Chicxulub crater' (Pre-Impact Target Rocks); Wikipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (2016 cores, near-complete absence of gypsum).

question: The crew of Expedition 364 drilled 1,334 metres below the seabed in 2016, into the ring of hills at the center of the buried Chicxulub crater, and pulled up 829 metres of core. The rock was granite, the kind that usually sits about ten kilometres down, lifted to the surface within minutes of the impact. What lets a mountain's worth of granite move like a fluid for those few minutes?
answer: shaking briefly cancels the friction inside the rock
choices: shaking briefly cancels the friction inside the rock
heat from the impact melts it into a thick liquid
pressure turns its quartz into a slippery glass
water boiling in its cracks floats the grains apart
context: The mechanism is called acoustic fluidization: seismic shaking temporarily cancels the internal friction that holds broken rock rigid, so for a few minutes a mountain's worth of granite behaves like a fluid, rises about 10 km, and slumps into a ring. Borehole M0077A reached 1,334.7 m below the sea floor with over 99 percent core recovery. Directly above the peak ring the cores held the largest known graded sand layer on Earth -- a megatsunami deposit dropped within hours as the ocean poured back into the hole; modelling puts rim waves near the crater above 1.5 km high, with run-ups of 100-300 m recorded onshore in Texas and Alabama. Source: Grokipedia, 'Peak ring' (Expedition 364; acoustic fluidization); Wikipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (granite peak ring; graded sand layer).

question: Dale Russell and Wallace Tucker said in 1971 that a nearby star had exploded, and as late as 1979 Russell still called a supernova the only real option for the great extinction. The idea made a checkable promise: an exploding star forges short-lived isotopes like plutonium-244 and iron-60, and those should still sit in the boundary clay today. What did the search turn up?
answer: none of those isotopes, at any boundary site
choices: iron-60, in amounts far above the prediction
none of those isotopes, at any boundary site
both isotopes, but only in deep-sea cores
plutonium-244 alone, and only in Denmark
context: No excess plutonium-244 or iron-60 has been detected at the boundary, and modelled iridium yields from a supernova at 10-20 parsecs fall orders of magnitude short of the 10-100 nanograms per square centimetre actually measured. The supernova idea died the honourable way -- on a test it had proposed for itself. Notice what the impact hypothesis then survived that it did not choose: the same spike, at the same stratigraphic level, is now confirmed at over 350 sections worldwide, from Hell Creek in Montana to China's Nanxiong Basin to Seymour Island in Antarctica. The boundary clay carries other independent markers too: nickel-rich spinels, glass spherules, soot from global fires, and an osmium ratio far off the crustal value. In 2024, ruthenium isotopes identified the impactor as a carbonaceous asteroid formed beyond Jupiter's orbit. Source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event research' (Russell & Tucker 1971; Russell 1979); Grokipedia, 'Iridium anomaly' (no short-lived radionuclides; global confirmations; 2024 ruthenium result).

question: Gerta Keller and her colleagues have argued for decades that the Deccan Traps of west-central India, erupting enormous amounts of lava across the same period as the Chicxulub impact, were responsible for most of the killing. Mark Richards and Paul Renne of Berkeley, working with Walter Alvarez himself, proposed a third position. What do Richards and Renne argue?
answer: the impact's shaking set off the largest Deccan eruptions
choices: the impact's dust smothered the eruptions for a century
the impact and the eruptions had a single deeper cause
the impact's shaking set off the largest Deccan eruptions
the eruptions weakened the crust the asteroid then struck
context: Richards, Renne and colleagues (2015) argue that seismic shaking from the impact -- felt 13,000 km away -- triggered the largest phase of Deccan eruptions 50,000 to 100,000 years later, and that the continuing volcanism is why marine ecosystems took so long to recover. Walter Alvarez is an active member of the team arguing that his own asteroid had an accomplice. The rival case is real science, not crankery: the geologist Dewey McLean proposed volcanism as the killer in 1978, two years before the Alvarez paper, and Keller calculates 7-9 degrees C of ocean warming during the biggest pulse. In 2010 Science published a review by 41 authors coming down firmly for the impact and ruling out massive volcanism -- and dozens of other scientists challenged its methods and its conclusions. The dispute is bitter enough to have earned a nickname, the 'dinosaur wars'. The argument has narrowed a great deal. It has not closed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (Alternative theories; Richards et al. 2015 GSA Bulletin; Schulte et al., Science 327:1214-1218, 5 March 2010); Grokipedia, 'Deccan Traps'; Grokipedia, 'Gerta Keller'.

question: A physicist brings an electron together with its opposite-charge twin, a positron from the antimatter family, and both simply vanish. No ash, no fragments, no debris are left behind, just pure light carrying the energy away. Which kind of light is it?
answer: gamma rays
choices: gamma rays
radio waves
visible light
microwaves
context: Electron + positron annihilation produces two gamma-ray photons, each about 511 keV -- the tightest E = m c-squared demonstration nature offers. Source: home.cern/science/physics/antimatter.

question: A young physicist wrote an equation for the electron in 1928, and it had a second answer he could not erase. That answer called for a partner particle with the opposite charge, an antimatter twin no one had ever seen. Who was he?
answer: Paul Dirac
choices: Paul Dirac
Niels Bohr
Max Planck
Erwin Schrodinger
context: Dirac was 25; the positron he predicted was found four years later. Source: ebsco.com/research-starters/physics/dirac-equation.

question: Carl Anderson caught one particle curving the wrong way in a magnetic field at Caltech in August 1932, while photographing tracks in a cloud chamber. That was the first sighting of the positive electron an equation had called for. What natural source made the particle that left the track?
answer: cosmic rays hitting the atmosphere
choices: cosmic rays hitting the atmosphere
the Sun's ultraviolet light
a lightning strike nearby
the Earth's magnetic field
context: Anderson didn't know Dirac's paper when he saw the track; he named the particle the positron. He shared the 1936 Nobel. Source: spark.iop.org/andersons-accident.

question: A girl counts stars from a dark field. The Big Bang should have made matter and antimatter in equal amounts, which would then annihilate into pure light, leaving no atoms behind. Yet she and the stars exist. Roughly what fraction of the first particles survived to build every atom in every star and person?
answer: about 1 in a billion
choices: about 1 in a billion
about 1 in a thousand
about half
none -- new matter appeared later
context: That one-in-a-billion excess is every atom in every star, planet and person; the photons from all that annihilation are still around as the cosmic microwave background. Source: home.cern/science/physics/matter-antimatter-asymmetry-problem.

question: The ALPHA-g team (Antihydrogen Laser Physics Apparatus, gravity setup) at CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research, let atoms of antihydrogen loose for the first time inside a tall magnetic bottle and watched which way the atoms went. Each was an antiproton with a positron in orbit. The team reported the end of its decades-long project in September 2023. What did the antihydrogen do?
answer: fell downward like ordinary matter
choices: fell downward like ordinary matter
floated upward
hovered motionless
shot out horizontally
context: Antimatter's acceleration matched ordinary matter's within about 20 percent, closing off the antigravity escape route from the asymmetry problem. Source: nature.com/articles/d41586-023-03043-0.

question: An astronomer scans the sky for a glowing seam, the border where a galaxy of antimatter would meet ordinary matter and the two would destroy each other in bursts of light. Telescopes have hunted such seams for decades, and detectors like the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer on the International Space Station have hunted for antihelium atoms drifting in from far away. What have all these searches turned up?
answer: no evidence of antimatter regions at all
choices: no evidence of antimatter regions at all
large antimatter clouds near the galactic center
one antimatter galaxy in Virgo
annihilation borders around every quasar
context: If the universe held equal amounts of matter and antimatter divided into regions, we would see gamma-ray borders; the sky is silent. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0211260.

question: A researcher adds one more result to the ledger: test after test says antimatter is a near-perfect mirror of matter. Gravity in ALPHA-g (the Antihydrogen Laser Physics Apparatus gravity experiment) checks out, the light spectrum of antihydrogen matches hydrogen's to great precision, and the antiproton's mass matches too. What does this growing pile of matched results do to the puzzle of why any matter survived at all?
answer: makes it harder to explain, not easier
choices: makes it harder to explain, not easier
solves it via leptogenesis
proves the universe is symmetric after all
removes the need for Sakharov's conditions
context: The tinier the differences experiments find, the harder it is to build up even a one-in-a-billion excess. No one yet knows the answer. Source: home.cern/alpha-experiment.

question: Robert Boyle hung a ticking pocket watch by a thread inside the glass receiver of his new air pump in 1660, to test whether sound could cross empty space. He pumped the air out and leaned close to listen. What did the watch do as the receiver emptied?
answer: Its ticking faded to nothing
choices: Its ticking faded to nothing
It stopped running and had to be rewound
It sped up as the pressure dropped
It kept ticking as loudly as before
context: This was Experiment 27 of 'New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall, Touching the Spring of the Air, and its Effects'. The ticking returned the instant Boyle let air back in. He built the pump with the young Robert Hooke; it was the first controlled test that sound needs a medium. Source: Royal Society blog, https://royalsociety.org/blog/2024/11/making-waves/

question: A girl shouts across a room to her brother, and the sound reaches his ear through the air between them. Scientists spent centuries arguing about what does the carrying at a small scale: tiny particles streaming out, an invisible 'ether' filling space, or something else. What is actually carrying the shout from mouth to ear?
answer: Patches of air squeeze and release, each pushing on the next
choices: Patches of air squeeze and release, each pushing on the next
Tiny sound particles stream out and drift into the ear
The room's walls flex outward and carry the message
Invisible waves in the ether pass across the space
context: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave: each layer of gas shoves its neighbour and springs back. That is why an empty jar goes silent (no neighbours to shove) and a rubber ball can bounce fine in a vacuum but a bell cannot ring. Source: Royal Society blog, https://royalsociety.org/blog/2024/11/making-waves/

question: Robert Boyle refused to declare the case closed in 1660. His ticking watch, hung inside the glass vessel of his new air pump, had hinted that sound cannot cross a vacuum, but he had two honest reasons for holding back a verdict. Which pair kept him cautious?
answer: His pump still leaked, and the suspending thread might be carrying the ticking itself
choices: His pump still leaked, and the suspending thread might be carrying the ticking itself
His watch was faulty, and Hooke had not verified the setup
Kircher outranked him, and the Royal Society had not yet met
The glass distorted the sound, and no one else had a similar jar
context: Boyle wrote up the demonstration as suggestive, not decisive, and named the leak and the thread as the two loopholes. The whole story is a lesson in the Feynman rule about fooling yourself first. Source: Journal of Applied Physiology overview, https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/japplphysiol.00759.2004

question: Francis Hauksbee closed a question at the Royal Society around 1705 that had stayed genuinely open for roughly 45 years since Robert Boyle's demonstration: can sound travel through a vacuum? What let him settle a debate that Boyle, Kircher and von Guericke could not?
answer: A far tighter air pump that reached a much better vacuum
choices: A far tighter air pump that reached a much better vacuum
A louder bell rung by a spring-loaded hammer
A larger glass jar that muffled outside noise
A new mathematical proof that vacuums must be silent
context: Better apparatus, not better argument, ended the debate. Hauksbee's improved double-barrelled pump reached low enough pressure that even a suspended bell went nearly silent, and he then reported that condensed (compressed) air made the same bell sound louder still. Source: Royal Society Philosophical Transactions, https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rstl/article/26/321/367/110425/II-An-account-of-an-experiment-shewing-that-actual

question: Andrew Fabian led a team in 2003 that used a 53-hour Chandra X-ray observation of the hot gas filling the Perseus galaxy cluster. They found real pressure waves rippling through it, driven by the central supermassive black hole. What pitch did those waves turn out to carry?
answer: A B-flat about 57 octaves below middle C
choices: A B-flat about 57 octaves below middle C
A C-sharp near the low end of a piano keyboard
A pure tone matching a low human whisper
A pitch matching the natural note of the cluster's brightest star
context: A grand piano covers about seven octaves, so the Perseus note sits more than fifty octaves below the lowest key any piano can play, and over a million billion times deeper than the human ear can hear. The vacuum of space really is silent, but the hot cluster gas is a medium, and sound obeys the rule of a medium there too. Source: Chandra press release, https://chandra.harvard.edu/press/03_releases/press_090903.html

question: A nurse draws blood from a man who never felt ill, for a 2020 survey that can find everyone ever infected with COVID-19. Set against one trait of the person infected, the death rate runs from near zero to several percent. Which trait shows that steep climb?
answer: age
choices: age
sex
blood type
weight
context: O'Driscoll and colleagues, in Nature in early 2021, found the lowest infection fatality rate in children aged 5-9 and a log-linear rise above age 30. That is the fact this whole story rests on: schools were closed for the age group least at risk from the disease. Source: O'Driscoll et al., Nature (2021).

question: A nine-year-old sits the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), the longest-running American check on learning, a test about fifty years old. The scores released in September 2022, after governments shut schools, show one subject down seven points, its first fall in the whole history of the test. Which subject?
answer: mathematics
choices: mathematics
science
civics
geography
context: The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) long-term trend found nine-year-olds' maths scores had fallen 7 points from 2020 to 2022 - the first-ever mathematics decline in the assessment's roughly 50-year history. Reading fell 5 points, the largest reading drop since 1990. Source: NAGB press release, 1 September 2022.

question: Bastian Betthäuser and his team published a big review in January 2023, a meta-analysis pooling 42 pandemic learning-loss studies from 15 countries into one headline number. When they broke that loss down by school subject, which subject had taken the bigger hit?
answer: mathematics
choices: mathematics
reading
science
history
context: A meta-analysis is a study that pools many earlier studies to give one combined estimate on a common scale. Betthauser and colleagues screened their 42 studies from a much larger pool using inclusion rules fixed before the analysis began, and reported that pandemic-era deficits were larger in mathematics than in reading. Source: Betthauser, Bach-Mortensen and Engzell, Nature Human Behaviour, 30 January 2023.

question: A teacher reads the headline of Bastian Betthäuser's review of learning during the pandemic: a Cohen's d of -0.14. Cohen's d is expressed in standard deviations, a unit that lets different tests be put on one scale, and typical schoolchildren gain about 0.4 of them in a normal school year. Roughly what fraction of a school year's learning does -0.14 represent?
answer: about a third
choices: about a third
about a tenth
about a full year
about two full years
context: Roughly 35% of a normal school year (0.14 / 0.4). The 95% confidence interval on the estimate ran from -0.17 to -0.10, so the honest range is roughly a quarter to two-fifths of a year - not the 'lost generation' rhetoric of the headlines, but not small either. Source: Betthauser et al., Nature Human Behaviour (2023); University of Oxford SPI summary.

question: Bastian Betthäuser took the overall loss of learning his team measured across the pandemic, d = -0.14 from 42 pooled studies, and broke it down by group. The deficit was not spread evenly across all children. Which group of children showed the largest deficit?
answer: children from low-income homes
choices: children from low-income homes
children in mathematics rather than reading
children in the pandemic's later months rather than its early months
children in countries with the longest school closures
context: Deficits WERE larger in mathematics than in reading, so that cut is a real finding - but the largest cut Betthauser and colleagues reported was by socio-economic background. The pandemic-learning-loss deficit also arose EARLY and then held steady rather than growing across later months, so the 'later months' cut is not where the largest loss sits. The gap the closures were often said to protect against was the one they widened most. Source: Betthauser et al., Nature Human Behaviour (2023).

question: Per Engzell and colleagues, writing in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in April 2021, measured about 350,000 primary-school pupils in one country across an eight-week school closure, and found a learning loss roughly matching the length of the closure itself. They picked that country as a best-case test: fast broadband, fair schools, and a short closure. Which country?
answer: the Netherlands
choices: the Netherlands
South Korea
Finland
Singapore
context: The Dutch primary system re-tested pupils on national exams before and after the eight-week 2020 closure, giving something rare in pandemic research: a genuine before/after measurement on the same test in the same country. Even so, pupils lost about a fifth of a normal school year, with losses up to 55% larger among children from less-educated homes. Source: Engzell, Frey and Verhagen, PNAS (2021).

question: A school counsellor opens a scientific brief from the World Health Organization (WHO), dated March 2022, on the mental-health toll of lockdowns and isolation. It estimates that worldwide rates of anxiety and depression jumped 25% in the pandemic's first year, a global figure with wide uncertainty. The brief then names the two groups the surge hit hardest. Which two?
answer: young people and women
choices: young people and women
the elderly and men
healthcare workers and teachers
urban residents and children under five
context: The brief also warned that mental-health services expanded far more slowly than need. This question cites the WHO's own headline figure and its own named groups; a critical reader should note the wide uncertainty in a global first-year prevalence estimate and the difficulty of disentangling closures from disease and disruption. Source: WHO scientific brief, 2 March 2022.

question: A parent asks a teacher whether her son will keep falling behind. Bastian Betthäuser's review of 42 studies of learning during the COVID-19 pandemic reported the shape of the deficit over time as well as its size. What did the deficit do over time?
answer: appeared early and then held steady
choices: appeared early and then held steady
grew steadily each pandemic month
vanished within one school year
reversed once schools reopened
context: Children hit a step down and then resumed the normal rate of learning from a lower baseline, rather than falling further behind each week. That shape is consistent with the Dutch finding that loss scaled roughly with time out of school. It also means catch-up is possible in principle but not automatic; nothing in the data shows the deficit closing on its own. Source: Betthauser et al., Nature Human Behaviour (2023).

question: A researcher lays Bastian Betthäuser's review aside and looks for what it cannot give: it measures the whole pandemic, not policy alone, since illness, fear and family stress were all in the mix. Which real-world comparison does the cleanest job of splitting school policy from the pandemic itself?
answer: Sweden's open primary schools vs its neighbours' closed ones
choices: Sweden's open primary schools vs its neighbours' closed ones
US states that reopened in autumn 2020 vs states that stayed remote
Nordic countries vs Mediterranean countries generally
private schools vs public schools within the US
context: Sweden kept its primary schools open through the entire pandemic while nearby countries closed theirs, giving a long, consistent policy contrast between culturally similar rich European nations. US-state reopening dates shifted mid-pandemic and were confounded with local politics; Nordic-vs-Mediterranean comparisons drag in enormous cultural, demographic and health-system differences; private-vs-public schooling within the US selects heavily on family background. Sweden's flat primary-reading line, set against the closed-school deficits measured across 15 countries in the Betthauser meta-analysis, is what lets a careful reader attribute the international loss largely to time out of school rather than to the virus itself. Source: Betthauser et al. (2023); Hallin et al. (2022).

question: Bari Weiss's thread on Twitter's private files named a Stanford professor whose account sat on a 'Trends Blacklist'. He had argued that COVID lockdowns would harm children. Twitter never banned him and never touched his follower count. Who was he?
answer: Jay Bhattacharya
choices: Jay Bhattacharya
John Ioannidis
Michael Levitt
Scott Atlas
context: Bhattacharya had co-authored the Great Barrington Declaration in October 2020. Twitter quietly kept him out of trends, the practice called shadow-banning. John Ioannidis and Michael Levitt, both Stanford professors, and Scott Atlas of Stanford's Hoover Institution were lockdown critics too, but Weiss's thread named Bhattacharya.

question: Bari Weiss quoted an internal note from one of Twitter's own engineers, out of the private files Elon Musk let her publish after he bought the company in late 2022. The engineer wrote that the company controlled what people saw and boosted content 'quite a bit.' He ended the note with an admission about ordinary users. What was it?
answer: They do not know how much we do
choices: They do not know how much we do
They can appeal any decision
They can buy their way to the top
They set their own reach limits
context: Verbatim: 'We control visibility quite a bit. And we control the amplification of your content quite a bit. And normal people do not know how much we do.' That admission is what turned 'shadow-banning is a conspiracy theory' into 'shadow-banning is a workflow'.

question: A Rhode Island book distributor in the late 1950s opens a state commission's warning letter on official stationery, listing 'objectionable' titles. No one is arrested and no law is passed, yet he stops selling the books. In 1963 the Supreme Court took up the letters in Bantam Books v. Sullivan. What did it rule?
answer: The letters were censorship even without any law behind them
choices: The letters were censorship even without any law behind them
The letters were the state's own speech, and so lawful
The letters were lawful, since he was free to ignore them
The letters were unlawful only because they named titles
context: The Court called the commission's notices a 'system of informal censorship': a government need not pass a statute to violate the First Amendment, and official pressure on a private party can be enough. Lawyers call that kind of pressure jawboning, and Bantam Books is the precedent the challengers in the 2022-24 social-media cases leaned on. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantam_Books,_Inc._v._Sullivan

question: Terry A. Doughty, a federal district judge, issued a sweeping preliminary injunction against most of the Biden administration on 4 July 2023. His ruling called the case, in one striking phrase, arguably the most massive attack against what in United States history?
answer: Free speech
choices: Free speech
Public health
Election integrity
Presidential authority
context: Doughty also wrote that the government 'seems to have assumed a role similar to an Orwellian Ministry of Truth'. These are the district court's own words, not a finding the Supreme Court adopted. The injunction blocked most of the administration from contacting social-media platforms about constitutionally protected speech.

question: The Supreme Court took up Murthy v. Missouri in 2024, after a lower court found that federal officials had pressed social-media platforms to take posts down. In June six justices ruled against the states and users who had sued. What did the six actually decide?
answer: That the challengers could not sue, so censorship went undecided
choices: That the challengers could not sue, so censorship went undecided
That the officials had persuaded the platforms, never coerced them
That the platforms had acted alone, with no pressure from officials
That the officials' pressure was lawful because it served public health
context: The ground was Article III standing, the threshold requirement to sue: a plaintiff must show a concrete injury a court can redress. Justice Barrett's majority held that the challengers could not tie particular takedowns to particular government demands, so the case never reached the merits; in a footnote she added that many of the lower court's factual findings 'unfortunately appear to be clearly erroneous.' Justice Alito, dissenting with Thomas and Gorsuch, wrote that the Court 'unjustifiably refuses to address this serious threat to the First Amendment.' Sources: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/23pdf/23-411_3dq3.pdf ; https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/the-supreme-court-rules-on-government-pressure-websites-to-moderate-content

question: Thomas Young, a London physician, stood in 1803 in a darkened room at the Royal Institution and let a thin sunbeam in through a small hole in the shutter. He split the beam by holding a slip of card less than a millimeter wide edge-on in its path. What did he see on the far wall?
answer: Alternating bands of light and darkness
choices: Alternating bands of light and darkness
A single bright stripe with crisp edges
Two beams bending back toward the card
A perfect circle of light with a dark rim
context: Two pieces of light overlapping to make DARKNESS is the one thing a stream of particles cannot do, and that is why the card-split sunbeam mattered. Young had stated the rule himself in 1802: the general law 'may be very easily deduced from the interference of two coincident undulations, which either cooperate, or destroy each other.' ACCURACY NOTE: what Young is documented as doing is this card-split beam plus a water ripple tank (a candle under a glass tank, viewed in a mirror tilted overhead). Wikipedia says flatly that 'it is not clear which experiments Young performed and which ones he described as thought experiments' -- the pristine 'double slit' of the textbooks is partly later tidying-up. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young%27s_interference_experiment; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Young_(scientist)

question: Augustin-Jean Fresnel, a road engineer for the French government, walked away from his post in March 1815, when the exiled Napoleon Bonaparte escaped from Elba and marched back on Paris. Fresnel sided with the royalists opposing Napoleon, and his bosses in the new government suspended him. How did he spend the forced time off?
answer: Running optical experiments at his mother's house
choices: Running optical experiments at his mother's house
Drilling with royalist volunteers near his old post
Surveying a valley road for a private client
Reading law in Paris until his reinstatement
context: The man who overturned Newton's optics was not a professor. Fresnel served in the Corps des Ponts et Chaussees and had been posted to Nyons in the Drome; the suspension sent him home to Mathieu, where he worked on light. Three years later he beat the Academy of Sciences at its own game. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustin-Jean_Fresnel

question: Fresnel had designed a lighthouse lens built from rings of separate glass prisms, and the commission that would pay for it wanted proof. On 20 August 1822 he assembled a rotating eight-panel apparatus in Paris. He lit it for observers standing 32 km outside the city. Where did he mount it?
answer: On the top of the Arc de Triomphe
choices: On the top of the Arc de Triomphe
On the north tower of Notre-Dame
On the great dome of the Pantheon
On the roof of the Louvre palace
context: A claim anyone can check beats a claim you must take on trust. Fresnel did not argue the commission into the stepped lens -- on 20 August 1822 he mounted a rotating eight-panel apparatus on the Arc de Triomphe and had it judged by observers standing 32 km outside Paris, with their own eyes. The first lens went into a lighthouse the following year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresnel_lens

question: Thomas Young told his 1803 audience that his experiments 'may be repeated with great ease, whenever the sun shines, and without any other apparatus than is at hand to every one.' He was right. Suppose you want to see light interfere with only your hand and a lamp. What do you do?
answer: Look through the gap between two almost-touching fingers
choices: Look through the gap between two almost-touching fingers
Look past the edge of one fingertip held close to the eye
Look through a fist closed loosely to leave a pinhole
Look through your fingers spread wide across the lamp
context: Hold two fingers close to one eye with a gap of about a millimeter between them and look at a bright window or lamp -- NEVER at the sun. Dark lines appear in the gap, running parallel to your fingers: those are diffraction fringes, light canceling light. No apparatus, no laboratory, no permission needed -- exactly the claim Young made to his audience in 1803, and you can settle it yourself in about ten seconds. Source: physicslens.com/single-slit-diffraction-using-fingers/

question: Siméon Poisson, a judge of the Paris Academy's 1818 prize, set out to crush Augustin-Jean Fresnel's wave theory of light by working through Fresnel's own math. Poisson was sure light was a stream of particles, not waves, and he was hunting for a result silly enough to sink the theory. He found one he thought clearly nonsense. What did Fresnel's math predict?
answer: A small round disc must show a bright spot in the center of its shadow
choices: A small round disc must show a bright spot in the center of its shadow
A straight razor's edge must cast a shadow with no boundary at all
A candle seen through a pinhole must appear as two separate flames
A beam crossing a second beam must be pushed sideways out of its line
context: Poisson meant it as a reductio ad absurdum -- a knockout blow, not a discovery. Fresnel's mathematics said the middle of the shadow would be 'illuminated as brightly as the exterior', as if the disc were not there at all. Physics World renders Poisson's reaction as: 'Obvious nonsense!' Arago tested it, the spot was sitting exactly where Poisson had said it could not be, and Fresnel won the prize. The spot has carried Poisson's name ever since -- named for the man who invented it to destroy the theory it went on to prove. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresnel%27s_physical_optics; physicsworld.com/a/the-spot-in-the-shadow/

question: Henry Brougham, one of the founders of the Edinburgh Review, tore into Thomas Young's work on light waves from January 1803, writing anonymously in the journal and calling it worthless. Young had published the work in 1802 and 1803. What did the attacks do to Young's work in optics?
answer: His publisher dropped the lectures and Young turned to medicine
choices: His publisher dropped the lectures and Young turned to medicine
The Royal Society refused to print his next Bakerian lecture
The Royal Institution canceled the rest of his lecture course
Young answered in print and the Review dropped the campaign
context: Brougham attacked anonymously, and the smear worked: the publisher who had agreed to print Young's Royal Institution lectures backed out, Young redirected himself toward medicine and later the Rosetta Stone, and the wave theory was 'generally ignored for more than a decade' until Fresnel and Arago revived it. English loyalty to Newton was part of the hostility. Young was no lightweight -- he had learned eleven languages by the age of fourteen, became physician to St George's Hospital in 1811, and by 1814 had worked through 86 demotic words of the Rosetta Stone, groundwork Champollion later built on. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young%27s_interference_experiment; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Young_(scientist)

question: Francesco Maria Grimaldi showed that light through a small hole spreads wider than straight lines allow, with colored fringes along the edges of shadows. He published the word 'diffraction' in 1665, so he had the effect and the name a century and a half before Young or Fresnel. What did Grimaldi take light to be?
answer: A very fine fluid, undulating like ripples in water
choices: A very fine fluid, undulating like ripples in water
A stream of hard particles, as Isaac Newton later argued
A pressure wave running through the air, like sound
A flow of heat, the same substance that warms a room
context: Grimaldi's 'Physico-Mathesis de Lumine, Coloribus, et Iride' (1665) gave the effect its name and showed it plainly -- but he read light as a substance, a fine fluid, with color arising from undulations inside it. Seeing an effect is not the same as having the theory that makes the effect mean something. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Maria_Grimaldi

question: A student shines a laser on a small ball bearing, and a bright dot appears right in the dead center of its shadow. The roundness itself is doing real work. One geometrical property of the circular rim explains why the light grazing the edge piles up at that single point instead of canceling. What property?
answer: Every point on the rim lies the same distance from the shadow's center
choices: Every point on the rim lies the same distance from the shadow's center
Every point on the rim aims its light straight at the shadow's center
Every point on the rim bends its grazing light by the same fixed angle
Every point on the rim has a twin directly opposite across the center
context: Because every point on the circumference is the same distance from the center of the shadow, light passing close by the edge all the way around travels exactly the same distance and arrives IN PHASE -- crest lining up with crest -- so it adds instead of canceling. That is also why the edge has to be smooth: rough corrugations on the rim smear the spot away, and they should stay under about 10% of the width of the neighboring Fresnel zone (roughly 77 micrometers for a 4 mm disc in the standard setup) or the contributions stop arriving together. You can see the spot for yourself: aim a laser pointer at a small ball bearing and a bright dot appears dead center in the ball's shadow. Physicists have since produced the same bright dot using beams of electrons and of neutral deuterium molecules. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arago_spot; web.physics.ucsb.edu/~lecturedemonstrations/Composer/Pages/84.12.html; Reisinger et al., 'Poisson's spot with molecules', Phys. Rev. A 79, 053823 (2009)

question: Joseph-Nicolas Delisle reported a tiny luminous spot at the center of a small ball's shadow in 1715, and Giacomo Filippo Maraldi did the same in 1723, both describing bright and dark rings around it. That was a century before the Paris Academy's 1818 prize for explaining diffraction. The reports sat in the journals for a hundred years and started no argument at all. Why not?
answer: Neither man had a theory of light that the bright point could test
choices: Neither man had a theory of light that the bright point could test
Both men blamed a flaw in the glass of their own telescope lenses
Newton's particle theory already explained it, so no one was startled
Maraldi's measurements contradicted Delisle's, and both were set aside
context: Arago himself pointed out the priority afterwards. This is the honest footnote to the whole story: an observation can be correct, published, and repeated, and still count for nothing for a century, because nobody yet has a framework that makes it a test of anything. Data alone does not decide; data plus a theory that could have come out wrong does. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arago_spot; grokipedia.com/page/Arago_spot

question: Augustin-Jean Fresnel could explain polarization only if light wobbled sideways to its direction of travel, a transverse wave shaking side to side as it moved forward. That put a hard demand on the ether, the invisible medium then believed to fill all of space and carry light. What did the ether have to be?
answer: As rigid as a solid, though the planets sailed through it untouched
choices: As rigid as a solid, though the planets sailed through it untouched
As thin as the finest gas, yet far stiffer close to the Sun
Two fluids intermingled, one carrying light and one carrying heat
Electrically charged throughout, though matter felt no force from it
context: Transverse waves cannot travel through an ordinary fluid -- they need a medium that resists being sheared sideways -- so the ether had to be stiff like a solid AND completely unobstructive to the planets at the same time. Nearly everyone found the picture repellent, and rightly so: the ether was abandoned about seventy years later. The predictions were still correct. A correct theory can ride for decades on a mental image that turns out to be wrong. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustin-Jean_Fresnel

question: Albert Einstein turned to the photoelectric effect in 1905, when Fresnel's waves had looked settled for most of a century. Light falling on a metal knocks electrons out of it, and on the wave theory the whole story was brightness: pour more light in, and each electron should come flying out with more energy. The experiments said otherwise. What did an electron's energy actually track?
answer: The color of the light alone, from deep red through to violet
choices: The color of the light alone, from deep red through to violet
The time the light had been shining on the metal beforehand
The temperature of the metal rather than anything about the light
The angle at which the beam struck the metal's polished surface
context: Color is frequency, and Einstein's 1905 argument was that light arrives in discrete packets of energy E = h x nu, proportional to frequency. Brightness turned out to set only how MANY electrons came out, not how hard each one was kicked: below a threshold color no amount of brightness helps, and above it even a dim light works instantly. Particles came back into the story and the argument Fresnel seemed to have closed reopened. That is the honest ending: the wave victory was real and earned, and it was not the last word. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers; grokipedia.com/page/History_of_quantum_mechanics

question: Augustin-Jean Fresnel had his first stepped lens lit at the Cordouan lighthouse in July 1823, replacing twelve big polished parabolic reflectors that had lit that tower since 1791. The lens was his practical monument, and his argument against those reflectors was blunt. What was wrong with them?
answer: Their mirrors never got half the light out of the tower
choices: Their mirrors never got half the light out of the tower
Their twelve frames were too heavy for the tower to turn
Their polished faces dulled within weeks in the salt air
Their beam spread so wide it faded within a few miles
context: A lens bends light where the light crosses its surface; the thick body of glass behind that surface is dead weight. Fresnel kept the surface and threw the bulk away -- his 1820 prototype panel was a square 55 cm on a side built from 97 separate polygonal prisms. The Cordouan lens was visible more than 32 km out to sea. The same idea now sits in overhead projectors, car headlamps and traffic lights. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresnel_lens; cordouan.culture.gouv.fr/en/cordouans-first-lens

question: A technician in a radiocarbon lab dates a mammoth tusk pulled from Siberian ice, then will not open the box holding a 66-million-year-old dinosaur bone. The bone is real, but the clock reads clearly only to about 50,000 years. Why won't any lab date it?
answer: Its carbon-14 ran out long ago, leaving none to count.
choices: Dinosaurs never took carbon-14 into their bones.
Its carbon-14 ran out long ago, leaving none to count.
Deep burial sped its carbon-14 decay past reading.
No counter can separate its carbon from the rock.
context: Carbon-14 halves away every 5,730 years, and radiocarbon runs out of signal at roughly 50,000 to 60,000 years, where so little is left that it sinks toward the detection limit. A 66-million-year-old bone sits about 11,500 half-lives past that wall, so there is nothing left to count -- which is a statement about the clock, not a hint that the bone is fake. The mammoth is well inside the window; the dinosaur is not remotely close. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Radiocarbon_dating).

question: An archaeologist lifts a wooden bowl, a linen shirt and a deer-bone needle out of one dry cave and sends all three for radiocarbon dating. Living things draw carbon-14 from the air, and the amount left in each object has been counting down since one particular moment. Which moment?
answer: When the tree, flax and deer died.
choices: When a craftsman shaped each object.
When the tree, flax and deer sprouted.
When the tree, flax and deer died.
When each object was buried in the cave.
context: A living plant keeps swapping carbon with the air and animals keep eating the plants, so everything alive carries roughly the same carbon-14 fraction as the atmosphere. Only when the organism dies does that exchange stop, and the carbon-14 begins to run down with nothing replacing it. A radiocarbon age is therefore the time since the sample ceased exchanging carbon with its environment -- which is why the beam of a house can date centuries older than the house. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Radiocarbon_dating).

question: A runner takes a deep breath at dawn. Carbon-14 decays away steadily, so every atom of it in the air should have vanished long ago, yet that breath holds a fresh supply, remade high overhead as fast as it drains away. Which atom up there becomes carbon-14, and how?
answer: Nitrogen-14, when a neutron knocks a proton out of it.
choices: Oxygen-16, when ultraviolet sunlight splits it apart.
Argon-40, when a cosmic ray shatters it into pieces.
Carbon-12, when it absorbs two extra neutrons.
Nitrogen-14, when a neutron knocks a proton out of it.
context: The reaction is 14N + n -> 14C + p: a cosmic-ray neutron strikes a nitrogen-14 nucleus, which takes in the neutron and throws out a proton, so nitrogen becomes carbon. The loop closes at the far end -- when that carbon-14 finally decays it emits an electron and an antineutrino and turns straight back into nitrogen-14. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Radiocarbon_dating).

question: To prove his numbers right, Willard Libby plotted his lab's dates against ages already known from other evidence. The plot became the star of his 1960 Nobel lecture. What did he run through his counters to build it?
answer: Egyptian tomb timber and rings from a felled sequoia.
choices: Bank notes and newsprint printed with their own years.
Egyptian tomb timber and rings from a felled sequoia.
Deep-sea mud and lake clay with their layers counted.
Whale bone and driftwood taken from dated shipwrecks.
context: Libby called the plot the 'Curve of Knowns'. Timber from the tomb of the pharaoh Zoser came back at about 2800 BCE +/- 250, against the Egyptologists' settled 2625 +/- 75; the tree rings came from the 'Centennial Stump', a giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) from California's Sierra Nevada. Even the paper title was the argument -- Libby and James Arnold, 'Age Determinations by Radiocarbon Content: Checks with Samples of Known Age', Science, December 1949. A clock earns trust by first retelling a story you already know. The first dedicated radiocarbon laboratory opened at the University of Chicago in 1949; the Nobel Prize in Chemistry followed in 1960. Sources: Pearson et al., 'Dendrochronology and Radiocarbon Dating', Radiocarbon (Cambridge University Press); Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating'.

question: Willard Libby built his whole method on counting decays, so his laboratory burned each sample down to pure carbon and sat it in front of a counter. Every living thing is faintly radioactive, with carbon-14 decaying inside it. How fast does one gram of modern carbon, a pinch the size of a pencil lead, tick?
answer: About fourteen times a minute.
choices: About fourteen times a second.
About fourteen times a minute.
About fourteen thousand times a minute.
About fourteen million times a minute.
context: Roughly 14 disintegrations per minute per gram of modern carbon (13.5 dpm/g in later measurements) -- about one decay every four seconds in a pinch of carbon the size of a pencil lead. An anti-coincidence circuit rings a second detector around the first: anything that trips both at once arrived from outside and is thrown away, leaving only the whisper from the sample itself. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Radiocarbon_dating).

question: A tree-ring scientist at Hohenheim in central Europe checks a date on an oak-and-pine chronology that now runs 12,460 years, with every ring pinned to its own year. The oldest bristlecone pines alive are about 4,000 years old, not enough to calibrate radiocarbon back toward the last ice age. How was the record pushed back that far?
answer: Overlapping ring patterns chained dead logs onto living trees.
choices: Radiocarbon dates on each log fixed its place in the sequence.
Growth-rate formulas restored the rings each log had lost.
Overlapping ring patterns chained dead logs onto living trees.
Peat layers buried above each log were counted down to it.
context: Crossdating is the trick. A run of fat and thin rings is a barcode that wet decades and droughts stamp on every tree in a region, so a dead log's pattern can be locked onto the overlapping years of a younger log, and that one onto a living tree -- no radiocarbon involved at any step, which is exactly what keeps the calibration from being circular. Hohenheim's oak and pine sequence reaches 12,460 years (Friedrich et al. 2004); bristlecone pine (Pinus longaeva) chronologies from California's White Mountains run past 8,800 years. Measure the carbon-14 in each calendar-dated ring and you have built the calibration curve. The modern curve, IntCal20, spans 55,000 years, its most precise stretch -- about the last 13,900 years -- resting directly on tree rings, with lake varves, uranium-thorium-dated corals and speleothems carrying it deeper. Sharpest of all are the solar spikes: a storm in AD 774-775 punched about 12 per mil of extra carbon-14 into the air in one or two years, visible in tree rings on every continent, and a second spike hit in 993. In 2021 Kuitems, Dee and colleagues found the 993 ring in Norse-cut wood at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, counted 28 rings out to the bark, and got a felling year of AD 1021 -- three separate trees agreeing. Sources: Pearson et al., 'Dendrochronology and Radiocarbon Dating', Radiocarbon (Cambridge UP); Grokipedia, 'Dendrochronology'; Kuitems et al., Nature (2021).

question: Physicists at Rochester and McMaster showed a new way to do radiocarbon dating in 1977, and it changed what a museum was willing to give up. A date used to eat a lump of pure carbon; now it could come from one flax seed, a single thread from a robe or a fleck of charcoal under a milligram. What do the new machines do that the old counters could not?
answer: They count individual carbon-14 atoms inside an accelerator.
choices: They run each sample for months to gather far more decays.
They concentrate the carbon-14 chemically before counting.
They chill the counters to near absolute zero to kill background.
They count individual carbon-14 atoms inside an accelerator.
context: Beta counting waits for atoms to decay, and with a half-life of 5,730 years almost none of them oblige while you watch. Accelerator mass spectrometry ignores decay altogether: it accelerates the sample's ions and sorts them by mass, so the carbon-14 atoms are counted one at a time. That drops the sample needed from tens of grams to under a milligram, which is why a single seed, a thread or a scraping of pigment can now carry a date. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Radiometric dating' and 'Radiocarbon dating'.

question: A geologist sets out to date a rock by uranium turning into lead and hits a wall: she must know how much lead the rock started with, and usually she cannot. So she reaches past the whole rock for one tough little crystal, zircon, which survives erosion, burial and even re-melting. What does a growing zircon crystal do that makes it such an honest clock?
answer: It takes uranium into its lattice but shuts lead out.
choices: It takes in uranium and lead in a fixed, known ratio.
It takes uranium into its lattice but shuts lead out.
It takes in only lead-204, never lead made by decay.
It takes in uranium and vents lead each time it reheats.
context: It is a size-and-charge mismatch. In zircon (ZrSiO4) a uranium-4+ ion of radius 1.05 angstrom can slip into a zirconium-4+ site of 0.87 angstrom, but lead-2+ is shut out: too big at 1.32 angstrom and carrying the wrong charge. A fresh zircon therefore starts with essentially no lead at all, so every lead atom found inside it had to be manufactured there by decay. The crystal starts its own clock at zero, and holds it up to a closure temperature near 900 C. Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Importance of zircon in uranium-lead dating'; Grokipedia, 'Radiometric dating'.

question: A graduate student in a radiocarbon lab computes a raw age with Willard Libby's half-life for carbon-14, 5,568 years, though the accepted value is 5,730. The age will then be calibrated against a curve built from tree rings. Why not simply switch to the correct figure?
answer: Because a date published in 1955 must still mean the same as one published now.
choices: Because switching would change every date by well over a thousand years.
Because the counters in every laboratory were built around his number.
Because a date published in 1955 must still mean the same as one published now.
Because the older figure gives ages that agree better with tree rings.
context: The Libby half-life of 5,568 +/- 30 years is retained by convention -- the constant 8033 in the age formula is simply 5568/ln2 -- rather than silently rewriting every age published before the correction. The genuine correction, which is larger than the half-life error anyway, is made openly at the calibration step. Radiocarbon dates are calibrated, not apologised for; the true Cambridge half-life is 5,730 +/- 40 years. The method also names its own blind spots.
