The Hallstatt plateau, roughly 800 to 400 BCE, is a flat stretch of the curve where a single date can be ambiguous by up to 400 calendar years, which genuinely muddles Iron Age chronology; and the marine reservoir effect makes ocean shells date about 400 years too old worldwide, because upwelling water carries carbon that has been out of contact with the air for centuries -- in hard-water lakes the offset can reach 2,000 to 2,700 years. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Radiocarbon_dating).

question: A researcher picks a zircon grain about two hairs wide from a rock in the Jack Hills of Western Australia. Dated in 2001 to 4,404 million years, it is the oldest dated piece of Earth, older than any surviving rock. It also holds a second reading: the ratio of its oxygen isotopes, which records the magma the crystal grew in. What does that ratio say about the young Earth?
answer: That the magma had already met liquid water near the surface.
choices: That the crust was still a worldwide ocean of molten rock.
That the magma had already met liquid water near the surface.
That the magma had been re-melted by a giant impact.
That the magma rose from far deeper than any magma today.
context: The grain's delta-18O of 8.5 to 9.5 per mil is heavier than mantle magma, the signature of rock that had been weathered by liquid water before being melted -- evidence for water at Earth's surface 4.4 billion years ago, within roughly 150 million years of the planet forming. Hadean grains older than 4.0 billion years make up as much as 12% of the Jack Hills zircon population. The site is now treated like a monument: Erawondoo Hill joined Australia's National Heritage List on 30 June 2020, and on 28 October 2022 the International Union of Geological Sciences named 'the Archean Zircons of Erawondoo Hill' one of the First 100 Geological Heritage Sites in the world. Source: Grokipedia, 'Jack Hills' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Jack_Hills).

question: A student raises the obvious objection to deep time: a rock spends aeons under crushing pressure and searing heat, so surely its decay clock must speed up or slow down. Laboratories have tested decay rates from -255 C to 1350 C, at pressures near 2,000 atmospheres and in magnetic fields of 8.3 tesla, and measured no change. What is the physical reason the rate is so hard to touch?
answer: Decay happens in the nucleus, while heat and chemistry move electrons.
choices: The crystal lattice around each atom shields it from outside conditions.
Heating speeds decay while pressure slows it, and the two cancel out.
Decay happens in the nucleus, while heat and chemistry move electrons.
Each atom's own internal heat drives its decay, and never changes.
context: The nucleus is about one hundred-thousandth the width of the atom around it, and heat, pressure and chemical bonding all act on the electron cloud far outside it. Marie Curie and Heike Kamerlingh Onnes made the point as early as 1913, chilling a radium sample to 20 kelvin and finding its decay constant unchanged to within 0.1 percent. Sources: Goodwin et al., 'Absence of low-temperature dependence of the decay of 7Be and 198Au in metallic hosts', arXiv:0805.0024; G. T. Emery, 'Perturbation of Nuclear Decay Rates', Annual Review of Nuclear Science 22 (1972) 165.

question: Kirsty Spalding, Jonas Frisen and colleagues at the Karolinska Institute measured the carbon-14 in the tooth enamel of 22 people. Nuclear tests in the open air up to 1963 had pushed the carbon-14 in the atmosphere to roughly double its natural level before it drained away. Every child alive then breathed that spike, and enamel is laid down in childhood and never replaced. What did the enamel give them?
answer: The calendar year each person was born in.
choices: The dose of fallout each had breathed as a child.
The hemisphere each of them had grown up in.
The main food of each one's childhood diet.
The calendar year each person was born in.
context: Atmospheric carbon-14 peaked in 1963-65 at nearly 100 percent above normal, then drained into the ocean and biosphere after the 1963 test ban; levels are now back near pre-nuclear values. That steep, precisely dated slope is the 'bomb pulse', and because it falls fast it dates recent things far more sharply than ordinary radiocarbon can. Spalding, Frisen and colleagues published the enamel result in Nature in 2005, recovering birth years to within 1.6 years. The same trick catches poachers: Kevin Uno, Thure Cerling and colleagues (PNAS, 2016) radiocarbon-dated tusks from 14 ivory seizures made between 2002 and 2014, pinning each elephant's death to about a year -- most of the ivory proved to be under three years old, recent killing rather than old stockpile. One seizure was the exception: a large fraction was over 30 years old, matching markings showing it had come out of a government stockpile. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Bomb pulse'; Spalding et al., Nature 437, 333 (2005); Cerling, Uno et al., PNAS (2016).

question: Physicists at the GSI (Centre for Heavy Ion Research) storage ring in Darmstadt took rhenium-187 and stripped every last electron off its atoms before letting them decay. Ordinary neutral rhenium-187 halves in 42 billion years, three times the age of the universe. Chemistry and environment can shift the decay rate of uranium in a rock by perhaps one part in ten million. What happened to the rhenium's half-life?
answer: It fell from 42 billion years to about 33 years.
choices: It fell from 42 billion years to about 33 million.
It fell from 42 billion years to about 33 years.
It rose from 42 billion years to about 400 billion.
It held at about 42 billion years, unchanged.
context: Fully ionized rhenium-187 nuclei at GSI decayed with a half-life of 32.9 +/- 2.0 years -- more than nine orders of magnitude faster than the neutral atom. In beta decay the emitted electron normally has to shove out past the crowd already surrounding the nucleus; strip the atom bare and it can drop straight into an empty orbital instead, a channel called bound-state beta decay, and it matters for how rhenium behaves inside stars. There is a smaller, honest cousin worth saying out loud: electron capture uses one of the atom's own electrons, so chemistry really can nudge it. Beryllium-7 sealed inside a carbon-60 cage has a half-life of 52.68 +/- 0.05 days against 53.12 +/- 0.05 days in beryllium metal, about 0.8 percent faster. Real, measured, tiny -- and irrelevant to uranium-lead, where environmental effects on alpha decay are estimated at one part in ten million or less. A rule you can state the exceptions to is stronger than one you cannot. Sources: Bosch et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. (1996), OSTI 404092; UC Riverside Physics FAQ, 'How to Change Nuclear Decay Rates'.

question: A geochemist counts the daughter isotope in a rock, the element the decay produces. To turn that count into an age she must assume how much of it was already there when the rock formed, and an assumption is not a measurement. So she takes several minerals from the same rock and plots each one's strontium against its rubidium. What does that plot hand her that a single sample never could?
answer: A line whose intercept gives the start and whose slope gives the age.
choices: A curve whose lowest point gives the start and whose steepness gives the age.
A line whose intercept gives the start and whose slope gives the age.
A cluster whose centre gives the start and whose spread gives the age.
A band whose lower edge gives the start and whose width gives the age.
context: This is the isochron. Plot strontium-87/strontium-86 against rubidium-87/strontium-86 for several minerals from one rock: if the rock stayed a closed system the points fall on a straight line whose slope is e^(lambda*t) - 1, which gives the age, while the y-intercept is the initial strontium-87/strontium-86 the rock was born with -- measured, not assumed. And the method polices itself: scatter off the line is the warning that the sample was disturbed. Zircon runs the same audit a different way. Wetherill's concordia diagram (1956) plots lead-206/uranium-238 against lead-207/uranium-235; a grain that stayed sealed lands on the concordia curve, while a grain that leaked lead falls below it along a straight discordia line whose upper intercept still recovers the crystallization age and whose lower intercept dates the disturbance. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Radiometric dating'; Wikipedia, 'Isochron dating'.

question: A museum guide tells a class that Lucy, the Australopithecus afarensis skeleton dug out of Hadar in Ethiopia, is about 3.18 million years old, and that nobody has ever dated Lucy. Her bones carry no usable clock at all. The number comes from somewhere else in the landscape around her. From where?
answer: Volcanic ash layers above and below her, argon-dated.
choices: Charcoal from the layer she lay in, radiocarbon-dated.
Volcanic ash layers above and below her, argon-dated.
Zircon grains in the sandstone around her, uranium-lead dated.
Minerals from the rock beneath her, rubidium-strontium dated.
context: Lucy is bracketed rather than dated: argon-argon ages on the volcanic ash layers that sandwich her set a maximum and a minimum, with the older ash lying about 18 metres beneath the fossil, and Lucy has to fall between them -- roughly 3.18 million years. Radiocarbon could not have touched her: it runs out near 50,000 years, and 3.18 million is far past its wall. The precise work followed Derek York's improved technique, applied by Aronson and Walter in 1992. Geochronologists also publish their own worst cases, which is how the traps got named: submarine basalts from eruptions witnessed in historical time have yielded potassium-argon ages as old as 22 million years, because argon trapped under water pressure never escaped the lava. Excess argon, inherited older zircon cores and entrained foreign crystals are the known routes to a wrong number -- which is exactly why step-heating and cross-method checks exist. On the Alder Creek Rhyolite, argon-argon on sanidine gives 1.1850 +/- 0.0016 million years while chemical-abrasion uranium-lead on zircon gives 1.1978 +/- 0.0046 million; when two independent methods disagree badly, that disagreement is itself the signal. Sources: Institute of Human Origins, 'About the Fossil Lucy'; Becoming Human, 'Geology and Dating'; Grokipedia, 'Radiometric dating'.

question: C. T. R. Wilson stood atop Ben Nevis in September 1894, a relief observer at its observatory, when the sun broke through and threw his own shadow onto the cloud below, ringed with colour. What did Wilson decide to do about what he had seen?
answer: Make the effect happen in a jar in his laboratory
choices: Make the effect happen in a jar in his laboratory
Return each summer to photograph it from the summit
Hunt other Scottish peaks for the same coloured rings
Work out how high the cloud must sit to show it
context: Wilson opened his 1927 Nobel Lecture with that fortnight on the summit, in his own words: the coronas and glories "greatly excited my interest and made me wish to imitate them in the laboratory." He was chasing weather, not particles. CERN's own build manual is blunt about it: he "wanted to study cloud formation and optical phenomena in moist air. He discovered soon, that by accident he had invented a particle detector." Sources: C. T. R. Wilson, Nobel Lecture 1927; J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, p.2.

question: A boy at sea level holds out his open palm. Muons, the electron's heavy cousins, are born about 15 kilometers up, when cosmic rays smash into the top of Earth's atmosphere. Physicists once hauled bulky detectors up mountains to catch them. About how often does one pass through his palm?
answer: About once a second
choices: About once a second
About once an hour
About once a week
About once a year
context: CERN states it flatly: "On average, 1 muon passes through the palm of your hand every second with an energy of typically 1 GeV to 1 TeV." At sea level muons are about 70% of all charged cosmic particles arriving, roughly one per square centimetre per minute, and there are 1.3 times more anti-muons than muons. They have been crossing you your whole life; a box of cold air is all it takes to see them. Source: J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, pp.11 and 14.

question: Trying to make clouds on a laboratory bench, C. T. R. Wilson filtered his air in 1895 until it was scrupulously dust-free. Physics in the 1890s held that a cloud cannot form without dust, since water vapour needs specks of dirt to condense on. Yet when he expanded the air hard enough, it clouded over anyway. What was seeding the droplets?
answer: Ions, molecules left carrying an electric charge
choices: Ions, molecules left carrying an electric charge
Salt grains too fine for any filter to catch
Scratches in the glass wall of the chamber
Cold spots where the air chilled the fastest
context: Droplets appeared only above a critical expansion ratio of about 1.25, corresponding to roughly fourfold supersaturation, and what they were growing on was electric charge. A meteorologist trying to explain rain had just found that ions make clouds, and with that, without meaning to, the first instrument that could show where an invisible particle had been. Source: Grokipedia, 'Cloud chamber' (History: invention and early concept).

question: An 87-year-old C. T. R. Wilson published his last scientific paper in 1956. He had invented the cloud chamber, a sealed glass box of damp air where a passing atomic particle leaves a visible white trail, and by the 1930s it was the fastest route in physics to spotting a new particle. What was that final paper about?
answer: The electricity inside thunderclouds
choices: The electricity inside thunderclouds
The tracks left by cosmic-ray particles
The rings of colour around a mountain shadow
A faster way to expand a chamber's air
context: The paper was 'A Theory of Thundercloud Electricity', 1956. Wilson was born on 14 February 1869 at Glencorse, Midlothian, the son of a sheep farmer, John, who died when Charles was four; he died on 15 November 1959, aged 90. He spent his whole working life on the weather. The particle detector that carried physics for forty years was the side effect. Source: Wikipedia, 'C. T. R. Wilson'.

question: A mother builds a particle detector at home from a manual by CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research): a clear plastic box about the size of a fish tank, a strip of felt, a black metal floor plate, a very bright torch and dry ice, handled in gloves in a ventilated room. The felt has to be soaked in the liquid that supplies the vapour. What is it?
answer: Isopropyl alcohol, over 90 per cent pure
choices: Isopropyl alcohol, over 90 per cent pure
Distilled water, warmed to blood heat
Liquid paraffin, thinned with white spirit
Glycerine, mixed half and half with water
context: CERN's shopping list in full: a clear box roughly 20 x 30 x 15 cm, 5 mm felt, a 5 mm black anodised aluminium plate (black so the white tracks show against it), dry ice at -78 C, isopropanol over 90% purity, and one tightly bundled bright torch. Safety, in CERN's own plain words: dry ice, "touching it directly will cause burns... only use in well ventilated rooms", and "dry ice in airtight containers will build up high pressure"; the alcohol, "never drink it, handle with gloves and goggles." Leather gloves for the ice, nitrile for the isopropanol. Source: J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, pp.3-5.

question: A student watches a white thread cross a cloud chamber and says she has seen a particle. C. T. R. Wilson never claimed that; he wrote only that the cloud condensed along the tracks. A charged particle tears electrons off the molecules it passes, and vapour grows droplets along that line until they are big enough to see. By the time she sees the thread, how long has the particle been gone?
answer: About a tenth of a second
choices: About a tenth of a second
About a millionth of a second
About ten full seconds
About a full minute
context: Roughly 100 ion pairs per centimetre for a fast minimum-ionising particle, thousands per centimetre for an alpha. The droplets grow to 1-10 micrometres across in about 100 milliseconds and last a few seconds. So the fog in the photograph is thousands of times fatter than the particle that made it, and it arrives a tenth of a second after the particle has already left the box. You are looking at a wake, not a thing, which is the more interesting claim. Source: Grokipedia, 'Cloud chamber' (Physics of supersaturation and ionization; Expansion and track formation).

question: A girl soaks the felt at the warm top of a home cloud chamber and sets dry ice under the floor. After about five minutes a layer holding more vapour than it should forms about a centimetre thick just above the plate at the bottom, and every track appears there. Why does the vapour gather down there instead of rising to the top?
answer: Isopropanol vapour is heavier than air, so it sinks
choices: Isopropanol vapour is heavier than air, so it sinks
The cold floor drags the vapour down by convection
The felt drips liquid alcohol onto the plate below
Evaporation drives the vapour away from the warm top
context: Alcohol evaporates off the warm felt, sinks because isopropanol vapour is denser than air, and gets chilled hard on the way down by dry ice at -78 C. That builds the thin supersaturated layer hugging the black plate, which is why every track you see runs along the floor. CERN: "The tracks look a little like spider's threads going along the chamber floor." Source: J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, pp.6-7.

question: A teacher watches threads cross the floor of a home cloud chamber. Most are thin and straight, muons made high in the atmosphere. Then one thread turns a sharp corner in mid-flight and carries on. What has just happened inside the box?
answer: A muon decayed into an electron and two neutrinos
choices: A muon decayed into an electron and two neutrinos
A muon glanced off the nucleus of an air atom
A muon crossed from the cold layer into warmer air
A muon knocked an electron loose from an atom
context: CERN's key to reading your own fog: a thin straight thread is a muon or anti-muon from the upper atmosphere; a thick straight stub about 5 cm long is an alpha particle from radon-222 in the room air; a curly wandering line is a slow electron; a Y-fork is a muon knocking an electron off an atom; and a sudden kink is a muon transforming in mid-flight into an electron plus two neutrinos. Particle decay, in your kitchen, for the price of a bag of dry ice. Source: J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, p.8 ('What can you see?').

question: Patrick Blackett filled a cloud chamber with nitrogen in 1925 and fired alpha particles into it from polonium, exposing his plates for weeks to catch the rare frame where one particle struck a nucleus head-on. Ernest Rutherford had claimed such a strike was possible. What did those plates record, for the first time in a photograph?
answer: Nitrogen turning into oxygen as a proton flies out
choices: Nitrogen turning into oxygen as a proton flies out
A nitrogen nucleus splitting cleanly into two halves
An alpha particle bouncing off a nitrogen nucleus
An electron being flung out of a nitrogen nucleus
context: N-14 + He-4 goes to O-17 + H-1. An alpha particle from polonium strikes a nitrogen nucleus, sticks to it, and knocks a proton out, leaving oxygen behind. Rutherford had claimed the reaction; Blackett's weeks of patient exposure are what turned the claim into a picture of one element becoming another. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Patrick Blackett' (Broader contributions to nuclear physics); Grokipedia, 'Cloud chamber'.

question: Caltech's Carl Anderson kept photographing tracks that were positive but far too light to be protons. One frame cannot show which way a thing was travelling, so each track might be an ordinary electron going upward or an unknown light positive particle coming down. Anderson settled it by adding one piece of hardware to his chamber. What did he add?
answer: A slab of lead laid across the chamber
choices: A slab of lead laid across the chamber
A second camera facing the opposite wall
A shutter timed to a single millisecond
Two counters, one above and one below
context: Six millimetres of lead. A particle crossing it loses energy, so its curve tightens on the far side, and the tighter half has to be the later half. A piece of metal is how you read the direction of time out of a still picture. On the evening of 2 August 1932 the frame came out: something entering from below at 63 million electron-volts, losing 40 MeV in the lead, leaving at 23 MeV. Anderson's logbook that night was deadpan: "Track 75. Thru Pb showing energy change or double ejection". He did not coin the name 'positron' either; he allowed it at the suggestion of the Physical Review editor. Sources: Per Carlson, 'Carl Anderson's 1932 upward going positron', PoS(ICRC2023)337; Science Museum Group Collection; Wikipedia, 'Positron'.

question: Carl Anderson developed a frame from his Caltech chamber on the evening of 2 August 1932 and found a track that should not exist: too faint for a proton, yet curving the wrong way through his magnet's field for an electron. Antimatter was not his first thought. He assumed instead that something mundane had gone wrong in his laboratory. What did he suspect?
answer: Students had reconnected the wires to his magnet
choices: Students had reconnected the wires to his magnet
The film had gone into his camera backwards
A scratch on the plate had faked the faint track
Someone had logged the field strength wrongly
context: Anderson told Luis Alvarez in 1934 that his first assumption was that students had reconnected the wires to the magnet and reversed its polarity; he checked the photographs taken just before and just after, nobody could have touched it, and only then did he believe the track. His boss Robert Millikan, the Nobel laureate everyone at Caltech called the Chief, pushed the safe reading: "...he repeatedly pointed out that cosmic ray particles travel downward, and not upward, except in extremely rare instances, and that these particles must be protons." Anderson admitted, "In the spirit of scientific conservatism, I tended at first toward the former interpretation." He had not read Dirac's antiparticle prediction at all. He had the Nobel Prize in 1936, at 31, sharing it with Victor Hess. Sources: Luis Alvarez interview by Charles Weiner, AIP 1967, and C. D. Anderson in 'The Discovery of Antimatter' (Weiss ed., 1999) p.29, both quoted in Per Carlson, PoS(ICRC2023)337; Grokipedia, 'Carl David Anderson'.

question: Seth Neddermeyer and Carl Anderson hauled a cloud chamber to the summit of Pikes Peak in 1936, with a slab of platinum set across it. They named the particle they caught, about 207 times an electron's mass, the mesotron, and physics spent eleven years taking it for the nuclear glue Hideki Yukawa had predicted. The clue had been on those first plates all along. What were the mesotron's tracks doing at the platinum?
answer: Punching through a centimetre of platinum almost undeflected
choices: Punching through a centimetre of platinum almost undeflected
Stopping dead inside the first millimetre of the platinum
Curling into tight spirals before ever reaching the platinum
Bursting into showers of secondary tracks below the platinum
context: Anderson and Neddermeyer's 1936 plates show the tracks punching through a centimetre of platinum almost undeflected. By the mid-1940s experiments had confirmed what that meant: muons barely interact with nuclei at all, so this could not be the glue holding a nucleus together. The mesotron was the muon, the same particle whose thread you can watch cross a kitchen table. Yukawa's real particle, the pion, turned up in 1947. For eleven years physics had the right measurement and the wrong identification, and nothing but further tests fixed it. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Carl David Anderson' (Identification of the muon); Grokipedia, 'Muon' (Discovery); Anderson and Neddermeyer, Physical Review 50(4), 263-271 (1936).

question: George Rochester and Clifford Butler ran a cloud chamber at Manchester for 1,500 hours, hunting cosmic rays, and took about 5,000 photographs. Two of them carried the prize: a pair of tracks that begin out in the middle of the gas and splay into a V, with nothing whatever leading in to the point where they meet. Why does the chamber show the fork but nothing arriving at it?
answer: Because the parent was electrically neutral and left no ions
choices: Because the parent was electrically neutral and left no ions
Because the parent arrived above the thin sensitive layer
Because the parent was moving too fast to ionise the gas
Because the parent's own track had already faded away
context: Two frames, out of five thousand, after 1,500 hours of running. A cloud chamber only draws what ionises the gas, so an electrically neutral particle crosses it invisibly and announces itself only when it decays in flight into charged pieces. That V was the decay: a neutral particle about a thousand times an electron's mass with a lifetime near 10^-10 seconds, the kaon, the first of the 'strange' particles. In 1949 the Manchester group carried their chamber up to the Pic du Midi observatory in the Pyrenees to catch more of them. Sources: Grokipedia, 'V particle' (Initial detection in cosmic rays); Grokipedia, 'Kaon'; Physics World, 'George Rochester'.

question: A girl counts thin threads in a home cloud chamber on her kitchen table. Each is a muon, made about 15 kilometres up, and it lives on average 2.2 microseconds before it decays. Even at nearly the speed of light the trip down to the ground takes about 50 microseconds, more than twenty lifetimes, so almost none should reach her. They arrive in floods. Why?
answer: At their own speed, their internal clock runs slow
choices: At their own speed, their internal clock runs slow
Decay is random, so out of vast numbers a few survive
Each decay makes a fresh muon that carries on down
Most are anti-muons, which take longer to decay
context: Special relativity, happening on a kitchen table. The 2.2-microsecond lifetime is measured on the muon's own clock, and at close to light speed that clock runs slow compared with yours, so the journey that costs the muon a fraction of its life costs the ground below far longer. Random survival cannot rescue the arithmetic: twenty lifetimes would leave a billionth of them, not floods. Every thin straight thread in a home chamber is a piece of evidence for Einstein that you collected yourself, with a fish tank, some dry ice and a torch. Source: J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, 'Test of special relativity', p.11.

question: Neal Nathanson and John Martin asked in 1979 why the first polio epidemics had struck where they did: Sweden in 1887, the American state of Vermont in 1894, Norway in 1905. Before the 1880s it had taken one child at a time, and then whole clusters fell ill at once. Those first-struck places shared one surprising thing. What was it?
answer: Unusually clean drinking water and sewers
choices: Unusually clean drinking water and sewers
Unusually crowded schools and shared classrooms
Unusually large dairy herds and raw-milk trade
Unusually damp and mosquito-rich summers
context: This is mainstream epidemiology, not a fringe claim. Sweden reported the first recognized outbreak in 1887; Vermont's 1894 epidemic counted 132 cases; Norway followed in 1905, and summer epidemics swept Europe by the 1920s. In poorer regions poliovirus stayed endemic and mostly harmless. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Polio; Neal Nathanson and John R. Martin, 'The Epidemiology of Poliomyelitis: Enigmas Surrounding Its Appearance, Epidemicity, and Disappearance', American Journal of Epidemiology, December 1979, 110(6):672-692.

question: Karl Landsteiner and Erwin Popper ground up the spinal cord of a nine-year-old boy killed by polio, in Vienna in 1908, and injected it into two rhesus monkeys. Both were paralysed, their cords damaged just as the boy's had been. One preparation step made the result decisive. Which step?
answer: Passing it through a bacteria-proof filter
choices: Passing it through a bacteria-proof filter
Boiling it until every bacterium was dead
Letting it settle and skimming the clear top
Mixing it with a recovered patient's blood
context: They used a Chamberland L3 porcelain candle filter, built to hold back every known bacterium, and injected what came through into the monkeys' brains and spinal fluid. One monkey died on the seventeenth day; the second was so ill it was put down on the twenty-fourth. Both showed destruction concentrated in the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, the same lesion as in the human cases. Whatever caused polio was smaller than any bacterium, could be passed on, and hunted nerve tissue. The work was done in 1908 and published the following year as 'Ubertragung der Poliomyelitis acuta auf Affen'. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Landsteiner; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erwin_Popper.

question: Philip Drinker and Louis Shaw, two Harvard professors, built a sealed metal tank in 1928 that breathed for kids whose chest muscles polio had paralyzed. On 12 October it saved a dying eight-year-old girl at Boston Children's Hospital, who woke up inside a minute. The pumps came from a pair of ordinary home appliances. Which?
answer: Two vacuum cleaners
choices: Two vacuum cleaners
Two kitchen refrigerators
Two hair dryers
Two electric fans
context: An electric motor drove air pumps taken from two vacuum cleaners, and the girl's recovery within less than a minute made the machine famous. An adult iron lung cost about $2,000 in 1930, roughly $39,000 in today's money. In 1959, 1,200 Americans were living in tank respirators; by 2004, 39. Paul Alexander of Dallas entered one at six and lived in it for 72 years, until his death on 11 March 2024. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_lung.

question: A B-25 bomber crew sprayed Rockford, Illinois, with dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) in August 1945. Rockford had called an emergency on 14 August, with 382 polio cases and 36 deaths in the county that season, most of them kids. Swimming was banned and schools opened six weeks late. What was the spray meant to kill?
answer: Houseflies breeding in rubbish and sewage
choices: Houseflies breeding in rubbish and sewage
Mosquitoes breeding in standing summer water
Fleas living on the town's rats and cats
Ticks carried in on dogs from nearby farms
context: The guess was wrong but it was not stupid. Polio arrived in a sharp summer and early-autumn wave, often inside a two-or-three-month window, and outbreaks tracked poor sewage disposal, swimming pools and food handling - exactly the signature of an insect-borne disease. San Antonio did the same thing in 1946: a Universal newsreel, 'City Gets D.D.T. Treatment', shows special vehicles laying a DDT smoke-screen over the streets. The epidemics came anyway. Sources: 1440wrok.com/rockfords-polio-epidemic-of-1945/; unwritten-record.blogs.archives.gov (Universal News, 1946); grokipedia.com/page/Polio.

question: A nurse rubs alcohol gel over her hands from a dispenser on a hospital wall. The gel destroys the viruses behind flu and the common cold within seconds, yet on hands carrying poliovirus it does almost nothing, and only real soap and running water will wash that virus off. What is it about the poliovirus particle that lets it beat the alcohol?
answer: It has no fatty envelope for alcohol to dissolve
choices: It has no fatty envelope for alcohol to dissolve
It has no surface proteins for alcohol to clot
It has a sugar coat alcohol cannot soak through
It has a DNA core alcohol cannot break apart
context: Alcohol works by dissolving the greasy membrane that influenza and coronaviruses wrap themselves in. Poliovirus has no such wrapping: it is a bare particle about 30 nanometres across, a twenty-sided protein shell built from 60 copies each of four proteins around a single strand of RNA, and it shrugs off acid and detergents alike. That is why it survives the stomach, and why the sink beats the dispenser. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polio.

question: Neal Nathanson and John Martin argued in 1979 that a delay turned polio from a common bug into a crippler. In five American epidemics between 1907 and 1912 most cases were children aged one to five; by the 1950s the average age had climbed to six. A later first meeting with the virus let a child outgrow a protection that infants have but older children do not. Which protection?
answer: Antibodies handed on by his mother, which fade within months
choices: Antibodies handed on by his mother, which fade within months
Antibodies made by his own gut bacteria, which fade within months
A gut lining too thick for the virus to cross in the first years
A body temperature too high for the virus to survive in infancy
context: Maternal antibodies have a half-life of roughly a month once breastfeeding ends. Meet poliovirus while they are still circulating and the infection is usually silent and leaves lifelong immunity; meet it afterwards and the odds of paralysis rise. Nathanson and Martin put it bluntly: epidemic polio appeared 'paradoxically' because of improvements in sanitation and personal hygiene. Sources: American Journal of Epidemiology, December 1979, 110(6):672-692; Nathanson and Kew, Am J Epidemiol 2010;172(11):1213; ourworldindata.org/polio.

question: A student reads the 1988 count of wild polio: about 350,000 kids paralysed a year in over 125 countries. Wild type 2 was last seen in 1999 and wild type 3 in 2012. In 2024 wild polio still spread in Pakistan and Afghanistan. How many wild cases were confirmed worldwide that year?
context: Seventy-four in Pakistan, twenty-five in Afghanistan. This stretch matters because the case definition did not change again across it, so the fall cannot be a bookkeeping effect - which is precisely why the 1988-to-now record answers 'did paralysis fall?' differently from the 1955-to-1957 record, and why the two must be argued separately. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polio.

question: Herman Kleinman, the state epidemiologist for Minnesota, said much of what his state logged as non-paralytic polio in 1956, plus a huge outbreak the next year, was really caused by two other viruses. Before labs could type a virus, a summer fever with headache and stiff neck often got called polio just by a doctor's judgement. Which two?
answer: Coxsackie B-5, then ECHO 9
choices: Coxsackie B-5, then ECHO 9
Coxsackie A-9, then ECHO 30
ECHO 6, then Coxsackie B-3
ECHO 11, then Coxsackie A-16
context: Kleinman's words in the record: 'In 1956 in much of our so-called nonparalytic polio, the etiology turned out to be Coxsackie B-5 virus, and in 1957 a staggering outbreak turned out to be Echo 9 virus.' Both are enteroviruses, cousins of poliovirus, and both can cause the same aseptic meningitis. Better laboratories did not cure those children; they moved them out of one column and into another. Source: Intensive Immunization Programs, Hearings before the House Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce, 87th Congress 2d Session, on H.R. 10541, May 1962 (govinfo CHRG-87hhrg84426), printed p. 98.

question: Bernard Greenberg told Illinois doctors in 1960 that health offices had changed how a paralytic polio case got counted in 1955. He led biostatistics at the University of North Carolina's public health school, and his talk was later entered into a 1962 House hearing. Until 1955, he said, the World Health Organization rule asked only for paralysis found on two exams. What did the 1955 rules add?
answer: Paralysis still present on re-examination about sixty days after onset
choices: Paralysis still present on re-examination about sixty days after onset
Paralysis affecting at least two separate muscle groups on both sides
Paralysis confirmed by a laboratory test isolating the poliovirus
Paralysis reported to the state within forty-eight hours of diagnosis
context: Until 1955 the definition asked for paralysis found on two examinations at least twenty-four hours apart; the new criteria asked for paralysis still present on re-examination about sixty days after onset. Greenberg's line: 'This change in definition meant that in 1955 we started reporting a new disease, namely, paralytic poliomyelitis with a longer lasting paralysis.' He was not arguing that the vaccine was worthless - two paragraphs on he wrote, 'Without doubt, the increasing trend has been reduced to some extent by the Salk vaccine,' and 'If there were no other vaccine, complete vaccination of all susceptible persons in the population with Salk vaccine would be justifiable.' His actual position was that the live Sabin-type vaccine should be adopted faster. Note the provenance: Greenberg never appeared as a witness. Clinton R. Miller of the National Health Federation, an opponent of the bill, asked that the reprinted 1960 panel discussion be inserted into the record. Source: Intensive Immunization Programs, Hearings on H.R. 10541, May 1962 (govinfo CHRG-87hhrg84426), printed pp. 90, 96-97.

question: Herman Kleinman said of the Salk vaccine at the 1960 panel, 'I am not against it.' The Minnesota epidemiologist was the one man there who had said in print that it worked: his 1957 paper with Leonard Schuman put two doses at 83 per cent protective against paralytic polio. Kleinman then turned to Bernard Greenberg's argument that part of the post-1955 fall in polio was really a change in what got counted. Which position did he take?
answer: He backed it: only unmistakable paralysis was now being reported
choices: He backed it: only unmistakable paralysis was now being reported
He rejected it: Minnesota's own criteria had never been changed
He allowed it for Minnesota alone: other states had not changed
He set it aside: the 1954 field trial had already settled it
context: Kleinman's words: 'It is no wonder then that the average doctor does not want to make a diagnosis of polio in the absence of frank lower motor neuron flaccid paralysis. As a result, the only polio that's being reported today are cases with frank paralysis.' He also called the new duration requirement 'absolutely silly'. That the counting changed is therefore not a claim only critics make; it is agreed across the argument. What remains contested is how much of the fall it explains. Source: Intensive Immunization Programs, Hearings on H.R. 10541, May 1962 (govinfo CHRG-87hhrg84426), printed pp. 90, 97-98.

question: Matthias Gromeier and Eckard Wimmer found the mechanism behind an old polio puzzle in 1998. From 1910 doctors had noticed that a child whose tonsils came out during a polio season was more likely to be paralyzed a week or two later, and more than two thousand case histories reviewed by Harvard's Infantile Paralysis Commission in the 1940s bore it out. What does an injury to tissue do that helps polio paralyze?
answer: It opens nerve pathways the virus can travel inward along
choices: It opens nerve pathways the virus can travel inward along
It leaves raw nerve endings where the virus can multiply
It strips the mucus that normally traps the virus in the throat
It floods the wound with white cells the virus prefers to infect
context: The effect is now accepted and has a name: provocation polio. Injured tissue - from certain operations and certain injections - gives poliovirus easy access to the nerve channels that lead to the spinal cord and brainstem. Anxiety peaked in 1950, when clinical evidence suggested tonsillectomy could treble the risk; the American Journal of Public Health ran an editorial on it in August 1954, and a 1957 paper cited nineteen studies reporting the association. A folk observation that sounded like superstition turned out to be a real biological effect - a reminder that 'that sounds like nonsense' is not a test. Sources: cam.ac.uk research feature, 'Polio provocation'; AJPH 1954;44(8):1065-1067.

question: Herbert Ratner, the health commissioner of Oak Park, Illinois, chaired the 1960 panel where Bernard Greenberg spoke, and said a second definition had moved too. Before the Salk vaccine, by his account, the National Foundation called it an epidemic when a town reported 20 or more polio cases per 100,000 people in a year. American towns had epidemics every year by that count. What became of that threshold after the vaccine arrived?
answer: It was raised to 35 cases per 100,000 in a year
choices: It was raised to 35 cases per 100,000 in a year
It was raised to 50 cases per 100,000 in a year
It was rewritten as 20 paralytic cases per 100,000
It was rewritten as 20 polio deaths per 100,000
context: Ratner's own gloss in the record: the higher rate produced 'not a real, but a semantic elimination of epidemics'. Clinton Miller then put the question to the House committee directly: 'Is a polio epidemic 20 cases per 100,000 or is it 35 cases per 100,000? Who decides upon what evidence what constitutes an epidemic?' Note the attribution: this threshold point is Ratner's, not Greenberg's - retellings routinely credit it to the wrong man, and the primary record does not support them. Source: Intensive Immunization Programs, Hearings on H.R. 10541, May 1962 (govinfo CHRG-87hhrg84426), printed pp. 82, 94 fn.2, 111.

question: Forrest Maready argues in his 2018 book The Moth in the Iron Lung that the pesticide era of dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT), and the lead arsenate sprayed on American orchards before it, shaped the curve of paralysis. It is one author's hypothesis. Researchers who reject it do not answer with credentials. They point to a single piece of evidence as the reason a poison cannot be the cause of the paralysis, at most something that alters the risk. Which one?
answer: Landsteiner and Popper injecting monkeys in 1908 with fluid from a dead boy's spinal cord
choices: Landsteiner and Popper injecting monkeys in 1908 with fluid from a dead boy's spinal cord
John Enders and his Boston team growing poliovirus in human tissue in the late 1940s
Herman Kleinman typing the other viruses behind Minnesota's polio counts in 1956
Harvard's Infantile Paralysis Commission reviewing two thousand case histories in the 1940s
context: This is how a hypothesis gets answered: not by ruling the author out of bounds, but by naming the evidence it has to get past. Landsteiner and Popper demonstrated a transmissible, sub-bacterial agent that produced the exact lesion of polio, decades before DDT existed. A toxin therefore cannot replace the virus as the cause; the most it could do is change who the virus paralyses - which is a real question, and an open one. Maready's book is one named author's argument, neither established nor suppressed. Sources: openlibrary.org (Maready, The Moth in the Iron Lung, 2018); grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Landsteiner.

question: A student studies a photograph of a hospital ward lined with iron lungs, and America's worst year seems to back it: 1952 reported 57,628 cases, 3,145 deaths and 21,269 left with paralysis. But a reported case was already a visibly sick child, and most people who met the virus never became one. Of all poliovirus infections, what share ended in any paralysis at all?
answer: About one in two hundred
choices: About one in two hundred
About one in two thousand
About one in fifty
About one in twenty
context: Roughly 70 to 75 per cent of poliovirus infections produced no symptoms at all, about 25 per cent a brief flu-like illness, and about 0.5 per cent - one in two hundred - acute flaccid paralysis, of which 5 to 10 per cent died of respiratory failure. Of paralytic cases about 79 per cent were spinal, 19 per cent bulbospinal and 2 per cent bulbar; the bulbar form, which takes out swallowing and breathing, is the one that filled the iron lungs, and it is the smallest slice. The photograph is true of a real ward and false as a picture of the disease - and 21,269 paralysed children in a single year is a real number too. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Polio; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_poliomyelitis.

question: James Lind split twelve sick sailors into six pairs aboard HMS Salisbury in 1747 and gave each pair one remedy. One pair got cider, one vinegar, one seawater, one a sour drink called elixir of vitriol, one garlic paste. The last got two of a certain fruit and one of another each day, and recovered fastest. What were they given?
answer: Two oranges and a lemon
choices: Two apples and a pear
Two oranges and a lemon
Two limes and a fig
Two peaches and a plum
context: Within six days one of the citrus pair was fit for duty and the other had nearly recovered; none of the other five remedies moved the disease. Source: https://www.usni.org/magazines/naval-history-magazine/2021/february/finding-cure-scurvy

question: Gilbert Blane persuaded the Admiralty in 1795, long after James Lind's shipboard trial, to give every sailor a ration of lemon juice each day. Within two years a disease that had killed more British sailors than French cannons ever did had all but gone from the fleet. Which disease?
answer: Scurvy
choices: Scurvy
Typhus
Malaria
Dysentery
context: Gilbert Blane, as Commissioner of the Sick and Wounded Board and drawing on Rodney's support, persuaded the Admiralty in 1795 to issue three-quarters of an ounce of lemon juice daily to every sailor -- and by 1797 scurvy had all but vanished from the fleet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Blane

question: Pierre Louis turned what he called his 'numerical method' on the most respected treatment of the day, in 1830s Paris. He simply counted who lived and who died, and the treatment had been in use since Galen. What treatment did his 1835 book find did not work for pneumonia?
answer: Bleeding the patient with lancets and leeches
choices: Bleeding the patient with lancets and leeches
Blistering the chest with heated cups
Purging with mercury and calomel
Applying poultices of hot linseed
context: Louis's 1835 book on bloodletting for pneumonia used the numerical method -- just count outcomes across matched cases -- to argue the 2,000-year-old treatment did not help. He is a founder of modern clinical epidemiology. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Charles_Alexandre_Louis

question: A kind physician sits with a very sick patient who could join the trial of a promising new drug. She steers him away from it and toward familiar care, and patient by patient the drug comes to look better than it is. Which enrollment method blocks this leak?
answer: Assign each patient to a group by chance
choices: Alternate patients by admission order
Let each patient choose an arm
Match on age and sex before assigning
Assign each patient to a group by chance
context: Selection bias is the reason 'matched groups' are not enough. Alternation is guessable, patient choice reintroduces the sicker/healthier tilt, and matching only balances what you thought to measure. Random assignment -- ideally with the sequence hidden from the enrolling doctor -- is what stops the leak. Source: https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/articles/why-the-1948-mrc-trial-of-streptomycin-used-treatment-allocation-based-on-random-numbers/

question: Muriel Bristol told her colleagues at Rothamsted one afternoon in the 1920s that she could taste whether the milk had gone into the cup before the tea or after. Ronald Fisher did not laugh. He laid out eight cups on the spot, four made each way and shuffled. His method became the template for what?
answer: The randomized experiment
choices: The randomized experiment
The double-blind trial
The peer-review system
The meta-analysis
context: Muriel Bristol's tea claim at Rothamsted in the 1920s prompted Ronald Fisher to design an eight-cup test in random order. He later made the design the opening illustration of The Design of Experiments in 1935. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_tasting_tea

question: Ronald Fisher poured eight cups of tea at the Rothamsted farm, four milk-first and four tea-first, shuffled them, and asked Muriel Bristol to sort them into the two groups. She had claimed she could tell which went in first. If she were only guessing, what are the odds of picking all four milk-first cups correctly by pure luck?
answer: 1 in 70
choices: 1 in 8
1 in 24
1 in 70
context: There are exactly 70 ways to choose 4 cups from 8, so a lucky guesser has a 1-in-70 chance of getting all four right. Fisher's colleague H. Fairfield Smith later said, as the statistician David Salsburg reports, that Bristol did in fact get all eight cups right, though Fisher's book presents the design without stating the outcome. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_tasting_tea

question: A patient with lung tuberculosis (TB) reached a British hospital, and a sealed envelope holding a random number sent him to streptomycin or to bed rest alone. The Medical Research Council published the trial in the British Medical Journal in 1948, the first proper randomized trial in medicine. Which statistician designed it?
answer: Austin Bradford Hill
choices: Marc Daniels
Austin Bradford Hill
Philip d'Arcy Hart
Richard Doll
context: Austin Bradford Hill of the MRC Statistical Research Unit designed the 1948 streptomycin trial for pulmonary TB; allocation used random numbers in a set of sealed envelopes, one per hospital, hidden from the doctors enrolling patients. Source: https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/medical-research-council-1948b/

question: A statistician sealed each patient's assignment in a numbered envelope at each hospital for Britain's trial of streptomycin against tuberculosis, to be opened only when the next patient walked in. This safeguard is called allocation concealment, and it is aimed at one person's judgement in the enrollment chain. Whose?
answer: The enrolling doctor deciding whom to admit next
choices: The patient deciding whether to consent
The ward matron assigning beds
The referring GP choosing which hospital to send the patient to
The enrolling doctor deciding whom to admit next
context: Allocation concealment protects against the enrolling doctor gaming the sequence: a doctor who can guess which arm the next envelope holds can quietly wait for a sicker or healthier patient before enrolling, and the whole trial rots. It is a separate safeguard from double-blinding, which hides which arm a patient is in AFTER enrolment. Source: https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/articles/why-the-1948-mrc-trial-of-streptomycin-used-treatment-allocation-based-on-random-numbers/

question: Officials in one European country chose to keep classrooms open through the whole spring wave of COVID-19 in 2020, while nearly every other Western government closed its schools. Children under sixteen went on attending with no closures, no masks, no distancing rules. Researchers later tracked 97,073 of its pupils in grades 1 to 3. Which country?
answer: Sweden
choices: Sweden
Denmark
Norway
Finland
context: Sweden's Public Health Agency, under state epidemiologist Anders Tegnell, chose recommendations over mandates for children in compulsory school (ages 1-15); upper-secondary schools (age 16+) did go remote from 18 March 2020. Its Nordic neighbours -- Denmark, Norway and Finland -- all closed their schools that spring. Source: The Local, March 2021.

question: Jonas Ludvigsson and his colleagues followed roughly 1.95 million Swedish children aged 1 to 16 who went right on attending class through the first COVID-19 wave of spring 2020, with no closures and no masks. They reported in the New England Journal of Medicine in January 2021. Of those schoolchildren, how many died of COVID-19?
answer: Not one
choices: Not one
Fifteen
Ninety-two
About three hundred
context: The NEJM letter (online 6 January 2021) reported 15 admissions to intensive care with COVID-19 or the related inflammatory syndrome across the whole cohort -- four of them children with a serious pre-existing condition such as cancer or chronic kidney disease -- and zero deaths in the 1-16 age group. Source: NEJM, Ludvigsson et al., 6 Jan 2021.

question: A teacher in Sweden faces a full classroom through the first COVID-19 wave, and the loudest worry about open schools is the danger to her. Jonas Ludvigsson's study compared the severe-COVID rate of the country's schoolteachers with the average across other jobs, health-care workers left out. Where did the teachers land?
answer: Below the average, at a relative risk of about 0.43
choices: Below the average, at a relative risk of about 0.43
About the same, close to 1.0
Somewhat above the average, near 1.5
Roughly triple the average, near 3.0
context: The reported relative risk for schoolteachers was 0.43 (95% CI 0.28-0.68) after excluding health-care workers -- meaningfully LOWER than the workforce average, not higher. Preschool teachers came in at 1.10 (0.49-2.49), essentially the same as average. Source: NEJM, Ludvigsson et al., 6 Jan 2021.

question: Anders Tegnell, Sweden's state epidemiologist, built the whole national response to COVID-19 around one core choice in early 2020, while most Western governments answered with hard lockdowns: closed schools, closed shops, orders to stay home. That choice set his country apart from almost every other Western government. What was it?
answer: Recommendations rather than enforced mandates
choices: Recommendations rather than enforced mandates
A single hard national lockdown at the first case
A universal mask order in all public spaces
A border closure to all non-citizens
context: Tegnell bet on sustained voluntary compliance -- stay home when symptomatic, avoid crowded indoor gatherings, keep distance from the over-70s -- rather than police-enforced orders. Later (2023) he said the decision NOT to close schools was the one he remained most pleased with. Source: Grokipedia; Irish Times, April 2023.

question: A Swedish reader opens the first report of the Corona Commission, an independent inquiry, on 15 December 2020. Sweden has refused hard lockdowns while its Nordic neighbours shut down, and for 2020 alone its excess deaths, the count of extra deaths over what a normal year would bring, are worse than those of Denmark, Norway and Finland. The report says plainly where the extra deaths concentrated. Where?
answer: In the country's nursing and care homes
choices: In the country's nursing and care homes
In the country's hospital intensive-care wards
Among the country's bus and taxi drivers
Among the country's primary-school teachers
context: The Corona Commission report of 15 December 2020 named hospital discharge policies that did not require testing, lack of PPE, and staffing and organizational problems as drivers; the government and the Public Health Agency both admitted the attempt to shield the elderly had failed. The other half of the ledger: across 2020 to 2022 taken together, most methods put Sweden, beside its Nordic neighbours, among the European countries with the lowest excess mortality, though the ranking shifts with the method. The school decision was vindicated by measurement; the care-home decision was not. Sources: The Local, Oct 2021 and March 2023; PMC PMC8436291.

question: A Swedish primary pupil sits the standard reading assessment after the spring 2020 wave, having stayed in class straight through it. This is the fair test of whether keeping the classrooms open cost the children something academically. What did the assessments show?
answer: No measurable learning loss on the reading tests
choices: No measurable learning loss on the reading tests
A drop of roughly one grade level, comparable to closure countries
A drop of nearly two grade levels, worse than closure countries
A small gain, credited to shrinking class sizes
context: Analyses of Swedish primary-school reading assessments spanning the pandemic period found no measurable learning loss in the pupils who kept attending school, while countries that closed classrooms recorded documented drops in reading and math attainment (the OECD/World Bank literature converged on roughly a third to half a year lost per closure period). The test the closures were meant to protect the children from -- the risk to their learning -- came back clean for the country that refused to run it. Source: PMC PMC9162440.

question: Wilhelm Ostwald, a celebrated German chemist, travelled from Berlin to Paris to see the shed where the Curies won their first tiny grain of radium from tonnes of ore. A caretaker let him wander the empty room alone. What did he later say the place looked like?
answer: A cross between a stable and a potato-cellar
choices: A cross between a stable and a potato-cellar
A workshop no better than a village blacksmith's
A glasshouse someone had emptied of its plants
A schoolroom with the desks pushed to the walls
context: Ostwald wrote: 'It was a cross between a stable and a potato-cellar, and, if I had not seen the worktable with the chemical apparatus, I would have thought it a practical joke.' The room was an abandoned wooden shed in the courtyard of the Ecole superieure de physique et de chimie industrielles, off the rue Lhomond - a former dissecting room for a medical school, with a leaking glass roof, a bituminous floor, worn pine tables and a cast-iron stove that barely worked. Summers turned it into a hothouse; winters dropped it below freezing. Marie Curie's own verdict on the same building: 'it was in this miserable old shed that we passed the best and happiest years of our life.' Both the shed and its adjoining workshop were demolished between the two world wars. (Ostwald quoted in R. Reid, 'Marie Curie', 1974, p. 95, via todayinsci.com; shed described by the Musee Curie, lamethodecurie.fr/en/article14.html; Marie Curie's line from 'Pierre Curie', 1923.)

question: Marie Curie, raised in Warsaw with strong feelings about the European empires, announced a new element with her husband Pierre in July 1898 and claimed the right to name it. Some historians call it the first element name meant as a political protest. What did she name it after?
answer: A homeland the empires had wiped off the map
choices: A homeland the empires had wiped off the map
An uprising the empires had put down in blood
A university the empires had shut by decree
A chemist the empires had driven into exile
context: Marie Sklodowska-Curie was born in Warsaw. When she named the element, Poland had been partitioned among Russia, Prussia/Germany and Austria-Hungary and appeared on no map of Europe as a country at all - so she put her erased homeland into the periodic table instead. Radium followed five months later, announced on 26 December 1898, its name taken from the Latin for ray. In the course of the same work the Curies coined the word 'radioactivity' itself. (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'; polonium's naming at wordorigins.org and Smithsonian, 'Six Secrets of Polonium'.)

question: Marie Curie wrote in her 1923 memoir of Pierre about a private joy of their leaky Paris shed: slipping back into the workroom after dark, no lamp lit and no work to do. What did she describe seeing?
answer: Faintly luminous silhouettes of bottles and capsules on the shelves
choices: Faintly luminous silhouettes of bottles and capsules on the shelves
The red glow of the iron stove sliding across Pierre's blackboard
Moonlight through the leaking glass roof lying on the pine tables
The courtyard lamps outside picking out the cracks in the walls
context: Her words: 'One of our joys was to go into our workroom at night; we then perceived on all sides the feebly luminous silhouettes of the bottles or capsules containing our products. It was really a lovely sight and one always new to us.' The passage is universally quoted with a closing line - the glowing tubes 'looked like faint, fairy lights'. She carried tubes of radium in her pockets and kept them in her desk drawers. Neither of them knew what the light was doing to them: Marie Curie died on 4 July 1934, aged 66, of aplastic anaemia - her bone marrow had stopped making blood cells - attributed to decades of exposure in the shed and to her wartime X-ray work. (Marie Curie, 'Pierre Curie', Macmillan, 1923; the autobiographical notes first ran in The Delineator, Jan-Mar 1922.)

question: Marie Curie tested every uranium-bearing mineral she could get in April 1898, with an electric meter she built to hunt the source of Henri Becquerel's 'uranium rays.' Pure uranium metal read 24. Pitchblende ore, only partly uranium, read 67 from Joachimsthal and 83 from Johanngeorgenstadt. What did she publish as the likely reason?
answer: That the ore might hold an element far more active than uranium
choices: That the ore might hold an element far more active than uranium
That pitchblende holds far more uranium than assayers had thought
That thorium in the ore was supplying the extra activity
That the rock around the uranium was concentrating its rays
context: Her printed table, in units of 10^-12 amperes: uranium 24; pitchblende from Johanngeorgenstadt 83; pitchblende from Joachimsthal and Pribram 67; natural chalcolite 52. Pitchblende is mostly other rock with uranium only part of it, so pure uranium metal should have been the ceiling - and instead the ores ran two to three and a half times hotter than the metal inside them. Her paper called that fact 'most remarkable' and printed the conclusion that it 'suggests that these minerals may contain an element much more active than uranium'. Thorium is a real wrong answer rather than a silly one: the same paper is titled 'Rays emitted by compounds of uranium and of thorium', and she reported thorium compounds active in it. The excess in pitchblende turned out to be two elements nobody had yet named. The scientific virtue in this story is what she did NOT do - blame the instrument, quietly round the number down, or set the odd sample aside. She went looking instead. (Marie Sklodowska Curie, Comptes Rendus 126, 1898; English translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/ea/curieann.html.)

question: Marie Curie boiled pitchblende in open cauldrons out in the courtyard beside her wooden shed off the rue Lhomond in Paris, sometimes for a whole day at a stretch. Her own account of the work names the one piece of equipment that left her 'broken with fatigue at the day's end'. What was it?
answer: An iron rod nearly as tall as she was
choices: An iron rod nearly as tall as she was
An iron mortar as wide as her two hands
A stoneware basin the length of her arm
A pair of iron tongs half her own height
context: 'Sometimes I had to spend a whole day mixing a boiling mass with a heavy iron rod nearly as large as myself. I would be broken with fatigue at the day's end.' She also noted there 'was no question of obtaining the needed proper apparatus in common use by chemists'. The boiling was done outdoors because the shed had no fume hoods: 'There were no hoods to carry away the poisonous gases thrown off in our chemical treatments, so that it was necessary to carry them on outside in the court, but when the weather was unfavorable we went on with them inside, leaving the windows open.' HONEST CAVEAT, from the American Institute of Physics' own historians: the heroic 'she did it all alone, by hand, in a shed' story is partly Marie Curie's own emphasis and served a fundraising purpose. The gross first-stage treatment of the first tonne of pitchblende was done at a factory, the Central Chemical Products Company; the Curies were reasonably well funded by the standards of French science; and Andre-Louis Debierne worked alongside them. The boiling cauldrons and the iron rod are real. Total solitude is not. (AIP exhibit, 'Marie Curie and Her Legend', history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/romleg_text.htm; ventilation quote via the Musee Curie, lamethodecurie.fr/en/article14.html.)

question: Marie Curie held roughly a tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride by 1902, less than a pinch of salt, after about four years of boiling, filtering and purifying sackfuls of Joachimsthal pitchblende in her Paris shed. All that labour existed to pin down one number about radium. Which one?
answer: The weight of a single atom of radium
choices: The weight of a single atom of radium
The heat that one gram of radium gives off
The temperature at which radium melts
The density of a lump of radium metal
context: She got her number: 225, fixed in 1902 from just 0.09 g of radium chloride and, she judged, good to within one unit. That figure is radium's relative atomic mass - how heavy one of its atoms is set against the lightest atom, hydrogen - and it is what tells a chemist where a new element belongs in the periodic table. She refined it to 226.45 in 1907 using 0.4 g of very pure salt; the modern accepted value is 226. Her earlier attempts on dirtier samples had given 138, then 146, then 174 - the number walking towards the truth as the salt got cleaner, which is exactly why the purifying had to be finished before the measuring meant anything. ACCURACY NOTE: the sources genuinely disagree on how much ore went in - Wikipedia says a tonne of pitchblende, the Musee Curie says thirteen tons, the American Institute of Physics says several tons - so only the yield, a tenth of a gram, is stated here as precise. (Musee Curie, 'Radium's atomic weight', lamethodecurie.fr/en/article27.html; 'Closing in on radium', EDP Sciences; history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/romleg_text.htm.)

question: A reader at the Bibliothèque nationale de France asks to consult one of Marie Curie's laboratory notebooks, kept in a lead-lined box. She handled radium salts bare-handed for years. What does the library require of him?
answer: Put on protective clothing and sign a waiver of liability
choices: Put on protective clothing and sign a waiver of liability
Read the pages through glass in a sealed viewing cabinet
Handle them with cotton gloves and a full face shield
Work from photographs, since the originals never open
context: You sign a liability waiver to read a chemistry notebook. The contaminant is radium-226, whose half-life - the time for half of a sample to decay away - is about 1,600 years. She has been dead more than ninety years, and roughly four percent of it has gone; the pages will still be hot when everyone reading this is a footnote. Her furniture and even her cookbooks are contaminated too, because she carried tubes of radium in her pockets and desk drawers. (Christian Science Monitor, 'Marie Curie: Why her papers are still radioactive'; Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'.)

question: Pierre and Marie Curie went hunting in 1898 for tiny amounts of a new element hidden inside pitchblende, a dark uranium-bearing ore. They needed tonnes of it and had no research budget to buy it. The Austrian government agreed to ship them 100 kilograms from the Joachimsthal mine at no charge, and it turned out to be exactly the material they wanted. What was in the free sacks?
answer: Residue left over after the uranium had been extracted
choices: Residue left over after the uranium had been extracted
Tailings from the mine's older silver workings
Sweepings from the floor of the ore-crushing house
Low-grade rock rejected before the ore was sorted
context: In the Curies' own words: 'we received from the Austrian government a shipment, at no charge, of 100 kg of a residue from the processing of Joachimsthal pitchblende.' The uranium - the part worth money - had already been pulled out and sold. The radium stayed behind in the discards, which is why the mine's waste was better raw material than fresh ore would have been, and why the Austrians were happy to give it away. Joachimsthal is now Jachymov, in the Czech Republic. The same paper reports the barium-bearing fraction they precipitated was already 'sixty times stronger than that of metallic uranium'. (P. Curie, Mme P. Curie and G. Bemont, Comptes Rendus 127, 1898; translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/curiesra.html.)

question: Henri Becquerel carried a tube of radium in his waistcoat pocket, and it burned a sore into his side. Pierre Curie decided a chance accident was not evidence. In 1901 he set out to produce the same injury deliberately and record how it developed. How did he do it?
answer: He bound a radium salt against his own forearm for ten hours
choices: He bound a radium salt against his own forearm for ten hours
He strapped a radium tube to a rabbit's shaved flank for a day
He sewed a radium tube into a coat and wore it for a fortnight
He fixed a radium tube inside a glove and wore it while working
context: Ten hours against his own arm, then a day-by-day chart of the wound as it reddened, blistered and scabbed like a burn; a grey scar was still there after about fifty-two days. Those two injuries - Becquerel's accident and Pierre Curie's deliberate copy of it - are where radiotherapy comes from. The reasoning is brutally simple: a thing that destroys healthy skin on purpose can be aimed at a tumour instead. (Reviewed in 'Pioneers of nuclear medicine, Madame Curie', PubMed 16868638; RSC Education, 'Radium - a key element in early cancer treatment'.)

question: Marie Curie measured a crystal of chalcolite, a natural uranium mineral, in 1898: it ran more than twice the activity of pure uranium metal. One experiment settled whether the extra activity belonged to the mineral itself or to something else hidden inside the crystal. What did she do?
answer: She built the same mineral from pure laboratory chemicals and measured it
choices: She built the same mineral from pure laboratory chemicals and measured it
She compared crystals of it collected from four different mines
She measured a copper phosphate mineral holding no uranium at all
She dissolved the crystal and measured each separated fraction in turn
context: She 'prepared chalcolite from pure reagents according to the procedure of Debray' - a counterfeit mineral with the identical chemical formula, assembled from clean chemicals so that nothing from the mine could be riding along in it. On her scale, plain uranium metal read 24, the natural chalcolite read 52, and her artificial copy read 9. Same formula, one-sixth the activity. So the extra was an impurity hiding in the real rock, not the compound. That is a control experiment in its purest form, run by someone who did not yet have a name for the thing she was chasing - and it is the move you can copy at any kitchen table: build the version WITHOUT the suspected ingredient and see what changes. (Marie Sklodowska Curie, Comptes Rendus 126, 1898.)

question: The Curies had concentrated a barium-bearing fraction of the pitchblende residue by December 1898 until it was sixty times more active than uranium. High activity alone proves nothing, though: an ordinary substance carrying an unknown contaminant would look the same. They sent a sample to the Paris chemist Eugène Demarçay. What did he find that let them announce a new element?
answer: A line in its light matching no known element
choices: A line in its light matching no known element
A crystal shape matching no known element
A melting point matching no known element
A flame colour matching no known element
context: The December 1898 paper puts it in one sentence: 'M. Demarcay has found in the spectrum a line which does not appear to belong to any known element.' Heat any element and the light it gives off carries a fixed pattern of bright lines - a barcode unique to that element. One unfamiliar line on a photographic plate is what turned 'an anomaly in our ore' into 'a new element'. Same paper: 'we propose to give the name radium.' The third author on it, Gustave Bemont, is almost always forgotten. (Curie, Curie & Bemont, Comptes Rendus 127, 1898; translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/curiesra.html.)

question: Gösta Mittag-Leffler, a Swedish mathematician, got word to Pierre Curie unofficially in 1903. Members of the Paris Academy of Sciences had named Pierre and Henri Becquerel for the physics prize, for the work on radioactivity, and left Marie Curie's name off the list. What did Pierre do?
answer: He wrote asking to be considered jointly with Marie Curie
choices: He wrote asking to be considered jointly with Marie Curie
He refused the prize outright unless her name was added
He asked the Academy to withdraw his own name in her favour
He said nothing and split the prize money with her later
context: His letter of 6 August 1903: 'I would very much like to be considered jointly with Mrs. Curie for our work on radioactive bodies', adding that 'her initial research led to the discovery of new elements, and she played a major role in it.' The committee could act on it only because Professor Charles Bouchard of the Paris Faculty of Medicine had already nominated her independently - a request from a nominee is not itself a nomination. The prize was split: half to Becquerel for discovering spontaneous radioactivity, half to the two Curies jointly. Neither Curie attended the ceremony on 10 December 1903, pleading teaching duties and Marie's health. In 1911 she took the Chemistry Prize alone, and remains the only person holding Nobels in two different sciences. (Association Curie et Joliot-Curie, 'The 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics'; nobelprize.org.)

question: Marie Curie faced two salts no filter and no ordinary trick would part. Radium sits directly below barium on the periodic table, and the two behave almost identically in the chemist's hands. She found one small difference between their chlorides and applied it thousands of times across four years until she had a pure salt. What was that difference?
answer: Radium chloride is slightly less soluble in water than barium chloride
choices: Radium chloride is slightly less soluble in water than barium chloride
Radium chloride is slightly denser as a solid than barium chloride
Radium chloride melts at a slightly lower heat than barium chloride
Radium chloride is slightly more stable in air than barium chloride
context: Dissolve the mixed chlorides, then let the solution cool so crystals form. Because radium chloride is a shade less willing to stay dissolved, the crystals that drop out first are slightly richer in radium and the liquid left behind is slightly poorer. Pour off the liquid, redissolve the crystals, do it again. That is fractional crystallisation, and she ran it several thousand times. The entire four years - the cauldrons, the iron rod, the ruined hands - is ONE small difference in solubility, applied over and over until a difference too small to see became a pure salt. (Musee Curie, 'Radium's atomic weight', lamethodecurie.fr/en/article27.html; Indian Academy of Sciences, 'Discovery of Radium'.)

question: Pierre Curie and Albert Laborde published a measurement in March 1903 nobody could account for: a radium salt sitting on a bench gives off heat, roughly 100 calories per gram every hour, and goes on giving it off month after month. Where is that heat coming from?
answer: The atoms themselves are coming apart, one element turning into another
choices: The atoms themselves are coming apart, one element turning into another
The salt is burning slowly in the air, a chemical reaction too faint to see
The salt soaked up light beforehand and is giving it back as warmth
The atoms are drawing in energy from the ether that fills all space
context: The three wrong choices were not silly - they were the live hypotheses of serious physicists in 1903: a slow chemical reaction, phosphorescence re-emitting stored light, and the atom absorbing energy out of the luminiferous ether. People reached for them because the alternative broke conservation of energy as it was then understood: heat pouring out forever with nothing going in. Two facts killed all three. The output was orders of magnitude beyond anything chemistry can supply, and the rate did not change with temperature, pressure or light - which is exactly how chemical reactions and phosphorescence DO change. Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy supplied the real answer with their transmutation theory: the atoms themselves are coming apart, and one element is turning into another. (P. Curie & A. Laborde, Comptes Rendus, March 1903; contemporary framing in 'A New Source of Heat: Radium', Popular Science Monthly vol. 63, May 1903.)

question: Doctors in California saw five children come down with paralytic polio in late April 1955, about a week after their shots of the new Salk vaccine. One thing the five had in common told the doctors this was no coincidence. What was it?
answer: All five were paralysed in the vaccinated arm.
choices: All five had been vaccinated at one clinic.
All five had a brother or sister with polio.
All five were paralysed in the vaccinated arm.
All five fell ill on exactly the same day.
context: Idaho State University's polio history records the detail that turned suspicion into evidence: 'It was found that all five of the California children became paralyzed in the left arm, which had received the vaccine.' Wikipedia's Polio vaccine article gives the same tell for the wider wave - the Surgeon General's reports described paralysis 'starting in the limb the vaccine was injected into.' A vaccine holding only killed virus cannot paralyse the limb it went into. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polio_vaccine; sites.google.com/isu.edu/polioinidaho/home/the-cutter-incident-1955.

question: A student reads down the list of the five American drug firms licensed in 1955 to make Jonas Salk's polio vaccine. One of them, Cutter Laboratories of Berkeley, California, was a small family firm with little skill in growing viruses at scale. Before polio, what had Cutter mostly made?
answer: Vaccines and medicines for animals.
choices: Vaccines and medicines for animals.
Blood plasma for army hospitals.
Insulin for diabetic patients.
Antibiotics for surgical wards.
context: Cutter Laboratories was a family-owned Berkeley firm best known for veterinary vaccines and general pharmaceuticals, with limited prior experience of large-scale virology compared with competitors such as Eli Lilly - an inexperience that, per Grokipedia, 'evaded detection during pre-licensing inspections by NIH's Division of Biologics Standards.' Its 1955 sales were $11,482,000. It stayed in business, bought Hollister-Stier in 1958, and was itself bought by Bayer AG in 1974. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cutter_Laboratories.

question: A doctor in Pocatello, Idaho, reported a case on 24 April 1955. Susan Pierce, seven, had been given the polio shot a few days before, and now had fever and paralysis. She died three days after her symptoms began. What did the officials running the local vaccine program first say about her?
answer: She must have caught polio before her shot.
choices: She must have been given a double dose.
She must have had a different illness.
She must have missed her second injection.
She must have caught polio before her shot.
context: Susan Pierce was the first reported death of the outbreak: fever and paralysis within days of her injection, then death from fulminating bulbar polio three days after symptoms appeared. Local vaccine administrators first dismissed the case as an infection she had already been carrying. Within days the Surgeon General was receiving the same kind of report from several states. Sources: history.com/articles/salk-polio-vaccine-shortages-problems; sites.google.com/isu.edu/polioinidaho/home/the-cutter-incident-1955.

question: A mother in Idaho was paralysed by polio in April 1955, though she had never had the shot. Her own two children had been given it.
