Some of Cutter Laboratories' batches of the Salk vaccine still held unkilled poliovirus, and Idaho's polio cases that week jumped fourteen above normal. How were unvaccinated people catching polio?
answer: The vaccinated children were shedding live virus.
choices: A wild epidemic had reached Idaho that spring.
The vaccinated children were shedding live virus.
Spilled vaccine had got into the town water supply.
Doctors were carrying the virus from house to house.
context: Wikipedia states the outcome plainly: 'The exposures led to an epidemic of polio in the families and communities of the affected children.' Children given Cutter's vaccine excreted live poliovirus and infected people who had never been vaccinated - a preventive shot starting an outbreak. Idaho alone reported fourteen extra cases that week, and the thirty-three-year-old mother caught polio from her own vaccinated children. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories; history.com/articles/salk-polio-vaccine-shortages-problems.

question: Cutter's vaccine had paralysed dozens of children by early May 1955 and been withdrawn. That was a breakdown in making and checking the vaccine, not proof that a killed-virus vaccine cannot work, and no other maker's lots were tied to any case. Surgeon General Leonard Scheele acted anyway on 8 May. What did he order?
answer: Every polio vaccination in the country stopped.
choices: Every polio vaccination in the country stopped.
Cutter's Berkeley plant closed by federal marshals.
All unused doses returned to the five makers.
Vaccination restricted to children over seven.
context: Scheele halted Cutter's vaccine on 27 April 1955 and suspended the entire national polio vaccination programme on 8 May until a cause could be determined; vaccination resumed in the autumn under a new testing regime. Sources split on which date to call 'the' suspension: Grokipedia gives 27 April for the immediate nationwide halt of Cutter's product and 8 May for Scheele's announced suspension, while history.com gives 8 May for the halt of all vaccinations. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Cutter_Laboratories; history.com/articles/salk-polio-vaccine-shortages-problems.

question: William Tripp and Karl Habel of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) went to Cutter Laboratories' plant in Berkeley, California, in 1955, sent by the US Surgeon General after live polio virus in its Salk vaccine paralysed children. They asked the workers questions and read the production records. What did their check find?
answer: Nothing was wrong with Cutter's production methods.
choices: Cutter had skipped a required safety test.
Cutter's monkey kidney cultures were contaminated.
Nothing was wrong with Cutter's production methods.
Cutter's records had been altered after the recall.
context: Wikipedia's sentence is verbatim: 'After a thorough investigation, they found nothing wrong with Cutter's production methods.' The flaw was real but invisible to an inspection of practice. A congressional hearing that June went on to blame the NIH's own Laboratory of Biologics Control for lack of scrutiny rather than the company. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories (citing Breakthrough: The Saga of Jonas Salk, Trident Press, 1966, pp. 313-315).

question: A worker at Cutter Laboratories leaves poliovirus, grown on monkey kidney cultures, in formaldehyde for about two weeks, the standard way to kill every particle. In some lots live Type 1 virus still reaches the bottles. Investigators argue over how. What has gone wrong?
answer: Clumped cell debris shielded virus from the formaldehyde.
choices: A poliovirus strain had grown resistant to formaldehyde.
Clumped cell debris shielded virus from the formaldehyde.
The monkey kidney cultures carried a second, unknown virus.
The formaldehyde had been neutralised days too early.
context: Grokipedia states the failure mode: 'formaldehyde penetration could be impeded by viral aggregates or tissue remnants.' Cell debris left behind by inadequate filtration wrapped poliovirus particles and kept the formaldehyde off them, so live Type 1 virus survived into the finished product; history.com puts it as proteins in the vaccine clumping together. Paul Offit traced the key manufacturing flaw to a change in the method of filtration - and found it at more than one company. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Cutter_Laboratories; gavi.org/vaccineswork/book-club/review-cutter-incident-paul-offit; history.com/articles/salk-polio-vaccine-shortages-problems.

question: Investigators pulled Cutter's own paperwork after the first paralysis reports of 1955, for the lots that had paralysed the children. Before a lot could be sold, the maker had to test it for surviving live virus and report the result. What did the paperwork show?
answer: The lots had passed every test the licence required.
choices: The lots had been shipped before testing finished.
The lots had been tested for strength but not safety.
The lots had come from an unlicensed second plant.
The lots had passed every test the licence required.
context: Wikipedia puts it in one clause: 'some lots of the Cutter vaccine - despite passing required safety tests - contained live polio virus in what was supposed to be an inactivated-virus vaccine.' Cutter's release testing was simply less sensitive than its competitors': other makers looked for residual live virus by inoculating animals, while Cutter relied on protein-nitrogen assays and monkey-kidney tissue-culture tests that could not detect a low viral load. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories; grokipedia.com/page/Polio_vaccine.

question: A nurse gives an American child a polio shot in the fall of 1955, under new federal controls. All five licensed makers had trouble killing every virus particle that year, though only Cutter's lots caused an outbreak. The next few years would test whether a killed-virus vaccine worked at all. What happened to polio in the United States between 1953 and 1957?
answer: Cases fell from about 35,000 to under 6,000.
choices: Cases fell from about 35,000 to under 6,000.
Cases fell from about 35,000 to about 25,000.
Cases held steady at about 35,000 a year.
Cases rose from about 35,000 to over 50,000.
context: Grokipedia's judgement of the incident is that it 'exposed manufacturing inconsistencies rather than flaws in the trial design or vaccine formulation itself.' Eli Lilly, Parke-Davis, Wyeth and Pitman-Moore all found complete inactivation difficult, and three of them were sued and settled out of court; only Cutter's lots caused paralysis. U.S. polio cases fell from roughly 35,000 in 1953 to under 6,000 by 1957. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories; grokipedia.com/page/Polio; grokipedia.com/page/Jonas_Salk.

question: Bernice Eddy of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) tested the makers' polio vaccines in eighteen monkeys in 1954, a year before the licence, and three of Cutter's six batches failed. She sent her superiors a report with one piece of evidence attached. What did she attach?
answer: Photographs of the paralysed animals.
choices: Statements signed by her laboratory staff.
Photographs of the paralysed animals.
Slides of spinal cord from her monkeys.
Samples of vaccine from the bad batches.
context: Wikipedia: 'in 1954, staff member Bernice Eddy had reported to her superiors that some inoculated monkeys had become paralyzed and provided photographs. William Sebrell, the director of NIH, rejected the report.' Her immediate superior, William Workman, head of the Laboratory of Biologics Control, invalidated her findings, removed her from polio research and reassigned her to flu vaccine. The problem never reached the licensing advisory committee. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories (citing Edward Shorter, The Health Century, Doubleday 1987, pp. 68-70); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernice_Eddy; grokipedia.com/page/Polio_vaccine.

question: Nathanson and Langmuir counted the Cutter cases in two separate groups for a 1963 study. Among the vaccinated children: about 40,000 with fever, headache and aching muscles but no paralysis, 56 paralysed, 5 dead. The second group was the brothers, sisters, parents and neighbours who caught polio from those children. What did that second count come to?
answer: 113 paralysed and 5 dead.
choices: 14 paralysed and 1 dead.
113 paralysed and 5 dead.
41 paralysed and 5 dead.
300 paralysed and 12 dead.
context: On this narrower per-group accounting the bystanders were about two-thirds of all the paralysis - 113 of 169 - so more of the paralysed were people who never received the vaccine than were vaccinated children. Keep it separate from the headline figure usually quoted (roughly 120,000 defective doses, over 200,000 children vaccinated in five states, about 40,000 ill, about 200 paralytic cases with over 160 permanent, 10 deaths), which counts vaccinees and contacts together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories, citing Nathanson N. & Langmuir A.D., Am. J. Hyg. 1963;78:29-60, and Offit P.A., N Engl J Med 2005;352:1411-1412.

question: Members of Congress at a June 1955 hearing blamed the National Institutes of Health (NIH) lab meant to be watching Cutter, not Cutter itself. The NIH director resigned, and so did the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. Later that year the lab was rebuilt as the Division of Biologics Standards. What power did the new division have?
answer: To test and release each lot before sale.
choices: To retest any lot after complaints arrived.
To test and release each lot before sale.
To license only firms with virus experience.
To publish each maker's own test results.
context: The Division of Biologics Standards held explicit authority over facility inspections, pre-licensing approval, and lot-by-lot federal potency and safety testing, replacing the earlier reliance on manufacturers' self-certification: no vaccine could be distributed until the DBS had verified it carried no live virus. The DBS ran until 1972, when its functions moved to the FDA's Bureau of Biologics. The officials who went: Secretary Oveta Culp Hobby, and NIH director William H. Sebrell Jr. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Cutter_Laboratories; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories (citing Edward Shorter, The Health Century, 1987).

question: Anne Gottsdanker took Cutter vaccine in her right thigh and was paralysed ten days later. At the Oakland trial, the lawyer Melvin Belli showed the jury that her lot had contained live wild Type 1 poliovirus. In January 1958 the jury voted ten to two that Cutter had not been negligent, since the company had made its vaccine as the industry and the federal licence required. What did the jury do next?
answer: It ordered Cutter to pay the families anyway.
choices: It cleared Cutter and awarded the families nothing.
It sent the case back to be tried a second time.
It divided the blame between Cutter and the NIH.
It ordered Cutter to pay the families anyway.
context: The same jury voted eleven to one that Cutter had broken an implied warranty - the law's presumption that a thing sold is fit for what it is sold for - and protested that the warranty law as the judge had spelled it out was 'extremely harsh.' The awards were $131,500 to the Gottsdankers and $15,800 to the Phippses, $147,300 in all. The California Court of Appeal affirmed on 12 July 1960, extending to vaccines and drugs the 'food exception' that lets a buyer sue a maker he never bought from directly: a company could be liable for harm with no negligence proved, even having made the product to industry standards under a federal licence. Paul Offit calls it liability without fault. Sources: TIME, 'Medicine: Cutter in Court', 27 January 1958; Gottsdanker v. Cutter Laboratories, 182 Cal.App.2d 602 (1960); discovery.org/a/2272/.

question: Jonas Salk told the Cutter court, 'I can produce safe vaccine with no live virus every time.' His safety standard was straight-line inactivation: if formaldehyde killed poliovirus at a steady rate, a maker could calculate the moment when none was left rather than hunt for survivors. The Nobel laureate Wendell Stanley then testified for the other side. What did Stanley tell the court?
answer: That he had often seen the curve depart from that theory.
choices: That formaldehyde had never killed poliovirus reliably.
That Cutter had grown the wrong strain of poliovirus.
That he had often seen the curve depart from that theory.
That the 1954 field trial had been too small to judge.
context: TIME reported the exchange from the 1957-58 trial. Salk: 'I can produce safe vaccine with no live virus every time.' Wendell M. Stanley, from the stand: 'I have seen many times where the curve does not follow that theory.' Straight-line inactivation let a manufacturer calculate an endpoint instead of measuring it - which is exactly what failed when clumped debris kept formaldehyde off some virus particles. Sources: TIME, 'Medicine: Cutter in Court', 27 January 1958; gavi.org/vaccineswork/book-club/review-cutter-incident-paul-offit.

question: Paul Offit set down the warning that was shelved, the lots that passed their tests and the liability without fault in The Cutter Incident, a 2005 Yale University Press book and the fullest account there is. What else is Offit known for in the vaccine world?
answer: He co-invented a rotavirus vaccine and advised the CDC.
choices: He argued the vaccine-injury cases in the federal courts.
He co-invented a rotavirus vaccine and advised the CDC.
He ran the NIH laboratory that licensed the 1955 vaccine.
He directed the March of Dimes fundraising campaigns.
context: Paul Offit directs the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, co-invented the RotaTeq rotavirus vaccine, sat on the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices from 1998 to 2003, co-edits Plotkin's Vaccines and holds the Albert B. Sabin Gold Medal - the most prominent public defender of vaccination in America. He also wrote the companion paper 'The Cutter incident, 50 years later' (N Engl J Med 2005;352:1411-1412). Offit was born in Baltimore in 1951; his family's pediatrician delayed his own polio vaccine because of Cutter, and at five, recovering from clubfoot surgery, he spent months in a ward beside polio patients in iron lungs. The 1955 record is not hidden: it was assembled and published by the movement's leading advocate. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Paul_Offit; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories.

question: Jack Rebok opened the valve on a cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene gas at DuPont's Jackson Laboratory in New Jersey on 6 April 1938. Nothing came out. The valve worked fine. Roy Plunkett ran one check before writing the cylinder off. What did he find?
answer: He weighed it: it was still as heavy as a full one.
choices: He weighed it: it was still as heavy as a full one.
He soaped the valve seat: no bubbles rose at all.
He warmed it in a bath: a thin trickle of gas came.
He tilted it slowly: nothing shifted or sloshed.
context: Plunkett's own account, via the Science History Institute: when he and Rebok prepared the cylinder for use, none of the gas came out - yet the cylinder weighed the same as before. The scale is the hero of this story: an anomaly is only an anomaly if somebody measured. Plunkett's first thought was not triumph. Asked in a 1986 oral history what his reaction had been, he said: 'Well, we have to start over now.' He tested the batch anyway instead of throwing it out. Source: Science History Institute, 'Roy J. Plunkett'; Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Long, Strange History of Teflon'.

question: Roy Plunkett, 27 and two years out of a doctorate, took on one job for DuPont at its Jackson Laboratory in New Jersey, and a new gas called tetrafluoroethylene was just the starting material for it. In 1938 he found the slipperiest solid ever measured, Teflon, without looking for a solid at all. What was the job?
answer: A non-toxic replacement refrigerant.
choices: A non-toxic replacement refrigerant.
A non-flammable dry-cleaning solvent.
A non-corrosive hydraulic fluid.
A non-toxic fumigant for grain stores.
context: Plunkett had no business recognising a polymer: his 1936 Ohio State doctorate was titled 'The Mechanism of Carbohydrate Oxidation.' His college roommate at Manchester College, Paul Flory, would win the 1974 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for exactly this field - the physical chemistry of polymers. The specific target DuPont set him was the compound CF2Cl-CF2H, chosen because Frigidaire already held the patent on Freon-114 and DuPont wanted a way around it; tetrafluoroethylene was only the feedstock. Source: Grokipedia, 'Roy J. Plunkett'; Science History Institute, 'Roy J. Plunkett'.

question: Roy Plunkett and his assistant Jack Rebok had made about a hundred pounds of the gas tetrafluoroethylene at DuPont's Jackson Laboratory by the spring of 1938. They packed every cylinder of it in dry ice. Why the cold?
answer: Warm, the gas would explode and burst the cylinder.
choices: Warm, the gas would explode and burst the cylinder.
Warm, the gas would leak past the valve packing.
Warm, the gas would corrode the steel from inside.
Warm, the gas would slowly turn poisonous to breathe.
context: Roughly 100 pounds of tetrafluoroethylene went into pressure cylinders packed in dry ice, specifically so the gas would not explode or rupture its container; one RSC account puts a single cylinder's contents at about 1 kg. Tetrafluoroethylene is documented as liable to explode when exposed to heat, light or contaminants. Both men already knew this gas was touchy before anything went wrong - which is what makes what they did next remarkable. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Long, Strange History of Teflon'; RSC Education, 'The discovery of Teflon'.

question: Two DuPont men, Roy Plunkett and Jack Rebok, took a saw to the steel shell of a tetrafluoroethylene cylinder in April 1938, because it would not give up its gas. That was a deliberate choice: both knew the gas often exploded. What did they find inside?
answer: A white waxy powder packed on the bottom and lower walls.
choices: A white waxy powder packed on the bottom and lower walls.
A clear oily liquid pooled in the bottom of the shell.
A grey metallic crust grown over the inside of the steel.
A dry brown scale ringing the throat of the valve.
context: Plunkett's own account: 'When he opened the valve - to let the TFE gas flow under its own pressure from the cylinder - nothing happened... we decided to cut open the cylinder. When we did, we found more of the powder packed onto the bottom and lower sides of the cylinder.' Another account has the first shake sending a whitish powder down onto the lab bench. The gas had polymerised itself into PTFE with nobody adding anything. Source: Plunkett's account via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_J._Plunkett; Grokipedia, 'Polytetrafluoroethylene'.

question: Marc Grégoire, a French engineer, was coating something of his own with Roy Plunkett's powder in the early 1950s. His wife Colette watched him work and told him to put the same coating on her frying pan. What piece of equipment had Grégoire been coating?
answer: His aluminium fishing tackle, to stop the line tangling.
choices: His aluminium fishing tackle, to stop the line tangling.
His bicycle chain, to stop the links from seizing.
His ski bases, to make them run faster on wet snow.
His garden shears, to stop sap gumming the blades.
context: Gregoire's French patent was granted in 1954 and he founded Tefal near Paris in 1956. The US FDA cleared PTFE for food contact in 1960, and Marion Trozzolo sold the first American-made version, the Happy Pan, from 1961 - twenty-three years after the cylinder was opened. Source: Grokipedia, 'Non-stick surface'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-stick_surface; Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Long, Strange History of Teflon'.

question: A chemist pours aqua regia, the acid mixture strong enough to dissolve gold, onto PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene), the slick white plastic Roy Plunkett stumbled on and DuPont later sold as Teflon. Nothing happens. The molecule is just a long chain of carbon atoms, but every carbon is wrapped in fluorine. What is it about that fluorine wrapping that leaves an attacker no place to start?
answer: Fluorine holds carbon in the strongest single bond carbon forms.
choices: Fluorine holds carbon in the strongest single bond carbon forms.
Fluorine gives the whole chain a charge that repels acids.
Fluorine packs the chains too tightly for acid to seep in.
Fluorine caps the chain ends so no reaction can spread.
context: The carbon-fluorine bond has a dissociation energy of about 485 kJ/mol - the strongest single bond carbon forms in organic chemistry, against roughly 413 for carbon-hydrogen and 348 for carbon-carbon. The consequences, in numbers: a coefficient of friction of 0.05-0.10, the lowest of any solid material; surface free energy of only about 18-20 mN/m, where untreated cotton is 40-50; water beading at a contact angle near 110 degrees; continuous service to 260 degrees C. Aqua regia and chlorosulfonic acid do nothing to it; the only things that attack it are molten alkali metals and certain fluorinating agents. Source: Grokipedia, 'Polytetrafluoroethylene'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon-fluorine_bond.

question: An engineer heats PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) and finds the price of its inertness: it never really flows. Its melt viscosity is around 10^11 pascal-seconds, so it barely moves at all. How do factories shape the loose powder into gaskets and sheet?
answer: They press the powder in a mould and bake it, the way a ceramic is fired.
choices: They press the powder in a mould and bake it, the way a ceramic is fired.
They dissolve the powder in solvent and pour it, the way varnish is poured.
They soften the powder in steam and roll it, the way rubber is rolled.
They compress the powder cold and glue the layers, the way plywood is pressed.
context: The process is called sintering: the powder is compacted in a mould and held at 360-380 degrees C, fusing without ever melting, exactly the way a ceramic is fired. Because its melt viscosity is on the order of 10^11 Pa.s, PTFE cannot be injection-moulded like an ordinary plastic. Its inertness was itself the first engineering problem it created. Source: Grokipedia, 'Polytetrafluoroethylene'; Grokipedia, 'Roy J. Plunkett'.

question: A student opens an account of Teflon's discovery and meets the usual photograph: three men in shirtsleeves, the young DuPont chemist Roy Plunkett among them, bent over a gas cylinder and cutting it open. The caption dates the picture to 6 April 1938, the morning Plunkett first found the solid at DuPont's Jackson Laboratory. The caption is wrong. Why?
answer: The picture was staged in 1966, with the three men posing.
choices: The picture was staged in 1966, with the three men posing.
The man holding the saw is Plunkett's supervisor, not Plunkett.
The picture shows a second cylinder, opened some weeks later.
The picture was taken in 1938 but at a different DuPont plant.
context: No photograph of the actual 6 April 1938 moment exists. The famous image was staged in 1966, with Plunkett, Robert McHarness and Jack Rebok posing over a cylinder. Plunkett went on to the John Scott Medal in 1951, the Plastics Hall of Fame in 1973 and the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 1985; he died on 12 May 1994, aged 83. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Long, Strange History of Teflon'; Grokipedia, 'Roy J. Plunkett'.

question: A fitter at a wartime government plant at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, seats a gasket of DuPont's still-secret PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) in a run of steel piping more than four hundred miles long. These seals will hold until the site closes in 1985. What is destroying the ordinary ones?
answer: Uranium hexafluoride, the gas the plant pushed through the pipes.
choices: Uranium hexafluoride, the gas the plant pushed through the pipes.
Nitric acid, the bath used to strip and replate the pipes.
Molten sodium, the coolant circulating in the plant's loops.
Chlorine gas, the by-product vented from the plating shop.
context: The plant was K-25, the gaseous diffusion facility; its converter shells and pipes were nickel-plated steel, and uranium hexafluoride was chewing through the gaskets and valve seals meant to contain it. In the words of one account, DuPont came saying 'we have this unique family of materials, we think it would make a good corrosion resistant gasket.' PTFE sealed that piping from 1942 until the facility closed in 1985. The material stayed a war secret: patent applied for 1 July 1939 and granted 4 February 1941 as U.S. Patent 2,230,654, 'Tetrafluoroethylene Polymers'; DuPont registered the name TEFLON only in 1945, and the first commercial sales came in 1946 - eight years after the cylinder was cut open. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; American Chemical Society, 'Uranium isotopes' landmark; Grokipedia, 'Tetrafluoroethylene'.

question: Patsy Sherman and Samuel Smith were chasing a rubber that jet fuel could not dissolve at 3M in 1953 when an assistant knocked a bottle of Sherman's experimental fluorochemical latex off the bench. It splashed the assistant's new white canvas tennis shoes, and Sherman watched that shoe over the following days. What had the splash done to it?
answer: The splashed patch stayed clean while the rest of the shoe grew dirty.
choices: The splashed patch stayed clean while the rest of the shoe grew dirty.
The splashed patch turned glassy while the rest of the shoe stayed rough.
The splashed patch went brittle while the rest of the shoe stayed soft.
The splashed patch faded grey while the rest of the shoe stayed white.
context: Sherman said the treated canvas shed liquid 'like water off a duck's back.' She and Smith spent about three years turning the ruined shoe into a product: Scotchgard, launched in 1956 and sold first to textile mills rather than shoppers. They ended up holding 13 joint patents in fluorochemical polymers. Sherman was the first woman named to 3M's Carlton Society, in 1974, and was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2001. Her line: 'Girls should follow their dreams. They can do anything anybody else can do.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsy_Sherman; Grokipedia, 'Scotchgard'; invent.org, 'Patsy Sherman and Samuel Smith'.

question: Bob Gore kept snapping heated PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) rods in 1969, after months of trying to stretch them by about ten per cent. One October night he changed a single thing about how he pulled, and the rod stretched roughly eight hundred per cent, opening into a solid that is about seventy per cent air. What did he change?
answer: He yanked the rod fast instead of drawing it slowly.
choices: He yanked the rod fast instead of drawing it slowly.
He chilled the rod first instead of heating it through.
He pulled in short repeated tugs instead of one long draw.
He twisted the rod as he pulled instead of pulling straight.
context: The result is expanded PTFE, or ePTFE: microporous, about 70 per cent air, and the basis of Gore-Tex fabric, vascular grafts and Elixir guitar strings. The trick was the speed of the pull - the opposite of what patience would suggest. Source: Science History Institute, 'Robert W. Gore'; invent.org, 'Robert W. Gore'.

question: Roy Plunkett poured nothing into his cylinder at DuPont in 1938, yet the tetrafluoroethylene inside turned itself into a solid polymer, against everything polymer science of the day predicted. Chemists have argued about what set the reaction off ever since. Which is the prime suspect?
answer: The iron of the cylinder wall itself.
choices: The iron of the cylinder wall itself.
The pressure of the compressed gas alone.
Heat left from the pump that filled it.
The jolt of the cylinder being moved.
context: Grokipedia records the white solid as forming 'due to spontaneous polymerization, likely initiated by trace impurities or the iron surface of the container.' Tetrafluoroethylene is separately documented as liable to explosive polymerization when exposed to heat, light or contaminants. An RSC piece notes that even now 'no one seems to have a clear explanation' of the exact trigger - the honest answer is that the leading suspect is the cylinder's own iron acting as a catalyst under pressure, and that it has never been proven. Grokipedia's note on the period is that the reaction ran against the predictions of polymer science of the day. Source: Grokipedia, 'Roy J. Plunkett' and 'Tetrafluoroethylene'; RSC Education, 'The discovery of Teflon'.

question: Researchers drew blood from a group of retired men who had worked in the fluorochemical plants and had taken in no PFOA (perfluorooctanoic acid) since, to measure what was left. PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) factories had used the chemical since 1951. How long did a man need to shed just half of the PFOA he already carried?
answer: About four years.
choices: About four years.
About four days.
About four weeks.
About four decades.
context: The same carbon-fluorine bonds that make PTFE untouchable are why the PFAS family does not break down in a river or a bloodstream either. In retired fluorochemical production workers the measured mean serum elimination half-life was about 3.8 years for PFOA and about 5.4 years for PFOS - years, not days, for the body to clear half of what it holds. PFOA was the processing surfactant used in making PTFE from 1951; US manufacturers phased it out by the end of 2015 under the EPA's PFOA Stewardship Program. Purified PTFE itself is a large molecule the body does not absorb, and has been FDA-cleared for food contact since 1960: the persistence problem is the small processing chemicals, not the finished pan. Source: Olsen et al., serum elimination half-life study, PMC1964923; Grokipedia, 'Polytetrafluoroethylene' and 'Non-stick surface'.

question: A grocer sets a weight on her scale, and the chain of checks behind it ends in a vault outside Paris, at the small cylinder that defined the kilogram until 2019. What was it made of?
answer: platinum-iridium alloy
choices: platinum-iridium alloy
polished tungsten carbide
sintered ceramic and gold
solid quartz crystal
context: The International Prototype of the Kilogram (nicknamed Le Grand K), a cylinder about the size of a plum, was 90% platinum and 10% iridium - chosen for hardness and chemical stability. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Prototype_of_the_Kilogram.

question: A staffer at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) in Sèvres comes to the safe that holds the cylinder fixing the kilogram, under three glass bell jars, one inside the next. No single staffer can open that safe. What does it take?
answer: three separate keys, held by three different custodians
choices: three separate keys, held by three different custodians
a written order signed by the French Minister of Science
an escort of French national police officers
a matching key issued to the visiting national laboratory
context: All three custodians had to be physically present. The cylinder was compared to its official copies only three times in about 130 years. Source: smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/redefine-kilogram.

question: A scientist outside Paris sets one of about 40 official copies of the kilogram on a balance against the master cylinder. In a century the copies and the master have drifted about 50 micrograms apart, close to the mass of a fingerprint. Nobody can say which has really changed. Why not?
answer: the prototype could not itself be weighed - it WAS one kilogram by definition
choices: the prototype could not itself be weighed - it WAS one kilogram by definition
the copies were kept in labs that no longer trusted each other's balances
the drift was below what any balance of that era could resolve
the older comparison records had been lost in the two world wars
context: By law and convention, Le Grand K WAS the kilogram; it could only be compared to something else. If it and the copies disagreed, the copies were 'wrong.' The direction of the drift is genuinely unresolved. Source: chemistryworld.com/news/game-over-for-the-original-kilogram.

question: A technician reads an atomic clock in a national laboratory, and its ticks trace back to one kind of atom. The second, the unit of time, was redefined in 1967 as a set count of oscillations of that atom's microwave radiation, while the kilogram stayed a physical object into the 2010s. Which atom was chosen?
answer: caesium-133
choices: caesium-133
hydrogen-1
krypton-86
strontium-87
context: One SI second = 9,192,631,770 periods of the transition between the two hyperfine levels of caesium-133's ground state. Krypton-86 was the atomic standard for the metre (1960-1983). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second.

question: Delegates to the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) redefined the metre in 1983 using a constant of nature, with a strange side effect. A quantity that used to be measured was now fixed by rule and could no longer be measured, even in theory. Which quantity?
answer: the speed of light in vacuum
choices: the speed of light in vacuum
the wavelength of the sodium D-line
the length of the equatorial degree
the local strength of Earth's gravity
context: The 1983 definition: one metre = the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Every improvement in measurement now refines the METRE, not c. This is the trick of every constant-anchored definition: fix a number of nature and let the unit float to it. Source: bipm.org/en/committees/cg/cgpm/17-1983/resolution-1.

question: Workers on the International Avogadro Project tried to count the atoms in a single object. They grew and polished a small sphere of nearly pure silicon-28, about 94 mm across and often called the roundest object ever made. Why did they insist on pure silicon-28 in particular?
answer: so nearly every atom in the sphere had the same mass, simplifying the count
choices: so nearly every atom in the sphere had the same mass, simplifying the count
so the sphere would not slowly release radiation into the lab
so the polishing lasers would not scatter off other isotopes
so the crystal would grow in a perfect body-centred cubic pattern
context: The spheres are about 99.9995% silicon-28. Surface deviations were below about 50 nanometres - if scaled up to Earth-size, the tallest mountain to deepest trench would be only a few metres. Source: nist.gov/si-redefinition/kilogram/kilogram-silicon-spheres.

question: A physicist reads a usable value for a constant of nature off a Kibble balance, which sets a mass against electromagnetic force. Even so, the 2019 rewrite of the kilogram is held up for years. What more proof does the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) want first?
answer: independent confirmation by the silicon-sphere atom-count to the required precision
choices: independent confirmation by the silicon-sphere atom-count to the required precision
a fresh 'periodic verification' of Le Grand K against its official copies
adoption of the Kibble balance by at least three national metrology institutes
reduction of the balance's uncertainty below one part in a billion
context: Two routes with entirely different error sources landing on the same Planck value is a stronger check than any single number: if two independent methods agree, unknown systematic errors are unlikely to be moving them together. Only when the Kibble and Avogadro projects converged did the CGPM lock in h. Source: physicsworld.com/a/new-definition-of-the-kilogram-comes-into-force.

question: A student copies down one number, 6.62607015 x 10^-34 joule-seconds, with no error bar. The International System of Units (SI) fixed it at that exact value on 20 May 2019, World Metrology Day, and the kilogram is now written in terms of it. Which constant is it?
answer: the Planck constant
choices: the Planck constant
the Boltzmann constant
the elementary charge
the Avogadro constant
context: Boltzmann's k, the elementary charge e, and Avogadro's N were also fixed at exact numbers on the same day, but the KILOGRAM keys off the Planck constant via the Kibble route. Those constants stopped being measurements and became definitions. Source: physicsworld.com/a/new-definition-of-the-kilogram-comes-into-force.

question: A lab director reads the 2019 notice that retired Le Grand K, the single cylinder kept in a French vault that had defined the kilogram for over a century, and rewrote the unit from a constant of nature. What does that give her in practice that a French cylinder never could?
answer: a properly equipped lab anywhere on Earth or Mars can realise a kilogram from scratch
choices: a properly equipped lab anywhere on Earth or Mars can realise a kilogram from scratch
the world's national kilogram copies could finally be replaced with fresh, undrifted platinum-iridium cylinders
the BIPM could ship certified 1 kg wafers of silicon-28 to any national lab on demand
atomic clocks became accurate enough to detect Le Grand K's drift in real time
context: The point of a natural-constant definition: no shipping, no borrowing, no French artifact. Give a lab a Kibble balance, the defined value of h, and the SI second, and it can build a kilogram out of physics. Source: nist.gov/si-redefinition/kilogram.

question: A boy weighs himself before bed and on waking, and the numbers differ. Santorio Santorio chased that gap in early-1600s Padua, weighing every meal, drink and waste from a hanging chair for about thirty years. Where did he conclude the missing weight had gone?
answer: Out through his skin and breath as an invisible loss
choices: Out through his skin and breath as an invisible loss
Into the growth of his own bones and muscles
Down into the wooden chair itself as absorbed sweat
Up into the air only when he laughed or shouted
context: Ars de statica medicina (1614) names the loss perspiratio insensibilis -- insensible perspiration. A kid with a bathroom scale can watch the same gap open overnight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santorio_Santorio

question: Werner Forssmann, a 25-year-old surgical trainee in Eberswalde, Germany, had been forbidden to try what he was about to try in 1929. He picked up a thin rubber tube used for draining urine and passed it 65 cm up a vein in his own arm, aiming for one specific place. Where did he stop?
answer: Inside the right side of his own heart
choices: Inside the right side of his own heart
In a vein at the back of his own throat
In the artery running to his own liver
Just above his own collarbone
context: Before that day, textbooks warned that any catheter reaching the heart chambers would trigger fatal spasm. Forssmann needed to prove otherwise, so he chose himself as the patient. Source: http://scihi.org/werner-forssmann-cardiac-catheterization/

question: Trainee doctor Werner Forssmann threaded a thin flexible tube up a vein into his own heart in 1929, in secret, a procedure his seniors had forbidden as suicidal. With the catheter still inside, he knew he needed a documentary record before anyone could dismiss what he had done. What did the trainee do next?
answer: Walked to the radiology department to have himself X-rayed
choices: Walked to the radiology department to have himself X-rayed
Photographed his own chest through a shaving mirror
Sent his nurse to fetch a chaplain as an eyewitness
Waited for a colleague to trace the tube on his skin in ink
context: The chest film, catheter tip clearly inside the heart, ran with his write-up in Klinische Wochenschrift in November 1929. His boss fired him and cardiology closed to him; he moved to urology. Source: https://www.mayoclinicproceedings.org/article/S0025-6196(18)30548-2/fulltext

question: Jesse Lazear of the US Army's Havana medical commission let mosquitoes that had bitten stricken patients bite him, in Cuba in the summer of 1900. The team was hunting a mosquito-borne plague ravaging the Caribbean, and he wanted to know whether the insect really carried it from patient to patient. What happened to Lazear?
answer: He caught yellow fever and died within weeks
choices: He caught yellow fever and died within weeks
He caught it and recovered in a fortnight
He never caught it and lived to publish his data
He caught malaria instead and pulled through
context: Lazear died on 25 September 1900, aged 34. The commission was later so shaken by his death that Walter Reed drew up written contracts, in Spanish and English, promising volunteers $100 in gold and $100 more if they took ill -- among the first written informed-consent forms in medical research. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_William_Lazear

question: Gerda Ditzen, a surgical nurse, lay down and let Werner Forssmann strap her arm to the table. His supervisor had forbidden the stunt and the catheter was locked away, so he had talked her into fetching the instruments, but she agreed only if he tried it on her, not himself. What did Forssmann do next?
answer: He slipped away and threaded the tube up his own arm instead
choices: He slipped away and threaded the tube up his own arm instead
He performed the catheterisation on Ditzen as she had asked
He untied her and confessed the plan to his supervisor
He waited until she dozed off, then began the puncture on her wrist
context: Ditzen only realised she had been tricked when she caught sight of him at a mirror, tube already in his vein; she then followed him to the X-ray room and helped push the catheter the rest of the way. Source: https://www.mayoclinicproceedings.org/article/S0025-6196(18)30548-2/fulltext

question: A New York pair, Andre Cournand and Dickinson Richards, made Werner Forssmann's stunt into the standard way of measuring pressure in a living heart, twenty-seven years after he was fired for pushing a tube into his own. What did the Nobel Committee do about that in 1956?
answer: Awarded the prize jointly to Forssmann, Cournand, and Richards
choices: Awarded the prize jointly to Forssmann, Cournand, and Richards
Awarded it to Cournand and Richards, passing Forssmann over
Awarded it to Forssmann alone as the original discoverer
Awarded it to the Eberswalde hospital where the first film was taken
context: Forssmann, then a small-town urologist, said he felt like the village priest who had suddenly been made a bishop. Every modern procedure that threads a wire into a blocked coronary artery -- angioplasty, stenting, ablation -- descends from his 1929 self-experiment. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Werner-Forssmann

question: Max von Pettenkofer swallowed a flask of cholera bacteria in front of colleagues in Munich in 1892, trying to prove the new germ theory wrong. Werner Forssmann threaded a thin tube up a vein into his own beating heart in 1929 to see if it could be done. Researchers today who wanted to try either on their own bodies could not simply do it: the rules changed after cases like these. What must they get first?
answer: Written approval from an outside ethics committee
choices: Written approval from an outside ethics committee
A signed waiver from their own medical insurer
A second doctor to run the same test on themselves
A patent on the technique they intend to try
context: Research authorities now treat an experiment on the researcher's own body as human-subject research needing outside review -- for exactly Feynman's reason: 'you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.' Source: https://hekint.org/2026/08/31/self-experimentation/

question: James Watson and Francis Crick announced the structure of DNA in a short note in the journal Nature on 25 April 1953. It ran barely more than a page and carried exactly one picture. What was that picture?
answer: a hand drawing of the helix made by Odile Crick, an artist
choices: a hand drawing of the helix made by Odile Crick, an artist
an X-ray photograph of DNA fibres taken by Rosalind Franklin
a chart of the four base amounts measured by Erwin Chargaff
a sketch of a single base pair drawn by Jerry Donohue
context: Odile Crick was Francis Crick's wife and a professional artist. In March or April 1953 she drew the two ribbons and their connecting rungs to her husband's spoken instructions — the first picture ever made of the double helix, and it has been called the most famous scientific drawing of the twentieth century. The paper itself ran under two pages, with that one illustration and no data at all. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odile_Crick; royalsociety.org/blog/2018/04/history-of-the-double-helix/; embryo.asu.edu (Watson and Crick, 1953).

question: Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins took the X-ray pictures of DNA at King's College London. Francis Crick and James Watson, working out its shape at Cambridge, did not run an experiment of their own. What did they spend their days doing instead?
answer: clamping metal parts into a model of the molecule
choices: clamping metal parts into a model of the molecule
hunting the literature for a matching molecule
deriving the shape by algebra from published angles
queuing for time on Cambridge's EDSAC computer
context: The parts came out of the Cambridge metal shop: cut plates for the bases, rods and clamps for the backbone. Watson gradually accumulated the list of pieces and assembled them while Crick advised. Every number came from somebody else — the X-ray measurements from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins at King's College London, the base ratios from Erwin Chargaff at Columbia, the chemistry advice from Jerry Donohue. Building a model out of other people's measurements is how a great deal of theoretical work gets done — and it is also why who was owed what credit for DNA has been argued over ever since. Sources: scientificamerican.com/blog/the-curious-wavefunction/the-structure-of-dna-61-years-later-how-they-did-it/; sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/francis-crick-rosalind-franklin-james-watson-and-maurice-wilkins/

question: James Watson wrote later that Francis Crick walked into a pub near their lab in 1953, after the two had figured out the shape of DNA, and told the whole room what they had just found. By that story, what did Crick say they had found?
answer: the secret of life
choices: the secret of life
the shape of the gene
the key to inheritance
the plan of the cell
context: The line survives only in Watson's telling. Crick said he had no memory of saying it, and nobody else recorded it at the time. Repeat a story often enough and it becomes part of the furniture — a good reminder that a famous quotation and a documented one are not the same thing. Source: scalar.fas.harvard.edu/the-river-divides-into-thousands-of-branches (chapter 7).  (Legend.)

question: Erwin Chargaff at Columbia broke DNA apart and measured each base. Before 1950 most scientists thought it too plain to carry genes, its four bases coming in equal amounts. In calf thymus he found about 30 percent adenine. What else did his numbers show in every species?
answer: adenine matched thymine, and guanine matched cytosine
choices: adenine matched thymine, and guanine matched cytosine
adenine matched guanine, and thymine matched cytosine
every species gave the amounts calf thymus gave
each base rose and fell with the animal's size
context: Chargaff hydrolysed DNA, separated the bases by paper chromatography and measured them by absorbance at 260 nanometres. Calf thymus came out near 30% adenine, 30% thymine, 20% guanine and 20% cytosine, and the A-with-T, G-with-C match held sample after sample. That killed the 'tetranucleotide' idea that DNA was a boring repeating unit — and the match only makes sense if A sits opposite T and G opposite C the whole way down the ladder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Chargaff%27s_rules

question: Francis Crick and James Watson closed their 1953 paper in Nature, just over one page long, with a single dry sentence. After describing how the bases pair across the ladder, they wrote that it had 'not escaped our notice' that this specific pairing 'immediately suggests' something. What did they say it hinted at?
answer: a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material
choices: a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material
a possible chemical basis for the mutation of genes
a possible route from a gene to a finished protein
a possible reason for the variety of living species
context: The sentence in full: 'It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.' — J. D. Watson and F. H. C. Crick, 'Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids', Nature 171, 25 April 1953. It is the punchline of the whole structure: because each strand spells out the complete instructions for building the other, the shape itself answers how a cell copies its genes. Source: annex.exploratorium.edu/origins/coldspring/printit.html (annotated full text).

question: A girl builds a paper model of DNA's ladder, every rung the same width, a large base always facing a small one. Each rung is clasped shut by hydrogen bonds, weak links where two atoms share a hydrogen between them, and those are the links that must let go when the strands part. How many hydrogen bonds hold a G-C rung, and how many an A-T rung?
answer: three across a G-C rung, and two across an A-T rung
choices: three across a G-C rung, and two across an A-T rung
two across a G-C rung, and three across an A-T rung
four across a G-C rung, and three across an A-T rung
two across a G-C rung, and two across an A-T rung
context: Two hydrogen bonds hold an A-T rung; three hold a G-C rung. G-C-rich DNA does melt at a higher temperature — for a short strand in standard salt, Tm = 69.3 + 0.41(%GC) − 650/length, so the melting point climbs about 0.41 degrees Celsius for every extra percent of G and C, and anyone designing PCR primers uses that every working day. The textbook then adds one step too many and credits the extra bond for the extra heat. When Yakovchuk, Protozanova and Frank-Kamenetskii measured the two forces separately in 2006, that G-C effect turned out to come from how neighbouring bases stack face to face rather than from the third hydrogen bond — the counting is right, the explanation usually hung on it is not. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Nucleic_acid_double_helix; Yakovchuk, Protozanova & Frank-Kamenetskii, Nucleic Acids Research 34(2):564-574, 2006.

question: A student at a microscope studies a human cell nucleus, only about six thousandths of a millimetre across. The DNA inside it, pulled out straight, would stretch about two metres, like packing 40 kilometres of very fine thread into a tennis ball. How does the cell manage to fit it all in?
answer: winds it in short lengths around millions of protein spools
choices: winds it in short lengths around millions of protein spools
folds it flat into sheets stacked like the pages of a book
cuts it into pieces stored in separate walled compartments
twists it into one tight rope coiled from corner to corner
context: Roughly 147 base pairs wind about 1.65 left-handed turns around each spool — a core of eight histone proteins, two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 — touching the protein every 10 base pairs and bending to a radius of about 4.2 nanometres. There are millions of these spools in a single nucleus. Alberts' Molecular Biology of the Cell states the problem as 'geometrically equivalent to packing 40 km (24 miles) of extremely fine thread into a tennis ball!' Sources: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK26834/; grokipedia.com/page/Nucleic_acid_double_helix

question: Linus Pauling submitted his own DNA structure on 31 December 1952. It appeared in a leading academic journal that February, weeks before Watson and Crick published theirs. Pauling had just solved the alpha-helix of proteins. He would win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry the following year. What model had he proposed?
answer: three chains wound together with the phosphates at the core
choices: three chains wound together with the phosphates at the core
two chains wound together with the sugars at the core
one chain folded back on itself into a flat pleated sheet
four chains braided around a core of trapped water
context: Pauling and Corey's 'A Proposed Structure For The Nucleic Acids' ran in PNAS 39(2):84-97: three chains around a central axis, the phosphate groups crammed inside and the bases sticking outward like the spokes of a bicycle wheel — exactly inside-out from the truth. Watson and Crick had built the same wrong idea themselves on 28 November 1951 and watched it collapse within days, when colleagues from King's College pointed out they had badly miscounted how much water the molecule carries. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Linus_Pauling; pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.39.2.84; royalsociety.org/blog/2018/04/history-of-the-double-helix/

question: James Watson pushed cut-out cardboard shapes of the four bases around his desk at the Cavendish for weeks, trying to fit them into a ladder of constant width. Nothing came out even. Jerry Donohue, a chemist who shared his office and had trained under Linus Pauling, looked at the cardboard and told Watson the textbook pictures he had copied were only guessing. What had Watson drawn wrong?
answer: hydrogen atoms drawn on the wrong side of each base
choices: hydrogen atoms drawn on the wrong side of each base
one extra ring on two of the four base shapes
the angle at which each base joins its sugar
the gap he left between one base and the next
context: Watson had copied guanine and thymine in their rare 'enol' forms; Donohue told him those molecules strongly prefer the 'keto' forms, which puts a few hydrogen atoms somewhere else entirely. Watson had also been trying to pair like with like — adenine with adenine, guanine with guanine — which can never give a ladder of one width. He recut his cardboard shapes, and A-T and G-C fell out on Saturday 28 February 1953. The paper thanks him in a single line: 'We are much indebted to Dr. Jerry Donohue for constant advice and criticism, especially on interatomic distances.' Sources: scientificamerican.com/blog/the-curious-wavefunction/the-structure-of-dna-61-years-later-how-they-did-it/; annex.exploratorium.edu/origins/coldspring/printit.html

question: James Watson and Francis Crick attacked one detail of Linus Pauling's early 1953 DNA model in print, weeks after it appeared. Pauling had packed the phosphate backbones so close together that their negative charges should have shoved the whole structure apart, and he had seen the problem and written in a fix. What was Pauling's fix?
answer: he left a hydrogen attached to every phosphate group
choices: he left a hydrogen attached to every phosphate group
he threaded magnesium ions between the three backbones
he angled every phosphate away from its neighbours
he packed a sleeve of water between the chains
context: A phosphate group carries its negative charge because it lets go of an acidic hydrogen into the water. Pauling drew those hydrogens still attached — which quietly meant that deoxyribonucleic acid, in his model, was not an acid at all. James Watson's verdict was that without ionized phosphates 'the chains would immediately fly apart', and he noted the sting: the correct chemistry was printed in Pauling's own textbook, General Chemistry. Watson and Crick put the objection in print, politely and lethally: 'We believe that the material which gives the X-ray diagrams is the salt, not the free acid. Without the acidic hydrogen atoms it is not clear what forces would hold the structure together, especially as the negatively charged phosphates near the axis will repel each other.' Pauling took it like a scientist — on 27 March 1953 he wrote that he was looking forward 'to finding out what the decision will be as to which is incorrect'. Sources: scarc.library.oregonstate.edu/coll/pauling/dna/narrative/page24.html; annex.exploratorium.edu/origins/coldspring/printit.html; paulingblog.wordpress.com

question: Frank-Kamenetskii's group built DNA with tiny gaps in 2006 and measured two forces separately. Every textbook said the hydrogen bonds across each rung hold the two strands together, and the old picture had the strongest force wrong. What supplies about 70% of the molecule's stability?
answer: the flat faces of neighbouring bases pressing together
choices: the flat faces of neighbouring bases pressing together
the salt ions the negative backbone pulls in from the water
the twist of the helix squeezing every rung inward
the sugars locking to one another along each backbone
context: Base stacking — flat faces pressed together by van der Waals attraction and by the hydrophobic effect of hiding those faces from water — accounts for roughly 70% of the free energy holding a duplex together. You can watch it happen: stacked bases shade one another, so double-stranded DNA swallows LESS ultraviolet at 260 nanometres than the same DNA taken apart. Heat a sample while watching that absorbance and it jumps as the helix melts — the hyperchromic effect, and the standard way melting temperatures are measured to this day. Sources: Yakovchuk, Protozanova & Frank-Kamenetskii, Nucleic Acids Research 34(2):564-574, 2006 (academic.oup.com/nar/article/34/2/564/2401647); grokipedia.com/page/Nucleic_acid_double_helix

question: A girl pulls one hair from her own head and tapes it upright across a red laser pointer's beam in her bedroom, never aiming it near anyone's eyes. The light lands on the wall a few paces away. What does that wall show?
answer: A row of bright spots split by dark gaps
choices: A row of bright spots split by dark gaps
A single crisp shadow with clean sharp edges
A soft red glow that fades evenly outward
A bright ring circling one dark centre spot
context: Babinet's principle: the diffraction pattern from an opaque body is identical to that from a hole of the same size and shape, apart from the forward beam. So a hair paints the same stripes a slit of its width would. The classroom demo uses a wire about 0.1 mm thick; a human hair is roughly 0.05-0.1 mm, the same scale. And it is measurable: bright-fringe spacing follows beta = lambda x L / d (wavelength times distance to the wall, divided by the separation), so with the pointer's wavelength and a pace-count to the wall, a ruler across the stripes lets the girl work back to the thickness of her own hair. Safety, per the standard protocols: avoid direct eye exposure, use a low-power pointer, block the beam past the wall. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Babinet's principle'; Grokipedia, 'Diffraction' and 'Double-slit experiment' (Standard Experimental Apparatus).

question: Thomas Young sent sunlight through a pinhole to make one clean beam, then split that beam in two so the halves overlapped further on. The pattern on a screen, reported in his 1803 lecture, gave him wavelengths close to modern values. What split the beam?
answer: A thin card held edgewise in the beam
choices: A thin card held edgewise in the beam
A pair of slits cut through blackened foil
A sewing needle stood upright in the beam
A fine wire of drawn gold stretched across it
context: Almost everyone pictures two slits. Young used a card about one-thirtieth of an inch wide, held edge-on in the sunbeam so its two sides acted as the pair of coherent sources. The card experiment and the wavelength calculations appear in 'Experiments and calculations relative to physical optics', his Bakerian Lecture read on 24 November 1803 (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 94, 1-16, printed 1804). His earlier Bakerian Lecture, 'On the theory of light and colours' (Phil. Trans. 92, 12-48), was read in November 1801, and Physics World notes Young published no full account of the experiments until his 1807 Lectures on Natural Philosophy. Sources: Phil. Trans. 94 (1804), 1-16; Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (reference list); Grokipedia, 'Thomas Young (scientist)'.

question: J. J. Thomson's research student at the Cavendish, 23-year-old G. I. Taylor, set a sewing needle in front of a gas flame in 1909 and choked the light with stack after stack of smoked glass, until his dimmest source was about as bright as a candle burning a mile away. How long did Taylor leave his photographic plate exposed at that setting?
answer: Three months
choices: Three months
Three hours
Three days
Three weeks
context: Each smoked screen absorbed a large fraction of the light and the screens could be stacked, so Taylor could push the attenuation as far as he liked. At his feeblest setting there was, on average, roughly one photon at a time inside the apparatus. Published as G. I. Taylor, 'Interference fringes with feeble light', Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 15, 114-115 (1909). Sources: Wikipedia, 'G. I. Taylor'; Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (candle quote and citation); Skulls in the Stars, 'Taylor sees the (feeble) light (1909)'.

question: Akira Tonomura's team at Hitachi filmed their detector in 1989 as electrons landed one at a time, each a single bright dot. Photos froze the picture at 10 electrons, then 200, then 6,000, then 40,000, then 140,000. What did the plate look like at 10 electrons?
answer: A few scattered dots in no pattern
choices: A few scattered dots in no pattern
A few dots along one narrow band
A few faint stripes already crossing it
A few dots crowded at the centre
context: Random speckle at 10, unmistakable stripes at 140,000 — the pattern is not in any single electron, it is in the statistics of many. Tonomura, Endo, Matsuda, Kawasaki and Ezawa, 'Demonstration of single-electron buildup of an interference pattern', Am. J. Phys. 57, 117-120 (1989). In May 2002 Robert Crease asked Physics World's readers to name the most beautiful experiment in physics; more than 200 replied, with nominations ranging from Schroedinger's cat to the 1945 Trinity test, and this won — the only entry in the top ten with no scientist's name attached to it. Sources: Am. J. Phys. 57, 117 (1989) figure series; Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (reporting Crease, September 2002).

question: Gottfried Möllenstedt and Heinrich Düker strung a conducting thread across an electron beam at Tübingen in the mid-1950s, to bend its two halves back together. No wire they could buy would do, so Möllenstedt made the thread himself, from a natural fibre coated in gold. What did he use for the fibre?
answer: Threads pulled from spiders' webs
choices: Threads pulled from spiders' webs
Threads unwound from silkworm cocoons
Hairs pulled from a horse's tail
Fibres teased from a cotton boll
context: The gold-coated fibre is the electron biprism, and it is what made electron interference practical. Physics World reports that Möllenstedt made the wires by coating fibres from spiders' webs with gold — 'indeed, it is said that he kept spiders in the laboratory for this purpose', a detail told as tradition rather than documented record. One of his Tübingen students, Claus Jönsson, would take the next step. Source: Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment'.  (Legend.)

question: G. I. Taylor shot five photographs of his fringe pattern, the bright and dark stripes, at wildly different light levels, the first at full brightness in minutes, the last from a source no stronger than a candle burning a mile away. What did he tell the Cambridge Philosophical Society about the plates made with the starved light?
answer: Their fringes had come out every bit as sharp as before
choices: Their fringes had come out every bit as sharp as before
Their fringes had shifted measurably closer together
Their fringes had faded into an even grey glow
Their fringes had inverted, bright bands turning dark
context: Taylor's own words: 'In no case was there any diminution in the sharpness of the pattern although the plates did not all reach the standard blackness of the first photograph.' Starving the light did nothing to the stripes. The sentence this result eventually led to is Dirac's, in The Principles of Quantum Mechanics (4th edn, p. 9): 'each photon then interferes only with itself.' Not particles of light jostling one another — one particle, doing it alone. Sources: Skulls in the Stars, 'Taylor sees the (feeble) light (1909)', quoting Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc. 15, 114; Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (Dirac quote and citation).

question: Pier Giorgio Merli filmed electrons landing one at a time in Bologna in the early 1970s, with Giulio Pozzi and GianFranco Missiroli, the first ever to do it, and slowly an interference pattern built up. They needed a special detector and had to borrow one. Where did their image intensifier come from?
answer: An anatomy institute in Milan
choices: An anatomy institute in Milan
A television studio in Rome
A military observatory in Turin
An astronomy institute in Bologna
context: The rig was a Siemens Elmiskop 101 and the intensifier was on loan from an anatomy institute in Milan. Their film 'Electron Interference' won the physics-category award at the International Festival on Scientific Cinematography in Brussels in 1976; the paper is Am. J. Phys. 44, 306-7 (1976), submitted May 1974 — fifteen years ahead of the famous Hitachi run, and still barely known. Merli's own account of how it happened: the first single-electron double-slit experiment 'was actually a by-product of research into the practical applications of electron interferometry.' Source: Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (letters from John Steeds and from Merli, Pozzi and Missiroli, May 2003).

question: Hitachi's Akira Tonomura sent electrons through his machine very slowly in 1989: fewer than a thousand a second, and never two at a time inside. The pattern took over twenty minutes to build up dot by dot. One small everyday problem could have wiped out the picture. What would have erased it?
answer: The apparatus drifting a fraction of a fringe's width
choices: The apparatus drifting a fraction of a fringe's width
The detector missing one electron in every hundred
The electrons arriving slower than one per second
The beam voltage rising by a few extra volts
context: Fringe spacing in the Hitachi rig was of order 900 angstroms, so a drift of a fraction of that over twenty minutes would have smeared every stripe into grey. Detection efficiency was almost 100% with error under 1%, using a fluorescent film plus a photon-counting image acquisition system adapted from Hamamatsu Photonics. The sparse beam was deliberate: physicists including Sin-Itiro Tomonaga had objected that fringes might come from electrons interacting on the way through, and Tonomura ran it 'from beginning to end with constant and extremely low electron intensities... so there was no chance of finding two or more electrons in the apparatus at the same time.' Sources: Tonomura's letter in Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (May 2003); fringe spacing from the matter-wave review arXiv:1211.3493.

question: Richard Feynman told readers of his Lectures on Physics that the double-slit experiment 'contains the only mystery' in all of quantum mechanics, then warned them off it: 'you should not try to set up this experiment. This experiment has never been done in just this way.' He began giving those lectures in 1961. That same year someone had run the thing for real: electrons, two slits, fringes on the far side. Who had already done it?
answer: Claus Jönsson, a physicist at Tübingen
choices: Claus Jönsson, a physicist at Tübingen
Gottfried Möllenstedt, a physicist at Tübingen
Lester Germer, a physicist at Bell Laboratories
Ernst Ruska, a physicist at Berlin
context: Jönsson, one of Möllenstedt's Tübingen students, ran the first actual electron double slit in 1961 with 40 keV electrons (de Broglie wavelength about 0.006 nm) — and did not stop at two, getting interference from up to five slits (Zeitschrift fuer Physik 161, 454-474). Because it was published in German it stayed obscure until the American Journal of Physics reprinted it in English thirteen years later, in 1974. Editors Anthony French and Edwin Taylor called it a 'great experiment' but noted there are 'few professional rewards' for doing 'real, pedagogically clean fundamental experiments', and admitted: 'Few such recent presentations acknowledge that the two-slit electron interference experiment has now been done.' Full quote of Feynman's larger claim, Lectures ch. 37-1 / Vol. III ch. 1-1 (1963): 'a phenomenon which is impossible, absolutely impossible, to explain in any classical way, and which has in it the heart of quantum mechanics. In reality, it contains the only mystery.' Sources: Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment'; Grokipedia, 'Double-slit experiment'; Feynman Lectures on Physics, ch. 37.

question: Markus Arndt, Anton Zeilinger and their Vienna team sent whole C60 buckyballs, cages of 60 carbon atoms, through a diffraction grating with 50-nanometre slits in 1999. Clear interference fringes appeared on the detector. What state were the buckyballs in as they flew through?
answer: Glowing at about 900 kelvin, fresh out of an oven
choices: Glowing at about 900 kelvin, fresh out of an oven
Chilled to about 3 kelvin in a jet of cold helium
Cooled to about 77 kelvin by a nitrogen-cooled nozzle
Held at about 300 kelvin, no warmer than the room
context: They made the beam by sublimating fullerene powder in an oven at about 900 K, so every molecule came through glowing hot and shuddering in 174 vibrational degrees of freedom — and it interfered anyway. Most probable velocity about 220 m/s; matter wavelength about 2.5 picometres, roughly 350-400 times smaller than the molecule itself, which is about a nanometre across. Molecules were counted by laser ionization. Arndt and colleagues: 'all these observations support the view that each carbon-60 molecule interferes with itself only.' Nature 401, 680-682 (1999). Sources: Physics World, 'Wave-particle duality seen in carbon-60 molecules'; Univ. Vienna QuantumNano, 'The Origin: C60 Diffraction'; review arXiv:1211.3493.

question: Yaakov Fein and Markus Arndt's Vienna team ran huge molecules through a two-metre interferometer in 2019, each of over 2,000 atoms, or more than 40,000 protons, neutrons and electrons. Each stayed spread over both paths at once for over seven milliseconds. Every moving object has a matter wavelength that sets how it interferes. How big was the wavelength of these molecules?
answer: About a thousandth of one hydrogen atom's width
choices: About a thousandth of one hydrogen atom's width
About the width of one whole hydrogen atom
About a thousand hydrogen atoms laid across
About the width of the whole molecule itself
context: The molecules were functionalized oligoporphyrins beyond 25,000 daltons; the largest single one was C707H260F908N16S53Zn4. Fein's own comment: 'Our experiments show that quantum mechanics, with all its weirdness, is also amazingly robust, and I'm optimistic that future experiments will test it on an even more massive scale.' Fein et al., 'Quantum superposition of molecules beyond 25 kDa', Nature Physics 15, 1242-1245 (2019). Sources: Nature Physics 15, 1242 (2019); phys.org, '2000 atoms in two places at once: A new record in quantum superposition'.

question: A teacher tells her class that G. I. Taylor's marathon 1909 exposure proved a single photon interferes with itself. Taylor's plates are real and his measurement was honest, but physicists today will not let that conclusion rest on them, because of what his light source was: a gas flame turned down behind smoked glass. What is the problem with a source like that?
answer: A dimmed flame emits its photons in random clumps
choices: A dimmed flame emits its photons in random clumps
A dimmed flame emits its photons in twinned pairs
A dimmed flame emits its photons in a strict even drumbeat
A dimmed flame emits its photons in one continuous stream
context: Attenuated thermal light keeps photon-number statistics that allow coincidences, so two photons could still overlap in the apparatus; by modern standards Taylor's conditions were not sufficient to demonstrate genuine single-photon interference. Safe phrasing for his run is 'on average roughly one photon at a time'. The airtight version came in 1986, when Philippe Grangier, Gerard Roger and Alain Aspect used heralded single photons — each one announced by the detection of its twin — in an interferometer equivalent to a double slit, with interference visibility close to 100%. Checking the strongest claim hardest is the point, not a footnote. Sources: Wikipedia, 'G. I. Taylor' (explicit caveat); Grokipedia, 'Double-slit experiment' (Single-Particle Interference).

question: Gerhard Rempe's group, with Simon Dürr and Thomas Nonn, built an atom interferometer in 1998, which splits an atom's path in two and folds it back together. A detector that reveals the path wipes out the fringes, and for decades the standard explanation was Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: pinning down position must kick momentum, and the kick smears the stripes. Their rig could measure that kick directly. What did the measurement show?
answer: The kick was far too small to wash the pattern out
choices: The kick was far too small to wash the pattern out
The kick was exactly the size the textbooks predicted
The kick grew larger as the two paths were separated
The kick reversed direction depending on the path taken
context: From the abstract of Dürr, Nonn and Rempe, Nature 395, 33 (1998): 'we report a which-way experiment in an atom interferometer in which the back action of path detection on the atom's momentum is too small to explain the disappearance of the interference pattern. We attribute it instead to correlations between the which-way detector and the atomic motion, rather than to the uncertainty principle.' In one sentence: the detector did not shove the atom hard enough to blur the stripes — the stripes died because the path became knowable. Berthold-Georg Englert's 1996 duality relation makes it exact: V squared plus K squared is at most 1, where V is fringe visibility and K is path distinguishability. Perfect path knowledge forces the fringes to zero; partial knowledge gives partial fringes. The relation is derived without invoking uncertainty at all — it is about information, not about kicks. Nothing here involves anyone looking, and no mind collapses anything. Sources: Nature 395, 33-37 (1998); Grokipedia, 'Double-slit experiment' (Which-Way and Delayed-Choice Experiments).

question: Yoon-Ho Kim's team made entangled pairs of photons in 2000, pairs whose measurement outcomes stay linked, and sent one of each pair through a two-path apparatus onto a screen. The partner's path information could be preserved or destroyed, the choice falling eight nanoseconds after its twin had landed. Destroy it and fringes seem to appear; preserve it and they are gone. Headlines called it the future rewriting the past. What does the screen's own raw record show?
answer: A smooth blur, with fringes only after the data are sorted
choices: A smooth blur, with fringes only after the data are sorted
Sharp fringes that fade away across the eight-nanosecond delay
Sharp fringes that appear the moment the partner is destroyed
A smooth blur that sharpens into fringes all by itself
context: This is the result that kills the myth. Kim's setup used entangled pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion and gave coincidence-counted interference with 95% visibility when path information was erased, and none when it was path-marked, despite the 8 ns delay. But as the sources put it, no information travels backward in time: the overall data show no interference until conditioned on the eraser outcome, reflecting the experimenter's choice of analysis rather than any alteration of past events. The signal-photon screen never shows stripes. The stripes appear only when hits already recorded are sorted by which detector the partner landed in. Nothing in the past was changed; a subset was selected. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Quantum eraser experiment'; Grokipedia, 'Double-slit experiment'.

question: James Ussher, an Irish archbishop, published an exact date in 1650 for the start of the world: the evening before 23 October, 4004 BC. He was a respected Trinity College scholar, and his tool was ordinary arithmetic. What was he adding up?
answer: The generations and reign-lengths listed in scripture.
choices: The generations and reign-lengths listed in scripture.
The sediment layers stacked in Ireland's sea cliffs.
The years between the oldest eclipses ever written down.
The coins struck by a long succession of kingdoms.
context: Ussher was not guessing at the far end of his chain. He pinned it to a date secular historians already accepted -- the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk in 562 BC, reached through 2 Kings 25:27 -- and counted backwards from there, even cross-checking the autumn equinox against Kepler's Rudolphine Tables of 1627. He measured nothing; he counted, carefully, on the evidence he had. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Ussher chronology'.

question: The Comte de Buffon had his own foundry cast iron globes in the 1770s, pulled them white-hot from the furnace and timed them with a watch. He wanted the age of a once-molten Earth from an experiment, not a Bible. What was he timing?
answer: How long a globe took to cool enough to hold bare-handed.
choices: How long a globe took to cool enough to hold bare-handed.
How long a globe went on glowing before its colour died.
How long a globe kept a wax seal beside it from melting.
How long a globe took to boil away a small dish of water.
context: Buffon repeated the trial with globes of different sizes, and with glass and stone, to find how cooling time scales with size, then scaled up to a globe the size of the Earth. In Les Epoques de la Nature (1778) he published the answer: 74,832 years. Wrong by a factor of tens of thousands -- but it was the first age of the Earth that came out of an experiment instead of a document. Sources: American Institute of Physics, 'Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon (1707-1788)'; Grokipedia, 'Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon'.

question: Harrison Brown gave his University of Chicago graduate student, Clair Patterson, the job of measuring the age of the Earth in 1948. 'It will be duck soup, Patterson,' he promised. How long did the job really take?
answer: Seven years.
choices: Seven years.
Eleven months.
Two years.
Nineteen years.
context: The obstacle was never the clock; it was the dirt. Lead was already in the beakers, the distilled water, the reagents, the dust and the air -- Patterson found it in his own hair. Before he could weigh the atoms he had to build a room clean enough to weigh them in, one of the first clean rooms in the world: filtered air, acid-washed apparatus, chemicals he re-distilled himself, visitors made to change their clothes. The contamination turned out to be real pollution. He later measured a 200- to 300-fold rise of lead in polar ice since the 1700s, traced it to tetraethyl lead in petrol, and spent the rest of his career fighting the lead industry until leaded petrol was driven out of American cars. Sources: Caltech Magazine, 'Duck Soup and Lead'; Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: John Joly, an Irish geologist, built a clock out of the saltiness of the sea in 1899. He measured how much sodium the world's rivers carry down each year, assumed the ocean began with none, and divided its whole load by that yearly rate. Out came 80 to 90 million years, close to the 98 million Kelvin preferred. What does sodium do that Joly's clock never allowed for?
answer: It leaves the sea again; it does not just pile up.
choices: It leaves the sea again; it does not just pile up.
It poured into the sea far faster in ages past.
