It rises chiefly from sea-floor vents, not rivers.
It sits in deep water that no ship had sampled.
context: Salt does not simply accumulate. Sodium leaves seawater again, so the sum Joly did -- how much sits in the ocean, against how fast it arrives -- gives the average time a sodium ion stays in the sea before something removes it. Oceanographers call that a residence time, and that is what Joly measured, beautifully, by accident. It is not the age of anything. Two clocks built on completely different principles, Kelvin's cooling rock and Joly's salt, now agreed on tens of millions of years, and both were out by a factor of about fifty. Sources: Wikipedia, 'John Joly'; Linda Hall Library, 'Scientist of the Day - John Joly'; Grokipedia, 'Geochronology'.

question: William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, turned the age of the Earth into a physics problem in 1862: assume a molten ball, then work the equations of heat backwards to find how long the cooling had lasted. His sum needed one measured fact about the real Earth to start from, something miners had known for years. What did he build his estimate on?
answer: Temperature climbs about one degree for every fifty feet down.
choices: Temperature climbs about one degree for every fifty feet down.
Deep rock carries heat away about twice as fast as surface rock.
Rock pressure roughly doubles every thousand feet of depth.
Water pumped from the deepest shafts comes up steadily warm.
context: Kelvin's 1862 paper states it exactly: 'there is, on the whole, about 1 degree Fahr. of elevation of temperature per 50 British feet' of depth. From that single gradient, plus Fourier's heat equation and a molten start, he concluded that the Earth's consolidation 'cannot have taken place less than 20,000,000 years ago... nor more than 400,000,000 years ago'. The whole age of the planet hung on how much warmer a mine shaft gets as you climb down it. Source: Lord Kelvin, 'On the Secular Cooling of the Earth' (1862), full text at zapatopi.net/kelvin/papers/.

question: Charles Darwin guessed 300 million years just to wear away the Weald valley in Kent, in the first 1859 edition of On the Origin of Species, since natural selection needed huge amounts of time. Critics loved to attack the number. Then Lord Kelvin argued Earth was much younger, and people believed him. What did Darwin do with the figure in later editions?
answer: Darwin halved it, then dropped the estimate altogether.
choices: Darwin halved it, then dropped the estimate altogether.
Darwin doubled it and defended it in a new closing chapter.
Darwin kept it and printed Kelvin's objection beside it.
Darwin replaced it with a range holding both men's figures.
context: Darwin said out loud what the conflict felt like: 'Thomson's views of the recent age of the world have been for some time one of my sorest troubles', and, thinking of the long ages natural selection needed, 'then comes Sir W. Thomson, like an odious spectre.' The best physics of the age was in open conflict with the best field evidence, and neither side was being dishonest. Sources: Darwin Correspondence Project, 'How old is the earth?'; Scientific American, 'When Lord Kelvin Nearly Killed Darwin's Theory'.

question: Henri Becquerel left uranium salts on a wrapped photographic plate in 1896 and later found the plate fogged, with no sunlight involved. He had accidentally found radioactivity, and it knocked out one of the two ideas holding up Kelvin's math. Which idea did it break?
answer: That the Earth only loses heat and makes none of its own.
choices: That the Earth only loses heat and makes none of its own.
That the Earth began as a molten ball rather than a cold one.
That heat crosses solid rock at a steady, measurable rate.
That the Sun has burned at roughly its present strength.
context: The consequence for Kelvin's model was direct: the Earth is not simply spending an inheritance of heat from a fixed start -- it makes heat, on the order of 20 terawatts of radiogenic heating, most of it in the crust. Becquerel's fogged plate is also about as close as a great discovery gets to being kid-repeatable in spirit: a wrapped plate, a mineral, and the patience to look at what came out. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Absolute dating' and 'Lord Kelvin'; Wikipedia, 'Age of the Earth'.

question: An engineer who had once served as Kelvin's assistant, John Perry, took on Kelvin's short-Earth calculation in the journal Nature in 1895. The arithmetic was flawless and rested on physics no geologist could match, but Perry showed that changing a single assumption about the deep Earth lets the very same cooling equations allow two to three billion years. What did Perry assume that Kelvin had not?
answer: That the interior stirs and circulates as it cools.
choices: That the interior stirs and circulates as it cools.
That the interior began far hotter than Kelvin allowed.
That the interior is layered, each shell holding heat in.
That the core keeps making heat as it slowly crystallizes.
context: Perry's assumption has a name: convection -- deep rock creeping and turning over like a pot on a stove, carrying its heat bodily upward instead of passing it from atom to atom through rock that never moves. Perry tried the polite route first: three weeks before going public he sent Kelvin his own solution for a cooling sphere whose conductivity changes with depth, and Kelvin brushed him off. Only then did Perry publish in Nature -- and he still opened by deferring to 'Lord Kelvin's letter'. He revered the man he was refuting. Note the date: 1895, before radioactivity was known to exist. The popular line that radioactivity proved Kelvin wrong is only half true, and the smaller half; Grokipedia's assessment is that Kelvin's 'primary shortfall stemmed not from ignorance of radioactivity... but from Kelvin's assumption of a rigid, homogeneous Earth conducting heat solely by diffusion, neglecting mantle convection.' Sources: John Perry, 'On the Age of the Earth', Nature 51 (1895); England, Molnar & Richter, GSA Today 17(1), 2007; Grokipedia, 'Lord Kelvin'.

question: Ernest Rutherford, lecturing at the Royal Institution in 1904, spotted Lord Kelvin in the audience and, by science's best-loved rescue story, quickly saved himself. Kelvin, he declared, had capped the Earth's age only 'provided no new source was discovered', radium being that new source. Kelvin did write such a caveat in 1862: his limit held 'unless sources now unknown to us are prepared in the great storehouse of creation.' Which of Kelvin's calculations does that caveat actually close?
answer: His estimate of how long the Sun could keep shining.
choices: His estimate of how long the Sun could keep shining.
His estimate of how long the Earth had been cooling.
His estimate of how long the Moon could hold its heat.
His estimate of how long the sea had been salting up.
context: The caveat closes 'On the Age of the Sun's Heat' (Macmillan's Magazine, March 1862), where Kelvin warned that the inhabitants of the Earth cannot expect light and heat for many million years longer 'unless sources now unknown to us are prepared in the great storehouse of creation.' Rutherford had borrowed a prophecy from the wrong calculation. The scene itself is no sturdier. It survives only in A. S. Eve's 1939 biography of Rutherford, page 107 -- printed thirty-five years after the lecture and two years after Rutherford's death -- where Eve records that Rutherford 'used to tell humorous stories about this lecture long afterwards', and the passage carries no quotation marks at all: it is Eve's recollection of Rutherford's much-repeated retelling. Kelvin, for his part, published no retraction of his age-of-the-Earth work before his death in 1907, conceding only privately to J. J. Thomson that radioactivity made some of his assumptions unworkable -- which makes the beaming-old-boy ending the least reliable part of the tale. Enjoy the story; do not cite it as evidence. Sources: Lord Kelvin, 'On the Age of the Sun's Heat' (1862); A. S. Eve, 'Rutherford' (1939), p.107; Paul Braterman, 'Kelvin, Rutherford, and the Age of the Earth: I, The Myth'.  (Legend.)

question: Bertram Boltwood published ages in February 1907 for minerals gathered around the world, running from 410 million years up to 2.2 billion for one crystal out of Ceylon, the first figures with the right count of zeros. The physicists' Earth was still a young one, and geologists had no number of their own to answer it. What had Boltwood measured inside the minerals?
answer: How much lead had piled up against the uranium still left.
choices: How much lead had piled up against the uranium still left.
How much helium had leaked out through the crystal's cracks.
How much heat the mineral still gave off as it lay there.
How far the crystal's colour had faded from the outside in.
context: Boltwood's figures ran about 20 percent high, but the order of magnitude ended the short timescale for good -- the Ceylon thorianite alone gave fifty times Kelvin's entire allowance. Arthur Holmes then spent a career pushing the number up: a Norwegian rock at about 370 million years in 1911, at least 1.6 billion in his 1913 book The Age of the Earth, and an upper limit of 3.0 billion by the 1927 edition. He argued for a billions-of-years Earth for four decades before anyone could prove it. Sources: American Physical Society, 'February 1907: Bertram Boltwood Estimates Earth is at Least 2.2 Billion Years Old'; Grokipedia, 'Arthur Holmes'; Linda Hall Library, 'Scientist of the Day - Arthur Holmes'.

question: John Perry showed Lord Kelvin in 1895 that the planet could be far older than Kelvin's physics permitted. Perry was right, and the paper was forgotten. England, Molnar and Richter argued in a 2007 re-assessment in the journal GSA (Geological Society of America) Today that the age question was not even the biggest thing lost. What else, by their account, did the neglect of Perry's paper cost?
answer: Decades of the continental-drift debate, argued with no mechanism.
choices: Decades of the continental-drift debate, argued with no mechanism.
A century of underrating how much heat the crust makes by itself.
An early route to dating the ocean floor, long before the drills.
A warning that the mine-shaft heat gradient varies from place to place.
context: England, Molnar and Richter put it plainly: a powerful argument in favour of a mobile Earth interior 'was overlooked during the first few decades of debate about continental drift.' Perry had handed geology a moving mantle in 1895 and nobody picked it up. The shape of the whole story sits in one line: Ussher counted generations in a text, Buffon counted minutes on a cooling iron ball, Kelvin counted degrees per fifty feet of mine shaft, John Joly counted grains of salt delivered to the sea, and Boltwood and Patterson counted atoms. Every estimate was honest for the evidence its author had, and every one fell to a better instrument rather than to a better argument. Source: England, Molnar & Richter, 'John Perry's neglected critique of Kelvin's age for the Earth: A missed opportunity in geodynamics', GSA Today 17(1), 2007.

question: Amy Cuddy stepped onto a TED (Technology, Entertainment, Design) stage in 2012 and told the crowd to hold one two-minute pose before their next job interview. Tens of millions of viewers watched the talk. What pose did she ask people to hold?
answer: Feet apart, hands on hips, chest open
choices: Feet apart, hands on hips, chest open
Arms crossed, chin tucked, eyes down
Both hands raised over head, palms flat
One knee on the floor, head bowed low
context: Cuddy called it the 'Wonder Woman' pose. By 2017 the talk was near 47 million views; today it is over 75 million. Source: TED (ted.com); Cuddy TEDGlobal 2012.

question: Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap ran an experiment in 2010 they called 'power posing', asking volunteers to stand for two minutes in wide, open, high-status poses, and claimed it changed the body's chemistry. Cuddy's popular TED (Technology, Entertainment, Design) talk was built on that one study. How many people were tested in it?
answer: 42 undergraduates
choices: 42 undergraduates
420 undergraduates
4,200 undergraduates
42,000 undergraduates
context: One study, 42 people, one lab, one afternoon -- and a TED sensation. Small samples let random noise look like a real effect. Source: Carney, Cuddy, Yap, Psychological Science 2010.

question: Dana Carney, first author of the 2010 power-pose paper, posted a note on her Berkeley faculty page in September 2016 and walked away from her own famous finding. The paper had claimed that two minutes in a wide, open pose changed the chemistry of the body, and it named a pair of hormones going in opposite directions. What was the pair?
answer: Testosterone went up and cortisol went down
choices: Testosterone went up and cortisol went down
Adrenaline went up and dopamine went down
Insulin went up and glucagon went down
Melatonin went up and serotonin went down
context: And risk-taking gambles went up. The claim was hormonal, not just psychological -- which made the later failure to replicate the hormones a serious matter. Source: Carney et al. 2010. Her statement said 'I do not believe that "power pose" effects are real', and listed the analytic choices in her own data that had produced them. Amy Cuddy still defends a milder version of the claim. Source: Carney, faculty page 2016; KPBS 2016.

question: Eva Ranehill and colleagues at the University of Zurich ran the power-pose experiment again in 2015 with a much larger sample, publishing in the journal Psychological Science. Amy Cuddy's 2010 claim covered how the body's hormones moved, how much risk a person took and how powerful a person felt. The results split that claim clean in half. Which part survived the retest?
answer: The self-reported feeling of power
choices: The self-reported feeling of power
The rise in salivary testosterone levels
The fall in salivary cortisol levels
The rise in monetary risk-taking behaviour
context: The hormones and the risk-taking did not survive. This is why it matters to say 'power posing does not do X', not 'power posing does nothing'. Source: Ranehill et al., Psychological Science 2015.

question: Roy Baumeister sat hungry students alone in a warm room at Case Western Reserve University in 1998, with fresh-baked cookies on a nearby tray. He told half of them they could eat only radishes from a bowl beside the cookies. Then he gave everyone a puzzle with no solution. What happened to the radish-eaters?
answer: They gave up on the puzzle sooner
choices: They gave up on the puzzle sooner
They kept working on the puzzle longer
They refused to try the puzzle at all
They solved a modified version faster
context: Baumeister concluded willpower was like a fuel tank that could run dry -- he called it 'ego depletion'. The idea would govern self-help and academic psychology for fifteen years. Source: Baumeister et al., JPSP 1998.

question: A psychology student reads a 2010 meta-analysis that pools 198 separate tests of ego depletion, the idea that willpower runs out like fuel in a tank. It calls the effect extremely unlikely to be absent. What later changed the picture?
answer: A 23-lab preregistered replication found essentially no effect
choices: A 23-lab preregistered replication found essentially no effect
A single new study in one lab found a much bigger effect
The original author confessed to having faked the 1998 data
A statistical error was found in the 1998 paper's coding
context: The 2016 Registered Replication Report coordinated by Hagger and colleagues ran one preregistered protocol on 2,141 participants across 23 labs; combined effect d = 0.04 (95% CI -0.07 to 0.15). Source: Hagger et al., Perspectives on Psychological Science 2016.

question: Carter and McCullough went back over the 2010 meta-analysis of ego depletion in 2014 and printed an early alarm. Once they corrected for one well-known distortion in the pool of studies, the effect shrank until nobody could tell it apart from zero. What was the distortion?
answer: Failed studies left unpublished in file drawers
choices: Failed studies left unpublished in file drawers
Students not split into groups at random
Lucky early results drifting back to average
Stopwatches running slow in some of the labs
context: The distortion is called publication bias: studies that do not work get filed in a drawer instead of printed. Once those missing studies are accounted for, the big pooled effect (d ~ 0.6) collapses to around d = 0.2 or lower. The signal was in the publishing, not the biology. Source: Carter & McCullough, Frontiers in Psychology 2014.

question: John Bargh, Mark Chen and Lara Burrows had New York University (NYU) students unscramble sentences in 1996, seeded with words like Florida, bingo and wrinkle. Hidden stopwatches then timed the students walking down the hall. What did the paper say those primed students did?
answer: Walked more slowly to the elevator
choices: Walked more slowly to the elevator
Walked more quickly to the elevator
Refused to walk out of the lab entirely
Turned back before reaching the elevator
context: It became one of the most-cited results in social psychology, and starred in Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow. Source: Bargh, Chen & Burrows, JPSP 1996.

question: Stephane Doyen and colleagues ran new students down the corridor in 2012, repeating John Bargh's elderly-priming walk. Bargh had reported in 1996 that unscrambling sentences full of words like 'gray', 'wrinkle' and 'Florida' changed how college students walked to the elevator afterwards. What did Doyen's team find?
answer: No difference in walking speed between the groups
choices: No difference in walking speed between the groups
A much bigger walking-speed difference than Bargh had
The primed group walked faster, not slower, to the door
Only the female participants slowed down after priming
context: They swapped the human stopwatch for infrared beams that timed the 120 walkers with no observer bias. The Bargh effect vanished. Source: Doyen et al., PLOS ONE 2012.

question: Stéphane Doyen ran John Bargh's elderly-priming walk a second time with ten experimenters, each holding a stopwatch while infrared beams timed the same corridor. Half had been told the primed students would walk slowly, half that they would speed up. What did the timings show?
answer: A slow walk only for experimenters who expected one
choices: A slow walk only for experimenters who expected one
A slow walk for every experimenter alike
A slow walk on the stopwatches but never on the beams
No slow walk for any of the ten experimenters
context: On the infrared beams the primed students walked slower (6.95 against 6.52 seconds) only with experimenters who expected slowness; with experimenters who expected speed there was no difference. On those experimenters' stopwatches primed students were even clocked as faster, which the team put down to errors in working the stopwatch. Doyen concluded that both priming and the experimenters' expectations were instrumental, as if the testers' beliefs reached the students. This is why every good behavioural test today is blinded -- neither subject nor tester knows the condition. Source: Doyen et al., PLOS ONE 2012.

question: Daniel Kahneman emailed the leading priming researchers in late September 2012, warning of 'a train wreck looming.' His own bestseller had praised their work. He urged them to act before outside skeptics did. What did he propose they set up?
answer: A chain of labs, each repeating a neighbour's result
choices: A chain of labs, each repeating a neighbour's result
A one-year halt on publishing new priming papers
A panel of senior editors to audit priming data
One giant priming study run by a single lab
context: Kahneman had praised priming studies in his own bestseller Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011). His own term was a 'daisy chain' of replications: each lab would try to repeat a priming effect from the next lab along, with someone from the original lab supervising. The letter went to leading priming researchers directly and became one of the founding documents of psychology's replication reform. Sources: Kahneman open letter, 26 September 2012; Nature news, 3 October 2012.

question: Investigators combed through the original labs' data, code and records, looking for cheating, after the power-pose, ego-depletion and elderly-priming results all failed on retest. What did those investigations find about Cuddy, Baumeister and Bargh?
answer: No fraud was found in any of the three
choices: No fraud was found in any of the three
Deliberate data fabrication in every one
Paid subjects producing the desired result
Students blocked from publishing replications
context: Cuddy, Baumeister and Bargh are real scientists who were not shown to have faked anything. Small samples, flexible analysis, and an audience that wanted the story were enough. Robust effects survive (the Stroop effect, the spacing effect, semantic priming). Fragile ones dissolve on retest. Source: BPS Psychologist, decade retrospective.

question: Paul Ehrlich, a biologist, mailed a cheque to Julian Simon, an economist, in October 1990. Ehrlich had spent 22 years warning that mass hunger was coming. What did the cheque settle?
answer: a public wager
choices: a public wager
a libel suit
an unpaid book royalty
a research grant repayment
context: The two men had agreed a ten-year bet in September 1980 about the price of natural resources. Ehrlich lost, paid on time and in full. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: Paul Ehrlich and Julian Simon turned their quarrel into a public bet on metal prices, adjusted for inflation. Ehrlich expected shortages to push them up; Simon expected ingenuity to keep them from rising. The materials and the span went to one man's free choice, so no one could call the terms rigged. Who insisted on that?
answer: Simon, offering Ehrlich free choice
choices: Simon, offering Ehrlich free choice
Ehrlich, offering Simon free choice
both men, in a joint agreement
a neutral referee they had chosen
context: Simon's move was what turned a public quarrel into a real test rather than a stunt: the loser could not later say the terms were rigged. Ehrlich then picked five metals and a decade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: Julian Simon offered Paul Ehrlich a public bet after Ehrlich warned that a growing human population would drain Earth's resources and drive up the prices of vital metals. On 29 September 1980 they signed a contract putting $200 on each of five industrial metals, $1,000 in all, at inflation-adjusted prices, with the payoff settled ten years later. Which five metals did Ehrlich and his colleagues pick?
answer: copper, chromium, nickel, tin, tungsten
choices: copper, chromium, nickel, tin, tungsten
iron, aluminium, zinc, silver, cobalt
gold, platinum, palladium, silver, rhodium
lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, graphite
context: These were core industrial metals in 1980. Ehrlich and his colleagues, including the physicist John Harte and the biologist John Holdren, made the selection. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: Paul Ehrlich, worried the world was running out of raw materials, staked $200 each on five industrial metals against Julian Simon, a $1,000 bet that their inflation-adjusted prices would rise as humans grew short of them. The ten-year clock ran out in September 1990. When the five metals were checked, where did they end up compared with 1980?
answer: all five cost less
choices: all five cost less
three of five rose, two fell
four of five rose sharply
all five had roughly held their value
context: A clean sweep. Chromium, copper, nickel, tin and tungsten each cost less in real, inflation-adjusted terms in 1990 than they had at the signing. The honest caveat is timing: a 2010 study by Kiel and colleagues reran the bet over every ten-year span from 1900 to 2008 and found Simon would have won only about 38 percent of them, and it ranked 1980 to 1990 among the fifteen worst spans in the whole record for Ehrlich's side. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: Julian Simon spelled out in The Ultimate Resource (1981) why he thought Paul Ehrlich would lose. Ehrlich, author of The Population Bomb, had bet him in 1980 that five metals would grow scarcer and dearer over ten years, after inflation. In Simon's account, what is a rising price of a metal?
answer: a signal that pays people to find substitutes and use less
choices: a signal that pays people to find substitutes and use less
a countdown to the exhaustion of the reserve
proof that population has outrun capacity
an accident of foreign-exchange movements
context: Simon's core mechanism. That is why he called the human mind 'the ultimate resource' -- more people, more problem-solvers, and each price rise pays someone to answer it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ultimate_Resource.

question: Julian Simon received Paul Ehrlich's cheque for $576.07 in October 1990, paid in full on their ten-year bet. Ehrlich did not concede the argument. He told the New York Times that December that 'the bet doesn't mean anything'. What did he tell the BBC (British Broadcasting Corporation)?
answer: it had been an excellent bet that his side happened to lose
choices: it had been an excellent bet that his side happened to lose
the metals had been secretly manipulated by traders
Simon had used inflation numbers rigged in his favour
he had never agreed to the bet in the first place
context: Documented at the time. Ehrlich paid promptly and in full, but held that the failed forecast proved nothing. The wager settled the price question and left the deeper argument untouched -- for him. Source: spiked-online.com/2015/09/29/the-simon-ehrlich-wager-25-years-on/.

question: A girl hammers a copper coin flat. The same blow shatters a lump of rock salt into flat-faced pieces. Both are neat stacks of tiny particles. Why does copper bend where salt breaks?
answer: The bond in a metal points in no particular direction; the bond in salt does
choices: The bond in a metal points in no particular direction; the bond in salt does
The copper is much warmer than the salt when the hammer falls
The salt is much more crystalline than the copper is
The copper is much denser than the salt and absorbs the blow
context: In a metal the outer electrons form a shared, non-directional glue, so layers of ion cores can slide and re-bond. In an ionic crystal the bonds link specific positive and negative neighbours, so once layers slip the wrong charges meet. Source: https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Chemical_Bonding/Fundamentals_of_Chemical_Bonding/Metallic_Bonding

question: Paul Drude drew the first simple picture of a metal's insides in 1900, to explain why copper carries a current, bends and shines. The picture is crude, and quantum theory has since replaced it underneath. What did he say the outer electrons of a metal's atoms do?
answer: Form a shared sea roaming the whole block, with the positive ion cores sitting in it
choices: Form a shared sea roaming the whole block, with the positive ion cores sitting in it
Orbit the nearest three neighbours in a fixed triangular pattern
Hop between just two atoms at a time as ordinary covalent bonds
Sit locked in place until heat knocks them briefly loose to carry current
context: This is the electron-sea model of metallic bonding. Drude's 1900 picture is classical -- quantum band theory has replaced it underneath -- but the sea image still explains conduction, malleability, thermal flow, and shine together. Source: https://www.ck12.org/flexi/physical-science/metallic-bond/describe-the-electron-sea-model-of-metallic-bonding./

question: A teacher slides one layer of a model metal over the next, and it simply bonds again, so the block changes shape without breaking. She slides one layer of a model rock-salt crystal by one atomic spacing, and something disastrous happens along the new plane. What?
answer: Like charges suddenly face like charges, and the layers repel and split
choices: Like charges suddenly face like charges, and the layers repel and split
The salt melts at the sliding surface from friction alone
The heavier atoms cluster on one side and the crystal tips over
The salt turns clear where the layer slid, opaque where it did not
context: Ionic crystals cleave along flat planes exactly because slipping brings like charges into contact. It is the SAME hammer blow and the SAME kind of orderly stack -- one mechanism, opposite outcomes. Source: https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Chemical_Bonding/Fundamentals_of_Chemical_Bonding/Metallic_Bonding

question: A boy at supper leaves a metal spoon in a bowl of hot soup for one minute, and the handle scalds his fingers. A wooden spoon in the same bowl barely warms. Both handles are the same shape and stick out into the same cool air. What inside the metal makes heat move down the handle so much faster than through the wood?
answer: The same free electrons that carry current also carry heat, quickly, all through the metal
choices: The same free electrons that carry current also carry heat, quickly, all through the metal
The metal is denser, so heat has more matter to conduct through per second
The metal's atoms are lighter and vibrate faster from the hot end onwards
The metal absorbs the soup's steam and warms from the outside in
context: The Wiedemann-Franz law, from 1853, gave the empirical clue: metals' thermal and electrical conductivities are locked together in a fixed ratio at a given temperature. Drude's 1900 free-electron picture explained why -- one carrier does both jobs. Test it at supper. Source: https://www.tutorchase.com/answers/igcse/chemistry/what-causes-metals-to-be-lustrous

question: A woman polishes a silver spoon in her kitchen until it acts almost like a perfect mirror, and she sees her face sharply in it. A piece of dry chalk cut and polished into the same spoon shape stays dull no matter how carefully she buffs it. Silver is a metal; chalk is not. What single fact about a metal is responsible for its mirror-like shine?
answer: Its free electrons respond to the light's electric field and re-radiate almost all of it back out
choices: Its free electrons respond to the light's electric field and re-radiate almost all of it back out
Its surface atoms are packed so tightly that no visible light can pass any gap
It emits a faint visible glow of its own at ordinary room temperature
Its polish makes the surface atomically smooth, so every ray reflects at one angle
context: Because a typical metal's plasma frequency lies in the ultraviolet, visible light drives the electron sea faster than it can lag, so almost all visible light is reflected. The 'atomically smooth polish' answer is the popular wrong one: many well-polished non-metals are dull because they lack the free-electron response, not because they are rough. Source: https://www.webexhibits.org/causesofcolor/9.html

question: An ancient smith mixes a few percent of tin into copper, long before anyone knows about atoms, and the bronze comes out far harder than the pure metal. A little carbon in iron does the same and makes steel. What do those added tin or carbon atoms actually do inside the crystal to make the alloy so much harder?
answer: The differently sized atoms jam the slip planes so the layers can no longer glide easily
choices: The differently sized atoms jam the slip planes so the layers can no longer glide easily
They fill the empty gaps between atoms and make the metal denser
They react chemically to grow tiny hard grains that pin the surface
They neutralise the shared electron sea in patches, stiffening the block
context: Solid-solution strengthening: solute atoms of the wrong size warp the lattice around them and block dislocation motion, the microscopic slip that lets pure metals bend. Bronze was humanity's first engineered material of this kind. Source: https://www.nuclear-power.com/nuclear-engineering/metals-what-are-metals/metalworking/solid-solution-strengthening-alloying/

question: A skilled beater hammers gold into leaf less than 100 nanometres thick, so thin that some visible light passes straight through the sheet. The light bouncing off it still looks gold. What colour is the light after it has passed through the leaf?
answer: Bluish-green
choices: Bluish-green
Deep red
Bright orange
Pure white
context: Reflected and transmitted light see the electron sea differently. Gold reflects the yellow-red end strongly; the wavelengths it does NOT reflect leak through, giving transmitted light a striking bluish-green tint. It shows in gilded stained-glass work and museum leaf demonstrations. Source: https://www.webexhibits.org/causesofcolor/9.html

question: Robert Liston took a leg off above the knee in twenty-five to thirty seconds, in Edinburgh and London, while strong assistants held the wide-awake patient down. Before 1846, speed was the surgeon's chief virtue. Why did it matter so much?
answer: Patients often died of the shock of the pain itself
choices: Patients often died of the shock of the pain itself
Assistants could hold a struggling man only briefly
A wound held open longer was likelier to fester
Bleeding could not be stopped once a vessel opened
context: Surgical shock was the killer. Many patients died not of the wound but of the pain and blood loss, sometimes within hours, so every second the knife spent in the body counted against them. Restraint was the other half of the arrangement: several strong assistants, or straps and iron frames. Liston's speed was not showmanship. Source: Grokipedia, 'Ether Dome' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Ether_Dome (section: 'Early Methods of Pain Relief').

question: The trustees of Massachusetts General Hospital took a gift in 1823 and stood it in their domed Boston operating room, opened two years before, as a fitting ornament. It is still there, after eight thousand operations. What is it?
answer: The mummified body of an Egyptian stonemason
choices: The mummified body of an Egyptian stonemason
A marble bust of the physician Hippocrates
An anatomical skeleton in a glass case
An oil portrait of the hospital's founders
context: His name is Padihershef, a stonemason from Thebes who died around 600 BCE. He was uncrated in 1824 and has stood in the room ever since, including on the morning of 16 October 1846; the hospital calls him its oldest patient. The theatre itself was designed by Charles Bulfinch and built of Chelmsford granite cut by state penitentiary inmates. It served as the hospital's main operating room until 1867, became a National Historic Landmark in 1965, and is still used for teaching. Source: Grokipedia, 'Ether Dome' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Ether_Dome (sections: 'Curated Displays in the Dome', 'The Bulfinch Building Amphitheater').

question: Edward Gilbert Abbott, twenty-one, lay on a Boston operating table on 16 October 1846 while John Collins Warren cut into his neck. He had breathed a vapour from a glass globe, and at the first cut he did not cry out. The hospital record sets down what he said he felt. What was it?
answer: Like the spot being scraped with a blunt tool
choices: Like the spot being scraped with a blunt tool
Nothing at all, from first cut to last stitch
A dull warmth spreading down from his jaw
A far-off ache belonging to somebody else
context: The hospital's own wording is 'a sensation like that of scraping the part with a blunt instrument.' The versions usually retold -- 'as if my neck had been scratched with a hoe' -- are later paraphrases of that line, not Abbott's words. Abbott had been admitted on 25 September 1846; he was born 2 September 1825 and died in 1855 of tuberculosis, unrelated to the surgery. Source: 'Ether Day Revisited: The Surgical Records of Edward Gilbert Abbott', Annals of Surgery Open (2022) -- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10431558/

question: William Morton held a plain device to his patient's face in the Boston theatre: a glass globe the size of a quart jar with an ether-soaked sponge inside, a narrow tube, a mouthpiece. It worked. Morton was back at his bench that night and had a modified version by the next morning. What had the first design got wrong?
answer: The patient breathed his own exhaled air back in
choices: The patient breathed his own exhaled air back in
The ether leaked out around the mouthpiece
The glass fogged over and hid the ether level
The sponge dried out before the cutting ended
context: Morton fitted one-way inhale and exhale valves on 17 October 1846, the day after the demonstration. The glass was the other clever part of the design: the operator could watch the ether level drop and judge the dose by eye. Source: Grokipedia, 'Ether Dome' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Ether_Dome (section: "Morton's Ether Inhaler").

question: Eben Frost walked into William Morton's Boston office on the night of 30 September 1846 with a toothache and let the dentist try something new. He breathed ether. The tooth came out. He felt nothing. Sixteen days later Morton stood in the operating theatre at Massachusetts General Hospital while the city's senior surgeons watched. What had brought that invitation?
answer: A paragraph in the next morning's Boston Daily Journal
choices: A paragraph in the next morning's Boston Daily Journal
A paper read to the Boston Society for Medical Improvement
A private demonstration for the hospital's trustees
A circular posted to every physician in the city
context: A reporter named Albert G. Tenney happened to be in the room that night. The Boston Daily Journal told its readers the next morning that the tooth had come out 'without giving him the slightest pain.' It was that newspaper paragraph, not a medical paper, that opened the hospital's doors to a dentist sixteen days later. Source: Countway Library, 'The Operation on Eben Frost' -- https://collections.countway.harvard.edu/onview/exhibits/show/introduction/morton-and-jackson/eben-frost-operation

question: Humphry Davy, a twenty-one-year-old English chemist, wrote about nitrous oxide in 1800. It had eased his own toothache. His book said the gas 'appears capable of destroying physical pain' and might 'be used with advantage during surgical operations.' What did nitrous oxide and ether become in the years that followed?
answer: Party entertainments for gentry and students
choices: Party entertainments for gentry and students
Industrial solvents for cleaning machinery
Preservatives for anatomical specimens
Veterinary drugs for quieting horses
context: Nitrous oxide fuelled 'laughing gas parties' among the British upper classes; ether fuelled 'ether frolics' among American medical students. Crawford Long got the whole idea from joining in -- he inhaled ether and nitrous recreationally with fellow students at the University of Pennsylvania in 1838-39, and noticed bruises he could not remember getting. For forty-four years the cure for surgical agony was a party trick. Sources: Humphry Davy, Researches, Chemical and Philosophical (1800), quoted in 'Nitrous oxide: are you having a laugh?', RSC Education -- https://edu.rsc.org/feature/nitrous-oxide-are-you-having-a-laugh/2020202.article ; Grokipedia, 'Crawford Long' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Crawford_Long

question: Horace Wells, a Connecticut dentist who had once shared a Boston practice with William Morton, went to a travelling showman's exhibition of laughing gas in December 1844. He was so struck that he had his own tooth pulled under nitrous oxide the next evening. Weeks later he arranged a public demonstration in Boston, and it went badly. What happened in front of that audience?
answer: The dose ran short, the patient cried out, and the room jeered
choices: The dose ran short, the patient cried out, and the room jeered
The gas bag split, the patient slept an hour, and the room panicked
The patient lost his nerve, refused the gas, and walked out
The tooth broke in the socket, blood ran, and the room emptied
context: The showman was Gardner Quincy Colton; Wells's own extraction was on 11 December 1844. The public attempt came in late January 1845, and Wells left disheartened. The right idea can fail its first public test. Where it happened is contested: popular accounts place it at Massachusetts General Hospital on 20 January 1845, but R. P. Haridas found no primary evidence it was ever held in that amphitheatre and argues for a public hall on Washington Street at the end of the month. Sources: Grokipedia, 'William T. G. Morton' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/William_T._G._Morton ; R. P. Haridas, 'Horace Wells' Demonstration of Nitrous Oxide in Boston', Anesthesiology.

question: Crawford Long, a country doctor in Jefferson, Georgia, soaked a towel in sulphuric ether, held it over James Venable's face and cut a tumour out of the young man's neck on 30 March 1842, four and a half years before anyone did such a thing in public. Long then kept it out of print for seven years. What was he afraid of?
answer: That critics would call the painlessness imagination or mesmerism
choices: That critics would call the painlessness imagination or mesmerism
That a rival doctor in Georgia would take the credit for it
That the state medical society would strip him of his licence
That Venable's family would sue him for experimenting
context: He also wanted more cases first, and a country practice did not supply many: between 1842 and 1845 he used ether in only about twelve to fifteen operations, including a toe amputation on 3 July 1842 and his own wife's childbirth on 27 December 1845. He finally published in December 1849, in the Southern Medical and Surgical Journal. Because 30 March is Long's date, the United States observes National Doctors' Day on 30 March, proclaimed nationally by President George H. W. Bush in 1990. Source: Grokipedia, 'Crawford Long' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Crawford_Long

question: William Morton filed for a patent on the vapour eleven days after the Boston demonstration, and to keep the secret he sold it under a name of his own invention, 'Letheon,' after Lethe, the mythological river of forgetfulness. US Patent 4,848 was granted on 12 November 1846 and never named the substance inside. Within a year the patent was worth nothing. What had defeated it?
answer: Anyone who opened a bottle could smell it was ordinary ether
choices: Anyone who opened a bottle could smell it was ordinary ether
A Paris chemist published the formula in a journal within weeks
The Patent Office struck it out as a monopoly on a medicine
Congress bought the method out and put it in the public domain
context: Ether was not new. Valerius Cordus mixed alcohol and sulphuric acid in 1540 and called the result 'sweet oil of vitriol.' The patent was unenforceable by 1847, and Morton spent the rest of his life chasing money for it: he asked Congress for $100,000 in December 1846, bills for up to $200,000 died in committee, and the French Academy of Sciences split its 5,000-franc Montyon Prize of 1850 down the middle between Morton and his rival Charles T. Jackson. He died of a stroke in a New York hotel room on 15 July 1868, aged 48, in poverty. Physicians had objected on ethical grounds too: in 1850 the new American Medical Association protested his 'unwarrantable assumption' of exclusive discovery. Sources: Grokipedia, 'William T. G. Morton' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/William_T._G._Morton ; Grokipedia, 'Ether Dome' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Ether_Dome

question: John Collins Warren turned to a sceptical Boston crowd on 16 October 1846 and said, by every retelling, 'Gentlemen, this is no humbug.' The line survives only as a remark witnesses recalled afterwards; no document from the day records it. Warren's own journal, written that evening, is the primary record. How does that entry begin?
answer: Did an interesting operation at the Hospital this morning
choices: Did an interesting operation at the Hospital this morning
Saw a great triumph over pain at the Hospital this morning
Performed a bold experiment at the Hospital this morning
Removed a tumour from the neck at the Hospital this morning
context: Warren's journal entry for that evening reads: 'Did an interesting operation at the Hospital this morning while the Patient was under the influence of Dr. Morton's preparation to prevent pain.' The surgeon who had just watched the end of surgical agony called it interesting. The 'no humbug' line is a reported remark, not a documented quotation; even Wikipedia flags its origin as questionable. The journal is the primary record of the day, and it names the drug plainly: 'the Substance employed was Sulphuric Ether.' A story can be true in spirit and still have no source -- worth checking before repeating. Sources: Massachusetts Historical Society, 'Ether Day, 16 October 1846: the Conquest of Pain' (Object of the Month, October 2016), reproducing Warren's journal entry -- https://www.masshist.org/object-of-the-month/october-2016 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Gilbert_Abbott

question: Builders in Boston put up a granite monument in 1868 to honor the discovery that ended surgical pain, but four different men each claimed it. One had done it earliest and stayed silent afterward. Another had attempted it publicly and failed. A third had only proposed the idea in advance, while the fourth had actually demonstrated it to the world. How did the builders settle whose name to carve on the stone?
answer: They carved no man's name anywhere on the stone
choices: They carved no man's name anywhere on the stone
They carved all four claimants' names in a row
They carved Morton's name alone, above the rest
They carved Long's name, the first to use ether
context: The priority quarrel was never settled, so the inscription commemorates a discovery and no discoverer: 'To commemorate the discovery that the inhaling of ether causes insensibility to pain; first proved to the world at the Bullfinch Building in the Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, October, A.D. MDCCCXLVI.' The claimant who only suggested it was the Boston chemist Charles T. Jackson, who had taught Morton and told him to use pure sulphuric ether; he staked his priority in a sealed letter to the French Academy of Sciences dated 13 November 1846, but he never once gave ether to a patient or demonstrated it publicly -- an idea without a trial. Oliver Wendell Holmes, who had proposed the word 'anaesthesia' to Morton in a letter of 21 November 1846, is said to have joked that the monument honoured neither Morton nor Jackson but 'either.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'William T. G. Morton' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/William_T._G._Morton ; https://theclio.com/entry/48248

question: Surgeons published a re-reading of the surviving Massachusetts General Hospital records in 2022. The old story has John Collins Warren removing a tumour from Edward Gilbert Abbott's neck under ether. The records show a malformation of the blood vessels under his left jaw: Warren cut in, found 'a congeries of large veins & small arteries,' and passed a tie around the mass. Abbott went home on 7 December 1846. What do the records say about the mass that day?
answer: It was the same size as when he came in
choices: It was the same size as when he came in
It had shrunk to roughly half its old size
It had gone, leaving only a healed scar
It had grown, and a second operation was set
context: The operative index entry reads 'Ligature of Erectile Tumor,' and the discharge note says the mass was 'of same size as on Entrance.' The anaesthesia was incomplete as well: Abbott 'did not shrink nor cry out' at the first incision, but 'during the insulation of the veins he began to move his limbs and utter extraordinary expressions.' The paper's authors argue the inscription in the operating theatre would be more honest if it read 'an influential experiment in producing insensibility to pain during a surgical operation.' What that morning proved was the anaesthetic, not the surgery -- and saying so out loud is what going back to the records is for. Source: 'Ether Day Revisited: The Surgical Records of Edward Gilbert Abbott', Annals of Surgery Open (2022) -- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10431558/

question: An anaesthetist takes a patient under and brings her back, as happens thousands of times a day, at a risk of about one death per hundred thousand operations. A 2024 review in Frontiers in Pharmacology still calls the mechanism 'elusive': nobody can yet say how these drugs switch off a person. One thing is solid: a single property of the drug molecule predicts its anaesthetic strength so closely that the pattern has its own name. Which property?
answer: How readily the molecule dissolves in fat
choices: How readily the molecule dissolves in fat
How readily the molecule dissolves in water
How tightly the molecule grips its receptor
How quickly the molecule breaks down in the liver
context: An anaesthetic's potency tracks how well it dissolves in fat so closely that the pattern has its own name, the Meyer-Overton rule. Much of the middle of the story has since been traced: propofol grips the GABA-A receptor and holds a chloride channel open so neurons will not fire, inhaled agents blunt the excitatory NMDA receptor, scans show the traffic between the thalamus, the brain's relay hub, and the cortex going quiet, and the EEG collapses from fast beta waves into slow delta and then into burst suppression. What is missing is the bridge from those molecules to the disappearance of the person: the review's own words are that 'a comprehensive understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying the induction of unconsciousness by general anesthetics remains elusive.' Nearly two centuries after the Ether Dome, nobody has it, and no one should pretend otherwise. Meanwhile the unexplained thing works: anaesthesia-related death runs at roughly 0.5 to 1 per 100,000 operations in high-income countries, lower than the risk of a car journey, while unintended awareness under anaesthesia still occurs in about 1 to 2 cases per 1,000. Sources: Frontiers in Pharmacology (2024), 'Recent advances in neural mechanism of general anesthesia induced unconsciousness' -- https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2024.1360864/full ; Grokipedia, 'General anaesthesia' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/General_anaesthesia

question: A surgeon of the 1840s leans over a patient lying quiet under ether and, with no screams to hurry him, cuts for longer and goes deeper into the body than ever before. Over the following twenty years, what happened to the share of survivors who died in the days after surgery?
answer: It rose, and went on rising
choices: It rose, and went on rising
It fell by roughly half
It stayed about where it was
It dropped, then climbed back
context: The era's word for it was 'hospitalism': wound infection killing patients who had survived the knife. Surgeons operated on far more people as well as for longer, still wearing the same coat from one patient to the next, on a table that was not cleaned between operations -- because painless surgery arrived roughly twenty years before germ theory reached the operating room. The freedom came first and the cleanliness came second. Joseph Lister's own figures show the scale of the correction: his operative mortality was 45.7 per cent in 1864-66, and fell to 15 per cent in 1867-69 after he began treating instruments and dressings with carbolic acid. Conquering pain was only half the problem, and the wrong half came first. Sources: Encyclopedia.com, 'Joseph Lister, 1st Baron Lister' -- https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/medicine/medicine-biographies/joseph-lister-1st-baron-lister ; Science Museum, "Lister's antisepsis system" -- https://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/medicine/listers-antisepsis-system

question: A psychology journal gladly prints a study that finds a striking effect and turns away one that finds nothing; many such studies are never even written up. Across thousands of studies, the published record ends up looking stronger than the evidence. Robert Rosenthal named this leak in 1979. What did he call it?
answer: The file drawer problem
choices: The file drawer problem
The publication paradox
The peer-review gap
The null-effect blackout
context: Rosenthal named it in Psychological Bulletin (1979). He worried that journals were filling with the 5% of studies that showed effects, while the other 95% sat unread, and he proposed a 'fail-safe N': a rough count of how many unpublished null studies would be needed to erase a meta-analysis's apparent effect. The name stuck. Erick Turner's 2008 comparison of FDA files with the journals caught the same filter at work, selective publication bias: an entire profession can be sincerely misled by a filtered shelf without one fabricated number. Sources: Rosenthal, Psychological Bulletin 86(3), 1979; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publication_bias; Turner et al., NEJM 2008.

question: Erick Turner and his team looked at 74 antidepressant trials, covering 12,564 patients, in 2008. Every trial had been logged with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) before anyone saw the results. Turner compared what was published with what was in that registry. What split did he find?
answer: 51% positive in the registry, 94% positive on the shelf
choices: 51% positive in the registry, 94% positive on the shelf
94% positive in the registry, 51% positive on the shelf
60% positive in the registry, 60% positive on the shelf
80% positive in the registry, 80% positive on the shelf
context: The registry could not hide -- every trial had been logged before the outcome was known. The published shelf could, and did. Source: Turner et al., NEJM 2008.

question: Erick Turner's 2008 study followed the 36 antidepressant trials that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had judged negative or questionable. Some of them vanished from the journals entirely. Others were published in a curious way. What happened to those others?
answer: Written up as though they had come out positive
choices: Written up as though they had come out positive
Retracted before they could reach typesetting
Combined into a single meta-analysis paper
Republished only in non-English translation
context: Of the 36 FDA-negative trials, 22 were never published at all and 11 more were spun as positive. Only 3 were published matching what the FDA had seen. Source: Turner et al., NEJM 2008.

question: Andrew Vickers reviewed medical trials from several countries in 1998 and asked one simple question of each: how often did the tested treatment come out useless? For two of the countries the answer was never: not one published trial reported a treatment as a failure. Which two countries were they?
answer: China and Russia
choices: China and Russia
France and Germany
Britain and Sweden
Brazil and Argentina
context: Japan hit 89%, Taiwan 95%. A 100% success rate is a publishing policy, not a scientific finding. Source: Vickers et al., Control and Clinical Trials 1998.

question: Annie Franco and her team tracked 221 government-funded studies in 2014, following each one from its grant to its final fate. The obvious suspects for hiding studies that found nothing were journal editors and peer reviewers. Franco's team found the real source of the hiding somewhere else entirely. Where did most of the null-result vanishing happen?
answer: The authors themselves never write up their null results
choices: The authors themselves never write up their null results
The peer reviewers reject null results at final review
The editors quietly kill null results before review
The funders demand null results be withheld from press
context: Strong results were 60 percentage points more likely to be written up at all, and 40 points more likely to be published. Correctly expecting rejection, most researchers spare themselves the effort. The censorship is largely self-administered. Source: Franco, Malhotra, Simonovits, Science 345:1502, 2014.

question: Tom Jefferson's Cochrane reviewers spent years pushing the drugmaker Roche for the full clinical trial data on its antiviral, Tamiflu. During the swine-flu scare, governments had spent billions of dollars stockpiling the drug on the strength of short published trial summaries alone. When the full data finally arrived in 2014, what had the drug's real benefit shrunk to?
answer: Roughly a day less of symptoms, with no drop in hospitalisation
choices: Roughly a day less of symptoms, with no drop in hospitalisation
Roughly a week less of symptoms and a large drop in deaths
Roughly two weeks less of symptoms and a full cure most times
No measurable benefit whatsoever in any age group
context: The claim that had justified the stockpiles -- fewer complications, fewer hospital admissions -- did not survive contact with the full trial data. Britain alone had spent around 500 million pounds. Source: Cochrane 2014; CEBM Oxford.

question: The world's major medical journals announced a repair for the file-drawer problem in September 2004, and it has actually worked. From then on a clinical trial had to do one specific thing before it began, or the journals would refuse to publish its results. What was it?
answer: Register publicly in a trial registry in advance
choices: Register publicly in a trial registry in advance
Post its full raw dataset in advance
Publish its statistical analysis plan in advance
Recruit an independent auditor team in advance
context: The ICMJE policy took effect on 1 July 2005. You cannot quietly bin a study you were required to announce. Source: ICMJE editorial, September 2004; DeAngelis et al., NEJM.

question: Robert Rosenthal warned in 1979 that studies which find nothing tend to be shelved, while studies with a striking result get printed. When a news report claims 'study after study shows X,' a careful reader has one question to ask. What is the question that matters?
answer: Not how many showed X, but how many were run
choices: Not how many showed X, but how many were run
Not how many showed X, but which authors ran them
Not how many showed X, but which country funded them
Not how many showed X, but which journals printed them
context: The shelf reports what worked. The drawer holds what didn't. Registries, when honoured, let you count both. Source: Rosenthal 1979; ICMJE 2004.

question: Robert Rosenthal named the file-drawer problem in 1979: studies that find nothing get shelved, while striking ones reach print. Since then statisticians have built several tools for spotting missing studies inside a meta-analysis. Which was Rosenthal's own original idea, rather than a later tool?
answer: Estimating how many hidden nulls would erase an effect
choices: Estimating how many hidden nulls would erase an effect
Testing whether a scatter of studies is asymmetric on a plot
Adding imputed missing studies to rebalance a meta-analysis
Ranking studies by their published p-values on a curve
context: Rosenthal's original 'fail-safe number' asked how many drawer-hidden nulls it would take to nullify a published finding. Funnel plots, trim-and-fill, and p-curve came later. Source: Rosenthal 1979.

question: Dmitri Ivanovsky, a young botanist in St Petersburg, pressed sap from mottled tobacco leaves through a porcelain filter in 1892, its pores far too small for any known germ. He brushed the clear juice onto healthy leaves. What did the juice do?
answer: Gave the plants the same mosaic disease as the originals
choices: Nothing - the filter had cleaned the sap completely
Killed the leaves faster than the raw sap ever had
Gave the plants the same mosaic disease as the originals
Cured leaves that already had the mosaic disease
context: Ivanovsky reported to the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences on 12 February 1892 that tobacco sap remained infectious even after passing through a Chamberland porcelain candle - the first hint that a disease agent could be smaller than any known bacterium. Source: https://www.lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/dmitri-ivanovsky/

question: Faced with clear juice that had passed his 1892 filter and still made tobacco sick, Dmitri Ivanovsky offered two rather plain guesses for what had slipped through. Which pair did he actually pick?
answer: A chemical toxin, or a bacterium small enough to slip the pores
choices: A brand-new category of agent, or a very small fungal spore
A chemical toxin, or a bacterium small enough to slip the pores
A plant enzyme leaking through, or an inorganic mineral trace
A bacterial spore, or a magnetic disturbance in the plant's vessels
context: Ivanovsky ran the experiment but did not make the conceptual leap. He assumed either that a bacterial toxin had come through with the sap or that the pores had leaked a very small bacterium. The idea of a genuinely new category was not his. Source: https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/medicine/medicine-biographies/dmitri-iosifovich-ivanovsky

question: Martinus Beijerinck redid Dmitri Ivanovsky's filter trick in 1898. Then he did one more thing: he passed the filtered juice through healthy plant after healthy plant in a row. What did that result push him to conclude that Ivanovsky had missed?
answer: That the agent was replicating inside the plant, not a fixed dose of poison
choices: That the agent could infect a plant at all, rather than only irritate its leaves
That the agent was replicating inside the plant, not a fixed dose of poison
That the agent could survive being dried and stored on a shelf for later use
That the agent was carried on the outside of the researcher's tools between plants
context: A fixed dose of toxin would dilute out across successive passages; Beijerinck's agent did not. He concluded it must be replicating inside the living plant, and coined contagium vivum fluidum - a contagious living fluid - to name a new category of agent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contagium_vivum_fluidum

question: Wendell Stanley pulled tobacco mosaic virus out of tons of sick plants, and in 1935 he held up a bottle of dry, needle-like crystals that could sit on a shelf like table salt. What happened when he dissolved the crystals and brushed the liquid on healthy leaves?
answer: The solution infected them just as vigorously as the raw sap had
choices: The solution was inert - crystallising had killed the infectivity
The solution was toxic but no longer produced the mosaic pattern
The solution infected them just as vigorously as the raw sap had
The solution worked only if a small amount of raw sap was added
context: Stanley published the crystallisation of TMV in Science in 1935 and won the 1946 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. An object that behaves like a chemical compound in a jar and like a living pathogen in a leaf broke the tidy line between chemistry and life. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1946/stanley/facts/

question: Timothy Rowbotham, a British public-health officer, pulled water from a cooling tower in Bradford in 1992, hunting the source of a pneumonia outbreak. Inside amoebae from that water he found something that took up the Gram stain like a bacterium, and he filed it away in his freezer as an unidentified bug he called Bradfordcoccus. A Marseille lab finally put it under an electron microscope in 2003. What did it turn out to be?
answer: A virus - but one so big it had been mistaken for a bacterium
choices: A new strain of Legionella bacterium, the classic cooling-tower bug
A tiny parasitic protozoan living inside the amoeba's cytoplasm
A virus - but one so big it had been mistaken for a bacterium
A prion, a misfolded protein with no genome and no reproduction
context: The Bradford microbe was named mimivirus (microbe-mimicking virus) - about 750 nm across, with a genome of roughly 1.18 million base pairs and about a thousand genes, including protein-building genes viruses were not supposed to have. It had been misfiled for eleven years because it was too big to be a virus. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1081867

question: A biologist dips a jar into the surface of the ocean, where viruses are no rarity. One class of them, the marine bacteriophages, is doing something huge to the bacteria in that water every single day. What are the phages doing to those bacteria daily?
answer: Killing 10 to 40 percent of them every day by bursting their host cells open
choices: Injecting them with useful genes fast enough to double bacterial populations every few days
Herding them into thin surface films where ultraviolet kills up to 50 percent daily
Killing 10 to 40 percent of them every day by bursting their host cells open
Fusing about 5 percent of them per day into large multicellular colonies
context: Marine bacteriophages lyse (burst) their host cells to release new virus particles, and estimates of the daily kill rate for ocean bacteria run from roughly 10 percent up to 40 percent depending on water and season. The biggest predator on the planet is one you cannot see. Source: https://asm.org/articles/2023/june/marine-viruses-submerged-players-of-climate-chang

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft shopkeeper with no science training at all, pressed a tiny microscope to his eye. It magnified about 275 times; the best of Robert Hooke's reached only 40 or 50. He never told anyone how he made such a thing. What was its working part?
answer: One glass bead clamped between two metal plates
choices: One glass bead clamped between two metal plates
Three lenses stacked inside a sliding leather tube
A lens and a mirror set facing in a brass box
Two lenses fixed either side of a water chamber
context: He ground over 500 lenses and built at least 25 microscopes; only about nine survive. The bead did all the work - the plates simply held the specimen at its focus, and the whole device was pressed against the eye. Gaynes notes that some may have reached 500 times. Leeuwenhoek kept the lens-making method to himself for life. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Antonie van Leeuwenhoek'; Gaynes, Emerging Infectious Diseases 32(6), CDC, 2026; George Dunea, 'Van Leeuwenhoek's discovery of animalcules', Hektoen International, 2018.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek looked at his teeth in a magnifying mirror and found them dirtier than he had assumed, for all his morning salt and his toothpick after meals. Before taking the scraping he described in his 1683 letter, he did one thing on purpose to set up the test. What did he do?
answer: He left his mouth uncleaned for three days
choices: He left his mouth uncleaned for three days
He scraped the same tooth on three mornings
He took the scraping before he had eaten
He fasted from all food and drink for a day
context: He also built a comparison group, which is what makes the letter an experiment rather than an anecdote: the same letter reports samples from two women who cleaned their mouths daily, a child of about eight, an old man of sober habits, and an old man who had never washed his mouth in his life - in whom he found an unbelievably great company of living animalcules, swimming more nimbly than any he had ever seen. Sources: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, Letter L-135 of 1683-09-17 to Francis Aston; University of California Museum of Paleontology, 'Antony van Leeuwenhoek (1632-1723)'.

question: O'Hara and Shanahan, two doctors, argued in 2006 that gut bacteria amount to an organ of their own, with up to a trillion of them in every gram of intestinal contents. Most people picture what leaves at the toilet as leftover food. What share of that weight did the two say is really bacteria?
answer: About 60 per cent
choices: About 60 per cent
About 10 per cent
About 35 per cent
About 85 per cent
context: O'Hara and Shanahan put bacterial concentration in the large intestine at 10^11-10^12 per gram of colonic content, 'which contributes to 60% of faecal mass'. Most of what you flush is not food you failed to digest; it is the organ's own population, shed and replaced. Source: O'Hara AM & Shanahan F, 'The gut flora as a forgotten organ', EMBO Reports 2006;7(7):688-693.

question: Three scientists at the Weizmann Institute, Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo, chased a famous figure back through the literature in 2016: ten bacterial cells in the body for each human cell. Textbooks, lectures and review papers all carried it, and every trail ended at one source. What was it?
answer: A sentence of rough arithmetic in a 1972 paper
choices: A sentence of rough arithmetic in a 1972 paper
A tally of gut samples in a 1930s survey
A count of bowel contents in a 1950s autopsy series
A rule of thumb in a 1965 bacteriology textbook
context: Thomas Luckey's 'Introduction to intestinal microecology' (American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 1972;25:1292-4) assumed 10^11 bacteria per gram of gut content and about a litre - roughly a kilogram - of alimentary tract, giving 10^14. Sender et al. describe a derivation that 'only consists of a sentence-long' calculation. The first public challenge came 42 years later: Judah Rosner of the US National Institutes of Health published a letter in Microbe in 2014 titled 'Ten Times More Microbial Cells than Body Cells in Humans?' - the question mark is his. Sender and his colleagues are not against estimating; they call such back-of-the-envelope Fermi problems 'effective sanity checks'. The sin was never re-checking the guess. Sources: Sender R, Fuchs S, Milo R, PLoS Biology 14(8):e1002533, 2016; Luckey T, Am J Clin Nutr 1972;25:1292-4.

question: Thomas Luckey imagined about a kilogram of gut with 100 billion bacteria in every gram, and out came 100 trillion. Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo checked the sum in 2016. The multiplying was sound; the trouble was where Luckey thought the bacteria lived. Which part of the gut holds almost none of them?
answer: The stomach and the upper small intestine
choices: The stomach and the upper small intestine
The lower small intestine and the appendix
The ascending colon and the transverse colon
The descending colon and the rectum
context: Bacteria do not fill the alimentary canal. Stomach acid and the fast flow of food hold the stomach and the upper two-thirds of the small intestine to about 10^3-10^4 bacteria per millilitre - essentially nothing. Nearly all of them live in the colon, which 'exceeds all other organs by at least two orders of magnitude', and MRI measurements put the colon's real content at about 0.4 litre, not the assumed litre. A quiet irony sits inside that: the mouth, where the hidden half was first seen, is one of the emptiest places in the body - Sender et al. put the whole mouth at less than 1 per cent of the colon's bacterial number. Leeuwenhoek found a kingdom's worth of creatures in the crumbs of the real thing. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016.

question: Ron Sender and his colleagues set two populations side by side in their 2016 recount: the roughly 38 trillion bacteria in the gut, and the mitochondria, power packs inside human cells that are thought to come from free-living bacteria swallowed whole and kept. How do the two groups compare?
answer: Several times more mitochondria than gut bacteria
choices: Several times more mitochondria than gut bacteria
Several times more gut bacteria than mitochondria
About ten times more gut bacteria than mitochondria
About equal numbers of mitochondria and gut bacteria
context: Most cell types carry hundreds of mitochondria or more - red blood cells, having none, are the exception - so the descendants of ancient captured bacteria inside your own cells probably outnumber the free-living ones in your gut several fold. Sender et al. flag it in a single sentence of their discussion, citing Robin ED & Wong R, J Cell Physiol 1988;136:507-13. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016, Discussion.

question: A lab technician tends a germ-free mouse in a sterile isolator. Reared on sterilised food and air, it has never met a microbe, and it has grown up visibly wrong: in this strain the caecum, the pouch where small and large intestine meet, has swollen to a fifth of the animal's whole body weight. She gives the animal an ordinary gut community. What happens to the swollen caecum?
answer: It shrinks back to normal size within a few weeks
choices: It shrinks back to normal size within a few weeks
It keeps swelling until the animal can no longer walk
It stays swollen for the whole of the animal's life
It shrinks by about half and then stops improving
context: The swelling has a known cause: mucopolysaccharides in gut mucus that bacteria would normally break down stay intact and hold water. In germ-free B6J mice cecal weight can represent up to 20 per cent of total body weight, about 5-10 per cent in NMRI and BALB/c strains; colonisation with intestinal bacteria 'normalizes the cecal size to the size observed in colonized animals within a few weeks'. That reversal is why germ-free animals are the field's causal tool: take the microbes away and something breaks, put them back and it mends - which is a test, not a correlation. Germ-free rodents also have smaller Peyer's patches, fewer intraepithelial lymphocytes and lower serum immunoglobulin, need more calories to hold their weight, and must be given supplementary B and K vitamins, the ones their missing bacteria would have made. Sources: 'The Genetic Background Is Shaping Cecal Enlargement in the Absence of Intestinal Microbiota', Nutrients 2023;15(3):636; O'Hara AM & Shanahan F, EMBO Reports 2006;7(7):688-693; Wikipedia, 'Germ-free animal'.

question: A team reporting in 2011 gave germ-free mice a normal gut community, to see whether strange behaviour could be reset. Raised in sterile boxes, those mice had grown up more active and less anxious than normal mice, with altered gene activity in brain regions for movement and worry. Which mice, if any, ended up acting like normally raised ones?
answer: Those colonised early in life
choices: Those colonised early in life
Those colonised as adults
All of them, whatever their age
None of them, at any age
context: Colonising germ-free mice early in life normalised the pattern; colonising adults did not. There is a developmental window, and once it closes the microbes arrive too late. The mouse evidence is real and specific - increased motor activity, reduced anxiety-like behaviour, and reduced PSD-95 and synaptophysin in the striatum. What it does not license is the leap to human mood, and researchers in the field draw that line themselves: a 2024 review of germ-free models in neuropsychiatric research by Delgado-Ocana and Cuesta urges 'extreme caution when interpreting experimental results as they may be influenced by the bias imposed by the germ-free condition', notes that the artificial rearing of these animals 'raises some questions about the direct generalizability of findings from germ-free studies to real-life contexts', and concludes there is 'no one model that fits all'. There is no germ-free human to compare against, so in people no one yet knows. Sources: Diaz Heijtz R et al., PNAS 2011;108(7):3047-3052; Delgado-Ocana S & Cuesta S, 'From microbes to mind: germ-free models in neuropsychiatric research', 2024.

question: Ron Milo and his colleagues replaced the famous ten-to-one figure in 2016, yet they never claimed the old number was simply a lie. It comes back almost exactly, they pointed out, under one change in what gets counted, and they said plainly that this is a question of definition rather than of measurement. Which change brings ten to one back?
answer: Counting only the human cells that carry a nucleus
choices: Counting only the human cells that carry a nucleus
Counting each mitochondrion as a bacterium of its own
Counting the bacteria of the skin and lungs as well
Counting the viruses of the gut alongside its bacteria
context: From the paper: 'if one chooses to compare the number of bacteria in the human body (3.8x10^13) to the number of nucleated human cells (about 0.3x10^13), the ratio will be about 10:1. This is because the dominant population of non-nucleated red blood cells is not included in the calculation.' The authors then turn the scepticism on themselves: whether cells without a nucleus should be included 'seems to be a question of definition. We view red blood cells as bona fide cells, as their name suggests. But it is also plausible to choose not to include them as some may think of them as bags full of hemoglobin.' A scientist naming which of his own assumptions could be argued with is the method in one paragraph. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016, Discussion.

question: Jonas Salk was already putting his killed-virus polio vaccine into human arms in 1953, one at a time, a year before the giant field trial. He needed brave first volunteers he could watch closely. Who got those very first injections?
answer: He injected himself, his own wife and their three sons
choices: He injected himself, his own wife and their three sons
He injected prisoners who volunteered at a federal prison
He injected Thomas Francis and his students at Michigan
He injected volunteers found for him by the March of Dimes
context: Salk inoculated himself, his wife and their three sons in 1953 as a demonstration of confidence, a full year before he asked any other family to volunteer a child for the field trial. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jonas_Salk.

question: Thomas Francis Jr. stood under bright television lights in Ann Arbor on 12 April 1955, before more than 500 scientists, to give his verdict on Jonas Salk's polio vaccine after the biggest field trial ever run. How did the press release open?
answer: 'The vaccine works. It is safe, effective, and potent.'
choices: 'The vaccine works. It is safe, effective, and potent.'
'The results are encouraging. Further study is needed.'
'The vaccine protects. Its duration remains unknown.'
'The trial is complete. Licensing should now proceed.'
context: The release, headed 'FOR RELEASE AT 10:20 E.S.T.', opened: 'ANN ARBOR: The vaccine works. It is safe, effective, and potent.' Francis read the result in Rackham Auditorium 'at a meeting of over 500 scientists and physicians and before the penetrating eyes of cameras and powerful spotlights'. It was ten years to the day since Franklin Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945 -- and it was Roosevelt's own charity, the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, that had paid for the trial. Sources: University of Michigan press release of 12 April 1955, sph.umich.edu/polio; theconversation.com/lessons-from-how-the-polio-vaccine-went-from-the-lab-to-the-public-that-americans-can-learn-from-today-145604.

question: A doctor in one of the strictest districts of the 1954 polio trial injected a 'Polio Pioneer' without knowing what was in the syringe. Only half the children there got Salk's vaccine, and no child, parent or doctor was told which half. What was in the other syringes?
answer: Culture fluid made to the vaccine's recipe, minus the virus
choices: Culture fluid made to the vaccine's recipe, minus the virus
Sterile salt water drawn from an unmarked glass bottle
A dose of the flu vaccine Francis had helped develop
A live poliovirus weakened by growth in monkey kidney cells
context: It was Mixture 199, a synthetic tissue-culture medium carrying antibiotics, formalin, red colouring and a buffer -- the vaccine's own formula with the poliovirus left out, so the needle, the sting and the look of the syringe were identical.
