A dummy treatment like this is called a placebo, and keeping everyone ignorant of who got which is called blinding. Each child in the course got three injections, and on the third a Polio Pioneers button and a March of Dimes membership card. Sources: vaxopedia.org/2024/08/11/the-1954-poliomyelitis-vaccine-field-trial/; sph.umich.edu/polio; americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object/nmah_1937859.

question: Jonas Salk's old teacher at Michigan, Thomas Francis Jr., agreed to judge the polio vaccine only on his own terms. Besides a matching group of children getting a dummy shot, he made one big demand of the charity paying for the whole trial. What was it?
answer: That it keep its hands off the evaluation entirely
choices: That it keep its hands off the evaluation entirely
That it publish every objection Salk had raised
That it double the number of children enrolled
That it pay for a second trial in Canada and Finland
context: Francis's stated conditions were that 'an equal or larger number of children were injected with an inert solution and followed in the same manner', plus a policy of non-interference by the National Foundation. The Foundation had put $7,500,000 of March of Dimes money into the trial, raised from contributions by over 80 million Americans -- which is precisely why Francis wanted the people who raised it kept away from the evaluation of it. Francis had founded Michigan's Department of Epidemiology in 1941, Salk did his postgraduate training under him there, and the two co-authored influenza-vaccine papers through the 1940s. Sources: polioplace.org/people/thomas-francis-jr-md; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1114166; sph.umich.edu/polio.

question: Jonas Salk fought Thomas Francis Jr. hard over the design of the trial, and not over credit. In the strictest districts half the enrolled children would get a dummy shot in the middle of a polio season. Francis did not budge, and Salk lost the argument. What was Salk's objection?
answer: That the paralysed dummy-shot children would be paralysed at his own hands
choices: That the paralysed dummy-shot children would be paralysed at his own hands
That parents would pull their children out once they heard of the dummy shot
That the donors had given their dimes for vaccine, not for a dummy shot
That one polio season was too short to prove the vaccine held up
context: Salk wrote that the design was enough 'to make the humanitarian shudder [and] Hippocrates turn over in his grave', and that 'I would feel that every child who [gets] a placebo and becomes paralyzed will do so at my hands.' He was not alone: the National Foundation's research director Harry Weaver and its scientific director Joseph Bell both left over the control-group design before Francis was brought in, while Basil O'Connor's foundation held that it had 'a mandate from its volunteers and donors to proceed'. Sources: Oshinsky, Polio: An American Story, quoted at blog.rootsofprogress.org/polio-and-the-controversy-over-randomized-clinical-trials; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1114166.

question: Thomas Francis Jr. set out a strict design: a random draw, a dummy shot for half the children, and nobody told who got what. Of 211 study areas across 44 states, 127 areas in 33 states refused to give any child a dummy injection and ran a different comparison. What did those districts do?
answer: Vaccinated the second grade and simply watched the first and third
choices: Vaccinated the second grade and simply watched the first and third
Vaccinated half of each grade and compared the two halves later
Vaccinated whole schools and compared them with the schools nearby
Vaccinated willing children and compared them with last year's figures
context: This was the 'observed control' design. 84 test areas in 11 states ran the randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled version; 127 test areas in 33 states ran observed controls -- 749,236 children in the placebo-controlled areas and 1,080,680 in the observed-control areas, 1,829,916 children in all, among whom 1,013 cases of polio were reported. The observed arm's own figures showed what it cost: 221,998 vaccinated second-graders at 17.1 paralytic cases per 100,000 against 725,173 first- and third-graders at 45.5. Sources: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1114166; sph.umich.edu/polio; randomservices.org/random/data/Polio.html.

question: Thomas Francis Jr. refused about 400 reporters what they were waiting for in Ann Arbor on 12 April 1955: one percentage for a headline. His report ran over 113 pages and gave them no such figure, because a single average would have hidden something the data plainly showed. How did the report break the result down instead?
answer: By poliovirus type, since the three types came out very differently
choices: By poliovirus type, since the three types came out very differently
By state, since polio rates varied enormously across the 44 states
By age, since younger children fared differently from older ones
By calendar month, since the trial ran across a whole polio season
context: Francis reported roughly 60-70% protection against Type I poliovirus, over 90% against Types II and III, and about 94% against bulbar polio; the finer strain figures are given as Type III 100%, Type II 92%, Type I 68%. The report also noted that 'in no area did Type II virus prevail. There was, however, prevalence in certain areas of Types I and III' -- so the single rounded headline number reporters wanted would have hidden the fact that the vaccine did worst against one of the two types actually circulating. Francis further reported that where good antibody responses were obtained 'the effect was maintained with but moderate decline after five months.' The university had set out four teletype machines and ten tables, and the Ann Arbor News lent the Associated Press its darkroom; the moment Francis finished, reporters grabbed the report and ran for the telephones. Sources: acsh.org/news/2016/02/23/62-years-ago-today-first-mass-trials-of-the-salk-polio-vaccine; vaxopedia.org/2024/08/11/the-1954-poliomyelitis-vaccine-field-trial/; sph.umich.edu/polio; aadl.org/features/polio.

question: Parents in the districts that used a random draw kept 338,778 children out of the trial, refusing to let them be injected. Those children had the same protection as the dummy-shot children, which is none, and paralytic polio struck the dummy-shot children at 57.1 cases per 100,000. What rate did the refused children come in at?
answer: 35.7 per 100,000 -- well below the dummy-shot children's rate
choices: 35.7 per 100,000 -- well below the dummy-shot children's rate
57.4 per 100,000 -- almost exactly the dummy-shot children's rate
81.2 per 100,000 -- well above the dummy-shot children's rate
16.9 per 100,000 -- roughly the rate among the vaccinated children
context: The full Francis Report table for the randomised districts: 200,745 vaccinated children, 33 paralytic cases, 16.4 per 100,000; 201,229 placebo children, 115 cases, 57.1 per 100,000 -- two groups matched to within 484 children out of four hundred thousand, which is what randomisation buys. And 338,778 not-inoculated children, 121 cases, 35.7 per 100,000. Francis's own report said out loud that the two kinds of family were not alike: 'Marked sociological differences were noted by the U-M's Survey Research Center among the participating and non-participating children in the study. For example, there was a higher proportion of children participating who had been vaccinated against small-pox, diphtheria, and whooping cough than among the non-participants.' Sources: randomservices.org/random/data/Polio.html; sph.umich.edu/polio.

question: Edward R. Murrow put Jonas Salk on his CBS television programme See It Now on the evening of 12 April 1955, the day the world heard that Salk's polio vaccine had worked in a trial on nearly two million American children. Murrow asked a question nobody had yet put to Salk in public: who owned the patent on the vaccine? What did Salk say?
answer: That the people owned it -- there was no patent; could you patent the sun?
choices: That the people owned it -- there was no patent; could you patent the sun?
That the March of Dimes owned it, having paid for every dose of it
That the University of Pittsburgh held it on the country's behalf
That he had signed it over to the National Foundation for one dollar
context: Verbatim: Murrow asked, 'Who owns the patent on this vaccine?' Salk answered, 'Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?' Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Jonas_Salk; retroreport.org/transcript/transcript-could-you-patent-the-sun/; libquotes.com/jonas-salk/quote/lbj2w7e.

question: Thomas Francis Jr.'s report found that the families who signed their children up for the 1954 polio trial were wealthier and better educated than those who refused. What did such a home do to an unvaccinated child's risk of paralysis, and why?
answer: Raised it: cleaner plumbing meant less early exposure and less immunity
choices: Raised it: cleaner plumbing meant less early exposure and less immunity
Raised it: more travel meant more contact with children from other towns
Lowered it: better food meant a stronger fever response to infection
Lowered it: bigger houses meant fewer children sharing the same rooms
context: It raised the risk, and the reason runs opposite to intuition: better sanitation delayed a child's first meeting with poliovirus past infancy, when infection is far likelier to paralyse, so the most comfortable families had the most vulnerable children. Volunteering families were not a random slice of the country, so a design that compares volunteers with non-volunteers compares unlike groups -- which is exactly why the observed-control districts' controls (45.5 per 100,000) sat well below the randomised districts' placebo children (57.1), diluting the measured benefit. Only the random draw makes the two groups alike in everything except the injection. Sources: blog.rootsofprogress.org/polio-and-the-controversy-over-randomized-clinical-trials; randomservices.org/random/data/Polio.html.

question: Jonas Salk gave one of the most quoted lines in the history of science when Edward R. Murrow asked who owned the patent on the polio vaccine. The line is true, and it is also not the whole story: the National Foundation's lawyers had already looked into patenting the vaccine before Murrow ever asked. What had they found?
answer: That it could not be patented anyway -- killing virus with formalin was old work
choices: That it could not be patented anyway -- killing virus with formalin was old work
That defending a patent would have cost more than the vaccine could ever earn
That the rights belonged to Salk personally and not to the Foundation at all
That a patent would have broken the terms of the March of Dimes appeal
context: Foundation lawyers concluded that the key techniques, such as viral inactivation with formaldehyde, built on too much prior scientific knowledge to clear the novelty bar. Salk's refusal was ethical conviction and legal reality at the same time -- which makes the story better, not worse, and is the sort of detail a good record keeps and a good soundbite loses. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Jonas_Salk; Jane S. Smith's archival finding as reported at slate.com/technology/2014/04/the-real-reasons-jonas-salk-didnt-patent-the-polio-vaccine.html.

question: A teacher shows a class a party balloon, an old diner sign and a light bulb. The gas in each sits in one column of the periodic table, long called the inert gases, since none seemed ever to react. Why do their atoms resist reacting?
answer: Their outer electron shells are already full
choices: Their outer electron shells are already full
Their atoms are too small to reach a partner
Their atoms carry a charge that repels others
Their atoms are too light to hold onto a bond
context: The balloon is helium, the sign is neon, and old-style incandescent bulbs were filled with argon to stop the tungsten filament burning up. A full outer shell has no electron to spare and no room to take one, so the atom gains nothing by bonding; that is why the column was called 'inert', and why textbooks printed before 1962 said these gases never react. After Bartlett they were renamed 'noble' instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_gas.

question: A student runs a finger down a table of first ionisation energies, the energy it takes to pull an element's outermost electron loose. One element grips that electron tighter than any other, and pulling it off takes more energy per atom than for anything else on the periodic table. Which element holds the record?
answer: helium
choices: helium
fluorine
hydrogen
iron
context: Helium's first ionization energy is about 2372 kJ/mol - the highest of any element - because its two electrons sit as close as any electrons ever do to a two-proton nucleus, both filling the tightest shell there is. Fluorine is high but not the highest; hydrogen has only one electron and it is easier to pull off; iron is a metal and gives up electrons cheaply. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionization_energy.

question: Neil Bartlett broke the seal between two flasks on the evening of 23 March 1962, working alone at the University of British Columbia. One held red platinum hexafluoride gas, the other a colourless noble gas. An orange-yellow solid formed at once, the first compound anyone had ever made from a noble gas. Which noble gas was in the second flask?
answer: xenon
choices: xenon
helium
neon
argon
context: Bartlett had already shown that PtF6 was strong enough to ionise an element with a comparable ionisation energy. Among the noble gases that pointed at xenon rather than the tighter helium, neon or argon - and the flask experiment confirmed it in seconds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Bartlett_(chemist).

question: Neil Bartlett had already used platinum hexafluoride to pull an electron off one common gas when he noticed a match: a noble gas whose outer electron took almost the same energy to remove, about 1170 kilojoules per mole to the other's 1175. Which molecule matched the noble gas's number?
answer: molecular oxygen (O2)
choices: molecular oxygen (O2)
molecular nitrogen (N2)
molecular hydrogen (H2)
carbon monoxide (CO)
context: The near-identity of the two ionization energies is the physicist's insight that made the chemist's reaction plausible on paper before he ran it. The other three sit much further away: N2 at 1503 kJ/mol, CO at 1352, H2 at 1488. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Bartlett_(chemist).

question: A Nobel-winning chemist predicted in print in 1933 that the heavier noble gases should form fluorides such as KrF6 and XeF6. In 1961, just one year before Neil Bartlett broke the seal on his flasks, the same man printed a fresh paper calling the gas Bartlett used 'completely unreactive chemically.' Who argued both sides of the question?
answer: Linus Pauling
choices: Linus Pauling
Robert Mulliken
Glenn Seaborg
Harold Urey
context: Pauling's 1933 prediction came from his own theory of the chemical bond, and that year, at his suggestion, Yost and Kaye tried to make xenon react with fluorine and failed. By 1961 he was writing that xenon was 'completely unreactive chemically'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_gas_compound.

question: Neil Bartlett wrote his 1962 product down as Xe[PtF6], a neat formula. Later analysis showed the orange-yellow solid was not what he wrote down. What did that analysis find?
answer: the solid was a mixture of two salts, not a single pure compound
choices: the solid was a mixture of two salts, not a single pure compound
the yellow colour came from an oxide of platinum; there was no xenon in it
the true product was krypton hexafluoride; the xenon flask had been contaminated
the reaction only ran at liquid-nitrogen temperature, never at room temperature
context: At room temperature the primary product reacts with more PtF6 to give a mixture containing [XeF]+[PtF6]- and [PtF5]-. The DISCOVERY - that a noble gas would react at all - stood on its own; the formula did not. Source: Graham et al., 'Neil Bartlett and the First Noble-Gas Compound', Structural Chemistry 21 (2010).

question: Neil Bartlett made the very first noble-gas compound in 1962 and broke a rule chemists had taught for sixty years: that these gases never react at all. The first compounds did not come from the whole column. Which noble gases formed them?
answer: the heaviest ones (xenon, krypton, radon)
choices: the heaviest ones (xenon, krypton, radon)
the very lightest one (helium)
the middle of the column (argon and neon)
only the artificial one (oganesson)
context: The old 'too small or too heavy to bond' story predicted the biggest atoms should be the LEAST reactive; instead they were the first to yield, because their outer electrons sit farthest from the nucleus and are easiest to persuade off. The full-shell / ionisation-energy explanation gets the direction right; the size story got it exactly backwards. Oganesson (element 118) is real but too short-lived for real chemistry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_gas.

question: Lord Kelvin, the most respected physicist of the Victorian age, calculated in 1862 that the Sun could shine for at most a few tens of millions of years. He then told Charles Darwin and the geologists that their slow Earth was impossible. What power source did Kelvin assume was keeping the Sun hot?
answer: the Sun slowly shrinking under its own gravity
choices: the Sun slowly shrinking under its own gravity
the Sun burning like an enormous coal fire
meteors constantly falling into the Sun
the Sun powered by an unknown chemical fuel
context: This is the Kelvin-Helmholtz mechanism: as a ball of gas contracts, gravitational potential energy turns into heat. Kelvin's math was correct for the physics of his day. What he could not know is that the atom hides an energy source Victorian physics had never imagined. Radioactivity, found by Henri Becquerel in 1896, was the first hint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_the_Earth

question: Francis Aston weighed hydrogen and helium nuclei in 1920 with his newly built mass spectrograph, a machine that could weigh atoms one kind at a time. Four hydrogen nuclei together came out about 0.7 percent heavier than one helium nucleus. If one turned into the other inside the Sun, what would that vanished mass become?
answer: Energy that powers the Sun
choices: Energy that powers the Sun
Extra neutrinos
Dark matter particles
Cosmic ray showers
context: A tiny sliver, but Aston saw its meaning at once. He wrote that 'if hydrogen is transformed into helium a certain quantity of mass must be annihilated in the process' and called out its 'cosmical importance.' That missing 0.7 percent, multiplied by c^2, is the fuel of every star. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_nuclear_fusion

question: Arthur Eddington stood up at a British Association science meeting in Cardiff, Wales, on 24 August 1920 and gave a bold answer to an old question: why do the stars shine? His talk was titled 'The Internal Constitution of the Stars.' What did he say powered the Sun?
answer: hydrogen nuclei joining together to make helium
choices: hydrogen nuclei joining together to make helium
helium nuclei splitting apart into hydrogen
heavy elements at the core slowly decaying
the Sun's rotation being braked by its magnetic field
context: Eddington was proposing what is now called hydrogen fusion, more than a decade before anyone worked out the reactions. His only clue was Aston's 0.7 percent of missing mass. Source: https://bfschutz.com/2020/08/24/eddington-in-cardiff-100-years-ago-today-the-first-proposal-that-stars-are-powered-by-fusion/

question: Critics told Arthur Eddington that the Sun's core, at only millions of degrees, was nowhere near hot enough for hydrogen nuclei to shove past their own positive electric charge, and their math was right. He had rested his 1920 account of the Sun's power on Francis Aston's weighing of atoms. How did he answer them in print?
answer: he told them to go and find a hotter place
choices: he told them to go and find a hotter place
he admitted the calculation was probably wrong
he proposed the Sun ran on gravity instead
he said the missing heat came from radioactivity
context: The full line: 'The helium which we handle must have been put together at some time and some place. We do not argue with the critic who urges that the stars are not hot enough for this process; we tell him to go and find a hotter place.' The wording is documented in Eddington's book The Internal Constitution of the Stars (1926); his 1920 Cardiff address carried the same title, which is very likely why the line is so often dated to 1920. The CLAIM is firmly 1920 — delivered 24 August 1920 at the British Association in Cardiff and printed in Nature a week later (vol. 106, p. 14). The wonder is that Eddington was right for a reason that did not exist yet. Tunnelling was not worked out until 1927–28, seven or eight years after he made the claim. In 1929 Robert d'Escourt Atkinson and Fritz Houtermans picked up Gamow's brand-new result and applied it to stars, showing that light nuclei could indeed fuse at the modest temperatures Eddington had calculated rather than the impossible ones his critics demanded. He won the argument before anyone knew why he should. Source: en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Arthur_Stanley_Eddington (exact wording, cited to The Internal Constitution of the Stars, 1926); Bernard Schutz, 'Eddington in Cardiff 100 years ago today' (bfschutz.com) — address 24 August 1920, Nature vol. 106, p. 14, Aston mass deficit about 1 part in 120; Atkinson and Houtermans 1929: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_d%27Escourt_Atkinson; the 1920 address as printed in The Observatory, October 1920.

question: A student takes the Sun's steady output, roughly 3.85 x 10^26 watts, and runs it through Albert Einstein's E = mc^2 on her calculator. The answer is how much of its own matter the Sun spends every second, and it has been shining for about 4.6 billion years. What figure does she get?
answer: about four million tonnes
choices: about four million tonnes
about four thousand tonnes
about four billion tonnes
about four trillion tonnes
context: Every second, roughly the mass of a small mountain vanishes from the Sun as energy (E = m c^2). It has been doing this since the Earth was young and will keep it up for billions of years more, because the Sun is a very large mountain. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun

question: Fred Hoyle stared in 1953 at a nasty snag in the way a star builds carbon. Two helium nuclei can crash together and stick as beryllium-8, but it splits back into two heliums almost the instant it forms, giving a third helium no time to arrive. Roughly how fast does it fall apart?
answer: about a ten-thousandth of a trillionth of a second
choices: about a ten-thousandth of a trillionth of a second
about a millionth of a second
about a thousandth of a second
about a full second
context: The measured half-life is about 8.19 x 10^-17 seconds. A third helium nucleus must arrive inside that vanishing window, or beryllium-8 splits back and no carbon is made. This is the triple-alpha bottleneck. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium-8

question: Fred Hoyle pressed William Fowler's Caltech nuclear lab in 1953 to look for something nobody had seen: a specific unknown energy level in carbon-12, close to 7.68 million electron-volts. It was one of the strangest successful predictions in the history of physics. What reason did Hoyle give for insisting the level had to be there?
answer: carbon is plentiful, so stars must have a way to make it
choices: carbon is plentiful, so stars must have a way to make it
the beryllium-8 measurement demanded a matching state
quantum mechanics forbade any other stable resonance
the Sun's spectrum showed a carbon line at that energy
context: Hoyle's argument was blunt: carbon is plainly here in vast quantity, so the nuclear physics must permit its formation. Reasoning of this kind is often called anthropic, since without the level there would be no carbon-based life to look for it. Within months Ward Whaling's team, on an old Van de Graaff accelerator in William Fowler's Caltech lab, found the level near 7.65 MeV, almost exactly where Hoyle had said; it is now called the Hoyle state. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple-alpha_process

question: Raymond Davis Jr set up an experiment nearly a mile underground in the Homestake gold mine in South Dakota in the late 1960s, to catch neutrinos, the ghostly particles the Sun's core should be producing. He meant to test whether the core really did what the fusion theory said, and he kept at it for over twenty years. What sat inside his tank?
answer: 100,000 gallons of ordinary dry-cleaning fluid
choices: 100,000 gallons of ordinary dry-cleaning fluid
100,000 gallons of ultra-purified drinking water
a block of solid lead the size of a small car
a chamber of extremely cold liquid helium
context: The fluid was perchloroethylene, filling a 380 cubic metre tank 1,478 metres down. Neutrinos from the Sun's core very rarely turn a chlorine atom into an argon atom, and Davis literally counted the argon atoms one by one. He shared the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physics. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestake_experiment

question: Raymond Davis Jr kept catching only around a third of the solar neutrinos that John Bahcall's carefully checked model of the Sun said his tank should. Either the model was wrong or the detector was, and neither team could find a mistake. The Sudbury Neutrino Observatory, with 1,000 tonnes of heavy water deep in a Canadian nickel mine, finally cracked it in 2001. What did Sudbury show?
answer: neutrinos change from one type to another as they fly
choices: neutrinos change from one type to another as they fly
the Sun's core is a little cooler than the model assumed
chlorine detectors miss most of the neutrinos that hit them
the Sun makes far fewer neutrinos than fusion predicts
context: Neutrinos come in three flavours (electron, muon, tau). Davis's tank could only see the electron flavour; SNO's heavy water could see all three, and the total matched Bahcall's prediction exactly. The 'missing' two-thirds had turned into the other flavours in flight. That change is only possible if neutrinos have mass. Kajita (Super-Kamiokande) and McDonald (SNO) shared the 2015 Nobel Prize. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudbury_Neutrino_Observatory

question: Astronomers watched in real time on 17 August 2017 as gold and platinum were forged in a blast that gravitational-wave detectors caught as event GW170817. Stars can fuse elements up to iron and no further, so the heaviest needed something else. What kind of event was it?
answer: the merger of two neutron stars
choices: the merger of two neutron stars
the core collapse of a single blue supergiant
a nova on the surface of an old white dwarf
a giant flare from a young magnetic star
context: The kilonova AT 2017gfo, seen 11 hours after the gravitational-wave signal, is estimated to have forged about 16,000 Earth masses of heavy elements, including roughly 10 Earth masses of gold and platinum alone. B2FH predicted this half a century earlier. Fowler received half the 1983 Nobel; Hoyle, controversially, was left out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B2FH_paper

question: Martin Kulldorff of Harvard, Sunetra Gupta of Oxford and Jay Bhattacharya of Stanford signed a one-page open letter in October 2020 with a different plan for COVID. Critics often called it 'let it rip.' What did the letter itself propose?
answer: Shield the old and sick harder; let others resume normal life
choices: Shield the old and sick harder; let others resume normal life
Let the virus spread freely so herd immunity comes fast
Keep schools shut but reopen shops, offices and gyms
Test everyone each week and isolate every positive case
context: The distinction matters: focused protection, the letter's name for its plan, called for HARDER shielding of nursing homes and the immunocompromised than generic lockdowns actually achieved, not for ignoring the virus. Critics often conflated it with 'let it rip'. The letter is named for the small Massachusetts town where the three met and signed.

question: Three epidemiologists wrote a public letter and were called 'fringe.' Yet one taught medicine at Harvard, one taught at Oxford, and one was a health-policy professor at Stanford. In about two weeks, how many other medical and public-health scientists signed onto the letter?
answer: More than ten thousand
choices: More than ten thousand
About one hundred
About five hundred
About one thousand
context: By 16 October 2020 the count was over 10,000 medical and public-health scientists, tens of thousands of practitioner signatures, and hundreds of thousands of citizen signatures. Whatever they were, they were not three.

question: Anthony Fauci and Clifford Lane received a private email days after the Great Barrington Declaration appeared. The sender was Francis Collins, then head of a top federal health agency. He called its authors 'three fringe epidemiologists' and asked for one very specific response. What did he ask for?
answer: A quick and devastating published takedown of the declaration
choices: A quick and devastating published takedown of the declaration
An invitation for the three authors to a Bethesda seminar
A formal ethics investigation of the three universities
A joint statement of areas of agreement with the authors
context: Collins's line, verbatim: 'There needs to be a quick and devastating published take down of its premises.' The emails came out later through a Freedom of Information Act request filed by the American Institute for Economic Research.

question: Another group of scientists answered the Great Barrington Declaration days later in the medical journal The Lancet: the John Snow Memorandum, a real scientific reply. It made two big objections, and one was that the declaration's plan could not really be carried out in practice. What was its second main objection?
answer: Uncontrolled spread would overwhelm hospitals
choices: Uncontrolled spread would overwhelm hospitals
Long COVID would disable a working-age generation
New variants would evade any acquired immunity
Vaccines were only weeks away and would end the epidemic
context: The John Snow Memorandum's two-pronged case was practical infeasibility of shielding plus health-system overload from uncontrolled transmission. Kulldorff, Gupta and Bhattacharya answered that generic lockdowns had ALSO failed to protect the vulnerable -- roughly 40 percent of early U.S. COVID deaths were traced to nursing homes anyway -- but the hospital-overwhelm concern was a genuine one, and one that being called 'fringe' did nothing to address.

question: Jay Bhattacharya and his two co-authors singled out one kind of closure as having the flimsiest risk case and the deepest measured cost. Sweden, under the epidemiologist Anders Tegnell, kept these places open through 2020, and the authors held it up as a real-world counterexample. Which closure did they condemn most sharply?
answer: Schools
choices: Schools
Indoor dining
Gyms and fitness centres
Houses of worship
context: Sweden kept most primary and lower-secondary schools open across 2020-21 and became the standing counterfactual. Measured learning loss and mental-health harm from U.S. and U.K. school closures now runs to multiple years in disadvantaged cohorts. Indoor dining, gyms and worship services were all closed in various jurisdictions, but the declaration's authors flagged schools as the sharpest case.

question: Senators voted on 25 March 2025 to put Jay Bhattacharya in charge of a top federal health agency, the same post Francis Collins had held when he called Bhattacharya and his co-authors 'three fringe epidemiologists' in a 2020 email. Which agency did Bhattacharya now direct?
answer: The National Institutes of Health
choices: The National Institutes of Health
The Food and Drug Administration
The Centers for Disease Control
The Office of the Surgeon General
context: The vote was 53-47, on party lines. Bhattacharya took office on 1 April 2025. Marty Makary, the Johns Hopkins surgeon, was confirmed to lead the FDA the same week. Whatever else it was, it was not vindication of the declaration as a whole -- but the man they had called fringe now ran the agency.

question: Francis Collins admitted in a 2024 interview that he had never actually seen the evidence behind one specific number from the US Centers for Disease Control (CDC). He had led a top federal health agency through the pandemic, when the CDC issued many rules for daily life in America, and this one was enforced for two years. Which rule was it?
answer: Six-foot social distancing
choices: Six-foot social distancing
The 14-day quarantine after exposure
The five-day post-symptom isolation window
The three-foot classroom-cohort rule
context: In a January 2024 transcribed interview with a House subcommittee, Collins said he did not recall seeing any evidence that supported the six-foot figure. Earlier, at a Braver Angels event in July 2023, he had called public-health leaders' neglect of the side-effects of their rules 'really unfortunate', and said of his response to the declaration, 'I regret that I used some terminology that I probably shouldn't.'

question: A student opens an old textbook and reads that the end-Permian catastrophe, about 252 million years ago, killed 96 percent of all ocean species. That number came from an older way of counting. Direct counts of species have lowered it, though this is still the worst extinction ever. What is the current estimate?
answer: About 81%
choices: About 81%
About 96%
About 55%
About 41%
context: The 96% number came from a genus-level 'reverse rarefaction' estimate; direct species counts now put the marine loss around 81%. The number changed because the METHOD improved, not because the crisis shrank -- it remains uniquely severe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian-Triassic_extinction_event.

question: A museum guide points to the rock layer that marks the worst extinction in Earth's history, about 252 million years ago. The prime suspect is written in one country's rocks: one of the biggest volcanic outpourings in the planet's story, burying a continent-sized area in lava at exactly this time. Which volcanic province is it?
answer: The Siberian Traps
choices: The Siberian Traps
The Deccan Traps
The Ontong Java Plateau
The Central Atlantic Magmatic Province
context: The Deccan Traps in India erupted at the end-Cretaceous, alongside the Chicxulub impact. Ontong Java is a mid-Cretaceous oceanic province. CAMP is the End-Triassic trigger. Only the Siberian Traps match the end-Permian date. Source: simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_Traps.

question: A geologist in the Tunguska basin traces the path rising magma once took up through the buried rock. The lava on top did not do most of the killing; what the magma cooked on the way up mattered more. Which buried rock, when cooked, gave off the carbon dioxide pulse that warmed the planet and starved the oceans of oxygen?
answer: Permian coal beds
choices: Permian coal beds
Evaporite (salt) beds
Organic-rich marine shales
Dolomite reef limestones
context: Field studies find charred coal fragments in the sills themselves -- direct evidence the intrusions burned through Tunguska coals. Evaporites and organic shales are also present in the basin and contributed halogens and hydrocarbons, but the measured coal-combustion signature is the biggest carbon source. CO2 rose toward ~2,500 ppm; temperatures climbed ~8 C. Source: pubs.geoscienceworld.org/gsa/geology/article/48/10/986.

question: A technician picks tiny crystals out of the volcanic ash beds of Meishan, China. For decades the end-Permian extinction could only be placed 'sometime late in the Permian.' A sharper radiometric clock, run on these crystals, tightened the main pulse to roughly 60,000 years, a geological instant. Which method delivered that precision?
answer: Uranium-lead dating of zircons
choices: Uranium-lead dating of zircons
Carbon-14 dating of fossil shells
Potassium-argon dating of feldspar
Optically stimulated luminescence of quartz
context: U-Pb via CA-ID-TIMS on zircons gives precision at the tens-of-thousands-of-years level even at 252 Ma. Carbon-14 dies at ~50,000 years old -- useless in deep time. K-Ar and OSL cannot approach this precision at this age. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian-Triassic_extinction_event.

question: A graduate student works through the review papers on the end-Permian extinction of about 252 million years ago. The trigger is agreed and the main killing pulse is timed, yet the case is far from closed: open questions are still live. Which one is the top open dispute?
answer: Ranking the several kill mechanisms by damage done
choices: Ranking the several kill mechanisms by damage done
Ranking intruded sills against surface lavas for the killing
Ordering the terrestrial pulse and the marine pulse in time
Setting full recovery closer to 5 million or 30 million years
context: The candidates -- extreme warming, ocean deoxygenation, ocean acidification, and ozone damage from volcanic halogens -- are all real, all measurable in the rock, and all argued over as to which killed the most species and in what order. The sills-vs-lavas, land-vs-sea timing, and recovery-length questions are also live in the literature but generate less contention. Source: academic.oup.com/nsr/article/11/1/nwad273.

question: Lucien Rudaux photographed the green flash in 1925, the tiny burst of green that some lucky watchers see for a second as the Sun's last sliver drops below the ocean horizon. A respectable rival explanation had held for decades that the flash was not in the sky at all but on the back of the observer's own eye. Which everyday visual effect did that explanation appeal to?
answer: The complementary-colour ghost the eye sees after staring at a bright red patch
choices: The complementary-colour ghost the eye sees after staring at a bright red patch
The persistence-of-vision blur that makes a spinning ember look like a solid ring
The Purkinje shift that makes reds fade to grey first as the light dims at dusk
The Troxler fading that erases a steady patch held in peripheral vision
context: A retina that has stared at a red Sun has bleached most of its red-sensitive photopigment, so a following white or dark scene reads as the complementary colour -- cyan or green. It is the same opponent-process effect that makes a red square leave a green ghost image on a white wall. The hypothesis was reasonable; it just happened to be wrong, and only the photograph could show that.

question: A girl on a beach waits for the very last instant of a clear sunset, careful never to stare at the Sun before it. Air bends green light a hair more than red at every sunset, so the green image of the Sun sets a fraction of a second after the red. Yet the flash is rare. What atmospheric condition almost always has to be present for her to catch it?
answer: A temperature inversion or mirage layer over the horizon
choices: A temperature inversion or mirage layer over the horizon
A high cirrus deck adding extra prismatic dispersion to the sunlight
A very dry stratosphere that stops scattering the shortest wavelengths
A viewer at high altitude looking down through less air than at sea level
context: The pure refractive green rim is only a few arcseconds thick and normally too thin to see. Warm air over cool water (or cool air over warm land) sets up a density gradient that behaves like a slow lens, stretching the last bit of the disc vertically until the green edge is thick enough to register. That is why a stable sea horizon, or a high desert horizon, is where amateurs actually catch it. And why 'blue flashes' are rarer still: violet and blue are bent even MORE than green, but they are scattered away by air along the long horizon path (Rayleigh scattering), so almost nothing at that end of the spectrum reaches the eye. Safety note: the flash is only safe to look for at the very last instant, when the disc is essentially gone -- do not stare at the Sun to catch it.

question: A team led by Zaichun Zhu added up 35 years of leaf counts in 2016, from a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration weather satellite (since 1981) and a NASA satellite (since 1999), which gauge how much leaf every patch of ground carries. The total showed something the models had not predicted. What had happened to Earth's plant cover?
answer: between a quarter and a half of the vegetated land had greened significantly
choices: between a quarter and a half of the vegetated land had greened significantly
the total leaf area had stayed within one percent of its 1982 value
the tropics had greened but the temperate zone had lost half its leaves
leaf area had shrunk by about a fifth as drought spread on every continent
context: The satellites were not looking for good news; they were counting leaves. NASA's own release put the extra leaf area at roughly twice the area of the continental United States. Source: Zhu et al., Nature Climate Change (2016); NASA Goddard release.

question: Zaichun Zhu's team ran the satellite counts through ten global ecosystem models to sort out what was driving the trend. The models, not a direct measurement, handed roughly 70 percent of it to one dominant driver, with three smaller runners-up. Which driver got the 70 percent?
answer: fertilisation by richer atmospheric carbon dioxide
choices: fertilisation by richer atmospheric carbon dioxide
extra nitrogen falling out of polluted air
longer growing seasons from a warmer climate
abandonment and regrowth of old farmland
context: The full split reported was 70% CO2, 9% nitrogen deposition, 8% climate change, 4% land cover. Co-author Ranga Myneni of Boston University stated the 70% figure publicly. The percentages are MODEL output, not a direct measurement. Source: Zhu et al., Nature Climate Change (2016).

question: Chi Chen led a 2019 study in Nature Sustainability that used the finer Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer satellite record to ask where the new leaves were actually appearing. The answer was awkward for a carbon-dioxide-only story. Two countries alone accounted for about a third of the new leaf area, mostly through tree-planting and intensive cropping. Which pair?
answer: China and India
choices: China and India
Brazil and Indonesia
the United States and Canada
Russia and Kazakhstan
context: China's greening was mostly forests (42%) and croplands (32%); India's was mostly croplands (82%). Those two countries hold only about 9% of Earth's vegetated land. So a large chunk of the greening is land MANAGEMENT, not the CO2 fertilisation the 2016 paper had highlighted. Source: Chen et al., Nature Sustainability (2019).

question: A technician checks the ring of vertical pipes around a sweetgum plot at Oak Ridge, pipes that feed carbon dioxide into the air all season. Instead of trusting models, this test grows real trees at raised carbon dioxide in the open air. After eleven years, what has happened to the early growth boost?
answer: it faded as soil nitrogen ran short and could not keep up
choices: it faded as soil nitrogen ran short and could not keep up
it accelerated, because the trees learned to use the extra CO2 better
it flipped to a loss, because the trees started shedding leaves early
it held perfectly steady across all eleven growing seasons
context: The Oak Ridge result is the textbook caution against extrapolating sealed-greenhouse gains to real forests: without extra nutrients, the CO2 boost hits a nutrient ceiling. It is exactly the kind of check a modelled 70% share needs. Source: Norby et al., PNAS (2010).

question: Samuel Myers led a team in 2014 that put wheat, rice, peas and soybeans through open-air carbon dioxide enrichment and measured what came out at harvest. The plants grew more grain and more leaf, as expected. What went down in the grain, compared with plants grown in ordinary air?
answer: the concentrations of zinc, iron and protein
choices: the concentrations of zinc, iron and protein
the concentrations of vitamin C and beta-carotene
the concentrations of calcium and vitamin D
the concentrations of omega-3 fats and folate
context: Bigger crops do not automatically mean more nutrition per bite -- a real cost of CO2 fertilisation in C3 grains and legumes, and the reason 'more leaf = pure good news' is a cartoon to refuse in both directions. Source: Myers et al., Nature (2014).

question: A patient lies in a hospital operating room. Just before the first cut, one doctor gives medicines that switch the patient's inner experience completely off; minutes after the operation the same doctor brings it back on. No one can point to the exact thing being switched. Which doctor does this?
answer: an anaesthetist
choices: an anaesthetist
a surgeon
a neurologist
a radiologist
context: General anaesthesia is the most repeated, most routine consciousness experiment on the planet, and neither the drug companies nor the neuroscientists can say what it is doing to the felt world. Source: iep.utm.edu/hard-problem-of-conciousness.

question: Thomas Nagel picked one animal for a famous essay in 1974. A person could learn every detail of how it sensed the world, he said, and still not know what sensing that way is like from the inside. Which animal did he pick?
answer: a bat
choices: a bat
an octopus
a honeybee
a mantis shrimp
context: The essay was 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' -- the animal chosen because echolocation is fully describable in physics, so any leftover is the leftover. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_Is_It_Like_to_Be_a_Bat%3F.

question: Christof Koch, a brain scientist, bet the philosopher David Chalmers a case of fine wine in 1998. Within a set number of years, he said, science would pin down the brain signature of consciousness. When the clock ran out at the 2023 consciousness science meeting, how did the bet end?
answer: Koch paid Chalmers
choices: Koch paid Chalmers
Chalmers paid Koch
the bet was called a draw
the wager was voided
context: The philosopher won; the neuroscientist handed over a case of Portuguese wine on stage and then immediately proposed a rematch on another 25-year clock. Source: scientificamerican.com/article/a-25-year-old-bet-about-consciousness-has-finally-been-settled.

question: René Descartes pointed to one small structure inside the head in the seventeenth century and named it as the spot where mind and body meet, where thought and matter touch. Which structure did he name?
answer: the pineal gland
choices: the pineal gland
the hippocampus
the corpus callosum
the medulla
context: Descartes picked it partly because it sits on the midline and does not come in a left-right pair; modern neuroscience has moved on, but the puzzle of where subjective experience 'happens' has not. Source: iep.utm.edu/hard-problem-of-conciousness.

question: Giulio Tononi built his Integrated Information Theory on one measure: how tightly a system's information is welded into one whole. Consciousness, he said, tracks that measure. Which part of the brain does his theory point to as the seat of consciousness?
answer: the hot zone in the back of the cortex
choices: the hot zone in the back of the cortex
the cerebellum at the base of the skull
the brainstem
the hypothalamus
context: The 'hot zone' spans temporal, parietal and occipital areas. IIT sits opposite Global Neuronal Workspace, which pushes the burden forward. Source: scholarpedia.org/article/Integrated_information_theory.

question: The COGITATE team staged a scientific tournament in the early 2020s between Global Neuronal Workspace Theory and Integrated Information Theory, two rival accounts of consciousness. Each camp had to write down its predictions before any brain scans were taken, a step called pre-registration. Then the team tested more than 250 people, using three different brain-imaging methods together. Which three?
answer: fMRI, MEG and intracranial EEG
choices: fMRI, MEG and intracranial EEG
PET, ultrasound and scalp EEG
CT, X-ray and near-infrared spectroscopy
fNIRS, DTI and single-cell recording
context: The intracranial EEG data came from epilepsy patients who already had electrodes placed inside their brains for clinical reasons -- the only ethical way to record neurons directly. Source: arc-cogitate.com/project.

question: Giulio Tononi's camp and its workspace rivals each sealed three predictions in advance for the COGITATE project's huge head-to-head test, and the result came out in Nature on 30 April 2025. How did Integrated Information Theory (IIT) and Global Neuronal Workspace Theory (GNWT) score on those sealed predictions?
answer: IIT 2 of 3 passed, GNWT 0 of 3 passed
choices: IIT 2 of 3 passed, GNWT 0 of 3 passed
IIT 3 of 3 passed, GNWT 0 of 3 passed
IIT 0 of 3 passed, GNWT 3 of 3 passed
IIT 1 of 3 passed, GNWT 2 of 3 passed
context: The paper's honest headline was that neither theory survived intact -- IIT scored better on the sealed predictions but neither camp got a clean sweep, and both have been forced to refine their claims. Source: psy.ox.ac.uk/news/a-landmark-experiment-published-in-nature.

question: Critics of Integrated Information Theory (IIT), the bold proposal that consciousness is a certain kind of joined-up information, measurable in principle with a single number, posted an open letter on the PsyArXiv preprint site in September 2023, and 124 researchers signed it. They argued that IIT should be publicly labelled a specific way, at least until it makes sharper testable predictions. What label did the letter demand?
answer: pseudoscience
choices: pseudoscience
unfalsifiable
religion
philosophy
context: Christof Koch, an IIT proponent, answered that the theory may be empirically wrong but states its assumptions clearly; Anil Seth, who is not an IIT proponent, still called the pseudoscience label inflammatory. This is a live public fight about where the border of science actually runs. Sources: nature.com/articles/d41586-023-02971-1; scientificamerican.com/article/prominent-consciousness-theory-is-slammed-as-bogus-science.

question: Roger Penrose, a mathematical physicist, and his collaborator Stuart Hameroff put forward a bold rival to the leading theories of consciousness. They placed consciousness in quantum-scale collapses happening inside one specific part of a brain cell. Which part of the cell did they pick?
answer: the microtubules
choices: the microtubules
the mitochondria
the ribosomes
the myelin sheath
context: Their theory is called Orchestrated Objective Reduction, or 'Orch-OR'; most consciousness scientists reject it, but it is a serious, real, published rival, not a joke. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_information_theory (rivals section).

question: Joseph Murray took a healthy kidney from Ronald Herrick in Boston in 1954 and sewed it into Ronald's dying identical twin, Richard. Earlier attempts on other pairs had failed within days. What was the first sign, right in the operating room, that this one was going to work?
answer: The transplanted kidney began making urine on the table
choices: The transplanted kidney began making urine on the table
Richard's own kidneys started working again beside it
Ronald's blood pressure held steady after the cut
The ward telephone rang with the wire service asking for the outcome
context: The organ pinked up, filled with blood and produced urine before the surgeons had closed. Murray later said the next day the patient was hungry with a sparkle in his eye. Source: https://www.harvardmagazine.com/alumni-profiles/harvard-joseph-murray-transplantation

question: Joseph Murray, a young surgeon on an Army burn ward in the Second World War, watched a piece of skin from a donor go onto a soldier scorched by an aircraft fire. The wound was too big for the man's own skin to cover. What happened to that graft once it was sewn on?
answer: It took hold, looked healthy for weeks, then was attacked and died
choices: It took hold, looked healthy for weeks, then was attacked and died
It knitted in cleanly and lasted the whole recovery
It never bled properly and greyed within hours
It slowly took on the patient's own skin colour
context: Grafts between identical twins on the same ward, by contrast, were kept for good. That difference told Murray the barrier was immunological -- the recipient's body could tell whose tissue was whose. Source: https://www.harvardmagazine.com/alumni-profiles/harvard-joseph-murray-transplantation

question: Joseph Murray's team met Ronald Herrick again and again before he agreed to give up a kidney for his dying twin. The 1954 operation meant cutting a healthy organ out of a healthy man who did not need surgery. On one point the team deliberately refused to help him. What did they refuse to do?
answer: Tell Ronald whether they thought he should go ahead
choices: Tell Ronald whether they thought he should go ahead
Bring the family priest into any of the meetings
Speak to Ronald without a lawyer present in the room
Give Ronald a written estimate of his own odds of dying
context: The team laid out the risks in full and even consulted clergy of several denominations and legal counsel, but stayed neutral on the decision itself -- the choice to give up a kidney had to be Ronald's alone. Source: https://collections.countway.harvard.edu/onview/exhibits/show/reconstructing-lives/transplantation/herrick-twins

question: Richard Herrick married one of his hospital nurses after Joseph Murray gave him the kidney of his identical twin, Ronald, in Boston in 1954, the world's first lasting organ transplant. Richard lived about eight more years and fathered two children. When he died in March 1963, what killed him?
answer: Heart failure
choices: Heart failure
Rejection of the transplanted kidney
Pneumonia caught from his brother
A stroke during a second operation
context: The transplanted kidney was still working at his death; some sources also note the underlying nephritis returning in it, but the immediate cause was cardiac. His donor brother Ronald lived to 79. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Herrick

question: Peter Higgs sent a short paper to the journal Physics Letters in 1964, on how tiny particles get their mass from an invisible field filling space. It said no. He added one paragraph and sent it to Physical Review Letters, which ran it. What did that paragraph point out?
answer: his idea implied a brand-new massive particle
choices: his idea implied a brand-new massive particle
his equations reproduced the orbit of Mercury
his mechanism replaced Einstein's theory of gravity
the maths could build a much better transistor
context: That paragraph is why the particle is called 'the Higgs boson'. Physical Review Letters accepted the second version. The other 1964 papers by Englert-Brout and by Guralnik-Hagen-Kibble had the mechanism but not the explicit prediction of a new particle -- Higgs's rejection-driven addendum put a target on the wall for the next forty-eight years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Higgs.

question: Peter Higgs was beaten into print in 1964. Three separate groups of physicists, in Brussels, Edinburgh and London, each figured out the same mechanism for how tiny particles could get their mass, and all three papers appeared within a few months. Which pair published first, back in August?
answer: Francois Englert and Robert Brout
choices: Francois Englert and Robert Brout
Gerald Guralnik and Tom Kibble
Steven Weinberg and Abdus Salam
Sheldon Glashow and Julian Schwinger
context: The proper name is the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism. Six people published it in 1964: Englert and Brout in Brussels in August; Higgs in Edinburgh in October; Guralnik, Hagen and Kibble in November. The 2013 Nobel went to Englert and Higgs; Brout had died in 2011 and Nobels are not awarded posthumously. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson.

question: A physics teacher writes on the board that the Higgs field 'gives things their mass.' That holds for basic particles like electrons and quarks. But of the mass of a single proton, only about one percent comes from the Higgs. Where does the other 99 percent of a proton's mass come from?
answer: the churning quark and gluon binding energy inside it
choices: the churning quark and gluon binding energy inside it
the total electric charge of its constituent quarks
the gravitational self-attraction of the proton itself
the sea of neutrinos passing constantly through it
context: A proton is three quarks and a boiling sea of gluons bound by the strong force. Einstein's E = mc squared runs both directions: the tremendous binding energy of that churn shows up as mass. So most of a person's body weight is not the Higgs -- it is quantum chromodynamics doing its work inside every proton and neutron in the body. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson.

question: Peter Higgs, 83, sat in a seminar room at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) near Geneva on 4 July 2012, forty-eight years after his 1964 paper. Two detector teams at the Large Hadron Collider showed the same bump at a mass of about 125 GeV. Asked for a reaction on camera as he wiped his eyes, what did Higgs say?
answer: That it was incredible it had happened in his lifetime
choices: That it was incredible it had happened in his lifetime
That it marked the beginning of a whole new physics
That it was the greatest find since the splitting of the atom
That the result still needed another year of checking
context: His words to the camera: 'It's really an incredible thing that it's happened in my lifetime.' Higgs, born 1929, was visibly emotional -- he wiped his eyes during the presentation. He shared the 2013 Nobel with Francois Englert; Robert Brout, the third author of the earliest 1964 paper, had died in 2011 and Nobels are not awarded posthumously. Higgs himself died in April 2024. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Higgs.

question: Peter Higgs asked people not to use 'the God particle,' the nickname still attached to the particle he predicted in 1964 and the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) finally detected in 2012. He hated it. Where did the nickname actually come from?
answer: the title of Leon Lederman's 1993 popular-science book
choices: the title of Leon Lederman's 1993 popular-science book
a Time magazine cover from the week of the 2013 Nobel
Peter Higgs's own religious upbringing in Newcastle
the Latin motto over the main entrance to CERN
context: Lederman, a Nobel-winning physicist himself, said he had wanted to call it 'the goddamn particle' because it was so hard to find; his publisher pushed the tamer title. Higgs, an atheist, objected because the phrase muddled people about what the mechanism actually claims. It claims something about how W and Z bosons get their mass, not about the origins of the universe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Higgs.

question: A physicist works a simple quantum calculation for the Higgs mass and gets a number a trillion trillion times too high; the measured mass is about 125 GeV. Nobody yet knows why. For decades the favourite proposed fix was a whole family of heavier partner particles, which the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has hunted and not found. Which framework predicted them?
answer: supersymmetry
choices: supersymmetry
loop quantum gravity
string landscape inflation
Kaluza-Klein extra dimensions
context: Supersymmetry pairs every known particle with a heavier partner whose quantum contributions would cancel the runaway drag on the Higgs mass. It was the leading candidate for decades and a major reason the LHC was built. As of the current runs the partner particles have not shown up in the expected energy range, and the hierarchy problem is more open, not less. Said plainly: no one yet knows. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson.

question: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson pointed the 20-foot antenna at the sky at Bell Labs in 1964, and they found the hiss. They were not out hunting for the beginning of the universe. They had a much more ordinary reason. What were they actually trying to do?
answer: calibrate the horn for radio astronomy
choices: calibrate the horn for radio astronomy
test a new design for a passenger radar system
search for signals from alien civilizations
map the Milky Way's spiral arms
context: The horn had been built in 1959 for Project Echo, NASA's passive communications satellite program. Penzias and Wilson wanted a quiet instrument for radio astronomy, and the mysterious hiss was a stubborn nuisance they were trying to make go away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmdel_Horn_Antenna

question: Robert Wilson and Arno Penzias chased the pigeons out of the giant Holmdel horn antenna in New Jersey in 1964 and cleaned out the mess. They suspected the droppings were behind the faint hiss they could not get rid of. They climbed back down and switched the antenna on again. What happened to the hiss?
answer: it stayed exactly as loud as before
choices: it stayed exactly as loud as before
it dropped by roughly half
it vanished within a few hours
it grew louder for several days and then faded
context: That is the whole point of the story: the noise was not coming from the birds. Whatever the source was, it was arriving through the sky itself, not from anything nesting in the metal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_cosmic_microwave_background_radiation

question: One by one, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson ruled out the sources of the strange hiss: New York City's radio noise, military radar, even the glow from a 1962 high-altitude nuclear test. Then they feared the horn's own metal joints might leak noise. What did they do to the antenna's aluminium seams?
answer: they taped over the seams
choices: they taped over the seams
they welded the seams shut
they repainted the seams with copper
they replaced the rivets with brass bolts
context: Nothing they tried made the hiss go away. What refused to leave was an excess antenna temperature of about 3.5 K, and it was the same in every direction they aimed the horn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_cosmic_microwave_background_radiation

question: Robert Dicke's team at Princeton, about forty miles from Holmdel, was already building an antenna to hunt for leftover heat from a hot early universe when Arno Penzias called about the strange noise at Bell Labs. When Dicke hung up the phone, what did he say to his team?
answer: 'Boys, we've been scooped.'
choices: 'Boys, we've been scooped.'
'Gentlemen, our instrument is obsolete.'
'We were right, and now we must prove it.'
'Then we shall build a bigger one.'
context: The radio astronomer Bernard Burke had heard about the Princeton work and told Penzias to call Dicke. That phone call connected two groups who had spent months chasing the same signal from opposite ends. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background

question: Two physicists worked from George Gamow's hot-start cosmology in 1948 and estimated that the early universe should have left behind a faint glow of about 5 degrees above absolute zero. No one built the instrument to look. Who were they?
answer: Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman
choices: Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman
Fred Hoyle and Thomas Gold
Hans Bethe and Edward Teller
Robert Dicke and James Peebles
context: Alpher and Herman's estimate sat in the physics literature for sixteen years before Penzias and Wilson stumbled into the signal. Their number -- about 5 K -- turned out to be startlingly close to what the horn measured. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Asher_Alpher

question: Andrew McKellar worked in 1940 from absorption lines W. S. Adams had recorded, and he noticed that one interstellar molecule was gently excited, as if warmed by something only a few degrees above absolute zero. It was an unrecognized clue to the leftover glow. Which molecule was it?
answer: cyanogen (CN)
choices: cyanogen (CN)
molecular hydrogen (H2)
hydroxyl (OH) radicals
carbon monoxide (CO)
context: McKellar's estimate for the exciting temperature was about 2.3 K -- eerily close to the modern value. No one at the time connected that gently warm interstellar cyanogen to a leftover glow from the beginning of the universe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_cosmic_microwave_background_radiation

question: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson had caught light in their horn, released when the early universe finally cooled enough for electrons and nuclei to combine into neutral atoms and the primordial fog cleared. Roughly how long after the beginning did that happen?
answer: about 380,000 years
choices: about 380,000 years
about 3 seconds
about 30 million years
about 1 billion years
context: At that moment the universe was around 3,000 K -- a fierce visible glare. Expansion has stretched that glare all the way down into microwaves, with a present-day temperature COBE measured at 2.72548 K. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background

question: A student pores over a sky map made by the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE), the satellite launched in 1989 to study the leftover glow with tools no ground-based horn could match. The map shows faint temperature ripples, about one part in 100,000. What are those ripples thought to be?
answer: the seeds that grew into galaxies, stars, and eventually us
choices: the seeds that grew into galaxies, stars, and eventually us
the imprint of gravitational waves from cosmic inflation
the shadows of primordial black holes forming
the boundaries between separate bubble universes
context: Where the sky was very slightly warmer, matter was very slightly denser -- and gravity pulled those denser patches into the first structures. John Mather and George Smoot shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for the COBE blackbody and anisotropy results. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_Background_Explorer

question: Alan Sokal, a New York University physicist, published a paper in May 1996 in a cultural-studies journal. It argued something a physicist would never actually argue. Three weeks later he said in Lingua Franca that he had done it on purpose, as a test. What did the paper claim?
answer: that physical reality is a social and linguistic construct
choices: that physical reality is a social and linguistic construct
that Einstein's relativity theory has been quietly falsified
that string theory is not falsifiable and so is not physics
that the Copenhagen interpretation is the true theory of mind
context: The paper was titled 'Transgressing the Boundaries: Towards a Transformative Hermeneutics of Quantum Gravity.' Sokal salted it with real physicists' terms used wrongly, plus claims a first-year physics student would refuse. The test was narrow and stated: would a journal print flattering nonsense if the jargon and the politics were agreeable? Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sokal_affair

question: Defenders of a leading cultural-studies journal spoke up after it printed Alan Sokal's nonsense article as a serious paper in 1996. They pointed out one thing about how the journal actually worked at the time, a detail the headlines mostly ignored. What was it?
answer: Social Text did not operate peer review and never sent the paper to a physicist
choices: Social Text did not operate peer review and never sent the paper to a physicist
Sokal had submitted the paper under a false name to hide his politics
the editors had asked Sokal to revise it heavily before publication
a physicist reviewer had approved the paper without spotting the errors
context: The editors accepted the paper on Sokal's NYU credentials and its ideological fit with a special 'Science Wars' issue. What the hoax actually demonstrated, then, was a failure of editorial judgement, not a failure of peer review - and Sokal's own stated claim was that narrower one. Getting the target right is part of getting the lesson right. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sokal_affair

question: Peter Boghossian, James Lindsay and Helen Pluckrose sent twenty fake papers to journals in 2017 and 2018, picking journals that ran peer review to fix the objection raised against Alan Sokal's test. How many were published or accepted before the project was exposed?
answer: four published and three more accepted
choices: four published and three more accepted
one published and one more accepted
twelve published and six more accepted
all twenty published outright
context: Six were rejected outright and the remaining seven were still under review when the exposure came. The trio called it 'Sokal squared.' They aimed at fields they termed 'grievance studies' where they thought only certain conclusions were welcome. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grievance_studies_affair

question: A peer reviewer called one hoax paper 'incredibly innovative, rich in analysis, and extremely well-written and organized.' The journal ran it under the name Helen Wilson. What was the paper actually about?
answer: rape culture and queer performativity in Portland dog parks
choices: rape culture and queer performativity in Portland dog parks
colonial legacies in the layout of Parisian arrondissements
toxic masculinity in the boardrooms of Silicon Valley
gendered patterns of household electricity consumption
context: The full title was 'Human reactions to rape culture and queer performativity at urban dog parks in Portland, Oregon.' The reviewer's words are documented: the three authors published the reviews with each paper. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grievance_studies_affair

question: James Lindsay, Helen Pluckrose and Peter Boghossian slipped one paper past the social-work journal Affilia, which accepted it as an original contribution to feminist theory. They had sent it in as part of their test of journals in what they called grievance studies. It was not original at all. What was it really?
answer: a passage of Hitler's Mein Kampf rewritten in feminist-theory language
choices: a passage of Hitler's Mein Kampf rewritten in feminist-theory language
a Marxist manifesto essay with the nouns swapped for gender terms
a chapter of Ayn Rand paraphrased into critical-theory prose
a chatbot's answer to a prompt about intersectional ethics
context: The passage was picked precisely because a competent reviewer should have recognised the source rhetoric. Affilia accepted it. The three authors published the manuscript record with each paper so the audit trail was public. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grievance_studies_affair

question: Someone at Gender, Place & Culture asked a simple question about one paper's author in October 2018, and the hoax project was over. No reviewer had brought it down by spotting the content of the papers. What was the question?
answer: was Helen Wilson a documented real person
choices: was Helen Wilson a documented real person
was Helen Wilson affiliated with an ethics board
was Helen Wilson listed in the copyright registry
was Helen Wilson current on the article-processing fee
context: She was not. The Wall Street Journal broke the story on October 2, 2018. The whole affair turns on this: the hoax survived peer review and died the moment someone asked for proof that the author existed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grievance_studies_affair

question: Alan Sokal fooled a cultural-studies journal into printing a nonsense paper in 1996, and the hoax has been used ever since to attack the humanities. A fair critic objects that a single hoax with no control group shows what the gatekeepers happened to miss, not whether the ideas of a field are true. What happened in 2014 to show the same trick works on hard technical journals too?
answer: Springer and IEEE withdrew over 120 computer-generated SCIgen papers
choices: Springer and IEEE withdrew over 120 computer-generated SCIgen papers
Nature retracted every paper from the Duke genomics group
a Chinese paper-mill was caught forging 400 peer-review reports
the Bogdanov brothers had their physics dissertations annulled
context: SCIgen is a random paper generator built at MIT using a context-free grammar; Cyril Labbe of Grenoble catalogued its output across more than 30 peer-reviewed conference proceedings from 2008 to 2013. The lesson: a hoax measures what a review system catches. It cannot, by itself, show whether the underlying field is right or wrong. The finding and the objection both stand, for a reader to weigh. Source: https://retractionwatch.com/2014/02/24/springer-ieee-withdrawing-more-than-120-nonsense-papers/

question: Stephen McIntyre asked Michael Mann in April 2003 for the numbers behind the most-argued-over graph in climate science, and was sent a spreadsheet. Ross McKitrick worked through the statistics with him. Neither man was a rival climatologist; both came from outside the field entirely. What did the two men do for a living?
answer: A minerals-exploration consultant and an economics professor
choices: A minerals-exploration consultant and an economics professor
A petroleum geologist and an applied mathematics professor
A television weather forecaster and a statistics professor
A software engineer and an experimental physics professor
context: Stephen McIntyre was a Canadian minerals-exploration and mining consultant whose working life was spent on the statistics of drilling data; Ross McKitrick was an economics professor at the University of Guelph. Neither was a climatologist. McIntyre downloaded the published 1999 data, then asked Mann directly for the 1998 dataset in April 2003, and found he could not reproduce the published result from the published description. That failure, not any opinion about the weather, is what set the whole audit going. Source: Wikipedia, 'Stephen McIntyre'; Wikipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)'.

question: Michael Mann built his famous temperature graph at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, with Raymond Bradley there and Malcolm Hughes in Arizona, and Nature published it in April 1998. Within three years it was a political symbol. What was Mann's job at the university while he built it?
answer: A postdoctoral fellow funded by the Department of Energy
choices: A postdoctoral fellow funded by the Department of Energy
A tenured professor in the department of atmospheric science
A visiting scientist on loan from a national laboratory
The director of the university's climate research centre
context: Mann held a US Department of Energy postdoctoral fellowship at UMass Amherst from 1996 to 1998, and the paper known as MBH98 came out of it: Mann, Bradley and Hughes, Nature, 23 April 1998, a Northern Hemisphere reconstruction reaching back to AD 1400. A follow-up in Geophysical Research Letters in March 1999 pushed it back to AD 1000. A long gentle decline ending in a sharp 20th-century rise looked like a hockey stick lying on its side, which is where the nickname came from. Source: Wikipedia, 'Michael E. Mann'; Grokipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)'.

question: Sir John Houghton stood in front of a huge print of the Mann, Bradley and Hughes curve in January 2001, launching a big report that the UN climate panel, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), had approved in Shanghai. The curve also went into the Summary for Policymakers, the short paper officials and reporters read. What claim did that Summary attach to it?
answer: That the 1990s was likely the warmest decade of the past thousand years
choices: That the 1990s was likely the warmest decade of the past thousand years
That human emissions had caused all of the warming measured since 1850
That the Medieval Warm Period had never happened anywhere outside Europe
That sea level would rise by a full metre before the end of this century
context: The wording was that it was 'likely that, in the Northern Hemisphere, the 1990s was the warmest decade and 1998 the warmest year' of the past thousand years. The 1999 paper itself had described the millennium as a long slow cooling of roughly 0.02 degrees C per century, interrupted by the modern rise. Once a research figure is a backdrop at a televised launch it stops being easy to revise, which is the whole trouble this fight is about. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)', quoting the IPCC Third Assessment Report Summary for Policymakers; Grokipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)'.

question: Nobody had a thermometer in AD 1400, so Michael Mann and his co-authors built their curve from things that grew or froze while the weather happened. There were 112 indicators in all: tree-ring widths, ice-core chemistry, coral growth bands and written records of glaciers. But the network was not the same size at every date. Roughly how many of those 112 series reached back to AD 1400, the oldest year the 1998 paper covered?
answer: About 22
choices: About 22
About 46
About 75
About 103
context: Roughly 24 series still run at AD 1820 and about 22 at AD 1400. The oldest end of the graph, the stretch people argued about most loudly, rests on the fewest records, and that is a structural fact about every long reconstruction rather than a fault of this one. The network also included maximum latewood density, borehole temperatures and a few early instrument series. Source: Grokipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)', section 'Mann, Bradley, and Hughes (1998-1999) Methodology'.

question: Stephen McIntyre and Ross McKitrick named the step they disputed in a 2005 paper. Before combining its North American tree rings, the 1998 Mann paper ran them through principal-component analysis, which boils many wobbly series down to a few summary patterns. Everything, the two argued, turned on which stretch of years that step was centred on. Which stretch did it use?
answer: 1902 to 1980, the window with thermometer records
choices: 1902 to 1980, the window with thermometer records
1400 to 1980, the whole length of the reconstruction
1000 to 1400, the stretch before the network thins
1961 to 1990, the standard meteorological baseline
context: 'Hockey sticks, principal components, and spurious significance' was received on 14 October 2004, accepted 17 January 2005 and published 12 February 2005 in Geophysical Research Letters. Centring on the 1902-1980 calibration window rather than on the full 1400-1980 record means every series is measured against its own 20th-century average, which pushes series that behave unusually in the 20th century toward the front of the queue. Their earlier 2003 paper in Energy & Environment had already argued the shape was 'primarily an artefact of poor data handling and use of obsolete proxy records'. Source: McIntyre & McKitrick 2005, GRL 32(3), doi:10.1029/2004GL021750; Grokipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)'.

question: Gerald North's twelve-member panel of the US National Research Council reported on the Mann, Bradley and Hughes curve on 22 June 2006. The panel agreed with the critics that the disputed statistical step was biased. Then it took up a second question: had that step actually changed the curve? What did the panel conclude?
answer: Reconstructions run without that step came out much the same
choices: Reconstructions run without that step came out much the same
Reconstructions run without that step lost the modern rise entirely
Reconstructions run without that step showed a warmer medieval peak
Reconstructions run without that step could not be produced at all
