context: The panel's sentence, in full: 'As part of their statistical methods, Mann et al. used a type of principal component analysis that tends to bias the shape of the reconstructions... In practice, this method, though not recommended, does not appear to unduly influence reconstructions of hemispheric mean temperature; reconstructions performed without using principal component analysis are qualitatively similar to the original curves presented by Mann et al.' Both halves are the finding. The critics were right that the step was biased; the referee judged the bias did not drive the answer. Source: National Research Council (2006), 'Surface Temperature Reconstructions for the Last 2,000 Years', ch. 11.

question: A tree-ring researcher takes a core from a strip-bark bristlecone pine, an ancient tree whose trunk is mostly dead, with a single surviving ribbon of living bark still laying down a ring each year. Such samples 'should be avoided' for temperature reconstructions, the US National Research Council panel wrote in June 2006. It then named something besides warmth that may be fattening the recent rings of such trees. What was it?
answer: Nitrogen from human sources settling out of the air
choices: Nitrogen from human sources settling out of the air
Desert dust settling on the slopes and feeding the soil
Deeper winter snowpack lasting later into the spring
Less competition as neighbouring old trees died back
context: The panel's tree-ring chapter says: 'While "strip-bark" samples should be avoided for temperature reconstructions, attention should also be paid to the confounding effects of anthropogenic nitrogen deposition.' Extra carbon dioxide in the air is a candidate for the same effect. The worry is simple and testable: if a ring gets fatter because the tree is being fertilised rather than because the summer was warm, then reading ring width as a thermometer reads the wrong thing. Source: National Research Council (2006), 'Surface Temperature Reconstructions for the Last 2,000 Years', ch. 4 'Tree Rings'.

question: Phil Jones, director of the Climatic Research Unit, sent a private email to Michael Mann and two colleagues on 16 November 1999 about a cover graphic for a World Meteorological Organization report. He said he had used 'Mike's Nature trick... to hide the decline.' The email leaked ten years later and the sentence went round the world. Among scientists a 'trick' is simply a technique, but the cover picture was not quite what it appeared. What did the graphic actually do?
answer: Swapped measured temperatures in for the post-1960 tree-ring values
choices: Swapped measured temperatures in for the post-1960 tree-ring values
Stopped all three plotted curves at 1960 and left the century blank
Dropped the two reconstructions that disagreed, showing only Mann's
Stretched the scale until the last forty years filled half the cover
context: The full sentence, typo and all: 'I've just completed Mike's Nature trick of adding in the real temps to each series for the last 20 years (ie from 1981 onwards) amd from 1961 for Keith's to hide the decline.' The graphic was the cover of the WMO Statement on the Status of the Global Climate in 1999, showing three reconstructions as smoothed anomalies from the 1961-1990 normal. The decline was in Keith Briffa's tree-ring values, which had begun falling after 1960 while thermometers rose. Splicing the measured temperatures on gave the reader one smooth continuous line, with nothing to show that a proxy had failed, and the caption said nothing about it. Source: FactCheck.org, 'Climategate'; WMO-No. 913 cover and caption.

question: Muir Russell reported in July 2010 on the emails taken from the Climatic Research Unit at East Anglia, one of eight inquiries, none of which found fraud or misconduct. His review said the scientists' 'rigour and honesty as scientists are not in doubt.' It then judged the 1999 cover graphic on the World Meteorological Organization report. What did it say about that figure?
answer: It was misleading, though splicing data is not improper in itself
choices: It was misleading, though splicing data is not improper in itself
It was sound, and the complaints about it rested on a misreading
It was improper, because reconstructions must never be spliced at all
It was outside the review's remit, so no judgement was offered on it
context: Muir Russell wrote both sentences and softened neither: 'The figure supplied for the WMO Report was misleading in not describing that one of the series was truncated post 1960 for the figure, and in not being clear on the fact that proxy and instrumental data were spliced together. We do not find that it is misleading to curtail reconstructions at some point per se, or to splice data.' The doing was allowed; the not-saying was not. Several of the same reports also criticised the unit sharply for poor data archiving and for resisting requests to share. Source: Independent Climate Change E-mail Review (Muir Russell), 7 July 2010, findings 13 and 23; Wikipedia, 'Climatic Research Unit email controversy'.

question: Edward Wegman, a statistician, led a review of the stats behind the temperature graph for a US Congress committee in July 2006, and it backed Stephen McIntyre's case. Part of it, a study of who co-authors papers with whom, was later republished in a stats journal. That journal pulled the paper in May 2011, and George Mason University then punished Wegman for research misconduct. What had been found in it?
answer: Passages copied word for word from textbooks and Wikipedia
choices: Passages copied word for word from textbooks and Wikipedia
Co-authorship links invented to make the network look tighter
Funding from an energy company that was never once disclosed
Calculations nobody at the journal could reproduce from the data
context: The Wegman Report, by Edward Wegman, Yasmin Said and David Scott, was announced on 14 July 2006, three weeks after the National Research Council reported. Its social-network section was published in Computational Statistics & Data Analysis and retracted in May 2011 for plagiarism. Auditing cuts in every direction: the people checking other people's work are checkable too, and the same standard that caught a sloppy statistical step also caught a copied paragraph. Source: Nature 473, 419 (2011), 'Copy and paste'; Retraction Watch; Wikipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)'.

question: Michael Mann and his colleagues published a fresh reconstruction in 2008 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, built from 1,209 proxy series, and reported that it still worked back to about AD 1000 with every tree-ring record dropped from the network. Near the end the paper carried one line the 1998 paper never had. What did that line say?
answer: That the data and the Matlab source code sat at a public web address
choices: That the data and the Matlab source code sat at a public web address
That the raw proxy series had been deposited in the PNAS archive itself
That the authors would send data and code to any reader who asked
That the code would be released once the follow-up paper appeared
context: The 2008 PNAS paper carried a line the 1998 paper never had: 'All data used in this study and Matlab source codes for implementing the algorithms described, as well as additional supporting information are available at www.meteo.psu.edu/~mann/supplements/MultiproxyMeans07'. That is what the whole fight settled: not a knockout argument but an address anyone could type in. The same paper reported a skilful reconstruction back to about AD 1000 with tree-ring data left out of the network entirely. The 2006 panel had put the remedy in one dry sentence: 'Improving access to data used in publications would also increase confidence in the results.' By 2017 the PAGES 2k Consortium was posting 692 records from 648 locations openly for anyone to download and check. Source: Mann et al. (2008), PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.0805721105; NRC (2006) Summary; PAGES2k Consortium (2017), Scientific Data 4:170088.

question: A student reads the published plan of the Human Genome Project, begun on 1 October 1990 to read the complete DNA of a human being, letter by letter. The plan allows fifteen years and three billion dollars. How did the finished project measure against it?
answer: It came in two years early, at about $2.7 billion
choices: It came in two years early, at about $2.7 billion
It came in on schedule, at about $5.4 billion
It came in six years late, at about $3.2 billion
It came in nine years late, at about $8.1 billion
context: Thirteen years instead of fifteen, and roughly $2.7 billion instead of three. James Watson, co-discoverer of the double helix, was the first director of the NIH genome centre. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: The leaders of the Human Genome Project picked 14 April 2003 on purpose for their big announcement, to send a message with the date. They could have made it on any day that spring. Which big discovery was turning fifty?
answer: Watson and Crick's description of the DNA double helix
choices: Watson and Crick's description of the DNA double helix
Beadle and Tatum's one gene, one enzyme rule
Avery and MacLeod's proof that genes are made of DNA
Meselson and Stahl's demonstration of DNA copying
context: Watson and Crick described the double helix in 1953, and the consortium timed 14 April 2003 to land on the fiftieth anniversary. The sequence they called finished covered about 92% of the genome and 99% of the gene-rich euchromatic portion, with fewer than 400 gaps and roughly one wrong letter in every 10,000. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: J. Craig Venter announced Celera Genomics in May 1998, a private company that would sequence the human genome itself and beat the public consortium to the finish. The consortium's plan was fifteen years and three billion dollars. Venter named his own deadline and price the same day. What did he promise?
answer: Three years and about $300 million
choices: Three years and about $300 million
Two years and about $150 million
Four years and about $900 million
Six years and about $1.8 billion
context: Venter founded Celera on 9 May 1998 with PerkinElmer and ran the sequencing on roughly 300 ABI PRISM 3700 machines at once. The public project he was racing had been running since October 1990 on a plan of fifteen years and three billion dollars, so Venter was promising the same result in a fifth of the time for a tenth of the money. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project; genengnews.com, 'From Sequencing to Sailing: Three Decades of Adventure with Craig Venter'

question: Five unnamed donors, three women and two men, gave the samples Craig Venter's team mixed into the genome of Celera Genomics, so the result was not one person's DNA. Venter left the company in 2002. What did he reveal about those five after he left?
answer: One of the five donors had been Venter himself
choices: One of the five donors had been Venter himself
None of the five donors had signed a consent form
All five of the donors had been Celera employees
Two of the five donors had withdrawn beforehand
context: After leaving the company in 2002, Venter revealed that his own DNA was one of the five strands blended into Celera's composite human genome. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Venter; dnalc.cshl.edu/view/15364-DNA-donors-for-sequencing-at-Celera-Craig-Venter.html

question: Craig Venter packed one building with about 300 top sequencing machines in 1998 and promised a finished human genome years before the public team could manage it. The machines alone were not enough; speed depended on how his company, Celera Genomics, chose to tackle three billion letters of DNA. Which approach did it take?
answer: Broke the whole genome into random fragments and had computers reassemble them
choices: Broke the whole genome into random fragments and had computers reassemble them
Read only the messenger RNA in cells and worked backwards to the DNA
Cloned each chromosome into bacteria and read the pieces in fixed order
Sorted the chromosomes one at a time and read each from end to end
context: This was whole-genome shotgun sequencing: blast the genome apart, sequence every fragment at once on those 300 machines, then let supercomputers hunt for the overlaps that put the puzzle back together. The public consortium had gone the other way, mapping each chromosome first, cutting it into known, ordered pieces, and reading those one at a time. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: A biology teacher writes the working number on the board before the human sequence comes in: 100,000 protein-coding genes or more, with some guesses at 120,000, on the thinking that a complex animal must need many genes. When the counting is done, how many protein-coding genes does a human really have?
answer: About 20,000
choices: About 20,000
About 55,000
About 140,000
About 400,000
context: The 2000-2001 drafts said 26,000-40,000; by 2005 it had fallen to 20,000-25,000; the finished 2022 sequence annotates 19,969 protein-coding genes. That is about what Caenorhabditis elegans carries - a soil roundworm one millimetre long whose whole body is 959 cells - and fewer than rice is annotated with (roughly 32,000-35,600, though plant counts are inflated by whole-genome duplication and annotation methods differ between species, so that comparison is loose). The count is always of protein-coding genes; counting RNA genes gives a larger number. Complexity is not gene count. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project; genome.gov roundworm education kit

question: Twenty volunteers, ten men and ten women, answered an ad in the Buffalo News in March 1997 and gave blood at Roswell Park in Buffalo, New York, for the human reference genome. The consent form promised that no more than 10 percent of the sequence would come from any one person. How much of the published 2001 draft came from a single donor?
answer: About 70 to 75 percent, from one anonymous man
choices: About 70 to 75 percent, from one anonymous man
About 40 to 45 percent, from one anonymous man
About 30 to 35 percent, from one anonymous man
About 20 to 25 percent, from one anonymous woman
context: The consortium promised each volunteer that no more than 10% of the final sequence would be his or hers, then drew roughly three-quarters of the published draft from one man. He is known to this day only by the code RP11, and most of the reference genome the world has used ever since is his. Source: statnews.com, 9 July 2024; undark.org, 9 July 2024

question: T. Ryan Gregory tests the assumption that a more elaborate creature needs more DNA with something anyone can pick up at a market: the common onion, Allium cepa. A human cell carries about 3.2 billion base pairs. How much DNA does an onion carry?
answer: About 16 billion base pairs, five times the human figure
choices: About 16 billion base pairs, five times the human figure
About 6 billion base pairs, twice the human figure
About 32 billion base pairs, ten times the human figure
About 130 billion base pairs, forty times the human figure
context: Gregory named this the onion test in 2007 and puts it as a question to anyone who insists nearly every stretch of non-coding DNA is essential: 'Can I explain why an onion needs about five times more non-coding DNA for this function than a human?' And the onion is no freak case - different Allium species carry more than fourfold different amounts of DNA from one another. Source: journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article?id=10.1371/journal.pgen.1004351 ('The Case for Junk DNA', Palazzo & Gregory 2014); grokipedia.com/page/Junk_DNA

question: Ewan Birney opened a betting pool in a bar at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in May 2000, on how many protein-coding genes a human would turn out to have. More than 460 researchers put money in over the next three years. Lee Rowen of Seattle won in 2003 with her guess of 25,947. Where did her winning number sit among all those bets?
answer: It was the lowest bet in the pool, and it was still too high
choices: It was the lowest bet in the pool, and it was still too high
It was the lowest bet in the pool, and it was slightly too low
It sat near the middle of the field, and it was slightly too high
It sat near the middle of the field, and it was still too low
context: Rowen, of the Institute for Systems Biology, placed the lowest bet in the pool - and the true count still came in under it. The highest wager was above 200,000 genes, and John Quackenbush staked his on 118,253; when Hugues Roest-Crollius entered 27,000, Birney remembered thinking, 'This guy's mad! There can't be 27,000.' Rowen took $600 of the $1,200 pot and an autographed copy of James Watson's The Double Helix; Paul Dear and Olivier Jaillon split the rest. The pool, called GeneSweep, charged $1 to enter in 2000, $5 in 2001 and $20 in 2002 as more sequence came in. Science reported the result on 30 May 2003 under the headline 'A Low Number Wins the GeneSweep Pool.' Source: genome.gov/virtual-exhibits/GeneSweep; science.org/doi/10.1126/science.300.5625.1484b

question: Beadle and Tatum made a rule textbook doctrine with their mould experiments: one gene, one protein. A gene is first copied into a working transcript, a messenger RNA, which the cell then reads to build a protein. Post-project analyses of human transcripts caught most human genes breaking that rule outright. What did those analyses catch a single human gene doing with its transcript?
answer: Cutting its transcript apart and rejoining the pieces in different combinations
choices: Cutting its transcript apart and rejoining the pieces in different combinations
Stitching its transcript onto a neighbouring gene's transcript to make hybrids
Slipping the cell's reading frame partway along its transcript by one letter
Reading its transcript straight through into several proteins in a row
context: The mechanism is called alternative splicing: one gene's transcript is cut into pieces and those pieces are joined back together in different combinations, so a single stretch of DNA yields many different proteins. Post-project analyses found that over 90% of human genes built from more than one coding block produce such variants, which retired the one gene, one protein rule that Beadle and Tatum's Neurospora work had made textbook doctrine. It is a large part of the answer to 'so few genes'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: Reporters took the word literally in April 2003, when the Human Genome Project announced that the human genome was complete. It was not true. Roughly 8 percent of it, some 200 million bases, had defeated every sequencing machine then built and was left out of the sequence called finished. Which parts were missing?
answer: The long repeated stretches at the centromeres and telomeres
choices: The long repeated stretches at the centromeres and telomeres
The stretches that vary most from one person to the next
The regions packed most densely with protein-coding genes
The mitochondrial DNA that sits outside the cell nucleus
context: Identical repeats are what break an assembly: a computer hunting for overlapping fragments cannot tell one copy from another. The Telomere-to-Telomere consortium - over 100 researchers using PacBio HiFi and Oxford Nanopore ultra-long reads on the CHM13 cell line - closed the last gaps on 31 March 2022, producing a gapless 3,054,815,472-base sequence with nearly 200 million bases nobody had ever seen. The Y chromosome, about 60% repetitive, held out until 2023. Source: science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abj6987; grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: Dan Graur and five colleagues fired back in print in 2013 at the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) consortium. More than 440 ENCODE researchers had published about thirty coordinated papers on 5 September 2012 and called at least 80 percent of the human genome functional, and newspapers had announced the death of junk DNA. What was Graur's objection?
answer: ENCODE counted molecular activity, not the jobs natural selection maintains
choices: ENCODE counted molecular activity, not the jobs natural selection maintains
ENCODE counted activity in cancer cell lines, not in healthy human tissue
ENCODE counted stretches twice, not once, wherever its datasets overlapped
ENCODE counted a sampled slice of the genome, not the whole three billion
context: Graur and five colleagues published in Genome Biology and Evolution in 2013 under the title 'On the Immortality of Television Sets: Function in the Human Genome According to the Evolution-Free Gospel of ENCODE.' Their line: claiming DNA stays functional without selection is like claiming 'a television set left on and unattended will still be in working condition after a million years.' ENCODE later clarified that by functional it had meant biochemical function specifically - observable molecular activity, not evolutionary selection or any proven job - and its 2013-2014 follow-ups adopted a tiered definition. Source: academic.oup.com/gbe/article/5/3/578/583411; nature.com/articles/nature11247

question: A geneticist who wants a number instead of an argument sets the human genome beside other mammals' and hunts for stretches that have stayed nearly unchanged for tens of millions of years. If a stretch has not been allowed to drift, something is holding it in place. A 2014 study did this, and a 2023 analysis compared 240 mammal species. What share of the human genome came out held that way?
answer: Roughly 8 to 11 percent of it
choices: Roughly 8 to 11 percent of it
Roughly 2 to 3 percent of it
Roughly 30 to 35 percent of it
Roughly 60 to 65 percent of it
context: What the studies measured is called purifying selection: mutations that land in a stretch the animal needs get weeded out, while junk drifts freely. The 2014 PLOS Genetics study put the human figure at 8.2%, with a 95% confidence interval of 7.1 to 9.2%; the 2023 comparison of 240 mammal genomes put it at 10.7%, about 332 million bases. Plenty of genuinely functional regulatory DNA exists beyond the protein-coding stretches. How much of the remainder does any job at all, no one yet knows. Source: journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article?id=10.1371/journal.pgen.1004351; grokipedia.com/page/Junk_DNA

question: Tony Blair, joining the White House by satellite in June 2000, called the draft human genome 'a revolution in medical science whose implications far surpass even the discovery of antibiotics.' The first draft cost hundreds of millions of dollars for one person's genome. Today it costs about $600. What has that cheap flood of sequences delivered for diseases caused by a single bad gene?
answer: Gene-therapy cures for fewer than one percent of them
choices: Gene-therapy cures for fewer than one percent of them
Gene-therapy cures for roughly a quarter of them
Gene-therapy cures for roughly two thirds of them
Gene-therapy cures for almost every one of them
context: The cost collapse is real: about $300 million for the first draft, under $1,500 by late 2015, roughly $600 by 2023. The medicine has arrived unevenly. Fewer than 1% of known single-gene (Mendelian) disorders have a gene-therapy cure, and the early SCID trials around 2000 restored immunity to several children only to give them T-cell leukaemia when the inserted virus landed in an oncogene, halting those protocols by 2003. For common diseases, genomics has produced risk statistics rather than cures. Source: genome.gov/about-genomics/fact-sheets/Sequencing-Human-Genome-cost; grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: Alexis Carrel cut a bit from a chick embryo's heart in 1912, dropped it in a flask at the Rockefeller Institute in New York and fed it every day. New York papers marked its birthday every January. About how long did the lab keep it going before quietly ending it?
answer: About thirty-four years
choices: About seven years
About fifteen years
About thirty-four years
About sixty years
context: The Rockefeller Institute maintained Carrel's strain 725 from January 1912 until 1946, roughly thirty-four years, on daily feedings of chick embryo extract. Source: https://www.gothamcenter.org/blog/alessandro-fabbri-the-rockefeller-institute-amp-the-immortal-chicken-heart

question: Alexis Carrel told reporters for over twenty years that his chicken-heart tissue, fed every day, was still alive and growing. He said it proved a very big claim about life itself. What claim did the papers repeat at every birthday?
answer: That cells given enough good food never age at all
choices: That cells given enough good food never age at all
That heart tissue can be moved between different animals
That French surgery was ahead of American surgery
That the chick embryo is the ancestor of every warm-blooded animal
context: Carrel used the culture to promote the view that cellular aging was not intrinsic, only a failure of nutrition and cleanliness. His stature (he had won the 1912 Nobel Prize for vascular surgery) gave the claim decades of authority. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_Carrel

question: Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead published a careful paper in Philadelphia in 1961 on normal human cells kept in a dish. Alexis Carrel had taught that healthy cells in a dish, rightly fed, would divide forever. The paper's result was the opposite. What did those human cells do?
answer: Divided roughly forty to sixty times, then stopped dividing
choices: Kept dividing indefinitely, faster than the chick heart
Divided roughly forty to sixty times, then stopped dividing
Turned into a different cell type after about a year
Died completely within a few weeks in every flask
context: Hayflick and Moorhead reported that normal human diploid cells go through about 40 to 60 population doublings and then enter a state biologists later named replicative senescence: still alive, still respiring, no longer copying themselves. Source: https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/serial-cultivation-human-diploid-cells-lab-1958-1961-leonard-hayflick-and-paul-s-moorhead

question: Paul Moorhead and Leonard Hayflick heard the charge from senior cell biologists: sloppy work, bad feed, dirty glassware, waste piling up. Their answer was one flask no outside excuse could survive. Male cells already at their fortieth doubling sat in the same feed as young female cells at only their fifteenth. Twenty doublings later, only female cells were left. What did that flask prove?
answer: That the counter was inside each cell, not in the shared medium
choices: That female cells outcompete male cells for glucose
That the counter was inside each cell, not in the shared medium
That fibroblasts secrete a poison that kills older neighbors
That cells need a second cell type nearby to keep dividing
context: Because the young and old cells shared everything in the flask, any external explanation (bad food, waste build-up, glass contamination) would have killed both populations together. Instead, each cell type stopped at its own scheduled doubling number. The clock had to be intrinsic. Source: https://gerontology.fandom.com/wiki/Hayflick_limit

question: Leonard Hayflick took up the puzzle of how Alexis Carrel's flask had kept the same chicken heart cells alive for decades, when no one else could get that result. He pointed at the daily feed, made by mashing whole chick embryos. What was his ordinary, unglamorous answer?
answer: The mash carried in fresh living cells that quietly replaced the old ones
choices: The mash carried in fresh living cells that quietly replaced the old ones
The mash contained an unknown hormone that reset the cells' age
Carrel had secretly restarted the culture from a new embryo every year
The chick heart tissue had accidentally become a cancer cell line
context: Hayflick argued that Carrel's chick embryo extract was almost certainly not sterile of cells: each daily feeding smuggled fresh living cells into the flask, so the culture was continuously restocked rather than endlessly self-renewing. The honest historical position is 'never replicated, most likely contaminated,' not 'proven fraud.' Source: https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/7644467B52FB7B4005F25283536B4667/S0025727300040126a.pdf/div-class-title-dr-carrelandapos-s-immortal-cells-a-href-fn01-ref-type-fn-a-div.pdf

question: Alexei Olovnikov went after the limit on cell division in 1971, working from the mechanics of how DNA gets copied. He predicted that a counter had to sit at a specific place on every chromosome, and had to shrink a little every time the chromosome was copied. Which place did he predict?
answer: At the very ends of the chromosome
choices: At the centromere, the pinched middle of the chromosome
At the very ends of the chromosome
At the origins where copying begins
At the nuclear membrane where chromosomes anchor
context: Olovnikov reasoned that the machinery that copies DNA cannot fully copy a linear template all the way to its tip, so a little of each end is lost per division. Sooner or later the end erodes into essential territory and the cell stops dividing. He called the idea marginotomy in 1971; the physical structures he predicted are now called telomeres. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1134/S0006297923110032

question: Carol Greider, a graduate student in Elizabeth Blackburn's Berkeley lab, found an enzyme in a pond ciliate in 1984. Alexei Olovnikov had predicted it in 1971: something must add fresh DNA back, or germ cells and single-celled life would run down and die. It is called telomerase. Which part of the chromosome does it rebuild?
answer: The tip
choices: The tip
The middle
The centromere
The histone core
context: Greider, then a first-year graduate student, ran the assays that identified telomerase in Tetrahymena thermophila in Blackburn's lab; she and Blackburn published the discovery in Cell in 1985. Greider, Blackburn and Jack Szostak shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for telomeres and telomerase. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/onc201015

question: A lab technician feeds a dish of cancer cells, and they keep dividing, long past the limit that stops normal human cells. Most cancers have broken that limit and will divide for as long as they are fed. What trick have these cells done to their own biology to make that possible?
answer: Switched telomerase back on so the chromosome tips get rebuilt
choices: Duplicated all of their chromosomes so there is always a spare
Switched telomerase back on so the chromosome tips get rebuilt
Stopped copying their DNA and started copying only RNA
Turned off their nucleus and split by budding instead
context: In healthy adult somatic tissue telomerase is largely silent, which is why the Hayflick limit exists. Roughly 85-90 percent of human cancers reactivate telomerase so that the chromosome tips are constantly rebuilt; the same mechanism that keeps HeLa cells growing for a lifetime is the mechanism the cell was supposed to keep switched off. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10522-006-9043-9

question: A girl catches measles once, gets better and never catches it again. Her immune system has kept two kinds of long-lived cells that know the virus on sight, ready to crush it within hours. A vaccine trains those same two cells without her getting sick first. What are they called?
answer: Memory B cells and memory T cells
choices: Memory B cells and memory T cells
Naive B cells and naive T cells
Plasmablasts and neutrophils
Regulatory T cells and NK cells
context: This is ordinary textbook immunology, uncontroversial since the mid-twentieth century. Memory B cells rapidly re-secrete antibody on a second encounter; memory T cells recognize protein fragments displayed on infected cells and kill them. Vaccines exist because they can train these two populations without exposing a person to the pathogen. Source: Cell/Immunity review S1074-7613(21)00037-6.

question: A woman recovers from COVID and asks two questions: will she catch it again, and will a second case put her in hospital or worse? A 2023 meta-analysis in the journal The Lancet pooled 65 separate studies from 19 countries and answered each question separately. Forty weeks on, even against the Omicron BA.1 variant, how well did a past infection guard against the serious case?
answer: About 88.9%
choices: About 88.9%
About 40%
About 15%
Essentially zero
context: The meta-analysis reported protection against severe disease of about 88.9% (84.7-90.9) at 40 weeks for Omicron BA.1, and about 90.2% for ancestral, Alpha and Delta; the T-cell arm of adaptive immunity holds up well against severe outcomes even as new variants appear. The other question had a different answer: protection against reinfection at 40 weeks fell to about 36.1% for Omicron BA.1, though it held at about 78.6% for ancestral, Alpha and Delta, because Omicron could slip past earlier immunity, an ability called immune escape. Both results were true at the same time; headlines in both directions reported only one. Source: The Lancet, IHME COVID-19 Forecasting Team, 16 Feb 2023.

question: Staff at the US Centers for Disease Control split California and New York into four groups by shot status and by prior infection, and in January 2022 they published the COVID case rates for May to November 2021. The group with both did best. Two others stood side by side in that autumn's Delta wave: a past infection but no shot, and the shot but no past infection. How did their rates of catching the virus compare?
answer: Past infection alone gave lower case rates than the shot alone
choices: Past infection alone gave lower case rates than the shot alone
The shot alone gave lower case rates than past infection alone
The two groups had almost exactly the same case rates
Both groups' rates matched those of people with neither
context: In the Delta-dominant week of 3 Oct 2021, unvaccinated persons with prior infection had case rates 29.0-fold lower (California) and 14.7-fold lower (New York) than unvaccinated persons without prior infection -- lower than the vaccinated-only cohort in the same weeks. The study covered 1,108,600 incident cases. The hybrid group (vaccinated AND prior infection) was lowest of all. Before Delta took over that summer, the order had run the other way: case rates were higher among survivors of a previous infection than among the vaccinated alone. Source: MMWR 71(4), 28 Jan 2022.

question: A worker hands her employer the record of her recovery from COVID, hoping it will meet a vaccine mandate. A bulletin from the US Centers for Disease Control in January 2022 would set the case rates of people like her beside those of people whose only protection was the shot. Through 2021 and 2022, how much credit did most US mandates give that record?
answer: None; it counted as zero
choices: None; it counted as zero
Half; it counted as one dose
A full course; it counted as complete
More than a full course; it counted as booster-equivalent
context: Prior-infection status was almost universally excluded from mandate compliance in the United States through this period, despite the MMWR and Lancet measurements; the European Union's Digital COVID Certificate, by contrast, accepted a documented recovery for a limited time. The US policy set aside a measured immune status that its own agencies were publishing. Sources: MMWR 71(4), 28 Jan 2022; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EU_Digital_COVID_Certificate.

question: A boy sits on a table edge with one leg hanging loose and taps the tendon just below his kneecap. The leg kicks before he can decide anything. The whole loop takes about eighteen thousandths of a second. Where does the signal actually turn around?
answer: The spinal cord
choices: The spinal cord
The base of the brain
The knee joint itself
The thigh muscle
context: The tap fires a sensory fibre that runs into the cord and comes right back out to the muscle; the brain is out of the loop for the kick itself. StatPearls, Physiology, Deep Tendon Reflexes.

question: A medical student traces the wiring of the knee-jerk in the spinal cord. The sensory fibre from the thigh's stretch sensor comes in low in the back and reaches the motor neuron that fires the thigh muscle. How many synapses, the junctions between nerve cells, sit between the two?
answer: One
choices: One
Three
Six
Twelve
context: This is the classic MONOSYNAPTIC arc; the withdrawal reflex, by contrast, is polysynaptic (multiple interneurons in the middle) and takes noticeably longer. StatPearls, Physiology, Deep Tendon Reflexes.

question: Charles Sherrington, at Cambridge, noticed something elegant hiding inside the knee-jerk. In the same instant the thigh muscle is told to contract, a different muscle is silenced so the two are not fighting. Which muscle goes quiet at the moment the thigh muscle fires?
answer: The hamstring at the back of the thigh
choices: The hamstring at the back of the thigh
The calf muscle at the back of the shin
The gluteus at the top of the hip
The abdominal wall at the front of the belly
context: Muscles can only pull, never push, so a smooth kick needs the puller ON and the opposite puller OFF. Sherrington called this reciprocal innervation and shared the 1932 Nobel for this whole family of discoveries. Oregon State Anatomy 2e.

question: A doctor taps a patient's knee and the kick is barely visible. She asks him to hook his fingers together and pull hard while she taps again, and the leg now kicks briskly. Ernő Jendrassik discovered this trick in the 19th century. What does its success show about the brain's part in the reflex?
answer: The brain cannot cause the kick but can turn its volume up
choices: The brain cannot cause the kick but can turn its volume up
The brain fires the kick directly along a second pathway
The brain overrides the spinal cord to abort the kick
The brain replaces the sensor signal with a stronger one
context: The finger-pull reduces the brainstem's normal damping of the reflex arc, so more motor units fire. It is the loop's volume knob, not its switch. Wikipedia, Jendrassik maneuver.

question: A student flips a fair coin ten times at the kitchen table and counts the heads, then works out the same test with a thousand flips. Which outcome is fairly common in the short run but essentially never seen in the long one?
answer: Landing 80 percent heads or more
choices: Landing 80 percent heads or more
Landing exactly half heads
Landing at least one tail
Landing more heads than tails
context: In ten flips, roughly one run in eighteen lands eight or more heads by pure chance; in a thousand flips, 800 or more heads essentially never happens. That is the whole law of small numbers in one demonstration -- small samples do not merely carry more error, they manufacture extremes at both ends. Elementary binomial probability; illustrated in Kahneman, 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' Ch. 10.

question: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky put a puzzle to their colleagues. A town has two hospitals: about 45 babies are born each day in the larger one and about 15 in the smaller one. Over a year, which hospital would record more days on which over 60 percent of the babies were boys?
answer: The smaller hospital
choices: The smaller hospital
The larger hospital
About the same in each
Cannot be determined without more data
context: 56 percent of the responding psychologists answered 'about the same'. The correct answer is the smaller hospital, and it is not close: with only 15 births in a day the daily proportion of boys wanders much further from 50 percent than it does with 45. Tversky & Kahneman 1971, Psychological Bulletin.

question: Howard Wainer and Harris Zwerling mapped kidney-cancer rates across the roughly 3,141 US counties. The counties with the lowest rates were rural and mostly in the Midwest, South and West -- and so were the counties with the highest rates. What actually produces that puzzling map?
answer: The extreme counties simply have very few people in them
choices: The extreme counties simply have very few people in them
Regression to the mean pulled the extreme counties back in
Simpson's paradox reversed the direction inside each county
Selection bias dropped the middle counties from the survey
context: Rural life cannot cause and prevent the same cancer. Rural counties simply have small populations, and small samples yield extreme results in both directions more often than large samples. Regression to the mean, Simpson's paradox and selection bias are real statistical ideas, but none is what is happening here. Kahneman, 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' Ch. 10, citing Wainer & Zwerling.

question: Harris Zwerling and Howard Wainer looked at 1,662 Pennsylvania schools. The best-performing fifty were heavily made up of small schools, and school reformers rushed to fund small schools on that basis. Where else on the same list were small schools showing up in unusual numbers?
answer: Among the worst-performing fifty schools
choices: Among the worst-performing fifty schools
Among the schools that had recently expanded
Among the schools with the most experienced staff
Among the schools in the wealthiest districts
context: Small schools were over-represented in the bottom fifty by a factor of six. Small schools are not better on average; they are simply more variable, and the reformers had ranked them by an unstable measure and read that instability as merit. Wainer & Zwerling, 'Evidence That Smaller Schools Do Not Improve Student Achievement'.

question: One American donor poured huge money into building small schools, sometimes by splitting big ones apart, on the very ranking pattern that Howard Wainer and Harris Zwerling later showed to be the noise of tiny samples. Which donor was it?
answer: The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
choices: The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
The Ford Foundation
The Rockefeller Foundation
The Carnegie Corporation of New York
context: Kahneman names the Gates Foundation in 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' Ch. 10 as the funder that acted on the small-schools ranking.

question: Jacob Cohen surveyed studies in a leading psychology journal in 1962 and reported a median statistical power, the odds of catching a real effect, of about 0.46 for a medium effect. Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer repeated the exercise across 1960 to 1987. Which way had the figure moved?
answer: It had dropped, to about 0.37
choices: It had dropped, to about 0.37
It had risen, to about 0.60
It had held roughly steady at 0.46
It had risen sharply, to about 0.80
context: Sedlmeier & Gigerenzer 1989, 'Do Studies of Statistical Power Have an Effect on the Power of Studies?' Twenty-four years after Cohen's diagnosis, more than half of real medium effects were still being missed by underpowered studies -- and the field had not corrected.

question: Katherine Button, John Ioannidis and their coworkers went through a stack of published brain-science studies in 2013 and measured each one's statistical power, the odds a study will catch a real effect if one is really there. The typical study came in at just 8 to 31 percent. In such a weak field, why does the average published effect end up bigger than the true one?
answer: Only results that chance pushed too far clear significance
choices: Only results that chance pushed too far clear significance
Reviewers prefer studies whose effects match prior findings
Authors round their reported effects up before submission
Journals publish only the largest study of each hypothesis
context: This is called the winner's curse. When power is low the only findings that reach the significance bar are the ones a lucky sample happened to inflate, so the published record is a filtered gallery of over-estimates. Button et al., 'Power failure: why small sample size undermines the reliability of neuroscience', Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2013.

question: American state legislators voted through the world's first compulsory sterilization law in 1907, in a normal democratic session. It let officials force certain people, judged 'unfit' to have children, to be sterilized against their will. There was no dictator and no foreign regime. Which US state passed it?
answer: Indiana
choices: Indiana
Georgia
Vermont
Nevada
context: Governor J. Frank Hanly signed the law on April 12, 1907, letting superintendents of state prisons and asylums sterilize inmates judged criminal, insane, or 'imbecilic.' More than thirty US states and about a dozen foreign countries later followed. Sources: Indiana Historical Bureau, in.gov/history/state-historical-markers; uvm.edu/~lkaelber/eugenics/.

question: An asylum superintendent judged an inmate 'unfit' to reproduce and had her sterilized, under one of the laws about thirty US states had on the books by the 1930s. Over all the decades these laws ran, about how many Americans were sterilized under them?
context: About two-thirds of those sterilized were women. Historians give a range rather than a precise total because state records varied in quality and completeness. Sweden's parallel welfare-state program sterilized a similar number -- about 62,000 -- from 1934 to 1976. Sources: The Conversation on forced-sterilization policies; uvm.edu/~lkaelber/eugenics/.

question: A student adds up the records of one American state: about 20,000 people cut, from 1909 all the way to 1979, with judges and doctors deciding who was 'unfit' to have children. That was roughly a third of the country's total, by far the biggest program of any state, and it ran in one of the most modern, progressive and science-friendly states of that era. Which state ran the program?
answer: California
choices: California
Illinois
New York
Massachusetts
context: California's program, authorized in 1909, sterilized patients in state hospitals for the 'feebleminded' and 'insane.' California was the third US state to pass such a law, after Indiana and Washington. Sources: Wikipedia, Eugenics in California; Foundation for Economic Education.

question: A student opens the record of North Carolina's Eugenics Board: about 7,600 forced sterilizations ordered between 1929 and 1974, each citizen judged on an IQ score and a social history. Many people assume such programmes faded after Nazi eugenics was exposed at Nuremberg in 1946. Compared with its pre-1945 work, what did the board actually do after the Second World War?
answer: It did more of its work after 1945 than before
choices: It did most of its work before 1945 and tapered off sharply after
It did roughly the same amount of work in each period
It did more of its work after 1945 than before
It did about a quarter of its work after 1945
context: This is the fact that breaks the comfortable story that Nazi revelations ended American eugenics. North Carolina's Board reviewed cases on IQ scores and social histories for nearly three more decades after the war. Source: NPR, 2013 coverage of NC compensation program.

question: The members of one American state's eugenics board ordered their last forced sterilization in 1981. Most states had shut down such panels by the 1970s, and this one, which judged citizens 'unfit' to have children, hung on longer than any other. It was not officially abolished until 1983. Which American state was it?
answer: Oregon
choices: Oregon
Alabama
Utah
Kansas
context: Oregon's State Board of Eugenics, created in 1917, was later renamed the Board of Social Protection. Then-Senator John Kitzhaber -- a physician who later became governor -- helped write the 1983 repeal. Sources: Arizona State Embryo Project; Oregon Encyclopedia.

question: A woman sterilized as 'unfit' under one of America's state laws reads Virginia's formal apology, the first from any US state government. Roughly 30 states had passed such laws in the first half of the 1900s, against the poor, the disabled, immigrants and unmarried mothers. The biggest program did not shut down until 1979. About how long after that did the first apology come?
answer: About 25 years later
choices: About 25 years later
Within the same year
About 5 years later
About 40 years later
context: Governor Mark Warner apologized in May 2002; Oregon Governor John Kitzhaber followed the same year, and California's Gray Davis apologized in 2003. In 2013 North Carolina became the first state to actually pay living victims -- a $10 million fund. Sources: UPI, May 2002; WUNC 2014.

question: Jonas Herby, Lars Jonung and Steve Hanke went back in 2022 through the government lockdowns of spring 2020, when whole countries were ordered to stay home in the hope of stopping COVID-19. They asked one narrow, checkable question about the entire effort. What was that question?
answer: by how much did they reduce COVID-19 deaths
choices: by how much did they reduce COVID-19 deaths
how much did they cost taxpayers
how did they affect mental health
how well were the rules obeyed
context: The narrow, quantitative framing is what made the whole project auditable; cost, mental health and compliance are real research questions too, but the three measured only deaths. Their paper is explicit that this is the BENEFIT side of a cost-benefit question - the other side was not their subject. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: Lars Jonung and his two co-authors set one strict rule for which studies of the spring 2020 lockdowns their meta-analysis would count. Under that rule even Imperial College London's famous Report 9 had to go. What kind of study did the rule exclude?
answer: Any study built on a computer simulation of the spread
choices: Any study built on a computer simulation of the spread
Any study written before the lockdowns had ended
Any study paid for by a government health agency
Any study counting deaths outside of hospitals
context: The rule was a design rule: they kept only studies using difference-in-differences, which compare the change in one group before and after a policy against the change in a comparison group that never got the policy, so any common time-trend drops out and only the policy effect remains. That excluded every study whose counterfactual was a model output - Imperial College's Report 9 among them. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: Public health officials had promised that the lockdowns of spring 2020 would slash COVID-19 deaths. Jonas Herby, Lars Jonung and Steve Hanke tallied every study using the Oxford stringency index for a meta-analysis in the journal Public Choice in November 2024. By how much did they find the lockdowns had actually cut deaths?
context: Their second, upper-bound estimate - built from nine specific interventions such as school closures and business closures - came out at 10.7 percent. Both numbers are on the low end of what supporters of mandates argued in 2020; both are far from zero. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice 203 (2025), 337-367, published online November 2024.

question: Jonas Herby and his co-authors turned their estimate into people: roughly 6,000 avoided COVID-19 deaths across Europe and 4,000 across the United States by 30 June 2020. To give a reader a scale, they set those figures against another annual cause of death the reader already knows. Which one?
answer: seasonal influenza
choices: seasonal influenza
road traffic accidents
lung cancer
heart disease
context: Ordinary-year influenza kills roughly 72,000 people in Europe and 38,000 in the United States, so the estimated benefit of the average spring-2020 lockdown came to about a twelfth of a year's flu deaths in Europe and about a tenth in the United States. The flu figures are the authors' own; a number without a scale is not information. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: Lars Jonung, Jonas Herby and Steve Hanke took a second pass at their question in the journal Public Choice in 2024. Their January 2022 working paper, on very similar data, had reported an average mortality reduction of 0.2 percent. How did their own headline number move between the two papers?
answer: upward by more than an order of magnitude
choices: upward by more than an order of magnitude
upward within statistical noise
downward to almost zero
downward into negative territory
context: 3.2 / 0.2 = 16, so more than an order of magnitude - and in the direction of admitting more benefit from the very policies the authors had publicly criticised. The revision is the best part of this story: same three authors, same question, refined method, published under their own names in a peer-reviewed journal. That is what self-correction looks like when nobody made anyone do it. Source: Herby-Hanke Johns Hopkins working paper (Jan 2022); Herby-Jonung-Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: Seth Flaxman and colleagues at Imperial College published the best-known estimate on the other side of the lockdown debate in Nature in June 2020, modelling 11 European countries. Through early May 2020, roughly how many deaths did they say the lockdown steps had prevented?
answer: 3.1 million
choices: 3.1 million
6 million
1.3 million
context: The Flaxman paper's central estimate was 3.1 million averted deaths across 11 European countries (95% credible interval 2.8-3.5 million). The Herby-Jonung-Hanke number for Europe was in the thousands. Both belong in the record; a record that hides the strongest opposing estimate has argued instead of taught. Source: Flaxman et al., Nature (2020).

question: Steve Hanke and his co-authors went through the whole pile of studies and found that the spring 2020 lockdowns had cut COVID-19 deaths by far less than officials had promised. Their own reading of that finding is not that nothing worked. They argue that something other than the government mandates did most of the real mitigation work. What was it?
answer: voluntary behaviour change
choices: voluntary behaviour change
warmer spring weather
prior natural immunity
faster hospital care
context: Their point is that when a virus becomes visible and dangerous, people change what they do - stop shaking hands, stop crowding indoors, avoid the sick - before and after any order tells them to; that voluntary shift shows up in the data. The finding is that the mandates added less than promised, not that the virus was mild. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: Jonas Herby, Lars Jonung and Steve Hanke wrote explicitly that their meta-analysis of COVID-19 lockdowns measures only one side of a two-sided question. They are careful about the limits of what it says. Which side?
answer: the benefit side only
choices: the benefit side only
the cost side only
both benefit and cost
the compliance side only
context: The costs - lost schooling, mental-health harm, business collapse, deferred cancer diagnoses, elderly people dying alone - were left for other researchers to measure. The paper's honest self-limitation is what lets it work as evidence rather than advocacy: it says what was measured and what was not, and gives a number a reader can check. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: Captain Sampson of the ship Norham Castle heard the volcano Krakatoa explode on the morning of 27 August 1883, about 40 miles away. When the shock wave hit his ship, he took up his log and wrote a single blunt line about the state of his crew. What did he report?
answer: the eardrums of over half the men aboard had been shattered clean by the noise
choices: the eardrums of over half the men aboard had been shattered clean by the noise
the men on watch had been thrown flat to the deck and could not stand for an hour
the helmsman had gone momentarily blind from the flash over the water
the cook and half the galley crew had been scalded by kettles thrown from the stove
context: Captain Sampson's log line, quoted in the contemporary Royal Society report: 'So violent are the explosions that the ear-drums of over half my crew have been shattered.' The Norham Castle was about 64 km (40 miles) from Krakatoa. Source: classicfm.com summary of Royal Society of London's 1888 report on the Krakatoa eruption.

question: A student reading about the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, heard across a fifth of the planet, finds it put at around 172 decibels and asks how anyone could know. No microphone that good existed yet. What tool at a gasworks in Batavia (now Jakarta), about 160 km away, really made that famous reading?
answer: a barometer, which registered a pressure spike of more than 2.5 inches of mercury
choices: a barometer, which registered a pressure spike of more than 2.5 inches of mercury
a seismograph, which registered ground displacement of more than 2.5 centimetres
a thermograph, which registered a spike of more than 2.5 degrees above ambient
an anemometer, which registered a wind gust of more than 2.5 times the daily average
context: The Batavia (now Jakarta) gasworks gauge spiked by more than 2.5 inches of mercury (about 8.5 kilopascals). Converting that pressure amplitude into a sound-pressure level at that distance gives roughly 172 dB. The '172 dB' number is therefore inferred from a pressure record, not measured as sound. Source: Nautilus, 'The Sound So Loud That It Circled the Earth Four Times.'

question: A physicist reads a viral internet post that lists the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa at '310 decibels.' That number cannot be right in principle, she says, because in ordinary air at sea level a sound wave tops out near 194 decibels. Why does the ceiling sit right there and not somewhere higher?
answer: at that amplitude the low-pressure half of the wave has already been pulled down to a vacuum
choices: at that amplitude the low-pressure half of the wave has already been pulled down to a vacuum
at that amplitude the wave breaks up the oxygen molecules and stops carrying any pressure at all
at that amplitude the wave heats the air enough to change the speed of sound and cancel itself
at that amplitude the wave saturates the human eardrum, which is what sets the top of the scale
context: A sound wave in air swings symmetrically around atmospheric pressure. The compression half can climb indefinitely, but the rarefaction half has a hard floor at zero pressure (a vacuum). At about 194 dB at sea level the rarefaction has reached that floor. Anything more energetic is no longer a sound wave; it is a blast wave, an asymmetric pressure jump moving faster than sound. The '310 dB' figure has no measurement behind it and could not describe a sound wave in sea-level air. Source: ScienceABC, 'What's the Loudest Sound Possible on Earth?'

question: A weather observer far from Krakatoa checks his barograph, an instrument that continuously records air pressure, in the days after the blast of 27 August 1883. By now the pressure wave has dropped below the roughly 20 Hz floor of human hearing and stopped being audible sound. But the barograph has caught it doing something remarkable. What does it record the wave doing?
answer: passing seven times as it travelled back and forth around the planet
choices: passing seven times as it travelled back and forth around the planet
reflecting off the base of the stratosphere and fading within a few hours
splitting into two waves that never rejoined and reached each pole separately
dying out at the first major mountain range it met and going no further
context: Beyond a few thousand kilometres the pressure disturbance dropped below the roughly 20 Hz threshold of human hearing and continued as infrasound. Weather-station barographs on several continents registered the pulse passing seven times over about five days as it circled the Earth (three and a half round trips). The same worldwide infrasound listening idea is what the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organisation now uses to catch clandestine nuclear tests. Sources: Nautilus, 'The Sound So Loud That It Circled the Earth Four Times'; historyfacts.com.

question: An editor from the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) sits down at a private meeting of the Trusted News Initiative, launched in 2019. Around the table are people from Reuters, the Associated Press (AP), Agence France-Presse (AFP) and the Washington Post. Which other kind of group was also a founding partner?
answer: The technology platforms that distributed the news
choices: The technology platforms that distributed the news
The national broadcast regulators in each member country
The universities that trained the members' journalists
The professional associations that certified those journalists
context: Google, YouTube, Facebook, Microsoft and Twitter joined the news outlets as founding partners -- the publishers and their distribution channels agreeing together about what would spread. That is the fact that makes the alliance recognisable as a piece of machinery rather than an ordinary press body. The alliance grew out of a June 2019 summit chaired by then-BBC director-general Tony Hall and was directed by BBC executive Jessica Cecil. Sources: Wikipedia 'Trusted News Initiative'; Influence Watch entry for TNI; Reuters Institute biography of Jessica Cecil.

question: The members of the Trusted News Initiative formally extended the alliance's remit to a new subject on 27 March 2020. The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) had set up the pact in 2019 to co-ordinate against what its members call 'disinformation', beginning with elections. Which subject did they add?
answer: COVID-19 information
choices: COVID-19 information
Anti-vaccine content on childhood immunisation
Climate change reporting
Deepfake video detection
context: The TNI had been founded in September 2019 to coordinate against election disinformation. The 27 March 2020 announcement pulled COVID-19 into the alliance's scope, and in July 2020 a second extension anticipated the US presidential election. Sources: Wikipedia 'Trusted News Initiative'; EBU announcement, July 2020.

question: Robert F. Kennedy Jr and Children's Health Defense sued the Associated Press, the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), Reuters and the Washington Post in January 2023 over the Trusted News Initiative. They filed not under free-speech law but under a different area of law. The suit stands as a claim, not a finding. Which area of law?
answer: Antitrust law, under Section 1 of the Sherman Act
choices: Antitrust law, under Section 1 of the Sherman Act
Consumer protection law, under the Lanham Act
Broadcast law, under the Communications Act
Election law, under the Federal Election Campaign Act
context: The theory is that competitors had agreed among themselves to suppress rival publishers -- a boycott. That is a filed claim, not a proven finding. In July 2025 the US Department of Justice Antitrust Division filed a 22-page Statement of Interest supporting the plaintiffs, arguing that antitrust law does play a part in protecting viewpoint competition in news markets. Sources: Bloomberg Law; Politico Pro, July 2025.

question: Alejandro Mayorkas, the US Homeland Security secretary, told a House committee on 27 April 2022 that he was setting up a brand-new working group. It was meant to help the federal government with one job. In plain terms, what job was it going to do?
answer: Helping judge which online claims were true or false
choices: Helping judge which online claims were true or false
Defending computer networks from foreign hackers
Investigating cross-border smuggling cases
Coordinating federal disaster relief
context: The board had no enforcement authority -- it was an internal coordinating working group inside DHS -- but its name, remit and choice of director drew immediate objection across the political spectrum. Sources: CBS News, May 2022; Wikipedia 'Nina Jankowicz'.

question: Critics from across the political spectrum called Alejandro Mayorkas's new working group, the Disinformation Governance Board, a 'Ministry of Truth' after he set it up on 27 April 2022. Its director quit, and the board was paused on 18 May 2022. What happened to the board within about four months of its launch?
answer: It was shut down
choices: It was shut down
It was greatly expanded
It was moved into the FBI
It was made permanent by Congress
context: The Homeland Security Advisory Council, co-chaired for this review by former DHS Secretary Michael Chertoff and former Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick, unanimously recommended dissolution. This is the honest end of the story: the machinery was stopped in public, by ordinary argument, in under four months -- and the ordinary body that stopped it is worth knowing by name. Sources: CNN, August 2022; First Amendment Encyclopedia (MTSU).

question: Paul Ehrlich watched a laboratory dye soak into one kind of cell under his microscope in late-1800s Berlin and leave the neighbouring cell untouched. A chemical that picks one cell out of a smear, he reasoned, might also pick out invaders inside the body. What did he name the drug he imagined?
answer: A magic bullet -- Zauberkugel in his German
choices: A magic bullet -- Zauberkugel in his German
An antitoxin -- like the diphtheria serum
A vaccine -- like Jenner's smallpox jab
An antiseptic -- like Lister's carbolic
context: Ehrlich called the goal a Zauberkugel -- 'magic bullet' -- and coined the word chemotherapy for the systematic chemical hunt that would try to find one. Source: https://centennial.rucares.org/index.php?page=Chemotherapy

question: Paul Ehrlich's Frankfurt laboratory made Compound 606 in 1907, the 606th of its numbered arsenic compounds, and set it aside on the shelf as a failure. It would one day be sold as Salvarsan against the deadly disease syphilis, but it was almost thrown away. What eventually rescued it?
answer: Sahachiro Hata retested it two years later at Ehrlich's insistence
choices: Sahachiro Hata retested it two years later at Ehrlich's insistence
Alfred Bertheim spilled it onto a rabbit that was infected anyway
Emil von Behring re-synthesised it and got the credit for the cure
Robert Koch retested it in Berlin and vouched for its safety
context: Ehrlich's Japanese bacteriologist Sahachiro Hata reran the test with more care and better records; the drug that had been called useless turned out to be the first real chemical cure. A 'negative result' can be a badly run test. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsphenamine

question: Gerhard Domagk gave one group of mice a red dye called Prontosil at Bayer in Germany in late December 1932, then hit both that group and an untreated control group with a dose of streptococcus known to kill mice reliably. When he opened the cages on Christmas Eve, what did he find?
answer: Every treated mouse alive; every untreated mouse dead
choices: Every treated mouse alive; every untreated mouse dead
Roughly half of each group survived, no clear difference
Every mouse in both groups dead by the second day
Only the untreated mice alive; the dye had killed the treated ones
context: Twelve mice given Prontosil all survived; fourteen untreated mice all died. Domagk began the run on 20 December 1932 and read it out on 24 December. Prontosil went on to save many lives from childbed fever, wound infections, and pneumonia -- years before penicillin was available in quantity. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/gerhard-domagk/

question: French chemists at the Pasteur Institute in Paris took up Prontosil in 1935 and 1936, the red dye the German company Bayer had shown could cure deadly streptococcus infections in mice. They compared how it behaved in a glass test tube with how it behaved inside a live animal, and one strange result would not go away. What did the red dye actually do in the test tube?
answer: Nothing -- it killed no bacteria at all in glassware
choices: Nothing -- it killed no bacteria at all in glassware
It killed streptococcus even faster than in the body
It turned the water pink but left the bacteria growing
It refused to dissolve in anything except living blood
context: Prontosil worked only inside a body. Jacques and Therese Trefouel and their team showed the animal splits the dye, releasing a smaller, colourless half -- sulfanilamide, a molecule already known and unpatentable -- which is the real antibiotic. If Domagk had screened in glassware, as was cheaper and standard, he would have thrown the winner away. Source: https://www.chm.bris.ac.uk/motm/sulfanilamide/sulfanilh.html

question: Gerhard Domagk won the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for showing that a red dye called Prontosil could cure deadly bacterial infections, but he would not collect his medal until 1947. What kept him from accepting the prize in 1939?
answer: The Gestapo arrested him and forced him to sign a refusal
choices: The Gestapo arrested him and forced him to sign a refusal
He himself judged the discovery too small for the honour
The Second World War had closed the Swedish border
The Nobel Committee had asked him to test the drug for another year
context: Hitler had forbidden any German to accept a Nobel Prize after the 1936 Peace Prize went to the concentration-camp prisoner Carl von Ossietzky. Domagk received his medal in 1947, though the prize money had by then been forfeit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_controversies

question: Ghirardi, Rimini and Weber added a real, mass-dependent breakdown of superposition to the equations of quantum mechanics in 1986, and Diósi and Penrose's gravity-driven proposal does the same. So they predict something the interpretations do not. What does that mean for their status today?
answer: some of their parameter ranges have already been ruled out by experiment
choices: some of their parameter ranges have already been ruled out by experiment
they were confirmed together by the 2015 loophole-free Bell tests in Delft
they were shown mathematically equivalent to many-worlds by a 2003 proof
they were withdrawn by their own authors after the 2020 underground results
context: Because objective-collapse theories predict a real, spontaneous breakdown of superposition, they leave a signature: a tiny radiation from charged particles as their wave functions collapse. Underground low-background searches published in 2020-2021 ruled out the simplest parameter-free version of the Diosi-Penrose gravity-driven collapse; matter-wave interference with heavier and heavier molecules continues to squeeze GRW-type parameters. A question that sounded like pure metaphysics turned into an experimental programme with a budget. Source: Quanta, 'Physics Experiments Spell Doom for Quantum Collapse Theory' (2022).

question: Charles d'Eslon secretly magnetised one tree in a garden at Passy in 1784, for a royal commission testing a healer's claim that an unseen force could flow from special objects into people. A blindfolded boy was led out to hug tree after tree. At which tree did he swoon?
answer: At the fourth tree, none of which had been touched
choices: At the treated tree, on his first try
At the fourth tree, none of which had been touched
At the second tree, which had been treated
At no tree at all, and the test was called off
context: In the Passy orchard trial, d'Eslon magnetized one tree and had a boy said to be sensitive to the force blindfolded and led to embrace trees one by one. The boy collapsed at the fourth tree, which had not been touched at all -- the belief did the work, not the fluid. Source: https://www.fibonaccimd.com/post/mesmer-frankin-mesmerism-placebos

question: Franz Mesmer, a Vienna-born doctor, set an oak tub, the baquet, in his Paris salon, with iron rods poking out of it. Patients gripped the rods while music played, and fell into fits. What did he say the tub moved through them?
answer: An invisible fluid he called animal magnetism
choices: The four humours of ancient Greek medicine
An invisible fluid he called animal magnetism
Nervous energy passed from one patient to the next
Blood, warmed and thinned by the tub
context: Mesmer taught that an invisible universal fluid he called animal magnetism flowed between all bodies; illness came when it dammed up. The word 'animal' meant living, not beasts -- from Latin anima, breath or soul -- to mark it off from ordinary iron magnets. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Mesmer

question: King Louis XVI grew tired of the mesmerist craze sweeping through his royal court in the spring of 1784 and named an official commission to test the doctrine. Its most famous member was the seventy-eight-year-old American ambassador, whose Passy house and garden hosted many of the trials. Who was this ambassador?
answer: Benjamin Franklin
choices: Thomas Jefferson
Benjamin Franklin
John Adams
John Jay
context: Franklin, then 78 and America's minister to France, was too weak from gout and a bladder stone to travel from Passy into Paris, so the commissioners held many of the trials at his own house and orchard. He is the reason the joint royal commissions are usually called the Franklin Commission. Source: https://benjaminfranklinhouse.org/benjamin-franklin-and-the-glass-armonica/

question: Franz Mesmer refused to have anything to do with the commissioners, so they tested the doctrine on the patients of his best-known Paris disciple, the court physician Charles d'Eslon. That switch strengthened the test. Why?
answer: The subjects were already believers, so a null result could not be blamed on stacked patients
choices: The subjects were already believers, so a null result could not be blamed on stacked patients
D'Eslon was known to be a fraud, so the trial would expose the trick
D'Eslon owned a baquet larger than Mesmer's, so more patients could be tested at once
The court paid d'Eslon well, so his cooperation cost the commissioners nothing
context: Because Mesmer cut off contact and d'Eslon offered his practice, the commissioners tested the doctrine on a believer's own patients -- people convinced the force was real. If the tests failed even there, no one could say the subjects had been picked to fail. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Commission_on_Animal_Magnetism

question: The American ambassador on the royal commission knew the eerie music at Franz Mesmer's Paris sessions. It floated over the sick patients from an unearthly-toned instrument, spun by a foot pedal. Why did he know it so well?
answer: He had invented that very instrument, the glass armonica
choices: He had commissioned Mozart to write pieces for it
He had invented that very instrument, the glass armonica
He had shipped one to Paris as a gift for Queen Marie Antoinette
He had heard it years earlier at a court in Vienna
context: Franklin invented the glass armonica in 1761, and its world premiere came in 1762; it became so popular that Mozart wrote for it, and Mesmer used its unearthly sound to help bring on the convulsive crises his patients treated as their cure. Source: https://benjaminfranklinhouse.org/benjamin-franklin-and-the-glass-armonica/

question: The commissioners printed some 20,000 copies of their public report in August 1784, and it found no sign of Franz Mesmer's fluid. But they were careful about the sufferers: the crises were real and worth explaining, they said, and they traced them to a single cause. Which cause did they name?
answer: The imagination of the patients themselves
choices: Fraud, deliberately staged by the mesmerists
A subtle drug added to the water in the baquet
A form of contagious hysteria unique to women
The imagination of the patients themselves
context: The August 1784 Rapport blamed the crises on imagination and imitation, not fraud or a hidden drug. This is the passage most historians treat as the first scientific description of what modern medicine calls the placebo effect. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Commission_on_Animal_Magnetism

question: A chemistry teacher sets a small silvery ingot on a student's warm palm. In about a minute the ingot has turned into a shining puddle running between the fingers. The metal's melting point is 29.76 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature - no other common metal is that easy to melt. Which metal is it?
answer: Gallium
choices: Gallium
Caesium
Indium
Tin
context: Gallium (element 31) melts at 29.76 C. Caesium melts even lower (28.5 C) but reacts violently with skin moisture and cannot be safely held; indium melts at 156 C, tin at 232 C. Source: Wikipedia, Gallium.

question: A chemist holds a beaker full of liquid gallium, the soft silvery metal that melts on a warm palm at about 30 degrees Celsius, and drops a small frozen chunk of the same metal into it. The outcome is what makes gallium unusual among the metals. What happens to the chunk?
answer: It floats on the surface
choices: It floats on the surface
It sinks straight to the bottom
It dissolves back into the liquid within seconds
It shatters into brittle silver crumbs
context: Gallium expands as it freezes, like water, so the solid is less dense than the liquid and floats. Only a handful of substances behave this way (bismuth and antimony are two other metals that do). Source: Wikipedia, Gallium.

question: A student lets a bead of gallium melt on her palm at 29.76 degrees Celsius. That is only one end of the metal's span. What is astonishing about the other end, the temperature at which gallium finally boils?
answer: It boils above 2,200 degrees Celsius, an enormous liquid range
choices: It boils above 2,200 degrees Celsius, an enormous liquid range
It boils at just above 100 degrees Celsius, like water
It boils around 357 degrees Celsius, the same as mercury
It skips liquid boiling and sublimates directly to a vapour
context: Almost nothing else stays liquid across so vast a span (roughly 2,000 degrees). This is why sealed quartz thermometers filled with gallium can read the interior of a furnace or a molten-metal bath, up to about 1,500 C, where a mercury thermometer would have boiled away centuries ago. Source: Wikipedia, Gallium; RSC Periodic Table.

question: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran was examining zinc ore from the Pyrenees in August 1875 when, within an hour, he became sure he had found a new element. He later named it gallium. What was the specific evidence that convinced him on the spot?
answer: Two violet lines in his spectroscope
choices: Two violet lines in his spectroscope
A grey powder left behind after roasting the ore
A magnet lifting silvery grains out of the ore
A vivid crimson flame in his Bunsen burner
context: Every element gives a unique fingerprint of coloured lines when its atoms are excited. Lecoq had built one of the best spectroscopes in France; the two violet lines belonged to no known element. He then isolated the metal itself by electrolysis. Source: Wikipedia, Gallium; Linda Hall Library biography of Lecoq de Boisbaudran.

question: In a materials lab a technician leaves a single droplet of liquid gallium on the edge of a heavy aluminium workbench overnight. The next morning the bench edge crumbles when he grips it, though nothing has burned and no visible pool of metal has formed. At the atomic scale, what has the gallium actually done to the aluminium?
answer: Seeped along the grain boundaries and destroyed the cohesion between the aluminium crystals
choices: Seeped along the grain boundaries and destroyed the cohesion between the aluminium crystals
Melted the aluminium into a soft gallium-aluminium alloy across the whole bench
Oxidised the surface layer, so the outer skin flaked away and exposed weaker metal beneath
Lowered the surface tension of the protective oxide, letting cracks propagate freely
context: Metallurgists call what just happened liquid metal embrittlement.
