Gallium atoms are small and mobile enough to diffuse into the microscopic seams between aluminium's crystal grains; once the grains no longer stick to each other, the bulk metal loses its strength while looking almost unchanged. Hydrogen embrittlement is a real cousin (hydrogen atoms doing something similar in steels). Source: PMC11901249 (2025 EBSD study of Al after Ga embrittlement); Wikipedia, Gallium.

question: A chemistry lecturer sets gallium on her warm palm and lets it melt at 29.76 degrees Celsius, but she would never do that with caesium, another soft silvery metal, though it melts lower still, at 28.5 degrees. What is the specific reason caesium cannot be held on bare skin?
answer: It reacts violently with the moisture on human skin
choices: It reacts violently with the moisture on human skin
It stains the skin a bright indelible yellow for months
It is one of the rarest metals on Earth and too costly to waste
Its liquid is opaque black and hides the melting moment entirely
context: Caesium is an alkali metal, one row below rubidium; even trace water on skin sets off a vigorous exothermic reaction that would burn the hand. Rubidium (melts at 39 C) has the same problem. Gallium, by contrast, is a post-transition metal that shrugs off skin moisture, which is why it, and not caesium, became the classic melts-in-your-hand demonstration. Source: Wikipedia, Caesium; Wikipedia, Gallium.

question: Kent Ford and Vera Rubin asked a simple question about Andromeda around 1970: how fast do its outer stars move? Around the Sun, Mercury zips fast and Neptune crawls, because gravity gets weaker far out. What did the outer stars of Andromeda do?
answer: orbited just as fast as the inner ones
choices: orbited just as fast as the inner ones
spiralled slowly inward toward the centre
orbited far slower, matching the Neptune pattern
drifted outward and escaped the galaxy
context: Rubin and Ford's 1970 paper 'Rotation of the Andromeda Nebula from a Spectroscopic Survey of Emission Regions' (Astrophysical Journal 159:379) plotted a rotation curve that stayed FLAT out to the visible edge. In a solar-system Kepler pattern the outer objects fall off. Andromeda's outskirts behaved like outer horses on a carousel keeping pace with the inner ones -- a hint that unseen mass was tugging them along. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_Rubin ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve

question: Vera Rubin walked into Palomar Observatory in 1965, the first woman ever given telescope time there, and saw there was no women's restroom at all: just a men's-room door with a painted man on it. What did she do?
answer: cut a paper skirt and taped it onto the stick figure
choices: cut a paper skirt and taped it onto the stick figure
insisted the observatory build a new restroom that night
held her observing run out in the parking lot
shared the men's restroom without saying a word
context: Rubin told the story herself; it is one of the more-told anecdotes in twentieth-century American astronomy. She got her observations. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_Rubin

question: Fritz Zwicky clocked the galaxies of the Coma Cluster in 1933 and worked out, with the virial theorem, that the cluster held some 400 times more mass than its glowing matter showed. Modern measurements still find hidden mass there, but far less. What had inflated Zwicky's figure?
answer: A value of the Hubble constant far too large
choices: A value of the Hubble constant far too large
Milky Way stars mistaken for cluster members
A slipped decimal point in his own arithmetic
Dim gas clouds counted as extra galaxies
context: Zwicky's paper 'Die Rotverschiebung von extragalaktischen Nebeln' appeared in Helvetica Physica Acta 6:110-127, and he called the missing stuff 'dunkle Materie', dark matter. His estimates were off by more than an order of magnitude, mainly because the era's value of the Hubble constant was much too large; modern Coma numbers put the mass-to-light ratio far lower (around 30 solar units, up to a few hundred by some estimates). The missing-mass problem itself is real. Jan Oort had hinted at unseen mass in the Milky Way disk in 1932. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter ; https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/Biviano/Biviano3_3.html

question: Fritz Zwicky saw his 1933 claim of missing mass sit mostly unused for about forty years: not proven wrong, not accepted, just ignored. In the 1970s a new kind of look forced astronomers to take the idea seriously. What kind of measurement did the trick?
answer: flat rotation curves of spiral galaxies
choices: flat rotation curves of spiral galaxies
the cosmic microwave background power spectrum
distant supernova brightness measurements
pulsar timing across the Milky Way
context: Rubin and Ford on Andromeda, and Morton Roberts, Albert Bosma, and Ken Freeman working the same problem on other spirals, all found outer stars and gas keeping pace with inner ones -- the same missing-mass signature Zwicky had seen in a whole cluster forty years earlier. Zwicky was a difficult, brilliant outsider whose ideas were often dismissed in his lifetime; he was famous for calling people he disliked 'spherical bastards -- bastards no matter which way you look at them'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Zwicky ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter

question: An astronomer sets a lensing map over an X-ray image of the Bullet Cluster, where two galaxy clusters are caught colliding. The X-rays show most of the ordinary matter, the hot gas, stripped and left glowing in the middle of the crash. Lensing of the galaxies behind the collision shows where most of the mass went. What does it reveal?
answer: most of the mass had sailed straight through with the galaxies
choices: most of the mass had sailed straight through with the galaxies
most of the mass had collapsed into a single black hole at the centre
the mass and the hot gas were still in exactly the same place
the mass had scattered evenly across the whole sky
context: Clowe et al. 2006 published the result as 'A Direct Empirical Proof of the Existence of Dark Matter' -- an eight-sigma offset between the visible mass (the X-ray gas) and the gravitational mass (the lensing). The 'bullet' subcluster smashed through the main cluster at roughly 4,500 km/s, more than one percent of the speed of light, creating a bow-shock visible in X-rays (Markevitch 2007, ApJ 661:L131). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullet_Cluster

question: Mordehai Milgrom put forward the main rival to the idea of unseen matter in 1983: Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). It tweaks gravity below a tiny acceleration and fits single spiral-galaxy rotation curves pretty well without any hidden matter. Where does MOND struggle most, giving most physicists a big reason to still favor unseen particles?
answer: galaxy clusters, including the Bullet Cluster
choices: galaxy clusters, including the Bullet Cluster
dwarf spheroidal satellite galaxies
wide binary star pairs
the cosmic microwave background power spectrum
context: MOND's tuning acceleration a0 is about 1.2 x 10^-10 metres per second squared -- roughly the acceleration of a car that speeds up by one metre per second every 260 years. Dwarf spheroidals, wide binaries, and the CMB power spectrum are all regimes where MOND has been argued about in the literature -- but rich clusters are the toughest case: a residual mass discrepancy remains even after MOND is applied, and the Bullet Cluster's clean separation of visible and gravitational mass is very hard for a pure gravity-modification story to reproduce. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics

question: A physicist reads the latest result from a giant vat of ultra-pure liquid xenon buried deep underground to shield out cosmic rays. He is hunting the leading candidate for the missing mass, weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs). Each detector from 2013 to 2023 has been more sensitive than the last. What have these underground hunts found?
answer: no confirmed detection
choices: no confirmed detection
a single confirmed WIMP
a steady confirmed signal
the axion instead
context: LUX (370 kg of xenon), XENON1T (3.5 tonnes), and LZ (multi-tonne) have each pushed the exclusion limits tighter without a confirmed hit. The remaining live particle candidates include axions -- very light particles independently proposed in 1978 by Frank Wilczek and Steven Weinberg -- and sterile neutrinos; both are still being searched for, neither confirmed. Said clearly: no one yet knows what dark matter is. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter

question: A cosmologist crosses ordinary neutrinos off her list of candidates for the bulk of the missing mass. They have a little mass, there are lots of them, and they barely interact with anything. What is wrong with neutrinos for the job?
answer: they move too close to light-speed for galaxy-scale structure to form
choices: they move too close to light-speed for galaxy-scale structure to form
they carry the wrong electric charge to bind gravitationally
they decay far too quickly to accumulate in halos
they are far too heavy to have escaped particle detectors
context: In cosmology talk, neutrinos are 'hot dark matter' -- they were still moving relativistically when structure began forming, so they would have streamed out of small clumps and smeared out the fine structure from which galaxies are actually seen to condense. The dark matter that fits the observed universe is 'cold': slow-moving, clumping easily. Vera Rubin herself did not treat any of this as settled -- she liked to say the ratio of dark to light matter in a spiral galaxy 'is about a factor of 10 -- that's probably a good number for the ratio of our ignorance to knowledge.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter

question: Friedrich Miescher was working in a makeshift chemistry lab inside the old kitchen of Tübingen Castle in the winter of 1869, trying to learn what living cells are made of. The young Swiss doctor needed a fresh batch of white blood cells every single morning. Where did he get them?
answer: Off used surgical dressings from the town clinic
choices: Off used surgical dressings from the town clinic
From salmon sperm shipped in from the Rhine fisheries
From calves' thymus glands ordered from the abattoir
From blood drawn by lancet from the medical students
context: Miescher soaked the pus off the bandages, washed out the leucocytes, and by the end of the year had precipitated a strange substance out of their nuclei he named 'nuclein' -- what we now call DNA. The stuff of genes was first scooped off used surgical dressings. Source: Dahm 2005 (Human Genetics); Univ. Tuebingen MUT exhibit.

question: At Tübingen Castle in 1869, Friedrich Miescher pulled a strange substance out of the nuclei of white blood cells and called it nuclein, the material later renamed DNA. It was full of phosphorus, and pepsin, the stomach's protein-digesting enzyme, could not break it down. What third clue told him it was not a protein?
answer: It contained no sulfur at all
choices: It contained no sulfur at all
It dissolved cleanly in pure alcohol
It turned bright green under iodine
It crystallized instantly on cooling
context: Two amino acids that proteins depend on -- cysteine and methionine -- carry sulfur, so any protein sample contains some. Miescher's nuclein contained none, which was chemically decisive. Source: Dahm 2008 (Current Biology).

question: Felix Hoppe-Seyler held back Friedrich Miescher's paper for two whole years. The young Swiss doctor had reported a strange phosphorus-rich substance from the nuclei of cells, the material later renamed DNA, and Hoppe-Seyler, his supervisor and the journal's editor, did not fully trust it. What did Hoppe-Seyler do before he let the paper out in 1871?
answer: Made his own students repeat the entire extraction themselves
choices: Made his own students repeat the entire extraction themselves
Sent a sealed sample to Louis Pasteur in Paris for arbitration
Presented the finding to the Prussian Academy under his own name
Struck Miescher's name from the byline and published it as his own
context: Replication before publication -- a supervisor's skepticism doing exactly the job skepticism is meant to do. The 1871 issue eventually carried Miescher's paper, a confirming paper by a second student, and an article by Hoppe-Seyler backing the finding. Source: Univ. Tuebingen MUT exhibit; Dahm 2005.

question: Erwin Chargaff met two young researchers at Cambridge in May 1952, James Watson and Francis Crick, and told them face to face what his lab had measured about the ratios of the bases in DNA. What did he later write about that meeting?
answer: That he had never met two men who knew so little and aspired to so much
choices: That he had never met two men who knew so little and aspired to so much
That they had already worked out the double helix on the blackboard in front of him
That they had grasped the base-pairing hint on the spot and thanked him warmly
That he shook their hands and told them the Nobel Prize was theirs to lose
context: Chargaff spent the rest of his life resenting the model that Watson and Crick built out of his numbers. His memoir Heraclitean Fire (1978) is the sourced record of the quote. Source: Chargaff, Heraclitean Fire (1978); CSHL DNA Learning Center.

question: Friedrich Miescher reached for the alphabet in 1892. Heredity, he suspected, might be written in chemical variety, the way 24 to 30 letters spell every word in every language. How did that idea reach the wider scientific world in his lifetime?
answer: It did not -- he confided it only to his uncle Wilhelm His and never argued it publicly
choices: It did not -- he confided it only to his uncle Wilhelm His and never argued it publicly
He announced it in a triumphant address to the Basel Academy of Sciences
He convinced Charles Darwin by mail and Darwin cited him in a late edition
He founded a research institute in Basel to prove the alphabet analogy
context: The 1892 letter to Wilhelm His speculated that the stereochemistry of asymmetric carbon atoms could encode hereditary richness -- an idea almost a century early. But Miescher published nothing of the sort, and for decades nuclein was written off as a mere phosphorus store. Source: Dahm 2008; Portin 2020.

question: Friedrich Miescher reported a strange substance from cell nuclei in 1871 and named it nuclein. For decades afterward, most biologists who thought about it at all called it chemically important but boring. What was their working guess about what nuclein did in the nucleus?
answer: It was a phosphorus storage compound the cell drew on when needed
choices: It was a phosphorus storage compound the cell drew on when needed
It was a scaffolding fiber that held the chromosomes in shape
It was a signalling molecule the cell released to trigger division
It was an energy currency the nucleus burned during mitosis
context: The phosphorus-storage guess is the reason serious biologists could look straight at DNA and see nothing important. It took Avery in 1944 and Chargaff in 1950 to force the field to look again. Source: Dahm 2005; Portin 2014.

question: Leo Baekeland set out in his New York lab to copy a natural varnish. By 1900 American electrical factories were coating their wires with it, gathered by hand overseas, and demand was outpacing supply. He ended up instead, in 1907, with Bakelite, called the first true plastic. Which varnish had he been chasing?
answer: Shellac, secreted by an Indian insect
choices: Shellac, secreted by an Indian insect
Beeswax, rendered from honeycomb
Gum arabic, tapped from acacia trees
Linseed oil, pressed from flax seed
context: The lac insect coats twigs across India with a resin that is scraped off, washed and dried into flakes - the wiring of the electrical age depended on insects. Baekeland's replacement, cooked under heat and pressure in a riveted steel vessel he called the Bakelizer, was sold as 'the material of a thousand uses'; its first mass-produced items included billiard balls, which replaced scarce ivory. The Bakelizer was made an ACS National Historic Chemical Landmark on 9 November 1993 and now sits in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. (Source: Grokipedia 'Bakelite', sections Invention, Commercialization, Cultural and Historical Significance.)

question: A chemist before 1920 measures the molecular weight of rubber and gets an answer in the tens of thousands, far past anything he can draw on paper. Almost nobody takes that reading at face value. What do the chemists of his day say rubber really is?
answer: A clump of small molecules clinging together
choices: A clump of small molecules clinging together
A crowd of tiny crystals too small to see
A jelly of small molecules trapped in water
A stack of flat sheets sliding over one another
context: This was colloid, or association, theory, and it was the ruling view: the huge measured weights were an illusion produced by ordinary small molecules stuck together by weak physical forces rather than by chemical bonds. Emil Fischer, who had mapped the sugars, and Heinrich Wieland both held it. It was not a stupid idea - nobody had ever seen a molecule with thousands of links - but it was wrong, and it took thirty years to dislodge. (Source: Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', section Origins of the Macromolecular Hypothesis.)

question: A girl at the kitchen table cuts a thin strip from a plastic grocery bag, grips both ends firmly and pulls slowly apart. Somewhere along the strip a narrow waist forms and turns cloudy white, the part engineers call a neck. She keeps pulling at the same steady rate, without yanking. What does the neck do next?
answer: It lengthens, swallowing the unstretched strip
choices: It lengthens, swallowing the unstretched strip
It tears through, leaving two ragged ends
It springs back and a new neck forms elsewhere
It crumbles into a brittle white powder
context: The neck refuses to be the weak point: it stops thinning and eats its way along the strip instead, so a whole strip can be drawn out to several times its length without parting. This is cold drawing, and it is how a synthetic fibre is made. In April 1930 Julian Hill, working in Wallace Carothers's DuPont laboratory, used a high-vacuum 'molecular still' to push a polyester to a molecular weight of about 12,000, drew filaments out of the hot melt like taffy, and found that stretching them cold turned them tough and elastic, with properties approaching silk. Stretching, not chemistry, made the fibre. (Sources: Wikipedia 'Necking (engineering)'; Grokipedia 'Wallace Carothers', section Development of Polyesters.)

question: A gardener rakes dead stalks onto a compost heap, a pile of long molecules no chemist made. Living things hold a billion-year lead over chemists at building them, and the most abundant of all makes up roughly a third of all the plant matter there is. Which substance is it?
answer: Cellulose
choices: Cellulose
Starch
Lignin
Pectin
context: Cellulose is a chain of glucose units and about 33% of all plant biomass, which makes it the most abundant organic polymer - repeating-unit molecule - on the planet. You are built of chains too: collagen is a chain of amino acids wound into a triple helix, which is what gives tendon and skin their tensile strength, and DNA is a chain of nucleotides. After his Nobel, Hermann Staudinger extended his macromolecular argument straight into biology, to proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids and polysaccharides. The fight over rubber decided how we read life's molecules too. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Polymer', section Natural Polymers; Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', section Extensions to Biological Macromolecules.)

question: Hermann Staudinger, a chemistry professor working in Zurich, published a paper in 1920 on polymerisation and turned almost every top German chemist against him. It took on what most of them taught about rubber and similar rubbery stuffs. What did Staudinger say rubber's molecules really are?
answer: Single molecules thousands of units long, joined by ordinary bonds
choices: Single molecules thousands of units long, joined by ordinary bonds
Ring molecules threaded through one another like woven chain mail
Sheet molecules one atom thick, stacked in parallel flat layers
Star molecules with short arms radiating from one central core
context: The claim was simple and enormous: the same valence rules that hold a small organic molecule together will hold a chain of ten thousand units. In 1922 Staudinger coined a word for them, 'Makromolekül' - macromolecule. He needed a new word because 'polymer' was already taken: Jöns Jacob Berzelius had coined it in 1833 from the Greek poly, many, and meros, parts, but he used it for compounds that share an empirical formula while their molecular weights differ by whole multiples. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', section Origins of the Macromolecular Hypothesis; Grokipedia 'Polymer', section Etymology.)

question: Heinrich Wieland, who won the 1927 Nobel Prize in chemistry, wrote to Hermann Staudinger that year and urged him to give up his idea of giant molecules. Staudinger had spent seven years fighting Germany's leading chemists over rubber, and he was losing. No organic molecule can weigh more than about 5,000, Wieland said; anything bigger would be as shaky as one famous structure. Which structure did Wieland name?
answer: The Tower of Babel
choices: The Tower of Babel
The Colossus of Rhodes
The walls of Jericho
The wings of Icarus
context: Grokipedia gives the 1927 letter as: 'organic molecules with a molecular weight higher than 5000 do not exist; they would be as unstable as the Tower of Babel.' The line circulates in several English wordings, so that is the sourced version rather than one to reshape. The fight had career teeth: Richard Willstätter, himself a Nobel laureate, is reported to have blocked Staudinger's academic appointments over the disagreement, deepening his isolation in post-war Germany. Carl Freudenberg started out against the hypothesis and later converted. (Source: Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', section Debate with the Scientific Establishment.)

question: Leo Baekeland made Bakelite in 1907, after Charles Goodyear's vulcanised rubber of 1839, Alexander Parkes's mouldable Parkesine of 1862, and the celluloid and rayon already in shops before 1900. Yet chemists still call his the first true plastic. What sets Bakelite apart from those four?
answer: It started from small manufactured chemicals
choices: It started from small manufactured chemicals
It started from a single ingredient, not a blend
It started from a liquid rather than a powder
It started from cheaper materials than the others
context: Vulcanised rubber, Parkesine, celluloid and rayon are all modified natural polymers - rubber and cellulose, treated with sulfur, nitric acid or solvents. Bakelite began from phenol and formaldehyde, two small chemicals made in a works, reacted under heat and pressure into a material with no natural parent at all. Baekeland filed on 13 July 1907 and was granted U.S. Patent 942,699 on 7 December 1909; he had funded the work with money from Velox photographic paper, which he sold to Eastman Kodak in 1899, and he eventually held over 400 Bakelite-related patents. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Polymer', section Historical Development; Grokipedia 'Bakelite', sections Invention, Key Patents.)

question: Hermann Staudinger answered his critics at the bench in 1922, working with Jakob Fritschi. If rubber's huge measured weight were an illusion, then breaking the chemistry behind it should leave only low-weight waxes. The two men chemically changed natural rubber. The product kept nearly the same stretch, solubility and thickness, and end-counts put its weight above 100,000. What had they done to the rubber?
answer: Added hydrogen to it, saturating every double bond
choices: Added hydrogen to it, saturating every double bond
Added sulfur to it, the way Goodyear vulcanised tyres
Added chlorine to it, making a rubber chloride
Added nitric acid to it, nitrating the rubber
context: Hydrogenation kills rubber's carbon-carbon double bonds, the very bonds association theory leaned on - yet the 'hydro-rubber' still behaved like rubber and still weighed over 100,000 daltons. Staudinger's other tool was thickness: a solution's intrinsic viscosity rises in step with chain length, and the telling result was that viscosity did not change when he chemically dressed a polymer in new side groups. It dropped only when bonds were actually cut. A clump would have fallen apart; a chain just wore a new coat. (Source: Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', section Key Experiments and Evidence.)

question: Theodor Svedberg built a machine at Uppsala that could do what no chemist had done: measure the weight of one dissolved molecule directly. He and Robin Fåhraeus turned it on haemoglobin in 1926 and got about 67,000 daltons for one uniform molecule, more than 13 times Heinrich Wieland's ceiling of about 5,000. How did the machine weigh a molecule?
answer: It spun the solution until molecules settled out by weight
choices: It spun the solution until molecules settled out by weight
It fired X-rays through the solution and read the pattern
It pushed the solution through a membrane and read the pressure
It burned the solution and weighed the gases given off
context: Svedberg's ultracentrifuge - a 1924 prototype built with H. Rinde reaching about 7,000 g, refined by 1926 to roughly 100,000 g at 42,000 rpm - drove molecules down through the solution at a rate set by their mass, so the sedimentation itself was the measurement. He took the 1926 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. Two other instruments from outside the quarrel pointed the same way: Herman Mark's X-ray work on stretched fibres, and membrane osmometry, which confirmed the high molecular weights independently. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Ultracentrifuge', section Invention and Early Advances; Wikipedia 'Hermann Staudinger'.)

question: A boy pulls a strip of plastic bag slowly, and a thin white neck forms and refuses to break. Everywhere else in engineering a thinned spot is the weak spot: a steel bar that necks snaps there within seconds. What makes the thinned plastic stronger than the plastic around it?
answer: Its tangled chains rotate into parallel alignment
choices: Its tangled chains rotate into parallel alignment
Its chains snap and re-form into shorter pieces
The stretching squeezes out trapped air pockets
The friction of stretching anneals the thin spot
context: In a ductile polymer, molecular orientation is a hardening mechanism that dominates at large strains: as the chains line up, the necked material carries more load than the tangled material beside it, so the neck stabilises and travels along the strip instead of tearing through. That is why drawing a fibre makes it strong, and why the effect is easiest to see in polyethylene - the plastic of a grocery bag. (Source: Wikipedia 'Necking (engineering)'.)

question: Hermann Staudinger and Johannes Hengstenberg fired X-rays at crystalline polyoxymethylene in 1927 to find its unit cell, the small repeating box whose copies, stacked in three directions, build the whole crystal. The box came out tiny: four to six units, no more. Yet viscosity measurements and end-group counting said the chains in that same solid ran well over a hundred units long. What did Staudinger read off that mismatch?
answer: The molecules run on through cell after cell
choices: The molecules run on through cell after cell
The unit cell is a fragment of a far larger one
The crystal holds only the shortest chains present
The viscosity had over-counted the chain length
context: A self-contained clump has to fit inside the box it sits in; a chain does not - it threads through many cells, which is exactly what the X-rays showed. This is the argument at its cleanest: two independent measurements, crystal geometry from diffraction and chain length from viscosity and end-groups, that cannot both be true unless the molecule is longer than its own crystal cell. Staudinger took the 1953 Nobel Prize in Chemistry at 72, thirty-three years after the 1920 paper. He had founded the journal Die Makromolekulare Chemie in 1939 and, in January 1940, the Freiburg Institute for Macromolecular Chemistry, the first institution in Europe devoted only to polymer science; Allied bombing destroyed it on 27 November 1944 and it was rebuilt after the war. (Source: Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', sections Key Experiments and Evidence, Nobel Prize and Vindication.)

question: Wallace Carothers's team at DuPont found that making a long chain is an arithmetic problem before it is a chemical one. Adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine, the two ingredients of nylon 6,6, had to be present in exactly equal numbers, because one spare molecule of either caps a growing chain and stops it dead. How did the chemists guarantee that one-to-one ratio?
answer: They crystallised the two together into a single salt first
choices: They crystallised the two together into a single salt first
They weighed each one out on an analytical balance
They titrated the mixture to neutrality before heating
They distilled the mixture until the ratio came right
context: Weighing is not good enough at 99.9%: a trace of moisture or a slightly impure batch throws the count off, and every stray monomer is a dead end. Crystallising adipic acid with hexamethylenediamine gives 'nylon salt', one compound holding exactly one of each, so the ratio is enforced by chemistry rather than by the balance. Nylon 6,6 was first made on 28 February 1935 and melts at 255-265 degrees C, high enough to survive a hot wash, which the earlier polyester was not. DuPont had recruited Carothers from Harvard in 1928, through Charles M. A. Stine, to do pure research with no products required, in a lab the chemists nicknamed 'Purity Hall'; Carothers hired Paul Flory in 1934 to work out the statistics of chain lengths, and Flory won the 1974 Nobel Prize. Carothers was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1936 and died in 1937, aged 41; the two key nylon patents were granted after his death, in 1938. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Wallace Carothers', sections Development of Polyesters, Exploration of Polyamides, Key Patents; Grokipedia 'Nylon', section Key Monomers and Polymerization Reactions.)

question: Erasto Mpemba, 13, was making ice-cream in a cookery class at Magamba Secondary School in Tanzania in 1963. The freezer was filling up, so he put his mix in while it was still hot, and he saw it freeze before his classmates' cooled mix. What did his teacher tell him?
answer: That he must have confused himself
choices: That he must have confused himself
That he had discovered a new effect
That he should redo the experiment tomorrow
That he had accidentally spilled another boy's mix
context: Mpemba was ridiculed by his teacher and classmates, and he kept asking anyway. The right lesson from this question is the shape of the reception a real observation can get from the people around it. Sources: PBS NOVA 'The ice cream that changed physics'; Skeptical Inquirer 'The Rise and Fall of the Mpemba Effect'.

question: Denis Osborne, a visiting British physicist from University College Dar es Salaam, gave a talk at a Tanzanian secondary school, and a student named Erasto Mpemba worked up the courage to ask him something. Hot ice-cream mix, Mpemba said, seemed to freeze faster than cold, the opposite of what every textbook said. Osborne was openly sceptical. What did he do instead of dismissing the boy?
answer: He went back to his laboratory and tested it
choices: He went back to his laboratory and tested it
He wrote to Nature reporting Mpemba's claim
He asked the school to repeat the observation
He looked up the earlier work of Francis Bacon
context: Osborne's controlled experiments back at the university appeared to confirm something, and in 1969 he and Mpemba jointly published 'Cool?' in Physics Education, with Mpemba credited as first author. Osborne wrote 'no question should be ridiculed'. Aristotle, Francis Bacon and Rene Descartes had all reported something similar in earlier centuries -- and been forgotten. Sources: Chemistry World; Physics Education 4, 172 (1969).

question: Henry Burridge and Paul Linden at Cambridge ran the most tightly controlled experiments to date in 2016 on whether hot water reliably freezes faster than cold. Sixty years on from Erasto Mpemba, physicists still argue, and a girl with two ice-cube trays can still run the test at home. What did the two men find?
answer: No evidence of any reproducible effect at all
choices: No evidence of any reproducible effect at all
Reproducible speed-ups only in salt-water samples
A clear effect once dissolved gases were removed
A larger effect than any earlier study had reported
context: Burridge and Linden defined freezing as cooling to zero degrees Celsius and found no consistent effect; other laboratories continue to report one, and the argument is not settled. Live candidate mechanisms include evaporation reducing the mass, dissolved gases, convection currents, differences in supercooling, and frost layers acting as insulation. This is an open mystery: the honest answer to what is really going on is still 'no one yet knows'. Try it at home with two ice-cube trays -- if you see nothing, that is a real result. Sources: Nature Scientific Reports 6, 37665 (2016); Quanta Magazine, June 2022.

question: A girl holds out her hand in the yard. Cosmic rays spray one kind of tiny particle down, and about one crosses every square centimetre of it each minute. Its journey is the classic school proof of Einstein's special relativity. Which particle is it?
answer: the muon
choices: the muon
the neutron
the neutrino
the positron
context: The muon is a heavier sibling of the electron, born about 15 km up. About one passes through every square centimetre of the ground each minute. Neutrinos also arrive but almost never interact; neutrons and positrons do not survive the trip through the atmosphere in anything like these numbers. Source: Wikipedia -- Experimental testing of time dilation; CERN HST 2000.

question: A student works out the fate of a muon born about 15 kilometres up and racing down at 99.5% of the speed of light. Its short lifetime says it should decay into lighter particles after about 660 metres. What happens to muons over that drop?
answer: they arrive at the ground in huge numbers
choices: they arrive at the ground in huge numbers
they all decay long before hitting the ground
they slow down and drift as cosmic dust
they merge with air molecules to form nitrogen
context: About one muon strikes every square centimetre of ground per minute -- a handful are going through the reader's hand every second. The mismatch between 660 metres and 15 kilometres is exactly what makes them a walking experiment in relativity. Source: CERN HST 2000 -- muon calc.

question: Frisch and Smith clocked about 563 muons an hour on top of Mount Washington in 1963, then took the counter down to sea level at Cambridge, Massachusetts. Physics with no relativity at all said only about 27 an hour should survive the trip. How many an hour did they count at the bottom?
answer: about 412 per hour
choices: about 412 per hour
about 30 per hour
essentially zero
about 4000 per hour
context: Frisch and Smith, Am. J. Phys. 31, 342 (1963). Twenty-seven predicted, four hundred and twelve arrived. The muons' internal clocks were running slow -- as measured from the ground -- by a factor of about nine. Source: Wikipedia -- Experimental testing of time dilation.

question: Two physicists beat the famous Mount Washington muon count by twenty-three years. In 1940 they compared muon counts at a mountain-top station and in a lower valley, and they found the faster muons outliving the slower ones. Which pair was it?
answer: Bruno Rossi and D. B. Hall, in Colorado
choices: Bruno Rossi and D. B. Hall, in Colorado
Robert Millikan and Carl Anderson, over Pasadena
Enrico Fermi and Emilio Segre, above Rome
Arthur Compton and Robert Oppenheimer, in Chicago
context: Rossi and Hall, 1940, compared Echo Lake, Colorado (3240 m) with Denver (1616 m). It was crude, but the direction of the effect was unmistakable. Frisch and Smith made the sharp quantitative check the textbook remembers. Source: arXiv:physics/0008012 -- Interpretations of time dilation experiments.

question: A teacher explains the muon's journey from two seats. From the ground, the muon lives long enough to cross 15 kilometres. From the muon's own seat, its clock runs normally, yet it still reaches the ground. What has changed instead, from the muon's point of view?
answer: the 15 kilometres of atmosphere is squashed to a few hundred metres
choices: the 15 kilometres of atmosphere is squashed to a few hundred metres
gravity is much weaker at that speed and pulls it less
the atmosphere becomes transparent to the muon's mass
the Earth is spinning fast enough to meet the muon halfway
context: Time dilation and length contraction are the same fact seen from two seats. From the ground, muon clocks slow; from the muon, our distances shrink. Neither observer sees both effects at once, but both agree on the final outcome: it arrives. Source: Open Book -- 'Consider the Muon's PoV'.

question: Dr Alexander, one of two American expert witnesses at the Nuremberg trial of Nazi doctors, wrote a memo of ethics rules that reappears, almost word for word, in parts of the judges' ten-point Code of August 1947. That Code's Point 1 opens with one plain sentence. What are its exact opening words?
answer: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.
choices: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.
First, do no harm -- above all else, spare the patient injury.
The interests of the subject must prevail over those of science.
Every adult has a right to decide what shall be done with his body.
context: The line is the whole Code in one breath: no matter what the science is worth, people deciding for their own bodies have to actually decide, and no one else may decide for them. Every research-ethics framework since -- Helsinki, Belmont, the Common Rule -- traces this principle back to Point 1. Alexander's April 15, 1947 memorandum, 'Ethical and non-ethical experimentation on human beings,' laid out six principles that ended up structurally inside the Code. The other expert witness, physiologist Andrew Ivy of the University of Illinois, was endorsed by the American Medical Association and contributed further principles. Authorship of the Code is genuinely shared between Alexander and Ivy. Sources: https://research.unc.edu/human-research-ethics/resources/ccm3_019064/; https://www.pedneur.com/article/S0887-8994(21)00242-3/fulltext

question: The judges at Nuremberg, after hearing what Nazi doctors had done in the camps, wrote Point 5 of their Code to rule out any experiment in which death or crippling injury is expected. Then they wrote one deliberate exception into that same point, hedged with the word 'perhaps.' Whom does the exception cover?
answer: the researcher who serves as his own test subject
choices: the researcher who serves as his own test subject
the terminally ill patient with no other treatment
the volunteer soldier under military orders
the prisoner offered a reduced sentence
context: The exact wording: 'except, perhaps, in those experiments where the experimental physicians also serve as subjects.' The judges wrote a special hole for the scientist who runs the risk on himself -- the same virtue this bank celebrates in Barry Marshall drinking his H. pylori beaker and the Wright brothers testing their own wing tables. Source: https://research.unc.edu/human-research-ethics/resources/ccm3_019064/

question: Jay Katz, a Yale professor of law and psychiatry, looked back on how American doctors took the Nuremberg Code and summed up their attitude in words of his own, not in any doctor's: the Code, they seemed to feel, was written for the sort of people they were not. How did Katz characterize the American view?
answer: a fine code for barbarians, needless for ordinary doctors
choices: a fine code for barbarians, needless for ordinary doctors
a set of rules for the defeated, not for the victors
a price of victory, paid once and then forgotten
a lawyers' document with no bearing on medicine
context: Katz, in his 1996 reappraisal in JAMA, wrote that the Code was taken as a 'code for barbarians' but unnecessary for ordinary physicians. That is a scholar's characterization of how American medicine behaved, not a contemporaneous quote from a named physician: it read the Code as a rule for Nazis, not for itself. The next twenty-five years of American research proved him right. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg_Code ; Katz J., 'The Nuremberg Code and the Nuremberg Trial: A Reappraisal', JAMA 276(20):1662-6 (1996).

question: A historian lays the record of American medicine beside the Nuremberg Code of August 1947 and looks for what changed. Research programs that violated its principles ran on for decades, and historians point to one pair above the rest as the sharpest measure of how little the Code changed U.S. medical practice. Which pair?
answer: the Tuskegee study and the Guatemala experiments
choices: the Tuskegee study and the Guatemala experiments
the Willowbrook hepatitis studies and the Fernald oatmeal study
the Human Radiation Experiments and the CIA's MKUltra program
the Holmesburg Prison trials and the Stateville malaria studies
context: The Tuskegee syphilis study ran for 25 more years after the Code was published in 1947. The Guatemala experiments (1946-1948) -- in which the U.S. physician John Cutler deliberately exposed roughly 1,300 Guatemalans to syphilis and other diseases -- were being conducted during the trial itself. The Code was moral force, not law; American medicine treated it as somebody else's problem. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatemala_syphilis_experiments

question: An American researcher reads the ten principles the judges at Nuremberg set down in their 1947 verdict on the Nazi doctors, and he goes back to work unchanged. For all its moral weight, the Code had one glaring weakness that explains why it was so easily ignored at first. What was the problem?
answer: It was not itself legally binding on anyone
choices: It was not itself legally binding on anyone
It applied only to experiments on prisoners
It made an exception for wartime research
It was kept secret until the 1960s
context: The Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 1964) gave its principles a medical profession's formal backing. The U.S. National Research Act (1974), passed after Tuskegee was exposed, created Institutional Review Boards. The Belmont Report (1979) codified respect for persons, beneficence, and justice as the framework for federally funded human research. The Code alone was moral force; the 1974 law and the federal rules built on Belmont are what gave its principles teeth. Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM199711133372006

question: Three American judges went on past the opening sentence of Point 1 when they wrote the Nuremberg Code in 1947, after the trial of the Nazi doctors who had experimented on concentration-camp prisoners. They required that a subject's decision be free of every 'ulterior form of constraint', and they opened their list of forbidden pressures with four words. What are those four?
answer: force, fraud, deceit, and duress
choices: force, fraud, deceit, and duress
coercion, pressure, threat, and reward
money, family, position, and duty
authority, custom, ignorance, and shame
context: The full clause: 'without the intervention of any element of force, fraud, deceit, duress, over-reaching, or other ulterior form of constraint or coercion.' The four words that open the list map directly onto how consent gets broken in real research settings -- and Point 1 says the duty to prevent all four cannot be delegated. Source: https://research.unc.edu/human-research-ethics/resources/ccm3_019064/

question: Albert Einstein sent a physics journal four papers in about six months of 1905, at twenty-six, with no laboratory and no university job. His day job in Bern gave him the rank of 'technical expert, third class'. What did that job have him doing?
answer: Examining patent applications for new inventions
choices: Examining patent applications for new inventions
Certifying weights and measures for shopkeepers
Drafting timetables for the federal railways
Testing telegraph gear for the postal service
context: The Swiss Patent Office in Bern. Einstein started there on 23 June 1902 at 3,500 francs a year, ranked 'technical expert, third class' (provisional), and stayed until October 1909. He divided his own day into three parts: 'eight hours work in the Patent Office, eight hours Allotria [fun] connected with scientific work, and eight hours of sleep.' The middle eight hours produced the four papers, which Annalen der Physik received on 18 March, 11 May, 30 June and 27 September 1905. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers; einstein-website.de/en/patent-office/

question: Albert Einstein wrote his burst of four papers in 1905 at home, in a rented second-floor flat at Kramgasse 49 in the Swiss city of Bern. He was not alone in those rooms. Who was living there with him?
answer: His wife Mileva Maric and their baby son Hans Albert
choices: His wife Mileva Maric and their baby son Hans Albert
His mother Pauline and his younger sister Maja
His schoolfriend Marcel Grossmann and Grossmann's wife
Two fellow clerks who rented the rooms with him
context: Einstein, Mileva Maric and their son Hans Albert lived at Kramgasse 49 from 1903 to 1905 — so the four papers were written in a second-floor flat with a baby in it, not in any laboratory. The flat is now the Einstein House museum: you can walk in and stand in the room. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_House

question: Carl Wilhelm Oseen, a member of the Nobel committee, picked the wording for Albert Einstein's 1921 prize. His words let the Academy honor Einstein without backing a theory many still doubted, and the word relativity never appears. Which of Einstein's results did the wording name instead?
answer: His work on the photoelectric effect
choices: His work on the photoelectric effect
His work on the dimensions of molecules
His work on the motion of suspended particles
His work on the specific heats of solids
context: The citation in full: 'for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.' Relativity is not named anywhere in it — Einstein never won a Nobel Prize for relativity, special or general. The prize was late as well: no physics prize was awarded for 1921 at all, and in September 1922 the Academy voted to hand Einstein the held-over 1921 prize and Niels Bohr the 1922 one. Einstein missed the ceremony on 10 December 1922; he was travelling in Japan, and the German minister Rudolf Nadolny read his speech at the Stockholm banquet. When he finally gave his Nobel lecture, at Gothenburg on 11 July 1923, he titled it 'Fundamental Ideas and Problems of the Theory of Relativity' — and lectured on the theory the prize had refused to name. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics; arxiv.org/abs/2112.13519; nobelprize.org

question: Robert Brown, a Scottish botanist, watched specks shaken out of pollen grains under his microscope in 1827. In water left to settle they jerked and wandered and never once stopped, and for nearly eighty years nobody could say why. Einstein's May 1905 paper named the culprit. What was shoving the specks about?
answer: Water molecules, battering them from every side
choices: Water molecules, battering them from every side
Faint currents from uneven warmth in the water
Electric charge gathering on the glass slide
A trace of life left in the pollen grains
context: Classical hydrodynamics said a particle in a fluid at rest should sit still, so Brown's endless jitter had been an embarrassment for nearly eighty years. Einstein's answer: a speck small enough gets struck unevenly by the molecules of the liquid from one moment to the next, and staggers under the imbalance. Anyone with a microscope can watch the same motion today. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: The twenty-six-year-old Albert Einstein sent the physics journal Annalen der Physik his four famous miracle-year papers of 1905: light quanta, Brownian motion, special relativity, mass-energy. A fifth piece he sent that same year to the University of Zurich instead. What did he send Zurich?
answer: His doctoral dissertation, on the size of molecules
choices: His doctoral dissertation, on the size of molecules
His application for a lecturing post in physics
A textbook on electrodynamics for schoolteachers
A review of Hendrik Lorentz's work, at Planck's request
context: 'A New Determination of Molecular Dimensions', approved by Zurich in July 1905. Einstein had no doctorate at all when the first papers went out: the March and May papers were posted by a man nobody could yet call 'Doctor', who had no professorship either. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: Maurice Solovine, a Romanian philosophy student, answered a small advertisement in a Bern newspaper in December 1901 and came round. Albert Einstein, still months away from his office job, was offering private lessons in mathematics and physics at three francs an hour. The first lesson ran nearly two hours. What happened to the three francs an hour?
answer: No money changed hands, and the lesson became an argument
choices: No money changed hands, and the lesson became an argument
Solovine paid the first hour, then never paid again
Solovine paid in books, which Einstein read and returned
Einstein raised the fee once the lessons ran long
context: No fee was ever paid: the two argued instead, and the lesson turned into a friendship that outlasted the papers. Solovine, Einstein and Conrad Habicht turned those arguments into a three-man club they named the Akademie Olympia, mocking the real academies that had no place for them; Einstein's joke title for himself was 'Albert Ritter von Steissbein' — Albert, Knight of the Tailbone. Over cheap suppers and three- and four-hour arguments they read Hume's Treatise of Human Nature, Spinoza's Ethics, Mill's System of Logic, Poincare's Science and Hypothesis, Karl Pearson's Grammar of Science, Ernst Mach's Science of Mechanics — and Cervantes' Don Quixote. Mach's attack on absolute space runs straight into the June 1905 relativity paper. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Olympia_Academy

question: Two top European scientists refused to say atoms were real when Albert Einstein published on the jiggling of tiny particles in 1905. One called them useless guesses about things nobody can see. The other said everything was really just energy changing form, with no hidden particles needed. Who were the two holdouts?
answer: Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald
choices: Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald
Hendrik Lorentz and Henri Poincare
Max Planck and Paul Drude
Ludwig Boltzmann and Jean Perrin
context: Mach the positivist would not admit unobservable things into physics at all; Ostwald the 'energeticist' wanted a physics of energy transformations with no particles in it. Neither man was a crank — they were two of the leading minds of the age, and whether atoms existed was still a live argument in 1905. Jean Perrin's patient measurements of suspended particles in 1908-09 matched Einstein's prediction and ended the argument; Perrin took the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics for that work. Consensus did not settle this one. A measurement did. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: Michele Besso, a Swiss-Italian mechanical engineer, joined the office in Bern in January 1904, taken on after Albert Einstein urged the director. The two ate lunch together and argued physics on the walk home, and Einstein's June 1905 relativity paper thanks no one else. What position did the office give Besso?
answer: A rank above Einstein himself
choices: A rank above Einstein himself
A rank below Einstein himself
A post in a different section
A temporary post with no rank
context: The office took Besso on as technical expert, SECOND class — one rank above the man who had recommended him — and he stayed above Einstein for more than two years: Einstein was still third class until his promotion on 1 April 1906. The paper's entire acknowledgement is its last sentence: 'In conclusion I wish to say that in working at the problem here dealt with I have had the loyal assistance of my friend and colleague M. Besso, and that I am indebted to him for several valuable suggestions.' Einstein later told his biographer Carl Seelig: 'I could not have found a better sounding-board in the whole of Europe.' The paper itself has no bibliography and cites no publication whatsoever; only five other scientists are named anywhere in it — Newton, Maxwell, Hertz, Doppler and Lorentz. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Michele_Besso; einstein-website.de/en/patent-office/; fourmilab.ch/etexts/einstein/specrel/www/

question: Albert Einstein sent the last of his four 1905 papers to the physics journal Annalen der Physik, and it ran to just three pages, about 1,500 words, the shortest of them by far. Its title does not announce a result. It asks a question. Which question?
answer: Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content?
choices: Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content?
Is the Speed of Light the Same for Every Observer?
Can the Motion of the Molecules in a Liquid Be Counted?
Does Light Travel as Waves or as Separate Grains?
context: 'Ist die Tragheit eines Korpers von seinem Energieinhalt abhangig?', received by Annalen der Physik on 27 September 1905 — three pages, volume 18, pages 639-641. Inertia is a body's resistance to being shoved: how hard you have to push to change its motion, which is what we usually call its mass. For contrast, the June relativity paper ran 31 pages. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annus_mirabilis_papers; grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: Albert Einstein gave a formula in his May 1905 paper tying how far a tiny speck wanders through a fluid in a given time to the temperature, the thickness of the fluid and the width of the speck. Argument alone had not moved skeptics who saw atoms as a convenient fiction. Now anyone with a microscope and a thermometer could directly measure a quantity that had only ever been guessed at. Which physical quantity?
answer: Avogadro's number, the count of molecules in a mole
choices: Avogadro's number, the count of molecules in a mole
The mean free path, a molecule's flight between hits
Molecular diameter, the width of one water molecule
Atomic mass, the weight of a single hydrogen atom
context: Einstein predicted the mean square displacement <x^2> = 2Dt, with D = kT / (6 pi eta r): temperature T, the fluid's viscosity eta, the particle's radius r. Track a speck's wandering under a microscope, measure the fluid's thickness, and the number of molecules in a mole falls out — without anybody ever seeing an atom. (A mole is just a chemist's counting unit: a fixed number of molecules, the way a dozen is a fixed number of eggs.) Jean Perrin did exactly this in 1908-09 and got about 6.0 x 10^23; his 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics was for confirming the patent clerk's arithmetic. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: A student opens the English translation of Albert Einstein's fourth 1905 paper online, three pages long, and hunts for the line that first ties mass to energy. Anyone can do the same. Which letters does she find there for energy and for the speed of light?
answer: L for energy and V for the speed of light
choices: L for energy and V for the speed of light
E for energy and c for the speed of light
L for energy and c for the speed of light
E for energy and V for the speed of light
context: Einstein's own words in the paper: 'The mass of a body is a measure of its energy-content; if the energy changes by L, the mass changes in the same sense by L / 9 x 10^20, the energy being measured in ergs, and the mass in grammes.' No E, no m, no c anywhere. That 9 x 10^20 is the speed of light in centimetres per second, squared. The famous shorthand came later — so when a book says the 1905 paper 'derived E = mc^2', that is a modernizing gloss, not what is on the page. Check it yourself: the English translation is online. Source: fourmilab.ch/etexts/einstein/E_mc2/www/

question: Albert Einstein closed his mass-and-energy paper of September 1905 not in triumph but by handing the idea to the experimenters. It is 'not impossible', he wrote, that the theory 'may be successfully put to the test', using bodies whose energy changes to a high degree. What did he tell them to try it on?
answer: Salts of radium
choices: Salts of radium
Ores of uranium
Foils of polonium
Crystals of thorium
context: The closing line in full: 'It is not impossible that with bodies whose energy-content is variable to a high degree (e.g. with radium salts) the theory may be successfully put to the test.' Einstein had no laboratory of his own; what he could do was state exactly what a test would look like and hand it to the people who did. That is the shape of the whole paper — a question for a title, three pages of argument, and a proposed experiment for a last line. Source (English translation): fourmilab.ch/etexts/einstein/E_mc2/www/

question: A twenty-six-year-old named Albert Einstein, with no university post, mailed a paper rewriting space and time to Annalen der Physik, Germany's top physics journal, in June 1905. No formal peer review stood in his way: one editor simply read it and let it through. Which physicist passed 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies' for printing?
answer: Max Planck
choices: Max Planck
Wilhelm Wien
Philipp Lenard
Arnold Sommerfeld
context: Annalen der Physik had no formal peer review in 1905. Its editors, Max Planck and Paul Drude, simply read what came in and decided. Nobody refereed special relativity; Planck read it and printed it. Worth sitting with: the most heavily tested theory in physics entered the world through no review process at all, and has been checked ever since by everyone who could get at it. Peer review is a filter, not a truth-detector — the test is what settles things. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: A collector near Manchester caught the first recorded coal-black form of a common speckled grey moth in 1848, while the city's coal-burning factories poured soot over every tree and wall. Fifty years later, almost the whole local population had turned the same coal-black. What is this moth's everyday name?
answer: The peppered moth
choices: The peppered moth
The luna moth
The cinnabar moth
The tiger moth
context: R. S. Edleston caught the first live carbonaria peppered moth near Manchester in 1848 and reported it in 1864, by which time it was already the commoner form in his garden. Before industrialisation the black form was roughly 0.01% of the population. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: A bird hunts along a sooty trunk near Victorian Manchester and spots a pale peppered moth with no camouflage left. Coal smoke has done two things: soot has blackened the bark, and one pollutant from the chimneys has killed the pale lichens that speckled it. Which pollutant is it?
answer: sulphur dioxide
choices: sulphur dioxide
carbon monoxide
methane
nitrous oxide
context: Sulphur dioxide, a major coal-smoke pollutant, killed the crustose lichens that gave clean bark its pale mottled look; combined with soot deposition on the bark, this destroyed the camouflage of the pale (typica) form and unmasked it to hunting birds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: Bernard Kettlewell marked and released peppered moths in the 1950s to show that birds were behind the colour change. He chose two English woods with opposite bark colours, sooty Birmingham and clean Dorset. Why two woods so unlike?
answer: So the camouflage advantage should flip between the two woods
choices: So the camouflage advantage should flip between the two woods
To count how many moths lived in each wood
To collect moths of every possible colour
To feed the moths a different local plant
context: Bernard Kettlewell's 1953-1956 mark-release-recapture work found birds took about 75% of light moths in polluted Birmingham and about 86% of dark moths in unpolluted Dorset. The mirrored result made bird predation the leading explanation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: J. B. S. Haldane did the arithmetic on Manchester's peppered moths in 1924. The black form had gone from about 2% in 1848 to about 95% in 1895, and he calculated that it must carry roughly 50% greater fitness than the pale form. What was he using the math to rule out?
answer: That the colour change could have happened by random chance
choices: That the colour change could have happened by random chance
That coal soot had simply dyed the moths' wings black
That dark wings merely kept the moths warmer in the gloom
That dark moths had simply flown in from other towns
context: Haldane's 1924 paper on the mathematics of selection used the peppered moth as a worked example, ruling out genetic drift and pinning a large selective advantage on the dark form long before Kettlewell went into the woods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: Judith Hooper, a journalist, turned real questions about Bernard Kettlewell's peppered-moth work into a much bigger charge in her 2002 book Of Moths and Men: fraud. Textbooks wobbled. Michael Majerus, Bruce Grant and other biologists checked the accusation. What did they decide?
answer: that the fraud charge was without merit
choices: that the fraud charge was without merit
that the raw data had been destroyed
that Kettlewell had confessed
that the Royal Society had already retracted him
context: Scientists including Michael Majerus and Bruce Grant went back through the record and rejected the fraud accusation while agreeing that the underlying methodological criticisms about release-in-daylight and placement on trunks were legitimate and worth answering with better experiments. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: Michael Majerus refused to argue with the public attacks on Bernard Kettlewell's peppered moth work and ran an experiment instead. From 2001 to 2007 he released nearly five thousand moths onto natural resting spots in his own garden, and he died in 2009 before the result came out. What was he doing all those summers?
answer: Personally watching birds take the moths off the bark
choices: Personally watching birds take the moths off the bark
Painting the moths new colours in the lab
Counting eggs on the tree trunks
Recording bird songs at dawn each day
context: Majerus (1954-2009) ran the largest predation experiment ever attempted on the species and confirmed that nine bird species differentially took the more-visible form. His colleagues analysed the data and published in Biology Letters in February 2012, closing the case. Source: https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsbl/article/8/4/609/49215

question: A moth surveyor tallies her catch at a British site decades after the Great Smog of London and the act Parliament passed in 1956. The peppered moth story is running in reverse: the black form has fallen from over 90% toward under 5%. What real-world change is driving that reversal?
answer: Cleaner air and lighter tree bark returning
choices: Cleaner air and lighter tree bark returning
New moth predators arriving in Britain
A change in the moths' own genes
Warmer summers each year
context: As soot cleared and lichens regrew, pale bark returned and pale moths regained their camouflage. Kettlewell reported the early turn in 1956, Bruce Grant tracked the decline in 1996, and Laurence Cook of the University of Manchester published the definitive long-term survey in 2003. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: Ilik Saccheri's team traced what makes a peppered moth black down to a specific piece of DNA in 2016: a stretch roughly 22,000 letters long, sitting inside a gene that shapes wing scales. The insertion dates to around 1819, before the first black moth on record was caught near Manchester in 1848. Which gene did it land in?
answer: cortex
choices: cortex
doublesex
optix
engrailed
context: The carbonaria allele is a large transposable element, a 'jumping gene', inserted into the first intron of cortex, a gene that regulates wing scale development across butterflies and moths. The estimated 1819 origin sits nearly thirty years, and so about thirty one-a-year moth generations, before R. S. Edleston's 1848 specimen, so the variant was already in the population, at low frequency, when the soot arrived. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature17951

question: A girl holds her smartphone in one hand: screen, chips, magnets, battery, camera, speakers. The periodic table lists about eighty stable, non-radioactive elements, and a share of them sit inside that slab, some in vanishingly small amounts. About what share of the stable elements is inside one phone?
answer: About two thirds of the stable elements
choices: About one in twenty of the stable elements
About one in ten of the stable elements
About one third of the stable elements
About two thirds of the stable elements
context: Element-audits of modern smartphones (Compound Interest 2014; various teardowns) put the tally at roughly sixty elements, close to two-thirds of the ~80 stable elements on the periodic table. Every one of those elements is doing a specific engineering job that no cheaper element would do as well. Source: https://www.compoundchem.com/2014/02/19/the-chemical-elements-of-a-smartphone/

question: A boy taps the glass face of his phone and it senses his finger. A signal has to cross the entire face without visible wiring, cheaply enough for billions of phones. Which conductor is coated as an invisible film across the glass?
answer: A layer of indium tin oxide
choices: A film of aluminium sputtered onto the glass
A grid of very fine copper wires
A layer of indium tin oxide
A coating of graphite ink
context: Indium tin oxide (ITO), roughly 90 percent In2O3 and 10 percent SnO2 by weight, is one of very few materials that conducts electricity while staying optically clear, which is why almost every touchscreen uses it. Copper and silver conduct better but are opaque, so a copper screen would be a mirror; aluminium films are used elsewhere in phones but block light too. Indium is a soft, silvery metal recovered mostly as a by-product of refining zinc. Source: https://www.chemistryworld.com/podcasts/indium-tin-oxide-ito/3008984.article

question: A woman feels her phone buzz in her hand and lifts its earpiece to her ear. The vibration motor and the speaker each have to move mass or air with a magnet only a few millimetres across, so the magnet has to be unusually strong for its size. Which family of permanent magnets does the job?
answer: Neodymium-iron-boron magnets
choices: Ceramic ferrite magnets
Neodymium-iron-boron magnets
Samarium-cobalt magnets
Ordinary steel bar magnets
context: NdFeB magnets are the strongest permanent magnets known, which is why a phone can be a few millimetres thick and still move enough air to be heard. Samarium-cobalt magnets are a real alternative, but weaker and much pricier; ferrite and steel magnets do not come close. Source: https://www.stanfordmagnets.com/use-of-ndfeb-magnets-in-mobile-phones.html

question: A teenager plays a long game on his phone, and it grows warm in his hands. Its tiny speakers and motors run on the strongest permanent magnets known, and makers add a small amount of a heavy metal called dysprosium to the mix. What does adding dysprosium do?
answer: Keeps the magnet strong even when it gets hot
choices: Keeps the magnet strong even when it gets hot
Makes the magnet many times stronger overall
Makes the magnet safe to hold against skin
Makes the magnet much cheaper to produce
context: Dysprosium (and, secondarily, terbium) is added to NdFeB magnets to raise the temperature at which the magnet gives up its field, which lets speakers and motors survive above 200 degrees Celsius during manufacture and shrug off ordinary use. Holmium, erbium and thulium are all heavy lanthanides sitting next to dysprosium on the periodic table, but none of them does the phone-magnet job. Dysprosium is one of the priciest and most supply-constrained elements in the phone. Source: https://www.arnoldmagnetics.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/Important-Role-of-Dysprosium-in-Modern-Permanent-Magnets-150906.pdf

question: A shopper looks at a bright red dress in a photo on her phone. Ordinary dyes give off a smear of colour wavelengths that would look muddy there, so her screen uses a phosphor, a powder made with the rare-earth element europium, in front of a white or blue backlight. What does the europium phosphor do to the light?
answer: Re-emits a pure, narrow red near 611 nanometres
choices: Re-emits a pure, narrow red near 611 nanometres
Blocks every colour except red from passing through
Adds a tiny mirror behind each pixel
Speeds up how fast the pixels change
context: Europium(III) doped into an yttrium-oxide or related host emits a sharp red line near 611 nm - it is the reason on-screen reds look like reds and not orangey mud. Terbium(III) does the analogous green job near 545 nm. These narrow lines are a quantum-mechanical trick of the rare-earth f-electrons. Source: https://www.snexplores.org/article/rare-earth-elements-electrons-properties-technology

question: A repairer opens a phone and finds its main board dotted with hundreds of tiny capacitors, parts that store electrical charge for a moment and hand it back on demand. Space is the constraint. One family packs a huge amount of charge into a tiny volume with an oxide layer as little as 20 nanometres thick, grown on a metal powder. Which metal's oxide is used?
answer: Tantalum, in a tantalum-pentoxide capacitor
choices: Aluminium, in an aluminium electrolytic capacitor
Titanium, in a titanate ceramic capacitor
Silicon, in a thin-film silicon-oxide capacitor
Tantalum, in a tantalum-pentoxide capacitor
context: Tantalum pentoxide (Ta2O5) grown on tantalum powder makes a dielectric only 20-400 nm thick, which is why a tantalum capacitor stores more charge per unit volume than the alternatives. Aluminium electrolytics can store more charge per dollar but need a much larger case, so they lose the space race inside a phone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantalum_capacitor

question: Dmitri Mendeleev wrote down a density and a melting point in 1871 for a blank square just below aluminium on his table, and called its element eka-aluminium. Phones now rely on that metal, gallium, for the two jobs silicon does poorly: giving off light and handling very high radio frequencies. What did his 1871 entry show about his periodic table?
answer: It could predict the properties of elements nobody had discovered yet
choices: It could predict the properties of elements nobody had discovered yet
It could turn one element into another in the lab
It proved that atoms had a fixed cubic shape
It explained how radioactive elements decay
context: Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated gallium from a zinc ore in 1875 and its properties matched Mendeleev's 1871 eka-aluminium prediction almost exactly - the first triumph of the periodic table as a predictive tool. Today gallium arsenide handles the Wi-Fi and cellular radio-frequency chips, and gallium nitride the blue LEDs. Germanium was Mendeleev's eka-silicon (found 1886) and scandium his eka-boron (found 1879). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendeleev%27s_predicted_elements

question: Galileo Galilei turned his new telescope on Venus late in 1610 and watched it change shape: a thin sliver, half, fat gibbous, almost full, and back again. Venus circles the Sun in about 225 days, yet that cycle of shapes takes about 584 days to come round. Why does it take so much longer than Venus's year?
answer: Earth moves too, so Venus must gain a full lap on it
choices: Earth moves too, so Venus must gain a full lap on it
Venus spins backwards, which slows its phases down
The Sun's glare hides Venus for months each cycle
Venus slows down whenever it swings far from the Sun
context: Venus's own year, its trip round the Sun, takes about 225 days, but Earth is circling the Sun the same way, so the Earth-Sun-Venus lineup repeats only when Venus has gained one whole lap on Earth: about 584 days, the synodic period, the way a clock's minute hand must gain a whole lap before it passes the hour hand again. Venus does spin backwards, and it is hidden in the Sun's glare for a while each cycle, but neither sets the length of the cycle. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Phases_of_Venus

question: A boy at a small telescope watches Venus swell and shrink as it changes shape. Near full it is a small bright dot, but at its closest to Earth it grows about six times wider. Which phase shines brightest in the night sky?
answer: the crescent
choices: the crescent
the fat gibbous
the exact half
the almost-full disc
context: Near Earth, Venus lies between Earth and the Sun and shows a crescent, lit along only part of its face, yet its sheer apparent size wins: its peak brightness comes in the crescent phase, not at full. The near-full disc is on the far side of the Sun and much dimmer. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Phases_of_Venus

question: Claudius Ptolemy built a model of the sky in Alexandria around 150 AD, with Earth at the centre and everything else circling it. Venus rode on a small circle called an epicycle, whose centre stayed on a line between Earth and the Sun, so the planet stayed trapped between the two. Through a telescope, what phases could such a Venus ever show?
answer: only crescent phases
choices: only crescent phases
only gibbous and full phases
an exact half, always
any phase, just like the Moon
context: Venus's lit face always points toward the Sun. In Ptolemy's system Venus sits between us and the Sun, so we see mostly its unlit night side with a thin lit edge - always a crescent. Galileo saw a fat gibbous Venus through his telescope, and a gibbous Venus is fatal to that geometry. Source: thonyc.wordpress.com/2014/06/09/the-phases-of-venus-and-heliocentricity-a-rough-guide

question: Galileo Galilei mailed Johannes Kepler a jumbled string of letters to stake his claim before he was ready to publish: 'Haec immatura a me iam frustra leguntur o y'. Unscrambled it read 'Cynthiae figuras aemulatur Mater Amorum', 'the Mother of Love copies the shapes of Cynthia'. The Mother of Love was Venus in Roman poetry. What was Cynthia?
answer: the Moon
choices: the Moon
the Sun
Mercury
Sirius
context: Cynthia was a poetic name for Diana, the Roman moon goddess, so the unscrambled boast reads: 'Venus copies the phases of the Moon.' The anagram let Galileo timestamp the discovery without giving it away, in case a rival beat him to publication. Source: eaae-astronomy.org/images/workshops/galileoandthephasesofvenus.pdf

question: Galileo Galilei wrote to Christoph Clavius, an old Jesuit in Rome, in December 1610. Galileo had just seen through his new telescope that Venus runs through a full cycle of phases, crescent, half, gibbous, almost full, and that contradicted the old Ptolemaic sky. Clavius had helped design the Gregorian calendar still in use today. Why did it matter that Galileo told Clavius?
answer: Clavius was the most respected astronomer in the Catholic world
choices: Clavius was the most respected astronomer in the Catholic world
Clavius was Galileo's own paying student in Rome
Clavius owned the largest telescope in Europe
Clavius was the personal astrologer of the Pope
context: Clavius, chief mathematician of the Collegio Romano, was the astronomer whose endorsement could shield or sink a claim inside the Church. Galileo's letter to him is dated 30 December 1610. Source: thonyc.wordpress.com/2014/06/09/the-phases-of-venus-and-heliocentricity-a-rough-guide ; grokipedia.com/page/Phases_of_Venus

question: Tycho Brahe had already offered a compromise cosmos when Galileo Galilei saw the phases of Venus: Earth fixed at the centre, the Sun circling Earth, and all the other planets circling the Sun. Many books say those phases proved that Earth moves. Through Galileo's telescope, what would a Tychonic Venus have looked like?
answer: exactly the same phase cycle as the Copernican Venus
choices: exactly the same phase cycle as the Copernican Venus
only crescent phases, exactly as Ptolemy had it
no phases at all - a steady bright disc all year
phases running backwards, gibbous shrinking to crescent
context: In both the Copernican and the Tychonic systems Venus orbits the Sun, so from Earth its lit face sweeps through the same cycle either way. The phases killed Ptolemy and left Tycho's compromise standing for another century - until Newton's gravity and Bradley's stellar aberration finally closed the case for a moving Earth. Source: thonyc.wordpress.com/2014/06/09/the-phases-of-venus-and-heliocentricity-a-rough-guide

question: A farmer who rises before dawn sees Venus blazing low in the east as the morning star, and months later it hangs in the west after sunset as the evening star. Never once in his life does he see it high overhead at midnight. What keeps Venus out of the midnight sky?
answer: Its orbit lies inside Earth's, so it never strays far from the Sun
choices: Its orbit lies inside Earth's, so it never strays far from the Sun
Its orbit lies outside Earth's, so it trails far behind the Sun
Its orbit is tilted steeply, so it dips below the horizon by night
Earth's shadow falls across it through the middle of the night
context: Venus's orbit sits inside Earth's, so from Earth it never appears more than about 47 degrees from the Sun, its greatest elongation: far enough to blaze in a dark sky after dusk or before dawn, never far enough to stand opposite the Sun at midnight. Mercury, closer to the Sun still, is held to about 28 degrees, which is why it is even harder to spot. Planets whose orbits lie outside Earth's, such as Mars and Jupiter, can stand opposite the Sun and ride high at midnight. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Phases_of_Venus ; earthsky.org/astronomy-essentials/greatest-elongation-definition-venus-mercury/

question: A Swiss physicist and his young helper lifted off from Augsburg, Germany, under a huge hydrogen balloon on 27 May 1931. They rose higher than any human beings ever had, the first people to reach the stratosphere, the calm layer of air above ordinary weather. Who rode up to 15,781 metres?
answer: Auguste Piccard and Paul Kipfer
choices: Auguste Piccard and Paul Kipfer
Wiley Post and Harold Gatty
Charles Lindbergh and Anne Morrow
Otto Lilienthal and Gustave Whitehead
