context: First manned flight into the stratosphere. Post and Gatty had just circled the globe the same summer; Lindbergh flew the Atlantic in 1927; Lilienthal was a 19th-century glider pioneer. Sources: history.com/articles/auguste-piccard-balloon-stratosphere; balloon.hu/new/2015/05/27.

question: Auguste Piccard flew a hydrogen balloon out of Augsburg in May 1931, up into air so thin that a person without protection will black out and die in minutes. His fix made the flight possible, and every airliner still carries its descendant. What did he invent?
answer: a spherical pressurized aluminium capsule
choices: a spherical pressurized aluminium capsule
a rubber suit fed by an air pump
a heated oxygen tent over the basket
bottled-oxygen masks for the crew
context: Piccard's gondola held sea-level pressure inside while outside pressure fell away -- the direct ancestor of every airliner cabin. Source: amusingplanet.com/2022/06/auguste-piccard-man-who-flew-to.html.

question: Auguste Piccard turned his own balloon upside down after the stratosphere flight. A balloon's basket hangs from a bag of light gas; his bathyscaphe Trieste hung a heavy steel cabin beneath a huge float, and the whole craft sank through the sea instead of rising through the air. What filled the float?
answer: gasoline
choices: gasoline
compressed air
fresh water
syntactic foam
context: Trieste's float held about 130 cubic metres of aviation gasoline. Gasoline is only about 0.7 times as dense as water and barely compresses (it shrank by roughly a tenth at full depth), so the deep cannot squeeze its lift away the way it would crush a pocket of air. Iron shot held on by electromagnets gave the weight to sink, and dropping it brought the craft home. Bathyscaphe is Piccard's own coinage, from the Greek for 'deep' and 'ship'. Syntactic foam, a solid of tiny glass spheres set in resin, is the modern answer, used in Deepsea Challenger. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trieste_(bathyscaphe)

question: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh heard a bang shake the Trieste about nine kilometres down on the way to Challenger Deep in 1960. They talked it over inside the pressure sphere and pushed on to the bottom anyway. What had broken?
answer: an outer Plexiglas pane on the entry tunnel
choices: an outer Plexiglas pane on the entry tunnel
the main viewport of the crew sphere
an electromagnet on the ballast hopper
the acoustic telephone to the surface ship
context: Their steel crew sphere was intact; the crack was on the flooded entry trunk they had climbed down through, so they were never in the same water as the crack. Source: sea-technology.com/60th-anniversary-of-deepest-ocean-dive.

question: Paul Yancey and his colleagues argued in 2014 that bony fish hit a ceiling near 8,200 metres, and biologists still doubt the flatfish Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reported at the bottom of Challenger Deep. One small molecule keeps a fish's proteins from being crushed, and its cells can pack in only so much of it. Which molecule?
answer: TMAO
choices: TMAO
myoglobin
haemoglobin
chlorophyll
context: TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide) stabilises folded proteins against pressure; fish need more of it the deeper they go, and near 8,200 m their cells would become isosmotic with seawater, past which they cannot easily go. What Piccard and Walsh actually saw remains argued about. Source: pnas.org/doi/pdf/10.1073/pnas.1322003111.

question: Don Walsh and Jacques Piccard sat the Trieste on the floor of Challenger Deep for twenty minutes in 1960, nearly 11 kilometres down in the Pacific Ocean near the island of Guam. It is the deepest known spot on Earth, and no crewed craft followed them. How long was the gap before a human being went back down?
answer: 52 years, until 2012
choices: 52 years, until 2012
12 years, until 1972
24 years, until 1984
38 years, until 1998
context: James Cameron dived Deepsea Challenger solo on 26 March 2012; Victor Vescovo's Limiting Factor (2019) was the first submersible built to make the trip REPEATABLE. A record is not a capability. Source: guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/613583.

question: An engineer sketches the crew cabin of a deep-sea craft and draws a sphere, as the builders of Trieste, Alvin, Deepsea Challenger and Limiting Factor did. Against uniform outside pressure the sphere alone answers with a single kind of stress in its wall, one that steel and titanium handle well. What kind of stress?
answer: pure compression
choices: pure compression
pure tension
torsion
shear
context: Any other shape develops bending stresses under uniform pressure, and bending is the failure mode both metals lose to first. A sphere loads the wall in compression alone. Source: engineering.org.cn/sscae/EN/10.15302/J-SSCAE-2019.06.018.

question: A researcher hands one trial patient a dummy pill and another patient two, and the two relieve pain better. A capsule beats a tablet of the very same fake, and the more a placebo looks like real treatment, the better it works. Which fake beats them all?
answer: An injection of salt water
choices: A pill that has been coloured bright red
A pill labelled with the name of an expensive brand
An injection of salt water
A drop of sugar water on the tongue
context: Placebo strength scales with the impressiveness of the ritual: injections outperform capsules, capsules outperform tablets, two dummy pills outperform one, and larger pills outperform smaller ones. Nothing at all, dressed up more, works more. Source: https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/306437

question: A doctor gives a new drug to a hundred people with sore knees, and eighty of them say the knee feels better afterwards. That number by itself does not prove the drug works. What missing comparison does she need before she can trust the drug?
answer: How many would have felt better without the drug
choices: How many kept taking their other medicines
How many would have felt better without the drug
How many knew they were getting the new drug
How many were on their worst day when tested
context: Because most people improve on their own -- illnesses come and go, and bad days are followed by better ones -- the honest question is never 'did the patients get better?' but 'did they get better than the ones who got the fake?'. That is why control arms exist. The other three choices are also real trial-design worries (co-intervention, blinding, regression to the mean) but only the control arm answers the missing comparison. Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM200105243442106

question: Leonard Cobb, a Seattle heart doctor, tested a popular operation for the crushing chest pain of angina in 1959: a surgeon tied off an artery behind the breastbone. Cobb compared it with a sham in which the surgeon only cut the skin. What did the sham do?
answer: It relieved angina about as well as the real surgery
choices: It did nothing, and confirmed that the real surgery worked
It relieved angina about as well as the real surgery
It caused more chest pain than doing nothing at all
It caused fatal complications and ended the trial early
context: Cobb's 1959 paper 'An Evaluation of Internal-Mammary-Artery Ligation by a Double-Blind Technic' in the New England Journal of Medicine compared the real ligation of the internal mammary artery to a sham in which only the skin was cut. The two arms did equally well; the operation, then widely used, was abandoned. Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM195905282602204

question: Bruce Moseley, a Houston surgeon, published a knee-surgery trial in the New England Journal of Medicine in July 2002. One group of patients was put to sleep and given real cuts on the skin, but the surgeon did nothing inside the knee. How did that fake-surgery group fare?
answer: About the same as the real surgery
choices: Much worse than the real surgery
Slightly worse than the real surgery
Slightly better than the real surgery
About the same as the real surgery
context: Moseley's 11 July 2002 NEJM trial randomized patients with knee osteoarthritis to arthroscopic debridement, arthroscopic lavage, or sham surgery (skin incisions only). At no point did either real-surgery arm report less pain or better function than the placebo arm. Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259

question: Asbjorn Hrobjartsson and Peter Gotzsche of Denmark gathered trials for a big review in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2001, choosing ones that compared a placebo, a fake pill or shot, against no treatment at all. Where did placebos reliably move the needle?
answer: On subjective reports, above all pain
choices: On subjective reports, above all pain
On measurable disease
On both, in equal measure
On almost nothing at all
context: Hrobjartsson and Gotzsche 2001, 'Is the Placebo Powerless?' in NEJM, reviewed trials with a no-treatment arm and found placebos reliably moved subjective outcomes (especially pain) but did not meaningfully change objective disease measures. Placebos mostly change how you feel, not what the disease is doing. Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM200105243442106

question: Henry Beecher fixed a number in the minds of doctors with his 1955 paper 'The Powerful Placebo': about one in three patients respond to a placebo. People still quote it. Kienle and Kiene looked again at his fifteen trials in 1997. What did they say really caused most of that response?
answer: Patients simply getting better on their own
choices: Deliberate cheating by the original researchers
Publication bias in which studies made it into print
Patients simply getting better on their own
The colour of the placebo tablets used at the time
context: Kienle and Kiene's 1997 reanalysis of Beecher's fifteen trials in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology found no evidence of a real placebo effect in the underlying data. Most of the improvement Beecher had counted as placebo response was just the natural course of illness -- people getting better anyway. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9449934/

question: Ted Kaptchuk at Harvard gave a bottle labelled 'placebo' to patients with irritable bowel syndrome in 2010 and told them openly that the pills inside were inert. The trial was small, it ran three weeks and it rested on what patients said they felt. How did that open placebo group do?
answer: Significantly better than no-treatment controls
choices: Significantly better than no-treatment controls
About the same as no-treatment controls
Significantly worse than no-treatment controls
The same as a fully-blinded placebo arm
context: Kaptchuk et al., PLOS ONE 2010: 80 IBS patients, three-week trial, one arm given pills openly labelled as inert sugar pills, one arm given no treatment with matched provider interactions. The open-label placebo arm improved significantly more. Caveat: small study, subjective outcomes, short follow-up. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0015591

question: A mother opens a free report on the World Health Organization (WHO) website, dated September 2019, months before anyone outside China had heard of COVID-19. It is the WHO's best advice on what governments should do the next time a killer respiratory virus sweeps the world. What is the report specifically about?
answer: non-pharmaceutical measures for pandemic influenza
choices: non-pharmaceutical measures for pandemic influenza
coronavirus outbreak response in the Western Pacific
vaccine stockpiling for future respiratory pandemics
hospital surge capacity in low-income countries
context: 'Non-pharmaceutical public health measures for mitigating the risk and impact of epidemic and pandemic influenza', WHO Global Influenza Programme, 2019, ISBN 9789241516839. NPIs are what a country has BEFORE a vaccine exists. Source: WHO publication page.

question: A student runs a finger along the summary table in the World Health Organization (WHO) guide of September 2019, written for flu, not the virus behind COVID-19. Four columns grade how bad a pandemic is, and one striking column sits beside them for a whole category of measures. What does its header say, word for word?
answer: Not recommended in any circumstances
choices: Not recommended in any circumstances
Recommended only in wealthy nations
Reserved for research use only
Under active scientific review now
context: The category column ran alongside the severity grid (Any, Moderate, High, Extraordinary) and gathered measures the evidence review had concluded should not be used at ANY severity. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, summary of recommendations.

question: A school principal opens the World Health Organization (WHO) pandemic-influenza guide of September 2019 at the page on schools. The guide sorts every non-drug measure into columns by evidence and severity, and planned school closures do not sit in its 'not recommended' column. What does its written language say about them?
answer: Suggested in a severe epidemic or pandemic, harms weighed, duration limited
choices: Suggested in a severe epidemic or pandemic, harms weighed, duration limited
Recommended at any pandemic level, as early as possible, to slow spread
Recommended only after two weeks of confirmed spread inside a school
Recommended for primary schools but advised against for secondary ones
context: The guide's words: 'Coordinated proactive school closures or class dismissals are suggested during a severe epidemic or pandemic. In such cases, the adverse effects on the community should be fully considered (e.g. family burden and economic considerations), and the timing and duration should be limited to a period that is judged to be optimal.' The 2020 US school closures ran far longer than that caveat contemplated, but the guidance itself did contemplate closures. Source: WHO, Non-pharmaceutical public health measures for mitigating the risk and impact of epidemic and pandemic influenza (2019), school-measures recommendation.

question: A journalist reads the World Health Organization (WHO) pandemic-influenza guide of September 2019, issued only months before COVID-19, and stops at quarantine: confining someone who feels fine but might have been near a sick person. The guide refuses to recommend it for exposed but well people, and gives its reasons in writing. What are they?
answer: no obvious rationale for the measure, and considerable difficulties in implementing it
choices: no obvious rationale for the measure, and considerable difficulties in implementing it
evidence from the 2009 H1N1 review showed no measurable slowing of transmission
modelling suggested contact tracing alone would substitute effectively for it
household transmission would still occur inside the quarantined home anyway
context: The evidence and practicality argument sits in the text; it is not a values statement. Note the document does not appeal to 'freedom' -- it appeals to evidence and to feasibility, which is what a public-health document should. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, contact management section.

question: A traveller steps up to an airport fever check and fills in a health form. The World Health Organization (WHO) pandemic-flu guide of September 2019, published months before COVID-19, refused to recommend screening at borders. What did the guide say was the flaw in airport screening?
answer: it cannot see infected people who are still pre-symptomatic
choices: it cannot see infected people who are still pre-symptomatic
symptomatic travellers can hide fevers by taking paracetamol before landing
the incubation window for influenza can exceed 14 days in some cases
screening sensitivity drops below 50% when local prevalence is low
context: The document phrased it as a 'lack of sensitivity' of symptom-based screening 'in identifying infected but asymptomatic (i.e. pre-symptomatic) travellers'. A hunting tool that cannot see the thing it hunts does not catch it -- an argument grade-schoolers can follow. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, travel measures section.

question: A factory owner opens the World Health Organization (WHO) pandemic-influenza guide of 2019, written before COVID-19, at the page on closing workplaces. The guide grades its measures by four levels of severity, and for workplace closures it uses a distinctive phrase. Which phrase?
answer: a last step only considered in extraordinarily severe epidemics and pandemics
choices: a last step only considered in extraordinarily severe epidemics and pandemics
recommended only where the community weekly attack rate exceeds five percent
suggested during moderate or above pandemics, with the closure kept under fourteen days
recommended only for high-risk industries and only during the pandemic peak
context: 'Extraordinarily severe' was the top of the document's four-level severity ladder; 'last step' was in the guidance's own language. Broad 2020 workplace closures did not observe that threshold. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, social measures section.

question: A nurse reads the World Health Organization (WHO) guide of September 2019 on non-drug measures for the next flu pandemic: masks, hand-washing, school closures. The guide scores the quality of the evidence behind each recommendation with a rating system called GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation). For nearly every recommendation, how does GRADE rate the evidence?
answer: very low
choices: very low
low
moderate
high
context: GRADE ratings run very low, low, moderate, high; nearly every line in this document was rated at the bottom. That is what makes the 2019 document important -- it is a public document being modest about itself. 'We are following the science' does not describe what a document rated 'very low' throughout can say. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, GRADE evidence-profile tables.

question: Protesters in yellow high-visibility vests filled roundabouts across France from 17 November 2018, answering a planned rise in the carbon portion of the fuel tax that fell hardest on diesel drivers in the countryside. The movement took the vest's French name, gilets jaunes. Why did that garment make an instant uniform?
answer: French drivers are required by law to keep one in every vehicle.
choices: French drivers are required by law to keep one in every vehicle.
The Elysee Palace staff had worn them during a recent strike.
It matched the color of the ruling party's campaign posters.
Truckers' unions had adopted it as their formal uniform in 2015.
context: The high-visibility yellow safety vest ('gilet jaune') has been mandatory in French cars since 2008. Because every driver already owned one, it worked as a leaderless, instant symbol - anyone could join by pulling one out of the glovebox. Source: International Budget Partnership, France: The Yellow Vests.

question: Edouard Philippe, France's prime minister, suspended a planned rise in the fuel tax for six months on 4 December 2018, as the gilets jaunes filled France's roundabouts and clashes with police spread through Paris. The next day he stood up in parliament. What did he do to the increase scheduled for 2019?
answer: Cancelled it outright for the coming year
choices: Cancelled it outright for the coming year
Doubled it and earmarked the extra for pensions
Tied it to a national referendum in 2020
Handed the decision to the European Parliament
context: Philippe suspended the rise for six months on 4 December; on 5 December he told the National Assembly it was gone from the 2019 budget, and the environment minister said it was scrapped for the whole year. On 10 December President Emmanuel Macron went on television and promised minimum-wage workers 100 euros more a month. Nothing about the physics of CO2 changed that week; the politics did. Sources: https://www.cbc.ca/1.4933806 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_vests_protests

question: Washington State voters went to the ballot on Initiative 732 in 2016. It would have taxed carbon dioxide emissions from $15 a tonne and cut the state sales tax from 6.5% to 5.5%, a revenue-neutral swap that libertarian and centrist economists praised. It lost 59% to 41%. Which coalition helped defeat it?
answer: State Democrats, labour leaders and environmental-justice groups
choices: State Democrats, labour leaders and environmental-justice groups
Chevron, ExxonMobil and the American Petroleum Institute
Audubon Washington, the Sightline Institute and James Hansen
The Federalist Society and the National Rifle Association
context: The Washington State Democratic Party voted to oppose it, as did the Washington State Labor Council and environmental-justice groups such as Front and Centered; the Sierra Club declined to support it. They objected less to taxing carbon than to handing the money back through a sales-tax cut instead of spending it on their preferred programs. Audubon Washington, the Sightline Institute and the climate scientist James Hansen backed it. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Washington_Initiative_732 ; https://planetizen.com/node/88665

question: Researchers at the Dutch consultancy CE Delft, working for Greenpeace, tallied aircraft movements at the airports serving Davos, the Swiss ski resort, during the 2022 meeting of the World Economic Forum (WEF). Presidents, prime ministers and the world's richest business leaders gather there for it. What did the researchers find?
answer: About 1,040 private-jet flights in and out of the airports
choices: About 1,040 private-jet flights in and out of the airports
About 40 chartered flights in and out of the airports
About 12,000 helicopter movements in and out of Zurich
About 300 commercial airliner arrivals into Zurich alone
context: The count covered the meeting week of 21 to 27 May 2022; the forum, usually held in January, met in late spring that year. An average week at those airports saw about half as many private-jet flights, and 38% of the meeting-week flights were under 500 km. The report was commissioned by Greenpeace International, and the researchers attributed about half the flights to the meeting itself. Sources: https://www.greenpeace.org/international/press-release/57867/hundreds-of-ultra-short-private-jet-flights-to-davos-world-economic-forum/ ; https://www.greenpeace.org/eu-unit/issues/climate-energy/46529/private-jet-emissions-quadrupled-during-2022-world-economic-forum/ (Greenpeace / CE Delft, January 2023).

question: Nicholas Stern priced a tonne of carbon dioxide at about $85 in 2006, and William Nordhaus, a mainstream economist of the same school, landed at a small fraction of that. The gap is not over the physics. What single modelling choice, applied over centuries, opens it?
answer: The discount rate they apply to harms falling on future generations
choices: The discount rate they apply to harms falling on future generations
Which damage function best fits observed 20th-century impacts
How to weight low-probability, high-severity catastrophic tails
Whether to price methane and nitrous oxide alongside CO2
context: Stern used a near-zero pure rate of time preference (about 0.1% a year); Nordhaus used about 1.5%. Damage functions and fat-tail weighting are real live disputes too, but it is the discount rate that drives the order-of-magnitude gap here. The fight about carbon taxes is over ethics and economics, not the infrared physics. Sources: PNAS, 'Agreeing to disagree on climate policy'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stern_Review (the $85 figure).

question: Ellen Goodman of the Boston Globe wrote in 2007 that 'global warming deniers are now on a par with Holocaust deniers.' The word then spread through the press, aimed even at people who accept the greenhouse effect but dispute policy. How did the Associated Press later update its stylebook?
answer: Advised its writers to avoid the label, and to avoid 'skeptic' as well
choices: Advised its writers to avoid the label, and to avoid 'skeptic' as well
Made 'denier' the required term for anyone questioning any climate claim
Kept 'denier' but told writers to flag the Holocaust link in a footnote
Replaced 'denier' with 'contrarian' as the AP's preferred neutral term
context: The AP asked reporters to avoid 'denier' (Holocaust connotation) and also 'skeptic' (which the AP said belongs to honest inquiry), suggesting 'doubter' instead. A word that makes a person unaskable is not an argument. Source: National Association of Scholars, 'AP Denies the Denier Label'.

question: Indian officials counted 8.3 million sterilisation operations in the twelve months from July 1976, most of them done without the patient's consent. The year before, the count had been 2.7 million. Under which crisis of government did that surge happen?
answer: Indira Gandhi's Emergency
choices: Indira Gandhi's Emergency
the Bengal famine relief
the Partition of Bengal
the Sino-Indian border war
context: The Emergency ran from June 1975 to March 1977; Prime Minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and ruled by decree. The Hindi word for sterilisation, 'nasbandi', became its lasting name in Indian memory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India).

question: Indira Gandhi, prime minister of India, suspended civil liberties and ruled by decree in June 1975. Her son took over the government's population campaign in September 1976, and India's sterilisation numbers shot up into the millions in a single year. Who was he?
answer: Sanjay Gandhi
choices: Sanjay Gandhi
Rajiv Gandhi
Morarji Desai
Jayaprakash Narayan
context: Sanjay Gandhi ran the drive as an unofficial parallel government. Rajiv was his elder brother, who kept out of politics until Sanjay's death in 1980. Desai and Narayan were the opposition figures who beat Congress in 1977. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India).

question: Paul Ehrlich, an American biologist, published The Population Bomb in 1968, predicting mass starvation in the 1970s and demanding drastic government action to cut births in poor countries. About India in particular, what did the book call for?
answer: compulsory sterilisation of men with three or more children
choices: compulsory sterilisation of men with three or more children
voluntary contraception funded by the World Bank
raising the legal marriage age to twenty-five
importing American grain to buy the crisis time
context: Ehrlich went further -- he proposed the United States supply helicopters and surgical instruments to speed the vasectomy programme. The recommendation is in his book; it is named here, and named as recommendation, not as cause. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Population_Bomb.

question: Officials handed sterilisation quotas down India's civil service while Indira Gandhi ruled by decree. The drive leaned on more than doctors: other state employees had to send in a set number of people for the operation, on pain of losing pay or a job. Which workers were they?
answer: teachers and clerks
choices: teachers and clerks
railway engineers
customs inspectors
postal sorters
context: Targets were passed down the civil service until schoolteachers were nudging parents into vasectomies and clerks were bringing in relatives. Attach a career to a number and the number is what you get -- honestly or otherwise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India).

question: Police in Muzaffarnagar, in northern India, held seventeen villagers for sterilisation on 18 October 1976, in a mass drive backed by police force. A crowd gathered around the police station and demanded their release. How did the day end?
answer: police opened fire and about thirty people died
choices: police opened fire and about thirty people died
the crowd freed the detainees and dispersed
the seventeen were quietly released overnight
a magistrate cancelled the operations by court order
context: One of the sharpest recorded incidents of the campaign. Muzaffarnagar became a byword for what a quota costs when it meets a village that says no. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India).

question: Indian voters threw out Congress in the general election of March 1977, after rule by decree since June 1975 and a mass sterilisation drive, and Indira Gandhi lost her own seat at Rae Bareli. Which single Hindi word did the winning opposition's slogans hammer over and over?
answer: nasbandi
choices: nasbandi
swaraj
satyagraha
ahimsa
context: 'Nasbandi' means sterilisation. The other three are famous words from earlier Indian politics -- swaraj (self-rule), satyagraha (truth-force), ahimsa (non-violence) -- Gandhi-era slogans, not 1977 slogans. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India).

question: Song Jian, a Chinese engineer, ran China's population through a family of equations at a meeting in Chengdu in 1980. Only a one-child rule kept up for decades could have reached the target his group set. What figure did his group give as China's 'ideal' long-term population?
answer: about 700 million
choices: about 700 million
about 1.5 billion
about 300 million
about 2.4 billion
context: Song and his team put the ideal at 650 to 700 million, roughly two-thirds of the then-population of one billion. To reach it required a one-child rule maintained for decades. He had encountered the cybernetic population theory of the Club of Rome at a control-engineering conference in Helsinki in 1978. Source: socsci.uci.edu 2010-09-23.

question: Wang Feng, Daniel Goodkind and other scholars have challenged a story often told about Song Jian, a Chinese engineer: that his population-model equations proved China had to cap families at one child, and the Party obeyed. What do they say happened instead?
answer: Party leaders had already decided on one-child restrictions before 1980
choices: Party leaders had already decided on one-child restrictions before 1980
Song's equations were sound but rested on a bad fertility estimate
the policy was pushed from below by provincial cadres, not Beijing
the policy was copied wholesale from India's 1976 Emergency campaign
context: Goodkind's phrase: Song's team functioned 'more like expert witnesses for a government already determined to prosecute'. The equations may have supplied authority rather than the decision, and that is its own lesson about the misuse of scientific prestige. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-child_policy.

question: Chinese officials imposed a one-child rule on most families from 1980, with fines and at times forced abortions behind it. Many wanted a son to keep the name. The sex ratio at birth rose from about 108 boys per 100 girls in 1981 to about 117 by 2000. Roughly how many more men than women did that leave in those generations?
answer: 32 to 36 million
choices: 32 to 36 million
3 to 4 million
300 to 400 million
under a million
context: The planners modelled births as a number. They did not model the preference, family by family, for a son to carry the name -- a preference that under a one-child rule crossed the modern ultrasound and became this gap. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-child_policy.

question: Walter Brattain and John Bardeen pressed tiny gold contacts onto a pure crystal at Bell Labs in the fall of 1947. On 23 December they showed a small device that made a voice signal a hundred times louder, and it would soon replace the vacuum tube. What crystal did they use?
answer: high-purity germanium
choices: high-purity germanium
single-crystal silicon
gallium arsenide
natural quartz
context: Silicon took over the industry within a decade, but the FIRST working transistor was point-contact germanium. Brattain's lab notebook for 16 December 1947 records the amplification; the 23 December demonstration played speech through the device so the audience could hear it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_transistor.

question: Max Tegmark and John Wheeler estimated in Scientific American in 2001 that about 30 percent of America's economy rested on inventions that only quantum mechanics made possible, the strange rules that govern electrons and photons. Their examples ran on to the magnetic resonance scanners in hospitals. Which two inventions opened the list?
answer: semiconductors and lasers
choices: semiconductors and lasers
atomic clocks and electron microscopes
digital camera sensors and solar cells
flash memory and superconducting magnets
context: Tegmark & Wheeler, '100 Years of Quantum Mysteries', Scientific American 284:2 (Feb 2001), pp. 68-75: the 30 percent rests on inventions 'from semiconductors in computer chips to lasers in compact-disc players, magnetic resonance imaging in hospitals, and much more.' Atomic clocks, electron microscopes, camera sensors, solar cells, flash memory and superconducting magnets are quantum technologies too, but the article's list opened with chips and lasers. Quantum theory sits inside a phone, a ceiling bulb and a barcode scanner all at once. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/100-years-of-quantum-mysteries/

question: Nick Holonyak ran current through a small diode at a General Electric lab near Syracuse, New York, on 9 October 1962. Grown from an alloy of gallium arsenide and gallium phosphide, it gave off light a human eye could see, the first visible light-emitting diode (LED). What colour did it glow?
answer: red
choices: red
green
blue
yellow
context: The alloy GaAs0.6P0.4 has a band gap that emits in the red. Green LEDs followed within a few years; blue took three more decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Holonyak.

question: John Bardeen shared a Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956 for the transistor, then shared a second in 1972 with Leon Cooper and Robert Schrieffer, which makes him the only person ever to win the physics prize twice. What was the second prize for?
answer: the theory of superconductivity
choices: the theory of superconductivity
the design of the atomic clock
the discovery of the neutrino
the invention of holography
context: The 1972 prize citation reads 'for their jointly developed theory of superconductivity, usually called the BCS-theory'. It explains why the electrons in certain cooled metals pair up and glide through the lattice with zero resistance - itself a purely quantum result. Source: nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1972.

question: William Shockley designed a rugged, layered transistor soon after his colleagues John Bardeen and Walter Brattain made the first working one at Bell Labs in 1947. Theirs, a tiny switch that blocks electric current or lets it through, was fragile and hard to make; his stacked three layers of treated crystal. What did Shockley's design become?
answer: The workhorse of early transistor radios and computers
choices: The workhorse of early transistor radios and computers
A curiosity shelved in favour of the fragile original
A rugged new kind of vacuum tube for radio sets
A magnetic memory cell for the earliest computers
context: Shockley's bipolar junction transistor (conceived in 1948) replaced the finicky point-contact geometry with three doped layers. It ran the transistor radios and computers of the 1950s and 1960s; the chips of today are built almost entirely from a later design, the metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET), invented at Bell Labs by Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng in 1959. Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel in Physics with Bardeen and Brattain 'for their researches on semiconductors and their discovery of the transistor effect'. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_transistor ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOSFET

question: Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura cracked one colour of light-emitting diode (LED) with gallium nitride crystals and shared the 2014 Nobel in Physics for it. White LED bulbs had waited thirty years longer than red ones, because the industry could not make that colour efficiently. Which colour was the missing piece?
answer: blue
choices: blue
green
yellow
infrared
context: The Nobel citation reads 'for the invention of efficient blue light-emitting diodes which has enabled bright and energy-saving white light sources'. Every white bulb in the house is a blue LED coated with a yellow phosphor (cerium-doped YAG) - the blue light pumps the phosphor and the eye adds the two into white. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-emitting_diode.

question: Theodore Maiman fired the very first working laser on 16 May 1960 at Hughes Research Labs in Malibu, California, with only his assistant, Irnee D'Haenens, in the room. A photo flash lamp coiled around a small rod pumped energy into it, and the rod produced the beam. What was the rod made of?
answer: synthetic ruby
choices: synthetic ruby
neodymium-doped YAG crystal
titanium-doped sapphire
neodymium-doped glass
context: Charles Townes and Arthur Schawlow had assumed a gas medium would come first; Maiman used a small cylinder of chromium-doped aluminium oxide - synthetic ruby - pumped by a spiral flashtube. Nd:YAG, Ti:sapphire and Nd:glass are all now-standard solid-state laser media, but each came later. The Nature paper 'Stimulated Optical Radiation in Ruby' appeared on 6 August 1960. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Maiman. ; laserfocusworld.com/home/article/16545957 (D'Haenens obituary: the two were the only people present).

question: A boy presses a button on a remote control and its status light comes on, a light-emitting diode (LED), the tiny solid-state bulb in most room lights too. Different colours of LED come from crystals with different energy gaps between the electron levels allowed inside them. When current flows, one electron does one specific thing in the crystal, and that fixes the colour. What does the electron do?
answer: falls from a higher band to a lower one and releases one photon
choices: falls from a higher band to a lower one and releases one photon
collides with another electron and both heat the crystal
spins in place and the magnetism of the spin glows
orbits the nucleus faster and radiates infrared
context: Electron energy = photon energy: E = h*nu, so a wider gap makes a higher-energy (bluer) photon. That is why an LED's colour is fixed by its material, not by voltage - and why blue took gallium nitride rather than a tweak to a red LED. This is a purely quantum result; classically an electron would radiate a smear of colours. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-emitting_diode ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_gap.

question: A student measures the wavelength of a cheap red laser pointer on her kitchen table instead of trusting the packet. She shines it at a shallow angle onto one everyday object whose surface holds long rows of tiny, evenly spaced tracks, what physicists call a diffraction grating. A row of bright spots appears on the wall, and their angles give her the wavelength. Which object is it?
answer: a CD or DVD
choices: a CD or DVD
a bathroom mirror
a sheet of aluminium foil
a printed newspaper page
context: CD track pitch is 1.6 micrometres; DVD 0.74 micrometres - both close enough to red-laser wavelengths (~650 nm) that the tracks act as a diffraction grating, and d*sin(theta) = m*lambda solves for lambda from the measured spot angles. A mirror gives a single reflection; foil scatters; newsprint is too irregular. Test it yourself: don't take the wavelength on the packet on trust, measure it. Reference: American Journal of Physics 65(9), 1997.

question: A science writer files transistors, light-emitting diodes and lasers under settled quantum technology, then turns to the much-hyped quantum computer. So far it has beaten ordinary machines only on narrow, specially chosen tasks, never on a problem people actually want solved. What stands in its way?
answer: Its qubits lose their quantum state before errors can be fixed
choices: Its qubits lose their quantum state before errors can be fixed
No one has yet written an algorithm it could run faster
Its chips cannot be cooled below the cold of outer space
Its answers can never be checked by an ordinary computer
context: Narrow 'quantum-advantage' demonstrations exist on contrived sampling and physics-simulation tasks, but a fault-tolerant machine that beats a classical one on a problem people want solved does not yet exist: qubits decohere too fast, and correcting their errors takes a huge overhead of extra qubits. The obstacle is not the algorithms (Peter Shor's factoring algorithm dates from 1994, and its answers are easy to check on an ordinary computer), nor the cold (the chips already run in dilution refrigerators about a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero, colder than outer space). Reference: Preskill, 'Quantum Computing in the NISQ era', arXiv:1801.00862.

question: A buyer filled a popular kitchen crock with water at bedtime, and its lining of radium ore 'charged' the water overnight for her to drink in the morning. Glowing radium sold across America as a health product for about thirty years after its discovery in 1898. What was the charged water supposed to give her?
answer: A daily health boost from the radioactivity
choices: A daily health boost from the radioactivity
Extra fluoride to protect her teeth
A year's protection against smallpox
A daily dose of iron to enrich her blood
context: The Revigator was patented in 1912 and sold in the thousands through the 1920s and 30s. Adverts promised the treated water would prevent arthritis, senility and flatulence, delivering 'the lost element of original freshness, radioactivity'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium_ore_Revigator

question: William Bailey styled himself a doctor without ever earning a medical degree, and he sold the radium tonic Radithor in 1920s America. He publicly offered $1,000 to anyone who could show that a bottle of it contained less radium than the printed dose promised. Why was he so sure he would never pay out?
answer: The bottles really did contain the radium the label claimed
choices: The bottles really did contain the radium the label claimed
Radium was too rare for anyone else to test for it
The tonic was actually just plain distilled water
The tonic contained no radium at all, only sugar
context: Bailey grew rich on Radithor. The Federal Trade Commission issued a cease-and-desist order against him in December 1931, and Eben Byers, his best-known customer, died three months later. Bailey was never a physician. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radithor ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eben_Byers

question: Eben Byers, the Pittsburgh industrialist and US amateur golf champion, hurt his arm in 1927, and on his doctor's recommendation he took Radithor and felt wonderful. He drank about 1,400 small bottles of it over the next three years and died in 1932. The Wall Street Journal told his story in 1990 under a very specific headline. What did the headline say the radium water had done?
answer: It worked fine until his jaw came off
choices: It worked fine until his jaw came off
It gave him a wonderful glow
It cured his ailments but ruined his stomach
It saved his life then broke his heart
context: By the end most of Byers' upper and lower jaw had been surgically removed, and holes were forming in his skull. He died on 31 March 1932. The headline topped a Wall Street Journal article by Ron Winslow on 1 August 1990, looking back on his case. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eben_Byers

question: A student runs a finger up one column of the periodic table on the kitchen wall, from radium to a common element the body needs each day. The body sorts swallowed radium the same way and files it into the same tissue, where radium-226, with a half-life of about 1,600 years, keeps firing alpha particles for life. Which everyday element is it?
answer: Calcium
choices: Calcium
Iron
Iodine
Sodium
context: Group 2 metals share two loosely held outer electrons and are chemically similar. The radium the gut absorbs follows calcium into the skeleton, and there it stays. That is why radium tonics did their damage inside people, not on the way through. Source: sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/radium

question: Company doctors at the US Radium Corporation in New Jersey gave sick dial painters two false diagnoses. The young women had hand-painted glowing radium numbers onto watch dials in the early 1920s, licking their brushes to keep a fine point, and they had begun losing teeth and breaking jaws. Which pair of diagnoses did the doctors use?
answer: Syphilis and phosphorus poisoning
choices: Syphilis and phosphorus poisoning
Tuberculosis and childhood rickets
Diphtheria and typhoid fever
Lead poisoning and mercury poisoning
context: The 'phosphorus poisoning' label came from a real occupational disease of the day (matchstick workers developed 'phossy jaw' from white phosphorus); the syphilis label was especially cruel because it also destroyed the women's reputations. In 1924 the dentist Theodor Blum first described the disease in print as 'radium jaw', and in 1925 the pathologist Harrison Martland showed that radium inside the women's bodies was to blame. Source: environmentalhistory.org/people/radiumgirls ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium_jaw

question: Grace Fryer, one of the sick radium dial painters in Orange, New Jersey, refused to accept the company's diagnosis. She recruited four old workmates and sued the US Radium Corporation in 1927, newspapers called the five doomed to die, and the case settled in 1928. What did her lawsuit help force people to recognise?
answer: That workplace radiation exposure is a real hazard
choices: That workplace radiation exposure is a real hazard
That radium must be banned from all medical use
That luminous dials must be painted by machine
That glowing watches must be sold with warnings
context: The chemist who had invented the Undark paint, Sabin von Sochocky, died of radium-induced aplastic anaemia in November 1928, having sawed off the poisoned tip of his own finger in an attempt to save himself. His autopsy helped confirm Fryer's case. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Fryer

question: A doctor draws up a monthly injection of radium-223, sold as Xofigo, which the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved on 15 May 2013. Radium really does kill cells, which is what poisoned the tonic-drinkers of the 1920s, and doctors have learned to aim that power on purpose. What cancer does radium-223 treat?
answer: Prostate cancer that has spread to bone
choices: Prostate cancer that has spread to bone
Skin melanoma on the face and neck
Leukaemia in the bone marrow of children
Brain tumours behind the eye
context: Radium-223 follows calcium into bone exactly like the old radium-226 did, but its half-life is only about eleven days, so it delivers a concentrated alpha dose to the tumours in the skeleton and is largely gone before it can do wider harm. The ALSYMPCA trial showed a 3.6-month survival benefit. Source: ecancer.org/en/news/4085-fda-approves-radium-223-dichloride-for-bone-metastases-from-castration-resistant-prostate-cancer

question: Supervisors at United States Radium in Orange, New Jersey, taught the young women who painted glowing numbers onto watch dials a three-word routine to keep a brush sharp before every stroke. Male chemists in the same building got lead aprons and tongs. What were the three words?
answer: Lip, dip, paint
choices: Lip, dip, paint
Trim, dab, stroke
Kiss, fill, brush
Wet, coat, mark
context: The routine put a little of the paint into the mouth on every stroke. The women, who ingested a little of the paint dozens of times a day, were told the material was safe; the men handling it in bulk downstairs were protected. Source: Wikipedia, 'Radium Girls.'

question: Some dial painters in Orange, New Jersey, and Ottawa, Illinois, mostly teenagers, kept their leftover radium paint, Undark, after a shift in the 1920s. They liked to decorate themselves before a night out. What did they mainly do with it?
answer: painted their fingernails and teeth so they would glow in the dark
choices: painted their fingernails and teeth so they would glow in the dark
used it to write love letters that only showed under lamplight
streaked it into their hair for photographs
poured it into perfume bottles as a party favor
context: Some also painted their eyelids. The brand name was Undark. Source: Wikipedia, 'Undark.'

question: A young woman at the US Radium Corporation in New Jersey paints a watch dial with Undark, the paint that glows in the dark. Radium by itself gives little light, so the makers mix it with a second substance that does the actual shining. What is that second ingredient?
answer: zinc sulfide
choices: zinc sulfide
phosphorus white
sodium borate
magnesium oxide
context: Alpha particles from the radium hit zinc sulfide crystals and excited them into giving off a faint blue-green light -- radioluminescence. Source: Wikipedia, 'Undark.'

question: Eben Byers, a rich Pittsburgh man, took a doctor's tip for a sore arm and drank Radithor, a radium tonic, for years. When he died in 1932, his coffin was lined with lead. Why did his coffin need a lead lining?
answer: His body was still so radioactive it was dangerous by itself
choices: His body was still so radioactive it was dangerous by itself
Lead was standard practice for a wealthy man's burial
To keep the smell of the tonic from escaping the coffin
To stop grave robbers from digging him up for the radium
context: Byers's upper and lower jaw had to be surgically removed before his death on March 31, 1932. He lies in Allegheny Cemetery in Pittsburgh in a lead-lined coffin. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eben Byers.'

question: Harrison Martland, the Essex County medical examiner, needed proof he could show a jury that radium was still inside the dial painters years after they left the factory. He used the women as the instrument. Which pair of measurements did he take?
answer: gamma rays from their living bodies plus radon gas from their exhaled breath
choices: gamma rays from their living bodies plus radon gas from their exhaled breath
urine samples analyzed for radium salts plus blood samples cultured for infection
spinal-fluid samples plus a controlled dose of iodine tracer
hair samples plus the temperature of their fingertips
context: He also laid bone samples from victims on unexposed dental X-ray film in the dark: the bones fogged the film by themselves. Source: Wikipedia, 'Harrison Stanford Martland'; Rowland, 'The National Bureau of Standards and the Radium Dial Painters.'

question: Catherine Wolfe Donohue, a dial painter too weak to sit up, produced a small box at her hearing on 10 February 1938 and set it down as physical evidence. The Radium Dial Company of Ottawa, Illinois, had kept its painters at the old brush routine long after the New Jersey settlement. What was in the box?
answer: fragments of her own jawbone that had come loose from her mouth
choices: fragments of her own jawbone that had come loose from her mouth
the last unopened jar of Undark paint from her workstation
a signed 1925 memo warning managers not to lip-point
a lead-lined necklace her doctor had made for her to wear
context: An Illinois Industrial Commission arbitrator ruled for Donohue on April 5, 1938; she died on July 27, 1938. Source: NPR Illinois, 'The Radium Girls: An Illinois Tragedy'; Northwestern University finding aid for Donohue, Catherine Wolfe.

question: Suppose you turn your back to a low evening Sun and spray a fine mist from a garden hose. A bright bow appears, a piece of a full circle cut off at the ground. That circle has a centre, a real spot in the world you can put your finger on. Where is it?
answer: At the shadow of your own head, out on the grass
choices: At the shadow of your own head, out on the grass
At the thickest part of the mist, just past the hose
At the point in the sky directly overhead
At the spot where the Sun's light first meets the water
context: That centre has a name: the antisolar point, the direction exactly opposite the Sun, and from where you stand it is marked by the shadow of your own head. Every rainbow anyone has ever seen was aimed personally at that spot. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antisolar point' ('from a person's perspective the antisolar point is the location of the shadow of their head on the ground'); corroborated at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow, which notes that in photographs the shadow of the photographer's head marks the centre of the rainbow circle.

question: Suppose you spray a garden hose at a cloudless July noon and get no rainbow, however you turn. At six that evening the first spray throws a bright bow, a slice of a full ring. The Sun's height decides where the ring sits. Where was the ring at noon?
answer: Below the ground: the whole ring lay under your feet
choices: Below the ground: the whole ring lay under your feet
Directly overhead: the ring rode high above the mist
Behind you: the ring had swung to the Sun's side
Inside the mist: the ring was there but far too faint
context: The ring's centre is driven downward as the Sun climbs, and the arc reaches about 42 degrees up from that centre. So once the Sun stands more than 42 degrees above the horizon, the whole ring has sunk below the ground and no amount of spraying will raise one -- at a July noon you are standing on top of your rainbow. TEST IT: try the hose at midday, then again an hour before sunset. Source: Atmospheric Optics, atoptics.co.uk/blog/low-and-high-rainbows/ ('If the sun is higher than 42 degrees you won't see a rainbow at all'); corroborated at livescience.com/30235-rainbows-formation-explainer.html.

question: A student lays three photographs side by side: a rainbow over an Icelandic glacier, one at a Hawaiian waterfall and one in her own garden sprinkler. Fat cold rain, thundering spray, fine mist. She measures how far each arc stands out from the centre of its own circle. What decides that figure?
answer: Every drop returns its light on a cone of one fixed width
choices: Every drop returns its light on a cone of one fixed width
Every drop returns a wider cone the bigger it happens to be
Every watcher stands about the same distance from the water
Every human eye takes in about the same width of sky
context: Every drop that sends red light to your eye lies on a cone about 42 degrees wide around the antisolar line; violet arrives from about 40 degrees. Drop size does not enter into it, which is why a bow in an Icelandic squall and a bow in your sprinkler are twins. Source: Grokipedia, 'Rainbow' -- the primary bow subtends 'an angular radius of approximately 42 degrees from the observer's shadow, with longer wavelengths (red) on the outer edge and shorter wavelengths (violet) on the inner edge'; corroborated at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow.

question: Two friends stand shoulder to shoulder in the same garden sprinkler mist with the Sun behind them, and each sees her own rainbow arching across the spray. One walks steadily out through the mist, still watching her bow. As she moves, which water is building the arc she sees?
answer: A different set of drops at every step she takes
choices: A different set of drops at every step she takes
The same drops that built it before she started walking
The drops falling closest around her as she walks
The drops that are building her friend's bow as well
context: A rainbow is a direction, not an object sitting at a place, which is why nobody has ever reached one: step sideways and the arc is rebuilt out of entirely new water. Two people standing shoulder to shoulder never see exactly the same rainbow -- their bows are assembled from completely different drops. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow (two observers 'never see exactly the same rainbow'); Atmospheric Optics, atoptics.co.uk/blog/opod-primary-rainbow/, adds that the bow 'forms a cone rather than a fixed location in space'.

question: A photographer at Cumberland Falls in Kentucky sets a tripod before a pale arch in the spray on a night near the full Moon. To her eye it is grey-white, barely a tint in it. She holds the shutter open, and the same arch comes out with its reds and greens plainly there. Why does the camera get colour her eye cannot?
answer: The eye's colour-sensing cone cells never wake in moonlight
choices: The eye's colour-sensing cone cells never wake in moonlight
The eye's pupil cannot open wide enough to take moonlight in
The eye's lens scatters such faint light before it registers
The eye's signals reach the brain too weak to read as colour
context: TEST IT AT NIGHT: a moonbow wants a full or nearly-full Moon lower than about 42 degrees, a properly dark sky, and spray or rain opposite it -- so two to three hours after sunset or before sunrise. Cumberland Falls, Victoria Falls and Yosemite Falls throw them reliably, and in Costa Rican cloud forest they appear almost every full moon from December through February. Aristotle already described one in the Meteorology around 350 BC. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonbow; corroborated at Grokipedia, 'moon rainbow'.

question: A boy on a porch watches a rain shower with the Sun behind him and sees a bow. Every drop splits sunlight into a full spectrum, the way a glass prism does, yet each sends his eye just one colour and the rest of its spectrum misses him. When his eye runs across the bow from one edge of the band to the other, what is it reading?
answer: A map of how high each drop sits: high ones give red, low ones violet
choices: A map of how high each drop sits: high ones give red, low ones violet
A map of how big each drop is: big ones give red, small ones violet
A map of how far off each drop is: near ones give red, far ones violet
A map of how fast each drop falls: slow ones give red, quick ones violet
context: A single raindrop hands you exactly one colour and flings the rest of the spectrum it made past your head, to land in front of you or behind you. The band of colour you see is therefore a map of drop height, not a spectrum from any one drop: the drops high in the arc are doing the red, the low ones the blue and violet. Source: sciencefocus.com, 'Why do millions of raindrops only make one rainbow'; corroborated at asu.edu/courses/phs208/patternsbb/PiN/rdg/rainbow/rainbow3.shtml.

question: A teacher draws one raindrop on the board and a whole sheet of parallel sunlight going into it. Each ray enters at a different height, bends, reflects off the curved back and bends again on the way out, and the rays leave spread across a wide fan of angles. Why then does a watcher see a sharp bright band, not a general glow?
answer: At one angle the rays from many entry heights pile up together
choices: At one angle the rays from many entry heights pile up together
At one angle the drop reflects nearly all the light instead of passing it
At one angle the light spends longest inside, gaining strength
At one angle the drop bends the light twice as far as at any other
context: The bend angle has a minimum near 138 degrees for red (140 for violet), and rays entering at many different heights all crowd into that minimum -- which is exactly what makes a bright arc instead of a smear. Do the subtraction: 180 minus 138 gives the familiar 42 degrees. That crowded ray is still called the Descartes ray. Source: Grokipedia, 'Rainbow' and 'Alexander's band' ('minimum deviations around 138 degrees for red and 140 degrees for violet, corresponding to the observed 42 degrees and 40 degrees angular radii from the antisolar point'); corroborated at reed.edu/math-stats/wieting/essays/Rainbow.pdf.

question: A girl walks a lawn on a clear, dewy morning with a low Sun behind her and sees a bow lying in the grass, not standing in the air: a dewbow, built in the beads of water on the blades. The returning light still comes back on the same cone it always does, and the flat ground simply slices through it. What curve does the slice draw across the grass?
answer: A hyperbola, opening wider the farther out it runs
choices: A hyperbola, opening wider the farther out it runs
A circle, closed neatly around the watcher's feet
A parabola, the curve of a ball thrown flat and low
A spiral, winding tighter toward the far hedge
context: A dewbow is a rainbow cone cut open where you can walk on it. Atmospheric Optics puts it exactly: 'The path on the grass of the dew forming the bow is a hyperbola or ellipse formed by the intersection of the rainbow cone with the ground. However the bow seen by your eyes at the tip of cone, is always circular.' Its apex sits at the lower end of your own shadow, and an ellipse rather than a hyperbola turns up when the geometry allows. Source: atoptics.co.uk/rainbows/dewbow.htm; corroborated at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewbow and glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/dewbow/.

question: A hiker looks up after a heavy shower and finds a second, fainter bow about nine degrees outside the bright one, a broader, softer band with its colours the other way round: red on the inside edge. What did the light that built that outer bow do differently?
answer: It reflected off the drop's back wall twice before it escaped
choices: It reflected off the drop's back wall twice before it escaped
It bounced off the bright bow itself, throwing back a mirror image
It passed straight on through a second raindrop behind the first
It entered through the drop's shaded side instead of the sunlit side
context: Two reflections inside the drop instead of one puts the secondary bow near 51 degrees, about nine degrees outside the primary, and flips the colour order so red faces inward. It carries only about 43 per cent of the primary's total brightness, spread over a band roughly 1.8 times wider -- which is why most people go a lifetime without noticing it. TEST IT: at the next double bow, check the colour order on the outer arc. Source: Atmospheric Optics, atoptics.co.uk/blog/secondary-rainbow/ ('Rays escaping after two reflections make a secondary bow with a radius of 51 degrees... it is broader, 1.8 times the width of the primary bow, and its colours are reversed'); corroborated at Grokipedia, 'Rainbow'.

question: Theodoric of Freiberg, a Dominican friar, shut himself in a darkened room some time between 1304 and 1311 with a single sunbeam and a water-filled glass sphere, and patiently traced where each ray came back out. He wrote the results up as De iride. In his model, what was that sphere standing in for?
answer: A single raindrop, blown up until he could follow rays through it
choices: A single raindrop, blown up until he could follow rays through it
A whole rain cloud, treated as one body reflecting the Sun
A patch of falling mist, its countless drops averaged into one
A curved sheet of water, of the sort a waterfall throws up
context: Everyone before Theodoric had reasoned about the rainbow by reasoning about clouds. Treating one water-filled globe as a single magnified raindrop let him trace the ray paths that build the primary bow and the secondary, and the colour reversal that follows. Kamal al-Din al-Farisi reached the same result independently in Persia within about two years, publishing it in Kitab Tanqih al-Manazir -- 'The Revision of Ibn al-Haytham's Optics'. Two men, two continents, no contact, the same glass sphere. TEST IT: a round glass of water on a sunny windowsill throws the same colours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodoric_of_Freiberg; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_optics; Grokipedia, 'Rainbow' (De iride, written between 1304 and 1310).

question: Alexander of Aphrodisias, who led Aristotle's school in Athens around AD 200, noted something about double rainbows that nobody had written down before, in his writing on Aristotle's Meteorology. It concerns the strip of sky between the two arcs, still called Alexander's band. What did he notice there?
answer: That strip of sky is darker than the sky on either side of the pair
choices: That strip of sky is darker than the sky on either side of the pair
That strip of sky shows a third arc, colourless and very faint
That strip of sky carries the two bows' colours in weak reverse
That strip of sky flickers as the falling drops cross through it
context: The gap is dark because the primary bow throws its light everywhere at angles LESS than about 42 degrees from the antisolar direction, while the secondary throws its light outward at angles GREATER than about 51 degrees. Nothing at all is aimed into the strip between them -- and the sky inside the primary is correspondingly brighter than the rest. TEST IT: on the next good double bow, compare the sky just inside the bright arc against the strip between the two. Source: Grokipedia, 'Alexander's band'; corroborated at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander%27s_band, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_of_Aphrodisias ('a date between 198 and 209'), and atoptics.co.uk/blog/secondary-rainbow/ for the brightness contrast.

question: A passenger at an airliner window, ten thousand metres up with a low Sun behind her, sees a rainbow whole: a closed ring, complete all the way round, as it never is from the ground. The bottom of the ring is built from drops below the aircraft, and those come into play only once the Sun is low enough. How low must it sit?
answer: Under about three degrees up, all but touching the horizon
choices: Under about three degrees up, all but touching the horizon
Under about fifteen degrees up, a fist held at arm's length
Under about thirty degrees up, a third of the way up the sky
Under about forty degrees up, not quite halfway up the sky
context: From an aeroplane the drops below your horizon suddenly come into play and the bow closes into a full circle -- on the ground it is the earth, not the physics, that cuts every rainbow in half. Grokipedia adds the number: at a typical cruising altitude of 10,000 metres the antisolar point clears the local horizon once the Sun drops below about 3 degrees of altitude. Window seat, low Sun, opposite side of the aircraft from the Sun. Source: Grokipedia, 'Rainbow' and 'Antisolar point'; corroborated at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow (full circles visible from aircraft).

question: Thomas Young offered an explanation in 1804 for the two or three faint fringes of pink, purple and green sometimes seen just inside the violet edge of a bright rainbow, the supernumerary bows. Careful ray tracing through a drop predicts nothing there at all. George Airy had to invent a whole new mathematical function in 1838 to get their spacing right. What are those fringes made of?
answer: Light that took two slightly different paths inside one drop, then combined
choices: Light that took two slightly different paths inside one drop, then combined
Light bent a second time by the flattened underside of a falling drop
Light from a much higher layer of drops, arriving a little behind the rest
Light thrown back down off the underside of the cloud above the shower
context: Young's 1804 answer was interference: two routes through the same drop arrive slightly out of step, reinforcing in some directions and cancelling in others. George Airy made it quantitative in 1838 in 'On the intensity of light in the neighbourhood of a caustic' (Transactions of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, vol. 6, pp. 379-403), inventing the function that now carries his name. Best part: the fringe spacing reports the DROP SIZE. You need drops about 1 mm across or smaller, and the smaller the drops, the broader and paler the bands -- so you can read the rain off the sky. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernumerary_rainbow; Airy (1838), ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1838TCaPS...6..379A; droplet range from Grokipedia, 'Rainbow'.

question: Frank Barmore went hunting in 1983 for a number physics textbooks like to repeat: that Rene Descartes found the rainbow's angle in 1637 by tracing some ten thousand rays through a raindrop by hand. Barmore found that textbook writers had simply copied it from one another. The real work needed nothing like ten thousand rays. How did Descartes pin the angle down?
answer: He stepped across the drop in tenths, then refined the strip near the edge
choices: He assumed one ray through the drop's centre and scaled the rest from it
He stepped across the drop in tenths, then refined the strip near the edge
He worked backwards from the bow's angle as he measured it in the sky
He derived the angle from the geometry and checked it against a few rays
context: Barmore's 1983 paper 'Descartes, the Rainbow and the Mythical 10 000 Calculations' traced the ten-thousand story to a line in Taylor's physics textbook and, further back, to a nineteenth-century claim by Grau. What Descartes did in 1637 was work through the deviation for entry points from 0.0 to 1.0 across the drop in steps of 0.1, see where the angle stopped changing, then go back and refine the interval between 0.80 and 0.90 -- using seven-figure trigonometric tables. A few dozen careful calculations, not thousands of brute-force ones; he found the answer by knowing where to look. His apparatus was 'a perfectly round and transparent glass ball filled with water' -- a raindrop you could hold. Source: F. Barmore, 'Descartes, the Rainbow and the Mythical 10 000 Calculations' (1983), opg.optica.org/abstract.cfm?uri=MO-1983-ThB3; method detail from Wieting, 'The Cartesian Rainbow', Reed College (2006).

question: Scheel, Schijen and Lakens, three psychologists, counted in 2021 how often psychology papers confirm their authors' first guess: 146 of 152 ordinary papers did, about 96 percent. Then they counted registered reports, where a journal agrees to publish before anyone knows the answer, while warning that two literatures are no controlled experiment. How did those reports compare?
answer: Fewer than half of them confirmed it
choices: Fewer than half of them confirmed it
Nearly all of them confirmed it too
About three in four of them confirmed it
Hardly any of them confirmed it
context: Scheel, Schijen and Lakens (2021), 'An Excess of Positive Results,' Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 4(2). 146 of 152 standard papers (~96%) reported a confirming result; 31 of 71 Registered Reports (~44%) did. IMPORTANT: this is a correlation between two different literatures, not a controlled experiment -- the authors themselves caution against a simple causal reading. The 52-point gap is still large enough to make any reader look twice at anything that comes back positive in the ordinary literature. Source: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/25152459211007467

question: Richard Feynman gave the whole reform movement its motto in his 1974 Caltech commencement address, later published as 'Cargo Cult Science.' He told the graduates in one sentence what the first principle of scientific integrity is. What did he tell them?
answer: Never to fool oneself, the easiest person to fool
choices: Never to fool oneself, the easiest person to fool
Always to trust the verdict of peer review
To treat a p-value under 0.05 as a discovery
To follow the leading authorities in a field
context: Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science,' Caltech commencement address, 1974. The line reads in full: 'The first principle is that you must not fool yourself -- and you are the easiest person to fool. So you have to be very careful about that. After you've not fooled yourself, it's easy not to fool other scientists.' This is why preregistration, Registered Reports, and adversarial collaboration exist: they are devices that keep researchers from letting themselves off the hook. Source: https://calteches.library.caltech.edu/3043/

question: Wasaburo Oishi sent up balloons from a Japanese observatory in the mid-1920s and tracked them with a telescope. High above him he found a narrow band of very fast wind, just below the top of the weather layer. What was that river in the sky later called?
answer: the jet stream
choices: the jet stream
the polar vortex
the Hadley cell
the Ferrel cell
context: Oishi's winter profile at Tateno is the first documented observation of the persistent upper westerlies. The polar vortex is a circumpolar low; the Hadley and Ferrel cells are meridional overturning cells, not bands of fast wind. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasaburo_Oishi; aos.wisc.edu/~aos610/HW2_Lewis_BAMS_Ooishi.pdf.

question: Wasaburo Oishi published nineteen careful reports on his balloon flights between 1926 and 1944, 1,246 pages on a great wind high over Japan. Almost nobody outside Japan read a word of them, because of the language he chose. What language was it?
answer: Esperanto
choices: Esperanto
Latin
German
French
context: Oishi was a devoted Esperantist and president of the Japanese Esperanto Institute; the very first report was titled Raporto de Aerologia Observatorio de Tateno. He picked Esperanto hoping to reach a wide foreign audience; the effect was the opposite. Source: smithsonianmag.com/air-space-magazine/as-next-may-unbelievablebuttrue-180968355.

question: American B-29 crews came over Japan late in 1944 planning to bomb from 30,000 ft and flew straight into winds of 200-300 mph, the high wind Wasaburo Oishi had measured, unknown to them. Under full throttle some aircraft made almost no ground speed, and bombs missed by miles. General Curtis LeMay changed one thing about how the B-29s flew. What did he do?
answer: he lowered their bombing altitude to about 25,000 ft
choices: he lowered their bombing altitude to about 25,000 ft
he grounded the daylight raids in favour of night bombing
he ordered new heavier propellers fitted to every airframe
he pulled the fleet back to India and cancelled the campaign
context: LeMay moved the B-29s to roughly 24,500-27,000 ft, out of the jet's core, and later to low-altitude firebombing entirely. Source: historyofwar.org/articles/weapons_B-29_combat.html.

question: Japanese soldiers began releasing roughly nine thousand paper balloons with bombs on 3 November 1944, aiming them at North America on the high wind Wasaburo Oishi had measured. The plan used a wind speed that was wrong. About how long did the crossing really take?
answer: about three or four days
choices: about three or four days
about ten hours
about two weeks
about six weeks
context: The fu-go crossings took roughly 72-96 hours rather than the shorter time the plan assumed; only a few hundred of the ~9,300 launched ever reached North America. Six civilians killed near Bly, Oregon on 5 May 1945 were the only WWII enemy-action deaths in the contiguous US. Sources: ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/japanese-balloon-bombs-fu-go/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fu-Go_balloon_bomb.

question: A traveller sees a New York to London flight listed about an hour shorter than the return. The high wind behind that hour screams in winter and slackens in summer. It lives where a horizontal temperature difference meets the top of the weather layer. Which difference is much sharper in winter?
answer: between equatorial and polar air
choices: between equatorial and polar air
between day-side and night-side air
between land and ocean surfaces
between wet and dry air masses
context: By the thermal-wind relationship, a sharp horizontal temperature gradient at the tropopause forces a fast westerly wind above it; the equator-to-pole gradient is steepest in winter. It is why an eastbound New York to London flight is routinely about an hour shorter than the westbound return -- something a kid can check on any departures board. Source: britannica.com/science/climate-meteorology/Upper-level-winds.

question: Michael Faraday set up a simple machine at the Royal Institution in London in 1831: a copper disc on a brass axle, its edge passing between the poles of a horseshoe magnet. He turned the crank by hand. What did the machine achieve?
answer: It turned steady muscle power into a steady electric current.
choices: It turned steady muscle power into a steady electric current.
It split water into hydrogen and oxygen without any chemical bath.
It sent a coded message down a wire from one room to another.
It boiled a beaker of water without any flame under it.
context: The device, later called the Faraday disc or homopolar generator, is the ancestor of every dynamo and every alternator on the planet. Feed a current back INTO the same disc and it spins itself -- the first hint that motor and generator are one machine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homopolar_generator .

question: A needle jumped on Michael Faraday's meter in 1831 as he pushed a bar magnet through a tight coil of copper wire. A common guess held that a magnet resting still beside the coil ought to give a steady current too. What did he find?
answer: The coil gives a current only while the field is CHANGING, never while it sits still.
choices: The coil gives a current only while the field is CHANGING, never while it sits still.
The coil gives a current the whole time the magnet is present, moving or not.
The coil gives a current only when the magnet is touching the wire directly.
The coil gives a current only when the magnet is aligned with the Earth's field.
context: A magnet at rest, even a strong one, produces no current in a nearby coil. Move it, spin it, or switch it off and the coil sees a pulse. This is Faraday's law: it is the RATE of change of flux that drives induction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faraday%27s_law_of_induction .

question: Hippolyte Fontaine ran a copper cable from one Gramme dynamo to a second about five hundred metres away at the 1873 Vienna World Exposition. Business partner to the Belgian inventor Zenobe Gramme, he meant to show that power could be sent over long distances. What unexpected thing did the second machine do?
answer: Its shaft started spinning under its own power.
choices: Its shaft started spinning under its own power.
Its coils caught fire and had to be doused with water.
Its output voltage climbed to twice what the first was producing.
Its galvanometer needle swung around and stayed at zero.
context: Nobody had meant to demonstrate that the machine was reversible, but there it was: pour current in, get rotation out. A dynamo run backwards is a motor. The Vienna accident is the moment industrial electric motors were born. Source: bie-paris.org Zenobe Gramme's electrifying discovery at Expo 1873 Vienna .

question: A cyclist pedals a bicycle whose front hub is a small dynamo, a coil spinning near a magnet that makes a current whenever the wheel turns. The moment she switches on her headlamp and current flows, the pedals get harder to push, because the lamp's power has to come from somewhere. Which physical law is doing the bookkeeping between wheel and lamp?
answer: The induced current always opposes the change that produced it.
choices: The induced current always opposes the change that produced it.
The induced current always adds to the change that produced it.
The induced current is proportional to the square of the wheel's speed.
The induced current only flows when the wheel is spinning downhill.
context: This is Lenz's rule, and it is really conservation of energy in disguise. The electricity in the lamp had to come from somewhere; the extra push your legs feel is exactly that energy leaving your body and going into the bulb. Source: spark.iop.org electromagnetic-braking-copper-pipe .

question: A driver takes an electric car down a long hill. Instead of pressing the friction brakes, which would waste the downhill energy as heat in the pads, she flips a switch that puts the drive motor into a different mode, regenerative braking. What does the motor do now, and where does the energy go?
answer: It acts as a generator; the current it makes refills the battery.
choices: It acts as a generator; the current it makes refills the battery.
It acts as a heater; the energy is dumped through a radiator.
It acts as a flywheel; the energy is stored as its own spin.
It acts as a transformer; the energy is stepped down to a lower voltage.
context: Regenerative braking is Faraday's principle sold as a feature: the shaft is being spun by the car's own momentum, so induction pushes current back INTO the battery instead of drawing it out.
