The kinetic energy that would have become brake-pad heat becomes usable charge instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regenerative_braking .

question: A student holds a small, strong neodymium magnet at the top of a length of thick copper pipe standing straight up. Copper is not magnetic, the magnet does not cling to it, and she expects a drop as fast as a pebble through open air. She lets go, and the magnet falls down the inside of the pipe. What happens?
answer: It sinks slowly, as if falling through honey.
choices: It sinks slowly, as if falling through honey.
It falls at normal free-fall speed, exactly as a pebble would.
It sticks to the inner wall of the pipe halfway down.
It shoots out the bottom faster than free-fall.
context: The moving magnet changes the magnetic field inside the pipe wall, and that changing field drives circulating eddy currents in the copper. Those currents make their own magnetic field, oriented to push back on the magnet by Lenz's rule -- a three-second home demonstration of conservation of energy. Source: phys420.phas.ubc.ca p420_2018 lalond72 .

question: Michael Faraday wound two coils onto one iron ring in 1831, the ancestor of the modern transformer: one voltage in and a different voltage out. Every high-voltage line coming into a town ends at a transformer that steps the voltage down for houses. There is one thing a transformer flatly cannot do. What is it?
answer: Transform direct current.
choices: Transform direct current.
Pass power between two coils that share no direct wire connection.
Work with an iron core instead of an air core.
Have more turns on the output coil than the input coil.
context: Induction needs a CHANGING flux, and a steady DC current produces a steady field with no change at all. That is why the domestic grid was built AC in the first place: only AC can be stepped up to high voltage for cheap long-distance transmission and stepped back down for your house. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer .

question: An engineer reads the textbook line that a motor and a generator are 'the same machine run backwards.' A motor turns electric current into spinning motion and a generator does the reverse, and she nods at the line, then adds a caveat about real hardware. What is her caveat?
answer: Each is wound, geared, and cooled for one job; reversibility is a schoolbook ideal.
choices: Each is wound, geared, and cooled for one job; reversibility is a schoolbook ideal.
The two use entirely different physical principles once you look inside the case.
Only Faraday's original disc was ever truly reversible; every later design broke it.
Reversibility fails because energy conservation is only approximate at large scale.
context: In principle the physics is symmetric; in practice a car's drive motor and a hydro plant's generator are built for opposite duty cycles, cooling loads, and torque profiles. 'Run it backwards' is true as a law and engineered around as a product. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_generator .

question: Alexander Glenny tried a salt called potassium alum on diphtheria toxoid at the Wellcome Laboratory in London in 1926, wanting only a purer preparation. It clumped the toxoid into a solid precipitate he could wash. He injected that solid into guinea pigs and compared them with animals given plain toxoid. What did he find?
answer: The precipitate produced a far stronger antibody response
choices: The precipitate produced a far stronger antibody response
The precipitate produced a far weaker antibody response
The precipitate produced a far quicker antibody response
The precipitate produced a far narrower antibody response
context: Glenny was chasing purity and caught the adjuvant effect instead: an ingredient that teaches the immune system nothing itself, but makes it pay far more attention to what it is taught. Aluminium salts have sat in vaccines ever since 1926, which is why aluminium is the ingredient in the childhood schedule that gets argued about most. Sources: 'Mechanism of Immunopotentiation and Safety of Aluminum Adjuvants', PMC3541479; 'Advances in aluminum hydroxide-based adjuvant research and its mechanism', PMC4514166.

question: A nurse sets out the American childhood vaccine schedule of 1986: eleven doses, seven of them shots and four given by mouth, covering seven diseases. She counts the 2025 schedule by the same rule, every dose from birth through age eighteen, with the yearly flu shot. How many doses is that?
answer: About 50 to 54 doses, against 16 to 18 diseases
choices: About 20 to 24 doses, against 16 to 18 diseases
About 50 to 54 doses, against 16 to 18 diseases
About 70 to 74 doses, against 16 to 18 diseases
About 95 to 99 doses, against 16 to 18 diseases
context: The counting rule is most of the argument. Change it - count injections only, stop at age two, leave influenza out - and the same schedule yields a different headline, which is how one campaign gets '11 to 70+' and another gets a modest rise. Neither side disputes that the schedule expanded; they dispute what the expansion means. The Institute of Medicine, counting its own way in 2013, said the under-six schedule 'is timed to protect children from 14 pathogens' and that children 'may receive as many as 24 immunizations by their second birthday and may receive up to five injections during a single doctor's visit.' The 1980s starting point is corroborated independently by the archived CDC schedules: in 1983, 'Eleven doses of four vaccines protected kids against seven vaccine-preventable diseases.' Sources: STAT News, 'How we know kids don't get too many vaccines too soon' (24 June 2025); IOM, The Childhood Immunization Schedule and Safety, Report Brief (January 2013); vaxopedia.org archive of historical CDC schedules.

question: A reporter looks up the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), the national early-warning system for vaccine side effects ordered by the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act of 1986, which opened on 1 November 1990. People argue about its numbers all the time and usually skip how a report gets in. Who may file one?
answer: Anyone at all, a patient or a parent included
choices: Anyone at all, a patient or a parent included
Anyone who was present, a parent or a nurse included
Anyone in health care, a nurse or a pharmacist included
Anyone required by law, a doctor or a maker included
context: In the CDC's own description, 'VAERS is a passive surveillance system, meaning it relies on people sending in reports of their experiences after vaccination.' Reports come from 'patients, family members, healthcare providers and vaccine manufacturers', and only providers and manufacturers are legally required to report certain events - nobody else is obliged to file anything. The open door is deliberate: a net meant to catch surprises cannot have a gatekeeper deciding in advance what counts as a surprise. It also means a VAERS entry is an account, not a verified injury. VAERS was built by merging the CDC's 1976 MSAEFI system with an FDA system. Source: CDC, 'About the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS)'.

question: A father raises aluminium, the vaccine ingredient parents ask about most. An American baby in 1986 received about 1.5 mg of it from vaccines in its first six months, and the 2025 schedule brought about 4.4 mg over the same span. How much does a formula-fed baby swallow in that time, by a different route?
answer: About 38 mg
choices: About 1 mg
About 12 mg
About 38 mg
About 120 mg
context: By age two the vaccine total is about 6 mg. The 38 mg swallowed figure is offered by the source 'for scale', and scale is all it is: it compares amounts, not routes into the body, and it settles nothing by itself - which is exactly why researchers went and measured vaccine aluminium directly rather than resting on the comparison. Three separate counts of the same schedule are now on the table - doses, antigens and milligrams of aluminium - and each answers a different question. Source: STAT News, 'How we know kids don't get too many vaccines too soon' (24 June 2025); cumulative ~4.4 mg by six months also stated at grokipedia.com/page/Vaccination_schedule.

question: A student reads two totals from the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS): roughly 30,000 to 50,000 reports in a typical year before the pandemic, and over 717,000 tied to COVID-19 vaccines by 31 December 2021. Writers on both sides of the argument quoted totals like those as the risk of being vaccinated. The CDC warns that no risk figure can be got from VAERS, and points to a number the system never collects. Which number?
answer: How many people received the vaccine in the first place
choices: How many people received the vaccine in the first place
How often that reaction strikes people who were never vaccinated
How many separate reports describe the very same patient
How many doctors saw such a case and filed nothing at all
context: A rate is a fraction. VAERS collects the top of it and never sees the bottom: in the CDC's words, 'It is usually not possible to use VAERS data to calculate how often an adverse event occurs in a population', because 'The number of people receiving a vaccine is usually not available.' A system with a numerator and no denominator can raise a flag; it cannot measure a rate. The CDC adds that 'VAERS data alone cannot determine if the vaccine caused the reported adverse event.' Both sides of the vaccine argument have published rates computed straight out of VAERS totals; the people who run the system say that arithmetic cannot be done. The 2021 pile of reports has at least three causes tangled together - the sheer number of doses given, expanded mandatory reporting under Emergency Use Authorization, and publicity, since the CDC notes that 'The number of reports submitted to VAERS can change in response to media attention and public awareness' - and no count alone can pull them apart. Source: CDC, 'About the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS)', Strengths and limitations.

question: A researcher sets the dose count aside and counts the load on a small immune system itself: antigens, the distinct molecules it learns to recognise. One whole-cell whooping-cough shot from the 1980s carried thousands of them. The whole 2025 childhood schedule, every dose added together, carried how many?
answer: Roughly 150 to 200 antigens in all
choices: Roughly 150 to 200 antigens in all
Roughly 1,200 to 1,300 antigens in all
Roughly 4,000 to 4,500 antigens in all
Roughly 25,000 to 30,000 antigens in all
context: Roughly a 95 percent cut in antigen exposure across the same decades in which the dose count roughly quintupled. Both numbers are true; they are answers to different questions, and each side of the argument quotes the one that suits it. 'Whole-cell' meant the entire killed bacterium went into the vial - thousands of distinct molecules in a single shot - where modern purified vaccines carry a short list of chosen ones. For scale in the other direction, Paul Offit and colleagues calculated that an infant could in theory respond to 10,000 vaccines at once while using under one percent of circulating B-cells, and infants meet an estimated 2,000 to 6,000 unique antigens every day from bacteria, viruses and food. Counts shift with the counting rule: STAT News (24 June 2025) puts the schedule near 165 antigens, and Grokipedia's 'Vaccination schedule' gives fewer than 150 for 2013. Sources: STAT News (24 June 2025); grokipedia.com/page/Vaccination_schedule.

question: Fifteen reports of one bowel problem in babies had reached the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) by July 1999, all after RotaShield, the first rotavirus vaccine, licensed on 31 August 1998. Part of the gut folds into itself, and in 13 of the 15 cases it came after the first dose. Just fifteen reports across the whole country. What came of them?
answer: The CDC urged suspension in days; the maker withdrew it that October
choices: The CDC urged suspension in days; the maker withdrew it that October
The CDC urged a label warning; the maker sold it for four more years
The CDC urged use after six months only; the maker narrowed the label
The CDC urged wider reporting; the maker paid for a follow-up study
context: The CDC and FDA called for suspension in mid-July 1999; ACIP voted on 22 October 1999 to drop the recommendation, and the manufacturer withdrew the product that month - under fifteen months from licensure to withdrawal, on fifteen reports. This is the strongest case for a system that cannot measure anything: it was built to notice, and it noticed. What it could not supply was the size of the risk. Once controlled studies were run they found roughly a 37-fold increase in the three to seven days after the first dose, amounting to 'The excess risk of approximately 1 intussusception case in 10 000 Rotashield recipients.' VAERS produced the hypothesis; epidemiology produced the number. A quieter case ran the same way: eight to ten VAERS reports of vaccine-associated paralytic polio fed the 1997 decision to move the American schedule off routine oral polio vaccine. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Vaccine_Adverse_Event_Reporting_System; 'Intussusception and Rotavirus Vaccination - Balancing Risk Against Benefit', PMC5715718; CDC MMWR 48(43).

question: An Institute of Medicine committee reviewed the American childhood immunization schedule in 2013 and made two findings, and both sides of the argument quote the report. The first was blunt: the committee found 'no evidence that the schedule is unsafe.' The second named a gap in the research literature. What gap?
answer: The number, timing, order and ages of doses had never been studied together
choices: The number, timing, order and ages of doses had never been studied together
The individual vaccines had never been compared against an inert placebo
The children studied had never been followed past their fifth birthday
The safety studies had never included children outside managed-care plans
context: Verbatim: 'Key elements of the entire schedule - the number, frequency, timing, order, and age at administration of vaccines - have not been systematically examined in research studies.' And: 'No studies have compared the differences in health outcomes that some stakeholders questioned between entirely unimmunized populations of children and fully immunized children.' Both halves belong in the same sentence, and the precise wording matters: 'no randomised trial of the whole schedule exists' is TRUE, while 'the schedule is unstudied' is FALSE - large observational comparisons exist and the same committee reviewed them, concluding it 'uncovered no evidence of major safety concerns associated with adherence to the childhood immunization schedule.' The committee also noted its report 'is unique in that it is the first to attempt to examine the entire childhood immunization schedule as it exists today.' Sources: IOM, The Childhood Immunization Schedule and Safety, Report Brief (January 2013), pp.2-4; Summary chapter, NCBI NBK206938.

question: A Danish team tracked 1,224,176 children born between 1997 and 2018 and matched 50 chronic disorders against how much vaccine aluminium each child had received by age two. The team found no raised risk of autoimmune, allergic or brain-development disease. But this was no trial: nobody assigned the doses at random. Where did the differences in aluminium between these children come from?
answer: Denmark kept switching brands, so the total depended on birth year
choices: Denmark kept switching brands, so the total depended on birth year
Denmark split supply between regions, so the total depended on address
Denmark paused doses one winter, so the total depended on start age
Denmark offered a lighter schedule, so the total depended on parents
context: Aluminium content per dose 'ranged from 0.125 to 1.00 mg', and procurement kept changing - pneumococcal vaccine added in 2007, supply substitutions, newer formulations - so a child's total depended on the year it happened to be born, for reasons having nothing to do with that child. The authors call it 'a natural quasi-experimental framework'. Adjusted hazard ratios per extra 1 mg by age two: 0.98 (95% CI 0.94-1.02) for any autoimmune disorder, 0.99 (0.98-1.01) for any atopic or allergic disorder, 0.93 (0.90-0.97) for any neurodevelopmental disorder. Lead author Anders Hviid: 'Our results are reassuring. By analyzing data from more than one million Danish children, we found absolutely no indication that the very small amount of aluminum used in the childhood vaccination program increases the risk of 50 different health outcomes during childhood.' The authors keep their own limits in view - 'small relative effects, particularly for some rarer disorders, could not be statistically excluded', individual medical records were not reviewed, and follow-up ran to a median age of five - and the design has a hard ceiling: only 15,237 of those children (1.2%) received no aluminium-adsorbed vaccine at all, so this is a study of more aluminium versus less, not of vaccinated versus unvaccinated. A CDC-funded study in the Vaccine Safety Datalink pulled the other way on one outcome: Daley and colleagues, 326,991 children, found aluminium 'positively associated with persistent asthma' (adjusted hazard ratio 1.19 per 1 mg in children without eczema) and wrote that 'additional investigation of this hypothesis appears warranted.' Reviewing that paper, Paul Offit noted the association vanished when the analysis was restricted to fully immunised children, was absent among breastfed children, showed no dose-response, and left dietary aluminium unaccounted for. Neither the Danish null nor the American positive is the end of the story, and that is what an open question looks like. Sources: Andersson NW, Svalgaard IB, Hoffmann SS, Hviid A, Annals of Internal Medicine, 15 July 2025, doi:10.7326/ANNALS-25-00997; Statens Serum Institut news release (July 2025); Daley MF et al., Acad Pediatr 2023; CHOP Vaccine Update.

question: Ross Lazarus and Michael Klompas of Harvard Pilgrim built an automatic detector to find out how much the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) was missing. One sentence of their 2011 final report to the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) is quoted in nearly every argument about the system: 'fewer than 1% of vaccine adverse events are reported.' Where does that figure come from?
answer: From studies published earlier, cited as the reason for the work
choices: From studies published earlier, cited as the reason for the work
From the team's own detector, run across 1.4 million doses
From a CDC estimate the team was contracted to test and confirm
From a match of VAERS entries against the clinics' own records
context: The famous line is background - prior literature summarised to justify the grant, not a measurement the project produced. What the project itself measured was something else entirely, reported on the same page: 'Preliminary data were collected from June 2006 through October 2009 on 715,000 patients, and 1.4 million doses (of 45 different vaccines) were given to 376,452 individuals. Of these doses, 35,570 possible reactions (2.6 percent of vaccinations) were identified.' The full background passage: 'Adverse events from drugs and vaccines are common, but underreported. Although 25% of ambulatory patients experience an adverse drug event, less than 0.3% of all adverse drug events and 1-13% of serious events are reported to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Likewise, fewer than 1% of vaccine adverse events are reported.' Checking the provenance of a number you like is the same move as checking one you dislike, and this is a number the schedule's critics like. Two further things sit in the same report. First, Aim 3 - a head-to-head test of the new detector against VAERS and the Vaccine Safety Datalink - never happened: 'there was never an opportunity to perform system performance assessments because the necessary CDC contacts were no longer available and the CDC consultants responsible for receiving data were no longer responsive to our multiple requests to proceed with testing and evaluation.' The report attributes that to 'restructuring at CDC and consequent delays in terms of decision making' and asserts nothing beyond it. Second, 'fewer than 1%' is not a universal constant: measured against active surveillance, VAERS captured 68-72% of vaccine-associated paralytic polio cases and 47% of intussusception after rotavirus vaccine, but only 13% of anaphylaxis after influenza vaccine and 12% of Guillain-Barre after one seasonal flu vaccine. 'No uniform underreporting factor exists across all events.' Sources: Lazarus R, Klompas M, 'Electronic Support for Public Health - Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (ESP:VAERS)', AHRQ Grant Final Report R18 HS 017045 (2011), p.6; grokipedia.com/page/Vaccine_Adverse_Event_Reporting_System.

question: A committee of the Institute of Medicine refused in 2013 to endorse the study that would settle the schedule question, calling it unethical: randomise children, leave one group unvaccinated, follow both for years. No such trial has been run on the whole schedule, which shows neither danger nor safety. The fallback compares the children America already has, some on the standard schedule and some on an alternative one. What flaw did the committee name in that?
answer: The two groups of children may differ in more ways than the schedule
choices: The two groups of children may differ in more ways than the schedule
The two groups of children may be too young for the illnesses at issue
The two groups' doctors may record the same illness under different names
The two groups' vaccines may vary in strength from batch to batch
context: Verbatim: 'children who are immunized with alternative vaccination schedules may differ in meaningful ways from children who adhere to the schedule, and these differences could make it difficult to tease out health differences that are attributable to the immunization schedule.' That is the healthy-user problem - when people sort themselves into the groups, whatever made them choose travels with them into the results - and the committee stated it by hand. It named a second wall on the same page: 'Fewer than 1 percent of Americans refuse all immunizations. Enrolling sufficient numbers of unvaccinated children and matching them with vaccinated children of the same age, gender, ethnicity, and geographic location - a necessary step to rule out chance findings - would be prohibitively difficult and time-consuming.' On the randomised trial the committee was explicit: 'The committee does not endorse conducting a new randomized controlled clinical trial that would compare the health outcomes of unvaccinated children with their fully immunized peers. Although this is the strongest study design type, ethical concerns prohibit this study, as unvaccinated individuals and communities intentionally would be left vulnerable to morbidity and mortality.' Note where the refusal rests: on ethics, not on power - the committee concedes the design is the strongest there is. What it recommended instead was the Vaccine Safety Datalink, a CDC collaboration with nine managed-care organisations then covering 'more than 9 million children and adults - roughly 3 percent of the U.S. population', which it called 'the best available system for studying the childhood immunization schedule'. The VSD has 13 member sites today and runs rapid-cycle analyses in near-real time: active surveillance, which goes and looks, rather than waiting to be told. Sources: IOM Report Brief (January 2013), p.3; CDC, 'About the Vaccine Safety Datalink'.

question: Yih and her team searched the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Mini-Sentinel records once RotaTeq, the vaccine built to replace RotaShield, had gone into use. It had been licensed only after a trial in 68,038 babies, which tracked one bowel problem, part of the gut folding into itself, and found no extra risk. How many extra cases did the team find in the week after a first dose?
answer: About 1.1 extra cases per 100,000 first doses
choices: About 0.1 extra cases per 100,000 first doses
About 1.1 extra cases per 100,000 first doses
About 4 extra cases per 100,000 first doses
About 11 extra cases per 100,000 first doses
context: Yih and colleagues estimated 1.1 excess intussusception cases per 100,000 first doses of RotaTeq in the seven-day window (95% CI 0.3 to 2.7) and 1.5 per 100,000 in the 21-day window (95% CI 0.2 to 3.2). Set that against RotaShield, whose excess risk worked out at 'approximately 1 intussusception case in 10 000 Rotashield recipients' - roughly ten times larger. RotaTeq's trial had been built for this exact question, and its sister vaccine Rotarix was trialled at similar size: the two 'each underwent large clinical trials of approximately 60 000-70 000 infants specifically to assess the risk of intussusception.' Neither trial found an increased risk - and a risk near one in a hundred thousand is precisely what a trial of 68,000 cannot see. This is the cleanest demonstration anywhere that 'the trial found nothing' and 'there is nothing to find' are two different statements. The mirror statement matters just as much: 'a real risk was found' and 'the vaccine should be withdrawn' are also two different statements. RotaTeq stayed on the schedule, because one in a hundred thousand is a different decision from one in ten thousand. The same split showed in 2010-11, when VAERS data mining flagged febrile seizures in children aged six to 23 months after influenza vaccine and the Vaccine Safety Datalink confirmed roughly 2 extra seizures per 10,000 vaccinations: the response was revised guidance on fever medicines and changed labels, not withdrawal. So three sentences that sound alike are not alike - 'no randomised trial of the whole schedule exists', 'it has been investigated and nothing was found', and 'therefore it is dangerous' - and treating any one of them as another is the error, whoever commits it. Sources: Yih WK et al., 'Intussusception Risk after Rotavirus Vaccination in U.S. Infants', N Engl J Med 2014; 'Evaluating the safety of a rotavirus vaccine: the REST of the story', PMC2602609; PMC5715718; grokipedia.com/page/Vaccine_Adverse_Event_Reporting_System.

question: Ian Donald took two cars to the Babcock & Wilcox boiler works at Renfrew on 21 July 1955, where an ultrasonic tester hunted cracks inside steel. A professor of midwifery at Glasgow, he had loaded both boots at his hospital. What was in them?
answer: fibroids and ovarian cysts cut from his patients
choices: fibroids and ovarian cysts cut from his patients
placentas saved from his own delivery room
jars of specimens from the pathology museum
blood and fluid drained from his own wards
context: The source puts it plainly: 'He took with him two cars, the boots of which were loaded up with a collection of lumps such as fibroids and ovarian cysts which had recently been removed from patients in his Department.' Donald had arrived in Glasgow in autumn 1954 with, in his own words, 'a rudimentary knowledge of radar from my days in the RAF' - he served as an RAF medical officer from 1942 to 1946, was mentioned in dispatches after pulling airmen out of a burning bomber, and was awarded the MBE. His question was as plain as he could make it: 'All I wanted to know, quite simply, was whether these various masses differed in their ultrasonic echo characteristics.' The rail worth remembering: Ian Donald did not invent ultrasound. He made the diagnostic application work, on borrowed industrial hardware, alongside the engineer Tom Brown and the clinician John MacVicar. Source: ob-ultrasound.net, Joseph Woo, 'A short History of the development of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology', Part 1 (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/history1.html); Wikipedia 'Ian Donald'.

question: At a boiler factory, Ian Donald ran a sound tester over samples from his hospital. To read the results he needed a comparison, healthy tissue tested that same day, which scientists call a control. The story goes that the firm kindly gave him one. What was it?
answer: a large lump of steak
choices: a large lump of steak
a slab of raw liver
a boiled ham hock
a whole plucked chicken
context: Joseph Woo's history records it with a Scottish deadpan: the tests were run '...on a large lump of steak which the company had kindly provided as control material. (No one had the appetite for the steak afterwards!)' Flagged as legend here because the detail survives in the telling rather than in a laboratory notebook. The idea underneath it is dead serious and is one of the oldest tools in experimental science: you cannot know what an odd reading MEANS until you have run the same test on something you already agree is normal. Try it yourself the next time you measure anything - measure something known first. Source: ob-ultrasound.net, Joseph Woo, Part 1 (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/history1.html).

question: Tom Brown, a 23-year-old engineer at a Glasgow instrument firm, picked up some odd gossip late in 1956 about a professor at the Western Infirmary. He looked up the man's number and called him out of the blue, and within a year they had built the first contact scanner. What was the professor said to be doing?
answer: using a flaw detector to detect flaws in women
choices: using a flaw detector to detect flaws in women
photographing unborn babies with old radar gear
listening to hearts through a submarine hydrophone
hunting tumours with a converted welding rig
context: Joseph Woo's wording: 'Quite by accident, Tom Brown had heard the strange tale of a professor who was attempting to use a metal flaw detector to detect flaws in women. He telephoned Professor Donald and suggested a meeting.' Flagged as legend because accounts differ on how the rumour reached him - Wikipedia has Brown coming across Donald while installing equipment at the Western Infirmary and then looking him up in the hospital directory - though both agree on the phone call. Brown, born 10 April 1933, had just been promoted to research and development engineer in 1956 and had already worked on an automatic flaw detector for industrial products. By late 1957 he and Donald had the first contact B-mode compound scanner in clinical use, its transducer running at 2.5 MHz, and Kelvin & Hughes patented the design that year with Brown named as inventor. Sources: ob-ultrasound.net Part 1; Wikipedia 'Tom Brown (engineer)'.

question: Jacques and Pierre Curie, brothers of 24 and 21, clamped crystals of quartz, sugar and salt in a small vise in a Paris lab in 1880 and pressed hard on the faces. Pierre would later share a Nobel Prize with his wife Marie. What appeared when they squeezed?
answer: a voltage across the crystal's faces
choices: a voltage across the crystal's faces
a flash of light inside the crystal
a rise in the crystal's temperature
a faint ringing note from the crystal
context: This is the direct piezoelectric effect: 'The first demonstration of the direct piezoelectric effect was in 1880 by the brothers Pierre Curie and Jacques Curie.' Quartz and Rochelle salt gave the strongest response; the brothers were then working under Charles Friedel at the Faculty of Sciences in Paris. A year later Gabriel Lippmann deduced the converse effect - feed a voltage in and the crystal deforms - mathematically, from fundamental thermodynamic principles, and the Curies immediately confirmed it in the laboratory. Those two halves are exactly the two jobs a probe does: the converse effect lets it speak, the direct effect lets it listen, and one crystal does both. A connective footnote: the sensitive piezoelectric quartz electrometer the brothers built for this crystal work is the very instrument Marie Curie later used to measure the radioactivity of pitchblende and isolate polonium and radium. Modern probes are not quartz but PZT, lead zirconate titanate, a ceramic developed around 1952 at the Tokyo Institute of Technology. Sources: Wikipedia 'Piezoelectricity', 'Jacques Curie', 'Pierre Curie', 'Lead zirconate titanate'.

question: A technician squirts cold gel onto a patient's skin, smears it flat and presses the ultrasound probe on top. The gel is not there for comfort: without it the screen shows almost nothing at all, just a black snowstorm. What physical job is the gel doing?
answer: shutting out the air, which bounces the whole beam back
choices: shutting out the air, which bounces the whole beam back
cooling the crystal, which heats up as it pulses
carrying the electric pulse from the probe into the skin
damping the probe so its own ringing dies away
context: Wikipedia's 'Medical ultrasound' states it directly: 'a water-based gel is placed between the patient's skin and the probe to facilitate ultrasound transmission into the body. This is because air causes total reflection of ultrasound; impeding the transmission of ultrasound into the body.' The mismatch behind it is brutal - acoustic impedance about 429 for air against roughly 1.6 million for soft tissue, which sends essentially the whole beam (about 99.9%) straight back off the first film of air it meets. StatPearls gives the working rule the same way: 'ultrasound waves cannot travel through the air, [so] probes must contact patients' skin through a coupling medium.' You can notice the same physics yourself: duck your head under the bathwater while someone talks above the surface and the voice all but vanishes, because sound crossing between water and air is thrown back at the boundary. Sources: Wikipedia 'Medical ultrasound'; StatPearls 'Ultrasound Physics', NCBI Bookshelf NBK570593; impedance values from OpenStax College Physics 2e 17.7.

question: A midwife times an echo with the very fast clock in her scanner, which carries no ruler. The echo arrives 100 microseconds after the pulse left the probe, having made the trip down and back, and sound crosses soft tissue at roughly 1,540 metres per second. How deep is the structure that threw it?
answer: about 7.7 cm
choices: about 7.7 cm
about 15.4 cm
about 3.9 cm
about 1.5 cm
context: 1,540 m/s multiplied by 100 microseconds is 0.154 m of travel; the echo went down AND back, so the reflector sits 7.7 cm below the probe. (15.4 cm is the trap - it is the round trip, not the depth.) Wikipedia's 'Medical ultrasound' states the principle bluntly: the scanner must determine 'how long it took the echo to be received from when the sound was transmitted. (Time and distance are equivalent.)' Delay fixes where the dot goes on the screen; the strength of the echo fixes how bright it is. Now the honest catch: 1,540 m/s is only an AVERAGE for soft tissue. Fat carries sound at about 1,450 m/s and muscle at about 1,590, so the machine's single assumed speed is itself a source of artefacts, and structures can be drawn slightly off their true depth. Sources: Wikipedia 'Medical ultrasound'; OpenStax College Physics 2e, section 17.7 'Ultrasound'.

question: Reginald Fessenden sailed on the Revenue Cutter Miami in 1914 with his new underwater oscillator, out to the Grand Banks off Newfoundland, into the ice lanes where the Titanic had gone down two years earlier. He sounded the depth of the sea below and caught the echo of an iceberg two miles off. The oscillator did a third job on that trip. What was it?
answer: tapped out Morse code through the water itself
choices: tapped out Morse code through the water itself
listened for a submarine running beneath the hull
measured the sea's temperature from its echoes
spoke by voice to a diver below the ship
context: Fessenden's 1914 demonstration covered depth sounding, underwater communications by Morse code and echo ranging, 'detecting an iceberg at a 2-mile (3.2 km) range' - in a year when radio was young and radar did not exist. Sending a coded message through the water itself was the third strand of that demonstration; the record credits it without saying who, if anyone, was listening at the far end, and without claiming it as a first - so this question does not claim one either. The point here is the ORDER of events: sound-ranging was a sea technology first, and medicine borrowed it decades later. Lewis Fry Richardson, a Quaker meteorologist who pioneered numerical weather forecasting and served the First World War as a conscientious objector in the Friends' Ambulance Unit, had patented iceberg detection by acoustic echolocation in air in April 1912, within weeks of the sinking, and filed a second patent for the same trick in water a month after that. Paul Langevin then built the first transducer that really worked, a submarine detector running at 150 kHz between 1915 and 1918, made from thin quartz crystals glued between two steel plates. Sources: Wikipedia 'Sonar'; Wikipedia 'Lewis Fry Richardson'; ob-ultrasound.net Part 1.

question: Ian Donald ran his ultrasound over the belly of a woman on his Glasgow ward, given up for lost by her doctors. X-rays and exams said she had stomach cancer that could not be cut out; his echoes disagreed. Surgery proved the machine right. What had it found?
answer: a huge ovarian cyst filling her whole abdomen
choices: a huge ovarian cyst filling her whole abdomen
a swollen liver, enlarged but not cancerous
a knot of scar tissue from an older operation
a mass of fibroids pressing on her stomach
context: The laparotomy confirmed a pseudomucinous cyst filling the entire abdomen - large, and removable. This is the case Ian Donald himself treated as the turning point: a woman told she would die, opened up instead and cured, because a borrowed industrial instrument disagreed with an X-ray. Donald's own account of what kept the work moving afterwards is worth keeping: 'As soon as we got rid of the backroom attitude and brought our apparatus fully into the Department with an inexhaustible supply of living patients with fascinating clinical problems, we were able to get ahead really fast.' The proof was published as Donald I, MacVicar J, Brown TG, 'Investigation of abdominal masses by pulsed ultrasound', The Lancet, 7 June 1958, 1(7032):1188-95. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ian Donald'; ob-ultrasound.net, Ian Donald biography (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/iandonaldbio.html); PubMed PMID 13550965.

question: Karl Dussik and Friedrich, his physicist brother, sat patients with the top of the head in a water bath in 1940s Vienna, trying ultrasound on the head before the belly. Karl read the pictures as the brain's fluid pockets, and his 1947 pictures were the first ultrasound images anyone had shared. How did Karl's machine work?
answer: the sound was sent through the head to a receiver on the far side
choices: the sound was sent through the head to a receiver on the far side
the sound was pulsed in and the echoes coming back were timed
the sound was made to resonate the skull and the ringing measured
two beams were crossed inside the head and the interference read
context: Dussik, born in Vienna on 9 January 1908, presented his first paper in 1941 and, with his younger brother Friedrich (a radio and mathematical physicist with a 1938 Vienna PhD) and the physicist L. Wyt, published the first ultrasound images in 1947. The method: 'a through-transmission technique with two transducers placed on either side of the head... Coupling was obtained by immersing the upper part of the patient's head and both transducers in a water bath.' He called it hyperphonography. Dating note: ob-ultrasound gives 1941 for the paper and 1947 for the images, while BMUS dates the first published work on medical ultrasonics to 1942, so 'the 1940s' is the honest span. Dussik was a serious pioneer, not a fraud - a test published years later showed that the pattern he had been reading came from somewhere other than the ventricles. Sources: ob-ultrasound.net, Karl Theodore Dussik biography (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/dussikbio.html); BMUS 'History of Ultrasound'.

question: John Wild, a surgeon, borrowed a US Navy radar trainer in Minnesota and aimed it at tissue instead of the sky. With the engineer John Reid he published in Science in 1952, and by 1956 their machine had checked 117 breast cases with better than 90% accuracy. What had Wild and Reid found that made the machine useful?
answer: cancerous tissue echoes more strongly than healthy tissue
choices: cancerous tissue echoes more strongly than healthy tissue
cancerous tissue carries sound faster than healthy tissue
cancerous tissue shifts the pitch of the echo as it grows
cancerous tissue swallows the beam almost completely
context: In the sources' own words, Wild and Reid found that 'malignant tissue was more echogenic than benign tissue' - malignant meaning cancerous, benign meaning harmless. Their landmark paper was 'Application of Echo-Ranging Techniques to the Determination of Structure of Biological Tissues', Science, 1952; Reid called it 'the first publication... on intensity-modulated cross-section ultrasound imaging.' By May 1953 they had real-time 15 MHz breast images. Their route - REFLECTION, listening for what comes back - is the road that won, and Ian Donald attended a lecture by Wild in 1954. On the same road, Douglass Howry at the University of Colorado built the first 2-D compound scanner in 1951 with engineers William Roderic Bliss and Gerald Posakony, mounting the transducer around the rim of a large metal tank of water; his 1957 Pan-scanner seated patients in modified dental chairs, and the AMA gave the work a Certificate of Merit in 1958. Source: ob-ultrasound.net Part 1 (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/history1.html).

question: A trainee watches a faint line form on the screen where fat meets muscle. Every boundary in the body throws some of the beam back, and how much depends on the jump in acoustic impedance, a tissue's density times its sound speed: here 925 against 1,075 kg per cubic metre, and 1,450 against 1,590 m/s. How much of the sound striking that boundary comes back?
answer: about 1.4 per cent
choices: about 1.4 per cent
about 7.2 per cent
about 26 per cent
about 64 per cent
context: OpenStax works the case out: the intensity reflection coefficient is a = (Z2 - Z1)^2 / (Z1 + Z2)^2, and for ultrasound crossing from fat into muscle a = 0.014 - 'only 1.4% of the incident intensity is reflected, with the remaining being transmitted.' An entire ultrasound image is assembled out of that 1.4%. The mirror image is why gel exists: air's impedance is about 429 against roughly 1.6 million for tissue, which throws essentially the whole beam back. Accuracy note, because the textbook version is routinely overstated: put the published bone impedance (5.7 to 7.8 million) into the same formula and a muscle/bone boundary reflects roughly 29-41% - a lot, but NOT 'almost everything'. Bone blanks out the picture mainly by ABSORBING the beam, whereas air really does reflect nearly all of it. Source: OpenStax, College Physics 2e, section 17.7 'Ultrasound'; Z = rho x c corroborated by Wikipedia 'Acoustic impedance'.

question: W. Guettner and colleagues at the Siemens laboratories in Erlangen published a paper in 1952 that ended Karl Dussik's pictures of the living human head. For a decade the field had read them as maps of the brain's fluid-filled ventricles, the most promising images anyone had. The pattern was real enough; it simply came from something other than the brain. From what?
answer: the varying thickness of the skull bone
choices: the varying thickness of the skull bone
the standing waves in the water bath
the folds of the scalp and its hair
the pulsing of the arteries in the neck
context: The paper: Guttner W., Fielder G. and Patzold J. (1952), 'Uber Ultraschallabbildungen Am Menschlichen Schadel' (On ultrasound images of the human skull), Acustica 2:148-156, out of the Siemens Laboratories at Erlangen. They showed that 'reflections within the skull and attenuation patterns produced by the skull were contributing to the attenuation pattern which Dussik had originally thought represented changes in acoustic transmissions through the cerebral ventricles.' In plain terms: a decade of pictures of the brain were pictures of bone. The honest reading is not that Dussik was foolish - it is that a promising method can produce beautiful, consistent, entirely artefactual results for years until somebody tests the assumption underneath it. The skull absorbs and reflects so strongly that sending sound straight through the head could never have worked. (Spelling note: this source prints 'Fielder'; other accounts write 'Fiedler'.) Source: ob-ultrasound.net, Karl Theodore Dussik biography (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/dussikbio.html).

question: An ultrasound operator sets her probe to 3 to 5 megahertz to scan a liver, though it can run anywhere from about 1 to 18. Higher frequency means finer detail, and at 7 MHz the wavelength in tissue is only about 0.22 mm, yet she gives that detail up on purpose. What goes wrong at 7 MHz?
answer: a 7 MHz beam is swallowed by tissue long before it gets there
choices: a 7 MHz beam is swallowed by tissue long before it gets there
a 7 MHz beam is scattered into noise by any flowing blood
a 7 MHz beam warms the tissue more than is thought safe
a 7 MHz beam fills the picture with grainy speckle noise
context: Acoustic absorption costs roughly 0.5 dB per centimetre of depth per megahertz, so a 5 MHz wave loses about 5 dB in the first centimetre and another 5 in the next; push the frequency up and the beam dies nearer the surface. Wikipedia states the trade directly: 'The attenuation of the sound wave is increased at higher frequencies, so penetration of deeper tissues necessitates a lower frequency (3-5 MHz).' OpenStax gives the other side: 'we will never observe details significantly smaller than the wavelength,' and at 7 MHz you 'can effectively scan to a depth of about 500 lambda' - around 11 cm. Resolution and reach are traded against each other in every single scan. The other honest limit: unlike a CT, image quality depends heavily on the hand holding the probe. What ultrasound has in exchange is exactly why it is the tool used on the unborn - nothing ionising ever enters the room, and randomised trials that followed children to ages 8 and 9 found no significant differences in developmental outcomes from ultrasound exposure. Sources: Wikipedia 'Medical ultrasound'; StatPearls 'Ultrasound Physics' NBK570593; OpenStax College Physics 2e 17.7; Wikipedia 'Obstetric ultrasonography'.

question: Chelyabinsk, Russia, was starting its working day on 15 February 2013 when a rock about 18 metres wide burst some 30 kilometres overhead, with about the force of thirty Hiroshima bombs. Nobody died, but 1,491 people needed treatment. What hurt almost all of them?
answer: Glass from windows blown in by the shock wave
choices: Glass from windows blown in by the shock wave
Burns from the heat of the fireball above
Masonry falling from walls and chimneys
The blast wind knocking people off their feet
context: 112 people were admitted to hospital, two in serious condition; the blast came shortly after the school day began. The shock wave damaged more than 7,200 buildings across six cities and shattered windows over an ellipse roughly 90 km long and 40 km wide along the ground track, and part of a zinc factory's roof caved in. Damage to buildings came to more than 33 million dollars. Source: Grokipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'; Wikipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'.

question: Divers raised the largest surviving piece of the Chelyabinsk rock from Lake Chebarkul on 16 October 2013 and put it on a scale. It had punched a seven-metre hole in the lake's ice, and of some 9,000 tonnes only four to six had landed at all. What happened on the scale?
answer: It broke the scale and split into three pieces
choices: It broke the scale and split into three pieces
It read 654 kilograms and was carted off intact
It weighed a tenth of what the hole suggested
It turned out to be iron rather than stone
context: It read 654 kilograms before the scale gave way; the largest of the three resulting pieces weighs 540 kg. About a thousand fragments totalling over 1,000 kg were recovered in all. Every one of them is a splinter: Chelyabinsk was an airburst, and the body that came in had already been destroyed tens of kilometres up. Laboratory work classified the meteorite as an LL5 ordinary chondrite at shock stage S4, carrying shock-melt veins and high-pressure jadeite formed above 1700 degrees C -- scars from a collision on its parent body roughly 100 million years ago. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor' and 'Chelyabinsk meteorite'; Grokipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'.

question: Residents of Chelyabinsk, Russia, walked to their windows on 15 February 2013 and were standing there when a shock wave arrived from a rock bursting about 30 kilometres up. They were not being careless. What had brought them to the windows first?
answer: The flash reached them at once, and the bang took over two minutes
choices: The flash reached them at once, and the bang took over two minutes
A small first burst drew a crowd, and a bigger one came later
The fireball took a full minute to cross the sky, and they watched
A glowing trail hung overhead for minutes after the fireball passed
context: Depending on distance, the shock wave took between 2 minutes 23 seconds and 2 minutes 57 seconds to arrive. The fireball itself was visible for roughly 30 seconds and could be made out 100 km away; twenty people afterwards reported ultraviolet burns like sunburn. You can measure the same gap yourself in the next thunderstorm: count the seconds between the lightning flash and the thunder, then divide by three for the rough distance in kilometres. Light outran sound over Chelyabinsk, and that gap is exactly why people were hurt. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'; The Planetary Society, 'What was the Chelyabinsk meteor event?'.

question: Survey telescopes swept the sky every night and had catalogued thousands of asteroids, yet not one of them saw the 18-metre rock that exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, on 15 February 2013. Why was every one of them blind to it?
answer: It came in from the direction of the Sun, lost in the glare
choices: It came in from the direction of the Sun, lost in the glare
It sat inside the Earth's own shadow on its final approach
It was moving too fast for a telescope to hold and track
It approached over the South Pole, where no survey looks
context: Its radiant -- the direction it came from -- lay close to the Sun, so it approached out of the daylight glare, where no ground-based survey can look. About sixteen hours later the tracked 30-metre asteroid 2012 DA14 passed 27,700 km above Earth, inside the ring of geosynchronous satellites. The two objects were completely unrelated, on different orbits from different populations, and the odds of such a same-day coincidence are put near one in a hundred million. The one they were watching missed; the one nobody saw hit. Source: Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'; NASA JPL, 'Additional Details on the Large Feb. 15 Fireball over Russia'.

question: People in Sweden and Scotland took photos of each other at midnight with no flash for several nights after 30 June 1908, when something burst far up over a Siberian river and flattened the forest below. In Britain, people read outside by natural light as late as 2 July. What was lighting up the night sky?
answer: About a million tonnes of fine dust, high above the clouds
choices: About a million tonnes of fine dust, high above the clouds
An unusually strong aurora, spreading south from the Arctic
The tail of a comet, passing between Earth and the Sun
Smoke from Siberian forest fires, drifting west over Europe
context: The dust was flung into the stratosphere and mesosphere -- the calm layers above our weather -- and polarisation measurements made at observatories of the day confirmed the glowing material was high, not low. Those bright nights were the first sign anywhere outside Siberia that something enormous had happened, and for years nobody in Europe connected the two. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tunguska event'; Grokipedia, 'Tunguska event'.

question: Jorge Zuluaga and Ignacio Ferrin, in Colombia, took under a week to work out the Chelyabinsk rock's speed, its path through the air and its orbit around the Sun. No telescope had been watching, so astronomers had no tracking data. What did the two men use to figure that out?
answer: Dashboard-camera video that Russian drivers keep running for insurance
choices: Dashboard-camera video that Russian drivers keep running for insurance
Seismic traces from Russian earthquake-monitoring stations nearby
Images from a weather satellite that passed overhead at the time
Radar echoes recorded by a Russian military tracking station
context: They used one camera in Revolution Square in Chelyabinsk, videos from the nearby town of Korkino, and the position of the hole punched in the ice of Lake Chebarkul, and they posted the result on 21 February 2013 -- six days after the event. The reconstructed orbit was an Apollo-type Earth-crossing path with a period near 2.1 years, from the Flora family in the inner asteroid belt, and it closely resembles the orbit of a known asteroid, 86039 (1999 NC43), raising the possibility that the two were once one body. Source: Zuluaga and Ferrin, arXiv:1302.5377; Borovicka et al., Nature 503, 235-237.

question: A listening station in Antarctica, some 15,000 kilometres from Chelyabinsk, picked up the blast as sound too low for the human ear. The station belonged to a worldwide network built for a different job, and twenty of its stations caught the blast in all. What was that network built to listen for?
answer: Nuclear tests carried out in secret
choices: Nuclear tests carried out in secret
Earthquakes far out under the ocean
Volcanic eruptions in remote places
Storms gathering over the open sea
context: It was the largest signal the CTBTO's monitoring network had ever recorded, until the Hunga Tonga eruption of 2022. The waves reached stations by paths running from 500 km to 87,000 km, meaning the sound travelled more than twice around the planet before the last detection. The infrasound alone, using period-versus-yield scaling and independent of every other method, gave about 460 kilotons; the estimate combining light curves, satellite sensors and seismic ground-roll gave 500 plus or minus 100 kilotons. Two utterly different instruments, one answer -- that agreement is what turns a number into a measurement. Source: Le Pichon et al., Geophysical Research Letters, 2013; Brown et al., Nature 503, 238-241.

question: Researchers travelled to the precise spots where the Chelyabinsk dashcam clips had been filmed. The clips were shaky, uncalibrated and pointed wherever the driver happened to be going, and the team needed the fireball's exact direction at every instant from each camera. What did the researchers do there?
answer: Photographed the night sky from the same spot and overlaid the stars
choices: Photographed the night sky from the same spot and overlaid the stars
Measured the height of every building that appeared in the frame
Re-filmed the whole scene with a surveyed and calibrated camera
Recorded the time showing on each camera's internal clock
context: Superimposing a night starfield on the daytime footage fixed the fireball's true position on the sky, frame by frame. They also measured the directions of the daytime shadows the fireball's light swung across the ground, a second and independent geometric handle on where that light had been. Ordinary consumer cameras, with the stars as a ruler. On the ground, Olga Popova's Russian Academy of Sciences team did the other half on foot: within a month they visited 50 villages, interviewed residents and photographed broken windows to build the damage map the energy estimate leaned on. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'; Scientific American, 'Chelyabinsk Eyewitnesses Help Scientists Resolve Meteor Mysteries'; Popova et al., Science 342, 1069-1073.

question: A student plots the last seconds of the Chelyabinsk rock: about 18 metres across, some 9,000 tonnes, hitting the air over Russia at 19 kilometres a second. It started to break at 45 kilometres up, with nearly all the air still below it, then broke about eleven more times over the next fifteen kilometres. What was tearing it up so high?
answer: The air piling up ahead of it pushed harder than the rock could hold
choices: The air piling up ahead of it pushed harder than the rock could hold
The heat of entry melted it steadily through from the outside in
The cold of the upper air cracked it the way ice cracks glass
Water frozen inside it boiled and blew the rock apart from within
context: Measured from the break-up altitudes, the body's bulk strength was only about 1 megapascal; Peter Brown's team called it 'a heavily fractured single stone'. The first major break came at 45 km, where the pressure of the onrushing air reached about 0.7 MPa, and roughly eleven more fragmentation events between 40 and 30 km, at 1 to 5 MPa, released most of the mass. A body that comes apart like that dumps nearly all its energy into a small volume of air in a fraction of a second. That is an explosion in the sky rather than an impact in the ground, and it is why such events usually leave nothing to dig up. Source: Brown et al., Nature 503, 238-241; Physics Today, 'Chelyabinsk: Portrait of an asteroid airburst'.

question: A visitor stands on the rim of Barringer Crater in Arizona, gouged out by a body of modest size. A similar body came down in eastern Russia on 12 February 1947 and left more than 200 craters, the largest 26 metres across and 6 metres deep, with over 23 tonnes later recovered. What did those two have that the Chelyabinsk rock did not?
answer: They were made of solid iron rather than stone
choices: They were made of solid iron rather than stone
They came in far more slowly than Chelyabinsk
They entered on a much steeper, near-vertical path
They were made of ice rather than solid rock
context: The 1947 fall was Sikhote-Alin, in eastern Russia, and the 23 tonnes recovered from its crater field were metal. Small stony asteroids preferentially burst before reaching the ground; small iron ones survive the passage and excavate real holes. Composition, not just size, decides whether you get a crater or an explosion in the sky. Source: Physics Today, 'Chelyabinsk: Portrait of an asteroid airburst'; Grokipedia, 'Tunguska event'.

question: Leonid Kulik reached the centre of the 1908 Siberian blast in April 1927, after a boat journey up the Podkamennaya Tunguska and days on foot and by reindeer through swampy forest. He had come for an iron meteorite lying in its crater, and he found neither. Over a zone about eight kilometres across at the very centre, what did he find?
answer: Trees still standing upright, scorched and stripped of every branch
choices: Trees still standing upright, scorched and stripped of every branch
Ground fused into a sheet of glass for kilometres in every direction
A ring of water-filled pits around a low mound of broken rock
Forest floor buried under a metre of fine grey ash and cinders
context: Kulik called it the telegraph-pole forest. Farther out the trunks lay flat in a vast radial pattern pointing away from the centre, about 2,150 square kilometres of taiga in a butterfly-shaped scar with a 70-kilometre wingspan. A blast directly overhead pushes straight down on the trees beneath it and strips their branches without toppling them; only farther out does the wave arrive slanting enough to knock trunks over. The absence Kulik came home with was itself the evidence. He led four expeditions across the 1920s and 1930s and never found the object; he volunteered for the militia in the Second World War, German troops captured him, and he died of typhus in a prisoner-of-war camp on 24 April 1942, aged 58. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tunguska event' and 'Leonid Kulik'; Linda Hall Library, 'Leonid Kulik -- Scientist of the Day'; NASA, '115 Years Ago: The Tunguska Asteroid Impact Event'.

question: Willard Libby, who invented radiocarbon dating, proposed in 1965 with Clyde Cowan and C. R. Atluri that the 1908 Tunguska blast had been a lump of antimatter. They said what it must have left behind: annihilation should have raised the amount of carbon-14 in the air that year by about seven per cent. Where did they go looking for that spike?
answer: In the yearly growth rings of living trees
choices: In the yearly growth rings of living trees
In ice cores drilled from the Greenland sheet
In peat cut from the bogs around the blast site
In museum air samples sealed before 1908
context: They measured tree rings including those of a 300-year-old Douglas fir in Tucson, and found only about 1 per cent for 1909; careful measurements on a tree nearer the blast showed no rise at all. The hypothesis died by the test its own authors had designed. A second wrong idea got the same treatment: in 1973 the physicists A. A. Jackson IV and Michael P. Ryan Jr. proposed in Nature that a tiny primordial black hole had punched through the Earth and out again, which predicted an exit shock wave over the North Atlantic -- and in 1974 Beasley and Tinsley replied that the microbarographs had recorded no such wave. Source: Cowan, Atluri and Libby, Nature 206, 861-865; Nature 208, 772 and Nature 212, 1226; Jackson and Ryan, Nature 245, 88-89; Beasley and Tinsley, Nature 250, 555.

question: A researcher lays out the Tunguska records, worked on for well over a century. Seismographs at Irkutsk, a thousand kilometres away, logged the blast at about magnitude 5.0, ordinary weather barographs from Germany to Washington, D.C. traced its pressure wave twice around the globe, and about 2,150 square kilometres of flattened forest have been mapped. No piece of the object has ever been confirmed. Where does the energy figure stand today?
answer: Published estimates still range from about 3 to 50 megatons
choices: Published estimates still range from about 3 to 50 megatons
Published estimates have converged on 10 megatons since 1960
Published estimates have narrowed to between 12 and 14 megatons
Published estimates agree on 30 megatons from the forest area
context: Recent calculations give 3 to 5 megatons, a 2019 paper argues for 20 to 30, and the figure most often quoted in the middle is 10 to 15. There is no settled number. Nor is there a settled object: no fragment of the impactor has ever been confirmed, only microscopic magnetite and silicate spherules and iridium anomalies in peat layers dated to 1908, and whether it was a stony asteroid or a comet is still argued -- a 2001 study by Paolo Farinella and colleagues put the odds near 83 per cent asteroidal against 17 per cent cometary, which is a good bet rather than a settled answer. The largest impact event in recorded history, and no one yet knows how big it was or what it was made of. Note also that the famous '80 million trees' is a preliminary guess, not a count: it came from multiplying tree density by an area overestimated fourfold. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tunguska event'; Grokipedia, 'Tunguska event'.

question: A physics teacher chills a small black ceramic tile on the desk, holds a rare-earth magnet just above it and lets go. The magnet does not fall. It hangs in the air over the tile, held in place. What kind of material has she just cooled?
answer: a superconductor
choices: a superconductor
a semiconductor
a permanent magnet
a piezoelectric crystal
context: This is the classic classroom demonstration of the Meissner effect: a superconductor cooled below its critical temperature expels magnetic field and locks a magnet in place above it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissner_effect

question: A student starts an electric current circling a loop inside a ceramic tile chilled to about 90 kelvin, colder than dry ice. The current runs on and on, which no copper wire can ever do. What is the tile's electrical resistance?
answer: exactly zero ohms
choices: exactly zero ohms
roughly one ohm
about one milliohm
close to copper's
context: The defining property of a superconductor below its critical temperature: current runs with no resistance at all -- a hard cliff, not a slope. Onnes phrased it 'practically zero'; the modern measurement is zero within any experimental limit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductivity

question: Two scientists at the Zurich lab of International Business Machines (IBM) tested, in 1986, a brittle ceramic that most metal physicists had written off. The lanthanum-barium-copper oxide became a superconductor at 35 K. They won the Nobel Prize just one year later, one of the fastest in physics history. Which pair was it?
answer: Georg Bednorz and Alex Muller
choices: Georg Bednorz and Alex Muller
John Bardeen and Leon Cooper
Brian Josephson and Alexei Abrikosov
Werner Heisenberg and Max Born
context: Bednorz and Muller's paper in Zeitschrift fuer Physik B (June 1986) opened the cuprate era; the 1987 Nobel followed within about nineteen months. Sources: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1987/press-release/ and https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2023/03/bednorz-muller-high-temperature-superconductivity

question: Maw-Kuen Wu at Alabama and Paul Chu at Houston swapped one element in a superconducting ceramic's recipe months after the International Business Machines (IBM) breakthrough, and the critical temperature jumped to about 93 K. That crossed a practical line: the coolant needed was now something a lab could pour from a flask. Which cheap coolant?
answer: liquid nitrogen
choices: liquid nitrogen
liquid helium
liquid hydrogen
liquid neon
context: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K and costs less per litre than milk; before YBCO, working superconductors needed scarce liquid helium at 4 K. Source: https://ethw.org/First-Hand:Discovery_of_Superconductivity_at_93_K_in_YBCO

question: A patient lies inside an MRI magnet built with copper-oxide ceramics, the breakthrough materials of almost forty years ago. Physicists have argued through dozens of pairing models for those ceramics. What is the current state of the theory of how they superconduct?
answer: No accepted mechanism yet exists
choices: No accepted mechanism yet exists
BCS phonon pairing was confirmed
String theory settled it in 1998
Bose-Einstein condensation explains it
context: The tiny or inverted oxygen isotope effect argues against a purely phonon mechanism; the pseudogap and stripe phases remain openly debated. The materials sit inside working MRI magnets and power grids while the microscopic theory is unsolved. Source: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0953-8984/13/29/202

question: Two Korean chemists posted preprints online on July 22, 2023, claiming a copper-doped lead apatite was a superconductor at room temperature and normal pressure. A video of a fragment tilting off a magnet went around the world. Three weeks later a Max Planck group in Stuttgart had grown clean single crystals of the stuff. What did those pure samples turn out to be?
answer: transparent purple insulators
choices: transparent purple insulators
genuine but weak superconductors
high-Tc superconductors above 200 K
ordinary metallic conductors
context: The Max Planck Institute for Solid State Research reported the pure crystals as transparent purple insulators with resistance in the millions of ohms. The apparent resistance drop in the original mixed samples came from a copper sulfide (Cu2S) impurity whose 385 K structural transition mimicked a superconducting drop; the partial lift came from ferromagnetic contamination. Science did not merely debate the claim -- it made the stuff. Sources: https://physicsworld.com/a/room-temperature-superconductor-lk-99-fails-replication-tests/ and https://www.sciencealert.com/lk-99-is-no-radical-superconductor-after-all-scientists-confirm

question: Mikhail Eremets and his team at Max Planck in Mainz saw superconductivity in lanthanum hydride at 250 K in 2019. That is only 23 K below the freezing point of water. Reporters called it a room-temperature superconductor. Why is that reporting misleading?
answer: It only worked near 170 GPa in a diamond anvil cell
choices: It only worked near 170 GPa in a diamond anvil cell
The measurement was later retracted
The Meissner effect was never seen
The temperature was in Celsius, not Kelvin
context: 170 gigapascals is roughly half the pressure at the centre of Earth's core; the sample sits between two diamond tips smaller than a pinhead. Hydride superconductivity is real and its temperature is genuinely remarkable, but it is not 'room-temperature' in any practical sense until the pressure comes down by orders of magnitude. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1201-8

question: Ranga Dias of the University of Rochester published two papers in Nature, each claiming a superconductor that worked at room temperature, one in 2020 and one in 2023. Jorge Hirsch, a theorist, challenged the data early, and both papers were retracted. Who asked Nature to pull the second one?
answer: Eight of his own eleven co-authors
choices: Eight of his own eleven co-authors
The editors of Nature, acting alone
A rival lab that failed to repeat it
The University of Rochester's inquiry
context: Nature retracted the 2020 paper in 2022 and the 2023 paper on 7 November 2023, the second at the request of eight of its eleven authors; their letter said the paper 'does not accurately reflect the provenance of the investigated materials'. Jorge Hirsch, a condensed-matter theorist at UC San Diego, had been first to question the published data and argued that some of it had never been measured in a laboratory. In March 2024 the University of Rochester reported that an investigation had found Dias engaged in research misconduct. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranga_P._Dias ; https://physics.aps.org/articles/v16/40

question: Paul Kammerer made midwife toads mate in water, not on land, in 1920s Vienna, and said he had proved a serious open claim: that acquired traits can be inherited. He said a change had appeared on the males and passed to their offspring. What did he say had appeared?
answer: dark, rough breeding pads on the fingers
choices: dark, rough breeding pads on the fingers
extra webbing between the hind toes
bright warning patches along the back
hardened claws for gripping wet rocks
context: Kammerer forced the toads to breed in water rather than on land, and reported that the males developed 'nuptial pads' - the dark, rasp-like grip patches other frogs use to hold a mate. If real, that would have been Lamarckism: environment writing itself into the germ line. It was a serious claim in a live debate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kammerer

question: G. K. Noble, an American herpetologist, travelled to Vienna in 1926 and put the last surviving specimen of Paul Kammerer's midwife toads under a microscope. Kammerer had claimed that the dark marks on its front feet came from unusual water and were inherited, proof, he argued, of Lamarckian evolution, in which traits an animal picks up in life pass to its young. Noble published his finding in Nature. What had the dark marks actually been made of?
answer: India ink injected under the skin
choices: India ink injected under the skin
a natural pigment triggered by tank temperature
a shellac coating brushed on before display
silver nitrate deposits from fixative chemicals
context: The microscope showed the pigment sitting where no living pigment sits. Noble's Nature paper was the ink. Kammerer blamed a lab assistant. The first move in every case that follows is the same one Noble made: someone looks at the physical thing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kammerer

question: William Summerlin, a skin doctor, showed off white lab mice at Memorial Sloan-Kettering in March 1974. He said they had accepted dark skin grafts from unrelated donors, with no drugs to block rejection. If real, it would be a huge breakthrough. Then a lab helper did one thing that ended it. What did the helper do?
answer: wiped a dark patch with alcohol and the colour lifted off
choices: wiped a dark patch with alcohol and the colour lifted off
checked the genotype and found the graft was the mouse's own skin
photographed the mice weekly and found the patches had shifted
traced the shipping records and found no donor mice had arrived
context: Summerlin had coloured the mice with a felt-tip pen. The five-person Sloan-Kettering committee led by C. Chester Stock found his conduct incompatible with science, and 'painting the mice' entered the language of research fraud. A cotton swab did what no committee had done. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Summerlin

question: Leon Kamin, an American psychologist, sat down in the early 1970s and read carefully through Sir Cyril Burt's published twin-IQ papers, one after another. Burt was Britain's most famous educational psychologist, and his data on identical twins raised apart was quoted in schools policy on both sides of the Atlantic. Kamin noticed something odd about the correlation numbers across the run of papers. What did those numbers do?
answer: they stayed identical to three decimal places as new twins were added
choices: they stayed identical to three decimal places as new twins were added
they climbed steadily upward as the sample size grew
they alternated exactly between two fixed values across papers
they matched the correlations of an unrelated German study
context: Adding fresh subjects to a real sample perturbs correlation coefficients in the fourth or fifth decimal at minimum; identity at three places across added waves is arithmetically impossible. The tell was not a beaker or a swab this time - it was a column of numbers added up by hand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Burt

question: Oliver Gillie of the London Sunday Times went hunting in 1976 for two people named on Sir Cyril Burt's papers as research assistants who had helped collect the twin data: Margaret Howard and J. Conway. Burt had been dead five years, and doubts about his twin-IQ studies were spreading. Gillie asked at the London campus where Burt had spent his career, and everywhere else Burt had worked. What did he find?
answer: no trace of them at University College or anywhere else
choices: no trace of them at University College or anywhere else
both had died before the studies they were credited with
both worked at a rival lab and denied any involvement
both had signed statements accusing Burt of fabrication
context: Gillie could not put Howard or Conway on any staff list, student register or address between 1914 and 1976. Names on paper are cheap; names attached to human beings are checkable. That is what Gillie checked. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Burt

question: Leslie Hearnshaw, a respected historian of British psychology and a friendly acquaintance of Sir Cyril Burt, took on the official biography at the request of Burt's family. Everyone expected the 1979 book to defend Burt against the fraud charges that had begun after his death. Robert Joynson and Ronald Fletcher later argued against the charges, and the case is still disputed. What did Hearnshaw actually decide about Burt's twin-IQ data?
answer: that they were unreliable or invented
choices: that they were unreliable or invented
that they were sound and the critics had misread them
that they were lost in wartime and could not be judged
that they had been faked by his assistants without his knowledge
context: Hearnshaw had full access to Burt's papers and diaries and started as a sympathetic biographer. His verdict was the tell that mattered most: the man's own defender, reading the man's own files, concluded the post-war numbers could not be trusted. Robert Joynson (1989) and Ronald Fletcher (1991) later argued the case was overstated, and independent twin studies by others have since found broadly similar heritability figures - so whether Burt's own papers were faked remains genuinely disputed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Burt

question: Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes, biostatisticians at MD Anderson, set out from 2007 to reproduce Duke University's much-praised genomic predictors of which chemotherapy would work for a given cancer patient. They rebuilt the whole analysis from the raw files. What did they find in the data?
answer: gene lists shifted by one row and patient samples mislabelled
choices: gene lists shifted by one row and patient samples mislabelled
batches of missing patients silently dropped from the training set
predictor genes hand-picked to hit a pre-set clinical target
the same tumour sample entered twice under different codes
context: Duke had already opened clinical trials assigning cancer patients to treatments based on the predictor. Baggerly and Coombes did not catch a lie - they found errors, in public writing, over three years. The trials were suspended in 2010 and eleven papers were eventually retracted. Source: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/deception-at-duke-fraud-in-cancer-care/

question: Paul Goldberg, editor of a small trade paper called The Cancer Letter, found something out about the Duke University oncologist Anil Potti in July 2010. Potti had built a shining career on gene-signature tests that promised to match cancer patients to the right chemotherapy, and Duke had put real patients on trials that used them. Two Texas statisticians had been raising alarms for three years, but nothing stuck. What had Goldberg found?
answer: he had claimed on grant applications a Rhodes Scholarship he never held
choices: he had claimed on grant applications a Rhodes Scholarship he never held
he had a second job at a private cancer clinic he had not disclosed
he had failed his oncology board certification twice under a former name
he had co-founded a company selling the very predictors he was validating
context: The Rhodes Trust had no record of him. Duke suspended Potti within days; he lost a $729,000 American Cancer Society grant and resigned in November 2010. The through-line of this story: an ink stain, an alcohol swab, a column of correlations added up by hand, an analysis rebuilt from raw files, a scholarship register checked. Not one authority announcing the truth. Every one somebody checking a physical thing. Source: https://cancerletter.com/the-cancer-letter/20100716_1/

question: William Gilbert, doctor to Queen Elizabeth I, carved a chunk of lodestone, the natural magnetic rock, in 1600 to test a guess: that the whole Earth is one giant magnet. Then he walked a tiny compass across it, watching the needle. What shape did he carve?
answer: A sphere
choices: A sphere
A flat disk
A long bar
A horseshoe
context: He called the little globe a terrella, Latin for 'little Earth'. On its surface a tiny compass did exactly what a ship's compass does at sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrella.

question: London compass-maker Robert Norman balanced a magnetised needle on a pivot in 1581. On deck a ship's compass hides what he saw, because it is set to swing horizontally. Freed from that constraint in his workshop, what did the needle do?
answer: Dipped its north end toward the floor
choices: Dipped its north end toward the floor
Spun in slow full circles
Pointed exactly at the Pole Star
Vibrated in time with the tide
context: Norman wrote it up in The Newe Attractive. Gilbert then reproduced the dip on his terrella and showed the angle grows the closer you get to the poles: a bench model that predicted a real shipboard measurement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dip.
