question: William Gilbert pulled apart two forces that everyone before him had lumped together as one. Rubbed amber picks up scraps of straw for a moment and then quits; lodestone pulls only iron, but pulls forever and points. He coined a brand-new Latin name for the amber-and-straw kind. What word did he coin?
answer: Electricus
choices: Electricus
Magneticus
Sideralis
Attractivus
context: Gilbert built the word from the Greek elektron, meaning amber. It took another 220 years, until Oersted's needle jumped near a current-carrying wire in 1820, for the two forces to be joined back together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gilbert_(physician).

question: William Gilbert put a common kitchen ingredient on his own compass needle to test a piece of sailor lore: the claim that rubbing it on a compass would destroy the compass's power. He watched the needle work perfectly. What was the ingredient?
answer: Garlic
choices: Garlic
Vinegar
Salt
Honey
context: The claim went back to ancient natural histories and was still repeated in Gilbert's day. He treated it the modern way: he tested it, and it failed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Magnete.

question: Kristian Birkeland, a Norwegian physicist, built a second little model Earth three centuries after William Gilbert's. He put a magnetised ball inside a vacuum chamber, painted its surface so it would glow, and fired something at it. Rings of light appeared around its poles. What did he fire at the ball?
answer: A beam of electrons
choices: A beam of electrons
A jet of steam
A stream of iron filings
A beam of visible sunlight
context: Cathode rays, in the vocabulary of the day. The glowing rings looked like the aurora, and that was Birkeland's point: he thought he was watching his model do what the sky does. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristian_Birkeland.

question: Sydney Chapman, the leading British geophysicist, led an objection that seemed to sink Kristian Birkeland's idea for fifty years. Birkeland had argued that the aurora was caused by charged particles from the Sun, funnelled onto the polar sky. What was the objection?
answer: Currents cannot cross the vacuum of space
choices: Currents cannot cross the vacuum of space
The Sun is too cold to shed electrons
The aurora comes from below, not above
Magnetised needles show no polar dip
context: The consensus of the day held vacuum as an insulator, so no solar circuit could reach the sky. Birkeland died in Tokyo on 15 June 1917 without an answer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristian_Birkeland.

question: Kristian Birkeland had been dead for fifty years when a US Navy satellite flew straight through the auroral zone in 1967, carrying instruments to sample the region directly. His aurora theory had still been called crank science when he died; the flight settled the argument in his favour. What did the satellite detect?
answer: Electric currents aligned with Earth's field
choices: Electric currents aligned with Earth's field
A ring of iron dust circling Earth
Micro-lightning between clouds and space
A layer of ozone glowing pale green
context: They are now called Birkeland currents. The auroral glow is the visible bottom end of a circuit reaching most of the way to the Sun. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristian_Birkeland.

question: A geologist samples a stack of old lava flows, Earth's own tape recording of its magnetic field, each one frozen with a copy of the field as it cooled. The stack shows north and south have fully swapped many times, the last about 780,000 years ago. When will the next swap come?
answer: No one can yet predict when it will come
choices: No one can yet predict when it will come
It is overdue, since flips keep a steady rhythm
Within two centuries, as the pole's fast drift shows
Never, since the core has cooled too far to flip
context: The last flip is called the Brunhes-Matuyama reversal. When the next will come cannot yet be predicted: reversals look statistically random on geological timescales, the gaps between them have run from under a hundred thousand years to tens of millions, and the mechanism is not settled, so the popular claim that a flip is overdue assumes a rhythm the record does not show. The magnetic north pole is moving fast enough to notice, though: from about 9 km a year in 1970 its drift sped up past 50 km a year, heading from the Canadian Arctic toward Siberia, before slowing lately to about 35. That drift and the aurora are two pieces of this story anyone can watch. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geomagnetic_reversal ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_magnetic_pole ; https://www.sciencealert.com/earths-magnetic-north-pole-is-officially-moving-scientists-just-updated-its-location

question: Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson, two French scientists, measured sunlight very carefully in 1913. Most of it matched the light of any hot glowing body, but a band of the Sun's ultraviolet light never reached the ground. What had they found?
answer: an invisible gas high in the atmosphere
choices: an invisible gas high in the atmosphere
a defect ground into their glass prism
sunspot activity dimming the Sun
the boundary of Earth's magnetic field
context: The shape of the missing-light spectrum would soon be matched to the lab absorption fingerprint of a single chemical -- ozone. Fabry and Buisson had detected an invisible gas overhead by the light it removed. Source: tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.3137/ao.460101.

question: Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson measured in 1920 how much ozone stands over one spot on the ground. A shield against sterilising sunlight sounds like a thick blanket, yet every ozone molecule above a person's head, squeezed down to sea-level pressure, forms only a thin film. About how thick is it?
answer: about three millimetres
choices: about three millimetres
about three centimetres
about thirty centimetres
about three metres
context: Fabry and Buisson's measurement of June 1920 gave a little over three millimetres; accounts of their first rough estimate in 1913 differ. The Dobson unit later baked it in: 100 DU is exactly 1 mm of pure ozone at sea-level pressure, and the global average column is about 300 DU. Sources: tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.3137/ao.460101; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobson_unit. ; repository.si.edu (history of the 1920 measurement)

question: Gordon Dobson, an Oxford weather scientist, built a ground tool that measures all the ozone overhead by comparing two ultraviolet wavelengths in normal daylight. Between 1928 and 1958 he did the thing that actually mattered. What did Dobson build besides the tool itself?
answer: a permanent worldwide network of matching stations
choices: a permanent worldwide network of matching stations
a set of matching detectors flown on high-altitude balloons
a chemical library of stratospheric samples returned by rocket
a theoretical model of ozone photochemistry from first principles
context: Dobson placed spectrophotometers at Arosa, Table Mountain (California), Helwan (Egypt), Kodaikanal (India), Christchurch (NZ) and many more; the network -- not any single instrument -- is his monument. One of its stations at Halley Bay was installed for the International Geophysical Year of 1957. Source: collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co54435.

question: A fisherman on the Bay of Fundy, on Canada's east coast, reads a printed chart. Twice a day the water there rises and falls by about 16 metres, as tall as a five-storey building, and he knows the exact times weeks ahead. What sets that clock so exactly?
answer: The gravity of the passing Moon
choices: The gravity of the passing Moon
The prevailing winds off the Atlantic
The current of the great Gulf Stream
The rotation of Earth on its axis alone
context: The Bay of Fundy holds the world's largest tidal range: on a flood tide roughly 160 billion tonnes of seawater flow in -- more than four times the combined flow of every freshwater river on Earth in the same six hours. The Moon does the scheduling; the Bay's funnel shape and 12.5-hour natural sloshing period do the amplifying. Sources: bayoffundy.com/about/highest-tides ; noaa.gov/ocean/fundy-max

question: A tourist on the Bay of Fundy watches the water pull a long way out at dawn and rush back over the shore by noon. She stays for one full lunar day, the roughly 24 hours and 50 minutes the Moon takes to return overhead. How many high tides does she count?
answer: Two, roughly twelve hours apart
choices: Two, roughly twelve hours apart
One, at the same time each morning
Four, one every six hours
Six, roughly one every four hours
context: Most coasts see two high tides in a lunar day (about 24 hours and 50 minutes long, because the Moon has moved on in its orbit) with a low in between. The two highs come from a tidal bulge on the near side of Earth AND a matching one on the far side -- and the far-side bulge is one of the finest puzzles in classical physics, one that even Galileo got wrong. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide

question: Galileo mocked Kepler's idea that the Moon pulled the seas as strange magic, in his 1632 book Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems. What did Galileo say really causes high and low tides?
answer: Water sloshing in its basin as the Earth spins and orbits
choices: Water sloshing in its basin as the Earth spins and orbits
Water flung outward by the Earth's daily spin toward the equator
Water rocked back and forth by the Earth's yearly orbit around the Sun
Water expanded by the Sun's heat as the Earth turns beneath it
context: Galileo's mistake is the loudest in his career: he had watched water slosh in the barges of Venice and generalised the picture to the whole ocean. Kepler, whom Galileo mocked, had already correctly guessed the Moon was doing the pulling. This is why the story is here at all -- a scientific hero being publicly wrong about his best evidence is the sharpest reminder that even the greatest names are checked by the TEST, not their reputation. Sources: pbs.org/wgbh/nova/galileo/mistake.html ; intellectualmathematics.com/blog/galileos-theory-of-tides

question: A student marks the tides on a globe and finds a second high on the far side of Earth at the same moment as the near one. A once-popular textbook explanation blamed centrifugal force from Earth-Moon rotation. That explanation is wrong. What actually creates the far-side bulge?
answer: The Moon pulls the solid Earth harder than the far water, so the far water is left behind
choices: The Moon pulls the solid Earth harder than the far water, so the far water is left behind
The Moon's pull curves around the planet and reaches the far side directly
The Sun's pull on the far side matches and reinforces the Moon's near-side pull
Water compressed by the near-side bulge is squeezed out and rises opposite it
context: Tides come from a GRADIENT, not a force. The Moon's gravity weakens with distance, so the water on the near side is pulled toward the Moon more than the solid Earth, and the solid Earth is pulled more than the far water. Subtract Earth's motion, and the near water bulges toward the Moon while the far water bulges away from it. Centrifugal accounts confuse the rotating reference frame with the underlying cause -- the two bulges are BOTH the Moon's gravity, seen as a difference. Sources: wtamu.edu/~cbaird/sq/2012/12/14 ; askanastronomer.org (near-far bulge explainer)

question: A sailor waits for the largest tides of the month, which arrive twice every month, in every season, at new moon and at full moon. Sailors call them spring tides, from the old verb meaning to leap, not from the season. Why do the biggest tides come at those two phases?
answer: The Sun and Moon line up, so their tidal pulls add
choices: The Sun and Moon line up, so their tidal pulls add
The Moon swings nearest to Earth at those two phases
The Moon moves fastest along its orbit at those phases
Earth's spin speeds up slightly at those two phases
context: At new moon the Sun and Moon sit on the same side of Earth; at full moon, on opposite sides. Either way they pull along one line, so the Sun's tide, a little under half the Moon's, adds to it. At the half moons they pull at right angles and partly cancel, giving the small neap tides, from an Old English word for scanty. The Moon's nearest approach in its orbit swells tides too, but it follows its own schedule, not the phases. Source: cosmicave.org/course/astronomy-of-planets/mod3/newtons-explanation-of-tides

question: An astronomer sets this year's distance to the Moon beside last year's, and the Moon has drifted farther off. Earth's rotation drags its tidal bulge slightly ahead of the Moon, and the bulge's own gravity tugs the Moon forward in its orbit, while Earth's day lengthens about 1.7 milliseconds per century. That drift is a direct measurement, not a model. What tool makes the measurement possible?
answer: Laser pulses bounced off Apollo retroreflectors still on the Moon
choices: Laser pulses bounced off Apollo retroreflectors still on the Moon
Radio signals timed across the Moon's shadow during eclipses
Optical parallax of the Moon against distant background stars
Gravity measured by tide gauges around the world's coasts
context: Apollo 11, 14, and 15 crews left corner-cube retroreflectors on the lunar surface; astronomers on Earth fire laser pulses at them and time the round trip to millimetre precision. Five decades of Lunar Laser Ranging give the recession as 3.83 cm per year, uncertainty about 0.09 mm. Every Moon-landing skeptic is met with the same clean answer: the mirrors are still on the Moon and still bouncing back light. It is a running scientific test, not an argument from authority. Sources: eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/SEhelp/ApolloLaser.html ; eos.org/features/seeing-the-light

question: A man takes strong antibiotics for a chest infection. Days later his colon burns with a nasty bug called Clostridioides difficile, or C. diff for short. The bug had been living in his gut all along, but only in tiny numbers. What did the antibiotic do to let it take over?
answer: Emptied out the neighbours that had kept it in check
choices: Emptied out the neighbours that had kept it in check
Weakened the immune cells that attacked C. diff directly
Damaged the colon lining and gave the bacteria an opening
Made the gut too acidic for the other resident bacteria
context: C. diff is caused by a VACANCY, not by an arrival. The commonest trigger for the infection is the treatment for a different infection. This is the mechanism that makes the disease so hard to break with more antibiotics.

question: Ben Eiseman, a Denver surgeon, had four patients dying from a colon disease in 1958, the lining of the colon falling away and nothing normal working. He and his team tried one more idea. What did they give the four patients?
answer: Enemas made from a healthy donor's stool
choices: Enemas made from a healthy donor's stool
Massive intravenous doses of penicillin
Radiation aimed at the inflamed section of colon
A blood transfusion from a recovered patient
context: All four recovered rapidly. The paper appeared as 'Fecal enema as an adjunct in the treatment of pseudomembranous enterocolitis' in Surgery, 1958. The idea then sat almost unused for fifty years, not because it failed but because of disgust.

question: Els van Nood and colleagues in Amsterdam ran the trial that finally settled whether donor faeces could beat the best available antibiotic for recurrent C. diff. They compared vancomycin against a single infusion of donor stool threaded through a nasal tube down past the stomach. Where did the tube's tip actually release the donor material?
answer: Into the duodenum, the first bend of the small intestine
choices: Into the duodenum, the first bend of the small intestine
Into the caecum, the pouch where the large intestine begins
Into the ileum, the last stretch before the large intestine
Into the jejunum, the middle third of the small intestine
context: The nasoduodenal infusion put the new community upstream so it could seed the whole gut. About 81 per cent of the infusion patients were cured by a single treatment. The paper appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine on 31 January 2013.

question: A doctor treating recurrent C. diff prescribes Rebyota, the rectally given product the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) licensed in December 2022, the first stool-derived product ever approved as an actual drug in the United States. A second product followed four months later, in April 2023, in a form most patients would find far easier to accept. What form did the second approval take?
answer: An oral capsule of purified bacterial spores
choices: An oral capsule of purified bacterial spores
A chewable tablet of freeze-dried whole stool
An intravenous drip of filtered bacterial extract
A nasal spray of live cultured bacteria
context: The product is called Vowst; the FDA licensed it on 26 April 2023 as the first oral fecal microbiota therapy. The whole journey from repulsive folk cure to prescribable medicine ran through one randomised trial.

question: Els van Nood's team cured about four patients in five of recurrent C. diff with a single treatment, and the success sent researchers rushing to try faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) for obesity, autism, inflammatory bowel disease and depression. Those follow-on results have been far less clear. Beyond mixed results, what does the science still not know about how FMT works?
answer: Which specific microbes in the donor stool are doing the healing
choices: Which specific microbes in the donor stool are doing the healing
Whether the donor's own gut community remains intact afterward
How long the transplanted community continues to protect the recipient
Whether children respond to FMT differently than adults do
context: The purified-spore products like Vowst are partly an attempt to answer this: strip the mixture down to specific spores and see which are enough. Donor screening also genuinely matters, because transmitted organisms have caused serious harm in FMT recipients.

question: A bat coronavirus called RaTG13 is the closest known cousin of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that caused Covid-19. Their genetic codes match by about 96 percent. But one small piece is missing from RaTG13 — a short insert that lets a human enzyme called furin cut the virus's spike protein and help it break into our cells. How long is that inserted piece in SARS-CoV-2?
answer: 12 nucleotides, coding four amino acids
choices: 12 nucleotides, coding four amino acids
24 nucleotides, coding eight amino acids
36 nucleotides, coding twelve amino acids
60 nucleotides, coding twenty amino acids
context: It is the only insertion larger than three nucleotides separating the two genomes. Twelve letters, one small insert, and a huge difference in how the virus behaves in a human airway. Sources: Insertion-and-Deletion Mutations between SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, and RaTG13 (PMC 2022); Frontiers in Virology 2022.

question: The coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2), which caused the COVID-19 pandemic starting in 2019, has on its spike protein a short stretch of amino acids called a furin cleavage site. A human enzyme called furin can snip that site, and the snip helps the virus break into our cells. Several wild coronaviruses carry such a site too, so the presence of one is not by itself proof of tampering. What is the odd thing about the site on SARS-CoV-2?
answer: It is absent from every one of the virus's own nearest wild cousins
choices: It is absent from every one of the virus's own nearest wild cousins
It sits inside a different subunit of the spike than any other coronavirus's does
It uses a run of four arginines rather than the usual two
It is the longest polybasic insert of any known virus
context: The sarbecovirus subgroup contains SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2 and hundreds of bat viruses. Sampling in Yunnan, Laos and elsewhere has turned up more than two hundred sarbecoviruses; RaTG13, the Laotian BANAL-52, BANAL-103 and BANAL-236, and the pangolin coronaviruses all lack the site. Other coronaviruses outside the sarbecovirus group (HKU1, MERS-CoV) do carry S1/S2 cleavage motifs -- the oddity is local absence in the nearest known relatives, not universal presence. Sources: Temmam et al. 2022 (Nature); Chan and Zhan 2022 (Molecular Biology and Evolution).

question: Thomas Peacock and colleagues at Imperial College tested what the twelve-letter insert actually does. They built a version of SARS-CoV-2 with the insert deleted and set up ferrets in adjacent cages, one infected and one clean, and watched. What did the stripped-down virus do?
answer: It shed much less virus and barely reached the clean ferrets in the next cage
choices: It shed much less virus and barely reached the clean ferrets in the next cage
It shed just as much virus but stopped reaching the clean ferrets by air
It reached the clean ferrets normally but no longer produced serious disease
It grew fine in the nose but not deeper in the lung tissue
context: The Peacock 2021 study (Nature Microbiology) showed that the small insert is a large part of what made SARS-CoV-2 spread the way it did. It changes tissue tropism toward the upper airway and boosts airborne shedding without changing receptor binding. Sources: Peacock et al. 2021.

question: The amino acid arginine can be spelled six ways in DNA. In bat viruses and in SARS-CoV-2, one of the six is rare. It shows up only about five percent of the time. Yet right at the furin cut site, both arginines side by side use that rare codon. Which one is it?
answer: CGG
choices: CGG
AGA
CGU
AGG
context: It is the only CGG-CGG doublet anywhere in the SARS-CoV-2 genome. CGG is common in human-codon-optimized laboratory expression constructs and rare in bat coronaviruses. The oddity is suggestive, not proof; natural CGG runs do occur in mammalian viruses. Sources: Sirotkin and Sirotkin 2021 (ACS Med Chem Lett); Dilucca et al. 2020 (Virology Journal).

question: In March 2018, over a year before COVID, a grant plan called Defuse reached the Pentagon's Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). EcoHealth Alliance wrote it with Ralph Baric's lab and the Wuhan Institute of Virology. DARPA said no. The paper leaked in 2021. What did Defuse plan to do?
answer: Add human-adapted cleavage sites to bat coronavirus spikes and test the result in the lab
choices: Add human-adapted cleavage sites to bat coronavirus spikes and test the result in the lab
Vaccinate wild bat colonies across Yunnan to break the sarbecovirus transmission chain
Screen human blood banks across southern China for prior sarbecovirus exposure
Sequence field samples only, with no laboratory work on any live coronavirus at all
context: DARPA rejected the proposal on biosafety grounds, so this specific experiment was PROPOSED, not funded. The document surfaced via a leak in September 2021, three years after submission. DEFUSE also proposed assembling synthetic viruses in six genome segments and screening for spikes adapted to human receptors. Sources: The Intercept September 2021; US Right To Know DEFUSE archive.

question: RaTG13, the bat virus the world now compares SARS-CoV-2 against, did not come from a routine field survey. It came from bat guano that a Wuhan Institute team collected in 2013 inside a mineshaft in Mojiang, Yunnan, where the year before six miners had gone in to clean out the droppings. What happened to those six miners in 2012?
answer: All six developed severe pneumonia and three of them died
choices: All six developed severe pneumonia and three of them died
All six recovered within a week and returned to work
None of the six ever showed symptoms; only their families fell ill
The six were quarantined but never sequenced or reported
context: The illness was documented in a 2013 Chinese Master's thesis that identified a SARS-like coronavirus from horseshoe bats as the likely cause. The full RaTG13 genome sat unpublished for years and was only deposited in GenBank on January 27, 2020, weeks after SARS-CoV-2 was sequenced. Sources: Rahalkar and Bahulikar 2020 (Frontiers in Public Health); Wikipedia RaTG13 entry.

question: Scientists grow the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2), which caused the COVID-19 pandemic, in monkey-kidney cells called Vero E6 for lab work. On the virus's spike sits a twelve-letter insert — the furin cleavage site that helps it enter human cells. Several studies watched what happened to that insert as the virus was passed from one flask of Vero E6 cells to the next, generation after generation. What did they see happen to it?
answer: It is repeatedly LOST through in-frame deletions and point mutations
choices: It is repeatedly LOST through in-frame deletions and point mutations
It is repeatedly LENGTHENED by an extra polybasic stretch each passage
It is faithfully copied at first, then tandemly duplicated by the tenth passage
It migrates from the S1/S2 boundary down into the S2 subunit
context: Davidson et al. 2020 (Genome Medicine) and later work on Calu-3 cells both showed the site disappears when the virus is grown in cells missing the TMPRSS2 protease. That is why no published coronavirus passaging experiment has ever produced a furin site DE NOVO in a virus that lacked one to begin with -- which is the single strongest natural-origin objection to a lab-leak account of the twelve letters. The counter-example is loud, and it is why the anomaly stays unresolved rather than settled either way. Sources: Davidson et al. 2020; Frutos et al. 2023 (Journal of Virology).

question: After the Covid-19 pandemic began, scientists argued for years over where the virus came from — a natural spillover from bats or a laboratory leak. Both sides paid special attention to a twelve-letter insert in the SARS-CoV-2 spike gene, the furin cleavage site that lets the virus break into human cells. Review papers by researchers on both sides of the origin debate — Harrison and Sachs 2022, Frutos and colleagues 2023 — reached the same one-line description of where those twelve letters came from. What do they say?
answer: An unexplained anomaly whose origin no one has yet demonstrated
choices: An unexplained anomaly whose origin no one has yet demonstrated
A recombination remnant from a bat coronavirus already deposited in GenBank
A relic from a much older ancestral coronavirus that the other sarbecoviruses lost
A convergent adaptation that appeared independently in an unsampled wild lineage
context: The insert has no known match in the closest wild relatives, no coronavirus passaging experiment has generated one, and the genome carries no recognisable engineering scars. Serious researchers on both sides now call the origin of these twelve letters an open question. For a real MYSTERY, the honest move is to say so out loud rather than pretend it is closed. Sources: Harrison and Sachs 2022; Frutos et al. 2023 (Journal of Virology); Chan and Zhan 2022.

question: A skinned frog's leg lay on Luigi Galvani's bench in Bologna in 1780, held by a brass hook. A spark machine crackled nearby, in contact with nothing. Then an assistant's steel blade touched the hook. What did Galvani see?
answer: The dead muscle twitched
choices: The dead muscle twitched
A spark leapt to the blade
The hook turned magnetic
The flesh gave off a glow
context: Galvani began systematic experiments on 6 November 1780 and kept at them for more than ten years before publishing anything. He soon found he did not need the machine at all: skinned legs hung from an iron railing by brass hooks kicked the instant hook met rail - no storm, no spark, no apparatus. Hooks of wood, glass or resin gave nothing at all; only conductors moved the dead legs. Source: Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Initial Observations and Experiments; Frog Leg Preparations and Electrical Stimulation); date corroborated Backyard Brains, 'The Galvani/Volta Experiment'.

question: Giovanni Aldini, Galvani's nephew, wired the body of the hanged killer George Forster to a battery before a crowd in London in 1803. He touched the wires to its face. What did the room see?
answer: Its jaw quivered and one eye opened
choices: Its jaw quivered and one eye opened
Its lips moved as if forming a word
Its chest rose in one long breath
Its head turned slowly to one side
context: The Newgate Calendar's own words: 'On the first application of the process to the face, the jaws of the deceased criminal began to quiver, and the adjoining muscles were horribly contorted, and one eye was actually opened. In the subsequent part of the process the right hand was raised and clenched, and the legs and thighs were set in motion.' Forster had drowned his wife Jane and their infant daughter Louisa in the Paddington Canal on 5 December 1802. Aldini's aim was medical, not monstrous - he was arguing that galvanism might revive the drowned and the suffocated, which is why he wanted a hanged man. Source: The Newgate Calendar, 'George Foster'; Grokipedia, George Forster (murderer).

question: Luigi Galvani published in 1791 after ten years of making dead frog legs kick, sure that it was real electricity. Alessandro Volta spent the next ten years fighting Galvani's answer to one question. Where did Galvani say the current was stored?
answer: In the animal's own body
choices: In the animal's own body
In the metals touching it
In the air around the bench
In the warmth of fresh flesh
context: Galvani called it 'animal electricity' and compared the animal to a Leyden jar, the charge-holding apparatus of his day: the nerve as the inner conductor, the muscle as the outer. His own 1791 words: 'a kind of circuit of a delicate nerve fluid is made from the nerves to the muscles when the phenomenon of contractions is produced, similar to the electric circuit which is completed in a Leyden jar.' The treatise was 'De viribus electricitatis in motu musculari commentarius', published through the Bologna Academy of Sciences. Source: Whipple Museum, University of Cambridge, quoting Galvani 1791; Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani.

question: Alessandro Volta pressed a strip of zinc and a strip of silver together and laid them on his own tongue. He wanted a demonstration that needed no frog, no dissection and no instrument, only his own body. What did he report sensing?
answer: A sharp, sour, acid taste
choices: A sharp, sour, acid taste
A sudden sweetness at the tip
A cold numbness spreading back
A prickling, like tiny pins
context: He was not the first to try it. In 1752 Johann Georg Sulzer laid lead and silver foil together on his tongue, felt the same acid tingle - and blamed vibration. Volta read it correctly as a current, one he could feel with his own body and no animal anywhere in the circuit. Two different metals plus something wet is the whole recipe; on the tongue, you are the wet part. Source: Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Volta's Criticisms and Alternative Explanation); Grokipedia, Galvanism (Early Observations - Sulzer 1752).

question: Nicholson and Carlisle built a copy of Alessandro Volta's battery in days, once his letter about it reached London in spring 1800. That May they did something no one had ever done before. What did they do with the current?
answer: They pulled water apart into two gases
choices: They pulled water apart into two gases
They pulled a metal out of a lump of ash
They drove a compass needle right around
They kept a frog's leg twitching for hours
context: Inflammable gas - hydrogen - bubbled off the negative wire, and breathable gas - oxygen - off the positive. Johann Wilhelm Ritter repeated the run, caught both gases and measured them: two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen. An argument about a frog's leg had, within weeks, opened a whole new chemistry. Source: Grokipedia, Electrolysis of water (Early Observations and Fundamental Discoveries).

question: Alessandro Volta read Luigi Galvani's 1791 book, praised it in private and attacked it in public. He did not just argue. He went to the bench and changed one thing in Galvani's setup, and the leg lay still. What had Volta changed?
answer: He had made both contacts the same metal
choices: He had made both contacts the same metal
He had warmed both contacts in his hand
He had shortened the wire between contacts
He had left the leg to rest a full day
context: Volta's answer was that the electricity came from the contact of two different metals, and that the frog was merely 'a sensitive detector, analogous to an electroscope.' He backed it two ways: the twitch died when both contacts on the frog were the same metal, and wet paper or leather worked perfectly well in the tissue's place. One myth worth dropping here - the taunt that rivals mocked Galvani as 'the frog's dancing master' appears nowhere in the record. Historians Marco Piccolino and Nicholas Wade traced it to nineteenth-century writers; the two men stayed personally civil, and it was their followers who got vicious. Source: Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Volta's Criticisms and Alternative Explanation); Grokipedia, Alessandro Volta; Piccolino & Wade, 'The Frog's Dancing Master'.

question: Napoleon set up a new republic in northern Italy in 1797, and it made every professor in Bologna swear a loyalty oath. Luigi Galvani, still defending his frog-leg work against Alessandro Volta, would not swear. What did the republic take from him?
answer: His chair, his salary, his pension and his house
choices: His chair, his salary, his pension and his house
His laboratory, his instruments and his notes
His passport and his freedom to leave Bologna
A year in prison and a fine he could not pay
context: Refusing the oath cost Galvani everything at once. He moved in with his brother Giacomo and died there on 4 December 1798, aged 61, with the quarrel still unsettled - he did not live to see the pile built or the argument resolved. The two men's endings invert the story: Alessandro Volta took a gold medal from Napoleon in Paris in 1801, the Legion of Honour in 1805, and was made a Count in 1810, and in 1881 an international congress named the volt after him. Source: Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Circumstances of Death); Grokipedia, Alessandro Volta (Retirement and Honors).

question: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley worked on the giant nerve fibre of a squid and took the 1963 Nobel Prize for what they found. A nerve cell at rest sits negative inside. When it fires, the inside flips briefly to positive, a swing of roughly a hundred thousandths of a volt. What moves to flip the voltage?
answer: Sodium rushes in, potassium rushes out
choices: Sodium rushes in, potassium rushes out
Calcium rushes in, sodium rushes out
Chloride rushes in, calcium rushes out
Electrons rush in, protons rush out
context: That flip has a name: the action potential. It is not electrons running along a wire - it is charged atoms crossing a membrane. Hodgkin and Huxley made the first intracellular recordings in 1939 and published the full mathematical model in 1952; the squid's nerve fibre was chosen because it is fat enough to push a wire inside. Every nerve in a reader's body is doing exactly this right now. Source: 'The Long Journey from Animal Electricity to the Discovery of Ion Channels', PMC11202063; Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani.

question: Alessandro Volta wrote to Sir Joseph Banks on 20 March 1800, describing a column of alternating zinc and silver discs, every pair parted by cardboard soaked in brine. About forty pairs threw sparks and delivered a shock. He had spent eight years arguing that Luigi Galvani's frogs proved nothing about animals. The words 'pile' and 'battery' came later, from other people. What did Volta himself ask that it be called?
answer: An artificial electric organ
choices: An artificial electric organ
A perpetual contact machine
A self-renewing electrometer
A permanent Leyden apparatus
context: The name was not a whim: Volta had deliberately copied the stacked, layered structure of a living creature's electric organ, and told Banks so - 'I have constructed it, in its form... to the natural electric organ of the torpedo or electric eel... I would wish to give the name of artificial electric organ.' The man who insisted electricity was not animal named his battery after an animal. His paper's title was a straight rebuttal of Galvani: 'On the Electricity Excited by the Mere Contact of Conducting Substances of Different Kinds.' And you can rebuild the thing in a kitchen, because all it ever needed was two different metals and something wet: copper and aluminium discs with raw potato slices between them, five cells for roughly 2 to 2.5 volts. Every lemon battery a kid has ever built is this letter, rebuilt. Source: Volta's 20 March 1800 letter to Banks, quoted in Trends in Neurosciences, 'The artificial electric organ'; Grokipedia, Voltaic pile; Backyard Brains.

question: Luigi Galvani answered Alessandro Volta in 1794 with a preparation that had no metal in it anywhere, though Volta's whole case rested on the metals: brass hook, iron railing, steel blade. Nothing was in the circuit but one frog and a second frog. The muscle contracted all the same, and Galvani published the result without putting his name on it. What had he laid against the muscle?
answer: A second frog's cut nerve
choices: A second frog's cut nerve
A second frog's fresh blood
A second frog's stripped skin
A second frog's bared bone
context: Galvani touched the cut end of one frog's sciatic nerve directly onto another frog's muscle, and the muscle contracted - no brass, no iron, no scalpel, nothing but animal against animal. He published it anonymously in 1794 as 'Dell'uso e dell'attivita dell'arco conduttore nella contrazione dei muscoli' (sources give slightly different wordings of the title). Source: Britannica, Luigi Galvani; Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Galvani's Responses and Further Experiments); PMC11202063.

question: Mary Shelley let Victor Frankenstein discover a 'principle of life' in her novel, then refused to say what the method was. Lightning cracking down a rod, electrodes bolted at the neck, the creature sitting up on the slab: she describes none of it, yet most people carry that version in their heads. Who put it there?
answer: James Whale, filming the novel in 1931
choices: James Whale, filming the novel in 1931
Mary Shelley, revising the novel in 1831
Giovanni Aldini, wiring a corpse in 1803
Percy Shelley, prefacing the novel in 1818
context: Galvanism does touch the book, but never in the story itself. It appears in Shelley's own 1831 introduction, recalling the ghost-story talk at the Villa Diodati in 1816: 'Perhaps a corpse would be re-animated; galvanism had given token of such things.' Even there, no lightning and no electrodes - those are Whale's, from his 1931 film. What is real is the galvanic fever of the age: Aldini had been wiring corpses in London in 1803, thirteen years before that evening at the Villa Diodati. When a scene everybody 'knows' turns out to trace back to a movie, that is worth checking before repeating - including the ones you are sure about. Source: Wikipedia, Frankenstein (animation method left deliberately ambiguous; 1831 introduction quote; electricity attributed to James Whale's 1931 adaptation).

question: Mr Pass, beadle of the Surgeons' Company, stood among the official witnesses in London on 18 January 1803 as Giovanni Aldini sent current through the hanged body of George Forster. The corpse's limbs moved. The Newgate Calendar's report of the day ends with a claim about Mr Pass that has been retold as fact ever since. What does it say happened to him?
answer: He died of fright soon after reaching home
choices: He died of fright soon after reaching home
He fainted and had to be carried out
He fled the room before it was over
He never entered a dissecting room again
context: The Newgate Calendar's full line names him: 'Mr Pass, the beadle of the Surgeons' Company, who was officially present during this experiment, was so alarmed that he died of fright soon after his return home.' Two centuries of retelling rest on that one sentence - no inquest, no second witness, no other account. The same reports cannot even agree on where Aldini worked on the body: the Newgate Calendar says only 'a house not far distant', while most modern retellings place it confidently at the Royal College of Surgeons. If the room itself is in doubt, the frightened beadle deserves the same doubt. Repetition is not evidence - a vivid detail everybody repeats is exactly the kind worth chasing back to its single source. Source: The Newgate Calendar, 'George Foster'; Grokipedia, George Forster (murderer); McGill Office for Science and Society.  (Legend.)

question: Emil du Bois-Reymond dipped his fingers into bowls of salt water wired to his own galvanometer in 1847. He had wound it with twenty-four thousand turns of wire and made electrodes to cancel the metal-contact effect Volta had exposed. The needle swung, the first time anyone had caught a living human's own electricity. What had he just done to make it move?
answer: He tensed the muscles of his own arm
choices: He tensed the muscles of his own arm
He held his breath for a full minute
He pricked his fingertip with a pin
He stared hard into a bright lamp
context: He contracted his own arm and the needle answered. He put it in the largest terms he could find, claiming he had realised 'the hundred-year-old dream of the physicist and physiologist: the identity of the nervous principle with electricity.' He had already detected the action current in frog muscle in 1843, and in 1848 he published two volumes of measurements, 'Untersuchungen ueber thierische Elektricitaet'. Those measurements settled the old dispute in the most awkward way possible - both men were right, each about a different thing. Volta had explained the frog-leg experiment correctly: the two metals really were making that current. And Galvani was right about the bigger thing: animals really do generate electricity of their own, as your own arm is doing now. Source: Grokipedia, Emil du Bois-Reymond (Foundations of Experimental Electrophysiology; Instrumentation Innovations and Methodological Advances); Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Long-Term Resolution in Favor of Galvani's Core Insight).

question: A student reads the popular name of the Right to Try Act of 2018 and finds no lawmaker in it. The Act opened experimental drugs to patients before full US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval, and it carries four other names: Trickett Wendler, Frank Mongiello, Matthew Bellina and Jordan McLinn. Who were those four?
answer: Patients or family of patients with terminal illnesses
choices: Patients or family of patients with terminal illnesses
Retired FDA commissioners who backed the bill
Physicians who first prescribed under state laws
Attorneys who wrote the model legislation
context: Three had ALS (Wendler, Mongiello, Bellina); Jordan McLinn was a boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy who lobbied Congress in person. Naming a federal statute after its patients rather than its sponsors was the whole point. Public Law 115-176. Source: congress.gov/115/plaws/publ176.

question: A campaigner ticks Alaska off her list, the forty-first state to pass a near-copy of the Right to Try bill. She has spent four years going state by state, and Congress has not yet acted. The bill would let dying patients try new drugs before full federal approval. Why start with the states?
answer: To build political pressure for the federal law
choices: To build political pressure for the federal law
Because state laws override federal drug rules
Because the FDA can only regulate one state at a time
Because the states run their own drug trials
context: Alaska became the 41st state to enact a Right to Try law before the federal Act. It is a case where the states moved first and Washington caught up rather than led. Source: goldwaterinstitute.org releases; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-to-try_law.

question: A woman with a fatal illness asks her doctor for a test drug under the Right to Try Act, before the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has finished approving it. The law opens the door only to certain test drugs: they must have passed one step in FDA testing, but not the whole process. Which step must the drug have passed?
answer: Phase I safety testing
choices: Phase I safety testing
Preclinical animal testing
Phase III efficacy trials
Post-marketing surveillance
context: The premise is narrow: a dying patient with no clinical trial option should be able to try a drug already shown reasonably safe in humans, without waiting for the full efficacy proof most patients never had time for. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-to-try_law.

question: A dying man with the Right to Try Act of 2018 behind him asks for an experimental drug the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not yet fully approved, and walks away empty-handed. A common gripe is that the law just clears the government's door and does not force anyone to hand over the drug. Three groups in the medical chain can still say no, and often do. Which three?
answer: The drug company, the insurer, and the prescribing doctor
choices: The drug company, the insurer, and the prescribing doctor
The FDA commissioner, the state medical board, and the hospital
The patient's employer, the pharmacy benefit manager, and Medicare
The clinical trial sponsor, the review board, and the patent holder
context: Right to Try is a permission, not a mandate: the manufacturer need not supply, the insurer need not pay, the doctor need not prescribe. Supporters answer that a permission is exactly what a dying patient needs, and that the FDA's older 'expanded access' pathway required the agency's leave rather than the patient's. Source: hklaw.com, 'Right to Try Law Enacted by Congress'.

question: Activists lay down at the headquarters of a federal agency on October 11, 1988, about 1,500 of them, for a nine-hour die-in. During the Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) crisis, life-saving test drugs had sat unused for years while that agency finished its testing. Which agency was it?
answer: The FDA
choices: The FDA
The CDC
The NIH
The Department of Defense
context: The Rockville, Maryland demonstration was ACT UP's first national action; 176 people were arrested. The point was blunt: patients wanted drugs already in trials and the wait was killing them. Source: washingtonpost.com, '1,000 Swarm FDA's Rockville Office'.

question: Frances Kelsey, a pharmacologist at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), kept sending back one drug's application in the early 1960s because the safety evidence was thin. Her stubbornness kept that drug, thalidomide, out of American pharmacies. It is the Right-to-Try debate's famous case of caution genuinely saving lives. What terrible effect did thalidomide later prove to cause?
answer: Severe birth defects in babies born to mothers who took it
choices: Severe birth defects in babies born to mothers who took it
Sudden heart attacks in older men
Blindness in young adults
Kidney failure in the elderly
context: Thalidomide disfigured at least 4,000 children in Europe (phocomelia); Kelsey's stubborn demand for evidence spared American children from that toll. Her demand was not 'ban it' -- it was 'show me the data'. That is the very rigor Right to Try's advocates say is missing on the other side of the ledger. The other scientists in the choices (McClintock, Franklin, Daly) are real contemporaries in different fields. Source: fda.gov, 'Frances Oldham Kelsey: Medical Reviewer'.

question: Elisabeth Bik, a Dutch microbiologist, began reading biology papers at night in 2013 with a sharp eye for doctored images. She has since flagged thousands of suspicious papers to journal editors and become one of science's best-known image detectives. What set her hunt off in the very first place?
answer: She discovered one of her own papers had been plagiarised
choices: She discovered one of her own papers had been plagiarised
A journal editor asked her to review a batch of images
She won a grant to build software for spotting fraud
A colleague was fired and asked her to clear his name
context: Bik went looking for other cases like her own and quickly discovered a much larger pattern. She left a full-time science job at Stanford to work on integrity full-time. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Bik

question: Elisabeth Bik and two co-authors had published a count in the journal mBio by 2016: 20,621 biology papers, every one checked by hand for doctored figures. About how many of those 20,621 papers had bad copied images?
answer: About one in twenty-five
choices: About one in twenty-five
About one in two hundred
About one in a thousand
About one in ten thousand
context: That number - 4 percent of the biomedical literature - shocked editors who had assumed peer review was catching this sort of thing. The paper had to be posted as a preprint on bioRxiv first; several journals were reluctant to touch it. Source: retractionwatch.com/2016/04/19/one-in-25-papers-contains-inappropriately-duplicated-images-screen-finds

question: Elisabeth Bik laid biology images side by side, looking for reused patches. A picture of a western blot, a lab test that shows dark protein bands on a gel, or of cells under a microscope carries something that a plain table of numbers never has. That extra thing is exactly what she hunts for. What is it?
answer: A unique random speckle pattern - a kind of visual fingerprint
choices: A unique random speckle pattern - a kind of visual fingerprint
A digital timestamp burned into every pixel by the camera
A machine-generated barcode in the lower right corner
A recorded audio note from the technician who took it
context: Rotate that pattern, mirror it, stretch it, drop it into another figure - the speckles still line up. Fabrication that would be invisible in a spreadsheet is visible in a picture, to a patient eye reading printed pages. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/2102.01874

question: A biologist types a published paper's DOI (Digital Object Identifier) reference code into a website and posts a comment on it. That site started in 2012 and lets anyone comment on any paper. A second site, launched in 2010, is a blog that tracks papers pulled back after publication. Between them the two do much of the checking after papers are already out. Which pair are they?
answer: PubPeer and Retraction Watch
choices: PubPeer and Retraction Watch
PubMed Commons and F1000Research
Publons and Faculty Opinions
For Better Science and Neuroskeptic
context: PubMed Commons and F1000Research both hosted post-publication commentary; Publons tracked peer reviews and Faculty Opinions (formerly F1000Prime) ran expert recommendations; For Better Science and Neuroskeptic are individual watchdog blogs. Neither PubPeer nor Retraction Watch is a journal, a university, or a government - both are largely volunteer. Source: retractionwatch.com/2015/08/31/pubpeer-founders-reveal-themselves-create-foundation

question: Matthew Schrag, a Vanderbilt neuroscientist, was hired in 2021 to look into a struggling Alzheimer's drug, and his investigation led him to a much bigger target: a landmark 2006 Nature paper by Sylvain Lesne, cited about 2,300 times. What did that famous paper claim?
answer: That a specific amyloid oligomer, Ab*56, directly caused memory loss in mice
choices: That a specific amyloid oligomer, Ab*56, directly caused memory loss in mice
That vitamin B12 injections halted memory decline in early Alzheimer's
That gut bacteria seeded protein plaques inside the brain
That sleep alone cleared the brain of Alzheimer's-related waste
context: Ab*56 became one of the most cited candidate molecules in Alzheimer's research. Investigative journalist Charles Piller laid out Schrag's evidence of image splicing and duplication in Science on 21 July 2022; Nature retracted the paper in June 2024. Source: science.org/content/article/researchers-plan-retract-landmark-alzheimers-paper-containing-doctored-images

question: Haruko Obokata, a young Japanese biologist, published papers in January 2014 claiming a simple acid bath could turn ordinary body cells back into stem cells that grow into anything. If real, it would have revolutionized medicine. Those papers were retracted only six months later, on 2 July 2014, with two independent checks converging on the same verdict at the same time. What were the two checks?
answer: Labs worldwide could not reproduce it, and readers on PubPeer found reused images
choices: Labs worldwide could not reproduce it, and readers on PubPeer found reused images
A rival RIKEN team replicated it once, and an internal audit cleared the figures
A senior collaborator confessed at a press conference, and Nature ran its own peer-review inquiry
A whistleblower emailed the journal, and a mass-spectrometry team spotted contamination
context: Failed replication and duplicated images pointing at the same answer from two different directions. Genetic testing later showed the 'STAP cells' were ordinary embryonic stem cells. Source: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519803

question: A horse threw Chuck Yeager, a US Air Force test pilot, two nights before his October 1947 try at the sound barrier in the rocket plane Bell X-1. He did not tell the Air Force, because it would have grounded him. A town doctor taped him up in secret. What had the fall done?
answer: It broke two ribs under his right arm.
choices: It broke two ribs under his right arm.
It cracked his right collarbone in two.
It tore a ligament in his right knee.
It broke two bones in his right wrist.
context: A civilian doctor in Rosamond taped the ribs; the flight surgeon was never told, because reporting them would have cost Yeager the flight. Two days later he flew the Bell X-1 past the speed of sound with them still taped. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Yeager

question: Chuck Yeager's Bell X-1 could not climb to its test height by itself on 14 October 1947: its rocket burned all its fuel in a few minutes, too little for the long climb from the ground. How did the X-1 get up there?
answer: A B-29 bomber carried it up in its bomb bay.
choices: A B-29 bomber carried it up in its bomb bay.
A C-54 transport towed it up on a cable.
A pair of jets in its wing roots lifted it off.
A booster rocket lifted it, then fell away.
context: The B-29 carried the X-1 in its bomb bay and dropped it at 20,000 feet; Yeager lit the rocket and climbed away, reaching Mach 1.06 at about 43,000 feet. Good sources differ slightly on the exact figures — the Smithsonian gives 42,000 feet, Wikipedia 45,000 feet at Mach 1.05 — which is itself worth noticing. He had painted the name Glamorous Glennis on the orange fuselage, after his wife. Source: airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/breaking-sound-barrier; grokipedia.com/page/Bell_X-1

question: Chuck Yeager lowered himself into the X-1's cockpit injured and hiding it. Sealing the rocket plane's side hatch meant bracing the hatch in place and driving a heavy locking lever home with his right arm, and his injury made that impossible. He told nobody but the project engineer, Jack Ridley. What did Ridley bring him?
answer: A sawn-off length of broom handle
choices: A sawn-off length of broom handle
A leather strap from a parachute harness
A long wrench from the ground crew
A padded brace to wear over the ribs
context: Ridley quietly sawed the handle off a broom in the hangar. Yeager slipped it through the hatch fitting and used it as a lever to force the lock home, sealing himself in — and the flight surgeon was never told. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ridley_(pilot)

question: Bell's engineers shaped the X-1 in 1947 with no flight data to work from, because nobody had ever flown faster than sound. But people had been sending things past the speed of sound for two hundred years, and those things were known to fly steadily while doing it. So the engineers copied one. What did they model the X-1's fuselage on?
answer: A Browning .50-caliber machine gun round
choices: A Browning .50-caliber machine gun round
A Hispano 20 mm aircraft cannon shell
A Lee-Enfield .303-caliber rifle bullet
A Bofors 40 mm anti-aircraft gun shell
context: Bell's designers called it 'a bullet with wings.' Nobody had flown supersonic, but people had been shooting supersonic for two centuries, so the engineers copied the one supersonic shape they trusted. The wings were made extremely thin, and a four-chamber Reaction Motors XLR-11 rocket gave 6,000 pounds of thrust. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_X-1

question: W. F. Hilton, a British scientist, showed a reporter his fast-flight work in 1935. The reporter cut one sentence down to two words that are still in use: 'the sound barrier.' What did Hilton mean by a barrier?
answer: The steep climb of a wing's resistance near the speed of sound
choices: The steep climb of a wing's resistance near the speed of sound
A wall of packed air standing in the sky at the speed of sound
A gap in his data that the wind tunnel could not reach into
A ceiling on engine power that no known fuel could beat
context: Hilton's actual sentence was: 'See how the resistance of a wing shoots up like a barrier against higher speed, as we approach the speed of sound.' He was pointing at a curve on a graph. The papers printed 'sound barrier,' and the public heard a wall hanging in the sky. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_barrier

question: A Spitfire pilot diving fast late in World War 2 pushed the stick sideways to roll out of the dive, and the plane did something strange. The 'barrier' name was wrong, but the danger was real: their own planes were killing pilots. What did the plane do instead?
answer: It rolled the opposite way, because the wings themselves twisted.
choices: It rolled the opposite way, because the wings themselves twisted.
It pitched nose-down hard, because the tail lost its lift.
It yawed sideways, because the rudder stalled in thin air.
It shook itself apart, because the wing skin tore away.
context: Engineers call it control reversal. The Spitfire's wings were torsionally soft, so at high speed deflecting an aileron twisted the whole wing the opposite way — and the wing won. Other fighters had other transonic killers: the P-38 Lightning suffered Mach tuck above about Mach 0.65, the nose pitching down while the elevator lost its grip, and it killed test pilot Ralph Virden in 1941. Thirteen months before Yeager's flight, on 27 September 1946, Geoffrey de Havilland Jr was killed when his DH 108 broke up at roughly Mach 0.9. The wall was imaginary; the danger was not. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_barrier; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mach_tuck

question: A boy stands 120 miles from the coast, directly under a fighter's flight path. The jet crosses the coast at 30,000 feet, pushes past Mach 1 as it does, holds Mach 1.5 for ten minutes and slows back below the speed of sound far inland. The boy hears a sharp crack. Where was the jet when it made the sound that reached him?
answer: Almost overhead, just short of the boy
choices: Almost overhead, just short of the boy
Back at the coast, where it went supersonic
Deep inland, at the end of the fast run
Halfway between the coast and the boy
context: The boom is not a doorway punched once. The shock cone trails behind the aircraft for the entire time it stays supersonic, dragging a 'boom carpet' along the ground; people each hear their own boom as the cone sweeps over them, far from wherever Mach 1 was crossed. The carpet runs about one mile wide for every 1,000 feet of altitude — roughly thirty miles across from 30,000 feet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_boom

question: A resident of Oklahoma City hears one more boom crack over the roofs in 1964 and fills in a claim form. Military jets are booming the city about eight times a day, 1,253 booms in six months, because the US government wants to know if Americans will put up with supersonic jets flying over. Residents file 9,594 damage complaints and 4,629 formal claims. How many claims does the government pay?
answer: 229 of them, for about $13,000 in all
choices: 229 of them, for about $13,000 in all
1,180 of them, for about $70,000 in all
2,400 of them, for about $300,000 in all
3,900 of them, for about $900,000 in all
context: Operation Bongo II ran from 3 February to 30 July 1964, flown by F-104s and B-58 Hustlers, with the overpressure deliberately stepped up partway through. 229 of 4,629 claims were paid, $12,845.32 in total — a 94% rejection rate. About a quarter of residents surveyed said they simply could not accept the booms. They brought a class action, and the government lost on appeal on 8 March 1969. In 1973 the FAA banned civil supersonic flight over US land, and that rule still stands — a rule about annoyance rather than damage: controlled studies found single booms below about 16 pounds per square foot did no significant harm to well-maintained buildings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_sonic_boom_tests; grokipedia.com/page/Sonic_boom

question: Ernst Mach and the photographer Peter Salcher photographed the cone of piled-up air trailing from a rifle bullet in mid-flight in 1887, sixty years before any aircraft could approach the speed of sound. The bullet crossed the picture in well under a thousandth of a second. How did they stop it dead on the plate?
answer: They lit it with an electric spark too brief to blur
choices: They lit it with an electric spark too brief to blur
They geared the shutter to a slotted disc spun fast
They left the plate open and let the bullet draw itself
They tripped a row of cameras with wires as it flew
context: Working at Charles-Ferdinand University in Prague, Mach and Salcher fired a bullet from a Werndl carbine and used a spark both to make the light and to freeze the motion. Their paper deduced and then experimentally confirmed a shock wave of conical shape with the projectile at its apex — the same cone a supersonic jet drags today. Mach did not name the Mach number: the Swiss aeronautical engineer Jakob Ackeret proposed naming the speed ratio after him in 1929, more than four decades later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Mach; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mach_number

question: Chuck Yeager pulled and pushed the stick on the X-1's eighth powered flight, and the aeroplane ignored him. At Mach 0.94, a hair under the speed of sound, the pitch control had simply died, and no amount of extra rocket thrust would have given it back. The project engineer, Jack Ridley, worked out an answer that almost every supersonic fighter since has carried. What did Ridley change?
answer: He made the entire horizontal tail pivot as one piece
choices: He made the entire horizontal tail pivot as one piece
He swept the wings sharply back to delay the trouble
He thinned the tail surfaces to slice the fast air
He moved the tail back and up, clear of the wing's wake
context: A shock wave was standing on the tailplane's hinge line, so deflecting the elevator behind it did nothing at all — worse, on a conventional tail the rearward-moving shock pushes the elevator down and steals the pilot's authority. Ridley's answer was to stop using the elevator for pitch and pivot the whole horizontal stabiliser: the all-moving tail, or stabilator. The crew flew it two flights later. Stabilators are now almost universal on military combat aircraft — 1947 engineering a kid can point at on any fighter overhead. Swept wings were a serious rival line of work at the time; the X-1 deliberately went without them because too little was yet known about them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ridley_(pilot); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stabilator

question: A farmer stands under Concorde's route and hears not one bang but two, about three tenths of a second apart, and then nothing. A pressure gauge on the ground draws the shape of the event: pressure jumps suddenly, falls smoothly to below normal, then jumps suddenly back. Each jump is a shock wave arriving. Where do the two jumps come from?
answer: One shock from the nose and one from the tail
choices: One shock from the nose and one from the tail
One shock from each wing, a moment apart
One shock from the nose and its echo off the ground
One shock from the engines and one from the nose
context: Engineers call the trace an N-wave, after the letter it draws: a jump at the nose, a smooth fall through the body to below-ambient pressure, a jump back at the tail. The positive and negative halves integrate to zero net impulse. A cruising supersonic aircraft lays down roughly 0.5 to 2 pounds per square foot on the ground, heard at about 105 to 120 decibels. NASA's X-59, unveiled on 12 January 2024, carries a needle nose more than 38 feet long precisely so its shocks never merge into a single N-wave — the aim is a 'sonic thump' rather than a boom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_boom; grokipedia.com/page/Sonic_boom

question: A student lays a protractor on one of Ernst Mach's spark photographs and reads the sharp angle at which the cone of piled-up air closes at a flying bullet's nose. A supersonic jet drags the same cone today. As an object flies faster and faster beyond Mach 1, what does that angle do?
answer: It narrows and sweeps further back
choices: It narrows and sweeps further back
It widens toward a nearly flat plane
It holds one angle at any speed
It narrows, then opens out again
context: The rule is sin(half-angle) = the speed of sound divided by the object's speed, which is 1 divided by the Mach number. At Mach 3 that gives about 19 degrees; just above Mach 1 the angle opens toward 90 degrees, and the shock is 'hardly a cone at all, but closer to a slightly concave plane.' Measure the angle on a photograph and you have measured the speed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_boom; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mach_number

question: Goriely and McMillen, two mathematicians, worked out the physics of a bullwhip's crack in 2002. The crack is a real sonic boom, a scrap of leather beating the speed of sound in a back garden. The tip ends up more than thirty times faster than the handle, though the arm makes just one slow swing. Where does the extra speed come from?
answer: A loop speeding up as it runs into the whip's thin end
choices: A loop speeding up as it runs into the whip's thin end
The leather stretching and snapping back like a bowstring
The plaited strands unwinding and whirling the tip around
The wrist adding a second, faster flick mid-stroke
context: Because a whip tapers, a travelling loop must speed up as it runs toward the thin end — the same energy carried by less and less leather. Goriely and McMillen found the tip can reach more than thirty times the handle's starting speed, and it is moving at roughly twice the speed of sound by the moment the loop goes supersonic. Scientific American reported the result as the crack coming from a loop travelling along the whip, gaining speed until it reaches the speed of sound. Humans were sending things past Mach 1 long before aircraft — in 1740 the British mathematician Benjamin Robins used a ballistic pendulum to measure musket balls travelling above Mach 1.5. Source: Goriely & McMillen, 'Shape of a Cracking Whip,' Physical Review Letters 88, 244301 (2002); Scientific American, 'True Cause of Whip's Crack Uncovered,' 28 May 2002

question: William Stanley, an engineer, wired up the small town of Great Barrington, Massachusetts, in 1886. He used a new invention that direct current could not use. What piece of gear made his demo work?
answer: A transformer that stepped voltage up for the wires and back down for the lamps.
choices: A transformer that stepped voltage up for the wires and back down for the lamps.
A vacuum tube that amplified the current at each customer's meter.
A rotary switch that briefly cut power to every home in turn.
A carbon-arc regulator that held every lamp at the same brightness.
context: Stanley's Great Barrington demonstration proved AC distribution in a real town two years before Tesla's motor patent even issued. The transformer -- an iron ring with two coils, right out of Faraday -- was the piece of hardware DC had no answer for. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_currents .

question: An engineer plans to send the same amount of power a hundred miles down a modest copper wire without much energy lost as heat. She has to watch the current inside the wire, because the physical relationship between current and heating loss is unforgiving. What does she want at the sending end?
answer: The voltage pushed as high as possible, so the current in the wire is small.
choices: The voltage pushed as high as possible, so the current in the wire is small.
The current pushed as high as possible, so the voltage in the wire is small.
The voltage matched exactly to the resistance of the wire between the stations.
The voltage kept low enough that no insulation is needed on the poles.
context: Power equals voltage times current, so for a fixed power a higher voltage means a smaller current -- and because heating loss in the wire goes as current SQUARED times resistance (I-squared-R), collapsing the current collapses the loss. A transformer takes AC from a modest generator voltage up to hundreds of thousands of volts for transmission and steps it back down at your neighbourhood -- the reason your street wire is AC. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_power_transmission .

question: Nikola Tesla filed US patent 381,968, granted in May 1888, for a new kind of electric motor. He fed several out-of-step alternating currents into separate coils arranged in a ring around a spinning iron rotor. What did those coils create between them that dragged the rotor around?
answer: A magnetic field that itself walked around the inside of the stator.
choices: A magnetic field that itself walked around the inside of the stator.
A pair of carbon brushes arcing continuously on a spinning commutator.
A ring of liquid mercury completing the circuit as the rotor turned.
A spring-loaded centrifugal governor holding the shaft at fixed speed.
context: This is the rotating-field induction motor. Because nothing physical has to slide against the rotor, there is nothing to wear out -- no brushes and no sparking whatsoever. Westinghouse licensed the patents from Tesla in July 1888, giving AC the one thing DC still had over it. Source: patents.google.com/patent/US381968A .

question: George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla underbid Edison's camp in 1893 for the contract to light a single event, and the war of the currents ended there, with a bid, not a duel or a court verdict. Their alternating current lit a sea of electric lamps across its grounds. What was the event?
answer: The World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
choices: The World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
The dedication of the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbour.
The Paris Exposition Universelle at the base of the new Eiffel Tower.
The inauguration of the transcontinental railroad at Promontory Summit.
context: On opening day, 1 May 1893, President Grover Cleveland pressed a golden telegraph key that set the fair's machinery running. About twenty-seven million people saw the White City glow on AC power over the six months of the fair. That contract, and the spectacle, won Westinghouse the Niagara Falls hydroelectric commission, which in November 1896 began sending power about twenty miles to Buffalo. Sources: teslauniverse.com 1893 tesla lights worlds fair ; worldsfairchicago1893.com/2018/05/01/opening_day_10/

question: Richard Harlan, an American naturalist, studied a huge fossil bone in 1834: one vertebra, a single bone from a backbone, dug up in Louisiana. From that one bone he named the creature Basilosaurus, or 'king lizard.' What kind of animal was it?
answer: A whale
choices: A whale
A sea cow
A giant seal
A sea turtle
context: Harlan compared the vertebra to the fossil sea reptiles Plesiosaurus and Mosasaurus, took the animal for a giant marine reptile, and wrote that it 'could not have been less than from eighty to one hundred feet' long. He had a whale. Under the rules of zoological naming the earliest published name has priority, so the largest whale of its age is stuck being called 'king lizard' forever. Basilosaurus cetoides is today the official state fossil of both Alabama and Mississippi, and Alabama law forbids carrying one out of the state without the governor's written permission. — Wikipedia, 'Basilosaurus'; Encyclopedia of Alabama, 'Basilosaurus cetoides'.

question: Philip Gingerich and Donald Russell dug up a fossil skull in rocks about fifty million years old in northern Pakistan, and named the animal Pakicetus. It is the earliest animal that scientists count as a whale, and its size is the first surprise. How big was it?
answer: About the size of a wolf
choices: About the size of a wolf
About the size of a horse
About the size of a bison
About the size of a rat
context: Pakicetus attocki was one to two metres long. Its sister species Ichthyolestes pinfoldi was smaller still: Hans Thewissen's 2001 Nature paper describes them as 'the fox-sized Ichthyolestes pinfoldi, and the wolf-sized Pakicetus attocki'. The earliest whales were not whale-sized, and telling them apart from any other small mammal of the period took real evidence rather than a glance. — Thewissen, Williams, Roe & Hussain, Nature 413:277-281 (2001); Wikipedia, 'Pakicetus'.

question: Richard Owen, Britain's leading anatomist, used a fossil skeleton on his bench, with no skin and no soft parts, to overturn a ruling that Basilosaurus was a giant sea reptile. He pointed to one feature and wrote that it was 'unknown in fishes and reptiles'. What was it?
answer: Molars carried on two roots each
choices: Molars carried on two roots each
Ribs curving in one unbroken arc
Neck bones locked into a single block
Finger bones sealed inside a flipper
context: Reptile teeth are simple single-rooted pegs, shed and replaced over and over through life; mammal cheek teeth are complex and anchored on more than one root. Owen proposed renaming the animal Zeuglodon cetoides — 'yoke tooth, whale-like' — and lost. Under the rules of zoological nomenclature Harlan's earlier name has priority, so the correct anatomy won and the correct name did not. — Wikipedia, 'Basilosaurus'; Encyclopedia of Alabama, 'Basilosaurus cetoides'.

question: Albert Koch, a showman, charged New Yorkers twenty-five cents in July 1845 to view a 114-foot 'sea serpent' he called Hydrarchos. The anatomist Jeffries Wyman needed one visit to call it a fraud. Koch sold it to the King of Prussia anyway. What was the monster actually made of?
answer: Bones from several Basilosaurus skeletons, padded with fossil shells
choices: Bones from several Basilosaurus skeletons, padded with fossil shells
Bones from one Basilosaurus skeleton, stretched with plaster spacers
Bones from three mosasaur skeletons, topped with a wooden skull
Bones from a mastodon skeleton, fitted with carved wooden ribs
context: Koch had assembled at least five or six different Basilosaurus individuals and padded the run of vertebrae out with ammonite shells to reach 114 feet. Wyman saw two things at once: the animal was a mammal, not a serpent, and the bones came from animals of different ages and sizes. Careful anatomy beat showmanship in a single visit — and the fake is why 'sea serpent' sat in the public mind as a live identification for these bones at all. — National Geographic, 'The Phrenology of a Monster'; Wikipedia, 'Basilosaurus'.

question: Philip Gingerich rested the whole claim on one feature when he and Donald Russell described a fifty-million-year-old skull from rock west of Islamabad in 1981, named it Pakicetus and declared it the oldest whale known. Nothing about the skull's outward shape looked remotely whale-like. That feature is still the founding mark of the whale group. What was it?
answer: A dense thickened lip of bone wrapped round the ear capsule
choices: A dense thickened lip of bone wrapped round the ear capsule
A bony plate that sealed the nostrils shut underwater
An oil-filled chamber hollowed out inside the snout
A ring of bone bracing the eye socket against pressure
context: The feature is the involucrum: a dense, thickened inner lip on the bony capsule that houses the ear, sitting on an auditory bulla formed from the ectotympanic bone alone. It isolates vibration so that sound can be located underwater, where an ordinary land ear is useless. When Gingerich and Russell described Pakicetus in 1981, the involucrum was found in whales and in nothing else then known, living or fossil — which is why one bump of bone could settle an argument the rest of the skeleton could not. — Wikipedia, 'Pakicetus'; National Geographic, 'Science Word of the Day: Involucrum'.

question: Hans Thewissen read the hunting style of Ambulocetus natans off its skull alone, though no one has ever watched one hunt. The animal came out of the Kala Chitta Hills of Punjab, Pakistan, in 1992: three metres of early whale, a quarter of a tonne. Which feature of the skull did he read?
answer: Its eyes sat high on the skull, aimed upward
choices: Its eyes sat high on the skull, aimed upward
Its jaw hinge slid forward, giving a huge gape
Its snout flattened out into a broad shovel
Its cheekbones flared into heavy bony shields
context: Large eyes set near the top of the head and looking upward are the eyes of an ambush predator lying just under the surface, watching the world above the waterline — the same arrangement a crocodile uses. Thewissen read Ambulocetus as a hunter that seized prey at the water's edge and held on while it struggled. The name Ambulocetus natans means 'the walking, swimming whale': the animal still carried four working legs, and its hind feet were enormous, probably longer than its twenty-nine-centimetre thigh bone, one toe alone running seventeen centimetres; feet that size suggest it swam like a river otter, with alternating beats of the back legs rather than a tail stroke. Holotype H-GSP 18507, described in 1994 by Hans Thewissen, Sayed Taseer Hussain and Mohammad Arif; about 48 to 47 million years old. — Wikipedia, 'Ambulocetus'; Grokipedia, 'Ambulocetus'.

question: Nikaido, Rooney and Okada, three biologists, came at the whale family tree a new way in 1999, after fossil hunters had spent decades arguing over it from bones alone. They used jumping genes, bits of DNA that slip into a genome, almost never come back out, and mark shared ancestry like a stamp that cannot be faked. Which living animals did their result put closest to whales?
answer: Hippos
choices: Hippos
Seals
Manatees
Otters
context: The method reads SINE and LINE insertions: mobile elements that land at a particular site in a genome and are, in practice, never removed. Two species carrying the same insertion at the same site is very hard to explain except by shared ancestry, which is why the technique is so hard to argue with. Seals, manatees and otters all went back to the water too, but each on its own separate line; the animal the insertions pointed to was the hippopotamus. That confirmed a case Graur and Higgins had already made from other molecular data in 1994 — that whales do not sit beside the even-toed hoofed mammals, the group of deer, pigs, camels and cattle, but INSIDE it. The fossil specialists had a different candidate entirely, and did not believe a word of it. — Nikaido, Rooney & Okada, PNAS 96:10261-10266 (1999); Graur & Higgins, Molecular Biology and Evolution 11:357-364 (1994).

question: Hans Thewissen's team dug up the rest of the Pakicetus skeleton in 2001.
