For twenty years the oldest animal that scientists count as a whale had been known from its skull alone, and the restoration drawn from that skull put it on the cover of Science: a sleek, crocodile-shaped hunter half-submerged in a river, chasing fish. What did the bones show?
answer: A long-legged land runner with four full working legs
choices: A long-legged land runner with four full working legs
A seal-shaped swimmer with paddle-like hind limbs
A squat river wader with broadly webbed feet
A heavy-bodied digger with spade-like front claws
context: Thewissen and colleagues wrote that the pakicetids were land mammals, 'no more amphibious than a tapir.' The first reconstruction had been an honest guess from a skull alone, and the guess was wrong — printed on a journal cover, then corrected by the same field that printed it. The bones did carry one aquatic signal, but not the one anyone had drawn: the limb bones are osteosclerotic, abnormally dense. Dense bone is ballast. It lets an animal sink and walk along a riverbed instead of bobbing on the surface, and heavy bones, not flippers, are the first aquatic signal in the whole sequence. — Thewissen, Williams, Roe & Hussain, Nature 413:277-281 (2001); Wikipedia, 'Pakicetus'.

question: Philip Gingerich, Holly Smith and Elwyn Simons reported a Basilosaurus fossil from the Egyptian desert in 1990: sixteen metres of animal, with its hind limbs still in place, joined together. Each hind limb was just thirty-five centimetres long. What did that little leg actually contain?
answer: A knee, an ankle of fused bones, and three toes
choices: A knee, an ankle of fused bones, and three toes
A thigh bone, a knee, and a shin fused into one rod
A hip socket, a thigh bone, and three flat paddle bones
A knee, a shin, and a single splint of a toe
context: A complete leg in miniature — knee joint, tarsal bones fused in the ankle, three digits — hanging off an animal sixteen metres long. The specimen came from Wadi al-Hitan in Egypt, 'the Valley of the Whales', about 150 km southwest of Cairo: roughly 1,500 marine vertebrate skeletons in rock 40 to 41 million years old, including hundreds of Basilosaurus isis and over 500 of the smaller whale Dorudon atrox. UNESCO listed it in 2005. Its fossils were the first archaeocetes ever found with hind legs, feet and toes at all. — Gingerich, Smith & Simons, Science 249:154-157 (1990); Wikipedia, 'Wadi El Hitan'.

question: Dr Friedlinde Obergfell handed Hans Thewissen the rocks that her late husband, the Indian geologist A. Ranga Rao, had collected in Kashmir. The Indohyus fossils inside had spent decades in storage. In Thewissen's laboratory they finally gave up the feature that makes this small deer-like plant-eater the closest known relative of whales. How did that feature come to light?
answer: A technician accidentally broke one of the skulls open
choices: A technician accidentally broke one of the skulls open
A CT scanner imaged the skulls inside their rock
An acid bath dissolved the rock away from the skulls
A student matched the skulls to an old monograph
context: The break laid the middle ear bare, and there was the dense thickened bony margin that had been the founding mark of whales alone. Thewissen and colleagues published Indohyus in Nature in 2007, establishing the Eocene raoellids of south Asia as the sister group of whales. Indohyus resembles whales, and no other even-toed hoofed mammal, in four things at once: ear structure, premolar shape, limb-bone density, and the oxygen-isotope signature locked into its teeth — a chemical record saying it spent much of its life in water. Its limb bones were thickened as ballast so it could sink and walk on a riverbed rather than swim. A slip of the hand found the whales' closest relative. — Thewissen, Cooper, Clementz, Bajpai & Tiwari, Nature 450:1190-1194 (2007); Wikipedia, 'Indohyus'.

question: Two teams published early whale ankle bones from Pakistan in the same month of 2001: Hans Thewissen's in Nature and Philip Gingerich's in Science. Molecular biologists reading DNA had placed whales inside the even-toed hoofed mammals; fossil specialists, following Leigh Van Valen, backed the mesonychians, extinct hoofed carnivores with odd triangular teeth. Both sets of bones carried the same astragalus, the bone that takes the body's weight at the top of the foot, and its shape ended the argument. What was that shape?
answer: An astragalus grooved like a pulley at both ends
choices: An astragalus grooved like a pulley at both ends
An astragalus grooved at one end only, flat at the other
An astragalus with a ball-shaped head riding in a socket
An astragalus with a smooth, ungrooved upper face
context: That double groove has a name: double-trochleated. In even-toed hoofed mammals — deer, pigs, camels, cattle — the astragalus is grooved like a pulley at BOTH ends, front and back, and it is found in that group and in no other mammal alive or extinct. Thewissen's pakicetid skeletons (Nature 413:277-281) and Gingerich's Artiocetus clavis and Rodhocetus balochistanensis, from 47-million-year-old Balochistan rock (Science 293:2239-2242), both carried it. The molecular biologists had been right; the mesonychian hypothesis was finished. Two methods that could easily have contradicted each other — one reading living DNA, one reading 47-million-year-old bone — were forced to the same answer. There is a sharper twist still: Gingerich's own 1990 Basilosaurus paper had read those fossil feet as 'consistent with derivation from mesonychid Condylarthra'. The man who found the feet was wrong about what they meant, and he is the one who published the bones that proved it. — Gingerich et al., Science 293:2239-2242 (2001); Thewissen et al., Nature 413:277-281 (2001).

question: A student hears that the hind legs of a sixteen-metre Basilosaurus isis, thirty-five centimetres long and no use whatever for walking, are vestigial, and takes the word to mean 'useless leftover'. It means only that a structure has lost its ancestral job. In their 1990 Science paper Philip Gingerich, B. Holly Smith and Elwyn Simons argued these legs still did real work, and named the job. What job did they propose?
answer: Guiding the two animals into position during mating
choices: Guiding the two animals into position during mating
Steering the body through tight underwater turns
Bracing the animal against the sea floor to rest
Anchoring a calf against the flank while it nursed
context: The 1990 abstract's own closing sentence reads: 'Hind limbs of Basilosaurus are interpreted as copulatory guides.' That is the part of the word vestigial most people miss. Vestigial means a structure has lost its ANCESTRAL job — walking — not that it does nothing at all. A sixteen-metre whale could no more walk on a thirty-five-centimetre leg than you could walk on a matchstick, and the leg was still not idle. — Gingerich, Smith & Simons, 'Hind Limbs of Eocene Basilosaurus: Evidence of Feet in Whales', Science 249:154-157 (1990).

question: Harry Coover's team at Kodak in Rochester wanted, in 1942, a clear plastic they could mould by the thousand instead of grinding each one from glass. The stuff they mixed stuck itself to the moulds and to the glassware, so they dropped it. What had the team been trying to mould?
answer: Gun sights for fighter planes
choices: Gun sights for fighter planes
Windows for bomber cockpits
Lenses for submarine periscopes
Viewing plates for aerial cameras
context: Kodak gave up and went on making gun sight lenses out of ground glass by the tens of thousands. Coover remembered the 1942 reject in Popular Science (February 1989): 'I was working with some acrylate monomers that showed promise... But everything they touched stuck to everything else. It was a severe pain.' The compound he threw away was cyanoacrylate - superglue - and this was the first of two times it would be thrown away. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Harry_Coover; popsci.com, 'How a shot at making better gunsights became Super Glue instead'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Coover.

question: Art Fry stood up to sing in his church choir in St. Paul, Minnesota, with the hymnal open at the wrong page. The 3M chemical engineer had set his places beforehand so he could turn straight to each hymn, but the same thing went wrong every service. What kept happening?
answer: His paper slips slid out of the book
choices: His paper slips slid out of the book
His pencil ticks rubbed off the page edges
The choir changed the hymn order late
The hymnal's damp pages stuck together
context: Fry had already sat through a seminar given by his 3M colleague Spencer Silver, who had an adhesive nobody wanted. In the choir stall he put the two halves together: 'I was thinking "I wish I had a bookmark that would stick to the paper but that couldn't pull it apart".' He then saw the key point - that the density of Silver's adhesive controls how hard it grips, so it could be tuned to hold paper and let go again. Sources split on the year: 1973 (The Chemical Engineer, MNopedia) or 1974 (Wikipedia, invent.org, Grokipedia). Fry worked the idea up under 3M's 'permitted bootlegging' policy, which let employees spend company time on self-directed projects.

question: An office worker peels a canary-yellow Post-it Note off a pad. The pads have stayed that colour ever since 3M first put them on sale across the United States in April 1980, and the reason is an unglamorous one. What actually settled on that yellow?
answer: The scrap paper stacked in the lab next door
choices: The scrap paper stacked in the lab next door
The shade a 3M designer judged most eye-catching
The one dye that survived contact with the adhesive
The colour the product's own sales team voted for
context: The lab beside the Post-it team happened to have canary yellow scrap paper on hand, so that is what the notes were made from. Nobody chose it for the product. The Post-it Note went national on 6 April 1980, reached Canada and Europe in 1981, and won 3M's Outstanding New Product award that year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-it_note.

question: Harry Coover took Kodak's new glue onto the TV panel show 'I've Got a Secret' on 15 January 1959, where the panel had to guess what a guest was hiding. He put a single drop between a metal bar and a cable. What happened next on live television?
answer: The host was hoisted off the studio floor hanging from it
choices: The host was hoisted off the studio floor hanging from it
The panel hauled at the bar in turn and could not part it
A stagehand hung the show's painted scenery from the joint
The bar took the weight of a barrel winched over the stage
context: One drop of Eastman 910 between the bar and the cable held Garry Moore's whole weight clear of the studio floor. Moore's line on air: 'Dr. Coover's secret is the only thing between my 150 pounds and that wire, will be one drop of glue.' Coover had filed his adhesive patent in 1954, and Kodak had put the product on sale in 1958 as the industrial 'Eastman 910', later licensed to Loctite and rebranded Super Glue. Sources cite different patent numbers for that 1954 filing, so the number is not worth quoting. Sources: cbsnews.com, 'Almanac: Super Glue'; lemelson.mit.edu/resources/harry-coover.

question: Fred Joyner loaded a sample into a tool for one routine check in 1951, and it cost Kodak the tool for good. The chemist was testing heat-proof plastics for jet canopies at the Kingsport, Tennessee plant, using the same sticky cyanoacrylate that Kodak had thrown out nine years before. What did Joyner wreck?
answer: A refractometer, its glass prisms welded together
choices: A refractometer, its glass prisms welded together
A viscometer, its narrow capillary plugged solid
A calorimeter, its sample chamber sealed over
A balance, its weighing pan cemented to the beam
context: Joyner was measuring how much the compound bends light, and to do it he spread ethyl cyanoacrylate in a thin layer between the prisms. The accident was identical to 1942; what had changed was the specification Coover was holding. This time he read the ruined instrument as a result rather than a mess: an adhesive that needs no heat, no clamping, no solvent and no drying time. There was no single eureka - the same compound had to be rejected twice before anyone accepted it. Naming note: Grokipedia and several trade retellings name Fred Joyner; the Wikipedia and Lemelson-MIT accounts describe the refractometer incident without naming the chemist. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ethyl_cyanoacrylate; popsci.com; lemelson.mit.edu/resources/harry-coover.

question: Spencer Silver added too much of one ingredient by mistake at a 3M lab in Minnesota in 1968, and the result stunned him. Before that, his job had been simple: make a sticky glue stronger than anything else on 3M's shelf. What was that stronger glue meant for?
answer: Holding panels together in aircraft construction
choices: Holding panels together in aircraft construction
Splicing lengths of photographic film in a lab
Fixing reflective road signs to metal posts
Bonding soles onto shoes on a factory line
context: Silver's own account, given to the Financial Times in 2010: 'I added more than the recommended amount of the chemical reactant that causes the molecules to polymerise. The result was quite astonishing.' The target had been a stronger pressure-sensitive adhesive for aircraft construction; what came out of the flask was the mirror image of Coover's compound, and it sat unused inside 3M for years. Sources: thechemicalengineer.com, 'Spencer Silver and Arthur Fry: in search of an application'; adhesivesmag.com obituary of Spencer Silver; grokipedia.com/page/Spencer_Silver.

question: A model-maker squeezes a drop of superglue onto a workbench, and it goes from liquid to hard solid in seconds as its molecules snap together into long chains. Nothing evaporates out of it. Something it meets on the way out of the tube starts that chain reaction. What is it?
answer: The trace of water sitting on almost every surface
choices: The trace of water sitting on almost every surface
The oxygen the liquid meets as the tube is opened
The warmth of the hand or bench it is squeezed onto
The pressure of the two surfaces pressed together
context: Coover put it plainly: 'all surfaces have at least a monomolecular layer of water on them. It's actually the water, or any weak base, that is the catalyst causing the polymerization.' Hydroxide ions from that trace moisture attack the molecule's carbon-carbon double bond and set off an anionic chain-growth polymerisation that zips the monomers into long solid chains. Compare the four glues a person would guess instead, each with a genuinely different mechanism: epoxy (a two-part chemical cure), hot-melt (cooling), rubber cement (solvent evaporating) and white PVA school glue (water evaporating). Skin is the worst thing you can touch, because fingers carry both moisture and amino acids and both start the reaction; acetone frees bonded skin because it breaks the polymer chains down. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanoacrylate; University of Bristol, Molecule of the Month, July 2009; popsci.com (quoting Coover).

question: Art Fry used the odd glue Spencer Silver had made by accident at 3M in 1968 to hold paper bookmarks in a hymnbook, and the Post-it Note was born. Peeled off a page, a note leaves the page undamaged; pressed somewhere else, it grips again, dozens of times over. What is on the back of a Post-it Note?
answer: A sparse layer of tough spheres touching the page at points
choices: A sparse layer of tough spheres touching the page at points
A soft film that stays half-set and grips the page lightly
A strong adhesive diluted down to a fraction of its grip
A mesh of fine fibres holding a strong adhesive off the page
context: Ordinary glue cannot do both jobs: it grips the paper fibres and tears them on the way off, or else it quits after a single use. What is on the back of the note is acrylate copolymer microspheres, roughly 1 to 250 microns across with most between 5 and 150. They will not dissolve in solvent (they only disperse and swell), will not melt or flow when heated, and spring back to round after being squashed. Coated on paper they form what their inventor Spencer Silver called a 'sparse monolayer', so the sheet touches the page only at scattered points - he compared it to sticking to a bunch of marbles. The geometry is the mechanism, not a thinner film of ordinary glue. Silver's patent US 3,691,140, filed 9 March 1970 and granted 12 September 1972, describes 'infusible, solvent-dispersible, solvent-insoluble, inherently tacky, elastomeric copolymer microspheres' and puts the film's tensile strength at 'less than about 10 psi' - a measured, deliberate weakness. Sources: patents.google.com/patent/US3691140A/en; C&EN, 'Sticky Notes'; thechemicalengineer.com.

question: A crime-lab technician seals a stolen laptop in a glass chamber, warms a few drops of superglue inside it until the glue fumes, and shuts the door. When she opens the chamber, fingerprints nobody could see on the plastic are plainly there. What did the fumes do to the prints?
answer: Grew a hard white polymer along every ridge of the print
choices: Grew a hard white polymer along every ridge of the print
Etched the bare plastic everywhere the finger had not touched
Stained the sweat left in the print a deep permanent blue
Baked a faint brown shadow of each print into the plastic
context: The vapour reacts with the invisible sweat residue a finger leaves behind, and white polymer grows along the ridges until the print stands out to the naked eye - that is how latent prints are developed in fuming chambers. The same chemistry has an ugly side: squeezed onto cotton, wool or fibreglass, superglue sets off a fast exothermic reaction violent enough to cause burns and to give off irritating white smoke, which is why it should never be tested on a cotton glove. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanoacrylate.

question: A tube of superglue sits on a shop shelf for months, though the trigger that sets the glue hard is all around it, even in the air above the nozzle. By that logic the tube ought to set solid long before anyone buys it, and it does not. What else is in the tube?
answer: An acid, which holds the reaction back until the glue meets a surface
choices: An acid, which holds the reaction back until the glue meets a surface
A solvent, which evaporates the instant the glue leaves the nozzle
A drying agent, which soaks up whatever water reaches the liquid
An inert gas, which fills the space above the liquid as it empties
context: Weak acids slow the polymerisation and strong acids stop it dead, so the monomer sits unreacted in the tube until it meets a moist surface; stabilisers used include sulphur dioxide, hydroquinone and organic sulfonic acid. A test anyone can run goes against common sense: a thin smear bonds better than a fat blob. The reaction is started at the surfaces, so a thick bead never polymerises all the way through - more glue makes a weaker joint. Sources: University of Bristol, Molecule of the Month, July 2009; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanoacrylate; grokipedia.com/page/Cyanoacrylate.

question: A clerk in one of four American test cities shelves pads called Press 'n Peel beside the notebooks and envelopes in 1977. Spencer Silver's low-tack glue, which sticks and unsticks cleanly, and Art Fry's paper pad are both ready, and sales are negligible. What has gone wrong?
answer: A shopper in the aisle could not work out what a pad was for
choices: A shopper in the aisle could not work out what a pad was for
The pads cost several times what a pad of plain paper cost
The adhesive lost its grip after a few weeks on a warm shelf
Shops shelved the pads too low for most shoppers to notice
context: The product had to be used to be understood, and nothing about a pad sitting in a stationery aisle explained it. The four test cities are usually reported as Richmond VA, Denver CO, Tampa FL and Tulsa OK, though the city names come from secondary retellings and are less firmly sourced than the four-city test itself. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Post-it_note; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-it_note; invent.org, 'The Invention of the Post-it Note'.

question: Geoff Nicholson and his boss Joe Ramey picked one city, Boise, Idaho, to save 3M's sticky-backed notepads after a four-city test launch flopped in the late 1970s. They saturated it, and what came back beat anything 3M had ever recorded. What did the two men do in Boise?
answer: Handed free sample pads straight to secretaries and office managers
choices: Handed free sample pads straight to secretaries and office managers
Paid every stationery shop in the city to stack the pads by the till
Ran a week of radio spots with a comedian demonstrating them
Put a free printed pad inside every newspaper delivered in the city
context: Roughly 90% of the people who were handed a sample pad said they would buy it - more than double the best rate any 3M product had ever recorded. The stunt is remembered as the 'Boise Blitz': stop selling it, start giving it away, and let people discover the use by using it. Sources give the year as 1978 (Wikipedia, MNopedia) or 1979 (Grokipedia and several business retellings), so the date is not worth anchoring on. The renamed Post-it Note launched nationally on 6 April 1980. Art Fry's own explanation of why it then spread so fast is itself a mechanism: customers stuck the notes onto documents they sent to other people, so every note advertised itself to its recipient. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-it_note; grokipedia.com/page/Post-it_note; mnhs.org/mnopedia; invent.org.

question: A chemist leaves a drop of cyanoacrylate on a benchtop beside an open dish of liquid resin. The resin sits there; the drop polymerises within seconds, its molecules snapping into long chains. The reason is the molecule's build: a cyano group and an ester sit crowded onto the same carbon, right beside the carbon-carbon double bond. What does that pairing do?
answer: They strip the double bond of electrons and leave it open to attack
choices: They strip the double bond of electrons and leave it open to attack
They twist the double bond out of shape so it snaps open on contact
They hold one hydrogen so loosely that plain water snatches it away
They lock the molecule into a strained ring that water prises open
context: The cyano group and the ester between them pull electron density off the carbon-carbon double bond, leaving it wide open to attack, and they also spread the negative charge on the growing chain across the whole molecule so it is stable enough to keep going. That double handicap is why even the feeble hydroxide ion in plain water is a good enough initiator, and why skin - which offers both moisture and amino acids - is the worst thing you can touch. Source: University of Bristol, Molecule of the Month, July 2009.

question: Spencer Silver pitched his odd invention at yet another internal 3M seminar: a weak adhesive that peeled cleanly back off paper without tearing it. It was the opposite of Harry Coover's superglue, which Kodak had thrown out in 1942 for being too sticky to be useful. Silver spent five or six years pitching it, with a catchphrase he used every time. What did he call it?
answer: A solution waiting for a problem to solve
choices: A solution waiting for a problem to solve
A glue that never found anything to hold
The adhesive that would not quite stick
A failure too interesting to throw away
context: Silver also admitted: 'I'd spun my wheels a long time trying to find a product I could put my adhesive on.' Neither compound was ever a chemical failure. The cyanoacrylate was worthless only against a specification that demanded an optically clear, non-sticky gun sight, and the microspheres were a failure only against a specification that demanded maximum bond strength for aircraft. Both men were eventually honoured for the compound each had once been unable to give away: Coover accumulated over 460 patents and received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation from President Obama in 2010; Silver earned 37 patents at 3M and entered the National Inventors Hall of Fame the same year. Sources: adhesivesmag.com obituary of Spencer Silver; popsci.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Coover.

question: Investigators looked inside Elizabeth Holmes's blood-testing company, Theranos, worth about $9 billion on paper in 2014. Its fridge-sized Edison box was said to run hundreds of tests from one finger-prick drop, and they found it handled only about a dozen of them. What ran the rest?
answer: modified commercial analysers made by Siemens
choices: modified commercial analysers made by Siemens
a network of Theranos boxes placed in Walgreens stores
a prototype microfluidic chip developed at Stanford
a mass spectrometer built in-house by Theranos engineers
context: The Edison was real and did run some tests, far fewer than claimed; behind the scenes the company was buying and quietly modifying standard clinical analysers from Siemens. Source: Grokipedia -- Theranos; John Carreyrou, Bad Blood.

question: Elizabeth Holmes claimed her company, Theranos, could run hundreds of blood tests from a single fingerprick drop. Forbes magazine valued it at about $9 billion in 2014, making her, on paper, the youngest self-made female billionaire in the world. Two years later, after reporters showed what her machines could not do, Forbes revised her net worth. To what number?
answer: zero dollars
choices: zero dollars
about one billion dollars
about five hundred million dollars
about fifty million dollars
context: Forbes had put Holmes's personal paper wealth at about $4.5 billion in 2014. In 2016, once the Edison story had broken, the magazine cut her estimated net worth all the way to zero. Source: Britannica -- Elizabeth Holmes; Forbes 2016 revision.

question: A nurse pricks a finger and collects one drop, only about 50 to 100 microlitres of blood. A routine glucose test alone uses roughly 15 microlitres of sample against 1,500 microlitres of reagent. Theranos advertised hundreds of tests from that drop. What breaks first?
answer: each aliquot falls below the chemistry's detection threshold
choices: each aliquot falls below the chemistry's detection threshold
the sample clots before it can reach the reagent chamber
the reagent volume overwhelms and destroys the analyser's optics
the finger wound bleeds so slowly that oxygen ruins the sample
context: The pitch broke analytical chemistry before it broke the law: divide 80 microlitres 200 ways and each test has less than half a microlitre of blood to work with -- well below the sensitivity of standard immunoassays. Source: C&EN, 'Blood tests at your fingertips', 2017.

question: A Theranos technician tops up a tiny finger-prick sample with saline to fill the volume that a machine built for a full vein draw needs. For narrow-range tests like blood potassium, where a small change in the number matters a lot, this is a disaster. Why?
answer: dilution drags the measured substance toward the instrument's noise floor and multiplies error
choices: dilution drags the measured substance toward the instrument's noise floor and multiplies error
the added fluid dissolves the red blood cells and destroys any signal
the potassium in the diluent overwhelms whatever came from the patient
salt in the diluent binds potassium and removes it from the sample entirely
context: A small pipetting error on a small sample is a huge percentage error after dilution. For an analyte with a narrow healthy range, that noise can push a normal patient into an alarm zone -- or hide a real crisis. Source: Kallidil Kalidasan, 'How good was Theranos' product?'.

question: At least one Phoenix doctor sent a patient to the emergency room over a bad Theranos reading. In May 2016 Elizabeth Holmes's startup took a step almost unheard of for a medical lab, finally facing what its Edison devices had really produced at Walgreens pharmacies. What did Theranos do to the results it had already sent to patients and their doctors?
answer: voided or corrected tens of thousands of results covering roughly two years
choices: voided or corrected tens of thousands of results covering roughly two years
asked doctors to keep the results and simply add a caution note
reran every voided sample on the same Edison devices for confirmation
sealed the results and offered patients a discount on a future test
context: The voided tests included calcium, estrogen and testosterone. At least one Phoenix physician had already sent a patient to the emergency room on a bad number. Source: TechCrunch, 'Theranos voids two years of Edison tests', 18 May 2016.

question: Inspectors from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), the federal lab regulator, went through the Theranos lab in Newark, California, in 2015 and wrote to the company on 25 January 2016. Their letter covered the lab's blood tests, including prothrombin-time tests, used to set doses for the blood-thinner warfarin. What did the letter formally say?
answer: the practices posed immediate jeopardy to patient health and safety
choices: the practices posed immediate jeopardy to patient health and safety
the practices required a routine follow-up visit within twelve months
the practices met standards but the paperwork was incomplete
the practices could continue under a temporary research exemption
context: 'Immediate jeopardy' is the most serious finding in the CMS toolkit; Walgreens ordered that no blood drawn in its stores be sent to the Newark lab until the issues were resolved. Source: CMS letter dated 25 January 2016.

question: A jury in San Jose, California, ended the criminal trial of Elizabeth Holmes, who led the Silicon Valley blood-testing startup Theranos, in January 2022. That November she was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison. Her Edison devices had produced badly wrong results for patients tested at Walgreens pharmacies. Whom did the jury decide she had defrauded?
answer: investors, but not the patients tested at Walgreens
choices: investors, but not the patients tested at Walgreens
patients tested at Walgreens, but not investors
both investors and patients on every count charged
neither investors nor patients -- the case was thrown out
context: The jury convicted Holmes on four counts of wire fraud on investors (wire transfers over $140 million) and acquitted on the counts of defrauding patients. Sunny Balwani, tried separately, was convicted on all twelve counts against him and sentenced to about 13 years. Source: US Attorney NDCA, U.S. v. Elizabeth Holmes.

question: J.J. Thomson measured how far a magnet bent a ray streaming off a metal plate inside a glass tube in 1897, when nobody knew what the ray was. Then he fitted a plate of different metal and measured again, then changed the gas in the tube and measured again. What number did the swaps give him?
answer: The very same number every time
choices: The very same number every time
A different number for each metal
A different number for each gas
Larger numbers for heavier metals
context: Thomson made the point twice in his 1897 paper: 'the value of m/e is independent of the nature of the gas,' and, of two tubes built with different cathode metals, 'the values of m/e were, however, the same in the two tubes.' A ray that was somehow a property of the metal it came from should have changed when the metal changed. It did not. Source: J.J. Thomson, 'Cathode Rays,' Philosophical Magazine 1897 (primary text, https://web.lemoyne.edu/giunta/thomson1897.html); corroborated at https://grokipedia.com/page/james_j_thomson

question: A Royal Institution audience heard J.J. Thomson out on 30 April 1897 and did not buy what his cathode-ray measurements had turned up. Forty years later, in his memoirs, Thomson set down what one distinguished physicist who had been there admitted to him. What had the man thought?
answer: That Thomson had been pulling their legs
choices: That Thomson had been pulling their legs
That Thomson had misread his own instruments
That Thomson had rushed into print too soon
That Thomson had borrowed a German result
context: Thomson wrote it down in Recollections and Reflections (1936): 'I was even told long afterwards by a distinguished physicist who had been present at my lecture at the Royal Institution that he thought I had been "pulling their legs."' The talk was a Friday Evening Discourse, the Royal Institution's showpiece slot. The disbelief was not stupidity: he was asking a room of professionals to accept, on one set of deflection measurements, that something existed underneath the atom. Source: J.J. Thomson, Recollections and Reflections (G. Bell and Sons, London, 1936), quoted at https://www.chemteam.info/AtomicStructure/Disc-of-Electron-Intro.html and https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2000/10/discovery-of-the-electron ; date from https://ethw.org/Thomson_Reveals_Electron

question: J.J. Thomson set the ratio of mass to charge for his cathode-ray particle, how much matter each unit of charge was dragging along, beside the same ratio for the hydrogen ion in 1897. Hydrogen was the lightest thing known, and the atom was taken to be the floor of the world. Against that floor, what did his paper claim for his particle's mass?
answer: About a thousand times lighter than a hydrogen atom
choices: About a thousand times lighter than a hydrogen atom
About a thousand times heavier than a hydrogen atom
Just about the mass of a hydrogen atom itself
About ten times lighter than a hydrogen atom
context: Thomson's paper spells out the comparison: his value of 10^-7 'is very small compared with the value 10^-4, which is the smallest value of this quantity previously known, and which is the value for the hydrogen ion in electrolysis.' Two cautions. Direction: the MASS-to-charge ratio was about a thousand times lower, so the charge-to-mass ratio was about a thousand times higher, and the two are easy to invert. Number: 'about a thousand' is Thomson's own 1897 claim - the familiar 1,836 comes from later and far more precise measurement, not from the announcement. Source: J.J. Thomson, 'Cathode Rays,' 1897 (https://web.lemoyne.edu/giunta/thomson1897.html); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Thomson

question: Ernest Rutherford wrecked J.J. Thomson's 1904 model of the atom with his alpha-particle scattering. When Thomson died in 1940, his ashes were laid in the nave of Westminster Abbey near Isaac Newton, a few steps from Rutherford's grave. What had the two men been to each other?
answer: Rutherford trained under Thomson, then took over his chair at the Cavendish
choices: Rutherford trained under Thomson, then took over his chair at the Cavendish
Rutherford taught Thomson, then handed over his chair at the Cavendish
Rutherford trained under Marie Curie, then took over her chair in Paris
Rutherford ran Manchester, then lured Thomson away from the Cavendish
context: Rutherford had arrived at Thomson's Cavendish Laboratory in 1895 as its first foreign research scholar, worked under him, produced the experiment that wrecked his atom, and then succeeded him in the Cavendish chair in 1919. So the 1904 atom was taken apart by the professor's own research student - and the two men now lie a few steps apart in the nave of Westminster Abbey. Thomson's Nobel lecture in 1906 had been titled 'Carriers of Negative Electricity.' Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/james_j_thomson (sections 'Death and Memorials' and 'Nobel Prize in Physics'); https://www.westminster-abbey.org/abbey-commemorations/commemorations/sir-joseph-john-thomson/

question: Alfred Marshall Mayer pushed magnetised needles through corks around 1878, floated them in a dish of water and held a magnet above the dish. Up to six corks, they shoved one another apart and settled into a single evenly spaced ring. Then Mayer floated a seventh, and J.J. Thomson later borrowed the result for his atom. Where did the seventh cork settle?
answer: Inside the ring, near the middle of the dish
choices: Inside the ring, near the middle of the dish
In the ring, which spread to make room for it
Outside the ring, in a loose second circle
Off the water, pushed clean over the dish rim
context: That is the whole seed of the shell idea, done with corks and a dish of water, and you can repeat it. Mutual repulsion plus a pull toward the centre does not produce one ever-larger ring; past a certain count the surplus is driven inward and a second, inner group forms. Thomson used Mayer's floating magnets as the physical analogy for how corpuscles would arrange themselves inside an atom, and hoped each new ring would correspond to a period of the periodic table. Source: 'A. M. Mayer's experiments with floating magnets and their use in the atomic theories of matter,' Annals of Science 33(1) - https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00033797600200141 ; https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-70626-7_9 ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Plum_pudding_model

question: Without raising the voltage others had used, J.J. Thomson got cathode rays to bend in an electric field in 1897. Physicists had bent the rays with a magnet for years, but every attempt with an electric field had failed, and that was the standard objection to calling the rays charged particles at all. What had been defeating everybody, himself included?
answer: Gas left in the tube was conducting and screening the field out
choices: Gas left in the tube was conducting and screening the field out
The glass walls were soaking up the field before it reached the rays
The rays were moving too fast for a field to act on them at all
The cathode metal held a charge that cancelled the applied field
context: Thomson names the objection in his own paper - 'An objection very generally urged against the view that the cathode rays are negatively electrified particles, is that hitherto no deflexion of the rays has been observed under a small electrostatic force' - and then answers it by pumping harder, down toward roughly 0.001 torr with improved mercury pumps: 'It was only when the vacuum was a good one that the deflexion took place.' The obstacle had been the apparatus, not the world. Worth carrying around: a null result can be a fact about your equipment. Source: J.J. Thomson, 'Cathode Rays,' 1897 (https://web.lemoyne.edu/giunta/thomson1897.html); vacuum figure from https://grokipedia.com/page/james_j_thomson

question: George Johnstone Stoney put the word 'electron' into print in 1891 without ever having seen such a particle. He had worked the quantity out in 1874 from measurements in a quite different corner of physics. J.J. Thomson, measuring his cathode-ray particle in 1897, refused the word outright and held out until 1914. Which measurements gave Stoney his number?
answer: Electrolysis - weighing the metal a current lays down
choices: Electrolysis - weighing the metal a current lays down
Spectroscopy - measuring the light a hot gas gives off
Calorimetry - measuring the heat a current produces
Electrostatics - measuring the pull between charged spheres
context: Stoney reasoned from the laws of electrolysis that electric charge comes in a fixed smallest lump, and in 1874 he calculated its size; his first name for it was the 'electrine,' and in 1891 he settled on 'electron.' So the name was coined for a unit of charge years before anyone caught the object that carries it. Thomson relented only by 1914, using 'electron' in his book The Atomic Theory. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Electron ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Thomson ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/George-Johnstone-Stoney

question: George Paget Thomson, son of J.J. Thomson, sent a beam of electrons through a thin crystal in the 1920s and caught them on a photographic plate behind it. Clinton Davisson was running a similar test in America, and in 1937 the two men shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for what those plates showed. What had the electrons done in crossing the crystal?
answer: Spread and interfered, the way light waves do
choices: Spread and interfered, the way light waves do
Passed through unbent, as if the crystal were empty
Scattered at random, an even fog on the plate
Bent all one way, as a magnet would bend them
context: The 1937 citation reads 'for their experimental discovery of the diffraction of electrons by crystals' - the electron behaving as a wave. Here is the family joke buried in it: J.J. Thomson had taken the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics for work showing that the electron behaves as a particle. Father and son, roughly thirty years apart and in the same household, won the same prize for opposite-sounding answers about the same object, and neither prize was ever judged a mistake. That is wave-particle duality. An electron is not a tiny ball that occasionally misbehaves; it is something our two everyday pictures each capture half of. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1937/thomson/facts/ ; https://grokipedia.com/page/james_j_thomson ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Thomson

question: Puzzled by the awkward 20.2 that neon came out at, J.J. Thomson sent positive rays of neon through crossed electric and magnetic fields around 1913 and let them fall on a photographic plate. Neon was a clean, unreactive, chemically pure element, and nobody could explain that measured atomic weight. What did the developed plate show?
answer: Two separate patches, at masses 20 and 22
choices: Two separate patches, at masses 20 and 22
One patch, sitting exactly at mass 20.2
A smear spread evenly from mass 19 to 21
A patch at mass 20, drifting as the tube warmed
context: Thomson's 'parabola method' made each mass-to-charge ratio trace its own curve across the plate, so two patches meant two different weights of neon atom: mass 20 and mass 22. Atoms of one element coming in different weights are what we now call isotopes, and this was the first evidence of them in a stable, non-radioactive element. It also cleared up the awkward 20.2 - that figure is the average of a mixture, not a property of a single kind of atom. Thomson's assistant on the work, Francis Aston, built the technique into mass spectrometry and took the 1922 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Thomson ; https://grokipedia.com/page/james_j_thomson (section 'Work on Positive Rays and Isotopes', citing Thomson's 1913 Bakerian Lecture 'Rays of Positive Electricity')

question: J.J. Thomson wrote in his 1897 paper that 'we have in the cathode rays matter in a new state', on the strength of two bends in a beam: one in a magnetic field, one in an electric field. Then he went much further, making a claim not about cathode rays but about every substance in the world. What did he claim?
answer: That all matter is built from one and the same kind of stuff
choices: That all matter is built from one and the same kind of stuff
That every element is a different knot tied in the ether
That the elements are still being manufactured inside stars
That the periodic table hides many elements yet to be found
context: His words: all matter 'is of one and the same kind; this matter being the substance from which all the chemical elements are built up.' Notice the size of the leap - two deflection measurements in one laboratory, and a claim about everything that exists. He turned out to be right, which is exactly why the caution of his critics was reasonable rather than foolish: nothing in the measurement itself guaranteed the conclusion. Kelvin's vortex atom, one of the wrong answers here, was a serious rival idea in which atoms were knots in the ether. Source: J.J. Thomson, 'Cathode Rays,' 1897 (https://web.lemoyne.edu/giunta/thomson1897.html)

question: Inside a sphere of positive charge J.J. Thomson worked out where corpuscles, his name for electrons, would sit and circulate: one at the centre, two at opposite ends of a diameter, three in an equilateral triangle, and rings of them further out. He gave those sums in a Royal Institution lecture the year after his 1904 atom. They were aimed at a puzzle that had baffled his contemporaries for decades. What was he trying to explain with the rings?
answer: Why the elements repeat their properties in regular periods
choices: Why the elements repeat their properties in regular periods
Why a heated element gives off its own pattern of bright lines
Why some heavy elements break down and throw off radiation
Why gases combine in simple whole-number ratios by volume
context: Thomson proposed that rings fill up and close, that the outermost ring fixes an element's combining power, and that a closed outer arrangement gives you the unreactive elements. Right or wrong, that is a picture with arithmetic attached - which is what makes a picture killable. Note also what the schoolbook cartoon loses: Thomson never wrote the words 'plum pudding,' and his 1904 paper describes 'a number of corpuscles moving about in a sphere of uniform positive electrification.' Moving. Its title investigates their 'stability and periods of oscillation.' Two papers argue the textbook version is a fabrication: Hon and Goldstein (Annalen der Physik, 2013) and Renstrom and Bomark (arXiv:2212.08572), who call it 'a mere caricature with almost no trace of Thomson's work.' Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Plum_pudding_model ; https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/14786440409463107 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08572

question: J.J. Thomson put his own working figure at about a thousand corpuscles, his name for electrons, per atom, and in 1906 he checked it three independent ways: how light spreads passing through a gas, how X-rays scatter, and how beta rays are absorbed. All three landed in the same place. Where did they land?
answer: About 1 for hydrogen and about 25 for an air molecule
choices: About 1 for hydrogen and about 25 for an air molecule
About 3 for hydrogen and about 50 for an air molecule
About 70 for hydrogen and about 900 for an air molecule
About 1,000 for hydrogen and about 28,000 for an air molecule
context: The rule the three methods pointed to was that the number of corpuscles is of the order of the atomic weight - about 25 per air molecule, against a molecular weight of 28. Thomson had been wrong by a factor of a thousand, and he was the man who proved it, in a paper of his own titled 'On the Number of Corpuscles in an Atom.' Three unrelated methods agreeing is also the strongest kind of evidence there is: a mistake in one would not survive in the other two. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Plum_pudding_model (section 'Electron Estimation in 1906', citing Thomson, 'LXX. On the number of corpuscles in an atom', Phil. Mag. 1906)

question: J.J. Thomson published the arithmetic of his own atom's downfall in a 1910 paper. He worked out what his design predicted for an alpha particle crossing gold foil about four hundred atoms deep. Positive charge smeared smoothly through an atom cannot shove hard, so the alpha would take thousands of feeble nudges, and those pile up into a bell curve. The measurement then came back with about one alpha in twenty thousand bending past ninety degrees. What was the largest bend his paper had allowed?
answer: About two degrees
choices: About two degrees
About twelve degrees
About forty degrees
About eighty degrees
context: Thicker foil gave about one in eight thousand coming back the way it came. On a bell curve, ninety degrees was not an unlikely outcome; it was off the bottom of the graph, and no amount of tinkering with the smeared-out positive charge could reach it. That is the point of the whole story: the plum pudding died because it had been made specific enough to be killed. A model that predicts nothing cannot be wrong, which is exactly what makes it useless. Being refuted by its own published prediction is a compliment to a model, not an insult. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Plum_pudding_model (sections 'Multiple Scattering Integration in 1910' and 'Geiger-Marsden Experiments', citing Thomson, 'On the Scattering of Rapidly Moving Electrified Particles,' 1910)

question: Steven Smale put a close cousin of the Thomson problem on his 1998 list of eighteen problems for the twenty-first century. Building his 1904 atom had forced J.J. Thomson to ask where N equal charges settle on a sphere so their repulsion costs the least energy. How far has anyone got in proving the answers?
answer: Proofs exist for a handful of small N and for 12
choices: Proofs exist for a handful of small N and for 12
Proofs exist for every N up to about a hundred
Proofs exist for all N, from one general formula
Proofs exist for no N at all, not even for two
context: The proved cases include the shapes a person would draw by instinct, an antipodal pair, a triangle, a tetrahedron, an octahedron and an icosahedron (N = 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12), and also N = 5, a triangular bipyramid, proved by Richard Schwartz with computer help (published 2013); a few more have been claimed since. Everything else is computer search and conjecture. Smale's seventh problem asks a close variant, with a logarithmic energy, about how the minimum grows as N gets large. A model can be flatly wrong about the world and still leave behind a question nobody has answered 120 years later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_problem

question: A digger on Neil Shubin's team looked up from the rock face at a quarry on southern Ellesmere Island in the 2004 field season. The team had flown into the Canadian Arctic five summers running and come back with nothing that mattered. Something was sticking out of the cliff. What was it?
answer: the tip of a flat, pointy snout
choices: the tip of a flat, pointy snout
a row of scales the size of coins
the curve of a jaw lined with teeth
a knot of small bones from a fin
context: Site NV2K17 had first been spotted by team member Jason Downs back in 2000; the 2004 season pulled three partial skeletons out of it, from about four to nine feet long. Accounts of who saw the snout first differ: the UCMP Berkeley newsletter credits Steve Gatesy of Brown University, noticing 'the tip of a flat, pointy snout peering out' of the face, while Shubin's own telling in Nature is first-person -- 'I looked over at a wall; there was a Tiktaalik snout looking out of the cliff at me.' Arctic field seasons ran from 1999 at roughly $100,000 each. Sources: UCMP Berkeley, 'Tiktaalik comes to UCMP' (Sept 2005); Nature News, 'The fish that crawled out of the water' (5 Apr 2006).

question: Neil Shubin's team dug Tiktaalik out of bare tundra on southern Ellesmere Island, more than 700 miles north of the Arctic Circle, with firearms kept close for polar bears. But continents move. Where on the globe did that ground sit when Tiktaalik was alive?
answer: about 30 degrees north, the subtropical belt
choices: about 30 degrees north, the subtropical belt
about 10 degrees north, deep in the tropics
about 60 degrees north, the cool northern belt
about 30 degrees south, the southern subtropics
context: In the Late Devonian that patch of Ellesmere sat near 30 degrees north, in a greenhouse world with atmospheric CO2 estimated near 1000 ppm -- warm, humid, low-lying country of shallow ponds and floodplains vegetated with primitive lycopods. Tiktaalik's neighbours in the same rock include the porolepiform fish Laccognathus embryi. The beds are fine-grained siltstone of the Fram Formation, late Frasnian, about 375 million years old; the team helicoptered in, camped on open tundra, and flew the fossils out in plaster jackets. Source: Grokipedia, 'Tiktaalik' (Habitat and Environment).

question: Neil Shubin pulled out, in the late 1990s, the thing that would end up choosing his dig site, to settle an argument about geology in his office. He and Ted Daeschler knew the age of rock they needed; what they did not know was where to look for it. What did he pull out?
answer: a first-year college geology textbook
choices: a first-year college geology textbook
a Canadian oil company's drilling survey
a nineteenth-century Arctic expedition's journal
a museum catalogue of Devonian fish fossils
context: Shubin: 'Everything changed one day in my office, back in the late '90s, when we had a geological debate. And to settle the debate, I pulled out a college geology textbook.' Its map of North America showed three belts of Devonian freshwater rock: Pennsylvania, which Shubin and Ted Daeschler had already worked; east Greenland, which Jenny Clack had already worked; and a strip across the Canadian Arctic that no paleontologist had ever searched for early tetrapods -- those Arctic rocks had been described only in oil-and-gas literature. Sources: iBiology, 'Finding Tiktaalik, the Fossil Link Between Fish and Land Animals' (Neil Shubin lecture); Harvard Gazette (2009); Nature News (5 Apr 2006).

question: Neil Shubin and his team chipped a 375-million-year-old flat-headed fish out of the frozen rock of Ellesmere Island in 2004, and it needed a name. They decided not to invent one. They asked outside, were offered several names, and took one. Whom did they ask?
answer: the Nunavut council of Inuit elders
choices: the Nunavut council of Inuit elders
the anonymous donors who funded the digs
the editors who published the description
the schoolchildren of the nearest settlement
context: The team put the naming to the Nunavut Council of Elders (Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit Katimajiit), who offered names; 'Tiktaalik' was chosen -- an Inuktitut word for a large freshwater fish seen in the shallows. The gloss varies by source: the 2006 Nature description reads 'large freshwater fish', Grokipedia gives 'large shallow-water fish'. The species name roseae honours an anonymous benefactor of Devonian paleontology, so the donors did get a name after all -- just the second half of it. Sources: Daeschler, Shubin & Jenkins, Nature 440 (2006); Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'Tiktaalik'.

question: Two dates told Neil Shubin's team the age band to search: lobe-finned fish are already common in rocks about 385 million years old, and animals with four limbs turn up by about 365. Age alone would not do. Two more things had to be true of a patch of rock before it was worth flying to it. What were they?
answer: laid down by fresh river water, and bare at the surface
choices: laid down by fresh river water, and bare at the surface
laid down in deep sea mud, and never folded since
laid down by desert wind, and rich in plants
laid down as reef limestone, and easy to split
context: Shubin's own framing of the window: 'we want something between 390 and 365 million years old. That's of a time period known as the Late Devonian.' Freshwater river sediment mattered because that is the setting where the transition happened; surface exposure mattered because a person has to be able to walk on the rock and see it. Shubin on the whole approach: 'We designed this expedition with the goal of finding this exact fossil. And we used the tools of evolution and geology as discovery tools to make a prediction about where to look. And the prediction was confirmed.' Sources: iBiology, Neil Shubin lecture; HHMI BioInteractive, 'It's a Fishapod'.

question: Ted Daeschler, Neil Shubin and Farish Jenkins described the Ellesmere fossil in Nature in 2006. Its skull is flat and crocodile-shaped, about 20 cm long, with the eyes set on top of the head instead of at the sides and spiracles opening just behind them. But the feature the specialists called decisive is one that every living fish lacks. Which is it?
answer: a neck
choices: a neck
a tongue
an eyelid
a voice box
context: In a fish, a chain of bony plates bolts the shoulder girdle to the back of the skull, so head and body turn as one unit. In Tiktaalik those plates are gone and the pectoral girdle is fully detached -- the earliest known fish that could turn its head without turning its body. Ted Daeschler: 'The head of these animals was becoming more solidly constructed and, at the same time, more mobile with respect to the body.' The team's own nickname for the animal was the 'fishapod'. Per Ahlberg's 2006 verdict: 'Tiktaalik substantially narrows the gap in the fossil record of the fish-tetrapod transition.' Sources: Daeschler, Shubin & Jenkins, Nature 440:757-763 (2006); Nature News (5 Apr 2006); Grokipedia, 'Tiktaalik'.

question: Jason Downs read the shrunken hyomandibula in Tiktaalik as the mark of an animal already leaning less on its gills. In a fish, that bone is a strut that braces the jaw against the braincase and drives the pump that pushes water over the gills. Suppose you look for the same bone in your own body, doing a different job. Where is it?
answer: in your middle ear, one of three tiny bones
choices: in your middle ear, one of three tiny bones
in your throat, the bone under your tongue
in your skull, the spike behind your jaw hinge
in your neck, the topmost bone of your spine
context: The bone is the stapes, smallest of the three bones of the human middle ear -- a fish's gill-pump strut, repurposed to carry sound. Jason Downs: 'The bony part of Tiktaalik's hyomandibula is greatly reduced from the primitive condition,' so these animals were 'already beginning to rely less on gill respiration.' Source: UChicago News, 'Fishapod reveals origins of head and neck structures of first land animals' (2008), reporting Downs, Daeschler, Jenkins & Shubin, 'The cranial endoskeleton of Tiktaalik roseae', Nature.

question: Grzegorz Niedzwiedzki, Piotr Szrek and Per Ahlberg published trackways from a quarry at Zachelmie in Poland in January 2010. Something walking on four legs had pressed its prints into rock about 395 million years old. Ahlberg called it the biggest discovery he had ever been part of. Neil Shubin's team had predicted the age of Tiktaalik's rock and found the animal there. What does that make Tiktaalik?
answer: a late cousin of animals that already walked
choices: a late cousin of animals that already walked
a direct ancestor of animals that later walked
a walker's descendant that had gone back to water
a true four-legged animal rather than a fish
context: The Zachelmie prints are roughly 18 million years older than the oldest known bones of any four-limbed animal, and 10 to 20 million years older than Tiktaalik itself: something with feet was already walking before Tiktaalik lived. The prediction still worked -- rock of the predicted age and setting held the predicted kind of animal -- but the word 'ancestor' did not. Tiktaalik is a late-surviving member of the transitional group, a cousin of the first walkers rather than their forefather. Per Ahlberg: 'I've been working on the origin of tetrapods for about 25 years, and this is the biggest discovery I have ever been involved in.' Jenny Clack: 'It's going to change all our ideas about why tetrapods emerged from the water.' Some isolated prints clearly show toes and ankles; the widest track is 26 cm across, implying an animal over 2.5 m long, while one trackmaker was only 40-50 cm. Sources: Niedzwiedzki, Szrek, Narkiewicz, Narkiewicz & Ahlberg, Nature 463:43-48 (7 Jan 2010); National Geographic (Ed Yong).

question: Thomas Stewart's team ran the best Tiktaalik block through a micro-CT scanner twenty years after it came out of the Arctic quarry, and read out vertebrae and back ribs still buried inside. Stewart said Tiktaalik was probably not walking on land yet, but was 'definitely doing something new'. What did the buried bones show it could do?
answer: prop itself up and push off with its hind fin
choices: prop itself up and push off with its hind fin
arch its back and lift its head clear of the water
flex its ribs and pump air down into its lungs
stiffen its trunk and swim in fast bursts
context: Micro-CT of the holotype NUFV 108 exposed sacral ribs 'expanded and ventrally curved', almost certainly tied by ligament to the expanded iliac blade of the pelvis -- a spine-to-hip linkage before limbs existed. The paper's conclusion: 'the origin of novel rib types preceded major alterations to trunk vertebrae, and linkage between pelvic fins and axial column preceded the origin of limbs.' Tom Stewart: 'This creature has so many traits -- large pair of hind appendages, large pelvis, and connection between the pelvis and axial skeleton -- that were key to the origin of walking.' Sources: Stewart, Lemberg, Hillan, Magallanes, Daeschler & Shubin, PNAS 121(15) (9 April 2024), 'The axial skeleton of Tiktaalik roseae'; Phys.org (Apr 2024).

question: Neil Shubin's team found a stout humerus inside Tiktaalik's front appendage, with a radius and an ulna of about the same length and a scatter of small irregular wrist bones, plus an elbow that bends through roughly ninety degrees. What the team still had to settle was how far toward a hand it had actually gone. What does its far tip carry?
answer: lepidotrichia, the segmented rays of an ordinary fish fin
choices: lepidotrichia, the segmented rays of an ordinary fish fin
phalanges, the jointed finger bones of a land animal
metacarpals, the long palm bones that spread a hand
ceratotrichia, the unsegmented rods of a shark's fin
context: Not a limb: a fin with a limb inside it. The humerus carries a broad deltopectoral crest and a spirally twisted shaft; the wrist bones include a radiale and an ulnare; preserved fins reach about 30 cm. John Maisey's reframe of the whole story in 2006: 'Tetrapods did not so much conquer the land, as escape from the water.' Sources: Shubin, Daeschler & Jenkins, 'The pectoral fin of Tiktaalik roseae and the origin of the tetrapod limb', Nature 440 (2006); Nature News (5 Apr 2006); Grokipedia, 'Tiktaalik'.

question: Spencer Lucas argued in 2015 that the Zachelmie trackways in Poland, in rock about 395 million years old, older than Tiktaalik, were not footprints at all. Per Ahlberg published a hard rebuttal in 2019, pointing to how closely they match the anatomy of four-legged feet. What had Lucas argued the marks really were?
answer: traces left by fish feeding and fish nesting
choices: traces left by fish feeding and fish nesting
cracks opened in drying mud and later filled
burrows dug by worms through soft sediment
scours cut by cobbles rolled in a storm
context: Ahlberg's 2019 reply was blunt: 'There is no way these could be formed by a natural process,' citing the marks' anatomical consistency with tetrapod feet. Neil Shubin, cautious even though the tracks had displaced his own animal: 'The skeletal anatomy, let alone evolutionary relationships, of a trackmaker is hard to interpret from a track' -- noting that Tiktaalik's own skeleton pressed into sand at different angles could leave prints like these. Later reanalysis also moved the setting from a marginal-marine tidal flat to ephemeral non-marine lakes. The argument is still live, which is the point. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Zachelmie trackways'; 'Non-marine palaeoenvironment associated to the earliest tetrapod tracks' (PMC5773519); National Geographic (Ed Yong).

question: Neil Shubin, Thomas Stewart and colleagues named a new animal, Qikiqtania wakei, in 2022, from a rock block collected days before Tiktaalik itself in the 2004 Arctic season. The block sat in storage for about fifteen years until a CT scan in 2020 found a jointed fin inside. The animal was about 75 cm long against Tiktaalik's nine feet, with a boomerang-shaped upper arm bone. What did that arm bone say the animal's line had done?
answer: gone back to paddling in open water
choices: gone back to paddling in open water
started walking short stretches on land
taken to burrowing in the riverbed mud
kept propping itself up in the shallows
context: Holotype NUFV 137. Its humerus is smooth and boomerang-shaped, missing the muscle ridges and processes that let Tiktaalik prop itself up; Shubin: 'it doesn't have the elements that would support it pushing up on land.' Qikiqtania's ancestors could already prop -- this line went back to the water. The group was experimenting in both directions, not marching toward land. Sources: Stewart, Lemberg, Daly, Daeschler & Shubin, Nature (2022), 'A new elpistostegalian from the Late Devonian of the Canadian Arctic'; UChicago News; Wikipedia, 'Qikiqtania'.

question: A hiker's phone finds her place by turning GPS clock readings into distances at the speed of light. Each satellite's atomic clock drifts about 38 millionths of a second a day from clocks on the ground. If nobody corrected that drift, how far off would the phone be after one day?
answer: About 11 kilometres
choices: About 11 kilometres
About 11 metres
About 11 centimetres
About 11 millimetres
context: A GPS receiver converts clock time into distance at the speed of light, so a timing error of one nanosecond is about 30 centimetres of position error, and one microsecond is about 300 metres. The daily discrepancy is 38,640 nanoseconds; multiplied by 30 centimetres, that gives roughly 11.6 kilometres, which is where the published figure of about 11.4 km per day comes from. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Error analysis for the Global Positioning System'; GIM International, 'GPS: Position, Time and Distance'; GNSS Metrics, 'Clock Error and Its Effect on Positioning'.

question: Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating won $8,000 from the US Office of Naval Research in 1971 to test Einstein's claim that a moving clock ticks slower than a still one. A single purchase took $7,600 of it. What did that money buy?
answer: Eight round-the-world airline tickets, two seats per flight
choices: Eight round-the-world airline tickets, two seats per flight
Eight caesium beam tubes to keep the clocks running
Eight weeks of priority time on the Naval Observatory's clocks
Eight days of chartered jet flying over the Atlantic
context: The published account records $7,600 of the $8,000 grant spent on eight round-the-world plane tickets, 'including two seats on each flight for Mr. Clock.' The four HP 5061A caesium-beam clocks were suitcase-sized and too delicate for the cargo hold, so they rode in the cabin as ticketed passengers on regularly scheduled commercial airliners. Eastward around the world first, then a week sitting side by side, then westward; the flights were completed on 7 October 1971, with the reference clocks left behind at the US Naval Observatory. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hafele-Keating experiment'.

question: An engineer checks a GPS satellite's atomic clock against two things Einstein said would each change its rate, and the two pull opposite ways. The craft circles 20,200 kilometres up, where gravity is weaker, and it travels at about 3.9 kilometres per second. Which wins, and what does it do to the clock?
answer: The height effect wins, and the clock runs fast
choices: The height effect wins, and the clock runs fast
The speed effect wins, and the clock runs slow
The height effect wins, and the clock runs slow
The speed effect wins, and the clock runs fast
context: Weaker gravity at 20,200 kilometres altitude makes the satellite clock GAIN about 45.8 microseconds a day. Its orbital speed of roughly 3.87 km/s makes it LOSE about 7.2 microseconds a day (7,214 nanoseconds). Gravity wins, and the net is a gain of about 38.6 microseconds a day -- which is why the common line that 'time dilation makes GPS clocks run slow' is exactly backwards. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Error analysis for the Global Positioning System'; Grokipedia, same article.

question: Physicists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology lifted one aluminium-ion clock just 33 centimetres above another in 2010. Two clocks at different heights tick at slightly different rates, so a man's head has kept different time from his feet his whole life. Over a 79-year lifetime, how far apart would the two clocks drift?
answer: About 90 billionths of a second
choices: About 90 billionths of a second
About 90 millionths of a second
About 90 thousandths of a second
About 90 trillionths of a second
context: NIST's 2010 experiment is the calibration anchor: two aluminium-ion optical clocks raised about 33 centimetres (roughly one foot) apart in height differ by about 90 billionths of a second over a 79-year lifetime. Run the arithmetic yourself -- g = 9.8 m/s-squared, h = your own height, c-squared = 9 x 10^16 -- and the answer comes out in the hundreds of nanoseconds for an adult standing up. The same team also caught velocity time dilation at walking-to-cycling speeds of a few metres per second. Sources: Chou, Hume, Rosenband & Wineland, 'Optical Clocks and Relativity', Science, 24 September 2010; NIST/ScienceDaily release; Grokipedia, 'Gravitational time dilation'.

question: Navy engineers launched Navigation Technology Satellite 2, the prototype for the whole GPS system, on 23 June 1977 with the first caesium atomic clock ever put into orbit. Einstein's theory predicted that clock would tick at a different rate up there, but some of the engineers doubted the relativistic effects were real. What did they build into the satellite's clock system?
answer: A correction circuit that could be switched on only after launch
choices: A correction circuit that could be switched on only after launch
A second, deliberately uncorrected clock running alongside as a control
A radio link that let the ground rewrite the clock's rate at will
A backup clock tuned to the old, pre-relativity frequency
context: Because some engineers doubted relativity was real, a frequency synthesizer was built into the NTS-2 clock system and left switched OFF at launch -- to be turned on afterwards only if the orbiting clock's rate really did match general relativity's prediction. They built an off switch for Einstein. NTS-2 launched on 23 June 1977 with the first caesium clock ever placed in orbit, and they ran it uncorrected for about twenty days before deciding. Sources: Neil Ashby, 'Relativity in the Global Positioning System', Living Reviews in Relativity 6 (2003) 1; leapsecond.com reprint; Gunter's Space Page; eoPortal TIMATION.

question: Glen Rebka and Robert Pound sent gamma rays from iron-57 climbing about 22 metres up a tower shaft at Harvard's Jefferson Physical Laboratory. Every ray scattered on the way up is one the detector never counts, and losing too many would have buried the faint shift the two men were hunting. What did the rays climb through?
answer: A Mylar bag filled with helium gas
choices: A Mylar bag filled with helium gas
A steel pipe pumped down to vacuum
A plastic tube flushed with nitrogen
A brass tube filled with argon gas
context: The gamma rays travelled up the tower inside a Mylar bag filled with helium, put there to cut the scattering that would otherwise have eaten the beam over 22 metres. The shift Pound and Rebka were reading was a few parts in a million billion, produced by gravity alone: ten days of data gave a fractional frequency shift of magnitude 2.56 +/- 0.25 parts in 10^15, first published in Physical Review Letters 3, 439 on 1 November 1959. A definitive run in April 1960 agreed with general relativity to about 10 per cent, and Pound's laboratory reached the 1 per cent level in 1964 with Snider. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Pound-Rebka experiment'; Pound & Rebka, Phys. Rev. Lett. 3, 439 (1959); Grokipedia, 'Pound-Rebka experiment'.

question: Richard Keating and Joseph Hafele flew caesium clocks all the way around the world going east. After a week's rest they flew them all the way around going west. Matching clocks stayed behind at the US Naval Observatory. When the westbound clocks came home and were compared with the ones that never moved, what did they show?
answer: They read about 273 nanoseconds ahead of the stay-at-home clocks
choices: They read about 273 nanoseconds ahead of the stay-at-home clocks
They read about 273 nanoseconds behind the stay-at-home clocks
They read about 59 nanoseconds ahead of the stay-at-home clocks
They read about 59 nanoseconds behind the stay-at-home clocks
context: Westward the prediction was +275 +/- 21 nanoseconds and the measurement +273 +/- 7 -- agreement to 0.09 sigma, the clean result of the pair. Eastward was the messier one, and honesty requires saying so: predicted -40 +/- 23, measured -59 +/- 10, agreeing to about 0.76 sigma. Close, not perfect. Four HP 5061A caesium-beam clocks made both trips on scheduled commercial airliners; the results appeared in Science on 14 July 1972. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hafele-Keating experiment'.

question: Carroll Alley's team at the University of Maryland flew five 15-hour loops above Chesapeake Bay, about 10 kilometres up, from September 1975 to January 1976, to pin the flying-clock result down much more tightly than Hafele and Keating had. Each loop carried a sealed box of three caesium and three rubidium clocks, and the answer agreed within about one percent. What let them compare the flying clocks with the ground clocks live?
answer: A pulsed laser link beamed between the aircraft and the ground
choices: A pulsed laser link beamed between the aircraft and the ground
A shortwave radio link relayed through a chain of ground stations
A television broadcast carrier used as a shared timing reference
A trailing wire antenna towed behind the aircraft on each pass
context: The pulsed laser link gave a live comparison between the airborne clocks and identical clocks on the ground, while radar tracked the aircraft precisely enough that the velocity effect could be separated out from the gravitational one. That separation is the whole trick: the two effects pull opposite ways, so you cannot check either unless you can tell them apart. Sources: C. O. Alley, 'Proper Time Experiments in Gravitational Fields with Atomic Clocks, Aircraft, and Laser Light Pulses'; Ben Crowell, lightandmatter.com, 'Historical photos and information about the Hafele-Keating and Alley experiments'.

question: Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew the same clocks in the same kind of aircraft at the same altitudes twice, eastward around the world and then westward, and the velocity part of their prediction did not simply repeat itself. It changed sign between the two flights, which is why the direction of travel mattered at all. What made flying west flip it?
answer: The plane's speed partly cancelled the spin of the ground beneath it
choices: The plane's speed partly cancelled the spin of the ground beneath it
The plane flew a longer path against the prevailing jet stream
The plane's speed was measured against the air, not against the ground
The plane's route bent nearer the poles, where the ground moves slower
context: The reference clocks at the Naval Observatory are themselves being carried eastward by the Earth's rotation at hundreds of metres per second. An eastbound plane adds to that motion, moves faster in the non-rotating frame, and loses more to velocity than the ground clock does. A westbound plane subtracts from it, moves more slowly than the ground, and therefore loses less -- so its velocity term comes out positive. Predicted components: eastward gravitational +144 +/- 14 ns and kinematic -184 +/- 18; westward gravitational +179 +/- 18 and kinematic +96 +/- 10. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hafele-Keating experiment'.

question: Robert Pound and Glen Rebka set out in 1959 to catch gravity's effect on time inside a single building, with gamma rays from iron-57 and about 22 metres of tower shaft at Harvard. The shift was a few parts in a million billion, five hundred times smaller than the width of the spectral line they read it against. They added a second, opposite shift they could control, and swept it until the two cancelled. What produced that opposing shift?
answer: A vibrating loudspeaker coil that moved the gamma-ray source
choices: A vibrating loudspeaker coil that moved the gamma-ray source
A spinning rotor that swung the source through a tight circle
A magnetic field tuning the iron-57 nuclei's energy levels
A heater shifting the source's temperature by a few degrees
context: A vibrating speaker coil imposed a continuously varying Doppler shift on the gamma-ray source, sweeping the absorption curve until the Doppler shift exactly cancelled the gravitational one -- they cancelled gravity with sound. The gamma rays travelled up the tower inside a Mylar bag filled with helium to cut scattering. Ten days of data gave a fractional frequency shift of magnitude 2.56 +/- 0.25 parts in 10^15. First published in Physical Review Letters 3, 439 on 1 November 1959; a definitive run in April 1960 agreed to about 10 per cent, and Pound's laboratory reached the 1 per cent level in 1964 with Snider. The coil ran at about 74 hertz with a peak speed of roughly 0.10 millimetres per second, swinging the source gently toward and away from the target. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Pound-Rebka experiment'; Pound & Rebka, Phys. Rev. Lett. 3, 439 (1959); Grokipedia, 'Pound-Rebka experiment'.

question: A team at the Joint Institute for Laboratory Astrophysics in Boulder chilled about a hundred thousand strontium atoms into a single cloud one millimetre tall in 2022, and watched the atoms at the top run faster than those at the bottom. Reading so small a gap took ninety hours of averaging, and it meant holding one fragile thing steady for a record 37 seconds. What had to survive those 37 seconds?
answer: Quantum coherence, the atoms all holding one rhythm
choices: Quantum coherence, the atoms all holding one rhythm
Entanglement, one shared quantum state across the cloud
The laser lock, its colour pinned to a reference cavity
The magnetic shield, its field steady around the trap
context: The JILA/NIST strontium lattice clock resolved the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample -- the top of the cloud running faster than the bottom -- with a fractional frequency uncertainty of 7.6 x 10^-21, a tenfold improvement on prior work, built from 90 hours of averaging. What the whole measurement rested on was the atoms' quantum coherence, held for a record 37 seconds: for that long the sample stayed in step with itself, which is what let so faint a gradient be read across one millimetre. Jun Ye on what it opens up: 'This a completely new ballgame, a new regime where quantum mechanics in curved space-time can be explored.' Sources: Bothwell, Kennedy, Aeppli, Kedar, Robinson, Oelker, Staron & Ye, 'Resolving the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample', Nature, 16 February 2022 (arXiv:2109.12238); NIST news release; phys.org.

question: A lab worker tests blood plasma and finds that about a fifth of its protein is antibodies. Each one was pumped out by a plasma cell. That is a B cell that has dropped every other job to work full time as an antibody factory. How many antibodies does one plasma cell release each second?
answer: About 2,000
choices: About 20
About 200
About 2,000
About 20,000
context: Alberts's Molecular Biology of the Cell calls it 'the astonishing rate of about 2000 molecules per second'. The same chapter notes that antibodies make up roughly 20% of the total protein in blood plasma by weight, and that a single B cell carries about 100,000 antigen receptors in its membrane. Source: Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 'B Cells and Antibodies', NCBI Bookshelf (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK26884/).

question: Susumu Tonegawa cracked one of biology's great puzzles in 1976, not at a university but at the Basel Institute for Immunology in Switzerland. The Swiss drug company Roche had built the institute and paid all its bills, at $24 million a year. What did Roche do about the science it was funding?
answer: Left the direction of the science alone
choices: Set yearly targets and reviewed each project
Claimed first rights to anything sellable
Left the direction of the science alone
Read and approved papers before publication
