The cube of its diameter
The cosine of its tilt
context: T squared is proportional to a cubed, published in 'Harmonices Mundi' (1619). Try Jupiter: 5.20 astronomical units cubed is about 140.6; 11.86 Earth years squared is about 140.7. Same trick works for Saturn: 9.54 cubed is about 868, and 29.46 squared is about 868. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_laws_of_planetary_motion

question: Tycho Brahe built his observatory-castle Uraniborg with tall towers on the small Danish island of Hven, and they swayed in the sea wind and blurred every reading he took with his biggest instruments. So in 1584 he built a second observatory about 80 metres away, on a very different plan, and named it Stjerneborg, 'Star Castle'. What was odd about it?
answer: Its instruments sat underground on solid bedrock
choices: Its instruments sat underground on solid bedrock
It floated on a raft in the harbour
It was built inside a hollowed-out sea cliff
It rotated as a whole to track the stars
context: Stjerneborg -- 'Star Castle' -- sank its largest instruments into five domed 'crypts' anchored on bedrock, so the wind could not shake them. Only the observers' heads poked above ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stjerneborg

question: Aristotle had taught that the heavens above the Moon never changed, and his word had stood for nearly two thousand years. Tycho Brahe tracked the new star of 1572 in Cassiopeia night after night, looking for daily parallax: a shift against the background sky as Earth turned. What did Tycho actually measure?
answer: No shift at all against the fixed stars
choices: No shift at all against the fixed stars
A shift twice as large as the Moon's
A shift that matched the Moon's exactly
A shift that grew larger every week
context: No daily parallax meant the new star lay far beyond the Moon, out in the supposedly unchangeable realm -- and yet there it was, brand new. Tycho published the finding in 'De nova stella' (1573). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SN_1572

question: Scientists exhumed Tycho Brahe's bones between 2010 and 2012 and analysed the green stain on the nasal remains. He had lost a bit of his nose in a student duel and worn a metal prosthesis, for centuries said to be silver and gold. What was the prosthesis actually made of?
answer: Brass
choices: Brass
Pewter
Lead
Iron
context: Roughly equal parts copper and zinc -- brass, an everyday alloy, not the silver-and-gold showpiece of legend. Tycho may have kept the gaudier one for banquets, but the working nose was brass. Source: https://muzeum3000.nm.cz/national-museum-news/research-of-the-tomb-and-remains-of-tycho-brahe

question: Tycho Brahe measured the great comet of 1577 against the fixed stars, while everyone else assumed it was weather, something in the air below the Moon. His parallax figure put the comet far beyond the Moon. What did that measurement destroy?
answer: The solid crystalline spheres carrying the planets
choices: The solid crystalline spheres carrying the planets
The idea that comets were made of ice
The Earth-centred universe itself
Aristotle's four elements below the Moon
context: A far comet on such a path would have had to smash straight through the transparent spheres the planets supposedly rode on -- so those spheres could not be solid, or could not be there at all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Comet_of_1577

question: Not quite able to set the Earth moving, Tycho Brahe proposed a compromise arrangement of the heavens in the 1580s. In the Tychonic system, what circles what?
answer: Sun and Moon circle Earth; the other planets circle the Sun
choices: Sun and Moon circle Earth; the other planets circle the Sun
Every planet including Earth circles the Sun
Every body including the Sun circles Earth
The Sun circles Earth; the other planets circle the Moon
context: Mathematically the Tychonic model is equivalent to Copernicus's, and it correctly predicted the phases of Venus that Galileo would later see through the telescope. Tycho kept the Earth still to satisfy scripture and common sense; the geometry did the rest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tychonic_system

question: Johannes Kepler was cast in some tellings as a poisoner, greedy for his master Tycho Brahe's data, and the rumour of poison ran for four centuries. The exhumation of 2010-2012 looked for the killer dose in Tycho's hair and bones. What did the test actually find?
answer: Far too little mercury to have killed him
choices: Far too little mercury to have killed him
A fatal dose of mercury in his beard hair
Arsenic well above any survivable level
Lead high enough to explain the symptoms
context: The mercury story collapsed. Modern doctors read the eleven days between his 1601 banquet and his death as uraemia and urosepsis from a bladder or prostate obstruction -- he could not urinate after the meal, and the poison in his body was his own. Source: https://phys.org/news/2012-11-mercury-poisoning-tycho-brahe-death.html

question: Johannes Kepler worked for years through Tycho Brahe's data on one stubborn planet and built a lovely circle-based model that matched almost everything, except two latitude points that would not budge. They were off by about eight arcminutes, a quarter of the full Moon's width, and Tycho's readings were reliable to one or two. What did Kepler do with those eight minutes?
answer: Threw away the circle and rebuilt astronomy from them
choices: Threw away the circle and rebuilt astronomy from them
Absorbed them with a small offset centre (an equant point)
Added one more epicycle to the circle
Blamed them on a small unknown perturbing planet
context: Tycho's data were reliable to one or two arcminutes, so the eight-minute residual could not be blamed on the observer. In 'Astronomia Nova' (1609) Kepler wrote: 'Now, because they could not be disregarded, these eight minutes alone will lead us along a path to the reform of the whole of Astronomy, and they are the matter for a great part of this work.' Any predecessor would have declared victory; Kepler let the tiny gap kill his own model. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomia_nova

question: A teacher numbers Johannes Kepler's three planetary laws on the board: first the ellipse, then equal areas (a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times), then the link between a planet's year and its distance from the Sun. History found them in a different order. Which of the laws did Kepler actually prove first, in his 1609 book Astronomia Nova?
answer: The equal-areas law
choices: The equal-areas law
The elliptical-orbit law
The period-squared-distance-cubed law
The nested-Platonic-solids law
context: Kepler proved his second law -- the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times -- in the earlier chapters of 'Astronomia Nova'; the ellipse itself came later. What actually betrayed the shape in Tycho's numbers was not a visible oval (Mars's orbit is only about 0.4 per cent flatter than a circle) but the Sun sitting about 9 per cent of the way off the geometric centre, so Mars runs measurably faster when it is nearer. History found the laws in the order 2, 1, 3. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomia_nova

question: John Tyndall shone invisible heat from a soot-blacked copper cube of boiling water down a long brass tube of gas at the Royal Institution in London in 1859. At the far end a needle swung across a scale to show how much heat the gas had swallowed. Some gases threw it right across. Which of these barely stirred it?
answer: Nitrogen
choices: Nitrogen
Ozone
Water vapour
Carbon dioxide
context: Tyndall's own words for the moment: "Dry air was now admitted into the tube, while the needle of the galvanometer was observed with all possible care. Even by the aid of a magnifying lens I could not detect the slightest change of position." In his Table V, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen and atmospheric air each moved the needle by only about ONE degree, while some compound gases swallowed more than four-fifths of the heat sent through them. The detector was a thermo-electric pile -- a stack of junctions that turns heat into a faint electric current -- wired to a galvanometer, a meter that shows that current as a swing of a needle. Nitrogen and oxygen together are about 99% of the air you are breathing right now, and Earth's outgoing heat sails straight past both of them. Source: John Tyndall, 'The Bakerian Lecture -- On the Absorption and Radiation of Heat by Gases and Vapours', Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. 151 (1861), pp. 172 and 176; Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900, 'Tyndall, John'.

question: An Irish scientist, John Tyndall, built a long brass tube in the 1850s to learn which gases in the air trap heat, and he shone the warmth of a boiling-water source straight through it. The caps at each end had to let those heat rays pass, and ordinary glass blocks them cold. What did he cut the end plates from?
answer: Rock salt
choices: Rock salt
Split mica
Polished quartz
Sheet gypsum
context: Rock salt is transparent to infrared -- the invisible heat radiation that any warm thing gives off -- while ordinary glass absorbs it. Choose the wrong window and the window, not the gas, becomes the experiment. The tube described in the 1861 paper was brass, polished on the inside, four feet long and 2.4 inches across, capped at each end with plates of rock salt; the source was a cube of cast copper filled with boiling water, its radiating face coated with lampblack. Tyndall used several tubes across the campaign, so there is no single canonical length -- and one of his radiant heat sets survives, catalogued as 1859/1861 and on display in the Royal Institution's Faraday Museum in London. You can go and stand in front of it. Sources: Tyndall 1861, Phil. Trans. 151, pp. 171-175; Royal Institution, 'John Tyndall's radiant heat apparatus'.

question: John Tyndall tested how tightly each gas gripped the heat crossing his tube. The winner was a gas that drifts in the sky in tiny amounts. It gripped at least thirteen times as much heat as the rest of the air put together. Tyndall wrote that any change in this gas must change the climate. Which gas was it?
answer: Water vapour
choices: Water vapour
Carbon dioxide
Nitrous oxide
Carbon monoxide
context: Undried air straight from the laboratory gave an absorption of about 15; the same air dried gave about 1. Tyndall's conclusion, verbatim: "the quantity of aqueous vapour diffused through the atmosphere on the day in question, produced an absorption at least equal to thirteen times that of the atmosphere itself." And the ranking, in his own sentence: "if, as the above experiments indicate, the chief influence be exercised by aqueous vapour, every variation of this constituent must produce a change of climate. Similar remarks would apply to the carbonic acid diffused through the air, while an almost inappreciable admixture of any of the hydrocarbon vapours would produce great effects..." Water vapour is Earth's strongest heat-trapping gas. That is Tyndall's measured result, and it is stated plainly here. In 1863 he wrote the line everyone remembers: aqueous vapour is "a blanket more necessary to the vegetable life of England than clothing is to man" -- take it away for one summer night and "the sun would rise upon an island held fast in the iron grip of frost." Sources: Tyndall 1861, Phil. Trans. 151, pp. 276-277; 'Heat Considered as a Mode of Motion' (1863).

question: Joseph Henry read a paper by Eunice Newton Foote to a science meeting at Albany, New York, on 23 August 1856, three years before John Tyndall built his tube. Foote had stood tall glass jars of different gases in the sun, a thermometer in each, and one held carbon dioxide. Her paper ends with a forecast. What did she say an atmosphere of that gas would do?
answer: Give the Earth a high temperature
choices: Give the Earth a high temperature
Shade the ground and cool it
Sink low under its own weight
Hold the Sun's light but not its heat
context: Foote's forecast, verbatim: "An atmosphere of that gas would give to our earth a high temperature; and if... the air had mixed with it a larger proportion than at present, an increased temperature... must have necessarily resulted." That is 1856, three years before Tyndall's tube. Her readings: hydrogen climbed to 104 degrees Fahrenheit, ordinary air to 106, oxygen to 108, and the carbon dioxide to 125 -- nearly twenty degrees clear of ordinary air. On that cylinder she wrote: "The receiver containing this gas became itself much heated -- very sensibly more so than the other -- and on being removed [from the Sun], it was many times as long in cooling." Her apparatus was two glass cylinders about 30 inches long and 4 inches across, fitted with mercury thermometers and an air pump so she could rarefy or compress the gas; she read them every two or three minutes over runs of 8 to 18 minutes. Joseph Henry of the Smithsonian read the paper for her at the meeting in Albany. Foote held two US patents in her own name (a rubber filling to stop shoes squeaking, 1860; a paper-making improvement, 1864) and was the fifth of the 68 women to sign the Declaration of Sentiments at Seneca Falls in July 1848. Sources: Eunice Newton Foote, 'Circumstances Affecting the Heat of the Sun's Rays', American Journal of Science and Arts, September 1856; Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Eunice Newton Foote'.

question: A police sergeant's son from County Carlow with no college behind him, John Tyndall took a job mapping Ireland for the Ordnance Survey in 1839. In November 1843 the Survey fired him. What had he done?
answer: Organised the other surveyors' complaints about their pay
choices: Organised the other surveyors' complaints about their pay
Falsified a whole set of measurements he had never taken
Published his employer's maps in Dublin under his own name
Refused a direct order to survey a landlord's estate
context: He organised his fellow surveyors' complaints about pay and working conditions, and the Ordnance Survey sacked him for it. What followed: railway surveying in Manchester and Halifax, then schoolmaster at Queenwood, then -- at twenty-eight, with no money and no degree -- off to Marburg in Germany to take a PhD under Robert Bunsen, finished in 1850. In 1853 he became Professor of Natural Philosophy at the Royal Institution, and in September 1867 he succeeded Michael Faraday as its superintendent. The Royal Society gave him the Rumford Medal in 1869 specifically for the researches on the absorption and radiation of heat by gases and vapours. Sources: Grokipedia, 'John Tyndall' ('Early Life', 'Leadership at the Royal Institution', 'Recognition in Physics and Atmospheric Science'); Wikipedia, 'John Tyndall'.

question: Borrowing John Dalton's idea of an atom as a single sphere, John Tyndall pictured his own results, which he could not yet explain. A ray of heat meeting a lone sphere, he reasoned, can do little beyond shoving it along. Gases whose atoms are grouped and bound together, he wrote, were the ones that drank the heat up, because a bound group can do something a lone sphere cannot. What can a bound group do?
answer: Move as a system, its parts flexing against one another
choices: Move as a system, its parts flexing against one another
Break cleanly into single atoms and then rejoin them
Spin end over end about its own centre of gravity
Swap one of its atoms for an atom of the gas nearby
context: Tyndall's wording, verbatim: "Taking Dalton's idea of an elementary body as a single sphere... the communication of motion... must be less than when a number of such atoms are grouped together and move as a system." He had the shape of it a lifetime before anyone could prove it. The modern account: infrared radiation makes the bonds in a molecule bend and stretch, and a molecule only absorbs if that flexing shifts its electric charge from side to side. Nitrogen and oxygen are each two identical atoms sharing their charge evenly -- flex them and nothing shifts, so the heat goes straight past. Carbon dioxide, water and ozone are lopsided groups, and every flex tugs their charge about. That is why 99% of the air is invisible to Earth's outgoing heat and the traces are not. Source: Tyndall 1861, Phil. Trans. 151, p. 283.

question: John Tyndall stood up at a Friday evening meeting of the Royal Institution in London in June 1859, more than a year before his numbers reached print. He packed his whole result into one sentence about the air and heat, and people still quote it today. What did that sentence say the air does to heat?
answer: The air lets the Sun's heat in, but checks its exit again
choices: The air lets the Sun's heat in, but checks its exit again
The air lets the ground's heat out, but checks the Sun's entry
The air checks heat entering and leaving in equal measure
The air lets heat pass freely, but holds it near the ground
context: Verbatim: "[T]he atmosphere admits of the entrance of the solar heat, but checks its exit; and the result is a tendency to accumulate heat at the surface of the planet." Two cautions worth carrying, because both are commonly got wrong. First, this line is NOT from the famous 1861 Bakerian Lecture -- it comes from Tyndall's Weekly Evening Meeting talk of 10 June 1859, 'On the transmission of heat of different qualities through gases of different kinds', printed in Notices of the Proceedings at the Meetings of the Royal Institution, Vol. III, p. 158. Second, the Bakerian Lecture itself was received by the Royal Society on 10 January 1861 and READ on 7 February 1861 -- not in December 1861, as several popular accounts state. Sources: Notices of the Proceedings of the Royal Institution, Vol. III (1858-1862), p. 158; Royal Society Publishing record for rstl.1861.0001; standupeconomist.com, 'Tyndall's solar heat quote: a definitive citation'.

question: Eunice Newton Foote dropped out of the history books after her 1856 paper on carbon dioxide and sunlight, never once cited by the Victorian physicists working on radiant heat. For 155 years nobody in the field had heard of her. Then in January 2011 someone pulled the paper back out of the archives and wrote up what she had really done. Who found her?
answer: A retired petroleum geologist reading old scientific annuals
choices: A retired petroleum geologist reading old scientific annuals
A graduate student cataloguing letters at the Smithsonian
A Royal Society librarian re-shelving old Transactions
A journalist researching a Seneca Falls anniversary feature
context: His name was Ray Sorenson, and he published his reconstruction in the American Association of Petroleum Geologists' 'Search and Discovery' series in January 2011. Scientific American and the New York Times followed; the University of California, Santa Barbara built an exhibit around Foote in 2019. No committee restored her -- a retired man with time and an archive did. That is a standing invitation: the primary sources are mostly scanned and online now, including Tyndall's own 1861 paper, and anybody patient enough to read them can check what the textbooks say. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Eunice Newton Foote' ('Historical Obscurity and 2011 Rediscovery'); Scientific American, 'The Woman Who Demonstrated the Greenhouse Effect'.

question: Watching his galvanometer needle, the meter that turned his heat detector's faint current into a visible swing, John Tyndall saw the main gases of ordinary air each nudge it by only about a single degree. Air was nearly invisible to the heat crossing his tube. He wrote that no fact in chemistry settled one long-argued question about air more firmly for him. What did that transparency prove?
answer: That air is a mixture of gases, not a chemical compound
choices: That air is a mixture of gases, not a chemical compound
That air is a compound whose atoms are only loosely joined
That air holds a light gas nobody had yet managed to isolate
That air's oxygen and nitrogen sit in a fixed proportion
context: Tyndall's line, verbatim: "no fact in chemistry carries the same conviction to my mind, that air is a mixture and not a compound, as that just cited." The reasoning is worth following, because it is the experiment turned into an argument. If oxygen and nitrogen were chemically joined into a compound molecule, that molecule would be a bound group -- and bound groups were exactly the things his tube caught drinking heat. Air drank almost nothing. Therefore the oxygen and the nitrogen are merely stirred together, not married. A needle that would not move told him what no chemical test of the day could. Source: Tyndall 1861, Phil. Trans. 151, p. 283.

question: Eunice Newton Foote got there first. She reported in 1856 that a glass cylinder of carbon dioxide standing in sunlight grew far hotter than a matching cylinder of ordinary air, and took many times as long to cool. Her result was real, three years ahead of John Tyndall. Yet the Royal Institution still credits Tyndall with the first unambiguous demonstration, on one specific ground about her apparatus, not about her. What was the limitation?
answer: Her cylinders took the Sun's whole spectrum, never infrared alone
choices: Her cylinders took the Sun's whole spectrum, never infrared alone
Her cylinders held gas she had not dried before a run
Her cylinders were read by eye, with no needle to steady the scale
Her cylinders stood in sunlight that passing cloud could dim
context: Glass passes sunlight but blocks long-wave infrared -- the low-grade heat a warm ground radiates back upward, which is the radiation the greenhouse effect actually acts on. That radiation never got inside Foote's cylinders at all. What she measured was the whole solar beam warming a jar of gas, with no way to tell which part of that beam was doing the work. Tyndall's tube had rock-salt windows and a source that was merely a cube of boiling water at about 100 degrees Celsius, giving off no visible light at all: long-wave infrared alone, nothing else in the beam. The Royal Institution's own wording is that Tyndall "demonstrated unambiguously for the first time the absorption and radiation by certain gases of what we now call long-wave infrared radiation", while Foote "did not differentiate between heat from the whole solar spectrum and what we now call long-wave infrared". That is a difference in apparatus, not a verdict on her. Foote's priority is real, her result was right, and Tyndall never cited her -- he cited Fourier, de Saussure and Pouillet, and there is no evidence he knew of her paper. Sources: Royal Institution, 'Who discovered the greenhouse effect?'; Roland Jackson, 'Who discovered the greenhouse effect?' (2019); Grokipedia, 'Eunice Newton Foote'.

question: Joseph Fourier argued in the 1820s that the air keeps the Earth warm, and John Tyndall showed by 1859 which gases do the absorbing. The first actual figure for how much a doubled load of carbon dioxide would warm the whole planet came in the 1890s, ground out by hand with pen and paper. Who did the sums?
answer: Svante Arrhenius
choices: Svante Arrhenius
Guy Callendar
Gilbert Plass
Charles Keeling
context: Svante Arrhenius made the first serious attempt in 1896; Guy Callendar came later still. Tyndall supplied the missing WHICH -- which gases do the absorbing -- and stopped there: he never computed a temperature for the planet. What he DID do is worth keeping straight, because popular accounts blur it. He named carbonic acid gas in print as an absorber of Earth's heat, he measured gases at small fractions of an atmosphere, and he gave a second Bakerian Lecture in 1864 ('Contributions to Molecular Physics: being the Fifth Memoir of Researches on Radiant Heat'), collecting the whole campaign into a book in 1872. Tyndall's biographer Roland Jackson puts it that the discovery "rest[s] on many shoulders": Fourier, Pouillet, Foote, Tyndall, Arrhenius, Callendar. Sources: Royal Institution, 'Who discovered the greenhouse effect?'; Roland Jackson (2019); Wikipedia, 'Royal Society Bakerian Medal'.

question: A teacher reads the carbon-dioxide monitor on a school corridor wall, a box that costs less than a phone, with no chemicals to replace and no moving parts. The same kind of device sits beside hospital beds reading a patient's breath one exhalation at a time. Millions of them are running right now, and every one of them would start printing nonsense tomorrow if the physics underneath were wrong. What does the box actually measure?
answer: How much infrared the air swallows in one narrow band
choices: How much infrared the air swallows in one narrow band
How fast a pulse of sound crosses the sample chamber
How far a beam of light bends passing through the air
How quickly a warmed wire inside the chamber cools off
context: It is called a non-dispersive infrared, or NDIR, sensor. 'Non-dispersive' means it does not split light with a prism or grating; it uses a narrow band-pass filter to look at one wavelength only -- 4.26 micrometres, where carbon dioxide absorbs hard and almost nothing else common in air absorbs at all. That is why the reading is specific to CO2, and it is, quite literally, John Tyndall's 1859 measurement sold by the million. Charles David Keeling began the Mauna Loa record in March 1958 with an infrared gas analyser of exactly this type and got 313 parts per million; NOAA still reads that mountain with an NDIR sensor today. This is why greenhouse absorption is among the firmest facts anywhere in the climate argument: it is not a model or a projection, it is re-measured commercially, every day, by instruments that would fail if it were false. You can buy one for the price of a video game and breathe on it. Sources: CO2Meter, 'How does an NDIR CO2 Sensor Work?'; Atlas Scientific; US Patents 6,969,857 and 8,143,581; Wikipedia, 'Keeling Curve'.

question: John Tyndall coated the walls and floor of a box with glycerine around 1875, until a strong beam shone through it lit up nothing at all: no floating motes, air he called optically pure. Boiled broths of beef, lamb and hay left open in that air stayed sweet for months, while the same broths open to dusty room air rotted within days. Then in 1876 a few of his boiled broths went bad anyway. What did he conclude from those failures?
answer: That some germs ride out boiling as heat-proof spores
choices: That some germs ride out boiling as heat-proof spores
That broth can spoil with no germ involved in it at all
That his glycerine had stopped catching the floating motes
That boiling had driven life out of the air into the broth
context: He treated his own failed runs as data rather than as embarrassments, and reasoned his way to heat-resistant spores that survive a single boiling. Then he beat them: tyndallization, repeated heating cycles with rests in between, so that spores which survive one round germinate into vulnerable cells and die in the next. It was the first effective method for destroying bacterial spores. The optically-pure-air broths were among the experiments that finished off spontaneous generation -- the old and entirely respectable theory that life simply arises in decaying matter. And it all came from the same obsession that drove the heat tube: what does a beam do when it meets stuff. In the 1860s he had sent concentrated beams through soap solution and dust-laden air and found the beam itself becomes visible, with blue scattering far more than red -- what is still called the Tyndall effect. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'John Tyndall'; Hektoen International, 'John Tyndall, FRS: The beauty of science'.

question: General Shiro Ishii ran a secret germ-warfare program for the Japanese Army from 1936, at a huge complex at Pingfang near Harbin in occupied Manchuria. The unit's official name on paper said the opposite of its real work. What was that cover name?
answer: Epidemic Prevention and Water Purification Department
choices: Epidemic Prevention and Water Purification Department
Bureau of Agricultural Research and Soil Analysis
Northern China Meteorological Survey Command
Kwantung Public Health Inspection Corps
context: The full title on the paperwork was 'Epidemic Prevention and Water Purification Department of the Kwantung Army.' The name was the disguise -- a euphemism a kid can learn to spot. Source: Wikipedia, Unit 731.

question: Shiro Ishii founded the Japanese Army's germ-warfare center at Pingfang, near Harbin in occupied Manchuria, and led it from 1936 until Japan's surrender in 1945. It is now called Unit 731. Historians agree it crossed a clear line most other wartime programs did not. What did it do?
answer: Tested weapons on live human prisoners
choices: Tested weapons on live human prisoners
Sold its data to enemy Allied scientists
Refused any government funding
Published all its results openly
context: Ishii was a physician and army surgeon who founded the unit in 1936 and led it until Japan's surrender. He was never arrested; he died in Tokyo of throat cancer in 1959, a free man. Source: Wikipedia, Unit 731; PBS American Experience.

question: Shiro Ishii's germ-warfare unit at Pingfang, in occupied Manchuria, entered its captured Chinese, Russian and Korean civilians in the files during World War II by a single Japanese word. The word, 'maruta', was chosen so the files would not read as records of people. What does 'maruta' mean?
answer: Logs
choices: Logs
Guests
Patients
Numbers
context: Filing prisoners as 'logs' was a bureaucratic disguise -- the same trick as calling a biological-warfare unit a Water Purification Department. Source: Wikipedia, Unit 731.

question: General Shiro Ishii's germ-warfare unit at Pingfang in Manchuria prepared a drop for Japanese planes, which flew over Ningbo, a coastal Chinese city, in November 1940 and released a strange mix of wheat grains, cotton scraps and sand. The wheat and cotton were only camouflage. What was actually hidden inside the drop?
answer: Fleas infected with bubonic plague
choices: Fleas infected with bubonic plague
Ceramic bombs of anthrax spores
Drums of cholera-tainted water
Capsules of mustard gas
context: The wheat and cotton were carriers for the insects. An outbreak of plague followed in Ningbo in November and December 1940 that killed more than one hundred civilians. Source: Wikipedia, Ningbo plague attack.

question: American officers at Camp Detrick in Maryland questioned Shiro Ishii and his scientists in 1947 and wrote up what they had learned. Ishii, a Japanese army doctor, had run the secret germ-warfare base Unit 731 in occupied Manchuria, and he fell into American hands after World War II. What did the American occupation give those Japanese scientists in return for their data?
answer: Immunity from war-crimes prosecution
choices: Immunity from war-crimes prosecution
Postwar research posts at Camp Detrick
Positions in the American zone civil administration
Amnesty from the Tokyo tribunal alone
context: The deal was authorized by General Douglas MacArthur as head of the American occupation, with payments drawn from a secret Army fund. The classified summary is known as the Fell Report, after Norbert Fell of Camp Detrick. Source: Asia-Pacific Journal, Christopher Reed on Payoffs and Amnesty.

question: Judges on the Tokyo war-crimes tribunal tried the surviving leaders of Imperial Japan from 1946 to 1948 for crimes across Asia. General Shiro Ishii's Unit 731 had run its germ-warfare program from a huge complex at Pingfang in Manchuria. What became of the Pingfang program at the Tokyo trial?
answer: It was never brought into the charges at all
choices: It was never brought into the charges at all
Ishii was convicted, but none of his officers
Eight of its officers were sentenced to death
Its officers were tried apart, at Yokohama
context: The exclusion was directed by the American occupation command; it was part of the same bargain that granted the scientists immunity. Japan had signed the 1925 Geneva Protocol banning biological and chemical weapons before the program began. Source: Wikipedia, Unit 731.

question: Twelve Japanese germ-warfare men faced a Soviet court at Khabarovsk in December 1949, and sentences ran from 2 to 25 years in labor camps. For decades, Western writers waved the whole trial off as Communist propaganda. How do historians today weigh the Khabarovsk confessions against that view?
answer: Its Stalin-era format has real flaws, but captured Japanese documents and the epidemics themselves independently confirm the substance of what was confessed
choices: Its Stalin-era format has real flaws, but captured Japanese documents and the epidemics themselves independently confirm the substance of what was confessed
Cold War timing shaped the early skepticism, but the confessions have never been corroborated by any independent source outside Soviet custody
Captured Kwantung Army records flatly contradict the Khabarovsk testimony on the plague attacks, so the confessions are treated as extracted fabrications
The Stalinist format so contaminated the record that mainstream historians now set the Khabarovsk material aside entirely
context: Khabarovsk lacked cross-examination and used Stalin-era confessions -- real reasons for caution. But it was the only Allied trial devoted entirely to Japan's bacteriological program, and independent documents and the epidemics themselves corroborate its core. Source: Journal of the History of Medicine, on the West's dismissal of Khabarovsk.

question: A five-year-old chews a stick of spearmint gum, then bites into a caraway-seed roll, and tells the two apart with one sniff. The molecule doing the smelling in each is called carvone, and the two versions share the same formula and the same connections between atoms. What is the actual difference between the two carvones?
answer: They are mirror images of each other
choices: They are mirror images of each other
They are packed at different densities
They vibrate at different frequencies
One is a heavier isotope of the other
context: Spearmint is (R)-carvone; caraway is (S)-carvone. Same formula, same connectivity, opposite hands - like a left and right glove. Source: Friedman & Miller, 'Odor Incongruity and Chirality', Science 1971 (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.172.3987.1044).

question: A chemist runs the two carvones of spearmint and caraway through her tests, and only one test separates them: they twist a beam of polarised light in opposite directions. Chemists call such pairs 'chiral', from the Greek for hand. A person's nose still tells spearmint from caraway in one sniff. Why can it?
answer: Smell receptors are chiral too, so only one shape fits
choices: Smell receptors are chiral too, so only one shape fits
Only one chiral form dissolves in nasal mucus
Each chiral form has a different electric charge
The nose senses the twist in polarised light
context: Smell receptors are built from proteins, and proteins are chiral. The binding pocket is a right glove - only a right hand fits. Source: Chiralpedia, 'The Chemistry of Taste and Smell' (https://chiralpedia.com/blog/the-chemistry-of-taste-and-smell-how-chirality-affects-senses/).

question: A 22-year-old graduate student published a short pamphlet in September 1874 and sent carbon's four bonds off the page into three dimensions. For most of the 1800s chemists had drawn those bonds flat, as Kekule did. The pamphlet explained at a stroke why Louis Pasteur's crystals had come in two kinds. Who wrote it?
answer: Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff
choices: Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff
Emil Fischer
Johannes Wislicenus
Adolf von Baeyer
context: Van 't Hoff's Utrecht pamphlet, Sept 1874. Joseph Le Bel in Paris published the same 3-D idea independently two months later. Source: 150 Years of the Tetrahedral Carbon (Wiley, 2024) (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/chir.70022).

question: Jacobus van 't Hoff, a young Dutch chemist, wrote a short paper in 1874 saying a carbon atom bonded to four groups should look like a tetrahedron, a pyramid shape, not a flat cross. Joseph Le Bel put the same idea into print in Paris two months later, on his own. What does it usually mean when two people find the same idea at once?
answer: The evidence was ripe enough that the field was ready
choices: The evidence was ripe enough that the field was ready
One of the two must have copied the other
The idea will probably turn out wrong
Neither one deserves credit
context: Le Bel's paper appeared in the Bulletin de la Societe Chimique in November 1874, two months after van 't Hoff. Pasteur had physically sorted mirror-image tartrate crystals back in 1848 but had no explanation for WHY. Source: 150 Years of the Tetrahedral Carbon (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/chir.70022).

question: Jacobus van 't Hoff, a Dutch chemist, won the very first Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1901, twenty-seven years after the short pamphlet he had published as a twenty-two-year-old student in Utrecht, in the Netherlands. What work did the Nobel citation name?
answer: Chemical kinetics and osmotic pressure
choices: Chemical kinetics and osmotic pressure
The tetrahedral carbon and its mirror images
The ring structure of the benzene molecule
The synthesis of urea from inorganic salts
context: The 1901 citation honoured him 'in recognition of the extraordinary services he has rendered by the discovery of the laws of chemical dynamics and osmotic pressure in solutions' - kinetics and solutions, not stereochemistry. Textbooks often imply the prize was for the tetrahedron; it was not. The tetrahedron paper had already been honoured on its own, with the Royal Society's Davy Medal in 1893, shared with Joseph Le Bel. Sources: NobelPrize.org, 'The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1901'; Wikipedia, 'Davy Medal'.

question: Nikolai Vavilov, a Soviet plant scientist, brought one kind of thing home to Leningrad by the hundreds of thousands. It came from about 115 expeditions through more than sixty countries, from Ethiopia to the Andes to Afghanistan, in the 1920s and 1930s. What was he collecting?
answer: seeds
choices: seeds
beetles
orchids
meteorites
context: Vavilov brought back roughly 380,000 seeds, grains, roots, tubers and fruits by the early 1930s, building the largest crop-diversity collection on Earth. His stated reason was singular. Source: Science History Institute; Crop Trust.

question: Crossing continent after continent from the 1920s onward, through the Andes, Afghanistan, Ethiopia and Central Asia, Nikolai Vavilov hunted wild and traditional varieties of wheat, potatoes and other food crops. He had grown up watching peasants starve when harvests failed. When he was asked why he was collecting on such a scale, what reason did he give?
answer: to end famine in Russia
choices: to end famine in Russia
to catalogue every plant on Earth
to prove Charles Darwin correct on inheritance
to prepare crops for interplanetary agriculture
context: Vavilov lived through the 1891-92 Volga famine as a boy; the stated purpose of the Leningrad collection was practical -- new crop varieties for Soviet fields. It is why he pushed on when Stalin later stopped his travel. Source: Crop Trust; Cornell exhibits.

question: Nikolai Vavilov steered his world seed hunts of the 1920s and 30s by one idea: each food plant had a 'centre of origin', a region where its oldest wild ancestors still grew. The wild old crops in those centres carry something that new farm crops often lose. What is it?
answer: disease resistance
choices: disease resistance
drought tolerance
higher protein content
frost hardiness
context: Modern crop breeding tends to select for yield and uniformity and to breed OUT the awkward wild traits -- so the centres are a library of answers to future plant diseases. Norman Borlaug used Vavilov-style landrace collections to build his Green Revolution wheats, whose stem-rust resistance came straight from wild relatives. Source: PMC review.

question: Stalin's leaders moved late in 1933 to stop the foreign trips of Nikolai Vavilov, who ran a worldwide seed-collecting programme and had built a global seed bank in Leningrad, hoping to breed crops that could feed the country in any climate. What single office act actually shut the collecting down?
answer: his passport was revoked
choices: his passport was revoked
the Party revoked his hard-currency travel funds
a Central Committee decree required Politburo approval for every trip
his chief patron Bukharin was arrested and could no longer protect him
context: The 1916 expedition to Iran had begun the collecting; by 1933 the Party's line under Lysenko no longer wanted a globe-trotting geneticist. Vavilov lost the passport, not (yet) the institute. Source: Nautilus, 'The Botanist Who Defied Stalin'.

question: Trofim Lysenko rejected genetics as 'bourgeois', won Stalin's favour, and helped have Nikolai Vavilov, builder of the world's largest seed collection, arrested. The story is no simple morality play. Before they became enemies, Vavilov had been Lysenko's boss at work. What had Vavilov briefly done?
answer: encouraged Lysenko's vernalization research
choices: encouraged Lysenko's vernalization research
written the pamphlet that made Lysenko famous
arranged Lysenko's first meeting with Stalin
co-authored a textbook with Lysenko in the 1920s
context: Vavilov valued vernalization's 'possible simplification of breeding work' and only withdrew his support when the method failed. That earlier goodwill is what makes the later denunciation so bitter. Source: Wikipedia on Trofim Lysenko.

question: Even as Trofim Lysenko turned the Party against him, Nikolai Vavilov kept hunting wild crop varieties. He was on a seed-collecting trip near Chernivtsi in western Ukraine on 6 August 1940 when he was arrested in the field. Who took him?
answer: the NKVD
choices: the NKVD
the Wehrmacht
the local militia
his own institute staff
context: The People's Commissariat of Internal Affairs -- Beria's secret police. He was taken to Moscow's Lubyanka prison, and over roughly 11 months was interrogated on 400 separate occasions. Charges: sabotage of Soviet agriculture and spying for Britain. Source: Nautilus; Wikipedia.

question: Nikolai Vavilov was sentenced to death in July 1941, a sentence later commuted to twenty years, and was transferred to Saratov Prison No. 1. He had once crossed sixty countries hunting crops. What did he do in his cell?
answer: lectured his fellow prisoners on plants and genetics
choices: lectured his fellow prisoners on plants and genetics
kept a hidden diary later smuggled abroad
traded seeds with the prison warden's kitchen garden
wrote weekly appeals to Stalin himself
context: Cornell's Vavilov exhibit records over 100 hours of prison lectures on plants and genetics -- the scientist teaching to the last. Source: Cornell exhibits, 'Cultivating Silence'.

question: Nikolai Vavilov fell into the hands of the Soviet secret police in 1940, arrested for opposing the state's approved biologist, Trofim Lysenko. He had crossed sixty countries and gathered 380,000 seed samples so that his homeland would never again face famine. He was held in Saratov prison, cut off from the collection he had built, and he died there on 26 January 1943. What killed him?
answer: starvation
choices: starvation
a firing squad
an infectious outbreak
beating by interrogators
context: The prison medical record lists pneumonia, dystrophy and oedema -- widely and honestly read, that is death from starvation and the conditions that accompany it. Vavilov was 55. His argument -- a library of seeds against famine -- outlived him. Source: Wikipedia; Science History Institute.

question: Trofim Lysenko, the Soviet farming official who rejected modern genetics as bourgeois science, took a state honour on 22 March 1943. Nikolai Vavilov, jailed for opposing his ideas, had died in a prison cell on 26 January. What did the Soviet state honour Lysenko with?
answer: a Stalin Prize of the first degree
choices: a Stalin Prize of the first degree
the presidency of Moscow State University
a Hero of Socialist Labour star of gold
an Order of Lenin for wartime civilian service
context: Cited officially for 'the scientific development and introduction into agriculture of a method of planting potatoes with the tops of food tubers'. The timeline is the story: prison starvation for the geneticist in January, Stalin Prize for the anti-geneticist in March. Source: Wikipedia on Lysenko.

question: The staff of Nikolai Vavilov's institute chose to starve through the 872-day siege of Leningrad rather than eat the collection they had been left to guard, and several starved to death at their posts. One of them, Dmitri Ivanov, died of hunger with his own specialist crop stored all around him. Which crop was it?
answer: rice
choices: rice
potatoes
maize
barley
context: Dmitri Sergeyevich Ivanov kept the institute's rice collection and headed its rice section; the institute's own roll of its siege dead lists him beside the oat keeper Lidia Rodina and the peanut keeper Alexander Shchukin. He died of hunger in the winter of 1941-42, and thousands of packets of grain were left in his office, uneaten. Sources: N. I. Vavilov Institute of Plant Industry, blockade memorial list (vir.nw.ru); Novaya Gazeta, 23 November 2012; Alexanyan and Krivchenko, Diversity (1991), as reported in Dawn, 4 October 2002.

question: Judges of the Military Collegium of the USSR Supreme Court opened Nikolai Vavilov's case in 1955, twelve years after his death in Saratov prison. Stalin had died in 1953, the Khrushchev thaw had begun, and Soviet courts were forced to revisit the sentences of Stalin-era victims. What did the judges do?
answer: vacated his sentence and rehabilitated him
choices: vacated his sentence and rehabilitated him
ruled his conviction final and unappealable
commuted his original death sentence posthumously to time served
transferred jurisdiction to a civilian court for a retrial
context: Rehabilitation came under Khrushchev's de-Stalinization; the institute became the N. I. Vavilov All-Russian Scientific Research Institute of Plant Genetic Resources (VIR). And the idea itself lives in the Svalbard Global Seed Vault (2008), inside an Arctic mountain -- Vavilov's library, in permafrost. Source: Wikipedia; Cornell.

question: A professor at a European medical school of the 1530s sat above the crowd in a raised chair, reading Latin aloud from the Roman doctor Galen. An assistant called the ostensor pointed to each part on the corpse as it was read out, and the professor never touched the body. Who actually held the knife and did the cutting?
answer: A junior barber-surgeon hired for the day
choices: The ostensor, once his pointing was done
A junior barber-surgeon hired for the day
The senior medical student of the year
The city executioner who supplied the body
context: The physician owned the text; the surgeon owned the knife. The manual being read was usually Mondino de' Liuzzi's Anathomia of 1316, printed in 1478 and reprinted in over forty editions. Andreas Vesalius broke the arrangement by climbing down off the chair and cutting the body himself - he had been handed Padua's chair of surgery and anatomy at 23, the day after taking his degree in December 1537. The frontispiece of his own book makes the argument in a picture: Vesalius stands at the table with his hand inside the opened abdomen, and the barber-surgeons are shoved underneath it, quarrelling, their razors idle. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Anatomical_theatre and /Medieval_medicine_of_Western_Europe (via search snippets); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Vesalius; pelviperineology.org, 'The frontispiece of Vesalius' Fabrica'.

question: Andreas Vesalius cut open a hanged man in public at Basel in 1543, wired the bones together and gave them to the school. That skeleton still stands in the city's museum, the oldest one like it in the world. What had the man been hanged for?
answer: Knifing his wife when she uncovered the second marriage
choices: Looting a church while garrisoned in the city
Forging silver coin in a cellar beneath his shop
Knifing his wife when she uncovered the second marriage
Poisoning the abbot of the house he entered as a monk
context: The man was Jakob Karrer von Gebweiler, a bigamist. Book I, chapter 39 of the Fabrica is where Vesalius set out in print, for the first time anywhere, the whole process of cleaning and mounting a skeleton - so the thing in Basel is his own written instructions carried out, and it is still there to go and look at, which is the point: a claim you can walk up to and check. Sources: historyofinformation.com, 'The Oldest Surviving Articulated Human Skeleton'; executedtoday.com, 12 May 1543 entry.

question: Andreas Vesalius checked the notes of Galen of Pergamon against the bodies on his own table at Padua, and error after error turned up. Europe had trusted Galen's anatomy for over 1,300 years, and he was no fraud: he dissected many carcasses and wrote up what he saw. Where had Galen's insides come from?
answer: Barbary macaques, pigs and dogs cut open in turn
choices: Skeletons lifted from Roman tombs after dark
Barbary macaques, pigs and dogs cut open in turn
Bodies unwrapped from Egyptian mummy cases
Gladiators' wounds glimpsed while patching them up
context: Roman law and custom barred the dissection of human bodies, so Galen worked on animals, favouring the Barbary macaque for its resemblance to us. He even recorded some ape-human differences in the face muscles and the vertebrae: the failure was extrapolating across species, not inventing. And Vesalius never treated him as a fraud - he edited the anatomical sections of Galen for the Giunta family's Latin edition, and historians call him a neo-Galenist who applied Galen's own observational method honestly. The method was Galen's; the corrections were that method used without flinching. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Galen (via search snippet); historymedjournal.com, 'The evolution of Vesalius's perspective on Galen's anatomy'; library.uab.edu on the Giunta edition.

question: On a real adult human skeleton at Padua, Andreas Vesalius counted the pieces of the breastbone. A finger run down the middle of the chest feels one solid strip, and the old books he had been raised on gave that bone seven separate pieces. What did he find?
answer: Three pieces, the last of a row fused in childhood
choices: Seven pieces, exactly as the books had it
Five pieces, joined down the line by cartilage
Three pieces, the last of a row fused in childhood
One piece, a single plate with no divisions at all
context: The three are the manubrium at the top, the long body, and the small xiphoid process at the bottom; a child has more, and they knit together as you grow. Seven was a real count - of a chest that was not human. Try it on yourself: press down from the notch at the base of your throat and feel for the small ridge where the manubrium meets the body, roughly level with your second rib. That join is one of Vesalius's corrections, on you. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Vesalius; biologyinsights.com, 'Andreas Vesalius's discoveries that changed anatomy'.

question: Head after head opened under Andreas Vesalius's knife, and he never found the rete mirabile, the wonderful net of fine vessels at the base of the brain where Galen said the vital spirit turned into the animal spirit of thought. He was not calling Galen a liar, because the net is real. Which animals have one?
answer: Sheep and cattle, cooling the blood on its way to the brain
choices: Sheep and cattle, cooling the blood on its way to the brain
Frogs and newts, feeding the brain while they lie under ice
Snakes and lizards, warming the head after a cold night
Moles and shrews, holding oxygen for the brain underground
context: In cats and in hoofed animals - sheep, pigs, cattle - the rete mirabile is a genuine mesh of vessels that makes up for underdeveloped internal carotid arteries and helps cool the blood heading for the brain. Galen saw a real structure; he saw it in the wrong species. And Vesalius was not even first to say so: Berengario da Carpi had already published that despite many attempts he could not detect the net in a human, so the looking-for-yourself method was spreading before the Fabrica made it famous. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Rete_mirabile (via search snippet); PMC6381050, 'Berengario da Carpi and the Renaissance of Brain Anatomy'.

question: Having opened bodies of both sexes at Padua, Andreas Vesalius printed his rib count in Book 1, chapter 19 of the Fabrica: twelve pairs in men, twelve in women, and the odd person at eleven or thirteen. Every home in Europe knew that a man has one less rib than a woman. What did he do with the old belief?
answer: He named Genesis in the text and called the belief plainly absurd
choices: He printed the bare count and left the old belief unmentioned
He named Genesis in the text and called the belief plainly absurd
He set the count beside the belief and left the reader to judge
He asked the theology faculty at Louvain to rule on the point
context: Vesalius wrote in Book I, chapter 19: 'It is commonly believed that men lack a rib on one side, and that men have one rib fewer than women. This is plainly absurd, even if Moses did say in the second chapter of Genesis...' He recorded the same twelve pairs in both sexes and noted genuine individual variation of eleven or thirteen. His move was anatomical rather than theological: the belief was a claim about what a count would show, and a count is something anybody can make. Sources: Fabrica Bk I ch.19 quoted at mistakinghistories.uk; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Vesalius.

question: A scholar finally looked properly at the fourteen muscle-men of Andreas Vesalius's Fabrica in 1903. Each is drawn with the skin off and posed in an Italian countryside of hills, farm buildings and Roman ruins, and for 360 years readers had taken the scenery for decoration. What had everyone missed?
answer: The backgrounds join into continuous stretches of country
choices: The ruins are Paduan buildings that still stand today
The shadows in every plate fall at the very same hour
The backgrounds join into continuous stretches of country
The artist's signature is hidden in the masonry of one
context: Set the plates side by side - reversing some, because of the way a woodblock prints - and the landscapes run on from one to the next. Precision worth having: scholars count TWO panoramas, not one long strip. A six-plate series shows the Euganean Hills between Padua and Venice; an eight-plate series shows country near Padua with the ruins of old Roman baths. The popular version, all fourteen in a single continuous landscape, overstates it. In London in 1545 the surgeon Thomas Geminus copper-engraved forty of the plates without permission and stripped the backgrounds out as superfluous - he had no idea what he was cutting up. Sources: clinicalanatomy.com/mtd/665, 'The landscape panorama of Vesalius' muscle men'; nyamcenterforhistory.org on Geminus; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Humani_Corporis_Fabrica_Libri_Septem.

question: Andreas Vesalius, as the story is told, came on the body of an executed criminal chained to a roadside gibbet outside the walls of Louvain in 1536, the flesh gone and the bones still hanging together by their ligaments. He carried off the arms and legs at once, came back after curfew to break the chain and take the trunk, and boiled the bones in secret. Then he built his first skeleton and lied about where it came from. What did he claim?
answer: That he had brought the skeleton with him from Paris
choices: That a physician in Cologne had left it to him by will
That the town had made him a gift of the bones
That he had bought it from a dealer in Venice
That he had brought the skeleton with him from Paris
context: LEGEND FLAG. The core is well attested - Vesalius took bones from the Louvain gibbet and assembled a skeleton, and Fabrica Book I chapter 39 gives his own method for preparing one. The night climb, the broken chain and the lie come from later biographical retellings and vary between them, so hold those details as the story told about him rather than the record. Bodies were the bottleneck of the whole enterprise: from 1539 Marcantonio Contarini, a judge of the Paduan criminal court, supplied the bodies of executed criminals and would even delay an execution to suit the anatomist, which Vesalius confirmed himself in 1546. Sources: encyclopedia.com, 'Vesalius'; libapps.libraries.uc.edu, 'The Illustrated Human' biography; Standring, 'A brief history of topographical anatomy'.

question: On his own table at Padua, Andreas Vesalius cut apart the thick muscular wall between the two sides of the heart. In Galen's heart, blood seeped from the right chamber into the left through passages in that wall, the step the whole system rested on. What did Vesalius set down in the 1555 second edition of his anatomy, the Fabrica?
answer: That he could not see how any blood at all gets through it
choices: That he found no passages except in the newly dead
That he could force a bristle through only in young bodies
That he could not see how any blood at all gets through it
That he traced them lower in the wall than Galen had put them
context: Translators render the line differently - one version runs 'I have not seen even the most obscure passages by which the septum of the ventricles is pervious' - and the 1543 first edition already doubted the pores before 1555 stated the denial plainly, so take the sense rather than one exact wording. Publishing that a textbook's promised structure is simply NOT THERE is one of the hardest results an observer can report, and it left a hole where Galenic physiology needed a mechanism. William Harvey, who studied at the same university, published his account of the circulation in 1628; historians treat Vesalius's vascular work as clearing the ground for it, not as anticipating it. Sources: hekint.org, 'The revolution of Andreas Vesalius'; PMC4462973, Vesalius 500 years (cardiovascular); Garrison translation note, faculty.wcas.northwestern.edu.

question: Andreas Vesalius's Basel printer held on to the Fabrica's pear-wood blocks, cut by hand, until 1568. They passed to the Froben family and were carted from one city to the next for three centuries after that, and they could still take ink when a last folio of the plates was pulled from them. Then one night ended the run. What happened?
answer: A bombing raid set fire to the library holding them
choices: A bombing raid set fire to the library holding them
A stove fire in the press room took them mid-printing
A river flood filled the cellar and pulped them past use
A gang of looters burned them through a hard winter
context: On the night of 30 March 1944 a raid burned the University of Munich library where the blocks were stored, and they were destroyed. That made the 1934 printing - Icones Anatomicae, produced by the New York Academy of Medicine with the Bremer Press and the University of Munich - the last impressions ever taken from the original blocks. Four hundred years of survival, ended in one night. Sources: PubMed 28038492, 'The Andreas Vesalius woodblocks: a four hundred year journey from creation to destruction'; codex99.com/anatomy/45.

question: Jacobus Sylvius put out a book in 1551 calling his old student Andreas Vesalius a madman, twisting the name into Vaesanus. It had twenty-eight rebuttals point by point and named Galen the sole parent of anatomy. Against the fixes Vesalius made at the table, what did Sylvius argue?
answer: That the human body itself had changed since Galen's day
choices: That copyists had slipped the errors in over the centuries
That Vesalius had cut up criminals rather than sound men
That the pupil's own knife had spoiled the parts he cut
That the human body itself had changed since Galen's day
context: Sylvius also denounced 'that insolent and ignorant slanderer who has treasonably attacked his teachers'. Notice the shape of his defence: he did not claim Vesalius had measured badly. He claimed that if the corpse disagrees with the book, the corpse must have changed. The book was the fixed point and the evidence was the thing that had to bend - which is exactly the move a claim makes when it will not be tested. Anyone could open a body and check; nobody could check the ancients' Rome. Sources: encyclopedia.com on Jacques Dubois (Jacobus Sylvius); Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), 'Andreas Vesalius'; clinicalanatomy.com/mtd/727.

question: A magistrate ordered the dissection shown in the frontispiece of Andreas Vesalius's Fabrica. Over a hundred spectators pack three tiers, and Vesalius stands at the table with his hand inside the opened body. The body is a woman's, hanged at Padua, rope marks still on her neck. What was the magistrate having checked?
answer: Whether the pregnancy she pleaded to escape the rope was real
choices: Whether the pregnancy she pleaded to escape the rope was real
Whether the hangman had botched the drop and killed her slowly
Whether the poison she was convicted of using was in her still
Whether the woman hanged was the woman named in the sentence
context: The woman had been executed at Padua after falsely claiming to be pregnant to escape her sentence, and the magistrate ordered the autopsy to test the claim. So the picture announcing the new anatomy shows a body opened to settle a question of fact, which is the argument of the whole book drawn in one scene. The rest of the plate argues the same way: Vesalius is down off the professor's raised chair with his own hand in the body, and the barber-surgeons are pushed underneath the table with their razors idle. Chained down in the crush are a live dog and a live monkey; scholars who read the plate take those for the animals the old anatomy was actually built on, though nothing in the picture labels them. Sources: pelviperineology.org, 'The frontispiece of Vesalius' Fabrica'; grokipedia.com/page/Galen (via search snippet); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Vesalius.

question: A girl steps outside on a cold morning and goosebumps rise on her arms. Tiny muscles under the skin, called arrector pili, pull each hair up straight. In a furry animal, what is this reflex actually for?
answer: Trapping a layer of warm air and puffing the animal up bigger
choices: Trapping a layer of warm air and puffing the animal up bigger
Cooling the animal by lifting the coat off the skin
Signalling to nearby predators that the animal is diseased
Draining excess sweat outward along the hair shafts
context: You kept the muscles and the sympathetic wiring on skin that no longer has a coat, so it doesn't warm you and it doesn't scare anyone. That is exactly what 'vestigial' means. Source: Wikipedia (Vestigial response); Biology Insights (Arrector Pili Muscle).

question: A doctor studies a human embryo at about week five or six of pregnancy, still smaller than a bean, and finds a body part longer than the tiny leg buds beside it. By about week eight it is usually gone again, reabsorbed back into the body. What did the embryo grow, and what does it leave behind in the adult body?
answer: A tail, which is reabsorbed leaving the fused coccyx
choices: A tail, which is reabsorbed leaving the fused coccyx
A gill slit, which fuses to form the eustachian tube
A yolk stalk, which resorbs leaving the umbilical ring
A pineal stalk, which retracts leaving the pituitary stem
context: Most of the tail vertebrae are cleared by programmed cell death (apoptosis) and the remaining segments fuse into the coccyx. In rare cases the tail persists to birth. Source: Jacob et al. 2014; Science Alert.

question: A surgeon takes a diseased coccyx out of a patient and finds no loose nub. Strong sheets of muscle and ligament are anchored to that small bone at the base of the spine, and they have to be cut free with care. What are those tissues doing for the patient?
answer: Forming the pelvic floor that supports the bladder and bowel
choices: Forming the pelvic floor that supports the bladder and bowel
Pumping venous blood back up the spinal column to the heart
Storing marrow that makes the body's red blood cells
Sensing balance signals feeding into the inner ear
context: 'Vestigial' means a structure has lost its ANCESTRAL job (being a tail), not that it has no job today. Whale pelvic bones anchor reproductive muscles, and python 'spurs' are used in mating -- all vestigial, none useless. Source: Wikipedia (Vestigial structure).

question: Robert Wiedersheim, a German anatomist, listed dozens of human organs in his 1893 book The Structure of Man that he claimed had no job, or only a partial one: the appendix, the tonsils, the pineal gland and many more. He called them 'vestigial', left over from animal ancestors. What did biology do with his list over the next century?
answer: Shrank it as most of the organs turned out to have jobs
choices: Shrank it as most of the organs turned out to have jobs
Grew it as more and more useless organs were catalogued
Threw it out because Wiedersheim was a discredited fraud
Left it exactly as Wiedersheim wrote it into the 21st century
context: The spleen was dismissed as vestigial into the 1950s and is now known to filter blood and mount immune responses. Wiedersheim's original list ran to about 86 organs; later editions grew to about 180 -- and most got quietly crossed out as anatomy caught up. Source: Wikipedia (Wiedersheim); Encyclopedia (Vestigiality).

question: Heather Smith's team mapped the appendix across the mammal family tree, and the strongest evidence against calling it a leftover with no job came from that tree and not from anatomy. What did they find that an organ with no job would never do?
answer: It has evolved independently at least thirty separate times in mammals
choices: It has evolved independently at least thirty separate times in mammals
It appears only in placental mammals with a diet of tough leafy plants
It shrinks in exact proportion to the length of the small intestine
It is genetically identical in every mammal species that carries one
context: Nobody re-invents a useless organ thirty-odd times. Smith's group also found the appendix has been lost only a handful of times. That is the fingerprint of an adaptive structure, not a leftover. Source: Smith et al. 2013 (C. R. Palevol); Smith et al. 2017.

question: A boy presses his thumb to his little finger and lifts his palm, and a thin cord, the palmaris longus, stands up in his forearm. About one person in seven has no such cord, and grip strength is the same either way. What do surgeons often do with it?
answer: Take it out to use as a graft elsewhere
choices: Take it out to use as a graft elsewhere
Shorten it to steady a loose wrist joint
Cut it to ease a stiff, aching wrist
Stimulate it to test the nerves of the hand
context: Because the cord is dispensable, surgeons harvest the palmaris longus for tendon grafts, using it to rebuild damaged tendons elsewhere in the body. It is one of the cleanest at-home checks for a vestigial structure: missing in about one person in seven, and nobody's grip suffers for it. Source: Britannica, 'Palmaris longus'; Everything Lowercase.

question: A team at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) followed embryos of Astyanax mexicanus, a fish of the dark caves of Mexico, as they started making normal eyes, with lens, retina and all. Then each eye was taken apart before the fish hatched. Which cause did the team pin the loss on?
answer: The lens undergoes massive apoptosis and skin grows over the shrunken eye
choices: The lens undergoes massive apoptosis and skin grows over the shrunken eye
The eye stops growing while the rest of the skull enlarges around it
Pigment cells fail to migrate to the eye, leaving it non-functional
The optic nerve fails to connect and the eye is reabsorbed as sightless tissue
context: The embryo runs the ancestral eye-building program and then dismantles it -- exactly what evolution predicts when eyes stop being selected for in permanent darkness. Ostriches and emus tell the same story with reduced wing bones and a shrunken keel. Source: NIH News 2018; UMD News 2018.

question: Yuri Gagarin, a Soviet air-force pilot, became the first human being to reach space on 12 April 1961, riding his capsule, Vostok 1, once around the Earth in 108 minutes. Something about his landing stayed a Soviet secret for the next ten years. What was it?
answer: he was not inside the spacecraft when it hit the ground
choices: he was not inside the spacecraft when it hit the ground
he touched down thousands of kilometres off target
he splashed into the Pacific rather than on Soviet soil
he landed hours later than the schedule had promised
context: At about 7 km altitude Gagarin was ejected from the descent module and came down under his own parachute; the empty capsule landed on its own chute nearby. This was the DESIGNED landing mode -- Soviet engineers had never developed a soft-landing system a person could survive inside -- but it was concealed because the Federation Aeronautique Internationale, the body that certified aviation and space records, required the pilot to land with the craft. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1 ; https://www.amusingplanet.com/2021/04/why-soviet-union-lied-about-yuri.html

question: Alan Shepard and later John Glenn came home from space in American Mercury capsules in the early 1960s, splashing down in the Atlantic Ocean, where a Navy ship fished the capsules out. The Soviet Vostok 1 capsule that had carried Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space, came home very differently. How did the Vostok 1 capsule itself come home?
answer: under its own parachute onto dry Soviet land
choices: under its own parachute onto dry Soviet land
on retro-rockets braking to a hover just above the ground
on a set of shock-absorbing landing skids like an aircraft
on inflated airbags that cushioned a hard bounce
context: Vostok's descent module carried its own parachute and floated down separately from Gagarin, hitting Soviet farmland fairly hard -- the reason engineers had planned pilot ejection at 7 km in the first place. Mercury's blunt cone splashed at sea for a Navy pickup; the American programme ran soft-water landings for years before switching to land landings with the Space Shuttle. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury

question: Engineers locked the cockpit's flight controls for the whole of Vostok 1's flight, since neither they nor the doctors were sure a human mind would function normally in weightlessness. A three-digit code that would unlock them was sealed in an envelope aboard the cabin. Which single system flew the spacecraft instead?
answer: the automatic programme with ground command
choices: the automatic programme with ground command
a purely mechanical clockwork timer
a live radio link to a chase plane
an onboard analogue computer set by dial
context: Vostok 1 was flown entirely by its onboard automatic sequencer with backup commands from ground stations, exactly because the medical staff would not commit to Gagarin thinking clearly in orbit. The sealed envelope was a fallback: if he found himself needing to steer, he could open it, read the code (most often reported as 1-2-5), and unlock manual attitude control. Engineers reportedly told him the digits ahead of time anyway. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1 ; https://spacedaily.com/t-for-the-first-space-flight-in-1961-soviet-engineers-locked-gagarins-manual-controls-behind-a-code-sealed-in-an-envelope-on-the-cabin-wall-because-they-were-not-sure-a-human-mind-would-function-in-orbit/

question: Yuri Gagarin fell back through the upper air in 1961 inside a small metal ball about two metres wide. Its heavy heat shield had to face the searing plasma of re-entry, or he would burn. The ball had to right itself in the airflow with no sensors, no computer and no steering thrusters. What one design choice let the sphere always fall heat-shield-first?
answer: the centre of mass was offset toward the heavy shield end
choices: the centre of mass was offset toward the heavy shield end
a spinning internal flywheel kept it pointed by gyroscopic force
a sacrificial nose cap ablated asymmetrically to nudge it around
a small tail fin trailed behind and dragged the shield forward
context: A sphere with the heavy end biased forward is passively self-righting: any tumble makes the aerodynamic torque swing the heavy end back into the airflow. That let the capsule reenter without a single thruster or attitude sensor. The price was a steep ballistic reentry -- concentrated deceleration on the pilot's chest -- but no attitude-control hardware to build or debug. Russian pilots nicknamed the capsule the sharik, 'little ball'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_(spacecraft)

question: Yuri Gagarin tumbled violently across half an orbit after Vostok 1's retro-rocket fired, because the equipment module failed to break cleanly away from his descent capsule. The two pieces stayed connected before finally coming apart. What had held them together?
answer: a bundle of wires that the main separation charge did not sever
choices: a bundle of wires that the main separation charge did not sever
a jammed docking latch that Gagarin punched open by hand
a frozen fuel line that snapped once the tanks warmed up
a stuck explosive bolt that a backup charge finally fired
context: The main separation mechanism fired but a cable bundle did not sever; the two modules stayed connected and the whole thing tumbled violently. Only as they hit the upper atmosphere over roughly Egypt did the wires finally burn through, letting the capsule right itself and reenter properly. The tumble did not injure Gagarin, but it was a real near-miss on the first crewed flight. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1 ; https://www.astronautix.com/v/vostok1.html

question: Friedrich Wöhler, a young German chemist in Berlin, sat down on 22 February 1828 and wrote an excited letter to his old Swedish teacher, Jöns Jakob Berzelius. He could not wait: Berzelius had not yet answered his last two letters. Something had happened at the workbench. What did Wöhler boast he could make?
answer: Urea, the main solid in urine — with no kidney of man or dog
choices: Urea, the main solid in urine — with no kidney of man or dog
Silk, the thread of fine cloth — with no worm of moth or spider
Lactose, the sugar of milk — with no udder of cow or goat
Gelatin, the jelly of bone — with no hide of ox or calf
context: Wöhler's words, from the manuscript held at the Center for History of Science, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences: 'I cannot, so to say, hold my chemical water and must tell you that I can make urea without the help of a kidney or even an animal, neither man nor dog. Ammonium cyanate is urea.' Translations differ — the Science History Institute renders the boast '...without needing a kidney, whether of man or dog.' He was writing from Berlin, where he lectured to industrial apprentices at the Gewerbeschule, a technical school, on about 400 thalers a year; he held a medical degree from Heidelberg and never practised medicine. Berzelius, his old teacher, was in Stockholm. Source: Yale Chem 125 (J. M. McBride) translation of the letter of 22 February 1828, chem125-oyc.webspace.yale.edu; Wikipedia, 'Friedrich Wöhler'.

question: Writing to Jöns Jakob Berzelius in 1828, Friedrich Wöhler named one small, ordinary thing as what had first set his urea experiment off. It was four years old and came from his student year in Berzelius's own Stockholm lab. What was it?
answer: A note in his own laboratory notebook, which he happened to reread
choices: A note in his own laboratory notebook, which he happened to reread
A jar of the old crystals, still sitting at the back of a cupboard
A remark of Berzelius's that he had copied onto a lecture card
A drawing of those crystals that he had pinned above his desk
context: Wöhler to Berzelius, 22 February 1828: 'Perhaps you still remember the experiment I carried out in that fortunate time when I was working with you, in which I found that whenever one tries to react cyanic acid with ammonia a crystalline substance appears which is inert, behaving neither like cyanate nor like ammonia. On leafing through my notebook this struck me again.' He had spent 1823-24 in Berzelius's Stockholm laboratory. A man rereading his own four-year-old lab note is what set the whole thing off — which is an argument for keeping a notebook. Source: Yale Chem 125 translation of the 22 February 1828 letter, chem125-oyc.webspace.yale.edu.

question: Jöns Jakob Berzelius sat down in Stockholm on 7 March 1828 to answer a letter from his former student Friedrich Wöhler, who boasted of making urea, a chemical from urine, in a dish with no living creature involved. Berzelius had argued since 1810 that living things run on a special 'vital force' that lifeless matter can never produce. How did he open his reply?
answer: With a joke: short supply could be topped up from the chamber pot
choices: With a joke: short supply could be topped up from the chamber pot
With a warning: the claim would be torn apart unless he repeated it
With a demand: he wanted the crystals sent to Stockholm at once
With a correction: he had made a salt, and not an animal substance
context: Berzelius, Stockholm, 7 March 1828: 'When one has begun his immortality with urine, there is every reason to end the trip to paradise in the same way... Aluminum and artificial urea, certainly two very different matters, following one another so closely, will, my Lord, be braided as jewels into your crown of laurels, and should the quantity of the artificial not suffice, one could easily make up the difference with a little from the chamber pot.' (The aluminium: Wöhler had isolated the first pure metallic aluminium on 22 October 1827.) Worth checking yourself — Grokipedia's 'Wöhler synthesis' article states that Berzelius 'initially responded with skepticism.' The letter itself does not support that. Source: Yale Chem 125 translation of the 7 March 1828 letter, chem125-oyc.webspace.yale.edu.

question: Friedrich Wöhler scraped a batch of white urea crystals out of a dish in his lab in 1828. Urea is now the most-produced synthetic organic compound on Earth, past 184 million tonnes in 2022, and not a tonne of it is made his way. Since 1922 the factories have all run the Bosch-Meiser process. What does that process start from?
answer: Ammonia and carbon dioxide
choices: Ammonia and carbon dioxide
Ammonia and limestone
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Hydrogen and carbon monoxide
context: The Bosch-Meiser process, patented in 1922, joins ammonia and carbon dioxide by way of ammonium carbamate, and it has supplied the world ever since — past 184 million tonnes in 2022, near 200 million tonnes in 2024. More than 90% of that goes out as nitrogen-release fertilizer, spread on fields to feed crops; the rest is scattered across many smaller uses. Wöhler's cyanate route survives only in the textbooks. Urea is still the main nitrogen-carrying substance in mammal urine, and it still melts at 132.4 C whether it came from a kidney, an evaporating dish, or a steel reactor. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Urea'; Grokipedia, 'Wöhler synthesis' (§Applications in Modern Synthesis).

question: Friedrich Wöhler mixed two lifeless chemicals, cyanic acid and ammonia, in a lab dish in 1828, and when the water dried out small white crystals were left at the bottom. Before he had run a single test on them he already had a guess, and he even printed it in his published paper. What did he expect the crystals to be?
answer: An organic substance, perhaps like the salt-forming bases of plants
