choices: An organic substance, perhaps like the salt-forming bases of plants
An inorganic salt, perhaps like the cyanates of lead and of silver
A vegetable acid, perhaps like the oxalic acid of the sorrel plant
An explosive salt, perhaps like the fulminates Liebig was studying
context: From the 1828 paper: 'I imagined that in the union of cyanic acid and ammonia there might be formed an organic substance, perhaps even a substance analogous to the vegetable salt-forming bases' — a plant alkaloid, in later language. He already knew from 1824 that the white crystals were not ammonium cyanate; the open question was what they were. One detail the textbooks get wrong: the standard telling has him mixing silver cyanate with ammonium chloride. Wöhler names two preparations and says the workhorse was the other one — 'By the latter method' (lead cyanate with ammonia solution) 'I have prepared a not insignificant amount of it for use in this investigation.' Source: Yale Chem 125 translation of Wöhler, 'On the Artificial Formation of Urea', Annalen der Physik und Chemie 88, 253-256, 1828.

question: Testing his crystals as a cyanate, Friedrich Wöhler got nowhere: no ammonia with caustic potash, no fizzing with acids, no lead or silver salts. Then nitric acid threw down bright flakes. Cleaned up again and again, the flakes tested sharply acidic, and he thought for a moment he had found a new acid of his own. What killed that idea?
answer: Neutralized with bases, the flakes gave plain nitrates and the old crystals back
choices: Neutralized with bases, the flakes gave plain nitrates and the old crystals back
Left to dry on the bench, the flakes went off with a crack, as fulminates do
Repeated with fresh crystals, the flakes could not be got a second time
Sent to Berzelius in Stockholm, the flakes were named an acid already known
context: From the paper: the nitric acid 'formed a precipitate of brilliant crystal flakes. After purification by repeated recrystallization, these crystals displayed a decidedly acidic character, and I was already inclined to consider them as a specific acid, when I found that they gave nitrate salts on neutralization with bases from which the crystalline material could be recovered.' A wrong guess, tested and dropped inside a single paragraph — that is what the method looks like from the inside. The failed cyanate tests are his words too: with caustic potash or lime the substance 'evolved no trace of ammonia', with acids it showed none of the ready decomposition of cyanate salts, 'and it even failed to give lead and silver salts as true cyanate salts do'. Source: Yale Chem 125 translation of the 1828 paper.

question: Friedrich Wöhler suspected the white crystals in his dish were urea, a chemical waste in urine that other chemists had been isolating and naming since the 1770s. Suspecting was not the same as proving, and no one in 1828 could see a molecule under any microscope. What did he do to settle whether his crystals really were urea?
answer: Isolated pure urea from urine and ran both through the same tests
choices: Isolated pure urea from urine and ran both through the same tests
Burned a sample and compared the elemental analysis with urea's
Grew bigger crystals and measured the angles between their faces
Sent a sample to Berzelius in Stockholm for a second opinion
context: From the paper: 'This similarity in behavior to urea led me to conduct analogous experiments with fully pure urea isolated from urine, with the completely unambiguous result that urea and this crystalline substance... are fully identical substances.' Many summaries — Grokipedia's among them — say he clinched it with an elemental analysis. His own letter says the opposite: 'I recently performed a small experiment... which I quickly completed and which, thank God, did not require a single analysis.' For composition he leaned on William Prout's published 1817 analysis of urea from urine and compared it with the calculated figures for ammonium cyanate. The identification rested on matched chemical behaviour, side by side. Urea had first been crystallized from human urine by Hilaire Rouelle in 1773; Fourcroy and Vauquelin gave it its name in 1799. Sources: Yale Chem 125 translations of the 1828 paper and letter; Wikipedia, 'Urea'.

question: Dissolving what he took to be ammonium cyanate, a plain lifeless salt, Friedrich Wöhler let the water evaporate in 1828. What crystallized out was urea, the very same chemical a living kidney makes. Chemists later worked out exactly what change the starting salt had gone through. What was that change?
answer: The atoms already there were rearranged; none was added or taken away
choices: The atoms already there were rearranged; none was added or taken away
One molecule of water joined on, as it does in most ammonium salts
Ammonia was driven off, and its nitrogen was taken up by the carbon
Two salt molecules joined into one, doubling the count of atoms
context: Ammonium cyanate NH4OCN and urea (NH2)2CO carry the same atoms in the same numbers — CH4N2O either way. Not a construction, a rearrangement. Wöhler had guessed as much in the letter, before there was a word for it: 'I supposed it possible that in combining cyanic acid with ammonia the elements might have come together in a different way, albeit in the same proportion.' Berzelius introduced the term isomerism for the phenomenon around 1830, from the Greek isos, 'equal', and meros, 'part'. One caveat about Wöhler's own printed page: in his 1828 notation he had to add an atom of water, 'as all ammonium salts contain water', so his formulas do not read as the clean modern pair — the anhydrous statement came later. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Wöhler synthesis'; Wikipedia, 'Isomer'; Yale Chem 125 translations of the 1828 paper and letter.

question: Jöns Jakob Berzelius, who taught that a 'vital force' inside living matter keeps it running, wrote back to Friedrich Wöhler on 7 March 1828: 'It is a truly important and beautiful discovery that the doctor has made, and it gives me indescribable delight to hear of it.' He then named the one thing in it he thought most enlightening for future theory. What was it?
answer: That the salt nature vanished when acid and ammonia combined
choices: That the salt nature vanished when acid and ammonia combined
That a substance of the animal body was built from mineral stuff
That a vital force was no longer needed for living chemistry
That cyanic acid had shown a power nobody suspected in it
context: Berzelius, 7 March 1828: 'But now enough raillery... It is a truly important and beautiful discovery that the doctor has made, and it gives me indescribable delight to hear of it. It is a unique situation that the salt nature so entirely disappears when the acid and ammonia combine, one that will certainly be most enlightening for future theory.' The founder of the vital-force doctrine was delighted — about salts. He does not mention vitalism at all, in this letter or in reply to the news. Source: Yale Chem 125 translation of the 7 March 1828 letter, chem125-oyc.webspace.yale.edu.

question: Friedrich Wöhler put the whole of what he published on his discovery into four pages of Poggendorff's Annalen for 1828, a paper called 'On the Artificial Formation of Urea'. Everything turns on how he closed it. What does the paper's final paragraph do?
answer: Declines to draw the conclusions that so naturally suggest themselves
choices: Declines to draw the conclusions that so naturally suggest themselves
Declares the doctrine of the vital force finished, and names Berzelius
Calls on chemists to make a living cell from mineral matter next
Claims priority over Liebig for this whole line of chemical work
context: The closing paragraph in full: 'I refrain from all the considerations which so naturally suggest themselves from this fact, especially in respect to the composition ratios of organic substances and in respect to similar elemental and quantitative compositions among compounds with very different properties, as may be supposed, among others, of fulminic acid and cyanic acid.' He steers the reader toward isomerism, not toward philosophy. What he did claim in print is exact and modest: the result is 'a noteworthy result in as much as it provides an example of the artificial production of an organic, indeed a so-called animal, substance from inorganic substances.' An example — not the end of vitalism, not the founding of organic chemistry. Sources: Yale Chem 125 translation of Wöhler, 'Ueber künstliche Bildung des Harnstoffs', Annalen der Physik und Chemie 88, 253-256, 1828; original scan at archive.org/details/ueberknstliche1221828whle.

question: Peter Ramberg, a historian of chemistry, traced the crusading version of the story, with Wöhler trying and trying to make something that would prove vitalism wrong until 'one afternoon the miracle happened', to a popular chemistry history from 1931. Wöhler's own paper had been in print since 1828 for anyone to check. Ramberg's 2000 study counted the organic-chemistry textbooks still handing students the crusading version. What share was that?
answer: Roughly nine in ten of them
choices: Roughly nine in ten of them
Roughly six in ten of them
Roughly three in ten of them
Roughly one in ten of them
context: Ramberg named it the 'Wöhler Myth' (Ambix 47, 2000). Wikipedia's summary of him: the 1931 popular history, 'ignoring all pretense of historical accuracy, turned Wöhler into a crusader who made attempt after attempt to synthesize a natural product that would refute vitalism and lift the veil of ignorance, until "one afternoon the miracle happened".' The author of that 1931 book is not named in the sources used here, so no name is claimed for it. You can watch the myth still running, in one sitting: Wikipedia's 'Organic chemistry' article says of 1828 that 'the event is now generally accepted as indeed disproving the doctrine of vitalism', while Wikipedia's own 'Vitalism' article says 'contemporary accounts do not support the common belief that vitalism died when Wöhler made urea.' Same encyclopedia, opposite claims — go read both. And the calendar agrees with the second one: Hermann Kolbe made acetic acid from inorganic starting materials in 1845, Marcellin Berthelot repeated the feat for many compounds through the 1850s, and only by about 1931 had biologists almost unanimously given vitalism up. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Vitalism', 'Wöhler synthesis', 'Organic chemistry'; Grokipedia, 'Wöhler synthesis' (§Criticisms and Reassessments).

question: Hans Krebs and his medical student Kurt Henseleit traced how a mammal makes urea in 1932: six enzymes across four linked reactions, mostly in the liver, the first metabolic cycle anyone had ever mapped. Friedrich Wöhler had got urea out of a dish of salts a century before. Two later researchers comparing that cycle with his dish pointed to the one feature that gives the living version its almost vitalistic look. Which feature?
answer: Its steps are split between the mitochondria and the cell fluid
choices: Its steps are split between the mitochondria and the cell fluid
Its enzymes are torn down and rebuilt before every single pass
Its reactions run only inside a cell that is still alive and whole
Its products pass straight into the kidney and never the blood
context: Krebs and Henseleit's ornithine cycle, 1932, was the first metabolic cycle ever discovered. It runs mostly in the liver across six enzymes, with one reaction inside the mitochondria and three out in the cytosol, the fluid filling the cell. Kinne-Saffran and Kinne argue that the cycle's apparently vitalistic character 'is caused by the compartmentalization of the various enzymatic reactions in mitochondria and cytosol, respectively' — the mystery is architecture, not a special force. Chemistry and biology are continuous; that does not make them identical. A closing note on the man: Wöhler pulled the first pure metallic aluminium out of its chloride in 1827 and isolated beryllium and yttrium in 1828, and in 1857 fragments of the Kaba meteorite, which fell on a Hungarian town on 15 April that year, were sent to him. He analysed the stone for two straight years. It became one of the first meteorites in which organic material was detected — 2% carbon by weight. The man who made an 'animal substance' out of salts went on to find organic matter in a rock from space. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Urea cycle'; E. Kinne-Saffran & R. K. H. Kinne, 'Vitalism and Synthesis of Urea: From Friedrich Wöhler to Hans A. Krebs', Am. J. Nephrol. 19(2):290-294, 1999; Wikipedia, 'Kaba meteorite', 'Friedrich Wöhler', 'Beryllium'.

question: Andrew Wakefield published a paper in The Lancet on 26 February 1998 describing twelve children, and hinted that the combined measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine might be linked to autism. The paper's own careful note, that it did not prove any such link, was drowned out by something that broke into the news the very same day. What blew the story up into a national panic in Britain?
answer: a press conference where Wakefield urged parents to switch to three single vaccines
choices: a press conference where Wakefield urged parents to switch to three single vaccines
a Cabinet Office briefing to health ministers, leaked to reporters that afternoon
a mass mailing of the paper to every general practitioner in Britain
a BBC Panorama investigation broadcast the same evening
context: The Royal Free's own PR film described the twelve-child work as a breakthrough. Wakefield's spoken recommendation went far beyond his printed paper. Source: Vaccinating Britain, NCBI Bookshelf; contemporaneous BBC news coverage.

question: Kreesten Madsen answered a twelve-child case series with no committee ruling but a much bigger test, a Danish study in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2002. It followed every eligible child born in Denmark from 1991 to 1998 and reported no association with autism. Roughly how many children was that?
answer: about half a million
choices: about half a million
about eighty thousand
about two hundred thousand
about fifty thousand
context: The exact number was 537,303, followed for more than two million child-years. The study found no association between MMR and autism. Source: Madsen et al., NEJM 347:1477 (7 November 2002).

question: Brian Deer, a Sunday Times reporter, started digging into Andrew Wakefield's finances in 2003. He found that since February 1996, two years before the 1998 Lancet paper, Wakefield had been paid 150 pounds an hour by a party preparing to sue over the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Who was paying him, and where did the money come from?
answer: Richard Barr, a UK solicitor building a lawsuit funded by the Legal Aid Board
choices: Richard Barr, a UK solicitor building a lawsuit funded by the Legal Aid Board
the American law firm Kirkland and Ellis, funded by a US class action
a UK parents' group that had pooled donations for a private prosecution
a rival British firm of solicitors funded by their own MMR claimant panel
context: The Legal Aid Board granted Barr 55,000 pounds in August 1996 to fund the clinical work. By 2006 Deer had documented 435,643 pounds paid to Wakefield through the litigation, none of it disclosed to The Lancet or its readers. Source: briandeer.com, Sunday Times exposure files.

question: Andrew Wakefield filed a patent in the years before his 1998 Lancet paper on the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine and autism. It later came out that lawyers preparing to sue vaccine makers on behalf of parents were paying him, and the patent was a second undisclosed interest that would have raised alarms at any medical journal. What was the patent for?
answer: a rival single measles vaccine and a related 'transfer factor' product
choices: a rival single measles vaccine and a related 'transfer factor' product
a laboratory test for detecting measles virus in gut biopsy tissue
a dietary supplement to be sold to parents of autistic children
an autism screening questionnaire for use in general practice
context: If parents dropped the combined shot for three separate single vaccines -- which Wakefield had recommended at the press conference -- the market for exactly the kind of product he had patented would open up. Source: Left Brain Right Brain, 'Andrew Wakefield's vaccine patent', 2010.

question: Fiona Godlee, editor of the British Medical Journal (BMJ), ran Brian Deer's line-by-line check of the 1998 Lancet paper in January 2011, setting its small case series against the real medical records of every child involved. What did the check show that made her call the paper 'an elaborate fraud'?
answer: five of the twelve children had developmental problems documented before their MMR shot
choices: five of the twelve children had developmental problems documented before their MMR shot
the histopathology grading of bowel biopsies had been altered to non-specific colitis
the reported time gap between MMR and symptoms had been shortened in eight of the twelve
the paper called the twelve consecutively referred when several were recruited through solicitors
context: Ten of Wakefield's twelve co-authors had already retracted the paper's interpretation in March 2004; The Lancet fully retracted the paper on 2 February 2010; the GMC struck Wakefield off the medical register on 24 May 2010. Source: BMJ, Brian Deer, 'How the case against MMR was fixed', January 2011.

question: Mr Justice Mitting took up John Walker-Smith's appeal in the High Court in March 2012. Walker-Smith, a paediatric gastroenterologist and the senior clinician on the 1998 paper, had been struck off the medical register alongside Andrew Wakefield. What did the judge do?
answer: quashed the GMC's findings against him and restored his name to the register
choices: quashed the GMC's findings against him and restored his name to the register
upheld the GMC's erasure and doubled the ban to a lifetime bar from medicine
sent the case back to the GMC for a second full hearing on the same charges
declined to hear the appeal on procedural grounds and left the erasure in force
context: Wakefield did not successfully appeal; Walker-Smith did. A disciplinary tribunal is not a laboratory, and can be wrong in either direction -- which is exactly why the load-bearing refutation of the MMR-autism claim is the counted evidence, not the erasure of a name. Source: Walker-Smith v General Medical Council [2012] EWHC 503 (Admin).

question: Andrew Wakefield held his press conference on the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in February 1998, though his paper had never survived a real test. Uptake in England stood at about 91.8% in 1996. To what low did it drop, before outbreaks followed in Yorkshire, Surrey, London and Cheshire?
answer: about 80% in 2003-04
choices: about 80% in 2003-04
about 88% in 2003-04
about 73% in 2003-04
about 65% in 2003-04
context: The precise low was 79.9% in 2003-04. That drop opened the door for measles to return. In no year between 1995 and 2001 had measles cases in England and Wales exceeded 177; from 2006 large outbreaks resumed, children were hospitalised, and some died. A claim that had never survived a test was paid for by people who never made it. Source: UK Parliament SN/SG/2581, 'Measles and MMR statistics', 2009.

question: Archaeologists have mapped some 500 Norse farm ruins around the roofless granite walls of Hvalsey Church, a metre and a half thick, on Greenland's southwest coast. The farms date from the four centuries the settlers held on. What did those farms keep?
answer: Cattle and sheep
choices: Cattle and sheep
Reindeer and musk oxen
Pigs and hunting hounds
Ponies and milk mares
context: European livestock farms in Greenland. The Eastern Settlement alone left roughly 500 groups of Norse farm ruins and 16 church ruins; the economy ran on sheep and cattle, with goats, plus some seal hunting, and the colony may have peaked at a few thousand people. Hvalsey Church - about 16 by 8 metres, holding 30 to 35 people, built in the Anglo-Norwegian style and thought to date to the early 1300s - is the best-preserved Norse ruin in Greenland. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hvalsey_Church; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Settlement

question: Hendrick Avercamp, a Dutch painter in the town of Kampen, took up a single subject from about 1608 and painted it over and over, the first in northern Europe to spend his entire career that way. Climate historians now read his art as a record of the Little Ice Age. What did Avercamp paint?
answer: Crowds of skaters on frozen canals
choices: Crowds of skaters on frozen canals
Fishing boats caught in winter gales
Villages buried under deep snowdrifts
Harvest fields flattened by hailstorms
context: Avercamp made winter 'ice scenes' his primary genre from about 1608, the first Northern Netherlandish artist to specialise in them systematically. Dutch winters in his lifetime averaged nearly 2 degrees C colder than modern norms, and those crowded frozen canals are among the Little Ice Age's most direct human records: a whole society out walking on ice that no longer forms. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Hendrick_Avercamp; grokipedia.com/page/Winter_Landscape_with_Skaters

question: A group of English friends, stuck indoors by cold rain at Lake Geneva in 1816, set each other a ghost-story challenge. Mount Tambora had blown up in Indonesia in April 1815, throwing so much sulfur into the sky that the next summer failed across the northern world. What came out of the challenge?
answer: Frankenstein and The Vampyre
choices: Frankenstein and The Vampyre
Dracula and The Raven
Wuthering Heights and Lamia
Faust and The Ancient Mariner
context: 'Eighteen hundred and froze to death', New Englanders called 1816. Tambora was a VEI 7 eruption that ejected at least 37 cubic km of rock; global temperatures fell 0.4 to 0.7 degrees C, frost struck in nearly every month across upland New England and New York, and Europe suffered its worst famine of the century. A second invention traces to the same year: with oats short and horses starving, the German inventor Karl Drais built the draisine, ancestor of the bicycle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer

question: John Evelyn watched coaches ply from Westminster to the Temple on the frozen Thames in the Great Frost of 1683-84, one of twenty-four winters the river froze right across between 1400 and 1831. The ice reached eleven inches thick and held for two months, with bull-baiting, horse races and puppet plays set up on it. A man named Croom took five pounds a day out there. What was he selling?
answer: Cards printed with the buyer's name and date
choices: Cards printed with the buyer's name and date
Roast ox carved off a fire built on the ice
Iron skates strapped onto the crowd's boots
Sledge rides along the length of the river
context: Croom hauled a printing press out onto the frozen Thames and sold souvenir cards carrying the customer's own name and the date, taking five pounds a day. Evelyn's diary catalogues the rest: 'sleds, sliding with skeetes, a bull-baiting, horse and coach races, puppet plays and interludes, cooks, tipling and other lewd places, so that it seemed to be a bacchanalian triumph.' The 1683-84 freeze sits inside the Maunder Minimum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames_frost_fairs

question: The Bishop of Geneva walked up the valley above Chamonix with about 300 people on May 29, 1644. The Glacier des Bois had been pushing downhill through the 1600s, and two small hamlets, Le Chatelard and Bonanay, had been wiped out. What had the Bishop's party come to do?
answer: Bless the ice and drive the spirits out of it
choices: Bless the ice and drive the spirits out of it
Say a mass over the hamlet buried beneath it
Plant a cross at the line the ice had reached
Carry the village church's relics down to safety
context: Villagers had already marched on the glacier in 1643, the year it destroyed Le Chatelard; two Chamonix residents alarmed the bishop, and his 1644 procession went up to bless the ice and drive out what locals took to be evil spirits living inside it. The glacier reached its maximum in the 1640s. Alpine glaciers hit their largest Holocene extent between about 1400 and 1850 - in Switzerland the Allalingletscher advanced far enough to dam the river Saaser Vispa and pond up the lake of Mattmark. Sources: chamonix.net, history of Chamonix glaciers; grokipedia.com/page/Little_Ice_Age

question: Icelanders carried the news home from Greenland, and that is the only reason the last surviving document from the Norse settlements, dated September 1408, survived. The Norse had lived there about four hundred years, with farms, churches and their own bishop, and then the written record simply stops. What does that final record describe?
answer: A wedding at Hvalsey Church
choices: A wedding at Hvalsey Church
A burial at Gardar cathedral
A cargo of tusks bound for Norway
A plea for grain sent to the king
context: On 14 or 16 September 1408 the Icelanders Thorsteinn Olafsson and Sigridur Bjornsdottir married at Hvalsey Church; two priests, Eindridi Andresson and Pall Halvardsson, had read the banns on three consecutive Sundays. Letters written back in Iceland - by a priest at Gardar and by several Icelandic witnesses - are why we know. The wedding party sailed home in 1410 on the last known voyage between Iceland and Norse Greenland, and after that there is silence. The date 1412, often quoted as the colony's last record, is not supported by the surviving documents. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hvalsey_Church; nunatsiaq.com, 'A wedding at Hvalsey Church'

question: Gilbert White, a naturalist in Hampshire, wrote that the sun at noon 'looked as blank as a clouded moon' after a fissure called Laki tore open in southern Iceland on 8 June 1783. It erupted for eight months, releasing some 120 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide and 8 million tonnes of fluorine. In Iceland the fluorine came down over the pastures where the sheep and cattle grazed. What did it do to them?
answer: It rotted their teeth and their bones
choices: It rotted their teeth and their bones
It blistered their mouths and tongues
It blinded them within a few weeks
It choked their lungs with ash and grit
context: Icelanders call the aftermath Modhuhardhindin, the 'Mist Hardships'. Fluorine poisoning rotted the animals' teeth and bones: 80% of the sheep died - 190,500 head - along with half the cattle and half the horses, and at least a fifth of Iceland's people died in the famine that followed. Benjamin Franklin noted that the haze over Europe was 'of a permanent nature; it was dry, and the rays of the sun seemed to have little effect towards dissipating it.' White logged 28 days of continuous frost that winter; an estimated 23,000 people died in Britain, and in North America the Mississippi froze at New Orleans. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki

question: A chemist tests the bones of Greenland's first Norse settlers for the carbon and nitrogen that food leaves locked in a skeleton, and about four-fifths of the diet comes back as farm food: beef, mutton, barley. She runs the same test on Greenlanders who died in the 1300s, and the reading has swung right over. What were they living on by then?
answer: Seal
choices: Seal
Cod
Reindeer
Whale
context: Carbon and nitrogen isotope work on Norse Greenlander skeletons shows the first settlers eating roughly 80% agricultural and 20% marine food; by the 14th century 50 to 80% of the diet came from the sea, chiefly seal. Read it both ways at once, because both are true: these were people adapting cleverly to their coast, and people eating seal because the cattle-and-barley life was failing. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Settlement; grokipedia.com/page/Norse_settlements_in_Greenland

question: Researchers ran ancient DNA on seven twelfth-century walrus tusks recovered at Kyiv. Walrus ivory was medieval Europe's luxury material, for chess pieces, crozier heads and reliquary panels, and a carved tusk tells nothing about where its animal was killed. Five of the seven traced back to one hunting region. Which?
answer: Western Greenland
choices: Western Greenland
Northern Russia
Arctic Norway
Eastern Svalbard
context: Five of the seven Kyiv specimens could be genetically assigned to a western Greenland origin, and were carved in the style typical of Greenlandic exports - a medieval trade route recovered from the DNA inside the tusk. The Norse held a near-monopoly on Europe's walrus ivory and hunted deep into the High Arctic, especially the North Water Polynya, and appear to have overharvested the herds. Sources: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6111184; grokipedia.com/page/Walrus_ivory

question: An ice-core team counts the yearly layers down a polar core and checks them against the sulfate line of Tambora in 1815. Every big eruption leaves such a layer, but it is faceless: the chemistry looks much the same no matter which mountain erupted. What else in the ice can be matched to one exact eruption?
answer: The ash shards
choices: The ash shards
The gas bubbles
The chlorine salts
The mercury traces
context: Volcanic ash - tephra - carries a chemical fingerprint characteristic of the volcano that erupted it, so a single shard in the ice can be matched to a mountain; the sulfate spike alone cannot. The highly conductive 1783 Laki sulfate horizon is a standard dating tie-point across Greenland cores from many locations, and Tambora's 1815 layer is the most prominent marker in West Antarctic cores. Sources: Annals of Glaciology, 'Laki and Tambora eruptions as revealed in Greenland ice cores from 11 locations'; geoinfo.nmt.edu ice-core research

question: A team of geologists set out in 2012 to find the year the Little Ice Age began, with no thermometers to ask. On Baffin Island the ice caps are shrinking back off ground they had covered for centuries, and the team gathered about 150 samples from the newly bared margins, radiocarbon-dating each one for a 'kill date', the year the advancing ice buried it. What were the samples?
answer: Plants still rooted where they grew
choices: Plants still rooted where they grew
Lichen still gripping the bare rock
Caribou bone still lying where it fell
Beetle shells still packed in the silt
context: Miller et al., 'Abrupt onset of the Little Ice Age triggered by volcanism and sustained by sea-ice/ocean feedbacks', Geophysical Research Letters, January 2012. About 150 radiocarbon-dated dead plants, collected with their roots still intact from beneath receding Baffin Island ice-cap margins, had been killed and buried where they grew - so each one dates the ice's arrival on that spot. The kill dates cluster at 1275-1300, with a second intensification at 1430-1455; the team argued that an unusual 50-year run of four massive tropical eruptions started the cold, with sea-ice and ocean feedbacks sustaining it. The largest of those, the 1257 'mystery eruption', was tracked down in 2013 to Samalas volcano on Lombok, Indonesia. Sources: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2011GL050168; pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1307520110

question: A student opens the telescope logbooks of about 1645 to 1715 and finds almost no sunspots: fewer than fifty in the 28 years to 1699, where a modern span that long would show forty or fifty thousand. The stretch is now known as the Maunder Minimum, and the Little Ice Age's coldest winters fall inside it. Why is the quiet Sun not enough to explain the cold?
answer: The cooling had begun before the Sun went quiet
choices: The cooling had begun before the Sun went quiet
A spotless Sun actually shines a little brighter
Sunspots change the Sun's light but not its heat
Nobody had logged sunspots before the gap began
context: The cooling began BEFORE the solar minimum, so the tidy solar story does not hold; the primary cause is believed to be volcanic activity. A spotless Sun is slightly dimmer, not brighter, because the bright patches called faculae that come with sunspots outweigh the dark spots, and the dip was perhaps 0.24 percent, roughly 0.82 watts per square metre averaged over Earth's surface: enough for about 0.1 to 0.3 degrees C of global cooling, against a Little Ice Age cooling of about 0.5 to 1 degree C. The Sun is part of this story, not the story - and one neat explanation should not be swapped for another. Telescopes had been logging sunspots since about 1610. The gap itself was dug out of the old logbooks by Gustav Sporer, who published in 1887 and 1889; Edward Walter Maunder wrote it up in 1890 and 1894; it then lay forgotten for most of a century until John A. Eddy revived it in a 1976 Science paper and gave it the name we use. Annie Russell Maunder did the sunspot-latitude research and received no public credit, women being barred from that recognition at the time. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maunder_Minimum; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cycle; swsc-journal.org, Space Weather and Space Climate 2017

question: Scientists of the Past Global Changes (PAGES) 2k consortium lined up proxy records (tree rings, corals, ice layers, lake mud) region by region across two thousand years in 2019. They were testing a disputed claim, that the medieval warm spell was a world event and not a North Atlantic one. Greenland ice cores and Sargasso Sea sediments both point to conditions about a degree C warmer around AD 1000. What did the consortium find about the timing of the warm and cold peaks?
answer: They land at different times in different regions
choices: They land at different times in different regions
They land in the same decades all over the world
They show up in the Northern Hemisphere only
They disappear once tree-ring records are dropped
context: PAGES 2k, 'No evidence for globally coherent warm and cold periods over the preindustrial Common Era', Nature 2019: the coldest century of the last millennium differs by region - the 15th in the central and eastern Pacific, the 17th in northwestern Europe and southeastern North America, the mid-19th elsewhere. The one exception to the patchwork is the 20th century, when warming shows up almost everywhere. The dispute is genuinely live, so hold it open: Grokipedia's Medieval Warm Period page reads multi-site tree-ring, ice-core and marine-sediment records as showing overlapping peak warmth around 950-1100 CE in both hemispheres - 'broad hemispheric coherence rather than isolated regional anomalies'. The IPCC's Third Assessment (2001) held that the evidence 'does not support globally synchronous periods of anomalous cold or warmth'. This bank does not claim the medieval period was globally warmer than today. What is not in dispute: the North Atlantic evidence for medieval warmth is strong - Hubert Lamb made that case in 1965 - and the climate swung hard, repeatedly, long before any smokestack. Sources: nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1401-2; grokipedia.com/page/Medieval_Warm_Period

question: A teacher tells the end of Norse Greenland as a clean climate parable: the world cooled, the farms failed, the colony died. The cooling was real, and it hurt. But historians who study the abandonment put a different pressure first, and say so flatly: not climate alone. Which pressure do they name as dominant?
answer: Economics: land opening at home, buyers falling away
choices: Economics: land opening at home, buyers falling away
Disease: plague brought in on the supply ships
Conflict: Thule Inuit hunters pressing down the coast
Isolation: Norway losing the ships that sailed there
context: More farmland was becoming available back in Scandinavia, and European demand for Greenland's exports was falling away - the walrus-ivory monopoly broke around 1200, when elephant ivory began arriving from Africa. Add overgrazing that eroded thin Arctic turf, walrus herds hunted out, and a diet swinging from beef to seal. Cooling was one genuine pressure among several, and the discipline runs both ways: a hard climate swing is not the whole explanation, and the cold did bite. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Warm_Period; science.org, 'Why did Greenland's Vikings disappear?'

question: A student takes Peter Wason's number game: she is told that the triple 2, 4, 6 fits a hidden rule, and she may test any triple for a yes or a no. She tries 8-10-12 (yes), 20-22-24 (yes), 100-102-104 (yes). Confident, she announces 'the rule is add two each time.' She is told: wrong. What was the rule?
answer: Any three numbers in increasing order
choices: Any three numbers in increasing order
Any three even numbers
Any three numbers that add to a multiple of six
Any three numbers where the middle one is the average
context: This is Peter Wason's 1960 2-4-6 task. Every triple you tested returned yes, because every triple you tested was ascending -- but so is 1-2-3 and 5-9-11, which you never tried. A string of yeses from tests that could never fail teaches you nothing. Source: P.C. Wason, 'On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task', Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1960.

question: Playing Peter Wason's 2-4-6 game, a student proposes triples of numbers and hears yes or no for each, trying to guess his secret rule. She has settled on 'add two each time' as her candidate. All four triples on offer are legal to try. Which is the strongest next test of her rule?
context: The winning move is a triple you EXPECT to be rejected. If 6-4-2 comes back 'no', direction matters. If it comes back 'yes', your rule is dead. The other three are all ascending sequences that 'add two each time' predicts a 'yes' for -- yeses that could never have been noes, and therefore teach nothing. This is the shape of a strong test. Source: Wason 1960; Nickerson, 'Confirmation Bias' review.

question: Peter Wason put four cards on a table for his second famous puzzle in 1966: 3, 8, blue, red. Each has a number on one face and a colour on the other. The rule: 'if a card shows an even number on one face, its opposite face is blue'. Which cards must a player turn over to test the rule?
answer: The 8 and the red card
choices: The 8 and the red card
The 8 and the blue card
The 3 and the blue card
Only the 8 card
context: The 8 checks whether an even number really is backed by blue. The red card is the ONLY other card that can break the rule -- if you flip it and find an even number, the rule is dead. Wason reported that fewer than one subject in ten picked correctly. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wason_selection_task.

question: A student at Peter Wason's card table reaches for the blue card. Four cards lie before her, red, blue, 8 and 3, each with a colour on one side and a number on the other, and the rule to test is 'If a card shows an even number, its other face is blue.' Almost every subject in his 1966 test wanted that card. Why is flipping it the classic wrong move?
answer: Whatever is on its back, the rule survives
choices: Whatever is on its back, the rule survives
It voids the experiment if flipped out of order
It matches two cards at once and is redundant
It always shows the number that started the rule
context: If the back of the blue card is even, the rule holds. If it is odd, the rule still holds -- the rule says only that even implies blue, not that blue implies even. The blue card is the confirmation trap: turning it can only add yeses, and yeses are exactly what the 2-4-6 game already showed you cannot trust. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wason_selection_task.

question: Griggs and Cox dressed the same logic as Florida drinking-age enforcement in 1982, with cards reading 'drinking beer', 'drinking coke', '16 years old' and '25 years old', and the rule 'if a person is drinking beer, the person must be over 19'. Peter Wason's abstract card task defeats roughly 90% of adult subjects. What happened to the success rate?
answer: It rose to about 74% -- roughly ten times the abstract score
choices: It rose to about 74% -- roughly ten times the abstract score
It stayed near 10%, because logic is logic
It fell close to zero, because the drinking rule was unfamiliar
It rose to exactly 100% in every published replication
context: The Florida rule is 'if P then Q', tested by checking P and not-Q -- the same conditional as the abstract card task. But 'catch the underage drinker' is a scene humans have circuits for; 'catch the even-backed non-blue' is not. Same logic, different context, ten times the accuracy. Source: Griggs & Cox, 'The elusive thematic-materials effect', Memory & Cognition 10(5), 1982.

question: Peter Wason watched people lose his 2-4-6 number game and his four-card task the same way: most kept testing cases that fit their guess. The two tasks teach one lesson about what a strong scientific test looks like. What separates a strong test from a worthless one?
answer: A strong test could have come out against the hypothesis; a worthless test could not
choices: A strong test could have come out against the hypothesis; a worthless test could not
A strong test uses larger numbers than a worthless test
A strong test involves at least three subjects; a worthless test involves one
A strong test always includes a control group; a worthless test never does
context: 'Add two each time', 'even numbers ascending' and 'the middle number is the average of the other two' all fit 2-4-6, and rules like these were announced by real Wason subjects. Their tests all came back yes and taught them nothing, because the tests could not come back no. A prediction that fits every result is not a prediction. Source: Wason 1960; Nickerson review.

question: Peter Wason ran a famous four-card puzzle in 1966 showing that people test their beliefs by looking for cases that would confirm them. The home version of his lesson is one sentence. Suppose you are about to argue for an idea in the world. What should you write down first?
answer: An observation, named in advance, that would make you drop the idea
choices: An observation, named in advance, that would make you drop the idea
The three closest experts who already agree with you
A list of previous cases where the idea worked
A friendly opponent's name to check the argument later
context: This is Wason's puzzle, aimed at yourself. If you cannot name an observation that would kill your idea -- a triple you EXPECT the world to answer 'no' to -- you are playing 2-4-6 alone, collecting yeses that could never have been noes. That habit is the difference between a scientist and a fan. Source: Wason 1960; Popper, 'Conjectures and Refutations', 1963.

question: A girl at home runs a five-minute test with two glasses. She drops an ice cube into water. Then she chills some olive oil in the fridge until a lump turns solid, and sets it into a glass of liquid olive oil at room temperature. Which way does each solid go?
answer: The ice floats and the solid oil sinks.
choices: The ice floats and the solid oil sinks.
The ice sinks and the solid oil floats.
Both the ice and the solid oil float.
Both the ice and the solid oil sink.
context: Almost every substance packs tighter when it solidifies, so its own solid sinks in it. As a fat melts its volume rises and its density therefore falls, which leaves solid fat crystals near 1.0 g/cm3 denser than the roughly 0.9 g/cm3 oil around them. Water is one of a small handful of substances that go the other way. Fair warning before you try it: olive oil begins solidifying somewhere around 37-50 F and thickens gradually into slush rather than forming a clean cube, so watch which way the solid parts drift instead of expecting a tidy sinking block. Sources: btsa.com, 'Physical properties of oils and fats'; centrafoods.com on solidified olive oil.

question: A boy drops a stone, a coin, a cork and an ice cube into a bucket of water. The stone and the coin sink, and the cork rides almost clear of the water. The ice floats too, but far lower than the cork. Roughly how much of a floating ice cube stands above the waterline?
answer: About a tenth of it.
choices: About a tenth of it.
About a third of it.
About half of it.
About three quarters of it.
context: Ice Ih measures 0.9167-0.9168 g/cm3 at 0 C against liquid water's roughly 1.00 g/cm3 -- about 8.3 percent less dense -- so a cube settles until only about a tenth of it clears the surface, and an iceberg does the same thing at ship-killing scale. Keep two numbers apart when you retell this: 8.3 percent is the DENSITY drop, while the VOLUME increase on freezing is about 9 percent. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice; grokipedia.com/page/Ice_crystal.

question: A cook slides a tray of water into the freezer, and as it freezes every water molecule locks onto exactly four neighbours, never three, never five. Nothing outside the molecule forces that count. Its own shape fixes it: one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, in a bent V. What about a single water molecule sets the number at four?
answer: It has two hydrogens on one side and two unshared electron pairs on the other.
choices: It has two hydrogens on one side and two unshared electron pairs on the other.
It has four unshared electron pairs on its oxygen, one aimed at each neighbour.
It has two hydrogens, each one able to hold two neighbours at once.
It has a bent frame with four open faces, one turned to each neighbour.
context: A hydrogen bond needs a donor and an acceptor. Water brings exactly two of each: two hydrogens it can offer, and two lone pairs -- unshared pairs of electrons -- on the oxygen that can receive. Four is the whole budget. A single hydrogen can donate only one such bond, and it takes a full PAIR of electrons to accept one, which is why the other counts do not work. The tetrahedral cage is not a design choice; it is arithmetic on a single molecule. In ice Ih those four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, with neighbouring oxygens about 2.75 angstroms apart. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water ('a maximum of four hydrogen bonds'); grokipedia.com/page/Hydrogen_bond; grokipedia.com/page/Ice_crystal.

question: A child watches a puddle freeze on a winter morning. Most liquids pack in tighter as they cool, and the solid comes out denser than the liquid was. Water does the opposite: the locked frame takes more room than the liquid did, its oxygen atoms a fixed distance apart in one repeating pattern. What pattern?
answer: Six-sided rings, with an oxygen at every corner.
choices: Six-sided rings, with an oxygen at every corner.
Cubes packed corner to corner, as in table salt.
Long parallel chains, like a bundle of threads.
Flat stacked sheets, like the layers in graphite.
context: Ice Ih is a hexagonal crystal: the oxygens sit at the vertices of open six-membered rings about 2.75 angstroms apart (lattice parameters a = 4.52 A, c = 7.36 A near 0 C; space group P6-3/mmc, a wurtzite-like oxygen lattice). That rigid cage holds the molecules further apart than the jostling liquid does. One cage, two famous consequences -- the float, and the six arms on every snowflake, which inherit the lattice's six-fold rotational axis. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ice_crystal; grokipedia.com/page/Snowflake; Kenneth Libbrecht, 'Snow Crystals', arxiv.org/pdf/1910.06389.

question: A plumber watches a drop hang from a tap before it falls, held by water's surface, which acts like a stretched skin. That pull is about 72 millinewtons per metre, well above the 20 to 40 of alcohol or cooking oil. Only one everyday liquid beats water, and it wins by nearly seven times. Which one?
answer: Mercury.
choices: Mercury.
Glycerine.
Liquid nitrogen.
Molten candle wax.
context: Mercury reaches about 485 mN/m, held together by strong metallic bonding between its atoms. Water's own 71.99 mN/m at 25 C is the outlier among ordinary molecular liquids, and the cause is the same hydrogen-bond network that floats ice: organic liquids get only weak van der Waals attraction and land at 20-40 mN/m. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water; grokipedia.com/page/Surface_tension.

question: A walker crosses a northern lake in February on a lid of ice, and underneath her the water is still liquid and the lake is still alive. Now suppose ice were the ordinary sort of solid, heavier than its own liquid. What would that lake do each winter instead?
answer: Fill from the bottom up and freeze solid, with nothing left alive in it.
choices: Fill from the bottom up and freeze solid, with nothing left alive in it.
Grow its lid downward twice as fast, with fish still wintering below it.
Stay ice-free all winter as sinking ice melted at depth, with its fish fine.
Freeze through in a single night, killing every living thing before dawn.
context: Floating ice 'prevents bottom-up freezing of the bodies of water', creating a sheltered environment for the life underneath. Wikipedia's counterfactual is blunt: if water were most dense at its freezing point, winter cooling at the surface would drive convective mixing all the way down and 'all life in it would be killed'. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water.

question: A runner finishing in August is drenched, and the sweat sitting on her skin has cooled her almost not at all -- it cools only as it leaves. Evaporating a single litre of sweat carries roughly 580 kilocalories off the body. What is that energy spent on?
answer: Snapping the hydrogen bonds that tie each molecule to its neighbours.
choices: Snapping the hydrogen bonds that tie each molecule to its neighbours.
Breaking the oxygen-hydrogen bonds inside each escaping molecule.
Heating the sweat the rest of the way up to its boiling point.
Pushing the surrounding air aside as the new vapour expands.
context: Water's heat of vaporisation is 40.65 kJ/mol, or 2257 kJ/kg at the normal boiling point: a molecule cannot leave the liquid until its hydrogen bonds to the neighbours are broken, and that bill is paid in heat taken from your skin. The bonds inside each molecule are untouched -- the vapour is still water. Thermodynamic measurement at body conditions puts the latent heat near 2,430 J/g at 30 C and 2,415 J/g at 37 C. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water; Ashworth et al., 'Sweat evaporation in humans: A molecular and thermodynamic perspective', Experimental Physiology.

question: Johannes Kepler, imperial astronomer in Prague and badly behind on his salary, could not afford a New Year's gift for his patron in January 1611. He wrote a small book instead, asking why every snowflake is six-cornered. Three centuries before anyone could see the lattice, he had to guess. What did he propose?
answer: The hexagon is one of the few shapes that tiles a surface with no gaps.
choices: The hexagon is one of the few shapes that tiles a surface with no gaps.
Six is the smallest number of arms a falling crystal can balance on.
Cold air currents spin the falling droplets into six-armed pinwheels.
Each flake grows on a speck of dust that has six flat faces to build on.
context: Kepler's book was 'Strena Seu De Nive Sexangula' -- 'A New Year's Gift, On the Six-Cornered Snowflake' -- and the question inside it was genuinely new. His packing guess reached for the right KIND of answer with three centuries too little equipment: the real one had to wait for X-ray crystallography to show the hexagonal ice lattice. The Charles Bridge walk and the phrase 'all with six corners and feathered radii' come from the traditional telling of the episode, so treat those details as story rather than record. Sources: keplersdiscovery.com; Kepler, 'The Six-Cornered Snowflake', Oxford University Press; softbites.org.

question: A homeowner finds a burst copper pipe inside the wall after a hard night's freeze, with water pouring through the drywall. Every plumber gives the same warning before such a night: leave one tap open, just a trickle running all night. Ice will still form somewhere in the pipe, and water still expands about 9% when it freezes. Why does that thin trickle keep the pipe whole?
answer: It gives the water squeezed between the ice and the tap an escape.
choices: It gives the water squeezed between the ice and the tap an escape.
It keeps the water moving fast enough that it cannot freeze at all.
It draws warmer water up from the main into the cold stretch of pipe.
It bleeds air out of the line so the pipe cannot pressurise at all.
context: Freezing pipes fail hydraulically, not by ice shoving the pipe wall. The growing ice plug blocks the pipe; the liquid trapped between that plug and a closed tap then keeps getting squeezed as more ice forms, and pressure climbs from about 35 psi to over 4,000 psi until the pipe lets go -- typically in the unfrozen stretch downstream. An open trickle gives that trapped water somewhere to go. Sources: jlconline.com, 'Understanding how water pipes freeze' (Journal of Light Construction); randrmagonline.com on water dynamics in frozen-pipe damage.

question: An angler drills through the ice of a frozen pond in January and lowers a thermometer on a string. Almost every liquid gets denser as it cools, right down to freezing, so its coldest part sinks to the bottom. Where in the pond does he find the coldest liquid water?
answer: Just under the ice, at the top
choices: Just under the ice, at the top
Lying on the bottom, in the mud
Spread evenly from top to bottom
In a band about halfway down
context: Liquid water is densest at 3.98 C -- Grokipedia gives the modern refinement as 3.98 plus or minus 0.0005 C at 1 atm. That anomaly is what makes the winter lid possible: as a pond cools past that point the coldest water is no longer the heaviest, so it stops sinking, stays on the surface, and freezes there. It also writes the lake's whole calendar. In autumn the chilled surface keeps sinking until the entire column sits at that temperature and goes uniform, and for a few days a moderate wind can then stir the lake top to bottom -- the 'fall turnover' that carries oxygen down to the deep water and lifts nutrients off the sediment. All winter the lake then runs upside down: near-freezing water on top, densest water resting on the bottom. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water; grokipedia.com/page/maximum_density; iisd.org/ela on lake stratification and turnover.

question: A chemist holds up a glass of water with two very different bonds at work in it. One is the covalent O-H bond inside a single molecule, holding its own hydrogens on. The other is the hydrogen bond reaching from one molecule to the next, the link that floats ice, lifts water's boiling point and keeps the oceans liquid. Which of the two is stronger, and by roughly how much?
answer: The covalent bond, by about twenty times.
choices: The covalent bond, by about twenty times.
The hydrogen bond, by about twenty times.
The covalent bond, by about twice.
The hydrogen bond, by about twice.
context: A hydrogen bond in liquid water is worth about 23 kJ/mol; the covalent O-H bond inside the molecule runs about 492 kJ/mol -- roughly 21 times stronger. The bond that makes the planet habitable is the WEAK one, about a twentieth the strength of the bond holding the molecule itself together, and it does the job only because every molecule makes four of them at once and they work as a network. Sources: Martin Chaplin, 'Water's Hydrogen Bond Strength', arxiv.org/pdf/0706.1355; water.lsbu.ac.uk on water hydrogen bonding.

question: A chemistry class draws a line through the boiling points of water's three cousins in the periodic table: hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen selenide and hydrogen telluride. They boil colder and colder as their molecules get lighter. Water is the lightest of the four, so the line predicts a boiling point far below zero. It boils at 99.98 C instead. By roughly how much are hydrogen bonds lifting it above the prediction?
answer: About 180 degrees.
choices: About 180 degrees.
About 120 degrees.
About 250 degrees.
About 300 degrees.
context: Extending the trend puts water's 'expected' boiling point far below zero, but the exact figure depends on how you draw the line: the University of Calgary textbook says about -80 C, other extrapolations reach -100 C, and extending the H2Te-H2Se line down to period 2 gives -130 C. Nobody has measured it -- treat the prediction as an estimate and the gap as roughly 180 degrees. The three cousins have no hydrogen bonding at all; they are held together only by London dispersion forces, which strengthen with molecular size, which is exactly why their boiling points rise down the group in the ordinary way while water's leaps out of line. Without that lift there would be no liquid water anywhere on Earth's surface. Sources: chem-textbook.ucalgary.ca on hydrogen bonding; docbrown.info; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water.

question: Engineers gave the James Webb Space Telescope a main mirror 6.5 metres across, wider than the payload bay of any rocket ever built. An Ariane 5 rocket lifted Webb off the pad at Kourou in French Guiana on 25 December 2021, and there was only one way to get the mirror into space. How did Webb fly?
answer: folded up, with the outer wings hinged back
choices: folded up, with the outer wings hinged back
in three launches, to be bolted together in orbit
wrapped around the outside of the rocket in strips
as loose panels for the crew to assemble on site
context: Webb launched aboard an Ariane 5 from French Guiana on Christmas Day 2021 with three of the mirror's outer segments folded back like the wings of a hinged panel. Once clear of Earth it spent about two weeks unfolding on the way to its destination. Sources: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/fact-sheet/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope

question: Space shuttle astronauts flew up to the Hubble Space Telescope five separate times, installing corrective optics for its blurry mirror in 1993 and swapping out worn gyroscopes and old cameras on later trips. Hubble's successor, the James Webb Space Telescope, was built on a very different rule from the start. What was that rule?
answer: no one would ever be able to service it
choices: no one would ever be able to service it
it would be brought home for repair every ten years
it would be replaced by a twin already on order
it would fix itself with onboard maintenance robots
context: Webb sits about 1.5 million km from Earth at the Sun-Earth L2 point, roughly four times as far as the Moon and far beyond the reach of any current crewed vehicle. Every mechanism on the observatory had to work without a possible repair mission. Sources: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope

question: Engineers walked step by step through the setup of the James Webb Space Telescope and counted every step that had no backup, no spare and no way to rescue it if it failed. Its 6.5-metre mirror and tennis-court-sized sunshield had to fly folded, with hinges to swing open, cables to release and five sunshield layers to stretch tight. What number did they arrive at?
answer: 344 single-point failures
choices: 344 single-point failures
12 single-point failures
about 1,800 single-point failures
roughly 40 single-point failures
context: The famous count -- 344 -- included latch releases, motor drives, spring hinges, cable spools, and the tensioning cords on the sunshield. About 80 percent of the 344 were tied to the deployment sequence; roughly 140 release mechanisms and 400 pulleys supported the sunshield alone. Every one of the 344 worked. Sources: https://interestingengineering.com/science/james-webb-has-344-single-point-failures-here-are-the-5-most-critical-elements ; https://keeptrack.space/deep-dive/jwst

question: The designers of the James Webb Space Telescope shaped the whole observatory around one strict demand. It was built to catch the faint light of the very first galaxies, stretched over billions of years from visible light into infrared waves that human eyes cannot see. Why did the telescope itself have to be kept extremely cold?
answer: a warm telescope glows in the same infrared band it is trying to observe
choices: a warm telescope glows in the same infrared band it is trying to observe
a warm mirror coating would slowly tarnish and lose its gold shine
a warm fuel tank would boil away the steering propellant
a warm instrument bay would overheat and shut down for safety
context: Anything warm radiates in the infrared. A room-temperature telescope trying to observe the infrared is like a floodlit stadium trying to observe candles -- the observatory's own emission is brighter than the signal. Webb has to be actively kept cold, which is why the sunshield, the L2 orbit and even MIRI's mechanical refrigerator all exist. Source: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/

question: The builders of the James Webb Space Telescope made a kite-shaped sunshield roughly the size of a tennis court from five separate layers of Kapton foil, each thinner than a human hair, held apart with empty space between them. It is not thick insulation. How do those five layers get rid of the Sun's heat?
answer: each layer catches some warmth and re-radiates it out the side
choices: each layer catches some warmth and re-radiates it out the side
the whole sandwich mirrors nearly all sunlight back at the Sun
the layers store warmth in the day and dump it during eclipses
a coolant pumped between the layers carries the warmth off to vent
context: Each Kapton layer, coated with aluminum and doped silicon, catches some incoming warmth and radiates it away edgewise rather than passing it to the layer behind. The temperature falls in five steps, from about 110 degrees C on the sun-facing side to roughly minus 233 to minus 235 degrees C on the telescope side -- a drop of over 300 degrees across five sheets of foil in space. Sources: https://jwst.gsfc.nasa.gov/content/observatory/sunshield.html ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.04869

question: Engineers set out to teach the mirror hexagons of the James Webb Space Telescope to act as one, once it was unfolded. They pointed it at one bright reference star in Ursa Major and looked at what came back. What did the very first alignment image show?
answer: eighteen separate images of the same star, one per segment
choices: eighteen separate images of the same star, one per segment
one perfectly focused star, sharper than expected
a total blank -- the sensor had not been powered on
a smear of light with no distinct star at all
context: Every mis-tilted segment reflected HD 84406 to a different spot on the detector, so the first mosaic showed eighteen ghost images of the same star scattered across the field. Over about three months tiny actuators moved each segment in fine steps of roughly 8 to 10 nanometres each until all eighteen images stacked into one crisp point. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HD_84406 ; https://www.universetoday.com/articles/heres-exactly-how-engineers-are-aligning-jwsts-segmented-mirrors

question: Engineers designed the James Webb Space Telescope with no possibility of a repair mission, but 'no repairs' is not the same as 'no damage'. One of its 18 gold-plated hexagonal mirror segments took a permanent hit between 22 and 24 May 2022, before its first science images had been released to the public. What hit it?
answer: a micrometeoroid larger than any pre-launch model predicted
choices: a micrometeoroid larger than any pre-launch model predicted
a stray fragment shed by the launcher's upper stage
a solar flare that briefly overheated the gold coating
a piece of orbital debris from a Russian satellite test
context: The particle struck segment C3 and left a local deformation Webb's actuators could reduce but never fully cancel; the segment's wavefront error jumped from about 56 to 258 nanometres RMS. There is no repair mission and there never will be, so the dent is part of the telescope for life. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/webb-telescopes-giant-mirror-struck-by-micrometeoroid/

question: Tom Jefferson and his team put out a Cochrane update on January 30, 2023, on ways to slow the spread of breathing viruses, pooling 78 studies and about 610,000 people. What phrase did the authors use for masks in public against no masks, for flu-like and COVID-like illness?
answer: Probably makes little or no difference
choices: Probably makes little or no difference
Cuts the illness roughly in half
Clearly helps adults but not children
Works only alongside a vaccine
context: 'Probably makes little or no difference' is verbatim from the authors' conclusions. It is a claim about the pooled trials, not about fabric physics. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36715243, factcheck.org.

question: Tom Jefferson's team asked a second question in their 2023 Cochrane review, which pooled randomised trials of masks against respiratory infection. When hospital workers do routine care, are they better protected by a fitted N95 respirator than by a plain surgical mask? A respirator stops more particles on a laboratory bench; routine care was a separate question. They pooled every trial that had put the two head to head. What did the authors report?
answer: No clear differences between the two
choices: No clear differences between the two
A large advantage for the N95 group
A clear win for the surgical-mask arm
Not one trial had ever compared them
context: 'No clear differences' is verbatim from the review. That is a claim about the pooled trials in routine care, and different from a bench filter test - bench tests DO show an N95 stops more particles. Source: cidrap.umn.edu, factcheck.org.

question: Researchers behind the trials in the 2023 Cochrane mask review randomised which villages, wards or households got the free masks and were asked to wear them. They then counted infections in each arm. Given that shape, what were those trials actually a test of?
answer: A recommendation to a population
choices: A recommendation to a population
The particle filtration of the cloth
One individual's own personal risk
How long the virus survives on fabric
context: The trials tested the intervention (asking people to mask) rather than the article (a mask on a face) - which is exactly what a mandate is. Adherence to the mask-wearing was often poor across the trials, and the authors said so in the paper. DANMASK-19 (Bundgaard 2020) and the Bangladesh trial (Abaluck 2022) both used this shape. Source: sciencebasedmedicine.org.

question: Karla Soares-Weiser, Editor-in-Chief of Cochrane, released a public statement on March 10, 2023. Within weeks of the January review of masks and breathing viruses, headlines had been reading it as saying 'masks don't work'. How did she describe that headline reading?
answer: Inaccurate and misleading
choices: Inaccurate and misleading
A fair summary of the paper
Supported by the plain-language text
A minority view within the field
context: Soares-Weiser also wrote the plain-language summary 'was open to misinterpretation, for which we apologize' and 'we take responsibility for not making the wording clearer'. The review's lead author answered back. Tom Jefferson told the journalist Maryanne Demasi that he had been given 'little workable notice' of the statement and that 'Cochrane has thrown its own researchers under the bus again'; the apology, he pointed out, was Cochrane's, not the authors'. The review itself was not withdrawn. Sources: cochrane.org statement, March 10, 2023; Maryanne Demasi, 'Did Cochrane sacrifice its researchers to appease critics?', March 15, 2023; Vinay Prasad, 'The Cochrane Mask Fiasco', Sensible Medicine, March 15, 2023.

question: Abaluck's team ran a cluster-randomised mask trial across 600 villages and 342,183 adults in Bangladesh, published in Science in 2022, and reported only a modest fall in symptomatic COVID. Subgroup analysis found one type of mask showed no significant effect at all. Which type?
answer: Cloth masks
choices: Cloth masks
Surgical masks
N95 respirators
KN95 masks
context: A real, modest, honestly reported effect - tripling mask usage across 600 villages moved symptomatic seroprevalence by roughly 9.5%. For contrast, the Danish DANMASK-19 trial (Bundgaard et al., Annals of Internal Medicine 2020) recruited 6,024 adults and found 1.8% of the mask arm vs 2.1% of the control arm tested positive after a month - a difference too small to call. Two honest trials, two different scales; a careful scientist reports both. Source: science.org, acpjournals.org.

question: A girl lay dying of diphtheria in a Berlin clinic at Christmas 1891, when the disease was killing 50,000 German children a year. The story goes that she was injected with something from a ram and a horse that had been made immune, and she lived. Which part of those animals held the protection?
answer: The clear serum that separates from their blood
choices: The clear serum that separates from their blood
The red marrow that fills their long bones
The soft tissue of their swollen lymph glands
The thin fluid drawn from around their spines
context: Emil von Behring's diphtheria antitoxin was not a drug at all: it was blood serum from an immunised animal, carrying something that animal's own body had manufactured. Before it, diphtheria killed 30 to 50 of every 100 children it struck; standardised serum therapy cut that to 1 to 5 by the early 1900s, and German paediatricians called Behring 'Saviour of the Children'. In 1901 the very first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to him 'for his work on serum therapy, especially its application against diphtheria'. The bedside details of that Christmas case have since been questioned by historians. Source: nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1901/behring/article/ and /facts/.

question: Gaston Ramon, a horse doctor at the Pasteur Institute, wanted his horses to make more serum against diphtheria in 1923. He found that adding plain dead stuff to the shot made them build far more antibodies, and he tried whatever was nearby. What did he stir in?
answer: Tapioca, potato starch and bread crumbs
choices: Powdered glass, chalk and fine sand
Beeswax, lanolin and pressed olive oil
Tapioca, potato starch and bread crumbs
Charcoal, saltpetre and quicklime
context: Ramon's junk worked, and it opened the field of adjuvants: substances that carry no protection of their own but make the immune system take the injected shape seriously. Three years later Alexander Glenny found the same effect with aluminium salts, which are still in vaccines today. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Immunologic_adjuvant.

question: Kitasato Shibasaburo was the first to grow the tetanus germ in pure culture, back in 1889, and in 1890 he and Emil von Behring wrote the paper that started serum therapy. The first Nobel Prize in Medicine for that work, in 1901, went to Behring alone. How did Japan honour Kitasato in 2024?
answer: It put his portrait on a redesigned banknote
choices: It made his birthday a public holiday
It issued a set of commemorative postage stamps
It renamed its national medical university for him
It put his portrait on a redesigned banknote
context: The Bank of Japan's redesigned 1,000-yen note, carrying Kitasato's face, entered circulation on 3 July 2024 - 123 years after the prize he was left off. Kitasato's deep-agar hydrogen tube was what made pure tetanus culture possible at all; the 1890 paper was 'Ueber das Zustandekommen der Diphtherie-Immunitaet und der Tetanus-Immunitaet bei Thieren', Deutsche Medizinische Wochenschrift, 4 December 1890. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Kitasato_Shibasaburo.

question: Archivists found a photograph in 1997 with a note scrawled across all four margins, and it muddied the 1891 Berlin diphtheria case told for a century as Emil von Behring's triumph. Behring's lab had not had enough serum for a full human dose, and Ernst von Bergmann, who ran the clinic, had banned its use, so someone went around him. The note dated the first treated child to December 22, 1891, and took the credit. Whose handwriting was it?
answer: Erich Wernicke, an assistant in Behring's laboratory
choices: Paul Ehrlich, a chemist measuring the serum's strength
Heinrich Geissler, a physician on Bergmann's ward
Erich Wernicke, an assistant in Behring's laboratory
Kitasato Shibasaburo, Behring's co-author on the serum
context: Wernicke immunised the rams and horses and harvested the serum himself. Christina Oedingen and Joseph Staerk of the Behring Archive found the inscribed photograph in 1997; Wernicke had written across its margins that on 22 December 1891 the first child was treated with serum he had produced, and was cured. The likeliest reconstruction is that Wernicke and Heinrich Geissler, one of Bergmann's house physicians, treated the child around the prohibition. Here is the traditional Christmas story AND its honest correction. Source: Don K. Nakayama, 'The Christmas Miracle of Emil von Behring', The American Surgeon (2023), doi:10.1177/00031348221129515.

question: Paul Ehrlich drew the immune system in a new way in 1897, showing living cells covered in side-chains: molecular arms, each shaped to lock onto one type of poison like a key. But the antitoxin, the protection in the serum, floats free in the blood and sticks to no cell at all. How did Ehrlich's picture say it got there?
answer: The cell overproduced its side-chains and the surplus broke off
choices: The cell overproduced its side-chains and the surplus broke off
The cell moulded fresh copies around the poison and released those
Dying cells dissolved and their surfaces drifted loose in the blood
The liver built new ones from fragments it filtered out of the blood
context: Ehrlich's side-chain theory was wrong in its details and right in its essential picture. He also made immunity measurable, defining one antitoxin unit as the amount of serum that neutralises 100 lethal doses of toxin in guinea pigs - a number you could stamp on a vial, which is what finally made Behring's serum reliable in the clinic. Behring and Ehrlich then ran large-scale production out of a laboratory under a railway arch in Berlin. Ehrlich shared the 1908 Nobel Prize with Elie Metchnikoff, whose rival cellular theory came from pushing rose thorns into transparent starfish larvae at Messina in 1882. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paul_Ehrlich.

question: Frank Macfarlane Burnet explained in 1957 where an army of cells comes from: a week after a vaccination, the blood holds hundreds of thousands of cells all making exactly the right antibody for a germ the body has never met. The vaccine itself was only a shape, a killed germ or one harmless piece of one. What does that injected shape actually do?
answer: It finds the few cells that already fit it and drives them to divide
choices: It orders the bone marrow to build fresh cells to that germ's shape
It folds a new antibody around itself, like clay pressed into a mould
It is copied into a cell's DNA and read back there as a blueprint
It finds the few cells that already fit it and drives them to divide
context: This is clonal selection - Frank Macfarlane Burnet's 1957 paper and, independently, David Talmage the same year - and it is the fact textbooks most often state backwards. Nothing is taught and nothing new is built: you already carry a lymphocyte for almost any shape before you ever meet it. The matching cell is rare, roughly 1 in 100,000 to 1 in 1,000,000, and one activated lymphocyte makes over 1,000 daughters within days. The 'mould' answer was the seriously held rival, proposed by Fritz Breinl and Felix Haurowitz in 1930 and backed by Linus Pauling in 1940; its supporting experiments could not be reproduced, and in 1958 Gustav Nossal and Joshua Lederberg showed in microdroplets that a single cell makes only ONE kind of antibody. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Clonal_selection.

question: Susumu Tonegawa and Nobumichi Hozumi went after a sum that did not add up: a human body carries about twenty thousand genes but makes hundreds of millions of antibody shapes. They found in 1976 that two markers for the ends of an antibody gene sat on separate fragments in mouse embryo DNA, and on a single fragment in DNA from a grown antibody cell. What had happened inside that cell?
answer: It had cut its own DNA apart and joined the pieces together
choices: It had folded its chromosome so the two stretches lay touching
It had copied the two stretches and stacked the copies end to end
It had cut its own DNA apart and joined the pieces together
A virus had spliced its own genes in between the two stretches
context: Every developing B cell physically cuts up and reshuffles the DNA it inherited from you - roughly 40 to 50 V segments, 25 D segments and 6 J segments recombined at random, with extra letters jammed into the joins by an enzyme called TdT - which can theoretically yield over a trillion different receptor shapes, while a rule called allelic exclusion makes sure each single cell ends up expressing exactly one. Your body invents receptors for germs that do not exist yet. Tonegawa took the 1987 Nobel alone 'for his discovery of the genetic principle for generation of antibody diversity'. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Susumu_Tonegawa; nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1987/tonegawa/facts/.

question: Alexander Glenny stuck a disarmed form of the diphtheria toxin onto aluminium salts in 1926, and said the aluminium pinned the antigen at the shot site and let it seep out slowly. Aluminium went into human vaccines in 1932. Then one guinea-pig test made Glenny's story very hard to hold. What did that test show?
answer: Cutting away the injected ear two hours later changed nothing
choices: A pump seeping pure antigen for weeks produced no response at all
Aluminium salts injected with no antigen raised the same antibodies
The antigen had drained out of the injection site within ten minutes
Cutting away the injected ear two hours later changed nothing
context: Removing the injection site within four days did block the response in one guinea-pig experiment - but removing the injected ear just two hours after injection changed neither the size nor the duration of the response, so slow leakage from a depot cannot be the whole story. The rival NLRP3-inflammasome explanation is no cleaner: NLRP3-deficient mice have shown marked suppression of antibody production, partial suppression, and no effect at all, in different studies. A century after Glenny, nobody can say cleanly why aluminium works - and it is better to say so than to pretend. Modern alum still raises seroconversion 2- to 10-fold over antigen alone. Source: 'Mechanism of Immunopotentiation and Safety of Aluminum Adjuvants', pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3541479/.

question: Maurice Hilleman was first to show and name the two ways flu rewrites itself, working on flu at Walter Reed Army Institute. Antigenic drift is a slow drip of small changes in the surface proteins, which is why the flu shot is yearly. Antigenic shift is a sudden swap of whole gene chunks, and that is what starts a pandemic. Measles barely does either, so one childhood shot holds. What lets flu drift so fast?
answer: Its copying enzyme has no proofreading step, so its mistakes stand
choices: Its copying enzyme has no proofreading step, so its mistakes stand
It replicates in cells whose repair enzymes cannot reach its genome
It carries a gene whose whole job is scrambling its surface coat
It copies itself several hundred times faster than measles does
context: Influenza's RNA polymerase errs at roughly 10^-6 to 10^-4 substitutions per nucleotide per replication, and the errors concentrate in five hypervariable antigenic sites on the head of the hemagglutinin protein - exactly the part your memory cells learned.
