Measles mutates at a comparable raw rate, about 9 x 10^-5, but is far more stable where it counts, minimising antigenic variation, so the coat your memory learned still matches decades later. In 1957 Hilleman spotted the new H2N2 subtype in reports out of Hong Kong, predicted it would reach the United States by early September, and drove 40 million doses out before the season peaked. He developed more than 40 vaccines - more than any other single scientist - and took the National Medal of Science in 1988. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Maurice_Hilleman; grokipedia.com/page/Antigenic_drift; grokipedia.com/page/Measles.

question: Jonas Salk made his polio vaccine from killed virus, injected into the arm; Albert Sabin made his from live weakened virus, swallowed on a sugar cube. Three doses of Salk's leave a child 99 to 100 per cent safe from paralysis, a number that makes the two vaccines look interchangeable. They are not. What is still true of a child who has had all three of Salk's doses?
answer: The child can still carry the virus and pass it to other people
choices: The child needs a fresh dose every ten years to stay protected
The child can still carry the virus and pass it to other people
The child is covered against only one of the three types of poliovirus
The child is left unprotected until months after the final dose
context: Protection from disease and blocking transmission are two different things, and the mechanism tells you which one you bought. The injected vaccine fills the bloodstream with a circulating antibody, immunoglobulin G, which intercepts poliovirus before it can travel to the nervous system - but poliovirus is swallowed, and it multiplies for weeks in the lining of the gut long before it ever reaches the blood. Grokipedia's polio-vaccine page states it flatly: the injected vaccine 'generates limited intestinal mucosal immunity, as it does not stimulate significant secretory IgA responses in the gut, allowing vaccinated individuals to potentially shed and transmit virus upon exposure despite protection from paralysis... This mechanism prioritizes individual protection over interruption of fecal-oral transmission chains.' The oral vaccine, replicating in the gut, does raise that secretory IgA and does interrupt the chain. Neither is simply the better one; each buys something different, and the immunology says exactly what. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polio_vaccine.

question: Alfred Wegener put forward continental drift in 1912, and geologists turned his idea down for about fifty years. His critics were no fools, and they raised several serious objections against it at the time. Which of those objections was the load-bearing one?
answer: He offered no mechanism for how continents could move
choices: He offered no mechanism for how continents could move
His matching fossils could be explained by ancient land bridges
His matching paleoclimates could be explained by shifting poles on a fixed Earth
His fit of the continental coastlines was too loose to be exact
context: All three other choices were real objections geologists raised, and each had a serious defender: sunken land bridges (to explain the fossil matches), true polar wander (to explain the paleoclimates), and the loose coastline fit. But the objection that STAYED alive for fifty years was the mechanism problem -- geologists could not see how solid continental rock could plow through denser oceanic rock. It stayed unsolved until seafloor spreading was measured in the 1960s. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'When Continental Drift Was Considered Pseudoscience.'

question: A glassblower drips molten glass into a bucket of cold water. Out comes a Prince Rupert's drop: a fat round head with a long thin tail. His heavy hammer does nothing to the head. Then he pinches the thin tail between two fingers and snaps it. What happens?
answer: The whole drop bursts into fine powder in an instant.
choices: The whole drop bursts into fine powder in an instant.
The tail breaks off and the head is left unharmed.
The head splits into two clean curved halves.
Fine cracks spread over the head but it holds.
context: This is a Prince Rupert's drop, and the two ends of one object behave in opposite ways. Purdue's Srinivasan Chandrasekar, on the 2017 result: 'The head can withstand hammering, and on the other hand, the tail can be broken with just the slightest finger pressure, and within a few microseconds the entire thing shatters.' You can watch it tonight — SmarterEveryDay filmed the disintegration at 130,000 frames per second (2013), and in a 2016 follow-up fired a bullet at the head: the bullet shattered and the drop survived. Sources: Purdue University News, 'Research solves centuries-old riddle of Prince Rupert's drops' (10 May 2017); Grokipedia, 'Prince Rupert's drop'.

question: A beachcomber watches lightning strike a sandy beach, pouring its heat into the ground in a few thousandths of a second. Days later she digs at the strike point. What does she pull out?
answer: A rough branching tube of glass, hollow inside.
choices: A rough branching tube of glass, hollow inside.
A shallow bowl of black fused sand, glassy on top.
A cluster of pea-sized glass beads welded together.
A flat plate of green glass a few inches across.
context: These are fulgurites: the bolt fuses the sand along the channel it takes underground, so the tube is a cast of the strike itself, branches and all. Nature makes glass in other ways too. Obsidian is silica-rich lava (65–80% SiO2) quenched too fast to crystallise; it breaks along smooth curved surfaces, which is why Stone Age knappers used it for their sharpest blades. Tektites are meteorite-impact glass — the Australasian field dates to roughly 0.8 million years ago, and some pieces were shaped into flanged buttons by re-entry at over 11 km/s. Source: Grokipedia, 'Glass' §Natural Occurrence.

question: King Charles II sent five Prince Rupert's drops to the brand-new Royal Society in March 1661, delivered by the courtier Sir Paul Neile. These teardrops came from molten glass dripped into cold water, and their fat heads shrugged off a hammer. Two days later the Society's assistant reported back to the meeting. What had he done?
answer: Made his own drops from scratch and got the effect.
choices: Made his own drops from scratch and got the effect.
Broke all five open and found every one of them hollow.
Weighed and measured each one, then read out the figures.
Reported them a glassmaker's trick, not worth study.
context: Thomas Birch's History of the Royal Society (1756) records the king's gift, delivered via Sir Paul Neile on 4 March 1660/1, as 'five little glass bubbles, two with liquor in them, and the other three solid.' The Society's amanuensis — its writing assistant — successfully reproduced them on 6 March 1661, two days after they arrived. That is the whole method in miniature: not 'take the king's word for it' but 'make one yourself and see.' Two of the five really were hollow with liquid in them, which is why a hollow drop is a fair guess — but a Prince Rupert's drop itself is solid glass throughout. Sir Robert Moray delivered the Society's full experimental report on 14 August 1661. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library, The Collation, '"Whose least part crackt, the whole does fly": early views on Prince Rupert's Drops'.

question: A guide at a medieval cathedral points up at the windows and says the panes are thicker at the bottom because glass is a very slow liquid that has crept down over six hundred years. That is a myth: the panes were uneven the day they were cut. What made them so?
answer: Each was cut from a big disc spun flat while still soft.
choices: Each was cut from a big disc spun flat while still soft.
Each was cut from a blown cylinder slit and unrolled flat.
Each was poured onto an iron table and rolled to size.
Each was ground down from a thick slab by hand.
context: This is the crown process: a blown hollow globe was reheated and spun until centrifugal force flung it out into a flat disc up to five or six feet across — thick at the centre around the pontil mark (the 'bullseye') and thinnest at the rim. Every pane cut from that disc was uneven. As for why the thick edge usually ends up at the bottom, John Mauro's explanation is human, not physical: 'Given non-uniform glass, it is only natural to orient the thicker part of the glass at the bottom, since it gives the appearance of being more stable.' A glazier's choice. Edgar Zanotto calculated that medieval glass would have to be held near 414 °C for centuries to flow measurably. And the Corning Museum of Glass answers it flatly: 'There are many glass objects thousands of years older than those windows that show no sign of flow.' Sources: ceramics.org, 'Glass viscosity calculations definitively debunk the myth of observable flow in medieval windows'; Corning Museum of Glass FAQ; Zanotto, Am. J. Phys. 66, 392 (1998).

question: Steve Jobs gave Corning's chief executive roughly six months to put a scratch-proof glass screen on the first iPhone. Bringing a new glass to market normally took the company close to two years, and it had never made a phone screen at all. Corning made the June 2007 date anyway. What did it reach for?
answer: A windshield glass carmakers had refused to buy.
choices: A windshield glass carmakers had refused to buy.
A cookware glass its kitchen brand had retired.
A television glass its own plants had wound down.
A telescope glass an observatory had turned down.
context: The glass was Chemcor, developed in 1962 under an internal programme called 'Project Muscle' and aimed at car windshields. Carmakers would not pay a premium over cheap laminated glass; Chemcor windshields reached little more than the 1970-model-year AMC Javelin and AMX, and by 1971 Corning had shelved it — where it sat for about forty years. What put Jobs on the phone: months before the June 2007 launch he pulled the prototype from his pocket and found its plastic screen scratched by his own keys — 'I don't know if it were my keys or what, but it scratched... we need glass.' Told it was not feasible, he answered that it would ship in June and it would be glass, then called Corning's chief executive, Wendell Weeks. Corning had no capacity and its board wanted a second supplier named; Jobs, in a private meeting: 'Do you know what your problem is? You're afraid' — arguing Weeks was protecting his own reputation and 'keeping your people from greatness.' Weeks's reply: 'You're right. I'm afraid. And I'll go fix that.' Corning converted its Harrodsburg, Kentucky plant, built in the 1950s for Cold War products, to make it. Corning's Gorilla division VP John Bayne notes the normal cycle is close to two years of R&D. Accounts differ on the exact interval between the scratched pocket and the call — Fast Company says the call came about six months before launch. Sources: Fast Company (2017); Fortune (23 Oct 2025); Grokipedia, 'Gorilla Glass'.

question: The Hydraulic Press Channel set the head of a Prince Rupert's drop, a glass tadpole made by dripping molten glass into cold water, between the hardened steel plates of a hydraulic press and squeezed. The round head was about the size of a marble, and the camera ran at 380,000 frames a second. What did the film show?
answer: The head pressed dents into the steel before it failed.
choices: The head pressed dents into the steel before it failed.
The head powdered the moment the plates first touched it.
The head crumbled slowly as the plates closed in.
The head shot out sideways from between the plates.
context: The Hydraulic Press Channel filmed the crush at 380,000 frames per second: the drop held out to roughly 20 tons of press force, denting the steel platens first, and then burst into large fragments rather than powdering — a different failure mode from the famous tail trick. The laboratory strength measurement used plates of tungsten carbide, the stuff of drill tips: individual samples held between about 11,000 and 19,000 newtons, roughly 15 kN in the middle of the range — near enough to a small car resting on a glass bead. Ordinary glass that size crushes in your hand. Sources: Aben, Anton, Ois, Viswanathan, Chandrasekar & Chaudhri, 'On the extraordinary strength of Prince Rupert's drops,' Applied Physics Letters 109, 231903 (2016); Grokipedia, 'Prince Rupert's drop'.

question: Sir Robert Moray went at a puzzle in 1661 by changing one thing at a time. Nobody could explain why molten glass dripped into cold water set into a tadpole whose head shrugged off a hammer, so he quenched identical melts in five different baths. Reporting to the Royal Society that August, he named one bath that spoiled fewer drops than cold water did. Which one?
answer: Salad oil
choices: Salad oil
Milk
Spirit of wine
Mercury
context: Moray quenched the same molten glass in salad oil, milk, spirit of wine, turpentine and mercury in turn, and reported that in salad oil the drops 'do not miscarry so frequently as in cold water.' Hold everything constant, change one thing, compare the results: that is a controlled-variable experiment, run in 1661 on a curiosity nobody understood. Notice what Moray did NOT do — argue about it. He made batch after batch and looked. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library, The Collation, on Prince Rupert's Drops.

question: Robert Hooke gave eleven pages of his Micrographia (1665) to the glass drops. His trouble was that the shattering ran far too fast for any eye to follow, and afterwards there was nothing left in one piece to examine. Hooke found a way to read the break anyway. What did he do to the drop first?
answer: Coated it in fish glue to hold the shards in place.
choices: Coated it in fish glue to hold the shards in place.
Sealed it in a bladder of water to slow the burst.
Blackened it with soot so the cracks would show up.
Bedded it in soft wax and snapped the tail beneath.
context: The glue was isinglass, made from fish swim bladders. Hooke coated the drop, snapped the tail, and the dried glue held the fragments roughly where they landed, so he could read the fault lines at leisure — a high-speed camera improvised out of fish glue, 250 years before high-speed cameras existed. The chapter is 'Observ. VII: Of some Phaenomena of Glass drops.' Hooke went on to reason from the mechanics of an arch and its keystone to an explanation that came remarkably close to the modern one, three and a half centuries before instruments could confirm it. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library, The Collation; Grokipedia, 'Prince Rupert's drop'.

question: A technician fires X-rays at fused quartz, glass made of pure silica, and finds the tiny pyramids that fill a quartz crystal: one silicon atom at the centre of four oxygens. They have the same shape and the same bond lengths, joined corner to corner into a network. How are the pyramids arranged in that network?
answer: In rings of many different sizes, mixed together.
choices: In rings of many different sizes, mixed together.
In rings all of one size, six pyramids to a ring.
In flat sheets that slide across one another.
In rings, but with one corner in six left unlinked.
context: Glass is an amorphous solid: real order close up, no repeating order at a distance. W. H. Zachariasen named the picture in 1932 — the 'continuous random network,' silicon-oxygen tetrahedra (the pyramid's proper name) linked corner to corner into rings of many different sizes. The local geometry is nearly what quartz has; what is missing is the repeat. Ordinary window glass is not this pure — the sodium and calcium added to it break some of those corner links, which is why the question named fused quartz, silica alone. And a glass is a genuine solid, not a slow liquid: Zanotto (Am. J. Phys. 1998) estimated the structural relaxation time of window glass at room temperature at more than 10^32 years, revised in 1999 to about 10^23 years — against a universe roughly 1.4 x 10^10 years old. Gulbiten & Mauro (2018) put it more vividly still: medieval cathedral glass would flow about one nanometre in one billion years. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Glass' §Atomic and Molecular Structure; Zanotto, Am. J. Phys. 66, 392 (1998) and 67, 260 (1999); ceramics.org (2018).

question: A researcher shines polarised light through the head of a Prince Rupert's drop, the glass tadpole that shrugs off a hammer. Its outer skin is locked in compression, squeezed so hard no crack can open in it, while the glass underneath is stretched taut. How deep does that squeezed skin go?
answer: About a tenth of the head's width, half a millimetre.
choices: About a tenth of the head's width, half a millimetre.
About a third of the head's width, two millimetres.
About half the head's width, three millimetres.
A hundredth of the head's width, fifty micrometres.
context: Why the drop is built this way: its outside hits the cold water and sets hard first, and when the still-molten interior then cools and tries to shrink it cannot pull the rigid skin inward with it, so it hauls that skin into compression and leaves its own core in tension — stretched. Integrated photoelasticity, which reads stress from the way polarised light passes through the glass, puts the surface compression at roughly 400–700 MPa and the interior tension at roughly 225–400 MPa, in a compressed layer only about 0.5–0.85 mm thick — around 10% of the head's diameter. That thin squeezed skin is the whole trick: a crack cannot open in a surface being pressed shut, so the hammer accomplishes nothing. The tail is the exception — too thin ever to grow that protective skin, so its stretched interior lies almost at the surface, and snapping it gives a crack direct access to all the stored tension. The drop is solid glass throughout. Sources: Aben, Anton, Ois, Viswanathan, Chandrasekar & Chaudhri, Applied Physics Letters 109, 231903 (2016); '10% of the diameter of the head' via Wikipedia, 'Prince Rupert's drop'; Grokipedia, 'Prince Rupert's drop'.

question: A girl thumbs the screen of her phone, glass that was toughened in a bath. Sheets of aluminosilicate glass sit in molten potassium salt at about 400 degrees C for hours, and come out with a surface far harder to crack than the glass that went in, with no hammer and no bucket of cold water. What happened to the glass in that bath?
answer: Potassium ions crowded into places sodium ions had left.
choices: Potassium ions crowded into places sodium ions had left.
A film of potassium salt fused onto it as a hard coating.
The heat drove out trapped water, closing tiny surface flaws.
Sodium ions drifted inward, leaving the surface pure silica.
context: This is ion exchange, and the point is size. A potassium ion is about 1.38 angstroms across; the sodium ion whose place it takes is about 1.02. Every incoming ion is wedged into a hole made for something smaller, and the jammed surface ends up in compression — reported up to about 900 MPa in a layer roughly 40–50 micrometres deep in early generations. That is Prince Rupert's trick performed with chemistry instead of quenching, and as of 2025 it is under the thumbs of users on more than 8 billion devices across 45+ brands. Keep the rival methods straight: annealing does the opposite (reheat, let viscous flow relax the stress out, cool slowly); thermal tempering gets there by blasting hot glass with high-pressure air, patented for flat glass by Francois Barthelemy Alfred Royer de la Bastie in 1874; lamination and wire mesh put nothing into compression at all — they just hold the fragments together. Source: Grokipedia, 'Gorilla Glass' §Chemical Strengthening Technique.

question: M. M. Chaudhri at Cambridge clocked the crack that races through a snapped Prince Rupert's drop, with framing photography running up to about a million pictures a second, hardware almost no school will ever own. The front runs tail to head at something like 4,000 mph, splitting into fresh cracks as it goes. Physicists have since published a way to time the same crack with equipment a high school can afford. What does their rig use?
answer: A resistive grid glued to the drop, its lines cut one by one.
choices: A resistive grid glued to the drop, its lines cut one by one.
A microphone at each end, timing the crack's sound arrival.
A laser beam across the head, broken as the drop bursts open.
A strobe lamp pulsed at a known rate, stepping the crack forward.
context: The published method glues a resistive grid to the drop and watches a digital oscilloscope as the traces sever one by one, each break marking the crack front's arrival; the authors note it 'can therefore be widely used in high schools and universities.' The speed itself: reported values run roughly 1,450–1,900 metres per second (about 3,200–4,300 mph); Purdue renders it as 'more than 4,000 mph.' Treat every one of these as a measurement range across papers, not a constant. What is left afterward is just as striking: a single millimetre-sized drop breaks into more than 20,000 pieces, and the fragment sizes follow an exponential distribution rather than the power law ordinary brittle fracture gives, with two characteristic sizes around 0.31 mm and 0.064 mm — a coarse population and a dust population. Sources: Chaudhri's framing photography (from 1994); Purdue University News (2017); 'Explosive fragmentation of Prince Rupert's drops leads to well-defined fragment sizes' (PMC8097073); arXiv:1602.06801.

question: Philip W. Anderson answered Science in 1995, when it asked for a problem worth the coming decade's attention. He picked the nature of glass and the glass transition, 'the deepest and most interesting unsolved problem in solid state theory.' It is still open. Suppose you cool a melt fast enough that it sets into glass without ever crystallising: one camp holds there was no genuine transition, only a liquid grown too sluggish to rearrange itself. Which measured oddity is that camp's best evidence?
answer: The temperature it sets at shifts when you cool it faster.
choices: The temperature it sets at shifts when you cool it faster.
Its heat capacity stays flat right through the setting.
The same melt sets tens of degrees apart from run to run.
The transition fades away if the glass is reheated slowly.
context: The glass transition temperature moves roughly 3–5 K for every tenfold change in cooling rate — and a transition whose temperature moves when the experimenter changes speed is a very strange transition. That is the kinetic camp's best argument: nothing special happens thermodynamically, they say; relaxation just slows until the liquid can no longer keep up with the experiment. The thermodynamic camp answers with the Kauzmann paradox (Walter Kauzmann, 1948): extrapolate the supercooled liquid's configurational entropy downward and it would fall below the crystal's at a finite temperature, which is impossible — so something real must intervene. Note too that unlike freezing, glass formation releases no latent heat and shows no abrupt volume change, which is why glass has a softening range instead of a melting point; what it does show is a step down in heat capacity, which is how laboratories locate the transition. Nobody has settled it, thirty years after Anderson called it out in Science. Sources: Science 267, 1615 (1995); Grokipedia, 'Glass transition'.

question: John Cook and colleagues read 11,944 climate paper abstracts from 1991 to 2011 and reported in Environmental Research Letters in 2013 that 97.1 percent 'endorsed the consensus'. A share of the 11,944 had been set aside for another reason before that percentage was computed. What roughly was that share?
answer: about 66 percent
choices: about 66 percent
about 3 percent
about 55 percent
about 70 percent
context: Cook 2013 reported that 66.4 percent of the abstracts - 7,930 papers - expressed no position on human causation at all. The famous 97.1 percent is a percentage of only the remaining third that did take a position. Source: iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/8/2/024024

question: John Cook's team sorted the abstracts of nearly 12,000 climate papers in 2013 by how strongly each endorsed the idea that human activity is warming the planet, into seven levels in all. The largest 'endorsement' bucket, by far, was a category the team labelled Level 3. What did a paper have to do to be scored Level 3?
answer: take a human contribution to warming for granted, without saying how much
choices: take a human contribution to warming for granted, without saying how much
state a specific percentage of warming caused by humans in its title or first line
recommend a specific climate policy such as a carbon tax or emissions cap
cite a named IPCC assessment report in its opening paragraph
context: Level 3 was called 'implicit endorsement': a paper about tree rings or Arctic sea ice that just assumed humans were part of the picture, with no number attached, landed in the same 97 percent as a paper explicitly saying humans are the dominant cause. Level 1 - the strictest 'explicit endorsement with quantification' - was a small minority. Source: iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/8/2/024024

question: Peter Doran and Maggie Zimmerman sent two questions by email in 2009 to 10,257 earth scientists, got thousands of replies and reported the survey in Eos. Then they narrowed to a smaller group they called 'climate specialists': people who called themselves climatologists and had more than half of their recent papers on climate. A second famous 97 percent comes from that group. How many people were in it?
context: Doran and Zimmerman's famous 97 percent is really 75 of the 77 climate specialists who answered the second question - out of a subgroup of 79 people. The 928 number is the abstract count from Naomi Oreskes's 2004 Science paper on the same question. Source: Doran & Zimmerman 2009, EOS, Transactions of the American Geophysical Union

question: Richard Tol wrote the hardest pushback to John Cook's 2013 paper, in the journal Energy Policy. He is an economist and Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) contributing author, and he himself agrees humans are warming the planet. His reply said Cook's team had skipped one quality-control check that critics could not rebuild from the paper. What did he charge?
answer: they never measured whether different raters agreed with each other
choices: they never measured whether different raters agreed with each other
they threw out papers written in languages other than English
they never trained their raters against a gold-standard subset before scoring
they refused to release their raw abstract ratings to critics
context: Tol argued that Cook's rating procedure lacked controls and any reported inter-rater reliability, so nobody could tell how consistently the same abstract would have been scored by different coders. Criticism from a working IPCC contributor on the same side of the physics is the strongest kind of published critique. Source: sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0301421514002821

question: A student writes climate science out as a stack of specific physical claims that each stand or fall on their own: some measured in the lab, some read off ice cores, some read off satellite data, some argued about in the journals. Serious publishing scientists broadly agree on some parts of the picture and dispute others. Which of these is a genuinely open question among them today, rather than a settled point?
answer: how much the planet warms per doubling of CO2 (the 'sensitivity')
choices: how much the planet warms per doubling of CO2 (the 'sensitivity')
whether the CO2 molecule absorbs infrared radiation in the laboratory
whether adding CO2 produces an approximately logarithmic warming effect per doubling
whether the mean global surface temperature has risen since the 1800s
context: The IPCC's own reports carry a wide range for climate sensitivity, and its size, the attribution of individual extreme weather events, and the economics of damage remain live disputes among publishing scientists. The logarithmic per-doubling shape of CO2 forcing is standard radiative-transfer physics; the open question is how much the whole climate system amplifies or damps that forcing. Source: IPCC AR6 WG1 Chapter 7

question: A volunteer at an American weather station reads a max-min thermometer, which holds only the high and low since it was last reset. He resets it when he writes the numbers down. Whether he does that at 5 pm or 7 am changes the U.S. temperature record. Why should the hour matter?
answer: One blazing afternoon gets logged twice, as today's high and tomorrow's
choices: One blazing afternoon gets logged twice, as today's high and tomorrow's
The dawn minimum is missed whenever the observer arrives after sunrise
Glass thermometers drift warm in afternoon sun and cool again by dawn
Readings taken before the daily peak are dropped and estimated later
context: This is called time-of-observation bias, and it is real. Zeke Hausfather: "If you change the observations times from afternoons to mornings, as occurred in the U.S., you change from occasionally double counting highs to occasionally double counting lows, resulting in a measurable bias." Reading in the early morning gives temperatures about 0.15 C cooler than a midnight reading; reading in the late afternoon about 0.45 C warmer. A thermometer can be perfectly accurate for 120 years and still hand you a step that has nothing to do with the climate. Source: Zeke Hausfather, 'Understanding Time of Observation Bias', Climate Etc. (Judith Curry), 22 February 2015 - judithcurry.com/2015/02/22/understanding-time-of-observation-bias/

question: An American weather observer got a new request from the U.S. Weather Service around 1960: stop reading the thermometers in the late afternoon and read them between 7 and 9 am instead. The change put a step into a century of temperature data, though no one at the Service was thinking about temperature. The observers tended several instruments, and the morning hour was chosen to make one of the others more accurate. Which one?
answer: The rain gauge, whose catch evaporated away through a hot afternoon
choices: The rain gauge, whose catch evaporated away through a hot afternoon
The snow board, whose fresh fall settled and packed down by evening
The soil thermometer, which runs hours behind the air above it
The wind vane, whose afternoon gusts swamped the daily average
context: In Hausfather's words: "starting around 1960 the U.S. Weather Service requested that observers start taking their measurements in the morning (between 7 and 9 AM), as that would minimize the amount of evaporation from rain gauges and result in more accurate precipitation measurements." A decision made to protect the RAIN record put a step in the TEMPERATURE record. Note the date: most U.S. stations were still reading in the late afternoon, generally between 5 and 7 PM, right up to the late 1950s - this was a post-1960 event, not a slow drift from 1900. Between the 1930s and the 1990s the share of stations reporting rainfall and temperature at the same morning hour rose from 56% to over 88%. Source: Zeke Hausfather, Climate Etc., 22 February 2015; Skeptical Science, 'Surface Temperature Measurements: Time of observation bias and its correction'

question: Luke Howard, the London chemist who named the clouds, set thermometers in the city against thermometers in the country around it through the 1810s, and he filled a 700-page book, The Climate of London, with the results. A driver can try the same check after sunset, watching her car's thermometer from town out into the fields. What pattern did Howard find?
answer: Warmer than the countryside at night, and a little cooler by day
choices: Warmer than the countryside at night, and a little cooler by day
Warmer than the countryside by day, and warmer still after dark
Cooler than the countryside at night, and much warmer at midday
Warmer than the countryside in winter, and cooler in high summer
context: The cooler-by-day half is the surprise: a city does not simply run hot, it runs SHIFTED. Howard reported London about 3.7 F (2.1 C) warmer at night; a second reading of his tables gives about 1.579 F as the annual average excess with peaks above 3 F on winter nights, so the safest way to say it is 'about 2 C warmer at night'. Why it happens: concrete can hold roughly 2,000 times as much heat as an equivalent volume of air, dark asphalt reflects little of the sun, there are no leaves giving off water vapour, tall buildings bounce sunlight between them, and cars and air conditioners add waste heat. Typical U.S. urban excess today is about 1-7 F by day and 2-5 F at night. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Luke Howard (meteorologist)' and 'Urban heat island'; Grokipedia, 'Climate of London'

question: A neighbourhood volunteer signs up to map her whole city's heat in one day, on a summer afternoon when one part of town can run up to 20 F hotter than a part a few miles away. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has paid for more than 70 such projects since 2017, and volunteers, not staff, do the work. How do they gather the readings?
answer: They strap sensors to their cars and drive fixed routes on the hottest day
choices: They strap sensors to their cars and drive fixed routes on the hottest day
They hang thermometers on lamp posts and photograph them all at noon
They read a handheld thermometer each hour at an assigned street corner
They fly small drones along set grids and radio the readings down
context: The sensors log temperature, humidity, time and GPS position as the car moves, and the campaigns run through NOAA's National Integrated Heat Health Information System. Which means the experiment is yours for the taking: pick a calm clear evening, watch the car thermometer as you drive from the middle of town out into open fields after sunset, and write the numbers down. That is the professionals' method, at your scale. Source: NOAA, 'Urban heat island mapping is revolutionizing how cities address extreme heat' - noaa.gov/education/stories/urban-heat-island-mapping-is-revolutionizing-how-cities-address-extreme-heat

question: Thomas Karl's team worked out a method in 1986, and Russell Vose's team re-checked it in 2003, for one correction to the U.S. temperature record. American volunteers had switched from reading their thermometers in the late afternoon to reading them in the morning, mostly after 1960, and the published record is not the raw station numbers: it is corrected for that switch first. What does that correction do to the U.S. record?
answer: It adds warming back - just under 0.3 C across the contiguous states
choices: It adds warming back - just under 0.3 C across the contiguous states
It takes warming out - just under 0.3 C off the contiguous-state trend
It cools the years before 1960 by about 0.3 C and leaves the rest
It moves about 0.3 C from summer into winter, with no net change
context: Here is the honest shape of it. Modelling the real 5 PM to 7 AM shift with synthetic data puts "a cooling bias of about 0.5 C" into the raw contiguous-U.S. record, because the early years double-count hot afternoons and the later years double-count cold mornings. Correcting it therefore ADDS "just under 0.3 C" of warming back - which is exactly the adjustment critics of NOAA quote most often. Concede the point, then finish it: the correction is documented, published, reversible, and it is fixing a step the thermometers themselves put there. Sources: Zeke Hausfather, Climate Etc., 22 February 2015, citing Karl et al. 1986 (J. Climate Appl. Meteor.) and Vose et al. 2003 (GRL, doi:10.1029/2003GL018111)

question: Anthony Watts, who doubted the U.S. temperature record, asked volunteers in 2007 to photograph the country's official climate stations one at a time. By 2009 about 650 of them had covered roughly 70% of the 1,221 stations, and the pictures showed thermometers beside air-conditioner exhausts, on tarred rooftops and in parking lots. One kind of facility turned up 68 times, and it is the finding people still quote. What was it?
answer: Wastewater treatment plants, whose tanks and pumps run warm
choices: Wastewater treatment plants, whose tanks and pumps run warm
Airport aprons, where jet exhaust washes across the concrete
Landfill sites, where buried rubbish smoulders and gives off heat
Power station yards, where cooling towers vent warm damp air
context: "We found 68 stations located at wastewater treatment plants," the 2009 report says - sewage plants run warm. The poster child was Marysville, California, where an official 'high quality' station sat in a fire station parking lot beside an air-conditioner exhaust, a cell phone tower and a barbecue grill. The report, 'Is the U.S. Surface Temperature Record Reliable?', concluded that "89 percent of the stations - nearly 9 of every 10 - fail to meet the National Weather Service's own siting requirements." Notice what kind of audit this was: amateurs, with cameras, checking the government against the government's own published rules. Source: Anthony Watts, Heartland Institute, 1 March 2009 - heartland.org/publications/is-the-us-surface-temperature-record-reliable/

question: A park ranger passes a weather station on clean ground in an empty field. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) built it for a second network from scratch, inside national parks and wildlife refuges, rather than keep fighting over badly placed thermometers. The first stations went in around January 2004, and by 2008 there were 114 across the lower 48 states. What stands in each empty field to measure the air?
answer: Three platinum thermometers, each inside its own fan-blown shield
choices: Three platinum thermometers, each inside its own fan-blown shield
One platinum thermometer, swapped each season for a freshly calibrated unit
Two mercury thermometers, read by a warden and averaged by hand
One infrared sensor, aimed at the ground and checked against orbit
context: NOAA's own words: "Air temperature, precipitation, and soil moisture and temperature are all primary variables measured using triple redundancy. In other words, three separate sensors measure each of these variables." Each thermometer reads every 2 seconds and is averaged every 5 minutes, and the official hourly temperature "is sometimes a median and sometimes an average of various combinations of the three observed values, depending on information about which instruments agree in a pairwise comparison within 0.3 C." The U.S. Climate Reference Network began as a prototype in North Carolina in 2000 and reached 137 stations by 2023. Building a new instrument to settle a dispute is the most scientific act in this whole story. Sources: NOAA NCEI, 'What's a USCRN Station?'; Wikipedia, 'U.S. Climate Reference Network'

question: Richard Muller, a Berkeley physicist, had said publicly that the problems he found in the existing temperature studies threw doubt on whether global warming was happening at all. He and his daughter Elizabeth founded Berkeley Earth in 2010 to redo the work from scratch, testing bad siting, city heat and cherry-picked stations across more than 1.6 billion readings. A Koch foundation gave part of the money, unrestricted. He announced his result in the New York Times in July 2012. What did he say?
answer: He called himself a converted skeptic: humans are almost entirely the cause
choices: He called himself a converted skeptic: humans are almost entirely the cause
He held to his doubts: half the land warming was measurement artifact
He split the verdict: the land record held up, but the ocean record did not
He blamed the fixes: the stations were sound, the adjustments were not
context: The op-ed opens: "CALL me a converted skeptic. Three years ago I identified problems in previous climate studies that, in my mind, threw doubt on the very existence of global warming. Last year, following an intensive research effort involving a dozen scientists, I concluded that global warming was real and that the prior estimates of the rate of warming were correct. I'm now going a step further: Humans are almost entirely the cause." Berkeley Earth's peer-reviewed figure was 0.91 +/- 0.05 C of land warming over the previous 50 years, matching NASA GISS, NOAA and the Hadley Centre. Name the money plainly: about $1,394,500 by December 2013, from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Bill Gates's FICER, the Bowes Foundation and the Charles G. Koch Charitable Foundation ($150,000) - nearly all unrestricted. The Koch Foundation's spokeswoman: "Our grants are designed to promote independent research. As such, recipients hold full control over their findings." Money that hoped for one answer paid for the other, and Muller published it anyway. Sources: Richard A. Muller, 'The Conversion of a Climate-Change Skeptic', New York Times, 28/30 July 2012; Wikipedia, 'Berkeley Earth'

question: A crewman on a working ship reads the sea's temperature from a thermometer set in seawater the ship is already drawing aboard for its own reason. Ships going about their normal work took the ocean's temperature for most of the twentieth century, and after about 1940 crews mostly stopped hauling buckets over the side. What is the ship doing with that water?
answer: Running it through the pipes that cool the engines
choices: Running it through the pipes that cool the engines
Running it into the ballast tanks to trim the hull
Boiling it in evaporators to make fresh drinking water
Holding it in the fire main that feeds the deck hoses
context: Engine-room intake readings carry an average WARM bias of roughly 0.1 to 0.5 C, from friction in the pipes and leftover engine heat. The method they replaced had the opposite fault: a canvas bucket hauled up on a rope loses heat to evaporation and wind on the way to the deck, and Folland and Parker (1995) put a typical U.K. canvas bucket about 0.4 C COOLER than the true sea surface, up to 1 C in some conditions. Wooden buckets, being insulated, lose far less - a Harvard test found a canvas bucket left on deck for three minutes cools about 0.5 C more than a wooden one. So the ocean record is stitched together from one method that reads too cold and another that reads too hot, and the seam is a genuine problem, not an invented one. Sources: Kennedy et al. 2011 (JGR, doi:10.1029/2010JD015220); RealClimate, 'Of buckets and blogs', June 2008; Harvard SEAS, 'The bucket list', July 2019

question: Anthony Watts's volunteers rated 1,007 of the 1,221 U.S. climate stations against the network's own five-class siting standard, and only 80 came out in the two acceptable classes. In 2011 those ratings were finally run through the numbers in a peer-reviewed paper - with Watts himself among its authors. What did the paper find when it compared temperature trends at the worst-sited stations with the best?
answer: The mean trends came out nearly identical, two opposite errors cancelling
choices: The mean trends came out nearly identical, two opposite errors cancelling
The mean trends at the worst sites came out roughly twice as steep
The mean trends at the worst sites came out flat, showing no warming
The mean trends parted only after 1990, as air conditioning spread
context: Verbatim: "Temperature trend estimates vary according to site classification, with poor siting leading to an overestimate of minimum temperature trends and an underestimate of maximum temperature trends... The opposite-signed differences of maximum and minimum temperature trends are similar in magnitude, so that the overall mean temperature trends are nearly identical across site classifications." Watts co-authored the paper that limited his own claim - that is what scientific honesty costs and what it looks like. NOAA's own re-analysis, Menne, Williams and Palecki (2010), used Watts's ratings and found "no evidence that the CONUS average temperature trends are inflated due to poor station siting"; counter-intuitively the badly sited stations trended slightly COOL, which is what nobody on either side expected. The siting really was bad, and the trend survived it. Sources: Fall, Watts, Nielsen-Gammon, Jones, Niyogi, Christy and Pielke Sr. (2011), J. Geophys. Res. 116, D14120, doi:10.1029/2010JD015146; Menne et al. (2010), JGR

question: David Thompson's team found a sudden drop of about 0.3 C in the world's sea-surface temperature inside the single year 1945, a step 40% as large as the whole century's warming trend. No volcano, no ocean current and no change in the sun accounts for it. What accounts for it is that the Second World War had just ended. What did that do to the readings?
answer: American ships went home, and European crews resumed hauling canvas buckets
choices: American ships went home, and European crews resumed hauling canvas buckets
Blackout rules ended, and crews went back to taking readings after dark
Convoy routing ended, and ships returned to the colder northern lanes
Naval crews stood down, and merchant officers logged their readings loosely
context: Through the war the ocean data came almost entirely from U.S. ships using warm engine-room intakes; when the fleets went home, measurement reverted to European ships hauling up cold uninsulated canvas buckets, and the global ocean appeared to cool overnight. Japan and the Netherlands were still using uninsulated buckets into the 1960s. A second warning from the same archive: before 1932 Japanese vessels logged whole-degree Fahrenheit readings that were converted to Celsius and stored to a tenth, and when U.S. Air Force personnel later typed the collection into a computer they truncated the decimals to whole degrees Celsius - a single keystroke habit that produced an apparent rapid cooling of the Pacific that never happened. Peter Huybers: "The data is rife with peculiarities." Sources: Thompson, Kennedy, Wallace and Jones (2008), Nature 453, 646-649; Harvard SEAS, 'The bucket list', July 2019

question: Berkeley Earth's team rebuilt the global land average using only sites far from any city and got the same trend. The worry was that a warming record built from thermometers in growing towns is really just measuring the towns, and the urban heat island is not in doubt: Luke Howard measured it over London in the 1810s. Why does a real and large effect vanish from the global number?
answer: Each station's trend is measured against its own past, not its neighbours
choices: Each station's trend is measured against its own past, not its neighbours
Urban stations are far too few among the world's thermometers to move it
A city correction is already subtracted from every urban station's record
Ocean readings outweigh the land stations and dilute the city heat away
context: A town that is 2 C warm and stays 2 C warm adds nothing to a trend built from each station's own change over time. Wickham et al. (2013) compared the land average from all sites against one built only from 'very rural' sites more than 0.1 degrees from any MODIS-classified urban area, over 1950-2010: the difference in slope was -0.10 +/- 0.24 C per 100 years, meaning the very rural sites warmed a hair FASTER, and statistically indistinguishable from zero. Berkeley Earth's conclusion was that the urban effect "is locally large and real, but does not contribute significantly to the average land temperature rise." Both halves are true at once, and the honest reader has to hold them together. Sources: Wickham et al. (2013), Berkeley Earth; Wikipedia, 'Berkeley Earth'

question: Zeke Hausfather set the adjusted global temperature record against the raw one for 1880 to 2016. The commonest charge against the record's keepers is that they adjust the raw readings until warming appears. The adjustments are real: at sea they correct for the change in how ships took their readings, on land for reading-hour and instrument changes, and every one of them is published and reversible. What do the adjustments do to the global trend?
answer: They shrink it - the adjusted record warms over 20% slower than the raw
choices: They shrink it - the adjusted record warms over 20% slower than the raw
They stretch it - the adjusted record warms over 20% faster than the raw
They shrink the ocean trend and stretch the land, cancelling to no change
They stretch the years before 1950 and leave the later decades alone
context: Broken out: ocean adjustments, dominated by the pre-1940 bucket corrections and "quite prominent at around 0.3C", produce "36% less warming since 1880 than in the raw temperature data", while land adjustments "increase the overall land temperature warming by 16% between 1880 and 2016". Since 1970 the adjusted data warms only 4% faster than raw. Two more checks point the same way. Over 2005-2022 the pristine reference network - no siting problems, no adjustments at all - shows 0.30 C per decade across the contiguous states against 0.23 C per decade for NOAA's standard adjusted network, so the clean record warms FASTER. And Hausfather, Cowtan, Menne and Williams (2016) found that adjustments "make both trends and monthly anomalies from USHCN stations much more similar to those of neighboring USCRN stations". Both slogans fail: 'the data is faked' is false, and so is 'the data needs no scrutiny'. Sources: Zeke Hausfather, 'Explainer: How data adjustments affect global temperature records', Carbon Brief; Hausfather et al. (2016), GRL, doi:10.1002/2015GL067640; Zeke Hausfather, The Climate Brink

question: Chinese researchers posted the genetic code of the new virus SARS-CoV-2 online in January 2020. Late on 31 January, Kristian Andersen, a virologist at Scripps Research in California, sent a short private email to Anthony Fauci, the US government's top infectious-disease official. What did Andersen tell Fauci?
answer: That some of its features potentially looked engineered
choices: That some of its features potentially looked engineered
That its receptor-binding domain was identical to a Wuhan patient sample
That it had already jumped four times independently from bats
That it was almost certainly the wild SARS-CoV-1 virus reappearing
context: The exact phrase Andersen used was 'some of the features (potentially) look engineered.' He added that he, Edward Holmes, Robert Garry and Michael Farzan found the genome 'inconsistent with expectations from evolutionary theory,' with the caveat that their opinions might still change with further analysis. The genome had gone public around 10 January; the email went out at 10:32 pm on 31 January. Sources: FOIA'd Fauci emails released 2021; Newsweek, 'Fauci emails: Kristian Andersen defends article' (June 2021).

question: Anthony Fauci and National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director Francis Collins joined a rushed conference call on February 1, 2020, to argue over what the SARS-CoV-2 genome meant. Kristian Andersen, Edward Holmes, Andrew Rambaut, Robert Garry and Christian Drosten were on the line too. Who set up and chaired that call?
answer: Jeremy Farrar, then director of the Wellcome Trust
choices: Jeremy Farrar, then director of the Wellcome Trust
Peter Daszak, then president of EcoHealth Alliance
Marion Koopmans, of Erasmus Medical Centre
Michael Farzan, of Scripps Research
context: Farrar later wrote in his memoir 'Spike' that he considered the discussions so sensitive that he used a disposable ('burner') phone for the surrounding communications. Four participants on that call, Andersen, Holmes, Rambaut and Garry, became authors of the Proximal Origin paper; its fifth author, Ian Lipkin, was not on Farrar's invitation list. Sources: Farrar, 'Spike' (2021); Farrar's 1 February 2020 invitation email, reproduced in the House Democratic staff report exhibits (usrtk.org).

question: Kristian Andersen, a virologist at Scripps Research in California, opened a private Slack channel with his co-authors in the first week of February 2020. They were drafting the paper later published as 'Proximal Origin', which would tell the public the new coronavirus had not been built, and the channel was there to coordinate the analysis. What did Andersen first title that channel?
answer: project-wuhan_engineering
choices: project-wuhan_engineering
project-wuhan_pangolin
project-wuhan_natural
project-wuhan_market
context: He renamed it 'project-wuhan_pangolin' on February 6, 2020, as the group moved toward a natural-origin conclusion. The channel name in the first week tells you what he thought was on the table. The subpoena that dragged these messages into daylight, from the House Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic, was issued in June 2023. Source: Intercept July 2023 (House-released Slack records).

question: Kristian Andersen typed one sentence into a private Slack channel on 1 February 2020 that became the most-quoted line of the whole affair, after the House released his messages. The Scripps Research virologist was weighing where the new coronavirus had come from, with the colleagues who would write the 'Proximal Origin' paper. What did his sentence say about a lab escape?
answer: That a lab escape was very likely, as such work was already under way
choices: That a lab escape was very likely, as such work was already under way
That a lab escape was unlikely, since the genome matched pangolin viruses
That a lab escape could be ruled out from the sequence alone
That a lab escape was possible but far less likely than spillover
context: His full sentence, from the messages the House Select Subcommittee released in July 2023: 'I think the main thing still in my mind is that the lab escape version of this is so friggin' likely to have happened because they were already doing this type of work and the molecular data is fully consistent with that scenario.' In his 2023 written testimony to Congress he said his view on engineering 'had changed after just a few days'. Sources: Public, 'Top Scientists Misled Congress About Covid Origins, Newly Released Emails And Messages Show' (July 2023); The Intercept, July 2023.

question: Kristian Andersen and his co-authors published a short paper in the journal Nature Medicine on March 17, 2020, titled 'The proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2'. It came about six weeks after their first private messages about the new virus, and the journal ran it as a correspondence, not an original research article. What did the paper's central sentence declare about the virus?
answer: That it was not built in a lab or deliberately manipulated
choices: That it was not built in a lab or deliberately manipulated
That it had most probably escaped a lab as a passaged strain
That it bore no likeness to any bat coronavirus yet known
That it had jumped straight from bats, with no animal between
context: The sentence itself: 'Our analyses clearly show that SARS-CoV-2 is not a laboratory construct or a purposefully manipulated virus.' The paper appeared as a Correspondence, not an original research article, and for the next three years it was the single most-cited scientific reference used to publicly dismiss any lab-related origin. Source: Andersen et al., 'The proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2', Nature Medicine, 17 March 2020.

question: A reader opens 'The Proximal Origin of SARS-CoV-2' in Nature Medicine in March 2020, by five virologists led by Kristian Andersen. Its argument is that the new coronavirus behind COVID-19 has a natural origin, and the paper has to actually argue the case, not just state it. Two specific technical arguments carry most of its weight. Which pair do the authors lean on hardest?
answer: A closer match of the receptor-binding domain to pangolin coronaviruses, plus awkward O-linked glycans around the furin site
choices: A closer match of the receptor-binding domain to pangolin coronaviruses, plus awkward O-linked glycans around the furin site
The discovery of a live progenitor virus in a Wuhan wet-market pangolin, plus a matching genome from a bat in Yunnan
A perfect RaTG13 match at the furin site, plus a published viral backbone signature they could rule out
A serology study of Wuhan Institute staff, plus a phylogeny placing the virus in Guangdong bats
context: Neither argument was a knockout: the pangolin match was partial and later disputed, and the O-linked glycan point rested on which lab scenarios you were willing to imagine. The paper's honest scope was narrower than its later usage suggested. Source: Andersen et al. 2020 (Nature Medicine).

question: House Republicans subpoenaed Kristian Andersen's emails and Slack messages in 2023, and he answered at a July hearing before the Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic. He had led the March 2020 Nature Medicine paper 'The Proximal Origin of SARS-CoV-2,' which told the public the new coronavirus had not been built. His defence rested on three concrete claims about how the paper actually came together. Which set of three did he put on the record?
answer: The paper came out 45 days after the February call; Fauci and Collins edited no draft; his NIH grant was awarded on a pre-pandemic application
choices: The paper came out 45 days after the February call; Fauci and Collins edited no draft; his NIH grant was awarded on a pre-pandemic application
The paper was drafted at Farrar's request; NIAID reviewed the manuscript before submission; the Slack channel was closed at Fauci's suggestion
The paper came out 45 days after the February call; Collins co-authored an early draft; his NIH grant was renewed just after the paper appeared
Andersen initially believed the engineering hypothesis throughout; Farrar chose the journal; the NIH grant was awarded specifically to fund the origin analysis
context: In his written testimony Andersen said the paper appeared on 17 March 2020, 45 days after the 1 February conference call, with a preprint posted 16 days after it; that neither Fauci nor Collins provided any edits, the only suggested change coming from Farrar, who asked for one 'unlikely' to become 'improbable'; and that the grant was applied for in June 2019 and scored in November 2019. He also wrote that his view on engineering 'had changed after just a few days'. Steel-man reading: changing one's mind on new evidence is scientific; the load-bearing question is whether the paper's confident public conclusion was proportionate to the still-live private uncertainty. Source: Andersen written testimony, House Select Subcommittee, July 11, 2023 (oversight.house.gov).

question: Otto von Guericke pumped the air out of two greased copper half-spheres at Regensburg in 1654, pressed rim to rim, no bolt and no glue. Two teams of horses hauled on opposite sides and could not part them. Then he opened a small valve, and the halves fell into his hands. What had held them shut?
answer: the outside atmosphere pressing them together
choices: the outside atmosphere pressing them together
an invisible cord of matter pulling from inside
static charge built up during the pumping
hot grease that had welded the two rims
context: The whole point of the show. With the inside emptied, the atmosphere outside -- about 15 pounds per square inch at sea level -- has nothing to push back against, and it presses the halves shut with the force of a small car. Open the valve, air rushes in, both sides equalize, the halves fall apart. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdeburg_hemispheres.

question: Otto von Guericke joined two big copper hemispheres around 1654, pumped the air out from between them and watched two teams of horses fail to pull them apart. He had built an early working air pump in his spare hours, around a demanding day job in the very city where he did his physics. Which office did he hold, from 1646 until 1678?
answer: chief burgomaster of Magdeburg
choices: chief burgomaster of Magdeburg
court alchemist to Emperor Ferdinand III
professor of natural philosophy at Wittenberg
abbot of the monastery of Saint Maurice
context: Guericke was elected chief magistrate of the ruined city in 1646 and held the office for thirty-two years. He rebuilt Magdeburg, brewed to raise a fortune, and did his physics in his spare hours. The hemispheres were funded, in part, out of the same civic purse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_von_Guericke.

question: Two teams of horses hauled in opposite directions on Otto von Guericke's evacuated copper hemispheres. In fact one team was enough for the physics, if he had changed what stood on the other side. What single swap would have proved exactly the same thing?
answer: a stout stone wall with the far hemisphere roped to it
choices: a stout stone wall with the far hemisphere roped to it
a heavy iron weight hung from the far hemisphere
a windlass cranked by a single ox on a treadwheel
a second team of oxen pulling twice as hard
context: The two-team pull was theatre. By Newton's third law, a fixed wall pushes back with exactly whatever force is applied to it, so one team against a wall matches two teams pulling on each other. The wall supplies the equal and opposite pull for free -- no second puller needed. The horses were spectacle; the air pump was the argument. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdeburg_hemispheres.

question: Otto von Guericke pumped the air from a jar with a candle inside, and the flame went out, one of his quieter demonstrations beyond the hemispheres. Then he put a heavy piston in a vertical cylinder and pumped the air out from underneath. What did the piston then do?
answer: it dragged a whole team of strong men off the ground
choices: it dragged a whole team of strong men off the ground
it floated in mid-cylinder and refused to move at all
it shot upward out of the top of the cylinder
it caught fire from the friction of falling
context: With a vacuum below and the atmosphere pressing down on top, the piston wanted to fall with a force equal to atmospheric pressure times the piston's area. Guericke had teams of men on ropes trying to hold it up -- and the air still won and lifted them. Same lesson as the hemispheres, no horses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_von_Guericke.

question: A cube-shaped vessel or a pair of flat plates would not do for Otto von Guericke, who wanted a vessel he could empty of air to show off his working air pump. He made his vacuum vessels spherical. Why did the shape have to be a sphere?
answer: a flat face would have crumpled inward under atmospheric pressure
choices: a flat face would have crumpled inward under atmospheric pressure
only a sphere can be pumped to a low enough interior vacuum
the air pump he had built only worked with round vessels
the horses could not have gripped a flat-sided iron frame
context: A curved shell spreads the load: every square millimetre of copper is pushed straight in toward the centre, and neighbouring copper resists it. A flat plate has nothing to lean on but its own bending stiffness, and 15 psi over a big flat area crushes it. Same reason submarines and pressure cookers are round. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdeburg_hemispheres.

question: A student reads that Otto von Guericke's evacuated hemispheres were about 50 centimetres across, and that the outside air held them shut with roughly 20 kilonewtons, around the weight of a small car. To get that number, she multiplies atmospheric pressure by which area of the sphere?
answer: the flat cross-section where the halves meet (pi r squared)
choices: the flat cross-section where the halves meet (pi r squared)
the full curved outer surface (4 pi r squared)
the curved area of one hemisphere (2 pi r squared)
the equatorial ring where the rims touch (a thin annulus)
context: On any curved patch of the shell the air presses toward the centre; those forces cancel sideways and only the components along the pull-apart axis matter. Sum them and the net comes out to atmospheric pressure times the cross-section of the seam -- pi times r squared, roughly 0.2 square metres for a 50 cm sphere, and 100 kPa times that is about 20 kN. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdeburg_hemispheres.

question: Madison Grant, a New York lawyer, wrote a race-science book that Hitler praised. The same man was one of the country's leading conservationists: he helped start the Bronx Zoo and campaigned to protect the land that became Glacier and Denali National Parks. Which animal did he help save from dying out?
answer: The American bison
choices: The American bison
The bald eagle
The California condor
The whooping crane
context: Grant was instrumental in forming the American Bison Society in 1905, which worked to bring the bison back from the edge of extinction, and he helped build the New York Zoological Society that opened the Bronx Zoo. The man behind those rescues and the man behind the race book were the same person. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Madison Grant'; National Park Service, 'Madison Grant.'

question: A leading American scientist of the day wrote an approving preface for Madison Grant's 1916 book, and one of New York's most prestigious publishers brought it out. This was no self-published pamphlet on a fringe press: it went through four revised editions. Which publisher, and which scientist wrote the preface?
answer: Charles Scribner's Sons, with a preface by Henry Fairfield Osborn
choices: Charles Scribner's Sons, with a preface by Henry Fairfield Osborn
Alfred A. Knopf, with a preface by Franz Boas
G.P. Putnam's Sons, with a preface by John C. Merriam
Harper and Brothers, with a preface by Charles B. Davenport
context: Osborn was president of the American Museum of Natural History from 1908 to 1933 and one of the country's most influential paleontologists. Boas was the Columbia anthropologist who publicly OPPOSED eugenics on scientific grounds; Merriam ran the Carnegie Institution; Davenport ran the Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor. All four are real contemporaries any of whom a reader might expect. Source: Archive.org, 'The Passing of the Great Race, 4th ed.'

question: Madison Grant, a New York lawyer and conservationist, published a race-science book in 1916. A story says that after it appeared in German in 1925, Adolf Hitler wrote to Grant calling it his Bible. Historians repeat the story to this day. What is it based on?
answer: An account from Grant's friends, with no letter surviving
choices: An account from Grant's friends, with no letter surviving
The letter itself, kept among Grant's papers in New York
A passage naming Grant in Hitler's book Mein Kampf
A thank-you note printed in a later edition of the book
context: The anecdote comes from people around Grant, and no copy of the letter is known to survive, so historians repeat it with a 'reportedly' attached, and so does this bank. What is documented: Karl Brandt, Hitler's physician, entered excerpts from the German translation into evidence at Nuremberg. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Madison Grant'; Wikipedia, 'The Passing of the Great Race' (citing Stefan Kuhl, The Nazi Connection, 1994).  (Legend.)

question: Margaret Sanger, founder of the group that grew into Planned Parenthood, published a eugenic program of her own in the April 1932 issue of her journal, Birth Control Review, under the title 'A Plan for Peace'. What exactly did the program propose?
answer: Intelligence tests for immigrants and sterilizing the feeble-minded
choices: Intelligence tests for immigrants and sterilizing the feeble-minded
Sterilizing black Americans as a group, chosen by race alone
Free abortion clinics opened in every large American city
A federal ban on marriage between people of different races
context: The article proposed intelligence-test requirements for immigrants, sterilization or segregation of the 'feeble-minded,' and government work camps for 'morons, illiterates, paupers, unemployables, criminals, prostitutes, and drug addicts.' It sorted people by condition, not by race or nationality, and Sanger herself opposed abortion. Sources: John Locke Foundation, 'Margaret Sanger and Eugenics'; FactCheck.org, 'Cain's False Attack on Planned Parenthood' (2011).

question: Clarence Gamble, a doctor, received Margaret Sanger's most-quoted line in a 1939 letter about the Birth Control Federation's Negro Project. In the letter, Sanger warned him about a problem she wanted black ministers to help solve. What was the problem?
answer: a rumor she feared would spread in the community that the project was an extermination plot
choices: a rumor she feared would spread in the community that the project was an extermination plot
a Congressional bill she thought was about to be introduced to shut the project down
a Catholic diocesan letter she believed the archbishop of New York had just written
a Klan meeting she said had been planned to intimidate the clinics
context: Sanger wrote: 'We do not want word to go out that we want to exterminate the Negro population and the minister is the man who can straighten out that idea if it ever occurs to any of their more rebellious members.' Gamble's own November 1939 memorandum had raised the concern that black leaders might suspect the project. Sanger's eugenic proposals in 'A Plan for Peace' were not aimed at particular ethnicities, and she opposed abortion. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Negro Project'; FactCheck.org, 'Cain's False Attack on Planned Parenthood.'

question: John Scopes, a biology teacher, went on trial in Dayton, Tennessee, in 1925 for teaching evolution, which broke the state's Butler Act. The book he was using had been the most popular high-school biology book in America for almost ten years. What other idea did that book teach?
answer: Eugenics
choices: Eugenics
Phrenology
Spontaneous generation
The four bodily humors
context: George W. Hunter's 'A Civic Biology: Presented in Problems' (1914) called large classes of Americans 'parasites' on the gene pool and praised European advances in eugenics. Truman Moon's 'Biology for Beginners' (1926), Peabody and Hunt's 'Elementary Biology' (1913), and Smallwood, Reveley and Bailey's 'New General Biology' were competing US high-school biology textbooks of the same era. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Civic Biology.'

question: Reginald Punnett, a Cambridge geneticist whose 'squares' still appear in biology textbooks, worked with the mathematician G.H. Hardy in 1917 to calculate how fast mass sterilization could eliminate 'feeblemindedness' if it were a simple recessive trait. What did their math show?
answer: It would take many generations to make even a small dent
choices: It would take many generations to make even a small dent
It could be wiped out in a single generation
It would roughly double the trait's frequency
It would have no measurable effect at all
context: Punnett -- famous today for the grid every biology student uses to work out Mendelian crosses -- published 'Eliminating Feeblemindedness' in the Journal of Heredity in 1917 and estimated it would take roughly 8,000 years for the sterilization program to make a serious difference. Source: Journal of Heredity 8:464-465 (1917), 'Eliminating Feeblemindedness.'

question: A genetics student works through the 1917 refutation of the sterilization program, granting that 'feeblemindedness' really was a simple Mendelian recessive, as the eugenicists claimed. The math comes from a rule every genetics class now teaches. Which mechanism made the program hopeless?
answer: Most copies hide in healthy carriers, beyond sterilization's reach
choices: Most copies hide in healthy carriers, beyond sterilization's reach
Population growth outran any rate of sterilization a state could run
A recessive trait returns by fresh mutation in every generation
Epigenetic change switches the trait back on within two generations
context: This is a direct consequence of the Hardy-Weinberg principle, worked out by Hardy in 1908; Punnett brought it to Hardy for exactly this problem. The refutation was in print, in the Journal of Heredity, in 1917. Nobody who mattered acted on it -- Buck v. Bell went the other way ten years later. Sources: ScienceDirect, 'Punnett Square'; Nature Heredity, 'Eugenics and the Genetics Society.'

question: Albert Sabin developed a rival to Jonas Salk's 1955 needle shot a few years later: a polio vaccine famously dripped onto a sugar cube and swallowed. He was aiming for protection right in the lining of the gut, where poliovirus first takes hold and multiplies. What very particular ingredient did he have to put inside those drops?
answer: poliovirus weakened by long passage through monkey kidney cells
choices: poliovirus weakened by long passage through monkey kidney cells
an aluminium salt that revs up the immune system's alarm response
a fragment of the viral protein coat glued onto a harmless carrier
a snippet of poliovirus messenger RNA wrapped in a lipid nanoparticle
context: Sabin grew the virus generation after generation in monkey-kidney cell cultures, selecting strains that had lost their appetite for nerve cells. Because it is still alive, it multiplies briefly in the child's gut before the immune system clears it -- and that gut replication is what Salk's killed injection cannot copy. Source: Sabin Vaccine Institute.

question: A boy who got Jonas Salk's polio shot later swallows wild poliovirus. He is safe from paralysis, but he can still carry the virus and shed it in his stool for weeks. Which type of antibody, mostly missed by a blood-only response, would have stopped that shedding?
answer: mucosal IgA
choices: mucosal IgA
circulating IgG
allergy-signal IgE
first-response IgM
context: IgA sits on the intestinal lining and blocks the virus from attaching there in the first place, which BLOCKS TRANSMISSION -- the vaccinated child cannot easily pass it on. Salk's shot raises IgG in the blood, so it protects the nervous system but leaves the gut open; Sabin's live oral drops replicate in the gut and do raise IgA. Source: Systematic Review, PMC3330118.

question: A child swallows Albert Sabin's drops in a place where too few other children get them, and the vaccine strain she sheds keeps passing gut to gut. It quietly builds up mutations, rebuilds the very genes bred out of it and spreads as a new epidemic. In 2020 alone, how many cases of paralysis did the reverted strain cause worldwide?
answer: about 1,000 cases across 26 countries
choices: about 1,000 cases across 26 countries
about 30 cases across 3 countries
about 12,000 cases across 90 countries
about 50,000 cases across 40 countries
context: The exact figure was 1,048 -- more paralysis in that year than wild poliovirus caused. The reverted strain is called circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus, or cVDPV. Source: CDC MMWR 69(16), 2020.

question: A health worker drips nOPV2 into a child's mouth, a re-engineered replacement for the old type 2 Sabin drops. Type 2 wild polio is gone, but the old drops keep seeding new outbreaks wherever coverage sags, and the World Health Organization (WHO) granted the replacement Emergency Use Listing in November 2020. What did the redesign mainly do to the virus?
answer: stabilised the RNA stem-loop 'domain V' in the 5' untranslated region
choices: stabilised the RNA stem-loop 'domain V' in the 5' untranslated region
swapped the outer protein coat for one from a harmless echovirus
replaced the RNA genome with a DNA copy that cannot mutate at all
added a suicide gene set to fire after one week in a human host
context: Domain V is the main determinant of Sabin-2 attenuation, so locking it down curtails drift-driven reversion. About a billion nOPV2 doses had been given across 35 countries by December 2023; sequencing shows the modifications largely hold, though reversion by RECOMBINATION with other enteroviruses is still possible. Source: PATH; PMC12872467.

question: Scientists from Peter Daszak's EcoHealth Alliance, a US-based group, went deep into limestone caves in Southeast Asia before the COVID-19 pandemic, swabbing the mouths of bats and scraping up their droppings. They were tracking one virus family behind a frightening 2003 outbreak, Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS), which killed hundreds of people worldwide. Which virus family were they tracking?
answer: Coronaviruses
choices: Coronaviruses
Filoviruses
Orthomyxoviruses
Lyssaviruses
context: The 2003 outbreak referenced is SARS, a bat coronavirus that jumped to humans; the field work was in part about spotting the next spillover early. EcoHealth's president was British zoologist Peter Daszak. Source: niaid.nih.gov, influencewatch.org.

question: Peter Daszak's EcoHealth Alliance received a bat-coronavirus grant of about $3.7 million from the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, running from 2014 to 2019. It passed a slice on to a partner laboratory in China so that partner could do part of the work, a pass-along called a subaward. Roughly how much money went to that Chinese partner over those years?
choices: About $60,000
About $1.5 million
About $3 million
context: The Chinese partner was the Wuhan Institute of Virology. The passed-along slice is called a 'subaward' - a subcontract inside a parent grant. The larger $3.7 million was the total EcoHealth received; only a modest fraction went to Wuhan. Source: HHS OIG audit 2023.

question: A senior scientist adds his name to a public letter in The Lancet in February 2020, as COVID begins spreading worldwide. He is one of 27 signers, and the letter calls any suggestion that the virus escaped from a laboratory a 'conspiracy theory.' It looks like an independent statement of the field's consensus, but it hides something about who actually drafted and organized it. What does the letter hide?
answer: The head of a non-profit that had long funded bat-coronavirus work in Chinese labs
choices: The head of a non-profit that had long funded bat-coronavirus work in Chinese labs
The director of the agency that had approved the bat-coronavirus grants
Press officers at the Chinese embassy in London, who wrote the first draft
The journal's own editor, who wanted a calm statement for the public
context: Daszak's own emails, later released, describe wanting the letter to look independent of his organisation. The Lancet added a competing-interest addendum in June 2021 after readers challenged the original no-conflict disclosure. Source: usrtk.org emails, thelancet.com addendum.

question: Senator Rand Paul and Anthony Fauci clashed in July 2021 at a Senate hearing about U.S.-funded coronavirus work in Wuhan, and the real dispute was over the meaning of one specific piece of technical jargon that Fauci himself called 'very nebulous.' What was the disputed jargon?
answer: Gain-of-function research
choices: Gain-of-function research
Dual-use research of concern
Passage in cell culture
Chimeric antigen construction
context: The federal 'P3CO' framework used the term without a single sharp definition, so the argument was partly semantic - with real consequences, because that label triggered extra oversight. Source: Senate hearing transcript, July 20, 2021.

question: Lawrence Tabak, National Institutes of Health (NIH) deputy director, sent Congress a letter in October 2021 about a Wuhan experiment paid for by the EcoHealth grant. A laboratory-made hybrid virus had been given to mice built to carry a human receptor. What happened next that the grant required to be reported quickly, but was not?
answer: The mice got sicker than with the parent virus
choices: The mice got sicker than with the parent virus
The mice cleared the virus faster than controls did
The mice bred a resistant strain of the modified virus
The mice died only when co-infected with a second virus
context: The grant terms required prompt reporting of any enhanced characteristics; EcoHealth reported this result in August 2021, roughly two years late. Source: Tabak letter to Rep. Comer, October 20, 2021; science.org coverage.
