question: American diplomats at the US Embassy in Beijing sent home two cables in January 2018 after a visit, two years before anyone had heard of COVID-19. The cables warned that a Chinese lab had poor training, too few staff and serious management problems. Which lab did the cables warn about?
answer: The Wuhan Institute of Virology's new high-containment lab
choices: The Wuhan Institute of Virology's new high-containment lab
A People's Liberation Army field station in Yunnan
The Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center
The Harbin Veterinary Research Institute
context: The cables were reported by Josh Rogin in the Washington Post in April 2020. The new lab was rated biosafety level 4, the highest containment level there is; much of the actual chimeric bat-coronavirus work at the institute, however, was done under the lower biosafety levels 2 and 3. Source: Washington Post, April 14, 2020.

question: Peter Daszak lost EcoHealth Alliance's government funding on May 15, 2024, when the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) suspended it. On January 17, 2025, HHS took a further formal step, running through 2029. What did HHS do to EcoHealth Alliance and to Daszak personally?
answer: Debarred both from receiving federal funds
choices: Debarred both from receiving federal funds
Referred both to a criminal grand jury
Ordered both to repay the entire grant
Revoked the organisation's tax-exempt status
context: Debarment blocks the recipient from ANY future federal contracts or grants. The debarment ends on May 14 and May 20, 2029 respectively. A separate May 5, 2025 executive order restricted federally funded dangerous gain-of-function work abroad in countries of concern. The transferable rule the whole story teaches: when the people who fund a line of work are also the people asked whether that work was dangerous, disclose the tie - that is what a conflict of interest is, and disclosure is the fix.

question: René Just Haüy, a priest in Paris, took a small hammer to sample after sample of calcite in the 1780s, deliberately breaking them on his workbench. Rock scientists have counted 2,544 different outward shapes for this one mineral: needles, blades, blunt pyramids, no two collector's drawers alike. What did the broken pieces show?
answer: Every piece split into the same slanted brick shape.
choices: Every piece split into the same slanted brick shape.
Every piece crumbled into a fine white powder.
Each piece split into a shape matching its own outside.
Each piece split along whichever face the hammer struck.
context: Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc, 'the prince of the curious', had noticed the same thing at Rians near Aix in the 1600s: the small pieces 'retain the Rhomboid figure'. Haüy drew the conclusion nobody had drawn — the outside can grow 2,544 different ways because the inside is stacking one shape over and over, and the flat faces and fixed angles are that stacking showing through. (Source: IUCr Newsletter Vol. 30 No. 4, 'René-Just Haüy and the birth of crystallography', quoting Haüy, Essai d'une Théorie sur la Structure des Crystaux, Paris 1784 — https://www.iucr.org/news/newsletter/volume-30/number-4/rene-just-hauy-and-the-birth-of-crystallography)

question: A student tips a little table salt onto dark paper and holds a hand lens over it. Table salt is the mineral halite, soft enough to scratch with a fingernail. She crushes one grain under a knife blade and looks again. What does she see?
answer: Smaller cubes, each one with flat square faces.
choices: Smaller cubes, each one with flat square faces.
Slivers with sharp, slightly curved edges.
Rounded grains, like very fine beach sand.
Thin flat flakes that peel apart in sheets.
context: This is perfect cubic cleavage on the {100} planes: halite does not shatter at random, it splits into smaller cubes, and those into smaller cubes again. Inside, each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions and each chloride by six sodium, in a face-centred cubic array — the shape you can see is the stacking you cannot. Halite is only 2 to 2.5 on the Mohs hardness scale, which is why a fingernail marks it. Under the lens the sugar bowl and the salt cellar are plainly different substances, not just different tastes. Go and look. (Source: Grokipedia, 'Halite' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Halite)

question: Nicolaus Steno collected quartz crystals in 1669, some the size of a grain of rice and some the size of a fist, and measured them carefully. He was patiently looking for the one thing that refused to change from crystal to crystal. Which measurement stayed exactly the same?
answer: The angle where two neighbouring faces meet.
choices: The angle where two neighbouring faces meet.
The ratio of the crystal's height to its width.
The share of the total surface each face covers.
The angle at which the crystal leaves the rock.
context: This is the law of constant interfacial angles, published in Steno's 1669 De solido intra solidum — the same book that founded geology. Examining rock crystal, chalcedony and agate, Steno found that the angles between corresponding faces hold no matter how big the crystal is, how lopsidedly it grew, or what it is made of; for quartz prisms he measured 120 degrees between adjacent faces. A rice-grain quartz and a fist-sized quartz meet at the same 120 degrees. That was the first hard clue that the outside shape follows the inside stacking — 112 years before Haüy's calcite. (Source: Grokipedia, 'Nicolas Steno', section 'Crystallography' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Nicolas_Steno; corroborated by IUCr Newsletter Vol. 30 No. 4, Fig. 11 caption)

question: René-Just Haüy, the story goes, was handling a friend's mineral cabinet when he had 'the happy misfortune' of dropping a fine group of calcite. He rushed home to smash more of it and cried 'Tout est trouvé!', everything is found. Which document first records that scene?
answer: A eulogy Georges Cuvier read to the Académie in 1823.
choices: A eulogy Georges Cuvier read to the Académie in 1823.
Haüy's own Essai on crystal structure, published 1784.
A letter from Haüy's friend Defrance de Croisset, 1781.
The mineralogy lectures of Gabriel Delafosse, from 1840.
context: Georges Cuvier added the dropped specimen — in the cabinet of curiosities of Haüy's friend M. Defrance de Croisset — in his 1823 eulogy at the Académie des Sciences, a year after Haüy died and about forty years after the work. The IUCr's own historians say flatly: 'The authenticity of this event has not been proved,' and shelve it beside Archimedes' bath and Newton's apple as a founding myth 'that a large consensus considers inelegant to contest.' Haüy's own 1784 Essai tells it soberly: a calcite prism that had come loose from a group and broken obliquely, giving a clean flat cut; then deliberate cut after deliberate cut until a slanted brick showed in the middle; then the same brick in every other calcite he tried. (Source: IUCr Newsletter Vol. 30 No. 4, section 'The birth of a myth', citing Cuvier, Éloge Historique de Haüy, Académie des Sciences, 1823 — https://www.iucr.org/news/newsletter/volume-30/number-4/rene-just-hauy-and-the-birth-of-crystallography)  (Legend.)

question: Arnould Carangeot, a beginner, tried in March 1783 to draw one strange rock crystal shape and could not get it right. He cut a scrap of something down until it wedged snugly into the notch between two faces. The same wedge then fit every other pair, and every other rock crystal he owned. What was he cutting?
answer: A slip of playing card.
choices: A slip of playing card.
A strip of whalebone.
A sheet of thin lead.
A slice of dried cork.
context: Carangeot turned the trick into an instrument — the contact goniometer — and wrote that any substance takes a polyhedral form 'whose angles are constantly the same in all crystals of the same species.' The IUCr's verdict on why a beginner with a playing card mattered: for centuries people had stared at crystal shapes and speculated, 'but no one before him had ever had the idea of systematically measuring the angles between faces.' You can repeat the whole thing tonight with a card, scissors and any quartz point. (Source: IUCr Newsletter Vol. 30 No. 4, section 'How measurements were introduced in crystallography', quoting Carangeot, 'Goniomètre, ou mesure-angle', Observations sur la Physique 22, 193–197, 1783 — https://www.iucr.org/news/newsletter/volume-30/number-4/rene-just-hauy-and-the-birth-of-crystallography)

question: A student cuts regular paper shapes at her kitchen table and tries to tile the top with copies of one shape at a time. At each meeting point the corners must add up to exactly 360 degrees: some shapes leave a wedge of bare table, and others ride up over a neighbour. A very short list of shapes works. Which list?
answer: Triangle, square and hexagon — and nothing else.
choices: Triangle, square and hexagon — and nothing else.
Triangle, square and octagon — and nothing else.
Square, hexagon and octagon — and nothing else.
Triangle, hexagon and dodecagon — and nothing else.
context: 360 ÷ 108 = 3.33…, and you cannot fit a third of a pentagon into the gap, so the failure is arithmetic, not clumsiness. Equilateral triangles (60 degrees), squares (90) and hexagons (120) all divide 360 exactly — six, four and three of them close a point — and no other regular shape does. Octagons need 135 degrees and dodecagons 150; neither divides 360. This is the tabletop version of a much harder rule about what can repeat in three dimensions. (Source: elementary geometry; interior angle 108° and the 324°/36° gap corroborated in Quanta Magazine, 'The (Math) Problem With Pentagons' — https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-math-problem-with-pentagons-20171211/)

question: Auguste Bravais finished counting all the ways points can stack in three dimensions by 1850, and crystallographers treated one gap in the list as closed business. A crystal is a pattern that lands back on itself after a slide of one fixed step, and the rotations that appear in minerals are always halves, thirds, quarters or sixths of a turn, never a fifth. What made the ban that firm?
answer: A fifth-turn would demand 0.618 of a step, never a whole one.
choices: A fifth-turn would demand 0.618 of a step, never a whole one.
A fifth-turn leaves a 36-degree gap that no stacking closes.
A fifth-turn needs a bond angle that no mineral's atoms hold.
A fifth-turn had never turned up in any mineral ever measured.
context: Rotate a lattice vector by +θ and by −θ; both results must still be lattice vectors, so their sum — 2cos θ times the original — has to be a whole number. That leaves θ = 180°, 120°, 90°, 60° or 0°, i.e. 2-, 3-, 4-, 6- and 1-fold rotations, and nothing else. Five-fold would need θ = 72°, and 2cos 72° ≈ 0.618 — not a whole number, so not a lattice. That is the crystallographic restriction theorem, and it is why the missing fifth was never just an unlucky run of specimens. Auguste Bravais enumerated the lattices in his 1850 memoir: exactly 14 distinct ways to stack points periodically in three dimensions, grouped into 7 crystal systems, giving exactly 32 crystallographic point groups and exactly 230 space groups. That finiteness is why crystallography works at all: you are never searching an endless catalogue, you are searching 230 possibilities. Johann Hessel had already derived the 32 classes in 1830, and Arthur Schönflies formalised the theorem group-theoretically in 1891. (Sources: Grokipedia, 'Bravais lattice' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Bravais_lattice; Grokipedia, 'Crystallographic restriction theorem' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Crystallographic_restriction_theorem)

question: Dan Shechtman, on sabbatical from the Technion, fired an electron beam through a ribbon of aluminium-manganese alloy at the National Bureau of Standards in Gaithersburg, Maryland, on 8 April 1982. The spots on his photographic plate carried a rotational symmetry no repeating lattice can make. In Hebrew he muttered 'Eyn chaya kazo', there ain't no such animal. Then, beside sample number 1725, he wrote in his notebook. What did he write?
choices: 'Contaminated?'
'Twins again.'
'New phase!'
context: The spots repeated every 36 degrees: 360 ÷ 36 = 10, ten-fold rotational symmetry, which no periodic lattice can carry. NIST holds the notebook page and has published a photograph of it — the entry reads '10 Fold ???', with three question marks. Shechtman did not write down a conclusion; he wrote down a question. The sample was 86 atomic percent aluminium and 14 percent manganese, made by melt spinning: molten metal squirted onto a spinning chilled copper wheel, cooling faster than a million kelvin per second, giving a ribbon 20 to 50 micrometres thick. The technician who made it was Frank Biancaniello, in the metallurgist William Boettinger's group. (Sources: NIST, 'The Nobel Moment: Dan Shechtman' — https://www.nist.gov/nist-and-nobel/dan-shechtman/nobel-moment-dan-shechtman; NIST image page 'Shechtman Lab Notebook'; Grokipedia, 'Dan Shechtman' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Dan_Shechtman)

question: John Cahn, a metallurgist, had a normal explanation ready in 1982 for Dan Shechtman's photo of a diffraction pattern with a rotational symmetry no repeating lattice can make: 'Go away, Danny. These are twins and that's not terribly interesting.' He meant several ordinary crystals grown together in a rosette. So Shechtman went back and tilted the sample through many angles, mapping every symmetry axis. What did the map show?
answer: Five-, three- and two-fold axes, in the pattern of an icosahedron.
choices: Five-, three- and two-fold axes, in the pattern of an icosahedron.
Five-fold axes alone, one for each crystal in the rosette.
Five- and two-fold axes, in the pattern of a ten-sided prism.
Five- and four-fold axes, in the pattern of a stretched cube.
context: Twinning can counterfeit one forbidden axis; it cannot fabricate a whole point group. As Shechtman tilted the specimen he found two-fold, three-fold and five-fold axes all present in the correct mutual arrangement — the full icosahedral point group, 120 symmetry operations. Cahn then reversed himself completely: 'Danny, this material is telling us something and I challenge you to find out what it is,' and he co-authored the 1984 paper. Note that twinning was the right first guess. It is exactly what an honest sceptic should propose, and killing it by test is what made the result stick. (Sources: NIST, 'The Nobel Moment: Dan Shechtman' — https://www.nist.gov/nist-and-nobel/dan-shechtman/nobel-moment-dan-shechtman; Grokipedia, 'Dan Shechtman', section 'Initial Analysis and Forbidden Symmetries' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Dan_Shechtman)

question: Dan Shechtman and his colleagues published their aluminium-manganese pattern in a leading physics journal on 12 November 1984. Their key sentence said the spots were 'as sharp as those of crystals but cannot be indexed to any Bravais lattice.' It was the sharpness that made the paper impossible to shrug off. What does a sharp diffraction spot say about a solid?
answer: Sharp spots mean long-range order; a disordered solid smears them out.
choices: Sharp spots mean long-range order; a disordered solid smears them out.
Sharp spots mean a pure sample; an impure one splits them in two.
Sharp spots mean a thin sample; a thick one washes them out.
Sharp spots mean a cold sample; a warm one jitters them wider.
context: A glass or any amorphous solid gives broad, diffuse haloes; sharp spots are the fingerprint of long-range order. So the alloy was simultaneously proving that it was ordered and proving that it had no repeating lattice — two things a century of crystallography said could not both be true. The paper's title said it outright: 'Metallic Phase with Long-Range Orientational Order and No Translational Symmetry', by D. Shechtman, I. Blech, D. Gratias and J. W. Cahn, Physical Review Letters vol. 53 no. 20, pp. 1951–1954, 12 November 1984. (Source: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.53.1951)

question: Roger Penrose, partly inspired by M. C. Escher's prints, ended the 1970s with a pair of tiles, their diagonals standing in the golden ratio of about 1.618 to 1, both carrying edge markings that force how they may meet. Laid down, they cover the whole plane, no gaps and no overlaps, forever. What does the finished tiling do when it is slid a fixed distance in any direction?
answer: It never lines up: no slide of any length brings it back.
choices: It never lines up: no slide of any length brings it back.
It lines up after about a hundred tile widths, never sooner.
It lines up along five directions, and never along the rest.
It lines up after one fat-tile diagonal, and never between.
context: This is aperiodic order — order without periodicity. Penrose's first aperiodic set appeared in 1974, in a paper titled 'The rôle of aesthetics in pure and applied mathematical research': six pentagon-based prototiles with edge markings. By 1978, in 'Pentaplexity' in the student journal Eureka, he had it down to two — the thin and fat rhombi, or the equivalent 'kite' and 'dart'. Every finite patch of a Penrose tiling recurs infinitely often, so it is thoroughly ordered; it simply never comes back onto itself by sliding, and it shows five-fold symmetry everywhere. And somebody had drawn the picture of the answer before anyone saw it in a metal: in 1981 the British crystallographer Alan Mackay published 'De Nive Quinquangula' — 'On the five-cornered snowflake', a deliberate nod to Kepler's 1611 essay on the six-cornered one — and in 1982 he decorated a two-dimensional Penrose tiling with atoms and took its optical Fourier transform, getting sharp spots with five-fold symmetry. Printed before Shechtman's paper appeared. Nobody connected the two at the time. Note that sources disagree on whether the two-tile set dates to 1974 or 1978. (Sources: Grokipedia, 'Penrose tiling' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Penrose_tiling; Wikipedia, 'Alan Lindsay Mackay'; Mackay, Physica 114A, 609, 1982)

question: Luca Bindi and Paul Steinhardt spent ten years hunting a natural quasicrystal by combing museum mineral catalogues, specimen by specimen. For twenty-seven years every known quasicrystal, every solid whose atoms pack in a way no crystal lattice can describe, had been made in a laboratory, which left the obvious objection standing: perhaps nature never makes them at all. In 2009 they found one. Where had it been sitting?
answer: In a drawer in Florence, in a rock labelled 'khatyrkite'.
choices: In a drawer in Florence, in a rock labelled 'khatyrkite'.
In a drawer in Vienna, in a rock labelled 'moissanite'.
In a drawer in Chicago, in a rock labelled 'wollastonite'.
In a drawer in Moscow, in a rock labelled 'perovskite'.
context: The rock was catalogue number 46407/G at the Museum of Natural History of the University of Florence. Inside were grains up to about 100 micrometres of a metal of composition Al63Cu24Fe13, with icosahedral symmetry. The International Mineralogical Association approved it in 2010 (IMA 2010-042) as icosahedrite — from Greek eikosi, twenty, and hedra, seat or face. It has no unit cell to quote: its lattice parameter has to be given in six dimensions, about 12.64 Å. In 2011 an expedition dug nine more grains, each under a millimetre, out of a clay layer about 7,000 years old in the Koryak Mountains of Chukotka; oxygen-isotope ratios show the metal is extraterrestrial, formed in a shock event about 4.5 billion years ago. The entire Khatyrka meteorite weighs 0.1 gram. (Sources: Wikipedia, 'Icosahedrite'; Wikipedia, 'Khatyrka meteorite'; Grokipedia, 'Icosahedrite' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Icosahedrite)

question: A crystallographer reads the new definition of 'crystal' in 1992, a single sentence from the International Union of Crystallography's Commission on Aperiodic Crystals. For a century the word had meant a solid built from a lattice that repeats, but by the late 1980s labs around the world were making alloys that no lattice could account for. The commission chose to define a crystal not by how the atoms are arranged, but by something anyone with the right instrument can measure. By what?
answer: By what it does to a beam fired through it.
choices: By what it does to a beam fired through it.
By the flat faces and fixed angles it grows.
By the sharp temperature at which it melts.
By the smooth planes along which it cleaves.
context: The 1992 sentence, published in Acta Crystallographica (1992) A48, page 928: a crystal is 'any solid having an essentially discrete diffraction diagram.' The field stopped defining a crystal by how its atoms stack and started defining it by what it does to a beam, because the beam was the thing everyone could agree on. And note carefully what did NOT change. Quasicrystals never violated the crystallographic restriction theorem. That theorem is a conditional: IF a structure is periodic, THEN its rotations are limited. A quasicrystal is not periodic, so the theorem has nothing to say about it either way. The mathematics was never wrong. What was wrong was an assumption nobody had examined and bolted on anyway — that ordered and repeating mean the same thing. The whole sequence: cleave a rock and infer the bricks (Haüy, 1784) → prove the bricks with X-rays under von Laue and the Braggs (1912) → find spots that bricks cannot make (1982) → change the definition (1992). (Sources: IUCr Newsletter Vol. 29 No. 2, 'Change to the definition of "crystal" in the IUCr Online Dictionary of Crystallography' — https://www.iucr.org/news/newsletter/volume-29/number-2/change-to-the-definition-of-crystal-in-the-iucr-online-dictionary-of-crystallography; Grokipedia, 'Quasicrystal' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Quasicrystal; Grokipedia, 'Crystallographic restriction theorem')

question: James Thomson, a young Glasgow engineer and older brother of the future Lord Kelvin, had an idea in 1849. Water expands when it freezes, so squeezing ice should push it back toward liquid and lower its melting point a little. What everyday winter thing did this idea seem to explain?
answer: Why an ice skater's blade appears to glide on a slippery film
choices: Why an ice skater's blade appears to glide on a slippery film
Why hot water freezes faster than cold in some experiments
Why sea ice floats but glacier ice can sink
Why lake ice cracks with loud booms in winter
context: James Thomson published the argument in 1849; his younger brother William, later Lord Kelvin, confirmed it experimentally. The effect is real, but as later work would show, far too small to explain skating. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premelting

question: An English chemist better known for his work on electricity pressed two blocks of ice together in a cold room in 1850. A thin neck of ice grew between them and fused them into a single lump. He proposed that the ice surface must already be coated with something liquid-like, even below freezing. Who was he?
answer: Michael Faraday
choices: Michael Faraday
James Joule
Humphry Davy
John Tyndall
context: Faraday's fused-blocks trick is called regelation, and it is why a snowball packs together while dry sand does not. The 'thin liquid film on every ice surface' idea he floated in 1850 turned out, roughly, to be right. Source: https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/58/12/50/394684/Why-Is-Ice-Slippery-In-1859-Michael-Faraday

question: John Joly, a young Dublin engineer, ran Lord Kelvin's equations for an ice skater in 1886. He calculated that a thin steel blade edge, carrying the skater's whole weight on a razor-thin line of contact, presses down on the ice at about 466 atmospheres. What story of ice skating did school textbooks teach for the next century because of his number?
answer: The skate's pressure melts a thin film of water beneath the blade
choices: The skate's pressure melts a thin film of water beneath the blade
Friction from the blade generates heat that melts the ice
Ice has a naturally slippery liquid layer on top of it
The skater's body heat radiates down through the blade
context: Joly's number is the one every textbook inherited. The awkward fact he never addressed is that competitive figure-skating ice is kept near minus 5.5 C, colder than his calculated melting depression could explain. Source: http://www.lptms.universite-paris-saclay.fr/membres/trizac/Ens/L3FIP/Ice.pdf

question: A physicist chills ice to around minus 10 degrees Celsius and aims an instrument at its very outer surface. A slippery, disordered film of water molecules sits on top of the solid crystal, the 'premelting layer' physicists have argued about for over 150 years. Roughly how many water molecules deep is that film?
answer: About three molecules deep
choices: About three molecules deep
About three thousand molecules deep
About three million molecules deep
A single molecule deep
context: Three molecules works out to a few nanometres (billionths of a metre). As the ice warms toward zero C the layer grows toward roughly ten nanometres and its molecules become far more mobile. Source: https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/10074321/1/Slater_NATREVCHEM-18-079-Clean_1542893503_15_clean.pdf

question: A student watches a molecular simulation of an ice surface, the kind several groups were running by the 2010s. The top water molecules are so weakly bonded to the crystal below that they do not really flow like a liquid at all, and rival pictures still have serious defenders. What did those simulations suggest the surface molecules are doing instead?
answer: Rolling over the ice like tiny spheres
choices: Rolling over the ice like tiny spheres
Freezing into an oriented ferroelectric layer
Locking into an amorphous glass phase
Standing on end in aligned dipole chains
context: The rolling-spheres picture is one of several live proposals; a genuine ultra-thin liquid film, a disordered pre-melted layer, and hybrid pictures all still have serious defenders. Which mechanism dominates at which temperature is openly argued in the current literature. Source: https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jpclett.8b01188

question: A boy sprinkles ground pepper on a bowl of water, and the flakes rest on the thin skin at the top. He touches the middle with a soapy fingertip, and the pepper flees to the edge of the bowl in an instant. Which everyday property of water did the soap just cancel there?
answer: Surface tension
choices: Surface tension
Air pressure
Static charge
Boiling point
context: The trick is a kitchen demonstration you can run tonight: water molecules cling to each other tightly enough at the top to hold a dusting of pepper up. Soap crashes into that clinging layer and drops the tension where it lands; the intact skin at the rim tugs the pepper outward. Source: Fizzics Education, Panicked Pepper (Science Fun).

question: Soapmakers boiled animal fat with lye from wood ash for thousands of years without knowing why the mixture turned to soap. In France in 1813 Michel Eugene Chevreul worked out what a fat is made of. What does the lye do to the fat?
answer: It splits off fatty acids, whose salts are soap
choices: It splits off fatty acids, whose salts are soap
It cooks the fat down into a hard, waxy glycerol
It burns off the fat's impurities, leaving it pure
It whips air into the fat until the fat turns foamy
context: Chevreul showed that a fat is fatty acids bonded to glycerol, and that the alkali splits those bonds and hands back a salt of each fatty acid: that salt is soap, and the glycerol is left over. Suddenly the ancient recipe made mechanical sense. He lived to 102 and gave lipid chemistry its vocabulary. Source: OCL Journal, Contribution of Chevreul to lipid chemistry (2023).

question: A girl lathers her hands with plain soap for twenty seconds during flu season. A flu virus on her skin wears a thin outer envelope that it stole from the cell it grew in, and the soap wrecks it. What do the soap molecules do to that envelope?
answer: Their greasy tails wedge into it and pry it apart
choices: Their greasy tails wedge into it and pry it apart
They eat through it the way a strong acid would
They dry it out until it cracks and crumbles
They glue its spikes down so it cannot grip a cell
context: Above a threshold called the critical micelle concentration, soap molecules gather into microscopic balls, greasy tails hidden in the core and charged heads facing out, and grease from a plate tucks into those cores and rinses away. The envelope of a flu virus or a coronavirus is grease too: fat taken from the membrane of the cell it budded out of. The tails slide into that fatty layer and pry it apart, and without its envelope the virus cannot infect. Soap is mildly alkaline, not acidic. Sources: Biolin Scientific on critical micelle concentration; Pall Thordarson, 'The science of soap - here's how it kills the coronavirus', The Guardian, 12 March 2020.

question: A girl home with the winter-vomiting norovirus scrubs her hands with soap under running water for twenty seconds. Norovirus and the common cold's rhinoviruses carry no lipid coat, only a tough protein shell. Alcohol hand-gel does very little against them, yet her twenty seconds help a great deal. What is doing most of the work?
answer: Soap lifts them off the skin so the rinse carries them off
choices: Soap lifts them off the skin so the rinse carries them off
The soap denatures their capsid proteins directly
Soap changes skin pH enough to inactivate them
The soap's charged heads bind and neutralise their RNA
context: For an unenveloped virus, twenty seconds of scrubbing under running water is mechanical work, not chemistry: the soap loosens the particles and the flow carries them away. It is why the CDC calls alcohol rub near-useless against norovirus and still tells you to wash your hands. Source: Infection Control Today, alcohol sanitizers ineffective against norovirus.

question: A girl watches the Sun sit right down on the horizon at sunset. At noon its light crossed roughly one thickness of atmosphere; now that beam has to plough sideways through roughly 38 times as much air. The Sun itself has not changed colour. What has all that extra air done to the sunlight?
answer: Scattered the blue and green out, leaving orange and red
choices: Scattered the blue and green out, leaving orange and red
Bent it downward, stretching its waves toward the red
Stained it orange with dust and smoke near the ground
Dimmed it until only its brightest colours are left
context: The Sun does not change colour at sunset; your line of sight does. Astronomers measure the path in air masses: 1 straight overhead, about 38 at the horizon at sea level. Over that long crawl the blue and green are stripped from the beam almost completely, which is why the Sun AND the clouds it lights redden together. Watch the next clear sunset and you are watching a measurement. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Air mass (astronomy)' ('the relative air mass at the zenith is 1... reaching a value of approximately 38 at the horizon'); Wikipedia, 'Sunset' ('the blue and green components are removed almost completely, leaving the longer wavelength orange and red hues').

question: A boy lies in a field on a cloudless day, and the whole dome of the sky glows a rich blue. Sunlight leaves the Sun essentially white, and no sheet of blue paint hangs over him, so something up there is redirecting sunlight's shorter blue wavelengths down to his eye. What is doing all that scattering?
answer: The nitrogen and oxygen that make up air
choices: The nitrogen and oxygen that make up air
Fine dust and soot from smoke and deserts
Water vapour and the tiniest of droplets
Ozone and the other trace gases of the air
context: There is no blue substance up there at all. The scatterers are the diatomic gases N2 and O2, ordinary air, not dust and not water vapour. The ozone answer is wrong for the daytime sky but far from absurd: Lange, Rozanov and von Savigny (Atmos. Chem. Phys. 23, 14829, 2023) modelled it and confirmed Edward Hulburt's 1953 result that ozone supplies only about 3% of the noon zenith blue, and yet at sunset, through its Chappuis absorption band near 600 nm, ozone supplies roughly two-thirds of the blue in the twilight sky. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Diffuse sky radiation'; UCR Physics FAQ, 'Why is the sky blue?' ('Molecules of oxygen and nitrogen, not dust or water vapor'); Lange, Rozanov & von Savigny, Atmos. Chem. Phys. 23, 14829-14845 (2023).

question: A woman stands in the shadow of a tall brick wall at noon under a completely cloudless summer sky. The wall blocks the Sun completely, yet the shadow is nowhere near black, and she can comfortably read a paperback in it. Where is the light inside the shadow coming from?
answer: From the whole sky, arriving from every direction
choices: From the whole sky, arriving from every direction
From the Sun's rays bending round the wall's edge
From the upper air, which glows faintly in daylight
From the wall itself, warmed by the Sun and glowing
context: Scattering knocks about 23% of the direct sunbeam sideways out of its path, and roughly two-thirds of that scattered share still reaches the ground as diffuse skylight. That is the light in your shadow, and the reason shadows on a clear day carry a blue tinge rather than going black. Test it: on a cloudless day photograph a white sheet of paper in full sun and again in shade, and compare the two colours. Source: Wikipedia, 'Diffuse sky radiation' ('approximately 23% of direct incident radiation of total sunlight is removed from the direct solar beam by scattering... about two-thirds ultimately reaches the earth as photon diffused skylight radiation').

question: Leonardo da Vinci saw that far-off mountains never look like the hills close by. He built a painter's rule out of it, written in the Treatise on Painting his pupil compiled around 1530. Nobody could explain the effect for three more centuries. What did Leonardo tell painters to do with the most distant hills?
answer: Wash them in pale blue-grey and soften their edges
choices: Wash them in pale blue-grey and soften their edges
Outline them in sharp dark lines against the sky
Warm them toward brown, like bare earth seen far off
Darken them steadily the further away they lie
context: Leonardo called it aerial perspective, and he painted with it: the mountains behind the Mona Lisa dissolve into blue-grey haze. It is the same scattering that colours the sky, worked over a horizontal path, with the air between you and the ridge throwing blue into your eye and scattering the ridge's own detail away. Look at any distant range on a clear day and you are watching the law by eye, centuries before anyone could write it down. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Aerial perspective'; Wikipedia, 'A Treatise on Painting'; Britannica, 'Aerial perspective'.

question: John William Strutt, who would later become Lord Rayleigh, published a paper in 1870 setting out the law by which air scatters sunlight, and the whole law hangs on wavelength. Across the visible band, wavelengths barely differ: violet's is a little over half of red's. How much harder does air scatter the violet end than the red end?
answer: About ten times as hard
choices: About two times as hard
About four times as hard
About ten times as hard
About a hundred times as hard
context: Run it yourself: red sits near 700 nanometres and violet near 400, and (700/400)^4 comes out near 9.4. Rayleigh's law climbs as the inverse FOURTH power of the wavelength, so a wavelength difference of under a factor of two produces an effect near a factor of ten, and that steep fourth power is the whole reason the sky has a colour at all. Rayleigh's paper ran with almost no changes as 'On the Light from the Sky, its Polarization and Colour', Philosophical Magazine vol. 41 (1871), pp. 107-120. Sources: UCR Physics FAQ, 'Why is the sky blue?' ('a factor of approximately 10, calculated as (700/400)^4'); Grokipedia, 'Rayleigh scattering'; Optics & Photonics News, 'Lord Rayleigh: A Scientific Life'.

question: Suppose you look up at a clear sky and reason that the shortest wavelengths scatter hardest, so the sky ought to be violet: violet sits beyond blue at the short end, and it is scattered even harder than blue is. Yet nobody has ever looked up at a violet sky. There are two honest reasons, and one is that sunlight simply carries less energy in the violet than in the blue. What is the other?
answer: Your eye has very few violet-sensitive cone cells
choices: Your eye has very few violet-sensitive cone cells
Your eye's rod cells, not its cones, catch violet
The upper air absorbs violet before it reaches you
Violet scatters so repeatedly it is lost to space
context: The short-wavelength (S) cones of the human retina peak near 420 nm and make up only about 5-10% of the cones in the fovea, the eye's sharpest patch. The sky's colour is set partly by your own retina. Note carefully what this question never claims: violet is NOT scattered less than blue. It is scattered more, and still loses. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Rayleigh scattering' and 'Visible spectrum' ('the human eye's greater sensitivity to blue wavelengths and the solar spectrum containing more energy in the blue than in the violet'); UCR Physics FAQ, 'Why is the sky blue?'.

question: John Tyndall, in the basement of the Royal Institution, sent a carbon-arc beam, the brightest artificial light the Victorians had, down a long glass tube seeded with the faintest mist of fine particles. Then he looked at the beam twice: once from the side, and once end-on, straight down the tube's length. What did he see?
answer: Blue from the side, orange-red from the end
choices: Blue from the side, orange-red from the end
Blue from the side, brighter blue from the end
Orange-red from the side, blue from the end
White from the side, pale green from the end
context: A blue sky and a sunset in one piece of glass, 1869. Tyndall also found the scattered light was polarized, and it stayed 'perfectly polarized' for as long as the cloud remained distinctly blue; he called these hazes 'actinic clouds', an artificial sky. But his tube needed particles, so he assumed the real sky did too. Rayleigh's 1899 extension of the mathematics to individual molecules, swapping molecular polarizability for particle volume and refractive index, showed that the air's own molecules alone are enough. Dust is NOT required, and 'the sky is blue because of dust and pollution' is simply wrong. Sources: J. Tyndall, 'On the Blue Colour of the Sky, the Polarization of Skylight...', Proc. R. Soc. Lond. 17 (1868-69) 223-233; Wikipedia, 'Rayleigh scattering' ('1899: He extended the theory to individual molecules').

question: Gustav Mie published the mathematics of the white cloud in 1908, with Ludvig Lorenz having reached it independently. A cloud is made of nothing but water, lit by the very same sunlight that turns the sky around it blue, and it comes out brilliant white. What is it about a single cloud droplet that takes it out of Rayleigh's blue-making regime?
answer: It is far larger than a wavelength of light
choices: It is far larger than a wavelength of light
It is liquid water rather than a gas at all
It is much denser than the air around it
It carries a small charge picked up in the cloud
context: Size, not substance. Cloud droplets run roughly 1-20 micrometres across; visible light's wavelengths run 0.4-0.7 micrometres. Rayleigh himself left the dividing line behind as a size ratio, x = 2*pi*r/lambda: below about one-tenth of a wavelength his law rules, and at cloud-droplet sizes you are in the Mie regime, where all colours are scattered nearly identically. Big droplets play no favourites, so what comes back to you is white. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Mie scattering' ('water droplets... scatter all wavelengths of visible light approximately identically'); Wikipedia, 'Rayleigh scattering' (the 1881 derivation from Maxwell's 1865 electromagnetism, and the size criterion).

question: Charles Braun and Sergei Smirnov tested the answer almost everyone gives, that the sea is blue because it reflects the sky, in 1993. They looked down instead of up, through a three-metre tube of pure water with white paper at the bottom, no sky involved at all, and the water was blue. Something about the water molecule itself is taking the red out of the light. What is doing it?
answer: The O-H bonds of the molecule, vibrating
choices: The O-H bonds of the molecule, vibrating
The electrons of the molecule, jumping levels
The molecules themselves, scattering light
The molecules themselves, spinning end over end
context: An O-H bond is the link between the oxygen and each hydrogen in H2O. In liquid water the red absorption is the short-wavelength tail of a band centred near 760 nm, a four-quantum overtone of the O-H stretching vibrations, with two weaker bands at 660 and 605 nm; the 698 nm often quoted is where one such overtone sits in water vapour, not in the liquid. Braun and Smirnov called it 'the only example from nature in which color originates from vibrational transitions'; every other colour you see is made by electrons. Water is most transparent at 418 nm, deep violet-blue, where its attenuation length is about 227 metres, which is why a glassful looks clear and a lake looks blue: you need metres of path before the absorption shows. Check it where no sky can reflect, in deep holes punched in fresh snow, in frozen waterfalls, in glacier ice. Sources: C. L. Braun & S. N. Smirnov, 'Why is water blue?', J. Chem. Educ. 70(8) 612 (1993), Table 1 (https://www.webexhibits.org/causesofcolor/ref/Braun-Smirnov.html); Wikipedia, 'Electromagnetic absorption by water'; Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, 'Why is the ocean blue?'.

question: A chemist swaps the hydrogen in normal water for deuterium, hydrogen's heavier twin, and has heavy water. The molecule keeps the same shape and the same electrons. Only the nuclei are heavier, and that shifts every vibration to a lower energy. Ordinary water's key absorption band sits at 760 nanometres. What does heavy water look like?
answer: Colourless, with no tint at all
choices: Colourless, with no tint at all
Blue, just as ordinary water is
Blue, but deeper than ordinary water
Green, like the tint in thick glass
context: Lower energy means longer wavelength. Ordinary water's 760 nm band sits just at the far red edge of human sight, close enough to bite the red out of what you see; in D2O that band moves out to about 1000 nm, well past the edge of vision, and the blue is simply gone. Same molecular shape, same electrons, heavier nuclei, colour vanished. It is about as clean a confirmation as chemistry offers that water's colour is vibrational rather than electronic. Source: C. L. Braun & S. N. Smirnov, 'Why is water blue?', J. Chem. Educ. 70(8) 612 (1993) ('D2O is colorless because all of its corresponding vibrational transitions are shifted to lower energy by the increase in isotope mass').

question: A photographer screws a polarizing filter onto her camera on a clear day, aims it at the sky and turns it. One stretch of sky goes dramatically darker while another barely changes: the sky's light is polarized, its waves lined up along one direction, and the effect is far from even across the sky. Where does the polarization peak, reaching about 80%?
answer: In a band right round the sky, 90 degrees from the Sun
choices: In a band right round the sky, 90 degrees from the Sun
In a tight ring within 10 degrees of the Sun itself
Straight overhead, within 20 degrees of the zenith
In a band within 20 degrees of the horizon, all round
context: The Rayleigh sky model puts maximum polarization in a circular band 90 degrees from the Sun, typically peaking near 80%. There are also three neutral points where the polarization vanishes entirely: the Arago point above the antisolar point, the Babinet point above the Sun, and the Brewster point below it. Test it yourself with one lens of a pair of polarized sunglasses: rotate it while sweeping across the sky, and the darkening bites hardest when you are looking at right angles to the Sun. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rayleigh sky model' ('The maximum degree of polarization occurs in a circular band 90 degrees from the Sun').

question: Albert Einstein worked out in 1910 why a gas scatters light at all. His answer arrived with a bonus nobody had gone looking for: the same equations would also yield a fundamental constant of nature, and it could be extracted from measurements of skylight itself. What was Einstein able to get out of the colour of the sky?
answer: Avogadro's number, how many molecules make a mole
choices: Avogadro's number, how many molecules make a mole
Planck's constant, the size of one quantum of energy
The electron's charge, the smallest unit of electricity
The speed of light, the fixed limit of the universe
context: The strangest part is the premise. Einstein showed that a PERFECTLY uniform gas would not scatter light at all; scattering exists only because molecules jostle and leave random density fluctuations behind. Marian Smoluchowski had pointed at fluctuations in 1908 without a formula, and Einstein supplied it in 'Theorie der Opaleszenz von homogenen Flussigkeiten'. The same mathematics gave a fresh, independent route to Avogadro's number (a mole being the chemist's standard counting unit for atoms and molecules). You can count the molecules of the air by looking at the colour of the sky. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Critical opalescence'; UCR Physics FAQ, 'Why is the sky blue?' ('Einstein (1911) calculated the scattering formula for molecules and verified Avogadro's number'; the paper itself is dated 1910).

question: A girl falls asleep and lies still, silent and helpless in the dark. That looks like a terrible plan for survival: a sleeping animal cannot eat, cannot mate and cannot flee predators. Yet almost every animal with a brain sleeps anyway. Across an 80-year human lifetime, roughly how much is spent asleep?
answer: about one third
choices: about one third
about one tenth
about one half
about one twentieth
context: Roughly eight hours out of every twenty-four -- about one-third of a life -- spent unconscious and vulnerable. Whatever sleep does, evolution keeps paying that steep cost, in humans and in essentially every animal with a nervous system. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0060106

question: Allan Rechtschaffen and Bernard Bergmann set out at the University of Chicago in 1983 to test what happens to an animal that never sleeps. They needed rats kept fully awake for weeks at a time, without electric shocks or drugs, which would have confused their results. What mechanical trick did their setup use to keep the rats awake?
answer: a divided disk over water slowly rotated whenever the rat fell asleep, forcing it to walk
choices: a divided disk over water slowly rotated whenever the rat fell asleep, forcing it to walk
bright overhead lamps flicked on whenever the rat closed its eyes for more than a few seconds
an automatic treadmill under the cage sped up whenever the rat's brain activity slowed
a technician on night shift pinched the rat's tail whenever it stopped moving
context: The famous 'disk-over-water' apparatus: two rats sat on halves of a divided disk above shallow water; when the experimental rat began to sleep, the disk rotated and it had to walk or drop in. The control rat could sleep whenever the experimental one was awake -- a yoked design that ruled out stress as the cause of what followed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disk-over-water_method

question: Allan Rechtschaffen, a University of Chicago sleep researcher, summed up his field's greatest puzzle in a single famous line. He wrote that if sleep does not serve some truly vital biological role, then it is the biggest mistake that one particular process has ever made. Which process was he talking about?
answer: the evolutionary process
choices: the evolutionary process
the circadian process
the homeostatic process
the metabolic process
context: Rechtschaffen's line -- 'If sleep does not serve an absolutely vital function, then it is the biggest mistake the evolutionary process has ever made' -- captures the mystery. The cost is obvious; the payoff is not. Source: Rechtschaffen 1971/1978, cited in Sleep Research Society retrospectives.

question: A rat learned a maze in an influential experiment while researchers recorded from its hippocampal place cells, neurons that fire when the rat sits at a particular spot. During the slow-wave sleep that followed, those same place cells did something that made sleep a live theory of memory. What did they do?
answer: fired again in the exact sequence they had used during the maze
choices: fired again in the exact sequence they had used during the maze
fell almost completely silent for the whole slow-wave phase
fired in the reverse of the maze sequence but far slower
fired at random with no relation to the maze at all
context: Neural replay in hippocampal place cells is one of the cleanest pieces of evidence for a memory role of sleep: the same firing sequences that ran during the day's task run again during subsequent slow-wave sleep, and sleep after learning beats an all-nighter on later memory tests. The mechanism is credible; that it is THE reason we sleep is not proven. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nrn2084

question: Andawei Miao, with Nick Franks and Bill Wisden at Imperial College London, injected fluorescent tracer into mouse brains and measured how quickly it moved out in animals that were awake, asleep or under anaesthesia. A famous 2013 result had said sleep cleans waste out of the brain. What did their paper in Nature Neuroscience report in May 2024?
answer: clearance was slower during sleep and anaesthesia than during wakefulness
choices: clearance was slower during sleep and anaesthesia than during wakefulness
clearance was faster during sleep, matching the 2013 Rochester result
clearance was faster only during REM sleep, not slow-wave sleep
clearance stopped almost entirely under anaesthesia but was normal in sleep
context: Miao et al. reported the opposite of the Nedergaard 2013 result: clearance in their experiment was reduced -- not enhanced -- during sleep and anaesthesia. The glymphatic 'sleep cleans the brain' story is now openly contested rather than settled science. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-024-01638-y

question: Alexey Guzey, an independent writer, put out a line-by-line critique of Matthew Walker's bestseller 'Why We Sleep' late in 2019. He found claim after claim that did not hold up, and even a bar quietly removed from a copied graph. What check does this show a curious reader can do on any popular science book?
answer: Follow the citations back to the original studies and see if they say what the book claims
choices: Follow the citations back to the original studies and see if they say what the book claims
Check the author's degrees, job and standing in the field before trusting a word
Compare its claims with what the other bestselling books on the same topic say
Look for the publisher's note that outside experts vetted the book before print
context: Guzey posted his critique on 15 November 2019. Within days the statistician Andrew Gelman took it up on his blog, and he went on to back it, above all on the graph with the missing bar; in 2020 the two wrote about it together in the statistics magazine Chance. Walker's professorship at Berkeley and the book's place on the bestseller lists had not caught the errors; going back to the cited studies did. Sources: https://guzey.com/books/why-we-sleep/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Walker_(scientist)

question: A student lists the five leading guesses for why animals sleep at all: consolidating memories, clearing waste products out of the brain, fine-tuning connections between neurons, saving metabolic energy and supporting the immune system. All five have serious researchers and real lab evidence behind them. Of those five, how many have direct, unquestioned proof from experiments in humans?
answer: zero of them are proven
choices: zero of them are proven
only memory consolidation is proven
memory and glymphatic are both proven
all five are proven
context: There is no single accepted answer to why animals sleep. Every candidate has supporting evidence, none has closed the case, and several may turn out to be simultaneously true. This is one of biology's most durable open questions. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0060106

question: William Smith, a young surveyor, walked the fresh cuts of the Somerset Coal Canal near Bath in the 1790s. In cut after cut the same rock bands appeared in the same order, and each band had its own signature. Even when two bands looked alike to the eye, Smith could still tell them apart. What was that signature?
answer: The fossils in the layer
choices: The fossils in the layer
The mineral hardness of the layer
The magnetic direction of the layer
The chemical smell of the layer
context: This is the principle of FAUNAL SUCCESSION -- each stratum has its own signature assemblage of fossils, so fossils identify the layer even when the rock type does not. It is still the way rock sequences on different continents are matched today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(geologist).

question: A collector lays out the 15 sheets of William Smith's 1815 map, a life's work of walking English hills. Together they make one map about eight feet by six, and historians call it the first of its kind to cover so large an area in such detail. What did the map show?
answer: The rocks and strata of England and Wales
choices: The rocks and strata of England and Wales
The soil fertility of the English counties
A gazetteer of mineral-ore locations
The canals and coalfields of the realm
context: The full title was 'A Delineation of the Strata of England and Wales, with part of Scotland'. Soil, mineral-locality and canal maps had earlier precedents, and William Maclure had published a rougher geological map of the United States in 1809; no one had yet mapped rocks by kind and age in such detail over so large an area. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(geologist)

question: William Smith laid the strongest tone right along one edge of each rock band on his 1815 map and let the pigment fade away as it crossed the band. That single trick let a flat sheet of paper convey a three-dimensional fact about the ground beneath. What did the graded shading reveal?
answer: Which way the strata dip underground
choices: Which way the strata dip underground
How deep coal seams reached
Where earthquakes had ruptured
The direction of past river currents
context: By making the base of each stratum darkest, Smith made the map read like a cutaway view: the reader could see at a glance which side of a band was on top and which way the layer slanted down into the earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(geologist).

question: A Bath stone quarry failed and left William Smith, ruined by a side venture, owing his co-investor Charles Conolly. To pay down the debt he sold his most personal scientific possession to the British Museum for 700 British pounds, and still came up short. What did he sell?
answer: His fossil collection
choices: His fossil collection
His original map plates
His country house
His surveying instruments
context: The collection was the physical evidence that had underwritten faunal succession -- Smith's hand-labelled specimens, tied to specific strata. The Museum bought it for GBP 700; the debt still swallowed him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(geologist).

question: The man who had mapped a nation was locked up in June 1819 in London's King's Bench, a notorious debtors' prison. William Smith served 11 weeks and was released on 31 August 1819, only to walk home and find one particular grim thing waiting for him. What had happened to his house while he was inside?
answer: The bailiffs had cleared it out
choices: The bailiffs had cleared it out
It had burned to the ground
His wife had sold it and left
The Geological Society had bought it
context: Smith returned to a house stripped by bailiffs against his outstanding debts -- a genuinely ugly moment in the biography of the man who had just published England's geology. Source: scienceblog.com/n-twenty-eight-years-of-surveying-then-ten-weeks-in-prison.

question: A popular telling of William Smith's fall says that George Bellas Greenough and the Geological Society brought out a rival copy of Smith's 1815 map, undercut his sales and drove him into a debtors' prison in 1819. Historians who went back to the record found that one link in that chain cannot hold. Which link?
answer: The rival map undercutting Smith's sales before his jailing
choices: The rival map undercutting Smith's sales before his jailing
The Geological Society putting out a rival map
Smith being sent to a debtors' prison in the summer of 1819
Smith's own map selling poorly in those years
context: Greenough's map is dated 1819 but came out only in May 1820, after Smith had left the King's Bench on 31 August 1819; it also cost more than Smith's and shared few of his subscribers, so it cannot have run up the debts that jailed him. Smith's map did sell poorly, but so did Greenough's. Smith's debts came from the failed Bath stone quarry and what he owed its co-investor. Much of the feud story traces to Smith's champion John Farey Sr., who used Smith's cause to air his own grievances against the Society in the Philosophical Magazine. In 1831 the Society gave Smith its first Wollaston Medal, and its president, Adam Sedgwick, called him the Father of English Geology. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(geologist)

question: A Shropshire family brewed a tea with over twenty herbs, and William Withering, a Birmingham doctor, heard of it in 1775. It really did ease an illness in which the body swelled with trapped fluid until the skin was tight and the lungs drowned. Bleeding, purges and mercury did nothing. What was that illness called in his day?
answer: the dropsy
choices: the dropsy
the consumption
the ague
the falling sickness
context: The dropsy was the eighteenth-century name for the massive fluid retention (edema) now most often traced to congestive heart failure. The consumption was tuberculosis, the ague was malarial fever, the falling sickness was epilepsy -- three real terrors of the era. Standard 1775 treatments for dropsy also included tapping (draining) the swollen abdomen with a hollow needle called a trocar -- none of it addressed the failing heart. Source: hektoen international -- Withering and the foxglove; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Withering.

question: William Withering, a serious botanist as well as a physician, did not just brew the Shropshire family's twenty-plus-ingredient tea. He set out to work out which single plant in the jumble was actually doing the work, and then he threw the rest of the recipe away. Which plant did he keep?
answer: the purple foxglove
choices: the purple foxglove
the deadly nightshade
the meadow saffron
the corn poppy
context: Withering identified Digitalis purpurea, the tall spike of hanging bells found in English hedgerows and gardens. The other choices are all real herbal-medicine plants of the period: deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna, a pupil-dilator and heart poison), meadow saffron (Colchicum autumnale, still prescribed for gout), and corn poppy (Papaver rhoeas, cousin to the opium poppy). Withering learned the recipe from 'an old woman in Shropshire'; the folksy 'Mother Hutton' name was invented in a 1928 Parke-Davis advertisement and is a myth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Withering.

question: William Withering published An Account of the Foxglove after ten years of dosing patient after patient with dried, weighed leaf. The 1785 book is counted among the founding works of drug testing. What did its 163 case histories do that earns it that place?
answer: included every patient the drug did nothing for or harmed
choices: included every patient the drug did nothing for or harmed
compared the drug against an inert pill from the same jar
gave every patient the very same fixed dose of the leaf
randomly assigned each patient to a different dose
context: Withering's 163 cases -- 156 from his own practice and 7 from the Birmingham hospital -- included the ones where the leaf did nothing and the ones where it made the patient worse. His preface says that giving only select cases would have been easy and flattering to his reputation, 'But Truth and Science would condemn the procedure.' Publishing negative results is the move that separates a drug from a nostrum. The book did none of the other things: Withering raised each patient's dose step by step, and comparison against a dummy pill and random allocation came much later (the Medical Research Council's streptomycin trial of 1948 is the landmark randomised one). Source: Withering 1785, Project Gutenberg 24886 (https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/24886).

question: William Withering wrote that his hedgerow flower could rescue a swollen, dying patient, yet a little higher up the dose it would kill. His 1785 book listed what very large, quickly repeated doses do, from sickness and giddiness to a pulse slowed to 35 beats a minute. One strange sign on that list is still a classic clue to overdose. What is it?
answer: objects appearing green or yellow
choices: objects appearing green or yellow
bleeding from the nose or the gums
ringing in the ears that will not fade
red blotches spreading down the arms
context: The 1785 book: 'The Foxglove when given in very large and quickly-repeated doses, occasions sickness, vomiting, purging, giddiness, confused vision, objects appearing green or yellow', and on through a slow pulse, cold sweats and convulsions to death. His stopping rule came well before that: give the leaf only until it acts on the kidneys, the stomach, the pulse or the bowels, and stop at the first appearance of any one of those effects. The yellow-green tint to vision is still a classic clinical sign of digitalis overdose. Bleeding from the nose and gums is a sign of too much blood thinner, ringing ears of too much aspirin or quinine, and spreading red blotches of a drug allergy. Foxglove is a common garden plant and eating any part of it can kill: this is a look-don't-touch wonder, never a try-it-yourself one. Source: Withering 1785, Project Gutenberg 24886 (https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/24886).

question: A reader of William Withering's famous 1785 book finds him writing down which organ he believed the foxglove leaf was really acting on. The dried leaves could ease the swelling and shortness of breath now called congestive heart failure, and he set down his own thinking honestly. Chemistry later proved him wrong. Which organ did he wrongly name as the leaf's true target?
answer: the kidneys
choices: the kidneys
the liver
the spleen
the lungs
context: Withering saw his patients pass enormous amounts of urine after taking the leaf and concluded it was a diuretic acting on the kidneys. In fact the leaf makes a failing heart contract harder and beat more slowly; only THEN does the returning blood flow reach the kidneys with enough pressure to drain the accumulated fluid. Right result, wrong mechanism -- honestly recorded. The other choices are the other Georgian go-to organs for fluid trouble (the liver was blamed for dropsy from cirrhosis; the spleen was blamed for almost anything obscure; the lungs were the seat of consumption). Source: cvpharmacology.com -- digitalis.

question: A doctor hands a digitalis drug to a patient with a weakened heart. Chemistry took more than a century and a half to catch up with William Withering's leaf. In heart-muscle cells, digitalis latches onto one specific membrane pump and jams it, letting calcium build up inside the cell so the muscle fibres pull harder. Which membrane pump does the drug jam?
answer: the sodium-potassium pump
choices: the sodium-potassium pump
the stomach acid proton pump
the muscle calcium reuptake pump
the sweat-gland chloride pump
context: Digitalis blocks Na+/K+-ATPase on the heart cell membrane. Sodium builds up inside the cell, which stalls a second exchanger that would normally pump calcium out in trade for sodium in; calcium therefore accumulates too, and calcium is what makes the muscle fibres contract harder. Hans Schatzmann showed in 1953 that cardiac glycosides block this pump, 168 years after Withering's book. The other choices are real membrane transporters: the proton pump is the target of omeprazole (heartburn); SERCA sequesters calcium after each beat (a mutation in it causes Darier disease); CFTR is the chloride channel broken in cystic fibrosis. Sources: cvpharmacology.com -- digitalis; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00210-021-02191-2

question: Dr Sydney Smith at Burroughs Wellcome isolated a purified cardiac glycoside in 1930 from the leaf of the woolly foxglove, a different species from William Withering's flower. Doctors still prescribe it today for heart failure and for slowing certain irregular heartbeats. What is that drug called?
answer: digoxin
choices: digoxin
warfarin
quinidine
atropine
context: Digoxin comes from Digitalis lanata; the closely related digitoxin comes from Withering's purple foxglove (Digitalis purpurea). The other choices are all real heart-era drugs: warfarin (a blood thinner from spoiled sweet-clover), quinidine (an antiarrhythmic from cinchona bark, cousin to the malaria drug quinine), and atropine (from deadly nightshade, used to speed a dangerously slow heart). A hedgerow flower is on the modern drug list because one physician measured it instead of believing it. Source: American Chemical Society -- Molecule of the Week: Digoxin.

question: Walter Friedrich and Paul Knipping aimed a narrow beam of X-rays through a small copper sulphate crystal in Munich on 21 April 1912, with a photographic plate set behind it. Nobody knew what would come out the far side. What did the developed plate show?
answer: A pattern of sharp spots ringing the central beam
choices: A pattern of sharp spots ringing the central beam
An even grey fog spread across the whole plate
A single blurred smear the width of the beam
A row of straight dark bands across the plate
context: The plate came out covered in well-defined spots arranged in intersecting circles around the central beam spot — patterns still called 'Laue diagrams' today. Copper sulphate was chosen simply because large pieces were easy to come by; zinc blende, tried soon afterwards, gave the cleaner four-fold pattern usually reproduced in books. Max von Laue, Friedrich and Knipping announced the result to the Bavarian Academy of Sciences on 4 May 1912. Sources: Wikipedia 'X-ray crystallography'; Physics World, 'One amazing moment'; Grokipedia 'Max von Laue'.

question: William Lawrence Bragg, 25 and serving as a British artillery officer at army headquarters in France, got the telegram from home: the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics had gone to him and to his father, William Henry Bragg, for using X-rays to map atoms inside crystals. What record does Lawrence Bragg's 1915 Nobel still hold today?
answer: The youngest laureate in any science category
choices: The youngest laureate in any science category
The first physics prize ever won by a Briton
The first Nobel Prize ever split between two people
The only physics prize awarded during the war
context: As of 2025 William Lawrence Bragg is still the youngest person ever to win a Nobel Prize in physics, or in any science category — he was 25, and the wording matters, because Malala Yousafzai was younger overall, at 17, for the 2014 Peace Prize. The 1915 citation reads 'for their services in the analysis of crystal structure by means of X-rays', and the Braggs remain the only parent and child ever to share a Nobel Prize in any field. It came in a bitter year: Lawrence's brother had been killed at Gallipoli on 2 September 1915, weeks before the announcement. Sources: Wikipedia 'Lawrence Bragg'; nobelprize.org 1915 prize pages.

question: Dorothy Hodgkin was 24 and new to X-ray work when arthritis swelled and twisted her hands. She would not give up the machine, and she kept solving crystal structures for the rest of her life, later from a wheelchair. What did she rig up so she could still start the X-ray machine herself?
answer: A lever fitted over the main switch
choices: A lever fitted over the main switch
A foot pedal wired to the main switch
A cord to the switch she pulled with her teeth
A clockwork timer wired to the switch
context: She made a lever to operate the main switch of her X-ray equipment. The disease eventually put her in a wheelchair and she kept working, taking the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry 'for her determinations by X-ray techniques of the structures of important biochemical substances'. Sources: Wikipedia 'Dorothy Hodgkin'; Royal Society, 'Scientists with disabilities: Dorothy Hodgkin'; nobelprize.org 1964 chemistry prize.

question: A student tilts a compact disc (CD) under a white lamp, and colours fan out across its face. The stamped spiral of data tracks, hundreds of tracks to the millimetre, does for lamplight what the atoms of a crystal do for X-rays. What splits white light into colours there?
answer: Waves bouncing off neighbouring tracks fall in and out of step
choices: Waves bouncing off neighbouring tracks fall in and out of step
The clear plastic above the tracks bends blue harder than red
A dye beneath the tracks soaks up one colour at each angle
The tracks are stamped in bands of slightly different metals
context: A CD's data tracks sit about 1.6 micrometres apart — roughly 600 to the millimetre, almost exactly the 1.667 micrometre line spacing of a standard laboratory diffraction grating. That is why a disc throws rainbows. TEST IT YOURSELF: shine a laser pointer of known wavelength at the disc, mark where the reflected spots land on the wall, measure the angles, and you can work out how far apart the tracks are without ever seeing one. Sources: Science Buddies, 'Using a Laser Pointer to Measure the Data Track Spacing on CDs and DVDs'; Phys. Rev. Phys. Educ. Res. CD diffraction guided-inquiry manual.

question: Dorothy Hodgkin solved penicillin in 1945. Vitamin B12 was a much bigger molecule, with a cobalt atom at its heart, and it took her about eight years from 1948. She got her first insulin crystal in 1934, when she was just starting out. How long before she had insulin's structure?
answer: Thirty-five years
choices: Thirty-five years
Twenty-seven years
Nineteen years
Eleven years
context: She got the structure in 1969, thirty-five years after that first crystal: a two-chain, disulfide-linked molecule resolved at 2.8 angstroms. She simply never let the problem go. Lawrence Bragg said her vitamin B12 result, published in 1955-56, was as significant an achievement as breaking the sound barrier. Sources: Wikipedia 'Dorothy Hodgkin'; Grokipedia 'Dorothy Hodgkin'.

question: Max von Laue argued in 1912 that nobody needed to rule a grating for X-rays, because nature had already ruled one. A diffraction grating is a plate scored with lines so fine that light striking it fans out into a spectrum, and no workshop could rule lines that fine for X-rays. What makes a crystal work as a grating for X-rays?
answer: Its atoms sit about as far apart as an X-ray wave is long
choices: Its atoms sit about as far apart as an X-ray wave is long
Its atoms are packed far more tightly than the wave is long
Its atoms swing in step with each passing X-ray wave
Its flat faces meet at the same exact angles again and again
context: X-rays have wavelengths of around an angstrom — about the size of the gaps between atoms in a crystal — so a crystal is already a three-dimensional diffraction grating, no ruling engine required. Friedrich and Knipping tested that reasoning in April 1912, and the 1914 Nobel Prize in Physics went to von Laue alone, 'for his discovery of the diffraction of X-rays by crystals'. The Braggs' prize, the following year, was for what they did with his spots — the discovery of diffraction itself is not theirs. Sources: Grokipedia 'Max von Laue'; nobelprize.org 1914 physics prize; Wikipedia 'X-ray crystallography'.

question: Lawrence Bragg, still a student, worked out on a walk by the river at Cambridge what nobody could yet say: what a single spot on Max von Laue's plates actually was. Crystallographers still use his reading. What is one bright spot on the plate?
answer: A reflection off one stack of parallel atomic sheets
choices: A reflection off one stack of parallel atomic sheets
A shadow cast by one heavy atom in the crystal
A glow given off by atoms the beam has excited
A gap where the beam passed through untouched
context: Bragg's reading: each spot is a reflection off one family of parallel sheets of atoms, and reflections from successive sheets only stay in step — only add up into a bright spot — at particular angles. The crystal sorts the beam for you. He presented his rock-salt work to the Cambridge Philosophical Society on 11 November 1912. Sources: Wikipedia 'Lawrence Bragg'; crystallography365, 'The structure that started it all: rock salt'.

question: William Henry Bragg built a new instrument he called an ionization spectrometer, and he and his son William Lawrence Bragg divided the work from there. What could the father's instrument do that a photographic plate could not?
answer: It read out each reflection's strength as a number
choices: It read out each reflection's strength as a number
It held the crystal steady while the beam swept past
It magnified the crystal until single atoms showed
It kept the crystal too cold for its atoms to shift
context: The reflected X-rays entered a gas-filled chamber, where they knocked electrons loose and produced a small electric current — so every reflection came out as a number, a measured strength, instead of a darker or fainter mark on film. Those numbers are what the son turned into atomic positions. The instrument is the ancestor of every diffractometer since. Sources: Grokipedia 'William Henry Bragg'; Grokipedia 'Diffractometer'.

question: Lawrence Bragg turned his reading of the spots into a rule anyone could compute with. A student sends in X-rays of a wavelength she already knows, turns the crystal until one reflected beam flares bright, and reads off the angle it came out at. What has that one angle just told her?
answer: The spacing between neighbouring sheets of atoms
choices: The spacing between neighbouring sheets of atoms
The spacing between neighbouring atoms within a sheet
The width of a single atom in the crystal
The thickness of the crystal along the beam
context: The rule is Bragg's law: n·λ = 2d·sin θ, where λ is the X-ray wavelength, d the distance between adjacent planes of atoms, θ the angle, and n a whole number. Angles in, architecture out — you measure something you can see and get back a distance you never could. Grokipedia dates the derivation to March 1913. Sources: Grokipedia "Bragg's law"; Wikipedia 'Lawrence Bragg'.

question: Lawrence Bragg was put on a wave problem of a different kind in France during the First World War. His crews spread microphones along a measured baseline, and when a German gun fired, the same boom reached each one a fraction of a second apart, so those tiny gaps fixed where the gun stood. But ordinary microphones could not hear the gun's low boom, only the sharper crack of the shell. What did Lance Corporal William Tucker rig up to catch the low wave?
answer: A heated platinum wire strung across a hole in a box
choices: A heated platinum wire strung across a hole in a box
A drumskin stretched over the mouth of a buried drum
A brass horn feeding a needle onto a wax cylinder
A tuning fork clamped to a field telephone earpiece
context: Tucker's hot-wire microphone was a heated platinum wire stretched across a hole cut in an ammunition box: the low-frequency pressure pulse from the gun cooled the wire and changed its electrical resistance, which the instruments could read. By September 1916 every British sound-ranging section in France and Belgium had one, and a gun could be fixed to within about 50 yards at a range of 10,000 yards — the same arithmetic of waves and spacing Bragg used on crystals, run on sound instead of X-rays. Sources: APS News, 'Bragg and sound ranging'; Royal Society Notes and Records, "Lawrence Bragg's role in the development of sound-ranging in World War I"; Wikipedia 'Lawrence Bragg'.

question: Henry Edward Armstrong, a past President of the Chemical Society, still would not have the Braggs' picture of table salt thirteen years later. It showed no NaCl molecules at all: sodium and chloride ions alternate endlessly, and the equal numbers of each come from the geometry of the stack rather than from atoms pairing off. How did he register his objection?
answer: He printed a protest in Nature headed 'Poor Common Salt!'
choices: He printed a protest in Nature headed 'Poor Common Salt!'
He printed a rival picture of salt in the Society's journal
He had the Chemical Society strike Bragg from its rolls
He asked the Nobel committee to take the 1915 prize back
context: Armstrong quoted Bragg's own sentences back at readers and objected to them: 'In sodium chloride there appear to be no molecules represented by NaCl. The equality in number of sodium and chlorine atoms is arrived at by a chess-board pattern of these atoms; it is a result of geometry and not of a pairing-off of the atoms.' Secondary accounts report that he called the chess-board pattern 'repugnant to common sense' and retorted that chemistry is neither chess nor geometry; the Nature page is paywalled, so treat those particular words as reported rather than confirmed. The measurements stood. Source: H. E. Armstrong, 'Poor Common Salt!', Nature 120, 478 (1927); quotation database todayinsci.com; Grokipedia 'Chemical structure'.

question: Dorothy Hodgkin put a penicillin crystal in an X-ray beam and photographed what came out. Penicillin was saving lives in every Allied hospital by 1945, and no chemist could say what its molecule looked like. Two Oxford camps had formed: Edward Abraham backed one shape for its atoms, and Sir Robert Robinson, the most eminent organic chemist in Britain and a future Nobel laureate, backed a rival one. Which shape did the pictures show?
answer: A four-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring
choices: A four-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring
A six-membered ring with a sulphur atom set in it
Two flat rings stacked face to face around a metal atom
A long unbranched chain with no ring along it at all
context: The pictures showed a beta-lactam ring — a strained four-membered ring, then unknown in any biological molecule, which is precisely why so many chemists had refused it — fused to a five-membered ring. That was Abraham's proposal; Robinson had championed a rival oxazolone-thiazolidine structure. Hodgkin had the answer in 1945 and published it in 1949. Sources: Wikipedia 'Dorothy Hodgkin'; EBSCO research starter, 'Hodgkin Solves the Structure of Penicillin'; biobasedpress.eu, 'Chemistry vs bacteria: the beta-lactam'.

question: A boy at the kitchen table sticks a paper straw into a tall glass of cold milk and takes a long sip. What actually sends the milk up the straw to his lips?
answer: The outside air, pressing down on the surface of the milk
choices: The outside air, pressing down on the surface of the milk
A pulling force generated by the tongue and cheeks
Surface tension between the milk and the straw wall
Capillary action wicking the milk up the narrow tube
