context: Suction is not a pulling force. The chest expansion lowers the pressure inside the mouth; the atmosphere, still at full pressure on the rest of the glass, does the actual lifting. Source: chem.libretexts.org, Introduction to Chemistry, Chapter 9: Straws.

question: A girl pokes a single pin-hole through the side of a straw, well above the surface of her drink, and tries to drink as hard as she can. A straw works because lower pressure inside it lets the atmosphere press the drink up the tube. What happens, and why?
answer: Nothing rises - air enters the hole, so the atmosphere no longer has to lift the drink
choices: Nothing rises - air enters the hole, so the atmosphere no longer has to lift the drink
The drink rises faster, because the hole gives an extra outlet for suction
The drink rises only as far as the pin-hole and then stops there
The drink rises briefly, then chokes off once the mouth pressure equalises
context: The pin-hole is the ten-second proof that nobody ever pulls the liquid - the atmosphere lifts it, and only when the tube is sealed above the liquid line. Source: tec-science.com, How does a drinking straw work.

question: A schoolteacher hands out plastic straws twelve metres long and tells the class to drink orange juice through them from a bucket on the floor. Every child fails, however hard each one sucks. What ceiling has the teacher run them into?
answer: The atmosphere can only push water up about ten metres, even against a perfect vacuum
choices: The atmosphere can only push water up about ten metres, even against a perfect vacuum
Surface tension holds the juice back once a tube passes ten metres
Juice viscosity is too high for a tube that long to conduct
Static electricity along a long plastic tube stalls the flow
context: At sea level, one atmosphere can balance a column of water roughly 10.33 metres tall - about a three-storey house. No lung, and no pump on Earth, can beat that ceiling by sucking. Source: scienceabc.com, How High Can A Pump Suck Water.

question: A pump salesman visits a farm and boasts that his new 20-horsepower pump can suck water up a 15-metre pipe from the bottom of an old well. A physics teacher listening in shakes her head: a suction pump can only raise water about 10 metres. Which quantities set that ceiling?
answer: Atmospheric pressure, water density, and the strength of gravity
choices: Atmospheric pressure, water density, and the strength of gravity
Motor horsepower, pipe diameter, and pump-seal tightness
Valve size, intake-filter mesh, and the shape of the pump casing
Impeller speed, pipe material, and the number of pump stages
context: Only three ingredients set the limit - and a manufacturer controls none of them. h = P / (rho * g) gives 101,325 / 9,810 = 10.33 m. Up a mountain the ceiling drops, because the air pressure itself is lower. Real pumps do worse, around 6-7 m, because of cavitation and friction; the 20 HP claim is snake oil. Source: scienceabc.com.

question: Galileo took up the complaint of well-diggers in Florence in his Two New Sciences of 1638, and he got it wrong. By one account they had carried it to the Grand Duke of Tuscany in the 1630s: their suction pumps refused to lift water past about ten metres, however well built. What explanation did Galileo publish for the ten-metre ceiling?
answer: That water, like a rope, has a breaking strength and snaps under its own weight
choices: That water, like a rope, has a breaking strength and snaps under its own weight
That the pump seals leak invisibly at any height above ten metres
That friction along the pipe walls drags the rising water back down
That the column grows too heavy for any pump handle to lift
context: Galileo put the limit near 18 braccia (~10.5 m) and treated the column as a self-hanging rope of water. It was a genius's wrong answer. The right one came from Torricelli in 1644: the weight of the air outside pushes the water up, and it can balance only about ten metres of it. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_New_Sciences; encyclopedia.com, Torricelli; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelista_Torricelli

question: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station (ISS) sips from a sealed squeeze-pouch, though straws work fine there because the cabin is pressurised. For open coffee, NASA engineered a special rimmed cup with a thin inner channel that needs no lid and no straw at all. What physical effect climbs the drink up that channel to the rim, on its own?
answer: Surface wetting along the narrow wedge, drawing the liquid up by capillary action
choices: Surface wetting along the narrow wedge, drawing the liquid up by capillary action
Centripetal spin from the station's rotation, throwing the drink outward
Electrostatic charge on the plastic cup, pulling the polar water molecules
A tiny suction pump built into the cup's base, lifting the coffee up
context: The ISS does not spin for gravity; in microgravity the atmosphere still pushes drinks up a straw, but stray droplets can float into electronics, so pouches rule. NASA's capillary 'space cup' uses the same wetting that pulls water up a paper towel - geometry, not suction, does the work. Source: chowhound.com, NASA Space Cup.
